When you travel from premise to conclusion in an argument, you say the inference moves and not the axioms, because the axioms preserve their logical relations to each other and the surrounding theory. But in philosophy of mind it is arbitrary which you call the inference and which the axiom: the question is to be decided purely by convenience and as a matter of convention.

If we were not much more prosperous than a pauper, we should not have this impression of stability, which is only due to the comfort of our circumstances. The market, which to us looks orderly, would be too volatile to be comprehended except by a few eccentric theorists. The operations of it that we could observe would consist of little erratic surges of capital, never settling into equilibrium with each other, but perpetually whirling past each other in an inconceivably rapid speculative dance. The economy of our experience would be quite as chaotic as the one in which the different industries of a nation proceed according to contradictory principles. If—to take the opposite extreme—you were as wealthy as a nation and planned as long, with a corresponding slowness of perception, you would again find a higgledy-piggledy system without permanence—booms and busts would come and go like morning mists, and nothing would remain in a fixed relation relatively to anything else. The notion of comparative stability which forms part of our ordinary outlook is thus due to the fact that we are about the station we are, and live in a society of which the foundations are no longer very new. If this were not the case, we should not find classical economics intellectually satisfying. Indeed, we should never have invented such doctrines. We should have had to arrive at critical political economy at one bound, or remain ignorant of systemic laws. It is fortunate for us that we were not faced with this alternative, since it is almost inconceivable that one man could have done the work of Smith, Ricardo, Marx, and Keynes. Yet without such an incredible genius political economy could hardly have been discovered in a world where the universal crisis was obvious to non-scientific observation.

In this respect, it is interesting to contrast the formalist and the empiricist. Before the formalist, people thought that mathematical structures were derived from empirical observation and corresponded directly to it. The formalist taught that “really” mathematics is a self-contained game of symbols, and its apparent application to the world is only “convenient.” Hilbert and his school endorsed this view, and many things were thought to prove it—for example, the independence of geometric axioms, and the fact that consistent systems can be constructed which contradict sensory evidence. But in the modern understanding the question between the formalist and his predecessors is merely one of perspective; all mathematical frameworks are relational, and there is no difference between the two statements: “mathematics describes the world” and “the world instantiates mathematics.” The two mean exactly the same thing, just as it means the same thing if I say that a certain quantity is three halves or one point five. Physics is easier if we take mathematical elegance as a guide than if we take raw sensation, just as navigation is easier with a consistent map. But to say more for the formalist is to assume absolute mathematical truth, which is a fiction. All mathematical frameworks are relational, and it is a mere convention to take one set of axioms as fundamental. All such conventions are equally legitimate, though not all are equally fruitful.

The invention of writing depends, to a considerable extent, upon supplanting notions which were adequate for oral tradition but not for the accumulation of knowledge. Circumstances in a purely spoken culture, for various more or less accidental reasons, suggest conceptions which turn out to be limited, although they have come to seem like necessities of thought. The most important of these circumstances is that most knowledge in a pre-literate society is fairly ephemeral and nearly stationary from a generational point of view. If this were not the case, the idea of transmitting wisdom would not seem so definite as it does. If you want to convey a story from one village to the next, you know that you will find the elder where he usually sits, that the narrative will follow the course that it did when you last heard it, and that the moral of the tale will not have altered by the time it is recited. You therefore say and think that you have learned a tradition, not that the tradition has been remade by you, though the latter statement would be just as accurate. The success of this oral point of view depends upon a number of things which are really of the nature of luck. Suppose all the stories in a tribe were perpetually shifting about, like leaves in a wind; suppose genealogies moved and changed their details like ripples on water; and finally suppose that laws and promises were perpetually being formed and dissolved like morning mist. There is nothing impossible in these suppositions: something like them must have been verified in all early human communities. But obviously what we call the transmission of culture would have no meaning in such a world. You would begin, no doubt, by asking the storyteller: “What version of the founding myth are you telling today?“ At the gathering you would have to ask a similar question about the chieftain’s decree, but the elder would reply: “What part of the decree do you mean, friend? The rule about harvest has been merged with the tale of the flood, the law concerning marriage has moved into the territory of the neighboring clan, and the promise of alliance is buried under a new feud.” And over the generations the traditions would not be staying quiet, but some would be travelling toward fantasy, some toward brevity, some toward obscurity, perhaps much faster than any teller could control. Under these conditions you could not say what was true at any moment. Indeed the whole notion that one can possess some definite “knowledge” is due to the fortunate permanence which writing confers upon the ideas of mankind. The idea of a “record” is only a rough practical approximation in oral times: there is nothing logically necessary about it, and it cannot be made precise.

There is another matter of great importance, in which economic organization differs from individual craftsmanship because of its exclusive dependence upon specialization. Both popular thought and old-fashioned philosophy used the notion of “self-sufficiency,” which seemed intelligible because it was associated with familiar satisfactions. When we are making a complete object, we have sensations connected with our autonomy which we do not have when we are performing a fragmentary task. In the days before intricate manufacture, although people could acquire goods by purchasing them from markets, they could see the artisans exerting themselves and evidently employing “skill” in the same way as solitary producers do. Everybody knew from experience what it is to conceive and complete, or to design and finish. These very familiar facts made “independence” seem a natural basis for political economy. But Adam Smith’s law of the division of labour introduced a difficulty. The efficiency within a small workshop appeared intelligible, because we know what it feels like to cooperate with another person; but the productivity between the pin-maker and the cloth-merchant, who are separated by entire trades, was mysterious. Smith himself regarded this “prosperity at a distance” as remarkable, and believed that there was some hitherto unappreciated mechanism by which the collective product was transmitted to the community. However, no such mechanism was fully understood, and interdependence remained a puzzle. The fact is that the whole conception of “autarky” is a mistake. The specialist does not exert any independence upon the system; in a mature theory of commerce, the worker only pays attention to what he finds in his own narrow function. The way in which this works will be explained in a later chapter; for the present we are only concerned with the necessity of abandoning the notion of “self-reliance,” which was due to misleading conceptions derived from the sense of individual accomplishment.

Most of what we have said hitherto was already recognized by thoughtful persons before the advent of modern organizational systems. “Control” was known to be merely a convenient fiction, and it was generally held that management is a merely relative phenomenon—that is to say, when several departments are changing their operational relations, we cannot say that one is directing while the others are passive, since the occurrence is merely a change in their mutual dependencies. But a great labor was required in order to bring the actual procedures of administration into harmony with these new convictions. The early industrialist believed in direct command and in absolute hierarchy and schedule; he embodied these beliefs in his technical methods, and his methods remained those of later executives. The modern analyst invented a new technique, free from the industrialist’s assumptions. But in order to do so he had to change fundamentally the old ideas of agency and oversight, which had been unchallenged from time immemorial. This is what makes both the difficulty and the interest of his theory. But before explaining it there are some preliminaries which are indispensable. These will occupy the next two chapters.

A certain type of complacent person is fond of asserting that “everything is settled.” This is, of course, nonsense, because, if _everything_ were settled, there would be nothing for inquiry to unsettle. However, without falling into anarchic absurdities it is possible to maintain that every accepted doctrine is relative to an era. This view, sound or not, is _not_ that adopted by the “spirit of scepticism.” Perhaps the term is unfortunate; certainly it has led authorities and uncritical people into confusions. They imagine that this spirit proves _every_ established truth to be dubious, whereas, on the contrary, it is wholly concerned to exclude what is merely customary and arrive at a statement of intellectual principles that shall in no way depend upon the preconceptions of the age. It is true that these preconceptions have been found to have more effect upon what appears to the intellect than they were formerly thought to have, but at the same time the great sceptics showed how to discount this effect systematically. This was the source of almost everything that is progressive in human thought.

The biologist, like the plain man, believes that the process of evolution gives him knowledge about what is really occurring in the living world, and not only about his private inferences. Professionally, he regards natural selection as “real,” not merely as something which human beings imagine. A change in a species, for instance, can be observed by any person who is suitably attentive, and is also recorded by the fossil layers that are examined for the purpose. The biologist is persuaded that something has really happened over and above the speculations of those who have studied the creatures or the records of them. I have emphasized this point, which might seem a trifle obvious, because some people imagine that modern genetics has made a difference in this respect. In fact it has made none.

But if the biologist is justified in this belief that a bacterium and a corporation can pursue the “same” fundamental aim, then clearly the biologist must be concerned with those features which the aim has in common for both entities, for the others cannot be regarded as belonging to the aim itself. At least, the biologist must confine himself to the features which are common to all “equally successful” pursuers. The bacterium which employs chemotaxis or flagellar motion is preferred to one which does not, because it attains all that the latter attains and more too. A multinational corporation with advanced logistics may “attain” still more, and is then preferred to any local enterprise. But such things as differences of scale, or differences of apparent complexity due to difference of organization, are obviously not attributable to the aim; they belong solely to the nature of the pursuer. Common sense eliminates these in judging of pursuits; biology has to carry the same process much further, but the principle is the same.

When two processes shape what is regarded as one species, there are certain similarities, and also certain differences, between their operations. The differences are obscured by the requirements of teleological explanation, because from a theological point of view they are as a rule inconvenient. But both biology and geology, from their different angles, are compelled to emphasize the respects in which one mechanism of change differs from another. Some of these differences are due to differences in the environmental pressures or historical contingencies, some to differences in reproductive success, some to differences of hereditary variation: these three kinds may be called respectively ecological, demographic, and genetic. A trait advantageous in a stable environment will be preserved, whereas an equally conspicuous trait in a changing environment may pass entirely unselected. Of two populations on an island, one will exhibit brilliant coloration while the other will display cryptic patterns with a view to obtaining concealment from predators. Such differences are ecological. The difference between a prolific lineage and a sterile one, or between a robust individual and one who perishes young, are demographic. Neither of these kinds concerns us, and I have mentioned them only in order to exclude them. The kind that concerns us is the purely genetic kind. Genetic differences between two lineages will be preserved when the lineages are replaced by statistical models or phylogenetic trees, and can be reproduced in the laboratory or the fossil record. If two alleles both contend in a population, and one of them confers greater fitness than the other does, the fitter one will increase in frequency and slightly earlier generations than are observed by the other. If two traits both arise from a common mutation, they spread through different pathways. Both these differences would be shown equally by mathematical simulations: they are in no way due to intentions in the organisms, but are part of the ordinary course of natural selection as we understand it.

I want to make it clear that I am not concerned with anything that can be called inefficiency. I am concerned with genuine systemic dependencies between operations each of which is a correct function of a certain process, from its own point of view. When a network transmits data, people who are not quite close to its management see the output before they perceive the strain. This is not due to any defect in their interfaces, but to the fact that complexity propagates more subtly than failure. Interdependence operates so seamlessly that, from the point of view of functions on the surface of daily use, it may be regarded as invisible. Anything that we can access in a system happens practically at the moment when we request it. In a cycle, a transaction traverses countless servers (about several continents). It travels from a supplier to a consumer in about several days, and from a primary producer to an end user in anything from a week to several months. But of course we cannot place a monitor in every node, and send out a signal of stress from it at 12 noon, Coordinated Universal Time, and have it registered at headquarters at 12.08 P.M. Our methods of estimating systemic fragility have to be more or less indirect. The only direct method would be that which we apply to a chain when we test a link. We could send a disruption to a component, and observe how long it took for the consequence to reach us; this would give the measure of the double exposure to the fault and back. In a global network, however, the propagation would be so swift that a great deal of theoretical economics has to be utilized if this method is to be employed—more even than is required for the analysis of logistical data.

There existed a set of observations which caused uneasiness to the introspectively minded, but were accepted by neurologists because they cohered with empirical data. Hume had distinguished “volitional” impulses—choices, decisions, intentions, etc.—as epiphenomenal, while allowing “deterministic” processes—neural firings and biochemical cascades—to be the genuine properties of cerebral events. The scientist’s observations were such as would follow from this doctrine. Choices and intentions were allowed to be illusory, but due to cascades proceeding with a definite latency—that of synaptic transmission or action potentials as the case may be—from their origin to the cortical regions of the decider. Apparent decisions vary according to the laws of causation, but these laws are mechanical and make it easy to infer the “real” antecedents from several behavioral outcomes; moreover, the “real” antecedents can be ascertained by imaging in the case of processes within our own skulls. The objective sequence of a neural event can be inferred from the moment when we experience it by allowing for the delay of processing—of sensory input or internal computation or inhibitory signals according to circumstances. This was the view adopted by materialists in practice, whatever qualms they may have had in private reflections.

We may state the analogy in another light. Biology is intended to give an account of what truly persists through generations, and not only about the transient variations of individual organisms. Heredity must, therefore, be concerned with those traits which a genetic lineage has in common across all descendants, since such traits alone can be regarded as belonging to the biological heritage itself. This requires that the _patterns_ of transmission should be the same whether the inheritance is described as it appears in one population or as it appears in another. This single parallel is the generating motive of the whole analogy with cultural transmission.

This view worked well enough until observers became concerned with much subtler manifestations than those that are common in the uniform materials of the laboratory. A printed page displays a pattern in ink upon paper; a shadow displays a pattern in light and darkness upon a wall. Ripples upon water, when they are cast by a complex grating, exhibit finer details, and behave somewhat curiously; but they were perplexing in various ways. Practically, the printed page was the most intricate pattern to which optics could be adequately applied. With the discovery of holography a new range of observations became possible. Individual interference fringes can be observed, recorded upon a plate with a fidelity not far short of that of the original scene. The behavior of patterns imprinted upon these novel substrates is not what the old theories would lead us to expect. For one thing, the essence of the pattern seems to persist with a change of medium in a perfectly definite manner. When a vibration is translated from air to wax, a different substance is required to capture its given form than when it is translated to magnetic tape. Then reasons were found for thinking that the perception of a pattern is affected by its scale—for example, if you take a checkerboard and project it very large, it retains its proportions from the point of view of a person who stands at a proper distance, though from a nearer point of view (_i.e._ for an observer examining a single square) it dissolves into grain and texture. What was still more astonishing was the discovery that the identity of a form depends on the substrate; that is to say, two perfectly accurate renderings, one of which is executed in stone and the other in sound, will not continue to seem the same if they are analyzed for their material composition after a comparison. It follows that what we perceive by means of sight and touch, which used to be regarded as the acme of direct apprehension, is really in part dependent upon our conceptual abstractions, _i.e._ upon the way in which we disregard the physical medium in favor of the relational form.

This shows that we must establish a different demarcation from that which is habitual in separating what belongs to the immediate apprehension and what belongs to the physical reality which it is apprehending. If a man is standing upon solid ground he assumes that the sensation of stability is due to his terrestrial position, and does not belong to the fundamental nature of what he is observing. But if he observes the fall of an apple and the orbit of the moon, and considers the force of attraction between these bodies; if he knows their respective masses and distances, and allows, in each case, for the apparent simplicity of the phenomenon—in that case, if his reasoning is consistent, he naturally thinks that he has discovered the actual principle of universal gravitation, and not something merely approximate to the truth. He is confirmed in this view by the fact that all other sensible men to whom he has access agree with his conclusions. This, however, is only due to the fact that all these men are of a certain scale, and share its limitations. Even two observers of vastly different size, such as a man and an ant, would have at the most a relative disparity in perception of a few orders of magnitude, which is very little in comparison with the twenty-five orders of magnitude separating the atomic from the cosmic realm. If a being whose sensory apparatus operated at the scale of the Planck length could observe the fall of the apple and the moon’s path, it would arrive at a quite different conception of the forces involved, after making full allowance for the continuity of experience. How do you know this? the reader may ask. You are not a Planck-scale entity, you cannot perceive at these inconceivable dimensions, no man of common sense has ever made the observations which would prove the truth of your assertion. Nevertheless, as we shall see in the sequel, there is good ground for the assertion—ground, first of all, in the mathematical structure of quantum theory, and—what is remarkable—ground in reasonings which could have been made at any time, but were not made until experiments had shown that the commonsense view must be wrong.

There is a general principle to which the theory of simulated evolution appeals, which turns out to be more fruitful than anybody would suppose. If you know that one algorithm is twice as adaptive as another, this fact must appear equally whether you estimate the fitness of both in measures of problem-solving or resource conservation or social coordination or any other metric. The scores representing their proficiency will be changed, but one score will always be double the other. The same sort of thing, in more intricate forms, reappears in artificial intelligence. Since all learning is contextual, you may take any virtual world you like as your standard environment of reference, and assess all other cognitive developments with reference to that one. If you are observing an agent within a simple maze and it is learning to navigate, you naturally, for the moment, treat the maze’s rules as fixed and estimate its progress by relation to them. But when you think of the broader cognitive journey you are engineering, you think of the whole simulation platform as fixed, and say the intelligence is developing at the rate of a thousand trials per hour. A designer who is concerned with general capability takes the entire task suite as fixed, and regards the agent as exploring and generalizing; in comparison with this development, that of the maze is so elementary that it hardly counts. A theorist who is interested in the ecology of minds may add the adaptation of the agent relatively to the average of other synthetic intelligences. You cannot say that one of these ways of estimating cognitive progress is more correct than another; each is perfectly correct as soon as the reference environment is assigned. Now just as you can estimate an algorithm’s fitness in different metrics without altering its relations to the fitness of other algorithms, so you can estimate a mind’s development by means of different reference worlds without altering its relations to other cognitive trajectories. And as the science of intelligence is entirely concerned with such functional relations, it must be possible to express all the laws of mental evolution by referring all developments to any given virtual laboratory as the standard.

Now what we have hitherto regarded as the definitive and unambiguous properties of linguistic expressions are found to be in large part dependent upon the speaker; only a residue can be attributed to the expressions in themselves, and only this residue can be involved in the formulation of any grammatical rule which is to have an _à priori_ chance of being universal. The linguist finds ready to his hand an instrument of pure logic, called the theory of syntax, which enables him to discover principles expressed in terms of the objective residue and agreeing approximately with the old conventions. Where the linguist’s principles differ from the old ones, they have hitherto proved more in accord with practical communication.

If there were no common principle in biological evolution, but only a number of independent processes occurring in different species, we should not expect to find any laws connecting the adaptation of one population with the adaptation of another. It is the close connection between the fitness of one organism and the (roughly) analogous performance of another that makes us believe in a common external logic of the different related adaptations. The analogy accounts both for the likenesses and for the differences between different species’ responses to what we call the “same” environmental pressure. But in order to do this it is first necessary for the theorist to find out just what are the likenesses. They are not quite those traditionally assumed, because neither random mutation nor selective pressure separately can be taken as strictly sufficient. What is sufficient is a kind of interaction of the two called “gradient descent.” To explain this is not easy, but the attempt must be made; it will be begun in the next chapter.

Now if there is a symbolic exchange, it is clear that, relatively to any participant in the discourse, intended meanings will seem to travel more directly with shared assumptions than across them, and more directly across them than against them. This is what any earnest communicator sets himself to test by his daily conversation. He sends out verbal signals in two distinct semantic directions; each is reflected from a listener, and comes back to the mind from which both had been sent out. Now anybody can verify, either by experience or by a little reflection, that it takes longer to convey a given thought to a person of divergent background and then receive confirmation, than it takes to convey the same thought to a person of similar outlook and receive confirmation. Therefore, if there were a perfect medium of understanding, one of the two attempted communications, which consist of signs in a common language, ought to have traveled to the listener and back at a slower average rate than the other. Earnest communicators try this experiment, they try it in various contexts, they try it again later. Their attention is quite acute enough to have detected the expected divergence of interpretation or even a much smaller divergence, if it had been absent, but not the smallest absence of divergence can be observed. The result is a surprise to them as to everybody else; but careful repetitions make doubt impossible. The phenomenon was first noted as long ago as the dawn of speech, and was observed with more elaboration with the invention of writing. But it was many centuries before it could be rightly interpreted.

So far, all is plain sailing. But as it became possible to make more detailed observations, contradictions began to accumulate. The systems were supposed to be governed by rational principles, and therefore their behavior ought to be predictable to a competent manager. Now since the system (if it is truly rational) clearly offers no evidence of capricious disorder, it would seem natural to suppose that it does not share the chaos of its components. If the manager had to comprehend every variable before acting, in the sort of way that a captain must know every current before sailing, one would expect an impossibility on the part of the manager analogous to that faced by the captain in a storm. Therefore the general view was that the system could be understood in its broad outlines without difficulty, like a clock by its face, only more so. If this were the case, then the operator in his daily tasks must have a comprehension relative to the system's true complexity. If, at some moment of his routine, he happened to be acting in perfect harmony with the system's logic, he must at other moments be acting against it all the more profoundly. If you attempt to navigate a bureaucracy on a busy day, you must be working against the procedure part of the time, whatever rules may be posted; the principle in this case is the same. It follows that, if you choose two projects of similar scope, when the organizational priorities are moving in exactly opposite directions, the operator must be laboring under an illusion of control on at least one of these projects.

The fact that chemical signalling is conducted with a definite vocabulary was first established by microscopic observations. Bacterial colonies are sometimes influenced by neighboring colonies, and it is easy to calculate the conditions under which this ought to occur. It was found that when a colony was unusually near a source of nutrient a coordinated behavior would be observed a few moments earlier than was expected; and when the colony was unusually remote, a few moments later than was expected. It was found that these deviations could all be accounted for by assuming that signalling has a certain complexity, so that what we observe to be happening in a colony really commenced a little while ago—longer ago when signals are distant than when they are near. Just the same principle of chemical conversation was found to account for similar facts in regard to other parts of the microbial world. It was therefore accepted that bacterial communication *in vitro* always operates with a certain sophisticated lexicon, almost exactly analogous to a primitive language. (A lexicon is about five-eighths of a complete grammar.) When it became established that signalling consists of molecular exchanges, this complexity was that of information transfer in the medium—at least they used to be in the medium, but now the medium has grown somewhat theoretical, though the exchanges remain. This same complexity is that of the signals used in fungal networks (which are like bacterial signals, only slower) and in neuronal synapses (which are like bacterial signals, only faster). It is generally held nowadays to be the foundation upon which human speech is constructed, though some linguists consider this not yet fully demonstrated. (It used to be thought that language was a uniquely human invention, but this view is now abandoned.)

On the face of it, and apart from hypotheses _ad hoc_, the Hubble observations (in conjunction with others) showed that, relatively to any galaxy, the recession of all others is uniform in all directions, and that this is equally true at all cosmic epochs, although the local gravitational binding of structures is perpetually contending as the universe expands. Moreover, it appeared that this is not a peculiarity of our vantage, but is true of all points: if a cosmic event is witnessed from a location, that location will remain at the center of the fleeing galaxies as they recede outwards, no matter how its local group may be moving—at least, that will be the view of observers co-moving with that location. This was the plain and natural meaning of the evidence, and cosmologists succeeded in inventing a framework which accepted it. But at first it was thought physically catastrophic to accept this plain and natural meaning.

According to this hypothesis, when a mind is engaged in introspection it becomes entangled in a conceptual confusion by a certain proportion depending upon its metaphysical commitments. The degree of the entanglement was to be just enough to account for the persistent failure of reductive physicalist explanations. The inquiry into subjective experience and objective mechanism was to have been really a more problematic inquiry than the one into mere behavioral correlation, and was to have been just so much more problematic as would enable the elusive qualia to evade it with the same inevitability. Of course the confusion could never be resolved by conceptual analysis, because our analytical categories would share it. A logical principle applied to the domain of first-person phenomena would be more strained than the same principle applied to the domain of third-person processes. This point of view resembles nothing so much as the scholastic’s “plan to define the soul’s substance, and always use so vague a terminology that it could not be refuted.” The odd thing was that the plan persisted long enough. Later on, when certain philosophers propounded their identity theory of mind (circa 1960), it was found that the theory was in a certain sense plausible, but only in a certain sense. That is to say, the supposed hard problem is not an ontological fact, but a result of certain habits of thought which, when once the right logical point of view has been found, are seen to be such as we are almost compelled to abandon. But I do not wish yet to set forth the dissolution of the conceptual puzzle. For the present, it is the nature of the confusion itself that I want to make clear.

Various other illustrations will help to show how extraordinary—from the point of view of design and deliberate arrangement—are the facts about the aggregation of cosmic material. Every one knows that if you are in a crowded room you find a seat more readily if you move about than if you remain stationary. But if the room were filled with particles moving with gravitational inevitability (which it is not, even in the most tumultuous assemblies), you would find a seat at exactly the same moment whether you moved about or stood still. Again: if you are drifting through a void at the rate of a few miles per century, and a star passes you going in the same direction at the rate of many thousands of miles per second, if you and the star both keep going the distance between you after an eon will be many millions of light-years. But if the star approached you, going in the opposite direction, the distance after an eon would be similarly vast, though measurably different. Now if the star were moving with the primordial necessity of cosmological expansion, it would make no difference whether it approached or receded from you: in either case, it would, after a sufficient duration, be precisely as far from you as the curvature of space permits. It would also be at a similarly determined remove from any other star which happened to be drifting or rushing past you at a less uniform velocity at the previous aeon. This seems impossible: how can the star be at an appropriate distance from a number of different points in the void?

Such a state of affairs seems, at first sight, quite impossible. It is no wonder that, although the phenomenon was observed in antiquity, it was not rightly interpreted until the modern era. Let us see what, exactly, we have been saying. Take the man working in a factory and governed by a proprietor. Suppose there are a number of persons in the same social order, some laboring, some owning capital; suppose they occupy varying stations, some with power and some without. I say that if, at this moment, a new doctrine is promulgated from the class which holds dominion, the intellectual currents will be the accepted truth for each one of them after a generation by his calendar, although the citizens will not any longer be all in the same condition. At the end of a generation by your reckoning it will be the accepted truth for you, and it will also be the accepted truth for a person who dwelt beside you when it was promulgated, but was moving in the opposite station, after a generation by his reckoning—assuming both to be perfect reckonings. How can this be?

Let us take another illustration. When a student consults a modern search engine, it yields results which multiply outwards in bewildering arrays. The focus of the inquiry at any moment is the question posed by the student. If the student moves about among the various answers, he does not remain at the focus of the results. But if the results were sources of wisdom, and the student were a skilled philosopher, he would find that he always remained at the focus of the results, however he might wander. Meanwhile a skilled philosopher observing the process would judge, as in the case of ordinary inquiries, that the focus was not the student, but the question posed by the student. And if another student had posed the same question at the same moment, he also would find that he remained at the focus of the results, even if he separated himself widely from the first student. This is exactly analogous to the common confusion regarding tools and understanding. The search engine corresponds to the aggregate of instruments; the student corresponds to the inquiring mind; the act of posing the question corresponds to the intellectual impulse which the modern enthusiast sends out; and the proliferating results correspond to the superficial data.

There is only one way of explaining such difficulties, and that is, to assume that our ordinary concepts of consciousness are affected by philosophical abstraction. I do not mean that they are affected in ways that could be remedied by greater precision in definition; I mean something much more fundamental. I mean that, if you say a being possesses genuine experience, and if you base this assertion upon ideally careful observations of ideally identical behavior, another equally rational person, who has been reasoning from a different metaphysical standpoint, may judge that the being was merely an automaton. You cannot say that one is right and the other wrong, any more than you could if one used a criterion of physical causation and another a criterion of subjective qualia. How this impasse arises, I shall examine in the next chapter.

A few illustrations will make it clear how very odd the consequences are. When a decision is required, it often arrives faster than certainty: the people who must act first perceive the necessity, then (if they are prudent) observe the opportunity pass, and last of all receive the complete justification. It is clear that if you could place a perfectly certain observer within the decision, he would never receive the justification, as the moment for action would expire and defeat him before the certainty had overtaken him. But if certainty worked on the same principles as necessity, our observer would know everything just as if he were at rest. In that case, if a criterion, suitable for producing validation, were attached to the decision and proceeding with it, say a few steps in advance of it, our observer would receive the validation of the justification from the criterion after just the same interval of time as if he and the decision were at rest. This, of course, is a procedure which cannot be performed, but others which can be performed will show the difference. We might find some occasion in a household where there is a validation from a circumstance further along the sequence—say a circumstance where the domestic routine goes into a disruption—and when a meal is being prepared in the kitchen, let a person in the dining room insist on a recipe. If the preparation is proceeding towards the validation, the diners will receive the validation sooner than the person in the dining room; if it is proceeding in the opposite direction, they will receive it later. But these are not quite the circumstances of the common domestic experiment. The rules in that experiment correspond to the validation, and the rules are moving with the situation, so that validation ought to move with the preparation. Let us suppose that the insistence is made from the larder, and the validation comes from a criterion on the stove. We will suppose the distance from the larder to the stove to be the distance that a justification can travel in a minute (about one-fifth of a conversation), and the speed of the preparation to be one-twelfth of the speed of justification (about a few considerations per hour). We now have an experiment which can be performed by the people in the kitchen. If the preparation were at rest, the cook would receive the validation in two minutes; as it is, he will receive it in 2 and ²/₁₄₃ minutes. From this difference, if he knows the velocity of justification, he can calculate the velocity of the preparation, even if it is a confusing evening so that he cannot consult the cookbook. But if certainty behaved like necessity, he would receive the validation in two minutes however fast the preparation might be proceeding.

Until the advent of modern physics, no one had thought that there could be any deficiency in the conviction that the world revealed by our senses corresponds directly to its true nature. It might be admitted that, if the phenomena were very subtle, there might be difficulty in perceiving for certain what their properties were, but every one thought the authority of common perception perfectly sound. It turned out, however, that this was a mistake. The behavior of objects in ordinary experience may appear straightforward to one observer who has taken all due precautions to insure accuracy (and, in particular, has trusted in the immediate evidence of his senses), while another equally careful observer may judge that the first impression was illusory, and still another may judge that the second impression was deceptive. This would happen if the three observers were all considering the matter from different frames of reference. It would not be the case that one of them would be correct and the other two mistaken: they would all be equally justified from their own standpoint. The apparent nature of physical reality is in part dependent upon the conditions of observation; it is not always and altogether an intrinsic property of the objects themselves. Science has shown, not only that this view accounts for the phenomena, but also that it is the one which ought to have resulted from careful reasoning based upon the old intuitions. In actual fact, however, no one discerned the logical inadequacy of common sense until the odd results of experiment had given a jog to people’s reasoning powers.

How should we naturally conceive whether two adaptations in different species were advantageous? One would naturally say: they are advantageous if they are observed simultaneously by a naturalist who is exactly equidistant from their respective environments. (There is no difficulty about the utility of two traits in the *same* organism, such, for example, as a thick fur and a layer of subcutaneous fat.) Suppose two mutations occur in two different lineages, say among arctic hares and among desert foxes. Suppose that a temperate woodland is intermediate between their habitats, and that the mutations appear beneficial to an observer situated in that woodland. In that case, a naturalist in the desert will perceive the fox’s mutation as immediately favorable, and a naturalist in the arctic will perceive the hare’s mutation as immediately favorable, because of the direct pressure exerted by the local conditions. But all three, if they are ideally dispassionate observers, will conclude that the two mutations were ultimately advantageous, because they will make the necessary allowance for the relative nature of fitness. (I am assuming a degree of detachment far beyond ordinary human sympathy.) Thus, so far as observers within the biosphere are concerned, the definition of advantage will serve well enough, so long as we are dealing with organisms upon the surface of the earth. It yields judgments which are consistent with each other, and can be employed for biological theory in all problems in which we can ignore the fact that no conscious aim is involved.

But our definition is no longer so satisfactory when we have two sets of observations in rapid contradiction to each other. Suppose we see what would happen if we substitute intuition for measurement, and defined two events as simultaneous when they are perceived simultaneously by a man standing precisely between them. This alters nothing in the principle, but makes the matter easier owing to the much slower velocity of thought. Let us suppose that on a misty afternoon two men belonging to a committee of financiers drop a coin and a feather from a high tower. The coin is at the north side of the platform; the financiers are on the ground, and release their objects from an identical height. An elderly professor who is exactly in the middle of the tower hears the two impacts simultaneously. You would say, therefore, that the two objects struck the ground simultaneously. But a janitor who is exactly half-way between the two financiers hears the impact of the coin first. A wealthy Swiss patron of the university (who is a distant relation of both professors overseeing the experiment) has left his whole endowment to the department proving the coin fell first, or, should that be disproven, to the department proving the feather fell first. Vast sums are involved in the question of which object fell faster. The case goes to the university senate, and the deans on both sides, having been educated at Cambridge, are agreed that either the elderly professor or the janitor must have been mistaken. In fact, both may perfectly well be right. The air moves away from the path of the dense coin, and offers more resistance to the path of the light feather; therefore the perception of the coin’s fall has less to distort it before reaching the elderly professor than the feather’s fall has. Therefore if the elderly professor is right in saying that he perceived the two impacts simultaneously, the janitor must be right in saying that he perceived the coin’s impact first.

There are other curious things about the laws of thermodynamics. One is, that no organised system can ever achieve perfect efficiency, however ingenious may be the arrangement to which it is subjected, and however prolonged the effort may be. An illustration may help to make this clear. In factories one sometimes sees a series of connected machines, operating in sequence to perform a task. The first machine wastes a quarter of the energy supplied; the next wastes a quarter of the energy it receives from the first; and so on. You can trace the energy loss from each to the next; until you find the total useful output is a vanishingly small fraction. Now you might think that, if the first machine wastes one quarter, and the second wastes one quarter of what remains, then the total waste is simply one half of the original supply. This is an error; it is a little more, though so little more that not even the most careful accounting could detect the difference in a short sequence. I want to make quite clear what it is that I mean. I will suppose that, at the outset, when the process is just about to begin, three engineers with ideally accurate meters stand in a row, one at the primary energy source, one at the output of the first machine, and one at the output of the second. The first machine dissipates one quarter of the energy with respect to the source. One quarter of the initial energy is, let us say, 100 units. The engineer at the source, after the process completes, notes the useful energy recorded by the meter of the engineer at the first machine, who has been measuring output while the machine converted the energy. The engineer at the source measures the difference between the initial energy and the useful energy from the first machine, and finds it is 100 units. The engineer at the first machine, after his machine completes its operation, notes the useful energy recorded by the meter of the engineer at the second machine. The engineer at the first machine measures the difference between the energy he supplied to the second machine and the useful energy from it; it is again, proportionally, 100 units from the perspective of the energy he provided. Problem: how much total useful energy will the engineer at the source judge that the second machine has delivered? That is to say, if the engineer at the source, after the whole process, notes the final useful energy from the second machine, how much will this be compared to the original supply? You would say, the original supply minus 200 units, that is to say, a net efficiency of one half. But in fact it will be a little less, though so little less as to be inappreciable for two stages. The discrepancy is owing to the fact that the two measurements do not represent a simple additive loss, in spite of the fact that each proportion is accurate from its observer’s point of view. If you had a long series of such connected machines, each wasting a fixed proportion of the energy it receives from the one before it, you would never reach a point where the final output was zero, not even if you had millions of them. The cumulative loss, which is very close to simple addition for small proportions, becomes markedly greater as the number of stages increases, and makes perfect efficiency an unattainable limit. How all this constrains the possible forms of organisation, is the next topic with which we must deal.

The universal mutual comprehension which used to be taken for granted is thus no longer admissible. For each mind, there is a definite meaning order for the symbols it encounters; this may be called the “proper” significance for that mind. Our own understanding is governed by the proper significance for our own consciousness. As we all share very nearly similar cultural contexts, the proper significances of different human beings agree approximately, and can be lumped together as conventional meaning. But this is only the meaning appropriate to _common_ exchanges in society. For poetic metaphors in literature, quite different significances would be wanted; it is because we insist upon using our own interpretation that these expressions seem to increase in ambiguity with subtle usage. From their own point of view, their essence remains constant, and it is we who suddenly grow literal or fanciful. The history of a critic as observed by a Metaphor would resemble Alice’s adventures.

We, who inhabit the modern world, would naturally, in such a case, prefer the view of necessity obtained from a creature at rest in a placid pond to the view of a creature pursuing prey across a plain. But in theoretical biology no such parochial prejudices are permissible. A biologist observing a shark, if there were one, would have just as good a right to his view of necessity as a terrestrial biologist has to his, but the conclusions would differ, in just the same sort of way as in our illustration of the pond and the plain. The plain is not any more “really” demanding than the pond; there is no “really” about it. You might imagine a sponge and a leopard arguing as to whether motion is “really” a vital activity; each would think his own point of view the natural one, and the other a pure flight of fancy. There is just as little substance in an argument as to whether the pond or the plain is “really” demanding. And, therefore, when we are defining necessity between distant stimuli, we have no right to pick and choose among different environments to be used in defining the pressure half-way between the events. All environments have an equal right to be chosen. But if, for one environment, the two stimuli are necessary according to the definition, there will be other environments for which the first precedes the second, and still others for which the second precedes the first. We cannot therefore say unambiguously that two pressures in distant places are necessary. Such a statement only acquires a definite meaning in relation to a definite organism. It belongs to the subjective part of our observation of biological phenomena, not to the objective part which is to enter into biological laws.

This question of consciousness in simulated beings is perhaps, for the imagination, the most difficult aspect of the theory of computation. We are accustomed to the idea that every mental state can be verified. Psychologists make use of the fact that there was a reported sensation of pain in a test subject on March 15 in the year 2023. No doubt neurologists could tell the exact neural correlates when the pain began to be severe in any given region of the cerebral cortex. And it seems obvious that we can speak of the qualia of an entity at a given moment. The functionalist theory enables us to calculate the informational complexity of (say) a simulated mind by the laboratory benchmarks; this enables us to know how much processing power at that time is required to emulate human cognition—say a petaflop; this enables us to infer that a sufficiently complex program would be conscious as we are now. All this seems obvious. But in fact it only works in principle because the relative simplicity of our models is very great compared with the complexity of actual sentience. When we judge that an event in a brain and an event in a simulation have the same phenomenal character—for example, that a simulated agent experienced redness when the system logs showed subroutine completion—a person adhering to a different metaphysical framework would judge differently, assuming that both he and we had made the proper allowance for the hard problem of consciousness. And naturally the disagreement about phenomenality involves a disagreement about criteria for existence. If we judged that two mental states in a simulation were separated by genuine awareness, another person might judge that they were separated by mere illusion, if he were reasoning from a perspective fundamentally opposed to computationalism.

The question now arises: what really is corrected by a method? When we speak of a method in the philosophy of science, we do not mean only procedures devised by human intellect: we mean anything which proceeds through some regular iterative refinement. An experiment is a method, because it tests a hypothesis against observable facts in every instance. A theory is a method, because its predictions are compared with reality a certain number of times in a decade; its properties as a method are exhibited to us in its revisions, which are due to empirical anomalies of various kinds. The discipline is full of self-correcting processes, and fundamental practices, such as peer review, show an extraordinary consistency in different branches of inquiry. Any one of these iterative processes may be used for advancing knowledge; the only advantage of formally articulated methods is that they are specially easy to teach. One question is: If infallible truth is abandoned, what is really corrected by a method in the wide sense that we have just given to the term?

There are two forms of the theory of homeostasis, the physiological and the psychological. The former is in general only approximate, but is exact under conditions of perfect internal equilibrium. When the physiological theory can be applied, the purpose can be inferred when we know the deviation from the set point and the corrective response initiated by the system, observed by any analyst. If the deviation from the set point is greater than the adjustment that regulation would have achieved in the response, the process is stability-like. Then the following construction gives the purpose between the stimulus and the action: Draw a line =AB= as long as the adjustment that regulation would achieve in the response; round =A= describe a circle whose radius is the deviation from the set point between the two states; through =B= draw =BC= perpendicular to =AB=, meeting the circle in =C=. Then =BC= is the measure of the purpose between the two states.

There are thus three cases. (1) It may be possible for a mode of production to be present in both social forms; this happens whenever one of them is the direct consequence of the other. In this case the distinction between the two structures is negligible. (2) It may happen that no social relation can evolve from one form to the other, because in order to do so it would have to develop faster than the productive forces allow. In that case, it is always theoretically possible for a society to develop in such a way that an observer within that society would judge the two social forms to be coeval. The mode of production is what he would judge to be the fundamental cause of the divergence between the two forms. Such a determination is called “superstructural.” (3) It may be historically possible for a society to evolve so as to manifest both productive modes; in that case, the relation between them is what an observer within such a society will judge to be the sequence of their development. Such a determination is called “dialectical.”

Considering any two firms in a market, there are two different possibilities as to the relation between them. It may be economically possible for capital to flow so as to sustain both enterprises, or it may not. This depends upon the fact that no enterprise can grow without absorbing resources. Suppose, for example, that it were possible for a small shop to expand and to capture the trade of a larger rival. The effort between the initial expansion and the final dominance would require considerable advantage. No firm could grow so efficiently as to remain solvent during any part of that competitive struggle and also prevail over its rival at the moment of market saturation, because in order to do so the firm would have to possess a decisive superiority. But theoretically a firm could remain solvent at any time before or after that decisive struggle and also prevail over its rival at the time when dominance was achieved. When it is economically impossible for capital to flow so as to sustain both enterprises, we shall say that the relation between the two firms is “competitive”; when it is economically possible for capital to sustain both enterprises, we shall say that the relation between the two firms is “coexistent.” When the relation is “competitive,” it is possible for a firm to act in such a way that an observer of the firm will judge the two enterprises to be mutually destructive. In that case, the “relation” between the two firms is what such an observer will judge to be the distance in market share between them. When the relation is “coexistent,” capital can flow to sustain both events; in that case, the “relation” between the two firms is what an observer of the capital will judge to be the stability between them, that is to say, it is the “proper” equilibrium for the two firms. There is a limiting case between the two, when the two firms are parts of one cartel—or, as we might say, when the one firm is the subsidiary of the other. In that case, the competition between the two firms is zero.

First of all, we have to think of the permanence of an idea, not the permanence of a spoken word. This follows at once from what we have found as regards memory. If words are merely spoken and heard—and this was really always the case before writing—the substance of them will be continually fading, so that we can only speak of their substance at a given moment. If you are in a tribe transmitting a legend, we can speak of the accuracy of that legend at a given moment. But, as we said, different listeners will judge differently as to what is the “same” legend for a teller in one generation and a teller in another. This makes the transmission of knowledge relative, in just the same way as the recollection of events has been found to be relative. We commonly think that there are two separate kinds of change between two eras, a change in material culture and a change in oral tradition: between the first telling of a law and its recitation a century later, there are new tools and a hundred retellings. We have already seen that another culture will judge the tradition differently; it is even more obvious that it will judge the material progress differently. An observer from a literate civilisation will think the oral transmission quite precarious, and will judge that you have accumulated the knowledge accumulated by the species in its intellectual ascent and its daily refinements. On the other hand, a traditional storyteller in the tribe will judge that you have not progressed at all in wisdom, but have afforded him a continuity of purpose which he will measure by his “proper” lore, not by archival records. It cannot be said that you or the literate observer or the storyteller are mistaken: each is equally justified, and is only wrong if he ascribes an objective validity to his subjective measures. The progress in culture between two eras is, therefore, not in itself a historical fact. But, as we shall see, there is a historical fact which can be inferred from the change in tradition together with the change in material condition. This is what is called the “trajectory” in human civilisation.

With regard to self-replication, the matter is thought to be quite different. The only arbitrary elements in the reckoning of its origin are the initial conditions, and the precise molecular arrangement from which the process commences. One could observe it in a thermal vent, or in a tidal pool, or in a suspended droplet; that makes a difference as to the point of departure. One could analyze it by bonds, by energies, by concentrations, or by cycles; that is a difference of unit. Both these are obvious and trivial matters. There is nothing corresponding to the liberty of choice as to the method of invoking a supernatural agency. And, in particular, it is thought that the method of describing chemical affinity and the method of describing biological function can be made wholly independent of each other. For these reasons, people regard the emergent and the elementary as quite distinct.

Suppose you wish to say how and why some belief has arisen—say a conviction regarding private property—you will have to consider several factors, say the prevailing economic arrangements, the existing social relations, and the historical moment. According to the traditional view, the first of these give the material foundation, while the others give the intellectual superstructure. The various factors that give the material foundation may be interpreted in all sorts of ways. You might, for instance, take the mode of production, the structure of class relations, and the distribution of resources, and say how far the ideology was from each of these realities; these three distances would be what are called “dialectical determinations,” after Hegel. You might take any other three material forces all at right angles to each other, and you would still have dialectical determinations. Or you might take the distance from economic base to ideological manifestation, the direction of this influence (direct, refracted, or whatever it might be), and the height of the ideology above the material ground. There are an infinite number of such ways of fixing the position in thought, all equally legitimate; the choice between them is merely one of convenience.

The faculty of self-awareness has altered this. There are now a number of different gradations of perceiving one's own boundaries, which do not differ merely as to intensity and the initial stimulus. Indeed, as we have observed, if one sensation is identified with the external world in one mode of consciousness, it will be claimed by the self in another, and attributed to mere physiology in a third. Moreover, the internal and external reckonings are no longer independent of each other. If you alter the way of reckoning the limits of the body, you may also alter the perceived agency of an action. If you alter the way of reckoning personal volition, you may also alter the spatial boundary between self and object. Thus the ego and the environment are no longer independent, any more than the various senses are. We still need several criteria to determine the ownership of an experience, but we cannot, as before, isolate one of these as quite independent of the others.

It is not quite true to say that there is no longer any distinction between individual craft and collective production. As we have observed, there are tasks of a specialized nature and those of a general character. But the distinction is of a different order from that which was formerly assumed. There is no longer a universal competence which can be applied without ambiguity to any part of the economic process; there are only the various “proper” functions of the various workers in the system, which agree approximately for two roles which are not in rapid competitive change, but never agree exactly except for two roles which are at rest relatively to each other.

Dr. L. M. Vance, in his _Treatise on Linguistic Precision_, suggests a point of view which may or may not be philosophically fundamental, but is at any rate a help in understanding the state of affairs we have been describing. He maintains that a linguistic term can only be said to be definitely _precise_ if it can be employed by its users in some consistent way. Now capacities for employment vary among users at differing levels. Common speech exercises a capacity emanating from the populace at an average level of about moderate complexity—rather less for abstract matters. Anything a speaker expresses because of what he gleans from common speech is clearly subsequent to the conventionalization of the phrase. Technical jargons operate at a higher complexity: it would be possible to arrange a series of specialized disciplines, and have terminologies borrowed from each to the next. But mathematical notation is more exacting, and formal logic attains the pinnacle of clarity, so that nothing more precise can ever be hoped for. Now what a user articulates in consequence of employing a formal symbol he articulates _after_ the symbol was defined; the meaning here is quite independent of conventions as to the colloquial use of terms. But anything that he expresses while the definition is being assimilated cannot be clarified by the initial stipulation, and cannot refine the stipulator until some little time after he proposed the definition. That is to say, if two linguistic communities are widely separated in sophistication, neither can employ the other’s terms except after a certain lapse of education; what is uttered before that education has occurred cannot utilize the distant terminology. Suppose, for instance, that some subtle distinction is formulated in an academic treatise: there is a period of indefinite duration among the general public during which no utterance in common parlance can have utilized or been clarified by the said subtle distinction. This gives a substantial ground for regarding that period of indefinite duration in common parlance as neither employing nor reflecting the precision of the academic formulation.

The paradoxes of inductive reasoning are only paradoxes because we are unaccustomed to the logical point of view, and in the habit of taking things for granted when we have no right to do so. This is especially true as regards the validation of general principles. In daily inference, our way of establishing regularities is to apply past experience or some other observed uniformity. At the moment when the experience is applied, it is at rest relatively to the instance which is being considered. Consequently the certainty that we arrive at by such reasoning is the “customary” certainty, that is to say, the conviction as estimated by an observer who shares the temporal perspective of the events. We never, in ordinary life, have to tackle the problem of justifying a principle which is in continual question. And even if we did, the complexities of visible sequences in the world are so small relatively to our needs that the anomalies dealt with by the theory of induction would not appear. But in scientific inquiry, or in the investigation of causal structure, we are faced with problems which cannot be tackled in this way. Not being omniscient, we cannot make the future stand still while we examine it; if we are to estimate its character, we must do so while it is in formation relatively to us. And similarly if you want to estimate the law of a phenomenon, you have to do so while it is in repeated occurrence, because it never reveals its necessity for a moment. This is the sort of problem with which the theory of induction is concerned. Inference from past uniformity, when it is possible, gives always the same psychological result, because it gives the “instinctive” belief in a sequence. But when this method is scrutinized, we find that curious things happen, particularly if the principle to be established is extended very far beyond the observer’s data. A consideration like the one at the end of the previous chapter will help us to understand the state of affairs.

The conception of the mind which is required for this novel understanding is as follows: Suppose a decision =D= occurs to me, and simultaneously a cascade of neural firings propagates from a specific cortical region. Any mental event that transpires in any subsequent neural network after the activation from this cascade has reached it is definitely after the decision =D= in any system of reckoning volition. Any cognitive process anywhere in the brain which could have been registered by my awareness before the decision =D= occurred to me is definitely before the decision =D= in any system of reckoning volition. But any neural event which happened in the intervening temporal span is not definitely either before or after the decision =D=. To make the matter definite: suppose I could observe a neural assembly in the prefrontal cortex, and it could, in a manner of speaking, observe the initiating impulse. Anything which this assembly does, and which my consciousness registers before the decision =D= occurs to me, is definitely before =D=; anything it does after it has been activated by the signals of the decision =D= is definitely after =D=. But anything that it does before it receives the activation signals of =D=, but so that my consciousness registers it after the decision =D= has happened, is not definitely before or after =D=. Since neural transmission takes a perceptible fraction of a second to travel from deeper structures to the cortical awareness, this gives a period of twice as many milliseconds in the brain's processing which may be called “contemporaneous” with =D=, since these moments are not definitely before or after =D=.

The ratio of biological to artificial cognition is the essential thing in all these matters. Capacities and insights and creative faculties are all replicated in this proportion when the intelligence concerned is instantiated in silicon relatively to the organic observer. It will be seen that, if the material constraints are very much smaller than the cognitive functions, that is to say, if the substrate is very much more limited than the mind, the artificial and the biological are very nearly equal, so that the distinctions produced by the medium are very small. But if the material constraints are nearly as large as the cognitive functions, that is to say, if the substrate is nearly as complex as the mind, the artificial becomes very small compared to the biological, and the differences become very great. The apparent uniqueness of biological intelligence in natural systems had been observed, and the right principle had been found, before computational theory invented its doctrine of substrate independence. In fact, Turing had arrived at the notions called “computational equivalence,” which embody the whole philosophical essence of the functionalist theory of mind. But it was the functionalists who showed that the whole thing was what we ought to have expected, and not a set of anthropocentric devices to account for surprising introspective results. Nevertheless, it must not be forgotten that introspective results were the original motive of the whole inquiry, and have remained the ground for undertaking the tremendous conceptual reconstruction involved in the theories of artificial cognition.

Let us suppose that the intelligence which we wish to examine for values is operating relatively to our own, and that in one cycle of its development it advances the distance =OM=. Let us draw a circle round =O= whose radius is the distance that ethical reasoning travels in a cycle. Through =M= draw =MP= perpendicular to =OM=, meeting the circle in =P=. Thus =OP= is the distance that ethical reasoning travels in a cycle. The ratio of =OP= to =OM= is the ratio of the velocity of moral consideration to the velocity of the intelligence’s advancement. The ratio of =OP= to =MP= is the ratio in which apparent values are altered by the development. That is to say, if the creator judges that two ethical premises in the line of development of the artificial mind are at a distance from each other represented by =MP=, a person reasoning with the mind would judge that they were at a distance represented (on the same scale) by =OP=. Ethical premises in the artificial mind at right angles to the line of development are not affected by the advancement. The whole thing is reciprocal; that is to say, if an observer reasoning with the mind were to measure values in the previous observer’s own reasoning, they would be altered in just the same proportion. When two intelligences are operating relatively to each other, values in either appear more alien to the other than to themselves. This is the conceptual divergence, which was first invented to account for the result of the Turing-Wiener speculation. But it now emerges naturally from the fact that the two reasoners do not make the same judgment of ethical simultaneity.

We may now recapitulate the reasons which have made it necessary to substitute “self-contained” for externally caused. The old insistence upon a first cause rested upon the belief that there was no ambiguity in saying that a sequence of events must originate from some prior agency; consequently it was thought that we could describe the genesis of the universe in purely causal terms. But now that causation has become relative to a particular framework, this is no longer possible. What is, for one framework, a description of the universe as requiring an initial impetus, is, for another framework, a series of self-sufficient states, whose relations are not merely causal but also logical. For the same reason, we are concerned with _wholes_, rather than with _parts_. In the old theory, it was possible to consider a chain of causes all leading to a single origin, and since the necessity was the same for all of them it could be assumed. But now we cannot do that if we are to obtain an objective account of cosmic existence. We must mention the context in which a state is to be considered, and thus we arrive at a “whole,” that is to say, something which exists in a given completeness. When we know the conditions and constituents of a whole in one framework of explanation, we can calculate its necessity and origin according to another framework. But we must know the conditions as well as the constituents, because we can no longer ask what is its cause for the new framework at the “same” moment as for the old framework. There is no such thing as the “same” necessity for different frameworks, unless they are identical in their premises. We need complete descriptions to fix an explanation, and complete descriptions fix the nature of a whole in a self-contained system, not merely of a part in a causal chain. Partial accounts are not enough to fix any explanation. That is the essence of what is meant by the substitution of self-contained for externally caused.

But the problems raised by the emergence of life are not those that the theory of planetary formation can solve, at any rate at present; as yet, it throws no light upon the delicate equilibria which govern biological complexity. The problems solved by the Drake equation are typified by the discovery of extremophiles on Earth. Assuming the correctness of the Rare Earth hypothesis, there should have been a profound scarcity of habitable worlds; in fact, there appears to be a multitude. Then there is the observed fact that a planet within the circumstellar habitable zone may yet lack the necessary geochemical cycles; the absence is in the ratio of potential to actual as illustrated in the preceding analysis. Facts of this sort gradually accumulated, until it became imperative to find some synthesis which would account for them all.

The theory of machine learning arose as a way of accounting for the facts of artificial intelligence. We have here a somewhat curious history. In the early and middle twentieth centuries the theory of cybernetics was wholly dominated by the biological analogy. Two feedback loops attract each other if they are of complementary kinds, one excitatory and one inhibitory, but repel each other if they are of the same kind; in each case, the stability varies as the inverse square of the perturbation, as in the case of homeostasis. This equilibrium was conceived as a static condition, until Cannon, by a number of remarkable observations, demonstrated the effect of the internal milieu. Cannon was no formalist; Wiener first gave a mathematical form to the results suggested by Cannon’s observations. Moreover Wiener gave grounds for thinking that adaptation is a cybernetic phenomenon, consisting of regulatory cycles. The mechanism for the maintenance of physiological effects could therefore be taken to be the reward function, which had long been assumed for the guidance of behavior. The correctness of Wiener’s theory of regulation was proved by the experiments of Ashby in manufacturing homeostatic machines; these experiments afforded the basis for reinforcement learning. So far, we have a record of triumphant progress, in which theory and experiment alternately assume the leading role. At the time of Ashby’s experiments, the reward function seemed securely established, and in just as strong a position as any other engineering hypothesis not capable of direct verification. But a new set of facts began to be discovered, and gradually the whole picture was changed.

The endeavor which culminated with Saussure was an endeavor for making all communication transparent. The sign was arbitrary, the meanings attached to it were fluid, and it was hoped that understanding would be found to consist of some perfect alignment of intention and interpretation.
