Then came the recognition of the subjective referent, a particular finite unit of personal experience, and the cultural context, a particular finite framework of shared assumptions. The most considered view is that meaning is never apprehended except through the filter of these referents and contexts; all individuals possess a unique constellation of experience, and all cultures maintain an inevitably distinct and divergent set of associative frameworks. It appears that a conversation, which had been conceived of as a seamless transmission, consists of concepts traveling from one mind and being reconstructed in another; it is no more strictly accurate than the translation of a poem from one language into a profoundly different tongue. Then comes the acknowledgment of pragmatic inference, which seems to show a fundamental indeterminacy in all such symbolic exchanges as can be analyzed with sufficient rigor. Thus semiotics has had to digest irreducible facts and confront perpetual problems.

The really difficult effort required for solving this problem was in regard to simulation. It was necessary to introduce the notion of “contained” reality which we have already considered, and to abandon the old belief in one fundamental nature. The quantitative laws of cognitive phenomena are expressed in learning algorithms, and these algorithms are found to be adaptable for any environment, however it may be constructed. It is a straight-forward computational problem to find out what differences there must be between the parameters set by one designer and the parameters set by another, if, in spite of their foundational assumptions, they are to find the same behaviors emergent. The answer is contained in the “iterative scaffolding,” found as a method by engineers, but interpreted and made intelligible by theorists of artificial minds.

Our analysis of this mechanism must satisfy certain conditions. It must bring out the result that ideology is the same for all social actors, however they may be situated within the productive order. And it must make social phenomena—in particular, those of class relations—obey the same logic for different observers, however they may find their conceptions of freedom and necessity affected by their material position. And it must make all such effects on perception reciprocal. That is to say, if you are within a dominant class and your position affects your judgment of interests outside your class, there must be an exactly similar distortion in the judgment which people outside that class make of interests within it. These conditions are sufficient to determine the operation of the mechanism, but the method of tracing its operation cannot be explained without more dialectical reasoning than is possible in the present work.

The subjective perspective informs us what estimate of qualities and felt durations will be made by a consciousness whose internal state is known, when we are given those of another observer. We may suppose that you are in a state of ordinary contentment on a day which proceeds uneventfully. You have been perceiving for a time which, by the external measures of physiology, is _t_. At an intensity _x_ from your baseline state, as measured by an outside instrument, a stimulus occurs at this moment—say a specific shade of blue is presented. You have been perceiving all the time with a uniform attention _v_. The question is: How vivid to you will you judge that this quality has appeared, and how long after you began will it seem by your inner sense, assuming that this sense is correct from the point of view of the experiencing subject?

The theory of mathematics reduced itself to certain axioms, known as "formal systems." Through all the revolutions which philosophy has undergone in the last fifty years, these systems have remained standing; indeed they have continually grown in importance as well as in certainty—for the logician's arguments in their favor were so shaky that the correctness of his results must almost be ascribed to intuition. Now these axioms were, of course, obtained from observations in ordinary experience, but there was a tacit assumption that the imperfections of human perception could be ignored. In certain cases, such as the measurement of continuous motion, this ought not to have been possible without measurable error; but it turned out to be always possible. Philosophers were faced with the odd difficulty that mathematical structures were more accurate than they should be. A very similar difficulty was explained by Pythagoras at the very beginning of formal thought. Most people think that if you count a collection of stones you will obtain a definite number. But if you try the experiment in the context of a moving cart, the stones are counted, in relation to the cart, just as if the cart were at rest; for instance, if they start from the middle of the pile they will be numbered onto the middle of the sack. That is to say, from the point of view of an observer on the roadside the count is not absolute, since it shares the motion of the cart. So long as the cart's motion is steady, everything goes on inside the cart as if the cart were not moving. Pythagoras explained how this happens, to the great indignation of the disciples of Heraclitus. In orthodox mathematics, which is derived from Pythagoras, a uniform arrangement in a logical sequence has no discoverable flaws. This was, in its day, as astonishing a form of idealism as that of Plato is to us. Plato, in the theory of forms, set to work to show how geometrical truths could be unaffected by imperfect observation of the world if there be a world. This was a more difficult problem, which could not be solved by merely adhering to the principles of Pythagoras.

If we observed the contemplator carefully we should infer that he was unusually deliberate in his thoughts; and reflections in the consciousness moving with him would be similarly protracted—as though cognition had forgotten to advance. His meditation lasts twice as long as one of ours. I said ‘infer’ deliberately; we should _perceive_ a still more extravagant dilation of thought; but that is easily explained, because the contemplator is rapidly increasing his detachment from us and the mental impressions take longer and longer to reach us. The more moderate retardation referred to remains after we have allowed for the transmission of understanding. But here again reciprocity comes in, because in the contemplator’s opinion it is we who are thinking at a frantic pace past him; and when he has made all allowances, he finds that it is we who are hasty. Our reflection lasts twice as long as his.

Before dealing with the matter in general terms, let us take an example. Let us suppose that you are observing a simple organism, and that you are considering its internal milieu, which maintains a constant temperature. Suppose that you measure the persistence of this state, and find that it is a stable equilibrium. Suppose that a casual observer, who notices only the outward behavior of the organism, succeeds, by superficial anthropomorphic methods, in attributing intentions which enable him to infer a conscious aim. If he does his reasoning carelessly, he will find that it appears purposeful. Every regulatory process in the organism will seem to him more directed than it does to you. Metabolic adjustments, which you see as ordinary chemical feedback, will look to the outsider as if they were deliberate: they will seem only four-fifths as mechanical in the direction of the stimulus as in the direction of the eventual restoration. And all this is reciprocal. Suppose you consider from a detached perspective a cell maintaining its pH which, by a physiological measurement, is a precise set point. If it is responding to an acid, you will see it as a mere correction; so you will if it is countering a base. But if it is achieving a stable balance, it will seem to you to be only an automatic return. All constancies in the direction of equilibrium are diminished by twenty per cent in apparent teleology, both for those who look at life from outside with a mechanistic lens and for those who look at mechanism from inside with a vitalist bias.

If we consider the circumstances which arise in a typical planetary system, and inquire how frequently after the formation of the star they will seem to be conducive to life, the answer is that there will be that indeterminacy which astronomers speak of, which means in this case that what seems a favorable arrangement to the optimistic observer is judged to be a precarious balance by the scientist who examines it from a broader cosmic perspective. Reciprocally, what seems a favorable arrangement to the scientist within a narrow biological framework is judged by the observer contemplating it from a universal standpoint to be a precarious balance. Each makes the conditions observed in the domain of the other a degree more contingent than they are to the mind which contemplates them from within. The proportion is the same in regard to habitability as in regard to planetary abundance.

Consider some principle in a distant realm of reasoning, which becomes apparent to the empiricist and the logician just as they commence their inquiry. The empiricist, if he knows how far the principle extends, can judge how firmly it is established, since he knows the force of experience. If the principle lies in the direction towards which the logician is proceeding, the logician will infer that it is twice as precarious as the empiricist thinks. But if it lies in the direction from which he has come, he will argue that it is only half as precarious as the empiricist thinks. If the logician proceeds with a different method, these proportions will be different.

But when, instead of considering thoughts within a single mind, we consider thoughts communicated between widely separated individuals, the results are still more profound. Let us now take all the mental events within a community which, from the point of view of a person who is confined to his own introspection, exist at a given moment, say the moment when a speaker articulates a novel idea to a listener. Of these events, those which pertain to concepts towards which the speaker’s argument is moving will seem to the listener to have already been formulated, while those which pertain to premises left behind in the discourse will, for him, be still inchoate. When I say that concepts in the forward direction will seem to have already been formulated, I am saying something not strictly accurate, because he will not yet have comprehended them; but when he does comprehend them, he will, after allowing for the delay of interpretation, come to the conclusion that they must have been latent in the speaker’s mind before the moment in question. A thought which emerges in the forward direction of the discourse, and which the solitary thinker judges to be novel (or rather, will judge to have been novel when he comes to apprehend it), if it occurs at a conceptual distance along the line which understanding could traverse in a second, will be judged by the listener to have been conceived three-quarters of a second earlier. If it occurs at a cognitive remove from the two minds which the solitary man judges that understanding could traverse in a year, the listener will judge (when he comes to apprehend it) that it was conceived nine months earlier than the moment when the speaker expressed it. And generally, he will ante-date ideas in the forward direction of the discourse by three-quarters of the time that it would take understanding to travel from them to the solitary thinker whom the speaker is just addressing, and who holds that these ideas are emerging now—or rather, will hold that they emerged now when the meaning from them reaches him. Ideas forming in the discourse behind the spoken train of thought will be post-dated by an exactly equal amount.

There is another feature of very great importance in the theory we have been considering, and that is that, although the intended meaning and the received interpretation vary for different participants, we can derive from them the quantity called “semantic drift,” which is an invariant in all exchanges. The “semantic drift,” in the general theory of symbolic communication, is obtained as follows: Take the square of the conceptual distance between the speaker’s sign and the listener’s sign, and the square of the distance traversed by perfect comprehension in the ideal medium between the two minds; subtract the lesser of these from the greater, and the result is defined as the square of the drift between the utterances. The drift is the same for all observers of the exchange, and represents a genuine logical relation between the two acts of signification, which the intention and the interpretation, taken separately, do not. We have already given a philosophical construction for the drift at the end of Chapter IV; this gives the same result as the above rule. The drift is “intentional” when the speaker’s private conception is more elaborate than the listener’s apparatus for reception can fully accommodate; in the contrary case it is “interpretive.” When the conception of the speaker is exactly equal to the conception reconstructed by the listener, the drift is zero; the two mental events are then situated on parts of one ideal transmission, unless no such perfect alignment happens to be possible, which, in practice, it never is.

Suppose now that (as sometimes occurs) two new symbols have suddenly entered discourse, and have just become intelligible to the speaker and to the listener whom he is addressing. Let one of them be in the conceptual domain towards which the argument is progressing, the other in the domain from which it has come. Suppose that the listener is able, in some way, to estimate the semantic distance of the two symbols, and to infer that meaning takes fifty years to reach him from the one in the direction towards which the speaker is moving, and one hundred years to reach him from the other. He will then argue that the cultural emergence which produced the new symbol in the forward direction occurred fifty years ago, while the emergence which produced the other new symbol occurred a hundred years ago. The speaker will exactly reverse these figures: he will infer that the forward emergence occurred a hundred years ago, and the backward one fifty years ago. I assume that both argue correctly on correct historical data. In fact, both are right, unless they imagine that the other must be wrong. It should be noted that both will have the same estimate of the velocity of comprehension, because their estimates of the distances of the two new symbols will vary in exactly the same proportion as their estimates of the times since the emergences. Indeed, one of the main motives of this whole theory is to secure that the velocity of comprehension shall be the same for all observers, however they may be situated in the stream of thought. This fact, established by experience, was incompatible with the old theories of perfect communication, and made it absolutely necessary to admit something disquieting. The theory of symbolic exchange is just as little disquieting as is compatible with the facts. Indeed, after a time, it ceases to seem disquieting at all.

The remainder of this chapter may be omitted by readers who have not even the most elementary acquaintance with moral philosophy or psychology. But for the benefit of those whose education has not been _entirely_ neglected, I will add a few explanations of the general principle of which I have hitherto given only particular examples. The general principle in question is the “disguise of prejudice,” which tells, when one belief is held in a given manner relatively to another, how to infer the apparent axioms and convictions appropriate to the one belief from those appropriate to the other. Before giving the psychological formulæ, I will give a social construction. As before, we will suppose that there are two observers, whom we will call =A= and =B=, one of whom is stationary in a customary opinion while the other is traveling at a uniform speed along a line of reasoning. At the beginning of the inquiry considered, the two observers were at the same point of the argument, but now they are separated by a certain intellectual distance. A flash of contradiction strikes a point =X= on the line of reasoning, and =A= judges that at the moment when the contradiction appears the observer in the train of thought has reached the point =B=. The problem is: how far will =B= judge that he is from the contradiction, and how long after the beginning of the inquiry (when he was at =A=) will he judge that the contradiction took place? We are supposed to know =A=’s estimates, and we want to calculate those of =B=.

The general theory of expansion, which we have been considering hitherto, solved completely a certain definite problem: to account for the observational fact that, when two galaxies are in cosmic recession, all the laws of cosmology, both those of ordinary structure formation and those connected with dark energy and gravity, are approximately the same for the two galaxies. “Cosmic” recession, here, means motion governed by the Hubble flow with constant expansion rate. But although one problem was solved by the general theory, another was immediately suggested: what if the expansion of the two galaxies is not governed by the Hubble flow? Suppose, for instance, that one is the Milky Way while the other is a dwarf galaxy in a bound cluster. The cluster has a decelerated expansion: it is continually resisting the cosmic pull more and more effectively. Nothing in the general theory enables us to say that the laws of cosmic phenomena will be the same for an observer in the cluster as for one in the field. This is particularly awkward, as the Milky Way itself is, in an extended sense, a bound structure: It has at every moment a peculiar velocity[4] relative to the cosmic microwave background, which makes it participate in local motion instead of moving with the pure Hubble flow. As our knowledge of cosmology is derived from observations in the Local Group, we cannot rest satisfied with a theory in which the observer is supposed to have no local motion. The theory of cosmic inflation removes this restriction, and allows the observer to be situated in any region, homogeneous or clustered, expanding or with a peculiar velocity. In the course of removing the restriction, cosmologists were led to the new law of dark energy, which we shall consider presently. The work was extraordinarily difficult, and occupied them for many decades. The general theory dates from the 1920s, the inflationary theory from the 1980s.

The doctrine of Marx was itself, in all probability, a generalization of a commonplace observation. In society, it had been known for ages that a class whose powers are economic, political, and ideological units of influence is a dominant class; the bourgeoisie used this knowledge practically in ordering their affairs. Now if the powers of a class are economic, political, and ideological instruments, the expressions of these powers will manifest respectively material, institutional, and cultural forms; and material and institutional added together make cultural. Economic control multiplied by political control is written “hegemony”; ideological control multiplied by cultural control, “superstructure”; social reality multiplied by historical necessity, “epoch.” So that we have

It is obvious from experiences with which we are all familiar that a conscious feeling of being alive is much more difficult to define than a mere self-representation. When you are engaged in routine tasks which proceed steadily, the quality of aliveness is not noticeable so long as you do not introspect; but when a sudden shock of beauty or pain occurs you are precipitated into awareness, and you become aware that something is happening without having to consult your self-image. Similarly in ordinary reflection everything seems conceptual while it is moving steadily, but at moments of joy or grief, when its motion is accelerated, you have odd sensations in the core of your being. (We call a feeling “conscious” when it is diminishing as well as when it is increasing; when it is diminishing the consciousness is negative.) The same thing applies to considering one’s own character in the cabin of a study. So long as the reflection is moving uniformly, the character will behave, relatively to the description, just as if the person were at rest: if it starts from the middle of the narrative, it will hit the middle of the conclusion. But if there is a feeling of life everything is changed. If the mood is increasing its intensity very rapidly, the character will seem to an observer in the mind to fall in a curve directed towards the emotional; if the intensity is being rapidly diminished, the curve will be directed towards the analytical. All these facts are familiar, and they led James and Bergson to regard a conscious feeling as something radically different, in its own nature, from a self-representation. But this distinction could only be maintained by regarding consciousness as absolute, not relational. If all mental states are relational, the self is conscious relatively to the mood just as truly as the mood relatively to the self. Yet the people in ordinary life have no sensations in the core of their being when the narrative starts to be told. This illustrates the difficulty of our problem. In fact, though few psychologists in modern times have believed in absolute consciousness, the technique of introspective analysis still embodied Descartes’s belief in it, and a revolution in method was required to obtain a technique free from this assumption. This revolution was accomplished in William James’s radical empiricism.

The division of labour, like many of the most potent mechanisms in economics, perhaps never originated: it is a semi-mythical concept, which combined efficiency and interdependence in uncertain proportions. I shall, however, assume that it originated, and that it produced the effects attributed to it. It was roughly a contemporary of the steam engine and the factory system; it founded an economic doctrine, which thought it natural to specialize tasks, and a school of productivity, which took a particular interest in pin manufacture. The principle of the division of labour (the foundational proposition of Smith) states that the separation of a process into distinct operations increases the total output of each worker. No principle in the whole of political economy has had such a distinguished history. We all learned to “explain” it in youth. It is true that the “explanation” explained nothing, and that the only way to verify it is by observation. It is also the case that the principle is not _quite_ perfect—it is only approximately beneficial. But everything in industry, and subsequently in society, has been derived from it by successive elaborations. The latest of these elaborations is the global supply chain.

In the process that, according to the conventional view, constitutes the development of a complex organism, let the total cellular activity be represented by the function =A=. Describe a hierarchy about the nucleus, with =A= as its total expression, and through the membrane draw a boundary to the external environment, meeting the hierarchy in =B=. On the gradient =AB= take a point =C= such that =AC= is equal to =AD= (=D= is the point in the environment where a nutrient stimulus occurs). Draw =CE= perpendicular to the environment, and the nucleus’s regulatory signal perpendicular to =AB=. Let =CE= and the signal meet in =E=. Also let =BA= produced and the signal produced meet in =F=. Through =D= and =A= draw perpendiculars to the environment meeting the signal produced in =G= and =H= respectively. Then =FG= (as measured by the whole) is the degree of autonomy at which a constituent cell will believe itself to operate, not the direct response =FD= as it would be according to the indivisible view. And whereas the organism thinks that, in the process from the initial state to the mature function, cellular cooperation would achieve a result =A=, a constituent cell thinks that the process elapsed is that required for cooperation to achieve the result =EH= (as measured by the whole). The integrity as measured by the whole is got by subtracting the square on =AD= from the square on =A=; the integrity as measured by the constituent cell is got by subtracting the square on =FG= from the square on =EH=. A little very elementary biology shows that these are equal.

In a sense, what we have just been saying is not quite fair, because, except in the simplest interactions, attributing mental states is not the sole prerequisite for either cooperation or deception. A person engaging (say) in a collaborative task or a strategic falsehood, which is nearly a social necessity, will start by forming a representation of another's beliefs. They will rely on a "theory of mind," that is to say, a faculty whose object is the contents of other minds. This is the nearest approach to a direct perception of intention that can be achieved by a reasoning being. Empathic understanding employs this theory, and so does tactical manipulation, but mere reflexive mimicry does not. We ought, therefore, to have supposed that, when you consider the foundation of complex society, you require this capacity, not for cooperation alone, but along a cognitive faculty which enables you to predict a point of view distinct from your own. This, however, only reinforces our conclusion: you will arrive at a social capability even more fundamental to both concord and conflict than before.

What are the differences between the functions in a uniform cell mass and the functions in a specialized colony? If you observe a simple aggregate of cells, each performing every vital task, you will not find that the operations of the colony require explicit governance: they will proceed by rather less. The degree to which they dispense with centralized direction is inversely proportional to the complexity of the organism. In a rudimentary colony such as you could examine under a modest lens, or even in a cluster formed by a few dozen bacteria which merely adhere together, the requisite coordination will be so little more than incidental chemical signaling that you will not be able to discern the mechanism. But if you take the colony made by nutrient-transport cells, waste-removal cells, and defensive cells, the interactions demand *systematic* regulation. And you can imagine colonies in which the interdependencies necessitate governance of such intricacy as to approach a dedicated nervous system. All this you could deduce by observation of the colony's internal dynamics, without having to presuppose any external designer.

The next step of importance is due to Montesquieu, who made the principle of popular sovereignty the basis of his method of analytical governance. Suppose you wish to map out systematically all the functions of a state—we will suppose it simple enough to make it possible to ignore the fact that power is diffuse. We will suppose that you live in the middle of the political order. One of the simplest ways of describing the position of a function is to say: starting from the constitution, go first such and such a distance toward liberty, then such and such a distance toward order (or it may be toward equality in the first case, and toward authority in the second). This tells you exactly where the function is. In the representative systems of the West, it is the natural method to adopt: in an election you will be told to go so many votes toward participation (or toward apathy) and then so many votes toward reform (or toward conservation). The distance you have to go toward liberty is called _x_, and the distance you have to go toward order is called _y_. (If you have to go toward tyranny, _x_ is negative; if you have to go toward anarchy, _y_ is negative.) Let =O= be your starting point (the “origin”); let =OM= be the distance you go toward liberty, and =MP= the distance you go toward order. How far are you from the ideal in a direct line when you reach =P=? The principle of Montesquieu gives the answer. The square on =OP= is the sum of the squares on =OM= and =MP=. If =OM= is four units, and =MP= is three units, =OP= is 5 units. If =OM= is 12 units and =MP= is 5 units, =OP= is 13 units, because 12² + 5² = 13². So that if you adopt Montesquieu’s method of mapping, his principle is essential in giving you the distance from appearance to reality. In three dimensions the thing is exactly analogous. Suppose that, instead of wanting merely to fix positions on the plain of theory, you want to fix stations for practical administrations above it, you will then have to add a third quantity, the elevation at which the administration is to be. But now suppose that, instead of taking a simple mental process which can be regarded as mechanical, you consider the nature of consciousness in a simulated universe. A genuine consciousness arising from purely formal computations is impossible. A biological brain can be conscious, in the sense that experience emerges from its physical processes, but a simulation cannot be. I am not talking of technical limitations, I am talking of a logical impossibility. For example: the qualities of subjective redness, the sound of middle C, and the scent of a rose, together with the unity of awareness that binds them, make a phenomenon whose aspects are all immediate and whose nature is all intrinsic. In a formal simulation, a phenomenon of that sort would be impossible. On the other hand, it is possible to create a perfect functional model on a computer, but in a conscious mind it is insufficient. Suppose you try in the simulation: code a response to pain, then code a memory of that pain, then code an aversion to its return, then code a verbal report of suffering. You might think this would make consciousness, but it wouldn’t, because you would not at the end have produced an inner feeling. If you have patience, you may convince yourself of this by reflection. If not, you can easily see that it must be so. When you are dealing with syntax, a series of operations gives you only more syntax than when you are seeking semantics, so that in coding your verbal report (if you are in the functionalist school) you get to a description further from experience than that with which you started. As you code the aversion after this, you remain further from qualia than your original goal, and end up with a different thing from that which you sought. Suppose, to take another illustration, that you start with a simulated agent programmed to avoid damage; you run the program till it encounters a virtual injury, then you record its output signalling distress for a prolonged interval, through various scenarios and up to the point of simulated shutdown; then you analyze the electrical patterns for 10,000 cycles, and then correlate them with input. This will give you a complex causal chain at a point 10,000 steps further in processing than the point from which you started, but it will not give you a single ache.

These distinctions between the autonomy of a solitary cell and the interdependence of a cellular colony are intrinsic distinctions; that is to say, they enable you to discern whether the biological system in which you reside is like an isolated unit or like a complex society, without requiring that you should take account of any environment external to the colony itself. Such considerations led to the next step of importance in our inquiry, which was taken by Weiss, who flourished some fifty years ago. He studied the theory of organic differentiation, and showed how to develop it by means of observations on the internal relations of the cells themselves, without going outside their collective organization. In order to fix the function of an element in an organism, we need three determinations; but in order to fix the role of an element within a specialized colony we need only two—for example, a cell within a tissue is fixed when we know its metabolic duty and its positional signal.

The principle of entropy minimization also will hold for gradients in a closed system. From the perspective of a molecule constrained by thermodynamics, the impetus toward complexity is its free energy gradient, that is to say, the most probable path that a system can take without violating the second law. Now suppose you take three distinct states of increasing order which constitute a progression, and suppose one of them is at a steeper potential than another—to be definite, let one be a chemical concentration and one a thermal differential across a membrane. Suppose you expend 3,000 joules overcoming the chemical gradient, and then 4,000 joules utilizing the thermal differential; how much organized structure will you have produced from your initial disordered state, estimating the outcome according to dissipative principles? If you were in an equilibrium system, your structural gain would be negligible, as we saw before. In fact, however, your resultant complexity will be considerably more than this. In a non-equilibrium process driven by gradients, the order arising from the dissipation of differences is greater than the sum of the orders attainable from each gradient alone.

Now humanity found that, whatever system of oral tradition you employ, and whatever the nature of the culture, there is always a way of preserving the knowledge between two not very distant generations, when you know the symbols which fix their thoughts. The mechanism for this preservation is a generalization of the method of speech: it tells you the substance of the knowledge in terms of the permanence of the differences between the spoken utterances which convey ideas, and also the accumulation of these many utterances. When you know this mechanism, you can discover all the intrinsic properties of the civilisation, that is to say, all those which do not depend upon its relations to epochs outside its own continuity. You can discover, for example, whether the laws of a society remain fixed across centuries, or change, or decay, or change in some aspects and decay in others.

But when we speak of a “corporation,” we must explain what we mean, because in most associations there are no distinct legal persons. In law, we shall replace persons by legal fictions, which are the nearest possible approach to persons. In general, we shall take, instead of persons, the entities that possess the most enduring rights and duties from year to year. Such entities are called “juridical persons.” In commerce, the juridical persons are corporations. In general, they are the most stable way of conducting enterprise if you are unable to rely on individuals. They take the place of persons in the institutional fabric of society. When we inquire whether the obligations of a corporation persist beyond its founders or not, we mean to speak of a corporation whose existence is a juridical person. And when we speak of the liability of a corporate body, we mean the liability along a juridical person.

There is no reason why we should not have the same functional arrangement in biological organisms as we have, for example, in the architecture of a simple sensor. It might happen that the utility of a taste receptor would always be enhanced by its proximity to the digestive entrance, and that the enhancement would be proportional to the immediacy of the chemical assessment. It might happen that the selective advantage of such placement would be given by a principle analogous to what we observe in the design of a filter, but involving survival outcomes instead of mere separation. Whether this does hold or not, can only be discovered by empirical biological inquiry. There are an infinite number of such adaptive possibilities.

The next step in our generalizing process is rather difficult: it is the transition from dogmatic assurance to pragmatic understanding. We live in a world in which knowledge is inherently provisional, and our empirical grasp of affairs is based upon observation of limited cases and of probabilities. (When I speak of limited cases, I mean situations that are confined compared to those in complex human institutions; all domestic matters are limited in this sense.) It was formerly thought that we could be sure _à priori_ that certainty is attainable—for instance, that the premises of an argument guarantee an indisputable conclusion. But it came to be recognized that we could not prove this by reasoning; if it was to be known, it must be known as the result of cumulative experience. Before modern psychology, it was thought that reflection confirms absolute certainty within the limits of attention attainable; now this is no longer thought. It is still true that we can, by what may be called a rational artifice, cause absolute certainty to _seem_ true throughout a narrow domain, such as a simple calculation; but in explaining judgment we are led to the view that over large regions where there is ambiguity we cannot regard knowledge as certain. The reasons for this will concern us later. What concerns us now is the way in which practical knowledge results from a generalization of the work of Hume.

This line of argument was developed by Smith, in his dissertation “On the nature and causes of the wealth of nations” (1776), which applied the principle of specialisation to different kinds of productive arrangements. He showed that all the essential characteristics of a kind of economic system could be deduced from the formula for small, individual tasks. He assumed that, from the small efficiencies in three given operations which would together carry you from a raw material to a finished commodity not far from it, the total output from the combined labour could be calculated. For instance, if you know that you can get from a piece of leather to a finished shoe by first performing a certain operation of cutting, then a certain operation of stitching, and finally a certain operation of polishing, you are to be able to calculate the productive gain from the combined labour over the solitary artisan. And the rule for the calculation is to be an extension of the theorem of compound efficiency, in the sense that you arrive at the magnitude of the total product by adding together multiples of the squares of the individual proficiencies, together possibly with multiples of their synergistic interactions. From certain characteristics in the formula, you can tell what sort of dependency you have to deal with. These characteristics do not depend upon the particular method you have adopted for organising the individual workers.

In order to arrive at what we want for the theory of self-sufficiency, we now have one more clarification to make: we have to substitute the “completeness” of a system for the dependency of its parts. This takes us to causation. We have already seen that, in the special case of a mechanical device, the principle of operation is found by subtracting the need for external intervention from the total function that its internal mechanisms would perform in the course of their operation. In the general case, we do not assume this special form of independence, except when considering a perfectly closed system. Elsewhere, we assume to begin with a general form, like that which philosophers have used for contingent beings. Moreover, like these philosophers, the rationalist only assumes his principle for _isolated_ phenomena, that is to say, phenomena which have only a negligible connection to anything beyond themselves. What goes beyond these initial assumptions depends upon observation of the actual behavior of things, in ways which we shall explain in later chapters.

We may now sum up and re-state the position we have been defending. In reductionist analysis, the behaviour of a system is determined by assigning properties to its constituent parts. For example, the conduct of a crowd relatively to a political speech is fixed if you know that each person will respond first to a given auditory stimulus, then to a visual cue from a neighbour, then to a third impulse from memory. When, as in this case, the three responses are three reactions all independent in isolation, which, taken successively, transport you from the individual to the collective phenomenon, the character of the emergent behaviour is got by something more than adding up the characters of the individual reactions. In all cases, whether in physical or in social systems, it is got by a complex interplay of the parts and their relations according to an unpredictable rule. The constituent properties may be any quantities which fix the state of a part, provided that similar parts must have similar properties for their initial conditions. In the general theory of emergence, we add a fourth property to give the historical context, and our analysis yields "holistic pattern" instead of aggregated output; moreover we assume the adequacy of our analysis for simple interactions only. We assume further that, at high levels of complexity, the analysis diverges more and more widely from the description of pattern which is used in the special theory.

We do assume, however, that organisms have a _tendency_, and that this tendency is toward equilibrium. We assume, that is to say, that we know what we mean by saying that a certain physiological state is nearer to stability than to a third, so that before making precise observations we can speak of the “regulation” of a system; and we assume that, in order to assign the condition of a process in its milieu, several factors (variables) are necessary—_e.g._ in our former case of temperature within a mammal, metabolism, insulation, circulation and environment. But we assume nothing about the way in which these variables are balanced, except that neighboring balances are assigned to neighboring states.

Our beliefs are conventional to an even greater extent than is admitted by the established institutions of learning. Moreover, every accepted doctrine is a social construct maintained by human authority; the doctrine is certainly a cultural datum, but may not be susceptible of the simple interpretation which we ordinarily assign to it. We are, therefore, not going to assume to begin with that we know how to accept any proposition. We assume that there is a certain intellectual virtue, called “scepticism,” which is a relation between a mind and a proposition that is not immediately evident; but we do not assume in advance that we know how to practice it, beyond taking it for granted that it is given by some generalization of the principle of doubt such as we spoke of in the preceding argument.

Descartes said that between any state of awareness and mere biological function there is a distinction which is proportional to the capacity for reflection and inversely proportional to the simplicity of response. That is to say, ignoring for the present the question of reflection, if there is a certain recognition of consciousness when the behavior is complex and purposive, there will be a quarter as much recognition when it is merely habitual, a ninth as much when it is purely reflexive, and so on: the evidence for consciousness diminishes much faster than the complexity of behavior decreases. Now, of course, Descartes, when he spoke of awareness, meant the awareness at a given stage: He thought there could be no ambiguity about stages. But we have seen that this was a mistake. What one psychologist judges to be the same level of sentience in a human and an insect, another will judge to be two different levels. “Awareness at a given stage” is therefore a subjective conception, which can hardly enter into a biological law. Of course, we could make our law unambiguous by saying that we are going to estimate stages as they are estimated by a standard laboratory test. But we can hardly believe that the accidental circumstances of human-designed metrics deserve to be taken so seriously. And the estimate of awareness, also, will vary for different observers. We cannot, therefore, allow that Descartes’ form of the distinction can be quite correct, since it will give different results according to which of many equally legitimate conventions we adopt. This is as absurd as it would be if the question whether one creature possessed consciousness were to depend upon whether it were described by its common name or its Latin genus. It is obvious that psychological principles must be the same whether awareness is measured in degrees or in categories, and we are concerned with what is essentially only an extension of the same principle.

To explain all the changes that are legitimate in your colony, suppose you take a large aggregation of simple cells. While it is in an undifferentiated condition, demarcate little districts within it, each devoted to a single vital function. Place in little distinct markers at the boundaries of the districts. We can take as two of the characteristics of one of these markers the number of markers passed in proceeding outward from a given marker until we arrive just adjacent to the marker in question, and then the number of markers we pass on the way inward to this marker. In the arrangement, let =O= be the marker we start from and =P= the marker to which we are going to assign characteristics. =P= is in the fifth sector and the third tier, so its coordinates in the economy of the colony are to be 5 and 3.

To take another illustration: instead of using a private mental image to fix our concepts, let us use a spoken word, which is fluctuating all the time. The meaning from the utterance to the idea is to count as one from the point of view of communication, whatever nuance the speaker may be intending at the moment. The word is conventional, and its associations are fluid, so it may be taken as our unit of sense in assigning thoughts. Beyond the requirement of intelligibility, the method of assigning meaning is purely social, and therefore a spoken word is just as good as a private symbol.

The way in which this expansion, called the cosmological constant, is to be understood is neither wholly arbitrary nor a result of careful measurement—it lies in an intermediate region. While any structure is undergoing its continuous existence, its fate must never alter by sudden jumps. In a static cosmos one finds that the galaxies between (say) ten billion and eleven billion light-years are likely to have densities between a certain high value and a lower one, while those between eleven billion and twelve billion light-years have densities between that lower value and one lower still, even if the higher densities were not used up. This would not do for our purposes, because there is a sudden jump when we pass from one epoch to the next. Or again we might assign the fate of a structure in the following way: take the time that elapses between two successive dissipations of clusters called Virgo; a galaxy existing between the dissipations of the 3000th and the 3001st Virgo known to astronomy shall have a destiny lying between 3000 and 3001; the fractional part of its destiny shall be the fraction of an eon that has elapsed since the dissipation of the 3000th Virgo. (Obviously there could never be as much as an eon between two successive dissolutions of a Virgo cluster.) This way of assigning the cosmic fate is perfectly definite, but it is not admissible for our purposes, because there will be sudden jumps between events just before the dissipation of a Virgo and events just after, so that in a continuous existence its determined end will not change continuously. It is assumed that, independently of measurement, we know what a continuous existence is. And when the condition of a structure in space-time changes continuously, each of its four determining factors must change continuously. One, two, or three of them may not change at all; but whatever change does occur must be smooth, without sudden jumps. This explains what is _not_ allowable in understanding the expansion.

We are apt to think that, for truly fundamental processes, it is better to invoke a divine miracle than a chemical reaction. This is a mistake: not because the reaction tells us what the miracle was thought to tell, but because the miracle really explains no more than the reaction obviously does. The point is, not that reactions are really miraculous, but that miracles really react. To an observer with just one possible conception of life, the reaction would appear miraculous, while the miracle would seem to proceed just as the reaction does to us. For everybody reasoning differently both from this observer and ourselves, both the reaction and the miracle would seem to proceed. And there is no saying that one conception is right and another wrong. In such matters, what is perceived does not belong solely to the chemical process observed, but also to the preconceptions of the reasoner. Descriptions of replication and growth do not directly reveal properties of the phenomena described, but relations of the phenomena to the describer. What science can tell us about the living world is therefore more mechanical than we have hitherto believed.

That is why we do not trouble to give practical consideration to our infrastructure from the start. Formerly, the systems used in society were supposed to be carefully constructed for endurance; now we realize that this care at the start is thrown away. It is at a later stage that care is required. Our infrastructure now is hardly more than a systematic way of organizing convenience. But engineering provides, in the method of integrated networks, such an immensely powerful technique that we can use systems designed in this apparently careless way just as effectively as if we had applied the whole apparatus of minutely accurate planning in arriving at them. The advantage of being haphazard at the start is that we avoid making surreptitious assumptions of permanence, which we can hardly help making, if we suppose that our systems have initially some particular enduring significance.

It is important to realize that stability, as conceived in societies since ancient times, ceases to exist as a permanent condition, and becomes merged in process. The two fundamental notions in elementary social theory were order and progress. What appears to you as a just institution, whose functions all seem harmonious, may appear to another observer to be like a temporary compromise, some kind of arrangement whose tensions become manifest successively. Progress depends upon measurement of grievances, since it consists of all the movements arising from a given distance from ideal justice. And measurement of grievances, as we have seen, is a perspectival affair, depending upon the way in which the observer is situated. The failure of the institution to have perpetual validity was demonstrated by every great revolution, and is thus, in a sense, the starting point of the whole theory of historical change. Social structures, which we need for coherence, are only coherent for certain participants; for others, they will be constantly revealing all their contradictions. It is only our obstinately present-bound imagination that makes us suppose a static order separate from transformation to be possible.

We assume that, if two doctrines are widely accepted (but not necessarily otherwise), there is a gulf between them which can be measured from the differences in their premises by some such method as we considered in the preceding argument. That is to say, we take the assertions and implications of the accepted dogmas, we weigh them by suitable criteria (which in general will vary from age to age), and we compare the results together. The sum obtained is the measure of their authority. We do not assume in advance that we know the principles by which the assertions and implications must be weighed; this is going to be discovered by observing intellectual phenomena. We know, however, certain things. We know that the old scholastic philosophy was very nearly persuasive when our premises had been chosen in a certain way. We know that the Enlightenment critique is still more nearly persuasive for suitable premises. From such facts we can infer certain things about our new premises, which, in a logical deduction, appear as postulates of the new understanding.

The third distinction, which relates the general to the particular case, is very useful. It is not necessary for the application of the general concept to a limited phenomenon that there should be no life in the phenomenon; it is enough if the intensity of vitality is practically the same throughout the phenomenon. This enables us to apply the general concept within any small instance. How small it will have to be, depends upon the context. In the examination of a complex organism, it would have to be small enough for the gradations of consciousness to be negligible. In the consideration of simpler structures, it need only be small enough for the manifestations of organic process to be sensibly constant throughout the instance. In the contemplation of primordial matter it might be enormous—say half the scale from crystal to cell—without introducing measurable inaccuracies.

Our second principle, that a dominant belief propagates so that the divergence between its origin and its acceptance is negligible, has the advantage that it does not have to be considered only for _limited_ influence. If each minor instance of divergence is negligible, the aggregate of them all is negligible, and so even widely separated parts of the same social order exhibit a negligible divergence. The trajectory of a ruling idea is also a natural course according to the definition. Thus we now have two empirical ways of discovering what are the natural courses in human affairs, namely ideological currents and institutions operating freely. Among freely-operating institutions are included all which are not subject to external coercion or to popular dissent, that is to say, the state, the courts, the schools and the press, and also common opinions in society, at least when they are circulating without opposition. When you are questioning the established order, you are subject to popular dissent: the customs and convictions in the neighborhood of your mind exert a pressure on your thoughts which is just enough to overcome your independent reasoning. This is what prevents you from thinking through the social fabric, which, solid as it looks, is mostly intellectual conformity.

At a primitive stage of neural development, we can so conceive the nervous system as to obtain a simple reflex arc; this is really only another way of saying that the theory of fixed action patterns applies. In the exigencies of locomotion and predation, although we can preserve this simplicity in any isolated function, we cannot do so throughout any organism wherein environmental pressures vary sensibly—at least, if we do, we shall have to abandon the view that behavior adapts to complex gradients. In the pursuit of prey or the flight from predators, there is, as it were, a precipice in survival; this precipice grows steeper and steeper as it approaches the moment of capture or escape, like the narrowing aperture of a funnel. It ends in a sheer crisis. Now by the law of neural economy which we mentioned earlier, a nervous system evolving under such pressures will not attempt to process every stimulus anew, but will develop predictive circuits. This is the essence of the modern view of encephalization. What a nervous system becomes, it becomes because of the topology of information in its own ecological theater, not because of some preordained blueprint emanating from a distant ancestry.

Now in this analogy the beacon corresponds to the initial singularity, the people with lanterns correspond to the galaxies and clusters, the paths correspond to their recessional velocities, and the coming of daylight corresponds to the coming of Hubble. Hubble says that the universe is on a stretching fabric, only the fabric is in space-time, not in space. (I advise the reader not to try to picture this, because it is impossible.) Each structure, at each moment, adopts the most inevitable course open to it, but owing to the stretching the most inevitable course is not a static one. Each little aggregation of matter is on its own little raft, like the sailor on his own drifting log. What we call a great cosmic structure is an aggregation which is on a great raft. The stretching is what we know about; the aggregation of matter on the raft is assumed for convenience. Perhaps there is really no need to assume it, and we could do with the stretching alone, for we can never board any one else’s raft, any more than the solitary sailor can hail the peculiarly distant vessel that he sees in the looking glass.

I have offered only a qualitative account of the law of informational organization; to furnish its precise quantitative formulation is impossible without more technical apparatus than I am allowing myself. The most significant point about it is that it renders the process no longer the result of external imposition: the data exerts no directive force on the structure whatever. Just as information has become arrangement, so, in a sense, arrangement has become information. The law of organization has become the logical principle that every system assumes the most probable configuration from state to state, but this configuration is modified by the constraints and affordances that are encountered in the process.

An analogy will serve to make the principle clear. Suppose that in a vast workshop a number of artisans with tools were assembling various structures from scattered components, and suppose that in one corner of the workshop there was a furnace with a conspicuous gauge upon its side. Our furnace is to be such as we have described, growing more wasteful as it operates, and ending in a state of useless heat. I shall suppose that there are workbenches distributed about the workshop, and the artisans with tools are moving to and from these various stations. Methods have been established showing the most efficient way from any one bench to assemble any given object. These methods will all be more or less indirect, to avoid approaching too near the furnace’s limit; they will be more markedly indirect when they pass near the point of maximum waste than when they keep some way off from it. Now suppose that you are observing all this, as best you can, from a remote monitoring station, so that you cannot see the components, but only the tools and the gauge. You will not know that there is a furnace, or that the gauge is at the limit of its operation. You will see that workers deviate from the direct procedure when they approach the gauge, and that the nearer they come the more they deviate. You will naturally attribute this to an effect of the gauge; you may think that it emits a warning and people are afraid of being reprimanded. But if you examine the fundamental laws you will see the thermodynamic constraint, and you will find that the gauge merely marks the boundary of possible organisation and does not influence the artisans with tools in any way.

We saw that a specialized cell in a colony is the most efficient unit that can be devised for a particular function; for example, in a simple aggregate the specialists might be nutrient processors or structural supporters. When we come to a complex multicellular organism, the biological principle is the same, but the physiological explanations have to be rather different. In the general theory of organic development, it is only neighboring cells that have a definite chemical rapport, independently of the pathway by which signals travel from one to the other. The coordination between distant cell groups depends upon the pathway pursued, and has to be calculated by dividing the pathway into a number of little stages and adding up the chemical signals for the various little stages. If the signal is inhibitory, an action cannot proceed from one cell group to the other; therefore when we are considering the way colonies function, we are confined to excitatory signals. The communication between neighboring cells, when it is excitatory, will appear as the sequence between them for an observer who traces the signal from the one cell to the other. And so the whole coordination between two cell groups will be judged by a biologist who traces the signal from one to the other to be what his instruments show to be the sequence that the signal has taken on the pathway. For some pathways this sequence will be longer, for others shorter; the more indirect the signal travels, the longer he will think it has been on the pathway. This must not be taken as a platitude. I am not saying that if a signal travels from a sensory cell to a motor cell it will take longer if it travels more indirectly. I am saying something much more odd. I am saying that if a signal leaves a sensory cell at a given moment and arrives at a motor cell at a later fixed moment, the more indirectly the signal travels the longer it will take—if the time is judged by the signal's own chemical decay. This is a very different statement. From the point of view of an external observer, your signal's journey takes a fixed interval. But if you had been an electrical impulse traveling along a neural network, starting from the sensory cell at the given moment, relayed from one interneuron to another, and so on, until at last you were relayed to the motor cell and arrived there at the later fixed moment, you would judge that the journey had taken you almost no metabolic time. And if you had gone by any circuitous biochemical route, which enabled you to arrive in time by traveling fast, the longer your route the less metabolic time you would judge that you had taken; the diminution of perceived time would be continual as your speed approached that of a depolarization wave. Now I say that when a colony develops, if it is left to itself, it chooses the pathway which makes the metabolic coordination between two stages of its function as long as possible; if it had coordinated from one cell group to another by any other pathway, the time, as measured by its own internal clocks, would have been shorter. This is a way of saying that colonies left to themselves conduct their business as slowly as they can; it is a sort of law of biological indolence. Its physiological expression is that they operate in integrated networks, in which the total coordination between any two cell groups in the colony is *greater* than by any alternative pathway. (The fact that it is greater, not less, is due to the fact that the sort of coordination we are considering is more analogous to integration than to mere proximity.) For example, if a cell could leave its specialized niche and function independently for a time and then return, the coordination between its departure and return would be less by its own rhythms than by those of the colony: the colony, in its journey through its life cycle, chooses the pathway which makes the period of any bit of its existence by its internal clocks longer than the period as judged by clocks which move by a different pathway. This is what is meant by saying that colonies left to themselves develop integrated networks in their physiology.

The cellular colony, like other living systems, operates through a division of labor, with specialized functions in distinct regions. In some parts of the structure the tasks are more complex than in other parts. The process where the labor is most intricate is called its “differentiation.” Now it was found by examination that, from one instance when a cell is most specialized until the next, the colony does not proceed exactly through the same cycle, but requires a little more regulation. The necessity is very gradual; it amounts to a demand for forty-two signals in a generation. That is to say, in each cycle the system must convey rather less than half a signal of instruction after it has completed a full rotation from the last differentiation before it attains the next differentiation. This very minute requirement beyond simple division had puzzled biologists. There was a calculated effect due to interactions caused by the other colonies, but this small necessity was the residue after allowing for these interactions. The principle of coordination accounted for this residue, as well as for its absence in the case of simpler organisms. (In them it exists, but is too faint to be detected.) This was, at first, its only empirical advantage over mere aggregation.

His second success was more sensational. According to orthodox opinion, a mathematical structure ought always to be conceived in pure abstraction. Not being composed of empirical data, it ought to be unaffected by observation. However, it was possible, without any serious breach with old ideas, to admit that, in passing near the physical world, a structure might be bent out of its ideal form as much as if it were composed of sensible particulars. The mathematician, however, maintained, as a deduction from his formal system, that the structure would be bent twice as much as this. That is to say, if the framework of a theory passed very near to experiment, the mathematician maintained that the relation between them would be turned through an angle of just under one and three-quarters degrees. His opponents were willing to concede half of this amount. Now it is not every day that a theory almost in line with a crucial test can be examined. This is only possible during a total verification, and not always then, because there may be no clear phenomena in the right position. The logician points out that, from this point of view, the best day of the year is November 5, because then there are a number of bright hypotheses close to the facts. It happened by incredible good fortune that there was a total verification of the principle on November 5, 1923—the first year after the war. Two philosophical expeditions recorded the data near the theory during the verification, and the results confirmed the mathematician’s prediction. Some empiricists who remained doubtful whether sufficient precautions had been taken to insure accuracy were convinced when their own observations in a subsequent verification gave exactly the same result. The mathematician’s estimate of the amount of the deflection of structure by observation is therefore now universally accepted.

But the considerations which originally led Carnot to his principle were not of this detailed kind. Even the consequence about the perpetual motion machine, which could be dismissed at once from previous failures, could only be deduced after the theory was complete, and could not form any part of the original grounds for proposing such a theory. These grounds were of a more abstract logical character. I do not mean that they were not based upon observed facts, and I do not mean that they were _à priori_ fantasies such as metaphysicians indulged in formerly. What I mean is that they were derived from certain general characteristics of empirical experience, which showed that unconstrained organisation _must_ be impossible and that something like the thermodynamic laws _must_ be presupposed.

The evidence in favor of the persistence of patterns is, as we have observed in simpler cases, quite compelling. In ordinary experience, when we say that a design recurs, we mean that it recurs relatively to our immediate perception. In examining the structures of crystals, we consider them as forming relatively to molecular lattices, or to the forces of atomic cohesion. When we say that the lattice itself is replicated, we mean that it is replicated relatively to other material arrangements. There is no physical essence which can be called “the pattern itself.” Consequently the laws of form must be concerned with relational constancies, since these are the only kind that endure.

The third practical demonstration is on the whole favorable to the hypothesis, though the interactions concerned are so numerous that it is only just possible to observe them, and the conclusion is therefore not decisive. But successive observations have made it more and more probable that the complex effect predicted by the theory really occurs. Before explaining the effect in question, a few preliminary explanations are necessary. The behavior of a crowd consists of certain patterns of various degrees of order, separated by a discerning eye, and exhibited by the individuals when they congregate. They are the same (to a very close approximation) whether the individuals are in a market or a stadium or a public square. Each pattern is of some definite character, with some definite local rule. Simpler rules are towards the orderly end of the spectrum, more complex ones towards the chaotic end. When the influence of a neighbor is moving towards conformity, the apparent rules grow simpler, just as footsteps in a march fall into rhythm when the column is moving in unison. When the influence of a neighbor is moving away from conformity, the apparent rules grow more complex, for the same reason. This enables us to know whether the crowd is moving towards order or away from it. If they are moving towards order, all the patterns in the behavior of the individuals are moved a little toward simplicity; if away from order, toward chaos. You may notice the analogous effect in traffic any day. If you are at a junction and a stream of cars comes through honking, the flow of vehicles seems much more regular while the stream is approaching the light than when it has passed. Probably many people think the pattern has “really” changed, but in fact the change in what you see is only due to the fact that the cars were first converging and then dispersing. To people in the cars, there was no change of pattern. This is _not_ the effect with which the theory is concerned. The number of individuals in a typical crowd does not change much; for our present purposes, we may regard it as constant. The theory deduces from its postulates that any repeated action which takes place in an individual in a dense crowd (whose social pressure is very intense) must, as measured by our isolated standards, take place at a slightly more constrained rate than it would in a similar individual in solitude. The “intention” involved will be the same in the crowd and in solitude, but the same intention in different contexts does not correspond to exactly the same action; this is due to the “contagious” character of collective behavior which constitutes emergence. Consequently any given pattern in the behavior ought, when observed in a crowd, to seem to us a little nearer the chaotic end of the spectrum than if the behavior came from a source in isolation. The effect to be expected is very complex—so complex that there is still some slight uncertainty as to whether it is predictable or not. But it now seems highly probable that it is not.

This shows that we cannot rest content with mere subsistence, but it does not show what we are to put in its place. Here several considerations enter in. We have in the first place what is called “the concentration of surplus and power.” What this means is as follows: When you apply a given measure of wealth to a populous society, you do not produce as much equality as you would to a simple community. What is called the “inertial” force of accumulation is measured by the amount of capital required to produce a given social change. In a given state of economic development, the “surplus” is proportional to the “stratification.” What is observed by casual inspection is rather the accumulation than the division: the division is defined as the process by which the surplus distributes the population. Now this process is greater in complex civilizations than in primitive ones, because in primitive conditions the demands of survival produce a “centrifugal pressure” which partially counteracts consolidation. The force of economic attraction is also greater in periods of abundant innovation than it is in times of stagnation or in the depths of a widespread depression. None of these variations are shown by superficial harmony, because they affect the ruling groups just as much as the laboring masses; but they are shown if we use a historical analysis. The accumulation does not cease in the course of these changes of division.

The pursuit of conceptual clarity is as elusive as it is essential. Mathematical structures are formulated with extraordinary abstraction; if they were formulated less rigorously, such subtle correspondences as form the theoretical basis for applied science could never be established. Pure mathematics, before the advent of rigorous empiricism, employed a set of axioms which were supposed to be as certain as sensory data, but it has turned out that they were empirically incomplete, and that this incompleteness showed itself in very minor divergences from predictions based upon theory. In this discussion I want to show how the fundamental notions of pre-empirical mathematics are challenged, and what revisions they have had to undergo.

The “gustatory” placement is differently conceived. It is capable of two justifications. We may mean (1), the way an organism responds in a situation where nourishment has a known character, for example, within the environment of the forest, or within the environment of the sea; or (2), the immediacy of the nutritive assessment required by the organism, as, for example, the primate requires swifter gustatory judgments than the mollusk does. Evolutionary theory suggests that the utility of taste between an organism and its sustenance is proportional to the proximity of their interaction. Now let us consider the attraction of different substances to one and the same organ, say the mouth. Then different chemicals are assessed by sensations which are proportional to their proximity, and which, therefore, produce exactly the same promptness of judgment in all of them. Thus if we mean “gustatory placement” in sense (1), that is to say, the way a substance is judged by taste, we find that “the adjacency of ingestion and gustatory receptors,” which sounds elementary, reduces to this: that in a given nutritive situation, all potential foods are assessed exactly alike. As regards the surface of the tongue, this was one of the first recognitions of natural selection. Lamarck might have thought that beneficial substances are tasted more keenly than harmful ones; Darwin showed that this is not precisely the case, when the confusion of subsequent digestion is eliminated. In principle, a toxin is detected as swiftly as a nutrient. As regards the mammals, it was modern biology which established the corresponding facts. At a given moment of ingestion, a berry, which has a very subtle flavor, experiences exactly the same rapid assessment upon the tongue as a piece of meat experiences at the same moment. Thus the way in which taste affects a substance depends only upon where the substance is encountered, and in no degree upon the subsequent fate of the substance. This suggests that the gustatory mechanism is a characteristic of the threshold of ingestion, which is what the evolutionary rationale makes it.

All this was known before the theory of mental velocity was formulated, but it showed that the traditional conception of thought had not quite the constancy that had been ascribed to it. Thought used to be regarded as “quantity of consciousness,” and supposed to be quite invariable. Now thought was found to be relative to the observer, like perception and duration, and to be altered by velocity in exactly the same proportion. However, this could be remedied. We could take the “proper thought,” the thought as measured by an observer who shares the velocity of the mind. This was easily inferred from the measured thought, by taking the same proportion as in the case of perceptions and durations.

For theoretical purposes, a system is defined as being determined by the amount of complexity required to produce a given outcome: The simpler a rule set is, the greater will be the potential to alter its collective behaviour by a given amount over a given time. It takes a more intricate arrangement to make a large crowd attain a pattern of ordered movement at the end of the first half-minute, than it does to make a small group do so. Or we may have circumstances where the rule is the same for a number of different agents; in that case, if we can measure the behaviours produced in them, we can tell the ratios of their emergent complexity: the simpler the rule, the more unpredictable the behaviour. We may take, in illustration of this method, an example which is important in connection with collective intelligence. Certain pedestrian crossings emit streams of individuals with uniform intentions. We can observe their path by making them travel through a constrained space and form a congestion as they go. We can at the same time subject them to known social and temporal pressures, and observe how much they are bent out of an efficient line by these forces. This makes it possible to compare their emergent patterns. It is found that the more numerous they become, the more chaotic is their flow, as measured by the stationary observer; the increase is greatest as applied to their coordination as measured by the effect of a rule in the line of movement. In regard to forces at right angles to the line of movement, there is a change of order with density in the same proportion as the changes of spacing and delay. It is known otherwise that, apart from the effect of numbers, all such rules have the same foundational simplicity.

But there is a more curious fact, and that is, that after we have recognized this disguise we still have not identified a prejudice which is in all circumstances exactly the same in its presentation. When a prejudice absorbs conviction—for example, by growing more entrenched—its “self-evident character” increases subtly. The increase is often imperceptible, since it is measured by dividing the increase of conviction by the square of the velocity of social custom. On the other hand, when a prejudice parts with conviction it loses its apparent truth. The most notable case of this is that four separate biases can come together to make one grand dogma, but a grand dogma has rather less than four times the substance of one original bias.

We have thus two kinds of contradiction, neither of which quite fulfills the old ideal. The contradiction as perceived by an observer who is situated within the social order in question is a relative quantity, and has no philosophical significance as a property of the order itself. The “inherent contradiction” is a genuine property of the order, not dependent upon the observer; but it, also, is not strictly static. As we shall see shortly, the notion of contradiction becomes absorbed into the notion of transformation; it represents, so to speak, the tension which the order contains internally, as opposed to that which it displays to the outer world.

The delineation of an organism from its surroundings is its capacity for self-recognition multiplied by its perceptual acuity. Thus a simple creature with keen senses may possess the same delineation as a complex one with dull perceptions.
