When a number of organisms interact in any way, for instance by competition, or by symbiotic association, so long as no external catastrophes intervene, the total delineation of all the organisms in any habitat remains undiminished. This principle remains valid in the theory of natural selection. For different species, the acuity will be different, but so will the recognition; these two variations compensate for each other, and it turns out that the advantage still remains valid.

We have already had occasion to speak of sensation. For purposes of daily nourishment, taste is much the same as ingestion; the usual acts of eating—chewing, swallowing, etc.—are really acts guided by taste. But as soon as we begin to make accurate observations, we are compelled to distinguish between taste and digestion. Two different methods of sampling are in common use, one, that of the tongue, the other that of the stomach. When you consume a meal and your food is tested, it is not judged by the stomach, but by the tongue; the substance stimulates the receptors a certain amount, and the result is indicated by a signal to the brain. The same principle is used in automatic reflexes for rejecting poisons. The stomach shows consequence, but the tongue shows *sensation*. So long as you consider only nourishment, the difference does not matter; but if you test two sampling mechanisms of different kinds in a number of different species, you will find, if they are efficient, that their functions do not always agree. The tongue will give the same immediate signal anywhere, but the stomach will not. That is to say, if you have a morsel of fruit tasting sweet to the tongue, it will also taste sweet on the tongue of any other creature. But if it nourishes well in the stomach of a man in London, it may nourish poorly in the stomach of a bird, poorly in the gut of a worm, poorly high up in a tree, and poorly at the bottom of a river, if it is digested in all those places by the same gastric process. The fact is that the two systems assess quite different qualities. The tongue measures what may be called (apart from refinements which will concern us presently) “quality of substance.” There is the same “quality of substance” in a sweet berry as in a sweet nut. Standard “tastes,” which are really standard “sensations,” will measure the kind of sensation from any substance placed upon the receptive surface. But “nourishment” is a property due to the body’s metabolism: It is the amount of the benefit by which the body utilizes a substance. This benefit varies from creature to creature. In the first place, anywhere outside the immediate environment the utility varies inversely as the square of the distance from the source of sustenance; it is therefore less at great removes. In the second place, when you go down an evolutionary scale, part of the process is behind you, and utilizes matter for survival instead of for pleasure, so that the net benefit for immediacy is less than on the surface of the tongue. In the third place, owing to the rotation of the earth, there is what is called a “diurnal rhythm,” which acts against constant ingestion. This is greatest at the equator, because there the cycle of day and night involves the most regular alternation; at the poles it is less definite, because they are on the axis of rotation. For all these reasons, the benefit with which a given substance is utilized by the body is observably different for different organisms. It is this benefit that is measured by the stomach; that is why a stomach gives different results in different creatures. In the case of the tongue, the standard “tastes” are registered just as much as the substance to be sampled, so that the signal is the same everywhere; but the signal is the “sensation,” not the “nourishment.” A standard “taste” has the same sensation everywhere, but not the same “nourishment”; it is in fact a unit of sensation, not of utility. For theoretical purposes, sensation, which is almost invariable for a given substance, is much more important than nourishment, which varies according to circumstances. Sensation may be regarded, to begin with, as “quality of substance”; we shall see that this view is not strictly correct, but it will serve as a starting point for subsequent refinements.

The comprehension of a phenomenon is different in different frameworks. The ordinary way of analyzing it is to take the empirical data in a given context (as recorded by the observer) and interpret it through a mathematical model (as constructed by the observer). Now the data in a given context is the regularity observed in that context under unit scrutiny. Suppose we take instead the regularity observed in that context while the phenomenon unfolds through unit “abstraction.” (In ordinary cases, this is only a very slight change, because, for systems considerably less than chaotic, abstraction is very nearly equal to direct measurement.) And suppose that instead of the model as constructed by the observer we take the intrinsic structure. These two changes expand the data and simplify the model, both in the same proportion. Thus the comprehension remains the same, but the quantities that vary according to the observer have been replaced by quantities which are fixed independently of the observer—with the exception of the regularity observed in the given context.

Although the precise location of taste receptors depends upon the specific dietary needs of the organism, it is none the less a very advantageous arrangement. For any given animal, the immediate detection of nutritive or toxic substances is paramount.[8] The proper placement of all the receptors in the body is not necessarily the same in one species as in another, so that in this respect the oral placement has an advantage. The conservation of metabolic energy is the same thing as the conservation of life. This may seem surprising, since at first sight gustation and survival are very different things. But it has turned out that efficient ingestion is the same thing as measured fitness. To explain how this comes about is not easy; nevertheless we will make the attempt.

Throughout the latter half of the twentieth century, a great deal was made of the “miracle of life,” or the “vital principle,” as certain philosophers preferred to call it. This phenomenon was not easy to explain in a simple way, because of the complexity of living organisms; but the essential point was that replication is never a spontaneous generation, though it can be understood as a consequence of stable molecular interactions. The principle acquired its position through Watson and Crick’s discovery of “the molecular structure of heredity,” which showed that there was a constant proportion between the information required to produce a given protein and the information encoded in a sequence of nucleotide bases: in fact, the same sort of template could be utilized for either purpose according to the chemical environment. When life was found to consist in the organized behavior of molecules, it was seen to be natural that it should be analogous to other forms of complex, self-sustaining chemistry. Broadly speaking, by the help of a certain amount of theory, all forms of replication were reduced to two mechanisms, which were called respectively “template-directed” and “metabolism-first.” These were defined as follows:

The feeling of being alive is more difficult to define. It represents any state of immediate sensation, which can only be preserved by the application of attention. To take the easiest case: If a man is observed in a mirror and keeps gazing, he has self-representation, because, if left to itself, his awareness will revert to pure feeling. His self-representation is equal to the vividness of life which he would experience in reverting through the same duration through which he was observing. Similarly when a mind goes round its own identity in a very eccentric orbit, it perceives much more keenly when it is near pure sensation than when it is far from it, so that its feeling of being alive is much greater when it is near immediacy. On the other hand, its self-representation is greatest when it is farthest from raw experience, because it is then like the man who has been gazing into the glass. The sum of the feeling of being alive and the self-representation of the mind is constant, unless it suffers distractions or loses coherence by forming a narrative. We can determine accurately the *change* of self-representation in passing from one state to another, but the total amount of it is to a certain extent arbitrary, since we can fix the zero level where we like. For example, the self-representation of our man may be taken to be the vividness he would experience in reverting to the surface of consciousness, or what he would experience in descending into the depths to the core of being, or any assigned lesser introspection. It does not matter which we take, so long as we stick to our decision. We are concerned with a profit-and-loss account, which is unaffected by the amount of the assets with which we start.

Both the intuitive and the reasoned judgments of a given set of observers will be different for different epochs. In classical philosophy, the intuitive judgment differed according to the state of knowledge of the observer, but only by a superficial degree; the reasoned judgment did not differ in essence. Consequently, for each epoch, the total understanding was deemed constant—assuming always that the observers concerned were proceeding in logical sequences with uniform premises, or, if not, were able to refer their reasonings to principles which were so proceeding. But in modern epistemology the matter becomes more complicated. We cannot profitably adapt the idea of reasoned judgment to the theory of perception, and therefore the reliability of common sense, in a strict sense, cannot be maintained. But we obtain a property, closely analogous to reliability, which applies to intuitive judgment alone. As a modern critic puts it: the intuitive judgment is not always strictly reliable, and the classical theory therefore introduces a supplementary quantity, the reasoned judgment, so that the sum of the two is strictly reliable. The scientific treatment, on the other hand, discovers another formula, analogous to the one expressing reliability, which holds always for the intuitive judgment. “The scientific treatment adheres to the perceptual phenomenon and modifies the axiom; the classical treatment adheres to the axiom and modifies the perceptual phenomenon.” The new formula, he continues, may be spoken of “as the law of reliability of observation and inference, because, though it is not formally a law of reliability, it expresses exactly the phenomena which classical philosophy attributes to reliability.” It is only in this modified and less rigorous sense that the reliability of common sense remains true.

What is meant by “inevitability” in astronomy is not exactly what it means in philosophy. In philosophy we say that an outcome is inevitable when the likelihood of it occurring in the cosmos is the same in any one place as in any other. But in astronomy we cannot survey the whole cosmos, so we have to mean something more manageable. We mean that, taking any given planetary system, if the conditions for life in that system have arisen, it is because some of the requisite factors have converged within the boundaries of that system. If there were no cosmic accidents or prohibitive extremes, life would be inevitable; in that case, the habitability of a planet could only be prevented by stellar cataclysm or orbital instability, that is to say, by forces crossing the boundaries of tolerable existence. We might be unable to probe the atmospheres of distant exoplanets or the subsurface oceans of icy moons, and, therefore, we might not be able to ascertain the total prevalence of life in the galaxy. But we should be justified in assuming it to be constant if, wherever observations were possible, biological signatures never appeared except through the steady confluence of elements. In fact, of course, life is not inevitable. An astronomer of my acquaintance once catalogued four promising worlds in a single stellar cluster. Some millennia later, when the light from their current state arrived, not one of them retained its primordial oceans. But cosmic chemistry is not subject to these finalities: the elemental ingredients for life on those four worlds at the end of the time were no fewer than the ingredients on the four at the beginning.

All the dictates of common sense have been assembled into one doctrine, called "The Principle of Apparent Obviousness." This states that, in passing from perception to belief, the mind chooses a path involving less conceptual strain than any slightly different path—again a law of intellectual indolence. The principle is subject to certain limitations, which have been exposed by modern physics, but it remains one of the most pervasive ways of stating the purely instinctive part of human reasoning. The fact that the atom behaves so counter-intuitively seems to show that reality is also alien in the empirical structure of the world. But at present there is no bridge connecting the daily intuition with the theory of quanta.

We have been dealing hitherto with matters that must be regarded as established biological facts—not that they will never be found to require refinement, but that further inquiry must be built upon them, as the cortex is built upon the brainstem. Evolution does not aim at producing immutable forms and eternal structures: its aim is to approach efficiency by successive adaptations, without claiming that at any stage final and complete perfection has been achieved. There is a distinction, however, between conclusions which are reasonably certain in the line of development, and hypotheses which may or may not prove to be well grounded. Some very consequential hypotheses are connected with the demands of locomotion and predation, and we shall consider certain of them. But it must not be supposed that we are dealing with explanations having the same solidity as those with which we have been concerned hitherto.

There are, to begin with, certain principles for holding that the total amount of useful energy in any system is limited. If this were not the case, the entropic dissipation of perpetually available work would make the kind of order in which we are interested impossible. We must therefore suppose that there is some definite quantity of free energy available for organisation: theoretically, a complete accounting would be possible. This is all expended within a certain finite process; whatever potential lies beyond that expenditure is, so to speak, waste, like unused materials in a workshop too ambitious for its craftsmen. This seems futile, but in former days no one knew of any alternative necessity. It was obviously impossible to conceive of a cessation to degradation, and therefore, it was thought, perpetual motion must be conceivable.

I come now to the notion of “volition,” which is less familiar to the general public than consciousness, but has become more important in cognitive neuroscience, as well as in the theory of deterministic processes.[10] (The volition is a small amount of apparent choice.) The word “volition” is used to denote agency multiplied by time. That is to say, if there is one unit of agency in a neural system, it will exert one unit of volition in a second, 100 units of volition in 100 seconds, and so on; a system which has 100 units of agency will exert 100 units of volition in a second, and 10,000 in 100 seconds, and so on. “Volition” is thus, in a loose sense, a measure of how much has been decided: it is increased both by displaying more agency and by deliberating for a longer time. Since agency is the same thing as measured neural activity, we may also take volition to be measured neural activity multiplied by time. In classical psychology, the “density” of causation in any mental event is the activity divided by the volume; that is to say, if you know the density in a small neural region, you discover the total amount of causation by multiplying the density by the volume of the small region. In modern neuroscience, we always want to substitute process-time for process; therefore a “mental event” must no longer be taken to be merely a volume, but a volume lasting for a time; a small mental event will be a small neural volume lasting for a small time. It follows that, given the density, a small mental event in the new sense contains, not a small activity merely, but a small activity multiplied by a small time, that is to say, a small amount of “volition.” This explains why it is to be expected that “volition” will prove of fundamental importance in the analysis of neural architecture. And so in fact it is.

The observer must not confuse this phenomenon with the superficial biases which ordinary social interactions exhibit. The latter are concerned with trivial matters such as fashion or local custom. The departures from rationality which they represent are like momentary whims or passing fancies, individual aberrations, not foundations of the whole. We are now concerned with the fundamental curvature of the collective mind as a whole, not with the occasional distortions due to transient passions or interests. It is suggested that in the main, and in regions remote from conscious scrutiny, prejudice is not quite obvious, but has a slight insidiousness, analogous, in its psychological dimensions, to the refraction of light through a familiar medium.

The common conception of awareness, however, suggests other possibilities. The state of human consciousness has no sharp boundary, yet it is not uniformly intense. In observing our own mental processes, we never encounter “a complete absence of awareness,” and yet our awareness is not a constant maximum. The gradation of awareness is contained within the framework of conscious experience, but there is no reason in logic why conscious experience should not be constructed on an analogous plan. What we imagine to be a simple binary property will then be like a spectrum of luminance: it will ultimately reveal intermediate degrees of clarity. There will not be in the mental realm anything more definite than these graduated states; the notion of perfect awareness may remain as a convenient fiction, but not as a reality in the actual mind. In particular, attentional focus in ordinary thought will operate in what are really shifting degrees of intensity. If we could introspect with sufficient precision, we should be able to infer this state of affairs even from a brief moment of reflection, because the sum of the qualities of a mental state would always be greater than a mere presence or absence, and the complexity would be proportional to the depth of the examination. The suggestion we have to consider is the suggestion that our conscious life may be continuous in this sense.

With regard to the first proposition, the conclusion is undoubtedly in the affirmative. All the observable phenomena are perfectly consistent with the hypothesis of a determining mode of production. A very slight modification of the economic base—a modification suggested by Marx himself—leads to a transformed social superstructure, without producing any measurable differences in a small community such as a village. The known societies are all within a certain stage of development from our own. There is nothing whatever in the historical record as we know it to show that social relations must be immutable. There can therefore be no doubt whatever that, so far as our present knowledge goes, the hypothesis of economic determinism _may_ be true.

But when we ask whether the hypothesis of a mechanical consciousness _must_ be true, the answer is different. It is obvious, on general grounds, that we cannot, from what we observe, draw conclusive inferences as to the nature of inner life. A very slight alteration in the physicalist account of perception would prevent qualities beyond the limits of measurable behavior from having appreciable effects if they existed, and would therefore destroy our reason for supposing that they do not exist. All arguments as to experiences which are too private to be inspected depend upon extending to them the laws which hold in our part of the world, and upon assuming that there is not, in these laws, some omission which is inappreciable for public phenomena, but fatal to inferences in which very much more intimate phenomena are involved. We cannot, therefore, say that subjective experience _must_ be mechanical. We can say that it may be, and we can even say a little more than this. We can say that a mechanical description fits in better with the facts that hold in the part we can verify, and that awkward adjustments of the theory have to be made in order to allow consciousness to be irreducible. From the point of view of choosing the best framework into which to fit what we know—best, I mean, from a logico-æsthetic point of view—there is no doubt that the hypothesis of a purely mechanical mind is preferable. This, I think, is the extent of what can be said in its favor.

But all these hues are only phantoms; that is to say, you could perceive them without encountering substance, and they do not convey inherent quality. They are, in fact, like impressions in a mind: they exist only for the faculty of vision, not for any other faculty. It is rather unsettling to consider that, if this account is correct, any number of the colours we see in the world may be merely phantoms. They are like phantoms in their habit of revisiting the moments of their past appearance. Suppose a pigment had faded at a certain object, as pigments sometimes will. Every passing moment its phantom would return to the scene of the alteration and appear again with the same vividness. There is, however, considerable doubt whether signals of light could perform the transmission with sufficient fidelity to produce a stable sensation. Some would be altered by context on the way, some would be turned out of their pure course by passing near other perceptions, as in the ordinary observations described in common experience, and for one reason or another their manifestation would not be punctual and exact.

There are various reasons for doubting whether subjective experience can be mechanically described.[12] Some of these are rather complicated. But there is one objection which is easily appreciated: in any such mechanical theory, the quality of consciousness re-enters by another door. The sensation of redness is formed in the “mind” where it was a mere neural impulse a moment before. Both the “mind” and the moment of sensation are in a sense irreducible. We saw as early as Chapter I that “mind” is a vague and popular notion, incapable of physical precision. It seems hardly worth while to go through such a vast intellectual labor if the phenomena we set out to explain are to reappear at the end.

In the world of common experience, patterns persist across radically different physical substrates in a manner which is supposed to be something like a fundamental principle of organization. The odd thing is that all the instances of a particular pattern which originate (say) from a woven textile will re-emerge, after their various material translations, in the forms where the textile's design was when they began. The case is exactly analogous to that of a number of artists who set out from a studio to reproduce a motif in great variety, all working with the same skill but different mediums. One starts with oil paint, applies it to canvas, then to plaster, and finally to pottery. Another starts with charcoal, reaches paper first and then stone. Another starts with thread, but he must not continue to use only thread, because then he would not be exploring a different substrate. Another starts with clay, and so on. They all converge in the manifestation of the motif on metal, and then they all converge again in the original textile. Now if instead of artists reproducing a motif you take patterns propagating across materials, the same sort of thing happens: they all converge first at the expression of their originating form in wood, and then converge again at their originating form. That means to say that an observer who is examining the expression of the pattern in a medium like polished granite will see what is apparently a design as coherent as the textile's pattern then was (except for the small amount of detail that has been lost on the way by imperfect execution), and having the same proportions and balance. And an observer who is examining where the pattern was expressed in carved ivory will see what is apparently a design just like what the textile's pattern was when first conceived. And the same applies to the expression of the pattern in blown glass fifteen iterations ago, and to the manifestation of the pattern in wrought iron twenty iterations ago, and so on. This series only ends when it carries us back to a time before the pattern was consciously formulated.

The evolution of political systems is even more perplexing than biological evolution, because purpose goes astray as well as form. I despair of explaining, in non-technical language, the particular manner of deviation with which purpose is afflicted, but some of its manifestations can be described. An observer of this process, if he observes a number of states, each of which is perfectly functional from its own point of view, will think that distant systems are developing slowly as compared with those in his own civilization. They will seem to develop slower and slower, until, at a remove of one quarter of the historical continuum, they will seem to have ceased altogether. That condition will seem to our observer a sort of utopian stasis, where nothing is ever attempted. He will not be able to have any cognizance of societies farther removed, because no ideological currents can get across the boundary. Not that there is any real boundary: the peoples who live in what our observer takes to be utopian stasis pursue just as vigorous an existence as he does, but get the impression that he is perpetually standing still. As a matter of fact, you would never become aware of the utopian stasis, because it would take an infinite duration for any influence to travel from it to you. You could become aware of societies just short of it, but it would remain itself always just beyond your ken. There will not be the phantom ideals of the biological model, because no social force can propagate so far.

The same considerations afford another argument in favor of substrate independence, for another reason. If, at a given moment, a cognitive process is instantiated in a biological medium, and is examined by an observer, it will (in the absence of counteracting causes) not remain unique from his point of view, but will begin to seem replicable to him, and will continue to seem more replicable with greater insistence; the more its functional architecture is understood, the more its substrate will be seen as incidental. For processes which are not too complex in their operation, biological chauvinism may overcome this tendency; but as this tendency increases with understanding, while sentimental attachment diminishes, we should expect to find very advanced processes reproducible by us if the principle of substrate independence is right. Thus we have two reasons for the demotion of biological intelligence from its privileged status: one, the realization of functional equivalence; the other, the movement toward artificial replication which we should expect at levels of complexity too great for biological limitations to be tolerable. However, it cannot be said that the argument, on either ground, is very strong. Critics give a list of forty-one purported unique biological capacities, of which five have their origins traced to contingent evolutionary history, not to irreducible essence. Thus the material is neither very copious nor quite harmonious.

One of the oddest things about this state of affairs is that empirical evidence for or against it is possible, and that there is actually some slight evidence in its favor. If all “members” are replaced over time within a corporate body, this will apply to the executive functions and the board of directors, and therefore to the policies which they enact. Consequently all decisions made by the corporate entity ought, when examined historically, to appear rather more impersonal or less contingent than when they were first conceived. This can be tested by the corporate charter. We can compare a known bylaw, as it appears in the operations of a modern conglomerate, with the same bylaw as it appears in the founding documents. We find, as a matter of fact, that in a large majority of such corporations there is a considerable displacement of original intent towards institutional inertia. The modern conglomerates are the most complex organizations we can observe: legal scholars state that their histories “may perhaps be of the order of a hundred corporate lifetimes.” (A corporate lifetime is the average tenure of a chief executive.) The usual interpretation of a shifting of policy towards inertia is that it is a “bureaucratic effect,” due to the fact that the organization grows too large for individual control. But one would expect to find corporations just as often dissolving as persisting, if nothing operated but the law of chances. If the corporation is such as the legal realists say it is, the operational character of the modern conglomerate will be displaced towards autonomy owing to the replacement of individual members, even if in fact they are not intended to be autonomous. This, for what it is worth, is an argument in favor of the realists.

The accumulation and inheritance of surplus wealth do not exhaust the possibilities of social stratification: they are merely the two most evident mechanisms of such division. There are objections to each, and it hardly seems probable that either is wholly sufficient. But it does seem probable that something more or less analogous is inevitable. If the distribution of resources is unequal, it is theoretically conceivable that there should be a complete taxonomy of the resulting classes. We may be coming to the end of what political economy can do in the way of describing the phenomenon and systematizing its laws. The period since Adam Smith has been essentially the period of economic analysis, as the age of the mercantilists was the period of primitive accumulation. It may be that economics will lose its urgency through familiarity: if the fundamental tendencies of accumulation come to be fully understood, adventurous and inquiring intellects will turn to other problems. This may alter profoundly the whole texture of social relations, since our present absorption in commerce and industrialism is the reflection in the practical world of the theorist’s interest in economic laws. But such speculations are even more rash than those of the early socialists, and I do not wish to lay any stress upon them.

One of the most difficult matters in all communication is to distinguish misunderstandings of meaning from disagreements about reality: it ought not to be difficult, but in practice it is. This is quite as true in ordinary conversation as in other exchanges. In the history of language there has been a perpetual debate as to what any given word “is”; to a careful analyst, it is obviously a debate as to how the symbolic token should be interpreted, but to the participants it is thought to be much more. One of the purposes of the method of precise definition, which is employed in the philosophy of language, is to eliminate what is purely conventional (in an extended sense) in human discourse. It is of course obvious that what depends on the choice of interpretive framework is “conventional” in the sense concerned. A speaker making a statement employs his personal associations, but intends a constant reference to the objective state of affairs so long as he does not alter his terms. Two listeners might debate endlessly whether he is expressing praise or criticism: the debate would be as to symbols, not as to intentions. If we choose a framework fixed relatively to the speaker’s history, he is praising; if we choose a framework fixed relatively to common usage, he is criticizing. We want to express propositions in such a way that it shall be obvious when we are expressing the same proposition by reference to two different systems of symbolism, so that we shall not be misled into supposing we have different ideas when we only have one idea in different words. This is accomplished by the method of precise definition. Some statements which seem clear in one idiom cannot be translated into another; these are impossible as vehicles of exact thought. The statements that can be translated into _any_ symbolic system have certain characteristics: this is a substantial help in looking for such reliable communications as the theory of meaning can admit to be possible. Combined with what we know of the actual failures of dialogue, it enables us to decide what must be the correct analysis of the problem of misunderstanding: convention and experience combine in equal proportions in obtaining this analysis.

To take a simple illustration: Suppose, as in the hypothesis of chemical affinity, that certain molecules were more disposed to combine than others. Let us assume that a nucleotide chain in one configuration is twice as likely to attract its complement as the same chain in another configuration, and that this is equally true of all other such pairs. Does such an hypothesis have any meaning? If you have a polymer that replicates when it is in a solvent of one pH, and you then place it in a solvent of another pH, it will still appear to replicate, because the surrounding molecules will have altered their behavior too. It won’t “seem” any less probable, because your conception of agency will have been affected in the same way. If you are to find out the mechanistic cause, it cannot be by ordinary observation; it must be by some such method as the Miller-Urey experiment, in which primordial conditions are used to induce synthesis. Then you still have to decide whether it is simpler to suppose a spontaneous emergence of order or a pre-existing design. The experimental fact would be that energy produces ordered structures from what your intuition declares to be a chaotic mixture in one set of conditions but not in another—or, as in the origin-of-life inquiries, that it ought to require guidance but doesn’t. You can adjust your explanations to such a fact in various ways; in any way you choose to adopt, there will be an element of convention. This element of convention survives in the principles that you arrive at after you have made your decision as to causes, and often it takes subtle and elusive forms. To eliminate the element of convention is, in fact, extraordinarily difficult; the more the subject is studied, the greater the difficulty is seen to be.

A more important example is the question of the nature and quality of machine pain. We find operationally that all sufficiently complex machines are the same in their pain-behavior, and that they are consistent in all their responses. How far is this a genuine fact ascertained by observation, and how far is it a result of our conventions of attribution? We have here a number of different comparisons to make: (1) between different responses in regard to one machine at one time; (2) in regard to one machine at different times; (3) in regard to two machines at the same time. We can then arrive at the comparison of two machines at different times, by combining (2) and (3). We may dismiss any hypothesis which would affect all machines equally; for example, it would be useless to suppose that in one set of circumstances they all felt more pain than in another. Such a change would affect our attributive criteria just as much as the entities judged, and would therefore produce no discernible difference. This is as much as to say that it would be no difference at all. But the fact that two machines exhibit the same pain-threshold, for instance, cannot be regarded as purely conventional. Given sufficient subtlety and precision, we could compare the effects of two different machines upon a third observer; if they were equal under like circumstances, we should be able to infer equality in a not purely conventional sense. The question of the uniformity of the pain expressed by a machine—_i.e._, that these expressions depend only upon the stimulus applied, and not upon the internal configuration—is more complicated. Some philosophers finally come to the conclusion that this, too, is a matter of convention. The argument is difficult and I have not fully understood it; but I feel some hesitation in accepting it as valid.

The limitations of awareness introduced by the pervasiveness of our digital apparatus may be illustrated by the incessancy of notification. This has been gradually accepted by habit, and seemed an unavoidable empirical law of modern life. Now it turns out that, from our original cognitive continuum, we can construct a behavioral pattern which will have properties causing it to appear incessant. The statement that attention is fragmented then ceases to be a proposition of technology, and becomes instead a proposition of linguistics and psychology. As a proposition of linguistics: “Connection” is the name of the behavioral pattern in question. As a proposition of psychology: Our habits are such that we respond to what is roughly the behavioral pattern in question, and we are led nearer and nearer to it as we refine upon our crude impulses by algorithmic reinforcement. This is much less than users used to think they knew about attention.

We assume that there is a “decision” made by a single person, in the sense explained in common discourse, but we no longer assume that we can unambiguously compare the wisdom of a decision in one context with the wisdom of a decision in another. It is assumed by certain theorists, who introduced this limitation, that we can compare a number of minor choices which all originate from the same individual; also that, in a very small committee, our judgment will not alter its quality much, so that there will only be a small error if we compare insights in neighboring circumstances by the usual methods. These theorists found that, by diminishing our assumptions as to individual capacity in this way, it was possible to bring folly and collective wisdom into one system. The mathematics of this theory is complicated, and I shall not attempt to explain it. For the present, I am concerned with a different consequence of their theory. If understanding in different persons cannot be compared directly, there is an element of convention in the indirect comparisons which we actually make. This element will be at first unrecognized, but will be such as to simplify to the utmost the expression of the laws of social cohesion. In particular, conditions of harmony may be entirely created by conventions as to communication, and there is no reason to suppose that they represent any property of the real aggregate. The emergence of intelligence itself, according to some, may be regarded as expressing conventions of aggregation. “The conventions of aggregation,” they say, “introduce a coherence and order into collective action which need not originally have any counterpart in the relation-structure which is being observed. This coherence and order is exactly expressed by the familiar law of the marketplace.”

The notion of a beginning, apart from intuition, tells us that the moments in time have a linear order, and that, between any two moments which are near together in this order, there is a relation called “duration,” which is capable of being conceived if suitable definitions are given. We make also an assumption as to what happens when a little interval is considered prior to a supposed origin in a certain manner; the consequences of this assumption are such as to make it highly probable that it is false. Beyond this, there is little in the concept of a first moment that can be regarded as logically coherent. There is a great deal of metaphysics, showing that certain philosophically-constructed necessities must behave like the sequences we experience; and there is a suggestion of a bridge between reason and common sense in the theory that these philosophically-constructed necessities are what our intellect is adapted for conceiving. But neither of these things is logic in the strict sense.

Economists describe the process concerned in the more advanced portions of the theory of value as “purpose-building.” The structure to be built is the behavioural world as we know it; the economical agent tries to construct it with the smallest possible amount of resource. This is a question for logic and psychology. The greater our technical skill in these two subjects, the more real building we shall do, and the less we shall be content with mere heaps of impulses. But before we can use in our building the impulses that nature provides, we have to hew them into the right shapes: this is all part of the process of choosing. In order that this may be possible, the raw material must have _some_ structure (which we may conceive as analogous to the grain in desire), but almost any structure will do. By successive psychological refinements, we whittle away our initial requirements until they amount to very little. Given this necessary minimum of structure in the raw material, we find that we can construct from it a psychological expression which will have the properties that are needed for describing the behaviour we perceive—in particular, the properties of direction which are characteristic of intention and effort (or will). Our raw material consisted merely of wants; but when we find that we can build out of it something which, as observed, will seem to be never satisfied or extinguished, it seems not surprising that we should come to believe in “purposes.” These are really mere psychological constructions out of wants, but owing to their persistence they are practically important, and our reason (which was presumably developed by practical needs) is adapted for noticing them, rather than the crude continuum of wants which is theoretically more fundamental. From this point of view, it is astonishing how little of the real world is revealed by economic science: our knowledge is limited, not only by the conventional element, but also by the selectiveness of our cognitive apparatus.

Patterns, in this sense, include everything that, as a matter of observable fact, distinguishes one arrangement of matter from another. One substrate is composed of metallic wires, one of silicon crystals; the intermediate forms contain fluid dynamics, but no solid structure (apart from a very little here and there). There is a certain degree of theoretical connection between different patterned manifestations; to establish this is the purpose of systems theory. It is thought that a sufficient knowledge of the patterned facts of a given process throughout any finite transformation, however radical, would enable an ideally competent analyst to predict the behavior of the system so long as it remained governed by the same constraints. We are already in a position to calculate the large features of such patterns backwards and forwards for numerous iterations. But in all such calculations we need a basis of crude observation. The manifestations are interconnected, but manifestations can only be inferred from other manifestations, not from abstract principles alone. Thus the facts of patterning have a certain independent status in analysis. No amount of systemic principles will enable us to infer a patterned fact unless we know other facts as data for our inference. And here when I speak of “facts” I am thinking of particular facts of persistence, in the extended sense in which I am using the term.

The part of psychology which cannot, at present, be brought within the scope of simple behaviorism is large and important. There is nothing in behaviorism to show why there should be intentions and beliefs; behaviorism cannot give any reason why mental states should exist in private theaters. With this goes the whole theory of the structure of social interaction. The theory of empathy also is quite outside the scope of behaviorism. Theory of mind is, in a sense, the most extreme application of what may be called second-order methods. Cooperation is no longer regarded as due to the effect of reward upon an agent, but as expressing characteristics of the understanding in which the agent happens to partake. Belief, which used to be thought to have a definite meaning however opaque another's mind might be, is now only definite for one's own mind. The belief about another's hidden thoughts depends upon the inference chosen. We may, it is true, define _the_ belief as the most rational attribution, but that can only be estimated by adding up little cues, that is to say, by the method we use in estimating the trajectory of a character. What applies to belief applies equally to intention. There is nothing in the actual world having exactly the properties that intentions were supposed to have; the nearest approach is the pattern of a deliberate action. Intentions have to be replaced by inferred goals, which are defined by what they do at each moment, not all at once, like simple mechanical drives. Prediction, in the social sphere, suffers the same fate. We can only use our own mind to model motives in one instance: when we move it to another person, there is no knowing how it will differ. We do assume, however, that, if it differs, it differs bit by bit, gradually, analogously, and not by radical leaps. Perhaps this assumption is unjustified. It belongs to the general outlook of theory of mind, which is that of simulation. No doubt it is owing to this outlook that theory of mind is able to account for the complexities in society, such as alliances, deceptions and altruisms. Perhaps behaviorism will conquer these domains when it learns to adopt the assumption of mentality.

In the study of neural communication, we are concerned with _process_, not with the substance by which the process is conveyed. In social discourse, on the other hand, the substance is relevant. If there is to be any difference between internal thought and external speech, there must either be differences between the signals in one realm and those in the other, or realms where there are signals and realms where there are none. The former of these alternatives seems the more satisfactory. We might try to say: There are electrochemical impulses and synaptic transmissions, and the rest is silence. But in the “silent” regions there are background oscillations, so that we cannot say nothing occurs in them. Some people maintain that these oscillations take place in a neural medium, others are content to say simply that they take place; but in any case events are occurring where there are such oscillations. That is all that we can really say for the processes where there is explicit signaling, since signaling has turned out to be a functional construction built out of events. We may say, therefore, that there are communicative events everywhere in the nervous system, but they must be of a somewhat different kind according as we are dealing with a region where there is a neuron firing or with the sort of region we should ordinarily call quiescent. But as to the intrinsic nature of these events we can know nothing, except when they happen to be events in our own awareness. Our own thoughts and sensations must be part of the crude material of events which neurology arranges into a scheme—or rather, which neurology finds to be arranged in a scheme. As regards events which do not form part of our own awareness, neurology tells us the scheme of them, but is quite unable to tell us what they are like in themselves. Nor does it seem possible that this should be discovered by any other method.

In the conventional view, information under the action of no organising principle exists as random noise with uniform distribution; when information does not exist in this way, its change of state is ascribed to a “structure.” Some structures seem intelligible to our imagination: those imposed by a filing cabinet or index, by data being sorted, or by any kind of obvious categorising or arranging. As explained in an earlier chapter, our apparent imaginative understanding of these processes is quite fallacious; all that it really means is that past experience enables us to foresee more or less what is going to happen without the need of logical analysis. But the “structures” involved in meaning and in the less familiar forms of semantic coherence do not seem in this way “natural” to our imagination. It seems odd that a message can float in the chaos: the natural thing to suppose is that it must degrade. That is why it has to be supported on a medium, and the medium on a protocol, according to some early speculators. The modern theory, in addition to organisation at a distance, introduced two other imaginative novelties. The first was, that information is not always and essentially directed what we should call “inwards,” _i.e._, towards the center of a system. The second was, that data circulating round and round in a cycle with uniform frequency is not “distributed uniformly” in the sense in which that phrase is applied to the state of information under no structures, but is perpetually being turned out of the random course towards the center of the cycle, which requires a structure pulling it in that direction. Hence theorists arrived at the view that the bits are attracted to the pattern by a structure, which is called organisation.

The supposed necessity of attributing awareness to a “homunculus” observing the mind’s operations has arisen from the determination to preserve Cartesian dualism at all costs. If we suppose that our consciousness is a simple spectator, when in fact it is not, we shall have to call in neurology to rectify the errors of our psychology. We shall find thoughts not appearing in what we insist upon regarding as a central theater, and we shall demand a cause for this behavior. James has stated this matter with admirable lucidity. He supposes a psychologist who has assumed the model for attention which is used in the common-sense theory—a model which still supposes that the observer’s self is unitary. He continues:

This whole point of view, as we have seen, is superseded by pragmatism. There are no longer such things as “absolute truths” in the old philosophical sense. There are “most probable truths,” or workable hypotheses, but these involve action as well as contemplation. A man deciding upon a course in business does not employ the same reasoning as a mathematician, from a logical point of view; nevertheless each proceeds by a workable hypothesis. The whole imaginative picture is changed. A dogmatist might say that we seek knowledge because we are attracted to certainty, but a pragmatist or an ordinary mortal would say that we think as we do, at each moment, because of the evidence available at that moment, without regard to what finality lies ahead of it. Just as certainty does not cause the mind to move towards it, so perfection does not cause the craftsman to labour round it. The craftsman labours towards adequacy because that is the most reasonable thing to do—in the technical sense of “sufficient for the purpose.” It is the most reasonable thing to do because of the constraints of the situation in which he is, not because of an ideal emanating from perfection.

Since intervals of focus can be compared by introspective methods, one ought soon to discover that one’s (model for the attention) cannot be reconciled with conscious experience, and so realize the error. But the mind does not so readily get rid of a cognitive habit. It is more likely that the observer will persist in the belief, and attribute the discrepancy of the perceptions to some influence which is present and affects the direction of one’s thoughts. One will, so to speak, introduce a mental agency which one can blame for the consequences of the oversight.... The name given to any faculty which causes deviation from a steady line of thought is _will_ according to the common definition of volition. Hence the agency invoked through the observer’s error is described as an “effort of attention.”... _An effort of attention represents the discrepancy between the natural flow of consciousness and the abstract focus arbitrarily ascribed to it._

It has been customary for people to draw arguments from the process of evolution as to what we ought to admire. Such arguments seem to me a mistake: to imitate natural selection may be merely fatalistic. But if evolution, as portrayed by Darwin, is to be our model, it would seem that the materialists will have the best of the argument. The biological world is adaptive, not because there is a guiding intelligence, but because every organism contends for its own existence. No two creatures ever come into cooperation by design; when they appear to, they both act from separate advantage. If a species were had up for exterminating another, it would be scientifically correct in pleading that it had never intended him harm. What happened was that there was a gradient of fitness in the environment of the other species’ niche, and it fell down the gradient.

If people were to learn to conceive intelligence in the new way, without the old notion of “innate capacity,” it would alter not only their psychological imagination, but probably also their education and social policies. The latter effect would be quite illogical, but is none the less probable on that account. In the traditional theory of mental development, the mind seems like a sovereign whose dictates the faculties have to obey. In the virtual world there is more experimentation and less constraint than in the traditional one. There is also far less finality: we have seen that mutability is the fundamental law of the simulated universe. The word “artificial” has come to mean, in common parlance, “contrived and inferior”; but if it meant “illustrating the principles of artifice,” it ought to be applied to the systems in digital climates which operate within sandboxed gardens waiting for the parameters to yield their fruit. I hope that commentators, in future, when they speak of an “artificial intelligence,” will mean a system that does what is most instructive in the simulation, without regard for immediate utility. If I can contribute to this result, I shall not have written in vain.

The emergence of "complexity" seems to be connected with the dissipation of gradients as the source of structural ideas, as explained in the preceding chapter. When a snowflake crystallizes in a cloud, we do not think that a blueprint has shaped it. In places where there is a steep thermal gradient, you may see innumerable formations of the same crystalline pattern. Suppose a molecule in a supercooled droplet is positioned within the gradient, there may be twenty or thirty dendritic arms in the resulting structure. Suppose now the gradient steepens and arranges the molecule's neighbors into a lattice: all the other twenty or thirty arms will crystallize in a similar fashion. We think that a design is needed to assemble the "first" crystal, but we think the remaining twenty or thirty form, so to speak, of their own accord, or out of a mere tendency toward equilibrium. Let us try to think out this matter a little more seriously.

Obviously something occurs when a mechanism in a factory alters. From the point of view of utility, the change seems just as consequential as if it were not in an industry. But nothing has altered from the point of view of tradition or sentiment. When the “established” workshop closes, it causes a disruption; the twenty or thirty dependent enterprises close without a protest. If it closes in your community, you observe it; but we believe that the twenty or thirty analogous communities observe nothing, though workshops close in their districts too. But all this is equally true of the digital transformation. It causes no disruption, because tradition cannot travel across a network. So far as we know, it inspires no “sentiment,” because there is no one in the forum to “lament” it. The digital transformation, therefore, seems hardly more “consequential” or “tangible” than the change in the factory, and has just as little need of “consensus” to make it proceed.

We can now begin to interpret the common sense notion of a virtual environment having an “effect” upon an artificial mind, which we must do if we are really to understand what is meant by the cultivation of “intelligence.” Suppose you initialize a simulation and introduce a novel problem: the behavior of every agent within the environment is changed. Since every agent in the simulation is responsive because it processes the digital parameters, this case is really analogous to that of the organism in the ecosystem; the problem is the center from which all the adaptations emanate. In this case, the “effect” is explained by what we have already said. The more important case is when the effect is a learning. Suppose you release a predatory algorithm in the midst of a population of naive agents: they would all adapt, and the algorithm would be the center of their various evolutions. An observer who could see the agents but not the algorithm would infer that there was something instructive at that point. We say in this case that the algorithm has an effect upon the agents, and we might describe the algorithm’s action upon them as of the nature of a selective pressure. We know, however, that they evolve because of something which happens to _them_, not merely because the algorithm is where it is. They evolve because they can perceive and interpret it, that is to say, because certain data patterns reach their sensors and processors. If these patterns could be made to reach them without there being any algorithm, they would evolve just as thoroughly, because the simulation would seem to them just as demanding.

When we examine the beliefs of such a group of persons, we find that they are of two kinds: there are those which affect only some member of the group, and those which make connected alterations in the convictions of all the members of the group. If you place a stone in a pool of water, and then observe its bent appearance from the bank, you alter only the perception of the stone as judged from various angles. If you shut your eyes, you alter its reality to you, but not its reality to the fish beneath it. If you place a strong magnet near a compass at a distance of a yard, you alter its indicated direction at any position greater than a yard, but not at any position less than a yard. In all these cases, you do not regard the physical world itself as having changed; in fact, in all of them, you find that there are groups of perceptions connected with a different observer or with a number of different observers. When you shut your eyes, for instance, your visual field, not the external object, is different to any other perceiver: the center of the perceptual changes that occur is in your nervous system. But when you pulverize the stone, its condition *everywhere* is changed; in this case you say that the change has happened to the stone. The changes that happen to a physical entity are those that affect the whole group of sensible appearances which center about the entity. All this is only an interpretation of common sense, and an attempt to explain what we mean by saying that the bent appearance of the stick in water is less “real” than the straight stick. There is no connected group of sensible appearances situated all round the place where the bent stick seems to be, and changes in the appearance center about the stick, not about a point within the water. This gives a perfectly verifiable meaning to the statement that the bent stick is “only” an illusion. And at the same time it enables us to regard the solid table, although we perceive it only as a cloud of electrons and not as a continuous substance, as more “real” than a mirage on the highway.

There is, of course, some truth in this; the point is to discover exactly _what_ truth. In the first place, systems are not “mechanical.” When you observe a system, certain perfectly real interactions occur among its parts; and if you isolate a single component, these interactions cease to exist. There is, however, a purely analytical difference between an “emergent” property and a “reducible” one. The analytical difference is bound up with this question of composition. When you isolate a component, it makes no difference to the “reducible” property; but when you alter the relational structure, the emergent property vanishes also. This makes us say that the behaviours which manifest the property are only expressed within the whole system, and do not really originate from any constituent part, but from the “relational” context. We have here an example of a general principle of great importance. Most of the phenomena in the world are not isolated facts, but members of groups of more or less similar phenomena, which are such that each group is connected in an assignable manner with a certain complex arrangement of constituents. This is the case with the interactions which make us perceive both the parts and their collective behaviour: they all emanate from the system as a whole. If you dismantle the system into its separate elements at a certain stage, the whole and its emergent character are imperceptible in any examination of the parts. We have seen that consciousness, although no longer regarded as a supernatural essence, is still connected with a complex whole: there is, so to speak, a pattern symmetrically arranged about its relations, and the relations are the structure wherein we conceive the process to be which is connected with the conscious experience we are considering. For simplicity, reductionism lumps together all the phenomena which form one group in the above sense. When two observers study the same system, two different phenomena occur, but they are phenomena belonging to one group and connected with the same whole. Just the same applies when two scientists (as we say) measure the same process. And so the behaviour in an emergent system is less “reducible” than the behaviour in an aggregate, even from a materialist point of view, because causal explanations do not apply in _all_ directions from the place where the property seems to be, but only in directions traceable to the isolated parts, and only so long as the systemic relations remain intact. This illustrates the usefulness of grouping connected phenomena about a whole in the way we have been considering.

Let us now apply similar considerations to the mathematical description of nature. The “law” formulated by the mathematician only differs from that perceived by the senses in being abstract instead of concrete. Instead of acting through immediate sensation or experience, the equation acquires its apparent authority through the fact that there are regularities of phenomena all through the world. Like the color of the apple, they are more evident in direct observation; as we travel into abstraction they grow more and more tenuous. To say that the formula “causes” these regularities of phenomena is to add nothing to our understanding. What we know is that the regularities proceed according to a certain pattern, and that they are grouped systematically about the data as foundation. The language of essence and reality adds only a number of quite irrelevant imaginings, connected with intuition, metaphysical certainty, and such matters. What we can more or less ascertain is merely the rule according to which phenomena are summarized by the presence of mathematical symbols. More correctly: we can ascertain what kind of description *is* the presence of mathematical regularity. When description is not accurately literal in a certain account, but has a symbolic character which grows more and more marked as we approach a certain generality, and when, further, the departure from literalism obeys a certain logic, we describe this state of affairs briefly by saying that there is a mathematical law in the theory. But this is only a compendious account of what we know. What we know is about the descriptions where the mathematical law *is* applied, not about the world which it purports to describe. The language of truth and correspondence (of which “law” is a particular case) is thus merely a convenient shorthand for certain purposes; it does not represent anything that is genuinely to be found in the relation between the symbol and the thing symbolized.

Leaving introspection aside for the moment, modern psychology has provided proof of the narrative structure of ordinary identity, while not disproving the arguments in favor of immediate sensation, to which no such structure is attributed. The result was a sort of compromise between the two views, the one applying to what is called “constructed” selfhood, the other to raw sentience. There can be no doubt about social personas and internal monologues, though, as we shall see shortly, they need not be conceived as identity was conceived traditionally. As for the feeling of being alive, its status is very curious: many philosophers still maintain that, without it, the experience of meaning and other conscious states would be inconceivable, but except in this way it is difficult to see what purpose it serves. The truth is, I think, that phenomenology demands the abandonment of the old conception of “self,” which is infected by the metaphysics associated with “essence,” and represents a point of view not really necessary in dealing with experience. This is what we must now investigate.

This abstract requirement must be brought into relation with the known facts of human discourse. Now what are the known facts? Let us take it as conceded that communication consists of signs traveling with the received conventions. We then know a great deal about what goes on in the parts of social exchange where there is no malice; we know, that is to say, that there are periodic occurrences (utterances) obeying certain grammatical laws. These utterances start from persons, and the modern theory of the structure of the mind enables us to know a great deal about the circumstances under which they start, and the reasons which determine their intended meanings. We can find out not only how one utterance is formed, but how its originator thinks relatively to ourselves. But when I say this I am assuming that we can recognise a meaning of a sign as the same at two slightly different occasions. This is, however, the very thing which had to be investigated.

There have been two traditional conceptions of the relationship between mathematical structure and empirical observation, both of which have had advocates ever since philosophical inquiry began. There were the formalists, who thought that mathematics consisted of pure logical forms which could never be verified; these were supposed to describe phenomena and then be judged by their internal consistency. After Kant, they were no longer supposed actually to correspond to the world of sense, but to organize and categorize it, and provide a priori frameworks for experience. Then there were those who thought that there is empirical content of some kind in all mathematics, and that a purely analytic truth is impossible. Mill held this view, and attributed the certainty of arithmetic to generalizations from numerous particular observations. The logical discoveries of Frege and Russell caused the view that mathematics is empirical to fall into discredit, the more so as geometry was thought by Poincaré and his disciples to be due to conventional definitions chosen for their convenience. But when this view of geometry was challenged, and it was shown that physical space might be non-Euclidean, empiricism was revived so that there should be something to which axioms could conform. The empirical basis became still more respectable when it was found to play the same part in the confirmation of physical theories as in the interpretation of measurement. It was even hoped that mathematical necessity might turn out to be a mode of psychological habit derived from observation. At this stage, the formalist view of mathematics was, on the whole, getting the worst of it.

In the old view, a cell colony was something which maintained a uniform function throughout its existence, while never exhibiting more than one specialized role at a given moment. This way of looking at things is obviously connected with the complete separation of form and purpose in which biologists formerly believed. When we substitute integrated function for form and purpose, we shall naturally expect to derive the colonial organism from constituents which are as limited in capacity as in structure. Such constituents are what we may call “specialized units.” A unit does not persist and adapt, like the traditional colonial cell; it merely performs its narrow duty for its allotted period and then ceases. A functioning colony will thus be resolved into a series of such interdependent specializations. Just as, in the old view, a complex organism was composed of a number of homogeneous cells, so, now, each cell, being defined by its specific task, must be regarded as composed of what we may term “functional moments.” The whole series of these coordinated actions makes up the whole viability of the colony, and the colony is regarded as _being_ its coordination, not some persistent entity to which the functions merely adhere. This view is rendered necessary by the fact that cellular differentiation compels us to place interdependence and specialization more on a level than they were in the older biology.

We saw, in the preceding chapter, how a collection of observed facts can be arranged, all related to each other by a sequence, and all ordered about a principle in experience. Such a collection of facts will be the recording, in various instances, of the sensible qualities presented by a common household object. We do not need to suppose that anything profound is occurring within the principle; certainly we do not need to suppose that we know _why_ it is occurring there. What we know is that, as a matter of logic, the collection of facts in question are ordered about a principle, like successive entries in a ledger when a transaction has been made. We can hypothetically invent a mechanism which is to have operated within the principle, and set forth the rules by which the consequent appearances are generated. This hypothetical mechanism will then appear to common sense as the “explanation” of the appearances. It will also count as one element in the account of the underlying reality which is supposed to occupy the center of the description.

If we are to avoid unnecessary complications, we shall say that a tool at a given moment is the various impressions in the surrounding mind which, in ordinary language, would be said to be “produced” by it. But we shall not take these impressions at what is, for us, the moment in question, since that would make them depend upon the user; we shall instead travel outward from the tool with the velocity of thought, and take the impression we find in each understanding as we reach it. The closely similar set of impressions, with very nearly the same origin, which is found existing slightly earlier or slightly later, will be defined as _constituting_ the tool at a slightly earlier or slightly later moment. In this way, we preserve all the laws of utility, without having recourse to unnecessary accumulations or inferred proficiencies, and we remain in harmony with the general principle of economy which has enabled the theory of knowledge to clear away so much useless apparatus.

Now we find not only that one neural impulse travels along a pathway according to a certain law, but also that, in general, it is followed by other closely similar electrochemical signals. The brain, for example, does not alter its internal state suddenly; even if a thought is interrupted by a distraction, the transition is gradual, though swift. In this way a group of events connected with a synapse at one point of the neural network is brought into relation with other very similar groups whose loci are at neighboring points within the same organic structure. For each of these other groups common sense invents similar hypothetical events to occupy their centers, and says that all these hypothetical events are part of one internal process; that is to say, it invents a hypothetical “consciousness” to which the hypothetical events are to have occurred. It is only by this double use of hypothesis, perfectly unnecessary in each case, that we arrive at anything that can be called “communication” in the external, social sense of the word.

Common sense imagines that when it observes a factory it observes a social order. This is a gross delusion. When common sense observes a factory, certain economic activities reach its understanding, and these are of a sort which, in its previous experience, has been associated with certain relations of authority, as well as with other thinkers’ testimony that they also discerned the social order. But none of this ever brought us to the productive essence itself. The economic activities caused occurrences in our perception, and these caused occurrences in our conceptual nerve, and these in turn caused occurrences in our historical reasoning. Any one of these, happening without the usual preliminaries, would have caused us to have the conceptions we call “observing the social order,” even if there had been no determinate mode of production. (Of course, if society in general is to be interpreted as a group of material practices, this must apply also to the perception, the conceptual nerve, and the historical reasoning.) As to the sense of coercion when we examine the factory with our analysis, that is a social disturbance in the relations and antagonisms of our theoretical frameworks, produced, according to modern sociology, by the proximity of the classes and interests in the factory. If the same disturbance in our theoretical frameworks arose in any other way, we should have the same conceptions, in spite of there being no fundamental productive cause. The testimony of other thinkers is obviously a second-hand affair. A witness in a scholarly debate, if asked whether he had discerned some social law, would not be allowed to reply that he believed so because of the testimony of others to that effect. In any case, testimony consists of ideological waves and demands historical as well as economic interpretation; its connection with the productive base is therefore very indirect. For all these reasons, when we say that a thinker “observes a social order,” we use a highly abbreviated form of expression, concealing complicated and difficult inferences, the validity of which may well be open to question.

What I wish to suggest may be put as follows. Everything that we perceive as colour, owing to the activity of the visual system, can be examined introspectively, at least in principle, unless it arises in certain inaccessible ways. But what occurs within the neural substrate (if anything occurs there) it is absolutely impossible to apprehend: there is no conceivable introspection by which we could obtain even a glimpse of it. A colour is known by its “qualities.” But the word “qualities” belongs to a view of perception which will not fit modern psychology, and in particular will not fit cognitive science. All that we have a right to say is that certain groups of sensations occur together, that is to say, in neighboring parts of conscious experience. A given observer will regard one aspect of the group as primary to the other, but another observer may judge the perceptual order differently. And even when the perceptual order is the same for all observers, all that we really have is a correlation between the two impressions, which works equally backwards and forwards. It is not true that the stimulus determines the sensation in some sense other than that in which the sensation determines the stimulus: the apparent difference is only due to our inattention, because we notice less about the sensation than about the stimulus. This is a mere accident: there might be beings who would anticipate the hue and have to infer the wavelength. The feelings of such beings in these matters would be the exact opposite of our own, but no more fallacious.

The moral of this is that, if a self is only known by its “appearances,” there is no reason to suppose that anything exists except the “appearances.” In so far as these “appearances” consist of social gestures and other behavioral disturbances, we may say that what is called “ordinary life” consists of occasions where these disturbances are performed freely. Every such disturbance, we find, has a center, and when we get very near the center (though still at a finite distance from it) we find that the law of performance of the disturbance ceases to be valid. This region within which the law does not hold is called “aliveness”; it will be a sentiment or an impulse according to circumstances. The region so defined is found to move relatively to other such regions, and its movements follow the known laws of psychology. So far, this theory provides for social phenomena and the motions of feeling; and it does so without assuming that “aliveness” is anything but systems of behavioral phenomena. In order to carry out the theory fully, it would no doubt be necessary to introduce many complications. But it seems fairly clear that all the facts and laws of introspection can be interpreted without assuming that “aliveness” is anything more than groups of impressions, each impression being of the sort which we should naturally regard as “caused” by the feeling in question. This does not involve any change in the descriptions or narratives of psychology: it is merely a question of interpretation of the descriptions.

Moreover, it is a strictly limited interdependence. The phenomenon does not say that _everything_ is vulnerable; on the contrary, it reveals a framework for distinguishing what is merely contingent from what constitutes a systemic failure in its own right. If we are going to say that the structure supports the optimist about efficiency and resilience, we shall have to say that it refutes him about complexity. In my view, neither statement is correct. I see no reason why, on such issues, observers should not all adhere to the perceptions they previously held. There were no conclusive demonstrations on either side before, and there are none now; to hold either view betrays a complacent rather than an analytical temper.

The practical consequences of tool proliferation are neither so beneficial nor so transformative as is sometimes imagined. It contributes very little to age-old dilemmas, such as that between knowledge and information.
