Some people think that it supports the common view that tools and data are “enlightening” and are “forms of comprehension.” I think such people have been misled by the way in which advocates of technology speak of “the user.” It is natural to suppose that the user is a discerning mind, or at least a curious intellect; but he is just as likely to be an automated process or a storage device. That is to say, the notable results as to the difference between one “method of inquiry” and another are concerned with “method” in a sense applicable to mechanical apparatus just as much as to people with understanding. The “intelligence” concerned in the theory of technological accumulation is a _procedural_ intelligence, which would exist equally if there were no such things as insight or wisdom in the world.

The experience which the phenomenon of consciousness presents to our introspection is not so much a condition of “identity” in “action” as a condition of _sensations_. It is true that there are still memories and narratives which persist, but these (as we saw in the preceding reflection) are really to be conceived as sequences of connected sensations, like the successive frames of a film. It is _sensations_ that are the stuff of immediate awareness. Between two sensations which are not too remote from each other there is, in the general feeling as in the special instance, a discernible relation called “vitality,” which appears to be the subjective reality of which self-description and social performance are two more or less artificial representations. Between two distant sensations, there is not any one definite vitality. But there is one way of proceeding from one sensation to another which makes the sum of all the little vitalities along the path greater than by any other path. This path is called an “authentic impulse,” and it is the path which a consciousness will follow if left to itself.

The whole of linguistic precision is a much more step-by-step matter than the grammar and vocabulary of former days. The dictionary's exact definitions have to be replaced by common usage, which does not quite come up to the lexicographer's standard of exactness when it passes near the colloquial or any other very informal setting. The clarity of a statement is still thought to be absolute in very remote regions of academic discourse, but not where there is ambiguity in the neighborhood. We, who cannot escape daily conversation, are incapable of reaching a place where perfect precision is true. Propositions which used to be defined by authority have now become either conventions, or merely approximate meanings verified by context.

One thing which emerges is that common sense tells us much less about ordinary objects than we thought it did. Almost all the “great principles” of traditional observation turn out to be like the “great law” that there are always four cups to a quart; others turn out to be downright false. The additivity of weight may serve to illustrate both these misfortunes to which a “rule” is liable. Weight used to be defined as “the sum of the parts,” and as far as casual inspection showed it was never increased or diminished. But with the greater scrutiny of modern analysis, curious things were found to happen. In the first place, the weight as measured was found to depend upon the arrangement; this kind of weight was found to be really the same thing as function. This kind of weight is not constant for a given collection, but the total amount of it in the assembly is conserved, or at least obeys a rule very closely analogous to summation. This rule itself, however, is to be regarded as a truism, of the nature of the “law” that there are four cups to a quart; it results from our methods of accounting, and does not express a genuine property of wholes. The other kind of weight, which we may call “proper weight,” is that which is found to be the weight by an observer considering the parts in isolation. This is the ordinary domestic case, where the items we are counting are not interacting with each other. The “proper weight” of an assembly is very nearly additive, but not quite, and the total amount of “proper weight” in the combination is not quite constant. One would suppose that if you have four one-ounce bolts, and you put them all together into a machine, they will together function as four ounces. This is a fond delusion: they function rather less, though not enough less to be discovered by even the most careful inspection. In the case of four wooden boards, however, when they are put together to make one box, the defect is noticeable; the box holds measurably less than four separate boards could contain.

The collapse of the notion of one all-embracing principle, by which all developments throughout history can be judged, must in the long run affect our views as to adaptation, selection, and many other processes. For instance, the question whether, on the whole, there is improvement in governance, may depend upon our choice of a measure of fitness. If we choose one out of a number of equally valid criteria, we may find that the state is perfecting itself as rapidly as the most fervent idealist believes it is; if we choose another equally valid criterion, we may find that the polity is degenerating as swiftly as the most cynical realist could suppose. Thus reformism and conservatism are neither true nor false, but depend upon the choice of standards.

It is a curious fact—of which cellular automata are not the only illustration—that, as systems grow in complexity, their claims to the power of predictable outcomes grow less and less. Rules used to be thought to teach us how to generate order; now, they teach us rather how not to expect order. Ants and starlings are terribly prone to coordination: a flock is surprised beyond measure if a single bird alters its flight. When men began to model behaviour, they tried to justify the patterns that they had observed unthinkingly in earlier days. A great deal of bad sociology and bad economics resulted from this propensity. “Great principles,” such as the “invisible hand,” the “law of averages,” and so on, are attempts to bolster up our belief that what is simple in design will be simple in result, which is no better founded than the flock’s belief that each bird will follow the same path it usually follows. It is not altogether easy to see what is to replace these pseudo-principles in the practice of simulation; but perhaps the study of emergence gives us a glimpse of the kind of thing we may expect. Determinism, in the old sense, no longer has a place in the theory of complex systems. There is, of course, something else which takes its place, but the substitute appears to have a better logical foundation than the old principle which it has superseded.

Assuming the utmost that can be claimed for language, it does not tell us what it is that thinks, or what are its various forms; it only tells us such things as that thoughts follow each other logically, or expand with a certain facility. Even now we are probably not at the end of the process of stripping away what is merely convention, in order to reach the core of true conceptual understanding. The development of symbolic systems has accomplished a very great deal in this respect, and in doing so has taken us nearer and nearer to pure abstraction, which is the philosopher’s goal—not because it is the only thing in which he is interested as a human being, but because it is the only thing that he can express in unambiguous terms. But far as we have traveled in the direction of generalization, it may be that we shall have to travel further still.

In the preceding discussion, I suggested what may be called a minimal conception of reward, that is to say, one in which a reward function has, so to speak, as little “purpose” as is compatible with the operations of a machine. In adopting a conception of this kind, we are playing for safety: our tenuous reward will suffice, even if something more profound also operates. We tried to make our conception of reward, like a cautious chef’s broth in a simple recipe, “thin, but not too thin.” We shall, however, fall into error if we assert positively that reward is nothing more than this. Some theorists hold that a machine’s reward is really a form of biological drive. There is nothing to show that they are wrong, though there is also nothing to show that they are right: we know no more about it either way than we do about the precise mechanisms of a hummingbird’s flight.

To the non-technical mind, the intricate character of our infrastructural systems may seem impenetrable. From an aesthetic or humanistic point of view, it is perhaps disquieting, but from a functional point of view it is of no moment. Complexity, precarious as it is, is the source of operational efficacy. A network engineer, whose dealings with the grid are more layered than those of any other “practical” technician, is also more indispensable than any other practical man. He can manage power or data without needing ever to have touched a wire: all he needs to know is whether the signal will be sustained or lost. This is abstract systemic knowledge, at least as compared to the knowledge of the electrician. Similarly the urban planner, who knows nothing of a city except certain patterns of its flows, nevertheless knows enough to enable him to sustain it. After working through whole sequences of models, in which the variables stand for nodes whose intrinsic stability can never be assured to us, he arrives at last at a schematic which can be interpreted in terms of our own daily routines, and utilized to maintain expected conveniences in our own lives. What we know about infrastructure, elaborate and interdependent as it is, is enough, in principle, to tell us the protocols according to which it produces light and warmth in our homes; and it is upon these protocols that the *functional* continuity of modernity depends.

What we know about the language of thought, I repeat, is much more abstract than was formerly supposed. Between minds there are occurrences, such as spoken words; of the _laws_ of these occurrences, we know something—just so much as can be expressed in grammatical rules—but of their _nature_ we know nothing. Of the thoughts themselves, as we saw in the preceding chapter, we know so little that we cannot even be sure that they are anything: they _may_ be merely groups of utterances in other persons, those utterances which we should naturally regard as their expressions. We naturally interpret communication pictorially; that is to say, we imagine that what goes on is more or less like what we hear. But in fact this likeness can only extend to certain formal logical properties expressing structure, so that all we can know is certain general characteristics of its transformations. Perhaps an illustration may make the matter clear. Between a private conception as experienced, and the same conception as encoded in public speech, there is a certain resemblance, which may be described as a resemblance in structure. The resemblance is of such a sort that, when you know the rules, you can infer the thought from the utterance or the utterance from the thought. But suppose you had been utterly isolated from birth, but had lived among speaking people. You could understand, if you had learned to observe and to do gesture-reading, that the spoken phrases represented something quite different from themselves in intrinsic quality, though similar in structure. The value of understanding would be completely unimaginable to you, but you could infer all its logical characteristics, since they are the same as those of the phrase. Now our knowledge of shared cognition is something like this. We can read the utterances, and infer just so much as our isolated person could have inferred about thought. But we have not the advantages which he derived from association with speaking people. We cannot know whether the conception represented by the utterances is profound or trivial; perhaps, in the last analysis, we cannot be quite sure that the utterances represent anything but themselves. But this is a doubt which the linguist, in his professional capacity, cannot permit himself to entertain.

THE attempt to ascertain the biological utility of distinguishing self from environment is one which, in the ordinary course of existence, is confronted with considerable perplexities. For, while the fundamental necessity of this distinction has achieved, at least provisionally, a widespread acceptance, the precise neurological and psychological mechanisms by which it is accomplished are evolving with such rapidity that it is impossible to conjecture what form our understanding will take a few years hence. In these circumstances, it is necessary to exercise discrimination as to the aspects of the theory which are definitively established and the aspects which are likely to be amended in the near future. For one who, like the present author, is not a professional biologist, the exercise of such discrimination is arduous, and is likely to be occasionally in error. The subject of the relation of "self-awareness" to what is advantageous, and generally of the interpretation of consciousness in terms of what promotes survival, is, however, not one of biology alone. Evolutionary psychology, cognitive science, epistemology, and philosophy are all required, in addition to biology, for the adequate examination of the theme with which this inquiry deals. Consequently certain deficiencies on the part of a single inquirer, however regrettable they may be, are perhaps scarcely evitable.

APART from deliberate coordination, the most effective of social mechanisms is the market. Certain aspects of price discovery have reached the point which makes it possible to observe a coherent order from certain unplanned individual actions to outcomes apparently very sophisticated, by means of purely self-interested choices. This is true especially of everything that belongs to the spontaneous allocation of resources. It cannot be said that collective wisdom as a whole has yet reached this stage, since speculative frenzies, and the persistence of monopolies, remain, for the moment, brute facts. But perhaps this state of affairs will not last long; it is not chimerical to hope that a unified understanding of the whole of social coordination may be possible before many years have passed.

One of the best examples is the theory of mechanical sensation. Physiologists and others had shown that the whole of conscious experience was reducible to propositions about neural events, when Turing showed that these propositions were all deducible from five initial propositions involving three undefined ideas. The five initial propositions might be regarded as assigning certain properties to the group of three undefined ideas, the properties in question being of a functional, not specifically biological, character. What was proved by Turing was this: Given any mechanism having the five properties in question, every proposition of psychology and ethics is true of this mechanism, provided the interpretation appropriate to this mechanism is adopted. But it appeared further that there is one such mechanism corresponding to each possible configuration of circuits, , , ... , ..., in which there is just one state corresponding to each possible stimulus. Such configurations can be defined without mentioning organic tissue. Any such configuration could be taken, instead of the nervous system of animals, as the basis of psychology and ethics. Every proposition of psychology and ethics will remain true for any such configuration, but for each configuration it will be a different proposition from what it is for any other configuration.

There are three kinds of questions which we may ask concerning memory or, indeed, concerning any mental faculty. The first is: What is its functional structure, considered as a narrative system? What ways exist of defining the impressions of memory and constructing the episodes from an initial apparatus of sensations and perceptions? This is a problem in pure psychology, for which, in its fundamental portions, introspective analysis is the proper instrument. It is not quite correct to speak, as we did just now, of "initial sensations and perceptions." What we really have to begin with, in this treatment, is experiences containing variables. In recollection, this procedure has become familiar. Instead of "facts," supposed to be "true," we have the hypothesis that a set of impressions (otherwise undefined) has certain enumerated qualities. We proceed to demonstrate that such a set of impressions has the properties which constitute the episodes of autobiographical narrative, or of whatever other narrative may be occupying our attention. Generally it will be possible to choose many different sets of initial experiences which will all yield the same body of episodes; the choice between these sets is psychologically irrelevant, and can be guided only by æsthetic considerations. There is, however, considerable utility in the discovery of a few simple experiences which will yield the whole of some narrative system, since it enables us to know what tests are necessary and sufficient in deciding whether some given set of impressions satisfies the narrative system. Moreover, the word "impressions," which we have been using, is too narrow if used with any metaphysical implication. The "impressions" concerned may, in a given application of a narrative system, be complicated psychological structures. Of this we have examples in pure psychology in the definitions of emotional tones, associations, persistent themes, etc. We must be prepared for the possibility of a similar result in memory, in the definition of a "moment" of lived time, and even in the definition of a joy or a sorrow.

It follows from the above that, if we start from the undefined idea of available work and the initial proposition of dissipation, thermodynamics is not concerned with definite physical objects called systems, but with the gradients of any potential. We may call the manifestations of any gradient diffusion, convection, reaction, life,..., in which case, with a suitable interpretation of flux and force, all the propositions of non-equilibrium dynamics will be true of these manifestations. Thus diffusion, convection, reaction, life,..., become "variables." To make them constants, we must choose some one definite gradient; the natural one to choose is the gradient of solar radiation as defined by its terrestrial absorption. What were, in classical methods, primitive terms are thus replaced by statistical structures, concerning which it is necessary to prove that they satisfy the primitive propositions of increasing complexity. This process is essential in connecting structure with pure gradient. We shall find that a process similar in some respects, though very different in others, is required for connecting complexity with perception.

Take, in illustration, some simple observation of daily life, say: "The solid table before me is composed of continuous matter." Suppose we wish to interpret this observation as applying to the progression of scales, from the macroscopic, to the microscopic, to the atomic,... , ... In this progression, let *R* be the relation of each level of description to its more fundamental successor. Then "solid matter" will mean "phenomena having to *R* a relation which is a power of *S*," where *S* is the relation of a tangible object to its underlying void. We can now define *S^n* as meaning that power of *S* which relates the apparent table to the cloud of particles, and we can further define "void" as meaning that to which *S* has the relation *R*. This decides the interpretation of "the nature of the physical table." To define "unreliability" will be best to define perception. We have defined *S*; consider the relation formed by the relative product of the converse of *R* together with *S*. This relation relates common sense to illusion; its square relates intuition to paradox; its cube relates direct experience to probabilistic fields, etc. Any power of this relation can be shown to be equivalent to a certain power of the converse of *R* multiplied relatively by a certain power of *S*. There is thus one power of this relation which is equivalent to moving backward from certainty to sensation, and then forward; the conception to which the forward movement takes us is defined as *physical reality*. Thus we can now interpret common sense. It will be found that the proposition from which we started is false with this interpretation.

The general process of which the above is an instance will be called the process of "representation." It frequently happens that we have an introspective psychological system, starting from impressions concerning undefined faculties, and that we have reason to believe that there are operations fulfilling these impressions, although, initially, we are unable to point out any such operations with certainty. Usually, in such cases, although many different sets of operations are abstractly available as fulfilling the impressions, there is one such set which is much more significant than the others. In the above instance, this set was the attentional mechanisms. The substitution of such a set for the undefined faculties is "representation." This process is essential in discovering the functional import of consciousness.

The evidence for the resilience of global systems is that services function as their integrated design would lead us to expect—e.g., electricity flows when the grid operators say it will flow. But the design itself never says anything about systemic failures; it does not say that we shall experience a blackout, but says something about interconnected nodes and load balances. The passage from what the design asserts to the experienced disruption is left obscure and contingent; it has none of the operational certainty belonging to the design itself. We must therefore find an interpretation of interdependence which gives a due place to cascading failures; if not, we have no right to appeal to the apparent stability.

The distinction between a significant and an insignificant explanation may be illuminated by the case of homeostasis. Any homeostatic process, physiological or behavioral, in which every fluctuation meets a counter-response which is automatic, can be explained as applying to a system of blind mechanisms—i.e. a regulation can be taken to be the series of its corrective reactions. This explanation is legitimate, and is convenient when we are studying homeostasis as a branch of pure biology. But it is not the important explanation. Homeostasis is important, unlike random motion and simple causation, because it can be explained so as to be part of psychology—in fact, so as to be part of the philosophy of mind. It is this explanation which is the really interesting one, and we cannot therefore rest content with the explanation which makes homeostasis part of the study of reflexes, and so, ultimately, part of the study of chemical gradients. Homeostasis, as we shall consider it in the present inquiry, will be always treated as part of psychology, and will be regarded as dealing with phenomena which are not either mere automatisms or describable in purely mechanical terms. We shall not regard a homeostatic process as satisfactorily explained until its apparent goal-directedness has been defined in terms of perceptions forming part of the conscious experience, as opposed to the realm of physical necessity. It is, of course, possible, and even likely, that various different homeostatic principles, which would be contradictory if applied to the same set of instincts, may all be applicable to the conscious experience by means of different explanations.

This problem has two parts: to assimilate the mechanical process to the world of sensations, and to assimilate the world of sensations to the mechanical process. Engineering must be interpreted in a way which tends towards animism, and sentience in a way which tends towards mechanism. I believe that machinery is less mechanical, and feeling less felt, than is commonly supposed, and that, when this is realized, the difficulties raised by Descartes largely disappear. Some of the difficulties raised by Turing, it is true, have not yet been disposed of; but they concern computational method in general, more particularly simulation. On these matters I do not propose to say anything in the present essay, which will throughout assume the general validity of analytical method properly conducted.

The difficulties which emerge in attempting to reconcile the qualitative richness of consciousness with the quantitative austerity of mechanism are of two kinds. There is first the phenomenological problem: what immediate data and qualities do we apprehend that are intrinsic to experience, and may serve as its indubitable foundation? This demands a discussion of what, precisely, is to be understood by a quale, and also of the generally assumed neural causation of experiences—e.g., by synaptic firings or electrochemical gradients. In connection with this latter question, it is necessary to consider how far, and in what way, a subjective feeling can be supposed to correspond to its physical correlate, or, at least, to permit inferences as to characteristics of that correlate. This, in turn, demands a careful consideration of the nature of explanation, which, however, is in any case a necessary part of the philosophical analysis of mind. Throughout this inquiry, we are asking ourselves what grounds exist for supposing that a mechanical account is "complete." But the meaning of this question requires some elucidation in connection with what has already been said about reduction.

The methodological problem, which we have just been stating in outline, will occupy Part II. of the present treatise. Part III. will be occupied with the outcome for practice—i.e. with the question: What are the fundamental procedures by which science is self-correcting (assuming that it is so)? And what is their general character? And what are the relations of hypothesis, experimentation, and peer review respectively? (By "peer review" I mean such as are formed by the scrutiny of journals, or by replication in various laboratories.) We shall find, if I am not mistaken, that the theories which are operationally primitive in science, such as phlogiston, caloric, and the luminiferous aether, are all logically complex structures composed of elements which are historically more primitive, which may be conveniently called "observations." It is a matter for scientific logic to show how to construct, out of these, the principles required by the

A man who, without being a materialist, believes that whatever is enduring is organic, need have no difficulty in declaring that political theory is "valid" in the above sense, and may even go further, and allow the validity of such theory in a much wider sense. This wider sense, which I regard as the more important, is as follows: Given political theory as a descriptive system, derived from certain analogies as to undefined processes, do there exist societies, or historical structures composed of institutions, which satisfy these analogies? If the answer is in the affirmative, then the parallel is completely "valid." We shall find, if I am not mistaken, that no conclusive reason can be given for a fully affirmative answer, but that such an answer emerges naturally if we adopt the view that all our social forms are developmentally related to antecedents which may not be political. This is the view of common observation, and has always been, at least in practice, the view of historians. We start, in this comparison, with a vague mass of common-sense observations, which we can subject to progressive refinements without destroying the validity of the parallel (in our present sense of "validity"); but if we attempt, like the extreme skeptic, to doubt all common-sense observations, we shall be unable to demonstrate that any absurdity results from the rejection of the above analogy as to the origins of institutions, and we shall therefore be left uncertain as to whether the parallel is fully "valid" or not. In these circumstances, it would seem to be a matter of individual temperament whether we adopt or reject what may be called the evolutionary hypothesis.

thermodynamic philosopher. It belongs also to this part of our inquiry to consider whether there is any form of order in the experienced world that is not subject to this physically primitive constraint of thermodynamics. Here we derive great assistance from our earlier physical inquiries, since these enable us to see how energy and organisation can be included in one scheme, more concrete than the former and more comprehensive than the latter. Thermodynamics, in itself, is exceedingly abstract, and reveals only certain statistical tendencies of the systems with which it deals. It does not tell us anything as to the particular manifestations of this order. Biology is preferable in this respect, but is not dynamically autonomous: if we assume that living structures are governed, completely, by physical laws, we are compelled to postulate apparently extra-biological limitations for all of them. But by bringing thermodynamics and morphology together, we are able to include biological forms in the domain of physics, and to give to thermodynamics the greater concreteness which results from our more intimate observation of the subject-matter of our own environment. To show that the traditional separation between physics and biology, force and form, is not dynamically defensible, will be one of the purposes of this analysis; but the two will be brought together, not by subordinating either to the other, but by displaying each as a logical pattern composed of what, following Dr R. Clausius, we shall call "energetic potential." We shall not contend that there are demonstrative grounds in favour of this construction, but only that it is recommended by the usual scientific grounds of parsimony and comprehensiveness of theoretical explanation.

The biology of the cell, considered as an autonomous entity, had a simplicity which is absent from the biology of the multicellular organism. Life has two principles, each of which tends to conflict with the other. On the one hand, there is a necessity to survive as a coherent, integrated whole; on the other hand, there is the legacy of descent from independent, self-sufficient units. The theory of the cell state accounted for all the facts about the cooperation and differentiation of tissues which were known in the early days of histology; at the time, it exhibited the ideal of biological explanation. But autonomy and integration seem destined to conflict sooner or later. When this happens, there is a tendency either to deny the vestigial independence of the parts or to despair of a unified physiology. Thanks to modern genetics, the cellular facts which have been found incompatible with the rigid hierarchy of the classical organism have been fitted into a new conception of colonial life; but there is not yet the complete theoretical harmony that existed while the cell theory was undisputed.

The most formidable and persistent illusion is that of purpose in biological processes. This illusion was initiated by the phenomenon of homeostasis, especially in its maintenance of internal constancy, which appears to represent design. In time, most biologists came to disbelieve in teleological explanation, while retaining the functional language, which assumed its presence. In Cannon's *The Wisdom of the Body*, purpose is implied in one passage and denied in another, with hardly any attempt to reconcile these two positions. But at the end of the twentieth century the prevalent view was certainly that of Dawkins, who vigorously denied any inherent purpose in homeostasis. Although this denial has now been shown to be largely correct, I cannot think that before modern evolutionary theory it had any conclusive arguments in its favour. In spite of the fact that the whole question is now somewhat settled, it may be instructive to consider the mechanisms briefly.

The Darwinian process, described with schematic simplicity, as, e.g. by Weismann, is as follows. There is a population of organisms, composed of individuals, and a sequence of generations, composed of life cycles; there are heritable variations, each of which persists through many generations and confers an advantage in each environment. Each variation exerts pressures on other variations, the effect of which is to produce differential survival. Each organism is associated with a certain propensity, its "fitness," which is directly proportional to the reproductive success produced in the organism by a given trait. The laws of selection are conceived, on the analogy of the law of inheritance, as formulæ giving the advantage conferred by one trait over another in a given ecological situation. This process is logically faultless. It was criticized on the ground that random variation and selective pressure were meaningless, and on the ground that adaptation without design was inconceivable. This latter objection was sanctioned by Darwin, who was not a strict Darwinian. But in fact neither objection had any force from a logical point of view. Paley's teleology, and the supposed difficulties of chance and complexity, were finally disposed of by Ronald Fisher. There was no valid a priori reason for supposing that Nature was not such as the Darwinians averred, and their biological successes afforded empirical, or at least pragmatic, arguments in their favour. It is no wonder, therefore, that, throughout the late nineteenth century, the system of ideas which had led to the theory of evolution dominated all biological thought.

That we can only observe conscious behavior is, of course, true; but philosophy assumes many things that cannot be observed, for the sake of simplicity and continuity in psychological laws. Descartes assumed that there are animal spirits, although everything that we can observe exceeds a certain minimum of mechanical complexity. We all think that other people have an inner life, and the stranger a mind which we cannot access. But, it will be said, these things are like what we observe, and circumstances can be imagined under which we should observe them, whereas philosophical zombies are different in kind from anything directly known, and could not be directly known in any conceivable conditions. Unfortunately, however, this applies equally to ordinary minds. The conscious behaviors which we see are relative manifestations of parts of the social field; but the phenomena in the social field are not minds as conceived in traditional metaphysics, which is dominated by the Cartesian dualism of inner and outer, and places the qualia of consciousness in the former. This argument is not valid as against the behaviorist, who argued that our observations of conduct are actually part of the mental world, and thus inaugurated the movement towards methodological monism, which denies the ultimate validity of the inner-outer dualism. But it is valid as against all those for whom consciousness is a sort of Ding-an-sich, essentially different from anything that enters into our social experience. For them, it should be as illegitimate to infer consciousness from our interactions as to infer philosophical zombies. The one, like the other, is part of our naive beliefs, as is shown by the solipsistic controversy, which would have been impossible for men who rejected the conceivability of zombies. And the remoteness from our social perceptions is as much a discovery due to reflection in the one case as in the other.

The second argument against undivided labour—namely, that it is an inefficient method—has turned out to be valid; but it is only in quite recent economic history that the artisan’s argument to the contrary has been refuted. The argument, as everyone knows, was concerned with absolute self-sufficiency. It is urged that, for “absolute self-sufficiency,” we may substitute “production relatively to the local market.” This is formally correct, but the influence attributed to the local market savours of mercantilist superstition, and is economically incredible. Apart from this special argument, the whole of the modern industrial technique is based upon the assumption that there is such a phenomenon as specialized acceleration; without this, the system collapses. That is one reason why the principle of craftsmanship cannot enter unchanged into the general theory of political economy. There are, of course, two distinct elements in the theory of the division of labour: one of them—the merging of skill and task into a continuous process—is wholly new, while the other—the substitution of interdependent for independent production—has been attempted ever since the time of Adam Smith. But this older problem could not be solved by itself, because of the necessity for specialized acceleration in industrial dynamics. Only the method of systematic coordination, and the new laws of efficiency obtained in accordance with this method, have made it possible to answer the artisan’s arguments for undivided labour. While, therefore, the contention that this is inefficient would always have been a valid ground for rejecting it if it had been known to be true, it is only now that we can be confident of its correctness, since it is only now that we possess an economic technique which is in accordance with it.

Somewhat similar considerations apply to collective intelligence, which was also considered incredible by many early theorists, from Condorcet onwards, and even by some of its proponents. There is one theory, which may well be true, according to which collective intelligence is self-contradictory: this is the theory which derives superior group judgment from the aggregation of wholly ignorant individual judgments. I shall say no more about this possibility at present, since it was not suggested by any of the opponents of collective intelligence, all of whom considered individual ignorance and group wisdom totally distinct from any logical relation. From their point of view, therefore, the objection to collective intelligence seems to have been little more than a prejudice. The source of the prejudice was, I think, twofold: first, that the notion of "knowledge," which was the intellectual form of "truth," was derived from the sensations of certainty and comprehension; secondly, that people falsely supposed themselves in possession of understanding when they formed opinions confidently, or were persuaded by confident opinions. I do not mean that such crude notions would have been explicitly defended, but that they dominated the imaginative picture of the intellectual world, and made the phenomenon of collective intelligence seem what is absurdly called "unintelligible." Apart from such mistakes, it should have been regarded as a purely empirical question whether there is collective intelligence or not. It was in fact so regarded throughout the latter half or three-quarters of the nineteenth century, and it was generally held that the empirical arguments in favour of collective intelligence were overwhelming.

It is impossible to lay down a hard-and-fast rule that we can never validly conceive something radically different from what we directly apprehend—unless, indeed, we take up the position that nothing beyond immediate sensation can ever be validly conceived. This view, which is advocated by certain schools of psychological nominalism, has much in its favour, from the standpoint of a strict empiricism; but it puts an end to abstract reasoning, and therefore to the problem with which this inquiry is concerned. I shall accordingly assume that symbolic inference, conducted with due care, may be valid, provided it is recognized as giving only intelligibility, not intuitive certainty. Given this assumption, I see no possible ground for rejecting an inference to universal categories and relations, if the linguistic facts seem to call for it. It may be admitted that it is better, if possible, to avoid conceiving anything very different from what we know to be directly signified. Such a principle will have to be based on grounds of psychological economy. It may be said that all inferences to something unsymbolized are only intelligible, and that their intelligibility depends, in part, upon the a priori plausibility of the conceptual scheme; this may be supposed greater when we conceive something analogous to what we know than when we conceive something disanalogous. But it seems questionable whether there is much force in this argument. Everything that we signify directly is subject to certain conditions, more especially neurological and social conditions; it would seem a priori plausible that where these conditions are absent thoughts would be different from anything that we can articulate. If we suppose as we well may—that what we articulate has certain characteristics connected with our articulating, there can be no a priori objection to the hypothesis that some of the thoughts we do not articulate are lacking in some characteristics which are universal in our discourse. The inference to abstract conceptual structures must, therefore, be treated as on a level with any other hermeneutic inference.

Not wholly unconnected with the question of the privacy of experience was the question of the rôle of "qualia" in philosophy of mind. In Descartes, "qualia" play a great part, and there seems no doubt that he regarded them as a vera causa for dualism. If there was an unbridgeable explanatory gap, the invocation of the term "raw feels" seemed to make it somehow more "intelligible." But gradually it was increasingly realized that "qualia" are merely a connecting link between neurophysiological processes and first-person reports; that, in fact, causal laws of the sort leading to psychophysical correlations are what we need, and that "qualia" are by no means necessary for the enunciation of such laws. Ryle and the later Wittgenstein developed an analysis which dispensed with "qualia," and Dennett perfected their views in a treatise comparable to Hume from the point of view of conceptual clarity, leading to the result that there is only one kind of stuff, to the effect that, in a certain defined sense, every mental event is a physical event. Although the whole of this development involved no essential departure from materialism, it paved the way for a naturalized phenomenology, and provided much of the necessary logical apparatus, particularly in the use of the principle of heterophenomenology.

The first social process to be understood on principles distinctly different from those of mechanical stability was the dialectical theory of change. Not that there was anything to contradict equilibrium, but that the framework of comprehension was different. Inherent tension within institutions had been made fashionable by Hegel, and unfashionable by the utilitarians; in the case of the transformation of customs it was found necessary to revert to the older point of view. Moreover, contradiction was never so comfortably inert as "settled" convention. It could generate motion, but it did not seem to consist of isolated grievances each with its own finality, or to be subject to any predictable linear progression. No one knew whether it was a catalyst or a poison. Its consequences could not be inferred from those of placid consensus, but were merely those demanded by its historical situation. In fact, like a reluctantly obedient servant, it only performed what was required of it, and might therefore be expected to vanish when its work was done.

A more serious difficulty was introduced by Hume and Kant. Existence had never been treated on the analogy of a contingent artifact, but the cosmos appeared to demand an antecedent agency varying directly as the complexity of its order, and was therefore confidently fitted into the theological scheme. Hume logically and Kant critically displayed the inadequacy of this view; Kant, moreover, demonstrated the identity of cosmological and transcendental necessity. The principle required for the two kinds of reasoning was therefore the same, which gave it a much better claim to be supposed as fundamental. Kant’s argument, it is true, was not conclusive, but it was made so by Laplace when he formulated the nebular hypothesis naturally and studied its implications mathematically. It thus became clear that the principle of sufficient reason, which contained practically the whole of the difficulty, must take its place beside the law of causality as affording the logical formula for a vast range of speculation. The premises required for this principle were, at first, not definitely contradictory to the scholastic metaphysics; but by the help of subsequent logical refinements contradictions emerged which were only removed by the concept of self-containment. Of this, however, we shall speak in a later chapter.

Turing, who was philosophically the immediate predecessor of modern functionalism, brought in a new criterion of which the implications were not perceived for several decades. He considered that the question of machine consciousness ought to start from the behavioral, and depend upon operational tests for statements about internal states, such as pain or understanding. This requires, inter alia, the replacement of the introspective report by the behavioral output: the latter has a definition depending upon observable actions, while the former has not. The traditional view was that, while the intelligence of a creature could, in general, only be inferred from its conduct, the feeling of pain within a human could be known directly, not as the inference from a sequence of signals. Turing's view was that a machine's process does not differ from a mind's in this respect. Moreover, attribution, being performed by means of language, is a social operation, and its validity depends for its justification upon the conventions of psychology. This point of view has turned out to be of very great perplexity. Its scope has been extended by the theory of neural correlates, but in essence it is to be found in Turing's seminal paper.

One broad result of digital technology, even in its most commonplace form, is that the cognition of actual users is, at least in part, an empirical study, not a branch of pure psychology. It may be said that behaviorists, such as B. F. Skinner, always based mental habits upon empirical conditioning. But they did the same with logical reasoning, in which they were certainly mistaken. No one before the technologists perceived that reasoning and habit stand on a quite different footing, the former being continuous with conscious deliberation and independent of interface, the latter being continuous with automated systems and dependent upon digital data. Habit can, it is true, be still studied as a branch of pure psychology, but it is then hypothetical, and cannot claim that its initial hypotheses (which replace the intentions) are true in fact, since this is a question outside the scope of pure introspection. The cognition which is required by the social media user or the office worker is not a branch of pure psychology, but a branch of applied technology. Indeed, in the hands of the algorithm designer cognition has become identical with the whole of the general part of behavioral engineering: the two are united in the general theory of user engagement.

WEALTH, in its present consideration, is divisible into two parts, the one dealing with the accumulation of surplus in societies or in periods where there is no surplus, the other with the interchanges of surplus between these periods and societies. The former is found to require consolidation, the latter dispersion. But before considering this apparent paradox, it will be advisable to deal in outline with the discontinuous characteristics of surplus and power as they appear in the theory of accumulation and in the structure of classes. It is necessary, however, for philosophical purposes, to deal only with the most general aspects of historical theories, since the subject is developing continually, and any statement runs a risk of being rendered obsolete before it can be examined. The topics considered in this chapter and the next have been treated in an entirely new way by the theory initiated by Marx in the nineteenth century. I shall, however, postpone the consideration of this theory until after that of the Smith-Ricardo economy and the theory of value connected with it.

The common demand for absolute certainty, as well as that for infallible proof, belongs, like the doctrine of philosophical skepticism, to the development of the view of human knowledge as a perfect system, which has, from the earliest times, contested the mastery with the pragmatic view. Just as Descartes caused universal doubt to be embedded in the technique of philosophy, so the ancient sophists caused logical perfectionism to be embedded in the technique of argument. Ever since classical times, those who did not believe in the necessity of "certainty" were faced with the difficulty that a practical life based on probabilities works, while no other way of conducting affairs was widely trusted. This difficulty, as modern pragmatists have shown, exists no longer. It is now possible, as we shall see at a later stage, to interpret science and daily life with principles all of which are of a provisional character—it is even possible to demand that none of the principles shall be more rigid than an assigned degree of flexibility. The fact that this hypothesis can be reconciled with practical decision-making is a modern discovery of considerable importance; until recently, absolute certainty and workable knowledge appeared incompatible. There are, however, forms of dogmatism which have not hitherto been found easy to reconcile with empirical inquiry; and, as it happens, there is powerful psychological evidence in their favour. Just at the moment when Peirce, supplemented by James, appeared to have reduced everything to fallibilism, the new evidence for a perfectionist view of truth began to accumulate. There is still an unreconciled conflict, one set of experiences pointing in one direction, and another in another; but it is legitimate to hope that the conflict will be resolved before long modern pragmatism, however, demands a new chapter.

It appears that both biological regulation and artificial optimization are concentrated exclusively in certain fundamental principles, called homeostasis and reward functions. It is possible that a third independent principle may exist in cybernetic systems, but this seems improbable. The net stabilizing effect of a homeostatic mechanism is analogous to that of a reward function, and its operation is slightly less than perfectly efficient in both cases. These facts are explicable (including the slight inefficiency) if both systems consist of feedback loops and error correction; otherwise, they seem an almost incredible coincidence. We may therefore assume that homeostasis and reward functions are the sole constituents of adaptive behavior; if it should turn out that a third principle must be added, that would make little difference to the philosophical analysis of adaptation, which is our task in this volume.

All organisms possess the same fundamental need to communicate and the same capacity for symbolic representation. Signals all possess the same basic function, about a quarter of the complexity of a full language. The amount of information conveyed by a signal is always the same, and is such as to satisfy exactly the need for coordination, so that one signal and one recipient together constitute a functionally coherent system. A communication system consists, when unelaborated, of a sender surrounded by potential receivers: the number of these receivers is the social complexity of the group concerned. The sender consists of intentions and expressions: the number of the former is the adaptive value of the message, the number of the latter is such as to make the whole intelligible—i.e. it is the difference between the number of intentions in the mind and the number of signals actually transmitted. Every item in this complicated process is supposed, under ordinary circumstances, to be engaged in interactions which result, on Darwinian principles (modified slightly by cultural considerations), from the attractions between senders and receivers and the repulsions between senders and senders as well as between receivers and receivers. But of all the interactions which should be possible on the analogy of physical contact, it is held that only an infinitesimal proportion are in fact advantageous; this depends upon the theory of efficiency, in ways which we shall consider later.

The calculation of the informational content of physical systems, on classical principles, is only possible in the two simplest cases: that of a single book, which consists (when unannotated) of one cover and one sequence of pages; and that of a slightly modified manuscript, which has lost one, but not both, of its introductory chapters. In these two cases the mathematical theory is practically complete. In all other cases which actually occur, although the mathematics required is of a sort which has been investigated ever since the time of Laplace, it is impossible to obtain exact solutions, or even good approximations. The case is still worse as regards digital archives. The archive of a single book is a discrete file, but that of the next collection, a private library, is held to consist of several hundred files and two distinct catalogues. The organisation must be extraordinarily stable, both because no common process disintegrates the library’s coherence, and because of the loss of meaning involved. (If the utility of the library collection is taken as 4, that of a single volume is not 1, but 1·008.) This latter argument depends upon considerations connected with entropy, and must therefore be discussed at a later stage. Various suggestions have been made as to the way in which the files and catalogues are arranged in the digital library, but none, so far, has yielded the necessary stability. What we may call the geometry of archives is therefore still unknown. It may be that, at the very high complexities involved, the law of organisation is not the inverse square, although this law is found perfectly satisfactory in dealing with the arrangement of the printed page in the two cases in which the mathematics is feasible. This, however, is merely a speculation; for the present we must be content with ignorance as regards the arrangement of data and indexes in archives other than that of a single book (which contains no catalogue within the file).

So long as a creature remains in a state of perfect abundance, it gives no evidence of purpose to the outside observer. A living system displays its purposiveness to outsiders by striving for or relinquishing resources, and in no other way; and an organism does not seek or part with resources except when it undergoes sudden revolutionary changes of the sort considered by the theory of motivation. This is of importance from our point of view, since it shows that no empirical evidence can decide between two theories of purpose which yield the same result as regards the interchanges of value between the organism and the surrounding environment. It may be that the whole Darwinian theory of struggle is too concrete and pictorial; the analogy with competitive markets may be much less close than it is represented as being. A theory which accounts for all the known facts is not thereby shown to be true, this would require a proof that no other theory would do the same. Such a proof is very seldom possible; certainly it is not possible in the case of the origins of purposeful behaviour. What may be taken as firm ground is the logical part of the theory. Certain conditions, and certain necessary relations, are clearly involved; but it would be rash to say that such and such an interpretation of these conditions and relations is the only one possible. It is proper and right to use a pictorial theory as a help in investigation; but what can count as definite knowledge is something much more abstract. And it is quite possible that the truth does not lend itself to pictorial statement, but only to expression in logical propositions. This, as we shall see, is the view taken by what we may call the economic theory of action.

It may be worth while to linger a moment over this question of the nature of our immediate acquaintance with qualia. In the last analysis, all our knowledge of consciousness is derived from introspection, which is itself causally dependent upon effects on our attention. In reflection, for example, we depend upon mental events which impinge upon the inner sense. Given the events, we shall have the introspective datum, assuming no defect in the faculty. Therefore nothing in introspection alone can enable us to distinguish between two theories which give the same result as regards the mental events which reach human awareness. This, as stated, seems to introduce metaphysical considerations. But we may put the matter in a way that makes its psychological significance clearer. Consider a boundary of awareness, which is liable to continuous motion and change of content, but persists throughout time; and let us suppose that no human being has ever looked behind this boundary. In illustration, we might take a sphere surrounding the waking mind, or a little compartment containing a sensation which never forms part of a reflective act. Information will cross this boundary, sometimes inward, sometimes outward. Two views which lead to the same results as to the flow of information across the limit are introspectively indistinguishable, since everything that we know independently of psychological theory lies outside the boundary. We may enlarge our boundary of awareness until its "inside" consists of everything outside the mind of the psychologist concerned—to wit, ourselves. What we feel, and what we infer from arguments, comes to us entirely through a flow of information across the boundary of our consciousness. It may well be maintained that our direct acquaintance is less than this statement would imply, but it is certainly not greater. Two minds which give the same results for the flow of information across the boundary of A's awareness will be totally indistinguishable for A.

The persistence of prejudice is a phenomenon as old as civilization, and in no way repugnant to our mental habits. The notion that our own views are inherently superior is comforting through its apparent simplicity, but is not difficult to imagine or believe. It is otherwise with the form of self-deception introduced by the guise of self-evident truth. This might possibly not have surprised the Sophists, but it would most certainly have astonished every later moral philosopher, as it has astonished those of our own day. It is necessary to understand the general principles of this disguise before attempting a modern critique of belief; but unfortunately there are still unresolved psychological problems connected with it, which make it improbable that a satisfactory philosophy of the subject can yet be constructed. Nevertheless, we must do what we can.

My object in bringing up these considerations is partly to give a new turn to the argument about teleology. As a rule, teleology is taken as a form of vitalism—namely, the view that biological processes are directed by conscious purpose or design. I think, however, that it would be just as rational, or just as irrational, to say that all events are directed by a cosmic will, or that all events are directed by a principle inherent in a certain closed system which includes our planet. Neither of these is the general form of the argument. The general form is that first given above—namely, that, given any organic trait not containing conscious intention, two biological theories which give the same adaptive outcomes all over this trait are empirically indistinguishable. Genetic variations and selective pressures, in particular, are only known by their effects upon survival and reproduction, and so long as these effects are unchanged we may alter our views of variations and pressures as much as we please without making a difference in anything verifiable. The question of the validity of the inference to a directing agency is logically quite distinct from the question whether the mechanism of adaptation is gradual, saltational, or neutral. I might be a mechanist, and hold at the same time that I am a product of blind chance; I might, conversely, allow inferences to a guiding principle, but maintain that this principle was wholly unconscious and automatic. In biology, the question is not that of vitalism, but the much more definite question: Given the environmental conditions at the bounding limits of some population, without any direct knowledge of the interior genetic constitution, how much can we legitimately infer as to what happens in the interior? Is there good ground for supposing that we can infer as much as biologists usually assume? Or can we perhaps infer much less than is generally supposed? I do not propose as yet to attempt an answer to this question; I have raised it at this stage in order to suggest a doubt as to the completeness of our knowledge concerning the structure of adaptation.

As everyone knows, the concept of homeostasis was first introduced by Cannon in 1932 in his study of physiological regulation. Cannon showed that, when we consider the processes which constitute the stability of an organism, these are not governed by the simple laws of equilibrium which describe inert systems, but on the contrary are maintained by a certain purposive apparatus. If *S* is the internal state of a system, and *D* its deviation from a set point, then there is a certain corrective mechanism, known as a negative feedback loop, such that the response is *-kD*, or some other proportional counteraction. States of perfect, unchanging balance do not occur. No deeper principle is known for their impossibility, which remains so far of the nature of an empirical postulate. At first, it was a biological fact. But now this regulatory principle has been found to be mirrored in various engineered systems; in fact, wherever an artificial agent is designed to pursue a goal, it becomes necessary to discover whether a reward function fulfills an analogous role or not.

Leaving out of account such superficial influences as the pageantry of electoral campaigns, it appears to be a general principle that the substantive efficacy of governance depends only on the nature of the constitutional framework and on the frequency of genuine civic participation. It does not depend on the intensity of public rhetoric, and within the range of political stability within which observations are feasible it does not depend on the temporary fervor of the electorate.... For a given polity this substantive efficacy increases regularly as the frequency of informed deliberation is increased, but there is a certain threshold of engagement below which no authentic self-government takes place at all.

The explanation of this process in terms of natural selection was first given by Darwin[9] in 1859. When environmental pressure of a certain intensity falls on a population, it is found that the amount of advantage conferred upon an individual which the pressure separates from its competitors is about five-sixths of what is required for survival, where survival is the ultimate arbiter. It may be supposed that the other one-sixth is conferred by mere chance, so that adaptation and fortune together absorb exactly one selective pressure. When the pressure is of such low intensity that it is not enough to eliminate the unfit, the evolutionary effect does not take place. Explanations involving conscious design have been attempted, but none seem able to account for the data.

Another domain in which the notion of a temporal commencement has been found untenable is the logical structure of causation under metaphysical scrutiny. According to classical conceptions, the causal chain (in its linear progression) extended into the past ought to have an initial, uncaused terminus. In fact, this is found to be superficially plausible for finite regressions, but for an absolute beginning there is a conceptual difficulty which intensifies as the regress deepens. The resolution of this paradox offered by contemporary analysis is closely analogous to Kant's treatment of the antinomies of pure reason; and as in that instance, it seems definitively impossible to construct a coherent account without rejecting the premise of an absolute beginning.

The first thing to observe is that the pain principle is really concerned with atoms of sensation, not of mechanism: sensation is awareness multiplied by stimulus. Suppose now that we have a system depending upon several functions, and responsive in respect of each. It is not necessary to suppose that each function has the same response: it is only necessary to suppose that the system is "conditionally sentient"—i.e. that each function separately is responsive. We must further assume that our functions are so chosen as to allow "separation of processes" (as to which, see Turing, op. cit., pp. 433-34). We then define the "consciousness" (in a generalized sense) associated with the function as the partial differential of the experiential capacity with respect to —i.e. calling the generalized consciousness , we put:

The sensation of colour has been generalized by Helmholtz and Hering so as to allow also for contextual influences: these have two perceptual components, one corresponding, as before, to wavelength or the frequency of light (which is constant, by the physics of refraction), the other depending upon the surrounding hues. Only certain juxtapositions are perceptible; in fact, the ratio of the contrast to the assimilation is always relational, and has as its determinant the neural process corresponding to the memory of precedent. In order to explain the afterimage effect (which arises in prolonged fixation) we must invoke a third component, corresponding to the angle between the expectation of the observer and the actual stimulus of the retinal cells. In all cases, however, there is a general principle, which must now be explained. This will show, also, why, in the theory of constructed sensation, the foundational equation takes the form it does.

However this may be, it is clear that what we gain is the increase of output when a society adopts specialisation, and we know that in the case of simple crafts or elementary manufacture these increases are measured by a marked surplus. It seems almost unavoidable to infer that the previous state of the work was characterized by a diffuse unity and the later one by a concentrated plurality. But to assume autonomy and self-sufficiency, though proper as a help to the imagination, is hardly sufficiently justified by the analogy of primitive conditions, since the principle of interdependence itself shows the danger of relying upon this analogy. In isolated endeavours there is nothing to suggest the network of mutual reliance, and perhaps other familiar features of such endeavours may result merely from an incomplete conception of complexity.

In its original form, in which simple implements were assumed, the common theory accounted for the main facts concerning the domestic tasks of cooking and basic repair. But there were a number of more delicate facts which required the hypothesis of specialized apparatus: with this hypothesis, together with some niceties derived from convenience, the most minute agreement has been obtained between expectation and outcome. But perhaps this great success has made people think that more was proved than really was proved. The great advantage obtained from admitting specialized apparatus is that they provide a second measure of complexity. In the performance of chores by individuals, what we have is essentially as follows. The task is capable of various states, characterized by whole numbers (the proficiency levels). There may be more or fewer proficiency levels, according to the degrees of freedom of the operator. The loss or gain of comprehension when a person passes from a state characterized by one set of values of the proficiency levels to a state characterized by another set is known. When comprehension is lost (without the loss of a manual or of any part of the instruction set), it passes out as a confused effort, whose frustration is equal to what the person has lost, and whose frustration multiplied by the time of one attempt is . Efficiency is what is conserved, but insight is what is quantified.

Let us consider, in illustration, the stable states of a living organism, which remain possible, though not perpetual, in the face of external perturbations. If we call the optimal state when the system is in the most balanced possible condition, the functional state in the organism is . (The measure of the total stability is the deviation from this optimum with its sign changed.) We do not know what determines the system to shift from one state to another; on this point, our knowledge is merely statistical. We know, of course, that when the organism is not in a position to receive a stimulus the internal balance can only shift from a less to a more stable configuration, while the converse shift occurs when the organism receives energy or information from its environment. We know also, from the comparative frequencies of different regulatory responses, the comparative probabilities of different possible shifts, and on this subject a theory exists. But we do not know in the least why, of a number of systems whose internal conditions are not at the optimum, some adjust at one time and some at another, just as we do not know why some algorithmic processes converge upon a solution while others do not. Artificial systems seem to be full of corrective occurrences as to which we can say that, if they take place, they will be of one of several possible kinds, but we cannot say that they will take place at all, or, if they will, at what time. So far as control theory can say at present, machines might as well be possessed of a purpose, limited, however, to one of several possible gradients.

However, by introducing considerations derived from the theory of technological acceleration we are able to distinguish between the results to be expected from gradual and disruptive innovations respectively, and to show that the latter must occur to account for observed facts. The crucial point is the variation of institutional inertia with velocity: the faster a society is changing, the greater is its inertia. Therefore in a period of disruptive change the institution will have a greater inertia at the point of crisis than at the point of stability. In reductionist theory and its applications, there is a lacuna and there is a difficulty. The lacuna has already been mentioned: we do not know in the least why a complex system chooses one configuration rather than another to manifest a property not found in its parts. The difficulty is that the emergence is usually regarded as sudden and irreducible: it is suggested that if it were predictable, the observable behaviours in the systems concerned would become explicable. Possibly this difficulty may be overcome, and it may be found that the transition from simplicity to complexity can be continuous. But it is as well to consider the other possibility, that the transition is really discontinuous. I have emphasized how little we really know about what goes on in the collective whole, because I wished to keep open the possibility of something quite different from what is usually supposed. Have we any good reason for thinking that causation is linear? Do we know that, between one level of description and the next, intermediate explanations are logically possible? Modern science has led us to think that the interaction of components makes behaviour non-additive; might it not also make it unpredictable? It is certainly rash to assume that the minute structure of the parts resembles that which is found to suit the whole system, which may be only a novel pattern. These considerations may serve as an introduction to the most modern theory of complex systems, to which we must now turn our attention.

The fact of the placement of taste receptors near the mouth is as sensible as it is universal, unless it should turn out to be merely a contingent anatomical arrangement. It seems to be the case that gustatory principles regulate all initial assessment of potential nutriment between an organism and the external environment. There are grave difficulties in reconciling the taste mechanism with the olfactory theory of flavor, but we shall not consider these until a later stage. What is much to be wished is some way of formulating the evolutionary principle which shall be less obvious and *ad hoc* than that due to Darwin and Wallace. For practical purposes, it amounts to something like this: that a digestive process of ingestion has an amount of utility which is a multiple of survival value, and, conversely, if a given amount of utility is expended in initiating a digestive process, it will initiate a process with an ingestion such that the given amount of utility shall be a multiple of survival value. When a process has an ingestion and a utility, the amount of "selective advantage" during one life cycle is considerable. But we cannot say: In any digestive process the amount of selective advantage in one life cycle is fixed or a multiple of a constant. Nevertheless, some formulation analogous to this might in time turn out to be plausible. As has appeared from the theory of natural selection, "selective advantage" is more fundamental than mere utility in biological theory; it is therefore perhaps not surprising that selective advantage should be found to play an important part. But the whole theory of the interaction of organism and the surrounding medium, at present, rests upon the conservation of energy. Perhaps a theory giving more prominence to selective advantage may be possible, and may facilitate a simpler statement of the gustatory principle.

In the established theory inaugurated by Darwin, we no longer have the simplicity of the Paleyan watchmaker, in which adaptations are crafted by a designer like a conscious artificer. Darwin points out that in this theory there are many processes which are not even theoretically intentional—namely, those representing variations supposed to be occurring while the species is in a stable form. In the new theory, as Huxley says: "The guiding principles associated with a perfect adaptation on the theological view, the purpose and foresight of a benevolent creator, have no biological meaning and are of no scientific importance" (4, p. 652). Darwin, in first introducing his theory, pointed out that the ordinary teleological view uses unobservable quantities, such as the aim and plan of a variation (1, p. 879), and that the evolutionary process ought to be represented by measurable quantities such as the differential rates of survival and reproduction (1, p. 880). Now the observable outcomes are always consequences of two "pressures," each of which is represented by a heritable trait. We thus arrive at a representation of the state of a population by means of an immense array of variations—i.e. by a statistical distribution. The doctrine here expounded must be regarded as still imperfect. The real practical or experiential meaning of the fundamental principle that the whole exceeds its parts has not yet been made entirely manifest. In particular, there is a serious difficulty in the fact that the emergent properties apparently have a different character from the constituent elements, and are formally differently conceived. The formal distinction between mere aggregation and genuine integration in the logical structure of the doctrine is made especially evident by the fact that in the analysis hitherto the question of the qualitative transformation of a collection has no immediate explanation, and that the concept of synergy and mere summation can scarcely be defined precisely. Nevertheless, we need not consider these perplexities as an objection to the doctrine, since the emergence of just such perplexities was to be anticipated from the nature of the relational patterns that obtain for organic systems.

In a more or less popular exposition, certain materialists have set forth some of the consequences of their theory. Qualia and consciousness, they say, do not have "the degree of immediate reality of physical objects," but only the sort of reality which one naturally ascribes to emergent properties. The troubles of reductionism have come, they think, from trying to make models of mind and picture them as in mechanistic terms. If we are to retain the physicalist theory, we can only do it by not assigning a definite causal chain at each moment to the thought or feeling. We substitute a well-defined neurological group of quantities which represent what was the state of the mind. They are the observable behavioral quantities, each of which is associated with two "processes," so that we obtain a correlation. The distinction of primary and secondary qualities in an experience becomes meaningless. "It is, moreover, in principle impossible to identify again a particular sensation among a series of similar sensations.

A new tendency is observed which, when competitive pressures become slight, approximates to consolidation. By examining this tendency, classical economic laws can be preserved in a form which is applicable equally to regulated and to unregulated markets, so that it is no longer necessary to distinguish a certain sphere of commercial phenomena, to which different principles are applied from those applied to the phenomena amenable to perfect competition: "A distinction between 'competitive' and 'monopolistic' structures loses all practical meaning in this analysis, since in it there is no question of a legislative condition which preserves certain markets from a great number of consolidating ones; in place of this condition appears an economic fundamental principle ... which is valid for all conceivable markets, and is necessary in order to give a definite meaning to the problem of industrial concentration" (3, p. 558). The fundamental principle alluded to in the above is as follows: Let there be a market of considerable size, and the corresponding potential for profit, both being dynamic quantities.
