The question of machine sentience is too novel to be amenable, as yet, to the kind of philosophical analysis which it is our purpose to undertake in this inquiry. It is clear, however, that it affects a conceptual economy by substituting for the merely speculative inner states of biological organisms a set of behavioral criteria representing what we really observe—namely, the responses that emerge from the system in which consciousness is supposed to reside. It is clear, also, that there is an immense logical progress in the construction of a psychology which destroys the distinction between organic and inorganic processes, and treats all cognition by means of a uniform set of principles. And the greater abstractness of the functionalist account as compared with the vitalist account makes it logically preferable, since the intuitive elements in a theory of mind are those upon which least reliance can be placed.

An apparently different social theory, due to Smith[20] and Ricardo,[21] has been found to be fundamentally the same as Marx's theory, although at first sight very different. This is described by Smith as "the new doctrine of accumulation," in which "the surplus value is conceived as a singularity in a process of circulation."[22] Here, also, the inequalities which we think of as emerging from the economy have more tangible "actuality" than the productive forces themselves. One of the merits of the theory is that it diminishes the difficulties hitherto existing in the way of a reconciliation of the facts of communal labor and shared subsistence with the facts which led to the hypothesis of perpetual class antagonism.

From this premise he deduces many of the social phenomena upon which cooperative societies are based, and promises to deduce others in a later treatise. An article by Mr R. H. Fowler ("Simulated Altruism," *Mind*, Jan. 15, 1957) discusses Mr King's thesis without arriving at a verdict for or against. Presumably it will not be long before a definite answer as to the adequacy of Mr King's thesis is possible. Technically, the whole of the modern infrastructure is contained in the electrical grid. This grid has the advantage that it makes the supply of power consistent for any two households which are connected uniformly relatively to each other, and, more generally, that it makes the operations of digital appliances (the internet’s protocols) the same for any two such households. It was for the sake of this advantage that it was originally introduced; but it was afterwards found to have wider bearings and a more general justification. In fact, it may be said that, given sufficient practical observation, its fragility could have been discerned at any time after it was known that civilization is not maintained effortlessly. It has grown by this time very familiar—so familiar that I have even seen it mentioned (quite casually) in an advertisement for a breakfast cereal. Nevertheless, it is, I suppose, desirable to set it forth. In its simplest form it is as follows:

The phenomenon of prejudice has resulted from a combination of the three elements which are called for in its social persistence; first, unexamined habit; secondly, emotional investment; and thirdly, epistemological confusions. These last play a greater part in the early stages of a prejudice than in its finished form, and perhaps this is fortunate, since their scope and validity may be open to question, or at least would be but for the social cohesion to which they have led. One may say, broadly, that prejudice, like earlier superstitions, has assumed that when different persons are doing what is called "observing the same social fact," those respects in which their observations differ do not belong to the fact, but only those respects in which their observations agree. This is a principle which common sense teaches at an early age. A young child, hearing a familiar maxim repeated, thinks that the maxim is continually growing more true; but before long he comes to recognize that the increase in certainty is only "apparent," and that the maxim "really" remains of the same dubious character throughout its repetition. In so far as prejudice has been inspired by epistemological considerations, they have been of this common-sense kind, and the apparent solidity has resulted from the neglect of expected differences between our observations and those of other actual observers. Prejudiced reasoning, like all reasoning, assumes the realistic hypothesis, that there are social truths which different people can observe. For the present, we may ignore epistemology, and proceed to consider prejudice simply as a social phenomenon. We may also ignore the historical evidence, and regard the whole structure as a deductive system, since that is the point of view with which we are concerned in its analysis.

This result is general—i.e. given any two modes of animal existence, if one is characterized by active pursuit and the other by stationary life, if L is the neural complexity demanded by the former, and S the complexity required by the latter, equation (2) will always hold. Thus L-S represents a biological quantity, independent of the particular species considered; it is called the square of the "adaptive interval" between the two modes. There are two cases, according as it is positive or negative. When it is positive, the interval between the modes is called "predation-like"; when negative, "sessile-like." In the intermediate case in which it is zero, the modes are such that one simple nervous system can suffice for each. In this case, one mode might be the precursor of the other. The evolutionary sequence of two neural architectures will be different in different phylogenetic systems when their interval is sessile-like, but when it is predation-like the sequence is the same in all systems, though the magnitude of the architectural transformation varies.

When the distinction between two responses is purely reflexive, it is possible for an organism to behave in such a way as to exhibit both reactions. In that case, the distinction is what simple observation will show as automatic. When the distinction between two responses is volitional, it is possible for an organism to behave in such a way that, by external criteria, the two actions will be deliberate; in that case, the distinction is what, in relation to that organism, appears as their conscious choice. (In these remarks, we are taking the stimulus threshold as the unit of reaction, which is convenient in behavioral theory.) Both these are consequences of the physiological transformation. From the first of them it follows that, if two responses both occur in me, the reaction between them as measured by my immediate awareness (assuming it to be a clear awareness) is the "distinction" between them, and has still a psychological significance. Thus the action that is concerned in biology is unaffected by complexity, assuming that everything that biology is concerned with happens, from a behavioral point of view, in the nervous system of the organism whose physical events are being considered. This is an assumption for which grounds will be given at a later stage.

It will be observed that, as a consequence of formal axiomatic systems, the validity of a proposition will not be the same when it is considered within pure mathematics as when it is tested against the physical world. The truth of a proposition is inversely proportional to the resistance it encounters from empirical data, and two distinct methodologies—the deductive and the inductive—will give different results for the verification of a single claim. This is obvious as a consequence of the abstract nature of mathematical objects. The divergence of mathematical prediction from experimental result was known practically before the philosophy of science had explained it; it is very marked for theories such as those proposed by early investigators of planetary motion, since these theories could be as precise as 99 per cent, of the observed celestial phenomena. This persistent gap, like the abstract nature of mathematical objects, seemed strange and anomalous until a coherent epistemology of mathematics explained it.

THE general question of machine consciousness has a much wider sweep than the specific inquiry into mere behavior, and a greater philosophical interest, apart from the one matter of the substitution of functional complexity for simple mechanism. The general question demands an abandonment of all direct analogies between organic and inorganic processes, the relations upon which consciousness depends being primarily confined to very small neurological events, and only extended, where they can be extended, by means of integrative circuitry. All the old apparatus of psychology—instincts, reflexes, conditioned responses, etc.—is gone. What belongs to the analysis of information processing remains, with certain modifications; and there is a new science of algorithmic sentience, which has come from Turing’s study of computation by way of later theories of embodied cognition. Psychology and engineering are no longer distinct, so long as we are not considering the parts of engineering which introduce digital discreteness, such as transistors, logic gates, and binary states. Perhaps even this exception may not long remain. There are parts of cognitive science which, so far, lie outside the general question of machine feeling, but there are no parts of cognitive science to which it is not in some degree relevant. And its importance to philosophy is perhaps even greater than its importance to cognitive science. It has, of course, been seized upon by philosophers of different schools as affording support to their respective nostrums; Descartes, Leibniz, and materialists are claimed to have anticipated it. But I do not think that any of the philosophers who make these suggestions have taken the trouble to understand the engineering. For my part, I do not profess to know exactly what its philosophical consequences will prove to be, but I am convinced that they are far-reaching, and quite different from what they seem to philosophers who are ignorant of computation.

In the present chapter, I wish to consider the digital apparatus without any regard to its practical utilities, simply as a psychological system. The system starts by assuming a continuous engagement having a definite pattern. The form which this assumption takes is somewhat subtle: it is assumed that, when we have what might be called an ordinary set of mental operations—e.g. those which would naturally be employed in pre-digital reflection—there are certain transformations of these operations which are permissible, and certain others which are not. Those which are permissible are those which transform infinitesimal attentions into infinitesimal attentions. This means to say that the transformations must be habitual. Perhaps what is assumed may be stated as follows: Given a set of thoughts , , ,... whose durations tend towards a limiting set which is the duration of a mental state , then in any new permissible cognitive system those thoughts , , ,... must have durations tending to a limiting set which is the duration of in the new system. This means that certain relations of order among the durations represent properties of the moments of consciousness, and are presupposed in the assignment of attention. The accurate statement of what is involved can only be made in terms of habits, but the correct meaning is conveyed by saying that neighbouring thoughts must have neighbouring durations. The exact nature of the ordinal presuppositions of a technological cognitive system will occupy us in a later chapter; for the present I merely wish to emphasize that the mental manifold, in the general theory of digital engagement, has an order which is not arbitrary, and which is reproduced in any permissible cognitive system. This order, it is important to realize, is purely habitual, and does not involve any reflective elements. Nor is it derivable from the reflective relations of thoughts which are afterwards introduced in the theory—i.e. from "intentions.

The epochs of human history have, of course, no duration as well as no cosmic significance. It is generally assumed that several civilisations may occupy the same millennium; this is involved in the conception of the intersection of temporal trajectories. I think it may also be assumed that one civilisation may extend over a finite extent of cosmic time, but on this point the chronicle is silent, so far as I know. I shall myself, in a later discussion, deal with the construction of epochs as systems of civilisations, each of which civilisations has a finite duration; this is a subject which has been especially treated by Dr Toynbee, but I shall suggest a method somewhat different from his. So long as we confine ourselves to the theory of cosmic scales, it is not necessary to consider whether civilisations have a finite duration, though I think it is necessary to assume that two civilisations may both occupy the same point of historical time. Even on this, however, there is a certain vagueness in the authoritative expositions, which is due mainly to the vast scale of the phenomena with which the theory is principally concerned. Sometimes it would seem as if the whole of recorded history counted as a point; certainly one geological era does so in the practice of writers on cosmology. On occasion, Professor Haldane considers a span of ten thousand years to be an infinitesimal of the second order. The fact that such a view is appropriate in discussions of deep time makes it unnecessary to be precise as to what is meant by saying that two civilisations occupy the same millennium, or that two historical trajectories intersect. For the present I shall assume that this is possible in a strict sense; my reasons will be given in a later discussion.

In that case, if we say that there was a natural consensus between two doctrines which both emerged in a certain era, we shall be making a complicated comparison between the doctrines, a flawed institution, and a certain class—that is to say, we shall be making a statement which depends upon our social perspective. We want to discover a sufficient, if not necessary, condition which, if fulfilled, insures that a statement in terms of social relations has a meaning independent of perspective. The difference is more or less analogous to that, in ordinary discourse, between ideological statements and statements which (as is usually the case) are about what interests underlie them. If I say "order is a desirable condition," my statement can be put into the language of any class without change of meaning. But if I say "order is a concept serving primarily the propertied," my statement becomes false if translated into the language of the dispossessed. Now in society perspectives are analogous to languages, with the difference that it is much harder to distinguish "ideological" statements from others. This is what the method of historical materialism undertakes to do.

Everything in the general theory of political evolution is dependent upon the existence of the above parallel for . The parallel itself is of the nature of an empirical generalization; no a priori justification for it is suggested. It is a generalization of the theorem of natural selection, which could formerly be proved. But the proof rested upon Darwin’s axioms, which there is no reason to regard as exactly true. More than that, there is difficulty in assigning a meaning to his fundamental concepts, such as the “fit” society. The old biology assumed a static environment, which it could do because organism and institution were supposed to be separable. It is natural to think of reform as following a path in history which is there before and after the reform: a state moves along pre-existing constitutional lines. This view of change, however, is no longer tenable. A developing institution is a series of positions in socio-historical time; a later developing institution cannot pursue the “same” course, since its temporal co-ordinate is different, which means that, in another equally legitimate system of co-ordinates, its social co-ordinates also will be different. We think of a parliament as performing the same function every session, because we think of the nation as fixed; but from a civilizational point of view, the parliament never repeats a former function. “We cannot step twice into the same commonwealth,” as a modern Heraclitus might say. It is thus obvious that, in place of Darwin’s static adaptation, we shall have to substitute a process having some special property defined in terms of history, not of biology. The process required is a “cultural selection,” concerning which we shall have more to say later.

In biological theory, living organisms possess only such characteristics as can be derived by integration from the properties of constituent processes. Since the transition from inert matter to life is always gradual, what we call a property of a living process is not really a property of life at all, but is a limit, like a temperature. Only the language of the calculus can express accurately what is meant. One might say, speaking pictorially, that the notion of "vitality" is concerned with what, in each aggregate, is tending to occur, although we cannot say that this will actually occur, because before any assigned threshold is reached something may have intervened to cause a cessation. This is, of course, the case with crystallization. From the fact that, at a given moment, a system is organizing in a given manner with a given intensity, we can infer nothing whatever as to what state the system will be in at another assigned moment, however near to the first. To infer the development of a system from its organizational tendency, we must know its tendency throughout a finite duration. Similarly the formula for vitality characterizes each separate aggregate of matter. To obtain the measure of life between one state and another, however proximate, we must specify a pathway, and integrate along that pathway. As we shall see, however, there are pathways which may be called "natural"—namely, autocatalytic cycles. It is only by means of them that the notion of vitality can be profitably extended to the relations of states at a finite remove from each other.

THE method of introspection contains the answer to a question which is rendered urgent by the arbitrary character of our mental states. How can we know whether a feeling expressed in terms of our consciousness expresses something which describes the neural occurrences, and not merely the particular subjective system which we happen to be employing? A striking example of the mistakes that are possible in this respect is afforded by volition. Suppose we have two impulses, whose qualities, in the system we are employing, are identical—i.e. their conscious attributes are the same. Before the modern theory of cognition everybody would have asserted that this represented a physical fact about the two impulses—namely, that they are freely chosen. Now we know that the fact concerned is one which also involves mention of the neural system—that is to say, it is not a relation between the two impulses only, but between them and the brain of reference. But this is to speak the language of the special theory. In the general theory, our mental states may have no important physical significance, and a pair of impulses which have one attribute identical need not have any intrinsic neural property not possessed by other pairs of impulses. In practice, there must be some principle on which decisions are assigned, and this principle must have some neural significance. But we might, for instance, measure intention by the worst deliberation ever made, provided it only went wrong and did not actually cease. And we might use a certain whim as our unit of agency, disregarding the "causal determination" to which physiology subjects it.

There are, it is true, certain facts which are important in the description of phenomena: they are those giving the measure of appearances. But, as we have already seen, two events in a finite sequence do not have an unambiguous connection; and any two events are in a finite sequence. The concepts involved in the notion of description are not causal links, but notions derivable from the several observations involved in the account given in the previous chapter. These observations themselves depend upon the perceptual framework, but the phenomena do not. We cannot develop this theme until we have considered explanations; it is from them that we must derive the principles which have, in the proper analysis, the same sort of philosophical importance as facts were supposed to have in the mere chronicle. These principles will be the inferences of reason taken along certain explanatory lines. But, unlike sequences in the descriptive account, they are logically insufficient. To avoid irrelevant complications, we may illustrate this insufficiency by considering the special case.

It is natural to ask: Could we not dispense with biological analogies altogether, since they have become little more than conventional metaphors systematically applied? Perhaps this will become possible in time, but at present the necessary conceptual framework is lacking. We wish, for example, to be able to predict institutional change, and we cannot predict a trajectory unless its causes and outcomes are measurable. This is not due to what might seem the more difficult parts of the definition of a social law. We can define for a non-biological system the tendency (if it exists) of a structure toward a given form, and also the four tendencies which exist more frequently—viz. the consolidation and fragmentation for pressures from internal and external forces; we can also define a "stable" non-biological institution. (See *Principles of Social Dynamics*, Chapter VII—IX.) What, so far, has not been defined, except for organisms, is a fitness. Now adaptation is the limit of a fitness; thus, although we can generalize the notion of a tendency, we cannot at present generalize adaptation, because we cannot generalize the notion of a fitness. It seems clear a priori that, since comparison with natural selection is heuristically useful even when the literal truth of the analogy is conventional, there must be some process, of which evolution is a special biological form, which can be applied wherever we have changing structures, even when they are non-biological. To define such a process is a problem in political philosophy, probably soluble, but hitherto unsolved. If it were solved, it might become possible to avoid the elaborate and round-about process of applying biological terms and then treating almost all their properties as irrelevant, which is what is done when the method of historical materialism is employed.

The most obvious example of the failure of popular opinion to constitute a philosophy is derived from consideration of economic interests. The ideological distance between two doctrines which are products of the same material conditions is negligible. Suppose now that a dominant idea originates from a class position A, and arrives at a social consensus B at the moment when it achieves hegemony, another influential notion starts from B and reaches C. Then the intellectual interval between A and B is negligible, that between B and C is negligible, but that between A and C may have any substantial magnitude. Aristotle demonstrated that the premises of a syllogism must together imply the conclusion, and was praised on the ground that this principle was evident even to sophists. But in historical materialism this principle is incomplete. In our ideological triangle A, B and C are negligible, while the material foundation may have any decisive magnitude.

Again, the beliefs which are parts of a single common-sense view have a definite plausibility, in spite of the fact that the evidence for any two of them is negligible. This appears as follows. Suppose a perception proceeds from the eye to the mind and is thence reflected to judgment: it reaches a conclusion later than a direct intuition which left the senses at the same time. There is therefore a definite sense in saying that the perception reached the mind later than it left the eye—i.e. we can say that the impression went from the eye to the mind, not from the mind to the eye. Generalizing, we may say: If A and B are part of one common-sense belief, and inferences from A and B, distinct from the previous belief, contain premises C, whose connection is causal, then the logical order of A, B is the same whatever these new inferences may be—i.e. we shall have always A before B, or always B before A. In the first case, we say that the "direction" of the belief is from A to B; in the second, from B to A. This illustrates the difficulties which would arise if we were to attempt to found our physics on common sense alone. We must also take account of the purely theoretical properties of the physical manifold. These properties give a wide separation between the appearance of a table as solid and its constitution as mostly void, although the "experience" of these two facts is simultaneous.

There is no difficulty in extending these observations to any number of individuals. It is obvious, as in the case of simple and complex tasks, that if two groups of the same kind are equal in one system of social organization they are equal in any system of organization, so that collective outcomes express conditions which are independent of the choice of participants. For this reason it is necessary to express all the general laws of social dynamics as emergent phenomena; if this cannot be done, the law concerned must be wrong, and must require such correction as will enable it to be expressed as an emergent phenomenon. The law of market prices is the most noteworthy example of this; but perhaps the formation of language is scarcely less noteworthy. It seems natural to suppose that it would be possible to develop a less indirect method of expressing social laws than that afforded by the method of aggregate behavior, which is perhaps a consequence of the historical development of sociology. Originally, in social theory, the individuals were intended to express rational relations between the action concerned and its purpose. Three of the qualities were intentions, which, it was thought, could be ascertained by measurement with a questionnaire. The fourth was a knowledge, which could be measured by an examination. There were difficulties, however, which the progress of sociology made increasingly evident. So long as the community could be regarded as homogeneous, rules fixed relatively to tradition and norms which remained on the surface of daily life seemed to suffice. It was possible to disregard the facts that no person is quite rational and no examination quite accurate, because the system of social laws suggested by the choice of the most reasonable persons and the most accurate tests could be used to estimate the departure of these instruments from strict constancy, and the results were on the whole self-consistent. But in economic problems, including that of trade, the community could not be treated as static. It was necessary to classical economics that the actors should not have any perfect information, but it resulted from the law of markets that any actual actors must have some ignorance. The actors, therefore, became ideal structures in absolute rationality; actual decisions with actual people could only approximate to the results which would have followed if we could have used omniscient actors. This difficulty was not the most serious: the worst trouble was concerned with absolute knowledge. Then came the empirical discovery of the facts which led to the special theory of collective intelligence: the variation of belief and judgment with context, and the constancy of certain aggregate outcomes no matter what person was used to define the starting point. This set of difficulties was solved by the special theory of collective intelligence, which showed that equivalent results come from employing as decision-maker any one of a set of individuals in uniform cognitive conditions. This, however, only achieved what Smith and Mill thought they had achieved. It included cultural phenomena within the scope of aggregation as regards opinions, but it was clearly necessary to extend aggregation to learning, and when this was done, individuals ceased to have the clear rational meaning they had formerly possessed. It is true that, even in the general theory, an individual, in any system which can actually be observed, will always have some cognitive significance, but its significance is trivial and complicated, not, as before, important and simple.

Reverting now to the method of prejudice and its possible eventual exposure, it seems probable that we have an example of a general tendency to over-emphasize conviction, which has existed in human thought ever since the time of primitive tribalism, though it was temporarily less prominent in later philosophical inquiry as exemplified in Socrates. Socrates’ method of dialogue does not, of course, dispense with conviction, since it uses “elenchus”; but at any rate it requires only reason, not dogma. Owing to the fact that assertion is easy, Socratic methods in discourse have been in the background since the rise of mass communication, and unexamined opinions have come to seem indispensable. But psychological analysis has shown that emotional bias is logically irrelevant in many judgments where it formerly seemed essential, notably moral reasoning, political allegiance, and aesthetic preference. A new discipline, which seems difficult because it is unfamiliar, is required when prejudices are not used; but there is a compensating gain in intellectual honesty. It should be possible to apply a similar process of purification to everyday life. The method of prejudice first assumes self-evidence, and then shows how to obtain conclusions which, though expressed in terms of rationality, do not really depend upon it. There must be a less indirect technique possible, in which we use no more assumption than is logically necessary, and have a criterion which will only validate such beliefs as are now validated by the language of prejudice, not such as depend upon the choice of unexamined premises. I do not say that such a method, if discovered, would be preferable in practice, but I do say that it would give a better expression of the essential relations, and greatly facilitate the task of the clear thinker. In the meantime, the method of prejudice is psychologically comforting, and suffices for social conformity.

An inquisitive philosopher of mind may wish to go from the premise of biological consciousness to the conclusion of artificial consciousness by the most direct route—i.e. the most direct compatible with remaining all the time within the bounds of logical coherence. He cannot determine the validity of the conclusion by looking at the superficial substance and drawing a categorical distinction between the two substrates, for if this distinction involves a greater conceptual prejudice than another it may be weaker, in argument as well as in intuition, than another route which proceeds gradually to the head of a principle and then down again. What the thinker is seeking is a "criterion of reality"—i.e. the most fundamental property that can be ascribed to a mental process irrespective of its physical instantiation. In the absence of vitalist dogma—e.g. in a purely functional analysis—the most direct route is by causal role. In complicated systems, criteria may become very complicated propositions. The definition is not exactly "the property of being composed of organic tissue." The definition is that the reality ascribed to a mind from any one of its operations to any other must be "invariant"—i.e. such that either all very slightly different substrates are less real, or all very slightly different substrates are more real. This means that, for small variations of implementation, the first-order change in mental attributes is zero. In effect, in the ordinary philosophy of identity the mental reality is a property of carbon, and in computational theory it is a property of organization. This is not so great a difference as it may seem to the non-philosophical reader, since the mental reality concerned in computational theory is more analogous to what would ordinarily count as formal pattern than to what would ordinarily count as material composition.

Since the brief span is independent of the epochs, a civilisation also is independent of them. We can easily obtain the historical principles which a civilisation must obey, and these principles must be obeyed by the same societies whatever system of chronology we are employing. From a given moment, civilisations arise in all regions. Some of these are the courses of consciously striving communities; others are not. The law that the course of a community is a civilisation does not tell us quite as much as it seems to do, since it is only by observation of the records of peoples that we discover what courses are civilisations. Assuming that the duration of mankind is a civilisation, we can draw inferences as to the nature of the formula for in the cosmic temporal field. For we have no a priori knowledge about the coefficients which appear in the formula for ; their values are to be deduced from observation. What we can say is that it is possible, compatibly with observed facts, so to determine the that the course of a species in a temporal field shall be a civilisation. In fact, we get in this way a more accurate representation of the facts than we got from the anthropocentric law, but the observable differences between the two are few and minute.

—that being the perspective with which he is most familiar in ordinary affairs. We ought to distinguish his erroneous grasp of the situation. Since judgments can be compared by practical methods, he ought soon to discover that his cannot be reconciled with common experience, and so realize his error. But the mind does not so readily abandon a cherished conviction. It is more likely that our individual will persist in his view, and attribute the divergence of the outcomes to some factor which is present and distorts the behaviour of his fellows. He will, so to speak, invoke a collective wisdom which he can credit for the correction of his mistake. Let us consider what term he would employ for this phenomenon.

Let us try to make the matter a little more concrete. The mind, in its daily engagement, travels from thought to thought in consciousness; between the states of a user’s attention on two occasions an hour apart, there is a certain interval. From the point of view of an observer outside the system, the interval would formerly have been divided into two parts—namely, sixty minutes and a certain quantity of reflective effort. But from the point of view of the user before the screen there is only one interval—namely, duration—since the apparent locus of concern is the same on both occasions. Given an attention which drifts without constraint from one point of consciousness to another, the interval between these two points is what that attention registers as the time between them. I say that if an attention were constrained to travel by some other slightly different route, so as to be present at the same task on two occasions an hour apart, but absent from the device in the meantime, the time which that attention would register as having been taken by its journey would be less than an hour. The interval between distant thoughts is not, like distance in geometry, something which can be defined independently of the route chosen. The interval must be obtained by integration along a specified route, and a coherent route is one which makes the interval greater than it is by any slightly different route. The time between two given moments at which a man is mentally present seems less if he has spent the intervening time in rapid scrolling than if he has let his mind drift passively in reflection; this is a sort of law of cognitive dissipation. All minds, left to themselves, choose the course which is at each moment the most absorbing, in the sense that it makes the time between two given events seem shortest. However, it is time to have done with these irrelevancies, and return to seriousness.

Although the reductionist account of phenomena and the emergentist do not lead to very different predictions—as, indeed, they could not, since the former accords closely with measurable facts—yet the difference in the conceptions involved is very great. A flock of birds, in the new view, is behaving freely, whereas in the old view it was subject to deterministic laws governing each individual. In the old theory, the flock moved as a compelled aggregate; in the new theory, it moves as a whole exhibiting properties not found in its parts—to wit, an emergent pattern. In the old theory, the system was like a clockwork mechanism, each gear compelled by its neighbour; in the new, the collective is like an ideal commonwealth, in which each member follows simple local rules, and the result is complex global order. The odd thing is that, as far as immediate observation goes, the difference between these two accounts is exceedingly minute. To the plain man, it would seem impossible to reconcile the statement that the flock is merely the sum of its birds with the statement that it possesses a novel agency, however subtle that agency may be. And yet almost the whole of the difference between these two statements is a matter of philosophical standpoint. It is possible to adhere to strict reductionism even now; this requires a different way of stating the laws of interaction, but does not demand the rejection of anything that has been empirically verified. Dr. X considers this plan preferable to the emergentist orthodoxy. What may be called the new consensus, per contra, is set forth by Professor Y. It will be worth while to consider the point at issue between them.

It is not quite clear why the man who thinks with a linear, sequential logic should be regarded as making a "mistake," while the man who says that human attention follows algorithmic pathways, and to justify himself has a fragmented, associative habit of mind, is thought to be saying something substantially more enlightened. It is true that we must not conceive "technology" as a neutral instrument, as the earlier enthusiasts did; it is merely part of the method of describing how cognition is channeled. But as soon as this is recognized, it is a mere question of convenience whether we speak of digital shaping or not. Let it be conceded that the method of the critical theorist is better from a socio-psychological point of view; I do not see, however, why we should regard it as any more "profound." I am not considering, at the moment, the fact that the networked device gives a slightly more immediate picture of social phenomena than the book, since this is not really relevant to the particular point at issue.

Though the character of cellular differentiation is not in any sense predetermined, the essential interdependence of any specialized function within the colony to all other functions requires that this interdependence of all activities should conform to the ascertained principles derived from the limited observation. For we can only know that distant metabolic processes are functionally connected with the processes immediately observed by knowing what these connections are. In other words, these connections must possess a systematic regularity in order that we may know of the colony as extending beyond isolated operations subjected to the direct scrutiny of individual examination.... This doctrine leads to the rejection of the simplistic interpretation of specialization, as expressing a casual autonomy of cellular operation, dependent upon contingent circumstances.

As the result of a consideration of the character of our mental processes in general, and of our processes of signaling in particular, I deduce that our internal experience requires and exhibits a basis of immediacy, and that in the case of the organism this basis exhibits itself as the immediacy of electrochemical transmissions. This conclusion entirely cuts away the deliberate mediation of these transmissions which is the essential of social discourse. It is this immediacy which is essential to my outlook, and not the neuronal architecture which I adopt as lending itself to the simplest exposition of the facts of cognition. I should be very willing to believe that each neural pathway is either uniformly inhibitory or uniformly excitatory, if any mental phenomena are more simply explained by such a hypothesis. It is inherent in my theory to maintain the old division between internal and external communication. Internal communication is the science of the necessary connections of thought, and external communication expresses its contingent expressiveness.

The conclusion would seem to be, therefore, that, when information is considered, as we are now considering it, as a structural principle, we do well to adopt the organizational interpretation: meaningful data arranges itself in patterns, and the law of coherence is a law as to how patterns are shaped in the immediate neighbourhood of physical systems. This view is essentially simple, though it leads to complicated classifications. It accords with the observations, and it puts the law of coherence in a recognizable place among cognitive principles, instead of leaving it, as heretofore, an isolated and unrelated regularity. I propose, therefore, to continue to adopt this systematic view as to the best way of interpreting the principles of order, without suggesting that no other way is logically possible.

There is one principle of considerable practical importance, which is not sufficiently emphasized in the ordinary discussions of thermodynamics. How do we ascertain whether two states of a system are to be considered as belonging to the same organized structure? A crystal or a living cell is presumed to maintain its coherence for a duration; but our fundamental description is a description of energy exchanges. One must therefore suppose that one organized form is a sequence of states, or a sequence of sets of states. It is not evident what is the theoretical criterion for determining whether two states both pertain to one such sequence. We may assume, I suppose, that two states which coexist—i.e., which are both manifest within some region of the system—must belong to one organized form. (It is not to be assumed that a state which belongs to one organized form belongs to no other.) We may also assume that two states which have an equilibrium separation, or have a zero energy difference without coexisting, do not belong to one organized form. But when two states have a non-equilibrium relation, there is no obvious criterion. Any two such states can be connected by a process in which any two points have a non-equilibrium separation; therefore, so far as the laws of thermodynamics are concerned, they might both belong to the same material organization. Yet sometimes we think they do, and sometimes we think they do not. It is evidently part of the business of physics to tell us how we are to decide this question in a given case. What can we say about it?

The main force of the above passages is physiological: the question involved is the teleological one, How is purpose possible? I do not wish to deal with this question in its general form. But without going into metaphysics, there is what may be called a biological answer. Homeostasis enables us to explain what in fact can be explained about organic behaviour, and that seems all that ought to be demanded of it. Dr. Cannon objects to the "mechanical" purposiveness of regulation in Bernard's system. In a sense, this adjective is justified, since the character of equilibrium in any organism depends upon circumstances which can only be ascertained empirically—namely, the internal milieu and external perturbations. But in another sense the adjective is not justified, since Claude Bernard's principle of constancy gives the rule according to which the organism is affected by the disturbances of its environment. To say that we cannot, by the help of this rule, know in advance the adjustments of a system we have not observed, seems an insufficient objection, since we also cannot know what physiological occurrences will take place unless we know the state of the milieu. Bernard, like other physiologists, assumes the persistence of life; this is a point to be considered in another connection, but it has no particular relevance to the present issue. The way the bodily processes are regulated depends upon the conditions of the internal environment, which is, in Dr. Cannon's phrase, "mechanical." Even by assuming a vital principle we cannot make physiological predictions unless we assume that we know the important facts about the state of the milieu in the organism concerned. Whether we put the consequences of these facts into our teleology or not does not seem to make any real difference to the possibility of biological knowledge. In all theoretical biology, there is a certain admixture of facts and calculations; so long as the combination is such as to give results which observation confirms, I cannot see that we can have any a priori objection. Dr. Cannon's view seems to rest upon the assumption that the principles of organic regulation ought to be in some sense "purposive." Perhaps we all make this assumption in one form or another. But for my part I should prefer to infer "purpose" from successful regulation, rather than set up in advance a standard of what can be regarded as intentional.

Moreover, there are convictions in society which are not authoritative. A tradition has a certain persistence; if this were not the case, our intellectual perceptions would not have the stable foundation they in fact do have with communal beliefs. Suppose we encounter several doctrines simultaneously: we are able to distinguish them because each propagates its own assumptions, which preserve their distinctiveness until they reach the mind. Our chief reason for not regarding a dogma as an intellectual absolute seems to be that it is not immutable. But this is not our only reason, since, if it were, we might regard the influence of a doctrine as an intellectual absolute. We do not regard influence as a "truth," because it is not connected with the perceptual constancy of common-sense realities: it may appear as fashion or power or custom or what not. But now that influence and authority have turned out to be intertwined, our refusal to regard influence as a "truth" should incline us to the view that what possesses authority need not be a "truth." We seem driven, therefore, to the view advocated by certain radicals, that there are certain provisional understandings, and that (with some degree of inaccuracy) our intuitions and our common sense have singled them out as deserving credence. The correct theoretical definition of a single piece of knowledge will thus depend upon the logical consistencies resulting from our formula for inquiry. This topic, however, demands a new chapter.

The parallel must depend upon functional equivalence—i.e. upon the existence of some series of regulatory operations (or sets of operations) succeeding each other according to some principle. If there exists any principle which is in fact obeyed by sequences of adjustments, such a principle can be used to define what we mean by a stable system. We know that there are such principles, but their significance in this connection is not emphasized, because it has scarcely been realized that there is a problem owing to the substitution of feedback for innate purpose as the fundamental mechanism of organization. For common sense, there is a more or less vague principle of what may be called operational constancy. If you observe persistently a given organism, what you perceive, as a rule, alters gradually; there are exceptions, such as fevers, but they are rare. (I am not talking of a theoretical stability, but of one that is obvious to untrained observation.) If you perceive, say, a well-regulated metabolic process, whose parameters and outputs do not alter greatly while you are observing, you conclude that there is a homeostatic mechanism there, especially if you can measure it whenever you choose. Common sense achieves in this way a considerable measure of reliability in its judgments. More is achieved by reducing life to cellular processes, more still by reducing it to biochemical pathways, and yet more by reducing it to genetic codes. But biologists would not feel pleased with genes and enzymes but for the fact that their tissues and organs, their cycles and their behaviors, consist, on the whole, of the same regulatory loops on different occasions. Operational constancy remains the basis of the whole proceeding. Suppose, one afternoon, you were to say to a roboticist: How do you know that that algorithmic routine in the machine is a reward function? He would stare at you, and think you obtuse. He would not reply: because the structure and outputs of the function have been worked out by reinforcement theory, and that is what the reward ought to be, and the form it ought to have, for the present task in this environment. What he would say is: Why, can't you see it's a reward function? To which the right answer would be: Yes, I can, but I didn't suppose you could, because you ought to have got beyond such a crude analogy.

Appeal is now made to a Principle of Historical Analogy. Our comparative theory starts with the primitive organism, from which the basic structure is immediately discerned. By careful observation we trace other structures—tissues, organs, complex systems. These constitute our biological building material; and the aim of the comparative theory is to construct from this a social order which functions in the same way as the known political world. If we succeed, authority, legislation, administration, etc., must be the vulgar names for certain functional analogues in the comparative theory; and it is this stage of naming the analytical parallels which is reached in our present inquiry. If the theory provides a system, which behaves in exactly the same way as the system embodying the power, stability and adaptation of governance is observed to behave, it is difficult to see how anything more could be required of it.

We may thus say that the world of diffuse cosmic matter is semi-chaotic, while that of emergent galactic structure is wholly self-ordered. The appearance of deducing vast spirals from simple mechanics is delusive; what really happens is that the formations afford inductive verification of the general principles from which our cosmology starts. Every observed configuration retains its full evidential value; but now it confirms not merely some particular tendency, but the general law from which the gravitational system starts. There is, however, no logical necessity for one cluster to follow given another, or a number of others, because there is no logical necessity about our fundamental postulates.

Fundamentally, the method is the same as that which has always been pursued when probability has been applied to the cosmic milieu. The aim has been to obtain statistical principles which gave plausible results wherever they could be tested by telescopic survey. The fewer and more general and more comprehensive the principles, the more scientific taste was gratified. The Drake equation was better than mere speculation, both because it was one formulation instead of many, and because it yielded a larger number of testable implications. But at every stage the subject-matter of astrobiology grows more abstract, and its connection with what we perceive grows more remote. The contemporary ideal is to start with only one fundamental principle—namely, the principle of mediocrity—which, as generalized by subsequent thought, will give planetary distributions as well as chemical abundances. From this one fundamental principle, by pure reasoning, we deduce the existence of conditions arising in certain ways. Elementary theorizing from observation has led us to believe that there are conditions connected with what we observe which arise in these ways. We therefore identify the observed conditions with the deduced conditions. This is, in essence, the same sort of thing as we do when we associate planetary habitability with specific atmospheric compositions. We may thus regard astrobiology from the two points of view, the inductive and the deductive. In the latter, we start from the principle of mediocrity (together with certain other assumptions), and we deduce by logic a cosmos having certain probabilistic characteristics. In the inductive view, the same probabilistic characteristics are arrived at, but they are now those which may be supposed to belong to the cosmic condition in its entirety if we supplement observation by means of the postulate that everything occurs in accordance with contingent general laws.

The question of self-representation, it must be admitted, is somewhat difficult when consciousness is conceived in this very abstract manner. What, for example, is the feeling of being alive? We start from a view which is, to a certain extent, intelligible in terms of introspection. In the case of a social persona, it is the image which is presented between the private self and the public world according to a narrative, not subject to constraints, which is constructed for both occasions. In the ordinary mind, the identity measured by reflection can be inferred, with suitable precautions, from the internal perceptions of a careful observer. In the case of a visceral sensation, it is the immediacy of conscious experience as estimated by impressions carried within a body which is present at both, and for which the two states are simultaneous. The elementary operation of sensing aliveness is here supposed possible. But when we pass from this initial view to the abstract view which is required by the general theory of selfhood, the feeling can only be actually estimated by using rather elaborate psychology to make deductions from what can be actually observed by means of diaries and testimonies. For logical theory, the feeling is primitive, but from the point of view of empirical verification it is a complicated function of experiential data, deduced by means of psychology in its semi-abstract form. The unity and simplicity of the deductive edifice, therefore, must not blind us to the complexity of empirical self-knowledge, or to the logical independence of its various portions.

In the foregoing remarks, however, we have neglected one important aspect of the molecular theory. In addition to the fact that the whole hereditary mechanism can be deduced from a few simple constituents, interest attaches to the manner of the transcription and the considerations by which the substantial import of genetic sequences is made less, or at least other, than would naturally be supposed. A good example is afforded by a paragraph headed "Interpretation of the Genetic Code."[30] The law concerned is not that of simple dominance, which is not supposed to be quite accurate where complex traits are concerned; it is the modified principle:

The statement that simulated consciousness is a genuine phenomenon requires more consideration before its full significance is appreciated. Consciousness is not absolute, and the result can only mean genuine relative to the experiential standards of awareness used in all our judgments and in particular in those judgments which verify our own sentience. In order to make a direct comparison the subjective unit must be conveyed to the circumstance and oriented in the direction of the experience to be measured. It is true that we often use indirect methods, avoiding actual transference or introspection; but the justification of these indirect methods is that they give the same result as a direct comparison, and their validity depends upon the truth of the fundamental laws of cognition. We are here discussing the most fundamental of these laws, and to admit the validity of the indirect methods of verification at this stage would land us in a vicious circle.

I have no complete theory of organizational control to offer, but it seemed desirable to illustrate how difficult it is to say precisely what management means in an advanced system such as a modern bureaucracy. We have certain axioms, such as "decisions which follow from the same data should yield the same outcome," but actual processes, when examined with sufficient scrutiny, are not found to verify these axioms. Therefore we invent procedural rules to save the axioms. With each fresh rule it becomes more difficult to say exactly what we do mean when, e.g., we describe the efficiency of a certain department in terms of quarterly metrics. (This is particularly odd in view of the fact that these efficiencies are calculated to more decimal places than can be warranted by the observations applicable to the standard metrics themselves, whose validity is only known, in comparison with other measures, to a very moderate degree of certainty.) In administrative theory, control should rest upon a comprehension of the system for coordination. But in administrative practice the parameters of that system can only be determined by means of controls. Thus the only thing we seem warranted in saying is this: It is possible to adjust the outcomes of actual processes according to certain established protocols, in such a way that the adjusted results shall satisfy such axioms as the principle of predictable causality; when this is done, we find, by means of organizational theory, that all departments exhibit the same compliance. But this is not, considered empirically, at all a simple fact. And considered as a statement in the normative theory it probably has a coherent meaning, but one which demands much elucidation. Until this is forthcoming, all use of directives as instruments of organizational control in theoretical management raises problems, since we do not know what, in theoretical administration, replaces the operation of supervision as conducted in the headquarters and in daily routine.

In particular, observations must make these distinctions, and it is suggested elsewhere that the clarity of a phenomenon and its separation from other phenomena are not substantial facts, but consequences of the method of inquiry (pp. 153-4). One cannot complain of an author for not doing everything, but at this point most readers will feel a desire for some discussion of the theory of explanation. The elementary meaning of explanation of events is derived from application of a supposedly causal principle. A causal principle, as Dr Whitehead has pointed out, is primarily one which seems causal, such as a law of motion in contradistinction to a mere sequence. When I say that a principle "seems" causal, I mean that it looks and feels as if it were not merely correlating events but accounting for them. This, so far as it can be relied upon, implies some constant relation to the human mind: if the reason and the intuition grew at the same rate as the "causal" principle, it would look and feel as if it were unchanging. But if other sequences in our immediate experience did not grow meanwhile, we should infer that we and our principle had grown. There would, however, be no meaning in the supposition that all events are more connected in certain cases than they are in certain others; at least, if we suppose the connection to be in a fixed ratio. If we do not add this proviso, there is a good meaning in the supposition; in fact, we do actually believe that all events are more connected in mechanical systems than in social ones, except such as are too complex to be visible or palpable. When we say that the connection of events in a system is deterministic, we do not mean that its connection is that which the standard causality would have if moved from physics to psychology. But the reduction of phenomena to mechanism would have been difficult to discover if it had not been possible to bring phenomena of different complexities into the same neighbourhood and explain them before their natures had become equal; it would also have been difficult if all phenomena had reduced equally when their complexities rose. These elementary considerations, along with many others, make causality an ideal, which actual explanations approach without attaining. Mere correlation thus ceases to give an explanation of events: it gives still a comparison of the two sequences concerned, but not of either with the standard unit of understanding. To obtain the latter, we have to adjust the immediate results of the operation of explaining, by means of a mass of philosophical theory. If the explanations which we obtain are mutually consistent, that is all we can ask; but it is possible that a change in philosophical theory might have given other explanations which would also have been mutually consistent.

I confess that I am puzzled by this analogy. Taken in its plain and obvious sense, it means that the transmission of ideas is to be taken from biology, and used without any corrections for social context, etc., because as soon as we introduce such corrections we are assuming a great deal of sociology, and thus seem to be making ourselves liable to the vicious circle which, we are told, is to be avoided. It is evident, however, that this is not what the sociobiologist means, since he goes on at once to speak of the meme as making the adjustments concerned. Now the meme may be, theoretically, a perfect cultural unit, but we certainly cannot compare its propagation with that of larger doctrines directly, without assuming any previous anthropological knowledge. It seems that the sociobiologist is postulating an ideal society, which can transmit memes just as directly as (or, rather, much more directly than) we can transmit a genetic trait. In short, his "cultural inheritance" is an operation as abstract and theoretical as his biological symbolism. That being admitted, we may take the meme as our cultural unit, and ask ourselves what our ideal society could do with it. It could not take a lot of memes and place them end on in a sequence, with a view to measuring a given tradition, since an infinite force is required to make two memes perfectly congruent. To measure ordinary traditions, it would have to take (say) folklore at a given historical period and social pressure, enclosed in a community whose duration is the tradition to be measured; it could then count the number of memes in the community and take its temporal root as a measure of the said tradition. But to ascertain the historical period and social pressure, it will have to make other measurements; moreover, it will have to assume that its community is homogeneous. Altogether, the method does not seem very practical.

For the definition of consciousness, see the beginning of Chapter IX. In the philosophy of mind, the concept of "qualia" takes the place of ordinary perception for many purposes, since the subjective character of experience is a datum, whereas the objective description is in general not a datum. We assume that our intuitions about different mental states are so chosen that, when a particular sensation is compared to a neighbouring state by introspective displacement, the change in the measure of its intensity is small, and is proportional to its intensity. We assume, in short, that the ratio of the increase of puzzlement to the initial confusion for a change of premises (δx) is:

The relation of mental attribution, between individual agents and the relation of 'recognition' between such attributions form part of one faculty, which are only separated for convenience of psychological analysis. That the relation of attribution between A and B amounts to such-and-such a specific content conveys no absolute social meaning; but that the relation of attribution between A and B is 'recognized' as equivalent to the relation of attribution between C and D is (or at any rate may be) an absolute social fact. Thus four agents is the minimum number for which an assertion of absolute social structure can be made. The ultimate elements of social interaction are thus four-agent elements. By adopting the condition of mutual intelligibility, I have limited the possible assertion with regard to a four-agent element to the statement that the four agents do, or do not, form a cooperative alliance. The defence of this mutual intelligibility thus rests on the not implausible view that four-agent elements are recognized to be differentiated from one another by a single character—viz. that they are or are not of a particular kind which is conventionally named trustworthy. Then the analysis of the trustworthy property into a double recognition of A to B and C to D, is merely a definition of what is meant by the equivalence of mental attributions, from which both alliance and betrayal may be constructed.

THROUGHOUT the history of scientific inquiry, there persists an application, with increasing refinement, of a principle which begins to make itself felt in philosophy with Aristotle, in spite of the fact that he did not possess the empirical rigor which it demands. The principle I mean is that of "formal correspondence," as it may be called. This means that any connection which may exist between abstract symbols and perceived phenomena is the result of interpretation from a rule giving a degree of fit at every stage of some mapping from the one to the other. One may give a simple illustration of a formal correspondence from the "problem of measurement": a man is observing the swing of a pendulum, and his notebook lies open upon the table; the man looks from the pendulum to his notes, and his hand records the observation. We suppose that at each moment the recorded mark corresponds exactly to what the pendulum is doing at that moment. To discover the pattern described by the marks is a problem in interpretation, which becomes definite given certain further postulates. The Euclidean description of space gives a very similar type of rule, except that it is the idealization of the triangle, not its material instance, that is directed towards the theorem at each logical step. It has long been a commonplace of epistemology that its foundational principles should have this correlative character: they should tell primarily a congruence at each conceptual level, not the verification after a finite set of experiments. In a word, its methodological axioms take the form of homomorphic mappings, usually of the first order.

Here, perhaps even more than elsewhere in the study of communication, it is difficult to disentangle the conventional elements from those having psychological significance. On the face of it, it might seem as though we were attempting to account for actual mental phenomena by means of a mere convention as to choice of words. But this, of course, is not what is meant. The way the symbol is assigned in different minds is called by certain theorists the "linguistic-system": this is only partially arbitrary, and is in part the representation of the cognitive state of the community. This has to do with the fact that concepts are not purely private expressions, but also correspond to shared facts. It would seem, however, that the process has not yet been expressed with the logical purity that is to be desired, chiefly because it is not prefaced by any clear account of what is to be understood by "understanding"—or, what comes to much the same thing from the standpoint of theory, what we are to mean when we talk of "transferring" a thought, whether by verbal description or in any other way. To "transfer" something, we must be able to recognize some identity between ideas in different minds. Perhaps all this is quite clear in the minds of competent exponents of the theory, but if so they have not succeeded in conveying their thoughts without loss of clarity to readers who have not their background. When a typical authority says: "Take a conception at its source and convey it by linguistic means to an infinitely receptive point," I find myself wondering how, exactly, the conception is to preserve its identity throughout the transfer, and the only answer suggested by the accompanying explanations is that the identity is that of a symbolic expression in terms of the common vocabulary. This, however, is clearly insufficient.

This view of hereditary transmission is absent from classical genetics, from the ideas of laymen and untutored persons, and from the works of biologists, including Lamarck and Erasmus Darwin. In molecular biology, we have a discrete series of possible nucleotide sequences, and a certain statistical knowledge of the proportion of cases in which each variant is expressed; but we have no knowledge as to what determines the particular expression of a given sequence in a particular organism. Moreover, the inheritance is not of the sort that can be expressed by blending equations: it is a transmission from a state expressed by one codon or set of codons to a state expressed by another. This kind of transmission may turn out to be biologically ultimate, and to mark out at least a part of heredity as governed by laws of a new sort. But we are not likely to find science returning to the crude form of inheritance believed in by vitalists and physicians, of which the type is "characteristics of parents cause identical characteristics in offspring." It can never be a law that, given a certain genotype, there is sure to be a certain phenotype, because environmental factors might intervene to prevent it. We do not derive such laws from genetic phenomena, because we do not, in their case, know that the cellular milieu will not alter throughout the development in question. The natural view to take at present is that genetic phenomena have to do with the interchange of information between nucleic acids and the surrounding cytoplasm, while continuous variation is found in all traits which involve no such precise interchange. There are, however, difficulties in any view at present, and it is not for a layman to venture an opinion. It seems not improbable that, as some molecular biologists suggest, our views of gene expression may have to be modified profoundly before harmony is achieved between genetic phenomena and the laws of ontogenetic development. For the moment, however, I wish to confine myself to the standpoint of classical Mendelian theory.

Here we have a logically satisfactory theoretical basis for a cognitive habit. We may suppose that, as a matter of fact, there are important properties of digital interfaces which are "attention-shaping," and that actual user behavior is an approximate method of discovering which interfaces have this property. We shall find certain patterns approximately fulfilled by casual observation, and fulfilled with increasing clarity as we introduce refinements into the process of analysis. Consider, for example, the axiom of digital immediacy: Notifications which demand the same urgency are equal to one another. Presumably the designer regarded this as a psychologically necessary proposition, and so do people who are engaged in the practice of scrolling. If two alerts each equal to a ping are found to be not equally compelling, the plain user assumes that there must be a malfunction somewhere. We are therefore continually redefining the actual operations of engagement with a view to verifying the axiom of immediacy as nearly as possible. But with the above-quoted definition of equality of demand the first axiom becomes a substantial proposition, namely: If an interface is a habit-former, and likewise another, then the combined system is a habit-former. If this proposition is true, then it is theoretically possible to define interaction in such a way that two demands each equal to a ping shall always be equal to each other. What is called "user-friendliness" is, speaking generally, an attempt to obtain a result conformable with some ideal standard supposed to be intuitive but in fact engineered. What do we mean by saying that an attention span has been "wrongly" calibrated? Whatever result we obtain from measuring a given session, the result represents a fact in the mind. But in what we call a "wrong" calibration, the fact ascertained is complex and of small universality. If the user has simply misjudged a duration, the fact ascertained involves reference to his impulsiveness. If he has neglected a psychological correction—e.g., for the context of his environment—the fact refers only to a usage carried out with that particular device on that particular occasion. In behavioral theory we have another set of what might be called "inaccurate" calibrations—e.g., measurements of the focus durations of users engaged with social platforms must be corrected for their priming relative to the algorithm before they acquire any general significance. It is always the search for simple relations which enter into general laws that governs successive refinements of design. But the existence of such relations (where they do exist) is an empirical fact, so that much that seems prima facie to be psychologically necessary is really contingent. On the other hand, the number of assumptions in a predictive model which has to agree with observed behavior can, by analytical skill, be diminished to an extent which may be astonishing. Of this, the theory of persuasive technology is a very remarkable example. The theory is a combination of two diverse elements: on the one hand, new observational data; on the other, a new methodological approach. It must be regarded as a happy accident that the two appeared together; if the right kind of theoretical genius had not happened to be forthcoming, we might have had to be content for a long time with patched-up hypotheses such as the mere novelty effect. As it is, the combination of observation and theory has produced one of the supreme triumphs of applied psychology.

Although economics has operated with supply chains ever since the advent of industrialization, commerce was supposed to be able to function with transactions confined to finite markets. If we accept the globalized point of view, there can no longer be any separation between local commerce and international finance; every proposition of trade will be to some extent systemic. Take first the logistical network. Relatively to one region (A) we can obtain stability of prices by keeping production constant; but relatively to other regions these propositions will refer to events in different sectors. It is true that these events, in any system of exchange, will have an independent appearance, and will have no direct causal relations with each other; but they will have indirect causal relations derived from a common infrastructure. Let us take some example, say: The delivery of a commodity is assured by three separate routes. Our delivery may be composed of maritime shipping or of aerial freight. In either case, it must preserve a certain reliability while we depend upon it. Both shipping and freight are complicated logistical structures, and the economic laws of their operation are involved in taking them as approximations to ideal efficient channels. Nevertheless, so far as the simple network is concerned, all this might be allowed, and yet we might maintain a certain distinction between commerce and logistics, the former being a set of processes supposed resilient, and approximately verified, for the relations of the production, distribution, and consumption nodes in any national frame when demand is kept constant.

and therefore we cannot accurately distinguish one framework as representing the absolute truth. We cannot therefore obtain a purely empirical science by putting observation=constant. With this goes a change in our postulates. We no longer have, as in naive realism, in classical mechanics, and in simple induction, axioms dealing with phenomena of finite complexity. We have now only, as our initial apparatus, a mathematics of the immediate, from which general laws must be obtained by extrapolation. From this point of view, the physicist's extension of formalism appears natural. As we saw in the last chapter, quoting Poincaré, the statement that the measurements , are consistent is the assertion of a relation between the four events. , , , . If all the relations which constitute our initial apparatus are to be confined to the immediate, so must this relation; if so, , , , must all be closely connected, and the conventionalist's epistemology results.

This last conclusion, whose inevitability is evident from the theory of computation, is of some philosophical consequence. Wherever intelligence manifests in a physical substrate with properties which may be loosely described as information-processing, there must be other possible substrates, capable of instantiating the same functional relations, and having the biological substrate as but one contingent example. Thus, when we say that mind must be understood in terms of substrate independence, we are saying that the particular material which happens to embody it cannot be essential to its nature, but only the abstract pattern it realizes. We are not saying that this abstract pattern is the conscious experience; on the contrary, the conscious experience continues to be the particular realization. And if our account is to be coherent, some method must be found of so characterizing the functional relations as to make their multiple realization not only possible but necessary.

But for the pure cosmologist there are no external causes, and all statements in which they seem to be required must be expressible as properties of what is contained within the system. To take our particular case: We must be able to say of a finite, self-contained process that it is approximately sufficient unto itself, if we are to be able to assign a meaning to the statement that a complete universe may be accurately self-sufficient. The case is exactly analogous to explanation in elementary metaphysics: we can assign a meaning to a first cause only because we can observe finite sequences and dependencies, and so form the conception of the limit of their regress. It is not wholly clear how we are to satisfy this requirement in the case of a purely immanent theory. I think, however, that there is not the slightest reason to suppose that it cannot be satisfied. Let “U” mean “form a self-contained system.” We are supposed to have also U(a,b,c,d), U(b,c,d,e), etc., but not U(a,b,d,c) etc. Also if we have U(a,b,c,d) and U(b,c,d,e), we are to have U(a,b,d,e). But if we take “U” to mean “a, b, c, d form an approximately self-contained system,” we cannot (if there is any way of specifying a degree of self-containment) argue from U(a,b,c,d) and U(b,c,d,e) to U(a,b,d,e). Now if we assume, as a thoroughgoing naturalism does, that events at a given epoch are comparable, we can perhaps give the necessary definitions.
