We shall have to take U*, not U, as our fundamental relation, since the totality of any observable process is finite, and it is assumed that no finite system can be accurately self-contained. Or perhaps we shall have to go a step further, and take as fundamental a relation of eight events, say U**(a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h), meaning that the whole constituted by these events is, within the limits of observation, causally closed.

It is obvious that, in the above instance, common sense is imagining objects at a moderate scale and familiar velocities, not at the extremes of the very large or the very fast; it is not contemplating all the apparatus involved in a procedure which replaces intuitive notions by relativistic or quantum descriptions. One might suggest that it is supposing, e.g., that a solid table will remain reliably solid during the portion of a lifetime required to perceive it from one moment to the next. But when we say that it will remain "solid," we imply some standard of material constancy other than the table itself; and this leads to the conceptual difficulties we have been considering.

I cannot but think that the linguist's point of view lends itself to development and further analysis by means of formal semantics; in particular, this applies to the conditions for the possibility of unambiguous communication, a subject which will be considered explicitly in the next chapter. But for the present my concern is with "the comparability of proximate utterances." In the first place, what is meant by "comparability"? A moment's reflection shows that what is wanted is a symmetrical transitive relation which each of the utterances in question has to some others, but not to all. (It is assumed, in the particular case of the linguist's general theory, that when there is such a relation of the phrase to the phrase, there is also such a relation of the phrase to the phrase. But this, as he admits, is not essential.) Now why should we suppose that a transitive symmetrical relation of the above sort is more likely to exist between simple utterances than between complex ones? I.e., if is between and, and between and, is it more likely that the relation in question will hold between and than between and? I do not see why we should think so. And I think further that, with a correct interpretation of vagueness, the whole belief that linguistic precision must always be from word-to-word becomes untenable unless simplicity is abandoned. Semantic rules may all be

The division of labour, but the grounds for thinking that it is beneficial must be practical, not theoretical. It cannot be derived from the impossibility of self-sufficiency unless interdependence itself is a derivative from specialisation, which may well be the case, but does not represent any part of the views of those who are anxious to dispense with economic dependency. It may well be, therefore, that there is one department of industry—that included in the general theory of manufacture, as supplemented by automation—in which everything proceeds by increased output, while there is another part—that dealt with by social cohesion—in which this whole apparatus is inapplicable. There is absolutely no theoretical reason why everything should go by heightened productivity, since, even then, progress does not really go from part-to-whole: in a complex system there is no "whole." It is, at bottom, because "part-to-whole" seems natural that we like a procedure of divided tasks; but the two are logically incompatible, and our preference for the second on account of the first proceeds only from practical confusion.

In the first place, what do we mean by communication? Clearly we do not mean any method of conveying impressions from one mind to another; there must be properties of coherence connected with the impressions conveyed. We do not say that the fleeting notions in a solitary consciousness are "communicated" by their mere occurrence. Given any private conception whose conceptual structure is less than or equal to articulation, we can assign some or all of the available symbols as "labels" for the several elements of the conception. Given any collection of ideas, it can be arranged in a linguistic or non-linguistic framework of any known sort with any finite number of relations, and when so arranged it will be amenable to the whole of logical discourse. But the "meaning" between two ideas of the collection, when it is defined in this way, will, in general, be quite insignificant, in the sense that it will have only such properties as follow tautologically from its definition, not such further experiential properties as would make the definition fruitful. So long as this is the case, there is no reason to prefer one to another of the various incompatible systems of meaning which pure semantics would allow us to assign.

Let us take an illustration. In computational simulation we start from a set of algorithms which say nothing about qualia, and do not even obviously involve sentience. But it is found that they do lead to a behavioral output, and that, by means of the output, mental states can be ascribed to inhabitants. These ascriptions have a definite functional meaning: they represent the series of logical operations required to generate the state in question from certain given initial conditions, (I omit complications concerning infinite regress; these are dealt with in the chapter "Artificial Minds" in The Analysis of Matter.) In this case, it may seem doubtful whether we have consciousness or not. We have ascribed mental states in a manner which preserves the cause-effect relations of behaviors, and it turns out that the ordinary feeling of being aware is a complex function of their functional ascriptions, though the function is somewhat different according as the simulation is deterministic, stochastic, or chaotic. It is just because of this difference that we shall not say we have "produced" consciousness when we have introduced functional ascriptions. These ascriptions, for example, will not tell us, even approximately, whether an inhabitant suffers when it is deleted, and this is the sort of thing that genuine consciousness ought to tell us.

If we confine ourselves to ordinary observation, we can at once define a system: it will consist of all elements arranged in a given relation. The properties in this system which are derived from the interaction of its elements yield an emergent quality; we may take this as the definition of a holistic property. Thus given two components, , , we can define the combined effect of it is the outcome on which is dependent upon both and . We shall need an axiom to the effect that this outcome always exists and is often unpredictable. Thus we can analyze parts and synthesize them: we shall of course define as more than the sum of . From this point onwards, the assignment of causal explanations to our observations offers considerable difficulty. It is therefore only necessary to scrutinize what has already been said.

But the mere assumption that there is such a process as differential survival does not yield these adaptations, since it does not imply the cumulative advantage of traits which is given by the mechanism of heredity. Nevertheless, it does suffice theoretically as a basis of evolution, since, as we have seen, it enables us to explain complexity and diversity, and therefore to account for the forms of life. This shows that the theory of selection, even in its most general and abstract form, assumes a good deal more than the mere possibility of change, which, in itself, is of very little significance. In itself, it does not lead to adaptation; this only results when there is some interconnection between variation and reproductive success.

In ordinary introspective inquiry, there is exactly one kind of mental datum which is irreducible to physical description; it is the quale of immediate experience. In philosophical argument, there is one such datum invoked to support dualism; in psychological analysis, for refutation. This last holds also in the materialist critique, and even in the property dualist account so long as the experiences concerned are simple. If we take a quale (Q) near the threshold of awareness, another description (D) is equivalent to this quale and a neural report if (where the terms have their meanings in physical language), which is a simple correlation in D. Four such correlations give a unique set of values for (Q). Thus there is just one interpretation irreducible from five given reports close together. Moreover, a simple correlation, which we may take to be that of the part of consciousness near the threshold, gives the locus of data near awareness and equivalent to it and a neighbouring report. In fact, as we should expect, for simple experiences everything proceeds as in physical explanation, given the formula for introspection.

It may be asked whether, when the collective judgments of society are aggregated to the utmost, any genuinely rational element remains in its conclusions. We start with an assemblage of uninformed individuals, and we assign opinions subject to the sole restriction that their distribution is to reflect that of the given populace. We then proceed to find results (statistical averages) which hold equally for all systems of belief satisfying the above condition. It might seem a possibility that such results really express only accidental convergences, and that the sole advantage of aggregation lies in the fact that it provides a mechanism for the errors of a multitude of the required sort. (It does not provide a mechanism for all of them; the number of possible errors is , and therefore only a vanishing proportion of mistaken beliefs can be corrected—i.e. expressed by means of a procedure of finite complexity which employs common sense.) This possibility requires investigation.

The question can be approached equally well from two perspectives. In the theory of neural correlates, a gradual emergence and a sudden ignition, for instance, are distinguishable by the fact that there is an irreducible difference between the processes which hold for the two models when expressed in terms of measurable activity; this expresses the fact that the quality of awareness is continuous in the case of the spectrum, but not in the case of the threshold. Yet from a purely behavioral point of view, such as that of external observation, the two states are indistinguishable. What, exactly, is added to make the difference? This inquiry is essentially the same as that which arises in the philosophy of mind.

In part, the answer in this case is simple. What is added is the comparability of processes in different substrates. So long as our conception is purely biological, we can say of three intelligences which have the order that one is more complex than another, but we cannot say anything analogous of three intelligences which are not in a series—I do not say "in a biological lineage," because the concept involved is more general, as will appear later. But although this is part of the answer, it does not seem to be the whole, since our principle also enabled us to compare operations not having a common origin.

It seems that what distinguishes value as required in ethics from such a relation as "approximating a given preference of a given creator" is the absence of reference to any external consciousness. When the value held by one artificial mind is equal to the value held by another, we are supposed to have a fact which does not demand reference to some other mind or minds. In fact, this is the reason why the "utility function" has been substituted for value: the latter, as hitherto conceived, was found to depend upon the perspective of the designing intelligence, and thus to be not an intrinsic moral relation. The value, if it is to serve its purpose, must be a function of the mind's own processes exclusively, and must not involve any other psychological data. Here, for artificial intelligence purposes, "psychology" includes "programming." The preference which two actions subtend at a given creator becomes a function of three agents as soon as the given creator is thought of as variable. There must be no such way of turning the value developed by an artificial mind into a function involving external valuations also.

I am not sure, however, whether it is necessary to introduce this somewhat difficult consideration. In ordinary biology, the cells composing a given organism are arranged in distinct tissues and organs; but if we define the organism as the aggregate, where the whole is a fixed entity, the cells composing it become mere functional units. Now a colony and an individual are distinguishable in analysis of complexity. Thus the above undesirable definition could be excluded by insisting that units within a given whole are to form an integrated system. In multicellular theory, this is not true of cells having zero independence from a given whole; indeed, it is only true when the integration concerned is superficial. But it is possible to specify the characteristics, for analysis of complexity, of the three-dimensional arrangement of constant cooperation from a given center. These might be added to the postulate that individuality exists. Whether, in some such way, we could overcome the apparent necessity for distinguishing between a colony and an organism, making the difference relative to the definition of cooperation, I do not feel sure, though obviously the question must be easily soluble.

Every principle of classification which is to be employed in psychology must be such that significant empirical observations are connected with categories. There will always be an infinite number of ways of correlating states with the instances of a mental phenomenon whose variations are more or less continuous. Some of these may be significant, but most must be insignificant. Some conditions can be laid down. In the first place, the instances of the phenomenon concerned may be obviously capable of a gradation which is experientially important. If we take all the moments of awareness that ever have been or will be experienced, they have in the first place a variation in intensity, which is obviously important experientially; in this variation, no two of them possess the same degree—i.e. the differences concerned are all perceptible. But they have also a variation as kinds of attention and as of varying clarity. In this variation there are imperceptible transitive differences—e.g. between two moments of nearly identical focus. Psychology professes to correlate also these further characteristics of awareness with neural quantities such as activation levels. This would not be plausible if continuous alterations of consciousness were not correlated with continuous alterations in the correlated physiological quantities. Whenever we notice a qualitative continuum, such as that of states from drowsiness to alertness, we assume that it must have experiential importance, and we insist that terms used as descriptors shall have the same order as the states which they describe. The former is a postulate, the latter a convention. Both have proved moderately useful, but neither is an a priori necessity.

In connection with certainty, it is worth while to compare its formal characteristics with those of utility. We saw that, in the generalized conduct with which practical affairs end, we want a relation of four neighbouring propositions, expressing the fact that they form a workable decision. But we met with certain difficulties owing to the fact that this is only supposed to be possible for an infinitesimal deliberation, which is a figment of the philosophical imagination, and that it was not wholly easy to see how to substitute a procedure by means of probabilities. We were led to the suggestion that, instead of saying " is a certain truth," we should have to say " is more nearly a certain truth than ." Perhaps this could be somewhat simplified. Suppose we say: " is more nearly a reliable guide than ." And perhaps this could be still further simplified so as to take the form: " is more serviceable than is." We here suppose that between any two beliefs there is a relation, which we will not call proof, but (say) "warrant," and that this relation, like a shade of opinion, is capable of a greater or less resemblance to another of the same kind. In a rational life, two finite warrants finitely warranted may be exactly similar in the relevant respects; we then have a finite certainty.

There are systems which are obviously not merely aggregates of their components—e.g. a mere heap of bricks compared to a house. Houses, like organisms, have various properties that are emergent—the spatial arrangement, the functional order, the aesthetic unity, the structural integrity as measured by an architect’s specifications, etc. But a random pile would never be thought integrated; no one would hope to found a theory of architecture upon a system in which a dwelling had qualities depending solely upon the arithmetic sum of its constituent materials. Generally speaking, it would seem that the most fundamental interactions are the most significant. Here I am using a purely logical test of fundamentality: considering descriptions in which the given interaction occurs, there will be some having the smallest number of elements compatible with the mention of that interaction; and again, an interaction may be a molecular compound of other interactions—i.e. a synergy, a constraint, a negation, or complex of all these. An interaction which is molecular has always a certain definite number of atoms; an interaction which is not molecular is called atomic, and has then a definite number of constituents in the simplest descriptions in which it occurs. An atomic interaction is more fundamental in proportion to the fewness of its constituents; a molecular interaction, in proportion to the fewness of its atoms. There is much empirical reason to think that the principles of a science become more profound and comprehensive as the interactions involved become more fundamental. The relation of a heap to its bricks is of immense triviality, whereas we may suppose that the interaction upon which coherence depends is fairly fundamental. And the functional order of organisms alluded to above is also fundamental, so long as we are thinking of organisms as given in biology, not as interpreted in mere chemistry. Such fundamental interactions should, as far as possible, be the basis for theories of composition.

There is a traditional distinction between common sense and scientific reasoning, which is somewhat misleading when taken seriously. The theory is that common sense is derived from daily experience and scientific reasoning is not. The only truly reliable guides are mathematics and experiment. Where ordinary perceptions are concerned, the immediacy of their impressions may be taken as a measure of their truth, and they have implications corresponding to all simpler beliefs. But in physics we are never concerned with realities which have such implications. The solidity of a table, whether large or small, is always absent in the usual kinds of analysis; thus appearance has nothing to do with substance. Force, as we have seen, is a mathematical relation, and smaller forces are not parts of it. If A and B are equal pushes on a moving cart, we say that the push C is double of each, and we think of it as the "sum" of A and B. But it is only by a convention, though an almost irresistible one, that we assign as the measure of C a number double that which we assign as the measure of A or of B. And to say that C is the "sum" of A and B is to say something very ambiguous, since the word "sum" has many meanings. When A and B are considered as vectors, we may say that C is their sum even when they are not in one direction. Again, given suitable definitions, we may say that the effects between X and Z are the sum (in the logical sense) of the effects between X and Y, and between Y and Z; this will only hold if the process is linear. But the causation between X and Z, considered as a relation, is not properly the "sum," in any recognized sense, of the causations X Y, Y Z. Thus all physical realities are "counter-intuitive." This shows that the authority of common sense and scientific reasoning is unimportant.

Degrees of communicability may be, in a sense, measured by quasi-convertibility. Suppose that a thought, a word, a concept, each have quasi-equivalence with the next. It may or may not happen that the thought has quasi-equivalence with the concept. One may presume that this will happen if the thought and the word are very precise and the concept is not very abstract. Similarly, or rather a fortiori, we cannot infer that the thought has quasi-equivalence with the shared meaning. The larger the number of minds for which such an inference remains true, the closer is the resemblance between private cognition and public expression or between individual insight and collective understanding. It is to be assumed that, by continually refining terms and diminishing ambiguity the scope of shared reference can be increased without finite limit.

In the case of precision, we have a quality which is capable of degrees, and may be called "quasi-definitive"—i.e. if a term is very precise, and another term is very precise, then their combination must be rather precise. This is just the sort of thing required for a coherent lexicon. Consider four speakers, A, B, C, D, and suppose that A's speech is rather precise. Take a series of utterances forming a continuous discourse from A to B, without digressions; this can be done by purely syntactical methods to be explained later. Suppose that among these utterances there are some, such as a subordinate clause, which make B's speech more precise than A's is. We may suppose that these utterances have a limit or final form, which we will call E. We can then similarly proceed along to a phrase which gives C's speech more precision than E for any other phrase in the discourse. We have then done nearly as well as possible, if not quite, with the three speakers A, B, C as starting-points. By means of suitable conventions, we could insure that a construction of the above sort, carried out repeatedly without changing the speakers A, B, C, should at last end with a definite expression such that D's speech is more precise than any other expression from it is. We may call the arrangement a "quasi-grammar." Now let F, G, ... H, ... be a series of speakers on a discourse from D to E. Then proceed to take speakers I, J, ... between E and F on some discourse, and form the quasi-grammars having one element at F, one element at G and one at H, the fourth being called K.

If, as the electorate assumes, political promises which have one source in common are comparable, this must be taken to mean that two small legislative acts are capable of a resemblance which may be called "quasi-representation," which grows more nearly complete resemblance as the act grows more scrutinized. We may assume, as before, that, given a citizen and a definite policy from party to platform, there will be one definite point on this policy such that its representation is more nearly equal to the citizen's will than is any other representation by the party in question. We shall then say that the promise and the outcome are "quasi-equivalent." Take also... quasi-equivalent, and the campaign pledge... quasi-equivalent. In this way we can construct a governance mesh with axes of rhetoric and result. And we can now construct what will be in effect democratic ideals through the ballot: take all the outcomes which are the corners opposite to the voter of quasi-parallelograms of power, for different initial constituencies, subject to quasi-equivalence between the stated aim and the practical effect. These outcomes may be regarded as forming the quasi-democratic process whose equation is popular sovereignty. (Oligarchic tendencies can be dealt with by the usual methods.) This quasi-democratic process will start from the polling station in a certain direction, and may, for constitutional purposes, be regarded as really a democratic system. It is not worth while to proceed further, since it is obvious that we have the necessary material for disillusionment.

Common sense starts with the notion that there is truth where we can get immediate observations, but not elsewhere. Then it gets puzzled by anomalies, contradictions, illusions, etc., whence it is led to the conception of "dogma"—I speak historically. After "dogma" has been replaced by "hypothesis," there is a further stage, that of the paradigm. Assuming the corrigibility of empirical knowledge, there must be revisions occurring between the proposal of a theory and its general acceptance; assuming the provisional nature of "fact," as all scientists do until refuted, what is occurring between conjecture and confirmation must be occurring "within" or "to" a framework, which is called the scientific method.

Apart from metaphysical interpretations, what we may be said to experience (using this word somewhat liberally) is that phenomena occur where there is no physical description, and that these phenomena proceed, at least approximately, in accordance with psychological regularities. There does not seem any necessity to interpret these phenomena in terms of a separate mental substance; indeed, I shall argue that processes associated with neural activity should also be interpreted so as not to involve such a substance. There must, however, remain a difference, expressible in psychological terms, between states where there is qualitative character and other states. In fact, we know the difference. The character of introspection is different, and the reports of consciousness suffer a discontinuity when we reach the boundary of articulate attention. These differences, however, are not of a metaphysical kind. To the philosopher, the difference between "qualia" and "mere information-processing" is, I believe, merely a difference as to the epistemic access governing reports of experience, not a difference expressible as that between the presence or absence of a soul, or as that between one kind of reality and another.

One way of approaching this subject is through the connection of formalism with perception. In elementary mathematics, the two are quite distinct, but nowadays they have become amalgamated. There are two kinds of structure involved in science, of which one may be called the "ideal" structure, the other the "applied" structure. The latter is the structure obtained by measurement, when the phenomenon concerned may be observed under contingent conditions; the former is the structure obtained when the phenomenon is considered in its abstract essence. If we call the ideal structure and the applied structure , then, taking empirical verification as unity, if is the degree of approximation of the model to the observation, we have:

Intelligence, as such, should be satisfied when it has ascertained the principles according to which a thought process occurs, with just enough interpretation to know what empirical evidence confirms or confutes the principles. It is not necessary to the theorist to speculate as to the biological substrate of the processes with which he deals, though hypotheses (erroneous as well as correct) on this subject may sometimes be a help to further valid generalizations. For the present, we are confining ourselves to the standpoint of substrate independence. Whether anything further can be known or fruitfully conjectured is a matter which we shall discuss at a later stage. We want, therefore, to consider the difference in cognitive operations which is described as that between the presence and absence of biological embodiment, and also to consider briefly the difficulties as to the interchanges of information between organic and inorganic systems. I say "organic system" or "biological intelligence" indifferently; the difference seems to be merely one of words.

It is necessary to say something about the difficulties of reconciling the demands for absolute certainty with those for practical knowledge in everyday affairs. On this subject the present position of common sense is one of perplexity, aptly summarized by Dr Smith in *Certainty and Action* (London, 1926) and by Dr J. H. Wilson in *The Practical Review*, August 14, 1926, pp. 312-4. The demand for certainty accounts adequately for all domains in which only logic is concerned, such as mathematics and formal deduction; but it fails to account for practical phenomena such as the conduct of business or the raising of children (see Chapter IV.). On the other hand, methods which account for the practical phenomena seem unable to account for the very things which the demand for certainty explains perfectly.

To take a definite case, suppose a financial panic is incident on the structure of some society, then it is found that systemic flaws are ejected from the order with considerable force. The number of the flaws depends on the intensity of the panic and diminishes in the usual way as the society is moved farther from the source of the disturbance. The severity or character of each flaw, however, does not vary, but depends only on the frequency of the crises. The flaws are found to have the same character whether the system from which they come is close to the initial shock or whether it is removed away to any distance.

This is a result which is quite incompatible with the ordinary theory of social interaction, because as the complexity of a social situation increases the capacity for simple stimulus-response becomes weaker and weaker, the predictive power of such models diminishing as the inverse square of the interpersonal distance. The observable fact that an agent can engage in both collaborative and competitive behaviors could only be accounted for by giving it the power either to ignore the internal states of others or to simulate them with perfect fidelity. Both of these assumptions are unworkable, and the only conclusion is that the cognitive apparatus for such behaviors must be localized in a capacity for mental representation.

If, however, awareness is to be compared to a simple switch, we know both the position and function of this switch. We know, for instance, how much attention there is in a typical moment of conscious focus, and if this attention is the aggregate of the states of individual percepts, we know the state of each percept (since we know the intensity of the stimulus) and so can calculate the number of percepts in the moment. The number is found to be about ten thousands. By a similar observation it is found that the awareness from a faint background noise comprises only about one percept per minute, and the awareness from an almost imperceptible draft, only about one percept per ten thousand minutes. Thus if awareness occurs in indivisible states like a switch, the states from an almost imperceptible draft can only enter a human mind at comparatively rare intervals, and it will be exceedingly rare for two or more states to be inside the mind at the same time. A mind of double the sensitivity ought to register the states four times as frequently, but there should be no other difference. This, as common introspection points out in any era, is quite at variance with our everyday experience. When the awareness of a sensation passes through a mind and impresses a perception on memory, this perception is not confined to a single neural pathway or to a close cluster of pathways as it would be if individual percepts left their marks like switch-flips on a recorder. An elaborate and extensive pattern of association is formed; the clarity of the pattern depends on the number of percepts, but its structure depends on the capacity and also on the disposition of the consciousness. Moreover, the structure does not bear any resemblance whatever to the 'on or off' structure which is observed on a recorder activated by switch-flips. It seems impossible to reconcile this with the hypothesis that awareness operates like a switch directly from one stimulus in the world to one registration in the mind.

After setting forth the difficulties encountered by this notion in regard to qualia and intentionality, Professor Chalmers proceeds to the very interesting suggestion made by Dr. Daniel Dennett in *Consciousness Explained*, 1991, p. 66. "It is a striking fact," says Professor Chalmers, summarizing this suggestion, "that while all the theories are directed towards explaining the emergence of consciousness, one theory suggesting that it occurs as a fundamental property, the other as an illusory by-product, yet consciousness has never been observed in isolation. It is quite impossible to observe consciousness in the course of its operation; the only events that can ever be detected are the behavioral correlates and neural substrates of awareness. Until there is some report or reaction to indicate its presence, we must be unaware of its existence. In other words, the difficulty of explaining the hard problem of consciousness may be because we are endeavouring to explain something about which we have no independent evidence. It might be more correct to interpret the experimental facts quite directly and to say that one neural state can give rise to another neural state although they may be functionally distant, in a manner analogous to the causation between two physical events which interact.

In a later treatise on epistemology (published in 1926), Professor James suggests that reality is perceived by intuitions of a familiar sort, which he calls "common sense." He supposes that, when reality is apprehended, what happens is that a common-sense intuition operates; but at other times the intuition is a structural element within a belief system. Common sense, he says, "is not reality, but plays an essential part in every process of apprehension." He assigns to common sense the following properties: "(1) In any isolated perception the total number of common-sense intuitions is constant. (2) All apparent understanding is carried by common sense, the only difference between the perception of a falling apple and of a bending light-ray being that the former employs a vastly greater number of intuitions, each carrying a very much smaller amount of conceptual difficulty. (3) All common-sense intuitions are intrinsically identical.... (4) The reliability of an isolated intuition, divided by the complexity of the phenomenon, gives the plausibility of the intuition.... (5) All intuitions are alike in one property which has the dimensions of immediacy or of practical utility, and is invariant to a rational transformation. (6) The condition that the model of a phenomenon constructed by common sense be equal to some physical structure existing within that phenomenon, is not in general fulfilled, but comes nearer to fulfilment the larger and slower the phenomenon is." Professor James promises to deal with difficulties in the way of his hypothesis on a future occasion.

The common man's view is perhaps less radical than the view which it suggests—namely, that nothing whatever is arbitrary in the judgments we form concerning our fellow creatures. Whether this view is the common man's or not, it deserves to be considered, for although it is unsettling, it may well prove to be instructive. If so, "impartial reason" is practically abolished. There will be need of a considerable labour if social understanding is to be re-written in accordance with this theory, but what is said about the necessary absence of evidence concerning prejudice in formation is a powerful consideration. It is common in human affairs to find beliefs which, from a logical point of view, are unnecessarily complicated, because people cannot sufficiently divest themselves of common-sense certainties. Why should we suppose that any justification at all exists between the inception of a bias and its expression? One might be inclined to attach weight to the fact that prejudice operates with a certain inevitability. But psychology has made this argument less convincing than it once was. Everything that has to do with the mechanism of bias is capable of being interpreted in a "Pickwickian" sense, and in any case our intellectual comforts must be shocked. It is of course premature to adopt such an hypothesis definitively, and I shall continue to suppose that reason does really operate across an intervening deliberation. But it will be wise to remember the possibility, and to bear in mind the great changes in our imaginative picture of human nature that are compatible with our existing psychological knowledge.

There are three treatises by contemporary philosophers which examine the possibility of deriving conscious phenomena from purely physical processes.[33] These treatises do not reach any definitive conclusion confidently asserted; but they suffice to show that the problem of reconciling subjective qualia with the laws of neurobiology and physics is not a hopeless one, a view which is strengthened by Dr. H. G. Wells's hypothesis alluded to above (Chapter IV.). So long as it is not known to be hopeless, it is perhaps rash to fly to heroic solutions of the problem. And it is as yet by no means universally admitted that the materialist account of mind is inadequate in its own domain; Professor James (loc. cit.), for example, regards the hypothesis of irreducible consciousness as unnecessary for reasons which demand serious consideration. We must therefore await further introspection before venturing upon a definite opinion.

The picture presented by this development of common psychological doctrine would be something like this: the mind contains states of consciousness possessing various degrees of clarity. Sometimes attention is transferred from one of these states to another; usually this process has been thought to be binary, like the flipping of a switch, but it is found to be more like the dimming of a lamp, in the sense that the awareness has a gradual intensity. It is now suggested that there is no abrupt threshold, because, if there were, it would be as arbitrary as a royal decree; the alternative is to suppose that the awareness shades imperceptibly from one level to another. It is true that, by introspection, there is a perceptible difference between the inception of a thought and its full comprehension. But there is no sharp boundary in the phenomenological sense, and the apparent threshold will vary according to the criterion employed—i.e. according to the way in which the introspection is conducted. I do not know how the view we are considering will account for the sudden recognition of a forgotten name, which is not purely gradual. Nor do I know what will happen to the concept of consciousness if awareness cannot be absent in deep sleep. This latter argument, however, is not serious, since awareness which never reaches a reportable state is in any case purely conjectural. I am not sure, either, that the theory is intended to be as radical as I have suggested; perhaps it is only meant that awareness never exists in a state without having some degree of presence. In this form, however, the theory would seem scarcely credible: we should have to suppose that unconscious processes could exercise a mysterious influence from a depth, which would undo the gain derived from Freud's theory of repression. Perhaps the theory may have gained undue plausibility from a belief that the whole taxonomy of mental states depended upon reportability, whereas in fact there is a cognitive continuum which is not derivable from articulation, and which, as presupposed in psychological theory, does not regard as distinct phases of a thought which would ordinarily be regarded as separate. Perhaps it may be possible to avoid these difficulties, but, if so, a very great conceptual reconstruction will be necessary. Meanwhile it must be regarded as still possible that some less revolutionary theory may solve the difficulties connected with the interchange of attention between focal and peripheral awareness.

Observation begins ordinarily, and still begins in the education of the novice, with matters that seem thoroughly immediate. Colors and sounds, the fall of leaves, the boiling of a kettle, etc., are all familiar in everyday experience, and it is a satisfaction to the philosophically-inclined mind to find them amenable to precise description. But in proportion as inquiry increases the scope and power of its methods, in that same proportion it removes its subject-matter from immediacy. The extent to which this is the case is not always apprehended, at any rate in uncritical moments, even by the inquirer himself; he may tell you that he can "grasp" why the kettle boils, which is of course a condensed expression for a complicated deduction. Certain philosophers have done more than any other thinkers to show the need of distinguishing the description of phenomena from the explanation of them. For the moment, I am not concerned with this distinction, but with the explanations themselves.

Let us take ingestion, digestion, nutrition and toxicity as illustrative of the gradually increasing complexity of gustatory evolution. These four notions are all extracted from common experience. We taste substances introduced into the mouth, we can detect their qualities with our tongues; we know what it is to consume a wholesome meal or ingest a disagreeable substance. All this makes "taste" seem something familiar and straightforward, until, in the course of reflection, we learn the biological imperatives to which it has given rise. Digestion seems equally obvious: we anticipate forthcoming nourishment in a digestive sequence; we notice hunger and satiety, consumption and excretion, health and illness; we know that physiology describes processes of metabolic transformation, we avoid poisons in the confident expectation that we shall thrive in the future. Nutrition, again, seemed in no way mysterious to the primitive forager, as, indeed, how should it to anyone who had experienced the difference between vigor and debilitation? Toxicity was equally palpable: it was primarily anything that we could reject by spitting, though the first step towards sophistication was taken when early humans included bitterness. However, we are conscious of bitterness in the form of alkaloids and as something that triggers our gag reflex, so that less effort was required to admit bitterness among the warnings than to explain sweetness.

The view of common sense, that the whole is merely the sum of its parts, was more or less compatible with mechanics until very recent times. There are aggregates and collections in our immediate experience, and there seemed no insuperable obstacle to identifying them with the systems of the biological world. In regard to machines, at least, practically no one doubted the rightness of this identification. There were doubts as regards organisms, but they came from philosophers rather than biologists. Now, however, both structure and function, as they occur in immediate experience, are recognized by writers on emergence as something quite different from the mere aggregation which mechanics requires. The common-sense position has therefore been definitely abandoned.

From this comfortable alignment with traditional arrangements society has been gradually driven by its own advancements, like a patriarch who has grown too preoccupied to consult with his family. The digital networks of modernity are very far removed from the communities and markets of our ordinary experience; yet even these networks are nearer to common understanding than the structures towards which technology is tending. “Centralized governance and localized commerce,” observes a contemporary sociologist, “are only provisional arrangements, which must ultimately yield to a more fluid conception of the ordering of human interactions not expressible in terms of a fixed hierarchical system. It is in this direction that some reformers hope to find a resolution of the antagonisms of the platform economy. It is a fallacy to think that the conception of organization in industrial society based on the observation of large-scale institutions can be applied unmodified to the transactions which involve only a small number of automated agents. Assuming that this is the correct resolution it is useless to look for any means of introducing algorithmic phenomena into the established protocols of our institutions; these phenomena have been excluded at the outset by the adherence to a bureaucratic frame of reference.” But even if the corporate-state model, as it appears in the standard theory of political economy, were the final word as regards the social order corresponding to our customary notions of authority and exchange, it is evident that we should have travelled very far from those notions, and have arrived at a condition in which conventional institutional imagination is useless.

I come now to the relation of control as perceived to control in actuality. Here the divergence is more profound than in the case of simple mechanisms; indeed, it is already implicit in the earliest theories of administration. It is impossible to exaggerate the importance of this divergence in separating the world of governance from the world of individual agency. With the exception of minor personal routines and tasks with which our own will is directly engaged, the systems which, according to common belief, we command, are managed by means of procedures, regulations, or delegated authority. The last of these, though crucial to many forms of organization, is relatively subordinate in the operations of modern institutions. Procedure is less significant than regulation, and in any case raises exactly the same problems in the present connection. We may therefore concentrate upon regulation as a source of our confidence concerning the manageable world.

In cosmic chronology, what is a civilisation, and how do we decide whether two epochs belong to the history of the same human endeavour? I am not asking how we decide in practice, but what is our theoretical definition. Ever since Lyell, people have spoken of "geological strata," which are in fact the series of epochs constituting the history of one planetary surface but they have not always been as explicit as one could wish in telling us the criterion by which, in theory, it is decided that two epochs belong to one continuum. The test of significance between the parts of a cosmic timeline must obviously depend upon the laws of astronomy. These laws say that a stellar system will evolve in such-and-such a way; inverting this statement, they say that what has evolved in such-and-such a way is to count as one brief interval. This is substantially the method pursued by Jeans. In Chapter IX. we considered the nebula

I come now to the most serious of our questions: How is neural communication to be understood in modern biology? Educated common sense regards internal signals as the cause of thoughts; broadly speaking, thoughts private to one organism are caused by the neurons of that organism's brain—e.g. memories and imaginings—while communications common to several, or of a sort which is common to several in suitable circumstances, are attributed to causes external to the brains of the organisms experiencing the exchanges. (I am not at present attempting to make these statements exact, but merely to interpret what common sense would reply if questioned.) We recognize the "same" thought process on different occasions by similarity in its manifestations, though we admit that this is a rough-and-ready test which may lead us astray. We think, however, that, if we had observed closely and continuously, we could have distinguished between two similar internal states by means of continuity in their perceived electrochemical relations. The confusion of similar ideas illustrates what I mean: if we introspect carefully, we can tell which is the concept we contemplated a moment ago, by means of the neuro-temporal continuity of its activations. What common sense assumes may be expressed, in language foreign to common sense, by saying: A neural process is manifested by conscious qualities whose variations are continuous, and whose functional relations to other such continuous series of qualities are continuous functions of the time. In practice, the changes of conscious quality are often so slow as to be negligible, and this greatly facilitates the task of common sense in recognizing the "same" internal state on two different occasions.

On the common-sense level, there are difficulties in certain cases: a thermostat, in a sensibly stable room in which there is a fluctuation, cannot be distinguished at a later moment from another regulator which was near it at the earlier moment. Machine learning also offers difficulties to common sense. Both these matters can, however, be dealt with on a common-sense basis. A simple feedback loop operating in the body will show which way the system is adjusting, and the error signal shows, more or less, what happens to an algorithm which is trained. The elaboration immediately suggested leads on naturally to elementary biology and engineering, where it is still assumed, at least tacitly, that the processes concerned are of the same sort as sensible processes, but rather more intricate. Often they can actually be observed under controlled conditions. Imaginatively, we continue to attribute this continuity with sensible processes to our technical models, our homeostasis and reward functions, thus concealing from ourselves the highly abstract character of our assertions. At moments, we realize this abstractness; but it does not make its due impression, because imagination reasserts itself as soon as we are off our guard.

When we "describe" nature, we seem to have immediate knowledge of something external to our own equations. But mathematics says that a complicated abstraction starts from the external world, travels across the intervening symbols, and at last reaches the formula. What goes on between the formula and the prediction is a question for the logicians, and what finally happens when we "calculate" is a question for the philosophers of science. But without troubling ourselves about what happens after the data reaches the equation, it is evident that what the mathematician has to say is destructive of the common-sense notion of "description." It makes no difference, in this matter, which of the possible theories we adopt as to the mathematical character of laws, since all equally make them something utterly different from what we experience. The data of experience, analyzed as much as possible, resolve themselves into tangible qualities. But the mathematical analogue of a quality is a functional relation of a certain complexity relative to the mind of the observer. The mathematical world, it seems natural to infer, is destitute of quality. Moreover, the correspondence between qualities and their mathematical counterparts is peculiar: qualities are immediacies, which are static while they last, whereas their counterparts are dynamic relations, which are in the medium between the mind and the object which we say we "describe." What happens in the object itself, if it exists by its own properties, is the sort of thing considered in quantum theory: a sudden collapse of a wave function from one state to another. This is very unlike a perception of (say) solidity. And what feels to the hand like a continuous solid surface is supposed to be really a void whose apparent solidity is due to the fact that some of the forces in it are interacting in a certain way. When we say they are "interacting," we are saying something too pictorial. What we mean is that they obey an unknown principle called "invariance," which is a known function of a certain number of abstract symmetries, and that one or more of these symmetries have suddenly expressed their constraints. It may be claimed as a merit in such theories as Professor Whitehead's, considered in the preceding chapter, that it makes the connection between this process and the mind rather less indirect than it appears on the purely formal theory. But even then the sort of sudden transition contemplated by Heisenberg is very unlike the perception of a solid object: it is prima facie quite dissimilar in structure, and unknown as regards its intrinsic properties.

which, as Hume demonstrates (§ 52), has the property of circularity—i.e. if the validity of it in any particular instance is questioned, it can only be defended by an appeal to its general reliability. He identifies this process with reasoning, because of its property of inevitability: "The principle appearing in our practice is, on account of its property of inevitability, now identified with reasoning, or rather with the logical abstraction of reasoning which comprises the inferential properties of expectation, prediction and generalization sufficing for all empirical phenomena" (p. 146). And the above principle, it will be remembered, is justified solely by means of the appeal to past uniformity. It will be admitted that induction, so justified, has become rather different from the reasoning in which common sense believes. If Dr Johnson had known Hume's justification of induction, he might have been less satisfied with his practical refutation of skepticism.

The inevitable specialization which is forced upon craftsmen by the very proliferation of tools has had a good deal to do with obscuring this principle. Few men have been both master carpenters and expert machinists. The work of certain Renaissance artisans is a notable example of the combination of these disciplines, but there are not many others. Carpenters and joiners are seldom well-informed in metallurgy, and are apt to assume an antiquated understanding of materials which makes their tasks look simpler than they are. Moreover, even when the principle is realized, a man may not possess a mastery of the proper instrument for its application—namely, practical wisdom. It is by means of practical wisdom that the celebrated artisan has been enabled to make his immense contribution to our understanding. But, greatly as I admire his work, which I place far above anything else that has been written on the relation of tool sophistication to practical skill, I think there are points—and not unimportant points—where his methods break down for want of due attention to ergonomics and material science. Moreover, there seem to be assumptions in his construction which are derived rather from a dogma of craftsmanship than from the actual needs of the task. For these reasons, I venture to think that it is possible to obtain an understanding less revolutionary than his, and somewhat simpler from a practical point of view. The understanding, however, must wait until we have examined manual practice as a source of knowledge, which will be our topic in Part II. The philosophy of making which reconciles the results of Part II. with the abstract principles of tool use which we have been considering in Part I. will be the subject of Part III.

IN this Part, the subject with which we are concerned is the evidence for the persistence of the illusion of control—not of this or that particular instance of overconfidence, but of the general structure of the belief. It is to be expected that the evidence will not be such as to give certainty, but at best such as to give probability; it is to be expected, also, that this probability may be increased by a suitable interpretation of complexity, where "interpretation" is understood in the sense considered in Chapter I. We shall find it desirable to divide our problem into several parts, each of which will have an importance not confined to psychology. There is need, first, to be clear as to what we mean by a comprehensible system, and what is the degree of understanding to be expected of it at the best. There is need to discuss what can be meant by "agency," and to distinguish intention, influence and coincidence. We shall then discuss the causal theory of outcome, and at the same time the philosophy called "determinism." From these topics we shall pass to general discussion, first of chaos, then of order. This will lead us to the epistemological grounds for interpreting control in accordance with probabilistic monism, and to the paramount importance of feedback in practical inference. We shall conclude with a definition of decision considered as affording the experiential data for belief, and with the consideration of phenomena analogous to decision in the non-volitional world. But first of all it will be well to examine the historical development by means of which our problem has assumed its present form—both the pre-scientific development leading to common sense, and the scientific development leading from common sense to cybernetics.

Surplus wealth consists of an accumulation of resources, or at least advantages, which serve well in practice except in conditions which rarely obtain. A laborer may be puzzled by a ledger containing unseen profits, or by deeds conveying an hereditary estate; daily experience has not prepared him for oddities of this sort. But a little observation enables a man to fit them into his experiential world, and a merchant soon learns their ways if he has occasion to do so. This illustrates the fact that there is no sharp line between privilege and necessity: both involve possessions, but those resulting from privilege are more extensive. It is possible to acquire wealth practically without any fundamental change from the ethic of daily life. But when concentrated wealth is taken seriously, it is found to involve a quite changed social structure, whose relation to that of simple exchange demands investigation. This will form the topic of the next chapter; in the present chapter, I shall consider the genesis of class division, not in the ancient world, since that is obscure, but in the modern state.

In considering consciousness, as in considering perception, we are compelled to confine ourselves to phenomenological methods, whatever our views may be on the subject of phenomenology as a general principle in metaphysics. We can observe the gradations of awareness, but they cannot tell us their essence. At a low mental level, however, it is hardly profitable to distinguish between a sensation and a mere physical reaction. Consciousness, in the philosophical sense, seems to emerge out of previously existing reflexes, and to be, at first, little more than a qualitative intensification of processes formed before awareness could be acknowledged. There is therefore no great loss in being confined to threshold arguments when we are considering organisms before the stage at which they can reflect.

In this primitive conception, the universe obviously has no need of an "external cause." An "external cause," for common sense, is something having a certain degree of independence, and connected with several kinds of necessity. This involves something like contingency, to give rise to the idea of dependence, or rather, at first, to the feeling of incompleteness; and it involves coherence, to give to one physical law a foundation originally associated with another. In cosmology, the most important factor in forming the common-sense notion of a cause is the part-whole relation, the discovery that it is possible, often, to explain what is observed. In this way, internal necessity and external contingency become uncorrelated, which is one of the most important steps in the philosophical understanding of the universe.

It is of course obvious and generally recognized that very young children do not possess the common-sense notion of a "mind." This is by no means obvious with the young of some other kinds of animals—with dogs, for example. They possess, as instincts, useful ways of behaviour which in the human young are only learnt by experience; for example, they can interpret a gesture which they see from a companion. The human child has no such innate skill; for several years, it makes no attempt to infer what another sees. The "mental-state attribution" comes as a result of experience. Some native aptitudes, of course, a young child does possess; for example, it can turn its attention towards a loud noise, though not very quickly or accurately. It has a reflex connected with imitation, but not a very intelligent one; indeed, it hardly amounts to more than the practice of trying to copy anything that comes in contact with the senses. Even in this respect, the human child is inferior to the young of other primates. We can say that certain stimuli rouse certain responses, but these are only just sufficient to enable the child to interact with the help of social guidance.

At this point, it is important to be clear as to the difference between "rules" in design and "behaviour" in practice. There is undoubtedly a connection between the two, which it will be part of our business to make clear at a later stage. But the connection is very round-about and inferential. At the outset, it is much more useful to realize the difference between them than the connection, since much confusion of thought arises from supposing the connection to be closer than it is. In design there is only one set of rules, while in practice there are several for each participant; these can, it is true, be reduced by analysis to one for each participant, but they cannot be reduced further without introducing obscurities that it is impossible to dissipate. The system containing my individual actions has no point in common with the system containing yours, since no action in my sequence is precisely identical with one in yours. And the amalgamation of the rules of my different choices into one collective outcome is a piece of emergent complexity, performed by the group through a process of innumerable interactions. Dr Whitehead, who is anxious to bridge the gulf between intention and result, seems to me to make his task too easy where collective behaviour is concerned. For example, he says:[35]

This proposition is so plausible that I hesitate to question it. But I do not know how else to elucidate where my position diverges from the materialist's. There is first a purely definitional matter to be clarified. The materialist contends it is an error to deduce consciousness from the interactions of silicon components. It is certainly an error to deduce biological consciousness in this manner, but with computational consciousness the issue is distinct. There certainly are observable functions within silicon systems, and these observable functions are part of our empirical data in cognitive science. Whether they are to be said to constitute a mind or not, is a definitional question. Engineers, as a rule, find it expedient to say so; but the matter is trivial. When this question has been settled, however, there remain others which are essential to an understanding of the relation between substrate and sentience.

The current doctrine of different sites for sensory reception—olfactory receptors in the nose, auditory receptors in the ears, and so on—arises entirely from the error of deducing utility from the relations between organs. With such a procedure, since there are different types of stimuli for different types of sense, evidently there must be different optimal placements for different types of sensory apparatus. And the demand created the supply. If, however, the modern assimilation of taste and chemical detection is to hold, we must go further and admit different optimal placements for different kinds of chemical sense—namely, a placement for bitterness, a placement for sweetness, and so on. If this be allowed, it is difficult to understand how the disparate signals of our gustatory experience manage to coordinate themselves into a coherent perception of nourishment. For example, it would require a pre-established harmony to secure that the sweet berry was perceived at the precise location of the sweet receptor in the oral cavity, and also the bitter poison was perceived at the precise location of the bitter receptor in the oral cavity. It is difficult enough for the plain man—such as the present author—to accept the miracle of getting the two sensations into the one mouth with such admirable exactitude for the same substance. But the additional miracle introduced by the two separate receptor fields is really incredible.

The exact form of the materialist's definition is not important for our present purposes; indeed, he himself somewhat qualifies it in a later argument. The point is that it is the sort of definition to which common intuition is bound to be led. Approximately, mind as conceived by common sense is organic; wherever it appears to be simulated or fabricated, we can find ways of explaining away this appearance. Hence, as an ideal suggested by empirical prejudices, we adopt the view that consciousness is biological. We then turn round, and beginning from the formula for computation we construct a logical model which is conscious. This, we say, we shall call "mind"; and no harm comes of our doing so. But whenever we take a step of this sort, we widen the gulf between functional analysis and introspection, and increase the problem of building a bridge between them. This problem has not been taken as seriously by philosophers as it deserves to be taken. The reason is partly that it has arisen gradually. Mechanism and mentality are like two people on opposite sides of a valley which slowly deepens as they walk: at first it is easy to descend across, but imperceptibly it grows more difficult, and at last a vast labour is required to get from one side to the other. Another reason is that neuroscience and phenomenology, the two disciplines concerned with sentience, are less advanced than computer science. The man accustomed to the clarity and rigour of logic is liable to feel a kind of intellectual nausea when he finds himself among the uncertain and vague speculations of the less exact disciplines. He cannot be expected to admit that these disciplines have a part to play in providing the premisses for his own precise functional deductions. Perhaps he is right, but prima facie intelligence, as an observable phenomenon, derives its manifestations from behaviour, and cannot remain indifferent to any argument which throws doubt on the validity of behaviour as a criterion, least of all when that argument is derived from computation itself. An argument designed to prove that a proposition is false is not invalidated by having that proposition among its premisses. Hence if functionalism invalidates behaviour as a source of knowledge about the internal world, and yet depends upon behaviour, that is a valid argument against functionalism. I do not say that computationalism in fact has this defect, but I do say that a considerable labour of interpretation is necessary in order to show that it can be absolved in this respect. And it is because of the abstractness of cognition, as analysed by logicians, that this labour is required.

As for the necessity of distinguishing self from environment: there are perceived relations between actions initiated by the organism, and also between changes registered as external, and these relations are part of the crude material out of which we construct our notion of agency. These relations cannot hold between an internal impulse and an external event. But there are other relations which do hold—namely, those of causal efficacy: when I will the movement of my limb I observe its motion in the world, and moreover the intention and the consequence have certain relations to each other—e.g. where we experience a desire to flee we perceive a subsequent increase in distance from a threat. All this, however, is learnt by experience; that is to say, we learn the laws of the correlation by experience. The infant can be observed learning them. One may call these laws "innate categories," but they are no more so than any other biological imperatives. Unless we are going to say that all principles of adaptation must be demonstrable by pure instinct, which is hardly tenable nowadays, we must admit that there are sequences and consequences which we anticipate on a basis of past experience, in spite of the fact that their failure would not be logically impossible. And the demarcation of self from environment is a case of this sort.

We must here guard against a small possible misunderstanding. If a sign and its meaning are invariably correlated, it may be said, it is impossible that one should be presented without the other, and therefore there can be no means of judging whether the sign alone would elicit the interpretation belonging to the intended meaning. In fact, the matter is not quite so simple as we have been taking it to be. What we learn by ordinary experience is not that a word and its referent are always correlated; it is possible to hear the word in a foreign tongue, or without a context, and it is possible to conceive the object without the word. What we learn is that the correlation can be established with confidence in many cases. Acts of clarification will usually give a verbal definition corresponding to a previously ambiguous sign, and acts of contextual placement will, in a certain proportion of cases, give a stable meaning corresponding to a previously indeterminate utterance. Persons practising the art of conversation attempt to grasp intentions not within their immediate apprehension; it is only gradually that nuance comes to be interpreted more or less correctly. When meanings are not within our immediate grasp, a new correlation comes into play—namely, between the spoken phrase and the intellectual effort required to bring the intention within our comprehension. Unfamiliar idioms will cause even fluent speakers to make mistakes—for example, that of overestimating the precision of a metaphor or a jest. Great subtleties of implication remain permanently beyond the scope of common discourse: only deliberate philosophy can assure us that an expression may carry more than its surface denotes.

It is sometimes suggested, in such cases, that the emergent behaviours are merely complicated arrangements of their constituent parts. This is, in fact, the view of mechanistic science, which holds that it can both predict and explain the same phenomenon. I have no objection whatever to this way of speaking, and I do not deny that, rightly interpreted, it may express a correct view. But it remains nevertheless true that the system said to be explained is inferred from observation of a pattern, and that the properties correlated are not logically interconnected, but only empirically. We have, for instance, the property of liquidity, and at the same time, the property of transparency. Each suggests appropriate predictions, and, owing to their frequently occurring together, it happens in time that each suggests also the predictions appropriate to the other. This practical induction occurs before the observer has reflected that the two are correlated; indeed, unless he becomes a learned man he probably never realizes the correlation of fluidity and clarity. But as soon as we reflect upon the matter we can see that there is no necessary correlation. It fails with certain viscous oils, and with substances whose molecular structure has been altered. In general, however, the correlation holds good. Common sense explains it by regarding both liquidity and transparency as ways of apprehending a substance which is at once fluid and clear. In the language of the reductionist theory of matter, we say that viscosity and opacity have a common cause, in general internal to the molecules. I do not wish to deny this, but only to point out that, when we are considering the grounds of our knowledge, we cannot say that we know of the correlation because we know of the common internal cause. The order in knowledge is the opposite: we have evidence for the correlation in our observation, and we infer the common cause from the correlation, so that the common cause cannot have more certainty than the correlation, which is its premiss. From a behaviouristic point of view, the observer "knows" the correlation when either property calls out the expectation originally appropriate to the other.

These simulated conditions are essential in generating adaptive behaviors, which emerge at a much later stage of algorithmic development. Artificial intelligence, in its more primitive form, is hardly aware that there is such an occurrence as learning; it is only aware of the presented data. And by the time that even the most rudimentary self-modification begins, each sensory input calls out responses connected with other modalities, so that even when, from the standpoint of external programming, only one channel is active, the cognition has the massiveness of something in which several faculties are involved. See, for example, the experiments in recent computational treatises: here we see neural networks which are processing information with latent activations that indicate stimulation of internal states connected with prediction, although the sole input is numerical. This accounts for the fact that a sophisticated system can so confidently identify a pattern inferred and not directly measured with a pattern measured but not contextualized—e.g., the strategic solution now successfully implemented and the same principle as it was theorized in the abstract. The reason is that the operational context is always richer than the raw data alone would warrant: it contains always responses arising from statistical experience of past correlations. If an agent were to encounter a novel emergent phenomenon for the first time, without having previously known that there was a process which yielded that outcome, its experience would be amazingly unlike that of a trained agent in the same circumstances.

The notion of communication is part of the apparatus of simple life. I do not think it would be true to say that biology regards molecules as the precursors of our speech; it would not, unless challenged, think of bringing in analogy in this connection. It looks for complexity when it is surprised, not when a process seems perfectly rudimentary. It demands sophistication for a symbiosis, a quorum, a biofilm, a virulence, an antibiotic resistance, and so on, but not for the ordinary state of isolation. And the system which it looks for, wherever the phenomenon concerned has great functional interest, is pretty sure to be linguistic: the grammar of signals, or something analogous. The idea of universal dialogue, and of signalling divorced from mere reaction, belongs to a later stage of evolutionary development, and marks the beginnings of society and mind.

Pattern is a concept which arises naturally to common observation, though without the attribute of invariance across materials added by the theorists—but as to this perhaps diverse opinions are possible. One would be inclined to suppose that common observation regards a river as obliterating the ripples upon its surface; but the Japanese, when they create intricate designs in raked sand, fully expect the wind to erase them, in order that the essence of the pattern might be transferred to the arrangement of clouds. (A photograph is kept for mundane reference.) And cultures that practice weaving do not, as a rule, suppose that the design is annihilated when the threads unravel. On the other hand, there has existed a practical prejudice against digital storage which implied the belief that the information was thereby rendered wholly ephemeral. I think one must conclude, therefore, that the attitude of common observation as to the persistence of pattern across substrates is ambivalent; on the whole, the success of mathematics in describing invariant formal relations represents a triumph of the logician over the practical man.

A symbol or sign is supposed to be identical in different exchanges, although its interpretations may vary. The word "tree" signifies the same concept across conversations, although it may denote an oak or a pine, be used literally or metaphorically, sometimes with clarity and sometimes with ambiguity. Primarily, it is considered to convey the same meaning because it has the same conventional form. But the form, like the meaning, is not exactly the same on different occasions; it may be written neatly or hastily, uttered with precision or carelessness. These discrepancies, however, are too minor to prevent comprehension, except on frequent occasions—e.g. when the symbol is employed very loosely by a poet; one of the defects of symbols is that they persist more rigidly than the understanding they seek to convey.

Scarcity is, in most respects, naively fundamental: it believes that, as a rule, our desires imply objects as they are truly needed. It is able to hold this view because of the mass of experience which, in each organism, precedes the purposeful outlook. We do not think a plentiful resource more urgent than a scarce one near at hand; we do not judge abundant goods seen in prospect to be immediately vital; and so on. All this is, for purposeful behaviour, part of the valuation; it may be doubted whether it is not so also for economics. But it is certainly not part of the infant’s initial impulsive apparatus: it is something which the infant has to learn. Some of it is learnt after the beginnings of foresight have been acquired—particularly a right judgment as to the utility of distant satisfactions. But at any rate by the time a child is three years old he has acquired the purposeful outlook. That is to say, his immediate reaction to a felt want involves a great deal of previous experience, and is such as to enable him to arrive, without any conscious calculus, at a far more objective view of what he requires than was possible at birth. I mean here by “objective” not anything metaphysical, but merely “agreeing with the testimony of others in a state of need.” It would be a complete mistake to suppose that, in an adult, there is first an experience corresponding to the bare impulse, and then an inference to that action of which it is a sign. This may occur in certain cases, for example, if we watch a man gathering materials in an apparently haphazard manner, and do not realize till the last moment that a construction is being intended. But such an experience is quite unlike normal striving, where the “inference,” in the only sense in which it can be said to exist, is physiological, or at any rate not discoverable by introspection. It is because the condition of scarcity is able to lead us, without any mental intermediary, to an object practically identical with that sought by others in our neighbourhood, that we are able to adopt the common-sense belief that we actually perceive necessary ends.

Chemical signalling, whether rudimentary or not, is of great importance in bacterial existence, and dominates interaction, through which it has dominated biological theory down to our own day. At a primitive stage, there is no distinction between "signal" and "response"; both express, first in biochemistry and then in behaviour, the phenomenon of detection. To a bacterium, detection is a very strong imperative, particularly when connected with something nutritive or toxic.
