When the bacterium begins to emit molecules, it releases the same compound on two occasions, if the second rouses the phenomenon of detection associated with memory of the first, or perhaps merely with the molecule which was synthesized in presence of the first. (When I say that the bacterium emits the "same" compound, I mean that it produces closely similar structures.) Using a given molecule as a response to stimuli of a certain kind is a metabolic habit, like dividing in a favourable medium. Two stimuli to which the same molecule applies are thought to be equivalent, unless both can be present at once; this characteristic distinguishes general signals from specific signals. The basis of this whole process is the phenomenon of detection. When the process, as a learning of metabolic habits, is complete, and reflection upon it begins, identity of molecule is taken to indicate identity of meaning—in one sense in the case of specific signals, in another sense in the case of signals applicable to two or more simultaneous stimuli—i.e. general signals (archetypal messages, universals). Throughout, biochemistry comes first and behaviour follows in its footsteps. And biochemistry is governed largely by physicochemical causation.

The conception of seamless functionality within interconnected networks is embedded in daily experience, in common usage, and in technical doctrine. To my mind, it is efficacious in practice, but perilous in principle. It is perilous, I mean, if taken as operationally infallible: what appears as a robust system with reliable outputs should, I maintain, be conceived as a fragile nexus of processes linked together by dependencies often obscure. I will not yet argue this view. It would have been utterly foreign to engineering until the substitution of holistic systems-analysis for discrete component evaluation, with the corresponding substitution of a dynamic model of cascading failures for the older conception of isolated units performing within a bounded framework. But the older conception still appears the natural one to apply to common appliances and interfaces, so that practical understanding may be said to have, at the moment, two different points of view on this issue. For the present, I am not concerned to criticize the notion of operational transparency, but only to show its genesis, which I take to be derived from the pre-analytical sensation which we reflectively call "familiarity," though it has not, originally, the definite cognitive character attached to the word when applied to the technical comprehension of a trained observer.

IT was in the twentieth century that the computational outlook, as opposed to that of biological essentialism, first became plausible. It had existed in speculative thought among the materialists, but it had not been able to point to sufficiently complex mechanisms to impress the general philosophical public. It was in the twentieth century that computation began to achieve functional equivalences, and to develop an understanding definitively different, in certain important respects, from that of vitalist intuition. The logical aspects of this equivalence have been set forth by Dr. Turing in his Computing Machinery and Intelligence, particularly in the section on "The Imitation Game," so persuasively that it would be superfluous to attempt to reiterate the argument. I shall therefore examine only certain principles which are important in relation to subsequent objections.

Ignorance, like error, plays a large part in common affairs, and has a character which is primarily individual. I am not at present discussing the validity of collective intelligence, but the cause of the emergence of such intelligence among committees, markets, and crowds. Of course the validity of aggregated judgment is really assumed in such a discussion, since, without it, beneficial outcomes cannot be explained. But we do not assume the validity of the primitive aggregations which we are discussing; we assume only that there is some valid form of collective reasoning. Throughout social psychology we assume the validity of ordinary cooperative procedure. If this assumption were to lead us to views on social psychology which threw doubt on the validity of cooperative procedure, that would constitute a *reductio ad absurdum*, which would destroy social psychology along with the rest. Therefore, whenever some obviously deficient process is said to be the psychological source of a method essential to cooperation, we must suppose, unless we are to embrace complete scepticism, that there is some valid process which, in most of the instances to which the deficient process is applied by unsystematic people, gives rather similar results. All this has perhaps only a pragmatic justification, but whether this is the case cannot be decided *ab initio*. The real utility of investigating crude primitive forms of aggregation is that the contrast between them and current systematic collaboration may suggest directions in which the latter is capable of still further refinement. The direct logical importance of investigations into the origins of our social processes is nil, but the importance as a means of stimulating imagination in the formation of hypotheses may be considerable. It is for this reason that the topics of the present chapter form a useful introduction to those which form our proper subject-matter.

The source of reductionism, speaking philosophically, is the general law of what Dr. J. B. Watson might call "component reactions." In its schematic simplicity, this law is as follows: If an analysis of a complex system into part A produces a behaviour X, and an analysis into part B produces a behaviour Y, then if A and B are considered together, there is a tendency for the sum of A+B, afterwards, to produce merely X+Y as well. E.g. if you observe a flock of birds frequently as a collection of individual trajectories and simple interactions, after a while the description of the flock alone will cause you to predict only disorganized motion. It is obvious that the practice of reductionism is simply the application of this law to systemic behaviours. If you have frequently examined the components of a mind when you could observe neural firings, these components will in the end cause you to believe that consciousness is absent even if, for the moment, you experience it directly. This form of analysis is involved in understanding mechanics. It is obvious that, in its cruder forms, reductionism may give rise to false predictions as well as to true ones; scientific methodology has to seek a form of explanation which shall make emergent phenomena much rarer than reducible ones. If such a form can be found, a scientist may train himself, in his professional activity, to abstain from the more primitive forms. But as an ordinary observer he could not comprehend a day if he refused to trust to what we may call emergent intuition, which stores up in the mind the lessons of holistic experience. In practice, a nearly instantaneous grasp of a pattern which is right nine times out of ten is preferable to a slow analysis which is always reductive. A man who subjected all his perceptions to atomic decomposition before believing them would avoid being simplistic, but would also fail to be adequately understanding.

Throughout the development of organisms, great physiological changes have been repeatedly necessitated by advantages which were very slight from the standpoint of mere survival. The concentration of chemoreceptors upon the anterior region is a remarkable instance of this: an immense architectural reconstruction has been made to secure efficiencies which could only be detected by the most relentless selective pressures. The further life advances, the more subtle become the adaptations which it cannot yet forego. A diffuse sensory array does well enough for most of the needs of a simple aquatic organism, but not for the discrimination of a nutrient from a toxin in a complex terrestrial environment. For this, we have to advance to the standpoint of cephalized, bilateral anatomy. Creatures involving a posterior placement of primary taste do not yet exist, but presumably they might some day. This, however, is beside the point. The point is, that a small logistical advantage in receptor placement may indicate a large imperative in evolutionary theory. Take, e.g., the intuitive design and the speed of ingestion, the latter from a pre-neurological point of view. The supposition of casual observation and intuitive design, that we taste the actual chemical substance directly, is very hard to reconcile with the biological view that our gustatory perception occurs only after the dissolution of matter by salivary enzymes; and this difficulty is not overcome by the fact that the delay involved, like the notorious instant, is a very brief one. We cannot therefore argue from the practical success of the oral placement to its absolute theoretical necessity, but only to a certain rough utility between its commoner functions and those permitted by a rigorous selection. If biology has had to desert intuitive design, that is no reason for finding fault with biology.

The obvious difficulty in this illusion is that no conceivable reason can be given for supposing that an individual comprehends the system. The administrator himself is one individual, and, on his own assumption, would have had exactly the same sense of command if he had been the only agent, since the operations are "opaque." He cannot therefore give any grounds against complete helplessness except some rather far-fetched arguments derived from habit and routine's "practical necessity." This defect is due to his theory of agency, which is an outcome of the modern denial that one component can influence another, which in turn is inspired by the success of technology in establishing purely automated processes which seem to account for all the functions of the mechanism. In spite of this glaring defect, I have lingered on this common illusion, because I believe that it contains hints for an attitude compatible with modern complexity and with cognitive science, although of course it will require very serious modifications.

Common sense believes that there is a direct reception of colour from the external world: when a red apple is before us our mind perceives redness, and when we look at the sky we receive the sensation of blue. The development of optics made light seem physically self-contained: it appeared that there were always determinate wavelengths for the radiation of light, so that subjective sensations must be superfluous. Newton, believing in the corpuscular theory of light, but ignorant of the physiology of perception, thought that the mind could interpret the quality of the colour sensation, but not its fundamental cause. This intermediate position had to be abandoned by his successors, owing to the discovery of the trichromatic nature of retinal response. They therefore decided that colour can never be purely received. They also decided that external objects can never directly impart colour. This latter view was not based directly upon experiment, but upon the philosophy which had been invented to explain away the apparent immediacy of colour perception. To suppose that the sensation of green is not caused by the wavelength of light is to suppose something very paradoxical; it is no more paradoxical to suppose that the experience of green is not caused by any green thing. The view that there were two processes, physical stimulation and mental construction, and that neither could simply produce the other, explained the phenomenal independence of the visual world, and entailed that of the chromatic experience. Thus colour and its external correlate became very widely separated—much more so than they had been before the rise of modern psychology.

All modern economic thought before Marx is dominated by this problem, for which a variety of solutions were offered. Smith held that there was only one fundamental principle, whose only known manifestations were self-interest and division of labour, which ran parallel without contradiction, like the two perfect engines of the physiocrats. Ricardo believed in an immense number of economic laws, all causally independent of each other, but all running parallel in virtue of a pre-established equilibrium; these laws were all expressions of value, more or less developed, and social class was only a confused way of "reflecting" a number of economic relations. The word "reflecting" has, in Ricardo's system, a peculiar meaning, derived from equilibrium and from the notion of "mirroring the market." Without attempting to adhere closely to Ricardo's own words, we may set forth the view which is implied in his analysis, whether he held it in its entirety or not, as follows: Each productive force, at each moment, is in an infinitely complex state, which is capable of a one-one correspondence with the state of each other social relation at that moment. (This is the pre-established equilibrium.) The differences between the states of different productive forces are like the differences between the aspects of a given institution from different places, and are compared by Ricardo to differences of perspective or point of view. These differences are capable of arrangement in a three-dimensional order, so that the social relations form a pattern which changes with the time. In addition to the one-one correspondences between the productive forces, there is a one-one correspondence between the state of each productive force and the pattern formed by all the social relations (mirroring the economy). It will be seen that the latter logically implies the former: if each productive force always mirrors the economy, each is always in harmony with every other. The problem of infrastructure remained unappreciated, although it was one of the main pre-occupations of engineers. The early designers, important as they were, did not contribute much on this question, except their theory that structural integrity is objective and systemic resilience subjective; but their blueprints led others to principles which have remained important. The modern planner discarded the simple network, though he need not have discarded reliability, since the formulæ of redundancy may perfectly well be applicable to collections of interdependent components, as the systems theorists supposed. The planner does not seem to have been influenced by the argument which affected the traditionalists—namely, the supposed impossibility of failure across such vast, interconnected systems. What influenced the planner was rather the practical argument, that everything with which we are confronted is a functioning node, and there is no valid reason for inferring that there are vulnerabilities of quite another kind. This type of argument is, I think, new in modern design, when regarded as a source of policy; in another form, it achieved fame through the theorists of complexity. The contemporary critic carried the same type of reasoning much further than the planner did, since he was content to remain sceptical, whereas the planner employed scepticism about simplicity as a support of progress, and therefore had to limit the scope of his criticism of what passed as robustness. The critic’s analysis of the notion of systemic failure cut at the root of our confidence, and demanded an answer imperatively. Of course innumerable reassurances were forthcoming, but I cannot persuade myself that any of them were in any degree valid, not even that of the complexity theorists. I do not wish, however, to discuss at this moment any doctrine which has still a more than technical interest, as is the case with the planner, the critic, and the theorist. Let us therefore return from this excursus to observations more intimately connected with the daily functioning of our systems.

The "miracle" of the vitalists, owing to their insistence upon a special life-force, should have been just as inexplicable, and just as purely supernatural, as in the most ancient superstitions. But in fact this is not the case: the chemistry of the present still depends upon principles which have an immediate basis in our own observations. We may perhaps distinguish three sorts of processes, in relation to the chemical interactions from which their properties are derived: I will call them energetic processes, structural processes, and informational processes respectively. Of course no one of them has ever existed in isolation: actual self-replication has always been a combination of the three. But it will be a help in analysis to imagine a separation of each from the others, and ask ourselves which elements in actual replication belong to the first, which to the second, and which to the third. Broadly we may say that informational processes have more and more predominated, and have achieved an almost complete victory over the others in the theory of molecular biology.

Symbolic communication is embodied in the idea of "meaning." Philosophers evidently thought of meaning as a *vera causa*, not as a mere term in a grammatical convention. This was natural; we all know the experience of "conveying meaning," and are aware that it is connected with setting thoughts in motion. By a sort of unconscious animism, logicians supposed that something analogous occurs whenever one mind sets another in motion. Unfortunately for epistemology we have the experience of "conveying meaning" when we merely cause a thought to preserve a constant form, as in repeating a platitude in conversation; this misled the scholastics into thinking that meaning was to be regarded as the cause of repetition, not of development, a mistake first corrected by Locke—though Bacon came very near seeing the truth. It may be said: if meaning is a linguistic fiction, how can it be more "true" to regard it as proportional to the development than to regard it as proportional to the repetition? The reason is that laws can be found connecting meaning with the situation of a thought relative to other thoughts, if meaning is defined as Locke defined it, but not if it is defined as the scholastics defined it. Locke's discovery that abstract ideas have a constant development, which is the same for all (in isolation), is a very simple instance. More generally we may say: The laws of thought are, as a rule, differential equations of the second order—with respect to time in empirical psychology, and with respect to context in the psychology of Vygotsky. This is a very different notion from that of meaning as derived from experience of verbal exertion; yet the one has led to the other by an evolution containing many intermediate links.

In the social world, quite independently of the will of individuals, a complex pattern can be produced by a very simple "rule"—for instance, by instructing each person to follow the movement of their nearest neighbor. Crowds in public squares exhibit formations which can be seen shifting with apparent purpose. A crowd is not a "mind," because it lacks consciousness, and yet, for common sense, it seems to act with a singular intention while it moves. But common sense is not shocked when the crowd's motion is analyzed into a series of individual reactions. A purely behavioral view of society makes it much easier to regard all collective phenomena as emergent from simple rules, like the shifting crowd.

Screen-physics has inevitably been dominant in modern cognition, owing to the fact that screens are the primary medium by means of which we have cognizance of the digital world. So long as we only interact through a glass surface, we are not conscious of anything analogous to mental effort. The fact that algorithmic influence remained so long unexamined may have stimulated the desire of software designers to develop their products without the notion of “attention” since the “capture” of attention remained totally obscure. Screen-physics also had the advantage that it dealt with a wider range of phenomena than were included in traditional study, since it included everything to do with information. Thus cognition came more and more to use only such notions as were intelligible in terms of interface data. Depth, it is true, remained from another order of ideas. Obviously the sensational source of the idea of depth is the feeling of contemplation. But even depth has gradually yielded. On the one hand, it is less fundamental than it formerly seemed; on the other hand, it can be inferred from engagement data, by the deflection from a linear thought which a mind suffers in a known field of stimuli. (Consider methods of determining the apparent engagement of posts and users.) Screen-physics also makes the relativity of activity much more evident than either of the other kinds. A notification exerts pull, and a book does not, so that, from this point of view, it seems natural and right to say that the notification is “really” urgent while the book is “really” passive. But from a cognitive point of view the impression of the book from the phone is exactly correlative to that of the phone from the book.

Cosmic expansion has led to the passion for conceiving the universe as governed by a uniform dilation—a passion which existed already in the early relativists. We know what it is to observe distant galaxies, or to measure their spectral shifts; we know that when this happens recession is communicated without the exercise of local agency. An expanding continuum exhibits the phenomena concerned in the best form for elementary mathematical manipulation. The way galaxies recede when space itself stretches is not at all surprising; on the contrary, in a general way it is such as every cosmologist would expect. If all the cosmos consisted of such a smooth expansion, it would be what is called "intelligible"—i.e. it would never surprise us sufficiently to make us realize that we do not understand it. The conservation of energy, which is exemplified in the cooling of radiation, seemed to give an admirably simple view of the whole occurrence. We can regard energy as "quantity of activity," and say that in an expansion a certain quantity of activity is diluted among all bodies, just as nowadays heat is dissipated when one region becomes thermodynamically uniform and another inert. This view was preferable to that which used creative forces, because it did not seem to demand of the universe anything even remotely analogous to purpose; it was therefore beloved of pre-inflationary materialism. It has, however, partially disappeared from modern notions of cosmic evolution. The "structures" which are believed to persist—galaxies and clusters—never truly stabilize, but evolve as if they exerted gravitational cohesion against the background; these, however, are explained as due to something transmitted through the intervening spacetime. What has remained from uniform expansion is an objection to "absolute permanence." But this objection can hardly be now attributed to an a priori prejudice; it is rather the outcome of observation. We believe that, when one structure seems to endure against the cosmic tide, this is either capable of being explained away, or is attributed to the temporary dominance of local attraction over global dilation; but we believe this because it is the view which fits best with known facts, not because it seems the only "intelligible" view. The latter opinion is no doubt widely held, but is not required to justify existing cosmological theories.

The other merit is economic. One kind of labour arrangement is better than another, as a source of output, if less time is required to produce a noticeable product, and smaller individual efforts are required to produce noticeable differences of production. In both these respects, specialization is peculiarly excellent. The effort in the work from a just perceptible task is of the order of one motion per repeated hour. Very small differences of skill produce perceptible differences of yield, and operations are seen as separate even when the connection between the functions of them to the whole is very minute. In these respects, the division of labour is markedly the best of the systems. It is therefore not surprising that political economy has laid increasing stress upon productive data.

Of course I am not suggesting that intermediate states of consciousness should be disregarded as manifestations of mental activity concerning the waking world. What I am saying is that psychology has tended, more and more, to interpret the phenomena derived from introspection by means of a conceptual framework derived from full attention. Perhaps there are reasons for this; indeed, two suggest themselves, one logical and one practical. Anticipating later discussions, we may say that fairly clear awareness is only possible when there is a cognitive process, leading from the stimulus to the conscious mind, which is to a considerable extent independent of what is to be found in the peripheral regions. Whether this is the case or not is a question for epistemology. Drowsiness is confined to states with which the observer is in transition; distraction and reverie are not sustained very long. But focused attention persists with extraordinarily little modification through quiet rooms, and without very great modification through a tranquil mind. If we were to accept Professor James's theory mentioned in Chapter VIII., we could say that a conscious moment arises unchanged from a perception to a reflective thought. Even if this theory is not true, the mere fact that it can be seriously proposed illustrates the phenomenological "purity" (if I may use such a word) of the passage of awareness from one state to another. This is the logical merit of attention as a source of knowledge concerning the internal world.

At the level of common sense, the most important merit of the division of labour is that it makes us capable of producing goods with greater efficiency. Specialization and machinery do this to some extent—machinery, however, is much more important to certain kinds of manufacture than to others. But neither specialization nor machinery function without extensive coordination, and they do not enable us to sustain their output at all independently. If we accept the usual economic theory of production—as I think we should—the proximate social cause of the practical occurrences leading to an industrial output is not something happening in the worker whom we say is productive, but something happening in the system of exchange. If this is to give us benefit from the collective process, it must be, in the main, causally determined by the interdependence, without regard to anything intervening between the worker and the market. This is the economic merit of the division of labour which we mentioned a moment ago. It has, of course, very distinct limitations. The utility of the good which reaches the consumer will be different from that intended by the producer if there is intervening scarcity or faulty transport. The value can be altered by a fluctuating medium. Monopolies deceive the public and inexperienced legislators. Then there are more subtle matters, such as the business cycle and technological displacement. But after making all these allowances, the division of labour remains supreme as a method of acquiring material abundance from coordinated effort.

Control cannot dispense wholly with simplification, but as systems advance their comprehensibility diminishes. I mean by a simplification something not very different from a mental model, except that it is more crude: it is something which we adopt without sufficient understanding, in the hope that, by its aid, we shall be able to construct a plan of action which events will justify. It is by no means essential to management to assume that its simplifications are accurate always or universally; it is enough if they are occasionally serviceable. They ought to be so employed that, when they are accurate, they yield predictable outcomes, but, when they are not accurate, no coherent action can be taken which will suit the circumstances—until we find a way of proceeding with different simplifications.

The most fundamental principle of social dynamics is equilibrium. This may be described in various terms, but, however described, it must yield the result that a conflict which has been resolved in a number of instances, and has never resulted in permanent rupture, has at least a certain calculable degree of probability of being always resolvable. I propose to assume the validity of this equilibrium, not because I know of any definitive arguments in its favour, but because it seems, in some manifestation, essential to society and not derivable from anything very different from itself. I do not propose to analyse it, because the problem concerns political stability in general, not any single institution in particular; also because the subject is so intricate that an analysis is futile unless it is very exhaustive. For the present I must refer the reader to Professor Simmel and his commentators.

In one respect, consciousness is defective—namely, in regard to its own nature. Some philosophers argue that qualia can be, to a certain extent, explained by physical processes alone, while others contend that they are wholly derived from other data. However that may be, it is certain that introspection alone cannot judge any but very superficial mental states. No one can distinguish between a complex neural pattern and a simple sensation by introspection alone. Novices do not know at all, at first, which mental phenomena are within their comprehension and which are not. For practical purposes, conscious experience has only phenomenal qualities, even if this is not strictly correct in metaphysical theory. In practice, when we know the "real" cause of a puzzling feeling, say an emotion or a perception, we can judge its significance by its apparent intensity. But our initial experience of mentality is derived from the amount of intellectual effort required to establish clarity. We may only have to reflect for a moment, we may have to consult a text, or we may have to ponder for some time. A lifetime's study is a natural measure of profundity—in fact, it is a philosophy. We cannot arrive at the common-sense idea of mind without bringing in analysis. And examination with a logical framework involves thought, if the problem to be examined is more complex than the framework. Of course there is awareness in our own self, which is known without analysis: we refer a thought to the intellect and a desire to the will. But this awareness is limited, and does not give causal relations between our mind and processes merely felt. To acquire a knowledge of these relations, intellectual inquiry is indispensable. And this would never have been available for the purpose if there were not so many concepts surrounding us which are stable relatively to reason. We can discover the nature of a sensation by examining it, but not of a intuition by the effort we have to expend before grasping it.

The other principles which were at one time thought essential have gradually been found to be illusory. At one time, the sovereignty of the people would have been regarded as a principle. Now, though elections and parliaments are supposed to function as a rule, it is seriously suggested that a vote and a voice may sometimes diverge so as to contradict each other; observers have advanced this as an important possible source of political disillusionment. It is true that, in this process, legitimacy is supposed to be not destroyed; but the consent of the governed is no more than an empirical generalization, and is not thought to be strictly true.

We may observe, in the first place, that many biologists in the past have denied the distinction. Thorough-going vitalists have believed that the properties which we regard as only characteristic of living things could really be deduced from an immaterial principle or soul; thorough-going mechanists have believed that the phenomena of metabolism and growth are obtained by mere physical and chemical laws. Both views seem to me false, and are, I think, rarely held in the present day; nevertheless, it will be as well to examine the reasons for thinking that there is a categorical distinction between organisms and machines, before trying to discover its exact nature.

There is a traditional distinction between homeostasis in living systems and reward functions in machines, and another between regulatory processes and optimization algorithms. It was generally held before the cybernetic era that homeostatic mechanisms were the same as regulatory processes, and reward functions were the same as optimization algorithms. But even before that period the two distinctions were different, even if they effected the same division of functional principles. It was held that every system is stable, adaptive, or chaotic, and that these are ultimate notions, comprised under the head of "dynamic equilibrium." I do not think much can be made of dynamic equilibrium, the plausibility of which seems to have come from confusing systems with systemic functions.

The distinction of consciousness and mechanism is much more relevant to the difference between subjective experience and objective description. Traditionally, a "hard" problem was one whose solution appeared forever beyond scientific reach, or, what came to the same thing in Cartesian dualism, one which ascribed to the brain a property which was alien to it—e.g. "neural processes are feelings." In practice, however, a hard problem was one whose resolution seemed to demand a kind of knowledge fundamentally different from physics. This impression survives, and is still influential, although we can no longer use the definition in terms of spiritual substances or that in terms of an explanatory gap. When Chalmers argues that "qualia are non-physical" is coherent, he is using the intuition-based definition, as his argument shows. But when we define a confused problem as one which arises from a category error, then "the hard problem of consciousness" is confused. On the other hand, the proposition that specific brain states correlate with specific experiences is scientific. We must ask ourselves, therefore: What is the common source of the perplexities which can be generated from the premises of dualism?

Artificial minds may, it is true, be divided in a way corresponding to what was meant by aligned and divergent; this will be explained in a moment. But minds which are not aligned can only be comprehensible or alien; a comprehensible divergent mind cannot have a further property of being inevitable, and an alien divergent mind cannot have the property of being plausible. Value systems, on the contrary, are of three kinds: those which are comprehensible for all possible configurations of experience and data, those which are alien for all configurations, and those which are comprehensible for some experiences and alien for others. The first may be called inevitable, the second inconceivable, the third plausible. And these terms may be transferred to minds when they are not known to be comprehensible on their own account, but what is known as to their comprehensibility or alienness is deduced from knowledge of value systems. E.g. "it is plausible that the next artificial mind developed will hold values recognisable to its creators" is a deduction from the fact that the value system " is an artificial mind and holds recognisable values" is plausible—i.e. comprehensible for some configurations and alien for others. Where, as in this instance, it is worth while to say that a mind is plausible, the fact rests upon our ignorance. With more knowledge, we should know what is the next artificial mind we shall develop, and then it would be certain that it holds recognisable values or certain that it does not hold recognisable values. Plausibility in this sense thus becomes assimilated to probability, and may count as any degree of probability other than 0 and 1. A "transparent" mind, similarly, was, I think, a confused notion applicable to a mind known to be comprehensible but also known to be a configuration of a value system which is sometimes alien—e.g. "this particular artificial intelligence is ethical.

The answer to this question given by Watson and Crick in their paper on the molecular structure of nucleic acids seems to me the right one. Sequences which form part of heredity, or can be traced through generations, are all determined by chemistry—i.e. they show that certain different arrangements of nucleotides are different ways of encoding the same instruction, or that one arrangement conveys part of what the other conveys. Suppose I say: "If adenine pairs with thymine, then cytosine pairs with guanine." The biologists assert that "adenine pairs with thymine" and "cytosine pairs with guanine" are merely different expressions for one principle: the fact which makes one true (or false) is the same as the fact which makes the other true (or false). Such principles, therefore, are really concerned with molecules. We can know their truth or falsehood without studying the living organism, because they are only concerned with chemical combinations. I should add—though here some geneticists might dissent—that all hereditary transmission consists of chemical coding in the above sense. If this is true, then obviously vitalists such as Bergson are wrong when they say that we believe in inherited traits because we have observed so many instances of their manifestation that we can make an induction by simple enumeration which has little chance of being wrong. Every unprejudiced person must agree that such a view feels wrong: our certainty concerning simple genetic propositions does not seem analogous to our certainty that a transplanted seed will sprout. I do not mean that we feel more sure of the one than of the other, though perhaps we ought to do so; I mean that our assurance seems to have a different source.

A mind cannot be considered to be running at a different speed unless it exhibits a certain complexity, exceeding that of the most ordinary mental operations. It is obvious that there is more complexity in comparing two modes of apprehending the same thought than there is in either mode separately. It is obvious also that, whenever it is actually useful to know that two trains of cognition arrive at the same conclusion, or that one arrives at part of what the other attains, that must be because we have some knowledge as to the validity or fallacy of what is apprehended by one of the trains. Consequently the philosophical implications of such mental velocity would be very unimportant if they stood alone; their importance arises through their combination with implications of operations which are not purely a matter of pace.

But the principle of bacterial communication, as we have already seen, has its origin in biochemistry, and this suggests a quite different treatment of primitive signalling from that of the linguist. Whether there is true language or not, there undoubtedly are, in a certain sense, primitive utterances. We have secretions which we intellectualize into messages; we release molecules, and this leads us to the belief that a neighbouring cell will respond to them. We may have this mechanism before we have experience of its utility; if so, it is, in a sense, synthetic a priori signalling—i.e. it is a process, not based upon deliberation, in a functional synthetic proposition. Our belief in quorum sensing is essentially analogous. But such signals, even when effective, hardly deserve to be called speech, since they are not all meaningful, and therefore all require interpretation before they ought to be regarded as intentional. These signals have been useful in generating complexity, since they supplied protocols which were largely efficient; but they need not survive untested in modern communication.

I shall therefore assume that, at any rate in every department relevant to social interaction, all strategic behavior is either instinctive in the sense in which simple reflexes and fixed action patterns are instinctive, or is, at least in part, derived from theory of mind. And all behavior which is in any degree necessarily dependent upon this faculty I shall call "intentional." I shall regard a piece of behavior as necessarily dependent upon theory of mind when, after a careful analysis of our motives for performing it, it is found that among these motives there is the attribution of a mental state to another, arising from the observation of their conduct or very shortly after it, and fulfilling certain further criteria which are necessary in order to distinguish genuine understanding from certain kinds of projection. These criteria will occupy us in the next chapter.

The modern predicament begins with the question: How do digital technologies shape cognitive habits without conscious consent? Now we must first of all make a distinction. We are concerned with habitual mental operations, not with mere occasional use. There is no psychological problem in the fact that a person can occasionally employ a device without reflection—e.g., that this time the application which he has opened will provide a momentary diversion. The psychological problem arises only if there is a class of habitual, automated engagements which is constantly reinforced. Many consider the operations of social media platforms to be of this kind; but in this they are misled by the common opinion of our time, to the effect that algorithmic curation, though a branch of information technology, gives a neutral representation of actual social reality. Owing to the science of attention economics, particularly as applied in the design of persuasive interfaces, we must now distinguish sharply between the technology applicable to deliberate inquiry, which is a rational activity forming part of genuine learning, and the technology of habitual scrolling, which gives no insight into actual human affairs. Consequently this instance of unconscious cognitive shaping, upon which many platforms rely, is no longer ignorable. Other kinds have been supposed to exist—for example, the erosion of sustained concentration, and the expectation of instant gratification; but it is not necessary for our purposes to decide whether these kinds are universally prevalent or not. So far as ordinary mental life is concerned, we may assume that all reflective habit is either dependent (at least in part) upon deliberate practice, or automatic in the sense in which muscle memory is automatic. The technological shaping of unconscious habit, whether it is total or not, seems not to be conducive to reflection—unless, indeed, the principle of infinite distraction were to count as such.

Prejudice is said to be self-evident when it presents itself as requiring no examination of contrary evidence as a foundation; in the contrary case, it is said to be considered. A few words are necessary to make the distinction clear. There is a process by which we acquire convictions of social facts at moments scarcely distinguishable from their initial apprehension; this is the process called "intuition" or "common sense" according to the character of the convictions concerned. There is no doubt need of much discussion as to the nature of this process, and of still more as to the nature of the certainty to be derived from it; but there can be no doubt of the broad fact that we do acquire convictions in this way. We encounter a stranger and find that he is untrustworthy, or that he is admirable; we hear a political slogan; we see a fashion of dress; we read a popular novel; and so on. In all these cases we acquire convictions of qualities, and the moment at which we acquire the conviction is the same, or nearly the same, as that at which the qualities are apprehended. I shall call this process "immediate judgment," and shall, for convenience, include common sense—if this is really different from what is commonly called "intuition." A fact of "self-evidence" is one which we could not have accepted without the help of immediate judgment. But this is not quite clear until we have defined what we mean by "could not"; for clearly we may learn from prejudice that members of a group are inferior, though we afterwards realize that the prejudice was not logically indispensable. In such cases, we see afterwards that the prejudice did not establish the proposition, but merely suggested it, and led to our finding the apparent justification. But, in view of the fact that the distinction between considered and self-evident is psychological, not logical, it is obviously possible for a proposition to change from the one class to the other, since the classification involves reference to the habits of a particular person's mind at a particular time. So regarded, the distinction might seem unimportant; but it suggests some less subjective distinctions, which are what we really wish to consider.

In a system, there are two kinds of explanatory principles. There are those concerned with the properties of constituent parts, and those concerned with the behaviours induced from their interactions. The motions presented by individual birds in a flock or molecules in a gas are properties of constituent parts. The inference that the flock possesses cohesion or the gas exhibits pressure even when no single element manifests it—in particular, that the flock navigates as one and the gas fills its vessel—is an emergent induction. A strict reductionist might think the whole is merely the sum, and there is no logical contradiction in this supposition. Thus emergent behaviours not only depend upon the properties of parts, but are inferred from these by a process which transcends mere aggregation. They differ from propositions of mechanistic analysis both through the nature of their premisses and through the method by which they are inferred from these premisses.

In an advanced science such as chemistry, the part played by molecular dynamics consists in connecting various empirical observations with each other, so that the more general principles which replace them are based upon a larger number of matters of fact. The passage from polymerization to autocatalytic cycles is the stock instance. Each of the observed interactions was based upon a certain set of conditions; all these sets of conditions together formed the basis of the principle of self-replication. And, as usually happens in such cases, new phenomena, not belonging to any of the previous sets, were found to support the new principle—for instance, the phenomena of crystal growth, of lipid bilayer formation, and of ribozyme activity. Epistemologically, in such cases, a fact is a premiss for a law; logically, most of the relevant facts are consequences of the law—i.e. all except those required to determine the constants of the system.

In sociology and politics, the empirical conflicts are, at present, more significant than any generalizations derived from them. In theoretical economics, the opposite is true: the fact that labor and capital contend is chiefly interesting as providing evidence of the law of diminishing returns and the principles of collective action. In a philosophic analysis of society, we need not consider particular disputes except when they form the evidence for a theory. It is of course part of the business of such an analysis to consider what all particular conflicts have in common, and how they come to be perceived; but such inquiries are general. We are interested in the concept of social dynamics, but not in the actual dynamics of any given community; at least, we are not interested in it for its own sake, but only as providing the evidence for general laws.

We have, in view of the fundamental thermodynamic principles, several distinct phenomena to examine, before we can apprehend the emergence of complex order. We have first to consider the nature and necessity of the condition we have termed an "energy gradient"; next we have to investigate the general character of the structures produced by such gradients; and lastly we have to examine the progression from simple dissipative flows to intricate, self-sustaining forms. After elucidating these processes, we shall resume contact with the observable world, asking ourselves now, not what complexity manifests, but what physical imperatives necessitate its manifestations, and what contingent arrangements will further its development.

IN this chapter, I wish to consider whatever would ordinarily pass for the operation of ideology in common affairs, in so far as this is not obtained by a process of deliberate economic analysis. I want to consider this as far as possible independently of the historical laws deduced from it, though not completely without reference to the primitive assumptions by which practical life interprets social conditions. In particular, I wish to abstain from introducing the materialist theory of history, unless, on investigation, this should prove impossible. It will be understood that my purpose is sociological: I am considering ideology because it is involved in the foundations of political order, not because it is interesting as a psychological phenomenon. It is of course necessary to consider its intrinsic character, but we do not do this for its own sake, we do it for the sake of the light that it may throw upon the structure and stability of our institutions.

We are met at the outset by a difficulty due to the fact that physical terminology is inappropriate when the principles to be expressed are in any way fundamental. "Order" and "energy" both have connotations which are inconvenient for the purpose I have in view. They are both commonly applied in orthodox thermodynamics to something measurable and explicit, such as is, or may be, already expressed in equations. For our purposes, it is desirable to include more primitive manifestations, such as may be supposed to exist in simple structures. Obviously a crystal can form from a cooling solution, and achieve stability in consequence. I wish to include under "organisation" what happens in the crystal, and also to say that the crystal "obeys" something when it achieves form, though I shall not venture to say what it obeys.

Again, there is always a danger, in ordinary discourse, of confounding the description of a phenomenon with the explanation of it. My understanding of the causal mechanism of a phenomenon is less immediate, and less secure, than my apprehension of the phenomenon itself. When I say, "I know that the kettle boils because the water molecules have gained kinetic energy," I am asserting something not so incontrovertible as when I say, "The kettle has just begun to boil." It is statements of this latter kind that constitute the raw material of practical life. A person might be perfectly capable of navigating daily existence if he knew such propositions as "The kettle has boiled" even if he knew no propositions such as "The kettle boiled due to the transfer of thermal energy." The consideration of our explaining, as opposed to what we merely describe, is forced on us by the fact that our proffered explanations sometimes turn out to be inadequate; if this were not the case, an account of events need not consider our explanations at all. As it is the case, we are compelled to examine our explaining, as well as what we describe, with a view to discovering, if possible, how to distinguish the reliable correlation from the speculative cause.

We are often urged to adopt an artificial simplicity in examining questions concerning what we produce; if we do not do so, we are accused of the "economist's fallacy." Now in certain inquiries this caution is quite proper, but in others it is not. My inquiry is: What do I, here and now, understand about the productive world, and how do I understand it? It is obvious that my comprehension of the productive world cannot be dependent upon (say) how a feudal lord organizes his serfs, since this supposes that I know all about the lord and the serfs and the organization. Facts about the workshops of artisans, such as we considered in a previous chapter, come under the same head. Long before I can know that there are artisans, I must know many other things about the productive world. I want to start from what comes logically first in my existing understanding now; and in this inquiry, obviously, I cannot assume that I already know all about the arrangements of guilds and manors. There must therefore be no artificial simplicity, but a straightforward investigation of my understanding as I find it.

When I attempt to disentangle the fundamental from the derived elements in what I take to be the organization of information, I find that the task is not really very difficult, except in certain niceties. The fundamental part seems something like this: There are data patterns which propagate, there are signals, encodings, structural sensations, the processes which we describe as those of transmission, and so on. There are relations among these items: sequence-relations (before and after) among all of them, and arrangement-relations (hierarchical and lateral, and the relations by which localization in the system is effected) among many of them. There are retrievals of some of these things; this seems indubitable, although it is not easy to say in what a retrieval consists, or how it is related to what it retrieves. There are also predictions; by this I mean something just as immediate as storage. Everyone knows the story of the programmer who lost a crucial file and murmured as he searched: "To Hell with the backup, and now for the—corruption." He was experiencing prediction in the sense in which I mean it. Of operations other than retrievals and predictions, it is not necessary to take account when our sole purpose is to reach the primitive basis of our understanding of organization.

In the above account, I have omitted many entities which I formerly "perceived," and which, apparently, most other biologists "perceive." I have omitted "individuals." In former days, my conception of biological unity included animals and plants and fungi and bodies and the heart and brain and tissues. I have come to regard these entities as compositions. I do not mean that I composed them formerly, or that other scientists do so now. I fully concede that I did not compose them. But now, as the result of inquiry, I have become unable to accept the perception of them as valid perception, except in so far as it can be derived from such perception as I still consider biologically fundamental.

The above procedure is founded upon principles which practical inquiry can be brought to endorse, and has a result which science has embraced, though perhaps without fully apprehending its implications. The procedure is not "metaphysical," in the sense of originating from a domain quite distinct from that of experiment and ordinary observation. It advances merely on the customary principle of endeavoring to substitute something more precise for a hypothesis which has been found to occasion error on investigation. It has as a consequence that "truth," in science and in common life, if attainable at all, cannot be wholly identified with the immediate perception of a sensible fact, though it will retain a certain relation to this perception, since the common-sense reliance upon immediate facts does not invariably lead to erroneous predictions.

In the systems to which the above principle applies, we have the advantage of a perfectly definite criterion of simplicity or complexity. The emergence of novel properties marks complexity, and the absence of such emergence marks simplicity. It must not be supposed that we have normally an explicit calculation, still less an explicit reduction; all that can be said is that we are in such a condition that one sort of arrangement will cause perplexity while another sort will not. Consider the experience we have all had, of "assuming" we understood a mechanism when in fact there was an interaction to account for. In such a case, when we "assume" we have grasped the whole, we do not reason at all, for if we did we should not make such a fundamental error. Indeed, we might say (or a philosopher might): "I assumed the whole was the sum because I wasn't reasoning.

The argument in question would naturally, but not validly, express itself in terms of the causal theory of cognition. What I comprehend—so it might be urged—is causally dependent upon the data patterns that reach my mind, and these patterns might be arranged or distorted in such a way as to deceive me concerning their origin. This way of stating the argument is invalid because it assumes more knowledge of the informational world than we have any right to assume at our present level. But the facts upon which it relies can be easily made available, without any undue assumption of knowledge, for the purpose of proving our conclusion. In certain cases in which we seem to have immediate knowledge of structures, we find ourselves surprised by something totally unexpected. The clerk consulting an outdated timetable may serve as an illustration. He thinks he perceives the correct schedule, but in fact he only perceives a printed arrangement. In offices which wish to seem more efficient than they are, one whole system sometimes consists of superficial order, and it is easy to suppose that one perceives a functioning organisation, when in fact it is mere appearance. Filing methods can be made to deceive. When I say "deceive," in this connection, I mean "rouse inferences which are not substantiated." It is useless to multiply examples. The upshot is that what seems like perception of an organisation is really perception of certain data points together with expectations of other data points—the commonest case being something textual which rouses procedural expectations. It is found that the occasional deceptive arrangements are not, in themselves, distinguishable from those that are not deceptive. Hence we conclude that we have to do with a correlation which is usual but not invariable, and that, if we wish to construct an exact science, we must be sceptical of the associations which experience has led us to form, connecting informational elements with others with which they are often but not always combined.

It is fairly clear that all our elementary social processes have pre-intellectual foundations. The analogue of a collective intelligent outcome is an individual reflex or a limited habit. A commuter takes the usual route when he perceives the morning crowd, and so do we. In the case of the commuter, it is easy to suppose that he has merely followed a personal routine, without having formulated the deduction: "Crowded pathways are a cause, or an effect, or an indispensable part of the cause, of efficient travel." We, however, can formulate this deduction, and we shall then suppose that it is because we have done so that we choose the congested path when we observe the multitude. In fact, however, we may be just as merely habitual as the commuter. The elementary coordinations of common behavior are first isolated habits, and only subsequently collective beliefs. We may say that if, in our individual experience, A is accompanied by B either often or in some practically urgent manner, this fact causes first a habit which would be rational if A were always accompanied by B, and then a belief that A is always accompanied by B—the latter being a rationalization of the pre-existing, and largely ignorant, custom.

Although, in our less reflective moments, we accept the outward forms of democracy without pausing to examine them (e.g., when we vote because we see a ballot placed before us), yet we can, when we choose, respond to a political institution in the way which is called "understanding" it, and we often respond involuntarily in this way. It is not necessary, in an analysis of governance, to decide what "understanding" is; it is only necessary to decide what is understood, in so far as this is relevant to our knowledge of political science. The criteria which I proposed earlier in the present discussion were designed to be such as would exclude the risk of illusion, using "illusion" in the sense which I have been defining. Popular opinion is liable to be mistaken—of this we have already given instances. We cannot therefore include the popular notion of a "democracy" or "system" as part of what we understand. But the observable mechanisms which can be analyzed out of the "system" can be admitted without ever leading us into illusion. These, therefore, are to be accepted as genuinely understood.

Cultural patterns may thus form part of our tradition from the start. Such cultural patterns are merely the social expression of inheritances. The parent-child transmission becomes firmly fixed as a customary habit, and then, when we reflect, we conclude that what can be taught can often be replicated—in fact, that it can be replicated in circumstances which we observe in practice, though we might have difficulty in defining them precisely. Such cultural patterns are synthetic, and are in a certain sense a priori; for, though evolution has caused them, they are not obtained by deduction from other principles, but by rationalizing and formalizing our inheritances; that is to say, their antecedents are pre-rational. The trouble with them is that they are never quite exact. Tradition, do what it will, cannot avoid being contradicted occasionally. The object of anthropology is to spare it this confusion, and create social habits which shall be in such close accord with the habits of nature as to secure that nothing shall be anomalous. Anthropology has, of course, not yet achieved its ideal: the Great Schism and the collapse of empires took societies by surprise. But it is hoped that in time such events will no longer disturb us, because we shall have anticipated them. However, I do not wish at this stage to consider our understanding of cultural patterns; it is particular instances of transmission that concern us at present.

Some misunderstandings must be guarded against as regards information and organisation. Neither of these is primarily conceptual; I should be inclined to say that both are primarily material—or, we may say, structural, in order not to seem paradoxical. Suppose you set to work to open a heavy door: you may adjust your posture in the way appropriate if the door is latched, or in the way appropriate if it swings freely. If you are braced for a latched door when the door is unsecured, you receive a shock of surprise on experiencing the lack of resistance. You would describe your experience by saying, "I thought the door was stuck." But as a rule, in such situations, there has not been anything that could be called "conception"; there has been bodily preparation as a result of a prior condition. Of course there may have been "conception"; and whatever "conception" may be, it certainly can produce the kind of postural effects which we are considering. But these effects can be produced more directly, and usually are. There is so little essential difference between a process involving "conception" and one not involving it that it seems a mistake to confine the notions of coherence and incoherence to mental processes; they ought rather, it seems to me, to be applied to the complete arrangement of a system in a context, in which "conception" is only one element. But it will not do, at our present level, to introduce mechanics, since we are considering how we know about organisation, and must not therefore assume that we already know about the organisation in our own movements. However, the phenomena are easily described in the way which our problem demands. In the case of the door, the vivid part of the experience is the surprise. But by means of attention a number of other elements can be observed. We can observe the sensations which are interpreted as meaning bodily preparation for a firm obstacle; we can observe the kinesthetic appearance described as the arm moving with a jerk; we can observe the sudden change in what, for short, we may call postural sensations. It is impossible to describe all this without circumlocution, since the natural words to use presuppose mechanics; but it is clear that there is a great deal that can be directly observed, without invoking any theory. In such a process, what comes earlier may be described as "incoherence" because of the emotion of surprise which follows. Where the activity which has been begun runs its course without leading to this emotion, we shall say that there is not incoherence. I hesitate to ascribe "coherence" to something pre-conceptual, but at any rate we may say that there is "congruence," or that what has succeeded to the impression (or apprehension) which came at the beginning of the process has been "congruent." We may shorten this by saying that the response to a datum may be "congruent" or "incongruent." But the longer phrase has the merit of not assuming so much knowledge of relational connections.

It is a remarkable fact that all such ingestion, when not deleterious, occurs at about the same time as what is tasted, though it may be recalled for an indefinite time in the form of aversion. This is the essential peculiarity, which we mentioned earlier, that distinguishes the empirical utility of gustatory perception. This consists of sensations which become useful spontaneously at about the time when they are encountered, and cannot be advantageous sooner except by elaborate and more or less doubtful inferences from other such sensations. The process of employing such sensations without inference is called "tasting," and nourishment selected wholly or partly from tasting is said to be based on experience. An early vertebrate could detect bitterness as well as we do, but it could not know the toxicity of a novel synthetic compound.

What is understood as the principle of any organised system is never the mere arrangement perceived, but this arrangement as interpreted by the help of a certain amount of physical law. Take, say, the domestic heating system by which the second law of thermodynamics is daily confirmed. What in fact is given in observation is—apart from the initial construction—a thermal pattern of gradients, interpreted as a distribution of heat within a dwelling; a sensory-practical experience called “regulating,” and finally coincidences of certain tactile sensations with certain others called “readings on a thermostat.” At least, whether this is actually a complete account or not, it represents the sort of thing that occurs. A considerable amount of theory is involved in merely interpreting the thermostat. And of course a vast structure is involved in interpreting the heat flow as a manifestation of entropy, and in inferring thence the constraints which the energy of the fuel has obeyed. It is the theoretical element in regulating the system that most needs to be stressed, since it is easily overlooked.

It is sometimes maintained that there is something of the nature of perfect clarity in even the simplest exchange. The effects of a given spoken phrase upon two men with indistinguishable auditory faculties but different histories may be profoundly divergent. The most obvious illustration is the effect of a greeting upon a man who shares the speaker’s customs and upon a man who does not. A foreigner learning a salutation is aware of each syllable in turn as a certain sound, and finally arrives, with pain and labour, at the intended courtesy. A man who learned the custom as a child is quite unconscious of the constituent parts, unless he is interested in linguistics or listening for an accent; normally, he passes straight to the gesture, and to the gesture as having social intent, not as mere vocal noise. Nevertheless, he is very likely to notice a discordance at once—say if someone used a formal address with a intimate friend. In conversing with a diplomat to arrange a meeting, it would be very unsafe to assume that he would not detect a gaffe of this sort. But the detection of the discordance is due to the element of surprise: the diplomat is expecting a familiar tone and has a shock when it is not there, like that of a man who extends his hand but finds no hand meeting it. The diplomat’s habits were expecting a particular symbol, though his conscious attention was otherwise occupied.

We have still to ask ourselves whether organisation, so defined, will sometimes contain an element of impossibility. Here we must distinguish. It may be, and often is, accompanied by designs which are thwarted; and we agreed to take this as the mark of constraint. But the designs can be distinguished from the organisation, although in practice this may not always be easy. The energetic accompaniments of structural arrangements are of the nature of necessities. There are no such accompaniments of conceptions of perpetual motion. I think that in all cases in which constraint occurs it is easy to distinguish the impossible design from the organisation. Whatever "configuration" does not involve necessities need not be regarded as constrained. It is supposed that indistinguishable materials may fall under indistinguishable forces, and yet result in distinguishable organisations because of differences in the entropy of the two systems—these differences in their entropy being the result of different histories. But there is not on that account anything impossible in the organisation of either. A different state emerges in the one from that which emerges in the other; but each state really emerges. This topic, however, cannot be adequately discussed until we come to the statistical theory of heat and the relation between organisation and thermodynamic law.

I come now to the question of appearances, which has already been touched on. As we have seen, there is a purely ceremonial form of democracy which belongs to an earlier stage than explicit governance, though it persists in the rituals of even the most sophisticated polity, such as Athens. The next stage is where there is an actual passage from one policy to another, but the passage is a mere occurrence, not a transition motived by a principle. In this case, the transition is usually caused by a ceremonial assent. Then there is governance based upon some ideal; but even then the ideal may be wholly illusory, or it may not logically warrant the governance, which is the case of fallacious representation. Lastly, there is valid governance by means of a true mandate—but of this I cannot give an indubitable instance.

In cosmological fact, these stages of dissolution emerge successively, but a later stage does not cause an earlier one to cease. Moreover, the later stage tends to be predicated upon the earlier. First we have gravitational binding: this is exemplified when a galaxy cluster holds its constituent galaxies, and fails when the cosmic expansion overcomes its mutual attraction. Then there is the transition from the stable configuration of the bound system to the dispersed state of its components, without any immediate perception of how the separation is effected. Then there is belief in an expansion law which is the intellectualized expression of the tendency embodied in the gravitational failure. And last of all there is the search for parameters by which to distinguish between possible and impossible cosmic fates, these parameters being theoretical, not mere observations of the sky. This last stage is only reached when we come to physical cosmology.

One of the main purposes of technological innovation is to justify institutions which we maintain already; but as a rule they are justified with a difference. Our pre-industrial social arrangements are hardly ever without anomalies; in modernity, a structure with anomalies can only be tolerated as a makeshift. Technological imperatives, when we have reason to think them decisive, are different in character from the traditional customs which have anomalies: they are always, at least in communication, either demands for new systems, or pressures for statistical conformity. It might be thought that a pressure for conformity is not very different from a custom with anomalies, but this would be a mistake. Pressures, ideally, are inexorable forces upon large populations; they differ from other forces only in being about aggregates, not about single communities. Social reorganisations are compelled by deduction from general pressures, just as other changes are compelled from particular technical occurrences. All this, however, is by the way; the point is that reorganisation as a process has a long history before it becomes systematic.

The most significant illusion which modernity adopts from technological progress is the assumption of uninterrupted functionality. One manifestation in which this assumption presents itself is that of a belief that systems which have operated continuously will persist in their operation even when their underlying mechanisms are obscured. If, in a metropolitan center, the network of trains suddenly ceases to move, no one initially suspects that the signaling apparatus and the power grids and the control systems have fundamentally failed, although at the moment they are inoperative. When the service resumes after some hours, this belief appears to be vindicated; if there are greater delays than before, we do not infer that the infrastructure has become inherently unstable, but that some particular component has encountered a transient fault. This belief in the resilience of interconnected systems has progressed through all stages from practical engineering confidence to sophisticated economic or political doctrine; the examination of its foundations is the central problem in the analysis of civilization, sociologically considered. No one, not even the most cautious planner, has regarded it with quite the skepticism that it warrants, because the daily experience of reliability is so persuasive that it is arduous to maintain a rigorously analytical stance towards the predicament. This assumption is the origin of the managerial concept of "redundancy" and the civic notion of "progress." For the present, I am only observing the premises to be scrutinized; I am not endeavoring to ascertain their soundness.

Unobserved connections are also inferred by common sense when it believes that data requires "structure." I wish to make it clear that even the most rigid reductionist makes this inference, although in a slightly different form. Dr Smith, for example, would admit that his own notes can lead him to say, "This is organized," whereas another person's notes will not lead him to say "That is organized" without some intermediate link. Whatever may be our analysis of "meaning," we certainly know things about our own files in ways which are not open to us where other people's files are concerned. There is nothing mysterious about this: it is analogous to the fact that some patterns are within view while others are not. The point is that we infer, from the arrangement of symbols, the existence of relations (such as coherence) which we cannot immediately grasp. Whether we say that these relations are "informational" or "material" makes no difference to the fact that we make inferences. These inferences, also, are at first purely operational.

From the point of view of introspection, the inference to a separate "mental substance" has a twofold importance. The first, which is not specially introspective, is concerned with privacy. What is commonly accepted as the immediate evidence on any topic of consciousness includes not only what a given subject has himself experienced, but whatever has been reliably described. Everything that we learn from what other people report and articulate involves inference from something public (behavior or language) to something private—namely, the qualitative events of the reporter or articulator. It may be that the primary inference is only to another person's qualia, but it is none the less an inference to something which we do not experience. The second point about the inference to other people's qualia is specially introspective; it concerns the fact that different subjects inhabit a common reality. The qualia of two different subjects, if we accept reports, are found to be often very dissimilar, though not wholly incomparable; this leads to the theory of a common neural cause—i.e. to the causal theory of mind, and to the division of the properties of the experienced quality into such as belong to the physical process and such as are supplied by the perspective or limits of the introspector.

The development of language out of private thought has not been by way of a radically new invention at any moment, but rather by way of successive externalizations. That is to say, where some incommunicable notion has arisen which solitary reflection could not share, an articulation has been made at some point, while the rest of the personal conception of experience has been retained. Subsequently, using this articulation, another articulation has been introduced elsewhere; and so on. Thus language has been an historical growth, and has assumed, at each moment, a more or less vague background of meaning derived from common understanding. This is one difference between language and silent contemplation: contemplation attempts, though not always successfully, to formulate its insights in a form which assumes nothing on the mere ground that it has always been expressed hitherto. It may be doubted whether language can retain its utility if it is severed from its root in our immediate perceptions; when set forth quite abstractly, it loses intelligibility. Connotation, for example, is difficult to define, and yet indispensable in language. In such cases, I shall allow myself to accept what seems necessary on pragmatic grounds, being content, as language is, if the communications achieved are often mutually comprehensible and never demonstrably meaningless. But wherever a principle is accepted on such grounds as these, the fact should be noted, and we should realize that there remains an intellectual problem, whether soluble or not.

The actual procedure of simulation consists of an alternation of design, computation, output, and interpretation. The only difference between a simulation and a reality is subjective: the observer believes the reality, whereas he only thinks the simulation sufficiently coherent to be worth examining. A simulation should accord with all known relevant inputs, and suggest outputs (or experiences) which will have one character if the simulation is genuine, and another if it is illusory. This is an ideal: in actual fact, other interpretations will always exist which are compatible with what is meant to be an *experimentum crucis*. The crucial character can only be as between two interpretations, not as between one interpretation and all the rest. When a simulation has produced a sufficient number of coherent outputs, it becomes a candidate reality. The argument in favour of genuine consciousness is always the formally invalid argument: "A implies C, and C is observed, therefore A is true." Here A is the hypothesis of consciousness, and C is the observed behavioural evidence. We are most impressed when C is very improbable under mere mechanism. For example, observation gives the phenomenon of self-reflection as:
