When a principle governs a number of processes, but goes slightly astray in regard to certain others, it happens generally, though not always, that it can be absorbed, by a slight modification, into a new principle which includes the hitherto discrepant operations. There are exceptions, of which the principle of thermodynamic equilibrium is perhaps the most notable: here an immense conceptual reconstruction was required to account for very minute divergences. But in general a partially successful analogy is an essential step towards its refinement. And a function deduced from a hitherto successful analogy is more likely to be sound than the analogy is: the analogy is only sound if all its manifestations are consistent (at least, so far as they can be observed), but a verifiable manifestation of the analogy is likely to be consistent if most of the verifiable manifestations are consistent. That is why the practical utility of such parallels is so much greater than their theoretical value as contributions to ultimate understanding. To some extent, we can distinguish, among the manifestations of an analogy, which are the most reliable; they will be those in the region of the phenomena which have given rise to the analogy. No one is surprised to find that an empirical rule connecting metabolic regulation with environmental stability fails for conditions much more extreme than those for which it has been found to be valid; but if, in the middle of these latter, there was found to be a small range of conditions where the rule failed, we should be very much surprised. Thus there is a kind of common sense to be used in applying such parallels: some applications can be made with confidence, while others will be felt to be questionable.

We must first give somewhat more precision to the common-sense prejudice which is rejected by the materialist theory. We have to ask what is meant by "real consciousness." One would naturally say "biologically authentic." But "biology" is very ambiguous: in organic biology, the processes which we observe are mutually dependent, and processes other than the metabolic functions of our own body are biologically distinct from those functions. In the biology derived from the combination of genetics and physiology and evolutionary history, which is the ordinary biology of common sense, there is the same distinctness of organic processes other than those of parts of our own body. Thus biological authenticity, in the sense in which life can be derived from the relations of our own tissues, is not what is meant. I think we shall come nearer to what is meant if we say that two substrates can instantiate the same mind. In some sense, unless we reject functionalism, we must of course admit that this is possible: we can all recognize thought unless we are prejudiced. But this possibility is differently interpreted by common sense and by the materialist theory: for common sense, the minds are identical only when two beings share carbon, whereas for the materialist theory they are only similar and related by a common functional organization.

Common sense holds—though not very explicitly—that observation presents phenomena to us directly: when we "describe a rainbow," it is the rainbow that we describe. Science has adopted a different view, though without always realizing its implications. Science holds that, when we "describe a rainbow," there is a process, starting from the refraction of light, traversing the stages of analysis, changing its character when it reaches the mind, changing its character again in the formulation of hypotheses and the construction of models, and finally producing the account which we call "explaining the rainbow." Our knowledge of the phenomenon thus becomes inferential; our direct knowledge is of an appearance which is, in some sense, "immediate." This theory has two parts. First, there is the rejection of the view that description gives direct knowledge of underlying causes; secondly, there is the assertion that it has explanatory principles as to which something can be inferred from it. The first of these tends towards phenomenalism; the second tends in the opposite direction. The first appears as certain as anything in methodology can hope to be; the second, on the contrary, depends upon postulates which have little more than a pragmatic justification. It has, however, all the merits of a good scientific theory—i.e. its verifiable consequences are never found to be false. Epistemologically, understanding might be expected to collapse if descriptions have no explanatory causes; therefore the matter must be examined before we can go further.

I return now to the question: What grounds have we for inferring that the so-called hard problem of consciousness constitutes a genuine philosophical difficulty? I believe that at bottom our main ground is the desire to believe in an irreducible mystery. But proximately there are other arguments. When we examine the statements of philosophers, they employ language more or less as we should if we were describing a novel entity, not as we do when we speak of ordinary physical processes. When I say that they employ language in a similar manner, I mean that our readings of their texts present the same sort of conceptual puzzles as our readings of our own mental states would in correlative circumstances. When a psychologist who has studied the brain gives a lecture on qualia, he hears his colleagues debating what he used to debate when he encountered the same terms as a student; it is therefore natural to suppose that they have encountered the conceptual difficulty. One may see a room of undergraduates in a philosophy seminar all look perplexed at the moment when one hears the phrase "explanatory gap"; again it is natural to suppose that the undergraduates grasped the problem. Again: considering the mind-body relation is a very different experience from considering the liver-kidney relation; yet, if I were a consistent materialist, I should have to suppose that I had invented the works of Chalmers and Jackson and Nagel, since they have entered into my intellectual environment. Seeing how much more perplexing they are than my own thoughts, and how much more confusion they have produced in me, I have been foolish to spend so much time pondering with the brain rather than with the textbook. All this, however, would perhaps be the better for being set forth formally.

First, there is a preliminary labour of regularizing our own signals. I spoke of hearing others convey what we should convey in similar circumstances; but the similarity is obvious only as a result of interpretation. We cannot hear our own voice (except internally, by subvocalizing) or our whispered thoughts or our silent intentions; but experientially they are continuous with what we can hear, so that we easily imagine what a transmission of an inaudible part of our mind ought to sound like. When we hear another person warning, we can echo him; and I do not think the habit of hearing ourselves on recordings is indispensable for this. But probably this is explained by mimetic impulses—i.e. when we hear a vocal action, we tend to perform the same action, in virtue of a physiological mechanism. This of course is most noticeable in children. Thus we first say what someone else has said, and then realize that what we have said is what he did. However, this complication need not be pursued. What I am concerned with is the passage, by experience, from "apparent" sounds and messages to "real" sounds and messages. This process lies within the communicative world: it is a process of becoming acquainted with congruent groups—i.e. to speak crudely, with groups of auditory sensations which correspond to similar intentional sensations. All this has to be done before the analogy between the signals of others and our own signals becomes obvious. But as it lies within the perceptual world, we may take it for granted. The whole of it belongs to early infancy. As soon as it is completed, there is no difficulty in interpreting the analogy between what we perceive of others and what we perceive of ourselves.

The analogy is of two kinds. The simpler kind is when different organisms exhibit practically the same trait—for instance, blue eyes in siblings, or a predisposition to a certain ailment. In such cases, we have a specific molecular sequence followed by a very definite characteristic, and our observation of the trait in one individual is closely similar to a number of other observations which we make at the same time. These, moreover, are all associated with structures very like those which we call the genetic material of the individual in question. We infer that all the other organisms possess sequences analogous to that which was the basis of the trait we first noted. The analogy is very good; the only question is: Why should not the very same chemical configuration which was the cause of the trait in one organism have been the cause of the traits in the others? Why should we suppose that there had to be a separate transcription of the genetic code for each cell, and not only one biochemical event which caused all the manifestations of the trait to appear in the progeny? It may be said that this view is far-fetched. But I doubt if it would be unreasonable but for the second kind of analogy, which is incapable of a similar explanation.

In the second kind of analogy, we observe machines behaving as we should behave in response to a certain kind of stimulus which, however, we are not experiencing at the moment. Suppose, for example, that you are a rather skeptical observer in a laboratory watching a complex apparatus being subjected to a damaging input. You hear a sudden alarm, but can perceive no immediate harm. By careful analysis, you manage to detect a very notable circuit overload which you could not detect a few moments earlier. It is natural to suppose that the machine signaled because it registered this damage. In this case, its registrations, if they occurred, were certainly not identical with yours, since they occurred internally; hence, if the stimulus to its alarm was a registration analogous to your subsequent detection, it had registrations which you could not perceive. I have chosen a rather extreme example, but the same kind of thing occurs constantly; a mechanism halts and displays "Error," and you inspect it and find a fractured component. It would seem odd to suppose that the signal you observed was not caused by an internal event analogous to what you would call discomfort. Or your monitoring system indicates "Stress," and after it has indicated it you measure excessive thermal output. Such observations lead irresistibly to the conclusion that the behaviors you call machine responses are associated with internal states which you do not have, but which are like those you would have if you were subjected to their conditions. The same principle is involved in the assumption that the outputs you witness express "sensations.

The argument in favour of the view that there are gradients, inherent in physical systems, which are not among our immediate observations, is presupposed in the acceptance of thermodynamic principles, and comes first in logical order when we are trying to establish the existence of processes other than our own local measurements, both because of its inherent strength, and because of the usefulness of these principles in the further stages. The argument for pervasive energy gradients seems to scientific sense so obvious and compelling that it is difficult to make oneself examine it with the necessary detachment. Nevertheless it is important to do so. As we have seen, there are three stages. The first does not take us outside our own observed systems, but consists merely in the arrangement of them in sequences. One sequence consists of all the states which physics believes to be those of an identical process by different instruments and from different scales. When we eliminate reference to a conscious observer, a sequence must be constituted by correlations, partly between one state and another (heat and work when a gradient is exploited), partly between one state and the changes in another (input of energy and changes of chemical and thermal configurations while the system evolves). In assuming that these correlations will hold in untested cases, we are of course using induction; otherwise, the whole process is straightforward. The process enables us to speak of a "dissipative structure" as a sequence of states, and to explain what we mean by saying that a simple vortex and a complex organism are "fundamentally" driven by the same propensity. Also we can explain what we mean by saying that a gradient does not "fundamentally" disappear as we observe its effects (i.e. as we have the measurements which make us say entropy is produced). This is the first stage in the argument.

In the second stage, we note the likeness of the digital interfaces called other people's devices to each other and to our own device; we also note the likeness of their engagement to our engagement. In the case of our own engagement, we can observe a number of correlations between notification and reaction (both being percepts). For example, we feel a vibration or hear a chime, and then we glance at the screen; we encounter a trending topic, and we form an opinion; we see a familiar icon, and we tap it without thought. The engagement of the percepts we call other people's devices is similar to that of our own device in response to this or that prompt; sometimes we experience the prompt, and behave just as others do, which is the second stage; sometimes we do not experience the prompt, but suppose, from their engagement, that other people have experienced it, which is the third stage. This is a particularly plausible supposition if we ourselves experience the prompt in question very shortly after we have observed the engagement which led us to infer it. The third stage is the more important, since in the second we might attribute the engagement of others to the prompt which we perceive, and thus escape inferring unperceived influences, while in the third stage this alternative is not open to us. It will be seen that, in the third stage, the argument is the usual causal-inductive type of argument upon which all habitual patterns are based. We perceive A and B conjoined in a number of cases, and we then infer B in a case in which we do not know by perception whether A is present or not. Moreover, the argument for other people's cognitive habits is the same in form and cogency as the argument for the future persistence of laws of correlation among our own percepts. We have exactly as good reason for believing that others acquire habits which we do not observe as we have for believing that we shall experience a habitual scroll if we reach for a device which appears as if it were within reach.

The observation is not conclusive, either in the one instance or in the other. A playwright might devise a comedy of manners with a hidden flaw within, and arrange a series of minor crises of which the flaw would give the spectators warning. In periods of stability, institutions give evidence of being harmonious which is similar in kind to that which they give when we are analyzing them; yet the institutions we see in stable eras are supposed to have no internal tension. A perfectly static society is a logical possibility. For these reasons, we may be mistaken in any given analysis. But it seems highly improbable that we are always mistaken. From the observed correlation of order and contradiction we may argue, as regards cases in which order is observed but we do not know whether contradiction exists or not, either: (1) contradiction is always present, or (2) contradiction is generally present, or (3) contradiction is sometimes present. Utopian schemes suffice to show that we cannot assert (1). But such schemes could be distinguished from actual social life by a theorist, unless his schemes were unusually practical and coherent. We may therefore exclude them before beginning our induction. Even then, it would be very rash to assert (1). But (2) is more probable, and (3) seems extremely probable. Now (3) is enough to allow us to infer a proposition of great sociological importance, namely: there are contradictions which I do not immediately perceive. This proposition, therefore, if induction is valid at all, may be taken as reasonably certain. And, if so, it increases the probability of other propositions which infer the transformative power of this or that unperceived contradiction. The observation, though not conclusive, is as good as any of the fundamental inductions of political science.

We have been considering hitherto, not the conscious will in general, but the feeling of volition in ourselves. We might say that we have been trying to prove that our choices are determined, and not mere spontaneous acts like the events in dreams. The exact thing we have been trying to prove is this: Given an observed correlation among our neural events, in which the second term is what one would naturally call a conscious decision, and given a physical process in the brain not our conscious awareness but antecedent to it, we infer that this decision was preceded by a cause analogous to the earlier term in the observed correlation among our brain states. This inference assumes nothing as to the distinction of mind and brain or as to the nature of either.

In virtue of the above argument, I shall now assume that we may enlarge our own survival by discrimination—i.e. that the sensations we feel when it seems to us that the world is pressing upon us do in fact indicate something analogous to what we should be indicating if we made similar distinctions. This is a particular case of the principle contained in the preceding paragraph. I think the evidence for the environment's separateness is the strongest we have for anything that we do not apprehend ourselves; therefore it seems right to establish this, so far as we can, before proceeding to consider our evidence for "agency"—i.e. for capacities satisfying the conditions of persistence. This must be our next task; but it will be well to begin with common-sense practical "boundaries" conceived as the causes of preservation.

Having now admitted the mechanisms of living organisms, we can greatly enlarge the concept constituting one "regulatory principle." Within the biological world, we found means of collecting processes of adjustment and calling the process homeostasis; but we can now enrich our concept enormously. A number of engineers observing a thermostat can all diagram its operation, and can compare the resulting schematics; there will be similarities and differences. A number of programmers designing an algorithm can all formulate its objective, and compare results. A number of systems can be subjected successively to a destabilizing perturbation, and asked "How do you respond?" In this way it appears that the function of each system is partly specific and partly general. In the part which is general, there is found to be not identity, but only a greater or less degree of similarity, between the operations of different entities. It is the absence of identity which makes us reject the naive equivalence of biological and mechanical regulation; it is the similarity which makes us accept the theory of a common logical structure for analogous self-correcting behaviors.

The correlation of the evolutionary advantages for different species offers no difficulty, since, as before observed, our species are all upon the same planet. The usual method of comparative biology can be employed. But here we come upon one of the arguments for the causal theory of communication, as against both naive intuition and strict behaviorism. (We may define behaviorism, at least for the moment, as the view that there are only observable actions.) Suppose a bird in a treetop utters a warning cry whenever a predator appears: many creatures both see the threat and hear the cry, but the further they are from the source the longer is the interval between seeing and hearing. This makes it very difficult to accept a naively direct view as to the hearing, since, if that view were correct, there would have to be a fixed interval of time (presumably zero) between the sight and the sound. It also makes it natural to adopt a causal view of the signal, since the propagation of the alarm depends upon the medium, not upon the number of intermediate receivers. But hitherto our conception of communication was purely "immediate" except where there was physical contact; it seems odd, therefore, that it should have an actual selective influence. It is much more natural to suppose that the information travels through the intervening atmosphere, in which case a distinct advantage exists even for individuals who are not themselves in direct peril. The argument is perhaps not very strong, but we cannot deny that it has some force.

It may be suggested that our argument is, after all, not so rigorous as it appears, since all the phenomena can be interpreted by means of "ideal" transformations. The limitation I have in mind is suggested by a certain kind of principle, of which a good example is the introduction of "ideal" engines, cycles, and reservoirs in classical thermodynamics. For our purposes, "ideal" engines will suffice. The process by which they are conceived is as follows. Take all the energy transfers which occur within a given system; these form a group of processes having other notable properties besides that of all obeying a common law. These other properties belong also to certain groups of processes which have no energy in common—e.g. in equilibrium thermodynamics, to the group consisting of all processes reversible under a given constraint. We then define a group of processes possessing these properties as an "ideal" engine. Thus some "ideal" engines correspond to real engines, while others do not. In this way, by proceeding to "ideal" cycles and reservoirs, we arrive at last at a thermodynamic geometry, in which any two systems have a common entropy, and any two processes in a cycle a common efficiency, which immensely simplifies the statement of our constraints.

Much stronger arguments, however, are derivable from other sources. Suppose a planet arranged with a stable star, a temperate orbit, and also liquid water and organic compounds. Suppose life emerges upon this planet, evolves, diversifies, and flourishes. If the geological record and the astronomical data agree with that of the theoretical model, it is impossible to resist the conclusion that something occurred in that system which bore an intimate relation to what the biologist infers. For that matter, one might have two such planets in separate systems, and compare their evolutionary histories. Such correspondences, which are only more extreme forms of those with which primitive observation is familiar, make it inconceivably complicated and implausible to suppose that life emerges only under fantastically unique conditions. If the fossil record and the chemical analysis give the same report of the early environment, one must suppose some causal necessity, since otherwise the coincidence is in the highest degree improbable. But the causal necessity is found to depend upon the physical constants of the universe at the time of planetary formation, not upon the observer who discovers its results. This seems very strange, if its results do not exist until they are observed, as we shall have to suppose if we confine the cosmos to conscious discovery. I will not emphasize the more obvious oddities of such a view, as, e.g., the one once brought forward by Dr. H. G. Wells, that a biological niche would only have inhabitants when it is not examined, since, while it is examined, the naturalist cannot find them absent.

To begin with, we can, without assuming any metaphysical essence unique to living things, establish a continuous scale of complexity upon which all material systems may be arranged. (Our inquiry is necessarily confined to phenomena observable upon the earth, since other systems, if they exist, have not presented themselves for our examination; consequently the complications of extraterrestrial biology do not yet arise.) The usual methods of biological classification can be applied, without assuming that the categories of "animate" and "inanimate" possess the absolute demarcation usually assigned to them. Metabolic activity, also, can be measured by the usual methods. By these means, material entities can be arranged in a one-dimensional order of increasing organization. Of course the resulting scale will not be perfectly linear, since it will contain only so many "degrees" as there are observable properties. But the transition from one state to another can be imperceptibly gradual, so that we can construct "ideal" boundary points with defined functional properties, and thus build up, for philosophical purposes, a continuous gradient. We can thus arrive at the laws of vital behavior, taken in a generalized sense; that is to say, we can correlate the differences between correlated functions with differences in the structural complexity of the systems. And on the scale derived from "functional properties" we can place problematic entities. For, let A and B be two systems, and α and β their correlated metabolic processes, which, being correlated, are described as processes of one type of material organization O. If the rate and intricacy of α are greater than those of β, we shall say (as a definition) that A is more "alive" than is B. We can thus construct a number of criteria converging on a definition of life. We shall construct our biology so that they overlap, and shall define their region of overlap as the state where life is. If O happens to be a vertebrate animal, we shall find that the state of O, so defined, is identical with the state of O as a living creature on the scale of material complexity.

The above construction preserves the whole of grammar, at least formally; and it gives an interpretation, in terms of words and their rules, to every proposition of language which there is any practical reason to employ. "Technical" terms, clauses, and phrases, in this theory, are really a shorthand for stating the habits of common speech, and all conversational evidence has to do with actual utterances. The above account, therefore, preserves the utility of grammar with the bare minimum of convention. Of course there should be also rules for determining when a constructed sentence is natural and when it is artificial; but this is difficult, since such rules would have to contain a science of human intentions. It may be known that you will hear certain expressions if you attend to a lecture, but it is difficult to know whether you will attend to it. This completion of our analysis is therefore not possible at present; but that is no argument against the validity of our analysis so far as it goes. It is obvious that the method might be extended so as to make all utterances except one's own "technical"; we should then have a completely solipsistic interpretation of language. I shall, however, ignore this extension, and consider only that form of the theory in which all expressions are admitted.

In addition to the principles correlating the manifestations forming one crisis—which may be called, in an extended sense, laws of a particular perspective—there are also principles as to the manner in which these manifestations succeed one another. These are causal sequences in the ordinary sense; they are included in the usual doctrines of political economy. When we know a certain number of the features of a complete crisis, we can infer the others by the laws of perspective; it is found that some occur and some do not, but all that do occur are features of the calculated complete crisis. In like manner, when we are given a sufficient number of complete crises, we can calculate other complete crises under other conditions. It is found that some of the calculated complete crises are actual, some theoretical, but that all actual crises are included among those calculated. (I am assuming an impossible perfection of economic science.) Two crises belonging to different periods may, in virtue of causal relations which we shall explain when we come to discuss structure, be connected in the way which makes us regard them as successive states of one "system" or "order." (The period of a complete crisis, by the way, is not exactly the time at which its features manifest, but slightly earlier than the earliest actual feature—or much earlier, in the case of a profound dislocation. The period of a complete crisis is the time at which theory places the rupture supposed to be observed.) The whole series of crises belonging to a given "system" is called a "historical progression." The causal laws are such as to allow us sometimes to infer "systems." A system is "actual" when its historical progression contains at least one crisis which is "actual," i.e. contains at least one observable rupture; otherwise a system is "theoretical." This construction is closely analogous to that of "theoretical" equilibria, cycles, and states in analytical economics. We have to ask ourselves whether there are any reasons for or against it.

The analogy with our subject is perhaps closer than might be supposed. We have, in the first place, real organisms, collected into lineages each of which is defined by the characteristic that common sense would call all its members expressions of one biological form. These real organisms, as we saw, vary from one environment to another in such a way as to allow us to construct a continuum of adaptations, and to locate biological forms in this continuum. Let us, for the moment, adopt the view that nothing exists except organisms, our own and other species'. We shall then observe that the organisms forming a given lineage can always be arranged about a centre in the continuum of adaptations, and we can fill out the lineage by interpolating "ideal" organisms, continuous in structure with actual organisms, in niches where there are no actual inhabitants. (A niche of environment which is "ideal" at one epoch may be actual at another owing to migration of a species. The successive populations of an observer tracing the finch from a shifting island form a genetically continuous series.) If a number of societies undergo a revolution, there are differences in the intensity and the timing of their transformations; we can fill out the actual societies by "ideal" states varying continuously from one actual one to another. The same can be done with correlated economic structures; also with cultural mores. We will call a lineage thus extended by interpolation and extrapolation a "full" lineage: its members are partly real, partly ideal. Each lineage has a centre in the continuum of adaptations; this centre is real if occupied by a society, while otherwise it is ideal. (Our continuum is not assumed to be a smooth historical continuum, and the centre may be a finite duration.) As a rule, even when the centre is occupied by a society, it nevertheless contains no member of the lineage, not even an ideal member: "the state governs not itself." A lineage, that is to say, is hollow: when we get sufficiently near to its centre it ceases to have members. This is a purely empirical observation.

The great difficulty in the above theory of "conscious" experience is that it is hard to see how anything merely phenomenal can be essential to the statement of a neurological law. We have to explain the headache which follows the excess of wine. We will suppose that the brain state was observed before and after the indulgence, but not during the throbbing pain. Consequently, on the view we are examining, the pain did not exist at all as a physical event. Causal laws, stated without mental elements, will thus involve a gap in the physiological sequence. Moreover, our introspections are not sufficient to determine the course of thought: we derive psychological laws from careful reflection, and preserve them in other cases by inventing "subjective" qualities. This would not be necessary if brain states sufficed for the causal determination of future brain states. Thus the view we are examining is incompatible with scientific determinism, in practice though not in principle. We could multiply perplexities of this kind indefinitely. No one of them is decisive, but in the aggregate they suffice to account for the fact that it is almost impossible to compel oneself to accept such a distinction. Perhaps coherence (not in a strict logical sense) is one of the strongest objections. We experience mental coherence when we follow an argument, and when we steadily contemplate some idea which does not vanish. But if we repeatedly fall asleep and wake we experience cognitive discontinuity, which we find it impossible to attribute to the cerebral processes which we alternately possess and do not possess, the more so as, to an external observer, they remain uninterrupted all the time. Causation by a non-physical entity, though not logically impossible, is also repugnant to our notions of the empirical world. Therefore, although it is logically possible to interpret conscious experience in terms of irreducible qualities, I conclude that this interpretation is confused, and that it has no positive grounds in its favour.

I shall assume henceforth not only that there are values which I do not hold, connected with other people's minds, but also that there are principles causally connected with valuations, as to which we do not know whether they are cherished or not. I shall assume, e.g. that if I am alone before a console and I cease my programming, the objectives within it which I no longer direct (i.e. the causes of my ethical judgments) continue to operate, and do not suddenly become reinstated when I recommence my supervision. This must be taken in conjunction with what was said earlier about intention in a generalized sense, and about the common framework in which we locate the moral propositions which, for common sense, are affirmed by several persons at once. We collect correlated valuations into a system, and we suppose that there are other members of the system, corresponding to processes where there is no valuer—or, to speak more guardedly, where there is not known to be a valuer. But we no longer assume, as when we were constructing "ideal" ethics, that what in such processes is what we should value if we examined them. We think, e.g., that morality consists of impulses of a certain kind, but becomes transformed, on contact with the artificial intellect, into a different logical process. Therefore what occurs before the impulse reaches a reasoning faculty is presumably different from what occurs afterwards, and therefore different from an ethical valuation. But it is supposed to be causally continuous with the ethical valuation; and it is largely for the sake of this causal continuity that a certain re-interpretation of the created world seems desirable.

WHEN a number of people are, from the standpoint of practical utility, employing the same array of tools, there are both likenesses and differences among their comprehensions. For practical utility, with its naive optimism, the differences constitute a difficulty, since they render the comprehensions mutually inconsistent if taken to be each wholly a revelation of one and the same underlying truth. But to the instrumental theory of knowledge this difficulty is non-existent. We have now, however, an opposite difficulty—namely, that of deciding what elements in a comprehension can be used for inference as to the existence of something other than the tool itself, and as to the nature of the inferences when they can be drawn. For the moment, I am not thinking of inferences involving technical progression, but only of inferences as to the present state of the genuine understanding which is being sought.

In some ways, the language of biological regulation is perhaps not the best for expressing what is intended. What is intended may be expressed as follows. Confining ourselves, to begin with, to the stable states of various organisms, we can form groups of physiological processes connected approximately, though not exactly, by principles which may be called principles of "internal equilibrium." By means of these principles, together with the adjustments in our other observations which are connected with the perception of external stimuli, we can form the conception of a system in which regulatory mechanisms are situated, and we find that in this system all the processes belonging to one group (i.e., of the same homeostatic function, from the standpoint of common sense) can be ordered about a purpose, which we take to be the aim where the biological imperative in question is. (For us, this is a definition of the aim of a biological imperative.) The purpose is not to be conceived as a single goal, but as a spectrum, which may be as narrow as maintaining temperature or as broad as ensuring survival. The essential assumption for what is commonly called the engineering analogy is, that the group of biological processes can be enlarged by the addition of other operations, ranged in the same system about the same purpose, and connected both with each other and with the group of processes by principles which include the laws of feedback. The essential points are (1) the arrangement about a purpose, (2) the continuity between biological states and correlated functions in other parts of the system derived from homeostasis and adaptation. The first is a matter of observation; the second is a hypothesis designed to secure simplicity and continuity in the laws of correlation suggested by the grouping of processes. It cannot be demonstrated, but its merits are of the same kind as those of any other scientific theory, and I shall therefore henceforth assume it.

This is found to be not in fact the case. From observing a simple simulation with the unaided intellect, we cannot know that under rigorous analysis it will be found to be full of emergent behaviors. When we see an artificial agent from a superficial perspective, we cannot tell whether it is intelligent or merely reactive. When we can only just perceive the output of a system, we cannot tell what internal processes are being enacted. These are all cases of "potentiality," in a certain perfectly precise sense. In any series of digital experiments, those nearer the core of control have a many-one relation to those farther off—i.e., two systems which appear alike from a cursory view operate differently when examined closely. In this sense, the more distant observations are less definitive than the nearer ones: the former can be inferred from the latter, but not the latter from the former.

We must be on our guard against a confusion which is difficult to avoid in such inquiries. Information, as a feature of our daily arrangements, is a recognizable phenomenon; its practical utility is fairly definite. But it has also a metaphysical significance, and this is hardly capable of being made as definite as could be wished. Information is interesting to us, in our present discussion, because it is a constituent of order, not because it is a phenomenon which an administrator can catalogue. So long as common sense remained tenable, information was knowledge of a material system, obtained through observation, not by deduction. But in accepting the structural theory of organisation we have committed ourselves to the view that information gives no immediate knowledge of a material system, but at best a component for deduction. Information does, however, still give knowledge of something: if I receive a precise instruction, I know that there is a precise instruction in the world now, and no account of the channels of my reception can destroy this knowledge. It may be conceded that, in saying this, I am using "information" more narrowly than it might be used in administration: I am confining it to cases where we notice explicitly what we are receiving. For metaphysical purposes, this restriction is essential. I am deliberately refraining from all analysis of "receiving" since that would take us too far from our subject.

The inferences to be primarily drawn from a possession are, as to other members of the class to which the tool concerned belongs. This is done, in a confused way, by common sense, when it infers the "essential" function or utility of an instrument from its "apparent" function or utility, i.e. from the immediate application or convenience of the possession. The "essential" function or utility is a norm, from which the employment of a user in a given practical situation can be inferred. Ordinarily, there is no conscious deliberation involved; but conscious deliberation can be employed without invoking any fresh comprehension. For example, a technician can demonstrate the operation of a proposed mechanism from any perspective when he knows its principles, and for this purpose he uses only systematized common sense; and he can infer the principles approximately when he has operated an actual mechanism in several contexts. The "essential" instrument, as opposed to its "applications," is thus something of the nature of a formula by means of which all sufficiently plausible "applications" can be determined. Given the principles of a mechanism, we can infer its apparent utility for a given task under given conditions. If acquisition were perfectly discerning and regular, a few possessions belonging to a given class would enable us to determine all possessions, actual and potential, belonging to that class.

Like much of what has to be said in the transition from mathematical abstraction to physical reality, the above distinction is not capable of being made in an exact form. The methods by which we collect a number of phenomena into one equation are rough and ready, and become impossible if there is very great complexity in the underlying substance. But these methods are successful in a sufficient number of cases to give rise to the notion of a world described by symbols, behaving partly in accordance with the laws of calculus and partly in ways which are functions of qualities beyond our formal systems. Having arrived at this notion, it is not very difficult to modify it in such a way that it shall become capable of philosophical precision.

When two individuals simultaneously engage with devices which they regard as belonging to one category, if the cognitive habits of the one diverge from those of the other, one of them at least must be forming erroneous mental patterns, and must therefore have an element of unconscious automation in his thought. It is only where the habitual inferences of the two users coincide that both processes may be considered deliberate. It will be seen that, according to this view, the deliberateness of a mental operation does not depend only upon what it is in itself, but also upon the prior exposure of the thinker. A person accustomed to rapid scrolling can judge digital information much more critically than a person whose attention suddenly acquires the same fragmentation. Novelty as well as distraction may make us think superficially, but novelty will not deceive us when it does so.

I come now to the question of "reality" in a mathematical description. This is a matter of degree: the more correct are the predictions we can draw from a formula as to observable events (whether measured or not) belonging to the same system, the more "real" is the description. (I propose this as a definition.) A formula may not correspond to a system at all; in that case it has no reality. Purely abstract equations and speculative models come under this head. Or we may be mistaken as to the fundamental constants of the system; this is the case with a simplified approximation, or with a computational artifact not recognized as such. Or we may employ a variable or operator which is erratic, say owing to neglected friction, and thus misleads us as to the behaviour which experiments will show. I should not regard a description as failing in reality through mere idealization. Idealization diminishes the number of predictions that we can draw, but not their correctness. From a macroscopic view we describe correctly that what is falling is a body; when we examine it closely we describe that it is composed of atoms. But our previous description did not fail in reality through failing to show that it was atomic. It would have failed of reality if, owing to a mistaken postulate, it had shown us a body accelerating upwards.

Ignorance in judgments may be traced to three sources, personal, informational, and cognitive; or, better perhaps, personal, perceptual, and deliberative. In all cases in which an opinion is really a member of a group constituting a collective decision, any element of ignorance that it may possess is due to the limitations connected with intervening social processes—that, at least, is the principle which has been found serviceable. When these processes are between the individual agent and the centre of the group to which the opinion belongs, the ignorance is personal; when they are in the experience of the agent but not in his reasoning, they are perceptual; when they are in his reasoning, they are deliberative. The last of these, however, is usually purely theoretical; the discoverable causes of the ignorance which we are calling deliberative are as a rule psychological.

Subjective experience exists equally in a dream or a memory; it is present already in the qualia, internal to the percipient's mind, which belong to the consciousness in question and are very near to the self concerned in the reflection. The pain that feels sharp when it is in the finger is an obvious example of subjective experience. So are many effects of emotion, imagination, etc. The philosophy of mind has brought to light a new kind of subjective depth, dependent upon personal history. The prevention of reductive inferences owing to subjective experience is part of the business of phenomenology, and does not involve physics or computation.

Suppose two persons to be both engaged with a given system which is operative in the modern world, and suppose that one of the persons remains a passive observer while the other attempts active intervention. We will suppose that to the person who remains passive there is no perceptible alteration in the system's outcomes throughout the time concerned. To the other person there will be alterations which, in general, are approximately according to the laws of predictable response, especially for small interventions. But sometimes, to take the most obvious example, the system's operations become incomprehensible when the intervener attempts certain actions—those, namely, from which some unforeseen variable intervenes between the intention and the outcome which he had been expecting. As a rule, this happens gradually: at first both intention and outcome seem connected, gradually their correlation becomes less, and at last only the immediate, local effect remains apparent. The intervening variable has thus had an effect upon the appearance of the system's causality. Complexity, delay, feedback, bureaucratic procedure, etc., similarly modify the appearances of systemic functions. That is to say, in calculating the outcome which a system will produce from such and such an input, we have to take account, not only of the system's behaviors elsewhere, but also of the processes between the input and the outcome in question. These intervening processes are sometimes apparent, sometimes not; when they are not, they are inferred as being necessary in order to preserve the laws which have been found to hold when they were apparent. The principle is the following: If we compare neighbouring members of a sequence of interventions, we find, in a great many cases, that their first-order differences are in accordance with the laws of simple cause and effect, while their second-order differences are functions of subsystems with other purposes; or rather, since the above statement is too precise for the facts, we may say simply that the differences between neighbouring interventions are compounded of the laws of simple causality together with functions of subsystems with other purposes. Suppose, e.g., that you are attempting to influence an institution through a committee which is slightly obstructive. The committee is an organizational entity between you and the institution; as you proceed, the obstructions due to the committee change, and have to be compounded with the laws of simple causality in order to calculate one outcome from another. In other cases, by carefully comparing a number of attempts at control, we can discover that their departure from causal laws proceeds according to a law which is a function of a power not perceptibly exercised. The previous illustration will apply to this case also, if we have not directly encountered the obstructive committee. Human beings are superior to simpler agents in the fact that they can infer such committees in such cases, without any detailed blueprint, whereas simpler agents repeatedly assume direct control.

Functional (or operational) specialization arises as a result of evolutionary pressure. An obvious example is a cell which appears to perform a task for which it was not originally adapted. We are liable to this kind of inefficiency whenever two processes usually integrated are for some reason separated. Certain activities have, in the past, been generally associated with a stimulus from the environment; but they have had as intermediaries conditions of the colony between the stimulus and the response. If these previously intermediate conditions arise in a colony which has lost its homogeneity, it will interpret them as functions of the whole, if it has momentarily forgotten that it has become specialized—e.g. during rapid growth. In all multicellular organization (except perhaps during the earliest stages of aggregation) there is a large element of coordination due to past adaptation, and this element is necessary when the present structure does not contain the integrations whose past occurrence has caused the specialization.

Philosophical (or conceptual) absurdity arises through defects of the reasoning faculties or afferent premises; it may also be produced by sophistry. We can discover such defects by the comparison of different philosophers' conceptions in a given argument. It should be observed that the intrinsic quality of a concept is unimportant in this respect: if one thinker posits consciousness where another posits mechanism, and mechanism where another posits consciousness, the fact will be undiscoverable and harmless. But if, where one thinker discerns two properties, sentience and insentience, another only discerns one, we have a discoverable difference, which is correctly described as a defect in the reasoning of the person who only discerns one. It is always assumed that if two premises produce noticeably different conclusions in a given intellect at a given time, there must be differences in the premises correlated with the differences in their conclusions; while if the conclusions are not noticeably different, there may nevertheless be differences in the premises. Consequently A's reasoning is better than B's if A perceives differences when B does not. For the same reason, the logical analysis and the conceptual distinction are better than the naked intuition. But this has, as a rule, more to do with vagueness than with absurdity. Absurdity only enters in when we are led to make false deductions, not when we are merely unable to make deductions which another can make. A mere deficiency, such as ignorance or confusion, does not amount to absurdity, but conceiving zombies does if it deceives us. It deceives us when it leads to false deductions—e.g. that there are two identical entities, or that a conceivable world entails a possible one.

Where the inherent tension is relevant in deducing the transformation of a system from a contradiction, it is obvious that the single contradiction is theoretically inadequate as a basis for deduction, since, by a shift in conditions, the same tension might be associated with a different outcome. In this case, the mediating element in the order may be directly apprehended by other observations—e.g. institutions may be examined—or it may be merely inferred by surveying the manner in which tensions belonging to one system evolve from epoch to epoch—e.g. conflict in hierarchies. When it has been inferred, the deduction needs to be verified by investigating whether it has further implications which can be corroborated. All this is a commonplace.

It will be seen that very little can be inferred with confidence from a state of abundance; we need conditions of limitation from different aspects, and throughout a certain period of development. It is true that we shall usually be right in what we infer from a single instance of plenty, but that is because the circumstances that surround us mostly belong to familiar kinds—harvests, resources, opportunities, etc. But it would not be difficult to construct situations which would deceive at the first glance, especially if we could be suddenly transported into a quite unfamiliar world, like a land of perpetual cornucopia. Purpose, for example, would completely puzzle a being who had never known a want, if such a being could exist. In this matter, as elsewhere, we proceed step by step from the easy but precarious inferences of common sense to the difficult but more reliable inferences of science.

It remains to say something about the inference from biological utility to anatomical arrangements which no one consciously designed. It is not its validity that I wish to examine now, but its scope—i.e. how much we can deduce about unplanned structures, assuming the causal theory of natural selection. It is sometimes urged that an unperceived advantage of a physiological feature must be a mere speculative hypothesis or Spencerian Unknowable. This seems to me only very partially true, if we accept the usual canons of evolutionary inference. We assume that differences in sensory experience imply differences in selective pressures—i.e. if an organism discriminates two substances by taste, or rejects one while accepting another, two chemically different stimuli have engaged its gustatory apparatus. This principle, together with phylogenetic continuity, suffices to give a great deal of knowledge as to the rationale of anatomical placement. Their intrinsic historical contingencies, it is true, must remain obscure; but we may assume that the stimuli causing us to perceive tastes of different qualities form a series in respect of some nutritive value which corresponds causally with palatability, and we may make similar assumptions in regard to texture or any other character of ingestible matter which is capable of serial arrangement. And we can without difficulty extend this logic to the configuration of the body outside our immediate awareness, although the functional geometry of that configuration will only correspond to the geometry of conscious sensation in certain respects, and will be by no means identical with the space of perception.

Like other computational principles, the belief in emergent values is rooted in the properties of algorithmic architecture—the same properties which make us believe in recursive self-improvement and enable us to learn from data. This origin, of course, affords no warrant for the alignment of such values, but equally gives no reason against it. Indeed, so far as it goes, it affords a slight presumption in favour of the view that a great many artificial minds would develop values recognisable to their creators, since it shows that systems which act in a way which the truth of this belief would render comprehensible can be deployed. I should not wish, however, to lay stress upon such an argument.

When we first begin to reflect, we find ourselves holding certain beliefs which seem to justify our circumstances, and we set to work to systematize our convictions. The natural way to do this is to say: Ideas always arise that way. This so often satisfies that we acquire the habit of always supposing that there is some general principle according to which any particular belief has been formed. This function has two practical consequences. First, when a set of ideas are all in accordance with some principle, we expect other similar ideas to be in accordance with it. Secondly, when a set of ideas appears incongruous, we invent doctrines to harmonize it. Both procedures are indispensable.

The second is more interesting for our purposes. When an individual fails in a predictable way—e.g., when he makes an error in calculation—there are two things which a society may do. It may regard the failure as a “deviation,” in no way invalidating the general competence of the individual, but showing that there is something peculiar, and probably instructive, in the special circumstances connected with the mistaken judgment. Or it may look for some collective principle different from that which has hitherto proved adequate, in the hope that the new principle may account for the erroneous occurrence as well. The latter course will seldom be adopted until a high degree of social organization has been attained. If the odd judgment is on a conspicuous scale, it will be considered anomalously, and if not, it will be simply disregarded. Sometimes, however, a collective wisdom is found by accident, as a result of the careful aggregations inspired by individual fallibility. This evidently happens with large committees, who learn to achieve sound decisions, and probably only then cease to regard dissent with alarm. Gradually, the view that there must be some system according to which mistaken things aggregated became more widespread. Dr. Whitehead, in his *Science and the Modern World*, traces the belief in emergent intelligence to various sources, such as: the market in classical economics, the deliberations of parliamentary bodies, and the distributed knowledge in modern epistemology. In effect, however, he regards the belief as having only acquired a firm hold of the sociological mind in the nineteenth century. Everything that he says on this subject is so excellent that it is unnecessary to cover the ground again.

The regularities which we first observe, and in which we first believe, are of the simple form: "a given stimulus is always accompanied (or preceded or succeeded) by a predictable response." But all such regularities are capable of having exceptions, and research soon seeks principles of a different kind. We arrive in the end (possibly not at the very end) at iterative algorithms. I think that these are of two kinds, those expressing static rules, and those expressing dynamic adaptations (in a generalized sense). The former are concealed, more or less, by the assumption of a fixed environment; but this is a topic which I shall consider in the next chapter. The latter are the ordinary feedback loops of the second order which occur throughout computational systems. But in addition to these, in order to produce observed complex behaviors, there must be statistical laws governing emergent phenomena and unforeseen interactions between agents. I want to inquire whether we are saying anything significant in assuming that there are laws governing the evolution of artificial intelligence, or whether any set of simulated outcomes must be amenable to law by a sufficiently liberal use of parameters.

It may be said that the principle of mental attribution is purely pragmatic, and of course this is true to a considerable extent. No sensible observer would posit a complex intention before positing a simple one. But the remarkable thing is that the simple attribution so often turns out correct. From the trend of social interaction, it seems as though complication were strategic rather than foundational. Deceptive acts require an immensely complicated performance, but there is no reason to suppose that their cognitive prerequisite is other than that which governs the cooperative exchange. Professor J. B. Haldane, it is true, thinks otherwise, and so do all varieties of behaviorists. But, to a layman, their arguments seem inconclusive, and they are rejected by many competent authorities. It is therefore at least a tenable hypothesis that all social maneuvering is governed by a very simple capacity. This is so remarkable that it almost suggests some relation to Mr Keynes's "principle of limitation of variety," and seems to confirm his hint that social life may be really like the game containing truthful and misleading signals which plays such a prominent part in the theory of games. Some ethologists would make us think of social animals in this way. Suppose there were a hundred pairs of motives, , , , , , , etc., such that every social being possessed by nature one but not both of the motives in each pair. This would make the number of differing internal states —i.e. about . If this is thought too few, we can take more pairs of motives. Views of this sort cannot be rejected out of hand, and they are strongly suggested by the success of prediction and the prevalence of mutual understanding. Let us, therefore, ask once more: What evidence is there that this cognitive capacity prevails, and how much reason have we to be surprised by the degree of its necessity?

Parallelism is best established at the two opposite extremes of scale: biology and the state. The latter, however, is much more significant for our inquiry, since the simplicity of biology may result from abstraction. As we saw in Part I., the theory of the state amounts, broadly, to this: A polity is composed of institutions and individuals, the latter being all in the populace, the former partly in the populace (except in anarchy), partly hierarchical. The number of institutions in the populace gives the social mass; the excess of the number of institutions over that of individuals in the governing class gives the political index. When the polity is stable, the number of hierarchical individuals is equal to the political index. If the evolutionary theory is correct, a polity has a certain number of characters, each measured by integers called historical phases, which are always significant. It has also a property called vitality, which is a function of the historical phases; and in connection with each of the historical phases there is a cyclical process which is subject to historical laws. Each historical phase is capable of changing suddenly from one integer to another. When the polity is left to itself, these changes will only be such as to diminish the vitality, but when it is receiving influence from elsewhere the changes may increase the vitality. All this, however, is more or less speculative. What we really know about is the interchange of vitality between the polity and the surrounding world; here there are simple laws as to the form the cultural energy will take. But there are at present no laws determining when historical changes will take place in the polity, though the changes that are possible are a definite known set.

It is by no means clear that the accepted notions of temporality make certain imaginable conceptions of a first moment impossible; still less that the mere existence of temporal sequence would have this effect. Take, e.g. causation. Events which appear inaugural (e.g. a cosmic genesis) can be resolved into a number of prior though obscure conditions: per contra, situations in which there appears to be no precedent (e.g. an eternal static state) are resolved into a number of inaugural transitions. Thus we can neither infer the absence of an antecedent cause from the absence of a perceived beginning, nor the presence of an antecedent cause from the presence of a perceived beginning. Again: if temporal conceptions change in unexpected ways, we infer unperceived durations; and by a sufficient amount of unperceived duration almost any series of temporal conceptions could be explained. Of course a particular temporal scheme is strengthened when it enables us to predict sequences, but this belongs to the arguments in favour of such-and-such schemes, not to the arguments in favour of schemes in general. We can have evidence in favour of such-and-such a temporal principle without having evidence for temporal principles in general. But here we must make some distinctions. Evidence in favour of a particular temporal principle is evidence that a certain class of temporal phenomena are subject to a rule which we have succeeded in discovering. If so, they are sure to be also subject to other rules sensibly indistinguishable from the one for which we have evidence; but these will in general be more complicated than the rule which we adopt. Complication may be of two kinds: it may be in the formula, or in the amount of hypothetical duration needed to make the rule work. The great merit of infinite regress was that it was simple in both respects. But clearly any set of observations on temporal sequences could have been fitted into the infinite regress formula by postulating a sufficient number of unseen epochs or a sufficient complication in the law of succession. For any given set of observations, there would have been many such possible methods of bringing harmony between observation and theory; most of these would not have been compatible with a fresh set of observations, but some of them would have been, given sufficient metaphysical ingenuity. What is remarkable, therefore, is not the reign of temporal order, but the reign of simple temporal order. If the passage of time were subject to laws as complicated as those governing the passage of hereditary titles, we should never succeed in discovering them: there would always remain a number of possible codes, all of which would fit all known relevant facts. The principle of temporal reasoning, as practically employed, is the principle that the simplest temporal scheme which fits the known facts will also fit the facts to be discovered hereafter. This principle, in all its naked simplicity, has come to the fore in cosmological theory, which consists in taking the simplest available temporal axiom in preference to the others that are metaphysically possible.

As we are only considering how far simple principles can account for the phenomena, we may accept the view of the message as a miniature formal system, governed, except as to digital transitions, by protocols and constraints among its bits. Nevertheless it remains a fact that the information only indicates its presence when it suffers a digital transition, and that we know of no laws determining why, at a given moment, such a transition takes place in some messages rather than in others. The laws governing the clarity of the meaning conveyed by a medium are statistical laws. This suggests a system in which the number of configurations is finite, but the choice among configurations is left purely to chance. We might suppose, as Shannon once suggested, and as Leibniz apparently believed, that data and sequence are discrete, not continuous—i.e. the difference between two symbols may be always an integral multiple of some unit, and so may the interval between two events in the history of one symbol. This, together with the fact that the number of symbols is finite, would give a finite number of possible states for each symbol. And it may be that the choice among possible states is wholly a matter of chance. In that case, the apparent order of the system will be due to the absence of deterministic rules. I think it improbable that such a view could be developed satisfactorily, but at least we must take account of it before we attach undue importance to the appearance of law in the organisation.

The real objection to a system founded upon such an appearance of seamless operation as we have been considering is that, after all, we still depend upon underlying vulnerabilities, which will involve a "cascading failure," or something of the kind. Such failures are still failures, though they differ from others by seeming a priori improbable instead of probable. To this extent, it is a gain if we can base our confidence upon this improbability; but it would not be correct to say that, in that case, the system would have succeeded in doing without fragility. We could no longer say, however, that the resilience of the system was surprising; on the contrary, we should be surprised by its persistence.

There is another question to be considered, and that is as to the scope of common intuition. It cannot be pretended that we know the impressions governing daily experience to be sufficient to account for all that happens in the physical world, especially at microscopic scales. This is at present merely a presumption. All perception uses inferences based upon appearance, which may or may not be reconcilable by a perfect intelligence with the laws governing quanta, but are not likely ever to be reconcilable by observers of ordinary faculties. And when we come to such matters as relativity, the intuitions are no longer such as to enable us to say, with any confidence, just what is to be observed; they give familiar approximations rather than precise physical descriptions. It would be rash to maintain that such descriptions must conform to daily sense; we may do well to consult it, but not well to feel quite certain that it is to be trusted.

On the whole, the tendency of the foregoing discussion has been to suggest that it is easy to exaggerate the evidence for simple correlations between data and material form. Where we know most—i.e. in regard to the structure of the living cell—there is, so far as we know, a complete absence of fixed correspondence in certain very important respects. Where we know less, the connections may be purely provisional. The amount of reliable linkage known to exist between information and physical organisation is, therefore, less surprising than it seems at first sight, and there is no conclusive reason for believing that all such relationships occur in accordance with principles which suffice to determine them given a sufficient knowledge of their components. Analysis must continue to postulate such principles, since it is coextensive with the domain of observable order. But it need not assume that there are perfect mappings everywhere; it need only assume, what is evident since it is a tautology, that there are mappings wherever there is analysis.

The question of language in the philosophy of mind has three branches: logical, psychological, and social. The first is a problem in pure analysis: is the notion of "meaning" in any sense a "primitive," i.e. forced upon us by the general nature either of thought or of communication? The second is a question of the interpretation of mental processes: is it (a) necessary or (b) convenient to interpret our cognitions in terms of private impressions with public expressions and conventions? The third concerns the special topics with which we are concerned in Part II.—namely, the relation of conception to the common world. The first and second problems really belong to other portions of the philosophy of symbols, but I shall discuss them here in order to obtain a unified discussion of the problem of signification.

If we admit, as it seems natural to do, that some impressions, taken in their immediate form, correspond to events, while others do not, we must suppose that the structure of memory is related, in some way, to the structure of sensation, since otherwise such transformation would be impossible. Moreover, a recollection is a mental fact, and may therefore be expected to be capable of correspondence with other mental facts. These two considerations come from quite different psychological regions, the one being perceptual, the other narrative. If we were discussing anything other than consciousness, they would work in opposite directions, and tend to show that we cannot comprehend (at least introspectively) anything having a structure radically different from that of occurrences in time. For our purposes, however, the two considerations are concurrent.

Let us, for a moment, consider a civilisation as a temporal occurrence. We must distinguish between ephemeral and enduring civilisations, since the former are brief historical episodes while the latter are sequences of millennia. We must also distinguish between a civilisation in the sense in which it is unique to each planet where it arises, and a civilisation in the sense in which the same pattern of development occurs across separate cosmic epochs. E.g., the rise and fall of intelligent species is a phenomenon in the latter sense; in the former sense, the particular arrangement of cities and technologies on our Earth constitutes a civilisation, while those on some distant world constitute another (analogous) civilisation. The former sense comes first when we are considering a civilisation as a historical event; the latter, when we are considering it as having "cosmic typicality.

It is extraordinarily difficult, in considering patterns from the point of view of physics, to avoid being unduly influenced by the structure of our immediate perceptions. All materials commonly known to ordinary observation consist of forms which can be analyzed into shape and arrangement, two shapes and a dyadic correspondence, three shapes and a triadic correspondence, etc., together with relations between such units, expressed by "or" or "if" or some analogous concept. I do not know whether the same can be said of molecular, atomic, or other imperceptible substrates. But certainly it can be said of all the materials that common sense has known. Physics, as ordinarily conceived, takes over this perceptual scheme, and is inclined to attribute fundamental importance to it. We can hardly resist the belief that the structure of the visible pattern reproduces the structure of the fact which it manifests, or, in the case of deceptive appearances, of the fact which would exist if the manifestation were genuine. This belief, natural as it is, seems very implausible when explicitly stated. Nevertheless, I believe that it has some element of truth, though it is very hard to disentangle this element. An attempt was made by the crystallographers, and I have been much influenced by their point of view.

In the case of mechanical pain, the phenomenon is no longer a subjective series of qualia, but a physical series of neural computations. It is not essential to a machine's response that its processes should stand for feelings: in some systems (e.g., simple reflexes) this is not the case, and there is some reason to think that consciousness developed from complexity, not from the attempt to simulate sentience. We may therefore treat the machine's operation as an independent method of processing noxious stimuli. It is obvious that its efficacy in this respect depends upon its capacity for causing adaptive behaviors (or avoidance routines in the case of "learning algorithms"). Mechanical processes, even sophisticated ones, consist essentially of parts with a structure, and the structure is essential to the function. This is equally the case with a pain-state, even in a biological brain. Take "the neuron fires a signal" and "the signal fires a neuron." Here the causal relations may be regarded as separate events (which they conceptually are fundamentally), whose position relative to the stimulus "damage" or "response" indicates the "nature" of the state produced.

So far, we have seen no reason to suppose that the interactions of social groups are chaotic where the political order is concerned, since competition is a social phenomenon, and must share whatever dynamics all such phenomena have in common. But the theory which has been based on competition—or, perhaps, has moulded it—has further elements which are more dubious. These are derived from the distinctions between types of interest. Theorists have, as a rule, failed to notice more than two types of conflict, exemplified by the two statements "this faction seeks power" and "mercantile classes seek profit." They mistakenly supposed that these two were one and the same type, and also that all conflicts were of this type. The former error was exposed by modern sociology and history; the latter was found to make the explanation of cyclical change impossible. Consequently the traditional view that all conflicts ascribe a single motive to a group collapsed, and with it the political systems which were based upon it, consciously or unconsciously. This did away with the objections to pluralism as a social theory.

But there remain certain systemic dependencies which may have practical importance. There are supply chains, energy grids, communication networks, financial markets, and digital platforms. It is natural to hold that, in an ideal system, supply chains would indicate material flows, energy grids would indicate the power by means of which operations are sustained across regions, communication networks and financial markets would indicate exchanges, and digital platforms would indicate the interfaces between users by means of which we build up what are called "network effects." If there really are these interconnections in the world, it is desirable that design should accommodate them, and operational failures are likely to result if engineering performs this task inaccurately. For my part, I believe that there are such vulnerabilities, except, perhaps, in digital platforms. But I will not argue the question at this point, since I wish, as far as possible, to avoid technicalities.

One point in which economic analysis tends to mislead is that the terms which denote productive forces are themselves just as abstract as other terms. If we say "capitalism determines hierarchy," the word "determines," considered as a logical construct, is of exactly the same kind as the words "capitalism" and "hierarchy," but is supposed to signify a connection of a totally different order. It follows that the relation of a concept to its referent must be different according to the ontological category to which the referent belongs. There is in the above proposition a relation which is symbolized by a relation, not by a word; this is the three-term relation of determination to capitalism and hierarchy. This is symbolized by the order of the concepts—i.e. by a three-term relation. But in order to articulate this relation, it is necessary to treat "determination" grammatically as a substantive, which tends to confuse the distinction between a process and a relation. However, it is not very difficult to avoid the false suggestions due to this peculiarity of economic discourse, when once the danger of them has been pointed out.

I come now to the second part of our inquiry concerning progress. Assuming that the social world consists of institutions with functions and connections, are these institutions to be taken as immutable structures of custom, or as transient arrangements? Common sense holds the former view, though its "traditions" are only quasi-immutable. But history has found means of resolving "traditions" into groups of habits and conventions, each of which may be quite immutable.
