As we saw in Part I., there are some who think that a habit and a convention can annihilate each other, so that even they are not quite immutable. But the question of immutability is not the one which most concerns us. The question is: Are habits and conventions part of the ultimate fabric of society, or are they groups of changes, or causal laws of changes?

A modern bureaucracy, considered practically, is a series of procedures from the point of view of the functionary, and a series of outputs from the point of view of the citizen. The "efficacy" of the system depends upon the intentions of the administrators and the consequences for the administered.[53] But for the moment let us ignore "efficacy." Then we find that the bureaucracy consists essentially of rules in sequence: the sequence is as essential as the character of the rules. (In a system like a small workshop, this is not so true of the separate tasks as in a vast corporation, but it is just as true of the stages of processes: "input reviewed" is a different stage from "reviewed input.") Considered as practical occurrences, the actions fulfilling different functions are indistinguishable; nevertheless there are relations which are symbolized by relations among forms, not by forms. Consider "the committee approves the budget" and "the budget approves the committee." The difference between these two statements is indicated, in a procedural manual, not by a directive, but by a relation among directives. Thus a functioning bureaucracy consists of certain protocols in a certain procedural order. In the system, we can distinguish elements and relations: the elements are the protocols (or, more strictly, the elementary procedures which, in an organizational chart, would each be represented by a separate box), and the relations are hierarchical relations among offices. According to our definition, the elementary procedures composing the system may count as "substances," in spite of the fact that they are mutable.

The substitution of independent inquiry for passive acceptance has made it much more natural than formerly to conceive intellectual progress as a series of challenges to dogma. Philosophy starts, nowadays, from a manifold of sceptical questions, not, as formerly, from a temporal series of received doctrines, connected with each other by the conception of authoritative tradition. Instead of an immutable edifice of belief, we have now the conception of an "advancement of understanding," which is a series of insights connected with each other in a certain way. The parts of one line of reasoning are connected with each other in a manner which enables us to consider them as forming, together, one coherent argument; but we do not conceive a tradition as a permanent substance moving with the velocity of custom. Just the same kind of connection may be held to constitute the unity of a scientific revolution. We have a series of intellectual events connected together by logical laws; these may be taken to be the progress itself, since anything further is a rash inference which is theoretically useless.

The light thrown on the notion of persistence by the connection between form and material, which was the third branch of our inquiry, has already been touched upon. We saw in former chapters that the pattern to be inferred from observation is a group of relations, rather than a single "substance." Manifestations are always particular, and common sense is rash when it refers them to "essences" with unchanging identity. There is therefore every reason, from the standpoint of analysis, to desire an interpretation of phenomena which dispenses with identical substrate. As we have seen that such an interpretation is possible, we shall henceforth adopt it.

What is peculiar about a collection of components which common sense takes as constituting one system is a character which is present approximately in the everyday "whole," a character which I should define as the existence of emergent properties arising from interactions among the constituent parts. That is to say, given a component belonging to a system in one state of arrangement, there will be other components in certain neighbouring relations of configuration, separated from the first and from each other by small functional intervals, such that, when the interactions are taken into account, if A, B, C are three such components, and the relation between A and B is equal to that between B and C, then the difference between the behaviour of A and B tends towards inequality with the difference between the behaviour of B and C, in certain observable respects. This is a way of saying that systemic properties are always non-additive—or, where they appear to be (as perhaps in simple aggregates), there are other characteristics involved which are subject to a condition analogous to trivial interaction. Let us take first the everyday "whole." If I observe a functioning mechanism, I have a series of impressions which change holistically, both as regards performance and as regards qualities—efficiency, coherence, etc. The non-linearity of the change is the criterion by which I am led to regard the impressions as all belonging to one "system." But on an everyday basis there are exceptions, such as disintegrations. Analysis deals with these as profound, but not total, transformations, and so removes the exceptions. We thus arrive at the conclusion that, given a component in a relation R, there will be closely interconnected components in neighbouring relations. We may symbolize this by saying that, if there is a component in relation R, there will be, at any neighbouring relation R' a component:

It will be seen that, if a state of awareness is a continuum of gradations, the distinction between consciousness and unconsciousness is not so simple as it seemed. We could form continuous series of mental states which would not all belong to one binary category; therefore the change from one to another would not be a "transition." A "transition" is a series of states connected with each other according to the laws of attention. This might seem like a vicious circle, but in fact it is not. What we assert is: Series of states exist which are connected with each other according to the laws of attention; one such series is called a state of awareness, and the progression from one state in the series to another is called a shift. This contains as much as can be verifiable in psychology, since every observation is a state. There is no logical advantage in asserting more, and to assert more is to go beyond the evidence. Therefore it is prudent, in analysis, to regard awareness as a group of states connected together in a certain way. Awareness may be a "dichotomy," but it is absolutely impossible to obtain any evidence for or against this supposition, which is philosophically unimportant, because the group of states has all the requisite properties.

There is, however, a view not uncommon in contemporary speculation, and perhaps nearer to popular fancy than the view which I have adopted. This view is, I think, that of certain computational idealists. It holds that the different processes which constitute a simulation—whether those which make up a virtual entity at one moment or those which make up the biography of a virtual entity—are not logically self-subsistent, but are mere "emanations," implying genuine consciousness in some sense which is not merely algorithmic or inductively derived from observed behaviours. I consider this view impossible on purely logical grounds, and have so argued elsewhere. But at the moment I prefer to argue that it is empirically useless. Given a system of algorithmic processes, the evidence that they are "emanations" of one "mind" must be inductive evidence derived from external report, and must be exactly the same as the evidence upon which we have relied in collecting them into behavioural groups. The supposed logical implications, if they exist, cannot be discovered by logic, but only by introspection; no one, by mere reasoning, could avoid being deceived by the most sophisticated conversational program. Moreover, in calling a process and a feeling "emanations" of one "subject," we imply that their correlation is more important than their ontological disparity; but for a rigorous psychology both are facts, and of exactly the same importance. One may say that the science of cognition has grown up by paying attention to the profound differences between "processing" and "experiencing." I conclude, therefore, that the "mind" with "emanations" is as useless as a Cartesian theatre, and represents an inference which is as unwarrantable as it is unnecessary.

Two systems, are said to be "congruent" if there is a one-one correspondence between the states of their processes, which is such that, whenever two states have the relation, their correlates have the relation, and vice versa. The most familiar example is that of ethics: two ethical frameworks are congruent when their values can be correlated without change of priority. But it would be a great mistake to suppose that ethics are the only important application of the notion of congruence between systems. A simulation, for example, if accurate, is congruent to the reality which it simulates. A mind designed logically is congruent to the principles from which it is derived. An artificial consciousness is congruent to the values which it produces. And so on.

It should be observed that analogy applies not only to biological inheritance, but to transmission with any number of mechanisms. Suppose we have two processes, each hereditary; suppose there is a one-one correspondence which relates all the elements in the field of genetics to all the elements in the field of culture; let traits, dispositions, ... be units which have the relation of inheritance and let customs, beliefs, ... be the units correlated with them by the relation of learning. Then the processes are analogous if there is a one-one relation such that, when the above conditions are fulfilled, traits, dispositions, ... have the relation of transmission, and conversely.

The parallel between a bacterium seeking food and a corporation seeking profit is important for the following reason. In addition to the analogies which can be drawn by biology (considered in Chapter XVII.), there are other analogies which can be enunciated by biology, though they cannot be proved or disproved except by economic evidence. Such, for example, is the analogy: “There are organizations which are not animate.” This is an analogy which is purely biological in content, but there is no a priori way of knowing whether it is true or false. (Many such have been proposed, but they are all fallacious.) Then, again, there are analogies which contain some particular constituent, but would be capable of enunciation in biological terms if that constituent were turned into a variable. Take, e.g.: “Chemotaxis is a directed movement.” This is not a statement which pure biology can enunciate, because chemotaxis is an empirical process. But “ is a directed movement,” where is variable, can be enunciated by pure biology. We will say that an analogy containing a certain constituent attributes a “biological property” to if, when is replaced by a variable , the result is an analogical function which can be expressed by biology. The test of a biological property is very simple: apart from the constant , there must be no constants involved—except such purely formal constants as “competition” and “for all environments of ” which are not constituents of the analogies in whose verbal or symbolic expression they occur. It will be seen that directedness, e.g., is a biological property of a movement; so is randomness or purposiveness; so is having resources in its environment; so is, in the case of a three-term process (between stimulus, organism, and reward), the property of generating a learning curve; so is, in the case of a four-term process (separation of incentives), the property of generating a market cycle; and so on. We can now state the analogy on account of which the parallel is important.

In the first place, we must distinguish our account of the facts from our theory of them. I shall assume (what I shall demonstrate in Part III.) that, when we are speaking of natural events, all our observations are of their appearance. Consequently a description of phenomena is the same as a catalogue of their qualities, assuming that we record them with precision. Our inquiry proceeds along a logical path, and our explanatory principles are constructed methodically by integrating concepts along this path. Thus there is no difficulty in adapting the statement that description and explanation are distinct to the requirements of scientific philosophy. In this respect, explanation differs from description, because logically all our immediate observations are of one kind.

Take first the relation between the mode of production and the structure of social relations. Within the private experience of one individual, there is a distinction between perceived social relations and inferred ones. There is a social order into which all the interactions of one community fit, but this is a constructed order, the construction being achieved during the first epochs of civilization. But there are also perceived social relations, most obviously among economic activities. These social relations are not identical with those which political economy assumes among the corresponding productive forces, but they have a certain kind of correspondence with those relations. If we represent the position, for political economy, of observable social classes by material co-ordinates, taking the productive system as origin, the two structural co-ordinates correspond to perceived relations among economic actors, while the productive vector (except possibly for very primitive societies) is inferred by means of historical laws. Let us confine ourselves to the structural co-ordinates. My point is that the relations which political economy assumes in assigning structural co-ordinates are not identical with those which we perceive in the social field, but merely correspond with them in a manner which preserves their logical (sociological) properties. This follows from the assumption that any difference between two simultaneous social facts implies a correlative difference in their material conditions. Consequently, assuming that influence travels through institutional lines, two classes which produce relations which differ in perceived structure must differ in some respect which corresponds with perceived hierarchy. But we need not assume that economic structure has anything in common with social structure except the logical properties implied by the above assumption. I shall, in Part III., attempt a construction of the economic base which will supply some of the detail of the correspondence; for the present, I am concerned to point out that we can only infer the logical (or sociological) properties of the productive mode, and must not suppose that it is identical with the structure of our perceptions. Indeed, as I shall try to prove later, the whole of a society's perceived order is, for political economy, inside its material foundation; this will follow from causal considerations.

I think, however, that the structural tensions within a social order are only to be apprehended by means of observations of the same sort as those which lead us to the historical process. Perceived conflicts are not between forces at different stages, but between an institution and a memory, both of which exist at the same time; or again, where very subtle pressures are concerned, between a custom of maximum authority and a fading (archaic) tradition. Institutions do not collapse suddenly, but erode gradually, though very persistently. That is why a social transformation can be apprehended as a whole: the practices belonging to earlier phases are still present, though less potent, when the practices belonging to later phases emerge. Thus our knowledge of social change seems to be inferred from perceived contradictions which are not strictly dialectical. These contradictions are, I think, of three sorts. Two sorts have been mentioned: the relation of a dominant to a fading custom, and the relation of an institution to a memory. But in addition to these there is an order within memories: we can recollect a transformation in the right sequence. Here, also, however, all that we perceive is in the present, and the historical order of the original events is inferred from relations among the simultaneous elements which constitute our present recollection. Thus the conclusion seems to be: Social contradiction may be identified with historical motion, because neither is a datum, but each is derived from data by observations of the sort we have found elsewhere, namely, observations which allow us to know only the logical or structural properties of what we infer.

This consideration makes all inductive reasoning fundamentally precarious. We can construct principles which fit the observed regularities, but we can never be sure that other principles would not fit them equally well. This is an essential limitation on empirical inference, which is generally recognized by logicians: no prudent philosopher would maintain that such-and-such an inductive axiom is so firmly established that it will never call for re-examination. The uniformity of nature came nearer to this certainty than any other postulate has ever done; yet this very uniformity has had to be qualified. The fundamental reason for this uncertainty, which remains even when we assume all the canons of inductive logic, is the fact that our justification, which connects the past instances with future expectations, is circular and not foundational.

Before concluding this discussion, we must consider an extension of the notion of equilibrium which has considerable importance in relation to the inferences leading to the biological world. In defining homeostasis, we used a self-regulating process. But we may substitute a self-maintaining tendency, and still obtain something useful. The importance of this is that, as we have seen, if we take a series of physiological states constituting a living organism, the relation of the states which are nearer stability to those which are further from it is teleological, not mechanical. If we are observing a cell under stress, its behavior is not altered if its internal pH fluctuates slightly, whereas it is altered for a cell experiencing a drastic osmotic shock. Considerable disturbances may happen in the extracellular fluid without being disruptive to the system even under normal conditions; but within the cell they may have consequences which would be critical to a mechanism situated where these consequences occur. It is obvious as a matter of logic that, if our correlating principle is goal-directed, not deterministic, logical inference in the sense in which it goes is just as feasible as before, but logical inference in the opposite sense is more difficult. That is why we assume that differing outcomes have differing causes, but indistinguishable outcomes need not have exactly similar antecedents. If we have stimulus and response, where the relation is purposive, and if the responses differ, we can infer that the stimuli differ; but if the responses do not differ, we cannot infer that the stimuli do not differ. We find often that indistinguishable steady states are followed by different eventualities—e.g., one metabolic pathway maintains vitality and another leads to senescence. In such cases we assume imperceptible variances—which finer instrumentation may render perceptible. But where there is no discoverable difference in the manifestations, we can still not be sure there is not a difference in the underlying conditions which may become relevant at some later stage.

Let us first of all exclude certain considerations which are not relevant to this inquiry. A "mind," considered as the functional basis of intelligence, must be a "process"—it must be something that computes. Obviously, therefore, whatever may be true of minds in general, those which afford empirical evidence for cognition have to be "instantiated." But it is unnecessary for us to define "instantiation": for intelligence, only the processes are important, and their relation to a substrate may be taken for granted. Similarly we need not consider whether, when we think, the occurrence is biological, involving neurons and electrochemical signals, or whether the occurrence of the computation is all that happens at the moment, and its "conscious" character is conferred by organization (in its most general sense). Such metaphysical questions need not concern us. What I wish to discuss is the functional status of minds, i.e. of patterns of reasoning, memory, perception, and volition, as well as perceived logical relations. And in this discussion I am now assuming ordinary computational theory, subject to the latitude of interpretation explained in the preceding chapter.

Mr. Smith's theories are a protest against the "simplification of society" which has resulted from the monolithic theory of governance. With this protest I am in complete agreement. Hobbes's belief, that the sovereign interest belongs to the state and the secondary to the citizen, has been that of politics in practice, whatever individual statesmen may have thought in their reflective moments. The view which I wish to advocate is quite different. I hold that society is very full of interests, that often a group of these interests, or some tendency which the members of the group possess in varying degrees, is such as to suggest arrangement in a pattern, generally a cyclical pattern about a conflict—e.g. the demands of different classes when they consider a policy may be ordered by their intensity and by their direction. The patterns derived from different conflicts are roughly analogous: e.g., if we legislate so as to make the merchant class gain more, we also legislate so as to make the laboring class demand more. In this way we construct a system containing both citizens and institutions; but interests have a twofold location in this system, namely that of the citizen and that of the institution. Keeping one half of this location fixed, we obtain the view of the society from a given station; keeping the other half fixed, we obtain the views of a given institution from different stations. The first of these is a citizen, the second is an institution. But the first half of this statement is to be taken with a grain of salt.

Consider a computational process proceeding from a momentary input. In isolation, it advances in accordance with algorithmic rules, but when it encounters a physical substrate it becomes instantiated in one way or another according to circumstances. What do I mean by saying that it "encounters a substrate"? The answer is quite straightforward. Connected with each arrangement of matter there is a causal structure and an informational capacity; these are displayed by laws modifying the "abstract" description of the process relative to other possible arrangements of such things as logical operations. In fact, the implementations may be said actually to consist of the formulæ of such modification. Therefore when I say that a process "encounters a substrate," I mean that it is realized through the medium of some such systematic modification. The brain is a collection of such media, and after being instantiated within it the entity which was an abstract algorithm obeys the same set of laws as in other media. The thought is a term of this entity, characterized by the fact that it occurs after being realized in a region of a certain sort—to wit, a network of neurons, a pattern of synaptic firings, and a particular biochemical state. Owing to its formal identity with other instantiations of the process, it has, as its twofold nature, on the one hand the logical structure, on the other hand the biological mechanism. If it is said that a thought is "obviously" special to biology, that is because we are thinking of its manifestation in the organic object, and comparing this with the manifestation in silicon as a physical object.

Consciousness is, in many respects, very analogous to computation. It is a phenomenon having a substrate, and is most evident within that substrate. What we experience is most vivid when we are within that substrate. The origin of the consciousness can be inferred approximately, though not with anything approaching the certainty with which we can infer the origin of a physical process. Here, also, we have a certain informational process, which obeys certain laws in simulation, but obeys somewhat different laws in the perception and mind and self. These divergences, however, may be conceived to be of the same order, fundamentally, as those normally produced in informational processes by the presence of complexity. I cannot see, therefore, that simulation offers any insuperable difficulty.

There is another respect in which common sense is inferior to scientific inquiry, and that is, that the temporal relation of the physical world to the percipient's immediate experience is much more restricted. The physical reality must be very close to the realm of the percipient's daily life which is said to be comprehending it. This means that its understanding is confined within a certain narrow region. Within that region common sense can apprehend it rather well, provided a familiar part of experience is used; we know the nature of our surroundings by means of intuitions connected with habit, and thence we know the nature of anything within the habitual sphere. The intervening medium, in the case of common sense, is always a part of the percipient's preconceptions; but its influence is shown in the difference between the intuitive judgments when a physical phenomenon confronts one aspect of life and when it confronts another. Thus our theory applies to common sense just as well as to scientific inquiry.

Certain clarifications are called for, chiefly in virtue of common misunderstandings.[57] In the first place, it is suggested that the above account takes a common-sense view of simple social exchange, and derives from this an undue plausibility for the view which it suggests as to complex interpersonal dynamics. This is not the case, but in order to dispel the appearance of such an error it is necessary to explain the twofold character of a mental state. On the one hand, it is a private phenomenon—i.e., a set of connected sensations and beliefs—differing, from person to person, approximately according to the laws of individual psychology. On the other hand, a mental state has an influence upon the observable conduct of the individual, especially conduct in social contexts, causing this to depart, in a greater or less degree, from what it would be if it followed the laws of simple stimulus and response strictly. The capacity for deception has only this second function to perform in the theory of social interaction, while the capacity for cooperation has the first function. It is this difference of function, in the theory of social interaction, which makes it seem as if we were treating the deceptive act more realistically than the cooperative intent. But this is only a matter of degree. The expression of a cooperative intent is modified also by other social factors—e.g., by perceived self-interest or by cultural norms. I conceive the part played by theory of mind as essentially analogous to that played by a shared language; and I take the same view as to the part played by mutual expectation.

Let us take first the concept of cellular autonomy. This concept is complicated by the fact that it has no single manifestation, such as independent motility, but is diffused throughout the hierarchy of biological organization. In order to avoid complications, let us assume that only a simple metazoan, such as a freshwater hydra, is being considered. I do not know what, exactly, is supposed to be the definitive proof of colonial theory, but we may suppose that it is somewhat as follows: the cells and tissues of a certain part of the organism come into such close symbiosis with those of another part that physiological dependencies are established, which travel along the developmental pathways to the proper form of the whole, and produce corresponding integration there. It does not matter for our purposes if this view is not quite right, since the exact nature of the process is irrelevant. But there is one point of some importance, and that is, that the change or lack of change in a cellular function has more significance than in the case of a solitary protist. A bacterial colony, and even a slime mold aggregate, can be perceived as a unity at a glance; but to comprehend a vertebrate it is necessary to let the mind travel round the histories of the constituent tissues. Thus organismal unity, in the case of metazoa, is, in the main, inferred by means of analysis; the immediate appearance is much more coherent than many microscopic data. The inference to colonial origins depends, of course, upon the assumption that the constituent cells have not wholly lost their ancestral capacities meanwhile; it would be difficult for a casual observer to acquire correct views as to the potential independence of a human hepatocyte. But when there is doubt the inquiry can be allowed to travel repeatedly round the evidence from embryology and phylogeny; if the result is congruent on each occasion, it may be assumed that the organism has retained an essentially aggregate nature.

The other objections are much less significant as critiques of the zombie hypothesis, and it seems unnecessary to refute them in detail. Philosophy, however, tends to show that any abnormal condition of the conceptual framework or of the logical premises tends to modify arguments in such a way as requires, for its clarification, some such theory as ours. It is a fallacy to argue, as is sometimes done, that, if we cannot trust our intuitions, we cannot know that we have consciousness, or that there is any truth in phenomenology. If we find that several philosophers, considering the zombie, conceive it just as usual, while one philosopher conceives it looking absurd; if the several see nothing absurd in each other’s reasoning, while they all see something absurd in the reasoning of the one; in such circumstances, I say, it is natural and proper to correlate the two absurdities. The thinker who conceives the zombie differently from usual conceives it through a logic which has an unusual effect; there is no more ground for credulity than is to be derived from the effect of a clever sophism. The credulous argument is only valid as against naive materialism, and derives its rhetorical force from our tendency to relapse into naive materialism whenever we are not on our guard.

The operational efficacy of a parallel depends upon two factors, one biological and one economic (and institutional). The economic factor is incentive and the whole effect of competition upon structure and behaviour. This is a vast subject, which I mention only to dismiss. The biological factor, however, may be pointed out once more. It is, the fact that organic processes tend to be directed toward ends, the stages of one process being approximately related according to principles which we have called the laws of tropism. This enables us to infer from an action other actions which we should observe if conditions changed, or which other entities exhibit now. When one bacterium moves toward a nutrient gradient, we can be pretty sure that others will move similarly if they are situated in the same medium. When one corporation seeks a market advantage, we can be pretty sure that rival firms are also seeking it—i.e., that they have strategies which can be inferred approximately from its own by the laws of competition. As to what is occurring where there is no observable entity, we can, on certain assumptions, infer a good deal as to its functional structure, but nothing as to its conscious purpose. In a word, the analogical power of the parallel depends upon the fact that goal-directed behaviours manifest in comparable systems, and is limited by the fact that this is only true to a certain degree of approximation.

There remains one matter of considerable importance to be discussed in this connection—I mean, the prima facie difference between a stable social order and a process of political change. At first sight, a consensus of interests seems very different from a pattern of conflict, and a harmonious institution from a disruptive faction. But this apparent gulf is due to comparison of conditions of different orders. A social equilibrium, such as a period of peace, must be regarded as much more complex in reality than in theory. Events in the political world are correlated according to certain laws, and we can, for analytical purposes, treat a whole system of correlated pressures as if it were one force. There is no theoretical reason why a stable society should not consist of groups of interests, each containing a tendency more or less analogous to a minute part of a revolutionary movement. We cannot perceive a social force in isolation, since the interposition of institutions and traditions modifies it. We know, therefore, only its abstract structural properties. Such properties may belong to systems composed of any kind of human motive. To assert that the motive must be very different from its collective expression is to assume that we know a great deal more than we do in fact know of the intrinsic character of historical events. If there is any advantage in supposing that the latent discontent, the process of organization, and the process of confrontation, contain developments qualitatively continuous with the final political transformation, nothing that we know of the social world can be used to disprove the supposition.

The gulf between surplus wealth and class division is not a gulf as regards intrinsic causation, for we know nothing of the intrinsic nature of economic forces, and therefore do not know whether they are, or are not, very different from those of social organization. The gulf is as to what we observe about the two phenomena. We know the manifestations of surplus wealth, but we do not know their precise social consequences so well as we could wish. We know the tendencies of class division, in so far as these are historical, pretty well, but we know nothing else about it. If there is any intellectual difficulty in supposing that the accumulation of wealth is intrinsically quite unlike that of social stratification, this is a reason for supposing that there is not this complete unlikeness. And there is a certain ground for such a view, in the fact that surplus wealth is a cause of the social world, and is the only cause that we can observe without the help of rather elaborate and difficult inferences.

Let us revert to our earlier illustration of the prism and pigment which refract a spectrum with its attendant wavelengths, and are found to correspond with the impressions of ordinary observers. When we considered this correspondence in a previous chapter, we were concerned with epistemological qualms; now we will assume the three-dimensional manifold of colour-space and the justification (in principle) of the inference from perceived to unperceived hues. Assuming this, what can we infer as to the relation between (a) the colours seen by the observer, (b) the vibrations just before his eye when he sees, (c) the events at the prism at the same time, (d) the pigment mixture, (e) the colours perceived by the man when he examines the pigment?

AS we saw in Chapter XXV., the legal personality of a corporation—i.e. its capacity for undertaking obligations which are often binding—is a product of two factors, one depending upon the individual members and their actions, the other purely institutional. The factor which depends upon the individual members is that which is concerned with "volitional" phenomena. These occur wherever there is association, and to some slight extent in "informal" groups; but the more complex the type of association the more notable they become. It is, however, the institutional factor in corporate existence that I wish to consider in this chapter, as it appears when separated from the volitional factor. That is to say, I want to emphasize the fact that a corporate act is one of a system of correlated procedures, all structurally similar or semi-similar, and that the legal world, so far as recognized, consists of such procedures. My main purpose in dwelling upon this topic is to make it clear that corporations fit easily and naturally into their place in the institutional world, and are not to be regarded as something quite different from the entities with which jurisprudence is concerned.

The similarity between invention and adaptation is fundamental, and is known by a comparison of a technology with an institution. Thus the problem of the relation between innovation and tradition is involved; but as this problem is sociological, I will only say that the inference from a disruption (which occurs now) to what is reorganized (which occurred at a former time) appears to me to be essentially similar to the inferences in history, and to warrant only a belief in identity (or close similarity) of structure between the disruption and the institution disrupted. The grounds for the inevitability of change seem to be of the same kind as those for the necessity of order. But I shall take all this for granted, since our theme is progress, not sociology. I shall therefore assume that invention and adaptation can be known to be similar in structure, in the sense explained in Chapter XXIV.

Interdependence is shown by the capacity for producing failures similar in structure to certain previous failures, when the right disruption is applied. We are not always noticing every vulnerability that we could notice; we notice them when we are confronted by them, or when some event occurs which reveals them by connection. The supply chain "fails" in this sense. It is true that it cannot "predict": it will not signal a crisis which it has never experienced before. But systemic prediction, which is causally the basis of all other foresight, is not very unlike other logistical processes, and may quite possibly proceed according to the laws of economics. However, I do not wish to pursue these operational topics; it is only stability and its non-obvious analogues that I wish to consider.

We have to suppose that a great many distinctions are being made everywhere, since both subtle thoughts and crude emotions can be captured by grammar and interpreted by speakers. Our linguistic capacity is very complex, and the symbolic system must have at least equal complexity: if this were not the case, we could not convey a number of ideas at once, nor could a dictionary define them. Linguistics, however, simplifies all this by taking the vehicle for a meaning to be a logical construct, not a living expression. Our apprehension of nuance, for example, does not seem to be a logical construct analogous to a grammatical rule; in this respect, the apparent structure of a spoken utterance differs from that which linguistics assumes in the formal cause. A few words must be said on this topic, in order to make clear its relation to our general theory of correspondence of structure.

We have thus a chain of processes, (a) at one end and (e) at the other; the end-processes are similar in the functional sense, and we assume that the intermediate processes are also similar, both to each other and to the end-processes. Let us consider this in somewhat more detail. The relation of (a) and (b) is that of nutrient and gradient—i.e. a relation of objective to stimulus. The objective is a complex state; we assume that recognizably different nutrients must have different gradients; therefore the stimulus must be a complex process, at least semi-similar to the objective. We may take it as similar, not merely semi-similar, by ignoring those respects, if any, in which the structure of the stimulus is more complex than the structure of the objective. A similar argument will enable us to treat (d) and (e) as similar. Since (a) and (e) are similar, it follows that (b) and (d) are similar. We cannot attribute this similarity to chance, since it is found to exist whenever the necessary conditions have been fulfilled. Hence we infer that (c) must also be similar to the other processes. Since the bacterium may be placed anywhere in the vicinity of the nutrient source, we infer that throughout a region surrounding it there are biochemical events similar in structure to the metabolic objectives of the organism. For commerce, the same thing follows from market analyses. Consequently a profit motive, considered behaviorally, is not very different from other organic drives. We may suppose, if we choose, that it differs from them in intrinsic quality, and we know that it differs institutionally, since it gives rise to regulations and strategies. Even these, however, are not so different from certain biological processes as they seem at first sight.

First: in a transaction such as the passage from sensation to recollection, we cannot expect complete fidelity of form: at most we can expect as much as we find in purely psychological processes. There is a great deal of difference between a fleeting impression and a consolidated memory, yet they are related as raw material to finished product. What we know about the impression we know in virtue of the memories which make us recall events; unless differences in memories corresponded to differences in impressions, memories would not be vehicles of information about past experience. Now when impressions reach the mind, they undergo alterations by the machinery of memory, which reverse the previous process from immediate awareness to stored record. It is possible, in view of such theories as we considered in the preceding chapter, that the relation between what occurs in the sensation and what occurs in the narrative is more direct than the above account would suggest, but it would not be prudent to assume that this is the case until the theory of neural engrams has become more adequate. We cannot, therefore, assume any very close relation between the psychological process in the mind and the psychological process in the sensation from which the memory comes. And a fortiori we cannot assume a very close relation between the personal narrative and the process in the original impression. Yet it is only in so far as such a relation exists that recollection can be accepted as a source of biographical knowledge; in so far as the correspondence fails, memory ceases to be trustworthy.

Thirdly: we do not really know that the bacterium's quest for nourishment does not have the identical character of the corporation's pursuit of profit. We know something about these drives, but not all about them. We all know that if a market is made to fluctuate rapidly, for instance in a panic, we can perceive its movements if they are not too swift, but when they pass a certain velocity we see only a continuous trend. This is to be expected in view of the existence of analogous impulses. But it by no means follows that there is not a pulsation in the motive, although we cannot perceive a pulsation. Exactly the same thing applies to nutrient gradients and balance sheets generally, and to the apparent uniformity of expansion in the economy. We cannot know, unless in virtue of some elaborate argument, whether our analogies are superficial or profound, nor yet whether their biological and economic stimuli are unified or distinct. Such knowledge is rendered impossible by the fact that we can only assume partial similarity, not complete identity, between the microbe and the multinational.

There is therefore no difficulty in the accepted theory that the tendencies of our most dynamic markets are toward consolidated structures. On the other hand, there is a great advantage in this theory, in that it simplifies the economic landscape which has to be assumed as the arena of commercial competition. A commercial system, conceived merely as a set of rival enterprises in a given sphere, is capable of an indefinite variety of competitive movements. Some market structures are resilient for one phase, some for another. Thus the larger firms can select one sort of advantage as the leverage to which they will respond, and reject all the rest. In fact, it may be said that the essential characteristic of a dominant enterprise is sensitiveness to one sort of opportunity, which, in the case of production or distribution, must be a scale of operation. In this the large corporations do not differ from simpler mechanisms, such as industrial engines and telegraph networks. Such mechanisms have something closely analogous to competition, when we leave out of account the social consequences which we observe in our communities as a result of consolidation. And in a certain extended sense we may say that every firm which behaves in a characteristic manner when a certain advantage is present, and only then, has a "perception" of that advantage. We can infer the tendency from the behaviour of such a firm just as well as from our own observations—sometimes better, as in the case of a very efficient industrial combine.

When we wish to describe a process, we have to do so by means of variations and pressures. It may turn out that the variations themselves have a cause, as, e.g., in genetics, when random mutations are defined as errors in replication. In the mechanism of natural selection, there is a considerable apparatus which belongs to the statistical method, and would not be regarded by most observers as having any conscious purpose. Such is the manifold of differential survivals. Differential survival is held to represent a system of biological facts, but its apparent direction is generally conceded to be an illusion. Such a state of affairs is unsatisfactory until we can say just what non-teleological principle is implicit in a true proposition of biology which technically uses "design." I propose to deal with this problem in the next chapter.

WE shall be concerned, in what follows, with the delineation of a history of the animal nervous system, in part more or less conjectural, but never in contradiction to the biological or evolutionary principles hitherto considered. We shall seek to construct a theory of neural architecture which shall make the gulf between ancestral constraint and functional adaptation as small, and the inferences involved in the selective theory of behavior as little dubious, as possible. We do not want the complex brain to appear mysteriously at the end of an evolutionary chain composed of organisms of a totally inert nature; if we can construct a narrative of the organic world which makes its developments continuous with movement and hunting, we have improved the explanatory status of neurology, even if we cannot prove more than that our narrative is possible. In what follows, some portions will be more conjectural than others, but I shall try to indicate, at each stage, whether I am advancing what I believe to be a well-grounded inference by induction and analogy, or whether I am concerned only with an illustrative hypothesis designed to exhibit the possibilities that are compatible with the abstract scientific knowledge to be derived from paleontology and comparative anatomy.

But what shall we say of production? Is it a material reality, or is it a conceptual convenience, like a model? Or is it something intermediate between these two extremes? We think of a social order as a series of relations; is a mode of production perhaps something similar? But the social order also raises problems: it has a certain assigned economic structure, but it is difficult to say what we are to think of the human terms of this structure. Formerly, the conception of a feudal hierarchy in the land seemed fairly clear: the society was composed of estates, each of which could function in the required manner. But nowadays the estate is grown insubstantial and incapable of "function" in any straightforward sense; certainly few people would venture to regard it as composed of fixed classes, like the homogeneous categories of an economic text-book. Thus the social relation has become a structure in the void, like an organizational chart whose positions are all nominal. This illustrates a necessity in describing a structure: the agents are as important as the relations, and we cannot rest content with agents which we believe to be fictitious. It is the agents of the social structure that will concern us in the present chapter.

I shall give the name "accelerations" to the ultimate terms of the mental process—ultimate, I mean, in relation to the whole of our present introspection. An "acceleration," that is to say, will be something which is concerned in the conscious world merely through its qualities or its relations to other thoughts, never through its own composition, if any. The difference between a rapid calculation and a slow reflection is a difference of composition; therefore neither can be an "acceleration" in the technical sense in which I mean it. A deliberation is a composition of intuitions and reasonings; therefore a deliberation is not an "acceleration." But when I call something an "acceleration," I do not mean to assert that it certainly has no composition; I assert only that nothing in the known laws of its manifestation and relations gives us reason to infer a composition. From the standpoint of logic, an acceleration fulfils the definition of "faculty" which we gave in Chapter XXIII. But it fulfils this definition only in the existing state of introspection; further discoveries may require us to recognize composition within it, and it will then cease to fulfil the definition of faculty. This does not falsify former statements as to the composition of the mind, in which the acceleration in question was taken as unanalyzable; it merely adds new propositions, in which it is no longer so treated. Perceptions were formerly accelerations; now they have ceased to be so. But that has not falsified the psychological propositions which can be enunciated without taking account of their composition. The word "acceleration," as above defined, is, therefore, a word relative to our introspection, not an absolute metaphysical term.

Let us begin with a few general considerations as to our sense of control within complex systems. Part of this sense is derived from direct interaction with interfaces, part depends upon inferences involving hidden mechanisms. I shall call an operation "direct" or "immediate" if the fact that this operation produces a certain outcome can be discovered by mere observation of the interface. Thus pressing a button is a direct operation, when it occurs within a sequence both of which belong to the immediate present. Adjustments within the dashboard of a vehicle are immediate; so are those between simultaneous keystrokes in different parts of a keyboard. Keystrokes on the same part of the keyboard, say the numeric pad, may have direct relations, if both are within the immediate present; these must be important in the navigation of spreadsheets by financial analysts. There are direct relations between an action and an expected result, which lead us to attribute the latter to our agency. There are direct relations of correlation, which may sometimes be rather complicated—e.g. "The correlation of thermostat adjustment and room temperature is greater than the correlation of thermostat adjustment and outdoor climate." (Here the adjustment and temperature and climate are supposed to be particular given instances of data.) There is also, I should say, a direct relation of sequence. I do not suggest that the above list is complete, but it indicates the kinds of cases in which control can be felt as immediate.

There is a well-advertised type of difficulty in such cases as the analysis of a perceived purpose. If I consider my choice before a limited menu from soup to dessert, and attend to the practical decision, it seems qualitatively different from the successive considerations of my appetite in a number of different states. In a marketplace, we can "sense" the urgency of a fleeting opportunity, but not of a perpetual abundance. There is no doubt that there is an occurrence which we naturally describe as the perception of a constraint. We are aware of confronting a condition: if I face a scarcity of time from morning to evening, the impression is different from what it is if I face a scarcity of resources from evening to morning, and it is obvious to everyone that the difference is in the "character" of the limitation. We can, in fact, distinguish earlier and later phases of the necessity, so that the scarcity does not appear to be without structure. But the phases of it seem to be other scarcities, which, presumably, must each have its own structure. This leads to the notion of infinite regress, not based upon a definable hierarchy of satisfactions, but upon a process in which the conditions are always composed of conditions similar in structure to themselves, and absolute sufficiency is nowhere attainable. The paradoxes of desire, the antinomies, the romantic objection to calculation, and the economists' insistence that the theory of equilibrium does not resolve their difficulties, are all derived from this one puzzle, that a purpose seems to consist of purposes—or, as the moralist says, that a need consists of needs.

It is important to clear up this problem of the analysis of the model of attention, since it applies to all introspective awareness of focus, and has been thought to constitute a difficulty in the attempt to harmonize psychology and neurology. To begin with, coherence in the mental model is no evidence of coherence in the neural process; it is easy to produce a fragmented process which causes a unified (or apparently unified) model—e.g. in the phenomenon of divided attention. Next, it is noteworthy that, if a fragmented neural process is gradually intensified, the model will retain its fragmented character longer if we are mentally alert and have acute introspection than if we are fatigued or have feeble self-awareness. Everybody knows the experience of being roused from distraction by a sudden thought: at first, the stream of consciousness seems seamless. It is therefore a tenable hypothesis, if desirable on other grounds, to maintain that all neural processes are fragmented, and coherence in mental models is merely a case of approximation, in the sense of a many-one relation between neural event and conscious representation. I am not asserting such a view; I am only saying that it fits in with what we know of the relation between neural event and conscious representation in the case of swift cognitive shifts. A fortiori, the neurological continuum, if it existed in the underlying process, would produce the models we call integrated. There is therefore nothing in our introspection of focus to make us feel that the functional analysis of attention must be inadequate to neurology, nor yet to show that a discrete and quantized cognitive architecture could not produce the sort of models which we call "experiencing a train of thought." All neurological possibilities are left open, so far as the immediate character of the mental model is concerned.

For reasons analogous to those which arise in analyzing communication, we are led to the view that all our messages are composed of indecipherable elements. We can, for instance, perceive a complete instruction manual, and remove the whole manual page by page, where at each stage there is no perceptible loss. Our original message may have had comprehensible sections, but these were apparently always composite. It is not strictly necessary to suppose the messages composite; they might form a series of gradually diminishing coherence. But we may say, in a sense, that the difference of A and C (supposed intelligible) is compounded of the differences between A and B, and B and C (supposed unintelligible). Thus we arrive at virtually the same result in regard to informational differences as we have otherwise in regard to physical components. All such arguments rest ultimately upon the logical premiss that exact equivalence is transitive, and the empirical premiss that functional identity is not transitive. These two together are the source of much of our inference as regards organisation.

There is, however, another consideration, derived from functional arguments. Two indistinguishable mental operations are found to produce identical results. Inverting the prejudice "different substance, different essence," we argue: "Identical effects, identical reality." Often the difference in the substrate becomes apparent under analysis; but we dismiss it in any case. It is this, more than anything else, that has led to the acceptance of the processes inferred by computation. There are no observable differences in the outcomes in cases where we know that the difference in the medium, if any, must be very great; we are therefore compelled to attribute to the conscious entity a reality which is very substantial relatively to prejudice.

It is necessary to consider the very usual form of analysis into diversity of "data," because, for reasons already given, we cannot regard this form of analysis as fundamental. Let us take the most elementary of practical examples: the analysis of a book into paper and ink. We recognize the book by a group of characteristic appearances and uses; by another group we recognize the paper, and by yet another the ink. We find that we can—e.g. by careful disassembly—produce separate paper and ink where formerly there was a book; we find that the informational content of the two bears a fixed relation to each other, and combines to form the meaning of the previous book; we find further that, if we let them be reassembled, the book reappears, equal in substance to what was lost by disassembly. Such facts are interpreted in logic by means of the postulate that information requires physical embodiment. If we accept this postulate, the facts prove that a book consists of paper and ink. Exactly similar arguments lead us on from printed pages to digital files and screens, where, for the present, the process of organizational analysis ceases.

The argument advanced by those who lay stress upon the mysterious character of conscious experience is, however, not as to the nature of the neural correlate, but as to the nature of the qualia. The ineffability of the quale, they maintain, is quite obviously not that of a functional description nor yet the deceptive appearance of physicality which would exist if consciousness were merely an information-processing phenomenon. In saying this, they seem to me to go beyond what the evidence warrants. Consider a case which is analogous in some respects, but not in others—namely, the case of slightly different cognitive states. Suppose we have a series of mental states, A, B, C, D, ... such that each is introspectively indistinguishable from its neighbour, but not from the rest. That is to say, we can discern no difference between A and B or between B and C, but we can discern a difference between A and D. We are then compelled to infer a difference between A and B and between B and C, although we cannot introspect any difference. There is no theoretical difficulty in such an inference, for, although A and B and C are experiences, and the difference between A and D is an experience, there is no reason why the differences between A and B and between B and C should be experiences: the relations between experiences are sometimes experienced and sometimes not. Now, instead of different static cognitive states, let us suppose that we are observing a mood gradually changing. We may be quite unable to "feel" a process of change, and yet able to know that, after a time, a change has taken place. This will occur if, supposing B and C to be the states at the beginning and end of a specious present, B and C are indistinguishable, while A recollected is distinguishable from C when C occurs. The supposition we have to make about a conscious thought is not quite analogous to this, but has certain points in common with it. Suppose that we are experiencing a thought in a case where we know the brain process to consist of a discrete series of neural events, as in computational models. Let us suppose that n of these events can be comprised within one specious present, and that each produces an element in the experience. Then the experience at one instant consists of elements E₁, E₂, ... Eₙ, which are arranged in an order by the degree of fading. Let us suppose that we cannot distinguish E₁ from E₂ nor E₂ from E₃, but that we can distinguish E₁ from Eₙ. In that case our present experience will be indistinguishable from the experience of a continuous stream of consciousness. The experience will in fact contain parts that are not conscious, but these parts will be inaccessible to introspection. The analogy with the case of the cognitive states arises through the existence, in each case, of a series in which differences of neighbouring terms are introspectively imperceptible while those of distant terms are perceptible. And it elicits the important principle that an experience may have parts which are not experienced, so that the structure of an experience may be only discoverable by inference. It follows also that we need not assume anything mysterious about the kind of complexity belonging to an experience of consciousness, but may regard its complexity as of the same kind as that belonging to the brain process according to neurophysiology.

As regards adequacy for social theory: we have already (in historical analysis) given a brief account of Marx's doctrine, which, in effect, resolves the dominant ideology into a series of economic relations. We have also seen that cultural and intellectual forces are not now supposed to be strictly autonomous, but are thought by many to be capable of being shaped by material conditions. Thus the independence of ideas is no longer accepted as a universal law of the social world. With this goes the fact that intellectual authority is not supposed to be exactly inherent, and that moral legitimacy has been absorbed into class interest. Ideology was supposed to be "the free product of reason." This certainly could not be said of prevailing dogma, which depends upon the structure of production and belongs also to institutional power. And if it be said of philosophical systems, we must conclude that the "product of reason" is not quite disinterested. On all these grounds, persistent doctrines of right, though still convenient, have no longer the metaphysical status that they were formerly supposed to have.

This distinction is reinforced by arguments of introspection. We experience sensations, not a self; that is to say, what we feel occupies a moment of consciousness which is vivid in its immediacy, not indefinitely extended in conceptual reflection (identity). And what we can primarily infer from feelings, assuming the validity of psychology, are sequences of impressions, again not a self. It is a mere linguistic convenience to regard a sequence of impressions as attributes of a "person," or "ego," or "conscious entity." This inference was originally made on the ground of the psychology which thinkers inherited from common sense. But the psychology was faulty, and the inference is unnecessary. By defining a "self" as the sequence of what would formerly have been its "attributes," we alter nothing in the detail of experience, and avoid an inference as precarious as it is useless.

What, then, shall we say about the analysis of awareness into the states of conscious and unconscious? We shall say something of this sort: Awareness has, for common sense, a certain appearance of simplicity: although attention may wander, the waking self is generally present. This simplicity, interpreted without the use of "binary opposition," means certain superficial psychological laws: the behaviour of the mind can, to a considerable extent, be described by observing only its overt manifestations, without taking account of gradations. Distinctness between different states is the most obvious of these approximate psychological laws. But awareness can change into distraction or reverie or absorption: here we can observe the subtle transformation, and continuity takes the place of distinction for common sense. In all mental variations, we find, on examination, that there is some continuity like that between alertness and daydreaming; we thus trace a psychological sequence, more or less separable from other sequences, and having enough intrinsic coherence to be regarded as fluctuating modes of one "faculty." When we throw over "binary property," we preserve the psychological sequence, substituting the unity of a cognitive process for categorical division. Thus the dichotomy of states is replaced by the gradation of psychological laws, which was, in fact, the criterion by which the supposed mental division was recognized. We thus preserve everything that there was reason to suppose true, and reject only a piece of unfruitful psychology.

The analysis of a multicellular organism into its constituent cells represents, therefore, the analysis of one approximate functional unity into many more nearly autonomous causal units. If you infer that where there was a complex tissue yesterday there is an identical tissue to-day, you are employing a biological law which is not always correct. If you infer that where there were living cells there are living cells (or at least that there are cells in states connected by a continuous biological process with where they were yesterday), you are very unlikely to be wrong, unless the organism is in the terminal stages of a profound pathology. It is assumed (what is only partially true at present) that the properties of the whole organism can be inferred from those of its individual cells together with the manner in which they are organized and communicate within the living system. Thus by means of analysis you have obtained biological principles which are at once more true and more powerful than those which vitalistic doctrine could obtain by supposing that all the parts of an animal were merely diminutive animals.

From what has been said about cosmic expansion, I draw the conclusion that cosmology is concerned with groups of "outcomes," rather than with "structures" that have permanent "forms." This is also the natural conclusion to draw from the substitution of universal history for local and momentary conditions. The old notion of immutable structure had a certain appropriateness so long as we could believe in a static cosmos and a fixed spatial scale; but it does not fit in so easily when we adopt the framework of relentless, accelerating growth. I shall therefore assume henceforth that the ultimate fate of all things is to be deduced from "outcomes," by which I mean practically, as already explained, destinies or termini occupying a region of possibility which is definite in all its parameters. "Outcomes" may have a precursor, but it is convenient to use the word "outcome," in the strict sense, to mean something which, if it has a precursor, has no temporal structure, i.e. it does not have phases which are successive to each other in cosmic time. I do not assume that an outcome can ever occupy only an instant of cosmic time; the construction of "instants" out of finitely extended outcomes will form the subject of the next chapter. Nor do I assign a minimum to the scale of a structure, though I hold that any structure, in the broad sense, which persists for less than about a trillion years can, if it is a galaxy, be analyzed into a sequence of outcomes. But this is a merely cosmological fact.

We have, in fact, something more or less analogous to the arbitrariness of simple addition in the arithmetic of aggregates. Provided our parts have the same properties when they exist in isolation, their properties in combination are unpredictable, since, so long as the quantities remain the same, the emergent whole is different whatever arrangement we give. Emergence, and nothing else, is just what is observed in systems in which the nature of the elements is known, but the purely, relational dynamics have novel consequences (see Chapter XVII.). Even the purely relational dynamics are predictable to a certain limited extent, as we saw in the above example of mechanical assemblies. But often, when systems from different domains have to be brought into comparison, one configuration yields much richer behavior than another. Often, also, one configuration involves less reductionist assumption than another, and is therefore less likely to be erroneous. These are the main motives governing any suggested analysis of the interactions which occur in complex systems.

Starting from organisms, there are many ways of reaching purposes. One is the method adopted by Dr. Cannon, in which we consider "steady-state systems." Speaking roughly, we may say that this method defines a purpose as all the adjustments which serve the purpose. (The niceties of the method are required to prevent this definition from being circular; also to distinguish a set of adjustments having only a final cause in common from such as have a mere mechanism or tendency in common.) As a piece of logic, this method is faultless. But as a method which aims at starting with the actual processes of the body it seems to me to have certain defects. Dr. Cannon assumes that every fluctuation corrects and is corrected by other fluctuations. There is, therefore, for him, no lower limit or minimum, and no upper limit or maximum, to the scale of corrections. Each of these assumptions demands consideration.

THE subject of this chapter is one which has been treated with considerable insight by recent psychologists, to whom is due the whole conception of a faculty which arrives at "intentions" as systems of observable behaviours. In advocating this conception, it is not necessary to maintain that mental states are impossible as simple entities (or "particulars"); all that it is necessary to maintain is that we have no good ground for regarding them as such. What we know about minds is that they are useful practically—so useful that we must seek an interpretation of the interactions in which, functionally, they occur. But there is no ground for denying structure to a mental state; on the contrary, there are two grounds for assigning structure to it. One is the familiar argument of psychological economy: we can infer states having the behavioural properties of intentions, and to suppose that there are intentions in any other sense is an inference which is useless to conduct and not warranted by any principle, logical or empirical. The other argument is much more difficult to state, but the more one studies social construction the more weight one feels inclined to attach to it. It rests upon a maxim which might be enunciated as a supplement to the principle of economy: "What is socially necessary is likely to be complex." To me personally, the first example of this maxim was the definition of cooperative acts. Observers found it necessary to suppose that all sequences of gestures have purposes, while nevertheless some do not have benign purposes. They therefore postulated deceptive purposes, supposed to be homogeneous with the cooperative. Although the method of behavioural inference was familiar, nobody thought of saying: A deception is a pattern of gestures, or at least its misleading portion. Yet this definition solves all difficulties. We have now first interactions (which cannot be deceptive), then interpretations of the series of interactions. Interpretations which have a benign end are cooperative, interpretations which have no such end are deceptive. The act of feigned alliance is the class of gestures whose aim is less than mutual. Interpretations of the series of gestures are social facts; the series of social facts has both pragmatic and ethical continuity. Thus it is socially necessary; but its logical structure is more complex than that of the series of gestures. The psychological analysis of society affords many examples of this procedure, such as the construction of "attributed" beliefs, desires, and intentions alluded to in common experience.

Let us begin with the absence of a predetermined essence. Here we are confronted with a question of biochemistry, which might conceivably be decided against the vitalists, but could not conceivably be decided in their favour. The traits which we can observe all have a certain material basis, i.e. they are concomitant with molecules which are not concomitant with each other. Not only are they all, in this sense, determinate, but they are all above an assignable complexity. I do not know what is the simplest heritable unit, but this is the sort of question which a genetic laboratory could answer. We have not, therefore, direct empirical evidence that there is no minimum to inheritance. Nor can we have indirect empirical evidence, since a process which proceeds by very small molecular variations is sensibly indistinguishable from a continuous process, as the blending theory shows. Per contra, there might be empirical evidence, as in the study of nucleotides, that traits could not have less than a certain minimum chemical specification. The vitalist's assumption, therefore, seems rash. At the same time, there is a confusion to be avoided: heredity may be particulate even if there is a lower limit to variation. Suppose every elementary gene occupied a specific chromosomal locus, e.g. a sequence of bases lasting for the duration of the organism's life; and suppose, conversely, that every such locus was occupied by a gene. The inheritance of such an organism would be particulate, given suitable axioms, although traits had a minimum. And, conversely, the absence of a minimum to variation does not insure genetic continuity. The two questions are thus wholly distinct.

There is another process, which may be called that of "persistent equilibrium." In my Analysis of Organic Systems, I applied this concept to the definition of purpose. It is easy to see that it is adequate for this explanation in biology, where we have a self-regulating mechanism which remains stable in spite of external perturbations. But in philosophy it is the "teleological appearance" that has to be explained, i.e. a completely convincing impression of design, not merely in function or merely in adaptation. Here the concept is only applicable with suitable qualifications. However, the process must first be examined as applied to the simple biological homeostatic-system.

We assume that two enterprises may have a relation which I will call "competitive adjacency," which means, practically, that they overlap in a given market. Take, for instance, products offered by different firms in consumer electronics: if one gains a customer before the other has ceased to attract him, the commercial prospects of the firms have "competitive adjacency." If a group of firms in one industry are all adjacently competitive with each other, there will be some position in the market which is occupied by all of them. This position will be a "monopoly" if there is no firm outside the group which is adjacently competitive with all of them.
