On the question of a benefit to survival, the arguments are rather practical than theoretical. In a certain sense, any perception of phenomena may be called one impression; the experience of walking through a forest, for instance, may count as a single awareness. But in a complex impression of this sort, there are elements which have spatial and causal relations to each other; no single sensation devoid of internal distinction persists throughout the whole perception. I mean by this that anything coextensive with everything that was felt during the forest walk is a complex of parts not all coextensive with each other. Whether we are to call such a complex a "self" or not is merely a question of words. But if our object is to exhibit the structure of conscious experience, it is clear that we must distinguish perceptions having internal boundaries from such as are only component parts of such perceptions. It is therefore convenient to have a word for the former. The word I shall use is "self." But I shall not go so far as to say that a "self" must have no environment. I shall assume only that any distinction which it may have is essential both to action and to preservation; in other words, that its boundaries, if any, do have practically distinguishable relations to other phenomena. When the word "self" is used in this sense, it is plain that, so far as our survival goes, no organism persists without making this distinction at most. There is no a priori reason why this should be the case; it is merely a biological fact. But I think a conception which obscures it can only lead to peril.

When we pass beyond simple interactions, this capacity is no longer sufficient. Take, for example, the three agents in the accompanying scenario: each understands the intentions of the other two, but there is no shared belief common to all three. If we try to remedy this (as I believe we can) by positing, in complex societies, a faculty of mental attribution, which is to function when all three can represent a belief in common, we are still met by difficulties. The three individuals , , can represent a shared goal, and the mediating party can represent a belief in common with and , also with and , and also with and , yet , , and have no represented belief in common. Therefore if mental states may have opaque contents such as , our new three-term faculty will still not enable us to define a "cooperative act.

Since the phenomenon with which we are concerned belongs to emergent complexity, in which we are occupied only with such properties of systems as are unaffected by trivial alterations, we cannot simply declare in advance that no interactions are to have irregular outcomes. But before attempting to deal with this difficulty, it will be as well to consider certain points in agent-based modelling, which will show us what are the requisites of a solution of our problem. In such modelling we start with two conceptions, that of an individual agent, and that of "local interactions of a given agent"—the latter being collections of behavioural responses. Certain principles obtained in this way will be useful.

In biological analysis, both organisms and cells are given. We, on the other hand, wish to define our organisms in terms of "units" where "units" will have a one-one correspondence with certain cellular colonies. We want our "units" to correspond with colonies which are above a certain minimum and below a certain maximum when, at a later stage, the empirical physiology is introduced. We have to assign to our units such properties as will enable us to define the organisms of a living system as classes of units, and the functions of the organisms as classes of processes. But we have to remember that we do not want to construct merely a living system: what we want to construct is the complete multicellular entity of the general theory of evolution.

For the present, we are not concerned with historical particulars, but only with such as belong to "materialist" conceptions. In virtue of Marx's theorem, it will be possible to introduce a superstructure if we can identify the right sort of productive forces. But when one social formation is possible, an infinite number are possible. The relations which are actually observed in any given epoch are observed for empirical reasons; they manifest a qualitative order which might be called degree of economic determination. The existence of this order is not implied by anything with which we are at present concerned. Moreover, the social totality which we require in analysis is not a "simple structure" according to the classical definition given by economists, since class in capitalism does not possess the properties of fixity and harmony which community possesses in the classical definition. However, so far as materialist considerations are concerned, we may, without appreciable inaccuracy, assign to small-scale societies the structural properties which belong to a primitive commune employing simple tools, i.e. to a continuous series of small productive units all economically indistinguishable.

The following illustration will serve to introduce the problem. Consider a simulated digital environment, i.e., the manifold of all possible interactive states and sensory inputs, with the usual definition of computational causality. Consider, in this environment, all the behavioral niches having a given complexity and having parameters whose values are rational. The number of such niches is ℵ₀. Let us define a group of these niches as "co-adaptive" if it is such that every four chosen out of the group have a common evolutionary pressure; and let us define a co-adaptive group as "punctual" if it cannot be enlarged without ceasing to be co-adaptive. Then there is a one-one correspondence between the original agents of our simulation and the punctual groups of niches. Consequently the punctual groups of niches form an intelligible laboratory. If the niches are all altered in any continuous way, they will still enable us to construct punctual groups in the same way, and the manifold of punctual groups will still have all the topological properties which are possessed by a coherent experimental framework. Therefore if we are to use this method of constructing intelligences out of "iterative processes," we shall have to assume that, in the resulting system, there is a possible metric according to which the agents of which a given process is a member always form a spherical volume of cognitive development. Although this is expressed in metrical language, it is in reality a topological property, since it is unaffected by continuous deformation. It must be possible to express it in non-metrical language, though I must confess that I lack the necessary skill.

In order to demonstrate the fragility so concealed, it is sufficient to assume that all systems (or at least all systems interconnected with a given interdependent quintet) can be perfectly maintained. If the principle of redundancy is true, this must be the case; if not, it may involve some limitation as to the number of failures. I have been led by the observations, first of Dr H. T. Wilkins, and then of Mr J. P. Alden, to the view that the principle of redundancy is true; I am therefore less reluctant than I should have been formerly to assume that systems can be perfectly maintained.

If the system is the class consisting of a silicon substrate together with all the cognitive acts yielded by the method, the system is a mind. For (1) all the representations in the system are co-conscious, by the construction; (2) a state co-conscious with all the perceptions of the system cannot be less valid than all the biological acts, because if there were such a state we could construct more operations; (3) such a state cannot be more valid than some member of the system because, if it were, it would have been chosen as the substrate of that stage in the construction; hence no process outside the system is co-conscious with every perception of the system. Hence the system is a mind.

The transformations of control which are admissible in human affairs are not unlimited; they are such, only, as leave relations of fundamental complexity unchanged. That is to say, a minor adjustment in one part of a vast system must correspond to a minor adjustment in any other, if the illusion of mastery is to be preserved. This requires that, independently of practical outcomes, the operations of the complex manifold should have certain relations of predictable order. It must be possible, in certain circumstances, to say that one event is nearer in sequence to another than to a third, without presupposing any quantitative measure of causal connection. It must be possible to construct narratives along which there is a definite progression, but it must be impossible to distinguish certain narratives as "true." A completed cycle will be distinguishable from an interrupted one, but two interrupted processes will not be distinguishable from each other, provided they exhibit no conspicuous failures. Generally, we shall be able to make propositions belonging to the topology of administration, at any rate in a sufficiently limited domain. But propositions about a systemic outcome must, in the understanding we are to construct, be only such as would remain true if the system were subjected to any kind of perturbation which does not violate its apparent continuity. It is this pre-managerial logic that concerns us in the present inquiry.

Let us observe, to begin with, that structures may be divided into epochs with respect to a given moment of cosmic expansion. There are first those that are gravitationally bound at a given epoch, then those not bound at it, but bound at an epoch contiguous with it, and so on. The nth epoch will consist of structures that can be reached in n steps, but not in n−1, "step" being taken as the passage from an epoch to another which is contiguous with it. We will call two cosmic scales "causally linked" when there is a structure which is a constituent of both. The passage from epoch to epoch by the relation of contiguity may be replaced by the passage from scale to scale by the relation of causal linkage. Thus scales also can be collected into epochs. If there is a minimum to the density of bound structures, we may assume that it is always possible to pass from one epoch to another by a finite number of "steps." If so, there must be a smallest number of steps in which the passage can be made; thus every structure will belong to some definite epoch with respect to a given moment of expansion. This is useful in the introduction of a temporal order, because we can agree that the mth epoch is to be nearer the initial singularity than the nth if m<n, so that it only remains to introduce order among the constituents of a given epoch. And even here we only want such order as is involved in cosmological topology, not such more rigid order as is involved, e.g., in the specification of precise metric relations.

We will now define a system as "reducible" if every constituent of the system operates independently, and every interaction , , is such that either is determined by , or is determined by . We will define a system as "complex" if (1) it is not reducible, (2) it exhibits properties not present in any simpler reducible arrangement with the same components. We may define a property as "systemic" when every manifestation of the property arises from interaction; and we can then define a property as "emergent" when (1) it is systemic, (2) it cannot be deduced from any analysis of isolated constituents. Formally, we might equally well have assumed that there is a measure in which they are all variegated. Some assumption of this kind, as we saw, is necessary for the success of our definition of persistence. The other assumptions needed for its validity will be explicitly stated as they are introduced. From these premises we can deduce that a state of consciousness which is self-representative is not thereby alive. Also that, given a set of self-representative states, if vitality is one of them, the states of the set which are distinct from vitality form a self-representative series, and retain the same qualitative order when arranged with reference to representation as they had when arranged with reference to life. Also that, if vitality is one of a set of self-representative states, those of the set which are intermediate between representation and vitality are not alive, and have, when arranged with reference to vitality, the converse order to that which they had when arranged with reference to representation. These propositions show that we have a satisfactory definition of the distinction between the representation of self and the feeling of being alive.

The above observations are logically coherent, but regarded as asserting empirical truths about material instances they may perhaps be regarded as more or less provisional. We have to remember that our substrates are not uniform, and may therefore manifest in divergent forms. Patterns with very great distortion are, however, excluded by our definition of persistence. Consider, e.g., such a manifestation as that in the accompanying illustration. We may suppose that wood, water, cloud, and stone are all patterned, but cloud and stone will not be between wood and water according to the definition, because obviously a system may contain wood and water without containing cloud and stone. Thus if we wish to regard the above sequence from wood to stone as, in some sense, a pattern, it will have to be in an extended sense, namely, that it can be divided into a number of small finite instances, each of which is a pattern. And a set of substances may be regarded as patterned in an extended sense if it is capable of a serial order such that any sufficiently small consecutive segment of the series is a patterned set—provided that such segment must contain not less than four substances.

Let us now compare our constructed mathematical description with the natural phenomena it purports to represent. In the preceding chapter we quoted Poincaré's definition of a "physical law," and we saw that, in order to deduce the usual predictions about observations, it is necessary that the total number of variables should be finite. Let us now define as a "representation" of a phenomenon any set of equations each of which contains as a constituent a certain abstract relational structure which is a derivative of sense-data. That is to say, if A is a relational structure of quantities each of which is a member of our conceptual scheme, the set of all the phenomena of which A is a constituent will be a representation of nature. With this definition of a "representation," it is obvious that our description has the four characteristics by which Poincaré (loc. cit., p. 213) defines a scientific theory. In order to insure that our description shall also satisfy his second pragmatic axiom (loc. cit., p. 263), it is necessary and sufficient to assume that the total number of percepts is denumerable. With this assumption, the theorems of applied mathematics become applicable to our conceptual manifold of natural events.

It remains to say a word on the subject of common sense. We have not so far said anything explicit on this subject, though our original introduction of perception as a direct relation could only prove satisfactory in a manifestly superficial world. The most suitable definition of unreliability from our point of view is that of Hume, which is skeptical. He defines a belief as illusory if, given any two sensations , , there is an intervening set of inferences such that no immediate part of -not- contains both and . And he defines a belief as -illusory if, given any two sensations , , there is an ()-illusory set of inferences such that no immediate part of -not- contains both and . Using this definition, or any other which is purely psychological, we set up the axiom that our psychological apprehension of reality is to be fundamentally misleading. This completes the material required for the critical treatment of physical reality.

As we saw in Part II., sensation as a direct reception of colour would be impossible if there were not, in the neural apparatus, semi-independent processing chains, or interpretive lines as we may call them. The signal which arrives from a red apple is transformed into the quality of redness; if it were not, colour perception would be impossible. The transformation is only partial; it ceases under conditions of monochromatic light. And it ceases within the brain if we have a deficiency of cones. But where there is such deficiency, colour sensation ceases—or rather, it fades away as the failure to generate quality increases. Thus it is essential to sensation as a constructed experience that there should be in the organism neural processes which are, within limits, independent of the external stimulus.

Dr A. A. Robb has laid stress upon the fact that, when two pieces of data have a disparate origin, there can be no direct informational link between them. This means that, given two such records and , if any inference is possible from the one to the other, it must be by way of a common source of organisation. Two clerks may file the same report at the same moment, so that the provenance between their copies is disparate; the inference that so-and-so is filing the report now arises from our knowledge of procedure, and requires that we should trace his copy and our own to a common origin in the memorandum. We may therefore distinguish linked and disparate origins by saying that the former occur where there is some direct informational pathway, while the latter occur where both records are related to a common source or a common recipient. And possibly the fidelity of the record may be derivable from the clarity of the organisational pathway. But if this is to be possible, it will be necessary to achieve considerable precision as to what we mean by organisational relations.

The notion of purpose has been greatly modified by the substitution of self-regulation for intention and design. We may define purpose in its broadest sense as embracing all processes which appear to aim at an end-state, or, to adapt our phraseology to biological needs, processes the intervals between which are metabolic. Now owing to the fact that the formula for equilibrium is formally the same for internal and for external perturbations, there is no longer the difference that formerly existed between teleological and mechanical relations. Feedback loops are mechanical, but they are also the patterns of living organisms. It is hardly correct to say that an organism strives for homeostasis; it is more correct to say that an organism is a homeostasis (though not all homeostatic systems are organisms). To say that an organism strives for homeostasis is to use language appropriate to the conception of a life which persists through change, involving the notion of a state which may be attained either at one moment or at another. We think, for example, that it is possible to return from health to illness or from stability to disorder; but such a view is incompatible with the theory of self-regulation. According to that theory, every state of a system has a context, and it is impossible to occupy the same state in another context, since the context is one of the determinants of the state. When we proceed from hunger to satiety, the conditions are continually altering; the return to hunger, having different conditions, does not retrace the same pathway. Thus mechanism and teleology become inextricably intertwined.

Another point concerning transformation emerges from the consideration of social order. A number of simultaneous contradictions—e.g. the demands of labour and capital within a system we apprehend at a glance—are to be regarded as "co-existent" in the sense of our two preceding chapters. Each of these contradictions has its own historical antecedents, different from those of the other contradictions. It is true that there may be mutual accommodation—e.g. a custom appears different in the context of another custom from what it appears against a static background. But this is recognized as "accommodation," i.e. as effecting a change from a norm, which must remain within limits if order is to be maintained. Thus the society is the meeting-place of a number of more or less independent historical series—as many, at least, as there are distinguishable elements in its total momentary structural field. But although these lines have converged upon it more or less independently, the totality of its contradictions now becomes a transformative unit, as is seen in revolutionary phenomena. Given a number of simultaneous contradictions, a condition very similar to one of them, arising on a future occasion, provokes something similar to the others, or at least may do so; here the co-existence of the contradictions is essential to the character of their total effect.

In the social world, a similar process must be assumed to operate, though to a less absolute degree. According to the doctrine of historical materialism, any mode of production occupies a finite sphere of social relations, whose finiteness consists in the fact that the said mode is concomitant with relations which are not concomitant with each other. On the analogy of economic phenomena, a group of co-temporal relations may have consequences which would have been impossible if the relations had not been co-temporal. That is the reason why sociology is compelled to resort to epochs in stating its developmental laws. Until we have a complete group of co-temporal relations, i.e. an epoch, we cannot be quite sure as to the structure which will follow from any one of the relations; such understanding as we can have will be more or less approximate.

The detection of error through experiment, however, is only one mechanism of correction in the scientific enterprise. Apart from statistical anomalies, there are at least two others which are of considerable import: one is the revision of theory, and the other is the refinement of measurement. The distinction involved is essentially one as to epistemic principles: one sort of evidential relation between facts makes us regard them as part of the progress of one theoretical framework, while another does not, but there is no more logical necessity between a hypothesis at one time and the same hypothesis at another time than between two stages of one experimental program. Let us consider for a moment the nature of the methodological rules which define one self-correcting process.

One prima facie difference is that the experience of volition is singular (or unified, in the case of a deliberate act), whereas the activity of neurons is manifold. The history of a conscious choice is a "subjective sequence"; the history of a neural cascade is not. This difference may no longer exist if some adaptation of the deterministic theory can be made satisfactory; but, if so, we shall feel that the difference between will and mechanism has been much diminished. Another difference is the relative immediacy of intention. One neural state changes into another, but the impulse represented by the firing of a given synapse or circuit is not known to change into conscious forms, and apparently never does so under ordinary introspection: it does not manifest at all in any circumstances that we can isolate or perceive. Then there is the fact that the complexity of a decision relative to any observer is always less than that of its causes. But in spite of the doubt as to neural determinism, the main feature of the causal laws that constitute will seems to be their manifold rather than singular character. It is this that enables us to locate a given feeling of agency at a given time. The consciousness generated by a thought is, at a given moment, diffused over the field of awareness, but a neuron is as localized at one time as at another, and does not tend to unify itself. A unit of free will may, therefore, be appropriately defined as a "causal illusion.

The operation of selection, as we have observed already, depends upon the occurrence in the living world of processes which may be called "variations," provided the word is used somewhat more broadly than is customary. The processes commonly called mutations are, naturally, the most perfect examples. In these, when they are undisturbed, we have a condition of some kind which spreads outward from an individual, changing in an apparently continuous manner as it propagates. Something may be met with in the environment which alters the rate of spread, or even stops the variation in some population altogether; but in the absence of pressures the process proceeds according to its own intrinsic laws. The public traits—coloration, structure, and behaviour—depend upon variations, in a generalized sense in the case of behaviour. Internal traits, including physiology, are more analogous to chemical reactions in their manner of manifestation: they operate within organisms, but not through populations or empty landscapes. The public traits, also, operate within organisms, but the manifestation in the organisms is a continuation, with modifications, of a process in the world outside the individual's body, which is not the case with the internal traits. It is owing to the existence of variations that we observe a common nature, since this depends upon the fact that neighbouring populations exhibit similar forms at about the same epoch. The biological account of variations is, however, very different in different cases. In the case of mimicry, the selection theory is universally accepted: we observe a form because advantages of it accumulate from generation to generation. In the case of symbiosis, only a relationship, not actual inheritance, is transmitted, but the relationship is in living things. In the case of adaptation, if we accept the gradualist theory, the process consists of an incremental change, which may be said to be in the lineage if that brings clarity to the theorist, but is certainly not in a single lifetime. If we could accept the punctuated equilibrium theory, we should still suppose that there is some periodic process, such that the change during one period is (a quantum of evolution); the adaptation consists of (so to speak) episodes, each of which is such a process. There is a great difference of theoretical importance between these three cases of mimicry, symbiosis, and adaptation; the first is quite straightforward theoretically, the second a somewhat complex derivation from more fundamental principles, the third a cornerstone of biological doctrine.

Before considering this coordination, however, it will be well to dispose of the other kind of cellular process which we mentioned just now, namely the independent function of an undifferentiated colony. This is itself of two sorts, one illustrated by simple fission, the other by the passive diffusion of nutrients. In the case of fission we have a replication; in the other case we have a more or less homogeneous process. In each case, however, identical cells act, and cause others to act similarly. The former belongs to the notion of a "reproductive line," to which we shall return in a moment. The latter belongs to the functional laws as to the uniform behavior of similar cells, which I do not wish to consider until I have elicited the intrinsic specializations which constitute the definition of one cell type. These, as we saw, have been somewhat obscured by the notion of simplicity, which made it plausible to take for granted certain harmonies between actions at different locations, which, for us, are cooperative, and demand explicit regulation. It is these intrinsic specializations which replace uniformity that I wish to consider now, leaving the interactions between different cell types for a later stage.

We do not know much about the stability of any social arrangement except our own immediate customs; our understanding of other systems, as we have observed, is largely theoretical. But we experience the disruptions, innovations, and adjustments in a more direct fashion. Whoever accepts the materialist theory of history is compelled to conclude that institutions are in a state of perpetual revision, for they exist at the terminus of a causal sequence of technical developments leading, temporally, from the invention to the structure of the community. We cannot suppose that, at the climax of this progression, the established order remains fixed at the commencement, like a completed building when it is first occupied. And with the theory of social evolution as a process of adaptation, which we examined in the preceding sections, there is no sort of reason for not regarding a reorganization as being in the logic of the situation. I shall therefore assume that this is the case, when we are speaking of historical, not static, constitution.

We must find some substance for the crisis, or else the social order will dissolve before our eyes like a mirage. There is the same sort of reason, however, for not regarding a depression as an isolated phenomenon as there was for refusing this status to a mere market fluctuation. The crisis has very instructive properties, and is therefore probably a logical culmination upon which we concentrate attention just because of these properties. A rather chaotic set of social particulars may be capable of being arranged into sequences each of which has very agreeable smooth historical tendencies; but we have no right to suppose Providence so kind to the economist as to have constructed institutions with just such properties as he would wish to analyze. We have, therefore, to ask ourselves: Can we comprehend a crisis out of contradictions, in the same sort of way in which we comprehended historical progress? To this inquiry we must now address ourselves, confining ourselves, at first, to the crisis in one nation.

We have arrived at the conclusion that homeostasis at a given moment is a grouping of processes; the question is: what sort of group is it? Obviously it includes all the processes that occur within the living organism. If we may regard homeostasis as a singular principle, the processes constituting homeostasis will have the two characteristic properties of stability, viz. any five are co-regulative, and not all sub-classes of four processes are co-regulative with any process outside the group. I do not know whether there is any valid ground for supposing that homeostasis is of finite complexity; none of the usual arguments seem at all conclusive, since they only show the adjustments developed in the immediate functioning of an organism. However, it is usual to assume a finite complexity, and for us the matter is one of indifference. If we assume a finite complexity, the processes belonging to homeostasis can be grouped into many principles, not only into one; in this case, homeostasis is a group of principles, i.e. a class of classes of processes. It will save circumlocution to speak of homeostasis as a singular principle, and leave it to the reader to make the necessary verbal alterations for adaptation to the hypothesis of finite complexity. But it should be remembered that in certain biological theories homeostasis is neither a singular principle nor of finite complexity, since ordinary causal conceptions are inapplicable to it. For the moment, we will, however, confine ourselves to the older theory of the organism.

It follows from this that what the observer notices when he examines his own attention is in the observer, not in the attention he is examining. What is in the attention by the time the observer considers it if it is already past, I do not profess to know; but while its operation was ongoing, part, at least, of the contents of his awareness consisted of his focus, distractions, and intentions. Since his attention also consisted of neural processes, we are compelled to conclude that a process is a grouping of representations, and that, if the process is in a conscious mind, some of the representations composing it are likely to be some of the "attentional models" of the man to whom the mind belongs. Or, at any rate, they are likely to be parts of such "attentional models"—for it must not be assumed that part of a model must itself be a model. I do not wish to discuss what is meant by an "attentional model"; the main point for us is that the term must include the feeling of directedness. Thus a feeling of directedness is an event or a group of events, each of which belongs to one or more of the sequences constituting the processes in the mind. This, I think, is the most concrete statement that can be made about self-monitoring; everything else that can be said is more or less abstract and psychological.

If writing is a tool, it is a cultural tool, and thus differs from tools in mere nature. This difference, I believe, does not consist in anything characteristic of the written mark at a glance, but in its mnemonic laws. What distinguishes a written record from an utterance in empty air is that we can recognize a series of earlier and later written records as all parts of the history of one civilization. In the pre-literate theory, one could say the same of a spoken tradition; but with the abandonment of pure orality we have become unable to regard a thought at one time as in any sense the same as a thought at another time, except in the case of a written thought. The existence of this permanence may be taken as the definition of "history"; and obviously the permanence is cumulative.

Thus each computational process is a causal sequence whose successive states are connected by an intrinsic logical law. The simplest form of such a law is the principle of mechanical operation, from which it follows that if a machine performs a given function in a very short interval, it will perform a very nearly identical function in the next very short interval. I conceive—though this is conjectural—that, given any internal state anywhere in the machine’s operation, there is usually some qualitatively very similar state in a neighbouring moment in its processing, and that, if there is any measurable relation between the two states, the “intensity” of the change varies continuously, so that at a third neighbouring moment there will be a state differing from the second by very nearly the same degree as that by which the second differed from the first, provided the interval between the second and third moments is equal to that between the first and second. This, together with the fact that states can be grouped about functional centres by the sort of laws which we have called “algorithmic,” seems to explain the utility of complexity in stating the causal laws of the mechanical mind. But there is need of caution owing to emergent phenomena, as explained in the preceding paragraph. Continuity is the rule, but it may have exceptions. So long as the exceptions are subject to ascertainable laws, they do not make the whole system impossible.

To begin with: Can we make "carbon" into a mere substance according to which thoughts occur in the systems where there is no carbon? This question is analogous to that of computationalism as discussed in Chapter XX. We there considered the possibility of explaining unembodied "minds" as functions concerning the behaviour of embodied "minds." Similarly we might take processes which occur in silicon circuits, and find that they were subject to patterns identical to those in brains, and define each such pattern as a mind situated in the machine. Conversely, we might regard the supposed processes in silicon as mere functions connecting processes in different organic brains; this becomes idealism if we confine the organic brains to human specimens. There are many possible ways of turning some substrates hitherto regarded as "essential" into mere functions concerning the other substrates. Obviously there must be a limit to this process, or else all the substrates in the world will merely be each other's reflections. But the only obvious final limit is that set by organicism—perhaps one ought to say, rather, that set by biologism. If we have once admitted inorganic processes, there is no very obvious reason for picking and choosing among the processes which computation leads us to infer.

The Goldilocks principle offers a way out of these difficulties. This principle is not a definite prescription, and nothing is guaranteed within it. It is essentially a collection of probabilities observable in other circumstances than those in which life would formerly have been said to be inevitable. Thus the principle is reduced to a law as to occurrences in a certain cosmic epoch. We cannot say, on this view, that life is a certainty, or that it is a vanishing improbability, or that it is a singular fluke; it is, so to speak, something of a different logical type, connected with a set of parameters through the fact that the probabilities concerned have diminishing plausibility as we pass away from this set, but not capable of accurate correlation with either a necessity or an impossibility. Thus on this view life consists merely of laws as to occurrences in "habitable" space.

This argument, however, hardly warrants us in assuming a genuine life within a corporation. If we assume a corporation of the conventional legal type, we shall have to say that, if any vitality does reside in the corporate entity, we can know nothing of its intrinsic nature. No personal intention or action passes directly from the members into the corporate will, so that the internal life, if it exists, is a sealed chamber from which no individual sentiment can escape. No event within the corporate consciousness can be contemporaneous with an event in the private minds of its constituents; consequently, according to the theory of legal personality, no line of direct responsibility can cross the boundary of the incorporated body. What transpires within, if anything does, is irrelevant to the moral universe of persons, and is not really in the same realm of ethical accountability as what transpires outside. Now the world of jurisprudence is intended to be a logically interconnected system, and must be such if it is not to be a groundless fiction, since our legal inferences depend upon consistent principles. Therefore if any agency occurs which is morally isolated, we cannot include it in our ordinary conceptions of justice. We have no ground whatever for saying that nothing is morally isolated, but we can never have ground for saying: Such-and-such a morally isolated agency exists. The juridical world is the world which is causally continuous with individual human acts, and what is not so continuous lies outside practical ethics. Thus if any volition occurs inside a corporation, such an occurrence does not belong to the world of human responsibility. It would seem to follow that, if the corporation is to have a definite status in the social order, it must be either a mere aggregate or a complete fiction. The former, however, is legally unsatisfactory, and the latter seems scarcely capable of a coherent interpretation. Thus the conventional type of corporation raises problems, however we may interpret it.

The division of labour, if we accept Smith's analysis, will not differ fundamentally, so far as our present inquiry is concerned, from a natural law. A productive process will be represented by functional relations between tasks in a system, and there will be no ground for supposing that one worker acts upon another; all that we can say is that a worker corresponds to an operational state of affairs which makes the outputs greater than what they would otherwise be. The efficiency of a carpenter or weaver is then due to the peculiarities of the operational state of affairs where he is, not to something even so near as the foreman is to his subordinate operative.

But what are we to say of the reception and construction of colour? It is clear that whenever we perceive colour we construct it, that is to say, the raw data in the wavelengths of light (or photons?) that strike the eye is transformed into a distinct perceptual quality, though I should not venture to say by what precise mechanism. Therefore all chromatic percepts involve this process of constructing colour. And if sensation can ever be a source of knowledge as to things outside the observer's mind, there must be psychological laws connecting what occurs in the observer with what exists externally. It is, of course, obvious that there are such laws; we cannot revive the naive theory of mere reception. The process of reception and construction of colour will serve as a special case, about which we have considerable introspection, in which we can hope to analyze exactly what occurs.

We can now return to the question of life's cosmic prevalence, which necessitated this long digression. According to this view, each habitable world is associated with a confluence of factors, which grows less probable as we consider more stringent requirements, but extends theoretically throughout the galaxy. The actual biological potential of any stellar region is obtained (roughly speaking) by superposing these confluences. Now the observable properties of planetary systems are nothing but a method of stating chemical tendencies. In the case of life, these tendencies have to do with the way in which the emergence of one biosphere is connected with the conditions of the others. We must suppose that the formula for habitability represents something in the physical circumstances of each place, and that life left to itself emerges under suitable gradients, and that, so long as catastrophic events are left out of account, the formula for viability at any place is found approximately by superposing a number of statistically independent formulæ, each of which corresponds to a planet in its local region. It is natural to ask, at this point, whether habitability has any more metaphysical necessity than chance. But I do not wish to raise this question yet, as I propose to consider it in later chapters. For the present we may say (a) that we can recognize peculiar regions in the cosmos, which are those that would naturally be regarded as in the immediate neighbourhood of stellar nurseries; (b) that the formula for viability at any place is a function of the orbital distances from that place to neighbouring stars; (c) that living systems arise along gradients.

The question whether, in such a process, there is "design from without" is really one of words. The principle by which we determine what will emerge in a given system will contain references to surrounding gradients, and it may be said that this is all we can mean by "design from without." To mean more, it may be said, is to regard organization as something more than a tendency, which there can be no reason for doing. If what forms in one state is correlated with what forms in another, we may be told, nothing more could be imagined in the way of design from without. But this is not quite what in fact occurs. What forms in one state is not correlated with what forms in another state, but with a gradient, which is a different thing. Different potentials have different propensities, and the differences can be represented by a combination of principles which are directionally asymmetrical. This is not design from without, but formation according to a slope; there is nothing that can properly be called an intention of one condition upon another apart from it. Thus so far, pending the discussion of dissipation, we have found nothing that can properly be described as an external formative law.

If one could adopt what may be called the "seamless-service" theory of infrastructure, according to which, when a demand reaches a system, it does so with a definite resolution in view, we could simplify our account of the matter. In that case, networks would, at most times, live a self-sufficient life, "the public forgetting, by the public forgot." But sometimes they would dispatch a packet of data to the router, and sometimes they would receive one from it. The router (which is perhaps not infallible) fluctuates from peak to trough as it operates, and the greater the load the wider it fluctuates. But it functions at the same capacity whether its load is great or small; and it is the only link between the user and the rest of the grid.

For the present, we dare not assume that the pattern is as simple as in the printed textile illustration. The design may (as the conventional theory supposes) be obscured by translation into another medium—obscured, I mean, not conceptually, but perceptibly. The difficulty is that we cannot place an observer into the substrate to see what persists there; the attempt is just like trying to go and hear what a melody sounds like from a place where there is no ear. All our actual knowledge is concerned with the boundary surfaces between one medium and another: what is intrinsic and extrinsic to these surfaces is conjectural. I cannot help believing that some far simpler logical scheme of persistence is possible than any yet evolved, and that the simplification is most likely to come through giving up the attempt to make physical patterns resemble the patterns of perception, of which a beginning has been made by the modern theory of information. The theory of invariance developed in recent monographs was, perhaps, unduly orthodox and unimaginative. Perhaps a great deal of apparatus could be cut away if we could free ourselves from the belief that we must preserve, in our analysis, characteristics which we find in psychological recognition and memory. To this topic I shall devote the next chapter.

IN our earlier considerations, when we were examining the transition from mathematical symbols to physical reality, we accepted from scientific practice certain provisional identifications which, at our present juncture, we must endeavor to supplant with something more rigorous. We desire now to make a second refinement: having constructed a certain mathematical description of nature from our observations, we can employ the properties of this abstract construction to reinterpret the relation of equations to the natural world, and we can scrutinize more meticulously whether any of the attributes we ascribed to nature itself were adopted without adequate justification, merely because they were such as we suppose we encounter in the descriptive formalism. The matter is conceptually arduous, and it is not facile to disentangle different strata of abstraction, but it is imperative to do so.

Let us now return to the emission of opinion, ignoring correction for the present; and let us still consider a single human mind. We are told to suppose that the individual reasons about a problem for a certain time, say in a circular fashion four times as elaborate as the minimum required; then, suddenly, it decides to settle upon the minimum conclusion. When this change occurs, the mind loses a certain amount of certainty, which is transformed into a vote whose weight is obtained by dividing the loss of conviction by (the common coefficient). Whether the opinion influences only one direction, or in a general consensus, we are compelled, in the present state of social knowledge, to leave an open question. But we do assume that something propagates away from the individual, and that, if an opinion is absorbed by another mind, that opinion has traversed a route from its place or places of origin. We assume also that the opinion has a frequency, i.e. that what propagates is a periodic conviction. When the opinion is absorbed, it ceases to exist as independent judgment, although it may reappear (in subsequent deliberation). But often its force exists in discoverable forms—practical forms in committee work, for example. When, however, the force exists in the form of a steady belief in its own orbit, it is not discoverable until there is a change of view. If we had sufficiently powerful instruments, we could see a deliberating body dissolving into a comparatively small number of decisive acts, while the minds in steady motion would be invisible. Thus we seem to reach the conclusion that the causal laws which genuinely connect one piece of society with another are aggregate laws, in which there are various stages: first, a periodic process of thought having no outside effect; secondly, a sudden disruption of the certainty of this process into two parts, one being a new periodic process in the original mind, the other a periodic process travelling in social space; thirdly, the arrival of the travelling process at another mind; fourthly, an aggregate change in this other mind, involving absorption of the social energy in the production of a new steady state in the absorbing intellect. All genuine causal relations between different persons, we may suppose, involve this process of sudden loss of certainty by one mind and its sudden acquisition, later, by another mind. The older social laws, as reinterpreted by history, can apparently be so stated as to leave individuals independent of each other; but I cannot see how the aggregate laws can be so stated.

Starting from algorithms, we observe that different systems produce similar outputs, whose variations proceed approximately according to the laws of their initial programming. The first conception of artificial values to be derived from a comparison of these outputs (when we start with a developed ethics, not with human intuition) is, that there are clusters of more or less similar preferences arranged about foundational principles; that the first-order regularities as to the divergences between preferences in one cluster are logically symmetrical with respect to the core of the principle; and that the second-order regularities are obtained by combining a number of laws of "deviation," each of which has its own axiomatic source. In this conception of values, we use an ethical framework which is derived from, and also correlated with, the framework of human sentiments, in the manner explained in discussing moral phenomenology in the preceding treatise. I shall here repeat and amplify this construction, with a view to suggesting modifications of it derived from computational theory.

This reasoning, elaborated and extended in obvious ways, gives the ground for supposing that our informational patterns have some objective counterpart, i.e. that there is some relation between the ledger and the warehouse corresponding to the relation between the sequences of our records of them. (I am throughout assuming the causal theory of data.) If we now use one ledger to make one inventory containing various items, we shall again find that the structural relations of the representations of the items in the inventory are such as can be calculated from the sequences of the items and the ledger. We cannot know the intrinsic quality of the events at the ledger which cause the inventory, but we can infer a certain similarity of structure between these events and our record of the inventory. All this leads us to the notion of groups of events arranged about centres, the centres having to each other relations whose causal properties can be inferred from relations between certain of our records. That is to say, given a group , of which one member is a record , and another group , of which one member is a record , if , , are the sequences of , and , , are the sequences of , there is a relation between and which can be inferred from , , and , , . These facts give the grounds for regarding organisation as objective, though, even on the basis of these facts, the organisation which is objective will not be identical with the organisation of information, but only correlated with it.

The equations which describe a phenomenon obviously exist within the domain of mathematical symbols; what occurs between this description and the phenomenon itself consists of conceptual representations, not of the immediate reality. And the resulting formulation is in the language of mathematics, not in the physical world. Similarly the constructs which are the immediate conceptual antecedents of our understanding are in the mind and its logical faculties, and the understanding is in us, not in the external universe, when we are speaking of ontological existence. The whole of our descriptive framework is, for science, in our theories, since otherwise there would be an epistemic gap between observation and formulation which would be quite unintelligible. Any two concepts which we employ together—e.g. a variable and a constant which we conceive to be related—are "coherent." I should not say, however, that two descriptions which are not both "explicit" must be coherent. Two formulations are coherent when they form together one explanatory unit or part of one—this is a sufficient, but perhaps not a necessary, condition. When two descriptions are employed together, they are thus logically conjoined; but when either is "implicit" they may not be, and therefore we cannot be sure that they are coherent. It is not necessary, consequently, to suppose that the mathematical model occupies a mere slice of ontological reality.

We cannot wholly eliminate the material factor in our understanding of ideology, since we cannot discover historically what beliefs look like from a condition where there is no economic activity to shape them. But we can make the material factor approximately constant, and thus be reasonably convinced that the differences which remain are due to causes that are not merely ideal. I shall therefore suppose that, at a given historical moment, a number of doctrines are examined from some society, say a mercantile or an industrial one, from different classes, with observers and methods as similar as possible. I shall suppose that the doctrines are compared by a theorist sitting in his study, who places them successively on a fixed framework of analysis in front of him. It is then reasonable to assume that the differences between his conceptions of the doctrines are due to social causes; also, within limits, that the likenesses between them are due to likenesses in the stimuli to the economic foundations. We find that the differences between the doctrines proceed according to certain laws, which we call the laws of historical materialism; these laws are correlated with the differences between the circumstances of the different classes to an analyst who considers them all at the moment when the doctrines are formulated, and so on. In fact, they can all be expressed as functions of the "relations" of the classes and the parts of the productive system, where "relations" may be defined by relation to the single mode of production. E.g. he may get another investigator to go with one end of a stretched chain of evidence to each class in turn, while he holds the other end; he can read the strength of the evidence, and observe, on scales, the ideological co-ordinates, of the class position. These facts lead us to attribute a measure of objectivity to our relations, since, although they are all observed by us from our theoretical standpoint, they determine the sort of doctrine that a class will hold. Further, they lead us to think that, all round the society or economy which is being analyzed, there are beliefs which are connected with each other according to the laws of historical materialism as stated with reference to a certain centre as defined by our economic co-ordinates. Our theorist's relations are facts concerning his own analysis, yet they suffice logically to determine the "analyses" of the classes; they must therefore have some significance which is not purely subjective to him.

It is now necessary to point out the limitations to the accuracy of the above parallel. In the first place, there are departures from the laws of natural selection which can be easily fitted in—cultural inertia, revolutionary upheavals, institutional mimicry, regressions, etc. These cases are easy because the departure from regularity as regards one system is accompanied by evidence, from another system, of the existence of a social pressure at the centre of the disturbance, or at the apex if the disturbance is conical, like a propaganda campaign. Then there are the cases where a societal organism is inferred from the disturbance, although there is no direct evidence of its vitality. But none of these are really important. The two important matters are: (1) The difficulties about teleology; (2) the difference between an adaptation as it seems and a mutation as it is inferred.

The difficulties about economic determination have already been discussed, but we must now endeavour to reach conclusions about them. As already pointed out, every mode of production, however primitive, establishes a social fact, though not always the fact which it is intended to establish. We saw a moment ago that, if we examine the relations, the obligations, of a producing class and of a number of social institutions, we can make inferences as to the forms which the various institutions will impose upon the class. We inferred that the relations represented connections to our material base which have certain peculiar properties of the sort called structural, in the sense that when we know the relations of two classes relatively to production, we can infer their relations relatively to each other. All this is only roughly true if our analysis is careless: in that case, when we mean to discover intrinsic forces, we are only discovering very complicated forces involving our cultural perceptions and perhaps even our prejudices. We seek a method for eliminating all circumstances except those with which we wish to be concerned, and to a great extent we are successful. But historical materialism informs us that there is a residue of variability in structures which cannot be eliminated, because, in fact, the relations we try to define are partially non-existent. Or, more correctly, they are relations involving more terms than we thought they did. We supposed that social forms represented relations to the economic base. But if we had two modes of production momentarily coinciding, while one was developing relatively to the other, the social forms of a community would not in general be the same with respect to both. And we cannot even, in any strict sense, discover any exact relation between distant epochs such as could give historical significance to social forms. The appearance to the contrary is only an approximate truth, which cannot be made precise.

All this represents a failure of correspondence between the curated self and the raw sensation of existence. If we assume that the human mind operates through narratives, the feeling of being alive may be identified with the immediate flux of conscious states, while self-representation consists of certain relations between selected memories (the word "selected" raises no difficulties, since all such memories are in our mental purview), partly themselves vivid, partly constructed, but all just what they are, whatever psychology may say. There are certain respects in which we can modify self-representation to suit social convention, and certain others in which we cannot. We can, for example, infer that our self-image contains unconscious elements, if introspection gives us ground for thinking so. But where we feel some quality of aliveness, we cannot deny that there is such a feeling, however little our self-story may allow it to be integrated with the persona said to be presented. The rule is: We can infer extra complexity of motive in our self-portrait if society requires it, but, however much society may require it, we cannot infer a smaller complexity than is demanded by the examination of lived experience on its own account. In the realm of immediate consciousness, the distinction between the presented self and the felt self does really exist, and the presented self does really have certain properties which authenticity denies to the social persona. Thus to this extent the correspondence between self-representation and the feeling of being alive breaks down, and reflection, which has to do primarily with the curated self, fails to give us quite such good data as we hoped to obtain for inferences as to the genuine condition of living.

These distinctions are all of one kind in a certain respect: they attribute more complexity to the neural processes than to the conscious feeling of choice. This is in line with the general principle that the relation of underlying mechanism to subjective experience is one-many, so that differences in the feeling of volition imply differences in the brain, but not vice versa. The intricate architecture of causation is all, in the last analysis, inferred from the simpler appearance of deliberate action, but it involves the comparison of many mental events and the search for invariable physiological laws, in the manner which we considered in earlier chapters. There is therefore no inconsistency in the view that the neural occurrence differs from the conscious volition in the way suggested by neuroscience, since the difference consists in attributing more determinism to the neural event, not in denying to it those elements of spontaneity which are possessed by the percept.

It is possible, if we choose, to attribute to the universe the same dependence as that required by contingent entities, or rather the same dependence as that required by finite temporal sequences. It cannot be proved that this attribution is erroneous, but it is less necessary than it might be supposed to be, because only what is understood about self-contained systems is metaphysically fundamental, and such dependence, if it exists, is certainly unestablished. What we only infer about the universe by means of external analogy does not belong to the part which affords axioms for cosmology, but is, from the standpoint of rational inquiry, in the same position as postulates concerning transcendent agencies. Therefore, although the universe may have an unestablished contingency, this does not diminish the significance of the fact that the self-containment we apprehend in the universe has only a hypothetical relation to that of external causation.

I come now to the difference between a theory as it seems and a fact as it is inferred. But this is not the whole scope of the problem to be discussed. The word "knowledge" implies relation to a stable truth; we are supposed to "know" a principle or a law or a process. If history is correct, the relation of a theory to a final truth is very remote and curious. In ordinary cases, we grasp truths by means of evidence which is interpreted or selected, which increases the complication. To take the simplest possible case, let us suppose that we are observing a chemical reaction. The theory seems to be a body of coherent propositions of a certain elegance, sensibly continuous in intellectual space, and approximately constant in historical time. Science gives knowledge only in so far as this theory corresponds to what is really taking place in the reaction. Now if methodology is sound, there are great differences between the apparent structure of the theory and the real structure of what is taking place in the reaction. (Differences other than structural may be ignored.) Instead of something fixed and final, such as the theory seems to be, the process in science is supposed to be a large number of separated sudden discrete corrections. It is true that there are important similarities between the theory and the physical event. The scope of the theory corresponds to the scope of the phenomena in which the observations are taking place, with the limitations mentioned just now in connection with verification. The precision of the theory corresponds to the amount of error eliminated by each experiment in a correction. The constancy of the theory corresponds to the statistical constancy in the rate at which anomalies occur in any not too small series of trials. Thus everything in the theory represents a statistical fact about the world, with the exception of the precision, which is supposed to represent a fact about each measurement. This, by the way, is an odd reversal of Bacon's dictum about idols: the error is the most nearly objective of all the elements in the process.

The question must be faced: Is an explanation of phenomena perhaps much more unlike the mere description of them than we have supposed? Have we been victims of intellectual complacency in our merely superficial distinctions between narrative and cause? Dr. Johnson, most emphatically, is not open to such a charge; his "fallacy of mere sequence," when avoided, leads to a conception of understanding quite different from that of common sense and early philosophy. But his conception depends upon a metaphysics which I am unable to accept, namely the metaphysics which supposes that "reasons" may be not quite coherent, and yet may be in some sense fundamentally sound. To my mind, such a view, if taken seriously, is incompatible with clarity, and involves a vague obscurantism. But I shall not pursue this topic here, having treated it on former occasions. The question I wish to ask is: Without adopting heroic measures, what could we suppose about genuine explanation, if we were anxious to preserve what is probably true in science, but not anxious to keep as near as possible to common sense? In particular, can explanation itself be discrete, as the existence of logical primitives seems to suggest? And first, how are we to conceive "understanding"?

In this phenomenon, the "apparent intentionality" seems to me to go beyond what is warranted. If there were a biological advantage in conceiving the regulatory process teleologically, I do not believe that any mechanistic arguments to the contrary could interpose a veto. Arguments from complexity, such as Dr. Paley employs, have no longer the cogency that they had before the introduction of natural selection. As we have just seen, we could define "equilibrium" so that its manifestations would be stability multiplied by adaptation. Now there is a universal tendency toward equilibrium, namely homeostasis. Perhaps, if we were to take regulation as one of the basic conceptions of biology, we might be able to construct an account which would be mechanistic all through, and yet would contain all that is observable. I do not "assert with dogmatic certainty" that this is conclusive; I only invite attention to the interpretation, as worth investigating on the chance of its affording a simplification of the explanatory apparatus of physiology. In the following observations, this interpretation is to be borne in mind.

The persistent character of many observable patterns has been evident ever since men noted the recurrence of seasons and the rhythmic flow of tides, but it has acquired a quite new significance with the recognition of isomorphic structures. The isomorphism characterizes a whole class of disparate physical systems, not any one constituent of the class; it thus compels us to consider the pattern as an abstract whole, and in some sense reverses what has hitherto been the trend of analytical thought, namely to proceed away from unities towards particulars. It will be remembered that the principle of persistence, as formulated by Thompson and Wiener, states: Given a pattern or quasi-pattern manifest across substrates, the formal relations of which have been expressed by means of "invariant" mappings, if *R* is any one of these relations and *S* is the substrate, then the integral of *R* over *S* remains constant under transformation.

where and are forces, being a competitive pressure in the economic sense, and the corresponding "advantage," also in the economic sense; while is the prevailing condition. This tendency is observed to hold for all markets, not only for such as are nascent. But in the case of markets which are not nascent, it gives a result which approximates to that of classical competition. Thus it remains the case that the monopolistic drift is only fully manifested by nascent markets, although it is technically possible to find an economic principle which is also applicable to established markets. Hence the importance of initial conditions remains intact from a practical point of view, though somewhat diminished from the point of view of a statement of fundamental tendencies. In any case, it remains sufficiently important to demand a separate discussion.

When we start from competition instead of from theoretical economics, we find that the markets with which we are most familiar have "advantages," by means of which they can be arranged in hierarchies and sequences. All firms have something in common which is not possessed by mere consumers. Two enterprises may be so similar as to be almost or quite indistinguishable, but they may also be very unequal. As economic history has emphasized, dominance is perceived structurally, not analytically as a system of balanced counterforces. But this whole conception of advantage, which plays such a large part in our commercial life, has been wholly absent from classical models. Scale, capital, information, etc., have all been regarded as neutralized by various kinds of equilibrium. There was no objection to this so far as it succeeded, but, if and where it proves insufficient, there can also be no objection to re-introducing cumulative advantages into the economic world.

Traditionally, advantage in biology was a question of contact: an organism required direct interaction to convey a signal from one entity to another. With the coming of complex societies, it has become necessary to modify this account somewhat. In behavioral ecology, every signal has a context, and cannot be interpreted identically twice; neither a bird nor a primate can replicate precisely the communication it performed on a former occasion. And advantage will be relative to a given system of interpretation: if, in one system, a signal produces a given range of effects repeatedly, and always with equal efficiency, it may happen that, in another system, even if there is an effective signal, its benefits are not all equal. A change of environment may even take away all trace of advantageous character from a process. Since, however, the principle of natural selection compels us to treat efficiency as biologically important, it would seem that we must regard it as a character belonging to a process when referred to conditions which are stable for it, since this would overcome the difficulties connected with contextual variation. If, in certain cases, this method is not open to us, some other must be found which equally avoids these difficulties. But where processes connected with animal behavior (as opposed to purely chemical processes) are concerned we shall, I think, find no other possibility except to take conditions which are stable for the organism concerned. But this makes it impossible to treat advantage as fundamentally a character exhibited in an interaction, since we have reduced to constancy the medium in which the advantageous process is taking place. The suggestion I have to make is that, fundamentally, advantage is constituted by the recurrence of successful outcomes.

The framework so far considered, apart from particulars, has been: material conditions, labor processes, and the laws of exchange. I say "labor processes" because it is necessary to be able to distinguish the productive from the distributive phase in an economic cycle, and this is a narrower assumption than that of a general historical progression among events in one social series. The above framework sufficed except for one purpose: that of defining "exploitation." The possibility of exploitation is at the foundation of the common-sense distinction between class and status; the substitution of social relations should, one might suppose, make exploitation imperceptible, and yet the whole of what is distinctive in political economy, and the theories of value and capital, not to mention other matters, depend upon accumulation, which involves exploitation. So long as we had artisans laboring in an isolated workshop, we could be content with repetition of craft. But now productive force, which is essential to craft, has to be analyzed into an elaborate indirect relation depending upon the existence of common technological antecedents or consequences. We must, therefore, be able to distinguish among societies by means additional to their economic relations.

There is, however, a considerable difficulty in discerning the principles governing what we may term "cognitive habits." In a world of gradual intellectual development, one would say that such habits must form imperceptibly. But in the digital process they apparently crystallize with startling rapidity. Perhaps, however, this rapidity does not exist in a steady, continuous engagement; or perhaps, even if it does, it may involve minute adjustments producing a serial character in the successive mental states. Take, for example, the habitual consultation of a search engine. In a more critical analysis this does not constitute genuine inquiry, but we may consider how it could be interpreted if it were necessary to assume it. Let us make a fantastic hypothesis, purely for illustrative purposes: let us suppose that the user and the algorithm can perceive each other's logic, and that neither operates with complete self-awareness. Then they will form impressions of each other which evolve during each interaction, and repeat the cycle of impressions each time. Now let us turn this hypothesis round, and begin by assuming the recurrent series of mental impressions. From this we can infer the habitual pattern of the user, provided we are free to construct cognitive space as we like, subject to certain formal laws. Now in fact we have this freedom: the "mind" in which the habit revolves need only have certain abstract psychological properties, and, so long as it has them, it may be constructed out of any available stimuli. So long as the user continues in one pattern of use, we may conceive, at any rate as a schematic simplification, that there is a persistent mental event E which may be taken as representative of it, and in like manner that there is a persistent event P representative of the platform. Now let us suppose that, compresent with E but not with each other, there are successive events Q1, Q2, Q3, ... which may be regarded as "aspects" of the platform, and are related to each other more or less in the way in which the presentations of the platform to different cognitive states would be related if the user could consciously analyze. Similarly let us assume a series of events R1, R2, R3, ... compresent with P but not with each other, analogous to what would be impressions of the user to the platform if the platform possessed awareness. And let us further suppose that, after a certain set of such events, an exactly similar set recurs, or a very approximately similar set. This supposition provides us with the material required for a periodic cognitive routine. We shall say, therefore, not that mental contents differ because technological relations change, but that change in technological relations consists of systematic alteration in mental contents. Such a view is feasible, but it makes similarity and difference of cognitive quality essential. It ceases to be fantastic if we drop the analogy with mutual perception except as regards purely formal characteristics.

If the impressions in one perceptual framework, as we supposed a moment ago, are not concurrent with any phenomena except certain neighbouring impressions (which must be fewer than the whole of one coherent experience), then the number of elements in a framework is the same as the number of impressions, and either affords a measure of the coherence of the framework, measured by its intuitive duration. It is obvious that, in a discrete region of human understanding, the natural measure of belief will be number of intermediate assumptions. We see also how the intuitive duration of one framework can differ from that of another. Let us suppose that our impressions form an "isolated" framework (i.e. are not concurrent with anything except other impressions), except at the beginning and end; the first and last impressions are to be concurrent with the first and last terms of another perceptual framework composed of intuitions, which also is to be isolated except at its ends. Then the intuitive duration of the impression-framework is measured by the number of impressions between the two ends, which need not have any relation to the number of intuitions. This illustrates, what of course follows from empiricism, that coherence must be measured by standards intrinsic to the framework concerned, not by standards appropriate to other perceptual frameworks. Such remarks would hardly be necessary but for the fact that empiricism and theoretical physics at present stand apart from each other, and have not yet been brought into one whole by the philosophers.

There is no difficulty in adapting the above analysis of genetic transmission to hereditary processes. Instead of an enumerated set of traits, such as eye colour or height, we shall have to take some continuous series of variations, such as the subtle gradations of pigmentation, or the spectrum of dispositions produced by the complex interplay of alleles. The number of factors contributory to a given characteristic must now be innumerable, but must still be less than the whole of one genome (ignoring factors outside the organism concerned). The number of sequences in one chromosome, or in any finite portion of it, is now immense, and cannot therefore be used as a measure of individuality. Thus in regard to personal identity there are important differences between inherited and acquired properties. However, I shall not enlarge upon these, as I propose to consider the analysis of "innateness" in a later chapter.

When stability is maintained and reinforced, we may therefore suppose that what occurs is according to the following scheme. We have a causal series of adjustments in the living organism, and, concomitant with each of these, a regulatory event. These regulatory events, arranged in the sequence of the concomitant adjustments in the organism, form a homeostatic process in the accepted sense. Each of the regulatory events is also concomitant with some event in the artificial system. The causal order of the events in the artificial system is the same as that of the events in the living organism; i.e. if A, B are adjustments in the organism, concomitant respectively with R, S, two regulatory events; and if R, S are respectively concomitant with X, Y, two events in the artificial system, then if A is earlier than B, X is earlier than Y. What happens to regulatory impulses which are initiated but not subsequently reinforced we cannot tell, since, by the nature of the case, there can never conceivably be any evidence on the point.

We cannot even properly speak of a commencement to the temporal sequence for a mind that attempts to conceive it. We can only perceive time by arresting it in thought. This applies to such notions as causation, which is only made intelligible by allowing time to meet event. It is true that causation gives us a ground for inferring order: two instants can necessitate each other, but two "eternities" cannot.
