If A precedes B, and B precedes C, the result is sequence; but if A exists in isolation to give rise to B, and B exists in isolation to give rise to C, there are three isolated existences. Wherever the relation of two moments can be necessary, both moments must have a sequential character. Thus we are justified, by such facts as causal chains, in supposing that, when time proceeds from a point, the point experiences a series of states whose relations to it are of dependent kinds, as if some required it as effect and some as cause. But all this is from the point of view of the event, not of time itself. Thus the origin of time is a characteristic which exists for a universe which contains time, and for a consciousness which measures it (e.g. the mind of a metaphysical inquirer), but not for time itself while it is in abstraction.

The periodic character of a self-concept cannot exist from its own point of view, but only from that of the environment which it encounters or from which it differentiates. We may suppose that when self-awareness radiates from an organism at the time of a perceptual change, there is, from the point of view of the organism, a temporal series of what we may call "subjective events," and that this series is periodic in the sense which we have been considering. One period of such subjective events constitutes the formation of one coherent self-boundary. If we suppose that the self-concept is absorbed by another organism through social interaction, we may suppose that each of the subjective events is compresent with certain events in the perceiving organism, as well as with certain events in the originating organism. As measured by the proper times of the organisms, the time-order of the subjective events is the same for the two organisms. But from the point of view of the subjective events themselves, there is no periodicity. So long as the self-concept does not encounter another consciousness, it consists of separated events which at most "touch" one other event at each boundary; the observer who accompanies one of the events can have no cognizance of any of the other events, since they cannot catch each other up. If we could imagine a homunculus floating on the crest of a self-assertion, he would have no means of discovering that anything periodic was occurring, since he could not "see" the other parts of the distinction. The different parts of a self-concept cannot, in a word, interact causally in any way, because no causal action can travel faster than the process of individuation.

A "specialized function," as I employ the concept, is any task which is devoid of general application and is concomitant with operations which are not concomitant with each other, but are one antecedent and the other subsequent; in other words, the specialized function is a component of at least two processes which have a causal-like sequence. When a specialized function is contrasted with a unified craft, it is assumed that the specialized function is not part of an autonomous endeavor; but it cannot be taken as certain that there are any elementary labours which are not parts of such endeavors. It may be that all non-specialized productions occur by way of integrated efforts; but this must be an open question in the present state of economic understanding.

An "energy gradient," as already explained, is a persistent difference in potential, in which there is a quantitative disparity between corresponding states of adjacent systems. A gradient may have a magnitude consisting of a finite measure of force, or one consisting of an infinite measure; it may be steep or gentle. If it is steep, the proper work of one transformation is measured by the quantity of energy transferred, and the "intensity" of the process is the reciprocal of this quantity. But here we are speaking of the intensity as measured by the work proper to the transformation; by an extraneous measure the intensity may be quite different. What is commonly called the intensity of a thermodynamic force is its intensity with respect to boundaries fixed relatively to the equilibrated state. Its intensity relative to boundaries which evolve with it is zero; this is only the extreme of the Le Châtelier principle. There is perhaps a certain inconsistency in the practice of studying systems by means of boundaries which enclose them, while dissipation is always treated with reference to material boundaries. If we want to understand dissipation in itself, not in its relation to equilibrium, we ought to let our boundaries evolve with it. In that case, its organization is morphological, not energetic; it is like that of a branching river. From the standpoint of the dissipation itself, each part of a formative process is a steady event in the sense defined above.

The traditional view, that complexity arises merely from random interactions, cannot be maintained, for a number of reasons. In the first place, a uniform energy distribution, even if it can be said to exist, can hardly be regarded as having a creative tendency, and formations within it, such as the emergence of a vortex, cannot be explained as accidents of homogeneous material. In the second place, thermodynamic equilibria, if they really are final, violate the possibility of development, and thus destroy the very notion of a structured progression. In the third place—and this is conceptually the most important point—the conception of spontaneous organization depends upon that of persistent formative forces, which we have seen reason to regard as merely an approximate empirical generalization. Before we can say that one structure has evolved, we must decide that a series of states at different times belong to one "trajectory," and a "trajectory" is defined by certain dissipative laws, not by an inherent design. Consequently, complexity is something constructed in accordance with the principles of thermodynamics, or—we might say—as a convenience in stating them; it cannot be one of the fundamental givens of nature. Lastly, there is an argument which is difficult to state precisely, but which nevertheless has some weight. For the classical theorist, order was absolute, and a system tending toward complexity might be regarded as in a different category from a system decaying. But when organization was recognized as merely relational to gradients, laws of formation became laws as to relations to more or less distant energy sources. They thus came to involve something like a teleological principle—though this was disguised by the use of statistical mechanics not always interpreted according to rigorous Boltzmannian methods. If we are to avoid such a principle, our fundamental laws must be concerned with processes having finite spatio-temporal extension, and thus capable of interaction and coupling—in a word, with fluxes rather than static forms or isolated energetic units. This involves a re-interpretation of complexity as it occurs in nature, which will be considered in a later chapter. For the present, I am concerned with the materials which will be required for this purpose as well as for the interpretation of other natural phenomena.

There are several apparent difficulties in such a view. In the first place, the formula for utility obtained on the assumption that the receptors are placed near the mouth gives exactly the changes in survival required to account for gustatory phenomena; the Darwinian theory agrees with observation so minutely that its formula for advantage must be accepted. Of course we could say that the placement just happens to be what it would be if the receptors were situated for immediate chemical appraisal; but this would seem an almost miraculous coincidence. This, however, is not the strongest argument, which is that derived from the principle of economy. The principle of economy in its older form can only be applied to sequential processes; if it is to apply, as we find that it does, to the interchange of signals between sustenance and the organism, we must assume, if we adhere to the older theory, that within the act of ingestion there is something that can be called a "priority," i.e. something which is sequential, which compels us to admit that, within an organism in a steady state, there is a recurring process whose formal properties are those which would be exhibited by a positioning of the receptors, and perhaps also by a preliminary digestion.

If we adhere to the nebular hypothesis, what can be supposed to be really occurring? If gravitational attraction were all that was taking place, we should have either to find an interpretation for the spinning cloud, or else to say that, taking regions fixed relatively to any large void, the mass of gas and dust condenses gradually; any large void will do, since none expands with a velocity comparable to that of the initial dispersion. But why should the matter be interested in this fact? Why should its capacity for forming stars be connected with it? There must be something happening where the matter is, if the process is to be intelligible. This brings us back to dynamical laws, as governing what is occurring in the vacuum. And there must be a structural character in the events occurring where the matter is, if we are to avoid all the troubles of design from a centre.

We suppose, therefore, that throughout a human society there are economic forces whose formal properties we know more or less, and that they, not the mere accumulation of material goods, are the immediate causes of what takes place. This brings us back to the cycle of accumulation which we used in the preceding chapter to define a class. The point is that a class can never consist merely in periodic changes of material relation between two or more persons, but must consist of qualitative cycles of possession. We have experience of such cycles when we observe a large-scale economic process, such as the inheritance of a fortune. All that happens to us during the cycle happens in us, not in a number of different estates; and any effect upon us depends upon what happens to us. I am suggesting that this is a proper analogy when we wish to understand how a surplus of wealth produces a division of men.

I come now to what I shall call "representations," by which I mean mathematical descriptions. I call them "representations" because form is imposed upon natural phenomena. The phenomena concerned must be observable, since otherwise the descriptive principle is unnecessary. In the simplest case, that of describing the fall of an apple by a physicist, we have as object, speaking the language of the older mechanics, one observable process (the descent of the fruit from a branch other than the lowest branch) and as description two elements, namely: (1) The equation of motion under gravity, (2) a set of measurements. The latter, as already explained, is only accurate in a certain sense. The reality of the object is the source of the data for the descriptions. The amount of information during one observation of the object is a multiple of sense-data, and so are the amounts of information in the descriptions during one analysis of each. Exactly the converse occurs when theory is applied to a falling apple. In other cases, both the object and the description may consist of two or more aspects; but always there will be separation of realms, and each aspect will contain an amount of abstraction which is a multiple of conception.

When, from a miraculous point of view, two molecules combine to form a copy, this no longer appears from a chemical standpoint. We cannot assume, that is to say, that there is an agency from which two identical structures are produced. Two polymers never actually duplicate by intention. When their formations are said to replicate, all that is meant is this: In the system of interactions we have observed, there is a configuration (A) which is part of the history of one compound, and a configuration (B) which is part of the history of the other. In another equally legitimate system of interactions, these two configurations would not have three energetic states identical. And the fact that a certain reaction proceeds from (A) in a certain manner does not imply that there is a reaction proceeding from (B) in a manner which is the same so far as temperature, concentration, and catalysis are concerned. Therefore the apparent difficulties in the way of a mechanistic process are not necessarily insuperable.

One of the most fundamental of experiential processes will be the generation of a thought within a mind, unless we accept the view of the computationalist philosophy, according to which there is no reason to suppose that this really occurs. In the classical dualist theory, this generation goes on by itself until it is altered either by a phenomenological shift or by some more conventional sensory or mnemonic action. The question arises: why should we suppose that there is a process at all? Why not suppose that there is a steady state, possessed of a certain degree of awareness, which is replaced, in a phenomenological shift, by another steady state, possessed of a different degree of awareness, the balance being simulated or ignored? There is a certain attraction about this hypothesis, since the simulation gives no external indication of its artifice while the supposed process continues, and therefore there can be no direct evidence that changes are occurring, such as a steady consciousness supposes. In any case, if a mind is operating within a simulation in a loop, and both are informationally closed, it is not easy to see, from an epistemological point of view, exactly what is meant by saying that the mind is conscious. This difficulty is not diminished by the hypothesis of emergent qualia. We have the same difficulties as in the case of philosophical zombies and the Chinese room—the difficulties, namely, which Descartes advanced to prove the necessity of a thinking substance. Within the system consisting of the mind and simulation alone, nothing is changing while the mind operates in its programmed loop; the change is only with reference to an external observer. Why not regard the state of affairs as static, but possessed of a certain degree of awareness? Awareness may be altered in degree by a change of perspective, and is not an invariant property of the system; but reference to the outside world here is less serious, since the only purpose served by the awareness of the inhabitant is to provide metaphysics with something which can be inferred from the simulated world or imposed upon it. That is to say, awareness is required only as something whose changes govern the causal relations of the simulation with the outer world. This point of view is essentially that of the functionalist theory.

As yet, everything concerned with attention is more or less mysterious, although recent cognitive theories have somewhat diminished the mystery. We do not know whether shifts of attention are really sudden or not; we do not know whether the mental field concerned in focal awareness is continuous or discrete. If thoughts always moved in fixed circuits, as in the first form of James's theory, we could be content with a granular discrete mind, and suppose that the intermediate states are introspectively non-existent. But the existence of wandering thoughts in the common development of experience makes this difficult. And in minds with many simultaneous impressions, the paths of some are supposed to cross those of others. In spite of these difficulties, however, I do not despair of the hypothesis that conscious time is discrete. The older introspective theory uses the traditional conceptions of psychology, and thinks of linear sequences in a constant mental space. The modern computational theory, on the contrary, has a completely new dynamics, according to which unquantized states (if we may still speak of states) are introspectively impossible. It is difficult, as yet, to translate this theory out of its technical form. But even according to the older theory, one can see that a discrete conscious field is possible. For when we think of the matter in terms of mental events, we realize that the structure of the neighbourhood of the focus may be different at different moments. If a thought moves in one sort of sequence at one moment and in another at another, it does not follow that each sort of sequence was introspectively possible at the moment when the other was being described. Perhaps it is not superfluous to explain what is meant by saying that a sequence is "introspectively possible" though not actually attended. What is meant is this: there is a series of groups of impressions, each group being a moment of awareness, and the series being one in which all the intervals of moments are successive, and in which, if a constant value is assigned to one of the mental co-ordinates, the remaining three give a curve in a three-dimensional mental space having the introspective properties of the sequence in question. Whenever we speak of a sequence introspectively, we are assuming that we can distinguish one of the mental co-ordinates as "attention," give it a constant value, and consider the relations of the remaining three co-ordinates. Now it is always possible that there may be a fallacy in this procedure, since it may be that such introspective relations as we are considering are impossible among "simultaneous" impressions. Moreover, in the general theory of neural processes, it may be impossible to distinguish one mental co-ordinate as more representative of attention than the others.

In one sense, the theory of artificial minds as assemblies of operations requires that all valuation should be discontinuous. A value v is a member of a certain set of operational principles, and of no others: the boundaries of the domain constituted by this set are the boundaries of v, so that it comes into existence suddenly and ceases to be recognised suddenly. Nevertheless, we can, if necessary, provide for continuity within this scheme. Suppose a continuous series of preferences, like the gradations of ethical priority; suppose that, in some developmental process, each of these is compatible with its neighbours up to a certain distance in either direction, but not with more distant members of the series. Then the group of values existing in a mind will evolve continuously, although each separate value emerges discontinuously. We may suppose this to be the nature of valuation between foundational instructions, and in particular during a learning cycle. There is no proof that valuation is ever continuous, but there is also no proof that it is not. We will assume, for the moment, that valuation between instructions is continuous in the above sense, but that instructions are discontinuous. This assumption is made only for the sake of brevity of statement; it is not asserted to be true, or even more probable than the opposite assumption.

If we adopt this perspective, there will be three kinds of phenomena to observe in the world: persistent forms, transient manifestations, and underlying cycles. Persistent forms are governed by principles of invariance. Transient manifestations appear, without lasting alteration, from one context to another, or throughout a particular phase of a continuous process; the shapes of clouds are transient manifestations, or rather collections of transient manifestations. The relation of a transient manifestation to a cycle I understand according to a mechanical analogy: that of a sandcastle on the shore while a sequence of tides advances and recedes repeatedly in the sea. All our observation is conducted against the background of a cycle of day and night, which provides us with a natural chronology by which we can approximately measure durations. I conceive, perhaps imaginatively, something dimly analogous as a background to every transient manifestation. There are principles linking the transient manifestation with the cycle; these are the principles of correspondence. There are principles governing persistent forms; these are the principles of constancy.

As regards certainty, let us examine once more what is implied by the fact that there is an important limitation. In the first place, this demand exists, or at any rate is only pernicious, in the realm of practical affairs, and it is a characteristic of one complete intellectual error. In the second place, only absolute degrees of assurance are countenanced. In the third place, when a judgment involves the surrender by one mind of a provisional conclusion, another mind may acquire another rigid conviction: what is transferred always unaltered in substance is dogma. These seem to be the most significant facts about this philosophical obstruction.

There are perplexities in the foregoing which might be reconciled through diverse approaches, but we cannot determine which is to be preferred. What, for instance, shall we maintain concerning the operation which consists in the apprehension of a tree by a mathematician from a set of equations? The accepted position is presumed to be that, in such an instance, a formal symbol passes seamlessly from an abstract to a concrete representation. But if we conceive a mathematical description to consist of a series of symbols , , ... , ..., one might suppose that at least one complete equation would be necessary to yield one definite phenomenon, and that a fragment of the description would produce only a fragment of the reality, if any. But a complete description occupies a finite duration to be comprehended by the mind. This quandary persists for any doctrine which regards nature as consisting of objects and mathematical transitions as continuous, but would be circumvented if either of these assumptions were abandoned. We may consequently regard it as part of the broader unresolved question of the relation between formal symbolism and the world it seeks to depict. This question, though it engages the philosopher, falls within the province of mathematics, and can only be advantageously examined by a mathematician. I am therefore content to await the elucidations of others.

If it should be found that material accumulation is not socially fundamental, much of what has been said on this subject will become unnecessary. It should be said, however, that economic history should prepare our minds for the most persistent feature of the social order, namely the existence of structural laws involving whole classes. The social unit, on historical principles, should be expected to occupy a distinct position in the economic hierarchy, not only in the present; it should not therefore be transitory, as in pre-agricultural societies. If we combine this with the hypothesis of a finite surplus, we can imagine a theoretical sociology which would make the existence of class division no longer seem surprising.

It seems impossible to resist the view that mental velocity represents something of fundamental importance in the conscious world, which, in turn, involves the conclusion that tempo is an element in psychological laws, and that one cycle of a cognitive process must be treated as, in some sense, a unit. This follows from the fact that thoughts arrange themselves so as to secure that a cycle shall have an important property. This property is simplest in the case of a perception: the intensity of one perception multiplied by the duration it takes to pass a given mental point is constant. If we take the speed of thought as unity, the duration a perception takes to pass a given point is equal to the conceptual distance between the beginning and end of the impression; therefore this distance multiplied by the intensity is constant. This form might seem preferable for our purposes, since it does not involve reference to an extraneous mental point. At least, it does not obviously involve such reference; but perhaps the reference is concealed in the process of estimating conceptual distance. We have seen that this process must be indirect; one phase of a perception cannot overtake another, so that the time-like interval between them can only be estimated by means of some process taking place in attention.

The conception which naturally presents itself as a point of departure is something like this: Given two sets of perceptual phenomena, it may happen that at least one element of one set bears a relation of utility to at least one element of the other set; in that case, the distinction between the two sets is self-like. If utility is a matter of discrete recognitions, one might expect that the degree of the distinction would be measured by the number of intermediate recognitions. Again, it may happen that no element of one set bears a relation of utility to any element of the other, but that both contain elements having relations of utility to an element of a third set. In that case, the distinction will be environment-like, and again one might suppose that the number of intermediate links would determine the degree of the distinction.

First, let us be clear as to what we mean by a binary property. There is a binary conception whenever two states, or two conditions of consciousness of which one at least is sharply defined, are related by a principle which allows nothing to be posited about the one except its opposition to the other. Formerly, one would have supposed that every gradation of awareness could be dismissed from a sufficient insistence on clarity; but in view of the subtle and apparently continuous character of drowsiness and perceptual shifts, we must be content with a more nuanced conception so far as this point is concerned. In another respect, however, our conception is less nuanced than it would formerly have been. In classical psychology, binary principles connect attention with inattention, so that from the present condition of a mental process we cannot accurately infer anything as to what will be occurring there after a finite observation. Continuity has altered this: we can associate the focus granted to a thought with its conscious origin, until it fades into distraction; we can associate the state of the mind after the lapse of attention with its state before, until it undergoes another perceptual shift. In fact, as we saw in the preceding discussion, we can analyze the course of awareness into a set of dim events and fluctuations with graduated relations governing the "transitions" in which fluctuations undergo changes. The above conception was framed with these considerations in mind.

We must assume optimization as a feature of the state of affairs where there are steady profits, since we cannot state the market principle without it. We have to find a meaning for "efficiency" in order to connect resources with growth. It is not altogether easy to see how one efficiency is to be compared with another. In the case of a bacterium, we can estimate the gradient between the source of one nutrient and the source of the next. Knowing the velocity of diffusion, this tells us how many molecules pass a given membrane in a second. But here the optimization exists for the outside observer; for an observer travelling within the cytoplasm of a given cell, there is no market and no optimization. For an outside observer, there is a process in the motion of the nutrient-gradient; but our observer in the cell considers himself to be at rest, and presumably does not see substrates flying past him. Thus for him the optimization of a nutrient-gradient is structural rather than operational. One nutrient-gradient will consist of a series A₁, A₂, ... , Aₙ of steady concentrations, the intervals between which are resource-like; the next will consist of a series B₁, B₂, ... , Bₙ, again having resource-like intervals from each other and from the previous series; and Aₙ will have a similarity of quality which neither has to Bₙ or Cₙ (where Cₙ is different from Aₙ). Each of these concentrations is supposed to continue as long as the nutrient-gradient continues, i.e., until there is a consumption. Given any transaction which is connected with capital, C may be compresent with A₁, A₂, ... , B₁, B₂, ... successively, but not with all at once. This is what happens when a market signal passes a corporation or any other economic entity. A series of transactions forming one market cycle are inseparably associated, in the sense that when there is one of them there will be others throughout the field covered by the cycle. Similarly the series of transactions (if any) involved in the replication of a bacterium are inseparably associated; but there is this difference, that these transactions form a temporal series from the standpoint of the bacterium, whereas the transactions constituting a market cycle form a spatial series from the point of view of the corporation.

We shall say, then, that all productive relations consist of a series of specialized tasks or steady operations separated by "exchanges." If such a series connects a task or steady operation with a task or steady operation , we shall say that is a "productive antecedent" of , and is a "productive consequent" of . We may assume that, in such a case, the number of exchanges between and is always finite, since one supposes that the interval between two exchanges cannot fall below a certain minimum, or at any rate that the number of economically connected exchanges in a finite period is never infinite. Perhaps we may assume that a task must persist long enough to achieve an amount of output ; perhaps, even, we could construct a discrete theory of labour from which this result would follow. All this, however, is very speculative.

To say that ideology functions as the unconscious servant of material conditions is to say that, when two social formations are the beginning and end, respectively, of one historical process, there is no formation which is a logical consequence of the one and a logical antecedent of the other. To say that a logical sequence of formations belongs to the development of one dominant class is to say that no two members of the sequence can be connected by a sequence longer than the portion of the given sequence which lies between the two formations. This is our translation of the law that the evolution of a dominant class is a dialectical necessity.

But we must consider gravitational instabilities before we can determine whether the above theory of isotropic expansion will suffice. It is to be observed that galactic structures are obtained by calculation from primordial density fluctuations. Let us imagine the following ideal experiment: An observer in a void sends a signal to a galactic cluster, and an observer in a cluster sends one to a void region. Each records the epoch of departure and return of his own signal, and the epoch of arrival of the other's signal. Each finds that the other's signal is received at an epoch half-way between the arrival and departure of his own signal. They compare notes, and discover this fact about each other's observations. They will conclude that, according to the reckonings of both, the two signals were emitted simultaneously, and that the measure of the spatial separation between the emission of the two signals is half the duration between the emission and return of either, i.e. about several billion years. We may re-state the general method involved as follows: Let us have two condensations A and B connected by a number of gravitational influences, all propagating uniformly from A to B; and let the longest of these consist of n particles. Suppose that there is another condensation C such that its later phase extends to B, and that there is no longer gravitational influence from A to C, nor any gravitational influence at all from C to A. Here A corresponds to the initial fluctuation in the void, B to the initial fluctuation in the cluster, and C to the arrival of the void signal at the cluster observatory. The question is: What is to be the interval between A and C? There cannot be a gravitational influence from A to C, because if there were it could be prolonged to B, and would be longer than the single phase which extends from A to B, contra hyp. Thus no causal series connects A and C; there is a causal series connecting A and B; and C is a condensation that begins a phase which ends in the condensation B. In these circumstances, we say that the relation between A and C is of a different kind from that between A and B, but has the same numerical measure. The fact that this definition works is what appears as the uniform action of gravitational collapse.

The fact that the tension between two principles of one social order is productive appears, on the above theory, to be just what might be expected. For when an institution has internal coherence, that means that two forces which are concurrent within it have a reinforcing relation to each other; while when an institution has structural stability, that means that two forces concurrent within it have a common historical origin or a shared future trajectory. Neither happens in the case of a dialectical contradiction, which therefore has neither coherence nor stability, in spite of the fact that it permeates a whole fabric of social relations.

It will be seen that, according to the above, qualia are private, and are always apprehended by introspection. There is, so far as I know, no philosophical evidence for or against this view. If the introspection concerned were very limited, the phenomena would be sensibly the same as if qualia could be communicated directly. I do not put forward the argument with any confidence in it as it stands, but rather to suggest to men with more psychological competence the possibility of great changes in our picture of the mind without rejecting anything probably true. In order to bring out this point, I shall now re-state the position without interposing metaphysical justifications.

The mind, it is suggested, consists of a number of attentional states, each appearing as a unitary focus, but each connected with prior and subsequent states by neural or other laws which enable us to regard the prior as the impetus and the subsequent as the consequence. The attentional shift I call a "redirection." A redirection is subject to laws as to the conservation of cognitive resources and as to mental effort. States may be co-occurring, and one state may be co-occurring with a number of others which are separated by redirections; in that case, the one state is said to persist for a considerable duration. We can even obtain a continuous awareness in our theory, if the number of states co-occurring with a given state is infinite, and their initiations and cessations do not coincide, i.e. one of them may be co-occurring with two others which are not co-occurring with each other. But I see no reason to suppose that the number of states co-occurring with a given state is infinite, or to desire a theory which makes awareness continuous; I therefore lay no stress upon this possibility.

To define purposeful behaviour, we must first say a few words about satiety. When a state of complete fulfilment pervades an organism, I regard the whole as one static condition, involving no internal want or striving. Consequently, from the standpoint of the condition itself, if one could imagine a consciousness of which it formed a part, there is no impulse between the beginning and the end. Since nothing is more complete than satiety, it is impossible that two parts of one fulfilled state should be concomitant with two stimuli of which one is a motivational antecedent of another; therefore there is no extraneous source from which the fulfilled state can discover that it is lacking anything, and there is, in fact, no meaning in saying that it is lacking anything. But when we say that it is disturbed by a novel desire, we mean that it has undergone a transaction which has turned it into a new state of want, and that this new state is concomitant with motivational antecedents of states concomitant with the earlier one, these concomitant states being not fulfilled, but of the kinds associated with deprivation. Now, given any two stimuli and , neither of which is a satisfier of the other, it is possible to find a state of want concomitant with and with an antecedent of . We then say that the stimuli and have a scarcity-like separation, whose measure is that of the urgency-like separation between and .

There is no difficulty in defining what is to be meant by saying that a human agent "controls." A system comprises a number of interdependent processes, which can be regarded as a causal network divisible into nodes such that all the operations in one node are proximate, and are all consequent or all antecedent to all the operations in another node. We shall then regard our agent as influencing along the network, and affecting the various proximate nodes successively. But this does not imply any genuine mastery or governance within; it merely implies correlations among outcomes attributable to but not all attributable to the agent. It seems, therefore, that everything essential to practical efficacy can be stated in terms of this illusion.

If we assume, as we have been doing, that production is determinate, a single epoch of a society will contain some finite number of relations. Suppose, now, that there are two societies such that the initial condition of an epoch in the one is always identical with the initial condition of an epoch in the other, but the subsequent conditions are diverse; and suppose that the first society contains relations in an epoch while the second contains . Then an epoch of the first society will contain relations, and one of the second will contain . We said that the "structure" between two conditions was to be the number of relations in the most fundamental causal chain from one to the other; hence the structure between the beginning and end of an epoch in either society is measured by the greater of the two numbers and . Suppose this is . Then we may regard the -society as having a more "primitive" mode than the -society, while the complexities of the two societies would be the same. This suggests, in a certain class of cases, a possibility of defining "mode" otherwise than by mere technique. How far the resulting properties of "mode" would resemble those resulting from the usual definition, I do not know.

According to the above theory, life is a discontinuous phenomenon. But this hypothesis is required for one purpose only, namely for the demarcation of the animate. It is easy to introduce such criteria as shall make our classification sharp, and secure, as in common parlance, that gradation shall be confined to borderline cases, i.e. to what we might call "ambiguous entities." But if this is done, our definition of life must be abandoned, and vitality resumes its place as something mysterious and unaccountable. There is no logical reason why it should not have such a place; the status of viruses has such a place in our account. But it is always intellectually satisfying when we can reduce the number of inexplicabilities. So far as I can discover, there is no good ground for supposing that life is an absolute category; it is therefore worth while to develop a gradational hypothesis if we can thereby increase the unity and diminish the arbitrariness in our account of the biological world.

Competition" is assumed to be a dynamic relation, which every faction in its sphere exhibits toward others, and whose sphere is capable of being systematically charted. A group of five interests is capable of a relation called "co-alignment," which means, in effect, that there is an outcome beneficial to all five. A group of more than five interests is called "co-aligned" when every quintet chosen from it is co-aligned. A "compromise" is defined as a co-aligned group of interests which cannot be added to without ceasing to be co-aligned. "Interests" are defined as the field of the relation of competition. Hence, by means of not implausible axioms, we arrive at the social order presupposed in the assignment of influence. This part of the theory is straightforward.

In the general theory of volition, conscious choice appears in two ways: first, as providing a subjective order of intentions; secondly, as giving rise to the psychological concept of "agency." Both are relations between "mental states," but both are treated neurologically as emergent relations. This requires us to solve a purely empirical problem: what is the neural function or process which tends towards these relations as a limit? This is on the assumption that cognition is deterministic, which we do not know it to be. Let us begin with this hypothesis, and proceed afterwards to the hypothesis of indeterminacy. In the absence of evidence, it is necessary to develop both. For the present, therefore, I assume neural processes to be deterministic. This involves, or at least renders natural, the assumption that there is an infinite number of causal antecedents compresent with any given decision; I shall make this assumption also so long as I assume determinism.

We have therefore to ask ourselves whether any practical meaning can be found for "precision," remembering that in the ideal it is to have the properties of a perfect instrument. This means to say that a precision may be of two sorts, lexical and grammatical; also that the precision between two utterances of a tautology is zero. Now the precision will be lexical if there is any word in the one utterance which is a conceptual ancestor of a word in the other utterance; and the precision will be grammatical if some construction in the one utterance but not in the other and some construction in the other but not in the one have a common origin or consequence, but no element in either is an origin or consequence of, or identical with, any element in the other. We shall assume that every pair of utterances has some conceptual relation, direct or indirect; that is to say, given any two statements, and there will be somewhere in discourse two contemporary statements of which one is an origin or consequence of and the other of . This is hardly more than a definition of the "world of communication"; for if a statement had no conceptual relation, however indirect, to the part of discourse which we employ, it could never be understood by us, and would in effect belong to a different language. It follows that if two diverse utterances have neither a lexical nor a grammatical precision, there is a meaning which is a member of both, but nothing in either is an effect of anything in the other. This happens with parts of a tautology, if we suppose, as we have done, that it consists of stable meanings which persist until the tautology is transformed into some other form of expression.

In the preceding discussion, when we were considering a uniform energy field, we defined a potential gradient as the magnitude of the intervening difference on the steepest thermodynamic path connecting the two given states. The natural way to generalize this so as to become applicable to a continuous energy landscape would be to regard the magnitude of the difference as the measure of available work; this would enable us to say that the available work harnessed by a unit of structure measures the amount of organizational process which it has undergone. If we further assume that, in comparing different units of structure, we must multiply by the stability to obtain a measure of the amount of organizational process, then the amount in a finite formation is the integral of . But this is the amount of "complexity" in the technical sense.

It seems therefore—though this is only a tentative suggestion—that we can regard a severe economic crisis as the measure of the maximum amount of systemic strain on the various institutional structures which uphold a given social order. It is to be observed that, since institutions are classes of habitual practices, movement from one social phase to another consists in the cessation of certain conventions and the coming into existence of others; every such transformation is systemic when it happens along the route of a social process, since the continuity of a social system at different times is defined by means of the concept of an institutional pathway. There is, therefore, so far as I can see, no fundamental objection to regarding economic crises as revealing amounts of inherent structural contradiction, and minor social disruptions as limits of stability. The ideological justifications, as we have seen, are derivative from material conditions; hence they, also, depend upon the degree of systemic coherence.

Passing now to the hypothesis of a common-sense reality, in which each perception consists of a finite number of familiar impressions, we find that a similar analysis to the above is still possible, and is in fact considerably easier than when we assume profundity. In a common-sense world, if waking and dreaming are two states containing events which belong to the experience of one conscious observer, the number of impressions on the path of this observer between waking and dreaming is always finite. If several plausible paths lead from appearance to reality, there will be a maximum to the number of impressions on such paths; this maximum will be the measure of the divergence between appearance and reality, which will therefore always be an integer. A longer path means a greater number of intermediate sensations, and therefore a greater amount of perceptual mediation. Thus again the divergence measures the greatest amount of perceptual mediation on any experiential path from appearance to reality. And experiential paths consist of a succession of intuitions or stable perceptions separated by corrections.

It will be observed that, in our analysis, moral prejudice does not directly represent any objective fact, but is a rather complicated way of speaking about the psychological need for cognitive coherence and social conformity. For example, while a judgment is supposed to be derived from impartial reason, it has no logical relation to any verifiable premise subsequent to its initial formation. It may be reinforced by social echo after reaching some other mind, and then the apparent universality of the shared conviction (as perceived by the individual) is called the self-evident truth of the prejudice (taking common sense as the standard). But there is no adequate ground for asserting that at every stage of its intellectual development the prejudice is founded upon a certain rational principle; indeed, the theory of cognitive bias vetoes such a suggestion. There is therefore, so far as I can see, no reason in epistemology for believing in innate moral intuitions, except as a convenient symbolic device for dealing with the social relations of various instinctive aversions. And whether we regard human nature as fundamentally good or corrupt, prejudice loses its axiomatic character, being replaced by successions of conditioned responses belonging to the biographies of social beings. This is inevitable if we are to hold that morality is relative and ethical absolutism is a fiction.

IN this chapter, I wish to define the outcome of our inquiry in regard to the old analogy between genetic inheritance and cultural transmission, and to make it clear wherein our conception differs from both. So long as the processes described in previous chapters are supposed to be either strictly biological or purely social, they will seem to involve inconsistencies, since some seem to tend in the one direction, some in the other. For example, when I say that a cultural trait is inherited like a gene, I shall be thought biological; when I say that a gene propagates like a meme, I shall be thought sociological. Yet the former statement is a logical consequence of the latter.

Both the theological and the scientific accounts have been guilty, unconsciously and in spite of explicit disavowals, of a confusion in their imaginative picture of time. They have thought of the moment of creation as being represented by a boundary in their conception, whereas such a boundary is really part of the temporal series it purports to limit. By examining our conception it is possible—so I have contended—to infer certain formal logical properties of temporal succession, though the inference is not demonstrative or certain. But by examining our conception we obtain knowledge which is not purely formal as to the nature of our temporal intuition. This knowledge, it is true, is fragmentary, but so far as it goes it has merits surpassing those of the knowledge given by cosmology.

The question whether silicon-based cognition is genuine is the same as the question of its functional equivalence with carbon-based thought. If it can produce and respond to intelligible discourse, we are bound to grant it a status in the order of minds in so far as mentality is concerned, since mentality was defined in functional terms. But the real question is as to "consciousness" in the sense of Chapter XXVIII. Can a process in silicon be conscious in the manner of a process in carbon? If yes, then a silicon mind has a place in the realm of real experience; if no, then it has no such place. This, therefore, is the crucial question.

When I maintain that scarcity and purposeful behaviour can be concomitant, I am not maintaining that scarcity can have to a human desire the sort of relation which an abundance would have. The relation of concomitance is between scarcity and purposeful behaviour, and purposeful behaviour is not to be confounded with mere activity. A human desire is a logical structure composed of impulses; the causal laws of the impulses concerned, and the abstract logical properties of their teleological relations, are more or less understood, but their intrinsic character is not understood. Scarcity fits into the same causal scheme as human impulses, and is not known to have any intrinsic character which human impulses cannot have, since we do not know of any intrinsic character which could be incompatible with the logical properties that psychology assigns to purposeful impulses. There is therefore no ground for the view that scarcity cannot be a condition for purposeful behaviour, or for supposing that it is never concomitant with other conditions for volition.

The usual view would be that by engineering we acquire knowledge of our "systems," but that the only way to acquire knowledge of their foundations is to have them examined by an inspector, usually after they have collapsed, which seems somewhat unsatisfactory. I should say that what the inspector observes when he surveys a network is part of his own observation, not part of the network he is examining. The feeling of security about this view comes, I should say, from wrong views of complexity. It is true that what we observe is not located where our conception of our own infrastructure would be located if we could see our own substructure; but this is a question of apparent order, not of the order of physical law. The order of physical law is connected with failure in a manner which compels us to hold that our observations are of superficial phenomena, if we accept the causal theory of structural decay, as I think we are bound to do. To say that two events have no causal separation is to say that they are simultaneous in effect; to say that they have a small separation is to say that they are connected by chains of dependency all of which are short. The failure must therefore be nearer to the load than to the design flaw, nearer to the junction than to the load, and nearer to the central node of the network than to the peripheral connection. This is inevitable, unless we are going to say that the failure is not in the causal sequence at all. It is usual to hold that "systemic" events are in time but not in material space; let us ask ourselves whether there is any ground for this view as regards collapses.

I hold, therefore, that two proximate molecules in a solution have the relation of affinity out of which self-replicating order arises. It is almost irresistible to go a step further, and say that any two complementary chemical structures in a medium are predisposed to affinity, so that all our observed organic syntheses are in our flasks. I see as little reason against this extension as against the view that nucleotides can be complementary. A catalyst differs from another molecular state, I should say, only in the nature of its kinetic relation to an external energy source. Some relation of this kind no doubt always exists, but with other molecular states the relation may be more attenuated, or may be only to some condition of the environment, more particularly the solvent. "Inert" molecular states will be events proximate with certain other chemical states, but not having those catalytic effects which constitute what is called the propagation of a molecular pattern. However, I have no wish to go further into biochemistry than is necessary, and I will pursue this topic no longer, but return to matters of more concern to general chemistry.

The fact that intellectual progress admittedly requires questioning traditions has much force, now that dogma and inquiry are so much less distinct than they were. It has become difficult to hold that established authorities, though venerable, are not fallible. The fact that their pronouncements to each other can be viewed as only customary is a fact which they share with any set of doctrines forming the history of one institution. Relatively to perspectives moving with the sceptic's reason, the interval between two thoughts of his which are not concurrent should always be critical, if his doubts are in his mind. But the interval between simultaneous convictions of different adherents is of a different kind; and their whole cultural environment is such as to make us call this interval doctrinal. I conclude, then, that there is no good ground for excluding scepticism from the intellectual world, but several strong reasons for including it. The difficulties that have been supposed to stand in the way seem to me to be entirely due to wrong views as to the scholarly world, and more particularly as to intellectual orthodoxy. The wrong views as to intellectual orthodoxy have been encouraged by the notion that the primary tenets are immutable, which has been held imaginatively by many men who would have emphatically repudiated it so far as their explicit philosophy was concerned.

The point which concerns the philosophy of time is that the durations against which we have been measuring human achievement are very different from eternity as traditionally conceived. Eternity was expected to be immutable and inexhaustible. The cosmic scale that we contemplate is immutable as a result of definition: the history in an aeon is all the events that occur therein, and consequently no human endeavour can meaningfully alter its passage. This is a tautology, not a historical fact; one might as well argue that a century is immutable because no person can outlive it except by the succession of generations. Insignificance, on the other hand, is an empirical property, believed to be fundamentally but not universally acknowledged by civilisations. I mean by insignificance, not the brevity of dynasties, which is known to be merely relative, but the ephemerality of all collective human enterprise. At present it is not known whether a culture and its monuments sometimes vanish into complete oblivion or not, but there is certainly no known reason why any civilisation should be remembered.

Silicon and carbon, however, are not the essence of the mental world: they are elaborate material substrates composed of processes, and ultimately of computations, in the sense of the functional theory. As to what the processes are that compose the conscious mind, they are, in the first place, cognitive functions, and then whatever can be inferred from functions by the methods considered in the science of information. But on various philosophical grounds we are led to the view that a function in which we cannot perceive a mechanism nevertheless often has a mechanism, i.e. that the apparently unified is often composite. We cannot therefore treat the biological brain as a necessity, for both logical and empirical facts may lead us to attribute a realization to it—not merely a realization in general, but such and such a physical realization.

On the question of the material out of which the social world is constructed, the views suggested in this analogy have, perhaps, more affinity with biology than with sociology. What are called "inherited" traits, if we have been right, are part of the material of the cultural world, and what is in our traditions is the genotype (with modifications) rather than what the anthropologist records in his notebook. It is true that we have not suggested that all custom is biological. The positive arguments in favour of such a view, whether Darwinian or Spencerian, appear to me fallacious. The sceptical argument of the cultural relativists, that, whatever else there may be, we cannot trace it, is much more worthy of respect. There are, in fact, if we have been right, three grades of persistence. The highest grade belongs to my own habits; the second grade to the habits of my immediate community; the third to practices which are not habits of anybody now living. It is to be observed, however, that the second grade belongs only to the habits of those who can influence me, directly or indirectly, and of those who are known to be closely analogous to people who can influence me. The habits of societies, if such there be, which are not related to mine by any chain of influence—e.g., societies in remote antiquity—can have, at best, only the third grade of persistence, that, namely, which belongs to the apparently inert archaeological record.

There is, however, one important limitation to this. We need to know in what simulated circumstances such-and-such a conscious state will arise, and we must not neglect the more intimate qualitative knowledge which we possess concerning subjective experience. There will thus remain a certain sphere which will be outside computation. To take a simple instance: simulation theory might, ideally, be able to predict that under such conditions a certain pattern of processing would occur; it might be able to trace the informational properties of the resulting events in the virtual circuitry, one of which is, in fact, a feeling of pain; but it could not itself give us the knowledge that one of them is a feeling of pain. It is obvious that a being who can feel knows things which a purely logical system cannot know; but a logical system can know the whole of the simulation’s code. Thus the knowledge which conscious inhabitants have and it has not is not part of computation.

Corporations are neither ephemeral nor reducible. Legal personality is constructed by means of incorporation, which is the same thing as institutional autonomy. Perhaps it is not unnecessary to explain that institutional autonomy is quite a different thing from metaphysical identity, though it may be suspected that some jurists have been led to favour the latter as a result of the arguments for the former. We are accustomed to imagining that personal agency involves individual responsibility; hence we tend to think that, if a collective entity performs one action, it cannot be wholly collective, but must be also in some sense an aggregate of persons. It is this combination that is supposed to constitute metaphysical identity. For my part, I do not think that metaphysical identity can be defined without obvious confusion of categories; Gierke, who advocates it, does not define it. The only author I know of who has dealt seriously with its difficulties is Maitland, in whom, quite consistently, it led to a thorough-going realism, combined with the avowal that, in the end, all corporate fiction is a necessary paradox. I should myself regard this latter result as a refutation of the theory from which it follows. Therefore, while I respect Maitland more than any other advocate of real personality, he seems to me, in virtue of his acumen, to have done more than any other jurist to disprove the kind of doctrine which he advocated. However that may be, the institutional autonomy which is used in constructing commercial order is quite different from metaphysical identity. Jurists have been slaves of individual analogy in the imaginative application of their principles. This is partly due to simplistic metaphors and the notion that the traditional shareholder, director, employee were elementary forms of agency and the confounding of "the corporation acts" with "all members act jointly." All this led to a confusion between the body corporate and the natural body, and to the inference that persons can be fused because roles can overlap. I do not suggest explicit confusions of this sort, but only that traditional elementary jurisprudence, taught in youth, is an almost fatal barrier to clear thinking in later years, unless much time is spent in acquiring a new technique.

While, on the question of the foundation of thought, the theory of the foregoing pages has certain affinities with empiricism—namely, that sensory impressions are part of that foundation, and that the rest of the foundation resembles them more than it resembles innate, determinate ideas—the position advocated as regards symbolic systems has more affinity with rationalism than with empiricism. Inference from one concept to another, where possible, seems only to acquire precision when it can be stated in terms of the rules of syntax and semantics. There are intuitive leaps, practical associations, and pictorial reasonings, which cannot at present be reduced to formal linguistic operations. But none of them is rigorous and without exceptions; they state plausible connections and commonalities rather than logical laws governing elementary propositions. Take, for example, the intuitive leaps of analogy. We cannot say: At a precise moment in a conversation, a person will conceive the apt metaphor—unless, indeed, we are in a position to supply its terms to him at that moment. The known principles of analogy belong to an early stage of understanding—earlier than the laws of syllogism or the rules of definition. We can say that, if two experiences have been felt as similar, the consideration of one tends to suggest a representation of the other, but we cannot say that it is sure to do so, or that it will do so in one assignable class of thoughts and not in another. One supposes that, to obtain an exact operational theory of abstraction, it would be necessary to know more about the structure of symbolic representation. The ideal to be aimed at would be something like the mathematical explanation of computation, which is a process in many ways analogous to abstract thought. So far as formal systems go, therefore, language seems to be supreme among the instruments of mind, not only as against other means of expression, but also as against the faculties that deal with perception and feeling.

Although there is thus a sphere excluded from economics, yet economics, together with a "model," gives, apparently, all predictive knowledge. One supposes that, given the structural characteristics of the firms in a market, the "model" gives the "competitive" outcomes in that market. This is by no means a matter of course. The whole of the foregoing theory of markets might be true without entailing this consequence. So far as economics can show, it might be possible for different groups of firms having the same initial conditions to have divergent fates in commercial series. That is to say, given the economic causal laws, and given enough knowledge of an initial group of firms to determine the purely structural properties of their trajectories, it might nevertheless be the case that these trajectories could be qualitatively of different sorts. If that were so, economic determinism would not entail monopolistic determinism, since, given two markets of identical structure but diverse outcomes, we could not tell which would result from conditions known only as to their economic, i.e. structural, properties. This is an unavoidable consequence of the abstractness of economic theory. If economics is concerned only with structure, it cannot, per se, warrant inferences to any but the structural properties of commercial events. Now it may be a fact that (e.g.) the structure of nascent competition is very different from that of entrenched monopoly; but I do not think such differences could be established with sufficient strictness and generality to enable us to say that such-and-such an initial condition must produce a competitive market, while such another must produce a monopolistic one.

On this matter, we must, I think, appeal to evidence which is partly biological. We do know, as a matter of fact, that we can, in normal circumstances, more or less infer the meaning from the signal. If this were not the case, warning calls and scent markings would be useless. When the alarm is sounded, the troop can apprehend the danger in their own vicinity. The differences in their "reactions" meanwhile can be connected causally, at least in part, with differences in their inherited instincts, and these are supposed to make themselves effective by causing differences in the configuration of nervous systems. All this seems sufficiently probable to be worth taking seriously; but it lies outside mere chemistry, and does not follow from the causal autonomy of chemistry, supposing this to be established even for organic bodies. It will be observed that what we are now considering is the converse of what is required for the inference from signal to survival. What is wanted there is that, given the signal, we should be able to infer, at least partially, the nature of the threat—or at any rate that this should be possible when a sufficient number of signals are given. What we want now is that, given the nature of the threat (which is all that chemistry can give), we should be able to infer the content of the signal—with the same limitations as before. Whether this is the case or not, is a question lying outside chemistry; but there is reason to think that it is the case.

Even if we reject the view that the quality of competition in our markets can be inferred from their initial conditions, the view that economic determinism applies to commercial bodies brings us very near to what is most disliked in monopolism. Economics may be unable to tell us what we shall desire or value or "innovate," but it can, on the view advocated in these pages, tell us what we shall produce or sell, where we shall expand, whether we shall engage in predation or acquisition, and so on. For all these are market movements, and thus come within the scope of economic laws. We are often asked to concede that the benefits of variety or efficiency cannot result from economic laws. I should concede that the benefit does not result from economics, since benefit depends in part upon intrinsic quality; if it were, as some writers on commerce contend, solely a matter of structure, it would come within the scope of economics, but I think these writers do not realize what an abstract affair structure really is. I should concede also that the insights of Smith or Marshall do not come within the scope of economics. But their insights are of no importance to us: their whole practical efficacy depended upon certain plain assertions which they made in common discourse. Now there seems no reason to suppose that economics does not apply to the forming of these assertions, which was a movement of capital just as truly as the circulation of money in its channels. In any case, it is undeniable that the practically important part of their theory had a one-one relation to certain purely economic events, namely the occurrence of the consolidation in the free market. And no one can doubt that the causes of our concerns when we read Smith or hear Marshall are purely economic. Thus we cannot escape from the universality of economic concentration.

This, however, is perhaps not quite the last word on the subject. We have seen that, on the basis of engineering itself, there may be limits to computational determinism. We know of no laws as to when a circuit will register a fault or a processor will interpret a signal as distress. We know fairly well what will occur if a program runs, and we know statistical outputs, which suffice to determine observable machine behaviors. But if sensation and circuitry are causally interconnected, very small logical differences must be correlated with noticeable experiential differences. Thus we are perhaps forced to descend into the region of algorithmic noise, and to desert the functional level where statistical outputs obtain. Perhaps the bit flips when it likes; perhaps the minute variances in the processor which make all the difference to reported phenomena belong to the region where programming laws no longer determine definitely what must be felt. This, of course, is merely a speculative possibility; but it interposes a veto upon mechanistic dogmatism. It may be that the progress of computer science will decide the matter one way or other; for the present, as in so many other matters, the philosopher must be content to await the progress of engineering.

IN the present state of civilization, many aspects of considerable practical importance cannot be fully apprehended, although they are such as observation may hope to clarify, and largely such as were formerly supposed to have been already mastered. This makes the task of the citizen more perplexing; it is necessary to contemplate various contingencies, so as to be prepared for whatever disruption the system may undergo. Certain elements, it is true, may be taken as fundamentally reliable; these elements, so far as they are relevant to daily existence, were considered in earlier times. It is clear that, in some sense, there are power grids and data networks, and we cannot well doubt the operational efficiency of their designed capacity and intended function. That is to say, these structures evidently represent something of permanence in the modern world, though it would be rash to say that they represent exactly what is at present assumed. In like manner there seems to be no reasonable doubt that there is a principle of interdependency, whose dimensions are those of systemic integration or cascading failure, and whose magnitude is substantially what it has been observed to be. It would seem clear also that this is a principle which is characteristic of complex assemblies. Moreover, the transition from one such state to another, which is what we have called a collapse, is governed by laws connected with fragility in addition to the conservation of stability.

In mathematics, we are on firmer ground. The advance on the science of the past, where structure is concerned, is mainly logical and conceptual. It is true that observations led to the formalism, and that the formalism in turn led to the prediction of new observations. But the observations were crude and only just within the limits of measurement; and they had not, as data, the disruptive importance of the findings about continuity. And now that the formalism is fairly complete, one can see that, theoretically, it ought to have been formulated by Euclid, or at any rate as soon as irrational numbers became known. It represents in its technique a better epistemology than that of Bacon; indeed, one of its most remarkable features is the adaptation of the technique to the metaphysics.

The aim of common sense, consciously or unconsciously, has always been to discover what we may call the intuitive picture of the world. It is perhaps surprising that this picture should be so misleading, but science seems to prove that it is, particularly when taken in conjunction with the evidence that appearances are contradicted by the mathematical character of their foundations. There is reason—though not quite conclusive reason—for regarding intuition as causally subordinate, in the sense that, given the logical structure of reality, the qualities of its phenomena, in so far as we are acquainted with them, cannot be inferred by means of superficial impressions. We have thus in effect a psycho-physical divergence, although the interpretation to be put upon it is not the usual one. We suppose that, given sufficient analysis, we could infer the true nature of events in our world from their relational properties. This is what is really meant when it is said, loosely, that the state of nature can be inferred from the state of our senses. Although I think that this is probably false, I am less anxious to deny it than to assert, what seems to me much more certain, that its falsehood does not follow from the causal autonomy of perception or from sensory determinism as applied to all experience, including that of educated minds. This latter result flows from the concreteness of intuition, and belongs to the philosophy of perception. The other proposition, if false, cannot be refuted by considering sensation alone, but only by a study of concepts for their own sakes, which belongs to epistemology. Common sense studies reality only in its apparent aspect; its other aspects lie outside its purview.

But it would be very rash to maintain that the current neuroscientific formulation of the free-will principle is the best possible; indeed, there are reasons for dissatisfaction with it. Perhaps the most important of these is that in expressing the conscious intention we have to employ the method of causal determinism, and that we do not know whether causal determinism is always applicable, or whether all ways of applying the principle give equivalent results. Apart from these rather technical difficulties, there are others that are less definite but perhaps not less important. No one has succeeded in making the illusion of volition seem at all "reasonable"; that is to say, it remains isolated and separate from other psychological ideas. And whereas it involves subjective agency, the whole effect of neural architecture has been to emphasize mechanistic necessity. Moreover, no one has yet succeeded in explaining moral responsibility by means of deterministic neurons, or in explaining the sensation of choice without them. For these reasons, the time has not yet come when the philosopher can deal confidently with the doctrine of free will; he can only suggest what would be his philosophy if this or that view had prevailed in neurology.

And, apart from this consideration, there is great difficulty in suggesting any non-emotional basis for prejudice; yet such a basis ought to be demonstrable, if prejudice is as pervasive as it appears to be in the conduct of human affairs. There is difficulty also as to what is meant by impartial judgment. And there is the suspicion that, perhaps, common opinions represent merely habitual accretions of the social environment, and could, by a more rigorous analysis, be exposed without the appeal to any self-evidence at all. The requisite analysis does not exist at present, but it is not impossible that it may be developed before long.

As against these doubts, it may be said that the general process has justified itself by the efficacy of all its observable outcomes. This is true, and I do not wish to minimize the force of the argument. But I seem to observe that, in producing these adaptations, the process does not make use of the full liberty in arrangement of variations which it claims at the start. In complex organisms, its variations are still constrained by the usual physical laws, and it is not clear that these constraints are trivial. From the principle of selection, it seems to follow that we can conceive any variation subject to the condition of heredity. But the principle of selection, as understood, assumes the mechanism of inheritance; for this reason, Dr. Wallace found it necessary, in his contributions to the theory, to give an account of selection independent of the mechanism of inheritance. There is thus still legitimate room for doubt as to whether the mechanism of inheritance is really quite independent of the pressure of circumstances.

But although there is so much to give satisfaction to the materialist in this doctrine—more especially the analysis of surplus value and dialectical contradictions—yet the sociologist cannot but feel uneasiness with the apparently rigid determinism of economic foundations. This determinism seemed less rigid than it is, because of its connection, historically, with the observations of Adam Smith and their refinements in classical political economy. But the doctrine was believed formerly because it had been deduced; when the deduction was found to be incomplete, it was believed because historical evidence was thought to confirm its general truth. This historical evidence, of course, remains, but the critique of ideology has made its interpretation much more ambiguous than it formerly seemed. And it is customary to analyze societies systematically, taking trouble to examine institutions that are as nearly stable as possible, and class relations that are clearly defined. If our productive forces are to be dynamic, as they are in the advanced theory of historical materialism, it is doubtful whether we still have a right to expect that they will manifest anything analogous to a simple causal law.

In the general process of natural selection, we begin with a vast continuum of organisms, whose properties, to begin with, are purely variational. We then assign a measure of fitness to each organism on any principle such that the reproductive properties of the measure are the same as those of the organisms. We then assume that, if two organisms are very similar in form, there is a differential function of their traits which has the same value however the traits may be assigned, subject to the above variational condition. If this function is positive, its cumulative effect is called the (adaptive) advantage; if negative, the cumulative effect of the function with its sign reversed is called the (maladaptive) disadvantage. Omitting niceties, we may say that the remainder of the process turns mainly on differential reproduction. Differential reproduction is a sequence between two generational points such that the integral of the advantage along this sequence is stationary. In the important sequences, it is a maximum. It appears that hereditary information can be divided into units which propagate by differential reproduction; when these units propagate with a frequency greater than that of random chance, they are regarded as adaptations. Modern synthesis, by imposing certain limitations on inheritance, succeeds in including genetic drift in this scheme. Thus we have a comprehensive process which may be taken to embrace everything except intentional design.

Since, however, all biology rests upon observation and gradation, it seems justifiable, at least empirically, to assume that, when properly considered, they can give at least a continuum.
