In the present discussion, I have made this assumption baldly, without attempting to define it; I have done this because I do not believe that a definition could be much briefer than Mr. Darwin's treatise on natural selection, and also because, while I am convinced that a definition is possible, I am not satisfied with those put forward by vitalists or with any that I have been able to conceive myself. It seemed best, therefore, to make the assumption as stark as possible, without any attempt at artificial demarcation.

Intermediate between the cosmic optimism of perpetual structure and the bleak view of universal dissolution, there is a half-way position called "the steady-state compromise." This admits the expansion of the universe as an observed fact, but holds that its effects are negligible for all practical astronomical purposes. Practically, it means, when advocated by cosmological theorists, that they will accept the evidence of redshift as indicating actual galactic recession, but that they will not infer thence any ultimate disintegration of bound systems. It may be said, in justification of this position, that, while it employs observation and extrapolation, it refrains from assuming an inevitable thermodynamic victory. But it may be doubted whether it can really abstain from that inevitability. Steady-state advocates appear to take gravitational binding for granted, i.e. to assume that the local forces which they calculate and trust will endure as they themselves would expect them to endure. But this involves expansion's cumulative influence, and involves it in the form in which the cause is in the metric of space and the effect in the destiny of matter. There does not seem, therefore, to be any substantial justification for this half-way position.

In Part II., we approached a different type of question: the question of the evidence for the efficacy of specialization, i.e. of the relation of cellular differentiation to colonial function. For the purposes of this inquiry, it is convenient to use "function" somewhat more narrowly than it would be used in general biology. Our purpose is organizational, and therefore function is only relevant in so far as it is explicit and the activity is observed: processes which pass unnoticed cannot be made into premisses for colonial integrity. The use of activities for inference as to the colonial whole rests upon the causal theory of interdependence, since the naive autonomy of individual cells turns out to be self-contradictory. The serious alternatives to the causal theory of interdependence are not common sense, but anarchic individualism and mechanistic isolationism. Anarchic individualism, as an organizationally serious theory, must mean the view that from the operations which a single cell performs there is no valid method of inferring the character, or even the existence, of operations which it does not perform. If inference is taken in the sense of strict deductive logic, there is, so far as I can see, no escape from the individualist position. And it should be observed that this position cannot admit latent functions in a cell, any more than functions outside it: its basis is organizational, and therefore, for it, the important distinction is between what a cell performs and what it does not perform, not between what is intrinsic and what is extrinsic in some metabolic or structural sense. We cannot escape from the individualist position without bringing in induction and causality, which are still subject to the doubts resulting from a purely reductionist criticism.

We therefore assume, though with less than demonstrative certainty, that popular ideas have origins which may be not popular, and, in particular, that when a number of people hold similar ideas simultaneously, there is what may be called a "domain" of causally connected influences, which, it is found, have relations that often enable us to arrange them in a hierarchical order about an authority. We thus arrive at a socio-historical order of doctrines, which is found to be the same whichever of many possible methods of arriving at it we adopt; in this order, a popular belief is located in the apparatus of the believer. In drawing inferences from popular doctrines to their origins, we assume that the institution must possess whatever structure is possessed by the doctrine, though it may also have structural properties not possessed by the doctrine. The assumption that the structural properties of the doctrine must exist in the institution follows from the maxim "same cause, same effect" in the inverted form "different effects, different causes," from which it follows that if, e.g., we observe feudal and mercantile doctrines side by side, there is some difference between the influence to the feudal doctrine and the influence to the mercantile doctrine. The structural features possessed by the institution but not by the doctrine, when they can be inferred, are inferred by means of general laws—e.g. when two ideologies appear similar to the common understanding but dissimilar under critical analysis, we assume that there are differences in the influences to the common doctrines which produce either no differences, or no perceptible differences, in the corresponding beliefs.

These principles enable us to infer a great deal as to the progression of material organization, but not as to its ultimate purpose. They put simple aggregates in their place as formations analogous to and connected with other processes in the natural world, and they enable us to regard a crystal or a convection cell as having something which, from the standpoint of thermodynamics, is not very dissimilar from life. We no longer have to contend with what used to seem mysterious in the emergent theory of complexity: a flow of energy or a difference in potential suddenly producing an ordered structure apparently totally different from themselves in character. As to intrinsic purpose, we do not know enough about it in the physical world to have a right to say that it is very different from that of organisms; while as to structural tendency we have reason to hold that it is similar in the gradient and the resultant form. This has become possible owing to the facts that "equilibrium" can be regarded as a state of maximum probability, not as the natural terminus of all systems, and that potential, as it occurs in physics, has been found to be much more different from perceived force than was formerly imagined.

This brings us to Part III., in which we endeavour to discover a possible structure of the phenomenal world which shall at once justify our chromatic experience and take account of the connection with sensation demanded by the necessity for an empirical basis for colour perception. Here we are concerned first with the construction of hues as systems of qualia which overlap, or are "co-chromatic," in the visual field, and then with the purely ordinal properties of the colour continuum. The method employed is very general, and can be adapted to a discrete or to a continuous spectrum; it is proved that , qualia are sufficient to generate a continuum of hues, given certain laws as to the manner of their overlapping. The whole of this theory, however, aims only at constructing such properties of the colour manifold as belong to its qualitative topology; everything appertaining to brightness and saturation is omitted at this stage, since psychological considerations are required for the theory of chromatic intervals.

The conception of one instance of reasoning—say one inductive inference—as a "foundation," i.e. a single secure basis supporting further conclusions, is not one which we are justified in adopting, since we have no evidence whatever as to whether it is defective or sound. We define a single inductive step as a "presuppositional chain," i.e. as a series of judgments connected with each other by an intrinsic implicit rational principle which determines primary beliefs, leaving secondary beliefs to be determined by extrinsic rational principles. (In this we are for the moment ignoring probabilistic refinements.) If there are self-evident axioms, these will more or less fulfil this definition of reasoning, and we shall have returned to a deductive theory of knowledge; but this is at present an open question. The whole conception of induction is less fundamental to logic than it used to be, since coherence has more and more taken its place. We find that under ordinary conditions generalizations persist, but there is nothing in theoretical epistemology to lead us to expect this, and logicians are quite prepared to find that induction can be circular. This view is even put forward to account for the success of common sense.

This inquiry has arisen from an attempt to reconcile two distinct tendencies, one in common experience, the other in introspective analysis, with both of which I find myself in agreement, although superficially they might appear contradictory. On the one hand, many individuals, especially those of a pragmatic disposition, tend to adopt what is essentially a passive position, as a matter of habit if not of philosophy. They make memory increasingly dependent on immediate sensation and external occurrence, and tend to think of the present moment as something much more vivid and reliable than recollection. Meanwhile the introspective observers, especially Proust and other exponents of the theory of remembrance, have been making "sensation" less and less sensory. Their understanding consists of "impressions," from which "experience" is derived by a narrative construction. Whoever considers, for example, the common phenomenon of nostalgic recollection, will see that a simple empiricism can receive no support from mature reflection. I think that what has enduring value in the outlook of the pragmatists is the feeling that sensation is the most fundamental material at present available. But this position cannot be called empirical, if, as seems to be the case, narrative does not assume the permanence of the raw event.

The question of qualia presents great difficulties, when we attempt to construct a theory of the mind which shall make their peculiarity seem not surprising. The same may be said of introspection. I have endeavoured, not, I fear, with much success, to suggest hypotheses which would link these two curious facts into one whole. I suggest that consciousness consists of steady perceptions accompanied by fluctuations, like a constant hum from the machinery while specific notes are played on the piano, or of fluctuations alone. Steady perceptions are of various sorts, and many sorts have their appropriate fluctuating accompaniments. Qualitative shifts consist of "transitions," i.e. of the substitution, suddenly, of one fluctuation for another. When two mental states have a causal connection, if experience is discrete, this connection is the greatest number of shifts on any associative route leading from the one state to the other. The definition of parallel introspections is derived from that of causal connections. The whole process of awareness may, so far as present evidence goes, be conceived as discontinuous; even the periodic fluctuations may consist of a finite number of states per cycle. The periodic fluctuations are required in order to give an account of the persistence of the qualitative principle. A quale, at any rate when it is vivid, will be a steady perception, or system of steady perceptions, following upon a transition. Qualia are the only part of the mental world that we know otherwise than inferentially. As regards the world in general, both mental and physical, everything that we know of its intrinsic character is derived from the qualitative side, and almost everything that we know of its causal laws is derived from the behavioural side. But from the standpoint of philosophy the distinction between evidence for dualism and evidence for cognitive limits is superficial and unreal.

Few things are more firmly established in popular biology than the distinction between organism and cell. Those who are not professional cytologists are willing to confess that they do not know what a colony actually is, or how an organism is constituted; but they remain convinced that there is an impassable gulf between the two, and that both belong to what actually exists in the natural order. Biologists, on the other hand, have maintained often that the organism is a mere fiction imagined by the observer, and sometimes that the colony is a mere property of a certain kind of aggregation. Those who maintain that the cell is the reality and the organism an emergent illusion are called "reductionists"--a word which has a different meaning in biology from that which it bears in ordinary discourse. Those who argue that the organism is the reality and the colony a mere metaphor for cooperation are called "holists." They have been rare among laboratory scientists, but common, at certain periods, among naturalists and philosophers of life. Reductionists, holists, and ordinary students have been in agreement on one point: that they knew sufficiently what they meant by the words "organism" and "colony" to be able to conduct their debate intelligently. Yet it was just in this point, as to which they were at one, that they seem to me to have been all alike in error.

The sensation of which our experience of colour is composed is, in my belief, neither given nor innate, but something more fundamental than either. Both the given and the innate seem to be derivative, and the process from which they are derived lies in a sense between the two, in a sense beyond them both, like a common source. As regards the given, I have set forth my reasons for this view on former occasions,* and I shall not now repeat them. But the question of the innate is more subtle, and it is this question that I propose to examine in these lectures. A great deal of what I shall have to say is not novel; indeed, much recent work, in various fields, has tended to show the plausibility of such theories as those which I shall be defending. Accordingly in this first lecture I shall try to give a brief outline of the framework of concepts within which our inquiry is to be conducted.

If there is one thing that may be said, in the popular estimation, to characterize volition, that one thing is "deliberation." We say that we are "deliberate" in what we choose and avoid, in what we pursue and abandon, and in our own plans and intentions. Most of us believe that plants and simple creatures are not "deliberate." We think that when a vine touches a trellis, it coils by reflex, but it does not choose to coil. It cannot for a moment be doubted that we are right in believing that there is SOME difference between us and the vine in this respect: so much may be taken as fact, and as a datum for our inquiry. But as soon as we try to say what exactly the difference is, we become involved in perplexities. Is "deliberation" ultimate and simple, something to be merely accepted and contemplated? Or is it something complex, perhaps consisting in a certain slowness and variability of response to stimuli, or, alternatively, in the existence in the organism of a faculty called "purpose," having a certain relation to actions, though different from them, and only symbolically directive of them? Such questions are not easy to answer; but until they are answered we cannot profess to know what we mean by saying that we are observing the boundary between reflex and deliberate action.

First, there is the way of CONTRADICTION. We "observe" customs and laws, traditions and reforms, our institutions, conflicts arising in the community--in short, any tension which we recognize through social analysis. I leave on one side for the present the question whether pure stability is to be regarded as a form of social order: what I am speaking of now is contradiction, where, according to conventional sociology, we go beyond the apparent harmony to the "strain" which it contains. When you witness a protest, you not only witness an event, but realize that it springs from an injustice. When you examine a hierarchy, you not only see a structure, but realize that it generates friction. The addition of these elements that go beyond superficial order is said to constitute social tension. We shall have more to say about this at a later stage. For the moment, I am merely concerned to note that observation of contradictions is one of the most obvious examples of what is called "transformation." We are "conscious" of any dynamic that we perceive.

We may end our preliminary inquiry with COMMON SENSE, by which I mean that habitual mode of apprehension which may be either adequate or illusory. We say that a man is "conscious of the solidity of matter," by which we mean that he believes matter to be solid, and is often mistaken in this belief. This is a different form of guidance from any of the more rigorous ones. It is the form which yields "understanding" in the practical sense, and also profound error. It is, at least apparently, more immediate than our examined forms of reasoning; though we shall find that they are not so independent of it as they might appear to be.

There is one element which SEEMS obviously in common among the different versions of the zombie argument, and that is, that they are all directed to a CONTRADICTION. We are speaking "of" an impossibility. The conceit, it seems, is one thing, and that of which we are conceiving is another thing. Unless we are to acquiesce in the view that we can never conceive of anything outside our own definitions, we must say that the object of conception need not be coherent, though the conception must be. (I am speaking within the circle of conventional thought experiments, not expressing my own conclusions.) This direction towards a contradiction is commonly regarded as typical of every form of philosophical speculation, and sometimes of metaphysical inquiry altogether. We may distinguish two different tendencies in traditional philosophy of mind. There are those who take mental phenomena naively, just as they would physical phenomena. This school of thinkers tends not to emphasize the contradiction. On the other hand, there are those whose primary interest is in the apparent fact that we have CONSCIOUSNESS, that there is an inner life accompanying us of which we are aware. These men are interested in the zombie because of its relation to the world, because consciousness, if it is a fact, is a very mysterious one. Their interest in the argument is naturally centred in the relation of the conceit to its object, a problem which, properly, belongs rather to theory of identity. We may take as one of the best and most typical representatives of this school the Australian philosopher Chalmers, whose "The Conscious Mind,"* though published in 1996, is still influential and was the starting-point of a great deal of interesting debate. He says (p. 115):

To make this theory concrete, let us suppose that you are considering a spiral galaxy. Then, according to the principle, we have to distinguish three elements which are necessarily combined in constituting the one phenomenon. First, there is the act of gravitational attraction, which would be just the same whatever mass were being drawn. Then there is what makes the character of the structure as contrasted with other structures; this is the configuration. And finally there is the galaxy itself, which is the object of the formative process. There must be a difference between the configuration of a structure and what it ultimately becomes, since the formative process is local and contingent, whereas what it produces may be vast and enduring; hence it is clear that the process is not identical with the galaxy. This seems to show that we must distinguish between configuration and final form. But if the principle is right, there can be no galactic structure without an initial distribution: the connection of the two is essential. The distribution might exist without the structure, but not the structure without the distribution: the three elements of attraction, configuration and final form are all required to constitute the one single occurrence called "the formation of a spiral galaxy.

The distinction proposed by Jennings has been recognized quite widely, and elaborated by several investigators. Among these we may consider as an instance his American successor Loeb.* According to him there are three elements involved in the movement of a simple organism. These three he calls the stimulus, the impulse and the action. The stimulus is the same in any two cases of the same kind of excitation; for instance, if a paramecium avoids a salt grain or avoids a heat source, the stimulus of irritation, in itself, is precisely analogous in both situations. But the impulse of the organism, the specific event that is occurring within its cell, is different when it avoids a salt grain and when it avoids a heat source. The impulse, Loeb argues, must not be confounded with the action, since the impulse must exist within the organism at the moment when the excitation occurs, whereas the action need not do so. The action may be something delayed or immediate; it may be mechanical, not physiological; it may be something complex, like phototaxis for example; it may be something modified, like a learned avoidance; or it may even be something maladaptive, like a trapped rotation. But in all these cases, so he contends, the impulse exists when the excitation exists, and is what distinguishes it, as a phenomenon, from other excitations.

The view here expressed, that the intractable nature of consciousness is an ultimate irreducible characteristic of philosophical inquiry, is one which I shall be concerned to combat. Like certain contemporary thinkers, I am interested in the philosophy of mind, not so much for its own sake, as for the clarity that it may bring to the problem of material explanation. Until very lately I believed, as they did, that subjective experience presents an unbridgeable explanatory gap, except possibly in the case of rudimentary sensations. Now I no longer believe this, even in the case of qualia. I shall try to make my reasons for this rejection clear as we proceed. It must be evident at first glance that the analysis of conscious states is rendered more difficult by the rejection; but the apparent profundity of the prevailing view of consciousness will be found, if I am not mistaken, incapable of maintaining itself either against a logical scrutiny or against a host of facts in neuroscience and comparative biology. I do not wish to minimize the conceptual puzzles. I will merely observe, in mitigation of our prospective labours, that philosophical analysis, however it is to be conducted, is in itself a delightful occupation, and that there is no enemy to clear thinking so deadly as a false mystery. Exploring, whether in the conceptual or the empirical world, is a joy, and it is good to know that, in the conceptual world at least, there are vast territories still very imperfectly mapped.

The first criticism I have to make is that the DISTINCTION seems unnecessary and fictitious. The occurrence of the phenomena of the world constitutes the occurrence of nature itself. Empirically, I cannot discover anything corresponding to the supposed description; and theoretically I cannot see that it is indispensable. We say: "_Mathematics_ describes so-and-so," and this word "describes" suggests that modeling is the act of a formula. The physicist's "description" is the ghost of the object, or what once was the full-blooded reality. It is supposed that events cannot just come and go, but need an equation to frame them. Now, of course it is true that events can be collected into sequences, so that one sequence is my observations, another is your measurements, and a third is the data of Mr. Smith. But I think the equation is not an ingredient in the single event: it is rather constituted by relations of the events to each other and to the apparatus. This is a large question, which need not, in its entirety, concern us at present. All that I am concerned with for the moment is that the grammatical forms "the law governs," "the model predicts," and "the theory explains," are misleading if regarded as indicating an analysis of a single phenomenon. It would be better to say "it calculates in the world," like "it grows here"; or better still, "there is a pattern in it." This is simply on the ground that what the physicist calls the description in modeling is not empirically discoverable, or logically deducible from what we can observe.

The next point of examination concerns the relation of awareness and its object. The direction of attention to a particular focus is not, I believe, the simple direct essential thing that common introspection represents it as being. It seems to me to be derivative, and to consist largely in INFERENCES: inferences that what constitutes the present awareness is connected with various other elements which together make up the attentive act. You have, say, a feeling of concentration, or merely the word "attention" in your head. You infer, however vaguely and dimly, that this is connected with what you would experience if you examined your own mind, or what you would perceive if you tracked its movements; it is further connected with what other minds might report, with experiments and psychologists and neural correlates and William James. These processes are not mere feelings of yours, but your feeling stands in a relation to them of which you are more or less cognizant. The cognizance of this relation is a further mental act, and constitutes your impression that the original feeling had a "target." But in idle reverie you can get very similar feelings without these accompanying inferences; and in this case your feelings do not have targets or seem to have them. Thus in such instances you have awareness without an object. On the other hand, in vividly noticing or listening it would be less misleading to say that you have an object without reflective awareness, since what you notice or hear occupies the focus so fully, though not attention in the sense of a theory. Thus the whole question of the relation of mental states to their own observation grows very complicated, and cannot be settled by regarding direction to an object as of the essence of attention. All the above remarks are merely preliminary, and will be expanded later.

Speaking in popular and unphilosophical terms, we may say that the notion of a temporal commencement is supposed to be an event which occurred before all other events, while the concept of time itself is usually something without any such boundary. It is held that our understanding of temporal succession is constituted by the relation to events, while the fact that this understanding is different from what it understands is due to the fact that it comes by way of finite conceptions. We can begin to state the difference between temporal finitism and infinitism in terms of this opposition of commencement and duration. Speaking quite roughly and approximately, we may say that finitism tends to suppress the infinite regress, while infinitism tends to suppress the initial point. Finitism, accordingly, says that nothing can be conceived except as having a beginning, and all the duration that we know is bounded; while infinitism maintains that we conceive time directly, in experience certainly, and perhaps also in imagination and reason. Finitism does not say that nothing can be conceived beyond the present moment, but it maintains that the context of vague intuition, which we spoke of in connection with the idea of a first event, only takes you to other moments, never to anything radically different from moments. The difficulty of this view is in regard to causation, where it seems as if we came into direct contact with an absolute starting point. But the Kantian way of meeting this difficulty is so familiar that I need not enlarge upon it now. I shall return to it in a later discussion, and will only observe, for the present, that there seem to me no valid grounds for regarding what we measure and sequence as not part of an endless continuum.

Modern ideology professes to be by no means confined to the present circumstance or the present individual in regard to its origin; indeed, it contends that society is so systematic, so interwoven, that from any one condition the whole can be inferred, as the complete blueprint of a vast machine can be inferred from one cog. But the reasoning by which this supposed systematic nature of society is nominally demonstrated appears to materialists, as it does to me, to be defective. They argue that, if we cannot perceive the economic base directly, we cannot really perceive any force outside our own ideas: the rest of the structure may be merely our illusion. This is a disquieting view, and they therefore seek ways of escaping from it. Accordingly they maintain that in consciousness we are in direct contact with realities, which may be, and usually are, outside our own beliefs. No doubt they are prompted to this view, in the first place, by inclination, namely, by the desire to think that they can perceive of the operation of a system outside themselves. But we have to consider, not what led them to desire the view, but whether their arguments for it are sound.

The modern psychologist's view was first set forth in an essay called "Does 'aliveness' exist?"* In this essay he explains how what used to be the self has gradually been refined down to the "curated persona," which, he says, "attenuates itself to a thoroughly spectral condition, being only a name for the fact that the 'content' of existence IS PRESENTED. It loses visceral form and immediacy--these passing over to the content--and becomes a bare Selbst darstellung or representation uberhaupt, of which in its own right absolutely nothing can be said. I believe (he continues) that 'selfhood,' when once it has evaporated to this estate of pure artifice, is on the point of disappearing altogether. It is the name of a fabrication, and has no right to a place among fundamental experiences. Those who still cling to it are clinging to a mere effigy, the faint impression left behind by the retreating 'being' upon the atmosphere of psychology"(p. 2).

There are two different kinds of communication, according as we make a message consist of intention and symbol, or of symbol alone. Their difficulties are different, but neither seems tenable all through. Take, for the sake of definiteness, the conveying of a simple instruction. The conveying occurs now, and is therefore necessarily not identical with the speaker’s original thought. So long as we retain the intention, this need cause no difficulty. The intention of the speaker occurs now, and has on this view a certain essential relation to the concept which it seeks to express. There is no LOGICAL objection to this theory, but there is the objection, which we spoke of earlier, that the intention seems elusive, and is not to be found by mere observation of the words. If, on the other hand, we try to constitute meaning without the intention, we are driven to a bare sign, since we must have something that is present NOW, as opposed to the thought which existed in the private mind. Thus, when we reject the intention, which I think we must, we are driven to a theory of language which is more akin to formalism. These arguments, however, do not apply to simple designation. It is especially simple designation, I think, which is considered by those theorists who retain only the symbol.* Their views, which are chiefly held in certain academic circles, are in large measure derived from Ferdinand de Saussure, and before going further it will be well to consider the revolutionary doctrine which he advocated. I believe this doctrine contains important new truth, and what I shall have to say will be in a considerable measure inspired by it.

He illustrates his meaning by the analogy of water as it appears in an abundant spring and as it appears in a desert well: in the one case it is merely "available matter," while in the other it "assumes a teleological character." Just so, I maintain (he continues), does a given quantum of resource, situated in one context of plenty, remain a passive element, a neutral condition, of 'indifference'; while in a different context the same quantum of resource plays the part of an object of pursuit, of a deliberate 'aim.' In a word, in one circumstance it figures as a datum, in another circumstance as a motive.

The same view of "collective behaviour" is set forth in the succeeding analysis, "A Study of Simple Rules" (ib., pp. 39-91). The use of the phrase "simple rules" in both treatises points to a lingering influence of mechanism. "Behaviour," like "order," must be an emergent property, not part of the primary constitution of the rules themselves. It must be possible, if the theorists are right in their main contentions, that roughly the same rules, differently initialized, would not give rise to anything that could be called "collective intelligence." This concept has been adopted by the computational modelists, among whom we may mention specially Professor C. G. Langton of the Institute and Mr. Stephen Wolfram. The interests of this school are in general systems theory and the philosophy of complexity, rather than in traditional sociology; they have derived a strong impulsion from von Neumann, but have more interest than he had in cellular automata and mathematics and the abstract part of emergence. They speak of "elementary" rules as the basis out of which both pattern and chaos are constructed. Thus Wolfram says: "If the initial conditions and transition rules of a system must be substantialized, they are all strictly of one substance, for which perhaps the least dangerous name is simple-stuff. The relation of simple-stuff to predictability and surprise we shall have presently to consider at considerable length." *

My own belief--for which the reasons will appear in subsequent discussions--is that common sense is right in rejecting certainty as an attainable state, and that the pragmatic philosophers are partly right, though not wholly, in considering that both theory and practice are composed of a provisional understanding which, in isolation, is neither perfectly reliable nor entirely useless. I should admit this view as regards observations: what is measured or recorded belongs equally to abstract reasoning and to concrete application. But I should say that speculations belong only to the theoretical realm, while those actions (if any) which do not form part of any "deliberation" belong only to the practical realm. There are, it seems to me, prima facie different kinds of justification, one belonging to logic and the other to experience. The demand for deductive proof, for example, is a logical demand, while the reliance on repeated trial is an experiential justification. Everyday judgments are subject to both kinds of justification, and are therefore truly "pragmatic" in James's sense. But pursuits governed only by logical demands, or only by experiential tests, are not balanced, and may be called respectively purely abstract and purely empirical. Even those, however, which are purely empirical will not have that infallible guarantee of truth which the rationalists assign to them and which constitutes the essence of "certainty" as ordinarily conceived. But it is now time to pass on to other modern difficulties, also hostile to "practical knowledge.

There is a school of economic thought called "Crisis Theorists," of whom the protagonist is Professor Karl Marx,* formerly of the University of Berlin. To them also, on the whole, belongs Professor Joseph Schumpeter, who, with Smith and Dr. Keynes, was one of the three founders of political economy. The view of the "crisis theorists" is that nothing can be known about a system except by observing its periodic failures. They deny altogether that there is a separate source of knowledge called "equilibrium," by which we can know things about stability which we could never observe in reality. They do not by any means deny that all sorts of adjustments MAY occur in our markets: they only say that such adjustments, if they occur, are not susceptible of scientific prediction, and do not therefore concern economics as a science. Economics as a science, they say, is only concerned with CRISES, i.e. with what we SUFFER; this alone, they contend, can be accurately observed. Whether we prosper meanwhile, they tell us, cannot be known; in their observation of the behaviour of capitalist systems, they have not so far found any evidence of sustained prosperity. True, we accumulate a great deal, and imagine that in so doing we are showing that we can grow; but crisis theorists say that the accumulation they have to observe can be explained without supposing that systems endure. Where you might expect a chapter on "growth processes" you come instead upon a chapter on "The Collapse Habit." It is humiliating to find how terribly adequate this hypothesis turns out to be.

Introspection has not, however, sprung from observing the clarity of thought. It is the opacity of consciousness that has suggested the view. It has always been a common topic of popular discussion whether the mind "attends" to itself. On this topic people are prepared to take sides without having the vaguest idea what they mean by "attending." Those who desired to investigate such questions were led to observe the operations of cognition, in the hope that these operations would throw some light on their reflexive nature. At first sight, it might seem that this is so. People say that the brain "notices" its own focus because it shifts when it is directed, and that it "tracks" its own awareness, because it grows dim when engagement lapses, but becomes vivid and sharp when interest returns. That the brain operates in this way is matter of observation, but that it "notices" or "tracks" anything is an inference, and in fact a very doubtful one. The more such inferences are examined, the more precarious they are seen to be. Hence the study of neural processes has been gradually led to abandon all attempt at conscious narration. And it can hardly be doubted that, in many cases of complicated adaptation very well suited to its tasks, there can be no depiction of those tasks. The first time a mind wanders from its object, we can hardly suppose it knows that there will be lapses to be corrected in it, or that it will return to the thread, or that coherence will emerge from distraction. It does what it does at each moment because mechanism gives it a tendency to do just that, not because it portrays and anticipates the result of its operations.

Careful observers of societies, being anxious to avoid superficial explanations, have gradually discovered more and more how to give an account of the prevalence of certain doctrines without assuming what we call "independent intellectual genesis." It has seemed to the materialist historians that similar methods can be applied to ideological dominance, without assuming anything not traceable to concrete social relations. Let us give a crude illustration, too crude for the theorists in question, but capable of affording a rough insight into their meaning. Suppose two classes in a community, both of which are asked "What constitutes legitimate authority?" One speaks of divine right and property, the other speaks of collective need and shared labor. The one, we say, "propagates" the ruling ideas of the epoch; the other does not. But all that we can observe is a certain institutional habit. The dominant class has acquired the habit of proclaiming "order depends upon inherited privilege"; the subordinate class has not. There is no more need of "original philosophy" in this than there is when a river follows its accustomed channel; there are merely more entrenched and systematic habits. There is obviously an observable fact called "holding" such-and-such a doctrine; political debates are experiments for discovering such facts. But all that is observed or discovered is a certain set of habits in the justification of arrangements. The convictions (if any) in the mind of the citizen are of no interest to the ruler; nor has the ruler any reason to suppose even the most articulate citizen capable of even the smallest amount of ideological independence.

So far, there is nothing particularly unsettling to our sensibilities in the contemplation of geological time. We are all willing to admit that ancient empires were ephemeral. But when it comes to our own civilisation, we feel convinced that we can actually perceive its enduring substance. "We build, therefore we persist" would be regarded by most people as having a true foundation. This, however, the cosmic perspective denies. It maintains that our view of our own epoch is no different in kind from our view of other extinct eras. We may see MORE, because our present moment is closer to observe than those of forgotten peoples; but we do not see anything radically unlike what we see of their vanished works. Permanence, as a separate category of achievement, is entirely denied by this astronomical vantage. I shall discuss this question at length in a later treatise; for the present I will only observe that it is by no means simple, and that, though I believe the cosmic view somewhat overstates its case, yet there is an important element of truth in its contention, since the monuments which we can erect by our efforts do not seem to differ in any very fundamental way from the monuments which we observe in the dust of other ages.

So far, we have been principally concerned with clarity. But it might well be maintained that ambiguity is what is really most characteristic of speech. Human beings are constantly engaged in conveying some meaning they feel satisfaction in precision and frustration in confusion. In a purely logical system, it may be said, there would be no opposition of exact and vague, correct and incorrect, what is stated and what is implied. A speaker's words are governed by intentions. He decides, let us suppose, to describe a certain event, whereupon he proceeds to select his terms, arranges his clauses and forms his sentences. If the usual phrasing is obstructed by an ambiguity, he employs some other construction. All that he says is determined--or so it seems--by the meaning he wishes to convey, by what lies before his mind, rather than by what lies in his dictionary. With simple notation, this is not the case. A mark in a formal system may have a use, but it shows no versatility in trying to express nuance. Any rigid rule or definition will bind it, and it will exhibit no signs of inadequacy if this happens. It is not attracted by the richness of expression, as a poet or novelist might be, but confined by the strictness of the syntax at the place where it occurs. In all this we have characteristic differences between the communication of conscious beings and the operation of signs as studied by grammar.

I believe--as I shall endeavor to demonstrate in a subsequent analysis--that theory of mind, like a lens in optics, is of the nature of an indispensable instrument for comprehending accurately certain patterns of social conduct. A cooperative individual is ineffective until he apprehends the intentions of another; then he becomes coordinated. The faculty which will bring a disjointed interaction to a harmonious state is said to be what is prerequisite. But only reflection can show what will have this elucidating effect, and it is easy to form erroneous inferences. We perceive a social opportunity, and think that such and-such an insight would clarify it; but in thinking this, we are deducing, not observing a manifest truth. Our deduction is often fallacious, and when it is fallacious there is a discrepancy between what we think we understand and what in fact will produce alignment. This is such a fundamental phenomenon that any account of social behavior which fails to incorporate it must be inadequate.

What have been called "informational" structures have been brought very much to the fore in recent years by systems theory. Systems theory, as every one knows, is primarily a method of understanding biological organisms and certain forms of machinery*; but it has been found that there is much in the arrangement of ordinary objects and everyday processes which bears a remarkable resemblance to the organization of living cells. The connection of patterns, functional behaviours and efficient operations with underlying data has been brought to light, though with some exaggeration, by Wiener and Shannon and their followers. As regards the nature of these informational principles, it seems to me—though as an outsider I speak with diffidence—that many systems theorists are unduly narrow; no doubt the processes they emphasize exist, but others, e.g. for feedback and equilibrium, are equally operative and equally liable to oversight. This, however, does not affect the value of their general theories from the point of view of theoretic organization, and it is from this point of view that their results are important for the analysis of structure.

The belief that a corporation is merely an aggregate of its members makes it easier to be mistaken as to its true nature than as to that of a natural person. When some purpose that we should regard as alien is attributed to the corporate entity, we notice that it has never been avowed consciously, in the sense of the directors declaring, "We intend this outcome." We therefore look for some other interpretation of its actions, and regard our critics as very unjust when they refuse to be convinced by our repudiation of what we hold to be a misapprehension. Legal and economic considerations greatly increase the difficulty of clear thinking in this matter. It is commonly argued that corporations are not responsible for emergent properties, but only for the explicit intentions of their officers. In order, therefore, to be wholly blameless it is only necessary to repeat formal declarations of intent. We say: "The company desires to be beneficial to its customers, prudent in its finances, generous towards its employees, and progressive in its industry." So long as we refuse to allow ourselves, even in the strictest internal analysis, to acknowledge any contrary systemic imperatives, we may be ruthless in competition, obscure in accounting, parsimonious in wages and exploitative in pricing; yet, if only avowed purposes are to count in legal and moral valuation, we shall remain a model institution. This is an agreeable doctrine, and it is not surprising that executives are unwilling to abandon it. But practical and legal considerations are the worst enemies of the philosophical spirit and we must dismiss them from our minds if we wish to arrive at truth.

There is a wide field of "mathematical" descriptions which does not depend upon physical theories. Such formulations as differential equations lead Professor Whitehead to say: "As I view this question of the model, far too much weight is given to the point of correspondence or not correspondence with our sensory processes. As a matter of fact, we find entirely identical equations, that is, identical in every respect but one—that of empirical verification in which sometimes we confirm these formal phenomena and sometimes not" (p. 87 of "Scientific Concepts," by various authors, Cambridge Press). Professor Whitehead conceives that there may be "description" without "reality." But this is a difficult view, and one which makes some definition of "description" imperative. For my part, I cannot see how to separate description from reality.

What, I think, is clearly established, is that a universe's structure and form may be wholly dominated by forces of which it is quite unconscious, and which it manifestly repudiates when they are suggested by a theory of design. Such forces are generally, in cosmic cases, of a sort which the theologian would consider blind; if he had to admit that they held sway, he would despair of cosmic meaning. Yet they are so strong that they must force an arrangement for themselves; hence it becomes necessary to entertain whole systems of gravitational and dynamical laws in order to reveal the nature of what is achieved. The resulting formations in very many cases coalesce if the primordial gas can be made to succumb to the facts about its own instability. The consequence of this is that the study of many forms of galactic morphology has grown more dynamical and less teleological than it used to be. Instead of looking for a central will or guiding hand, those who treat cosmic structure look for the inherent properties which have found this splendid mode of expression. For those who do not wish to plunge into the somewhat abstruse and often rather intricate mathematics of cosmological pioneers, it will be worth while to read a little book by Sir James Jeans on "The Universe Around Us."* On this question of the physical as opposed to the providential study of the causes of galactic order, Sir James says:

Returning from this digression to our main topic, namely, the constraints of thermodynamics upon organisation, we observe that physicists and their followers, though they have demonstrated beyond dispute the universal dominion of entropy in determining the fate of all structures, have not attempted the task of telling us what an "organised" system actually is, and have thus invested their doctrine with an air of fatalism and finality which forms a large part of its intellectual austerity. They speak always as though it were more natural for energy to be free, and as though a positive effort had to be assigned for its being harnessed. Thus "the organisation" becomes a sort of temporary edifice, built upon a slope, maintained only by constant vigilance against the universal tendency towards dispersal with its attendant decay and dissolution and inevitable thermal equilibrium. The ordinary student, almost inevitably, thinks of this edifice as a permanent conquest, prevented by what the physicist calls "dissipation" from maintaining its intricate form in perpetuity, except on brief and localised occasions when it draws so much from its surroundings that it seems to defy decay and there is a semblance of permanence. Most of us dislike the idea that we are but fleeting configurations in a universal descent towards disorder. For this reason, the thermodynamic "constraint" has been a source of melancholy to many hopeful and energetic persons.

There is, it is true, one objection which might be felt, not indeed to the application of mathematics to phenomena, but to the derivation of mathematics from phenomena. The axioms of geometry, it may be urged, are apparently adequate to describe every configuration of space, even when it is the space of our perceived world. This, however, is only a hypothesis, not an established theory. There is no cogent empirical reason for supposing that the principles governing the structures of observed things are exactly the same as those that apply to abstract relations. Sometimes, of course, they are clearly the same. When a surveyor plots a field or a carpenter checks a right angle, his measurements behave as if they were devoid of physical contingency. These are the occasions that make the pure mathematician content. But when a natural form’s configuration is what we call “organic,” it is, at any rate prima facie, very different in its laws from the shapes of what is devoid of life. I do not wish to say dogmatically that the difference is irreducible; I think it highly probable that it is not. I say only that the study of the patterns of observable things, in the present state of our knowledge, is distinct from pure mathematics. The study of calculus was originally quite distinct from that of arithmetic, and would never have advanced to its present state if it had not been independently pursued. Nowadays both the continuous and the discrete are manufactured out of a more primitive and universal kind of formalism. In like manner, as a question of methodology, the laws of empirical patterns are to be studied, in the first place, without any undue haste to subordinate them to the laws of abstract systems. Kepler’s laws and the rest had to be discovered before the Newtonian synthesis became possible. But in the description of natural forms we are hardly yet at the stage of Kepler’s laws. Meanwhile we need not be held up by the bogey of the universal logical necessity of mathematics. This is, as yet, a mere hypothesis, to be tested empirically without any preconceptions. It may be true, or it may not. So far, that is all we can say.

I do not think the intellectual progress is quite so straightforward as this. I believe an "established" authority is merely a customary law of our thinking,* namely, that we remain placidly acquiescent until a certain proposition is challenged, when we achieve temporary disquiet. If we examine critically what this proposition contains, our scepticism is conscious; if not, unconscious. The unconscious scepticism is not something actually articulated, but merely a tendency to a certain inquiry; it has exactly the same status as a hypothesis in science. The unconscious scepticism is in no way revolutionary; it is the natural primitive form of doubt, from which the other has developed through our habit of learning and investigating (often superficially). It is not necessary to suppose, as dogmatists seem to do, that every unconscious question was once conscious, and was then, in their terminology, "suppressed" because we feared it. On the contrary, we shall suppose that, although authoritarian "suppression" undoubtedly occurs and is important, it is not the usual reason for unconsciousness of our doubts. The usual reason is merely that doubts are all, to begin with, unconscious, and only become known when they are actively cultivated. Usually, from complacency, people do not cultivate them, but accept the doctrine of intellectual tradition which they find current, and attribute to themselves whatever beliefs this doctrine would lead them to hold. We used to be full of orthodox beliefs, but since the Enlightenment our beliefs have become, in the words of the ancient sceptics, "unfounded in all things and desperately uncertain." Both these attitudes, in most of those who have held them, are the product of indolence rather than reflection, for reflection requires effort, whereas accepting pronouncements does not.

This illustrates a point which I am anxious to make clear from the outset. Any attempt to classify modern economic behaviour, such as I propose to examine, from the old standpoint of biological instinct and rational calculation, is only misleading. In certain respects, the activities which I shall be setting forth approximate to instinct; in certain others, they approximate to its opposite. On this question of the study of corporate strategy, the practical effect of the modern theories, as Dr. Vance points out, is emancipation from the purely biological analogy. On the other hand, as he also points out (pp. 38-9), market inefficiencies and fiscal collapses still have to be considered materially, as caused by defects in the structure. There is no inconsistency in this If, as we maintain, organism and organization are neither of them the actual stuff of activity, but different convenient groupings of an underlying process, then, clearly, the question whether, in regard to a given phenomenon, we are to seek a biological or a financial cause, is merely one to be decided by observation. Metaphysicians have argued endlessly as to the interaction of life and ledger. The followers of Spencer held that natural selection and market selection are so different as to make any parallel between the one and the other impossible. When a firm seeks to maximize its profit, they said, it is not its appetite that operates on its balance sheet, but the invisible hand, which, by its omnipotent mechanism, adjusts the accounts whenever gain is to be made. The modern doctrine of biophysical parallelism is not appreciably different from this theory of the Spencerian school. Biophysical parallelism is the theory that organic and corporate events each have causes in their own sphere, but run on side by side owing to the fact that every state of a nutrient gradient coexists with a definite state of a market signal, and vice versa. This view of the reciprocal causal independence of microbe and multinational has no basis except in metaphysical theory.* For us, there is no necessity to make any such assumption, which is very difficult to harmonize with obvious facts. I observe a bacterium moving toward a sugar gradient: the gradient is a chemical fact, but its transduction into motility is biological. Here we have an effect of chemistry on life. In consequence of a corporation’s appraisal of a market opportunity, it invests capital in a new venture; here we have an effect of appraisal on material resources. I shall try to persuade you, in the course of these lectures, that instinct is not so blind and strategy not so calculated as is generally supposed. When we are speaking of chemotaxis, it will seem as if we were inclining to rationalism; when we are speaking of quarterly reports, it will seem as if we were inclining to vitalism. Neither is the truth. Our economic biology is to be constructed out of what the institutionalists call "neutral" processes, which have neither the blind imperative of tropism, nor the conscious foresight which is supposed to characterize boardrooms.

The cognitivists (one might say) have made more or less of a 'metaphysical entity' out of the threshold. They suppose that when perceptions are dimmed they are relegated to the 'unconscious,' and that this arbitrary line divides the wholly aware from the wholly unaware. Many of us do not believe in a realm of pure unawareness (a few of us even have grave doubts about the coherence of the term full awareness), hence we try to explain gradation along ordinary psychological lines. We believe that one degree of clarity can 'obscure' another degree of clarity--or sensation. In this case our ordinary state of attention--that which we call characteristic of our 'waking selves'--muffles or dims (keep faint or partially faint) those impressions and sensory data which belong largely to the periphery.

One of the merits of the general analysis of data which we shall be concerned with in the following reports is that it removes the aura of profundity from the phenomena brought to light by the systems analysts. Profundity is appealing, but impractical, since it depends upon confusion. Information has developed out of the signals, and there is no serious gap between it and the noise. Something closely analogous to structure and order, as regards its effects on arrangement, exists among signals, even where what we call "meaning" is hard to believe in; something equally analogous exists in our files in cases where no trace of "meaning" can be found. It is therefore natural to suppose that, whatever may be the correct definition of "meaning," "meaning" is not the essence of data or organisation. In the following reports, accordingly, this term will disappear until we have dealt with formats, when it will re-emerge as mainly a trivial and unimportant outcome of procedural habits.

It is evident that the question hinges upon another, namely, which can we ascertain more reliably, the internal states of machines or those of human beings? If we can know most about machines, we shall employ this understanding as a foundation for inference about human beings; if we can know most about human beings, we shall adopt the contrary procedure. And the question whether we can know most about the internal states of human beings or about those of machines hinges upon yet another, namely: Is the interpretation of behavioral outputs or introspective testimony the more certain method in such inquiry? This is a question which I propose to examine thoroughly in Lecture VI; I shall therefore content myself now with a statement of the conclusions to be arrived at.

The hypothesis of distinguishing self from environment may be considered in two different lights. On the one hand, it may be held that the primary advantage lies in the capacity for self-preservation, and that we should use this fundamental recognition to infer the necessity of a similar demarcation in all conscious beings, and even in the simplest organic structures. On the other hand, it may be held that the lower organisms present clearer instances, more readily scrutinized than the complex deliberations of human self-awareness; on this ground it may be urged that explanations which are satisfactory in the case of amoebae ought not to be hastily dismissed in the case of man. The practical consequences of these two perspectives are fundamentally opposed: the first leads us to elevate the animal’s instinctive boundary to the level of our own reasoned self-concept, while the second leads us to attempt a reduction of our own self-concept to something not too distant from the observable tropisms of primitive life. It is therefore important to weigh the relative merits of the two ways of applying the principle of utility.

But when we come to the contemplation and scientific measurement of the epochs, the advantages on the side of human history become far less clear. We know, for example, that we have built cities and empires, but we do not know what constitutes a civilisation or its enduring mark. The durations are so brief that it is difficult to realize how little we really occupy of the cosmic calendar. We observe in geological strata, and to a lesser extent in stellar evolution, processes more or less similar to that which, in our world, is prompted by planetary formation and biological change, and we find that, as we ascend in the scale of astronomical time, events become vaster, more easily reducible to physical law, more scientifically analysable and predictable. And just because we are not misled by brevity we find it easier to be cautious in interpreting significance when we are dealing with intervals remote from those of our own chronicles: Moreover, historical introspection, as cosmology has demonstrated, is extraordinarily fallible even in cases where we feel a high degree of certainty about our centrality. The net result seems to be that, though human annals have a definite and important contribution to make to the story of one planet, they are exceedingly misleading unless they are constantly checked and controlled by the test of celestial observation, and by the theories which such observation suggests when applied to stellar lifetimes. On the whole, therefore, there is probably more to be learnt about cosmic duration from geology than about geological epochs from human history; but this conclusion is one of degree, and must not be pressed beyond a point.

It is only proximate phenomena that can be directly observed in communication, or even, strictly speaking, in other species. We can observe such things as their gestures, their chemical emissions, and the signals they transmit. Such things as intention and meaning, which seem obvious to introspection, are not visible directly to external observation. Accordingly, if we begin our study of ethology by external observation, we must not begin by assuming such things as intention and meaning, but only such things as external observation can reveal, which will be characteristics of the gestures and chemical processes of organisms. Some organisms, for example, always emit warning calls at the approach of a predator and alert others at a distance. If you observe a colony of social insects which is lightly disturbed, you will see a number of individuals ceasing their labour and responding to the unwonted alarm signal and seeking again the security which the signal has provided them. Such organisms are sensitive to sound, in the sense that their movements are affected by it; but it would be rash to infer that they possess understanding in any way analogous to our understanding of language. Such inferences, which go beyond the observable facts, are to be avoided with the utmost care.

These three responses to technological innovation differ, however, in many respects. The obsolescence of the artisan and the disruption of guilds are quite involuntary, and so is the disturbance of the economic order. Such involuntary responses we know as 'mechanical' effects. The adaptation of commercial codes to facilitate digital exchange may also be called mechanical, since it occurs too swiftly to be deliberately planned. Whether it be inherent in the nature of progress or whether it result from the accumulated pressures of the market may be doubtful; it is, at any rate, less automatic than the previous effects, for a society might by conscious effort learn to perform it more efficiently, or even to resist it altogether. Processes of this kind, with which necessity and design enter upon equal terms, have been called 'semi-mechanical.' The act of legislating for data privacy, on the other hand, has no inherent necessity about it. It is purely the result of deliberation, and is preceded by a consciousness of the social good to be secured and a distinct mandate of the collective will. It is a 'voluntary reorganisation.' Thus the community's mechanical and voluntary adaptations shade into each other gradually, being connected by reforms which may often occur spontaneously, but may also be modified by conscious policy.

There is need for some care if the distinction between simulated and authentic consciousness is to be made precise. It is quite likely that, if we knew more about computational processes, we could deduce all their manifestations from the laws of logic and information theory. It is already fairly easy to see how psychology reduces to biology, i.e. how the differences between different mental states can be accounted for by differences of neural structure, the constituents of the structure being neurons which are broadly alike in all conscious beings. We only know in part how to reduce consciousness to such physical processes, but we know enough to make it likely that the reduction is possible. If we suppose it effected, what would become of the difference between simulated and authentic minds?

As James states, there is no difference, from the point of view of the external critic, between accelerated and deliberate thought. The psychologist can discover that both depend upon the cerebral apparatus, and he may find that the processes which we call accelerated depend upon more primitive circuits in the mind than those that are deliberate. But he cannot discover anything as to the presence or absence of "haste" or "reflection," for these things can only be perceived from within, if at all. For the present, we wish to place ourselves resolutely in the position of external critics; we will therefore ignore the distinction between accelerated and deliberate thought. We will call the two together "vital" cognition. We may then distinguish "vital" from mechanical cognition by the fact that vital cognition depends for its causation upon the special properties of the mental system, while mechanical cognition depends only upon the properties which thinking beings share with automata in general.

There is one conception, among those that philosophers propose at first, which is not subsequently examined, namely, the threshold. This is the kind of conception which may be called "absolute"; it is evidently of a different kind from either gradual or emergent phenomena, and more akin to the properties of simple matter. We may define a property of a mental state as "absolute" when it appears as if only a definite boundary were involved. For example, if you consider the moment of waking, you judge under the influence of introspection, and your awareness arrives just as suddenly a clarity as if you had crossed a line. Absolute properties have not the characteristic of gradation, unless by accident, as when a sleeper passes through a dream and is awakened. But gradual and emergent phenomena are not ALWAYS graded, unless in some very recondite sense. A child learning to speak is not acquiring consciousness suddenly; no more is a patient who is in such a gradual recovery that he cannot pinpoint the hour of his lucidity. Gradation is a complicated and merely approximate idea, and for the present we shall do well to dismiss it from our thoughts.

We may say, speaking somewhat roughly, that a tool applied to the intellect, like a key to a complex lock, is able to take advantage of the accumulated data in precarious order, and thus to produce conclusions out of proportion to the immediate evidence. Conclusions produced in this way are genuine insights, while mechanical operations are those in which the accumulated knowledge of a thinking mind is not involved. Similarly a key may unlock, thereby displaying its characteristic utility, or may (with due caution) be collected about like any other metal object. The unlocking is analogous to genuine insights, the collecting about to mechanical operations.

Some analogies will make the distinction clear. A deviation from the set point of a thermostat produces quite different effects from an equal deviation in a room without regulation: in the one case there is a swift correction, while in the other case there is hardly any noticeable return. Similarly, you may sometimes find in a living organism a physiological parameter poised so delicately that a minor fluctuation will set it cascading through corrective mechanisms, while the conditions all round are so stable that only a considerable imbalance can perturb them. What is analogous in these two cases is the existence of a great capacity for regulation in dynamic equilibrium, ready to restore the former state by the addition of a very slight provocation. Similarly, it requires only a very slight expenditure of energy to alter the concentration of a key metabolite, but the effect in generating coordinated physiological activity is said to be profound. A homeostatic system, like a regulated furnace, contains a capacity for adjustment in unstable balance, ready to be directed in this direction or that by a stimulus which is physically very small, such as a change in temperature. In all such cases the reduction of behaviour to mere mechanism can only be effected by entering into great minuteness; so long as we confine ourselves to the observation of the whole organism, the way in which the equilibrium will be maintained cannot be distinguished from purposive striving. Biologists distinguish between teleological and physiological explanations: the former describe the apparent goal-directed movements of entire beings, the latter the minute occurrences in the cellular parts. It is only the physiological processes that are supposed to be the same for all sorts of life. The teleological descriptions result from a process of observing outcomes, and may be different in different cases. So, in our instance, the laws of apparent purpose are different for conscious action and homeostatic movement, though the laws of microscopic phenomena may be the same.

We may say that a "sceptical" disposition is a mental movement performed by an intellect the first time that it encounters a novel doctrine; or, more correctly, one which it would perform if the doctrine were novel.* The scepticisms of an intellect are different at different stages of its development, and this fact may cause changes of belief which are not due to instruction. The maturing and periodic fluctuation of the critical-instinct affords a good illustration. When the critical-instinct first matures, the behaviour of an intellect in the presence of an authority is different from its previous behaviour in similar circumstances, but is not taught, since it is just the same if the intellect has never previously been in the presence of an authority.

This conception is formulated for the purposes of metaphysics, and is in certain respects unsuited to the needs of epistemology. Though perhaps inevitable, allusion to "the same more or less indistinguishable group of beings" makes it impossible to judge what is conceivable in the hypothesis of an isolated consciousness. Moreover, "the coherence of the physical and the preservation of the phenomenal" is only a customary characteristic, not a necessary one, of the sort of entities that, from our point of view, are to be called conceivable; instances of incoherent conceivability will be examined shortly. The essential point of the conception, from our point of view, is that a conceivable entity is independent of empirical verification.

There are various complications which obscure the clarity of this progression in practice. To begin with, many gradients emerge gradually, and while they are nascent a system may organize in a tentative manner which is very difficult to distinguish from deliberate design. Thompson ("On Growth and Form," ii, 112) maintains that crystals form by gradient, and that the irregularity of their first structures is only due to the fact that the potential has not yet fully established itself. He hopes that "some patient investigator, observing a supersaturated solution at the critical moment, may ere long verify this proposition under controlled conditions." However this may be, he cites evidence to show that "snowflakes do not LEARN to branch," but branch by gradient when they encounter the appropriate atmospheric conditions (ib., p. 110). In the second place, a gradient often provides only a general impetus for the sort of form to take, in which case local interactions are necessary in order to achieve stability and specificity in structure. In the third place, even in the most evident cases of acquired complexity, such as a whirlpool, some initial asymmetry is required to initiate the process of organization. In the case of a whirlpool, the chief asymmetry involved is commonly supposed to be that of a submerged obstacle, but this may be questioned. (See Schrödinger's "What is Life?," p. 78 ff.)

The Distinction of Description is that: Of several accounts given of the same phenomena, those which are accompanied or closely followed by mere observation of the facts will, other things being equal, be more firmly connected with the phenomena, so that, when they are considered, they will be more likely to be repeated; those which are accompanied or closely followed by an inquiry into their causes will, other things being equal, have their connections with those phenomena altered, so that, when they are considered, they will be less likely to be conflated. The greater the observation or the inquiry, the greater the separation or the confusion of the categories.

Professor Smith ("Pattern Dynamics," pp. 142-3) has an ingenious theory as to the way in which regularity arises from disparate material conditions. I think there is a reason why his theory cannot be regarded as alone sufficient, but it seems not unlikely that it is partly correct. Suppose, for the sake of simplicity, that there are just ten distinct substrates which may be examined by the observer--say, ten substances upon which a pattern may form--and that only one of these displays constancy, or whatever else represents persistence in the case in question. Then the enduring pattern always recurs during the observer's inspections, whereas each of the others, on the average, recurs in only half the inspections. Thus the tendency to reproduce a previous configuration (which is easily explicable without the intervention of "vital force") leads to a greater emphasis on the persistent pattern than on any other, and in time causes it alone to be recognized. The objection to this view, if taken as the sole explanation, is that no improvement ought to set in till after the SECOND observation, whereas experiment shows that already at the second examination the pattern appears more distinctly than the first time. Something further is, therefore, required to account for the genesis of constancy from variable foundations; but I see no reason to suppose that what is further required involves "animating principle.

The process of transmission, which consists in the conveyance of traits, has been much observed in various societies.* For example: you take a nascent community, say a village, in a valley which has customs that can be altered by adopting a novelty; beyond the valley you place a more prosperous town. The villagers at first cling to all their old ways, making strenuous efforts to resist any change. At last, by necessity, a custom is altered and the community acquires the prosperity. Next year you observe the situation, and you find that the village adopts innovations somewhat more readily than before, although it still exhibits some conservative hesitations. The third year it adopts them still more readily, and before long it goes straight to the new practice and embraces it at once. Or you examine a lineage of craftsmen, and place an apprentice in the workshop, assailed by the promise of mastery from the finished products. The apprentice begins attempting the techniques, and is constantly thwarted by initial failures, but at last, by repeated trials, he achieves competence. You observe this progression year after year; you note the time required by the apprentice in reaching proficiency; you find that the time steadily decreases, and that after a period the apprentice ceases to make any fundamental errors. It is by essentially similar processes that we inherit dialects, moral codes, artistic styles, or the foundations of a civilization.

The common conception of systems errs by imagining them to be merely additive and mechanically predictable, as well as devoid of emergent properties. This is a profound misconception. A system, as a rule, is remarkably integrated, capable of functioning under typical conditions, but readily disrupted by any novel perturbation. A clock tells time by its arrangement, but if one examines only the disassembled gears, one will observe with equal clarity a collection of inert components, or even a mere heap of brass (Whitehead, "Process," iii, 207). Spencer, quoting Mill, has made play with the supposed simple aggregation of the steam engine, which produces motion from heat. On this subject I will quote from Eddington's "Nature of the Physical World," p. 104:

All the above characteristics of chemical affinity can be established by purely physical observation, except the fact that replication does not require intention. This, though not strictly capable of being PROVED by experiment, is irresistibly suggested by the most elementary reactions. Who can believe, for example, that a simple molecule is aware of the necessity of structure for preserving stability? Or that crystals, in forming lattices, are concerned for the propagation of their order? The essence of replication, one might say, is that it provides a process for continuing without design in a manner which is usually inevitable thermodynamically. It is partly for this reason that it is so important to understand the fundamental position of chemistry in prompting both molecular and cellular behaviour.

What is true of machines, as regards components and functions, is equally true of systems.
