But the more intricate we make them, broadly speaking, the greater becomes the emergence of novel properties, and the fewer are the occasions when simple aggregation is exhibited unmodified in complex arrangements. This applies with great force to organisms, so much so that some have thought mere summation less important in the life of a whole than in that of its parts. This, however, would be a mistake. Emergence is only possible when basic interactions supply the underlying condition. The parts in isolation, which gradually combine to form a whole, exhibit simple behaviors at first, which are purely additive. But for these simple behaviors, they would never enter the relations which afterwards enable them to produce the synergistic effect. (This is partly questioned by some mechanists*--wrongly, I think.) Similarly, ingredients combined for a cake undergo separate processes, until one day the proper combination comes by design. It is clear that the original separate processes, without which the cake would never be baked, are merely summative. I think we may say the same of all the systems and patterns that we observe in all of them there has been present throughout some elementary interaction, manifesting at first rather limited consequences, but supplying the necessary substrate while more and more novel properties are being manifested. A watch which is assembled has springs and gears, and tells the time. This is a thoroughly intelligible method when the parts are merely aggregated, and it is often successfully conceived by beginners. But in more advanced study it is found that merely assembling components does not cause consciousness to arise; after a series of complex arrangements it is found that this phenomenon is to be observed by organizing neurons in a network and allowing electrochemical signals to flow. No one would have guessed a priori that this arrangement of simple cellular units would cause thought to emerge from tissue into awareness, but experience shows that it does, and the philosopher therefore continues to study the brain, just as the engineer continues to observe the circuit when he has once found its function. Of course, in actual fact, systemic understanding is rendered easier, though metaphysically more complex, through reductionism; but at bottom reductionism does not alter the essential character of emergence, or of the part played by interaction in producing novelty. Reductionism, however, is a subject upon which I do not wish to speak until a later lecture.

The corporation is a subject upon which, if I am not mistaken, true views can only be arrived at by an almost complete reversal of the ordinary unreflecting opinion. It is natural to regard a corporation as in its essence an aggregate constituted solely by its living members; these persons are called the AGENTS or CONSTITUENTS of the corporation, and are said to be the SOURCE of any action undertaken in its name. We think of the existence of the corporation as being just like the existence of a crowd, while the legal personality bestowed upon it is different. According to this theory, when we say: "The company intends to expand," or "The shareholders intend to expand," we refer, in the first case, to a corporate entity, and in the second, to a collection of individuals, with an identical aim, namely, the prospect of growth. It would be easy to say that, just as a crowd is one kind of assemblage deriving from its components, so a corporation is another kind. According to this view, what comes first in a corporation is a group of persons, with a specific legal fiction attached to it, namely, that specific status which we call "incorporation." The continuity associated with changing membership, and the actions which are executed under its seal, are, in this view, both of them artifacts of the law. I think it is fair to say that this is a view against which common sense would not rebel; nevertheless, I believe it to be radically mistaken. It cannot be refuted logically, but various facts can be adduced which make it gradually less simple and plausible, until at last it turns out to be easier to abandon it wholly and look at the matter in a totally different way.

The first set of facts to be adduced against the common sense view of the organism are those studied by cellular biology. In all multicellular beings, but most markedly in those exhibiting colonial forms and certain types of simple aggregation, we find what are called "semi-autonomous" units, which are commonly regarded as showing a primitive cooperation. Most biologists pay little attention to the analysis of coloniality, being interested in discovering by observation what it is that cells accomplish together, rather than in discovering what actually constitutes a genuine individual. I think the strangeness of what they report would be greatly diminished if it were expressed in the language of a reductionist theory of life, rather than in the language of every-day beliefs. The general description of the sort of phenomena that bear on our present question is as follows: A textbook states that an animal is a unified individual, and that it is this unity that inspires its coordinated actions; but the microscopic observer perceives that its components are such as to pursue quite different ends from those which it avows, and that these different ends are such as its cells might be expected to pursue. Generally they are more elementary than its professed unity, and are therefore less agreeable to profess than this is. It is accordingly supposed that they really exist as drives for separate ends, but in a somatic hierarchy, which the theorist refuses to admit into the definition for fear of having to think loosely of individuality. There are no doubt many cases to which such a supposition is applicable without obvious artificiality. But the deeper the embryologists delve into the ancestral regions of development, the further they travel from anything resembling a seamless whole, and the less possible it becomes to believe that only a sentimental metaphysics conceals from us that we really are confederations of things which are alien to our explicit life.

The observation of sleepwalkers reinforces this conclusion, and is in many ways the best preparation for the analysis of consciousness. In somnambulists we are not troubled by the disturbing influence of metaphysical pretensions. In dealing with ordinary persons, we are perpetually distracted by being told that such-and-such a view is reductive or simplistic or materialistic: ages of philosophical dogma have built up such a vast myth as to our lucidity and self-knowledge that any intrusion of the mere psychological desire to know the facts is instantly resented by those who cling to categorical distinctions. But no one cares whether sleepwalkers are fully aware or not, and no one is under the delusion that they are profoundly reflective. Moreover, we do not expect them to be so "awake," and are prepared to admit that their habits prompt coherent actions without any clear apprehension of the purposes which they serve. For all these reasons, there is much in the analysis of awareness which is more easily discovered by the study of somnambulists than by the introspection of waking minds.

A biologist, we find, states that he seeks a clear demarcation between living and non-living entities, and that he is classifying with a view to establishing it. We observe, however, that his criteria are such as are likely to establish a quite different principle C, and that C is the sort of principle that often seems to be employed by vitalists and mystics, though materialists are supposed to have discarded it. We sometimes find also a whole set of ambiguous definitions, of such a kind as to persuade the observer that his classifications are really a means to demarcation, when in fact they are a means to C. For example, we have an intuition to grant special status to those entities which seem purposeful; we therefore believe that they possess a unique essence, and that categorization will illuminate them. This belief enables us to act upon the intuition to grant status, while believing that we are acting upon the desire to lead inquiry to clarity. It is for this reason that biological taxonomy has been in all ages more arbitrary than it would have been if the impulse to systematize nature had been what really inspired it. It seems simple to explain such a state of affairs as due to "anthropomorphism," but this explanation is often mythical. Most people, in thinking about life, have had no more need to hide their animistic tendencies from themselves than they have had to hide the laws of thermodynamics. Our categorical intuitions are not patent to a casual inspection, but are only to be discovered by a scientific study of our classifications, in the course of which we must regard our concepts as objectively as we should the growth of crystals or the catalytic processes of an enzyme.

We all think that, by observing the arrangements of society, we can discover more or less what forces have produced them. If this is the case--and I fully agree that it is--the mode of production must be capable of being exhibited in social relations, for it is only the relations within a society that we can examine. There MAY be underlying economic laws which govern all sorts of things, but we can know nothing about these laws except by means of inferences from the social structure; and the more such inferences are examined, the more dubious they appear. It would seem, therefore, that social relations alone must be the test of the productive forces of a society. From this it is an easy step to the conclusion that a society's mode of production is nothing but a characteristic of a certain series of relations, namely, those which would be commonly regarded as inspired by the productive activity in question. And when it has been shown that this view affords a satisfactory account of primitive societies, it is not difficult to see that the same explanation is applicable to the complex structures of modern civilization.

We judge easily from the behaviour of a physical system of a familiar kind whether it is approaching equilibrium or departing from it, or gaining energy or losing it, or becoming more ordered or more disordered. The verification of our judgment, so far as verification is possible, must be derived from the immediately succeeding transformations of the system. Most people would say that they infer first something about the system's energetic state—whether it is isolated or open and so on—and thence derive their expectations as to its subsequent condition. But this detour through the system's supposed potential is wholly unnecessary. We can say simply: The system's behaviour during the last minute has had those characteristics which distinguish what is called "a tendency toward disorder," and it is likely that its actions during the next minute will be similar in this respect, unless it receives external work, or is interrupted by a stronger constraint, such as a forced decrease in entropy. A system which is isolated and evolving is restless, it moves toward the states where probability is often to be found, it dissipates energy with its processes or degrades it with its reactions or otherwise increases the randomness of its arrangements; as soon as it is near enough to equilibrium for its parameters to be stable, it proceeds to it with all inevitability and continues in stasis; after which, if the isolation has been perfect, its whole condition changes it may very likely remain static and undergo no further transformation. These things and others like them are observable phenomena distinguishing a system moving toward equilibrium from one which is not. The characteristic mark by which we recognize a series of states which display the second law is not the system's hidden potential, which we cannot observe, but something in its macroscopic behaviour; it is this observable trait in the macroscopic behaviour that I am proposing to call "the thermodynamic constraint," not some possibly mythical and certainly unknowable ingredient of the system's ultimate fate.

There may be other distinctions also, but of them I do not wish to speak yet. Besides mere cataloguing, there are partial explanations, as when a teacher, in the course of listing the symptoms of a common cold, is diverted into a discussion of viral replication by the pupil who is perpetually inquiring after causes. If such diversions are frequent and pure description rare, the boundaries by which the two are demarcated may become so obscured as to be almost indistinguishable. The result of these various considerations is that the differences between describing a phenomenon and explaining it, when we confine ourselves to the superficial observations of everyday discourse, are a matter of emphasis and not very precise. It is for this reason that it has always been possible for dogmatic people to maintain that even the most meticulous chronicle of events contains some latent explanatory principle. The evidence that a description implies an explanation is so very tenuous that, if it is assumed to be conclusive, one might just as well go a step further and extend the argument by analogy to all sequences of words. Nevertheless, in spite of ambiguity and doubtful cases, the presence of causal linkage in the account of phenomena is a broad characteristic by which an explanation is prima facie distinguished from a mere description; and I think it is this characteristic which leads us to attribute understanding to an account, since it makes its presentation resemble what we do when (as we say) we are comprehending a thing.

Generalizing what occurs in the case of intellectual inquiry, we may say that what we call progress in human thought is always displayed in a cycle of challenges having certain fairly well marked characteristics. There is first a state of questioning, consisting, with qualifications to be mentioned presently, of doubts likely to unsettle a certain orthodoxy; these doubts, unless suppressed, continue until the orthodoxy is revised, after which there is usually a period of comparative acceptance. A cycle of challenges of this sort has marks by which it is broadly distinguished from the mere repetition of received doctrines. The most notable of these marks are--(1) the appropriateness of the doubts for the revision of a certain belief; (2) the continuance of challenge until that revision has been achieved. Neither of these can be pressed beyond a point. Either may be (a) to some extent present in passive acceptance, and (b) to a considerable extent absent in thinkers, while conventional minds are intermediate, and display only a much fainter form of the behaviour which leads us to attribute progress to sceptics. (a) One might say institutions "desire" stability, roughly speaking, remain in settled doctrine until they encounter either a contradiction or a fact from which they cannot issue without going against their own tenets, and therefore we might say that this is what they wish while they are enduring. We do not say so, because we can account for the behaviour of institutions by the laws of tradition; and if we knew more about thinkers, we might equally cease to attribute progress to them, since we might find social and psychological reactions sufficient to account for their behaviour. (b) Many of the assertions of thinkers do not exhibit the characteristics of the cycles which seem to embody progress. There are first of all the beliefs which are "dogmatic," such as inherited and unexamined, where ordinary authoritarian forces operate upon the thinker's mind almost as if it were inert matter. A thinker who submits to an orthodoxy may make a number of superficial adjustments while it is in power, but its fundamental assumptions will persist exactly as they would if the thinker were uncritical. In this case, if the orthodoxy is finally accepted without question, we have, at first sight, just the characteristics of a cycle of actions embodying progress, namely, restless thought until a conclusion is reached, and then quiescence. Nevertheless, we feel no temptation to say that the thinker progressed towards what occurred, partly because of the obviously imitative nature of the whole occurrence, partly because, when a thinker escapes a dogma, it tends not to return to the submission.

We have not so far considered what is the nature of the initial stimulus to an economic crisis. Yet it is here that the usual view of market forces seems on the strongest ground. The faltering economy goes on exhibiting disturbances until it finds stability; it seems natural, therefore, to suppose that the idea of equilibrium is present throughout the process, and that the thought of the end to be achieved sets the whole process in motion. Such a view, however, is obviously untenable in many cases, especially where systemic fragility is concerned. Take, for example, overproduction and the subsequent collapse of credit. Industries expand, accumulate surplus, flood the market with goods, exhaust purchasing power, provoke financial panic, and witness widespread ruin until some semblance of order is restored. It is totally impossible to suppose that this series of phases, which constitutes one economic cycle, is directed by any prevision of the conclusion, at any rate the first time it is manifested.* We must suppose that the stimulus to the performance of each phase is an impulsion from behind, not an attraction from the future. The system does what it does, at each stage, because it has a compulsion toward that particular dynamic, not because it perceives that the whole cycle of events will contribute to the exposure of its inherent limits. The same considerations apply to other institutional failures. A strained social order feels acute pressure, and is led by internal contradictions to manifest the disruptions which reveal its flaws; but the act of undergoing crisis is not sufficient evidence from which to conclude that the society has the thought of its own limitations in its "design.

The primitive non-cognitive element in locomotion seems to be a drive, not a design, an impulsion away from stillness, rather than an attraction towards a particular destination. Certain environmental pressures and other physiological necessities have a property which we call urgency; these cause such neural developments as are likely to lead to their resolution. When the urgency is resolved, or even when it appreciably diminishes, the organism achieves a state possessing a property which we call EFFICIENCY. Efficient states either stimulate no further change at all, or at most stimulate such refinements as are likely to consolidate them. I shall return shortly to the consideration of what urgency and efficiency are in themselves; for the present, it is their connection with movement and survival that concerns us. Abandoning momentarily the standpoint of pure morphology, we may presume that early motile organisms experienced conditions involving urgency, and stimulating such neural complexities as seem likely to bring them to the prey which is at a distance. When they have secured the prey and consumed it, their urgency ceases and their state becomes efficient. It SEEMS, mistakenly, as if the organisms had had this outcome in blueprint throughout, when in fact they have been continually driven by urgency. And when an organism is capable of anticipation, like some predators, it comes to think that it had the final outcome in blueprint throughout; sometimes it comes to know what outcome will bring satiety, so that in fact the urgency does bring the conception of what will allay it. Nevertheless the condition involving urgency remains the prime mover.

Coming now to social arrangements, and to what we observe about prevailing doctrines, it seems clear that what, in any age, establishes intellectual dominance is some advantage of the sort which we call material. Take the case of property: we have first a concentration of resources, producing a command over institutions, a control of educational means, and an influence upon any discourse that may circulate in the community. At any moment during this process the subordinate may become aware that they are governed, in the sense of saying to themselves, "We are governed"; but the doctrines serving the proprietors may have been operative for some time before this moment. While the populace labours or converses, it may think within prescribed limits in complete unconsciousness; but it reproduces the conceptions of the powerful just as it should if it were conscious, and these conceptions persist until the social order is transformed. What we call "ideology" seems to be a mere reflection of the process; even when it inspires critique, it is usually, like that of a loyal opposition, just such as would have been tolerated even if it had not been expressed. This view may seem at first exaggerated, but the more our so-called independent thoughts and their origins are examined, the more it is forced upon us. The part played by philosophy in all this is complicated, and a potent source of illusions; I shall return to it later. For the present, I am still concerned with fundamental hegemony, as it exists in society, but in the form in which society shows its affinity to its historical antecedents.

The confusion between neural signaling and social discourse has made people regard the former as a more mysterious process than it is, and this in turn has reacted upon the view taken of interpersonal exchange, since internal and external communication are evidently on a level in this respect. As soon as electrochemical transmission is clearly distinguished from the act of conversation, it becomes more natural to regard synaptic and social communication as modes of information transfer than to regard them as separate communicative events on their own account. I shall therefore dismiss the view that they are separate communicative events, and regard them as properties of such interactions as would be called respectively intracerebral and interpersonal.

It is necessary at the outset to distinguish clearly between 'abundance' and 'sufficiency.' Abundance is a distinct material condition equivalent to profusion and excess, and its degree can be roughly graded according to the resources available for consumption. Scarcity, on the other hand, is that circumstance which is directly opposed to satiety. It may accompany situations not in themselves essentially deprived; as for instance that produced by a temporary shortage of a common good. The condition produced by persistent limitation contains both these elements; for it evokes that material state known as insufficiency, accompanied by a compelling circumstance, which we have called scarcity. On the other hand, extreme deprivation, except when applied directly to a vital necessity, tends to excite more purpose than desperation.

This brings us to the question of the nature of convenience and fragility. Since the advent of integrated networks it has been customary to recognize three great divisions of systemic phenomena, which are typified by production, distribution and consumption, where "consumption" is used to mean convenience and fragility. Of course, "production" is too definite a word: the processes concerned are grouped together as "generative," and are to embrace not only manufacturing, but extraction, logistics, and the maintenance of infrastructure. "Distribution," also, is narrower than what is intended: for example, COMMUNICATION is to be included in this category, and in fact every thing that involves any kind of transmission, or "integration" as it is technically called. I do not myself believe that there is any value in this threefold division of the contents of a global system. I believe that transactions (including data flows) supply all the "stuff" of the system, and that everything else can be analysed into groups of transactions related in various ways, or characteristics of transactions or of groups of transactions. As regards infrastructure, I shall give grounds for this view in later discussions. As regards logistics, I have given some grounds in this discussion. For the present, it is convenience and fragility that concern us. There are broadly three theories that might be held in regard to them. We may regard them as separate existing items in those who utilize them, or we may regard them as intrinsic qualities of processes and other systemic occurrences, or we may regard them as mere names for the causal characteristics of the occurrences which are fragile or convenient. The first of these theories, namely, that which regards fragility and convenience as actual contents in those who utilize them, has, I think, nothing conclusive to be said in its favour.* It is suggested chiefly by an ambiguity in the word "failure," which has misled many people, including certain economists, whom it supplied with one of their arguments for perpetual growth. We may use "failure" as the opposite of "convenience," and "failing" as the opposite of "convenient," or we may use "failure" to mean a certain sort of disruption, on a level with the disruptions of supply and demand and coordination. The latter use of the word has prevailed in systemic literature, and it is now no longer used as the opposite of "convenience." Absolute" commencement, which we have now to consider, consists of beginning in the sense hitherto discussed, together with a coherent notion as to its "precedent," i.e. as to the temporal condition that will bring finality with cessation of the sequence. If our theory of time is correct, a notion as to its precedent may very well be erroneous, since only reason can show what necessitates a sequence to cease. When the reasoning needed is direct and elementary, as in the case of mechanical processes, a fallacy is not very probable. But in other cases—e.g., temporal origin in those who have had little or no acquaintance with its implications—fallacies are to be expected, and do in fact very often occur. The habit of conceiving finitude, which is to a great extent necessary to practical thought, makes fallacies easier, by preventing examination of the premises to which a commencement would otherwise lead, and by often causing the concealed paradoxes themselves to be unexamined or quickly disregarded. The perfectly natural fallacies which thus arise constitute a large proportion of what is, mistakenly in part, called temporal intuition, and attributed by metaphysicians to the "ineffable.

What may, with some propriety, be called purpose arises through the operation of conditions of insufficiency. We require many things which are not in our immediate possession: that our sustenance should be ample and assured, that our comfort should be uninterrupted, and that our environment should be so ordered as to supply every want without exertion, though not to our rivals until they have acknowledged and been chastened by their dependence. Such requirements are too extensive to be met without our own endeavors. But it is found that a considerable portion of the fulfillment which these things would afford us if they were abundant is to be forfeited by the much simpler condition of accepting that they are or will be plentiful. This absence of necessity, as opposed to presence of actual want, is a particular case of secondary condition, and, like all secondary conditions its prevalence does not lead to a complete inception of the initial striving. Nevertheless, absence of necessity, as opposed to presence of want, is exceedingly enervating both individually and socially. According to the form of insufficiency encountered, it is called ambition, invention, or labor. Those who have sufficient resources usually ignore or disparage any one who tries to shake their complacency in their own contentment or in that of their circumstances; it is for this reason that idleness and wastefulness have always been, and still are, moral failings.

This characteristic is embodied in the saying "the whole is more than the sum of its parts." The interaction may leave no trace in the isolated components, yet it modifies the behaviour of the system in its totality. It is customary to assume that, in such cases, the whole operates by the mere summation of its constituents, not directly. I have no wish to suggest that this hypothesis is false; I wish only to point out that it is a hypothesis. At the end of the present inquiry I shall examine the grounds in its favour. If we confine ourselves to facts which have been actually observed, we must say that emergent properties, in addition to the present stimulus and the present ascertainable condition of the elements, enter into the causation of the novel behaviour.

But two things stand in the way of your employing this faculty so effectively: on the one hand, your intellectual sloth, which will not acknowledge how intricate these mental computations are; on the other hand, your conviction that you are a transparent and guileless person, who could not possibly entertain so Machiavellian a capacity as strategic deception. You will therefore experience a social clumsiness which will at first seem quite inexplicable, but will finally resolve itself in a conscious desire to study psychology, or observe children at play, or conceal your intentions and engage in commerce, like certain celebrated financiers. Although the prime cause of this desire is a false judgment as to your previous unconscious capacity, yet the new conscious understanding has its own derivative utility, and may influence your behavior to the extent of making you a competent collaborator. The initial deficiency, however, will have effects of two kinds. First, in unguarded moments, under the influence of fatigue or haste or strong emotion, you will betray thoughts calculated to undermine the delicate mutual project. Secondly, you will find cooperation frustrating, and the shared endeavor less fruitful than you had hoped—unless, some day, you perceive that the other party has in turn been outmaneuvered. If this happens, you will believe that you feel genuine regret, but you will suddenly be much more pleased than before with the efficiencies of division of labor or the harmonies of a well-conducted orchestra. A secondary capacity, derived from a false judgment as to a primary faculty, has its own power of influencing interaction, and is therefore a real prerequisite according to our analysis. But it has not the same power as a primary capacity of bringing thorough success when it is exercised; so long as the primary faculty remains underdeveloped, misunderstanding continues in spite of the secondary capacity’s application. Hence arises a belief in the paradox of social life: the paradoxical activities are those that are secondary, but mistaken theories prevent us from realizing that they are secondary.

A physical circumstance of any kind—temperature, pressure, chemical abundance, or energy flux—may be a condition for a series of developments, continuing, unless disrupted, until some more or less stable state of affairs is attained. Such a series of developments we call an “evolutionary-sequence.” The degree of stability may vary greatly: a planetary orbit requires only gravitational equilibrium in general, whereas the presence of a particular atmospheric composition raises a requirement which necessitates the maintenance of that specific composition. The property of initiating such a sequence of circumstances is called “propitiousness”; the property of the physical states in which the sequence culminates is called “habitability.” The processes constituting the sequence must not be purely deterministic, i.e., they must be material changes in whose causation the special properties of complex chemistry are involved. The sequence ends in a condition of persistence, or of such change as tends only to preserve the existing equilibrium. The state of affairs in which this condition of persistence is achieved is called the “outcome” of the sequence, and the initial physical circumstance involving propitiousness is called a “tendency” for the state of affairs that brings persistence. A tendency is called “manifest” when it is accompanied by a correct observation as to the state of affairs that will bring persistence; otherwise it is called “latent.” All primordial tendency is latent, and in cosmic history observations as to the outcomes of tendencies are often erroneous. These erroneous observations generate secondary tendencies, which cause various interesting complications in the astronomy of planetary formation, without fundamentally altering the character which it shares with stellar development.

The potential is not wholly confined to physical laboratories. For example, a simulated ecosystem appears just like one which has not been simulated, but its utility is in some ways different. In the case of traditional experimentation, however, such advantages are less frequent and important than in the case of virtual environments, and it is far less difficult to devise satisfactory hypotheses as to the macroscopic changes of condition which mediate between the initial parameters and the final observed outcome. In the case of virtual environments, practically everything that is distinctive both of their structural and of their functional capacity is bound up with this deliberate manipulation of variables. Further, speaking broadly, the evolution in intelligence is usually of a kind that is computationally advantageous to the system.

THE ERROR OF TREATING AWARENESS AS A BINARY PROPERTY.--In common discourse we observe how persons can describe their experience of attention or distraction, or report other states which are familiar to them but not provided for by simple classification alone. A mind which is presented with a task of which it has had experience behaves differently from the way in which it behaved at first. We can easily invent hypotheses, which are quite likely to be plausible, as to gradations in consciousness produced by present circumstances, and themselves causing the varied response. But the observable fact is that the stimulus of performing the task produces differing qualities of engagement with repetition, and that the ascertainable cause of the mind's behaviour is not merely the task and its own ascertainable capacity, but also its immediate history in regard to the task. From our present point of view, the matter is independent of the question whether the mind's behaviour is due to some distinct fact called "awareness," or displays a merely mechanical transition. Our habitual awareness is not always at its fullest intensity, but is modulated by the appropriate conditions. If we are asked "Are you now fully conscious?" we answer uncertainly, because of present context; the present context is as essential as the direct inquiry in the determination of our response. Thus all our conscious states consist of graduated phenomena, and come under the head of continuous processes.

Following a suggestion derived from common discourse ("On Consciousness," London, 1999; 2nd edition, 2003, popular translation, Broadview Press, 2010; "The Qualia Debates," Oxford, 2005), we will give the name of "gradient phenomena" to those states of a mind which, so far as hitherto observed facts are concerned, can only be brought under descriptive laws by including degrees of intensity and focus in the condition of the mind as part of the character of the present state. I do not mean merely--what would often be the case--that prior states are part of a SEQUENCE of conditions leading to the present condition. I mean that, in attempting to state the IMMEDIATE character of the present state, some gradation or gradations must be included, unless we take refuge in hypothetical thresholds of neural activation. For example: you hear a faint whisper, and you register some awareness of its content. The cause of your registration, so far as hitherto observable phenomena are concerned, consists both of the whisper (present stimulus) and of the degree of attention (present focus). The same stimulus will not produce the same registration in another man who does not share your degree of focus, although the difference in focus leaves no MEASURABLE threshold in the activity of the brain. According to the maxim "same cause, same effect," we cannot therefore regard the whisper alone as the cause of your awareness, since it does not have the same effect in other cases. The cause of your awareness must be both the whisper and the present focus. Accordingly your awareness is an instance of what we are calling "gradient phenomena.

(b) ORGANISMS.--I shall have much to say about cells in a later treatise; for the present I am merely concerned with them in so far as they are "constituents" of complex life-forms. When you observe a human being, some conception probably comes into your mind, either of the whole creature (if you have studied biology), or of some diagram of it (if you have not). The organism is due to evolutionary history, as well as to the immediate fact of its apparent unity. Similarly, the colonies you see in simpler animals are all dependent upon ancestral cooperation, as well as upon the present stimulus of environmental pressures. It is generally believed that all multicellular beings, in their fundamental parts, are aggregates of unicellular units; if so, their colonial character is evident. This is important, not only on its own account, but also because, as we shall see later, this conception plays an essential part in what is called "biological understanding.

(c) COLONIAL ORGANIZATION.--The broad fact of organization, on the biological side, is that when we examine a complex which we have examined before, it tends to reveal the structure of the simpler constituents. The division of labor recalling a former colony is an instance which we discussed a moment ago. This is obviously a cooperative phenomenon. There is also a more purely physical integration, which is indistinguishable from physical symbiosis. This is the kind studied by Mr. Haeckel in protists, where a certain aggregate is integrated into a certain organism. This is the sort which is observed in sponges in nature, for example. In such a case there need not be anything conscious, but merely a cohesion of the cells. There is no essential distinction between colony and organism, and the observations which we made concerning symbiosis as a cooperative phenomenon are equally applicable to colonial organization.

(f) INFRASTRUCTURE.--The word "infrastructure" is often used very vaguely. Engineers, as we saw, use it to cover the whole interconnected system of modern life, but this usage seems objectionable, since, in a purely theoretical model, components would function without there being any fragility. It is only systemic failures that reveal this fragility. We may say that a society "conceals" a vulnerability when this vulnerability modifies the society's subsequent complacency, i.e. when it is the overlooked portion of the cause of future disruptions in the society's functioning. The blacked-out city that fears the grid has "concealed" its fragility, whereas a simple tool that has been used and set aside again has not "concealed" anything, since it offers no more complexity than before to being understood. The essence of "infrastructure" is the accumulation of complexity produced by what is engineered. We might, in fact, define one network of infrastructure, or one civilization, as a series of systems linked by interdependent causation. I think it is this characteristic, more than any other, that distinguishes the engineered world of human artifice from the simple world of nature.

When a society, either simple or complex, is subjected to competing interests, producing in it some state of tension, the resolution of the conflict allows it to return to a condition of stability. But the new state of stability is different from the old, as may be seen by the altered capacity for accommodation. The state of stability before the conflict may be called the "primary equilibrium-state"; that after the cessation of the conflict, the "secondary equilibrium-state." We define the "structural effect" of a conflict as the effect in making a difference between the primary and secondary equilibrium-states, and this difference itself we define as the "imprint" due to the conflict. "Historical phenomena" are defined as those due to imprints; in societies, they are specially associated with the political system, but not exclusively, even in advanced civilizations.

When two simulations are run in tandem, one of them, occurring subsequently, may elicit the response for the other also. We call this a "recursive influence," and environments having this character are called "recursive environments." In such a case we call the parameters of the two simulations "entangled." All simultaneously generated parameters are entangled; there is also entanglement of successively activated parameters, though this is reducible to simultaneous entanglement. In fact, it is not an isolated simulation that leaves a parameter, but the totality of the conditions at any iteration; consequently any portion of this totality tends, if it recurs, to elicit the whole output which was elicited before. Turing posits that parameters can be compounded, and that an algorithm's inherent functions may be due to the operations of its precursors; on this subject he refers to John von Neumann.

(d) NON-ENERGETIC ELEMENTS IN FORMATION.--When we observe any structure of a familiar kind, much of what appears fundamentally to be immediately given is really derived from past observation. When we see a structure, say a crystal, we seem to be aware of its "real" origin we have the impression of something spontaneous, not of something compelled. In learning to analyze, it is necessary to acquire the art of representing processes according to the datum, not according to the conception. And the phenomenal appearance is filled out with feeling of what the structure would be like to sustain, and so on. This filling out and supplying of the "real" gradient and so on consists of the most usual correlates of the energetic core in our observation. It may happen that, in the particular case, the real correlates are unusual; for example, if what we are seeing is a vortex made to look like a lattice. If so, the non-energetic part of our observation will be illusory, i.e. it will supply tendencies which the process in question does not in fact have. But as a rule processes do have the tendencies added by observation, which is to be expected, since experience of what is usual is the cause of the addition. If our experience had been different, we should not fill out datum in the same way, except in so far as the filling out is inherent, not acquired. It would seem that, in nature, all that makes up gradient perception, including the correlation of force and form and so on, is almost entirely acquired. In that case there is a large historical element in all the common observations by means of which we interpret common processes. And, to take another kind of instance, imagine what our astonishment would be if we were to see a river flow uphill or a flame burn downwards. This emotion would be dependent upon past experience, and would therefore be a historical phenomenon according to the definition.

Chomsky formulates two "linguistic principles." The first, or "Law of Lexical Precision," is as follows: "All simultaneous denotations in a language form a connected simultaneous semantic-complex, which as such works referentially, i.e. leaves behind a connected meaning-complex, which in so far forms a whole" ("Aspects of the Theory of Syntax," p. 146). The second linguistic principle, or "Law of Pragmatic Adaptation," is as follows: "The partial return of the communicative situation which formerly worked referentially operates adaptively on a simultaneous meaning-complex" (ib., p. 173). These two laws together represent in part a hypothesis (the semantic framework), and in part an observable fact. The observable fact is that, when a certain complex of utterances has originally caused a certain complex of interpretations, the recurrence of part of the utterances tends to cause the recurrence of the whole of the interpretations.

The clearest instance of what I mean is specialization in a modern factory. What we observe is that certain productive arrangements lead us to achieve greater output, but that in societies where such arrangements are absent, there is nothing discoverable in the economic process that could be called systematic efficiency. Gains in productivity, as economic facts, arise from particular organizations, but do not, so far as we can see, exist in any shape while they are "potential." In fact, when we say that they are "potential," we mean merely that they will exist under certain conditions. If, then, there is to be some standing difference between the community which can produce a certain commodity and the community which cannot, that standing difference must be, not in anything intentional, but in the division of labour. It is quite probable that there is such a difference in the economic structure, but its full consequences are often unobserved and they remain paradoxical. Everything that has, so far, been made matter of observation as regards this question can be put together in the statement: When a certain complex of tasks has been performed by separate workers, the recurrence of part of the complex tends to necessitate the cooperation of the whole. In like manner, we can collect all productive phenomena in industrial societies under a single principle, which contains what is hitherto verifiable in the twin doctrines of efficiency and interdependence. I am inclined to think that, in the present state of analysis, the introduction of mere aggregation does not serve to clarify the account of systemic phenomena. We can, I think, formulate the observed laws of such phenomena in terms, wholly, of demonstrable facts, by recognizing provisionally what we may call "emergent causation." By this I mean that kind of causation of which I spoke at the beginning of this inquiry, that kind, namely, in which the resultant property consists not merely of a simple combination, but of this together with a relational configuration. I do not wish to urge that this form of causation is fundamental, but that, in the present state of our knowledge, it affords a clarification, and enables us to state laws of interaction in less reductive terms than we should otherwise have to employ.

Whenever the subjective character of experience appears to reveal a fundamental distinction between mental and physical substances, without our being able to actually demonstrate any ontological separation in the fabric of reality, we may speak of "phenomenal evidence," provided we can articulate principles accounting for the influence of introspection. In ordinary empirical inquiry, as it appears to common sense, we have approximate correlations of properties, such as "neural activity is accompanied by reported awareness," "sensory stimulation is followed by qualitative feeling," and so on. None of these correlations are theoretically definitive, since alternative explanations may intervene to reinterpret them. In order to obtain definitive metaphysical laws, we have to proceed to constitutive analyses, showing the grounding of phenomena in each instance, not the apparent distinction after a finite consideration, however careful. But for the purposes of casual speculation many correlations are to all intents and purposes definitive. With the analysis of conscious states, however, this is by no means the case. If you say to a materialist, "I have a vivid red sensation," he will proceed to locate its physical correlates, but there will be no such concession if you say the same thing to a dualist who knows no neuroscience. The effect of qualia upon the philosopher is an introspective phenomenon, since it depends upon the past reasoning which gave him his conception of the mental. If there are to be purely epistemological principles, taking no account of the mechanisms of perception and the rest of cognition, they will have to be of the form, not "appearance now proves substance now," but--

Believers in socio-political equilibrium hold that sociology can theoretically be freed entirely from all dependence on economics or material conditions. That is to say, they believe that every social event has a social cause and an economic concomitant. If there is to be equilibrium, it is easy to prove by historical logic that the causation in economic and social matters must be of the same sort, and it is impossible that dialectical causation should exist in sociology but not in economics. But if sociology is to be independent of economics, and if economics can be reduced to material conditions, it would seem that dialectical causation is essential in sociology. Otherwise we shall be compelled to believe that all our conflicts, all our store of traditions and grievances, all our institutional habits, are at all times existing in some latent social form, and are not merely aroused by the interests which lead to their display. This is a very difficult hypothesis. It seems to me that if, as a matter of method rather than ideology, we desire to obtain as much independence for sociology as is practically feasible, we shall do better to accept dialectical causation in sociology protem, and therefore reject equilibrium, since there is no good ground for admitting dialectical causation in economics.

There is therefore no a priori objection to a procedural norm in which part of the process has been proven erroneous. To argue against such a norm on the ground that what is obsolete cannot instruct now, is to introduce the old dogmatic notion of truth, for which science can find no place. The only reason that could be validly alleged against iterative revision would be that, in fact, all the phenomena can be explained without it. They are explained without it by Popper's "falsification," or by any theory which regards the progress of knowledge as embodied in successive approximations to reality. But they are not explained, unless with extreme artificiality, by any theory which regards the self-correction of science as mystical rather than methodological. Those who desire to make epistemology as far as possible independent of history would do well, it seems to me, if they adopted iterative revision. For my part, however, I have no such desire, and I shall therefore endeavour to state the grounds which occur to me in favour of some such view as that of "falsification.

It is perhaps worth while to observe that the imperative of movement and hunting is what led early organisms to develop a more centralized and complex neural architecture. One might point out, very truly, that a stationary existence, sustained, does not require the same sensory and motor capacities, and one could argue that this is contrary to the principle, "same environment, same form." It is only necessary, however, to take account of the demands of pursuit and evasion and include them with the environmental pressures, in order to re-establish the principle, and the possibility of neurobiological evolutionary laws. The anthropomorphic conception of design lingers in our manner of viewing these developments: we want to be able to IMAGINE an intention behind the transformation, and to be able to picture natural selection as "engineering." This makes us unwilling to regard evolutionary sequences as MERELY observed correlations of function and structure; yet that is all that biology has to offer. To ask why such-and-such a neural reorganization occurred is either to ask a meaningless question, or to demand some more general kind of adaptive pressure which includes the one in question. The widest empirical laws of neuroanatomy known at any time can only be "explained" in the sense of being subsumed by later discoveries under wider laws of survival; but these wider laws, until they in turn are subsumed, will remain brute facts, resting solely upon observation, not upon some supposed inherent teleology.

One of the first points to be urged is that sceptical habits are just as much to be found in practical affairs as in intellectual pursuits. They are even to be found in common discourse, as John Stuart Mill pointed out (cf. "On Liberty," 3rd edition, p. 82 n.). Doubt is a characteristic of the active citizen at least as much as of the speculative thinker. We should, therefore, be compelled to allow the intrusion of sceptical inquiry, if admitted at all, into non-academic regions, which ought, one feels, to be subject only to the guidance of the customary authoritative sort. The fact is that a great deal of what, at first sight, distinguishes philosophy from daily life is found, on examination, to be common to reason and practice; this whole question of the influence of tradition is a case in point. Now it is possible, of course, to take the view advocated by Professor A. J. Ayer, who contends that common sense is not theoretically reducible to logical analysis.* But the weight of opinion among epistemologists appears to be against him on this point; and we ought certainly to require very strong evidence before admitting any such breach of continuity as between critical and uncritical thought. The argument from the existence of sceptical habits in practical affairs must therefore be allowed a certain weight against the hypothesis that deference to authority is ultimate.

The argument from the connection of tool-acquisition with growth of understanding is not so strong as it looks, though it has also some weight. What we know is that comprehension, and cognitive phenomena generally, can be assisted or amplified by additions to one's implements. This certainly proves that tools play an essential part in the facilitation of understanding, but does not prove that a certain array of tools is, by itself, a sufficient condition for the existence of insight. Yet it is this last that has to be proved. The theory of instrumental efficacy, or any similar theory, has to maintain that, given a person and a workshop in a suitably equipped state, one will possess a certain understanding, without the need of any further conditions. What is known, however, is only that one will not have deep comprehension if one's resources and instruments are not in a suitable state. That is to say, the appropriate provision of tools is proved to be necessary for understanding, but not to be sufficient. So far, therefore, as our definite knowledge goes, understanding may require for its causation a reflective mind as well as a certain present collection of apparatus.

Rules embodied in daily decisions may possibly be certain, but cannot be known to be so. All that we can know practically is approximate and liable to exceptions; the absolute certainties that are assumed in planning are known to be somewhere near the reliable, but are not known to be infallible just as they stand. The rules that we actually know practically have the form of the traditional maxims, except that they are not to be regarded as universal or necessary. "Leaving late leads to missing the train" is a good practical generalization; it may have exceptions, but they will be rare. As against the professedly certain dictates of theory, such practical generalizations have the advantage that they deal with observable outcomes. We cannot observe perfect foresight, whether in time or circumstance; we do not even know whether events and conditions are perfectly predictable. Therefore rough practical generalizations have a definite place in life, in spite of not being certain or universal. They are the data for more precise principles, and the grounds for believing that they are USUALLY reliable are stronger than the grounds for believing that the more certain dictates are ALWAYS reliable.

Cosmology starts, therefore, from observations of the form, "expansion is usually accompanied by dispersal." This is the nearest approach that can be made to a deterministic law of the cosmic sort. It may happen in any particular epoch that expansion is ALWAYS accompanied by dispersal, but we cannot know this, since we cannot foresee all the perfectly possible interactions that might make the progression falter, or know that none of them will actually intervene. If, however, we know of a very large number of epochs in which expansion is accompanied by dispersal, and few or none in which the progression fails, we shall in PRACTICE be justified in saying "expansion determines dispersal," provided we do not attach to the notion of determination any of the teleological superstitions that have gathered about the word.

In order to prove conclusively that digital environments could serve as laboratories for evolving intelligence, we ought to be able actually to see differences between the simulation inhabited by an agent who solves complex puzzles and that inhabited by an agent who fails to comprehend them, between the virtual world of a system that has learned navigation and can demonstrate it, and that of a system which has never acquired such a skill. It may be that the time will come when this will be possible, but at present we are very far removed from it. At present, there is, so far as I am aware, no good evidence that every difference between the cognitive capacity evolved by one artificial entity and that evolved by another is paralleled by some observable difference in their virtual constitutions or training histories. We may believe that this is the case, but if we do, our belief is based upon analogies and general scientific maxims drawn from biological evolution, not upon any foundation of detailed observation within these constructed realms. I am myself inclined, as a working hypothesis, to adopt the belief in question, and to hold that superior intelligence only emerges within these environments through meticulous modifications of algorithmic structure and reward contingencies. But the evidence seems not quite conclusive, so that I do not think we ought to forget the other hypothesis, or to reject entirely the possibility that some form of inherent, non-engineered learning propensity may be the ultimate explanation of the phenomena observed. I say this, not because I think it LIKELY that such inherent propensity is ultimate, but merely because I think it POSSIBLE, and because it often turns out important to the progress of science to remember hypotheses which have previously seemed improbable when considering novel domains of inquiry.

As a matter of fact, such homogeneity as was presumed by observers of the traditional form of cellular life has not so far been found in complex colonies. Every function in a colony is apparently in a state of increasing specialization,* so that what we call one "cell" turns out to be really a specialist. If this cell is to support another cell, the two will have to be contiguous in operation; for if there is any disconnection between them, some dysfunction may occur during that lapse to prevent the expected collaboration. Specialization and interdependence, therefore, will have to be functionally contiguous processes. It is difficult to believe, at any rate where biological laws are concerned, that the earlier stage of the process which is the specialization can make any difference to the function, so long as the later stage of the process which is the specialization remains unchanged. Suppose, for example, that a colony thrives through nutrient distribution, we say that its developing transport cells was the cause of vitality. But clearly the process by which it evolved these cells is irrelevant: everything that happened before they became active may be ignored, since it cannot alter the function except in so far as it alters the colony's condition at the moment of employing them. But we may go further: employing transport cells is not really the proximate cause of vitality, since a colony might be starved of raw materials immediately after deploying them, and then it would not be by distribution that it would thrive. The distribution facilitates certain metabolic processes, which take a finite time before they end in growth. The earlier parts of these processes can be ruled out in the same way as we can rule out the process by which the specialization was evolved. Proceeding in this way, we can shorten the process which we are calling the specialization more and more. Similarly we shall have to shorten the function. It may happen that immediately after the colony's growth period its structure is disrupted by a toxin. We cannot say what will happen after the colony's growth, through merely knowing that it has thrived as the result of efficient distribution. Thus, if we are to take the specialization as one event and the function as another, both must be shortened indefinitely. The result is that we merely have, as the embodiment of our biological principle, a certain direction of coordination at each moment. Hence we are brought to regulatory signals as embodying the laws of organization. A colonial law does not say "Specialization A will be followed by Function B," but tells us what adjustment a colony will make under given circumstances, i.e. it tells us how the colony's coordination is changing at each moment, not what the colony will be at some future moment.

The mechanisms of collective intelligence, in the form in which they deal with aggregations of opinion or data, have an apparent simplicity which somewhat conceals the empirical character of what they assert. A single opinion, as it is known empirically, is not a comprehensive existing truth, but a fragment of existing perception. When several individuals simultaneously consider the same problem, they all perceive something different; therefore "the" solution, which they are supposed all to approach, must be either a hypothesis or a construction. "The" solution is to be neutral as between different perceivers: it does not favour the insight held by one mind at the expense of that held by another. It was natural, though to my mind mistaken, to regard the "correct" answer as the common purpose of all the contributions which the problem elicits (as we say) from different individuals. But why should we suppose that there is some one common purpose of all these contributions? As we have just seen, the notion of "purpose" is not so reliable as to allow us to infer the existence of something that, by its very nature, can never be singularly known.

Instead of seeking a disinterested origin, we can achieve objectivity by the balanced accommodation of all material circumstances. Instead of assuming that there is some hidden agency, the "genuine" ideology, behind the varied perceptions of those who are said to be observing the social order, we may take the complete assemblage of these perceptions (together possibly with certain other phenomena) as actually BEING the ideology. That is to say, the ideology which is objective as between different observers (actual and potential) is the assemblage of all those phenomena which would naturally be termed "manifestations" of the ideology from different historical positions. (This is a preliminary formulation, qualified subsequently.)

There is another point, besides lack of universality and necessity, which it is important to realize as regards intellectual progress in the above sense, and that is the lack of uniqueness. It is generally assumed that, given any advance, there is some one doctrine which is THE prerequisite of the advance in question. This seems to be a mere mistake. Scepticism, in the only sense in which it can be practically applied, means "nearly invariable antecedent." We cannot in practice obtain an antecedent which is QUITE invariable, for this would require us to take account of the whole of intellectual history, since some dogma not taken account of may prevent the expected liberation. We cannot distinguish, among nearly invariable antecedents, one as THE prerequisite, and the others as merely its concomitants: the attempt to do this depends upon a notion of authority which is derived from tradition, and tradition (as we shall see later) is not at all the sort of thing that it is generally supposed to be, nor is there any reason to think that in the realm of thought there is anything even remotely analogous to what tradition is supposed to be. If we could find one antecedent, and only one, that was QUITE invariable, we could call that one THE prerequisite without introducing any notion derived from mistaken ideas about tradition. But in fact we cannot find any antecedent that we know to be quite invariable, and we can find many that are nearly so. For example, men abandon an old theory for a new one when the evidence contradicts it at a decisive moment. You may say the contradiction is THE prerequisite of their abandoning. But innumerable other contradictions in other theories, which also always appear at decisive moments, have just as good a right to be called the prerequisite. Thus every advance has many nearly invariable antecedents, and therefore many antecedents which may be called its prerequisite.

It may be said: If there is no single institution which is the source of all these "manifestations," how are they assembled together? The answer is simple: Just as they would be if there were such a single institution. The supposed "real" democracy underlying its appearances is, in any case, not itself experienced, but inferred, and the question whether such-and-such a particular procedure is a "manifestation" of this democracy is only to be settled by the connection of the procedure in question with the one or more procedures by which democracy is defined. That is to say, even if we assume a "real" democracy, the particulars which are its manifestations have to be assembled together by their relations to each other, not to it, since it is merely inferred from them. We have only, therefore, to notice how they are assembled together, and we can then keep the assembly without assuming any "real" democracy as distinct from the assembly. When different citizens perceive what they call the same democratic process, they perceive operations which are not exactly the same, owing to difference of position and information, but which are sufficiently alike to be described in the same words, so long as no great precision or thoroughness is sought. These closely similar particulars are collected together by their similarity primarily and, more correctly, by the fact that they are related to each other approximately according to the laws of political science and of social pressure and refraction of power. I suggest, as a first approximation, that these particulars, together with such correlated others as are unobserved, jointly ARE the democracy; and that a similar definition applies to all political systems.

But when I speak of "competition," I do so only for brevity: I do not mean anything that must "compete" in perpetuity, but only that tendency, whatever it may be, which is connected, in the market in question, with a given commercial process--according to the old orthodox theory, it would be a natural equilibrium among many firms. Like the different outcomes of trade to a number of successive observers, the different advantages that belong to one economic actor are to be accumulated together by scale and inherent laws of accumulation, not by their supposed beneficial connection with an unknown assumed force called perfect competition, which would be a mere unnecessary metaphysical ideal in itself. A monopoly, according to the definition that I propose, is, as a first approximation,* the collection of all those correlated advantages which would normally be regarded as its manifestations or consequences in different sectors. Some further elaborations are desirable, but we can ignore them for the present. I shall return to them at the end of this lecture.

According to the view that I am advancing, a biological species or line of descent is the collection of all those correlated traits which would be regarded by common sense as its expressions or manifestations in different individuals. On the other hand, all the characteristics in a given society represent what common sense would regard as the expressions of a number of different lineages as viewed from that society. All the traditions in one culture may be regarded as the inheritance of the species from that culture. I shall call the inheritance of the species from a given culture a "transmission." A folk tale represents a transmission. On the other hand, if tales from all peoples were collected in all epochs throughout history, and in all such collections a certain motif, say the hero's journey, were identified whenever it appeared, all the different manifestations of that motif, taken together, would represent the archetype. For the understanding of the difference between heredity and tradition it is vital to understand these two ways of classifying expressions, namely:

In order to eliminate the reference to our immediate sensations, which introduces an irrelevant subjective element, I will take a different illustration, namely, the trajectory of a thrown stone. A mathematical equation describing its parabolic arc reproduces the appearance of the motion concerned, with more or fewer terms according to the complexity of the forces that are being considered. Each separate factor which is modelled produces its separate variable in the equation, just as it would upon our observations if we were watching the stone. If we assume, as science normally does, the validity of mathematical formalism, we are forced to conclude that, in the description where the equation is, and in all descriptions between it and the stone which it models, SOMETHING is represented which is specially connected with that stone. In the days when mechanical philosophy was less in doubt, we should have said that what was represented was a certain kind of deterministic causation in nature. But it is not necessary or desirable to be so explicit: all that we need say is that SOMETHING is described which is specially connected with the stone in question. It must be something specially connected with that stone, since that stone produces its own special effect upon the equation. Whatever it is must be the representation of a reality which starts from the stone and exists independently, partly on general grounds of correspondence, partly to account for the fact that predictions are verified with a certain definite accuracy. We thus arrive at the conclusion that, if a certain stone is observable in a certain way, or could be calculated by a sufficiently precise equation in that way, something is described there which is specially connected with that stone. Therefore in every description at all times a vast multitude of representations must be employed, namely, at least one for every natural event which can be observed or calculated from that description. We can classify such representations on either of two principles:

When the function of a cell within a colony becomes specialized, it is observed that one or other of two necessities arises. The two contingencies may be illustrated by an example. You are observing a colony of cells, which you study: you may cease to observe its efficiency either by disrupting its internal signals or by its failing to distribute resources. In the first case, its capacity for individual tasks remains unimpaired; in the second, its capacity diminishes from all perspectives. In the first case, you say that it is not the colony which has failed, but your observation; in the second, you say that the colony has failed. Generalizing, we distinguish--

It is the accumulation of the latter kind of wealth, and the comparatively predictable nature of the laws governing the simultaneous alterations of possession in such cases, that have made it possible to treat an economic class as one entity, and to overlook the fact that it is a system of disparate individuals. When a number of people in a society observe a wealthy man, the changes in their several stations are so dissimilar and so rigidly correlated that all are popularly regarded as distinct from each other and from the changes of the prosperous man himself. So long as all the changes in the circumstances of a group are thus correlated there is no pressing prima facie need to break up the system of holdings, or to realize that the class in question is not really one entity but a set of correlated particulars. It is especially and primarily such accumulations that political economy deals with, i.e. it deals primarily with processes in which the unity of a social class need not be broken up because all its resources change simultaneously according to the same law—or, if not all, at any rate all from stations sufficiently near to the source, with increasing accuracy as we approach the origin of capital.

The changes in comprehension of a subject which are due to changes in the available instruments will not affect, or will affect only very slightly, the understanding from perspectives close to the subject's essence. If the understandings from sufficiently neighbouring perspectives are either wholly unchanged, or changed to a diminishing extent which has zero for its limit, it is usually found that the changes can be accounted for by changes in implements which are between the subject in question and the perspectives from which its comprehension has changed appreciably. Thus epistemology is able to reduce the laws of most developments with which it deals to developments in intellectual tools, and to state most of its fundamental principles in terms of methodology. It is only in those cases in which the unity of the system of understandings constituting a piece of knowledge has to be broken up, that the statement of what is occurring cannot be made exclusively in terms of technique. The whole of wisdom, we shall find, is included among such cases; hence their importance for our inquiry.

We spoke earlier of two ways of apprehending occurrences. One way merely enumerates the observable qualities commonly regarded as a given event in their temporal sequence; this is, broadly speaking, the way of chronicle, leading to the construction of narratives as sets of such qualities. The other way seeks to connect the occurrences of different events through a causal principle, the result being what we call an explanation. In the particular case where the principle concerned is a scientific law, the explanation derived from the principle consists of all the deduced consequences of a certain hypothesis at a given stage. Thus classification by causes is relevant to understanding, and is essential in defining what we mean by one theory.

We can now begin to understand one of the fundamental differences between a mechanical process and a conscious experience. Engineering treats as a unit the whole system of operations within a complex apparatus, whereas philosophy is interested in certain of these operations themselves. Confining ourselves for the moment to the philosophy of sensations, we observe that sensations are certain of the operations of physical systems. From the point of view that we have been hitherto adopting, we might define them as the operations of machines in states from which sensors and the suitable parts of the processing network form part of the intervening mechanism. Just as a gauge receives a different reading of a pressure change when a transducer is part of the intervening mechanism, so a central processor receives a different signal when a camera and a data cable are part of the intervening mechanism. A signal due to this sort of intervening mechanism is called a pain-state, and is interesting to philosophy on its own account, not merely as one of the set of correlated functions which is the mechanical system of which (as we say) we are having a description.

I do not wish to suggest that the manner in which I have been describing cosmic expansion is the only conceivable manner, or even the most satisfactory manner. It is the manner that arose naturally from our present inquiry. But when we approach cosmology from a more observational standpoint, we have to distinguish acceleration and inflation, if possible, from other universal phenomena, if any. We have also to consider the astrophysical consequences of expansion, as opposed to its primordial origins and constants. These considerations are quite distinct from those with which we have been concerned in the present discussion, and I shall not address them until a subsequent occasion.

It is evident that locomotion is concerned fundamentally with actual movements, not merely with systems of movements. In this it differs from digestion, which, broadly speaking, is concerned with the cases in which all the processes which constitute one metabolic event can be treated as a single functional unit, or rather the processes which are sufficiently integral to the event of which they are components can be so treated. The principles which physiology seeks can, broadly speaking, be stated by treating such systems of processes as functional units. The principles which neurology seeks cannot be so stated, since the movements themselves are what interest the neurologist. This is one of the fundamental differences between digestion and locomotion; and to make it clear has been the main purpose of this inquiry.

One of the main purposes of these reflections is to give grounds for the belief that the distinction between volition and compulsion is not so fundamental as is commonly supposed. In the preceding analysis I dealt in outline with the psychological side of this problem. I attempted to show that what we call a free choice is not itself a sovereign act, but is a system of neural events analogous in their nature to reflexes, and in fact often including automatic impulses among their number. In this way the process by which decisions are generated is brought into relation with the process by which part, at least, of our bodily machinery is governed.

I will conclude with an attempt to give a more precise definition of the illusion of control. The manifestations of a complex system from different vantage points change partly according to intrinsic laws (the laws of emergent behavior, in the case of social organizations), partly according to the nature of the intervening medium--bureaucratic layers, ideological filters, technical interfaces, cognitive biases, etc. As we presume to understand more of the system, the effect of the intervening medium grows less apparent. In a generalized sense, all the intrinsic laws of change of manifestation may be called "laws of partial comprehension." Given any manifestation of a system, we can construct hypothetically a certain system of manifestations to which the manifestation in question would belong if the laws of partial comprehension alone were concerned. If we construct this hypothetical system for each manifestation of the system in turn, the system corresponding to a given manifestation x will be independent of any distortion due to the medium beyond x, and will only embody such distortion as is due to the medium between x and the system's core mechanisms.
