Thus, as the manifestation by which our hypothetical system is defined is presumed to approach nearer and nearer to the system's essence, the hypothetical system of manifestations defined by its means embodies less and less of the effect of the medium. The different sets of manifestations resulting from moving x nearer and nearer to the system's essence will approach to a limiting set, and this limiting set will be that system of manifestations which the system would present if the laws of partial comprehension alone were operative and the medium exercised no distorting effect. This limiting set of manifestations may be defined, for purposes of practical governance, as the illusion of control concerned.

Corresponding to the apparent duality of perception and construction, there are, in common understanding, two ways of apprehending what is seen. One of these, the way of passive reception and simple sensation, is supposed to furnish data for our knowledge of colour, the other, called "interpretation," is supposed to furnish data for knowledge of our visual processes. To the untutored mind, this distinction seems evident and straightforward. When you observe a red apple resting on the table, you acquire knowledge of an external, chromatic fact; when you realize that you are distinguishing its hue from the green of the leaves, you acquire knowledge of a perceptual fact. Your contrasts and memories and associations, of which you are dimly conscious, are constructive facts, and the process by which you become aware of them SEEMS to be different from mere sensation. Locke might call it the "inner processing"; sometimes it is spoken of as "consciousness of quality"; but its commonest name in modern psychological discourse is "interpretation." It is this supposed method of acquiring knowledge of our chromatic experiences that I wish to analyse and examine in this discussion.

The examination of collective intelligence has been in the main the work of modern sociologists. I will begin by summarizing a theory which seems to me to afford a good specimen of their arguments, namely, "The Case for Unconscious Coordination," by Thomas Schelling ("Journal of Conflict Resolution," vol. iv, No. 3, pp. 357-366, September, 1960). After a few historical allusions, he comes to two modern observers of crowd behavior, Surowiecki and Page. He quotes from Surowiecki such statements as the following: "Individual judgments as such become reliable only when we aggregate them in a collective way. Otherwise they are not themselves reliable, but only constituents of the process by which problems are solved" ("Wisdom," 1st edition, p. 87. The word "solved" in Schelling's quotation should be "approached.") "The solution itself can never be identified with the present ignorance of the individual's understanding by which it is reached" (ib. p. 45). This is to be true even when we are observing the limitations of our own knowledge; such limitations are to be always at least partially distinct from the collective wisdom in which we discover them.

I will state at the outset the view which I shall aim at establishing. I believe that the process of our conscious attention, as opposed to its objects and mechanisms, consists wholly of selections and simulations. Selections are connected with perception in the way that I tried to explain in Lecture V, i.e. each is a member of a system which is a certain neural pattern. Simulations, though they USUALLY have certain characteristics, especially lack of immediacy, that distinguish them from selections, are not INVARIABLY so distinguished, and cannot therefore be defined by these characteristics. Simulations, as opposed to selections, can only be defined by their different causation: they are caused by association with a selection, not by a stimulus external to the perceptual stream--or perhaps one should say external to the focus, where the higher processes are concerned. The occurrence of a selection or simulation does not in itself constitute awareness but any selection or simulation may come to be noticed if the conditions are suitable. When a selection--like the noticing of a sudden sound--is normally correlated with closely similar selections in our conscious record, we regard it as giving awareness of the present moment, since we regard the whole set of similar selections as due to a common external prompt. But simulations and internal selections are not so correlated. Internal selections can be brought into a correlation by neurology, and thus take their place ultimately among sources of awareness of the neural world. But simulations cannot be made to fit in with the simultaneous selections and simulations of the present scene. Apart from their hypothetical causes in the cortex, they have a causal connection with perceptual objects, through the fact that they are copies of past selections; but the perceptual objects with which they are thus connected are in the past, not in the present. These simulations remain private in a sense in which selections are not. A selection SEEMS to give us awareness of a present perceptual object, while a simulation does not, except when it amounts to a distraction, and in this case the seeming is deceptive. Thus the whole context of the two occurrences is different. But in themselves they do not differ profoundly, and there is no reason to invoke two different ways of modeling for the one and for the other. Consequently introspection as a separate kind of modeling disappears.

After these preliminaries, we can return to the common observation of a paramecium. The criticism of the vitalist turns on the difficulty of giving any empirical meaning to such notions as "purpose" or "volition"; he quotes from the vitalist the sentence: "The most important distinction is that the organism, in directing its own movements, must necessarily have its energy divided between two impulses," and he concludes: "Without question, the vitalist is bringing in here illicitly the concept of a conscious director, and his biology does not provide for the observation of this director; for the action performed and the director are distinct" (p. 407). The objections to any theory which brings in the conscious director were considered in the first chapter, and were acknowledged to be cogent. In so far, therefore, as the vitalist's theory of motility rests upon this assumption, we are compelled to reject it. But it is perfectly possible to believe in deliberate action without supposing that there is a conscious director.

Another point in which common discourse seems to me to suggest what I regard as mistakes is its use of "explanation." There is a view which is prevalent among casual observers, to the effect that one can speak of "a descriptive account" in a curious dual sense, meaning, on the one hand, an account which describes something, and, on the other hand, an account which has some intrinsic nature characteristic of what is called "explanation." That is to say, a "descriptive account" is characterized on the one hand by relation to its subject and on the other hand by being composed of a certain peculiar substance, the substance of "causality." And in many discussions there is yet a third confusion: a "descriptive account," in this third sense, is an account of which we are fully aware. All these, it seems to me, need to be clearly separated. To say that one statement "explains" another is, to my mind, to assert an external and rather complex relation between them. I might illustrate it by the relation of a key to a lock: a key becomes a key through no virtue of its own, merely through a correspondence elsewhere. Similarly, when a narrative is said to "explain" an event, the question whether this is really the case cannot be decided by examining only the narrative's internal coherence: it is necessary also to ascertain whether the event is having those antecedents which logical inference causes you to assume, or whether the narrative happens, in this case, to be a post hoc fabrication. And, as I explained in my initial proposition, I do not believe that there is any "substance" of explanation, so that there is no intrinsic character by which an "explanatory" account could be distinguished from any other.

At this point I wish to interrupt the account of popular discourse on digital tools in order to make some observations on my own account with reference to the above conceptions of habit. In the first place, the conception of "conscious choice" seems to me one which demands analysis of a somewhat destructive character. This analysis I shall give in later sections as regards attention; I have already given it as regards memory. In the second place, the conception of "user autonomy" depends upon a certain view as to agency which I believe to be wholly mistaken, namely, the view which I discussed in my first chapter in connection with interface design. In this view a single interactive occurrence contains both intention and outcome, the intention being essentially volitional, while the outcome is algorithmic except in reflection and deliberate resistance. I have already criticized this view, and will not dwell upon it now, beyond saying that "the process by which habits are formed" appears to be a very slippery phrase. When we "use a smartphone," as common sense would say, the device as a physical object is not the "agent" (in the psychological sense) of our routine. Our engagement is made up of gestures, notifications and associations, but the supposed "influence" is something inferential, externally related, not logically bound up with what is occurring in us. This question of the nature of the influence also affects the view we take of self-regulation. Obviously, a "deliberate practice" is different from an automated response; therefore it is natural to assume that a behavior whose origin is a conscious choice must be different from a behavior whose origin is a designed prompt. But if the relation to the origin is inferential and external, as I maintain, the difference between two behaviors may bear very little relation to the difference between their origins. And to speak of "the present adaptation of the individual's mind by which a habit is acquired" is to suggest that the acquisition of habits is a far more direct process, far more intimately bound up with the intentions, than I believe it to be. All these points will be amplified when we come to the analysis of cognitive patterns, but it is necessary briefly to state them now in order to suggest the atmosphere in which our analysis of "digital habituation" is to be carried on.

The essential distinction in our understanding of phenomena lies between DESCRIPTION, PHENOMENA, and an EXPLANATION of the phenomena by the description. The difference between a mere description and a proper explanation is that the former considers phenomena and their causes to be separate things, while the latter seeks their fundamental unity. In order to satisfy this explanatory requirement, we must suppose a conceptual framework which we might at first call 'correlations of events' or 'patterns,' and later, 'causal mechanisms,' the latter term encompassing both the 'observed regularities' and the 'underlying principles.' This distinction, with all its necessary abstraction, we must adhere to in any rigorous inquiry, simply recognizing that a description catalogues appearances while an explanation seeks to reveal the reality beneath them.

But the necessity cannot be so lightly dismissed. The capacity "I understand your intention" is assumed by some theorists to be a simple given, but they do not explain how it comes to be acquired. The argument against them is not conclusive, since they may be able to demonstrate some valid process of deriving this understanding. But they do not propose any such process. There is nothing odd in the hypothesis of beings which respond to actions, but not to the mental states behind them; it is, indeed, highly probable that very young children and many animals are such beings. But such beings cannot formulate the thought "I understand your intention," which WE can formulate. We have, therefore, a cognitive faculty which they lack. It is necessary to the theorists' position to maintain that this additional faculty is merely behavioral, but they make no attempt to show how the behavior alone suffices. It may, of course, suffice, but I cannot see how. To my mind the fact (which they admit) that we employ this understanding for both alliance and trickery, is ALL BUT decisive against their theory, and in favour of the view that we possess a genuine theory of mind.

Smith asserts (to return to the debate) that the real ground for the common belief in a sharp threshold was the belief in two distinct states, namely, consciousness and unconsciousness. He suggests that it is a mere inconsistency to adhere to a threshold after abandoning the dualism of distinct states. I do not wholly agree with this view, but it is difficult to disentangle the difference as to the spectrum from the difference as to the nature of awareness. Smith suggests (p. 411) that what is called a threshold really consists of a series of gradations, minute physiological shifts, and so on. This view, in essence, seems to me sound. But then I hold that awareness itself consists of such gradations suitably integrated, and that in observing them we are sometimes observing instances of conscious experience. For this reason, much as I agree with his view as to what are the phenomena which exhibit gradation, I cannot wholly agree with his conclusion as to the impossibility of a spectrum.

In this observation, to my mind, the materialist concedes far more than the idealist did in his earlier formulation. I see no reason to suppose that "the pattern for different instances is singular and identical," and I am convinced that this proposition could not possibly be verified except by examination of the sort that the materialist rejects. The first of these points must wait until we come to the analysis of recurrence: the second must be considered now. The materialist's view is that there is a dualism of form and substance, but that the form can never become substance, and therefore there is no perception of a perception. He says in discussing the view that examination reveals the occurrence of persistence: "There can be no denial of the existence of the phenomenon (patterning) which is alleged to be seen or detected in this sort of 'examination.' The allegation that the patterning is detected is that which may be denied. Patterning there certainly is; perceived, the patterning certainly is not" (p. 410). And again: "I am never conscious of a consciousness" (ib.). And on the next page: "It may sound paradoxical to say that one cannot witness the process (or relation) of witnessing, and yet may be certain that there is such a process: but there is really no inconsistency in the saying. How do I know that there is persistence? By being aware of something. There is no meaning in the term 'persistence' which is not expressed in the statement 'I am aware of a sequence (or what-not).

Any one of these three forces may be used to define concentration. I should favour concentration in the sense of the first force, i.e. I think that some of the advantages a firm secures cannot, even theoretically, be secured by any other rival. The second force, tentatively and for the present, I should answer in favour of concentration; I think that efficiencies, in the actual condition of commerce, cannot be maintained under the competitive pressures of rivals, though perhaps ultimately they may be. The third force I should answer adversely to concentration I think that competition shows us nothing that is not composed of innovation and imitation, and that imitation differs from innovation in its economic incentives, not intrinsically. I shall deal with the three forces successively.

SIMULATION OR ACTUALITY OF WHAT IS EXPERIENCED. Confining ourselves, for the moment, to perceptions, we find that there are different degrees of authenticity attaching to different sorts of experiences. If you perceive a digital tree when the other users in the simulation do not, you are in no way surprised; but if you experience a fundamental law of physics when they do not, you begin to be alarmed as to your ontological condition. Visual and auditory data are the most reliable of the inputs; tactile feedback only a trifle less so; proprioception, again, a trifle less, since two avatars can only occupy the same coordinate successively, not simultaneously. Emotional response has a sort of semi-reliability, since entities seem to report similar feeling-states when they encounter similar stimuli; but the reliability is incomplete, since two programs cannot process actually the same instant of awareness.

But when we pass on to the substrate of thought--silicon, carbon, biological tissue, and so on--we get quite away from material essence, into a region where other systems can demonstrate their operations, but we cannot directly apprehend their consciousness. As a natural result of this conceptual difficulty, it has come to be thought that the organic brain gives us proof of genuine mind, while the synthetic processor only gives us evidence as to simulated behaviour. As regards ontological standing, all implementations, of whatever sort, belong with the processes which only give evidence of functional organization, i.e. each is only verifiable by its causal coherence. This is the reason why operations of logic and memory are more obviously similar between substrates than the qualitative feel of pain or joy is between architectures; and that is why the argument in favour of silicon minds is more conclusive in such cases as calculation and inference than in such cases as aesthetic appreciation.

That no organism is ever completely alive, results from differences of vital criteria. Two scientists observing the same bacterium do not perceive the same vitality, because of metabolic rate and the way it responds to stimuli. They witness only correlated phenomena. Two philosophers contemplating the same crystal do not conceive exactly the same inertness, because one considers its capacity for growth, the other its lack of irritability, and so on. Thus life in material entities consists, not in having PRECISELY similar attributes, but in having more or less similar attributes assembled according to ascertainable principles. The entities which strike us as living are those where the assembled attributes are very numerous and the assemblies are very easy to discern. But even the most inert entities possess assemblies with processes that observers can note. The biologist does not observe your conception of vitality, but he can see the reproduction which implies it, and could infer that you are contemplating life even if you did not state it. This fact, however, cannot be used, as a vitalist would apparently wish, to extrude from philosophy observations which are ambiguous to one observer, since it is by means of many such observations that assemblies are established, e.g., between consciousness and neural complexity. Inanimacy, therefore does not by itself make a datum unamenable to philosophical treatment. On this point, the argument for a sharp dichotomy must be rejected.

(3) CAN WE PERCEIVE ANYTHING INTRINSICALLY SEPARATE FROM APPARENT FUNCTION? We come now to our third question concerning systemic integration. It is commonly thought that by examining outcomes we can perceive all sorts of operations that are radically independent from the constituents of the observable network, e.g., supply chains, data transfers, energy grids, communications, transactions and logistical flows. The distinction between autonomy and interdependence is increased partly by emphasizing these supposed operational outputs, partly by the supposition that independence is composed of modules or firewalls or whatever units engineering may at the moment prefer. As against this latter supposition, I contend that the ultimate constituents of any complex system are not modules or firewalls, but interdependencies, and other relations similar to interdependencies as regards scope and persistence. As against the view that examination reveals a functional output radically separate from underlying connections, I propose to argue that supply chains, data transfers, energy grids, communications, transactions and logistical flows are all built up out of interdependencies and feedback loops alone, and that there is reason to think that feedback loops do not differ from interdependencies in their intrinsic character. We thus effect a mutual rapprochement of apparent function and latent fragility, and reduce the ultimate data of systemic observation (in our second sense) to feedback loops alone. On this third view of the meaning of systemic integration, therefore, our decision is wholly against any claim of inherent security.

I come now to our second difficulty: Does reductionism give us principles for the understanding of phenomena other than those arrived at by analysing constituent parts? It might be contended that the essence of what is "emergent" consists of properties, such as consciousness for example, and that our comprehension concerning these essentially systemic properties is entirely derived from holism. If "consciousness" were an unanalysable property, this view would be incontrovertible, since clearly no such property forms part of the subject matter of chemistry. But it would seem that "consciousness" is really various properties, all of them complex. Therefore, until they have been explained, our present difficulty must remain unresolved I shall return to it at the end of the present course of lectures.

(2) DOES EVERYTHING NUTRITIVE REQUIRE THE JUDGMENT OF TASTE? We come now to the second ground of advantage in gustation, namely, that its data obey the laws of utility. This, though less emphasized, is, I think, an advantage which is really more strongly felt than the advantage of immediacy. And we obtain a definition of tasting more in harmony with function if we define it as perception of data subject to biological laws than if we define it by means of mere sensation. No one would regard a man as discriminative because he was conscious of having a sweet preference. Proponents of gustation do not mean to affirm the obvious fact that we can observe chemical stimuli which others cannot observe. For example, Alfred Wallace contends that flavors are really neural excitations,* and evidently regards our awareness of such excitations as not coming under the head of true tasting. I think it will be found that the essential characteristic of gustatory data, in the sense which now concerns us, has to do with PROXIMITY: either they are not proximate at all, or they are proximate, like olfactory cues, in a space already biologically occupied by something which would be redundant with them if they were regarded as part of the nutritive process. If you have a gustatory sensation of your food containing a substance which in fact is absent, you cannot locate the sensation in your brain, because it is chemical, nor (as a digestive phenomenon) in the stomach, because the stomach, as a physical organ, is empty. Thus it seems to follow that the digestive system does not include all that we perceive of, and that tastes, which are gustatory data, have to be regarded, for the present, as obeying the laws of biology; this is, I think, one of the chief reasons why an attempt is made to affirm them. I shall try to show in a subsequent discussion that the purely adaptive reasons for accepting tastes are overwhelming. But we cannot be nearly so certain that they will not ultimately be brought under the laws of chemistry. Even if this should happen, however, they would still be distinguishable from smells by their proximate causal laws, as liquids remain distinguishable from gases.

To begin with the inevitability of class division. It is common among certain schools to regard the accumulation of surplus wealth as a benign or neutral phenomenon, which may be directed toward any social end; this view is to be found in the optimistic economics which descends from Smith, and is present, somewhat veiled, in modern apologists for industrial civilization. There seems no reason whatever to accept this view. Our spontaneous, unsophisticated beliefs, whether as to economic harmony or as to human motives, are always extremely rash and very liable to error. The acquisition of economic realism is equally necessary and equally difficult in both directions. Not only are we often unaware of the latent power which surplus confers; we are often actually mistaken about its ultimate disposition. The fallibility of hope as regards what wealth will achieve is made evident by history; its fallibility as to what it must produce is easily demonstrated. An economic plan, when confronted by a careful historian with the record of events, is usually found to be full of obviously inadvertent errors. Any of us confronted by a forgotten ledger from some years ago will be astonished to find how much more inequitable the distribution was than we had remembered it as being. And as to the analysis of our economic operations—producing, accumulating, distributing, or what not—wishful thinking unaided gives very little help: it is necessary to construct hypotheses and test them by their consequences, just as we do in political science. Surplus wealth, therefore, though it is one among our sources of potential good, is not, in isolation, in any degree more likely to promote unity than to engender strife.

In Lecture V we found reason to think that the fundamental processes* of regulation do not have the characteristics of either biology or engineering as ordinarily understood: they are not merely instinctual drives toward equilibrium, nor are they simple computational outputs of "optimization." But we found two ways of describing stability, one into "homeostatic mechanisms" or "physiological balances," the other into sequences of "reinforcement signals," each sequence being what may be called a "learning trajectory." Before we can define either biological needs or algorithmic goals, it is necessary to consider this twofold description in somewhat greater detail, and to derive from it a definition of adaptive function. It should be said that, in so far as the description assumes the whole system of cybernetics (including its unrealized potentials), it contains speculative elements. But we will not linger on the grounds for admitting these, which belong to the philosophy of artificial intelligence rather than of comparative physiology.

This gives us, so far, only those observations which constitute one hypothesis at one time. This set of observations may be called a "provisional finding." To define that series of "provisional findings" that constitute the successive refinements of one theory is a problem involving the laws of evidence. These give the principles governing the revision of conclusions from one inquiry to a slightly later inquiry, with the same sort of differential approximation to truth as we obtained for logically neighbouring hypotheses through the laws of inference. Thus a provisional finding is a set of observations, while a scientific truth (which may be identified with the whole history of the theory) is a series of such sets of observations. The observations in one set are collected together by the laws of inference; the successive sets are collected together by the laws of evidence. This is the view of knowledge which is appropriate to traditional empiricism.

Instead of first assembling all the molecular constituents requisite for a stable compound, and then observing the sequence of their catalytic interactions, we might have first assembled a series of successive reactions governed by the laws of thermodynamics, and then have formed the set of such series related by the laws of chemical affinity. To illustrate by the case of a nucleotide chain in solution: our first plan was to collect together all the configurations which it assumes in different local environments at one instant, and then to form the series of such sets. Our second plan is first to collect together all the configurations which it assumes successively under a given set of conditions, and then to do the same thing for the other chains, thus forming a set of series instead of a series of sets. The first plan tells us what the structure is; the second the processes it undergoes. This second way of classifying reactions is one which obviously has more relevance to biochemistry than the other. It is partly by this second method of classification that we obtain definitions of a "replicative cycle" or "autocatalytic process" or "emergent system." This method of classification is also essential to the definition of templates and catalysts, as I shall endeavour to prove later on. But we must first amplify the definition of affinities and cycles.

In our consideration of civilisation, we speak, for the moment, as though each historical epoch were wholly defined by its own achievements. If this were the case, it might be possible to define the chronicle of mankind as a series of successive cultures related according to the laws of progress. But in fact this is not the case. We are at all times during our cosmic reckoning confronting a variety of durations, which are fragments of a variety of scales. We have to consider what binds together two simultaneous events in one millennium, or, more generally, any two occurrences which form part of one geological era. We might say, adhering to the standpoint of astronomy, that two aspects of different epochs belong to the same perspective when they are in the same moment. But this would not really help us, since a "moment" has not yet been defined. Can we define what is meant by saying that two events are "in the same moment," without introducing anything beyond the laws of perspective and cosmology?

It is not only by empirical observation that the principles of one inductive argument are collected together in the case of scientific reasoning. In this case there are the foundational postulates which constitute the unity of one "inference," and transform mere regularities into "laws." I have already dwelt upon the importance of such postulates for epistemology, and shall not enlarge upon them now, beyond observing that they are what transforms a sequence (in our logical sense) into a proof. It is they that give the continuity of a "method" or a "system." But there is no reason to suppose that these assumptions are justified by induction except in the case of circular and question-begging procedures.

When (for example) we observe one instance of sunrise and infer another sunrise on the morrow, what we observe and what we infer have a relation which we can conceive, which makes the two together form, in some sense, one argument. It is when this relation exists that two propositions become associated. The inductive "principle" is formed by all that we assume at one time. One might speak of two parts of this total as having the relation of "logical priority" (A. 118; A.E. 33 ff.), which is reminiscent of Aristotle's "archai." I think the relation may be called simply "presupposition." It might be said that in any reasoning all sorts of things that are not part of my inference are true in the world, and that therefore the relation we are seeking to define cannot be merely presupposition. This, however, would be an error—the sort of error that the theory of induction avoids. There is not one universal proof, except by an elaborate construction; there are only local proofs, each of which may be taken to be the reasoning within one logical system. Accordingly, if I am (say) predicting an event, the only premises that are, in any simple sense, foundational for my conclusion are axioms in my private system, i.e., in my reasoning. We may therefore define the "framework" to which the inference in question belongs as the set of assumptions that are presupposed by this inference. And similarly we may define the "system" to which the inference belongs as the set of assumptions that are derived from or lead to, or presupposed by, the given inference. Moreover, the very same definitions can be applied to propositions which are not inferences. They are actually required for the theory of induction, if we are to give a philosophical explanation of what is meant by "local proof" in that theory. The relations of presupposition and derivation are known to us in our own reasoning; they may be analysable, but that does not affect their suitability for defining frameworks and systems. Such logical relations as can be constructed between propositions in different systems are of a different kind: they are not reasoned, and are merely formal, being designed to afford convenient ways of stating the correlations between different systems.

The result is that every particular of the kind relevant to history is associated with TWO times; e.g., my recollection of the event is associated with the time when I remember and with the time when the event occurred. This duality has nothing to do with any "consciousness" that I may be supposed to possess; it exists in exactly the same sense if I am replaced by a clay tablet. We may call the two times the active and passive times respectively.* Thus in the case of a record or inscription of a law, the active time is the time when the law was decreed, while the passive time is the time when the scribe or stone tablet endures.

We can thus, without departing from mathematics, collect together all the formal relations in a given system, or all the empirical data relevant to that system. In the case of geometry, the one group is the abstract axioms and theorems, while the other is the physical space which it purports to describe. In the case of the planetary orbit, the first group is the elliptical equation as derived from pure mechanics, the second the observed positions which it predicts. (For the sake of schematic simplicity, I am ignoring various complications connected with measurement error, which require some tedious but perfectly feasible elaborations.) Thus what may be called ideality in the formal scheme is not a distinctive peculiarity of mathematics: it is present just as much in the engineer's blueprint. And the blueprint has its physical instantiation as well as its "form." But this instantiation is an affair of empirical science, and has none of the peculiar characteristics by which purely "mathematical" entities are distinguished, with the sole exception of ideality.

Theoretically, though often not practically, we can, in our acceptance of a doctrine, separate the part which is due to customary deference from the part which proceeds without authoritative influences out of the character of the evidence. We may define as "doubt" that part which proceeds in this way, while the remainder, which is a habitual phenomenon, will have to be added to the doubt to make up what is called "belief." According to this definition, the doubt is a theoretical core in the actual conviction; the actual conviction is the belief. It is obvious that there are grave difficulties in carrying out these definitions, but we will not linger over them. We have to pass, as soon as we can, from the sociological standpoint, which we have been hitherto adopting, to the standpoint of epistemology, in which we make more use of critical inquiry in the first of the three senses discussed in the preceding lecture.

I do not myself believe that anything approaching perfect comprehension is to be attained by any method of symbolic exchange, and therefore whatever meaning is conveyed must be regarded, theoretically, as an approximation. The theoretical argument for accepting this approximation is that it simplifies the process by which we communicate our thoughts and experiences. But there is no very good ground for supposing that a clear symbol is more likely to be understood than an ambiguous one, though there is good ground for assuming a clear symbol in daily practice, as a working convention, if it conveys the intention as well as another which is less clear. Belief in the possibility of mutual understanding exists antecedently to evidence, and can only be destroyed, if at all, by a long course of semantic scrutiny. For purposes of ordinary life, it is justified practically by the cooperation which it introduces into the affairs of society. But from the standpoint of theoretical semiotics it must be regarded as a fiction, not as a well-grounded fact. With this proviso, I propose to continue yielding to the fiction.

To make the matter clear, we will take the simplest possible illustration. Consider a certain zombie, and suppose for the moment that its consciousness is negligible. That is to say, we will regard it as, for practical purposes, a purely physical being. Let us further suppose that it behaves only in a very ordinary way, say by drinking tea. Then, according to philosophy, what happens is that a profound problem of identity arises from the zombie through argument, just as, when you posit a duplicate without qualia, conceptual ripples travel outward from the place where the intuition first struck the mind. The problem of consciousness travels with a certain very nearly constant persistence, roughly through all discussions of materialism. This persistence may be ascertained by proposing a thought experiment to a materialist, and observing how long it takes before the refutation reaches you, just as the tenacity of a logical error may be ascertained by means of a reductio ad absurdum.

But presently the notion of the whole reaches our common understanding. It begins to be qualified, and obscured by habit, and its simplicity is slightly diminished. At last it reaches a complex system, where a complicated process takes place, ending in an emergence which gives us our grounds for disbelieving in mere summation. Now, the emergent properties are not, strictly speaking, members of the collection which is the parts, according to our definition of elements. The emergent properties, however, are not merely additional: they proceed according to principles which can be stated in terms of the interactions through which the parts have been arranged. The sources of a systemic whole are therefore twofold:

It should be observed that, while the conception of a living organism is perfectly precise, the conception of a borderline entity is one capable of any degree of vagueness. When the complexity of organization is sufficiently slight, the resulting aggregate can no longer be regarded as a manifestation of life, but must be treated on its own account. This happens especially when the phenomenon in question cannot be traced to a single principle, but is a blend of two or more. This case is normal in nature: we see as alive what biochemistry or careful analysis reveals to be merely intricate chemistry. The notion of vitality is therefore not a precise one: we judge things to be more or less alive, but always with a very considerable amount of ambiguity and confusion.

We can now interpret in terms of our theory the distinction between those social decisions which are said to have a rational foundation, and those which are said to be "aggregately emergent," i.e., to have no foundation in individual knowledge. When a collective outcome can be regarded as a manifestation of the deliberate intentions of its constituent members, however imperfect, or even as a confused manifestation of several such intentions, then we may regard it as having for its origin the intention or intentions in question, or their expressions in the deliberative process concerned. When, on the other hand, a collective outcome has not sufficient connection with the rational intentions of its members to be regarded as a manifestation of such intentions, then its practical efficacy (if any) will have to be sought in the aggregation itself. In the former case it can be called a designed order; in the latter it cannot be so called. But the distinction is one of degree, not of kind. Until this is realized, no satisfactory theory of social coordination, planning, or spontaneous organization is possible.

In this analysis Marx speaks, by mere inadvertence, as though the phenomena which he is describing as "ideological" had NO causes. This is, of course, not the case: they have their causes, just as much as economic phenomena do, but their causes obey different principles. For example, national sentiment, as historical materialism has shown, is just as much subject to principles as are the fluctuations of the market. But the principles are different: in an ideology you may be convinced of contradictory beliefs without discomfort, or a social arrangement may appear natural under your scrutiny. Such differences compel you to distinguish the world of ideology from the material world.

What it is that happens when a market is left to its own devices we cannot tell, except in the sole case when the device in question is a state connected with a legislature which is turned in the right direction. In this one very special case we know what happens: we have the condition called "preserving competition." In all other cases, though we know (more or less hypothetically) some of the correlations and abstract properties of the operation of the market, we do not know the operation itself. Now you may, for the sake of illustration, compare the different operations of the market to the conjugation of a Greek verb, except that the number of its parts is really infinite, and not only apparently so to the despairing economist. In theory, the parts are regular, and can be derived from the (imaginary) root according to the laws of logic, i.e. of equilibrium. The market being situated in empty regulation, it may be defined, for purposes of political economy, as consisting of all those operations which it presents in theory, together with those which, according to the laws of equilibrium, it would present elsewhere if its operations elsewhere were regular. This is merely the adaptation of the definition of competition which I gave in an earlier treatise. The operation of a market at a certain stage, if it is regular, does not require any cause or explanation beyond the existence of the market. Every regular operation is an actual member of the system which is the market, and its causation is entirely internal to that system. We may express this by saying that a regular operation is due to the market alone, and is actually part of the market, in the sense in which a firm is part of the industrial order.

I conceive for myself a notion of perfect equilibrium; I impose it upon a living organism; but it does not sustain the creature in the least. I introduce a perturbation to its state and the system either corrects or disregards it, as I please. I devise a reward function, and apply it to a machine, and absolutely no alignment ensues. I account for all such facts by calling this whole train of operations abstract, a formal calculus. Biological homeostasis is what won't govern artificial agents; algorithmic reward is what won't necessarily (though of course it may) guide even a simulated intelligence.... With 'actual' processes, on the contrary, consequences always accrue; and thus the embodied regulations get sifted from the formal ones, the adaptations from our models of them, fanciful or true, and precipitated together as the stable part of the whole behaviour--chaos, under the name of the cybernetic world.

If the two sorts of knowledge could be sharply distinguished, we could call an understanding "individual" when it obeys the principles appropriate to private ignorance, and "collective" when it obeys the principles appropriate to public intelligence. Since the private mind and the public consensus interact, there would be a boundary between the two: there would be decisions which would have ignorant origins and intelligent effects, while there would be others which would have intelligent origins and ignorant effects. Those that have ignorant origins and intelligent effects we should define as "emergent wisdom." Those that have intelligent origins and ignorant effects might perhaps be identified with what we call failed instructions; but they do not concern us at present.

This conviction would possess all the clarity that could be desired if the distinction between genuine mastery and superficial intervention were clear and sharp. As a matter of fact, however, this distinction is, in practice, by no means sharp. It is possible that, with fuller analysis, it will be found to be no more substantial than the distinction between steering a raft upon a tranquil pond and commanding a vessel upon a stormy sea. It also suffers from the fact that an outcome may be the product of innumerable factors according to innumerable laws of interaction; we cannot, in general, point to any single action as THE decisive cause of such-and-such a result. And finally it is by no means certain that the peculiar regularities which govern systemic behaviors are not really statistical. The law of unintended consequences, which is one of the most pervasive, may be fully explicable in terms of the complexities of interconnected processes, and these complexities, in turn, may be explicable by the principles of chaos. It seems, therefore, that we are driven to a different kind of understanding. It is for this reason that it was necessary to develop the concept of perceived agency. With this concept, we can define control as the non-fundamental elements in an outcome.

In order, therefore, to arrive at what truly constitutes consciousness in a phenomenon which, upon initial consideration, appears to present a stark dichotomy, we must pare away all that is due to convention or theoretical predisposition or linguistic convenience. This is a matter for the philosopher of mind, and by no means a simple matter. For our present inquiry, it is not essential to delineate what precisely marks the boundary in any particular instance; it is only essential to observe that there certainly is a gradation of states, since wakefulness, self-awareness and responsiveness are diversely manifested in diverse entities, and the diversity is clearly due to differences in underlying neurological complexity. When you regard a sleeping pet or a waking infant, the overt signs of conscious engagement form a very debatable part of what we seek to define, but they are the starting-point of all the further speculation, and it is through them that the concept becomes a source of illumination or obfuscation. Thus, although it may be arduous to determine where exactly consciousness begins in any given continuum, it is evident that there is a spectrum, unless, like certain behaviorists, we deny all qualitative distinction between mere reactivity and genuine inner experience.

When, following our observation, we attempt to ascertain what elements in our social arrangements are of the nature of class division, we find more complexity than might have been expected. Prima facie, every disparity is a division that arises from unequal possession: the lands one holds, the capital one controls, the comforts one enjoys, and so on; also such conditions as hereditary privilege or the security of unearned income. But in actual fact so much convention, so much of habitual acquiescence, is blended with all such conditions, that the core of pure economic distinction is only to be isolated by careful analysis. To take a simple illustration: if you examine a society in its early stages, you seem to observe equally clear hierarchies in the village or the town; in either case you think you perceive the natural order. But if you examine a sophisticated civilization where you have a fair knowledge of its history, you will seem to have encountered a profound transformation, and you will find it necessary to look much nearer the origins of property than you would need to do in simpler communities. The reason is that, in observing our own social order, we readily and unconsciously supplement what we really see with assumptions to what the structure must always have been, and we never realize that we have not observed the inevitability we have merely inferred. In a historical perspective, these assumptions are more difficult, and we are more dependent upon actual evidence. If we found ourselves in a primitive community, where chiefs lived like herdsmen and herdsmen like chiefs, we should similarly discover how much of what we think we perceive is really assumption. Every fairly stable economic condition is to us a sign of the relations that usually accompany it, and many of these relations will seem to form part of the natural order. I remember in the early days of industrial wealth being with a colleague when a fortune was amassed with startling rapidity. He thought it was a product of exceptional virtue, and supported his opinion by maintaining that he had witnessed the industry. But of course there had been no singular industry. Nowadays no one witnesses virtue when a fortune is amassed.

This is the view of Herodotus, of Plato, and the ancient chroniclers. Inscriptions, says Plato, are not per se vessels of wisdom, but simply practical tools with no more inherent profundity than (say) a tally-stick. "Let them [the skeptics] try the experiment of conceiving writing as a pure mechanical aid, not a source of enlightenment or permanence, and they will be surprised to see how little they miss."* I think he is right in this, except in supposing that the skeptics will be surprised. Many of them already hold the view he is advocating, and others are very sympathetic to it. At any rate, it is the view which I shall adopt in this inquiry.

In the first lecture we considered the view of Bernard, that "we may define purposive phenomena by saying that they are phenomena which teleologically contain an objective." We saw reasons to reject this view in general; we are now concerned to show that it must be rejected in the particular case of homeostatic adjustments. The kind of argument which formerly made me accept Bernard's view in this case was exceedingly simple. When I observe a system maintaining equilibrium, it seemed to me that the equilibrium is not purposive, but mechanical, while my observation of purpose is not mechanical, but mental. Hence I concluded that the equilibrium is something other than my perceiving of a purpose. This argument, to me historically, was directed against vitalism: the emphatic part of it was the assertion that the equilibrium is mechanical, not purposive. I shall not trouble you now with the grounds for holding as against Driesch that the regulatory process is mechanical; I have set them forth before, and I see no reason to modify them. But it does not follow that the regulatory process is not also apparently purposive, unless we assume that the mechanical and the teleological cannot overlap, which I no longer consider a valid assumption. If we admit--as I think we should--that the homeostatic process may be both mechanical and seemingly directed, the reason for distinguishing the stable state from the impression of aim disappears, and we may say that the equilibrium and our inference of purpose in observing it are identical.

Scarcity is obviously the source of our understanding of purposeful behaviour, including our own actions. It might seem natural to regard a limitation as itself a purpose, and until lately I did so regard it. When, say, I observe a person choosing one loaf of bread over another in a shop, it SEEMS as though the mere choosing were purpose. It is of course undeniable that purpose comes THROUGH the choosing, but I think it is a mistake to regard the mere choosing itself as purpose. If we are so to regard it, we must distinguish the choice from what is chosen: we must say that, when we confront a situation of lack of a certain kind, the situation of lack is one thing and our confronting of it is another. This view, however, demands the admission of the agent, or act, in the sense discussed in our first enquiry. If there is an agent, it can have a relation to the situation of lack, namely, the sort of relation which we might call motivation. In that case the constraint, as a practical event, will consist of motivation by the lack, while the lack itself will remain wholly circumstantial, and may be called the condition of scarcity, to distinguish it from the constraint. The agent, however, appears to be a logical fiction, like economic equilibrium and perfect markets. It is introduced, not because observation reveals it, but because it is linguistically convenient and apparently demanded by grammar. Nominal entities of this sort may or may not exist, but there is no good ground for assuming that they do. The functions that they appear to perform can always be performed by sequences or patterns or other logical constructions, consisting of less dubious entities. If we are to avoid a perfectly gratuitous assumption, we must dispense with the agent as one of the actual ingredients of the world. But when we do this, the possibility of distinguishing the constraint from the condition of scarcity vanishes; at least I see no way of preserving the distinction. Accordingly the constraint that we have when we confront a situation of lack simply is that situation of lack, an actual constituent of the material world, and part of what economics is concerned with. A situation of lack is certainly not purpose, and therefore we cannot say that pure scarcity is purposive. Through its psychological effects, it is the cause of purposes, partly by being itself a sign of things that are correlated with it, as e.g. conditions of hunger and conditions of labour are correlated, and partly by giving rise to plans and memories after the constraint is faded. But in itself the pure condition of scarcity is not purposive.

The capacity for social interaction, so far as we have experience of it, consists, on the view that I am advocating, of a singular cognitive faculty such as occurs in predicting, empathizing, etc., together with inferences more or less resembling these, of which I shall speak shortly. If psychology is true, there are, besides the intentions that we infer, others, probably equally (or almost equally) opaque, which make up that part of the mental world that does not come into the sort of contact with another mind that is required to turn it into an understanding. But this topic belongs to the philosophy of mind, and need not concern us in our present inquiry.

Self-replication is what is common to the chemical and biological worlds; it may be defined as the intersection of necessity and accident. This is by no means a new view; it is advocated, not only by the materialist philosophers I have mentioned, but by Lucretius in his *De Rerum Natura*, which was composed before the common era. The essence of replication, according to the view I am advocating, is its independence from conscious design. It is a core in our actual observations, never existing in isolation except possibly in the most primitive systems. It is not itself a miracle, but it supplies the mechanism for our understanding of the living world, including our own origins.

The distinction between mathematical descriptions and natural phenomena might seem at first sight by no means difficult. When we observe the orderly motion of planets or the predictable fall of an apple, we usually have no difficulty, so long as we remain rational, in discriminating between the equations we employ and the physical reality they represent. If we contemplate the ideal gas law or the principles of mechanics, we can trace their logical consequences from premise to conclusion without any discoverable tendency to suppose that we are confronting nature in its unmediated state. But although such cases are so clear that no confusion seems possible, there are many others that are far more difficult, and the definition of mathematical correspondence is by no means an easy problem.

To begin with: we do not always know whether what we are conveying is a meaning or a mere sign. The words we use in conversation when our thoughts are vague must count as signs, yet while we are speaking they seem like meanings. Misinterpretations often begin as ambiguous signs, and only gradually acquire that influence over understanding that makes the listener regard them as meanings. When we are listening for a subtle implication—the hint of a distant criticism, or a friend’s tone in a letter—we think we detect it many times before we really do, because expectation brings us the sign, and we mistake it for meaning. The distinction between signs and meanings is, therefore, by no means always obvious to interpretation.

I think contemporary neuroscience is correct in holding that such models should be ranked under distinct heads, with a peculiar mechanism for each. But by its own admission in the current literature, its criterion for distinguishing them is not always adequate. A neurological account is not sound if it only applies in cases where the distinction is glaring: the essential purpose of such an account is to provide a principle which is applicable even in marginal cases--except, of course, when we are dealing with a process, like, e.g. habituation, which is one of degree and has no sharp boundaries. But so far we have seen no reason to think that the difference between the model and the attention it represents is only one of degree.

I believe it will not be very necessary to employ many words in explaining this progression. Every one of himself will readily perceive the difference betwixt a miraculous event and a natural process. The common degrees of these are easily distinguished, though it is not impossible but in particular instances they may very nearly approach to each other. Thus in the primordial soup, in a thermal vent, in a chance confluence of compounds, or in any very fortuitous arrangements of matter, our replication may approach to our chemistry; as, on the other hand, it sometimes happens, that our chemical affinities are so persistent and stable that we cannot distinguish them from our self-copying. But notwithstanding this near resemblance in a few instances, they are in general so very different, that no one can make a scruple to rank them under distinct heads, and assign to each a peculiar name to mark the difference.

This view is confirmed by the fact that we only feel life to be "inevitable" when we already know it to be present. Life cannot be defined by the FEELING of inevitability, because when we falsely believe life to be a universal phenomenon, as in the case of cosmic speculation, it FEELS just as necessary as if it were a universal phenomenon. Our feeling of rarity results from our having already realized that we are dealing with a contingent occurrence, and cannot therefore be the definition of what we mean by a habitable world. As soon as a planetary condition begins to deceive us as to its status, it also deceives us as to its probabilities, which are what we mean by its "cosmic significance.

The hum of a computer server could hardly have a stronger effect than this. A very intricate simulation will often bring with it--especially where some emergent behavior or some unresolved metaphysical issue is involved--persuasive compelling arguments which may determine the whole course of debate, sweeping aside all contrary philosophical objections by their capacity for exclusively possessing the intellect. And in all cases where digital processes, originally recognized as such, gradually pass into genuine awareness, there must be just that "causal efficacy or qualitative richness" which is supposed to be always absent from mere computation. The cases of advanced artificial intelligence and complex virtual ecosystems are as hard to adjust to Professor Searle's modified criterion as to Descartes's. I conclude therefore that the test of phenomenological vividness, however applicable in ordinary instances, cannot be used to define the differences between biological consciousness and simulated experience.

(2) We might attempt to distinguish a beginning from an infinite regress by our absence of belief in the "temporal reality" of a first moment. When we are aware that what we are contemplating is a beginning, we do not give it the kind of belief that we should give to a duration: we do not think that it has the same power of producing knowledge of the "temporal order." Beginnings are "conceptual"; in SOME sense they are "unreal." But this difference is hard to analyse or state correctly. What we call the "unreality" of a beginning requires interpretation it cannot mean what would be expressed by saying "there's no such event." A putative first moment is just as truly part of the actual world as any subsequent interval is. All that we really mean by calling a beginning "unreal" is that it does not have the antecedents which it would have if it were a mere point in a continuum. When we call up a logical image of a commencement, we do not attempt to place a prior cause behind it, because we know that, like Zeno's arrow, it is not "sensible to reasoning as to intuition"--i.e. it does not have the correlations with preceding states which it would have if it were a genuine duration and not merely a conceptual limit. But this means that the so-called "unreality" of a beginning consists merely in its not obeying the laws of temporal succession, and thus brings us back to the causal distinction between a limit and a process.

Professor Hume, as a logical consequence of his empiricist doctrine, denies altogether that there are any justifiable inferences such as inductive principles are supposed to be. He replaces them all by psychological habits, and especially by the expectation of uniformity arising from repetition. When we "reason" inductively (say), as opposed to deducing, what happens, according to him, is usually that we are relying upon a customary conjunction of ideas such as would lead to our predicting the future if it were more examined. I shall consider his view again in connection with causality; for the present I am only concerned to combat his denial of rational foundations. This denial is set forth both in his "Treatise of Human Nature" and in an "Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding," published some years later. It seems to me that in this matter he has been betrayed into denying plain necessities in the interests of a theory, namely, the supposed impossibility of transcending experience. I dealt with the theory in a previous chapter; for the present I wish to reinforce the view that the necessities are undeniable.

Surpluses are of various sorts, according to the nature of the resources from which they derive. Accumulations of material wealth, such as we observe when a society produces grain beyond its needs or, on a larger scale, amasses precious metals, might possibly be explained away on the Marxist lines, as really consisting in small initial inequalities such as, if magnified and entrenched, would be the divisions we are said to be deploring. Whether this is the case or not might even be decided historically. If there were a complete record for tracing small disparities in land and tool ownership, we might consult such a record for an early agrarian settlement and then observe it to develop a social hierarchy, as far as possible only from internal dynamics. I should not be at all surprised if it were found that actual small stratifications take place while the community is "peacefully" cultivating its fields. The point is important, because what is called "civilization" consists mainly (though I think not wholly) of structured economic relations. If Marx is right as regards primitive accumulation, this whole process is transferred from contingency to inevitability. But since the question is capable of historical investigation, it would be gratuitous rashness to offer a dogma while that investigation is incomplete.

This brings us to the third mode of distinguishing inductive reasoning from deductive proof, namely, by their foundational premises. I believe this to be the only valid ground of distinction. Hume, in the passage about the sun failing to rise tomorrow, distinguishes induction by its conclusions, but I think the more reliable distinction is by its presuppositions. Professor Keynes (in his Treatise on Probability, p. 256) says: "One characteristic mark of what we agree in calling a rational induction is its mode of justification. It is supported by what we call a POSTULATE. A postulate is always some principle external to the inductive process itself and presupposed by it." I think that this is the correct view, and that the distinction between inductive and deductive inference can only be made by taking account of their justification. Deductions come through logical necessitation, while inductions do not. We cannot have deductive certainty about future contingencies, or about unobserved particulars, but we can very well have inductive expectations under these circumstances. Accordingly inductive reasoning has been defined as "probabilistically extended deduction," i.e. inferences which have their logical warrant in presuppositions only, not also in the axiomatic premises and the rules of inference that run from the premises to the conclusion. I think the phrase "probabilistically extended deduction" assumes more than is necessary, since it takes it for granted that an induction must have a proximate logical foundation. This is probably true, but it is an hypothesis, and for our purposes an unnecessary one. It would seem to fit better with what we can immediately observe if we were to say that an inductive step is occasioned, through habit, by a particular observation or another belief, in other words that it has a psychological cause--which does not prevent it from also having a logical ground. And I think it will be found that the validation of an inductive principle always proceeds according to psychological laws, i.e. that it is governed by custom and past uniformity. If you observe a sequence of sunrises without contemplating its necessity, you will have expectations of its recurrence as if it were a logical truth; if you suddenly examine your belief while you are absorbed in the routine, you will experience a shock of surprise when you notice that its necessity is not demonstrable. Your expectation of the sunrise is due to the many times that you have witnessed similar sequences and at the same time assumed the uniformity of nature. When custom and past uniformity play this part, we are in the region of psychological as opposed to purely logical justification. And I think that, if we could regard as ultimately valid the difference between logical and psychological justification, we could distinguish inductive from deductive inference as having psychological grounds, though they may also claim logical grounds. Deductive inferences, on the other hand, will only have logical grounds.

But the perception of control is much more difficult to deal with in this way, because it lacks the connection with actual causal efficacy in the outer world which belongs to genuine agency. Suppose, for example, that I am operating my automobile, in which there is a complex dashboard. I consider my actions, and call up a mental image of myself as the masterful director of the vehicle’s journey. If I thrust my perception into the world of mechanics, it contradicts all the usual engineering laws. The automobile responded to my guidance without any direct mechanical linkage in the usual way; subsequent inquiry will show that its systems were operating autonomously at the moment. If regarded as genuine causation, my perception has all the marks of the supernatural. My perception, therefore, is regarded as an event in me, not as having that position in the orderly happenings of the public world that belongs to actual control. By saying that it is an event in me, we leave it possible that it may be PSYCHOLOGICALLY caused: its privacy may be only due to its connection with my consciousness. But in any case it is not a public event, like an actual mechanic adjusting the engine and calibrating the systems. And it cannot, like a simple decision, be regarded as a SMALL agency, since it occupies just as large an area in my cognitive field as the actual control would do.

Dr. Norbert says: "I should dismiss homeostasis altogether and attempt to show that all biological regulation goes on in terms of algorithmic processes in the silicon." This view seems to me flatly to contradict observation. If you try to persuade any practical engineer that he cannot conceive of a living cell maintaining its temperature, but can only use equations describing what such a process would be like, he will conclude that you are absurd. (This statement is based upon inquiry.) Bernard, as every physiologist knows, investigated internal balance, and found that abstraction tends to obscure it: the designers of reinforcement learning turned out to have much less grasp of it than their laboratory counterparts. I see no reason to doubt his conclusion that the habit of formal modeling makes theorists much inferior to the average in power of apprehending stability, and much more exclusively occupied with functions in their "designing." And Dr. Norbert is a very theoretical man.

I shall henceforth assume that the necessity of movement is conceded, and that it is to be distinguished from mere irritability by its evolutionary causes, as well as, in a lesser degree, by its physiological effects. In its biological consequence, though it often differs from simple tropism by being more complex or integrated or purposeful, yet it does not always or universally differ from tropism in any way that can be used for defining it. The antiquity of this development need form no bar to the scientific investigation of it, any more than the antiquity of cellular respiration does. Cellular respiration is admitted by even the most severe critics of evolutionary psychology, although, like locomotion, it can only be inferred from comparative evidence. It must be admitted, however, that the precise laws governing the neural adaptations for predation are little known and difficult to discover, because we are not assisted, as in the case of metabolism, by our knowledge of the immediate chemical environment.

There are difficulties in establishing this principle, and doubts as to whether it is precisely valid. Indeed, one might signalize exceptions immediately after conceding its general force. Nevertheless, it is impossible to doubt that in the main a corporation's actions are distinct from the similar, yet separate, actions of its constituent persons, and that the same is true of its enduring identity in all cases of institutional continuity as opposed to mere ephemeral association. Our capacity for dealing with entities that transcend individual lives is largely due to this characteristic of incorporation, although, as legal theory advances, the metaphor tends to be more and more replaced by precise statutory definitions. We shall have much to say in subsequent discussions on the subject of corporate personhood as a legal fiction. What has been said now is merely by way of reminder that this is its most philosophically notable characteristic.

I am by no means confident that the distinction between self and environment is ultimately fundamental, and I should be glad to be convinced that self-awareness can be reduced to a peculiar kind of environmental perception. I think it is clear, however, that, at any rate in the case of practical navigation and social interaction, this distinction does confer a marked advantage upon the organism, and therefore constitutes a recognizable class of beneficial adaptations, even if it should prove that they can be regarded as a sub-class of reflexive responses. This is all that is necessary to validate the evolutionary utility of self-differentiation to be considered in the sequel.

In investigating colour-sensations, there are certain points which must be borne in mind. In the first place, everything constituting a colour-experience is happening within the mind, not in the external object to which the sensation is said to refer. It is not logically necessary to the existence of a colour-sensation that the wavelength perceived should have objective reality, or even that an external world should have existed at all. There is no logical impossibility in the hypothesis that the chromatic world is generated by the brain, exactly as it appears, with an observer that "perceives" a wholly constructed spectrum. There is no logically necessary connection between external stimuli and internal qualia; therefore nothing that is measured instrumentally or described physically can disprove the hypothesis that colour is manufactured by consciousness. Hence the occurrences which are CALLED perception of hue are logically independent of the object; they are wholly analysable into neural processes, which might, theoretically, be just what they are even if no coloured things had existed.

I do not myself believe that the comprehension of reality can be achieved entirely by means of purely intuitive apprehension, such as the plain man employs. I shall discuss this question in a subsequent treatise. In the present analysis I shall attempt the examination of common-sense convictions, both as an introduction to the problem of reality in general, and because common sense, in some form, is presupposed in almost all practical activity. Immediate appearance, we decided, is not a form of truth. It might, however, have been expected that we should begin our discussion of reality with EXPERIENCE, i.e. with that integral encounter with objects in the world, out of which appearance is extracted by philosophical analysis. What is called experience differs from mere appearance by the fact that the apparent ingredients bring up habitual inferences--assumptions and expectations of their customary properties--all of which are subjectively indistinguishable from the direct impression. The HABIT of past observation is essential in producing this elaboration of appearance, but not the KNOWLEDGE of past observation. The non-apparent elements in experience can be wholly explained as the result of custom, produced by frequent conjunctions. Common sense, according to our definition in Chapter III, is no more a form of understanding than appearance is, except in so far as it involves predictions. The purely practical difficulties which it presents are not very formidable, though they have sometimes been rendered artificially perplexing by unwillingness to admit the fallibility of the non-apparent elements of experience. On the other hand, physical reality raises many subtle and very profound problems, which it is necessary to consider at the first possible moment.

One reason for treating expansion at this cosmological stage is that it seems to be involved in the fact that structures are recognized as "consequences" of prior physical conditions. In the preceding discussion I alluded to Hubble's principle "that all our galactic observations in their first appearance are derived from receding motions, which are correspondent to them, and which they exactly measure." Whether or not this principle is liable to exceptions, everyone would agree that it has a broad measure of truth, though the word "exactly" might seem an overstatement, and it might seem more correct to say that observations APPROXIMATELY represent motions. Such modifications of Hubble's principle, however, do not affect the problem which I wish to present for your consideration, namely: Why do we believe that structures are, sometimes or always, approximately or exactly, products of expansion? What sort of evidence is there? And what sort of evidence is logically possible? The difficulty of this question arises through the fact that the condition which a structure is supposed to follow is in the past when the structure exists, and can therefore only be known by inference, while, on the other hand, inference of past conditions seems only possible by means of present structures. How, then, are we to find any way of comparing the present structure and the past condition? The problem is just as acute if we say that structures differ from their antecedents as if we say that they resemble them; it is the very possibility of comparison that is hard to understand.* We think we can know that they are linked or separate, but we cannot bring them together in one state and compare them. To deal with this problem, we must have a theory of cosmic evolution. In this way the whole status of structures as "consequences" is bound up with the analysis of expansion.

In the second place, equations without physical referents are insufficient to constitute a description of nature; and symbols are still more insufficient. The mathematician, who attempts to make physics a manipulation of formulae, has to trust his observation in making the connection. "Model" is a concept involving the correspondence of abstract terms to sensible phenomena; if the mathematician feels confident that there is such a utility as a model, that can only be because he trusts his perception, when it assures him that there have been other instances. And the same applies to equations. If we are to know as it is supposed we do—that mathematical descriptions are "representations," faithful or unfaithful, of natural events, something more than the mere manipulation of symbols must go to constitute this knowledge. For their mere manipulation, by itself, would not suggest any connection with anything that had occurred externally.

I come now to the other characteristic which material patterns must have in order to account for our recognition of persistent forms. They must have some characteristic which makes us regard them as referring to more or less disparate physical substrates. That is to say if we suppose that X is the original pattern, Y the subsequent manifestation, and s the difference in substance between X and Y, there must be some characteristic of Y which is capable of degrees, and which, in accurately identified patterns, varies as s varies. It may increase as s increases, or diminish as s increases. The question which of these occurs is not of any importance for the theoretic serviceability of the characteristic in question.

Our confidence or lack of confidence in the permanence of a spoken utterance must, in fundamental cases, be based upon a characteristic of the utterance itself, since we cannot preserve the spoken word bodily and compare it with the written record. It might be suggested that brevity is the required characteristic, but I do not think this is the case. We sometimes have utterances that are by no means peculiarly brief, which yet we do not trust--for example, under the influence of passion we may hear a political promise vividly and clearly, but horribly misleading. In such a case we distrust our utterance in spite of its being unusually distinct. I think the characteristic by which we distinguish the utterances we trust is the feeling of PERMANENCE that accompanies them. Some utterances, like some thoughts, feel very permanent, while others feel ephemeral. Permanence is a feeling capable of degrees.
