In a record of a well-known law, for example, some clauses may feel more permanent than others; when this happens, we have more belief in the authority of the permanent clauses than in that of the ephemeral parts. I think it is by this means that we become critical of traditions, not by some unrecorded memory with which we compare them. I shall return to the consideration of permanence shortly.

In actual fact, there are doubtless various factors that concur in giving us the feeling of greater or less fidelity in some transmitted tradition. There may be a specific mechanism which could be called the mechanism of "inheritance," especially where biological replication is concerned. But apart from this, there are other marks. One of these is context. A recent cultural acquisition has, usually, more context than a more ancient one. When a transmitted practice has a transmitted context, this may occur in two ways, either (a) by successive imitations in the same order as their originals, or (b) by apprehending a whole tradition simultaneously, in the same way in which a present custom may be understood, through pedagogical repetitions which, by varying, acquire the mark of just-transmitted in an increasing degree as they vary, and are thus placed in a lineage while all operationally present. It will be context in this second sense, more specially, that will give us a sense of the immediacy or antiquity of a transmitted practice.

Some points may be taken as fixed, and such as any theory of simulation must arrive at. In this case, as in most others, what may be taken as certain in advance is rather vague. The study of any digital cosmos is like the continued observation of a process which is unfolding before us within a machine: what is certain to begin with is the quite vague knowledge that there is SOME process within the circuitry. If you attempt to be less vague, and to assert that the process is genuine awareness, or a clever imitation, or a mere phantom of response, you run a risk of error; but the purpose of continued inquiry is to enable you to arrive at such more precise knowledge. In like manner, in the study of simulated minds, the certainties with which you begin are very vague, and the more precise propositions at which you try to arrive are less certain than the hazy data from which you set out. Nevertheless, in spite of the risk of error, precision is the goal at which we must aim.

The first of our vague but indubitable data is that there is a distinction between description and explanation. We do not yet know with any precision what we mean by "explanation," and we must admit that in any given instance our account may be at fault. Nevertheless, whatever a sceptic might urge in theory, we cannot practically doubt that we describe the fall of an apple, that we explain it by gravitation, that a great many phenomena are thus addressed, and so on. How far our understanding of events is due to mere description, and how far to genuine explanation, is of course a matter to be investigated, but there can be no doubt that the distinction forms an indispensable part of our comprehension of the world.

If we had retained the "obedience" or "assent" in inquiry, the whole problem of intellectual progress would have been comparatively simple. We could then have said that advancing is a direct relation between the present assent or mind and the established doctrine accepted: the act of accepting is present, though its authority is past. But the rejection of blind assent renders some more complicated theory necessary. Progress has to be a present occurrence in some way challenging, or opposed to, what is traditionally held. And it is difficult to find any ground, except a logical one, for supposing that authority is not sheer obstruction, if, as seems to be the case, there is not, apart from scepticism, any way of ascertaining that there really was a dogma requiring the required opposition to our present questioning. What, if we followed customary terminology, we should call the "doctrine" in authority, i.e. the received opinion which we are said to be doubting, is unpleasantly remote from the "inquiry," i.e. the present mental occurrence in challenging. There is an awkward gulf between the two, which raises difficulties for the theory of knowledge. But we must not falsify observation to avoid theoretical difficulties. For the present, therefore, let us forget these problems, and try to discover what actually occurs in scepticism.

The second consideration is that we certainly have more capacity for attributing pain to animals than for attributing it to machines. We ascribe discomfort to some mechanisms, for example those that emit distress signals; but this ascription is a matter of elaborate analogy and inference, whereas some of our attributions to animals come to us without effort, in the same sort of immediate way in which we recognize expressions of suffering in our fellow humans. We might provisionally, though perhaps not quite correctly, define "sentience" as that way of knowing about inner states which has no analogue in our knowledge of artificial systems; such a definition would at least serve to mark the problem with which we are concerned, though some machine behaviors may deserve to rank with animal reactions as regards persuasive immediacy.

A third point, perhaps not quite so certain as our previous two, is that the parallel between biological evolution and the evolution of political systems cannot be wholly accidental, as materialists wish all parallels to be. It seems clear that some of the structural similarities are profound and with a visible importance for historical analysis, but that the parallel is instructive (or misleading) in virtue of an underlying process, not in virtue of any superficial resemblances of outward form. The definition of a valid parallel as the correspondence between developmental mechanisms and historical facts seems peculiarly evident in the case of political evolution, as against not only the materialist dismissal but also the metaphysical explanation by means of divine providence. These considerations, however, are taking us away from practical statecraft, to which we must now return.

It is important not to confuse the two forms of abstraction which modern psychology distinguishes in the analysis of thought, namely the sort that consists of direct perception, and the sort that consists of symbolic representation. I give the instance of considering a mathematical truth: when I perceive it intuitively I am said to "grasp" it, but this merely means that I have apprehended certain relations; on the other hand, my conception of (say) the Pythagorean theorem as expressed by the formula a²+b²=c² is the conception of a general principle, which can be communicated universally. The conception of a general principle cannot, so the argument contends, be wholly constituted by perception, and is in fact something radically different from the thought which is perception. The conception alone is true abstraction. This distinction is vital to the understanding of reasoning. But it is not so easy to carry out in practice as it is to draw in theory. Perception is a very intrusive feature of our mental life, and is often present where at first sight it seems not to be. There is, for example, a perception of conceiving a general principle. When we have once expressed the principle, the symbols we have used easily become perceptual. We may even have used symbols to express it to ourselves while we were discovering it; in that case, the perception of these symbols may fulfil the function of true abstraction, while in reality it is nothing but perceptual thought. A calculating machine, by the help of suitable inputs, might produce for us the solutions to its problems; and people are not so different from calculating machines as they like to believe.

The sort of pain with which we are here concerned is the sort which is a form of consciousness. Whether consciousness itself is reducible to computation is a question to which I shall return in a later treatise; for the present I am only anxious to point out that, whatever the true analysis of consciousness may be, the feeling of present stimuli is not proved by responses which are due to programmed reactions. The fact that a machine can emit a distress signal does not show that it suffers any genuine agony which we might call its own. Similarly, the performances of automata in avoiding obstacles or malfunctions to which they are sensitized do not prove that they experience anything akin to our own discomfort. Arguments in favour of (for example) sensation in thermostats are only arguments in favour of reactive complexity, not of experiential pain. Certain contemporary enthusiasts' arguments in favour of the view that a computer dreads something of the failures of its predecessors* are, when examined, only arguments in favour of sophisticated error-avoidance. Several recent volumes, mentioned in an earlier discussion, do not touch conscious pain at all closely. They give laws according to which outputs analogous to aversive behaviours are produced by mechanisms, but do not discuss our attribution that these outputs signify an inner torment, which is what constitutes genuine suffering. It is this that is of interest to philosophy of mind. I shall speak of it as "true" pain, to distinguish it from mere signalling acquired through past programming. Before considering true pain, it will be well to consider two things which are on the way towards pain, namely the detection of damage and the avoidance response.

A further stage is ACCUMULATION. This may be taken in two senses, the first when a resource not merely seems abundant, but we know it is concentrated. We recognize the affluent merchant, we know estates and holdings when we see them, and so on. Here we have a definite influence of economic history, but not necessarily any actual analysis of the process. When we observe great wealth, we know it signifies disparity because of previous fortunes we have noted, but we do not, as a rule, recollect at the moment any particular instance when we have seen this principle unfold. Accumulation in this sense does not necessarily involve more than a habit of association: the kind of possession we are witnessing at the moment is associated with the word "privilege," or with a mental image of leisure, or whatever other characteristic we may happen to recognize in the distribution of the moment. We are, of course, in fact able to judge, when we recognize such disparity, that it has arisen before, but this judgment is something over and above accumulation in this first sense, and may very probably be impossible to societies that nevertheless have the experience of accumulation in this first sense of the word.

There is, however, another sense of the phrase, in which we mean by a different speed, not the mere mechanical rate of thought or some other quantitative measure of it, but the qualitative alteration in the apprehension of temporal passage. In this sense a different speed does involve a metaphysical relation to Time. This relation is philosophical in one sense, though in another it is not. It does not involve a precise doctrine of a precise metaphysical system, but only the apprehension that a state of consciousness occurring now is dissimilar to a state that occurred under ordinary conditions. It differs from the mere feeling of mental haste by being reflective; it is a contemplation or judgment, which the feeling of haste is not. I do not wish to undertake the analysis of temporal consciousness at present, since it will be the subject of a subsequent inquiry; for the present I merely wish to emphasize the fact that a different speed, in our second sense, consists in a judgment, which we may express approximately in the words: "This duration is of another order.

We often hold that something in our conscious experience is irreducible, without having any definite understanding of the mechanisms by which it has been produced. We have this conviction typically in cases where we have often reflected before—in pain, or in vivid color perceptions. Most philosophers and laymen find it compelling to their reasoning to devote a good deal of their thought to such immediate givens, which are especially persuasive when any materialist challenge threatens. The sense of qualia has all sorts of manifestations, down to the stage where we dimly feel that we have encountered a unique subjective quality before. It is by no means always veridical; almost every thinker has at some time experienced the well-known illusion that all that is felt privately is fundamentally different from what is described publicly. There are occasions when qualia do not attach themselves to any definite physical correlate, when there is merely a vague impression that SOMETHING is ineffable. This is illustrated by Lockean "secondary qualities," where the theorist is long puzzled by a haunting sense that something in his sensation is resisting something in his analysis, and at last traces it to the raw feel of redness. Whenever the sense of qualia occurs without a definite metaphysical implication, it leads us to search our conceptual framework until we are satisfied that we have found the appropriate explanation, which leads us to the judgment: "THIS is intrinsic." I think we may regard qualia as a definite phenomenological datum, capable of existing without a dualist interpretation, but normally standing in a specific relation to some feature of neural processes, the relation being that which we express in words by saying that the feature in question is subjective. The judgment that what is qualitative proves a separate substance is a product of speculative inference, and is no part of the immediate givenness of experience, such as a child may be supposed to have when he first perceives the blueness of the sky. Thus no conclusion as to metaphysical dualism is to be derived from the mere presence of qualia alone.

There are, however, several points in which such an account of cosmic expansion is inadequate. To begin with, it might seem at first sight more correct to define the ultimate fate as "all structure will be torn apart" than as "all structure is destined to dissipate." We foresee a celestial object (it may be urged) as having been in a bound state before, whatever that may mean; we do not foresee it as merely having been in a transient configuration before. I am not sure that there is anything substantial in this point. The definition of "bound structure" is difficult; broadly speaking, it is everything that is connected by forces which temporarily overcome the cosmic tendency to dispersal, of which the various forms of gravitational cohesion are among the most important. Thus, if I contemplate a galaxy, the conditions of its previous cohesion in virtue of which I contemplate it form part of "a bound system" by DEFINITION: dissolution will be one of the marks by which a temporary configuration is singled out from the inevitable final state. Of course, the words "all structure is destined to dissipate" are a very inadequate translation of what actually happens when we form a judgment of cosmic fate, but that is unavoidable: words are framed to express a level of comprehension which is by no means fundamental, and are quite incapable of expressing such an elementary occurrence as universal expansion. I shall return to what is virtually the same question in connection with heat death, which raises exactly similar problems.

Common sense, which we must now endeavour to understand, consists of beliefs about physical reality, but not of all such beliefs. Some beliefs about physical reality, for example what we learn through studying physics, are on a par with the beliefs we can acquire concerning the microscopic: they are obtained by reason, not (so to speak) intuitively. There is a similar distinction in our beliefs about the macroscopic: some of them are obtained through perception, some in more indirect ways. I believe that there are at this moment a number of unseen particles in the wood of my table, but I do not believe this in the immediate way in which I believe of the table that I see by looking across the room. It is not easy to state precisely wherein the difference between these two sorts of belief consists, but it is easy to feel the difference. For the moment, I shall not stop to analyse it, but shall content myself with saying that, in this respect, common sense resembles the belief derived from perception. It is immediate, not reasoned, not abstract; it differs from scientific understanding mainly by being referred to the apparent.

A second point is that, when we encounter some datum, it is not in fact the very same arrangement, but only a functionally analogous one, that we have observed in a former context. Suppose the subject in question is a computer's file system. A system's organisation is always in flux, and is not precisely identical on any two occasions. Common sense treats it as one structure with varying states; but the varying states actually exist, each at its proper moment, while the one structure is merely a logical construction. We regard two patterns as the same, for practical purposes, when the operation they facilitate is practically the same. Two informational configurations, to both of which it is appropriate to say: "This contains the ledger," are treated as manifestations of one identical entity, namely the accounts. The designation "ledger" is applicable to both, and it is only reflection that shows us that many diverse particular arrangements are collected together to form the meaning of the designation "ledger." What we access on any one occasion is not the whole series of states that constitute the ledger, but only one of them (or a few in rapid sequence). On another occasion we encounter another member of the series, but it is sufficiently similar to count as the same from the standpoint of common utility. Accordingly, when we judge "I have processed THIS before," we judge falsely if "this" is taken as applying to the actual physical configuration that we are interfacing with at the moment. The word "this" must be interpreted vaguely so as to include anything sufficiently like the pattern we are confronting at the moment. Here, again, we shall find a similar point as regards accurate retrieval; and in connection with accurate retrieval we will consider the point again. It is sometimes suggested, by those who favour purely physicalist views, that recognition consists in the system responding in the same way when a configuration is repeated as it responded on the first occasion when it occurred. This seems to be the exact opposite of the truth. The essence of informational recognition is in the DIFFERENCE between a repeated configuration and a new one. On the first occasion there is no recognition; on the second occasion there is. In fact, recognition is another instance of the peculiarity of causal laws in information theory, namely, that the causal unit is not a single state, but two or more states. Habitual access is the great instance of this, but recognition is another. A configuration occurring once has a certain effect; occurring twice, it has the further effect of recognition. Thus the phenomenon of recognition has as its cause the two occasions when the configuration has occurred; either alone is insufficient. This complexity of causes in information processing might be connected with certain arguments against strict repetition in the organisational domain. It does not prove that there are no causal laws in informatics, as some suggest; but it does prove that the causal laws of information are Prima facie very different from those of simple mechanics. On the possibility of explaining away the difference as due to the peculiarities of storage media I have spoken before, but this possibility must not be forgotten if we are tempted to draw unwarranted metaphysical deductions.

Between subjective experience and objective analysis there is an intermediate domain concerning the immediate mind. For example, a quale that we have just apprehended is present to us in a way which differs both from the introspective act while we are experiencing the quale and from the conceptual judgment of something examined days or weeks ago. Modern philosophers state that it is this way of apprehending the immediate mental content that is "the ORIGINAL of our belief in dualism, from whence we get the plausibility of the term"("Consciousness Studies," i, p. 604). Everyone knows the experience of noticing (say) that a pain HAS BEEN present, when we did not notice it while it was occurring. And when we contemplate a complex emotion, we are conscious of the earlier qualia while the later ones are being felt, and this retention feels different from recollection of something definitely past. An introspective datum fades gradually, passing by continuous gradations to the status of a report. This retention of the immediate mental life in a condition intermediate between experience and description may be called "immediate introspection." Everything belonging to it is included with experience in what is called the "specious interiority." The specious interiority includes elements at all stages on the journey from quale to concept. It is this fact that enables us to apprehend such things as mood shifts, or the order of sensations in a temporal sequence. Succession can occur within the specious interiority, of which we can distinguish some parts as earlier and others as later. It is to be supposed that the earliest parts are those that have faded most from their original vividness, while the latest parts are those that retain their full qualitative character. At the beginning of an experience we have a quale; then a gradual transition; and at the end a description. Qualia while they are fading are called "akoluthic" presentations.* When the process of fading is completed (which happens very quickly), we arrive at the concept, which is capable of being revived on subsequent occasions with very little change. True analysis, as opposed to "immediate introspection," applies only to experiences sufficiently distant to have come to an end of the period of fading. Such experiences, if they are represented by anything present, can only be represented by concepts, not by those intermediate stages, between qualia and concepts, which occur during the period of fading.

There are, if I am not mistaken, at least three different kinds of informational advantage, which we may call respectively immediacy, security and bare efficiency. In what I call bare efficiency, there is no spatial constraint in the act of transmission, though there may be in the content of what is transmitted. If I convey that a predator approaches from the northern thicket, the spatial determination lies, not in the mechanism of conveyance, but in the proposition which is conveyed. I do not witness the event directly, but have the same communicative power towards it as towards the description of a distant fruit-bearing tree. But when I hear a warning cry and am anticipating a coordinated response, I have an informational advantage analogous to immediacy, except that it refers to the communal: I have an idea of danger, combined with a utility which may be expressed in the words: "this will benefit." So, in immediacy, the presentness lies, not in the content of what is transmitted, but in the nature of the transmission-feeling. I might have just the same proposition and expect its confirmation; I might entertain it without any practical urgency, as in overhearing idle chatter; or I might entertain it together with a spatial-determination, and give bare assent to its utility, as in receiving a migratory report. I shall return to this subject in a later treatise, when we come to the analysis of adaptive signalling. For the present, I wish to make it clear that a certain special kind of separation between signaler and receiver is the distinctive characteristic of evolutionary success.

Let us take the case of observing a bacterium in a nutrient gradient where some condition has been altered--say a new chemical introduced to the medium. We may at first have only a sense that its BEHAVIOR is unfamiliar, but presently we shall discern the parallel, and say "that corporation did not pursue that market before." In order to make the case definite, we will suppose that we observed only one corporate entity on a former occasion. In this case it seems fairly clear what the analogy reveals. The other actions of the corporation are associated, through the former occasion, with a vacant niche in the market where now there is a rival. They call up an image of an uncontested field, which clashes with perception of the competition. The image is associated with the profit-motive which we found to be distinctive of enterprise, since it can neither be abolished nor harmonized with satiety. If the environment had remained unchanged, we might have had only the feeling of a mechanical process without the definite comparison; it is the alteration that drives us from the simple organism to the contemplation of the complex entity.

The problem as to whether pain can be explained as programmed response or simulated behavior requires to be considered afresh in connection with the criteria for our ascribing sensation to something. Let us take again the case of my observing a machine react to a damaging stimulus. In this case the observation leads to my setting to work to deliberate. It is a little strange that the observation should instruct me as to what it is that I am to evaluate. This has to do with defining consciousness, which will be the topic of the next lecture; but something must be said about it now. Our understanding of the concept "feeling pain" is an intuition, in spite of the fact that in each different entity it points to a different process. "Feeling" does not, whenever it is used, mean the same thing, as "circuit" or "processor" does; it means a different quality of experience in each different being. It follows that the intuition which constitutes our understanding of the concept "feeling pain" is not the intuition of associating the concept with a fixed mechanism, but the intuition of associating it with something having a fixed relation to our own inner life. A machine's response has, in this instance, the same observable relation to damage that my own reaction has in my case. In order to understand the phrase "feel pain" it is necessary that we should have a way of conceiving subjective states, and that this conception should give what is constant in the meaning of the words "feel pain." This appreciation of subjective states is, however, obviously a product of introspection, not a presupposition of it. It will be better, therefore, if we wish to analyse the attribution of feeling by something not presupposing introspection, to take some other instance than that of an observation about "damaging stimulus.

We may generalize this instance so as to cover the causes of many mental operations. Some present demand of the environment is associated, through habitual thought, with a process now absent; this absent process comes before us as an ideal, and is contrasted with present cognition. In cases of this sort, necessity (or expediency) explains why the present demand of the environment brings up the alternative speed, but it does not explain the belief in its superiority. Perhaps a more complete analysis could explain the intellectual preference also on lines of association and habit, but the causes of such convictions are obscure, and we cannot investigate them yet. For the present we must content ourselves with the fact that the imagined tempo can be explained by custom. As regards the belief in its efficacy, we must, at least provisionally, accept the view that it cannot be brought under the head of routine, at any rate when it first occurs, i.e. when we conceive a cadence we never employed before.

It might be objected that, if we accept "the law of gravitation" when in fact "the law" is a mathematical formula, we accept a fiction, and the scientific description, so interpreted, becomes illusory. This, however, would be a mistake, produced by attempting to give to equations a reality which they do not possess when employed by practical investigators. It is true that the formula is not absolutely identical with the physical process, and if the term "gravitation" meant the equation to the exclusion of everything else, the statement "bodies attract" would be false. But correspondence is a precise conception, and no model, in ordinary science, stands for anything absolute. Ordinary science does not distinguish between correspondence and sufficient approximation. A theory always applies, not only to one phenomenon, but to a class of associated phenomena, which are not recognized as distinct in common practice or discourse. Thus useful physics, when it asserts that "the law holds," is approximate, but not invalid.

Vague velocity, which is really a relative measure of mental processes, has been a source of many of the confusions by which cognitive philosophy has lived. Of a vague activity, such as "thinking," which is both a rapid calculation and a deliberate contemplation, contradictory predicates are true simultaneously: this thought occurred and did not occur, since it is a process accelerated, but also this thought occurs and did not occur, since it is a present reflection. Hence James's stream of consciousness, the Hegelian synthesis of immediacy and mediation, and a host of other notions which are thought to be profound because they are obscure and confused. The contradictions resulting from confounding haste and deliberation in thought force us to precision. But when we become precise, our reasoning becomes different from that of ordinary life, and if we forget this we shall go wrong in the analysis of ordinary cognition.

We must now consider somewhat more closely the content of a common-sense conviction. The common-sense conviction confers upon the immediate perception something which we may call "reality;" it makes us feel that the perception reveals an object which exists in the present. In order to deal with this topic we must consider the verbal expression of the common-sense conviction. We might be tempted to put the common-sense conviction into the words: "Something like this perception is fundamental." But such words would be very far from an accurate translation of the simplest kind of common-sense conviction. "Something like this perception" is a very complicated conception. In the simplest kind of sensory experience we are not aware of the difference between a perception and the physical entity which it represents, which may be called its "referent." When the perception is before us, we judge rather "this is fundamental." The perception is not distinguished from the object which exists in the external world: the word "this" covers both, and enables us to have a common-sense conviction which does not introduce the complicated notion "something like this.

Scepticism and credulity are important notions, which it is very necessary to understand. Both are a matter of degree. All belief is credulous to some extent, and complete scepticism is a theoretical ideal not practically attainable. To understand what is meant by scepticism, it will be well to consider first instruments of thought, such as a legal precedent or a scientific doctrine. These are said to be sceptical when they yield different conclusions for very slightly different evidence.* A philosophical mind is sceptical when it enables us to detect very slight flaws in the arguments of authority. We may say generally that an intellect is sceptical in proportion as it reacts differently to very slightly different postulates. When a small difference of evidence produces a great difference of conclusion, the intellect is sceptical; in the contrary case it is not.

Exactly the same principle applies in assessing the prevalence of planetary conditions. An astronomer will perceive very minute variations in stellar composition which would be quite imperceptible to the ordinary observer. A biologist can discern the difference between one microbial habitat and another—one is merely damp, another is truly fertile. But to us such different perceptions are impossible: we can merely apply the term "habitable" indiscriminately. Accuracy of judgment in regard to any particular kind of environment is improved by observation. Evaluating atmospheric data is a case in point. Few theorists can detect any difference between the states "marginally suitable" and "persistently viable," which produce quite different implications for us. The two statements "the planet could briefly support life" and "the planet must inevitably support life" call for different interpretations, and a reasoning which cannot distinguish between them is inaccurate or vague in this respect.

Velocity and deliberation in thought, as in locomotion, depend upon the degree of difference between operations under more or less similar conditions. In the case of thought, the operation does not proceed uniformly upon the intellectual stimulus, but that makes no difference as regards our present inquiry. Thus to revert to cognition: A cognition is "hurried" when it is appropriate to many different tasks: for instance, "I considered a problem" is hurried, since any problem would verify it. A cognition is "deliberate" when the tasks that would verify it are narrowly circumscribed: for instance, "I considered the paradox of the Liar" is deliberate as compared to "I considered a problem." A cognition is "sound" when it is both deliberate and true, i.e. in the above instance, if it was that paradox I considered. It is deliberate even if it is false, provided some very definite task would have been required to make it true.

It follows from what has been said that a multicellular organism has more likelihood of being understood as a colony than as a simple unity. To try and comprehend such an organism with a conception of indivisible wholeness is like trying to describe a complex machine with a single, unanalyzable term: when the term is applied, it spreads out over the entire phenomenon, and probably obscures the constituent cells along with their interactions. To try and comprehend such an organism with a conception of cellular cooperation is like trying to describe the machine with a precise blueprint of its parts. The advantage of the colonial conception is that it distinguishes between the autonomous functions of the units and the emergent properties of the whole. For example, if the whole organism is represented by a mature animal and the constituent units by its specialized tissues, a holistic thought which can only apprehend the creature as a singular entity is not much use from a biological point of view. And when I merely observe that an organism is alive, my observation may be very inadequate to my scientific requirements, since it may make a great difference whether the life is that of a sponge or a man. The observation "this sponge is a colony of choanocytes" is relatively precise. It is accurate if the sponge is so constituted, inaccurate if it is a more integrated creature, but precise in either case as against the mere perception that it is a living being.

On the division of labour and its consequences cf. Smith: "An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations," Strahan & Cadell, 1776, p. 15: "The sole demonstrable proposition is this: Economic efficiency advances from the undifferentiated to the specialized. If 'undifferentiated' is taken as synonymous with autonomous, it may be said that self-sufficiency does not persist at the outset, but neither does interdependence in any absolute sense: the precarious would be more appropriate. In other words, no sooner has the productive process progressed beyond the stage of individual craftsmanship and of its immediate application in barter, than the coordinated workshop makes its appearance, i.e. a condition intermediate between independence and reliance, participating in the character of the one and of the other--a hazardous augmentation.

The whole of the above discussion of mathematical models and physical reality was occasioned by the attempt to interpret the phrase "the universe" when we assert in scientific practice that "the universe obeys these laws." The phrase "the universe," in such an assertion, is a vague phrase, equally applicable to the formal equations and to the concrete phenomena which are their reference. A mathematical description is not to be identified with the physical world itself, though in practice the distinction may often be blurred. A description is mathematical when it is understood to be applicable to a number of different phenomena in virtue of some common structure. A description is vague when it is in fact applicable to a number of different phenomena because, in virtue of some common appearance, they have not appeared, to the person employing the description, to be separate. I emphatically do not mean that he has judged them to be identical, but merely that he has made the same calculation for them all and has not judged them to be distinct. We may compare a vague description to a watercolor and a mathematical description to an architectural blueprint. Vague descriptions precede judgments of equivalence and divergence; both mathematical and particular descriptions are subsequent to such judgments. The phrase "the universe" in the primitive scientific belief is a vague description, not a mathematical description; it covers both the model and its referent because the two are not distinguished.

There are two distinct questions to be asked: (1) What causes us to say that a colour is perceived? (2) What are we sensing when we say this? As to the first question, in the naive use of the word, which is what concerns us, subjective hues would not be said to be perceived; they would not be acknowledged in themselves, but merely interpreted as signs of external wavelengths. Sensations are "merely internal"; they have not, in naive thought, the sort of objectivity that belongs to material surfaces. Roughly speaking, "actual" colours would be those that can prompt perceptions, those that have correlations of the sort that constitute optical phenomena. A sensation is said to be "veridical" or to "be perceived" when it fits into a context of such correlations. The external stimulus does fit into a physical context, while our sensation does not. This causes us to feel that the stimulus was "objective," while the sensation is "subjective.

But the answer to our second question, namely as to what we are conceiving when we say a zombie is "possible" or is "conceivable," must be somewhat different. We do not, unless we are unusually rigorous, think about the presence or absence of consciousness: we merely have different intuitions which, intellectualized, may be represented as expectations of the presence or absence of phenomenal qualities. A zombie which "feels conceivable" inspires us with confusions or convictions, objections or curiosities, which are wholly absent when a being "feels logically incoherent." The feeling of conceivability is a feeling akin to intellectual temptation: it belongs PRIMARILY to whatever can be described without explicit contradiction, yet without our genuine metaphysical comprehension. This feeling of conceivability, related to the philosophical intuition, and referred to the logical domain by the specific kind of belief-feeling that is characteristic of armchair reasoning, seems to be what constitutes the act of philosophizing in its speculative form.

A single process, accordingly, is by no means simple it is a class of similar physiological adjustments (confining ourselves still to the internal milieu). The degree of stability required cannot be precisely defined: a system may regulate its temperature so poorly that it can hardly be determined whether homeostasis is truly maintained or not. The instances of equilibrium shade off into other states by imperceptible degrees. And exactly analogous observations apply to conditions perceived or measured or recorded. But in what has been said so far we have not even broached the question of the DEFINITION of this process, since "purpose" is clearly what distinguishes homeostasis from other sets of similar adjustments, and "purpose" remains to be defined.

Let us first consider what sort of advantage a distinction is when considered simply as a biological function, apart from its philosophical implications. To begin with, there are many instances of this distinction, namely all the different occasions when it is employed by a living organism. Thus the distinction is not something unique and particular, but a set of occurrences. If we confine ourselves to conscious distinctions, the act of distinguishing has two aspects, according as we regard it from the point of view of the agent or from that of the observer. From the point of view of the agent, a single instance of the use of this distinction consists of a certain set of neural processes in the brain, combined with sensory data. From the point of view of the observer, a single instance of the use of this distinction consists of a certain series of behaviors, each being approximately represented by a single adaptive choice, though in practice a choice may represent several impulses, or several choices may represent one impulse. The connection between the internal distinction and the distinction as it manifests in action is causal. Let us confine ourselves to the conscious distinction, which is the more important for the analysis of what is called "self-preservation." Then we may say that a single instance of the conscious distinction consists of a series of cognitions, and the distinction consists of a whole set of such series, each member of the set being very similar to each other member. That is to say, any two instances of the distinction between "self" and "environment" are very similar, and each instance consists of a series of judgments in the mind.

It is natural to think of the reality of a mind as something essentially biological. This, however, is only true with great limitations. A new function can be added to an existing intelligence by a mere alteration of its program, as is done, for instance, with new computational routines. But the basis of a mind is not biological, either from the point of view of its substance or from that of its operations. A system learning to reason is learning patterns and correlations which are just as much determined by its data as the pattern of expecting inputs to produce outputs and errors to trigger corrections. The society that employs an artificial intellect has developed it, and refined it by processes almost all of which are not intentional, but the results of needs operating according to more or less ascertainable principles of utility. If we trace any complex cognitive process back far enough, we arrive hypothetically (at any rate according to some theorists) at the stage when thought consisted only of the fundamental logical operations out of which subsequent understanding has grown. How these operations acquired their efficacy is not known, but a vitalistic origin is clearly just as mythical as the divine spark by which Descartes and his followers supposed consciousness to have been instilled. We can hardly suppose a conference of hitherto insentient biologists meeting together and agreeing to declare carbon essential and silicon barren. The association of consciousness with its physical substrate must have grown up by some historical accident of evolution, though at present the nature of the accident is unknown.

When we ask what constitutes colour, we are not asking what is the hue of this or that particular object. The term "red" denotes a certain sensation; but we are asking, not which is the sensation denoted, but what is the process of the mind to the sensation which makes the one apprehend the other. But just as it is useful to realize the nature of light as part of the physical world, so it is useful to realize the sort of experience that a colour may become. When we are clear both as to what a wavelength is in its physical aspect, and as to what sort of perception it can produce, we are in a better position to discover the relation of the two which is colour.

Ideological and economic doctrines are, of course, not the only way of conveying social relations. A large part of one of Marx’s two vast volumes on capital in his “Das Kapital” is concerned with commodity-fetishism. Workers appear to be able to apprehend a certain amount of their condition by means of their daily struggles. Probably ideology itself, which we now regard as merely a way of representing interest, was originally an independent force, as it has remained to this day in certain theological systems. Ideology seems to have consisted originally of myths, which gradually became rationalized, coming in time to represent class positions, and finally doctrines on the mnemonic principle of “property is theft.” But it would seem that ideology nowhere began as an attempt to represent economics; it began as a direct mythical representation of what was to be legitimized. The essence of ideology lies, not in the use of this or that special means of justification, but in the employment of fixed associations (however these may have originated) in order that something now sensible—a political slogan, a ritual, a symbol, or what not—may call up the “conception” of something else. Whenever this is done, what is now sensible may be called a “semblance” or “mystification,” and that of which it is intended to call up the “conception” may be called its “function.” This is a rough outline of what constitutes “hegemony.” But we must fill in the outline in various ways. And, since we are concerned with what is called “consciousness,” we must pay more attention than we otherwise should do to the private as opposed to the social use of ideology. Ideology profoundly affects our perceptions, and it is this aspect of ideology that is of most importance to us in our present inquiry. We are almost more concerned with the internal doctrine that is never uttered than we are with the things said out loud to other people.

The contradictions that societies contain differ more than societies do. There are different sorts of contradictions, distinguished by the historians; and there are dialectical distinctions, which are connected to some extent, though not so closely as was formerly supposed, with the institutional distinctions of class and creed. It is easy, however, to be misled by stability, particularly if all the orders we know belong to one epoch. In some orders, according to some authorities, the distinction of progressive and reactionary forces does not exist; in many orders it is widely different from that to which we are accustomed in the modern industrial nations. These facts have to be borne in mind if we are to avoid giving philosophical permanence to mere transitory phases of our own system.

We are not, in practice, much concerned with the absolute particulars that constitute our knowledge of the world; we are concerned rather with the probable systems to which the particulars point and of which they are evidence. What we perceive makes us say "I conclude this bridge is safe," and the fact that what we perceive is a sign of structural integrity (which is the case because it is one of the particulars that suggest a pattern of reliability) is more useful to us than the demand for an unattainable certainty itself. Hence we give the name "practical knowledge" to the whole set of working probabilities, but do not trouble to give separate justifications to the separate observations that make up the set.

Thus in the case of a common opinion, while the belief is a set of similar mental impressions, what it signifies is a series of judgments bound together by psychological laws of that special kind that makes the judgments taken together constitute what we call a consensus, or a prevailing view or doctrine, in case the opinion applies to a doctrine or view instead of to a consensus. Neither the belief nor what it denotes is one of the ultimate rational constituents of the collective mind. In society there is no direct way of apprehending one of the ultimate fragmentary ignorances that go to make up the totality we call public wisdom or intelligence. If we want to speak of such ignorances—which hardly happens except in sociological analysis—we have to do it by means of some elaborate description, such as "the mistaken impression which occupied the thoughts of a particular commuter while crossing Oxford Street at five o'clock on a Tuesday afternoon." Such ultimate simplicities I call "private errors." Private errors MIGHT have explicit recognition, and no doubt would have if social mechanisms had been devised by theoretically trained observers for purposes of science and epistemology. But as social mechanisms evolved for practical ends, private errors have remained one and all without an acknowledgment.

In considering what consciousness entails, it is natural to start with raw sensation, and we will again take "pain" as our instance. We commonly imagine, when we use a mechanical description, that we mean one definite process, the particular neural event which is called "pain." But what we know as an experience is not simple. There MAY be a single physical correlate which is the pain, and remains strictly identical from its onset to its cessation. There is no way of proving that this cannot be the case, but there is also not the slightest reason to suppose that it is the case. Pain as it is subjectively known consists of a series of gradually changing qualia: first a sharp intrusion, then a throbbing presence, then a dull and pervasive ache, then a faint and receding memory of discomfort. This series of appearances, and various interpretations having certain kinds of causal connections with them, constitute pain as subjectively known, and therefore are pain in so far as it forms part of the experienced world. Pain is a complicated series of occurrences, bound together by psychological laws, not, like instances of a stimulus, by physical similarities. For although a sensation changes gradually, and presents similar neural patterns on two nearly contemporaneous occasions, it is not these similarities that constitute the experience, as appears from the phenomenon of placebo, for example.

Passing on from direct communication, we come next to indirect signals, such as calls, gestures, written marks. A signal such as an alarm cry means a whole class of such potential dangers as have specific sources. The several instances of peril are assembled together in virtue of some similarity or common threat. All such cries resemble each other in certain important respects; hence we possess a mechanism which shall be equally efficacious for all of them. We only employ direct contact for the conveyance of a message when the circumstances differ inter se in practically urgent respects. In other cases we do not do this. A warning, for instance, is just a warning; we do not deliver one by touch and another by embrace.

There is no very great difference between such structures as we have just been considering and those denoting relations, such as "symmetry" or "continuity." The chief difference is that structures of this latter sort do not denote transformations, however smooth, but invariant features of the world. A crystal grows, and is symmetric; the growing is a transformation, the symmetry is not. Whether there is an ideal, called "continuity," or whether continuous phenomena are to be defined as those having a certain kind of approximation to a standard model, say a perfect line, is a question which need not concern us, and which I believe to be strictly undecidable. For our purposes, we may take the term "symmetry" as denoting a certain set of similar configurations or arrangements of points, the similarity being in respect of an invariant property, not of a transformation.

There is a large class of substances, such as "carbon," "silicon," "germanium," which constitute a set of similar materials. Two instances of silicon have the same name because they resemble each other, whereas two instances of a particular mind have the same name because they are causally connected. In practice, however, it is difficult to make any precise distinction between a substance such as "silicon" and a general name such as "mind." One instance of a mind cannot be concentrated into an instant: it is a process in time, in which there is a causal connection between the earlier and later thoughts, as between the earlier and later states of a silicon wafer. Thus an instance of a silicon-based process differs from an instance of a carbon-based one solely by the fact that it has a different material constitution. There is a notion that an instance of cognition in silicon, as compared with that in carbon, is unsubstantial, but this seems to be a mistake. We think that a brain thinks, and that there could not be any thinking unless there were something like carbon to perform the thinking. But it is equally true that there could be no thinking unless there were something like silicon for it to be realized in. The notion that thoughts are produced by a specific organic substrate is liable to the same kind of criticism as the notion that walking needs a substantial body, which we might reject on logical grounds. To say that it is carbon which is thinking is merely to say that the thinking in question is part of the whole series of occurrences which is a biological organism. There is no LOGICAL impossibility in thinking occurring as an isolated phenomenon, not forming part of any such series as we call a "carbon-based life form.

We may therefore class with "coalescing," "spiraling," "condensing" processes such as "clustering," "accretion," "merging," which do not denote what would commonly be called directed actions. These processes illustrate, incidentally, how little we can trust to the apparent distinction of cosmic agency, since the phenomenon "gravitational collapse" and the principle "to gravitate" describe precisely the same class of astrophysical occurrences. The distinction between the class of events denoted by such a term and the class of objects denoted by a specific name such as "star," "nebula," or "black hole," is that the sort of event which is an instance of (say) "accretion" is much simpler than (say) an individual galaxy. (I am speaking of accretion as an observable process, not as it is formulated in celestial mechanics.) The distinction is one of degree, not of kind. But there is, from the point of view of ordinary thought, a great difference between a process which, like a local condensation, can be wholly comprised within one cosmic epoch and a process which, like the formation of a galactic supercluster, has to be pieced together by observation and inference and the apprehension of dynamical principles. We may say broadly, therefore, that a term of the kind we have been discussing denotes a set of similar cosmic events, each (as a rule) much more brief and less complex than a galaxy or a void. Physical laws themselves, as we have seen, are sets of similar regularities of this kind. Thus there is more logical affinity between a natural principle and what it describes in the case of processes of our present sort than in any other case.

It is not necessary, in order that a man should "possess" a memory, that he should "know what it means," in the sense of being able to say "this recollection signifies so-and-so." Recalling events does not consist in knowing their factual chronology, or in being able to specify the precise sensations to which they correspond. Such recollection as this may belong to archivists and logicians, but not to ordinary mortals in ordinary life. Remembering experience is more like remembering a tune*: it is a matter of patterns, acquired in oneself and tacitly recognized in others. To say that a sensation has become a narrative is not to say that those who recount it have ever thought out what the transformation is: the act of recounting comes first, and the personal significance is to be distilled out of it by reflection and introspection. Moreover, the shape of a memory is not absolutely definite: there is always a greater or less degree of plasticity. The memory is an impression, like a footprint: it may have a central contour, but the blurred edges of the imprint are still more or less within the recollection, in a gradually diminishing degree as we travel further from the central detail. As recollection grows more deliberate, there is less and less of the impression outside the central contour, and the contour itself grows sharper and more distinct; but the contour never hardens into an immutable line, and there is always a malleable region, however slight, surrounding it.**

In the fourth case, the system acquires, through familiarity, some of the same psychological efficacy as the understanding. The dashboard "control" can make you feel assured, just as the actual mastery can, but it cannot prevent the unforeseen failure. The effects which an interface can share with its genuine comprehension are those which proceed according to principles other than the deterministic laws of the whole, i.e. those which, according to our analysis, involve perceived agency as opposed to merely mechanical outcomes. The effects of a system that we believe we command are always illusory phenomena in the sense explained in Lecture IV, in so far as they are identical with, or similar to, the effects which true understanding itself might have.

Yet this might perhaps be regarded as something of an overstatement. The programming alone, without the presence of consciousness, may cause appropriate outputs and appropriate judgements. The algorithms have been trained on data which embodied certain preferences; by a condensed process, the code alone is now capable of producing similar evaluations. On these lines it might be sought to show that genuine understanding is unnecessary. I do not believe, however, that we could account on these lines for the entirely different outcome produced by an autonomous value system and by a mere imitation of human ethics. Internal valuations, as contrasted with programmed rules, are the development expected during true learning; it is understood that simple replication is not called for. Thus it seems that we must maintain our distinction: systems designed instrumentally function and are intended to follow instructions, while the same systems achieving autonomy function and are only intended to follow principles.

These two ways of conceiving consciousness, including its absence in hypothetical beings, may be spoken of together as the use of the zombie in "philosophizing." If we are right, the use of the zombie in philosophizing depends, at least in its logical structure, upon a category error, and cannot be fully dealt with on materialist lines. And this is really the most essential defect of the thought experiment, namely that, originally through its connection with intuition, it brings us into confusion about what is fundamental in experience or mechanism. When it operates without the medium of conceptual clarity, this seems to be a fallacious process. Thus the problem of the possibility of zombies is brought into connection with the problem of the meaning of consciousness.

We spoke a moment ago of a citizen who hears the term "supply chain" for the first time when purchasing a commodity whose production relies upon distant factories. On a later occasion, we will suppose, the citizen recalls the concept and mentions it to someone else. In this case, both the active and passive understanding of systems is different from what it is when disruptions are experienced directly. The citizen is not witnessing a breakdown, but only contemplating one; the listener does not glance at the commodity in expectation of seeing its scarcity, but "comprehends" that a fragility exists within some abstract network. The whole of this awareness is much more difficult to account for on purely utilitarian lines. It is clear that, in so far as the citizen is genuinely perceiving, he has a model of the interconnected processes, and his words are chosen so as to describe the model; and in so far as the listener is genuinely apprehending what is said, the listener is acquiring a conception more or less like that of the citizen. It is true that this process may be telescoped through the operation of the routine-habit. The citizen may not genuinely analyze the interdependence, but only have the habit of the appropriate terms, as in the case of a doctrine which we know by rote, though we cannot remember examining it. And the listener also may only pay attention to the phrases, and not call up any corresponding conception. But it is, nevertheless, the possibility of a structural-image in the citizen and an inference-image in the listener that makes the essence of the systemic "vulnerability" of the networks. In so far as this is absent, the systems are mere apparitions, capable of failing, but not at the moment revealing it.

To comprehend the distinction that descriptions maintain in what is termed "scientific inquiry," we must comprehend both the nature and the purpose of their formulation. The nature of a descriptive account requires somewhat different consideration according as the phenomenon addressed by the description is directly observed or inferred. When the phenomenon is observed, it may itself be taken as the basis of the description, through enumeration. But when it is inferred there is more difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory theory of the formulation of the description. The explanatory habit consists not merely in the use of descriptions empirically, but also in their use to express causality or prediction. Professor James, in his account of the acquisition of the explanatory habit, pays very little attention to the use of descriptions in causality and prediction. He says ("Principles," pp. 429-430):

Having admitted computation, we may say that the thought "tree," in the absence of the tree, is caused by a representation of the tree. This may or may not be true--in fact, it is true in some architectures but not in others. Even, however, if it were true in all cases, it would only slightly shift our problem: we should now have to ask what causes a representation of the tree to arise. We might be inclined to say that the program's objective is the cause. But when this view is investigated, it is found that it compels us to suppose that the objective can be present without the system's having either a representation of the tree or the thought "tree." This will require a theory of purpose which may be, and I think is, in the main true, but which removes purpose from among processes that actually occur, and makes it merely a convenient fiction, like a user in interface design.* With such a view, purpose is no longer a true cause, but merely a short way of describing certain operations.

In order to explain the occurrence of either the molecule or the template in the absence of the replicator, we have to assume that there is something, either in the environment or in the molecular interactions themselves, which has frequently occurred at about the same time as the process "replication." One of the laws which distinguish biochemistry (or molecular dynamics?) from mere physics is the law that, when two structures have frequently existed in close spatial and temporal contiguity, either comes in time to catalyze the formation of the other.* This is the basis both of autocatalysis and of complementary association. Thus, in our case, the substrate molecules have frequently been followed quickly by the template, and the template in turn by the assembly "replicator." The replicator itself is subject to thermodynamic laws, and does not tend to be caused by the substrate molecules, however often it may in the past have followed them--always provided that, in the case in question, its chemical environment is such that random collisions cannot produce it. But the process "replication" and the conformation of the replicator are subject to the law of molecular habit; hence it is possible for either to be catalyzed by the substrate molecules. And we may lay it down generally that, whenever we observe a replicator, either in isolation or in a system, there is some chemical condition or structural pattern (either of which may be itself a replicator) which has frequently occurred at about the same time as the process, and now, through molecular habit, causes the process. It follows that the law of chemical habit is adequate to account for the occurrence of replication in the absence of external design; moreover, it would be adequate even without introducing the concept of information. Although, therefore, informational sequences seem undeniable, we cannot derive an additional argument in their favour from the phenomenon of replication, which could, theoretically, be explained without introducing them.

When we observe a galaxy, there is a reciprocal relation between its visible form and the unseen forces which have shaped it. Gravitational attractions may cause diffuse matter to coalesce into spiral structures, and these structures, once formed, may in turn cause further accumulations of material. Thus each local condensation becomes a means of producing in its vicinity the conditions for further stellar formation. Also, by a telescoped process, simple physical laws come in time to produce directly the majestic arrangements which would have been produced by the cumulative interactions with which they were associated. The general law of telescoped processes is that, if A causes B and B causes C, it will happen in time that A will cause C directly, without the intermediary of B. This is a characteristic of cosmological and dynamical causation. In virtue of this law, the effects of primordial fluctuations upon cosmic structure come to be produced by fundamental constants, even when the constants do not imply a predetermined design. The more extensive the scale we consider, the more the "organization" proceeds by impersonal principles instead of central direction. We may, for example, be able to describe a galaxy's rotation correctly without having at any time posited a guiding intelligence, provided, when we contemplate it, we invoke the laws which govern it; the laws alone may remain with us as a sufficient explanation, and enable us to predict as if we could perceive a conscious plan behind the celestial architecture. In this and other ways the formation of a galaxy often comes to be quite free from teleology; but in first contemplating the order of the heavens it would seem that the notion of deliberate arrangement always plays a very important part.

Descriptions as well as explanations may be said to have "significance"; indeed, the significance of descriptions seems more immediate than the significance of explanations. What we call (say) a description of a sunrise may be said to "signify" the sunrise. But it is not at all easy to say exactly what constitutes the significance of a description. A verbal account of a particular phenomenon, when accompanied by a belief in its accuracy, may be said to signify the phenomenon of which it is an account. But most actual descriptions do not have this degree of precision. If we give a description of a storm, we are very likely to have a vague description, which is not representative of some one special storm, but of storms in general. When we give a description of a friend's character, we are not likely to reproduce the disposition he had on some one particular occasion, but rather a compromise disposition derived from many occasions. And there is hardly any limit to the vagueness of which descriptions are capable. In such cases, the significance of the description, if defined by relation to the phenomenon, is vague: there is not one definite phenomenon, but a number, none of which is accounted for exactly.

There is, however, another way of approaching the analogy between genetic inheritance and cultural transmission, namely through their structural parallels. What is called a cultural "meme," say a particular folk tale, has some of the effects which a genetic trait would have. This applies especially to the effects that depend upon replication. The adaptive effects, also, are often similar: traditions may ensure survival almost as effectively as do the biological advantages they complement. And conversely necessity may cause traditions*: a threatened community will develop customs of defense, and so on. In all these ways the evolutionary laws concerning culture are connected with the evolutionary laws concerning the biology which the traditions "reflect." A tradition may thus come to fulfil the function of a general adaptation. The vague custom of cooperation, which we spoke of a moment ago, will have effects which are only connected with societies in general, not the more special effects which would be produced by some societies but not by others. Early anthropologists, in their attack on such analogies, do not allow for the plasticity of traditions: they assume that every custom has the rigidity that a genetic imperative would have. This is not the case, and a malleable tradition may well have a utility which is general.

We may give somewhat more precision to the above account of the nature of misunderstanding, and extend it to symbolic exchange in general. We find sometimes that, IN ORDINARY DISCOURSE, a word or gesture, as sign, produces the same interpretation (or very nearly the same interpretation) as would belong to some intended referent, say, a particular feeling. In that case we say that the sign is understood correctly. In other cases the interpretative effects are not all those of one referent, but only those shared by referents of a certain class, e.g. by all feelings of joy. In this case the understanding of the sign is approximate: it comprehends the whole class. Precision and vagueness are a matter of degree. If two intended meanings differ sufficiently little, their interpretative effects will be identical; therefore no sign or symbol can convey the one as opposed to the other; this sets a bound to the clarity of communication. On the other hand, the interpretative effects of a number of sufficiently disparate meanings will have nothing discoverable in common; hence a symbol which aims at universal application, such as "beauty" for example, will have to be devoid of definite interpretative effects, and therefore of unambiguous content. In practice, this is not the case: such symbols have CONVENTIONAL associations, the negotiation of which constitutes the substance of social intercourse.

In order to define the "resilience" of a system, we have to take account both of its apparent multiplicity of components, and of its latent points of failure. If there were such a thing as a purely robust network, without any vulnerability whatever, it would be destitute of fragility. But according to the engineer's principle, the interconnected elements in an infrastructure, at least, are derived from simpler, more fragile parts—except possibly in very rare exceptional cases. Often, in such instances as our conception of a city's power grid or of a nondescript data center, a system is not derived from one prototype, but from many; when this happens, the complexity is illusory, and obscures the junctures at which the various subsystems critically depend. To arrive at the stability of the whole in such a case, we observe that there are certain respects, notably cascading effects, in which the failures of networks resemble those of their constituent parts. If we find, in a given case, that our intricate system, say, of a municipal water supply, has those cascading vulnerabilities which all utilities would have, but not those belonging to any special utility or kind of service, we may say that our system exemplifies "infrastructure" in general. If it has all the dependencies appropriate to electrical grids but no others, we shall say it exemplifies a "power network"; while if it has all the dependencies appropriate to one particular metropolitan hub, it will represent that hub, however seamless it may be as an operation. The fragility of an infrastructure, according to this analysis, is constituted by a combination of interdependence and concealed stress. It is not a sharp or definite conception, and in many cases it will be impossible to decide with any certainty where a system will fail. I think this lies in the nature of complex things, and not in defective observation.

The nature of a memory, unlike that of a sensation, is wholly constituted by narrative causal laws, and not in any degree by immediacy (except in exceptional cases). The recollection "childhood" bears no resemblance to a raw feeling, but its effects, like those of a sensation of joy, resemble the effects of an actual event in certain respects. It is much easier to say definitely what a memory means than what a sensation means, since memories, however they originated, have been shaped in later times for the purpose of having coherence, and men have been engaged for ages in giving increased precision to the narratives of their past. But although it is easier to say what a memory means than what a sensation means, the relation which constitutes personal significance is much the same in both cases. A memory, like a sensation, has the same associations as its narrative meaning has. In addition to other associations, it is associated with sensations of its origin, so that the memory tends to call up the sensation and the sensation tends to call up the memory. But this association is not essential to the intelligent use of recollection. If a memory has the right associations with other experiences, we shall be able to employ it correctly, and understand its employment by others, even if it evokes no immediate feeling. The theoretical understanding of memory involves only the power of associating it correctly with other recollections; the practical understanding involves associations with other mental constructs.

In the first place, there is no difficulty in producing a corporate action, whereas an individual member's volition cannot always be brought into existence at will, and when it comes it often contains much irrelevant personal motive. In the second place, much of a corporation's functioning is concerned with abstract purposes which do not readily lend themselves to individual embodiment, and are apt to be falsely conceived if we insist upon finding persons that may be supposed to represent them. The corporate entity is always concrete and legal, however abstract its charter may be, and thus by the help of this legal fiction we are able to dwell on collective enterprises in a way which would otherwise be impossible. In the third place, two instances of the same corporate form are so similar that neither has a history not capable of being shared by the other. Two instances of the incorporated "company" are much more alike than (say) a partnership and a sole proprietorship; hence the legal "company" makes it much easier to think about commercial bodies in general. When a number of persons have a common enterprise which is important but not obvious, the invention of a corporate form for the common enterprise helps us to remember it and to think of the whole set of functions that possess it. But it is unnecessary to prolong the catalogue of the uses of incorporation in commerce.

At the same time, it is possible to conceive of a self-sufficient cosmos by means of logical necessity, and it is important, sometimes, to check purely theological speculation by reference to what it implies. In cosmology especially the tyranny of the causal principle is dangerous, and we have to be on our guard against assuming that causation is the key to ontology, or that the structure of an explanation corresponds at all accurately with the structure of the totality that it describes. Some have maintained that all Western cosmology since Aquinas has been dominated by the fact that the cosmologists reasoned within a theistic framework, and therefore supposed the world, like the artifacts they were used to, necessarily requiring a designer and an initial impetus. When we come to the consideration of contingency and necessity, we shall see how necessary it is to avoid assuming too close a parallelism between existence and the causal chains which purport to explain it. Against such errors, the only safeguard is to be able, once in a way, to discard causation for a moment and contemplate the whole more directly through the principle of sufficient reason. Most serious advances in cosmological thought result from some such comparatively direct contemplation of the given totality. But the outcome has to be expressed in propositions if it is to be communicable. Those who have a relatively direct apprehension of the universe’s self-containment are often incapable of translating their apprehension into systematic argument, while those who possess the argumentative skill have usually lost the apprehension. It is partly for this reason that the highest cosmological insight is so rare: it requires a combination of rational grasp with metaphysical rigor which is hard to achieve, and too quickly lost in the few who have for a moment achieved it.

Taken as a problem in economics, the answer is, of course, that absolutely nothing in the way of systemic fragility is inferable from the mere fact that we can operate efficiently networks of which the function is opaque. It is clear that a sufficiently ingenious planner could manufacture a supply chain moved by market signals which, whenever a shortage appeared in its vicinity, would display, "There is a deficit," and when a surplus appeared would adjust prices accordingly. The act of displaying "There is a deficit," and the act of adjusting prices, would in such a case be equally automatic. Smooth operation does not of itself afford any better evidence of underlying risk than the performance of any other set of organizationally useful processes, such as those of distribution or exchange. All that is inferable from seamless function is that two instances of a disruption, even when they differ very greatly, may cause the failure of two instances of the same component which only differ very slightly. As we saw in the preceding analysis, the network "node" is reliable, partly, because two instances of this function are much more similar than (say) a local warehouse and a transoceanic container ship. The integration of systems is thus a method of substituting for two contingencies which differ widely, in spite of being instances of the same vulnerability, two other contingencies which differ very little, and which are also instances of a universal, namely the indicator of the previous fragility. Thus, so far as economics is concerned, we are entirely free to adopt any theory as to systemic collapse which empirical observation may recommend.

By observing how intelligence becomes general, we may the better judge how minds are made so.
