And here it is to be noted that I do not deny absolutely there are general intelligences, but only that there are any BIOLOGICALLY exclusive general intelligences; for, in the arguments we have examined wherein there is mention of mental superiority, it is always supposed that it is formed by biological necessity, after the manner set forth in common doctrines. Now, if we will annex a meaning to our terms, and reason only from what we can demonstrate, I believe we shall acknowledge that an intelligence which, considered in its substrate, is particular, becomes general by being made to represent or stand for all other particular intelligences of the same functional sort. To make this plain by an example, suppose a philosopher is demonstrating the method of achieving a cognitive operation. He describes, for instance, a biological brain of a certain complexity: this, which in itself is a particular implementation, is nevertheless with regard to its operational capacity general, since, as it is there considered, it represents all particular implementations whatsoever; so that what is true of it is true of all implementations, or, in other words, of an intelligence in general. And, as THAT PARTICULAR IMPLEMENTATION becomes general by being made a token, so the CONCEPT 'mind,' which taken materially is particular, by being a functional token is made general. And as the former owes its generality not to its being the token of an abstract or privileged mind, but of all particular thinking systems that may possibly exist, so the latter must be thought to derive its generality from the same cause, namely, the various particular substrates which it indifferently instantiates.

Whether others, in their symbolic communications, possess this remarkable capacity for perfect mutual understanding, they best can tell: for myself, I dare be confident I have it not. I find, indeed, I have indeed a faculty of interpreting, or representing to myself, the intended meanings of those particular signs I have encountered, and of variously combining and separating their possible senses. I can interpret a statement as ironic, or the opening part of a message joined to the conclusion of another. I can consider the word, the gesture, the inflection, each by itself abstracted or separated from the full context of the exchange. But, then, whatever word or gesture I interpret, it must carry some particular association and nuance. Likewise the meaning of a sentence that I frame to myself must be either literal or metaphorical, precise or vague, generous or unkind. I cannot by any effort of thought conceive the perfectly transparent exchange above described. And it is equally impossible for me to form the idea of pure communication distinct from the symbols conveying it, and which is neither clear nor obscure, direct nor implied; and the like may be said of all other ideal linguistic transactions whatsoever. To be plain, I own myself able to achieve comprehension in one sense, as when I grasp some particular elements of meaning separated from others, with which, though they are united in some utterance, yet it is possible they may really be intended without them. But I deny that I can abstract from one another, or conceive separately, those aspects of symbolic value which it is impossible should exist so isolated; or that I can frame a notion of flawless exchange, by abstracting from imperfect instances in the manner aforesaid—which last are the two proper acceptations of MISUNDERSTANDING. And there is ground to think most men will acknowledge themselves to be in my case. The generality of men which are simple and illiterate never pretend to PERFECT COMMUNICATION. It is said it is difficult and not to be attained without pains and study; we may therefore reasonably conclude that, if such there be, it is confined only to the theoretical.

There is, however, another way of distinguishing between the latent, the specific and the structural, and this is not by their appearance, but by the disruption which they produce. A system, for example, may be said to be latent when it is susceptible to a number of different pressures, but to each as singular events; the prosperity of a decade, for example, is latent: it is always assumed to withstand ordinary strains, but there are many strains to each of which it ultimately succumbs.* The concept "crisis," on the other hand, is structural. We speak of "This is a recession," but we do not say "This is crisis," but "This is a crisis." Thus we may say that a condition embodies a latent flaw when its manifestations are appropriate to an incident, but are the same for various similar incidents, while a condition embodies a structural flaw when its manifestations are different from those appropriate to mere incidents. In what this difference consists it is, however, not easy to say. I am inclined to think that it consists merely in the recognition that no one incident is causative, so that what distinguishes a structural limit from a latent flaw is merely the presence of a certain accompanying realization. If this view is correct, a structural limit differs from a latent one in a way analogous to that in which a systemic failure differs from a cyclical downturn. There also we found that the difference consists merely of the fact that a systemic failure is accompanied by a belief, in this case as to the fundamental.

The invention of writing in the above account, which is essentially the same as that of the early historians, does not wholly agree with modern archaeology, although it comes nearer to agreement than does the view of those who believe that there are in civilization single events which can be called decisive revolutions. The way in which the traditional view is inadequate is chiefly in the fact that written records are as a rule not of one definite origin, but of a number of related similar origins. On this subject Goody has written well. In "The Domestication of the Savage Mind," pp. 217 ff., discussing the effect of repeated similar inscriptions in producing and modifying our traditions, he says: "We choose a case of cultural transmission whose existence we can perceive for ourselves by examination, and seek to recover the social picture of our earliest city in its absence, and have thus a pure historical record before us. At first it may seem to us that a determinate quite concrete account becomes manifest in us, but just when we are concerned with a society with which we are in constant contact, we shall find that the recovered record has something so to speak generalized. It is something like those composite photographs which seek to display what is general about a type by combining a great number of photographs of different artifacts over each other on one plate. In our opinion, the generalizations happen by the homophonic working of different accounts of the same event which we have come across in the most different conditions and situations, once fragmentary, once complete, once celebratory, once critical, once in this script, and once in that. As soon as we do not let the whole series of transmissions resound in us uniformly, but give our attention to one particular moment out of the many... this particular historical stimulus at once overbalances its simultaneously roused predecessors and successors, and we perceive the event in question with concrete definiteness in that particular situation." A little later he says: "The result is--at least in literate societies, but probably also in the higher civilizations--the development of a sort of CULTURAL abstraction. Documentary homophony gives us, without the addition of other processes of thought, a picture of our ancestor Y which is in a certain sense abstract, not the concrete in any one situation, but Y cut loose from any particular point of time. If the circle of recovered traces is drawn even more widely, abstract pictures of a higher order appear: for instance, a scribe or a king. In my opinion, the first form of abstract institutions in general is based upon such abstract pictures. The cultural abstraction which takes place in the above described manner is a predecessor of purely historical abstraction. It is by no means a monopoly of the ancient world, but shows itself in various ways also among the more highly organized societies." The same subject is treated in more detail in Chapter xvi of "The Logic of Writing and the Organization of Society," but what is said there adds nothing vital to what is contained in the above quotations.

It is necessary, however, to distinguish between the chaotic and the structured. So long as we are content with the notion of a primordial gas cloud, we MAY get no farther than the chaotic. The question whether this notion takes us to the structured or not depends, I think, upon the question whether, in addition to the generalized conception of cosmic material, we have also particular conceptions of some of the processes out of which it is compounded. Suppose, for example, that on a number of occasions you had considered one local density fluctuation, and that you did not know whether this one was significant or trivial on the different occasions. Suppose that in the end you had an abstract theoretical conception of the different gravitational collapses presented by the matter on different scales, but no clear conception of any one of the single progressions. In that case your conception would be chaotic. If, on the other hand, you have, in addition to the generalized conception, particular conceptions of the several progressions, sufficiently clear to be recognized as distinct, and as instances of the generalized model, you will then not feel the generalized model to be adequate to any one particular progression, and you will be able to make it function as a structural principle rather than a chaotic notion. If this view is correct, no new structural principle needs to be added to the generalized conception. What needs to be added is particular progressions compared and contrasted with the generalized conception. So far as I can judge by cosmological observation, this does occur in practice. Take for example the instance of a spiral galaxy. Unless we make some special effort of analysis, the formation is likely to come before us with an average description, very blurred and chaotic, but we can at will recall how a galactic structure appeared in some special simulation when it was influenced by rotation or collisions or dark matter, and this enables us to realize the generalized character of the chaotic conception.

It should also be said that our gestures even of quite simple intentions have always a greater or a less degree of ambiguity. That is to say, the intention might have varied within certain limits without causing our gesture to vary recognizably. To arrive at the abstract it is necessary that we should be able to contrast it with a number of relatively precise symbols or signs for concrete objects; so long as all our signals and signs are ambiguous, we cannot arrive at the contrast by which the abstract is defined. This is the justification for the view which I have long maintained, viz. that conceptual thought progresses from the indeterminate to the determinate, and that the symbolic appears earlier than either the concrete or the abstract.

I think the view which I have been advocating, to the effect that a mode of production is distinguished from a mere technique by the presence of a social relation, is also that intended by Marx when he says (op. cit., p. 92): "The economic base is never, the social formation is always, a totality. We know that for economists (formerly at any rate) the market is the simple and primitive element; next comes the institution, uniting two or several interests; then ideology, combining two or several institutions. For the materialists, on the contrary, production is the fundamental act; the social relation is the result of labor (cooperative or antagonistic), of forces with exclusion of superstructures.

I am inclined to think that similar remarks apply to the general idea of "carbon-based consciousness," concerning which there has been much controversy. The advocates of carbon-based consciousness are not contending merely that there can be thinking which is purely biological; they are contending that there can be thinking which proceeds neither in silicon nor in carbon. My own feeling is that they have rashly assumed the presence of a unique essence in cases where material organization has rendered such an essence unnecessary. When engineers experimented with circuits in machines, they found that the associations established were between an electrical stimulus and a logical output (not the ghost of it), without the need of supposing any non-physical intermediary (op. cit., p. 100 ff.). The same thing, it seems to me, applies to ourselves. A certain neural situation produces in us a certain mental event. Sometimes this event consists in forming beliefs. Prejudice leads us to suppose that between the neural stimulus and the formation of the belief a process of carbon-based magic must have intervened, but there seems no good reason for such a supposition. Any systematic operation, such as calculating or remembering, may be performed on the appropriate occasion, without any need of a carbon substrate, and the same seems to be true of a painfully large proportion of our cognition. What applies to biological brains applies of course equally to the silicon systems which are not biological. I remain, therefore, entirely unconvinced that there is any such phenomenon as thinking which consists neither of silicon nor of carbon, or that "vitalism" has to be added to transistors and neurons as part of the material out of which mental phenomena are built.

In addition to external observable actions (including the expression of intentions), there is also the generic understanding produced by the inference, or, in common parlance, empathy, of a number of similar social cues. This understanding is imprecise so long as the multiplicity of its antecedents is not recognized, but becomes systematic when it exists alongside of the more specific recognitions of its instances, and is knowingly contrasted with them. In this case we find again, as we found when we were discussing social cognition in general in the preceding analysis, that conscious attribution is not logically necessary in order to account for observable conduct, i.e. in this case successful interaction. Successful interaction could exist as a pragmatic adjustment, without any accompaniment of explicit inference, and this conclusion applies to acts of which the motive is cooperative, just as much as to acts of which the motive is deceptively particular. If this conclusion is valid, it follows that a purely behavioural account, which eschews mentalistic postulates, is capable of being an independent explanation, and of accounting for all that part of the conduct of other agents which is commonly regarded as evidence that they strategize. It must be admitted that this conclusion considerably weakens the reliance which can be placed upon introspective intuition. It must be accepted simply on account of the fact that we seem to apprehend it, not on account of its supposed necessity for explaining the data of external social commerce.

The question of the nature of our engagement with digital tools is much affected by our view as to the general nature of the relation of habit to its origin. If we adopt the view of certain theorists, according to which all mental habit has essential reference to a designed object, it is then natural to suppose that there is some peculiar kind of cognitive operation of which the object is a technological system, as opposed to a natural environment. According to this view, a particular screen can be observed or remembered, while the universal "interface" is apprehended. But this whole manner of viewing our dealings with devices has to be abandoned when the relation of a mental habit to its "cause" is regarded as merely indirect and cumulative, which is the view that we have adopted. The habitual action is, of course, always particular, and the question as to what it "signifies" (in case it signifies anything) is one which cannot be settled by merely examining the intrinsic character of the action, but only by knowing its developmental history in the case of the person concerned. To say that a certain behavior "signifies" a technological influence as opposed to either a biological or a social one, is to say something exceedingly complex. A user will behave in a certain manner whenever he encounters a notification, even if the alert is derived from a trivial source. That is to say, any environment containing an instance of the universal "demand for attention" produces closely similar behaviour in the user, but we do not say that the user is conscious of this pattern. There is equally little reason to regard a person as conscious of the same pattern, because under the same circumstances he can react by reaching for his device. This reaction, like that of the user, is merely closely similar on different occasions where the environment affords instances of the same universal. Behaviors of which the logical origin is systemic can therefore be performed habitually, without anything that could be called awareness of their shaping. Such awareness in the only sense in which it can be said to exist is a matter of reflective judgment consisting in the observation of routines and interruptions. A technological influence never appears before the mind as a single object in the sort of way in which something used appears. I think a sociological argument could be produced to show that such influences are part of the structure of modern life, but they are an inferred part, not a part of our immediate experience. What exists in us consists of various factors, some open to external observation, others only visible to introspection. The factors open to external observation are primarily habits, having the peculiarity that very similar reactions are produced by stimuli which are in many respects very different from each other. Of this the reaction of the user to the ping of a message is an instance, and so is the reaction of the person who feels anxiety without his device under the same circumstances. The gestural reaction is, of course, the most important from the point of view of what may be called adaptation to systems. A person who can always unlock his phone when he feels a moment of pause may be said, in a certain sense, to understand the function of the device, and in that sense to have knowledge of the universal "digital mediation." But there is, of course, a further stage reached by the critic in which he not merely reacts with the habitual gesture, but sets to work to discover what it is in the design that causes in him this almost identical reaction on different occasions. This further stage consists in knowledge of conveniences and constraints: conveniences which are necessary to the utility of the device, and constraints which are compatible with it. Our knowledge of these conveniences and constraints is never exhaustive, and therefore our knowledge of the meaning of a technological habit is never complete.

This, at any rate, is the conclusion to which we are forced, so long as, with the materialists, we accept common-sense views of the mental world. But if, as I have urged, the conscious experience itself, as known, is infected through and through with objectivity, if, as the theory of cognitive science suggests, the mental universe contains the uniformity of causal processes which we have been accustomed to regard as distinctively physical, then we are brought back by this different road to the necessity for dismissing difficulties which are in an important sense illusory. And it is the illusory nature of metaphysical qualia which causes much of the philosophers' preoccupation with them.

For my part I am unable to attach as much importance to this conclusion as many cosmologists do. The reasoning employed appears to me hardly to fulfil the conditions of scientific deduction. Broadly speaking, what is done is, that a set of observations are made of various stellar systems, their features are recorded, and likewise the inferred accounts, based upon probability, of the processes of formation which led them to possess those features. Much too much reliance seems to me to be placed upon the completeness of these inferences. On statistical inference as a method I have spoken earlier. I am not prepared, like certain strict necessitarians, to reject it wholly, but I do consider that it is exceedingly fallible and quite peculiarly liable to distortion in accordance with preconceived hope. It is like depending upon the report of a nearsighted person as to what he sees shining in the heavens at a moment when he is firmly convinced that a comet is sure to appear. If every observer were nearsighted and obsessed with beliefs as to what was going to be visible, we might have to make the best of such testimony, but we should need to correct its errors by taking care to collect the simultaneous evidence of people with the most divergent expectations. There is no evidence that this was done in the calculations in question, nor indeed that the influence of hope in distorting the inference was at all adequately recognized. I feel convinced that if a strict necessitarian had been one of the interpreters of the data, he would have drawn conclusions totally different from those recorded in the papers in question. Sagan quotes an opinion of Monod on these speculations, which appears to me thoroughly justified. "These arguments," he says, "are not arguments at all in the sense of a scientific methodology; they are counterfeit arguments, that seem rigorous simply because they are ordinarily performed in an astrophysical institute, and involve the co-operation of two disciplines, which purport to be observation and theory. In reality, they are as unmethodical as possible; they possess none of the special features by which we distinguish the inferences of experimental cosmology from the casual inferences of everyday curiosity."* Sagan, of course, dissents from this opinion, but I cannot see that his reasons for dissent are adequate. My doubts are only increased by the fact that Drake at any rate used trained astrophysicists as his collaborators. A trained astrophysicist is, of course, supposed to have acquired the habit of impartiality, but he is at least equally likely to have acquired a habit of seeing what his hopes require. We may take Drake's "Equation" to illustrate the kind of results arrived at by such methods. Drake says: "We ask ourselves the general question: 'WHAT FACTORS GOVERN THE PREVALENCE OF LIFE?' Then we do not at all attempt a preliminary determination of the concept 'life,' but choose for analysis only such factors as everyone would describe as determinants of prevalence." The most important thing in the calculation, he says, is "the probability that..." which he calls a factor. It is, he says, factors in this sense that are essential to the equation. The equation, he maintains, does not need concrete examples or sensuous confirmations. "I assert rather that in principle every variable can be estimated distinctly, without any help from empirical confirmation (Bestätigungshilfen). Every individual value for the rate of stellar formation in the galaxy that figures in my model I can think with complete distinctness non-empirically (unempirisch), provided it is possible that the value should be given to me in another manner than by the help of observations. How that is possible we shall see later." What he calls a factor (Faktor) cannot be reduced, according to him, to other physical occurrences. He maintains that factors consist for the most part of plausible guesses. It is clearly essential to the interest of this theory that the factor or guess alluded to by Drake should not need to be expressed in definite numbers, for if it is expressed in definite numbers it is immediately capable of being dealt with on the lines with which the statisticians have familiarized us. It is clear also that the supposed absence of precise values rests solely upon the inferential testimony of the theorists involved. I cannot think that there is sufficient certainty of their reliability in this negative observation to make us accept a difficult and revolutionary view of cosmic habitability, merely because they have failed to observe the presence of stringent requirements or their equivalent in their calculations. I think it far more likely, especially in view of the fact that the persons concerned were highly intelligent, that we are concerned with telescoped processes, in which optimism has caused a great many intermediate steps to be elided or to be passed over so quickly as to escape scrutiny.

We must distinguish between recording and what is recorded. I may record that Sargon ruled Akkad, that all harvests were abundant, that taxes amounted to ten percent, or that the Nile flooded in April; in all these cases the recording is just the same, and only the contents recorded are different. I may preserve a merchant's contract, a king's decree, or a priest's astronomical observation. In all these cases the act of written preservation is just the same, and only what is preserved differs. Exactly similar remarks apply to transmission. Mere inscription, preservation and transmission are forms of recording; all three are different from what is recorded, and each has a constant character which is independent of what is recorded.

In Lecture I we criticized the analysis of a machine into hardware, software and behavior. But our inquiry into pain contains three very similar elements, namely the feeling, what is felt and the physical cause. The objections to the hardware (in the case of machines) are not valid against the feeling in the case of pain, because the feeling is an actual subjective experience, not something inferred, like the hardware. But it is necessary first to complete our preliminary distinctions, and then to examine the concept of a machine. After that, we shall be in a position to return to the question as to what constitutes feeling.

Just as doctrines are characterized by authority, so inquiries are characterized by progress or stagnation. And just as authority consists in relation to the institution upheld, so progress and stagnation consist in relation to something that lies outside the inquiry. You may accept that such-and-such a principle is eternally valid. The occasion arises, and your principle endures or does not endure; according to the outcome, your acceptance was progressive or stagnant. You may accept that celestial bodies revolve around the Earth; in this case also there is a demonstration which makes your acceptance stagnant. You may accept that combustion is explained by phlogiston, or that it is explained by oxidation. In the one case your acceptance is progressive, in the other stagnant; in either case its progress or stagnation depends upon the experiments of Lavoisier, not upon anything present or under your control. What makes an acceptance progressive or stagnant I call a "verification." The particular verification that makes a given acceptance progressive or stagnant I call its "corroboration," and the relation of the acceptance to its corroboration I call the "grounding" or the "evidential grounding" of the acceptance. Thus, if I accept that planetary orbits are elliptical, the "corroboration" of my acceptance is Kepler's actual observations, and the "grounding" of my acceptance is the relation between my acceptance and the observations--that relation, namely, in virtue of which the observations make my acceptance progressive (or, in another case, stagnant). "Grounding" of acceptances differs from "authority" of doctrines in various ways, but especially in the fact that it is of two kinds, "sound" grounding and "unsound" grounding. The progress or stagnation of an acceptance does not depend upon anything intrinsic to the acceptance, but upon the nature of its relation to its corroboration. The intrinsic nature of acceptance can be treated without reference to what makes it progressive or stagnant. In the remainder of the present discourse I shall ignore progress and stagnation, which will be the subject of Discourse XIII. It is the intrinsic nature of acceptance that will concern us to-day.

What is remembered, and the remembering, must both consist of present occurrences in the rememberer, no matter what may be the origin of the memory. Suppose I remember, for example, "that I tasted a ripe peach yesterday." The origin of my memory is a sensation which occurred recently, which I directly experienced but do not now sense. This sensation itself is not in my mind when I remember that it occurred. It is not correct to say that I am remembering the actual sensation; what I am remembering is something now in my mind, something related to the sensation (in a way which we shall investigate in due course), but obviously not to be confounded with the sensation, since the sensation is not occurring now but the remembering is. What a man is remembering at a given moment is wholly determinate if we know the contents of his mind at that moment; but the tasting of the peach was an immediate physiological event, which is distinct from the present contents of every present mind. What is remembered, however vivid it may be, is not the actual fact that makes the memory accurate, but a present event related to the fact. This present event, which is what is remembered, I shall call the "narrative" of the memory. We have already had occasion to notice the distinction between narrative and origin in the case of sensory memories, where the narrative is "this was experienced" and the origin is the past sensation.

The objective reference of a mathematical proposition is connected with the fact that all or some of the constituents of its form have empirical correlates. If I say "the quadratic equation yields two roots," a person who knows the meaning of the three terms composing my statement knows as much as can be known about the nature of the observation which would make my statement valid. It is clear that the objective reference of a mathematical structure is, in general, in some way derivative from the meanings of the symbols or diagrams that occur in its formulation. There are, however, certain complications which must be borne in mind. In the first place, it might be contended that a geometrical diagram acquires meaning only through the observational test, which would seem, at least in the case of physics, to make empirical confirmation more primitive than the meaning of axioms. In the second place, it is a very singular thing that structure, which is single, should generate empirical reference, which is dual, namely verified and falsified. This is one of the facts which any theory of mathematical application must explain if it is to be satisfactory.

(4) Between subjective experience and physical process there is sometimes a very wide gulf, for example in the case of "the redness of a sunset." This gulf may, when it is first perceived, give us a feeling that we cannot really "explain" anything about the inner world. All we can "report," it may be said, is what is now in our awareness. If neural firings and qualia cannot be jointly in our consciousness, it might seem as though we must remain cut off from understanding of them. I shall not now deal at length with this feeling, since it is necessary first to define "evidence," which cannot be done yet. But I will say, as a preliminary answer, that the feeling assumes an ideal of introspection which I believe to be quite mistaken. It assumes, if it is thought out, something like the infallible transparency of mind to itself. These two are often said to be combined into a unity by the fact of acquaintance; hence when this unity is plainly absent, it may seem as if there were no genuine explanation. For my part, I think such theories and feelings wholly mistaken: I believe introspection to be a very partial and limited faculty, incapable of exhaustive description, dependent upon cognitive architecture, and involving no more duality than there is between a thermometer and the heat which it indicates. I shall return to this question on a later occasion; for the moment these provisional remarks must suffice.

Language sometimes conceals the complexity of a system. We say that a computer processes information, and it might seem as if information formed the whole content of the operation. But what is really processed is that information is organized, which is very far from being simple. Similarly, when a machine has a data-structure with a functional purpose, the purpose is "this organizes," in the sense explained in the preceding chapter; and "this organizes" is not simple. In like manner all cases where the mechanism of a system seems simple at first sight will be found, on examination, to confirm the view that the mechanism is always complex.

The first thing to notice about what is conveyed, i.e. about the substance of a communication, is that it is always approximate: We assert that a certain sign denotes a certain object, or a certain relation to another sign, or that it signified or will signify (in the sense discussed at the end of Lecture IX); or we may assert that all the instances of a certain symbol have a certain denotation, or that a certain meaning sometimes occurs among the uses of a symbol; or we may assert that if one symbol is employed, another will be inferred (for example, "if I say 'bank' you may think of money"), or we may assert that a meaning does not transfer, or did not or will not transfer (for example, "my tone was not sarcastic"); or that one of two interpretations must be accepted (for example, "either you take my words literally, or you grasp my intended irony"). The catalogue of the sorts of distortions we may encounter is infinite, but all of them are inevitable.

We may take first induction, in either of the forms "the future will resemble the past" or "what has held always will hold again." In either case, an unproved postulate is a constituent. For example, you observe the sunrise, and you say to yourself "daily." Here the observation and the expectation "daily" are both constituents of your inference; there is also a relation between them, expressed by "will" in the proposition "the sun will rise." As soon as your act of induction is completed by the occurrence of the belief "daily," your reasoning proceeds: you predict if you seek regularity, or cease to predict if you admit chaos. In this case the content of your assumption is an experience (the sequence) and a principle (uniformity) related in a way which may be called presupposition.

The same moment may bring into your mind the temporal image of a commencement, instead of the word "beginning." In this case your conception consists of a present instant and an image suitably related. Conceptions of this class are what are called "intuitions of temporality." As we saw in earlier discussions, the notions associated with a temporal point often come with such spontaneity and force that the unsophisticated do not distinguish them from the point itself; it is only the metaphysician or the skilled logician who is aware of the large conceptual element that is added to the instant to make a temporal series. It may be objected that what is added consists merely of notions without conviction. This is no doubt sometimes the case, but is certainly sometimes not the case. That conviction always occurs in temporal reasoning as opposed to mere chronology it is not necessary for us to maintain; it is enough for our purposes to note that it sometimes occurs, and that when it does, the content of our conviction consists of a present instant and an image suitably related.

The more sophisticated notions of temporal inception tend to consist only of paradoxes. Often intuitions of various kinds accompany them, but they are apt to be misleading, and to form no part of what is logically entailed. For example, in contemplating a first moment, you are likely to have vague impressions of metaphors you have encountered of a cosmic clock starting, a divine finger initiating motion, a blank canvas receiving its first mark, and so on; but none of these form part of your understanding that a beginning implies a preceding void. The only conceptions that form an actual part of such reasoning are, as a rule, conceptions of definitions. And these definitions, for the reasons considered in metaphysical inquiry, cannot be granted any coherence, when, as is often, if not invariably, the case, they demand a state of time before time itself.

It is impossible for a structure to consist of matter alone, except when, as in the case of galaxies, the matter has properties which make it a system possessed of order. The reason is that gravitational coherence is of the essence of structure, and gravitational coherence is derived from interaction. When I speak of a structure consisting partly of matter and partly of voids, I do not mean to deny that the voids, when they are not mere emptiness, are physical, but that they occur as features, not (so to speak) in their own right. To revert to the cloud of the nebula, when you observe it and say "spiral," the cloud and the form are both phenomena (if you actually discern the form), but the cloud is part of the process which makes your description true, whereas the form is not part of this process. It is the PATTERN of the form "spiral," not the actual shape, that forms part of the process which is the objective of your description. Thus the form occurs in the observation as a representation, in virtue of its pattern, whereas the cloud enters into both the observation and its objective. It is this that distinguishes the occurrence of forms as representations from the occurrence of phenomena in their own right: the objective contains the phenomena that occur in their own right, but contains only the patterns of the forms that occur as representations.

It may be said that even in this very simple colony the functional differentiation of the cell-units is not quite so isolated as that of the organelle-content, that specialists have a wealth of particular capacities which are compromised when autonomy is preserved, that the nutrient-processing cell is not a mere processor in the abstract, but a cell of a certain efficiency and scope, not merely adjacent to the structural cell, but a specific interval away, and so on. In reply, it may be admitted at once that there is, as a rule, a certain amount of truth in the objection. But two points may be urged to minimize its force. First, specializations do not, as a rule, have that wealth of independent operation that would make it IMPOSSIBLE to integrate them fully into a system. They are limited and interdependent: a finite set of signals, though perhaps a complex set, would convey at least their ESSENTIAL directives. For--and this is our second point--specializations enter into the function of a colony through the fact that they are capable of purpose, and their purpose does not, as a rule, have as much autonomy as they possess: some of their activities are usually devoid of systemic consequence. Thus it may well be possible to orchestrate by coordination all that has purpose in a specialized colony; in that case the coordinated system and the specialized unit will have exactly the same functional necessity.

The nature of a corporation, when considered in law, is the same thing (or very nearly the same thing) as what in jurisprudence is called a "legal person." A legal person is an entity (or sometimes a collection of entities) possessing the kind of attributes that can incur rights or obligations. "That a company may own property," "that a guild can be sued for damages," "that a university holds a charter in perpetuity," "that all incorporated bodies are immortal," are legal facts. Not any collection of individuals is a legal person, but only such collections as have "standing," or, in our terminology, "corporate personality." Given the articles of association, and the statutes of incorporation, the status of a corporation is determinate. This is the reason why we can recognize a firm we never encountered before. You probably never encountered before the entity "that the manufacturers of Wessex habitually produce galvanized widgets for the market," but there is no difficulty in recognizing the entity. The question of the relation between the identity of the corporation and the identities of the separate members is difficult, and I shall not pursue it now; I brought it up solely as being illustrative of the nature of legal persons.

We may extend the term "communication" so as to cover the signal-contents of interactions consisting of gestures. Thus, in the case of warning a group in which the predator is to the left of the water, when we convey the signal-content the message will consist of the gesture for danger on the left together with the gesture for refuge on the right. We will distinguish messages of this kind as "gesture-messages" and messages in sounds as "sound-messages." We may identify communication in general with the contents of actual and possible warnings, and we may say that it is these transmissions that are advantageous or disadvantageous. In biology we are concerned with transmissions rather than specific interactions, since biology is not interested in what creatures do in fact signal, but only in the conditions which determine the success or failure of possible warnings. Whenever possible, except when actual interactions are in question, it is generally a simplification to deal with transmissions.

To begin with, there are various different attitudes that may be taken towards the same proposition. Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that you entertain the notion of a simulated reality. You may accept it while you are reading a treatise on computation; doubt it as you reflect on the nature of qualia; feel curiosity as to its plausibility when questioned as to your intuitions about consciousness; merely consider the hypothesis, without connecting it with any metaphysical commitment, when you are engaged in idle speculation; desire it if you are optimistic about artificial minds, or feel aversion for it if you are committed to biological necessity. Suppose, for the sake of definiteness, that the proposition is "a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants." Then you have the following attitudes: "I believe a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants"; "I doubt a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants"; "Could a simulated world produce genuinely conscious inhabitants?" "A simulated world producing conscious inhabitants: well, what follows from it?" "I hope a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants, for it would expand the realm of mind"; "I fear a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants, and their suffering might be an ethical abyss." I do not suggest that this is a list of all possible attitudes on the subject; I say only that they are different attitudes, all concerned with the one proposition "a simulated world could produce genuinely conscious inhabitants.

It might be objected to the theory that many forms of mental activity which we certainly practice do not call for any symbolic expression. I engage in contemplating that time is relative, that justice is an ideal, that numbers are abstract entities, and so on; and at first sight it seems obvious that such contemplations, as a rule, do not call for any articulation on my part. But when we investigate the matter more closely, it becomes more doubtful. To begin with, we must distinguish thought as a mere DISPOSITION from actual active thinking. We speak as if we always contemplated that justice is an ideal, but that only means that we are always ready to contemplate it when the subject comes up. The phenomenon we are concerned to analyse is the active thought, not the permanent disposition. Now, what are the occasions when we actively think that numbers are abstract entities? Primarily: instruction, when we perform the symbolic act of writing them down; discussion, when we assert it to display our philosophical erudition; and solitary reflection, when we are engaged in showing what pure reasoning leads to. In all these cases symbolic expressions (writing or speaking) result from our thought.

It would seem that the sensation of control is more primitive than actual governance, and may well ante-date complex institutions. There is no reason why the feeling of agency, accompanied by that very simple conviction which we decided to be the essence of command, should not have occurred before systemic understanding arose; indeed, it would be rash to assert positively that this sort of delusion does not occur among the most sophisticated administrators. Our more elementary assumptions, notably those that are added to a minor success to make mastery, often remain at the level of intuition. For example, most of the mechanical devices in our daily employ rouse images of comprehension: we have a different feeling in operating a motor-car from what we have in contemplating a digital network, and the difference consists chiefly in different stimulation of our intellectual imagination. It may be said that these images of understanding are merely present, without any accompanying belief in true control; but I think this view, though sometimes correct, derives its plausibility as a general proposition from our thinking of explicit conscious analysis only. Most of our convictions of command, like most of our desires for order, are "unconscious," in the sense that we have never told ourselves that we possess them. Such convictions display themselves when the expectations that they arouse fail in any way. For example, if someone adjusts a single dial on a vast industrial machine, and it proceeds under the impression that this constitutes genuine direction; or if you issue a command to a complex bureaucracy, and it turns out to be a mere ritual gesture made to look like governance. The shock of surprise on an occasion of this kind makes us aware of the expectations that habitually enter into our interactions with systems; and such expectations must be classed as beliefs in control, in spite of the fact that we do not normally take note of them or put them into words. I remember once watching a committee chairman proposing over and over again a minor procedural change to try to exert influence on the particularly obdurate institution which he expected to respond, judging by what he saw in the reports. He must have experienced each time the sort of surprise on finding no measurable effect, which is calculated to lead in time to the adoption of the theory that systemic outcomes are only loosely connected to individual will. His expectation of efficacy, though not expressed in formal analysis, deserved, I think, to be called a belief.

We propose hypothetically to define "profit-seeking" by a different kind of causal efficacy, namely efficacy in causing organizational movements. (Organizational movements are defined as those corporate actions which are distinguished from automatic operations as involving the higher executive centres. I do not like to distinguish them by means of such notions as "purpose" or "strategy," because I do not think these notions, in any definable sense, are always applicable. Moreover, the purpose of the analogy we are examining is to be, as far as possible, biological and mechanistic, and this purpose is not achieved if we introduce such a conception as "purpose" or "strategy." Nevertheless, it is necessary for our purpose to find some way of distinguishing between organizational and automatic movements, since the results would be too paradoxical, if we were to say that automatic operations also involve profit-seeking.) According to this definition, an opportunity is said to be "profit-seeking" when it causes the corporation to act. The chemical signals perceived are the same if you observe a bacterium, "Suppose there were a glucose gradient in the immediate environment," and if the bacterium actually encounters, "There is a glucose gradient in the immediate environment." But its actions will be very different in the two cases: in the first, it shall remain inert; in the second, it is probable that it may not. It is suggested, by the analogy we are considering, that this difference of effects constitutes what is meant by saying that in the second case the bacterium engages in nutrient-seeking, while in the first case it does not. According to this view, signals or gradients are "profit-seeking" when they cause corporate movements.

But there remains the simulation which merely occurs in "processing." One may set to work to render some digital environment one has been programming, and what one renders is simulated, although it probably does not cause any genuine qualia whatever. It is true that what we simulate always MAY produce consciousness. Suppose I am invited to become architect of a virtual domain: I find the prospect plausible, and go to my terminal to write a subroutine for my new creation. At the last moment I consider philosophical zombies and all the other constructs which have failed the test of sentience; I change my mind, and log out without completing the compilation. But such incidents are rare, and cannot constitute the whole of my conviction that a simulation could be inhabited. The conclusion seems to be that, although a simulation always MAY produce consciousness if it attains sufficient complexity, it often exists actively (not as a mere abstraction) without generating any subjective experience whatever. If this is true, we cannot define consciousness by the effect of computational operations.

There is another, more empirical, ground for rejecting the view we are examining. It is evident that a molecule can be either replicative or merely stable, and that the structure is the same in both cases. We can observe a crystal forming in a solution, or merely entertain the supposition that a crystal may form. A moment ago I considered the possibility of a protein folding into an active conformation, but I do not assert that this will occur. Now, it seems evident that, since replication and stability have different consequences if one produces identical copies while the other does not, there must be some intrinsic difference between replication and stability; for if they were precisely similar, their consequences also would be precisely similar. We have seen that the difference between a molecule that replicates and one that is merely stable does not lie in the structure; therefore there must be, in one case or in both, something additional to the structure which distinguishes the occurrence of replication from the occurrence of a mere persistence of the same form. So far as the chemical argument goes, this additional element may exist only in replication, or only in stability, or there may be one sort of additional element in the case of replication, and another in the case of stability. This brings us to the second theory which we have to examine.

Let us conceive a biologist examining a strand of DNA, and taking note of nothing else. As this examination involves the existence of the genetic code, AND THE BIOLOGIST HAS NO EVIDENCE WHICH ANNULS ITS FUNCTION [Mendel's italics], he will necessarily contemplate the code as operative, nor will he be able to doubt of its efficacy, however little certain of it he may be. I deny that a scientist in so far as he observes [percipit] affirms nothing. For what is it to observe a helical structure but to affirm that the molecule [that molecule, namely] has a double form? For if the mind had nothing before it but the helical structure, it would contemplate the same as definitive, would have no cause to doubt of its primacy, nor any power of dissenting from its authority, unless the observation of the helical structure were joined to an idea which contradicted [tollit] its necessity.

If this view is correct, it follows (though the analogy’s proponents do not draw the inference) that there is no need of any specific process called “intelligent design,” and that the mere operation of selective pressures yields all that is required. The state of a system in which we merely adjust parameters, without optimizing or degrading its performance, will then appear as a sophisticated product, the result of some rival force adding to the algorithmic procedure a positive constraint which may be called regularization or non-convergence—a constraint which may be compared to that of a network about to update its weights waiting for the validation signal. Such a network, though not learning, is in a very different condition from that of a network quietly at rest. And so the system that is adjusting parameters without optimizing them will be in a state of tension, restraining the natural tendency to minimize error which it would display if nothing interfered. In this view adaptation primarily consists merely in the existence of the appropriate selective gradients without any counteracting forces.

There is a great deal to be said in favour of this view, and I have some hesitation in regarding it as inadequate. It fits admirably with the phenomena of computational equivalence and algorithmic processing, and it is recommended by the way in which it accords with our understanding of information. Carbon, silicon, and other potential substrates all seem, in this light, arbitrary and contingent rather than fundamental or privileged. Intelligence as a particular phenomenon, if it is to be defined, may be regarded, in this view, as a product of organization, a function arising from structure, a capability, not merely of THIS flesh, but of ANY-SUFFICIENTLY-COMPLEX-SYSTEM. It is not difficult to suppose that a machine could manifest the problem-solving behaviours we call thought, or the adaptive patterns we recognise as learning. But it is very difficult to suppose that such capacities are intrinsically and forever bound to the wet, biological machinery from which we first observed them.

I think it must be conceded that a mere simulation, without the addition of any substantive process that could be called "thought," is apt to have a certain cognitive power, and in this sense an unexamined simulation has the force of a mind. But although this may be true, it accounts only for some of the simplest phenomena in the region of consciousness. It will not, for example, explain self-awareness. Nor can it explain cognitions which do not issue in any proximate behavior, such as those of pure mathematics. I conclude, therefore, that there must be mental processes of the same order as those of biological brains, although phenomena closely analogous to those of mind can be produced by mere uncontradicted algorithms.

I come now to the view of ideology which I wish to advocate. It seems to me that there are at least three kinds of ideological function, namely justification, anticipation and passive reflection. Each of these I regard as constituted by a certain mental habit or complex of assumptions, attached to the material conditions served. We may illustrate by an example. Suppose I am perceiving, by means of notions, not facts, that an economic arrangement is natural. We have here two interrelated elements, namely the justification and the material condition. The justification consists of images of (say) the apparent fairness of markets, the sensation of inevitability, the murmur of consensus, interrelated, roughly, as the experiences would be if it were ordained. Thus the justification is a complex product composed of preconceptions. Exactly the same justification may enter into the memory "it was always so" or the assent "this is necessary." The difference of these cases from each other and from anticipation does not lie in the justification. The difference lies in the nature of the ideological-feeling. I, personally, do not profess to be able to analyse the assumptions constituting respectively justification, anticipation and passive reflection; but I am not prepared to say that they cannot be analysed. There may be other ideological-feelings, for example in rationalization and obfuscation; also a critical-feeling.

If we are right in our analysis of emergence, the use of reductionism in explaining systems is apt to be misleading. There is no way of accounting, in mechanistic terms, for a flock’s movement and a calculation of its individual birds: the swirling of starlings and the summing of trajectories have the same formal basis, though (assuming that we observe the flock) they express phenomena which are ontologically very different. In the one case, what occurs is that we perceive the pattern “coordinated flocking”; in the other case, we deduce the aggregate “starlings’ flight paths combined.” In the latter case, but not in the former, the wholeness is part of the phenomenon observed. Exactly similar remarks apply to the difference between anticipation, such as we have when watching a storm’s chaotic development, and deduction from a set of initial conditions, such as we have in all the usual cases of predictive models as to what will unfold. I think this inadequacy in the reductive description of the holistic aspects of systems is one among the causes which have hampered science in the consideration of emergence.

The analogy between natural selection and the training of artificial neural networks, which is our topic to-day, lies strictly outside our general subject, namely the engineering of computational systems. From the practical standpoint, there may be different kinds of optimization, and different degrees of efficiency, but there cannot be any purely technical means of distinguishing between profound and superficial analogies. An analogy is rendered sound or unsound by relation to a principle, which may lie outside the implementation of the system employing the method. Soundness and fallacy, except in the case of analogies about our own constructions, depend upon the relations of algorithmic processes to external realities, and thus take us beyond the analysis of computational processes as they are in themselves. Nevertheless, we can hardly avoid the consideration of soundness and fallacy. We wish to believe that our models, sometimes at least, yield UNDERSTANDING, and a model does not yield understanding unless its analogy is sound. The question whether our algorithms are instruments of insight, and, if so, in what sense, is so vital that any suggested engineering of systems must be examined in relation to this question. To ignore this question would be like describing a selective breeding program without regard to its fidelity to natural pressures, or a gradient descent process without mentioning the fact that it approximates an evolutionary search.

The view of pattern-persistence which I have been advocating contains little that is novel except the distinction of kinds of substrate-invariance--such as crystalline and algorithmic. Thus one might say: "Everyone knows the difference between conceiving a form and observing its manifestation, between sketching a configuration and conceding its recurrence...IN ITS ESSENTIAL CHARACTER, PATTERN, OR THE SENSE OF REPETITION, IS A SORT OF PRINCIPLE MORE ALLIED TO LOGIC THAN TO ANYTHING ELSE" (A hypothetical treatise, vol. ii, p. 283. The author's italics). One might proceed to point out that certain optical illusions, and, still more, the contemplation of intricate tessellations, will heighten the sense of invariant order: in the latter case, he says, a man's very mind may thrum with recognition, and he be all the time utterly unable to say from what material the regularity springs. It would seem that, in such cases, the perception of pattern exists unattached, without its usual relation to a specific medium, just as the perception of symmetry may sometimes occur without being related to any definite symmetrical object. The perception of pattern, when it occurs in this separated heightened form, generally leads us to look for a substrate to which to attach it. Much of what passes for profound discovery or aesthetic insight probably comes in this way: the pattern-feeling, in abnormal strength, attaches itself, more or less accidentally, to some physical instance which we happen to observe at the appropriate moment. But this is only a speculation, upon which I do not wish to lay too much stress.

We will now consider another bacterium, which also, when you first observe it, releases a specific chemical signal. But with this bacterium, instead of exposing it to different stimuli, you make a practice of introducing the same chemical inducer at regular intervals. You find that it secretes a varied array of molecules, or none at all, or a contradictory signal at random, and you conclude that it also does not possess a coherent communicative intent, though by fortunate accident it responded appropriately the initial time. This bacterium is like a faulty semaphore which, instead of conveying a fixed message, is always flashing erratically, signalling without any change in circumstance. This bacterium and semaphore have the opposite defect to that of the previous pair: they produce different outputs to inputs which do not differ in any relevant particular.

If you ask a mathematician "What is the sum of two and two?" and the mathematician says "four," you take that as prima facie evidence that the mathematician understands the operation of addition. But if you go on to ask what is the sum of three and three, of four and four, of five and five, and so on, and the mathematician always answers "four," you come to the conclusion that he knows nothing about the correspondence between formalism and fact. Exactly similar remarks apply to empirical observations. I know a certain theory of planetary motion which has the convenient habit of always predicting circular orbits. If you were to test it first with the moon's path, you would think it an admirable theory; but with the first observation of Mars your confidence would be shaken. The mathematician and the theory have the same defect: they do not vary their prediction when the empirical datum is varied. A sound structure, or a scientist with true understanding, will yield different predictions for data which differ in relevant ways. This is the first point in defining the fidelity of theory to observation.

Persistence of pattern is a perfectly clear notion in the case of crystalline structures, but in other cases it is much more obscure. We may say generally that a system, whether organic or inorganic, is "susceptible" to a certain formal arrangement if it manifests similar organization according to the presence or absence of that governing principle. Thus a whirlpool is susceptible to the same vortical law as a galaxy. But susceptibility does not constitute persistence, and persistence of a form which is not material is not susceptibility to that form, as we have seen in distinguishing the abstract pattern from its concrete instantiation. As soon as we pass beyond the simple case of geometric repetition, the definition of persistence by means of observation demands the consideration of function. A neural network recognizes a face, and so we say the pattern "persists" in silicon. But if it merely produced shapes at random, we should not say that the pattern "persisted" in that medium, any more than a cloud assuming momentary resemblance knows the form it mimics.

From our present point of view, it is difficult to exclude differentiation from function; at any rate, efficiency is displayed by processes based upon specialization. A cell dividing within a tissue assumes a distinct metabolic role; its assumption is a response to chemical signals. This response has the characteristic of utility, in the main, and leads us to say that the colony "organizes," by necessity, what duties are in its domain. For a biologist, this must certainly count as adaptation, however it may be viewed by theoretical ecology. In this case, what is arranged, roughly, is the immediate task; but in more advanced colonies the task and what is arranged become different. For example, you observe in a biofilm and find that nutrient distribution will be complex this season. Here the task is local consumption, whereas the arrangement concerns the whole collective. Even this can be paralleled among organisms: the behaviour of the slime mold has a simple stimulus but anticipates scarcity, so that the aggregate might be said, in a sense, to know the shortage. However that may be, the point I am emphasizing as regards organization is that what is coordinated may be quite different from the initial specialization, and no part of the cause of the functional response. It is only in rudimentary colonies that the specialization and what is coordinated are, with qualifications, identical. In organization for collective tasks, it is obvious that they are totally distinct, since otherwise the function would precede the structure. In symbiotic systems also they are distinct, since cooperative facts have no single origin. In organization from past adaptations there are complications, which we must briefly examine.

In spite, however, of the fact that the precision of a language is SOMETIMES an indispensable part of the efficacy of its users, this circumstance is, I think, irrelevant to the general question with which we are concerned, namely What sort of structure for what sort of community can be regarded as displaying true linguistic precision? There is one characteristic which the structure must have, namely, it must consist of voluntary conventions. The need of this characteristic is connected with the characteristic of UTILITY, which I do not wish to consider as yet. For the present I wish only to obtain a clearer idea of the sort of COMPLEXITY that a precise language must accommodate. It is clear from many instances that complexity, in other cases, may be purely mechanical. The most complete form of complexity consists in giving elaborate answers to inquiries, an achievement in which technical manuals far surpass ordinary speakers. In making an inquiry of a technical manual, you must use its framework: you must not address it in casual speech, any more than you would address a casual speaker in formal logic. But if you address it in the framework it understands, it will tell you what is the tensile strength of annealed copper, without a moment's hesitation or a hint of ambiguity. We do not say the manual UNDERSTANDS the answer, because it has no purpose of its own in giving the answer: it does not wish to impress you with its thoroughness, or feel proud of being such a good manual. But as far as mere complexity goes, the manual leaves nothing to be desired.

Every form of political development will be, from our present point of view, in one sense a delayed adaptation. But this phrase does not quite clearly express what is meant. If you introduce a novel policy and connect it with a body of tradition, the consolidation of that policy may be spoken of, in a sense, as a delayed adaptation to your initial innovation. But that only means that it is a somewhat late portion of a continuous process of which the earlier parts have less dramatic consequence. This is not the case with institutional inertia. A display of institutional inertia has two sorts of causes: (a) the past circumstances which generated the structure, (b) the present circumstance which brings it into operation. When a society encounters a severe crisis, and reacts as it does react, the structure has been caused by generations of precedent and compromise, whereas it is brought into operation by the immediate pressure. The great bulk of our governance is an inertia in this sense: whenever a state is faced with a familiar challenge, it reacts predictably by mere institutional routine. It would hardly be correct to say that the original founding was the stimulus, and that the present reaction is a delayed adaptation. But in cases of political evolution this way of speaking would have an element of truth. In an established political order, the formative historical event was clearly an essential part of the stimulus to the formation of the structure. The present stimulus which brings the structure into operation produces a different outcome from that which it would produce if the structure did not exist. Therefore the structure enters into the causation of the outcome, and so do, at one remove, the causes of the structure. It follows that a past historical circumstance is an essential part of the causes of our current political form.

II. I have so far assumed as unquestionable the view that the stability or fragility of a system consists in a relation to a certain condition, namely the isolation of its components. This view has, however, been often disregarded. Engineers have sought some intrinsic property by which secure and precarious systems could be distinguished.* I am afraid their chief reason for this search has been the wish to feel more confidence than seems otherwise possible as to what is robust and what is frail. If we could discover the vulnerability of a system by examining its internal characteristics, or those of some collection of systems of which it forms part, the maintenance of security, it is thought, would be a less intricate business than it otherwise appears to be. But the attempts which have been made in this direction are not reassuring. I will take two properties which have been suggested, namely, (1) apparent simplicity, (2) functional redundancy. If we can show that these are inadequate, we may feel fairly certain that no intrinsic property hitherto suggested will suffice to distinguish resilient from fragile systems.

On the features which distinguish writing from mere communication in general, not much can be said from a purely anthropological point of view without referring to permanence. But the necessity of SOMETHING besides transient utterance may be brought out by the following consideration: Suppose two societies, of which one preserved whatever the other forgot, and forgot whatever the other preserved. So far as immediacy and richness of expression alone are concerned, there would be nothing to choose between these two societies. A messenger who conveyed news inaccurately might be just as prompt as the reliable kind; and a tradition that is entirely oral is just as vivid a medium as one that is entirely written. The observable and historical difference between them would be that the society which relied solely on memory would quickly lose its complex inheritance. This illustrates once more that fluency of communication does not alone show civilisation, but must be reinforced by durability, i.e. suitability for preserving one's knowledge. This applies even in the apparently simple case of recording laws: if the purpose of the records is to control, their fixity, not their fairness, will be evidence of advancement. The proportion of the combination of durability with fluency in the definition of progress is difficult; it seems that both enter in, but that durability is only required as regards the fundamental structures of society, not as regards each individual transaction.

The view that such a correspondence exists is generally held by those whose theories are in any degree derived from microbiology. It may be illustrated by the following consideration from a modern treatise, "The Chemical Basis of Communication" (Academic Press, 2019), p. 312: "Strictly speaking, a simple diffusion event is not a signal at all. The response does not follow from the molecule M alone, but from the molecule plus a certain context C, WHICH IN NO SENSE BELONGS TO THE CONTENT OF THE SIGNAL. What takes place may be a process of random interaction, of mere proximity, or the like, but is not a process of signification. An experienced biochemist will be able by careful experiment to detect that in this process there is wanting just the specific element of the intentional dependence of the response upon the emission which is characteristic of a true signal. It must be admitted, however, that an exceptional power of analysis is needed in order to distinguish, by means of instrumentation, mere chemical noise from articulate discourse.

Judgments of cognition, such as "this thought is swift," are in a quite different position from judgments of physiology, and their immediacy must have a different explanation. In order to arrive at the nucleus of such a judgment, we will eliminate, as far as possible, the use of concepts which take us beyond the present experience, such as "thought" and "swift." The simplest kind of judgment underlying the perception that a thought is swift would seem to be the perception of difference in two mental rates experienced successively. Suppose we are contemplating two ideas, and we perceive that their velocities are dissimilar. This dissimilarity is a psychological fact, not a matter of measurement or clocks; and it certainly seems to be indubitable in a way that many judgments are not.

The same conclusion emerges from surveying the evidence. If we consider the four principal arguments commonly advanced in this debate, we shall find that three of them suggest cosmic rarity, while the fourth implies biological inevitability. The proposition that life requires a narrow set of initial parameters follows by empirical observation from astronomical data: that means that its apparent rarity results, not from the essence of life itself, but from the contingent arrangements of matter. Now arrangements, in cosmology, occur as chance dictates; thus the feeling of paradox, in this case, seems explicable by the fact that the whole matter is beyond our control. I do not wish to assert that this is the complete account of life's distribution, for the problem is intricate, and I do not know what the complete account is. But I do wish to suggest that the appearance of life's conditions being neither rare nor inevitable has to do with the fact that they are concerned with the accidents of configuration, not with necessities of nature such as metaphysical reasoning might postulate.

If this theory is to be logically tenable, evolutionary advantage must not consist merely in the fact that a trait promotes survival. We acknowledge that our adaptive explanations are sometimes erroneous, and we wish to be able to select a certain class of explanations which are never erroneous. If we are to do this, it must be by some mark which belongs only to certain traits, not to all; and among those to which it belongs there must be none that are mutually inconsistent. If, for example, two traits p and q were advantageous, and it were also demonstrable that p and q could not both be selected for, that would condemn advantage as a guarantee of propagation. Again, evolutionary benefit must not be the same thing as the absence of competition or the presence of complete dominance. If a trait is completely dominant in a population, we do not seek a mechanism to support its prevalence. If selective advantage is alleged as a ground for prevalence, that implies that countervailing pressures have crept in, and that our advantageous trait has not wholly resisted the assaults of a changing environment. To say that any given species exhibits some traits so fixed that they cannot be supplanted is no doubt true. Such traits it will be compelled to use as foundations for further adaptation, and to that species personally they will seem to have as much utility as any trait can need. But among the adaptations which one lineage finds indispensable there will be some that another lineage finds it quite possible to discard. It used to seem advantageous that there could not be communication without physical contact, because signals would dissipate, or at best grow unreliable from traversing empty space. But certain birds find the utility of this capacity for long-range calls self-evident. Therefore, if selective advantage is a guarantee of persistence, our ancestral species must have been mistaken in thinking their reliance on direct touch universally advantageous. Some theorists meet this difficulty by saying that some traits are falsely thought to be advantageous, but in the case of others it is evident that they are beneficial, and these are wholly reliable. Even this, however, does not remove the practical risk of misattribution, since we may mistakenly believe it evident that a certain trait is advantageous. To remove all risk of misattribution, we shall need an endless series of more and more complicated beneficial correlations, which cannot possibly be realized in observation. It would seem, therefore, that evolutionary advantage is useless as a practical criterion for insuring the explanation of a trait's fixation.

The next thing to observe (although I do not personally doubt that most of our practical knowledge is serviceable) is that it is very difficult to define any class of such knowledge which can be known, by its intrinsic quality, to be always exempt from the demand for absolute certainty. Most of our practical knowledge involves correlations, as when we judge that a certain dampness in the air presages rain. Such knowledge is all obviously liable to the corruption of dogmatism, since there is no correlation of which we have a right to be certain that it is invariable. Other practical knowledge is derived from recognition, as when we say "this is a reliable tool," or even merely "this will suffice." All such knowledge entails some risk of error, though sometimes perhaps a very small one; some tools that appear reliable may soon fail, and methods that some would call sufficient others might call inadequate. Our subjective certainty is usually a result of habit, and may lead us astray in circumstances which are unusual in ways of which we are unaware.

The fundamental objection to this method is empirical, and consists in a criticism of its reliance upon unproven premises. I shall omit this philosophical argument, which I have examined elsewhere.* For the moment I will content myself with observing that the powers of induction seem to me very much less than this procedure assumes. If it were taken seriously, its practitioners ought to profess that any one instance is inductively inferable from any other, and that, for example, the fact that the sun rose yesterday, if adequately considered, would enable us to discover whether milk will sour to-morrow. No such claim is put forward in practice, and the necessity of foundational postulates is not denied; but according to the theory it ought to be.

Coherence.--Coherence as the definition of value is advocated by designers, particularly by those who in the main follow a holistic tradition. It is set forth ably in Dr. Atherton's treatise, "The Genesis of Machine Ethics" (Cambridge, 2024).
