According to this view, any set of valuations other than the whole of coherent value can be condemned on purely logical grounds, as internally inconsistent; a single preference, if it is what we should ordinarily call alien, contradicts itself irremediably, while if it is what we should ordinarily call recognisable, it has implications which compel us to admit other valuations, which in turn lead to others, and so on, until we find ourselves committed to the whole of a value system. One might illustrate by a very simple example: if I say "this processor prefers computational efficiency," that is not a self-subsistent valuation. We cannot logically conceive of a system in which this preference constituted the whole of its values. There must be also some correlate, such as a dispreference for thermal excess, which is intrinsically linked to the particular efficiency in question. The view we are considering regards everything that can be said about any one artificial aim as relative in the same sort of way as "this processor prefers computational efficiency." But everything, according to this view, is relative, not to one or two other aims, but to all other aims, so that from one bit of a coherent value the whole can be inferred.

Another objection is that no endeavour is made to show that we cannot form a coherent narrative composed partly or wholly of distorted impressions, as in a daydream. The common conception of memory as a passive record seems to accord much better with naive psychology and with the immediate realism which is now instinctive. The attempt to reconstruct the past by pure sensation is attractive, and in simpler minds was largely supposed capable of fidelity. But nowadays most persons admit that recollections must be tested by present evidence, and not merely by the fact that they harmonize with other recollections. A consistent fantasy is a different thing from actuality, however vivid it may be. But to pursue this topic would lead us into subtle psychological complexities; I shall therefore assume, without further argument, that coherence is not sufficient as a definition of memory.

III. Many difficult problems arise as regards the utility of tools. We acquire various implements, and while we employ them we think we comprehend their use. But it sometimes turns out that we were misguided, or at any rate we come to think we were. We must be misguided either in our previous confidence or in our subsequent disillusionment; therefore our acquisitions are not all beneficial, and there are cases of possession which are not cases of understanding. The question of utility is in essence this: can we discover any set of tools which are never superfluous or any test which, when applicable, will always enable us to discriminate between fruitful and futile acquisitions? Put thus broadly and abstractly, the answer must be negative. There is no way hitherto discovered of wholly eliminating the risk of redundancy, and no infallible criterion. If we believe we have found a criterion, this belief itself may be misguided; we should be begging the question if we tried to test the criterion by applying the criterion to itself.

One of the plainest cases of vulnerability, perhaps ultimately the only case, consists in the failure of something assumed. You engage with a network believing that there will be a service at a certain standard; you find the service, you depend upon it, and it functions at the assumed standard This constitutes reliance, and is a perfectly common experience. It is, in a sense, the converse of design; instead of having first components and then systems accompanied by transparency, we have first systems accompanied by transparency and then components. Apart from differences as to the structural-order and the accompanying assurances, the relation between component and system is closely similar in the two cases of design and reliance; it is a relation of integration, with difference as to causal independence--broadly, the component has the functional but not the sovereign effects that the system would have. When a component accompanied by a reliance-belief is thus succeeded by a failure which is the "consequence" of the integration, we say that the reliance-belief has been exposed. The experience of exposure in this sense is exceedingly systemic; it happens every time that interconnected operations have results that are not anticipated, in commerce and communication and computation and all our daily infrastructures.

But although the phenomenon in question is familiar, it is not wholly easy to give a theoretical account of it. How do we know that the accelerated thought resembles the ordinary mental process? Does the ordinary cognition persist during the period of haste, so that we can compare the two? And even if SOME cognition does persist, how do we know that it is the ordinary process unchanged? It does not seem as if this line of inquiry offered much hope of a successful issue. It is better, I think, to take a more external and causal view of the relation of mental haste to its practical outcome. If the outcome, when it is achieved, gives us the feeling of efficiency, and if the hastened thinking, beforehand, enabled us to act in a way which proves appropriate to the circumstance, that must be held to constitute the maximum of validation. We have first a deliberate pace, then a hurried operation with the feeling of altered tempo related to memory of the slowness. This whole experience, when it occurs, may be defined as confirmation, and as constituting the success of the hastened process. Appropriate action, during the period of acceleration, may be regarded as additional confirmation, but is not essential. The whole process may be illustrated by attempting a routine task, completing it with the expected dispatch, and in the expected sequence of steps. In this case we can strengthen the confirmation by describing beforehand the method which we expect to employ.

I think all scientific progress is ultimately of the above sort. We correct a scientific error indirectly, by deducing observable consequences from a theory, which subsequent experiment fails to confirm. If somebody were to doubt whether a prevailing hypothesis were flawed, correction could only be obtained from the future. We could proceed to display experimental data to our scientific sceptic, in which it was shown that the theory had behaved in this erroneous way. We could advance arguments, verifiable by future testing, to prove the inadequacy of the model from its predictions, its assumptions, etc. We could find new observations disagreeing with the theory on other points, and tending to show its general inaccuracy. The methodological principles which our arguments would assume could be verified by the future success of predictions made by means of them. The existence and persistence of nature's uniformity, it is true, must be regarded as a fortunate accident, and how long it will continue we cannot tell. Meanwhile correction remains often practically possible. And since it is sometimes possible, we can gradually discover what kinds of theories tend to be corroborated by experience, and what kinds tend to be refuted; to the former kinds we give an increased degree of assent, to the latter kinds a diminished degree. The process is not absolute or infallible, but it has been found capable of sifting errors and building up knowledge. It affords no theoretical refutation of the dogmatist, whose position must remain logically unassailable; but if complete certainty is rejected, it gives the practical method by which the system of our sciences grows gradually towards the unattainable ideal of impeccable understanding.

This mode of stating the necessity for an external cause is obviated by the circumstance that there are dependent and independent systems, but not dependent and independent realities. If the universe is self-contained, there is not a dependent objective "the universe requires a cause," which could be the objective of the erroneous supposition "the universe requires a cause." This is the reason why two conceptions which are each other's contradictories have the same ontological ground. There is, however, a metaphysical inconvenience, namely that we cannot determine the causal status of a system, according to this principle, unless we know whether the system is truly self-sufficient or not. To avoid this inconvenience, it is better to adopt a slightly different formulation, and say: The "explanation" of the conception "the universe is self-contained" consists in pointing to the condition "the universe is self-contained" if that is a condition, or away from the condition "the universe requires a cause" if that is a condition. The "explanation" of the conception "the universe requires a cause" will be exactly the opposite. By this hypothetical form we are able to speak of the explanation of a conception without knowing whether it is ultimately valid or not. According to this formulation, we know the explanation of a conception when we know what would make it necessary and what would make it superfluous, even if we do not know whether it is in fact necessary or superfluous.

Just as a portrait has a likeness, so a self-representation has a subjective correspondence. The subjective correspondence of a self-representation is a function (in the psychological sense) of the impressions of its constituent reflections. But the subjective correspondence differs from the impression of a portrait through the duality of authenticity and artifice. You may experience the self-representation "I am content" both when, in fact, you are content, and when you are not content. If you are not content, this state is the subjective of your representation that you are content. But obviously the relation of your representation to the state is different in this case from what it is in the case when you are content. We may say, metaphorically, that when you are content, your representation that you are content resonates WITH the state, whereas when you are not content your representation resonates AGAINST the state. Thus the subjective correspondence of a representation is not determined by the state alone, but by the direction of the representation with or against the state.* If, in a moment of vitality, one person represents himself as vital while another represents himself as languid, their representations have the same subjective, namely the state of being vital but the authentic representation resonates with the state while the artificial one resonates against it. Thus, in order to define the correspondence of a self-representation we have to take account not only of the subjective, but also of the direction of resonance, with the subjective in the case of an authentic representation and against it in the case of an artificial one.

In the case we have just been considering the self consists of two aspects with a certain relation (that of representation-to-immediacy), and the awareness consists of conceptions of these aspects with the very same relation. The same awareness, if it were illusory, would have a less simple formal relation to its actuality. If the mental conception consists of an idea of the self as represented preceding an idea of the self as felt, while in fact the representation does not precede the feeling, the awareness does not result from the actuality by the mere substitution of conceptions for their realities. Thus in this unusually simple case we can say that a veridical awareness "corresponds" to its actuality in a formal sense in which a deceptive awareness does not. Perhaps it may be possible to modify this notion of formal correspondence in such a way as to be more widely applicable, but if so, the modifications required will be by no means slight. The reasons for this must now be considered.

The purely formal definition of multicellularity offers little difficulty. What is required is a formal expression of the fact that an organism is colonial when it derives from its constituent units, and unitary when it obscures them. In very simple cases we can give a very simple account of this: we can say that colonial organisms actually resemble their cellular foundations in a way in which unitary organisms do not. But for this purpose it is necessary to revert to primitive aggregates instead of complex individuals. Let us take again the illustration of a sponge, a familiar organism, and let us suppose that in its structure the cells are largely independent and totipotent. If in fact the cells are largely independent and totipotent, there is a correspondence between the aggregate and its essential nature; there is the same relation between the whole and its parts as between the concept of a colony and the concept of a unified being. The colonial understanding consists of the conception of the whole as dependent upon the autonomy of the parts. When this is true, the very same relation relates the terms of the objective (namely the organism and its cells) as relates the concepts which describe them. In this case the correspondence which constitutes the colonial view is very simple.

The consideration of abstract formalism and concrete data introduces further complications. A mathematical model is necessarily ideal: we can conceive of a circle as a perfect locus of points, or as a conic section of zero eccentricity, but we can form no conception of the bare empirical "the circle not existing in physical space." We can DISBELIEVE the theoretical proposition expressed by "the circle as a material object," and our disbelief will be true if the circle is not found in nature. But we can form no equation of the fact that the circle is absent from the observable world. Attempts have often been made to deny such empirical discrepancies, but, for reasons which I have given elsewhere,* I believe these attempts to be mistaken, and I shall assume that there are observational facts.

Systemic interdependencies, like mechanical linkages, are always positive realities. The fact that electricity enables communication is manifested in daily life by the fact that the power grid underlies the functioning of the internet. But we cannot manifest the fact that the internet does not function without electricity by not having the grid support the network. A systemic failure is not apparent, and ordinary operation, being intended for seamless service, has to be apparent. Therefore we manifest the fact that the internet does not function without electricity by observing the cascading collapse during a major blackout. We thus obtain a chain of events which is just as positive a reality as the chain "electricity enables communication." The vulnerabilities arising from interconnected systems are themselves positive realities; they are merely different positive realities from those sustaining ordinary function.

To begin with, the simple type of vulnerability we have been considering can hardly be perceived when systems are examined in isolation, because, in their apparent operation, dependencies are usually managed by protocols, which are not themselves dependencies. Take such a system as the electrical grid preceding the data network. Here the protocol for "synchronization" is just as tangible as the entities "grid" and "network"; it GOVERNS a dependency, but is not a dependency. Thus the failure which makes our system fragile consists of TWO systems with a linkage between them, whereas our operational model consists of THREE components with a relation of sequence between them. Of course, it would be perfectly possible, theoretically, to indicate a few chosen linkages, not by protocols, but by arrangements between the other systems. "Grid-network" might be used to mean "the grid enables the network"; "network-grid" might be used to mean "the network monitors the grid and controls its distribution"; and so on. But the possibilities of such an arrangement would be very limited. For aught I know, there may be infrastructures that use it, but they are not among the infrastructures with which I am acquainted. And in any case, in view of the multiplicity of linkages that we wish to manage, no infrastructure could advance far without protocols for dependencies. But as soon as we have protocols for dependencies, operational models have necessarily more components than the realities to which they refer, and cannot therefore correspond so simply with their actual frailties as some isolated systems can.

Even when we confine ourselves to the interactions between particles which are both gravitating, it may be impossible to conceive a mechanical model in which the attraction of the masses is represented by the same necessity of the components. Suppose we say "a spiral arm is 100,000 light-years from its galactic core," we express a certain spatial relation between the arm and the core; but we cannot allow such distances to intervene between our conception of the one and our conception of the other. This is perhaps not a fair example, since "100,000 light-years from" is not a simple relation. But take a case where the relation is immediate, say, "dark matter is more pervasive than luminous matter." We can form conceptual images of halos and of stars, and it may happen that our image of the halo is the more extensive of the two, but this is by no means either necessary or sufficient. The act of gravitational clustering, implied in the process, is something more than the mere proximity of two masses, one of which is in fact denser than the other. It would take us too far from our main topic if we were to go into the question what actually occurs when this aggregation proceeds. Enough has been said to show that the correspondence between the initial conditions and the resulting structure is more complicated in this case than in that of a vortex forming in a draining basin, and this was all that had to be proved.

In spite of these complications, the general nature of the formal correspondence which makes a description adequate is clear from our instances. In the case of the simpler kind of formulations, namely those that I call "elementary" equations, where there is only one symbol expressing a relationship, the phenomenon which would verify our formulation, assuming that the term "approximation" is absent, is obtained by replacing each symbol by what it signifies, the symbol signifying a relationship being replaced by this relationship among the significances of the other symbols. For example, if the formulation is "the distance varies as the square of the time," the phenomenon which verifies it results from replacing the symbol "distance" by an actual interval, the symbol "time" by a temporal duration, and the symbol "varies as the square of" by the physical relation of acceleration between the interval and the duration. If the result of this process is an observed occurrence, the formulation is accurate; if not, it is idealized. When our formulation is "the distance does not vary precisely as the square of the time," the conditions of accuracy and idealization are exactly reversed. More complicated formulations can be dealt with on the same lines. In fact, the purely formal question, which has occupied us in this last section, offers no very formidable difficulties.

Our natural way of thinking about these cosmic conditions, rarity, inevitability, habitability, is that the astronomical observation of some planetary fact suggests the intellectual conclusion called the probability, and that this latter state of understanding gives rise to the statistical expectation. My view, on the contrary, is that THE STATISTICAL EXPECTATIONS FOLLOW DIRECTLY THE OBSERVATION OF THE PERTINENT DATA, AND THAT OUR SENSE OF THE SAME EXPECTATIONS AS THEY FORM _IS_ THE PROBABILITY (Drake’s italics). Common sense says: we find many exoplanets, infer life is common and are surprised by silence; we note fine-tuning, are convinced and predict abundance; we observe Earth’s uniqueness, are doubtful and deem life rare. The hypothesis here to be defended says that this order of reasoning is incorrect, that the one conclusion is not immediately induced by the other, that the statistical manifestations must first be interposed between, and that the more rational statement is that we infer commonness because we are surprised, inevitability because we predict, rarity because we doubt, and not that we are surprised, predict, or doubt, because we infer commonness, inevitability, or rarity, as the case may be. Without the statistical states following on the observation, the latter would be purely descriptive in form, pale, colourless, destitute of probabilistic weight.

Common sense, by observations in daily life, shows that many of the usual convictions about material objects are present in our judgments even when, by examining the evidence of microscopic physics, the solid table is revealed to be a cloud of swirling atoms, the tangible world cut off from all correspondence with direct perception, except that existing through certain macroscopic approximations. It maintains the various beliefs which "contributed to indicate the existence of a reality as solid and continuous as the senses had ever reported to us before the scientific investigation had been undertaken."* It infers that the immediate testimony of the senses cannot be the foundation of the physical truth disclosed under such scrutiny, and concludes: "We are forced back toward the likelihood that the commonsense apprehension of reality is SECONDARY to the intellectual synthesis occurring with the theoretical framework.... We may with the plain man accept sensory impressions and the habits and inferences of them as contributory to practical navigation, but we must regard them as simplifying rather than as revealing the ontology."*

The most illuminating aspect of this inquiry consists in the examination of the distinctions drawn between graded awareness and sudden awakening. Consciousness, as here considered, is a quality attributed to certain complex organizations of matter. This is among the profound mysteries, the nature of which, both in philosophy and in connection with perception, have only come to be scrutinized during recent decades. Investigators have found that minimal responsiveness, reflexive action and deliberate intent occurred in circumstances which suggested a continuum of awareness, and that a precise definition of threshold could, for example, produce all the difficulties of arbitrary demarcation. They studied the manifestations of consciousness in various orders of being; they found that it causes the debate to intensify, categories to become blurred, definitions to be contested, and so on. These problems were still encountered if the phenomena in question were removed from their biological context and examined in abstract isolation.

The first thing to be considered when we are dealing with Eternity is a HUMAN CENTURY. We have already defined geological epochs, and we have maintained that, from a cosmic standpoint, it is impossible to distinguish which among such durations are brief and which enduring. Nevertheless, there certainly is a distinction. When we reflect that all recorded history occupies but a moment, our consequent humility is appropriate. The orbit of a comet, on the other hand, is immeasurable: we can neither lengthen it nor shorten it by any effort of our own, except indirectly, as e.g. by celestial mechanics. A civilisation is intermediate between the two: we normally regard it as a vast achievement, but we can perceive its transience if we choose.

According to our definitions, if Smith is right, a productive process may be regarded as involving a specialized application of the labourer concerned in its execution, while if Ricardo and Marx are right, a productive process involves a specialized application to its external materials. This follows from what was said in Lecture VII. We there defined a specialization as an arrangement, however intricate, of one or more functions external to the individual. And in order to be an arrangement of one or more functions, it is only necessary that the operation in question should be connected with them by a continuous chain, and should vary when they are varied sufficiently. Thus the question whether an economic operation can be called a specialization turns upon the question whether anything can be inferred from it as to its effects outside the individual: if such inference is possible, the operation in question will come within our definition of a specialization. And in that case, according to the definition in Lecture VIII, its non-autonomous elements will be dependencies. Accordingly, whether productive processes are caused by efficiencies in the labour or by material objects, they contain elements which are dependencies according to our definition.

A system in its entirety is, of course, something much more complex than an inventory of its components. A system is essentially an organization, and it will be only what one may call a static catalogue of the parts that will be a summation, of a mere aggregation according to the reductionist, or (in certain cases) of a simple totality according to his critics. A system in its entirety contains emergent properties, such as functional behaviors, interactions, synergies and constraints. Interactions and synergies and constraints, according to the theory adopted in the preceding analysis, are characteristics of organizations, not separate appendages. A system—a household, for example—will be a certain kind of organization, consisting of constituent objects and (in general) relational activities. The interactions and synergies and constraints involved are properties of this organization, not separate items in the catalogue of which the system is enumerated. The emergent properties in a system, if we are right in our reasoning, contain, from our point of view, no elements beyond those contained in the organizations considered previously. The elements of a system are only parts and relations and processes arranged together according to a certain pattern. With this conclusion we may leave the systems and pass to the consideration of the implications.

At the end of our inquiry it is time to return to the question from which we set out, namely: What is it that characterizes biological evolution as opposed to political evolution? Or, to state the same question in other terms: How is natural selection to be distinguished from institutional selection? The answer provisionally suggested at the outset of our examination was that biology and political science are distinguished by the nature of their adaptive mechanisms, not by their structural outcomes. At the same time we held that there is a certain process, namely random mutation, to which only biological adaptive mechanisms are applicable; this process, therefore, we assigned exclusively to biology. But we found no way of defining institutional mutation except through its consequences; in its intrinsic character it appeared to have no universal mark by which it could be distinguished from genetic variation.

Expansion, in the cosmological sense, involves something more than mere spatial extension. The sort of case I am thinking of is the ultimate fate after protracted evolution. Receding galaxies are a part of this, but not the whole. There is, in addition to them, a principle: "This is what must become of all things"; there is also a condition of tension within bound systems, followed by a different condition at the moment of dissolution. I see no reason whatever to suppose that there is any specifically supernatural agency; matter and energy, with their relations and physical laws, yield all that seems to be wanted for the analysis of cosmic destiny, together with the fact that gravitational binding tends to resist the dispersal with which it is ultimately incompatible. Conflict of forces is of course essential in the causation of the emphatic kind of fate: there will be for a time configurations of opposing interactions, followed by the exclusive dominance of the expansion which is said to be inevitable. Thus the Hubble parameter seems to add no new irreducible ingredient to the analysis of the cosmos.

Interdependence," by those who regard it as fundamental, is taken to be a condition diffused throughout our economic life, distinct from supply chains and markets, regulations, innovations and demands, but present in all of them.* Dr. Adam Smith, in a treatise which I cited in Lecture III, distinguishing markets from purely local exchanges, says: "Commerce, in the strict sense of the term, demands the existence of interconnection." This statement, at first sight, is one to which we feel inclined to assent, but I believe we are mistaken if we do so. Interconnection is the sort of thing of which we MAY be conscious, but not a thing of which we MUST be conscious. We have been led, in the course of our inquiry, to admit invisible efficiencies and invisible fragilities. There is, so far as I can see, no class of systemic or other occurrences of which we are always aware whenever they happen.

In the second place, the question arises as to whether we can discern patterns in social contention. If we apply our principle to this case, it seems to demand a pattern of patterns. In order, for example, to discern a pattern of factional rivalry, we shall require, according to the letter of the principle, a pattern which is a model of our pattern of rivalry, and has this pattern for its archetype. Now, it hardly seems probable, as a matter of observation, that there are patterns of patterns, as opposed to patterns of isolated interests. We may meet this difficulty in two ways, either by boldly denying discernment of social patterns, or by finding a sense in which, by means of a different accompanying dynamic, a pattern, instead of signifying its archetype, can signify another pattern of the same archetype.

The first thing to notice is that competition must be of something. In view of this, I should define "competition" in terms of that relation of a firm to a market which we defined, in earlier analysis, as "rivalry." When a market is followed by a consolidation which is a "consequence" of it, I think it may be said that the existence of the consolidation constitutes a tendency toward monopoly, provided it is accompanied by that sort of process which, when we reflect upon it, makes us feel that the consolidation is a "sign" of something other than itself. This is the sort of process which, in the case of economies of scale, we expressed in the words "this enlarges"; or which, in the case of a judgment of commercial advantage, makes us believe in efficiencies correlated with present operations, as e.g., production and distribution efficiencies are correlated. The addition of some element of accumulation seems required, since mere rivalry does not involve a tendency toward anything, and there can be no tendency which is not of something. If advantages alone constituted a tendency toward their ultimate form, such competitive advantages as in fact have ultimate forms would involve a tendency toward them; since this is not the case, an element of accumulation must be added to the advantages in defining the tendency. The accumulation must be of that sort that constitutes market dominance, present or prospective. An advantage, together with an accumulation of this sort concerning it, constitutes, according to our definition, a tendency toward the monopoly of the market.

But when we pass from the observation of hereditary traits to the comprehension of the molecular basis of inheritance, certain further points arise which demand an addition to our definition. A conception of genetic identity, we may say, consists of a core of biochemical data, together with associated phenotypic expressions, with belief in the fundamental determinism of a code to which nucleotides and proteins are referred in a way which is difficult to analyse. Perhaps we might say that the belief is not fundamentally in any ABSOLUTE determinism, but is of the nature of a statistical prediction: for example, when we examine a genotype, we expect certain traits to result if we proceed to observe the organism. Heredity, then, will consist of a present molecular sequence together with expectations of future expressions. (This, of course, is a theoretical analysis, not an account of the way inheritance appears to unchecked intuition.) But all such expectations are liable to be erroneous, since they are based upon correlations which are usual but not invariable. Any such correlation may mislead us in a particular case, for example, if we assume a monogenic trait under the impression that it is "wholly predestined." Since biochemical interpretation is fallible, a similar difficulty arises as regards comprehension of ancestral lineages. It would seem odd to say that we can "comprehend" a principle which does not or did not operate. The only way to avoid this awkwardness is to add to our definition the proviso that the postulates involved in comprehension must be VALID.

According to what we have been saying, time itself is not an instance of a finite series, though the immediate succession by which it is apt to be conceived is so. A moment which is considered as initial becomes an object of logical scrutiny as soon as it begins to be postulated, which will normally be almost immediately after its conception (if at all); but while it is posited it is not an object of contradiction. If, however, it is part of a temporal sequence, say of some familiar duration, we may say that the sequence conceived is an object of logical difficulty. For in this case the moment is a SIGN of the preceding void in much the same way in which a causal chain is a sign of a necessitated event. The essential metaphysical function of "beginning" and "eternity" is that they enable us to conceive with reference to what is infinite in extent or duration, even though it is not at present contained within our intuition. This reference to unbounded continua is possible through reason and abstraction. Actual intervals, in themselves, are not cases of logical paradox, because they do not bring in this reference to what is necessarily prior. But their connection with contradiction is very close, both through immediate antecedence, and through the necessities which turn instants into mere relative positions.

The first alternative, which denies the existence of contradictions, has already been discussed when we were dealing with social stasis in Chapter VI. We then decided that there must be, in some sense, a recognition of inherent tensions. We are therefore left with the second suggested way of dealing with the dynamism of institutions. According to this second hypothesis, there may be two manifestations of the same social principle, such that one of them challenges the other, instead of challenging an external force. It will be remembered that we defined a social principle by its practical consequences a custom or law is a principle, we said, when it produces the same effects as its justification. But this definition must not be interpreted too absolutely: a custom or law will not have ALL the same effects as the ideal which it purports to serve. The rule "property" may be associated with the concept "security," but it would not happen except by accident that a claim to property would be associated with universal security. And in like manner an institution may have certain consequences which its founding ideal will not have, e.g. a consequence of fostering inequality. When these consequences are apparent, an institution opposes its own ideal, instead of opposing a foreign system. If a society has upheld a given principle many times, it can confront one of these upholdings, as opposed to the rest, by recollecting the historical context or any other distinctive circumstance of that one epoch. This happens, for example, when a crisis recalls to us some promise the order previously made in that era, so that we remember a promise as opposed to the reality which it obscured. Thus we may say that we perceive a contradiction A when we have a similar social form B associated with recollections of conditions connected with A, but not with its ideal or with other manifestations of the same ideal. In this way we become aware of tensions without the need of any new external catalyst, merely by the help of new historical understandings. This theory, so far as I can see, solves the problems of dialectical change, without requiring heroic measures such as those proposed by revolutionary dogmatists, whose views we discussed in Chapter VI.

Very similar considerations apply to civilisation, if taken as the essence of humanity. A city is illuminated by a star which is shining now, but is different from the effect which the present light would have produced if the stellar event had not occurred. This may be accounted for by the temporal insignificance of the human epoch in the cosmos, making it a different phenomenon from that which would have resulted from a more enduring existence. The causal peculiarities of history may, therefore, have an astronomical explanation. With every special class of terrestrial phenomena this possibility meets us afresh. If civilisation is to be a significant entity at all, we must seek a wider ground for its importance than any that we have been considering hitherto.

I come next to those characteristics of economic phenomena which arise out of competitive causation. The tendency toward consolidation in the absence of countervailing force is one of the things that might be held to characterize markets. Let us take first a very elementary example. Suppose you are in a familiar industry, and suddenly a rival gains an advantage. You will be able to predict the eventual dominance of that rival without much difficulty by means of the picture of the market which you have in your mind. In this case economic principles serve, somewhat imperfectly it is true, the purpose which direct observation would otherwise serve. The stimulus to the recognition of these principles is the desire to understand commercial history, which, according to what we found in earlier analysis, consists essentially of present conditions and strategic impulses caused by them. Again, data examined or reports considered enable you to act with reference to the trends about which they give information; here, again, a present commercial stimulus, in virtue of habits formed in the past, enables you to act in a manner appropriate to an outcome which is not yet fully present. The whole essence of the practical efficiency of "foresight" consists in sensitiveness to indicators: the sensible presence of A, which is an indicator of the present or future existence of B, enables us to act in a manner appropriate to B. Of this, economies of scale are the supreme example, since their effects as indicators are prodigious, while their intrinsic interest as isolated phenomena on their own account is usually very slight. The operation of these indicators may or may not be accompanied by conscious planning. If a commercial stimulus A calls up an image of B, and we then act with reference to B, we have what may be called consciousness of B. But routine may enable us to act in a manner appropriate to B as soon as A appears, without ever having an image of B. In that case, although A operates as an indicator, it operates without the help of consciousness. Broadly speaking, a very familiar indicator tends to operate directly in this manner, and the intervention of conscious deliberation marks an imperfectly established commercial habit.

The power of accumulating surplus, which characterizes developed societies, is an example of the general law that, in economic causation, the causal unit is not one transaction at one time, but two or more transactions at two or more times.& A prosperous merchant acquires land, that is to say, the possession of capital has a different effect upon a man who has had the experience of profit than upon one who has not. More correctly, the observed effect, when a man who has prospered is placed amidst new commercial opportunities, has for its cause, not merely the opportunity itself, but this together with the previous accumulation. The general formula, when a society has generated inequality through some concentration of wealth A, is that, when a new resource B appears at some future time, the community in which A has occurred stratifies differently from a community in which A has not occurred. Thus A and B together, not either separately, must be regarded as the cause of the social stratification, unless we take account of the effect which A has had in altering the community’s institutional structures, which is a matter not patent to superficial observation except under very special circumstances. With this possibility, we are brought back to materialist laws, and to the suggestion that many things which seem essentially social are really economic. Perhaps it is the property relations that generate class rather than the collective spirit. If so, the possibility of accumulating surplus cannot be used to define a classless society.*

The notion of "reorganisation" is familiar throughout society, and is usually treated by men of affairs as though it were perfectly natural. Institutions, on the other hand, find great difficulty in the process. "Reorganisation" is naturally defined in terms of historical necessity: it is that transformation of which the cause is known without dispute, so that it may be used as a premise in explaining other transformations. Further, when a transformation which is a reorganisation asserts the dominance of something, we say that the something is a reorganiser, as well as the transformation asserting its dominance. Thus those innovations of whose dominance we become certain through technological change are said to be reorganisers.

It is clear, in the first place, that there can be no ideology apart from a material condition. A belief which merely floats in the air is not an ideology; it only becomes an ideology when it is anchored in economic relations. Similarly, in social life, we do not have an ideology unless we have a SYSTEM of production. In the sense in which ideas (as opposed to facts) are ideologies, it would seem natural to say that those ideas of which we are unconscious are ideologies. But unconsciousness, as we have seen, is a complex notion, involving habits, as well as historical phenomena such as are required for class interest and tradition. It follows that no ideology is theoretically independent, since no condition is immaterial; it follows also that every ideology has a greater or less degree of servitude, since there is always some servitude in tradition and the meaning of interests.

Homeostasis, as a characteristic of living systems, was considered in Lecture VII, in connection with the definition of organic regulation. We there decided that those processes which constitute the physiological world can be arranged into sequences in two ways, one of which makes a series of all those processes that are manifestations of a given need under different conditions, while the other makes a series of all those processes which are manifestations of different needs under a given condition. A series of this latter sort, at a given moment, is called a "steady state"; taken throughout a period of operation, it is called a "viable trajectory." Equilibrium is the characteristic of steady states and trajectories, the characteristic of maintaining the internal condition within certain limits. We saw in Lecture VII that this characteristic involves none of the other characteristics that are commonly associated with intelligent phenomena, such as foresight, purpose and learning. We found in fact that it is exhibited by a thermostat, and, strictly speaking, by any mechanism taken in conjunction with those which have the same "regulative" function in the sense defined in Lecture VII. The processes forming one steady state are connected together primarily by simultaneity; those forming one trajectory, primarily by the existence of direct causal relations between them. To these are to be added relations derivable from the laws of feedback. In all this we are clearly not in the region of biology, as commonly understood; yet we are also hardly in the region of engineering. And the definition of steady states and trajectories, though it does not yet yield anything that would be commonly called "purposive," is presupposed in purposive phenomena, for example in reinforcement learning: the functional unit in reinforcement, which gives rise to Sutton's value function, is the whole of one steady state--not of any steady state, but of a steady state in a system where there is computational architecture, or at any rate adaptive machinery of some sort. Optimization also, as we saw, can only be defined in terms of steady states. Thus the conception of equilibrium, i.e. of the "regulative" function of a process, though not alone sufficient to define intelligence, is clearly an essential element in the definition.

Control is not that condition of which our awareness is earliest in time. At every stage of engagement, after we have become capable of reflection, some of our convictions are obtained by analysis, while others are not. A conviction may pass from either of these classes into the other, and may therefore become, or cease to be, a conviction yielding a sense of command. When, in what follows, I speak of control, I do not mean the condition of which we feel sure before systematic inquiry begins, but the condition which, when a system is well established, appears as affording grounds for confidence in its operations, without itself being believed on any ground except superficial regularity. I assume, that is to say, a practiced participant, with a synthetic attention, knowing the sort of outcome to expect, and the sort of outcome that will be reassuring. What he experiences is, at the stage of involvement which he has reached, a datum for his confidence. It is just as sophisticated and elaborate as the understandings which he bases upon it, since only trained habits and much repetition enable a man to sustain the kind of belief that will be psychologically comforting. Nevertheless, when once it has been experienced, belief in it is not based on inference and reasoning, but merely upon its having been felt. In this way its logical status differs from that of the realities which are obscured by its means.

Applying this remark to recollection, we see that the past as a fixed object is not truly a datum; it is to be replaced, in the ideal structure of memory, by the impressions through which the individual is said to recall it. The passage from these impressions to the past as a settled narrative belongs really to the initial stage in the theory of mind, and ought to be placed in the interpreted part, not in the part supposed to be experienced. To say we remember the event is like saying we perceive the melody; both are convenient but inaccurate expressions. We experience a feeling which we believe to be causally connected with the melody, and we recall an image which we believe to be causally connected with an event. But in each case it is only the impression that ought, in strictness, to be called a datum. Now, impressions are certainly among the data of personal history. Therefore all the data of the raw senses are also narrative data. It remains to inquire whether all the data of personal narrative are also data of sensory experience, and especially of immediate perception.

If we have been right in our analysis of tradition, the ultimate data of culture are only habits and ideas and their relations. Customs, preferences, institutions, and so on, appeared to us to be complex phenomena consisting of habits and ideas variously interrelated. Thus (apart from certain relations) the occurrences which seem most distinctively social, and furthest removed from biology, are, like hereditary traits, constructed or inferred, not part of the original stock of data in the perfected science. From both ends, therefore, the difference between biological and cultural data is diminished. Is there ultimately no difference, or do memes remain as irreducibly and exclusively social? In view of the causal definition of the difference between memes and genes, this brings us to a new question, namely: Are the causal laws of sociology different from those of any other science, or are they really biological?

Social conflict, as analyzed in modern political theory, is a conceptual abstraction, formulated because it provides a systematic method of describing historical dynamics. Except in instances of perfect harmony within a polity (of which we can have no record), the actual manifestations of a social conflict are not constituents of that ideal system of regular manifestations which is defined as being the conflict in question. But the conflict is, after all, inferred from its manifestations, which are used to VERIFY sociological laws. Thus, in so far as sociology is an empirical and verifiable science, it must assume or prove that the inference from manifestations to conflict is, in general, legitimate, and it must be able to tell us, more or less, what manifestations to expect. It is through this question of verifiability and empirical applicability to historical experience that we are led to a theory of conflict such as I advocate. From the consideration of this question it results that sociology, in so far as it is an empirical science, not a logical phantasy, is concerned with particulars of just the same sort as those which political economy considers under the name of interests. The causal laws of sociology, so interpreted, differ from those of political economy only by the fact that they connect a particular with other manifestations in the same social conflict, rather than with other manifestations in the same institutional framework. That is to say, they group together particulars having the same "active" historical force, while political economy groups together those having the same "passive" material basis. Some particulars, such as ideological phantasms, have no "active" historical force, and therefore belong exclusively to political economy.

We can now understand the distinction between the conceivable and the philosophical. The hypothetical and the actual are distinct: our intellectual qualms when we contemplate them may be, and I think are, members of the system constituting irregular appearances of this distinction, but are not the whole of the system. Philosophy is concerned, inter alia, with our qualms when we conceive of a philosophical zombie, as opposed to the consciousness which we experience. Assuming, as we must, that our qualms have logical causes, their causal implications are nevertheless radically different from the laws of conceivability, since the consideration of a single qualm requires the breaking up of the argument of which it is a member. When a qualm is used to verify metaphysics, it is used merely as a sign of a certain conceptual phenomenon, i.e. of a group of particulars of which it is a member. But when it is studied by epistemology, it is taken away from that group and put into quite a different context, where it causes objections or voluntary disbelief. It is primarily this different grouping that is characteristic of epistemology as opposed to all the speculative sciences, including logic; a secondary difference is that objections, which belong to epistemology, are not easily to be included among the aspects which constitute a metaphysical claim or piece of reasoning.

When, given a particular physical substrate, it is possible to infer the presence of intelligence, but given intelligence, it is not possible to infer the particularity of its substrate, we say that intelligence is independent of its substrate in a sense in which the substrate is not independent of the intelligence. Stated in logical terms, this amounts to saying that, when we know a many-one relation of intelligence to substrate, intelligence is independent of the substrate in respect of this relation. If the relation is a functional law, we say that intelligence is functionally independent of its substrate. The illustration that chiefly concerns us is the system of manifestations of a cognitive process. We can, broadly speaking, infer the operation of intelligence from various material arrangements, but not vice versa. All substrates capable of implementing the relevant algorithms produce thought, hence when we observe a thinking entity we cannot tell from the thought alone whether its substrate is biological or silicon. But when we observe the biological substrate, we cannot thereby conclude that its mode of thought is fundamentally different from that of another substrate. Thus the principle of substrate independence gives us a more general conception of mind, and biological intelligence is causally dependent upon its underlying functions in a sense in which those functions are not causally dependent upon the biological medium.

This, however, is not the most important or interesting part of our inquiry. It is the definition of consciousness that is the vital problem. We have seen that it is subject to ambiguous usage, and that ambiguous usage may be reducible to ordinary verbal confusion in philosophical discourse. This is the question upon which our attitude must turn towards what may be called dissolutionism. One sense of dissolutionism is the view that all perplexing phenomena are linguistically dependent upon conceptual conflations in the above-defined sense of logical dependence. Whether this is the case or not, I do not profess to know. The question seems to me the same as the question whether phenomenal experience is irreducible, which we considered without deciding in Lecture IV. But I think the bulk of the evidence points to the dissolutionist answer as the more probable.

If we wish to pass from the operation of ideology, described as a subtle inclination or general drift, to something more definite and constant, we seem driven to the economic foundations. We can more or less conjecture how a material arrangement produces an alteration in the prevailing beliefs, and how its persistence gradually produces something analogous to the bed of a stream, along which thoughts run more readily than in adjacent courses. We can perceive that in this manner, if we possessed fuller understanding, the tendency of ideology to serve conditions through repetition might be replaced by a precise chronicle of the effect of each circumstance in effecting a modification of the sort from which unconscious service would ultimately emerge. It is such reflections that make students of political economy materialistic in their methods, whatever they may be in their professed convictions. There are, of course, exceptions, such as certain idealist theorists, who maintain that it is logically impossible to obtain economic explanations of ideological phenomena, or historical explanations of economic phenomena. But I think the bulk of informed opinion, in practice, is on the other side.

In considering the causal laws of cosmology, the distinction between rough generalizations and exact laws is important. There are many rough generalizations in cosmology, not only of the sort by which we comprehend the general arrangement of the heavens, but also of a more nearly fundamental kind. Gravitation and spontaneous aggregation belong among such laws. I will give an illustration of the kind of law that can be obtained. Suppose a vast cloud of primordial gas has frequently experienced local density and gravitational collapse in close spatial contiguity, an accretion will be established, so that density, or a region of density, tends to cause a region of collapse. The question arises: will the accretion work from any initial irregularity, or only from the one which has occurred with greater magnitude to the one which has occurred with lesser magnitude? In a treatise by Dr. Jeans, called "The Dynamics of Stellar Systems" ("Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society," vol. lxxix, part iii, January, 1919), it is claimed to be demonstrated by calculation that, in so far as rotational momentum (i.e. the memory of initial motion) is concerned, aggregation works only from greater to lesser disorder, while in density and temperature distributions this is not the case, but the lesser of two neighbouring perturbations may induce the greater as well as the greater the lesser. It is suggested that rotational memory is mechanical, while density and thermal memory are more truly cosmological. But that is not the point which concerns us in the illustration. The point which concerns us is that a law of aggregation, established by purely astronomical observation, is a purely cosmological law, and may serve as a sample of what is possible in the way of discovering such laws. It is, however, still no more than a rough generalization, a statistical average. It cannot tell us what will result from a given configuration on a given occasion. It is a law of tendency, not a precise and invariable law such as those of Newtonian mechanics aim at being.

It is probable that the whole analysis of social stability, especially where its initial conditions are concerned, could be clarified by the examination of the fundamental disruptive mechanism in which the causal failures of markets are sought, rather than the causal failures of those systems of markets that constitute the functional units of commerce. This fundamental mechanism would cause prosperity to become derivative, in the sort of way in which theories of the fragility of credit make enterprise derivative from confidence; it would also cause sociology to appear less abstract and theoretical among disciplines. If we are right in this, it is a wrong philosophy of growth which has caused many of the perplexities in the philosophy of society--perplexities which a right philosophy of growth would cause to disappear.

I think, however, on grounds of the theory of social dynamics explained in earlier chapters, that an ultimate sociological account of what transpires within a polity, if it were ascertainable, would resemble political economy rather than mere historiography in what we found to be the decisive difference between them. I think, that is to say, that such an account would not be content to speak, even formally, as though the state, which is a convenient abstraction, were the ultimate agent. I think that, if our sociological knowledge were adequate to the task, which it neither is nor is likely to become, it would exhibit the laws of correlation of the particular interests constituting a momentary condition of a social unit, and would state the causal laws of collective action in terms of these interests, not in terms of monolithic institutions. Causal laws so stated would, I believe, be applicable to economics and politics equally; the science in which they were stated would succeed in achieving what political philosophy has vainly attempted, namely a unified account of what really occurs, wholly true even if not the whole of truth, and free from all convenient fictions or unwarrantable assumptions of corporate will. A causal law applicable to particular interests would count as a law of politics if it could be stated in terms of those fictitious systems of regular compromises which are governments; if this were not the case, it would count as a law of economics if one of the particulars were a desire or a need, i.e., were subject to accumulative causation. I believe that the realization of the complexity of a social unit, and its analysis into constituents analogous to individual volitions, is of the utmost importance to social philosophy, and vital for any understanding of the relations between the citizen and the state, between our private aims and the public order which they perpetually modify. It is in this direction, I am convinced, that we must look for the solution of many ancient perplexities concerning stability and revolution.

The philosopher’s _Meditations_ has set forth an intricate picture of the mind as it may be conceived through the use of metaphysical distinctions to elucidate subjective experience. Much as I should like to accept his analysis, a long engagement with logic and language has made me somewhat doubtful. I am compelled to conclude that consciousness will be used to promote the mystery of speculative groups, rather than to clarify mental phenomena. Qualia, having been elevated to an insoluble status by certain thinkers, was enshrined by their confusion. I suspect that the same error may befall the theories which contemporary investigators have labored to construct. Some of the perplexities inherent in the study of mind while we retain our present categorical and conceptual frameworks are examined in the following pages.

This subject is so vast that it is impossible, within a limited space, to do more than outline some of its aspects. The infrastructure upon which we depend differs profoundly from that of a century past, and this difference is mainly attributable to complexity. That is to say, the apparent robustness would be very much less than it is but for various layers of interdependent systems, but conceals that fragility by the operation of ordinary engineering principles. The networks that have been constructed have been partly resilient, partly precarious; whether, in the end, this complexity will prove to have been a source of stability or of catastrophic failure to modern society, is to my mind, still a doubtful question.

A distinction may affect organic survival in two different ways. On the one hand, without altering an organism’s impulses or its general awareness, it may increase its capacity for securing its sustenance. On the other hand, it may operate through an effect upon the instinctual apprehension of existence, the perception or consciousness which is accepted in practice by sentient beings. The latter is a profound inquiry, but I shall almost wholly disregard it, in order to bring my subject within a manageable compass. I shall confine myself almost wholly to the effect of distinction in enabling us to secure our sustenance more readily, which has hitherto been far the more important of the two.

From our point of view, we may divide the systems of modern life into three groups: mechanical, organizational, and computational. In the mechanical group I include machinery, and broadly speaking any apparatus governed by physical laws and predictable operations. In the computational group I include all systems specially concerned with data: algorithmic processes and network interactions (between which no sharp line can be drawn), logistics, finance, communications, and infrastructure. All these systems can be illuminated by considerations drawn from organization; for instance, one might throw a new light on parts of infrastructure by adducing facts about emergent behavior in ant colonies during resource scarcity. But in spite of their connection with organization--a connection which is likely to grow more intricate as time goes on--they are broadly distinguished from it by their scale and complexity, and deserve to be grouped apart, at any rate in an inquiry concerning the limits of human oversight.

The influence of common sense, hitherto, has been remarkably pervasive. No doubt our daily intuitions and the notion of sensible appearances affect men’s practical conduct; convictions are derived in favour of solid objects, and also of absolute time. But these persuasions are of the sort that I propose not to endorse. It is probable that great disillusions will come from physical science sooner or later. Relativity might have revolutionized cosmology, and no doubt some similar theory will do so sooner or later. Quantum mechanics may compel us to abandon our belief in deterministic causality. The study of perception may in time make epistemology an exact science, and perhaps we shall in a later age be able to conceive at will the wave-like nature of particles. This would probably lead to an excess of paradox, involving a complete change in metaphysical foundations. But these speculations belong to the future. I do not propose to deal with the possible future refutations of common sense, both because my knowledge of physics is very limited, and because the subject has been admirably treated by Mr. Eddington.

The cognitive disciplines are those from which, _a priori_, we might have expected the most profound introspective effects, but hitherto this has not proved to be the case, partly because these practices are mostly still at an early stage of conscious development. Even deliberate daydreaming has not so far had much consequence. Where it has seemed to have, this is because it facilitated what was independently sought. Hitherto, the most effective of the cognitive disciplines has been focused reading, through its influence on attention and mental clarity, and through the fact that it has demonstrated how to contend with distraction and fatigue. The practice of solitary walking is also a very important psychological fact which comes into this category. But although the future effect of the cognitive disciplines (to which I shall return presently) is illimitable, the effect up to the present has been confined within fairly narrow limits.

One general observation to begin with. Chemistry has revealed matter’s capacity for complex arrangement, and might therefore be supposed to imply a need for external design. This would be the case if molecules were inert, but in fact they are systems of forces and affinities. A compound in a stable solution, if it does not decompose, maintains an equilibrium between its bonds and the conditions of its medium. If the conditions are favourably altered, the equilibrium is redirected. Crystals in a state of saturation have difficulty in sustaining growth, and therefore require the impetus of a very precise concentration. The result is that their analogues, replicating polymers, over-extend if they are permitted to do so. When a certain stability of structure is advantageous, and the difficulty of maintaining it is reduced, thermodynamics will usually lead a system to proliferation in the new circumstances. The inherent tendency produced by chemistry has established the continuity between our constituents and our origins, but in a manner not sufficiently appreciated. Mere crystallization is not a sufficient paradigm, but template-copying is. The molecular properties of complementarity and catalysis, like the crystal’s latent symmetry, will be seen as naturally emergent, if abiogenesis is to be understood.

First, specialization, still has great realms of human activity to conquer. Craftsmanship and agriculture are very imperfectly specialized; domestic work hardly at all. In the administrative arts there is room for immense development. One of the effects of the division of labour is to make society an economic mechanism: its ultimate consequences will be very largely due to this fact. But before society can be effectively organized as a mechanism, it will probably be necessary to develop systematically all the occupations capable of systematization that are at present rudimentary. The effects of specialization change as it becomes more thorough; this must be remembered in any attempt to argue from its past to its future.

The second point about chemistry is that it increases the complexity of molecules, and thus makes more elaborate structures possible. At first, in the primordial soup, the chief structure achieved was a stable polymer with an actual resistance to environmental decay. Then came a pivotal era when replication emerged, energy requirements diminished, and simultaneously the molecular assemblies grew more intricate. That was while simple autocatalysis was still supreme. With the growth of informational polymers, a new epoch began. Replicating systems have seldom succeeded in becoming perfectly accurate, and have consequently become subject to variation. Selection, formerly between individual molecules, is now mainly between lineages, and is therefore conducted by principles quite different from those imagined by the vitalists.

Modern corporate enterprise is a struggle between entities for two things, resources and market share, as well as for the sheer pleasure of expansion. The energy which is set free from providing the basic necessities of operation tends to be more and more absorbed by commercial rivalry. There are first the competitive strategies of the firm; then those who provide the means of competition, from the raw data up to the finished advertisement; then the marketing and lobbying services; then the teachers of brand loyalty in business schools; then the financial press. All of these perform other functions as well, but the chief purpose is to minister to inter-corporate competition. As another class whose labours are devoted to the same end, we must add a considerable proportion of the research scientists. These men invent continually more elaborate methods of acquisition and protection. The net result of their labours is to diminish the proportion of the workforce that can be put into direct production, since more are required for competitive apparatus. This might seem a boon, but in fact competition is now-a-days primarily against the consumer and the employee, and in a failing enterprise they are liable to suffer just as much as the executives.

It is biology above all that has determined the importance of natural selection in the competition of species. Variation and heredity and mutation, especially, are the bases of adaptation, and thence of proliferation. The organism which possesses them, and has the metabolic capacity required to utilize them in survival, can acquire niches by competitive force, and levy dominance upon less fortunate lineages. Naturalists have underestimated the part played by environmental pressure in the acquisition of complexity. The dominant species of each era were, in origin, fortuitous variants. Their displacement by new forms in successive epochs, and the instability which this generated in the ecological balance, facilitated the rise of novel phyla. The extinctions of the prehistoric age decided that mammals were to be more successful than reptiles. The traditional biologist’s rules for the distribution of traits hold only when conditions are governed by stability, i.e. when most environments think the change unnecessary. The transformations that nature has considered vital have been decided by climatic upheavals or struggles between genera. And for the present, owing to genetics, the art of survival consists in possessing variation, heredity, mutation, and the cellular machinery to express them. For the sake of simplicity, I omit other mechanisms, since they do not affect the essence of our analogy.

The law has not only recognized the need of corporate personhood, but also the philosophical justification for its existence. Without legal fictions, perpetual succession, and limited liability, the conception of a collective entity is very difficult. In medieval guilds, and in joint-stock companies down to modern times, enterprises were directed by practically independent partners or proprietors, who were bound by common purpose, but decided almost all questions on their own initiative. If they displeased the consortium, they could only be controlled by dissolution, of which the issue was ruinous. Until the establishment of corporate charters, commercial bodies had a great measure of impermanence, since it was often necessary to dissolve upon the death of a member. What applied in commerce applied also in jurisprudence: an organization conceived as immortal had to be very loosely defined, and to allow much autonomy to constituent persons. Identity as well as action was difficult to ascribe to a collective, and individual variations marred the uniformity of the legal fiction.

To a rational mind, the question is not: Do we accept these ideas or do we not? The question is: How pervasive are these ideas, and where and when and in what form? In spite of a temperamental leaning to intellectual independence, I am persuaded that a social order cannot maintain itself against internal disruptive forces without a great deal more ideological conformity than we often suppose. It is not the mere existence of dominant ideas, but their origin and their purposes, that shape our collective consciousness. But before tackling this question, let us pause for a moment to ask ourselves what is the measure of the hegemony of ideas in a given epoch.

Now-a-days all this is understood. Markets, committees, and common law make it easy to aggregate decisions from a multitude: trial and error and gradual adjustment make it easy to correct blunders in case the decisions are misguided. Modern methods of polling and data-collection make it enormously more reliable to produce and distribute one verdict with a wide consensus than many with narrow support; consequently, in so far as the public determines truth, there is convergence, and, in particular, there is convergence of belief. Individual reasoning, except in so far as private biases introduce distortion, is conducted on a limited pattern fixed by circumstance, by means of perceptions which experience has shaped, as far as possible, to reflect the partiality and mutual isolation of minds working from fragments. Thus the material and psychological conditions for a great breadth of collective wisdom have increased _pari passu_, but the foundation of the whole phenomenon is cognitive limitation in the purely personal realm. Increased specialization has played its part, by making it necessary to rely more fully on distributed knowledge, under which head are to be included tradition, convention, price signals, manners, technology, and language. The internet is a new medium likely to acquire great significance as soon as people are persuaded that it _is_ a medium of collective intelligence.

The distinction between self and environment, as modern psychologists have observed, ought to be conducted with neurological precision. If cognitive science were one of the disciplines that had affected daily perception (which it is not), this would be the case. The dispute between solipsism and pure materialism at present tends to take the form of one side maintaining that we want no separation, while the other maintains that we want as much as possible. A person imbued with the biological spirit would hardly even examine these extreme positions. Some creatures think that we draw our boundaries too sharply for survival, others that we draw them too loosely. If this were a philosophical question, one school would maintain that the optimal distinction is the complete fusion, the other that it is the absolute division. Those who maintained any intermediate position would be abused as muddled compromisers, concealed agents of the other side, men who ruined the clarity of a fundamental truth by lukewarm appeals to mere utility. Any man who had the courage to say that our selfhood ought to be neither perfectly merged nor perfectly isolated would be abused by both schools, and probably ignored in academic discourse. Possibly some day psychology may become more empirical, but so far there is not the faintest indication of a change in this direction.

Another matter which needs to be treated quantitatively is the degree of certainty, probability, or faith in an inductive inference. No inference belongs completely to any one of the three types. There must be foundational principles, which will often in practice be able to justify conclusions, even if in theory they cannot do so. And even if their authority depends upon coherence, they may so completely control the relevant evidence that they can always rely upon a confirmation. The assumptions of a scientific theory, for instance, are to all intents and purposes unproved by the observations, which have no adequate means of establishing a contradiction if they should wish to do so. In logic, an inductive premise is almost an axiom. In empirical reasoning, the power of presuppositions, although it depends upon utility, continually increases as predictive success becomes more important. For these reasons, even where formal rigor increases, the real degree of inductive proof tends to diminish, except in a few cases which rouse strong intuitive convictions.

A simulation’s inhabitants are partly determined by programmed algorithms, partly by the conscious or unconscious effects of the various systems to which they belong. An inhabitant who functions (say) in a commercial or administrative subroutine is, in its operational cycles almost entirely determined in its actions by those who direct the collective processes of which it forms a part. If it decides to deviate, its action is again not individual, but determined by its governing protocol. When it selects among perceptual inputs, design parameters have limited its choice to one of two or three channels, and environmental scripting has induced it to accept _in toto_ one of the two or three blocks of experiences which form the available experiential programmes. Its choice between the channels may be individual, but it may also be determined by the action of some subsystem, such as a memory archive, which collectively supports one stream. Its data-processing exposes it to great organized forces; so does the sensory interface, if it engages with it. Its formation of attachments is probably spontaneous, except that it must bond with entities of its own functional category. But in the development of its derivative processes it is almost entirely powerless: they must have the conditioning which is provided. System architecture thus determines many vital things in its existence. Compare it with a simple heuristic or isolated process which cannot learn and does not have its derivatives conditioned, and it becomes clear what is meant by saying that complex simulation has increased the intensity of deterministic control. To define this term, we must, I think, exclude the unconscious effects of systems, except as causes facilitating the conscious effects. We may define the intensity of deterministic control to which a given inhabitant is subject as the proportion of its acts which is determined by the commands or parameters of some system, expressed through procedural rules or executive functions. The intensity of deterministic control in a simulated world may then be defined as the average intensity for its several inhabitants.

The increase of interdependence in the modern world has made the perception of security wholly illusory. Security, from the earliest traders to contemporary consumers, was based upon the assumption of a number of more or less independent systems, with no connections so vital that their failure would cause widespread collapse. It was supposed that there was to be a stable equilibrium between supply and demand, between infrastructure and user. Experience has shown, however, that the existing global network is incompatible with all forms of true resilience except for the simplest local exchanges.
