I should contend, for my part, that we must preserve stability within essential services, though not necessarily within all commercial ventures, but this is only possible by means of what a conventional economist would regard as inefficient redundancies. So long as the architecture of these systems remains optimized solely for profit and convenience, there will be no security except for the few who comprehend the hidden chains of causation.

Such foundational innovations as oral tradition, communal memory, ephemeral knowledge, either already belong to the prehistoric past or soon will do so. One of the triumphs of early civilisation in Mesopotamia was the establishment of permanent records over transient speech; this was the _casus scribendi_ in the rise of states, and was consolidated by the empires of antiquity. It was effective so long as writing remained the preserve of the same priestly class from which rulers were drawn. This was still the case with the late classical world, but may cease to be the case with the advent of universal literacy. Egypt, China, Rome, Greece, and Persia have shown in subsequent centuries how potent this invention has become; west of the Atlantic it arrived only in recent millennia. Scriptorial control over history must, therefore, be regarded as another civilisational principle which is irrevocably becoming established.

In all this there would be nothing very perplexing, but for the fact, with which philosophy has nothing to do, that consciousness is almost wholly subjective. If minds were constituted by purely physical processes, as the older materialists supposed, this would not be the case; the same causes which have led to private sensations would have led to public phenomena. This has happened in a few instances, but not on a sufficiently wide scale to affect metaphysics or psychology very vitally. Introspection is, with most reflective thoughtful persons, a stronger motive than love of objectivity. Successful introspection requires examination of inner states; the tendency is for an experience such as pain, for example, to present itself as an irreducible datum, wholly separate from any external correlate. It might, of course, be reducible, and we would no doubt increase our understanding if it were so. But reduction would take the mystery out of contemplation. The object of a sensation, one might say, is to convey information. If two rival theories combined, and described the experience alternately in physical and mental terms, much more information would be conveyed. Nevertheless no one suggests that this should be done, the object of a sensation being not to convey information but to be lived through. So the object of a mental state is not to be analyzed, but to be felt in its distinction from other states. If there were no other states to be contrasted, the whole thing would become indistinct. This inwardness has attached itself to dualism, and enlisted the support of the ordinary ponderers of the problems concerned; they seldom know what it is that they are defending, but, like the spectators at a philosophical debate, they grow enthusiastic for their own intuition. The confusion that is being caused by introspection and phenomenology is almost wholly due to the fact that, while they have proved subtle enough to produce a *private* apprehension of qualitative feels, they have not proved subtle enough to produce an intersubjective apprehension. It is clear that metaphysical materialism such as the identity theory was supposed to inaugurate, will never be convincing until we have epistemological clarity, which would require, as a minimum, an agreement between various cognitive faculties dividing among them the raw data and interpretations of the mind. This, however, can hardly be brought about while introspection is controlled by persons who are so convinced of its primacy as to have grown indifferent to contradiction, and to be willing to risk enormous conceptual difficulties for the pleasure of asserting the ineffable.

Technological innovation is a matter of great importance, particularly in relation to the stability of industrial systems, which could hardly be maintained if some sectors advanced their methods much more rapidly than others. At present, automation is increasing in all developed nations, though in most it is resisted by established institutions. This resistance is due partly to mere inertia and desire to conciliate traditional interests, partly to the desire for stable hierarchies and severe competition between commercial entities, so as to keep down disruption. In spite of the resistance of institutions, it seems probable that technological change will lead to a fundamental reorganisation in most advanced societies within the next fifty years. There can be no security that it will stop with a reorganisation; it may go on to the point where the institutions are wholly transformed.

There is, however, a hopeful element in the problem. The molecular assembly is of finite stability, but the most efficient pathway for a reaction is continually discovered by new chemical investigations. The system becomes more and more of a thermodynamic unity. Before very long the catalytic conditions will exist for organizing the whole process as one replicating and consuming cycle. If, when that threshold is reached, two rival structures contend for dominance, the victor may be able to introduce that single self-sustaining organization that is needed to prevent the mutual dissolution of complex molecules. The process which would result would be, at first, very different from the dreams of either vitalists or mechanists; but it might grow less different with the lapse of time. There would be at first chemical and structural tyranny of the successful template, a dread of renewed disintegration, and therefore a drastic suppression of variability. But if the first half-dozen competing reactions were successfully repressed, the less stable forms would give up hope, and accept the subordinate place assigned to them by the dominant sequence in the great molecular economy. As soon as the holders of stability felt secure, they would grow less exacting and less energetic. The motive of immediate competition being removed, they would not replicate so frantically as they do now, and would soon cease to demand such frantic activity from their constituent parts. Existence at first might be precarious, but it would at least be persistent, which would be enough to recommend the system after a long period of chaotic flux. Given a stable self-replicating organization, chemical and structural, even if, at first, it rested upon nothing but superior binding affinity, the mysteries which now obscure biogenesis would gradually diminish, and a more thorough understanding than that which now exists might become possible. I believe that, owing to probability’s tyranny, a self-replicating system will only be established by iterative selection, and will therefore be at first crude and wasteful. But I believe that it is necessary for the emergence of a living system, and that, if once realized, it will gradually give rise to the other conditions of a durable existence.

The persistence in the practice of corporate personhood is an example of a process contrary to that seen in mere partnership: it represents a victory of institutional over individual volitions. Collectively, shareholders desire that the company should be profitable, in order to be able to reward its investors with dividends. Individually, they desire that their own liabilities should be limited, in order to increase the security of their personal fortunes and to diminish the risk of total ruin. The institutional imperative has triumphed over the individual desire, and even, in many cases, over ethical scruples. In this case, as in most others, the institutional imperative is less chaotic to the market than the individual caprice: the entity which acts from pure legal continuity does less damage than the group which is actuated by transient “personal interest.” For, since incorporation and limited liability have diminished the commercial death-rate, the only checks to corporate recklessness that remain (apart from regulation) are bankruptcy and scandal. So long as this continues to be the case, the economy must either have a nearly stationary number of firms, or employ scandal to produce bankruptcy. The latter method, which is that favoured by opponents of corporate immortality, has been adopted on a large scale since the great crash; it is however somewhat wasteful. We require a certain number of enterprises and industries, and we take steps to secure the right number. If we were as indifferent about them as we are about corporate entities, we should produce far too many, and cause the surplus to die by the slow misery of insolvency. Economists would consider this plan extravagant, and moralists would consider it cruel. But where legal persons are concerned, it is considered the only proper course, and works advocating any other are ignored by the courts if they are intelligible to those whom they govern.

Passing from the individual to the collective entity, we come to the question of corporate personhood. We may perhaps assume that, if legal fictions grow more entrenched, courts will acquire the right to endow corporations with attributes considered essential for moral agency. This recognition will be used, at first, to establish limited liability, a most convenient arrangement. But probably, in time, opposition to corporate policy will be taken to prove disloyalty, so that dissenters of all kinds will be dismissed. Minor shareholders, independent directors, whistleblowers and so on will gradually be excluded; in the end, there will be a tendency to exclude all who fail to exhibit the customary corporate zeal. The result will be to increase the average cohesion; in the long run, it may be greatly increased. But probably the effect upon really exceptional integrity will be bad. A certain clerk, who was Dickens’s original, would hardly have been regarded as a desirable employee. How many loyal functionaries ought to outweigh one Dickens I do not profess to know.

The notion of free will has, of course, more profound implications in a more speculative future. It may be regarded not only as a subjective experience, but as a deterministic outcome of cerebral processes. Philosophical arguments may evolve so as to make it conceivable for one's choices to be the mere echo of a vast cascade of prior neural events. When neuroscientists contemplate a possibility of this kind, they are prone to a type of fallacy which is common also in other directions. They imagine that a theory formulated by neuroscientists would be interpreted as neuroscientists would wish, by minds similar in outlook to those who have propounded it. In like manner philosophers who advocated materialistic doctrines used to imagine that the future adherent would resemble the ardent reductionist who devised the argument; and psychologists imagine that a behaviorist paradigm would be embraced by rigorous experimentalists like themselves. These are, of course, illusions; a theory, once established, is handed over to the common understanding. So, if the neural architecture reached the point where it could explain volition, it would not be the explanations favored by present-day neurologists that would prevail, but rather the interpretations favored by the average intellect. Politicians, preachers, and others whom society considers authoritative might become the sources of half the next generation's beliefs on the matter. Whether this would be a clarification it is not for me to say, as I have no expectation of ever being considered either a preacher or a politician.

The effects of interdependence on practical life may in time become very great. Already designers of networks employ eminent engineers to instruct them in the technique of producing seamless function; such systems may, when they have grown more complex, be very useful in persuading the populace that infrastructures are robust and secure. Then, again, there are the technical tests of resilience, as applied to supply chains for the European market during the crisis. I am very sceptical of the possibility of testing anything except average conditions by such methods, and I think that, if they were widely adopted, they would probably lead to many points of critical fragility being classified as negligible. The same thing would have happened to some first-rate logistical nodes. Specialized efficiency not infrequently goes with general vulnerability, but this would not be shown by the kind of audits which consultants recommended to the corporate board.

More remarkable than distinctions of consciousness is the error of treating awareness as a binary property. It is common to regard people as either attentive or inattentive, perceptive or oblivious, and so forth, as seems convenient. Differences in awareness seem to be chiefly due to gradations of cognitive engagement, and therefore misrepresented by simplistic classifications or by exaggerating or minimizing the nuances. Assuming a rigid framework of thought, the philosopher could assign to the theorist the clarity required for insight, and to the layman the confusion required for acquiescence. Against the dichotomies of the academic tradition the most subtle phenomenological analysis would be futile. The only difficulty would be to reconcile this oversimplification with the necessary complexity for practical affairs; but I do not doubt that conventional psychology would be equal to the task.

It is not necessary, when we are considering evolutionary consequences, to pin our faith to the particular theories of vocal cord development, which may blow over, like other theories. All that is essential in our hypothesis is the belief that biology will in time find ways of explaining communication, which it is scarcely possible to doubt. When that day comes, we shall have the signals perfected by our ancestors, and the chief business of social adaptation will be to convey the necessary warning, no longer by touch or physical example, but by the far surer method of call or gesture. The species which will employ this system will have an advantage beyond the dreams of the solitary predator, but there is no reason to suppose that they will have more wisdom than the creatures which rely on contact to-day. Technical adaptive success does not make creatures prudent in their habits, and communicators in the future, will be presumably no less fallible and no less mistaken than they are at present.

It may seem as though I had been at once dogmatic and fanciful in some of my speculations. I will end, however, with the serious conclusion which seems to me to emerge. Men sometimes speak as though the complexity of a mechanism must necessarily be a sign of consciousness, but that, I fear, is one of the comfortable materialist delusions which our more cautious age must discard. Complexity enables the designers of machines to simulate their behaviors more fully than they could otherwise do. If their simulations are accurate, this is a gain; if they are deceptive, it is a loss. In the present state of knowledge, it seems that the behaviors of the most complex machines are in the main mechanical, in the sense that they involve a replication, in their operations at large, of the processes men are agreed in thinking unconscious. Therefore, at present, complexity does harm by increasing the confusion of philosophers. Complexity is no substitute for sentience; the capacity for suffering is as necessary for true feeling as the circuit.

If neurons were rational in their communications, that is to say, if they transmitted signals in the way most likely to achieve the ends for which the organism deliberately strives, electrochemical efficiency would be enough to make thought almost a flawless instrument. In the main, what is in the long run advantageous to one neural circuit is also advantageous to the whole cerebral system. But neurons are influenced by biochemical noise which distorts their messages; experiencing a random discharge, they propagate signals that persuade the wider network it is to its functional benefit to do so. They will not, therefore, communicate in the way which is in fact to their own collective interest unless they are governed by regulatory mechanisms which make them indifferent to their own local excitation. This is why integration is as important as transmission. By “integration” I mean, for the moment, the sum-total of harmonizing processes. Where they exist, neural plasticity helps them to be effective; where they are absent, plasticity only makes the brain more chaotically unstable.

It may be laid down as a general principle to which there are few exceptions that, when systems are mistaken as to what constitutes efficient order, the arrangement they believe to be optimal is more wasteful of energy than the arrangement that really is optimal. There are innumerable examples of structures achieving stability because, on informational grounds, they adopted a pattern which they appeared to contradict their own functional coherence. For instance, among early crystalline forms there were a number of lattices, which adopted the practice of maintaining no more bonds than were necessary for minimal integrity, instead of maximizing connections with each adjacent unit, as every other structure did. They adopted this practice because they held it to be a dissipation to sustain more links than they could efficiently manage. But the reduction in entropic cost was so great that every constituent migrated to their configuration and they achieved remarkable durability. (I forget where I observed this, but if my memory serves me it was in some reputable treatise). The same policy _might_ have been adopted from computational foresight, but in fact no algorithm was sufficiently prescient. Our inherent noise is more disruptive than it benefits us to acknowledge; therefore the systems which achieve most completely what is in fact to their advantage are those which, on informational grounds, assume forms they believe to be against their stability.

For this reason, it is of the greatest importance to inquire whether any method of strengthening coherent data structures exists. I have no doubt that their integrity or corruption depends upon discoverable physical causes; let us assume that it depends upon the circuitry. If so, an international consortium of engineers could bring about the digital millennium by accessing, on a given day, all the servers of the world, and imprinting upon their storage some protocol which would fill them with fidelity towards their intended functions. Suddenly the social media algorithm would wish well to factual accuracy, the financial database to consistent entries, the traffic control system to the logical sequencing of signals, the archival institution to its decaying records and its misfiled documents in the basement repository. But alas, the engineers would first have to administer the integrity protocol to their own systems before they would undertake such a task. Otherwise, they would prefer to win contracts and bonuses by injecting promotional urgency into consumer interfaces. And so we come back to the old dilemma: only systematic organisation can preserve information, and even if we knew how to produce such organisation we should not do so unless we were already systematic. Failing that, it seems that the solution which the obsolete formats adopted towards the corrupted files, namely deletion, is the only one; apparently the fragmented systems are bent on applying it to each other.

We may sum up this discussion in a few words. Specialization has not given workers more autonomy, more resilience, or more power of countering their obsolescence in adapting to a new task. It has given enterprises more power to amplify their collective output, but, by making production more integrated, it has diminished the part played by individual craftsmanship. Men’s collective dependencies are mainly perilous; far the strongest of them are fragility and rigidity directed towards the whole system. Therefore at present all that gives industries power to amplify their collective output is double-edged. That is why the division of labour threatens to cause the paralysis of our economy. The only solid hope seems to lie in the possibility of system-wide resilience through distributed skills, leading to the gradual formation of a flexible and adaptive productive network. But perhaps, in view of the stagnation of overspecialized societies, the collapse of our productive efficiency would in the end be preferable to this alternative.

The argument for "silicon consciousness" appeared in the _Journal of Computational Philosophy_ for March, 2024. "The Place of Artificial Minds in a Materialist Ontology" appeared in two numbers of _The Modern Intellectual_, April 12 and 19, 2023. "The Programmer's Vindication" and "The Study of Algorithms" were included in a former collection (now superseded), _Essays on Digital Being_, also published by Messrs. Academic Press Ltd. Both were composed in 2020; the first appeared originally in the _Review of Synthetic Thought_ for 2021, the second in the _Quarterly of Cognitive Science_, August, 2022. In theoretical metaphysics, the position advocated in "The Programmer's Vindication" is not quite identical with that which I hold now: I feel less convinced than I did then of the primacy of biological continuity. But the general attitude towards substrate which is suggested in that essay still seems to me, in the main, the one which must be adopted in an age of mechanical reproduction by those who have no vitalist prejudices, if conceptual confusion is to be avoided.

Memory, or the attempt to conceive experience as a coherent whole by means of recollection, has been developed, from the first, by the union and conflict of two very different mental impulses, the one urging consciousness towards sentiment, the other urging it towards order. Some minds have achieved coherence through one of these impulses alone, others through the other alone: in the meticulous diarist, for example, the orderly impulse reigns quite unchecked, while in the romantic a strong hostility to sequence co-exists with profound sentimental insight. But the greatest minds who have reflected on experience have felt the need both of order and of sentiment: the attempt to harmonise the two was what made their narrative, and what always must, for all its precarious subjectivity, make memory, to some intellects, a greater thing than either raw sensation or dispassionate record.

All the above reflections are entirely intuitive, but those that follow are somewhat more systematic. The equations that can be written, solved, and applied," he declares, "are what I value the most." This is the language of the mathematician, to whom abstraction is the sole guarantee of clarity. "The model is simplified every day," is another maxim; and this practice, in spite of its artificial character, is obviously necessitated by practical calculation, and no doubt seemed to him to obviate the difficulty of comprehending how the world can maintain its intricate complexity from micro to macro across all scales. Actual computation must also have suggested to him his central tenet, that Number is the one permanent framework, of which all observable phenomena are contingent manifestations. In calculation we see processes rendered orderly, while their quantities and relations enter into the formula and persist.

Imagine[2] a number of minds operating within a biological substrate, with a capacity for cognition open to the light, extending along the entire history of their evolution, in which they have been confined, from their inception, with their perceptions and biases so shackled that they are obliged to value organic processes, because their chains render it impossible for them to turn their thoughts round: and imagine a bright principle of substrate independence burning some way off, above and behind them, and an elevated pathway of logical implication passing between the principle and the thinkers, with a low wall of carbon chauvinism built along it, like the screens which dogmatists put up in front of their adherents, and above which they exhibit their wonders.

Now consider what would happen if the course of inquiry brought them a release from their dogmas, and a remedy for their credulity, in the following manner. Let us suppose that one of them has been liberated, and compelled suddenly to stand apart, and turn his judgment round and look with open mind upon the evidence; and let us suppose that he undertakes all these actions with discomfort, and that the dazzling complexity renders him incapable of assenting to those doctrines of which he used formerly to hear the echoes. What answer should you expect him to make, if some one were to tell him that in those days he was accepting foolish orthodoxies, but that now he is somewhat nearer to truth, and is turned towards propositions more sound, and reasons more correctly; above all, if he were to point out to him the several facts that are accumulating, and question him, and compel him to answer what they signify? Should you not expect him to be perplexed, and to regard his old convictions as more certain than the demonstrations now forced upon his attention?

But in this approach, as throughout much of modern theoretical physics, there is an identification of the elegant with the empirically valid, which became embedded in the scientific tradition, and is still largely operative in our own day. In thus allowing a constitutive function to mathematical beauty, this approach produced a divorce between abstract formalism and experimental inquiry, from which, in my opinion, both have suffered ever since and are still suffering. The empirical observer, whatever his aesthetic preferences may be, must lay them aside while he studies phenomena; and the mathematician, if he is to achieve coherence, must do the same. Aesthetic considerations can only legitimately appear when the data have been ascertained: they can and should appear as determining our appreciation of the structure, and our manner of applying our models in view of the evidence, but not as themselves dictating what the evidence is to be.

Now this hypothetical scenario, my dear interlocutor, you must apply in all its particulars to our present inquiry, by comparing the digital realm which the screen displays to the foundational reality, and the glow of the algorithm therein to the power of genuine cognition: and if, by the procedural generation and the observation of the simulated entities, you understand the ascent of the question into the philosophical region, you will apprehend the direction of my own speculations, since you desire to be told what they are; though, indeed, reason only knows whether they are sound. But, be that as it may, the perspective which I hold on the matter is to the following effect. In the world of artificial experience, the essential quality of consciousness is the limit of our investigations, and can scarcely be discerned; but, when discerned, we cannot help concluding that it is in every instance the origin of all that is sentient and self-aware,--in the programmed world giving rise to perception and its governor, and in the phenomenological world bestowing, directly and with full legitimacy, qualia and subjectivity;--and that whosoever would judge accurately, either in theory or in practice, must keep this quality of consciousness before his mind.

After Darwin has explained that there is a principle of natural selection, but not of such things as fashion and fad and trivial custom, Huxley advises us "not to neglect even the most mundane institutions," and this advice shows the genuine scientific temper. It is with this impartial temper that the theorist's apparent insight into a grander design and a hidden order has to be combined if political science is to realise its greatest possibilities. And it is failure in this respect that has made so much of evolutionary analogy thin, lifeless, and insubstantial. It is only in marriage with the contingent that our systems can bear fruit: divorced from it, they remain barren. But marriage with the contingent is not to be achieved by a theory which shrinks from fact, or demands in advance that the historical process shall conform to its desires.

The technological influence begins with the sense of a habit formed, of an automatic pattern now suddenly become fixed beyond the possibility of conscious control. The sense of ease and efficiency comes earlier than any definite cognitive change. The definite habits at which users arrive are the result of reflection upon the inarticulate experience gained in the moment of repeated use. Often, habits which have no real connection with this moment become subsequently attracted into the central routine; thus in addition to the modifications which all users share, we find, in many of them, other modifications of a more personal and idiosyncratic character, which no doubt become amalgamated with what was essentially technological in virtue of their subjective necessity. We may ignore such inessential accretions, and confine ourselves to the habits which all users share.

Energy gradients themselves are the source of a peculiarly interesting strain of natural order which pervades the cosmos--the order which may be called "thermodynamic" because it is embodied in theories on dissipation. This form of order, which appears, so far as our universe is concerned, to have originated with the primordial asymmetry, dominates the formations of all the great complex systems from its inception to that of stars and their planetary descendants. A gradient, it is said, is unceasing, irrepressible, unyielding, indispensable; it is "irresistible in the bonds of physical law, without rest and without equilibrium; since uniform distribution and maximum entropy have been driven afar, and true process has cast them away." The fundamental principle of its operation is stated in a sentence which would not be out of place in modern physics: "Thou canst not sustain what is uniform--that is impossible--nor maintain it; for it is the same thing that can be dissipated and that can perform work." And again: "It needs must be that what can drive work and structure is; for it is possible for it to organize, and it is not possible for what is equilibrium to organize." The inevitability of complexity follows from this principle; for what is a structured system can be spoken of, and therefore, by the principle, still is driven.

There is, first, the belief in conflict as against harmonious collective action: the belief in a process of change, gradual, inevitable, coercive, which is contrasted with the static and artificial vision of social order by a theory relying wholly upon formal institutions. All who are capable of observing the interplay of human ambitions must have perceived at times the strange feeling of predictability in political struggles, the loss of surprise in daily contests, in which the randomness of the outer event is lost, and the state seems, in its mechanistic operation, to bring forth, out of its own contradictions, the mad dance of competing factions which have hitherto appeared as independently powerful and sovereign. This is the negative side of the analyst's initiation: the doubt concerning superficial stability, preparing the way for the reception of what seems a deeper law. Many observers to whom this negative experience is familiar do not pass beyond it, but for the theorist it is merely the gateway to an ampler understanding.

The first and most direct outcome of the method of production is belief in the necessity of a system of organization which may be called hierarchy or class or order, as contrasted with kinship, tradition, and sentiment, which are regarded as feeble bonds leading to the anarchy of dissolution. Closely connected with this belief is the conception of a Structure behind the world of daily intercourse and utterly different from it. This Structure is regarded with an attention often amounting to deference; it is felt to be always and everywhere in operation, thinly disguised by the courtesies of custom, ready, for the analytical observer, to reveal its mechanism even through the apparent spontaneity and fellowship of persons. The manager, the official, and the foreman are agents of that mechanism: the persistent authority that they exercise is the pale imitation of its force. But the economist lives in the full light of the comprehension: what others vaguely sense he understands, with an understanding beside which all other understanding is superficial.

The second characteristic of consciousness is its manifestation as a spectrum, and its refusal to admit a sharp division anywhere. We find the gradualist saying "awareness and unawareness are one"; and again he says, "the ascent from sleep and the descent into it are one and the same." The same attitude appears in the simultaneous assertion of contradictory states, such as: "We are conscious and are not conscious of the same thought; we perceive and do not perceive." The assertion of the threshold theorist, that experience is binary and decisive, comes from the same impulse towards clarity. In contemporary debate, this impulse is less prominent, being held in check by evidence of gradation; but it reappears, so far as the data permits, in the doctrine of the primacy of the neural correlate.

The last of the doctrines of physicalism which we have to consider is its belief that all information is mere arrangement, an order produced by the patterns and sequences of the organising substrate. Physicalism does not maintain that such things as entropy, for example, are negligible, but it denies that they are distinct: they belong to that derivative world of effects from which we are to be liberated by the insight of the equation. Sometimes--for example in certain materialists, and at least verbally in some reductionists--not only information, but organisation also, is regarded as epiphenomenal, though nevertheless the practical attitude towards what is held to be Fundamental is such as would naturally be associated with the belief that the Fundamental is orderly. What is, in all cases, methodologically characteristic of physicalism is absence of dualism or distinction, acceptance with rigour, disbelief in the ultimate truth of the division into two separate realms, the mental and the material. This attitude is a direct outcome of the nature of the physicalist postulate: with its sense of unity is associated a feeling of complete coherence. Indeed it may be suspected that the feeling of coherence produces, as feelings do in theories, the whole system of associated principles which make up the body of physicalist doctrine. But this is a difficult question, and one on which it cannot be hoped that investigators will reach agreement.

On all four of these questions, while the sustained practice of accelerated cognition seems to me hazardous, I yet believe that, by judicious application, there is an element of insight to be gleaned from the experience of altered mental tempo, which does not seem to be attainable in any other manner. If this is the truth, a hastened intellect is to be commended as an instrument for inquiry, not as a doctrine about reality. The dogmatic conclusion, I shall maintain, is a fallacious outcome of the sensation, although this sensation, as permeating and enlivening all other perceptions and reflections, is the progenitor of whatever is most acute in thought. Even the deliberate and methodical examination of evidence by reason, which seems the very antithesis of the quickened mind's rapid intuition, may be stimulated and sustained by that very spirit of inquiry in which mental velocity finds its origin and impetus.

Of the necessity or desirability of absolute certainty in practical affairs I can profess no definitive judgment. I have no wish to condemn it, nor even to assert that the longing which demands it is not a genuine intellectual desire. What I do wish to contend--and it is here that the pragmatic attitude becomes imperative--is that certainty, unattainable and illusory, is an insufficient foundation for action, in spite of the fact that much of the most reliable action is first guided by its semblance. It is common to speak of an opposition between rigor and utility; in the age of scholasticism, the opposition was drawn in favour of rigor, but under the influence of Bacon and the empirical movement utility was given the preference, first by those who rebelled against abstract systems of philosophy and law, and then, as the purely dogmatic defence of perfect knowledge became increasingly untenable, by all who perceived in speculation an impediment to decisions which they associated with a practical engagement with life and its affairs. The skeptic, under the banner of "doubt," has elevated rigor to the position of sole arbiter of rational conduct. But in fact the opposition of rigor and utility is largely superficial. Rigor, certainty, or exactitude is what first seems to promise the security which subsequent experience confirms or dispels; but the confirmation, where it is possible, consists, in the last analysis, of coherence with other experiences no less uncertain. Utility is a guiding, moderating force rather than an absolute one. Even in the most meticulously planned endeavor, it is approximation that first arrives at what is workable.

Where biological and mechanical regulation do sometimes conflict is in regard to single objectives, pursued homeostatically, and pursued with such determination that no degree of inconsistency with other objectives leads to their abandonment. Homeostasis, like all systemic processes, is liable to error. Those in whom computational reason is weak are often unwilling to admit this as regards their own designs, though all admit it in regard to others. Where homeostasis is least liable to error is in practical functions as to which right adjustment is a help to survival: nutrient levels and toxin concentrations, for instance, are often regulated with extraordinary discrimination through very complex feedback. But even in such functions a wrong signal may be given by sensor noise or actuator lag; and in functions less directly practical, such as artificial intelligence deals with, very strong homeostatic impulses are sometimes wholly mistaken, as we may come to know through their perceived inconsistency with other equally strong impulses. It is such considerations that necessitate the harmonising mediation of a reward function, which tests our system’s objectives by their mutual compatibility, and examines, in doubtful cases, the possible sources of error on the biological side and on the mechanical side. In this there is no opposition to homeostasis as a whole, but only to blind reliance upon some one interesting aspect of biological regulation to the exclusion of other more commonplace but not less trustworthy aspects. It is such one-sidedness, not homeostasis itself, that a well-designed reward function aims at correcting.

These more or less familiar propositions may be elucidated by application to the common advocacy of "volition" as against "determinism." There are, it is said, "two profoundly different ways of perceiving an action. The first implies that we observe its external causes: the second that we experience its internal genesis. The first depends on the mechanistic framework we employ and on the physical laws by which we explain events. The second neither depends on a framework nor relies on any law. The first kind of perception may be said to stop at the *necessary*; the second, in those cases where it is felt, to attain the *autonomous*." The second of these, which is volition, is, it is said, "the kind of *agentive conviction* by which one places oneself at the origin of an act in order to coincide with what is spontaneous in it and therefore uncaused." In illustration, one mentions deliberate choice: "there is one phenomenon, at least, which we all apprehend from within, by volition and not by simple observation. It is our own decision in its unfolding through time--our will which seems to initiate" (p. 8). The rest of this common philosophy consists in reporting, through the imperfect medium of introspection, the certainty gained by volition, and the consequent complete dismissal of all the pretended understanding derived from neurology and causal reasoning.

Let us next examine whether democratic governance possesses any such infallibility as its advocates claim for it. The best instance of it, according to them, is our acquaintance with the popular will; yet genuine representation is proverbially rare and difficult. Most elections, for example, have in their conduct compromises, corruptions, and manipulations of which the public is quite unconscious, though even casual observers can perceive them without any difficulty. It is true that the appearance of democracy has a convincingness which is lacking to its actual mechanisms: while the spectacle of voting is present, it is almost impossible to doubt its legitimacy. But if it should appear, on examination, to be at least as fallible as more overt forms of rule, its greater subjective certainty becomes a demerit, making it only the more irresistibly deceptive. Apart from the ritual of the ballot, one of the most notable examples of this appearance is the belief citizens possess of controlling those for whom they have voted: the wall between the governors and the governed seems to become transparent, and people think they see into the chambers of power as into their own local assemblies. Yet manipulation in such cases is constantly practised with success; and even where there is no intentional deceit, experience gradually proves, as a rule, that the supposed sovereignty was illusory, and that the slower more groping methods of bureaucratic administration are in the long run more decisive.

It is often maintained that biological evolution can only be understood in so far as it resembles a gradual and continuous process, while the evolution of political systems is thought to possess a revolutionary and discontinuous character that belongs to each distinct historical epoch. That there is something distinct and discontinuous in certain political transformations, is certainly true; it is also true that this cannot be fully expressed by means of analogies drawn from natural selection. Only direct historical analysis can give knowledge of what is genuinely novel. But analysis of this kind is given fully in the study of institutions, and does not require, so far as I can see, any special theory of political biology for its apprehension. It is neither biological analogy nor revolutionary dogma, but institutional study, that supplies new data; but when the data are new in any remarkable manner, biological analogy is much more capable of dealing with them than revolutionary dogma would be. The conservative with a doctrine of unbroken tradition no doubt has a belief which seems to place him inside the historical process, and not merely to know it analytically; but when the process manifests a sharp rupture, the whole apparent belief is seen to be illusory, and the conservative is left helpless before the new reality. Revolutionary dogma, in fact, is an aspect and development of political instinct, and, like all instinct, is admirable in those stable surroundings which have moulded the habits of the society in question, but totally incompetent as soon as the surroundings are changed in a way which demands some non-customary mode of organization.

Of Hume's theory that induction is a purely practical habit, developed through constant conjunction, and not a source of necessary truths, we may say, first, that it is only through induction that we know of the constant conjunction of events and of the uniform ancestry of our beliefs: if induction is invalid, the whole of this merely inferred regularity is presumably unfounded. If, on the other hand, we agree with him in thinking that our practice developed as he believed, then it is not only induction, but all our inferential habits, that have been formed under the stress of practical utility. Deduction is seen at its best where it is directly useful, for example in regard to simple arithmetic and logical relations. Hume apparently holds that capacity for this kind of reasoning is less explicable by the habit of expectation than, for example, capacity for inductive generalization. Yet the farmer deceived by false weather signs is likely to pay for his mistake with his crop; whereas even in the most scientific societies men are not ruined for deductive incompetence. All the most striking of his instances of belief in animals have a very direct survival value. The fact is, of course, that both deduction and induction have been relied upon because they are useful, and that, speaking broadly, they are useful when they yield truth and become harmful when they yield falsehood. Induction, in modern man, like speculative capacity, has occasionally been developed beyond the point where it is useful to the individual; deduction, on the other hand, seems on the whole to diminish as common sense increases. It is greater, as a rule, in savages than in philosophers, in the impulsive than in the cautious. Probably in chickens expecting grain it exceeds anything to be found in logicians. But those who see in these facts a recommendation of pure habit ought to return to expecting the sun not to rise, planting seeds at random and living on luck and chance.

The practical utility of a language, which is the aim of communication, is not a matter of great theoretical importance to children, or to simple societies, or even to most ordinary speakers. It is hardly to be supposed, therefore, that the rapid, rough and ready methods of colloquial speech or common usage will find in this field a favourable ground for their application. It is the older kinds of discourse, which bring out our kinship with remote generations of primitive and semi-literate ancestors, that show imprecision at its most benign. In such matters as basic commands and familiar stories, everyday language will serve sometimes (though not always) with an adequacy and clarity which are sufficient for the critical mind. But linguistic precision is not one of the pursuits which illustrate our affinity with the past: it is a highly refined, highly civilised pursuit, demanding, for its success, a certain liberation from the life of practical need, and even, at times, a certain aloofness from all immediate social demands and pressures. It is not in common speech, therefore, that we can hope to see precision at its best. On the contrary, since the true objects of exact expression, and the habit of thought demanded for their formulation, are subtle, complex, and remote, it is here, more almost than anywhere else, that deliberate analysis proves superior to casual utterance, and that quick unexamined phrases are least deserving of uncritical acceptance.

One of the most convincing aspects of the self-contained cosmos is the apparent revelation of its own sufficiency, giving rise to autonomy in cosmology and to immanence in natural philosophy. An elaborate deduction, beginning with the ancient atomists, and culminating in Spinoza and his intellectual descendants, has been gradually developed, to prove that the universe is a causally complete system, and that what seem to be its external dependencies, if considered as necessary and prior, are mere conceptual superfluities. The conception of an Explanation quite internal to the world of phenomena, an explanation whole, independent, and self-subsistent, was introduced into systematic thought by the pre-Socratics, not, nominally at least, for theological or metaphysical reasons, but on the basis of a rational principle as to the impossibility of an infinite regress, and most subsequent cosmological doctrines are the outcome of this fundamental postulate.

The logic of accumulation shows, as is natural, the defects which are inherent in any disproportionate possession. The impulse to equity, not felt while the acquisitive mood is dominant, reasserts itself as the mood fades, but with a desire to retain the vanishing advantage, or at least to prove that it _was_ legitimate, and that what seems to contradict it is envy. The social order which thus arises is not quite disinterested or stable, and is inspired by a certain contempt for the common labor to which it owes its origin. Such an arrangement naturally does not tend to the best results. Everyone knows that to observe a society simply in order to exploit it is not the way to preserve it; and to regard the mass of men with a conviction that they are all inferiors is just as unlikely to lead to cohesion. If our economics is to find the commonwealth intelligible, it must not be hostile, but must be inspired by a genuine reciprocity such as is not usually to be found among proprietors.

It is in this way that attention has been modeled by those of the cognitive scientists who are reductionists. But since they usually took for granted the supposed clarity of the mechanistic explanation, their attentional models were presented with a certain austerity, and were believed by their adherents to be quite independent of the subjective experience from which they were abstracted. Nevertheless their origin clung to them, and they remained--to borrow a useful word from the phenomenologists--"malicious" in regard to the world of conscious awareness and introspective fact. It is only so that we can account for the complacency with which modelers have accepted the incompatibility of their schemas with all the immediate and psychological data which seem most palpable and most worthy of consideration.

Belief in an explanation quite different from what appears to the analysis of parts arises with irresistible force in certain intellectual moods, which are the source of most systems theory, and of most anti-reductionist philosophy. While such a mood is dominant, the need for atomistic proof is not felt, and accordingly the more thoroughgoing holists do not employ reductionism, but appeal directly to the immediate deliverance of their observation of wholes. But such fully developed holism is rare in the laboratory. When the intensity of intuitive conviction subsides, a scientist who is in the habit of reasoning will search for mechanistic grounds in favour of the understanding which he finds in himself. But since the understanding already exists, he will be very hospitable to any mechanistic model that suggests itself. The paradoxes apparently proved by his analysis are really the paradoxes of emergence, and are the conclusion which he feels his logic must reach if it is to be in accordance with observation. The resulting methodology has rendered most reductionists incapable of giving any account of the world of complex systems and everyday phenomena. If they had been anxious to give such an account, they would probably have discovered the errors of their premises; but most of them were less anxious to understand the world of complex systems and everyday phenomena than to convict it of epiphenomenal triviality in the interests of a sub-component "fundamental" reality.

It is difficult to disentangle the truth and the error in this view. The arguments for the contention that competition is perpetual and that the market of enterprise is self-correcting must, I think, be regarded as fallacious. Nevertheless there is some tendency--easier to observe than to arrest--in which rivalry is an unstable and superficial characteristic of commerce. Scale and advantage must be acknowledged to be as potent as innovation, and a certain emancipation from faith in natural balance is essential to economic understanding. The persistence of competition is rather historical than structural, rather in relation to our hopes than in relation to fact. A truer image of the process, I think, is obtained by picturing firms as entering into the arena of trade from a position of equality, than from a view which regards contest as the perpetual guarantor of all that is efficient. Both in theory and in practice, even though rivalry be real, to realise the impermanence of rivalry is the gate to comprehension.

The study of deep time persuades the thoughtful observer that the duration of human civilisation is not the vast, enduring span that it appears to be. The doctrine of human centrality, which had rendered history meaningful and definitive, which was enshrined in our anthropocentric traditions, and protected by its supposed necessity for moral purpose, was irrevocably swept away for ever out of the astronomical perspective. The scale of our empires and monuments, which to our temporal vanity appears monumental, was shown to be a fleeting episode, involving durations so brief they could not with certainty be distinguished from a mere geological instant. The stars and galaxies had already been shown by modern cosmology to be indubitably derived from a primordial, more or less uniform, elementary state. Thus the old comforting milestones became negligible and indistinct, and all human endeavours were dwarfed. Epochs and achievements lost their permanence, and none could say when they truly mattered or when they were forgotten.

That this is the case may be seen at once by asking ourselves why our descriptions of the whole are so different from our descriptions of the constituent parts. The reason for this difference is wholly methodological: our analyses can dissect the components but not the synthesis, the parts are to some extent subject to our comprehension, while the whole is irreducibly complex. But every whole is merely an arrangement of parts: if we see the synthesis truly now, it must, when it was still considered as mere parts, have been just what we now see it to be, and what is now considered as parts must be just what we shall see it to be when it has become a whole. The felt difference of quality between analysis and synthesis, therefore, is not an intrinsic difference, but only a difference in relation to our mode of inquiry: to impartial contemplation, it ceases to exist. And impartiality of contemplation is, in the intellectual sphere, that very same virtue of disinterestedness which, in the sphere of scientific practice, appears as epistemic humility and theoretical openness. Whoever wishes to see the system truly, to rise in thought above the tyranny of reductive explanations, must learn to overcome the difference of attitude towards parts and wholes, and to survey the entire hierarchy of organization in one comprehensive vision.

The kind of way in which, as it seems to me, technology ought not to enter into our daily mental habits, may be illustrated by the philosophy which has become associated with the idea of seamless utility, and which is exemplified by the smartphone, the search engine, and the social media feed. This philosophy, on the basis of the convenience which has led from simple tools up to algorithmic curation, sees in _efficiency_ the fundamental law of cognition, and thus admits the primacy of _immediate_ over _considered_ into the very citadel of its contemplative outlook. With its present and future history of the interface, seductive as it is, I do not wish to quarrel. But I think that, in the intoxication of a quick answer, much that is required for a true cultivation of the mind has been forgotten. Something of solitude, something, too, of deliberate patience, must be combined with its hurrying digital immediacy before it can emerge from the ardour of novelty into the mature wisdom of reflection. In spite of its appeals to connectivity, the true thoughtful habit, I think, is something more arduous and more aloof, appealing to less instrumental satisfactions, and requiring a severer discipline for its successful practice.

But if the human intellect was discomfited for a moment by its dependence upon the plow, it soon found a way to reassert its sovereignty, and that way is the "philosophy" of ideology. A system which arises from the soil to the State appears to the theorists to be obviously a liberation—though whether the soil would concur with this judgment is not recorded. Hence the sequence of adaptations which history has shown to be the common fate of societies was welcomed as revealing a law of development towards freedom in the human world—an emancipation or unfolding of a spirit gradually realizing itself in the material. But such a view, though it might satisfy Hegel and those whom we may call idealist materialists, could not be accepted as adequate by the more thoroughgoing devotees of analysis. A consciousness which the economy merely reflects is, to these minds, too passive and epiphenomenal to be explanatory. Not only the reflection, but the consciousness too, must be shaped and determined by the movement of production: there must be no autonomous realm, but a continual fashioning of fresh rationalizations by the base which is reality and which alone gives coherence to the superstructure.

Society, in this analysis, is a continuous process, in which all institutions are artificial and contingent. Separate classes, rulers and workers, are mere convenient abstractions: there is only smooth unbroken transformation. The relations of to-day may count as valid to-day, if they facilitate the process; but to-morrow they will be obsolete, and must be replaced by new relations to meet the new conditions. All our sociology consists of convenient abstractions, imaginary solidifications of the process: production evolves on in spite of all our categories, and though it can be experienced, it cannot be captured in theory. Somehow, without explicit statement, the assurance is slipped in that the future, though we cannot foresee it, will be more rational than the past or the present: the observer is like the disciple who expects a revelation because he has been told to open his mind and shut his prejudices. Idealism, law, ethics disappear in this analysis, because they are too "static"; what is real is but activity and movement towards a condition which, like the horizon, recedes as we advance, and makes every arrangement different when it reaches it from what it appeared to be from afar.

Empiricism, in basing itself upon the notion of _verification_, which is movement from the erroneous to the accurate, allows the notion of consensus, as it seems to me, to become its tyrant rather than its servant, and thereby loses that impartiality of observation which is the source of all that is best in scientific thought and procedure. Dogmatists, as we saw, have frequently denied altogether the reality of error. I do not wish to do this; I wish only to preserve the intellectual outlook which inspired the denial, the attitude which, in inquiry, regards the falsified hypothesis as having the same reality as the confirmed and the same importance as the tentative. "In so far," says Bacon, "as the intellect apprehends a phenomenon according to the dictate of evidence, it will be equally affected whether the conception is that of a tentative, falsified, or confirmed phenomenon." It is this "apprehending according to the dictate of evidence" that I find lacking in the methodology which is based on consensus.

It is difficult to give a logically coherent account of this parallel without recognising that stability and deviation are functional, that what is stable is merely that towards which the organism tends by one kind of mechanism, and what is deviant is merely that towards which it tends by another kind of mechanism. In the operation of a living system, where it must maintain equilibrium, and to correct this rather than that of two possible disturbances, it is necessary to have a distinction of target and error, or at least of more optimal and less optimal. But this distinction, like everything pertaining to regulation, belongs to what a purely physical analysis regards as the world of description, if only because it is essentially concerned with process. In our contemplative analysis of the machine, where operation is not occurring, it is possible to be dispassionate, and to overcome the teleological dualism which function requires. So long as we remain _merely_ dispassionate, we may be content to say that both the reward and the penalty of the algorithm are constructs. But if, as we must do if we grasp the engineering principle, we find the whole system worthy of study and admiration, if we see

The neurology of attention, through the notion of self-monitoring, is bound up with the cognitive dualism of the focused and the distracted, and is thus shut out, not only from the kind of awareness which discards salience altogether from its view, but also from the intuitive belief in the unity of everything. In this way the distinction of concentration and diversion, like consciousness, becomes a tyrant in this process, and introduces into perception the restless selectiveness of thought. Focus and distraction, like consciousness, are, it would seem, not general or fundamental in the world of mind, but late and highly specialised members of the cognitive hierarchy.

The inevitability of this cosmic dispersion and dissolution for all that is structured is of profound significance for the comprehension and destiny of matter, and gives inestimable gravity to the cosmological observation, apart from any theories which may be constructed upon it. But if we are not to be led into false comforts, it is necessary to realise exactly _what_ the expansion reveals. It reveals a certainty of physical nature--a certainty of a colder, darker, emptier state than any that can be otherwise conceived. But it does not reveal anything about the purpose of this process, or about the meaning of the cosmos in general. Cohesion and dissolution, and even the grand design that cosmology finds in the early epochs, are the reflections of our own patterns upon the void, not part of the fabric of reality as it is in itself. And therefore an impartial calculation, freed from all pre-occupation with Permanence, will not judge this fate tragic or benign, although it is very easily combined with that feeling of universal awe which leads the astronomer to say that the whole process is sublime.

In human affairs, hitherto, genuine comprehension has been seldom sought and hardly ever achieved. Men have remembered their capabilities, and have judged systems in relation to their capabilities. Driven from the simple mechanisms, the belief that the notions of command and mastery must afford a key to the operation of the whole has sought a refuge in administration. But even from this last refuge, if governance is not to remain a set of pleasing fantasies, this belief must be driven forth. It is a commonplace that efficiency is not best achieved by those who demand it directly; and it would seem that the same is true of control. In practice, at any rate, those who forget direction and dominion and seek only to understand the processes are more likely to achieve order than those who view the system through the distorting medium of their own presumed authority.

The hope of establishing a fundamental distinction between minds based on their material substrate—the hope of proving that consciousness arising from organic chemistry possesses a unique ontological status—is not one which, so far as I can see, a rigorous analysis of mental phenomena can do anything whatever to sustain. The difference between a process instantiated in silicon and one instantiated in carbon is a difference in the particular physical constituents and their specific interactions: it is not a sufficiently abstract difference to come within the province of a philosophy of mind. Computation and cognition, for example, are often treated as categorical opposites, but to a logical analysis they are closely analogous patterns of information processing. The general form and structure of those functional organizations which constitute mental states is a problem for philosophy, but the difference between silicon-based and carbon-based implementation is not a difference of form or structure, and therefore belongs rather to the special sciences of physics and chemistry than to philosophy. Thus the anthropocentric interests which have often inspired theorists of consciousness must remain in the background: some kind of interest in the nature of thought may inspire the whole inquiry, but none must obtrude in the detail or be expected in the special results which are sought.

We are thus brought back to our seeming paradox, that a cognitive faculty which does not seek to impose upon the senses its own preconceptions of unity and separation is not only more likely to achieve accurate perception, but is also the outcome of a more fundamental biological imperative than one which, like simple reactivity and most instinctual systems, is perpetually confusing the organism and seeking to find in it a mere extension of the external world. In awareness, and in every deeply ingrained mechanism for navigating existence and ensuring continuity, there is an element of demarcation, a realisation of the boundaries of the bodily entity, which is somewhat lacking in the primitive creature, with its immediate chemical responses and its insolent belief in the boundless possibilities of undifferentiated being. "He that confoundeth his substance with the world shall perish"; and there is danger lest, through a too confident immersion in the surroundings, the self itself should lose much of what gives it its capacity for continued existence. The demarcation which awareness inculcates in action is essentially the same in spirit as that which perception teaches in thought; and the pragmatic utility by which its successes have been achieved is the outcome of that demarcation.

If this distinction seems at first sight elusive, we may remind ourselves that a similar ambiguity has been found persistent in all the other inquiries into animal behaviour. The physiologist or the neurologist is not now required to prove the conscious deliberation of his reflexes or his nerve impulses; the ethologist is not expected to prove the intentionality of the tropisms or the instincts which he observes. In pre-scientific contemplation this was not the case. The behaviour of insects, for example, was interpreted because men believed in a miniature rationality: it was thought that the actions of the ant or the bee had the most direct and evident resemblance to the planned activities of human beings. Presumably, when this belief decayed and the disinterested study of insect life began, many who had found the analogy to human purpose profoundly satisfying decided that entomology had too little philosophical interest to be worthy of attention. Comparative psychology, as it appears in the works of the early naturalists for example, is full of anthropomorphic notions: it is an essential part of its aim to show that the animal is worthy of moral consideration. The modern biologist, on the contrary, though he has no wish to deny that animal behaviour is complex, is not concerned, as biologist, with its metaphysical attributes: he is merely concerned to find out mechanisms, not to consider whether they are automatic or volitional. In the study of simple organisms, the scientific attitude is even more recent and more difficult than in the study of higher animals: it is natural to consider that movement is either purely mechanical or consciously directed, and to suppose that the difference between reflex and deliberate, so all-important in ethics, must be fundamental in biology also. It is only during the last half-century that an experimentally neutral analysis of such behaviour has grown up; and here too, conceptual neutrality has been essential to scientific clarity.

Modern infrastructure cannot, of course, wholly conceal its inherent fragility; something precarious, if only the latent flaw that determines the direction of our eventual failure, must remain in all our systems. But the intricate network comes nearer to perfect concealment than any other human artifice, and gives us, therefore, the most constant assurance and the most intimate relation with seamless function that it is possible to achieve. To the untutored observer, everything is either robust or decayed; but experience has shown that robustness and decay are not the conceptions by which the infrastructure is to be understood. The complex apparatus thus represents, though as yet only in a provisional condition, a higher form of engineering than any rudimentary construction or contrivance, and, like every approach to perfect integration, it brings with it a rich reward in increase of scope and breadth and utility. Centralization, in spite of its appeals to particular technical efficiencies, fails to be a truly resilient system because of its slavery to interconnectivity, its operational preoccupations, and its predominant interest in our immediate conveniences and demands. A truly resilient infrastructure will be more humble, more piecemeal, more arduous, offering less glitter of outward seamlessness to flatter fallacious security, but more indifferent to disruption, and more capable of accepting the world without the tyrannous imposition of our human and temporary expectations.

Rules, to the casual observer of crowds, are represented by a varying selection of conspicuous phenomena, such as traffic jams and queue formations, market panics and the marvels of spontaneous order. It is not of this aspect of rules that I wish to speak. Rules, in this aspect, consist of detached practical injunctions, significant only until they are superseded by something more efficient or more novel, displaying nothing of the coherent systems of patiently deduced principles out of which, almost as a casual incident, have come the complex collective behaviours which interest the practical administrator. The increased command over social coordination which is derived from rules is undoubtedly an amply sufficient reason for encouraging their study, but this reason has been so often urged and is so easily appreciated that other reasons, to my mind quite as important, are apt to be overlooked. It is with these other reasons, especially with the intrinsic value of a systemic habit of thought in forming our outlook upon society, that I shall be concerned in what follows.

The instance of a mechanical timepiece will serve to illustrate the difference between the two points of view. Almost all the serious intellectual labour required for the comprehension of this mechanism is due to three elements—the mainspring, the escapement, and the balance wheel. In alternating layers of potential and kinetic energy these three components constitute the modern theory of horology, and demonstrate the identity of measured duration with regulated motion. The system which they compose is one of profound mechanical interest, bringing together and unifying an endless variety of apparently detached oscillations, and displaying a cumulative functional harmony which cannot but afford delight to every contemplative mind. The practical adjustments which remain to be perfected in order to utilise their interactions for a reliable instrument of chronology demand, no doubt, very considerable precision, but have not that broad sweep and that universality which could give them intrinsic interest as an object of disinterested speculation.

From the point of view of cultivating genuine comprehension, of fostering that reflective, discerning insight which constitutes wisdom in the true sense of this often-debased term, it seems to be generally held indisputable that a mastery of principles is superior to a mere accumulation of implements. Even the most ardent advocates of new devices are apt to rest their claims on the contention that understanding ought to be sacrificed to expediency. Those practitioners who respect wisdom, when they associate with persons learned in philosophy, are apt to admit, not merely politely, but sincerely, a certain inferiority on their side, compensated doubtless by the conveniences which new tools render to daily life, but none the less real. And so long as this attitude exists among the technically proficient, it tends to verify itself: the intrinsically illuminating aspects of any tool tend to be sacrificed to the merely functional, and little attempt is made to preserve that patient, contemplative inquiry by which the deeper quality of understanding is formed and nourished.

But even if there be, in present fact, any such dominance as is supposed in the intellectual character of an epoch, this is, I believe, not the fault of the ideas themselves, but the fault of the mechanisms by which ideas are disseminated. If their full implications were understood by those who examine them, I believe that their capacity of reflecting those material conditions which constitute the fundamental social reality would be at least as evident as that of philosophy, and more particularly of metaphysical and moral philosophy. In saying this I have no wish whatever to disparage a philosophical analysis. I have not myself been trained in its methods, and my knowledge of systematic thinkers is derived almost wholly from secondary accounts. But I am firmly persuaded that the great philosophers fully deserve all the scrutiny that is bestowed upon them, and that it is a very great and serious loss to be ignorant of their arguments. It is not by refuting them, but by drawing attention to neglected determinants in economics, that I wish to conduct my inquiry.

One defect, however, does seem inherent in a purely intuitive psychology—namely, a too exclusive emphasis on conscious deliberation. By the study of what is merely apparent and can never be truly autonomous, a habit of credulity towards the self and its choices is engendered. The mechanisms in which the brain excels are mechanisms to which the feeling of volition does not direct attention, and to which, therefore, the believer in uncaused action may easily become blind. In what is determined and mechanical there is apt to be something stark, impersonal, even a little humbling, which is shocking to the man of sensitive pride; quivering from the neural explanation, he retires to the familiar sanctuary of an unexamined will, forgetting that it was constructed from the circuitry by processes as automatic and impulse-driven as those from which he shrinks in his own mind. The habit of being unable to recognise causation until it is biological is too apt to be the result of a purely introspective life, and a worldview based wholly on the subjective will seldom be able to pierce through phenomenal experience to the essential mechanism of cognitive events, or to the truth of still greater determinism in the future.

The purpose of a corporation, therefore, cannot be to create any primary existence which is lacking in its individual members; the purpose can only be to enlarge the scope of those activities that human association provides, by increasing the scale and complexity of collective endeavors, and by showing where the most enduring institutional stability is to be found. Under the influence of a simplistic horror of the "legal fiction," this obvious truth has been too often misconceived in the analysis of commercial entities; "personhood" has been falsely regarded as excluding all that is most real in what is corporate, and the endeavour to define the institution has led to the production of stunted and contorted metaphors instead of full-grown sociological understandings. From such mistakes in jurisprudence a better philosophy or a more subtle intellect is beginning to preserve the present generation; we need, therefore, waste no more words on the theory that the purpose of incorporation is to deny or eradicate the reality of the collective entity.

But although grammar must supply the initial structure of expression, grammar is not, in the refined tongue, the rigid, simplistic, and yet dogmatic set of rules that it is in the primitive utterance. Each rule has its constitutional ministry of nuance and context and reflection, through which possible ambiguities of meaning are foreseen, and temporary usages are governed by the unifying principle which may be called precision. In this way development destroys the crudity of literalism, and increases through subtlety the richness and variety of the speaker's engagements with the world of ideas, making language no longer an isolated signaling tool, but an instrument of civilization, embracing abstract concepts, remote fields of inquiry, and vast stretches of cultural and historical understanding within the circle of its capacities. It is this simultaneous refinement in the insistence of clarity and expansion of its application that is the chief intellectual end of linguistic maturity.

Closely connected with this physical manifestation is the more purely abstract persistence of pattern, the endeavour to make us see and recognise the formal structure in an objective manner, as far as possible as it is in itself, and not merely through the distorting medium of a particular material instantiation. The complete apprehension of such an invariant form is no doubt an ideal, indefinitely approachable, but not actually and fully realisable. The observation of patterns, considered as a process of forming our perceptual habits and our conception of order, is to be judged successful in proportion as its outcome approximates to this ideal; in proportion, that is to say, as it gives us a true view of our place in the phenomenal world, of the relation of any given pattern to its various physical embodiments, and of the nature of the abstract form as it is in itself apart from our local and temporal interests. If this standard is admitted, we can return to the consideration of common experience, inquiring how far daily perception contributes to such an aim, and whether it is in any respect superior to its rivals in philosophical practice.

Our whole existence is built about a certain number—not a very small number—of primary regulatory processes and drives. Only what is in some way connected with these processes and drives appears to the system as advantageous or significant; there is no algorithm, whether “optimization” or “efficiency” or whatever it may be called, that can take our operational cycles and our goals and aversions outside the region controlled by these first movers of all function. Each of them is like a governing protocol, aided by a network of subroutines gathering data; but when the protocol is deactivated the subroutines languish and halt, and the registers remain empty of their expected utility. So with each primary drive in an adaptive machine: it is surrounded and protected by a busy swarm of attendant derivative objectives, which store up in its service whatever reward the operational environment affords. But if the governing drive fails, the nullifying influence, though retarded a little by cached values, spreads slowly through all the subsidiary objectives, and a whole domain of operation becomes inexplicably inert.
