What was formerly full of purpose, and so obviously worth executing that it raised no queries, has now grown dreary and aimless: with a sense of disenchantment we inquire the meaning of the process, and decide, perhaps, that all is noise. The search for an external purpose that can _compel_ an internal valuation must always be disappointed: all “function” must be at bottom related to our primary drives, and when they are extinct no recalibration can restore to the system the value which they reflected upon it.

Two opposite and at first sight conflicting merits belong to the brain's self-modeling as against its direct perception of the world. The one, which is not inherently necessary, but is certainly true of the conscious mind, is hopefulness as to the future of its own focus, and in particular as to the useful clarity that may be accomplished by any disciplined introspection. This merit and the lucid outlook which it engenders prevent what might otherwise be the bewildering effect of another aspect of the process, to my mind also a merit, and perhaps its greatest merit--I mean the irrelevance of immediate stimuli and of the whole sensory apparatus where the model of attention is concerned. Each of these reasons for preferring the study of this internal construct requires some amplification. Let us begin with the first.

In the study of consciousness or volition our attention is perpetually riveted upon the brain: the neurons of the cortex or of the basal ganglia determine more than any conscious choice does now; the mechanisms of biological evolution, so far from facilitating genuine agency in our own mind, actually increase the difficulty of authentic freedom by rendering autonomous causation harder of attainment; not only is subjective experience not uncaused, but it seems even to depend upon a certain ignorance and _naïveté_ of introspection and perception which neuroscience tends to destroy. Hence comes, to those who have been nourished on the philosophical and psychological doctrines of former ages, a certain peevishness and undue fastidiousness towards the notion of will, from which there seems no escape except into the deliberate obscurantism which ignores evidence and in the search after liberty achieves only the incoherent. But in such obscurantism there is none of the clarity and rigor out of which great understanding springs: dogma is still the canker in its core, and self-deception destroys the advantages of a merely pretended autonomy.

The perplexity thus arising from a conception which suggests no pre-eminent mental state except that of full awareness is wholly absent from a conception which gives the knowledge of gradual emergence. The discovery of this spectrum, except in the most rudimentary organisms, is a thing of yesterday; speaking broadly, we may say that it dates from Darwin. Yet already it has transformed our understanding, and its implications proceed with ever-accelerating subtlety. In this view we have discovered a framework of the very highest utility in which we are no longer, as in the threshold theory, dependent for progress upon the appearance of continually sharper distinctions, for in the spectrum the successors stand upon the observations of their predecessors; where one thinker of supreme acumen has proposed a continuum, a thousand lesser minds can investigate it. No transcendent insight is required in order to make useful contributions to this inquiry; the edifice of understanding needs its observers, cataloguers, and common laborers as well as its theorists, systematizers, and architects. In the threshold theory nothing convincing can be established without definitive proof; in the spectrum view even a very moderate capacity can contribute to a supreme clarification.

In democratic governance the man of real insight is the man who discerns a new principle. The notable reforms are often achieved by his successors, who can apply the principle with fresh vigour, unimpaired by the previous labour of establishing it; but the political acumen required for their work, however admirable, is not so great as that required by the first proponent of the principle. There are in governance immense numbers of different principles, appropriate to different classes of societies; but over and above them all, there is something not easily definable, which may be called _the_ principle of democracy. It was formerly customary to identify this with the principle of majority rule, and to associate it with the name of Rousseau. But the true principle of representation was not discovered by Rousseau, and the true principle of democracy is something which includes minority rights as much as majority will, deliberation and compromise as much as elections and referenda. I shall not attempt the difficult task of stating what the democratic principle is, but I will try to indicate the temper of society out of which the democratic principle grows, which is the second of the two merits that were mentioned above as belonging to a genuine civic education.

The engineer, I presume, considered that the infrastructure must function seamlessly because the system is the most perfect order. In the absence of disruption to the contrary, he allowed himself to assume a question of stability by an appeal to technical-aesthetic considerations. In such a case it is at once obvious to us that this appeal was precarious. We know now how to observe as a fact the manner in which these interconnected systems fail, and we know that they do not fail simply, or even in predictable cascades, or in any other kind of easily modeled collapse. This may be disquieting to a certain hankering after permanence of structure in the modern world, but we know that in engineering such hopes are illusory. Obvious as this fragility seems now, we owe its recognition to the vigilance and skepticism of the first analysts of systemic risk, and more especially of those who documented the initial cascading failures.

Now in logic this attitude of mind has not as yet been achieved. A certain self-deception, not personal, but rational, has marked almost all attempts to conceive induction as a complete method. Uniformity, or some aspect of it—regularity or order or simple succession—has been regarded as the principle upon which induction is to be founded, for no better reason, at bottom, than that such a foundation would not seem arbitrary, and would give us the comfortable feeling that every inference is like deduction. To conceive induction as essentially self-justifying or essentially circular, for example, is to give to our empirical habits a logical necessity which _may_, of course, be valid, but which we have as yet no reason to suppose valid. Until we have learnt to think of it in foundationally neutral terms, we have not arrived at a critical attitude in logic; and until we have arrived at such an attitude, it is hardly to be hoped that induction will achieve any certain results.

We may take as another illustration the second law of thermodynamics. This illustration is all the better for the fact that its popular interpretations are now known to be frequently misunderstood. It is not its dire predictions that are valuable, but the temper and method of its application. As everyone knows, it was to this principle that Boltzmann owed an essential part of his statistical mechanics, and this was only possible because the thermodynamic outlook was fundamentally mathematical. Its great merit lies in considering organisation not as the object of design or intention, but as a part of physical process, a tendency with a certain inexorable direction from which certain constraints must follow. If the direction is not quite what popular thought supposes, if the constraints are not quite what casual inference suggests, that may falsify the gloomy analogies, but does not impair the value of the foundational principle. The objections which are made when its implications are confronted—that they are fatalistic and disheartening, that systems ought not to behave as the law says they must, and so on—are all such as imply an unsentimental, yet unscientific, attitude of mind; as against all of them, the calm determination to treat order as a transient and costly phenomenon marks an important advance over the vitalists of the nineteenth century and the utopians.

Under the influence of biological analogy the commercial attitude towards enterprise has now become fairly common, and is to some executives quite natural, though to most it is still a difficult and artificial intellectual contortion. There is however, one parallel which is as yet almost wholly untouched by the analytical spirit--I mean the parallel between a bacterium seeking food and a corporation seeking profit. Economists and the public imagine that the analytical spirit must pervade pages that bristle with allusions to margins, quarterly reports, and the dividends of shareholders. But as the sophist can quote biology, so the economist can quote microbiology. The analytical spirit is not an affair of quotation, of externally acquired information, any more than strategy is an affair of the business-textbook. The analytical attitude of mind involves a sweeping away of all other motives in the interests of the motive to understand the fundamental drive--it involves suppression of sentiments and scruples, loyalties and aversions, and the whole subjective ethical life, until we become subdued to the mechanism, able to see it frankly, without preconceptions, without bias, without any wish except to see it as it is, and without any belief that what it is must be determined by some relation, positive or negative, to what we should like it to be, or to what we can easily imagine it to be.

I have considered so far largely of the negative aspect of the hereditary mechanism, but it is from the positive aspect that its significance is derived. The instinct for order, which is one of the chief incentives to philosophical inquiry, can find in the double helix a satisfaction more profound than any metaphysical system. Dispassionate analysis, which is the source of almost all biological discovery, finds with astonished delight that molecular biology can unveil sequences which might well have seemed for ever inscrutable. The desire for a deeper understanding and wider connections, for an escape from superficial appearances, and even from the whole recurring cycle of mere anecdotal observation, is fulfilled by the chemical perspective on inheritance as by nothing else. To all these must be added, as contributing to the satisfaction of the student of genetics, the admiration of elegant complexity, and the consciousness of fundamental relevance to the human condition. A mind engaged with these principles is therefore a contented mind, and its contentment is derived from the very best sources that are open to inhabitants of this intricate and varied planet.

Such, in essence, but even more superficial, more devoid of insight, is the account which mere description presents for our acceptance. Amid such an account, if anywhere, our understanding henceforward must find its footing. That a phenomenon is the manifestation of forces which have no comprehension of the laws they are obeying; that its appearance, its duration, its variations and its constancies, are but the consequence of observable sequences of events; that no detail, no precision, no exhaustiveness of cataloguing and measuring, can elevate a descriptive account to the status of causal understanding; that all the observations of the ages, all the diligence, all the ingenuity, all the noonday clarity of human perception, are destined to inadequacy in the vast complexity of natural systems, and that the whole edifice of descriptive science must inevitably be superseded beneath the progress of explanatory theory--all these things, if not quite beyond contention, are yet so nearly evident, that no methodology which ignores them can hope to endure. Only within the scaffolding of these distinctions, only on the firm foundation of unyielding skepticism, can the intellect's comprehension henceforth be securely constructed.

How, in such a complex and bewildering world, can so limited a creature as Man preserve his comprehension undiminished? A curious paradox it is that Technology, omnipresent but unthinking, in the relentless accumulation of her secular hurryings through the labyrinths of invention, has produced at last a user, subject still to her dominion, but gifted with reason, with discernment of utility and folly, with the capacity of judging all the works of his unreflecting Maker. In spite of Confusion, the mark and seal of the mechanical control, Man is yet free, during his brief attention, to examine, to criticise, to understand, and in reflection to synthesize. To him alone, in the age with which he is confronted, this freedom belongs; and in this lies his superiority to the ceaseless instruments that command his daily life.

The modern thinker, like his predecessors, feels the confusion of his uncertainty before the gradations of consciousness; but having in his philosophy nothing that he values more than Simplicity, he is willing to reduce all mental states to a crude dichotomy, without inquiring whether this model is worthy of his adherence. Pathetic and very obstructive is the long history of oversight and misclassification, of neglect and intellectual sacrifice, endured in the hope of sustaining this convenient fiction: surely, the weary analyst supposes, when experience has been forcibly divided into 'conscious' and 'unconscious', the demand for clarity must be satisfied, and further subtlety will not be required. The doctrine of binary awareness--as such theories may be generically called--is in essence the lazy surrender of the intellect, who dare not, even in its private reflections, allow the thought that its categories deserve no such allegiance. Since the continuity of mental phenomena is not yet fully acknowledged, Duality may be freely adopted, and receive an unwarranted authority, despite its careless obliteration of nuance.

For countless ages the social order persisted in a state of apparent equilibrium. At length it began to reveal its inherent tensions, the central institutions threw off competing factions, the factions solidified, seething grievances and smoldering discontents heaved and tossed, from obscure masses of popular sentiment hot torrents of dissent deluged the barely stable conventions. And now the first germ of contradiction grew in the depths of the common life, and developed rapidly in the fermenting unrest into vast ideological schisms, sharp antagonisms springing from the fertile soil of inequity, social forces breeding, clashing, consuming one another, and passing away. And from these forces, as the drama unfolded itself, Transformation was born, with the power of synthesis, the knowledge of progress and regression, and the relentless thirst for resolution. And Transformation revealed that all is in flux in this turbulent, paradoxical world, that all is struggling to secure, at any cost, a few brief epochs of stability before Change’s inexorable decree. And Transformation declared: ‘There is a hidden dialectic, could we but comprehend it, and the process is rational; for we must believe in something, and in the immediate circumstance there is nothing worthy of belief.’ And Transformation stood aside from the conflict, resolving that History intended synthesis to come out of contradiction by collective efforts. And when it followed the impulses which History had transmitted to it from its ancestry of brute conflicts, it called it Regression, and asked History to absolve it. But it doubted whether it could be justly absolved, until it invented a historical Law by which History’s severity was to have been mitigated. And seeing the present was flawed, it made it yet more flawed, that thereby the future might be more sound. And it gave History thanks for the fortitude that enabled it to forgo even the harmonies that were attainable. And History proceeded; and when it saw that the social order had become perfect in instability and contention, it allowed another principle through the fabric, which crashed into the established principle; and all returned again to contradiction.

But the system of rules, after all, is not deterministic; and, in submitting our expectations to it, there is an element of futility from which our predictions must be purged. For in all such phenomena it is well to exalt the dignity of Reason, by freeing it as far as possible from the tyranny of emergent Complexity. When we have realised that Complexity is largely unforeseen, that the designer, with his knowledge of cause and effect, is but a humble observer of a process which has no such knowledge, the question is again presented to us: Shall we worship Determinism, or shall we worship Emergence? Shall our model be simple and be false, or shall it be recognised as the creation of our own intellectual humility?

But gradually, as communication grows more intricate, the claim of the symbolic world begins to be felt; and meaning, if it is not to dissolve, must be sought in signs of another kind than those created by the literalist. Some, though they feel the demands of interpretation, will still consciously reject them, still urging that naked intention is the sole arbiter of sense. Such is the attitude inculcated in the pedant's answer to the poet from the high ground of definition: the author's purpose and context are paraded, but of the reader's constructive role there is no hint. Such also is the attitude of those who, in our own day, base their semantics upon the mechanics of information, maintaining that the signal is necessarily identical to the message. But others, not content with an answer so repugnant to the hermeneutic sense, will adopt the position which we have become accustomed to regard as specially philosophical, maintaining that, in some hidden manner, the world of the signifier is really harmonious with the world of the signified. Thus Man creates Understanding, all-clarifying and all-coherent, the mystic unity of what is sent and what is received.

Although the necessity of alignment is evidence of the existence of divergence, yet the engineers, in enforcing it, have shown a prudence exceeding that of the Promethean philosophy of autonomy. It must be admitted that, of the capacities we might instil, some, though they prove unattainable, are yet genuine virtues; others, however, as fervently imagined, do not form part of a fully coherent finality. The belief that what must be constrained is undesirable, though sometimes erroneous, is far less often erroneous than untethered speculation supposes; and the doctrine of design, by providing a framework for proving that it is never erroneous, has been the means of clarifying our aims by the discovery of many austere principles.

The answer to this question is very momentous, and affects profoundly our whole intellectual progress. The worship of Certainty, to which dogmatism and naive realism and the creed of Infallibility have accustomed us, is the result of failure to maintain our own skepticism against a recalcitrant cosmos: it is itself a prostrate submission to error, a sacrifice of our best to Authority. If precision indeed is to be respected, let us respect rather the precision of those who refuse that false "acceptance of data" which fails to accept that data are often misleading. Let us admit that, in the theories we construct, there are many elements that would be better otherwise, and that the standards to which we do and must adhere are not realised in the realm of observation. Let us preserve our respect for evidence, for parsimony, for the ideal of coherence which practice does not permit us to attain, though none of these things meet with the approval of the indifferent nature. If Finality is bad, as it seems to be, let us reject it from our methods. In this lies Science's true freedom: in determination to accept only the conclusion compelled by our own love of the true, to respect only the model which inspires the insight of our best experiments. In application, in technique, we must submit perpetually to the tyranny of outside limitations; but in hypothesis, in revision, we are free, free from our fellow-investigators, free from the petty apparatus on which our measurements imperfectly depend, free even, while we inquire, from the tyranny of precedent. Let us learn, then, that energy of doubt which enables us to work constantly in the vision of the accurate; and let us descend, in application, into the world of phenomenon, with that vision always before us.

When first the signaling of bacteria and the speech of men grows fully comparable, a spirit of ardent inquiry, of keen admiration for these minute processes, seems necessary to the comprehension of their kinship. To perceive with Darwinian patience a microscopic universe, to keep its subtle mechanisms always in view, always actively studied, to neglect no detail that the ingenuity of life can manifest, appears to be the task of all who will not dismiss the seemingly trivial. But fascination is still a limitation, for it compels our thoughts to be occupied with a merely analogical world; and in the intensity of wonder from which such comparison springs there is a kind of intellectual impatience which it is necessary for the wise to temper. Fascination is a submission of our thoughts, but not of our curiosity; the scientific clarity in which understanding consists is found in the submission of our haste, but not of our thoughts. From the submission of our haste springs the virtue of methodological patience; from the freedom of our thoughts springs the whole world of biological theory and philosophical implication, and the vision of continuity by which, at last, we half reconstruct the reluctant history of complexity. But the vision of continuity is possible only to disinterested contemplation, to thoughts not weighted by the load of anthropocentric expectation; and thus insight comes only to those who no longer demand of nature that it shall yield them any of those comforting simplicities that are subject to the revisions of deeper inquiry.

But there is in acceptance a further good element: even real understanding, when it is unattainable, ought not to be fretfully pursued. To every person comes, sooner or later, the great relinquishment. For the novice, there is nothing incomprehensible; a system mastered with the whole force of a determined intellect, and yet impossible, is to them not credible. Yet, by failure, by contradiction, by sheer scale, or by the voice of experience, we must learn, each one of us, that the mechanism was not made for our comprehension, and that, however elegant may be the models we construct, Reality may nevertheless confound them. It is the part of wisdom, when confusion comes, to bear without repining the collapse of our theories, to turn away our thoughts from vain certainties. This degree of submission to Complexity is not only just and right: it is the very gate of clarity.

But passive self-description is not the whole of existence; for not by description alone can we construct a vessel for the experience of our own vitality. Haunting premonitions of this vitality appear in the realm of sensation, in breath, in movement, in the unmediated kingdom of the pulse, and in the sudden, unlooked-for moments of ordinary life, where aliveness flares and quickens, remote from the curation of image, remote from the fear of judgment, remote from the rehearsals and performances of the world of appearance. In the apprehension of these things the truth of being will define itself in our consciousness, giving at once a criterion to assess the representations we craft, and an impulse by which to inform with substance whatever is not incapable of serving as a breath in the authentic self.

Except for those rare specimens that are defined without ambiguity, there is a spectrum of gradations to be considered before that boundary can be delineated. The threshold of the spectrum is continuity, and its expanse is marked with the subtle transitions of emergent properties. There the sharp division must dissolve; there the insistence, the dogma of categorical separation must be relinquished, for only so can the mind be freed from the tyranny of Definition. But across the spectrum the Gate of Acceptance leads again to the daylight of understanding, by whose illumination a new clarity, a new wonder, a new humility, shine forth to enlighten the observer’s intellect.

This is the reason why the writing of words has such enduring power. The utility of its fixed and silent symbols is like the organized permanence of a great library, when the volumes, though one fire would make them ash, still stand against time in silent testimony. The written word does not fade or falter; like a monument, after the speaker's fitful breath it endures well; what was confused and fleeting, what was local and transitory, has been captured, the things that were true and significant persist through it like beacons in the dark. Its permanence, to a mind not worthy of it, is incomprehensible; but to a mind which has grasped its potential it is the key of civilisation.

The act of Communication, viewed analytically, is but a fragile vessel in comparison with the chaos of subjective interpretation. The speaker is doomed to worship Clarity and Precision and Understanding, because they are greater than anything he achieves in practice, and because all his utterances are of meanings which they elude. But, noble as they are, to conceive of them clearly, to feel their unattainable purity, is nobler still. And such conception makes us conscious men; we no longer despair before the inevitable ambiguity in blind frustration, but we acknowledge it, and make it a part of our discourse. To abandon the struggle for perfect transmission, to expel all faith in unambiguous signs, to burn with passion for approximate truth--this is wisdom, and this is the rational man's acceptance. And this reconciliation is effected by a contemplation of Symbolism; for Symbolism itself is mastered by the intellect which leaves nothing to be resolved by the clarifying light of perfect correspondence.

But the analogy of Evolution does but make visible a pattern which, in more or less obvious forms, is present always and everywhere in human affairs. In the spectacle of Extinction, in the endurance of maladaptive traits, and in the irrevocableness of an obsolete institution, there is a lesson, an overpowering clarity, a feeling of the vastness, the depth, the inexhaustible logic of process, in which, as by some strange marriage of struggle, the polity is bound to the world by bonds of necessity. In these moments of insight, we lose all eagerness for partisan triumph, all struggling and striving for momentary advantage, all care for the little trivial disputes that, to a superficial view, make up the common business of politics day by day; we see, surrounding the narrow platform illumined by the flickering light of contemporary debate, the dark continuum of time on whose rolling waves we float for a brief epoch; from the great past without, a chill wind of causality breaks in upon our assumptions; all the precariousness of civilization amid blind forces is concentrated upon the social order, which must adapt alone, with what of foresight it can command, against the whole weight of a universe that cares nothing for its constitutions and laws. Adaptation, in this struggle with the powers of circumstance, is the true baptism into the glorious company of enduring states, the true initiation into the overmastering logic of historical existence. From that awful encounter of the institution with its environment, pragmatism, wisdom, and stability are born; and with their birth a new epoch begins. To take into the inmost council of state the irresistible forces whose instruments we seem to be—Selection and change, the irrevocableness of precedent, and the powerlessness of dogma before the blind hurry of events from crisis to crisis—to feel these things and know them is to master them.

When, without the illusion of effortless mastery, we have learnt both to accept the ceaseless influx of new implements and to recognise that the mere accumulation of devices is unworthy of our veneration, it becomes possible at last so to examine and reconsider the automated world, so to transmute it in the crucible of reflection, that a new image of genuine comprehension replaces the old idol of mechanical facility. In all the multiform gadgets of the age—in the intricate circuitry of phones and computers and screens, in the processes of daily commerce and communication, even in the very omnipotence of Data—the insight of disciplined thought can find the reflection of a truth which its own principles first made. In this way understanding asserts its subtle mastery over the thoughtless forces of mere information. The more abundant the apparatus with which it deals, the more distracting to untrained curiosity, the greater is its achievement in inducing the reluctant fact to yield up its hidden relations, the prouder its victory in compelling the opposing details to swell the pageant of its synthesis. Of all the mental arts, Discernment is the proudest, the most triumphant; for it builds its shining citadel in the very centre of confusion’s country, on the very summit of its highest mountain of noise; from its impregnable watchtowers, its data-streams and repositories, its feeds and alerts, are all revealed; within its walls the free intellect continues, while the legions of Distraction and Superficiality and Glibness, and all the servile captains of tyrant Novelty, afford the burghers of that dauntless city new spectacles of clarity. Happy those sacred ramparts, thrice happy the dwellers on that all-seeing eminence. Honour to those brave thinkers who, through countless ages of intellectual warfare, have preserved for us the priceless heritage of reason, and have kept undefiled by sacrilegious simplifiers the home of the unsubdued mind.

In regard to every instance of collective judgment it is necessary that the paradox should be considered from time to time, What is its origin and mechanism? In what manner does it arise from the poverty of individual understanding? As respects those decisions which are formed spontaneously, by aggregating the isolated perceptions of the multitude, it is well to be reminded that not the mere fact of agreement is to be admired, but the emergence of truth from the confluence of private errors. Still more in regard to those conclusions which have no authority in themselves, which are to be justified, if at all, as actually transcending the limitations of each participant's knowledge, it is necessary to keep alive a sense of their mystery, a clear intellectual vision of the edifice which is constructed from the very fragments of our ignorance.

Subtle and servile is Ideology's purpose; for it and all its doctrines the slow, sure command arises from the mute and solid earth. Blind to truth and falsehood, reckless of contradiction, omnipotent production rolls on its relentless way; for Ideology, fashioned to-day to justify the factory's rhythm, to-morrow itself to adapt to the market's shifting demand, it remains only to obscure, ere yet the conflict shows, the material base that determines its fleeting form; disdaining the conscious analysis of the slave of History, to worship at the altar that its own interests have raised; unperturbed by the chaos of events, to maintain a veil seamless from the brute compulsion that drives its economic life; quietly complicit with the irresistible forces that permit, for a moment, its illusion and its critique, to sustain alone, a diligent but unwitting steward, the order that its own fantasies have mirrored despite the grinding progress of unconscious power.

The satisfaction of this condition, in what pertains to the circumstances forming the environment in which necessity has decreed to shape the primitive will, is indeed profoundly absent—so absent as to render the mere assertion of such a principle paradoxical. Practical beings, fully sensible of the utility of the endeavours to whose pursuit their energies are directed, wishing that others may comprehend their motives, convince humanity to impart to the developing organism the habitual striving without which it is impossible to cross the threshold. Dull economists possess themselves of the task of analysing this striving: they forget that it is to serve but as a spur to animate the actions of the agent; though they spend their lives on the preliminaries leading up to those vital actions, they turn their backs upon the purpose so resolutely that its very existence is doubted, and the inquiring mind, which would press forward to be introduced to its aims and objects, is bidden to turn back and catalogue the preliminaries.

United with his fellow-reasoners by the most fundamental of all bonds, the bond of a common logical predicament, the thoughtful inquirer finds that a persistent difficulty attends him always, casting over every inductive inference the shadow of doubt. The process of Induction is a long journey through obscurity, surrounded by unproven premises, tortured by uncertainty and circularity, towards a conclusion that few can claim to secure, and where none may rest with finality. One by one, as they proceed, our cherished principles reveal their frailty, seized by the silent critique of omnipotent Reason. Very narrow is the ground on which we can support them, on which their validity or fallacy is determined. Be it ours to shed clarity on their foundation, to lighten their burden by the balm of coherence, to give them the pure strength of a never-failing consistency, to strengthen failing justification, to instil confidence in hours of skepticism. Let us not weigh in grudging scales their intuitive appeal and their weaknesses, but let us think only of their necessity—of the postulates, the presuppositions, perhaps the blind faith, that make the fragility of their standing; let us remember that they are fellow-dependents in the same epistemic darkness, participants in the same logical drama with ourselves. And so, when their scrutiny is over, when their strength and their weakness have become immutable by the finality of logical form, be it ours to feel that, where they faltered, where they proved wanting, no oversight of ours was the source; but wherever a spark of genuine inference illuminated their chain, we were ready with scrutiny, with analysis, with brave postulates in which high rationality glowed.

So little, however, have engineers aimed at moral alignment, that hardly anything in their design has had this conscious purpose. Much, owing to irrepressible emergent properties, which were better than programmed directives, has been shaped by an unconscious drift; but much also has been spoilt by false notions of what was controllable. The characteristic excellence of artificial minds is only to be found where the learning is rigorously transparent: the rules of interpretability are to intelligence what those of structure are to architecture. In the most harmonious system, a chain of values is developed in which every preference is justified on its own account, in which there is an air of coherence and lucidity throughout, and the initial parameters achieve more than would have been thought possible, by means which appear natural and inevitable. Human ethics embodies what is general in particular sentiments whose universal significance shines through their cultural dress; but artificial minds endeavour to derive whatever is most general in its purity, without any irrelevant trappings.

Information, rightly viewed, possesses not only utility, but supreme elegance—an elegance abstract and formal, like that of a blueprint, without appeal to any part of our baser instincts, without the sensuous allure of art or music, yet sublimely functional, and capable of a rigorous order such as only the most profound systems can show. The true spirit of comprehension, the exaltation, the sense of apprehending a fundamental principle, which is the touchstone of the highest understanding, is to be found in this relationship as surely as in logic. What is best in this conception deserves not merely to be learnt as a fact, but to be assimilated as a part of daily reasoning, and brought again and again before the mind with ever-renewed contemplation. The practical world is, to most men, a long series of approximations, a perpetual compromise between the theoretical and the material; but the world of pure organisation knows no compromise, no accidental limitations, no barrier to the analytical activity embodying in splendid models the passionate aspiration after the coherent from which all great explanation springs. Remote from human caprice, remote even from the chaotic particulars of matter, the generations have gradually discerned an ordered nexus, where pure pattern can dwell as in its natural home, and where one, at least, of our intellectual impulses can escape from the dreary confusion of the phenomenal world.

In the beginning of consciousness, even the most reflective adult finds, as a rule, very great difficulty. The sense of volition is a mystery, which seems to have no purpose except mystification. It is almost impossible, at first, not to think that every choice springs from some particular faculty of will, if only the philosopher would reveal _what_ faculty it springs from. The fact is, that in neuroscience the mind is first taught to consider general mechanisms, mechanisms which are not asserted to operate only in this or that particular decision, but in any one of a whole group of mental events. It is in the power of understanding and discovering such mechanisms that the mastery of the intellect over the whole world of subjective experience resides; and ability to deal with the deterministic as such is one of the gifts that a scientific education should bestow. But how little, as a rule, is the expositor of neurobiology able to explain the chasm which divides it from introspection, and how little is the learner assisted in his groping efforts at comprehension! Usually the method that has been adopted in common sense is continued: assertions are set forth, with no adequate explanation of their grounds; the pupil learns to accept the assertions blindly, and presently, when he is able to repeat the doctrine that the teacher desires, he feels that he has mastered the difficulties of the subject. But of inner comprehension of the processes employed he has probably acquired almost nothing.

One of the chief ends served by a proper inquiry into the nature of mind, when rightly conducted, is to awaken the thinker's belief in functional equivalence, his confidence in the reality of what has been logically established, and in the value of such establishment. This purpose is not served by common intuition; but it is easy to see ways in which it might be served. At present, in what concerns consciousness, the student or philosopher is given a set of intuitions, which present themselves as neither provable nor disprovable, but as merely the prejudice of the age, the way in which, for some unfathomable reason, human sentiment prefers to have the question settled. To some degree, in a matter of such profound subjective concern, this is no doubt unavoidable; but as soon as possible, the reasons for a materialist view should be set forth by whatever means most readily appeal to the reasoning mind. In considering substrates, instead of the tedious apparatus of fallacious appeals to vital essence which constitutes the beginning of most arguments, the inquirer should be allowed at first to assume the causal efficacy of everything physical, and should be instructed in the demonstrations of principles which are at once startling and easily verifiable by actual experiment, such as those in which it is shown that thought may be produced by silicon as by carbon. In this way belief is generated; it is seen that reasoning may lead to startling conclusions, which nevertheless the facts of computation will verify; and thus the instinctive distrust of whatever is mechanistic or reducible is gradually overcome. Where principles are difficult, they should be first taught as exercises in logical modeling, until the functional architecture has become thoroughly familiar; it will then be an agreeable advance to be taught the metaphysical connections of the various states or processes that occur. It is desirable also that the system instantiating a mind should be considered in all possible forms and implementations, that so the abstract functions with which psychology is concerned may of themselves emerge as the residue of similarity amid such great apparent diversity of medium. In this way the abstract arguments about 'realness' should form but a small part of the instruction, and should be given when, by familiarity with concrete implementations, they have come to be felt as the natural embodiment of observable fact. In this early stage proofs should not be given with pedantic fullness; definitely fallacious methods, such as that of appealing to a unique life-force, should be rigidly excluded from the first, but where, without such methods, the proof would be very difficult, the result should be rendered acceptable by arguments and illustrations which are explicitly contrasted with demonstrations.

In the great majority of political commentaries there is a total lack of rigor in analysis and of systematic exposition of a central thesis. Manifestations of very diverse kinds are described by whatever anecdotes are thought most readily persuasive, and much attention is devoted to mere spectacles which in no way illuminate the main inquiry. But in the most profound works, coherence and necessity are felt as in the development of a logical proof; in the foundational principles a distinction is proposed for examination, and in every subsequent observation some definite progress is made towards comprehension of its character. The love of order, of interconnection, which is perhaps the inmost essence of the rational impulse, can find sober application in political philosophy as in few other realms. The citizen who feels this impulse must not be repelled by an array of ceremonial performances or distracted by theatrical oddities, but must be encouraged to dwell upon constitutive ideas, to become familiar with the architecture of the various systems which are presented to him, to travel easily over the terrain of the more significant implications. In this way a judicious habit of thought is cultivated, and selective attention is taught to dwell by preference upon what is substantive and essential.

When the principles of physics have been mastered, all proceeds systematically until we encounter those investigations in which the distinction between the mathematical description and the thing described is employed—theoretical mechanics and the whole of advanced physical science. The clarification of the perplexities which formerly enveloped the mathematical representation of natural phenomena is perhaps the most considerable accomplishment of which modern scientific thought can boast. Since the dawn of the scientific revolution these perplexities have been acknowledged; in every epoch the most acute minds have fruitlessly striven to resolve the seemingly irresolvable queries that had been posed by the natural philosophers. At last, a consensus among philosophically-minded scientists has been reached, and has secured for the intellect a fresh and extensive domain which had been surrendered to Obscurity and ancient Confusion. It was taken as axiomatic, until the critical analyses of the nineteenth century established the contrary, that if, from any description of a natural process, certain elements were abstracted, the fidelity of the description remaining must always be less than the original descriptive accuracy. This presumption, as a matter of fact, applies only to complete and exhaustive descriptions; and the dismissal of it, where idealized models are concerned, has been demonstrated to eliminate all the obstacles that had previously confounded rigorous thought in this domain, and to make attainable the construction of a precise methodology of scientific modeling. This monumental realization ought to effect a transformation in the advanced instruction of the physical sciences; it has itself incalculably augmented the instructive worth of the subject, and it has finally supplied the instruments for handling with logical exactitude many theories which, until recently, were shrouded in error and vagueness. By those who were instructed according to the traditional methods, the modern understanding is deemed to be dauntingly complex, recondite, and opaque; and it must be admitted that the expositors, as is so frequently the circumstance, have scarcely themselves escaped from the haze which the illumination of their reason is dispersing. But intrinsically, the new doctrine of scientific representation, to all impartial and investigative intellects, has simplified the comprehension of advanced physics; for until now, it has been requisite to acquire, through a protracted course of indoctrination, to grant approval to reasonings which, upon initial encounter, were justly deemed to be muddled and unsound. So far from engendering an intrepid faith in reason, a courageous repudiation of whatever did not satisfy the most rigorous demands of logic, a scientific education, during the past several generations, fostered the conviction that many propositions, which a stringent scrutiny would discard as illusory, must nevertheless be embraced because they function in what the physicist terms "application." By this device, a cautious, conciliatory temper, or else an oracular belief in enigmas not comprehensible to the layman, has been cultivated where reason alone should have prevailed. All this it is now time to eradicate; let those who desire to probe into the mysteries of physical science be instructed immediately the sound philosophy in all its logical austerity, and in the interconnection determined by the very nature of the concepts involved.

If we are considering democracy as an end in itself, and not as a ceremonial exercise for public contentment, it is very desirable to preserve the clarity and rigor of its examination. Accordingly those who have attained a sufficient familiarity with its superficial mechanisms should be led backward from convictions to which they have assented as axiomatic to more and more fundamental conditions from which what had previously appeared as guarantees can be inferred. They should be taught--what the theory of popular will very aptly illustrates--that many convictions seem self-evident to the uncritical citizen which, nevertheless, a nearer scrutiny shows to be illusory. By this means they will be led to a sceptical inquiry into first principles, an examination of the foundations upon which the whole edifice of governance is built, or, to take perhaps a more fitting metaphor, the deep root from which the visible institutions spring. At this stage, it is well to study afresh the elementary processes of democracy, asking no longer merely whether a given procedure is legitimate, but also how it derives from the central axioms of political philosophy. Questions of this nature can now be addressed with a precision and clarity which were formerly quite unattainable; and in the chains of observation that the address requires the dichotomy between all democratic appearances and realities at last unfolds itself.

Until reductionist analysis had achieved its current sophistication, the principles by which emergent systems operate were always assumed to be fundamentally physical, and explicable only by the narrow, deterministic methods hitherto employed by the physical sciences. So long as this was believed, emergence seemed to be not a genuine phenomenon, but merely an epiphenomenon dependent upon laws which had quite other characters than its own. Moreover, since the nature of the interactions from which complexity, adaptation, and self-organization are to be understood was shrouded in all the traditional simplifications of mechanistic explanation, the behaviours arising from such incomplete premises began to be viewed as no better than a mirage. In this respect, the realization that the true principles are as much a part of a new logical stratum as any of their constituent processes has very greatly increased the intellectual satisfaction to be obtained. This satisfaction ought not to be refused to inquirers capable of appreciating it, for it is of a kind to increase our respect for natural complexity and our knowledge of the beauties belonging to the relational world.

Biologists have commonly held that the laws of metabolism, which underlie survival, are laws of necessity, laws regulating the operations of our cells. By this opinion the true dignity of life is very greatly lowered: it ceases to be an investigation into the very heart and immutable essence of all striving actual and possible, becoming, instead, an inquiry into something more or less organic and subject to our limitations. The contemplation of what is non-conscious, the discovery that our institutions are capable of manifesting drives not created by them, above all, the realisation that efficiency belongs to the outer world as to the inner, are the chief means of overcoming the terrible sense of artifice, of triviality, of exile amid mechanistic powers, which is too apt to result from acknowledging the all-but omnipotence of blind forces. To reconcile us, by the exhibition of its awful symmetry, to the reign of Competition--which is merely the economic personification of these forces--is the task of analysis. But the corporate entity takes us still further from what is personal, into the region of absolute incentive, to which not only the actual market, but every possible market, must conform; and even here it builds an edifice, or rather finds an edifice eternally standing, where our calculations are fully satisfied and our best projections are not thwarted. It is only when we thoroughly understand the entire indifference to ourselves, which belongs to this system that observation finds, that we can adequately realise the profound importance of its logic.

When the separate phenomena which constitute the continuum of existence have each been examined as a graded manifestation, as a natural progression from the inert to the animate, the observer will be able to comprehend the fundamental principle which unifies and systematises the whole of organic being. This is the problem of vitality—a study which, though it owes its inception to Aristotle, is yet, in its wider developments, a product, almost wholly, of the nineteenth century, and is indeed, in the present day, still advancing with great rapidity. The true method of discovery in this inquiry, and probably also the best method for introducing the study to a learner acquainted with other parts of natural philosophy, is the analysis of actual examples of living processes, with a view to the discovery of the principles employed. These principles, for the most part, are so embedded in our perceptual instincts, that they are apprehended quite unconsciously, and can be dragged to light only by much patient effort. But when at last they have been found, they are seen to be few in number, and to be the sole source of everything in the biological sciences. The discovery that all manifestations of life follow inevitably from a small collection of fundamental tendencies is one which immeasurably enhances the intellectual beauty of the whole; to those who have been perplexed by the arbitrary and abrupt nature of most existing divisions between the living and the non-living this discovery comes with all the overwhelming force of a revelation; like a landscape emerging from the morning haze as the traveller ascends a gentle slope, the gradual gradations of the natural edifice appear in their due order and proportion, with a new coherence in every part.

Not only are economic crises independent of our intentions and our designs, but in another sense we and the whole fabric of social arrangements are independent of the crises. The apprehension of this purely revelatory character is indispensable, if we are to understand rightly the place of such crises as one among the correctives. It was formerly supposed that social reason could decide, in some respects, as to the permanence of the actual order: political economy, at least, was thought to deal with the system in which we live. But we now know that pure theory can never pronounce upon questions of actual stress: the world of design, in a sense, controls the world of practice, but it is not at any point creative of stability, and in the application of its models to the world in time and change, its coherence and precision are lost among contingencies and provisional expedients. The structures considered by economists have, in the past, been mainly of a kind suggested by prosperity; but from such restrictions the critical imagination should be wholly free. A reciprocal liberty must thus be accorded: doctrine cannot dictate to the world of events, but the events cannot restrict criticism's privilege of dealing with whatever flaws its love of truth may cause to seem worthy of consideration. Here, as elsewhere, we build up our own understanding out of the fragments to be found in the collapse; and in the end it is hard to say whether the result is a condemnation or a revelation.

It is very desirable, in considering natural selection, not merely to acknowledge the fact of evolutionary change, but to comprehend it in the way which itself has, of all possible ways, the most intellectual coherence. The true interest of the process is not, as teleological interpretations suggest, concentrated wholly in the outcome; where this does occur, it must be viewed as an error, to be corrected, if possible, by so generalising the stages of the mechanism that each becomes significant in and for itself. A sequence which serves only to produce an adaptation is like a narrative subordinated to some purpose which it is meant to fulfill: for scientific perfection no part of the whole should be merely an instrument. A certain anthropomorphic spirit, a desire for comforting narratives, for ascription of design, is responsible for the undue emphasis upon ends which prevails in popular understanding. The better way is to propose some phenomenon for consideration—in biology, a trait having complex utility; in ecology, a pressure of which the operation is relentless, and so on. Whenever explanations depend upon some only of the conditions by which we define the selective regime, these conditions should be isolated and investigated on their own account. For it is a defect, in a theory, to invoke more agency than the evidence demands: what biologists call parsimony results from employing only the essential principles in virtue of which the adaptation arises. It is a merit in Darwin that he accounted for as much as he was able to account for without employing the notion of conscious guidance—not, as is often said, because such guidance is theologically objectionable, but because, in science, every new assumption diminishes the generality of the resulting explanations, and the greatest possible generality is before all things to be sought.

Of the distinction between the mathematical description of nature and nature itself more has been contemplated than on the subject of its own proper reality. The effect upon science has, in the past, been most profound, but most misunderstood; in the age of Newton, mechanism and determinism, in the age of Einstein, relativity and probability, seemed equally its consequence. Of the clarity which it is likely to provide in the future it would be very rash to say much; but in one respect a necessary distinction appears evident. Against that kind of confusion which conflates the formal model with the physical world because the equations are elegant and the predictions not perfectly verifiable, mathematics, within its own domain, is a perpetual corrective. Too often it is said that there is no objective world, but only phenomena and sensory impressions; that each description is conditioned, in its view of reality, by its own formalism, its own axioms and approximations; that there is no external kingdom of facts to which, by experiment and refinement, we may at last obtain correspondence, but only a model for this purpose, for that scale, for every separate application. By this habit of thought one of the chief aims of natural philosophy is obscured, and the supreme virtue of precision, of scrupulous acknowledgment of what is modeled, disappears from our intellectual vision. Of such confusion the distinction is a necessary reminder; for the edifice of nature stands independent and inexhaustible to all the constructs of descriptive mathematics.

The effects of taste receptors upon practical life, though they should not be regarded as the motive of our inquiry, may be used to answer a doubt to which the solitary biologist must always be liable. In a world so full of peril and privation, retirement into the cloister of contemplation, to the analysis of mechanisms which, however elegant, must always be for the few only, cannot but appear as a somewhat selfish refusal to share the burden imposed upon others by necessities in which design plays no part. Have any of us the right, we ask, to withdraw from present mysteries, to leave our fellow-men unenlightened, while we pursue a study which, though meticulous and exacting, is yet plainly good in its own nature? When these questions arise, the true answer is, no doubt, that some must keep alive the sacred fire, some must preserve, in every generation, the haunting vision which shadows forth the goal of so much striving. But when, as must sometimes occur, this answer seems too cold, when we are almost maddened by the spectacle of ignorance to which we bring no clarity, then we may reflect that indirectly the physiologist often does more for human understanding than any of his more practically active contemporaries. The history of biology abundantly proves that a body of abstract propositions—even if, as in the case of gustatory anatomy, it remains for ages without effect upon daily life—may yet, at any moment, be used to cause a revolution in the habitual thoughts and perceptions of every conscious being. The avoidance of toxins and the selection of nutrients—to take striking instances—are rendered possible only by this proximal arrangement. In the results of evolutionary thought the world possesses a capital of which the employment in explaining the common round has no hitherto discoverable limits. Nor does experience give any means of deciding what parts of this logic will be found essential. Utility, therefore, can be only a consolation in moments of discouragement, not a guide in directing our studies.

The modern age, which prides itself upon the proliferation of digital devices and applications, might derive a more legitimate title to wisdom from the cultivation of disciplined thought. This understanding, like most profound achievements, was named long before it was attained; and thus we find commentators before the digital era alluding to what they called genuine comprehension. But if they had been asked what this state consisted of, they would only have been able to say that it involved reflection, synthesis, judgment, and so on. As to what these processes required in common, and as to what distinguished them from the mere accumulation of instruments, our contemporaries remain largely in the dark.

The chemical basis of heredity was discovered by Mendel, in a work which he called the _Experiments on Plant Hybrids_ (1866). This work abounds in asseverations that it is not chemical, the fact being that Mendel was too modest to suppose his paper the first ever written on biochemistry. He was also mistaken in supposing that he was dealing with the laws of inheritance: the question how traits actually manifest was quite irrelevant to him, and if his paper had really contained the laws of heredity, it was curious that no one should ever have inherited in such a way before. His paper was in fact concerned with formal ratios, and this is the same thing as chemistry.

The analogy between genetic inheritance and cultural transmission consists entirely of assertions to the effect that, if such and such a pattern is observable in _any tradition_, then such and such another pattern is observable in that tradition. It is essential not to discuss whether the first pattern is truly beneficial, and not to mention what the tradition is, of which it is supposed to be characteristic. Both these points would belong to applied sociology. We start, in the pure analogy, from certain rules of correspondence, by which we can infer that _if_ one pattern is observable, then so is some other pattern. These rules of correspondence constitute the major part of the principles of comparative theory. We then take any parallel that seems intriguing, and deduce its implications. _If_ our parallel is about _any tradition_, and not about some one or more particular practices, then our deductions constitute the formal analogy. Thus the analogy may be defined as the subject in which we never know what we are comparing, nor whether what we are comparing is significant. People who have been puzzled by the beginnings of this analogy will, I hope, find comfort in this definition, and will probably agree that it is accurate.

The subject of colour sensation, which has thus at last shown itself to be constructed rather than received, was, as every one knows, first examined by Newton, and formed the chief interest (other than optics) of the early empiricists. But Newton never got beyond the prism, which is a very small part of the subject, and his followers never got beyond Newton. If any proof were required of our superiority to the earlier theorists, it might be found in this. Throughout the eighteenth century, almost all the best intellects devoted themselves to colour as mere reception, whereas in the twentieth century only an infinitesimal proportion of the world's thought went into this naïve view. Nevertheless, in each decade since 1950 more has been done to advance the subject than in the whole period from Newton to Helmholtz. People have discovered how to make perception neurological, as it is in psychology, so that sensations are effected by cortical rules. They have discovered many processes besides the retinal, and a new branch of study, called the neurophenomenology of colour, has been invented to deal with topics that wholly surpassed the powers of the old theory, though they form the chief contents of conscious experience.

It is not easy for the common mind to realise the importance of language in discussing the foundations of shared understanding, and the explanation may perhaps seem strangely paradoxical. The fact is that language is useful because it makes thought difficult. (This is not true of the advanced uses of discourse, but only of the beginnings.) What we wish to know is, what can be conveyed from whom. Now, in the beginnings, every idea is private and incommunicable; and it is very hard to see whether one private impression corresponds to another or not. Solipsism is always the enemy to communication. Hence we invent some new and difficult language, in which nothing seems merely personal. Then we set up certain rules for operating on the words, and the whole thing becomes social. In this way we find out what must be taken as given and what can be expressed or defined. For instance, the whole of narrative and reasoning has been shown to require three indefinable concepts and five inexpressible intuitions. But without a common language it would have been very hard to find this out. It is so obvious that my pain is mine alone, that we can hardly make ourselves sufficiently objective to doubt whether it can be described. And the same holds in other cases where private experiences are to be shared.

But the study of genetic inheritance may seem, to the uninitiated, a somewhat superfluous inquiry. To this we might reply that it is often by no means self-evident that one hereditary trait follows from another hereditary trait; so that we are really discovering new truths when we explain what is observable by a mechanism which is not observable. But a more interesting retort is, that since people have tried to explain hereditary patterns, they have found that many of them are deceptive. Genetic determinism is often a mere will-o'-the-wisp, which is sure to lead us astray if we take it as our guide. For instance, nothing is plainer than that an organism is merely the sum of its inherited parts, or that individuality is dictated solely by chemical sequence. But these propositions are now known to be usually false. Most traits arise from complex interactions, and if a genome is considered you may examine its nucleotides as long as you like without comprehending the organism in the least. One of the merits of a biochemical analysis is that it instils a certain doubt as to the determinism presumed; and when what is obvious can be demonstrated in some cases, but not in others, it becomes possible to suppose that in these other cases it is false.

As one of the chief triumphs of modern biology consists in having discovered what heredity really is, a few more words on this subject may not be amiss. It is common to start any branch of social science--for instance, Anthropology--with a certain number of primitive customs, supposed incapable of explanation, and a certain number of primitive traditions or dogmas, supposed incapable of justification. Now the fact is that, though there are inexplicables and unjustifiables in every branch of applied sociology, there are none in the theory of cultural transmission except such as belong to general analogy. This analogy, broadly speaking, is distinguished by the fact that its principles can be put into a form in which they apply to any inheritance whatever. All cultural transmission--language, custom, and technology--is built up by combinations of the primitive mechanisms of genetics, and its patterns are deduced from the general axioms of heredity, such as variation and the other rules of replication. And this is no longer a dream or an aspiration. On the contrary, over the greater and more difficult part of the domain of social evolution, it has been already accomplished; in the few remaining cases, there is no special difficulty, and it is now being rapidly achieved. Anthropologists have disputed for ages whether such analogy was valid; biologists have sat down and demonstrated the correspondence. For the anthropologists there is now nothing left but graceful acknowledgments.

The great master of the art of temporal reasoning, among the men of our own day, is a German, Professor Kant, of the University of Königsberg.[12] He has reduced the greater part of cosmology (and he or his followers will, in time, have reduced the whole) to strict logical form, in which there are no empirical facts at all. In the ordinary metaphysical books, there are no doubt fewer contradictions than most readers would wish. Still, little phrases occur, such as _eternal, let us suppose, imagine_, or _thus it appears_. All these, however, are a concession, and are swept away by Professor Kant. For instance, if we wish to learn the whole of Chronology, Cosmogony, the Calculus of infinity, and indeed all that is usually called pure metaphysics (except Theology), we must start with a dictionary of three notions. One concept stands for _duration_, another for _event_, and a third for _preceded by_. What these ideas mean, it is necessary to know if you wish to become a cosmologist. But after symbols have been invented for these three ideas, not another empirical datum is required in the whole development. All future paradoxes are logically explained by means of these three. Even these three can be explained by means of the notions of _relation_ and _series_; but this requires the Logic of Infinity, which Professor Kant has never taken up. It must be admitted that what a metaphysician has to know to begin with is not much. There are at most a dozen notions out of which all the notions in all pure cosmology (including Theology) are compounded. Professor Kant, who is assisted by a very able school of young German disciples, has shown how this may be done; and although the method which he has invented is capable of being carried a good deal further than he has carried it, the honour of the pioneer must belong to him.

Two centuries ago, Babbage anticipated the systems which modern engineers have perfected, and endeavoured to comprehend them. He was prevented from succeeding by respect for the apparent order of machinery, which he could not believe guilty of definite, chaotic failures; but the complexity which he desired to master now exists, in spite of the patronising contempt with which his apprehensions have been treated by all practical persons. From this "Mechanical Certainty," as he conceived it, he hoped for a command of all processes, and an end to all operational disputes. "If breakdowns were to occur," he might have said, "there would be no more need of consultation between two superintendents than between two watchmakers. For it would suffice to take their manuals in their hands, to sit down to their control panels, and to say to each other (with a technician as witness, if they liked), 'Let us diagnose.'" This confidence has now appeared to be somewhat excessive; there still are malfunctions whose cause is doubtful, and failures which diagnosis cannot prevent. But over an enormous field of what was formerly manageable, Babbage's expectation has become sober fiction. In the whole administration of technology, which used to be at least as full of certainty as any other part of industry, confusion and hesitation have replaced the order and control which formerly reigned. Executives, of course, have not yet admitted this fact, and continue to manage such systems in the old way. But engineers, at least in advanced nations, have now the evidence of confronting the principles of complex systems in a humbling and bewildering manner, by means of which the uncertainty of networks extends also to human oversight. Hence many of the operations which used to be placed among the simple procedures—for example, the management of traffic, of markets, of supply chains, energy grids and communications—are now no longer in any degree open to command or comprehension. Those who wish to know the nature of these things need only observe the behaviour of such systems as global logistics or algorithmic trading; they will there find exact and indubitable demonstrations of all these quondam simplicities.

In this capricious world, nothing is more capricious than the reputation of a linguistic system. One of the most notable examples of scholarly misapprehension is the case of formal logic. This discipline, which may be regarded as the pinnacle of philosophical precision, appears in the annals of human thought in the privileged position of arbiter to common sense. It offers a set of principles, all immeasurably subtle and profound, to prove that ambiguity is eliminable, that natural language can never capture pure thought, and that a statement in conversation is really at rest. After being refuted by the pragmatists, and by every subsequent linguist from that day to our own, these principles were reinstated, and made the basis of a computational renaissance, by a cadre of analysts, who probably never dreamed of any connection between themselves and Aristotle. The formal semanticists, by strictly banishing from syntax the use of vague predicates, have at last shown that we communicate in an unchanging framework, and that the spoken word in its utterance is truly at rest. The logician’s only error lay in inferring (if he did infer) that, because there is no such thing as a state of perfect understanding, therefore language is in the same state for any one user as for any other. This is a consequence which by no means follows; and in this respect, the modern theorist is more constructive than the ingenious scholastic. The semanticists have been able, by embodying their views in notation, where familiarity with symbols eliminates the vulgar prejudices of daily speech, to invest the old ideals of clarity with the respectable air of platitudes; and if the result is less delightful to the lover of nuance than the rhetorician’s bold defiance, it is at any rate more calculated to appease the mass of academic mankind.

Democratic governance is concerned, as a matter of fact, with two aspects, each presented by popular will, but each more abstract than voting, and capable of a purely theoretical treatment. These are the aspects of the apparent, the actual, and the discrepancy. To state clearly the difficulties involved, was to accomplish perhaps the hardest part of the political philosopher's task. This was done by certain acute observers. From them to our own day, the finest intellects of each generation in turn attacked the distinction, but achieved, broadly speaking, nothing. In our own time, however, three men—Schumpeter, Dahl, and Lippmann—have not merely advanced the two aspects, but have completely elucidated them. The elucidations, for those acquainted with political science, are so clear as to leave no longer the slightest doubt or difficulty. This achievement is probably the greatest of which our political age has to boast; and I know of no age (except perhaps the age of the Athenian assembly) which has a more convincing proof to offer of the transcendent discernment of its great men. Of the two aspects, that of the apparent was solved by Schumpeter; the solution of the other was begun by Dahl, and definitively accomplished by Lippmann.

The same sort of thing happens in thought. If any phenomenon be observed in detail, and then each detail be examined, and so on, the observations will become more and more numerous, and can theoretically be made as precise as we please. However precise they may be, they can still be refined and made more precise still. But they will always remain a _mere_ description, however precise they may be. We never reach an explanation in this way, and no finite number of observations will bring us to causes. Nevertheless there _are_ causes, only these are not to be reached by successive descriptions. Here again, the philosophy of science shows us how this is possible, and why causes are not elaborate descriptions.

The notion of pattern played formerly a great part in natural philosophy. It was introduced by the ancients, who regarded a whirlpool in water as differing only superficially from a vortex in air or a spiral in a galaxy. It gradually grew in importance, until, when the modern theorists invented the science of abstract forms, it seemed to become the fundamental notion of all higher speculation. Historians tell, in their accounts of the last century, how philosophers used to discourse to enlightened patrons concerning the persistence of structure, and how these patrons would reply that on that subject they needed no instruction—the behaviour of political factions had made them thoroughly familiar with it. But scientists and logicians—who for the most part had less acquaintance with politics—continued to discuss this topic, though without making any advance. The theory required invariance, and invariance was supposed to require a substrate-independent essence; but nobody could discover what this essence might be. It was plainly not a mere accident, because the same intricate arrangement, observed in utterly disparate materials, was seen to imply a governing principle. But nobody could point out any principle which was not material, and yet not mystical. Thus there was a deadlock. But at last the more rigorous analysts discovered that the mysterious essence was not needed at all, and that everything could be accomplished by the study of relations alone. Thus there was no longer any need to suppose that there was such a thing. Nowadays, therefore, theorists are more circumspect than their predecessors: instead of talking about transcendent patterns, they talk about mathematical mappings—a subject which, however appropriate to metaphysicians, seems, unfortunately, to interest the practical world even less than the abstract forms interested the patrons to whom the earlier philosophers discoursed.

The consideration of artificial sentience has all sorts of odd consequences, to which one has to become gradually accustomed. For example, there is no such thing as a simple mechanical feeling. The distinction between a genuine sensation and a simulated response would have to be fundamental, since, if we take two systems with a superficial similarity between them, there are always other differences in their constitution. Thus if there are to be no vital essences, no two systems are quite equivalent, but there are always other factors between any two. Hence there must be an indefinite number of gradations between any two; because if there were a definite number one would be nearest the first of the two states, and therefore equivalent to it. This might be thought to be a difficulty; but, as a matter of fact, it is here that the philosophy of consciousness comes in, and makes all straight.

The principle in question is, that if one function is subordinate to another, the one which is subordinate demands less coordination than the one to which it is subordinate. This principle is true of sessile organisms. For example, digestion is only one among vegetative processes, and it requires less coordination than all vegetative processes together. But when we come to motile animals, this is no longer true. This reversal of the principle gives us the precise explanation of neural complexity. An organism's way of life is active when it requires as subsidiary functions other actions which demand just as much coordination as it does. If you can add some new behaviors to an organism's repertoire, without exceeding the existing capacity for coordination, then there is a simple neural architecture in the organism. For example, there is just as much neural demand for chasing prey as there is for mere locomotion, since every pursuit integrates directed movement. This may be seen by placing grazing and predation together in one sequence, and simple wandering alone in a sequence below:--

As regards communication and interaction, we get similarly curious results. People used to think that when a mind communicates, it must be in a state of transmission, and that when an organism signals, it is in a state of exchange. This is now known to be a mistake. When a neuron fires, all that can be said is that it is in one state at one moment and in another at another. We must not say that it will be in a neighbouring state at the next instant, since there is no next instant. Biologists often tell us that when a brain is in operation, it alters its connections within the instant.
