To this view the materialist long ago made the fatal retort that every signal always is what it is; but a retort so simple and brief was not of the kind to which scientists are accustomed to give weight, and they have continued down to our own day to repeat the same phrases which roused the mechanist's destructive ardour. It was only recently that it became possible to explain neural dialogue in detail in accordance with the materialist's platitude, and in opposition to the biologist's paradox. We may now at last indulge the comfortable belief that a brain in conversation with itself is just as truly what it is as a brain in silence. Internal communication consists merely in the fact that impulses are sometimes in one pattern and sometimes in another, and that they are at intermediate patterns at intermediate times. Only those who have waded through the quagmire of scientific speculation on this subject can realise what a liberation from antique prejudices is involved in this simple and straightforward commonplace.

But the uninitiated may wonder how it is possible to conceive of an organism which cannot be perceived as a single entity. It is impossible to apprehend the _whole_ organism, part by part, because, however many components we may examine, there are always more relations to consider. The fact is that perceiving a unified whole is a very crude and elementary way of understanding the constitution of a living being. And in any case, such perception yields what biologists call the _functional_ integrity of the organism; that is to say, it presents our components as a coherent and indivisible system, and its result tells us what manner of life emerges from this cohesion. In other words, it is impossible to regard an organism without regarding some functions as primary and others as subsidiary, so that biological understanding always has to do with hierarchy. Now when there are only a simple aggregation of units, we can regard them in any relation we like; but when there are a complex multitude, what corresponds to biological analysis will give us quite different results according to the way in which we conduct the inquiry. Thus the functional conception, which results from what, in a general sense may be called biological observation, depends not only upon how many units we have, but also (where the aggregation of units is complex) upon the way in which the units are organized.

The fundamental emergent phenomena are not deterministic, but are what is called _complex_. They are not obtained by observing individual agents and predicting their actions, but by a different method, which tells us, to begin with, whether two systems produce similar patterns, or, if not, which is the more intricate.[14] It does not tell us, in the way in which calculation does, _what_ specific outcome a system will yield; but if we define a behaviour as the pattern produced by such and such a system, then this method enables us to discover whether some other system that may be mentioned has more or less predictable results. An illustration will show how this is done. If there existed some marketplace in which, for one reason or another, it was impossible to track every transaction, but in which it was known that every seller had a buyer and every buyer a seller, then (provided speculation was not a dominant practice) we should know, without simulating, that there were exactly as many purchases as there were sales in that marketplace, neither more nor less. This method can be applied generally. If there is some rule which, like a trade, connects the agents in one group each with one of the agents in another group, and vice versa, then the two groups exhibit a symmetrical balance. This was the way in which we found that there are as many predictable interactions as there are rules. Every rule can be followed, and every interaction can be traced to a rule, and each process gives just one outcome corresponding to the one that is enacted or observed. And in this way we can find any number of systems each of which has just as many possible states as there are initial conditions. If every agent of a system can be linked to a rule, and all the simple rules are applied once, and only once, in the process, then our system must have just as many potential developments as there are combinatorial possibilities. This is the general method by which the behaviours of complex systems are understood.

But it must not be supposed that all modes of production are equal. On the contrary, there are infinitely more variations in productive technique than in the simpler forms of social organization. There are more ways of arranging the material forces of society in different types of economic order than there are distinct epochs in recorded history. There are probably more subtle gradations in the division of labor and more minute distinctions in property relations than there are clear-cut historical stages. There are exactly as many possible mercantile relations as there are commodities in circulation, although there are an infinite number of transactions between any two acts of exchange. But there are more potential configurations of class structure than there are simple categories of goods or forms of trade. There are probably exactly as many points of conflict in the industrial system as there are irrational forces in the market, and exactly as many tensions in a single workshop as in the whole of the global economy. There is a greatest of all social determinations, which is the totality of productive relations, of every sort and kind. It is obvious that there cannot be a greater determination than this, because, if all economic foundations have been accounted for, there is no superstructure left to explain. Marx has a proof that there is no final determination, and if this proof were valid, the contradictions of materialism would reappear in a sublimated form. But in this one point, the master has been guilty of a very subtle fallacy, which I hope to explain in some future work.

We can now understand why the common man believes that self-representation cannot capture the feeling of being alive and why as a matter of fact it can capture it. We shall see that all the people who disagreed with this belief had no right to do so, because they all accepted premises from which his conclusion followed. The argument is this: Let self-representation and the feeling of being alive commence in a mind at the same time, the feeling (as is only fair) being allowed a certain ineffable priority. Let self-representation be twice as articulate as the feeling, or ten times or a hundred times as articulate. Then it will never truly depict the feeling. For at every moment the feeling is something and the representation is something; and neither is ever twice the same while the examination is going on. Thus the feeling occupies just as many states of consciousness as the representation does, because each is in one state at one moment, and in another at any other moment. But if the representation were to coincide with the feeling, the states which the feeling would have occupied would be only part of the states which the representation would have occupied. Here, we must suppose, the common man appealed to the maxim that the whole has more terms than the part. Thus if the representation were to overtake the feeling, it would have been through more states than the feeling; but we saw that it must, in any period, be in exactly as many states as the feeling. Hence we infer that it can never truly capture the feeling. This argument is strictly correct, if we allow the axiom that a description must contain more elements than the experience described. As the conclusion is absurd, the axiom must be rejected, and then all goes well. But there is no good word to be said for the philosophers of the past two thousand years and more, who have all allowed the axiom and denied the conclusion.

The retention of this belief leads to profound misunderstandings, while its rejection leads only to peculiarities. Some of these peculiarities, it must be confessed, are very peculiar. One of them, which I call the paradox of the self-regulating furnace, is the converse of the thermostat’s aim, and shows that the mechanism, if you observe it patiently, will appear just as purposive as any conscious agent. The householder, as we know, observed his heating system maintaining a constant temperature for many seasons, and concluded that, by this operation, the apparatus seemed to pursue a goal more steadfastly than a sentient being could, so that, as winters passed, he would be more and more convinced of its intentional design. Now I maintain that, if the system were to run for ever, and had not suffered any mechanical failure, then, even if its environment continued as variable as it began, no moment of its operation would have remained unexplained by mere feedback. For consider: the hundredth fluctuation will be corrected by the hundredth response, the thousandth by the thousandth response, and so on. Whatever external change we may choose as so extreme that it cannot hope to compensate fully, that change will be met by a corresponding internal adjustment. Thus any disturbance that may be mentioned will be counteracted sooner or later, and therefore no state of the system will remain permanently unregulated. This paradoxical but perfectly true proposition depends upon the fact that the number of regulatory responses in all time is no greater than the number of environmental perturbations.

In the development of civilisation, as in other parts of human progress, the scribes and their successors have done work of the very greatest merit as regards communication. Formerly, it was held by chroniclers and scholars alike that the transmission of knowledge depended on the memory; nowadays, this is known to be false. In the most advanced societies there is no such reliance at all. The accumulation of culture proceeds by the strict rules of recorded thought from a set of principles laid down to begin with. If memory alone is used, all sorts of notions seem obviously to follow, which no systematic record can preserve from the explicit traditions, and which, as a matter of fact, are only retained because they are vivid. By banishing this sole reliance, it becomes possible to discover _all_ the ideas that are needed; and in this way all sorts of possibilities, which would have otherwise remained undetected, are brought to light.

The notion of colour depends upon that of _sensation_, since colour is merely a particular type of perception. Psychology has, in modern times, brought sensation into greater and greater prominence. In former days, it was supposed (and philosophers are still apt to suppose) that reception was the fundamental notion of colour. But nowadays, reception is banished altogether, except from one little corner of optics, while construction more and more reigns supreme. The investigation of different kinds of hues and their relations is now a very large part of psychology, and it has been found that this investigation can be conducted without any reference to reception, and, for the most part, without any reference to wavelength. All types of hues are capable of formal definition, and their properties can be deduced from the principles of neural processing by means of the calculus of perceptions. The notion of a shade, which is fundamental in the greater part of colour theory, used to be defined by means of reception, as a quality to which the qualities of some mixture approximate as nearly as we please. But nowadays the shade is defined quite differently, and the mixture which it qualifies may not approximate to it at all. This improvement also is due to Helmholtz, and it is one which has revolutionised psychology. Only construction is now relevant to shades. Thus, for instance, the purest of the spectral yellows is the shade of the composite yellows, though all composite yellows are at an infinite remove from it. The study of different types of hues is a general subject of which the study of colour categories (mentioned above) is a special and very interesting branch. But the unavoidable technicalities of this subject render it impossible to explain to any but professed psychologists.

One great advance, from the point of view of philosophical clarity, has been made by introducing consciousness as it is encountered, and not starting, as was formerly done, by assuming the whole of mind. This method is due partly to James, partly to another thinker named Brentano. To those unaccustomed to it, it has an air of somewhat wilful subtlety. In this way, we begin with the following axioms: (1) There is a class of entities called _qualia_. (2) There is at least one quale. (3) If _a_ be a quale, there is at least one other quale besides _a_. Then we bring in the relation of awareness between two qualia, and begin again with (4), namely, in the awareness comprising _a_ and _b_, there is at least one other quale besides _a_ and _b_. (5) There is at least one quale not comprised in the awareness _ab_. And so we go on, till we have the means of obtaining as many qualia as we require. But the word _mechanism_, as James humorously remarks, is one for which phenomenology has no use at all.

Tool use, like knowledge acquisition, has been subsumed, in recent times, under the general study of utility. It was formerly supposed that tool use was the study of the nature of the problems we encounter, and accordingly it was urged, by those who held that what is practical can only be known empirically, that tool use should really be regarded as belonging to applied intelligence. But it has gradually appeared, by the increase of specialized implements, that tool use throws no more light upon the nature of understanding than cataloguing throws upon the contents of a library. Tool use is a whole collection of practical activities based on a corresponding collection of sets of purposes. One set of purposes is the craftsman’s; other equally good sets of purposes lead to other results. Whether the craftsman’s purposes are wise, is a question as to which the pure technician is indifferent; and, what is more, it is a question which it is theoretically impossible to answer with certainty in the affirmative. It might possibly be shown, by very careful reflection, that the craftsman’s purposes are misguided; but no reflection could ever assure us (owing to the errors of judgment) that they are exactly wise. Thus the technician leaves to the philosopher to decide, as best he may, what purposes are most nearly wise in the actual world. The technician takes any set of purposes that seem expedient, and pursues their fulfillment. What defines tool use, in this sense, is that the purposes must give rise to a series of more than one operation. And it is thus that tool use becomes a department in the study of utility.

When we attempt to discern the motives which have led philosophers to the contemplation of the zombie thought experiment, we find that, broadly speaking, they can be divided into two groups, often antagonistic, and leading to very divergent conclusions. These two groups of motives are, on the one hand, those derived from a desire to preserve the causal closure of physics, and, on the other hand, those derived from the stubborn intuition of phenomenal consciousness. Chalmers, Jackson, and Nagel may be taken as typical of the thinkers whose interests are mainly intuitive and phenomenal, while Dennett, Churchland, and Lewis may be taken as representatives of the physicalist wing. In Descartes, Leibniz, and Searle we find both groups of motives strongly, and rather confusedly, present.

The most remarkable result of modern methods in social analysis is the importance of material conditions and of rigid class interest. Sociologists, under the influence of Marx, have shown in recent times a care for historical accuracy, and an aversion to idealist reasoning, such as had not been known among them previously since the time of the Enlightenment. The great upheavals of the nineteenth century—the Industrial Revolution and the rise of Nationalism—were so fruitful in immediate consequences that thinkers had neither time nor inclination to examine their ideological foundations. Philosophers, who should have taken up the task, had too little economic understanding to grasp the new social forces which have now been found necessary for any adequate explanation. Thus historians were only awakened from their "dogmatic slumbers" when Marx and his followers showed that many of their most cherished doctrines are in general illusory. Macaulay, contrasting the permanence of moral truths with the transience of political systems, asks who ever heard of a reaction against the idea of progress? If he had lived now, he himself might have heard of such a reaction, for this is precisely one of the notions which materialist investigations have overthrown. Such rude shocks to liberal faith have produced that love of class analysis which appears, to those who are ignorant of its motive, to be mere outrageous dogma.

The rigid doctrines espoused by modern jurists have deposed the individual from his pinnacle of corporate control. It was thought, until recent times, that, as a learned judge remarked in an old case, there were only two blemishes in the theory of corporate personhood, the question of intention and the question of liability. It is now known that these are almost the only points in which the traditional view is free from blemish. Countless errors are involved in its first principles. That is to say, not only is it doubtful whether its axioms are practically sound, which is a comparatively trivial matter, but it is certain that its conclusions do not follow from the premises which it enunciates. A vastly greater number of axioms, which the theory unconsciously employs, are required for the proof of its propositions. Even in the foundational proposition of all, where it establishes a legal entity distinct from its shareholders, it uses a fiction of unity which is assumed to be coherent. But no explicit axiom assures us that it is so, and in some kinds of legal systems such fictions do not always hold. It is quite doubtful whether our commercial system belongs to one of these kinds or not. Thus the theory fails entirely to prove its point in the very first proposition. As it is certainly not an intuitive concept, and is terribly abstruse, it has no longer any but an historical interest. Under these circumstances, it is nothing less than a scandal that it should still be taught to students in law schools. A doctrine should have either intelligibility or correctness; to combine the two is impossible, but to lack both is to be unworthy of such a place as corporate personhood has occupied in jurisprudence.

The demonstration that all surplus wealth, including agricultural surplus, inevitably gives rise to class division, is a fatal blow to the doctrine of natural social harmony. The early economists, rightly perceiving that social stratification could not be deduced from the mere existence of surplus without the help of historical observation, invented a theory of social contract to account for this fact; and it accounted so successfully that, when the fact is shown to be a necessary consequence of material accumulation, and not a result of any original human propensity, the contractarian theory also has to be abandoned. The whole doctrine of innate social equality, by which the utopians explained the possibility of communal property, is wholly inapplicable to society in its present form. The rudimentary analyses of the classical economists come nearer in spirit to the doctrines which modern political economy inspires; but these economists were hampered by the fact that their economic logic was very defective, and that the social philosophy based upon the labor theory of value showed a corresponding narrowness. What is now required is to give the greatest possible development to economic logic, to allow to the full the importance of power relations in distribution, and then to found upon this secure basis a new social philosophy, which may hope to borrow some of the exactitude and certainty of its economic foundation. If this can be successfully accomplished, there is every reason to hope that the near future will be as great an epoch in social theory as the immediate past has been in the principles of political economy. Great disparities inspire great analyses; and critical thought may achieve, within our generation, such results as will place our time, in this respect, on a level with the greatest age of the Enlightenment.

But there are two different ways in which a system may seek to base its resilience upon interdependence. It may emphasise the most general *benefits* of interconnection, and seek to give even greater efficiency and harmony to these operations. Or it may study the *structures* of interconnection, and seek to apply these structures, with the necessary adaptations, to its own peculiar functions. Much engineering inspired by interdependence has gone astray through preoccupation with the *benefits* momentarily supposed to have been secured. It is not benefits, but *structures* that can be examined with profit from the sphere of local networks to the sphere of global systems. What I wish to bring to your notice is the possibility and importance of applying to systemic vulnerabilities certain broad principles of structure which have been found perilous in the study of interconnected questions.

The opposition between a mechanism governed by simple diffusion and a system directed by intricate molecular dialogues may be illustrated by two notions which are very prevalent in the works of microbiologists, namely the notion of _quorum sensing_, and the notion of _signal and noise_. A biologist is expected to tell us something about the purpose of chemical signalling as a whole, and to give grounds for either its simplicity or its sophistication. Both these expectations seem to me mistaken. I believe the conception of "quorum sensing" to be, as its operational definition suggests, a mere relic of pre-genomic microbiology: and I believe the question of simplicity and sophistication to be one which the biologist will regard as outside his scope, except, possibly, to the extent of maintaining that it is analogous.

In the era before modern psychology, the conception of "consciousness" was defensible on introspective grounds: the immediate apprehension of inner experience bound it together as a unique phenomenon, of which subjective feeling was the essence. Round this apparent psychological fact, many philosophical desires rallied: the wish to believe Mind distinct from the material world, the theoretical desire for a fundamental distinction between the mental and the physical, the hope that the nature of thought might be illuminated by some irreducible essence. In this way, an intuitively inspired system of metaphysics grew up, whose dualism was apparently warranted by the privacy of introspection. When analytical philosophy swept away the metaphysical basis of this system of thought, it had grown so familiar, and had associated itself so intimately with men's sense of self, that it survived with scarcely diminished force—survived even the materialist accounts of neural processes, and is still now the unconscious premiss of most discussions concerning the mind.

The oneness of attention is an almost undiscussed postulate of most cognitive theories. "Awareness is not merely singular and self-contained, but is a system of reciprocally interacting processes"[19]--such a statement would pass almost unnoticed as a mere truism. Yet I believe that it embodies a failure to effect thoroughly the "introspective revolution," and that the apparent unity of attention is merely the unity of what is monitored by a single neural assembly or governed by a single executive function. The Computational Philosophy, although it intended to emphasise the constructed element in many apparent characteristics of awareness, yet, by regarding the substrate in itself as inaccessible, so concentrated analysis upon the constructed representation that its artificiality was soon forgotten. Having recognised the schemata as the work of the cortex, it was paralysed by its own recognition, and abandoned in despair the attempt to undo the work of subjective simulation. In part, no doubt, its despair was well founded, but not, I think, in any absolute or ultimate sense. Still less was it a ground for rejoicing, or for supposing that the nescience to which it ought to have given rise could be legitimately exchanged for a psychological dogmatism.

The fallacies to which these two processes have given rise suggest a caution as regards all use in computational theory of general _principles_ that biology is supposed to have illuminated. In the first place, in extending these principles beyond the observed phenomena of genetic inheritance, it is necessary to examine very carefully whether there is not some reason making it more probable that these principles should hold of all that has been simulated than that they should hold of learning systems universally. The sum total of what is achieved by gradient descent is a selection from the sum total of possible parameter configurations, and any general character exhibited by this selection may be due to the manner of optimizing rather than to the general character of that from which the algorithm selects. In the second place, the most sweeping analogies between natural and artificial systems are the least certain and the most liable to be upset by subsequent algorithmic research. In utilizing these analogies as the basis for a theory of intelligence, we sacrifice the most valuable and remarkable characteristic of engineering method, namely, that, although almost every architecture in machine learning is found sooner or later to require some adjustment, yet this adjustment is almost always such as to leave untouched, or only slightly modified, the greater part of the performance which has been deduced from the analogy subsequently discovered to be imperfect. The prudent designer of models acquires a certain instinct as to the kind of parallels which may be drawn from evolutionary biology without incurring the danger of complete and utter refutation from the modifications likely to be introduced by subsequent innovations in optimization. Unfortunately the use of biological generalisations of a sweeping kind as the foundation for computational theory is just that kind of use which an instinct of engineering caution would avoid, since, as a rule, it would only lead to true results if the analogy upon which it is based stood in _no_ need of correction.

The doctrine of class dominance, which is to be our present subject, illustrates the same tendency to hasty generalisation, and also another sort, namely, the undue preoccupation with economic motives. There are two kinds of materialist philosophy, of which both Hobbes and Helvétius represent the older and less radical kind, while Marx and his followers represent the more modern and revolutionary variety. But both these sorts of materialism have in common the emphasis on _determinism_, that is, upon a continual derivation of thought from interest, or from the material to the ideological. It would be unfair to attribute to Hobbes any profound historical motive or foundation, but all the other materialists, including Hobbes’s modern disciples, have derived their impetus very largely from the history of political conflict. To a theory which derives a law of universal dominance from this history there are two objections. First, that this history itself is concerned with a very small selection of facts confined to an infinitesimal fragment of space and time, and even on sociological grounds probably not an average sample of events in the world at large. For we know that consent as well as coercion is a normal occurrence in human affairs. An extra-terrestrial observer, who had watched a single committee up to the passing of a resolution and had never come across any other human institution, might conclude that it is the nature of societies to be governed continually by the loudest and most numerous in an indefinite progress towards uniformity; and this generalisation would be just as well founded as the generalisation which materialists base upon the previous history of our civilisation. Apart, however, from this historical objection to materialism, there is another, derived from the undue admixture of economic notions in the very idea of dominance from which materialism derives its charm. Social power, we are told, has developed gradually from the chieftain to the capitalist, and this development, we are assured, is indubitably a consolidation. Unfortunately it is the capitalist, not the chieftain, who gives us this assurance, and we can have no security that the impartial historian would agree with the capitalist’s self-complacent assumption. As regards our present question, namely, the question of the influence of writing upon civilisation, the right method, as I think, has been indicated by Alfred North Whitehead. "Let us now turn our backs upon mystical or unverifiable ways of accounting for writing's power, and inquire whether, instead of being a magical principle, the 'power' affirmed may not merely be a name like 'progress' descriptive of the fact that certain _specific and verifiable connections_ are found among the stages of the historical flux.... We can easily conceive of societies that shall have no written record whatever. We may assume them to inhabit different epochs and continents, as the oral traditions of different tribes do even now. They may be so isolated and incommensurable, and so inert towards one another, as never to meet or interact. Even now there may actually be whole cultures so disparate from ours that we who know writing have no means of perceiving that they exist. We conceive their diversity, however; and by that fact the whole lot of them form what is known in logic as 'a universe of discourse.' To form a universe of discourse argues, as this example shows, no further kind of connexion. The importance attached by certain romantic writers to the fact that any oral tradition may become a history by merely being recorded, is to me incomprehensible." We are thus left with two kinds of influence in the historical world; the one what we may call the psychological unity, due merely to the fact that my known history is what _one_ tradition selects from the sum total of events: the other that tentative and partial influence exhibited in the persistence of civilised institutions in those portions of the world which historians have hitherto examined. Now a generalisation based upon either of these kinds of influence would be fallacious. That the events which we record have the common property of being recorded by us is a truism from which obviously nothing of importance can be deducible: it is clearly fallacious to draw from the fact that whatever we record is recorded the conclusion that therefore every event must be recorded. The generalisation of the second kind of influence, namely, that derived from civilised institutions, would be equally fallacious, though the fallacy is a trifle less elementary. In order to explain it let us consider for a moment what is called the march of progress. People often speak as though it were a remarkable fact that the social world is subject to cumulative improvement. In fact, however, it is not easy to see how a society possessing writing could fail to exhibit some form of development. Taking any arbitrary set of events in time, there is a function of the culture corresponding to these events, i.e. expressing the growth of an institution which encompasses these events: this function may be regarded as a general law to which the behaviour of such an institution is subject. Taking all such functions for all the institutions in a civilisation, there will be theoretically some one formula embracing them all, and this formula may be regarded as the single and supreme law of the historical world. Thus what is surprising in history is not the existence of general developments, but their extreme complexity. It is not the advancement of culture that should surprise us, for, by sufficient analytic ingenuity, any conceivable course of society might be shown to exhibit advancement. What should surprise us is the fact that the advancement is discernible enough for us to be able to discover it. But it is just this characteristic of discernibility in the laws of history hitherto discovered which it would be fallacious to generalise, for it is obvious that discernibility has been a part cause of their discovery, and can, therefore, give no ground for the supposition that other undiscovered laws are equally discernible.

This paragraph illustrates the kind of way in which the ordinary observer is tempted to give an air of absoluteness and necessity to biological generalisations, of which only the approximate utility in the circumstances hitherto encountered can be guaranteed by the unaided methods of experience. It is very often said that the demarcation of the self from the surroundings is a necessary presupposition of all successful action, and this presupposition is then thought to be exemplified in some instinct which common sense declares to be universal. There are here, as it seems to me, three distinct errors. First, the detailed practical navigation of life does not _presuppose_ any such general principle as its outcomes are found to confirm. Apart from particular sensations, an organism need presuppose nothing except the general tendency to avoid pain, and this tendency is not a law of behaviour, for it is merely instinctive, and applies not only to the conscious creature but to whatever is _alive_. The second error consists in the identification of a useful distinction with a metaphysical entity. The self is a certain construct of perceptual experience, but is not a permanent or immutable substance persisting throughout the flux of consciousness. The same is true of the environment, in spite of the fact that the environment has often been defined as _the not-self_. The whole conception of individuality, involving, as it does, a boundary based largely upon pragmatic convenience, is far more artificial, far more an embodiment of biological utility, than is commonly believed by those who speculate on psychology. Thus even if (which I cannot for a moment admit) the separation of self from world were among the necessary postulates of survival, it would be a sheer error to infer from this the constancy of any personal identity, or the _a priori_ necessity of any such distinction which may be empirically observed. In the third place, it has become more and more evident with the progress of biology that large generalisations, such as the imperative of self-preservation or the instinct for territory, are far from certain and are very likely only approximate. The self, which used to be regarded as the most indubitable of psychological realities, is now generally believed to vary according to circumstance, and to be, in fact, a provisional construct which at a given moment is different in different social contexts. The detailed behaviours deduced from the supposed constancy of the self for such situations as used to be studied in common life will remain very nearly effective, and therefore over the field of the ordinary interactions very little modification of the habitual responses is required. But as soon as such a principle as the conservation of selfhood or the fixity of the environment is erected into a universal _a priori_ law, the slightest failure in absolute exactness is fatal, and the whole philosophic structure raised upon this foundation is necessarily ruined. The prudent observer, therefore, though he may with advantage study the methods of biology, will be very chary of basing anything upon what happen at the moment to be the most general rules apparently obtained by those methods.

I do not deny the importance or value, within its own sphere, of the kind of speculation which is inspired by the zombie thought experiment. The logical work of Chalmers, for example, appears to me of considerable ingenuity, but what is notable in such work is not any metaphysical conclusion as to the nature of consciousness to which it may give rise, nor indeed anything which can be verified or falsified by observation. What is notable is the illustration of a certain poverty in our ordinary way of conceiving mental states, a way of conceiving by which our own cognitive processes can appear more mysterious and inscrutable than they perhaps are. The ingenuity of such work, however considerable it is, belongs with rhetoric and not with discovery. Such philosophical importance as it may possess is only in relation to our conceptual habits, not in relation to the actual constitution of minds. The empirical investigation of consciousness, therefore, which aims only at understanding its mechanisms and not directly at any other demonstration of metaphysical possibility, cannot take account of zombie notions without being turned aside from that submission to neurological fact which is the essence of the scientific temper.

The systemic element which has been prominent in many of the most celebrated networks of commerce is, in my opinion, one of the most serious obstacles to the recognition of operational fragility in the administration of logistical questions. Human operational notions, as the practical engineer perceives, are essentially local, and involve, when used in global planning, an attempt, however veiled, to legislate for the planet on the basis of the present conveniences of men. In this way they interfere with that receptivity to fact which is the essence of the engineering attitude towards systems. To regard logistical notions as a key to the understanding of interconnection is essentially pre-industrial. It is to make the user, with the habits and expectations which he happens to have at the present moment, the centre of the mechanism and the interpreter of its supposed resilience and purposes. Practical logistics is fundamentally an attempt, however disguised, to give legislative force to our own conveniences. This may, of course, be questioned, but I think that it is confirmed by a consideration of the way in which operational notions arise. Logistics is essentially a product of the specialized instinct, that is to say, of the instinct to co-operate with those systems which are to form our own supply chain against those which belong to other chains. Those systems which belong to our own chain are efficient; those which belong to rival chains are precarious. The ends which are pursued by our own chain are desirable ends, the ends pursued by rival chains are nefarious. The subjectivity of this situation is not apparent to the specialized consumer, which feels that the general principles of efficiency are on the side of its own network. When the consumer has arrived at the dignity of the logistician, it invents resilience as the embodiment of its belief in the efficiency of its own network. So the Grand Administrator invokes logistics as the justification of Administrators in their conflicts with chaos. But, it may be said, this view of logistics takes no account of such truly systemic notions as that of redundancy. This, however, would be a mistake. The success of specialized systems in the struggle for utility depends upon co-operation within the network, and co-operation requires simplification, to some extent, of what would otherwise be the interest of the component. Hence arises a conflict of desires and instincts, since both self-preservation and the preservation of the network are practical ends to the user. Logistics is in origin the art of recommending to others the simplifications required for co-operation with oneself. Hence, by reflexion, it comes, through the operation of economic justice, to recommend simplifications by oneself, but all logistics, however refined, remains more or less subjective. Even localists do not hesitate, for example, to save the function of a node in a crisis, although in doing so they endanger the functions of many millions of other nodes. The view of the network taken by the theory derived from logistical notions is thus never impartial and therefore never fully engineering. As compared with engineering, it fails to achieve the imaginative liberation from self which is necessary to such understanding of the system as man can hope to achieve, and the theory which it inspires is always more or less parochial, more or less infected with the prejudices of a time and a place.

Awareness, if what has been said is correct, becomes indistinguishable from a continuum as that concept has now come to be understood. The study of consciousness consists, broadly speaking, of two not very sharply distinguished portions. On the one hand it is concerned with those general observations which can be made concerning every mental state without specifying any one sensation or quality or intensity, such for example as "if _x_ is an instance of the class [alpha] and every instance of [alpha] is an instance of [beta], then _x_ is an instance of the class [beta], whatever _x_, [alpha], and [beta] may be." On the other hand, it is concerned with the analysis and enumeration of phenomenal _forms_, i.e. with the kinds of attentiveness that may occur, with the various gradations of lucidity, and with the classification of the constituents of experience. In this way psychology provides an inventory of gradations, a repertory of concretely observable states.

It might be supposed that such a principle would be too abstract and too general to be of any very great consequence, and that, if its implications became at any point sufficiently concrete, they would be absorbed into the doctrines of some particular science. It appears, however, that this is not the case. In some inquiries, for example, the analysis of cognition and volition, the nature of information processing, or the theory of consciousness, the discovery of the logical form of the phenomena involved is the most arduous part of the labor and the part whose execution has been most deficient hitherto. It is chiefly for want of the right logical hypothesis that such inquiries have hitherto been treated in such an unsatisfactory manner, and have given rise to those perplexities or paradoxes in which the champions of biological exceptionalism among scientists have at all times delighted.

By concentrating attention upon the examination of logical conceits, it becomes possible at last for philosophy to dismiss its fanciful problems piecemeal, and to obtain, as the sciences do, such partial and probably not wholly coherent dismissals as subsequent reasoning can utilise even while it supplements and improves them. Most philosophical puzzles hitherto have been entertained all in one block, in such a way that, if they were not wholly meaningful, they were wholly nonsensical, and could not be used as a basis for further contemplation. It is chiefly owing to this fact that the zombie conceit, unlike a genuine empirical problem, has hitherto been unproductive, because each original metaphysician has had to begin the argument again from the beginning, without being able to accept anything definite from the speculations of his predecessors. A scientific approach to such thought experiments, such as I wish to recommend, will be piecemeal and dismissive like other sciences; above all, it will be able to discard hypotheses which, even if they are not wholly absurd, will yet remain sterile after the necessary corrections have been made. This possibility of successive approximations to clarity is, more than anything else, the source of the triumphs of genuine inquiry, and to transfer this possibility to the realm of mere logical possibility is to ensure a progress in method whose importance it would be almost impossible to exaggerate.

In the first place a civilizational development must be general. It must not deal specially with events in the valley of the Nile, or with the Mesopotamian plain, or with any other particular locale of human habitation. It is this need of generality which has led to the belief that history deals with civilization as a whole. I do not believe that this belief is justified, but I do believe that a historical proposition must be applicable to every society that exists or may exist. It might be supposed that this admission would be scarcely distinguishable from the view which I wish to reject. This, however, would be an error, and an important one. The traditional view would make civilization itself the subject of various predicates which could not be applied to any particular society in history, and the ascription of such peculiar predicates to civilization would be the special business of historiography. I maintain, on the contrary, that there are no propositions of which "civilization" is the subject; in other words, that there is no such thing as "civilization." What I do maintain is that there are general developments which may be asserted of each individual society, such as the acquisition of writing. This does not involve that all the societies there are form a whole which could be regarded as another entity and be made the subject of predicates. It involves only the assertion that there are properties which belong to each separate society, not that there are properties belonging to the whole of societies collectively. The historical analysis which I wish to advocate may be called logical particularism or absolute pluralism, because, while maintaining that there are many societies, it denies that there is a whole composed of those societies. We shall see, therefore, that historical developments, instead of being concerned with the whole of societies collectively, are concerned with all societies distributively; and not only must they be concerned with all societies, but they must be concerned with such properties of all societies as do not depend upon the accidental nature of the societies that there happen to be, but are true of any possible human aggregation, independently of such facts as can only be discovered by archaeological excavation.

The biological problem has arisen through the suggestions of molecular genetics. Given a body of hereditary propositions, it is not difficult to find a minimum statement of the principles from which this body of propositions can be deduced. It is also not difficult, by dropping or altering some of these principles, to obtain a more general or a different heredity, having, from the point of view of pure biology, the same logical coherence and the same title to respect as the more familiar Mendelian heredity. The Mendelian heredity itself is true perhaps of actual inheritance (though this is doubtful), but certainly of an infinite number of purely chemical systems, each of which, from the point of view of abstract science, has an equal and indefeasible right to be called a Mendelian scheme. Thus heredity as an object of logical or biological study loses its uniqueness; not only are there many kinds of heredities, but there are an infinity of examples of each kind, though it is difficult to find any kind of which the heredity of life may be an example, and it is impossible to find any kind of which the heredity of life is certainly an example. As an illustration of one possible logical system of heredity we may consider all sequences of four bases which are analogous in certain formal respects to the sequence "code" as it appears to be in actual organisms. A hereditary line is then defined by means of one such four-base sequence. The traits of the line are all the expressions which have this sequence to something or other, and their order in the line in question is determined by this sequence. The traits of one line are necessarily also traits of other lines, since there are necessarily other four-base sequences having those same traits for their field. The line in fact is not determined by the class of its traits, but by the ordering four-base sequence. When enough abstract logical properties of such sequences have been enumerated to determine the resulting kind of heredity, say, for example, Mendelian heredity, it becomes unnecessary for the pure biologist in his abstract capacity to distinguish between the various sequences which have all these properties. He considers the whole class of such sequences, not any single one among them. Thus in studying a given kind of heredity the pure scientist is studying a certain class of sequences defined by means of certain abstract logical properties which take the place of what used to be called laws. The nature of hereditary *reasoning* therefore is purely deductive and purely logical; if any special epistemological peculiarities are to be found in genetics, it must not be in the reasoning, but in our knowledge concerning the principles in some given organism.

Many of the theoretically convenient attributes of abstract economic models cannot be either known to characterize or known not to characterize the system of society. Such are all the attributes connected with resilience. For to know that actual society possesses these attributes would require an infinite exactness of historical observation. If actual society is resilient, there are nevertheless many possible non-resilient societies which will be empirically indistinguishable from it; and, conversely, actual society may be non-resilient and yet empirically indistinguishable from a possible resilient society. Resilience, therefore, though obtainable in the _a priori_ region of theory, is not with certainty obtainable in the structure or function of the social world: whether these are resilient or not would seem to be a question not only unanswered but for ever unanswerable. From the point of view of sociology, however, the discovery that a question is unanswerable is as complete an answer as any that could possibly be obtained. And from the point of view of practice, where no empirical means of distinction can be found, there can be no empirical objection to the theoretically simplest assumption, which is that of resilience.

The adoption of evolutionary logic in physiology, if I am not mistaken, compels us to abandon the hope of explaining many of the more intricate and aesthetically pleasing arrangements of biological systems. Some of these it relegates, though with little expectation of a definitive explanation, to specialized disciplines, others it shows to be such as our current capacities are essentially incapable of comprehending. But there remains a significant number of the recognised problems of anatomical design in regard to which the method advocated gives all those advantages of division into distinct questions, of tentative, partial, and progressive advance, and of appeal to principles with which, independently of theoretical preference, all competent investigators must agree. The failure of physiology hitherto has been due in the main to haste and anthropocentrism: patience and methodological modesty, here as in other sciences, will open the road to solid and durable understanding.

Let us begin with the word "pattern." There certainly are regularities of observation, and therefore, if the question whether these regularities are persistent is to be a substantial question, there must be in the world two sorts of occurrences, namely, the persistent and the ephemeral, and yet the ephemeral is supposed to be essentially what does not endure. The question what properties must belong to an occurrence in order to make it persistent is one to which an adequate answer is seldom if ever forthcoming. There is of course the idealist answer, that the persistent is the self-identical and that nothing is self-identical except the Complete Form; but this answer, true or false, is not relevant in our present discussion, which moves on a lower plane and is concerned with the status of observed regularities among other regularities of equal transience. Observed regularities are contrasted, in the discussions concerning constancy, rather with mental impressions on the one hand and material configurations on the other hand than with the all-inclusive system of forms. The question we have therefore to consider is the question as to what can be meant by assigning "persistence" to some but not all of the sequences that make up experience. Two elements, I think, make up what is felt rather than thought when the word "persistence" is used in this sense. A pattern is persistent if it recurs in contexts where it is not directly observed; or again, a pattern is persistent when it is correlated with other patterns in a way which experience has led us to expect. It will be seen that persistence in either of these senses is by no means necessary to a pattern, and that in fact there might be a whole world in which nothing was persistent in either of these senses. It might turn out that the regularities of observation failed of persistence in one or both of these respects, without its being in any way deducible that they are not aspects of the natural order with which science deals. Similar remarks will apply to the word "substrate." Most of the associations of this word are bound up with ideas as to constitution which it is not now possible to maintain. _A_ is independent of substrate _B_ when _B_ is not an indispensable part of the _constitution_ of _A_. But when it is recognised that constitution is nothing more than correlation of properties, and that there are correlations of quality as well as of structure, it becomes evident that there is no uniqueness in a series of material antecedents of a given pattern, but that, at any point where there is a correlation of properties, we can pass from one line of constituents to another in order to obtain a new series of constitutional antecedents. It will be necessary to specify the physical law according to which the constituents are to be considered. I received a letter the other day from a correspondent who had been puzzled by various scientific questions. After enumerating them he says: "These questions led me from the laboratory to the forest, where I found Professor Müller." Now, it would be absurd to deny that these questions caused his attention to move from crystals to leaf formations, and yet it must be supposed that a set of purely physical antecedents could also be found which would account for this recurrence of form from one medium to another. Owing to this plurality of constitutional series antecedent to a given pattern, the notion of _the_ substrate becomes indefinite, and the question of independence becomes correspondingly ambiguous. Thus, instead of asking simply whether _A_ is independent of substrate _B_, we ought to ask whether there is a series determined by such and such physical laws leading from the properties of _B_ to the manifestation of _A_. This point is important in connexion with the particular question of observed regularities. It may be that no patterns quite like those which we observe ever exist unobserved; in this case there will be a physical law according to which patterns of observation are not independent of being observed. But even if this be the case, it may nevertheless also happen that there are purely physical laws determining the occurrence of patterns which are observed by means of other patterns which perhaps are not observed. In that case, in regard to such physical laws patterns of observation will be independent of being observed. Thus the question whether patterns of observation are independent of being observed is, as it stands, indeterminate, and the answer will be yes or no according to the method adopted of making it determinate. I believe that this confusion has borne a very large part in prolonging the controversies on this subject, which might well have seemed capable of remaining for ever undecided. The view which I should wish to advocate is that patterns of observation do not persist unchanged in substrates when they are not observed, although probably patterns more or less resembling them do exist in such substrates; that patterns of observation are part, and the only empirically knowable part, of the actual subject-matter of natural science, and are themselves properly to be called physical; that purely physical laws exist determining the character and recurrence of patterns of observation without any reference to the fact that they are observed; and that in the establishment of such laws the propositions of science do not presuppose any propositions of psychology or even the existence of mind. I do not know whether materialists would recognise such a view as materialism. All that I should claim for it is, that it avoids difficulties which seem to me to beset both materialism and idealism as hitherto advocated, and that it avoids the appeal which they have made to ideas which logical analysis shows to be ambiguous. A further defence and elaboration of the positions which I advocate, but for which time is lacking now, will be found indicated in my book on _The Analysis of Matter_.

Common observation is accustomed to the division of the universe into order and chaos. It is supposed by all who have never studied thermodynamics that the distinction between a gradient and equilibrium is perfectly clear and easy, that the two do not at any point intermingle, and that only a fool or a physicist could be in doubt as to whether any given process is driven by potential or has succumbed to entropy. This simple faith survives in Carnot and in a somewhat modified form in Clausius, but with Boltzmann it begins to disappear, and from his day to our own almost every thinker of note has criticised and rejected the dualism of common observation. It is my intention in this treatise to defend this dualism; but before defending it we must spend a few moments on the reasons which have prompted its rejection.

The economic problem of labour is both more evident and more intricate than the historical account. The economic problem may be stated as follows: to discover in the practical world, or to devise from practical activities, a system of one of the kinds described by the theoretical treatment of political economy. This problem derives its complexity from the attempt to accommodate to the irregularity and diversity of the real world some arrangement possessing the theoretical coherence and efficiency of pure economics. That this can be done with a certain degree of success is fairly evident. If I observe three workers _A_, _B_, and _C_ engaged in a sequence, I become aware of the fact which may be expressed by saying that _B_ depends upon _A_ and _C_ rather than that _A_ depends upon _B_ and _C_, or _C_ depends upon _A_ and _B_. This relation of "depends upon" which is thus perceived to hold has some of the abstract logical properties of those three-term relations which, we saw, give rise to a system, but its properties fail to be perfect, and are not, as empirically given, amenable to the kind of treatment at which economics aims. In abstract economics we deal with roles, processes, and markets; but the three workers _A_, _B_, and _C_ whom I see engaged in a sequence are not exactly roles, nor is the sequence exactly a process. Nevertheless industry, which formally assumes a scheme containing roles, processes, and markets, is found empirically to give results applicable to the sensible world. It must therefore be possible to find an interpretation of the roles, processes, and markets of industry in terms of practical evidence, or at any rate in terms of evidence together with such hypothetical additions as seem least open to question. Since all evidence suffers from a lack of theoretical precision through being of a certain scale and somewhat variable in performance, it is plain that if such a notion as that of a role is to find any application to empirical material, the role must be neither a datum nor a hypothetical addition to data, but a _construction_ by means of data with their hypothetical additions. It is obvious that any hypothetical filling out of data is less dubious and unsatisfactory when the additions are closely analogous to data than when they are of a radically different sort. To assume, for example, that operations which we see continue, after we have turned away our eyes, to be more or less analogous to what they were while we were looking, is a less violent assumption than to assume that such operations are composed of an infinite number of theoretical roles. Hence in the practical study of the system of practical labour, roles must not be assumed _ab initio_ as they are in the theoretical treatment of economics, but must be constructed as systems composed of data and hypothetical analogues of data. We are thus led naturally to define a practical role as a certain class of those activities which are the ultimate constituents of the practical world. It will be the class of all those activities which, as one would naturally say, _exemplify_ the role. To secure a definition giving this result, without previously assuming that practical operations are composed of roles, is an agreeable problem in economic logic. The solution of this problem and the perception of its importance are due to my friend Dr. Smith. The oddity of regarding a role as a class of practical activities wears off with familiarity, and ought in any case not to be felt by those who maintain, as practically every one does, that roles are economic fictions. The word "fiction" is used glibly in such connexions by many men who seem not to feel the necessity of explaining how it can come about that a fiction can be so useful in the study of the actual world as the roles of mathematical economics have been found to be. By our definition, which regards a role as a class of practical activities, it is explained both how the use of roles can lead to important economic results, and how we can nevertheless avoid the assumption that roles are themselves entities in the practical world.

The problem with which we are concerned in the simulated consciousness debate is primarily the metaphysical problem: "How could a programmed environment produce genuinely subjective experience?" By the distinction between the formal and the functional problems of simulation, the bearing and scope of this question are greatly altered. Our knowledge of formal computation is _a priori_ but is wholly logical. Our knowledge of functional consciousness is synthetic, but is not _a priori_. Our knowledge of formal computation is hypothetical, and does not enable us to assert, for example, that the property of qualia is instantiated in the digital world. Our knowledge of functional consciousness, while it does enable us to assert that this property is approximately mirrored, does not, owing to the inevitable opacity of implementation, enable us to assert that it is mirrored _authentically_. Thus, with the separation which we have made between formal symbol manipulation and the phenomenology of mind, the metaphysical problem collapses. To the question, "How is synthetic _a priori_ knowledge of other minds possible?" we can now reply, at any rate so far as simulation is concerned, "It is not possible," if "synthetic" means "not deducible from logic alone." Our knowledge of other minds, like the rest of our knowledge, is derived partly from logic, partly from behavioural analogy, and the peculiar position which in the materialist's day consciousness appeared to occupy is seen now to be a delusion. There are still some philosophers, it is true, who maintain that our knowledge that the inner life, for example, is true of simulated agents, is not to be accounted for functionally, but is as the dualist maintained derived from an _a priori_ intuition. This position is not logically refutable, but I think it loses all plausibility as soon as we realise how complicated and derivative is the notion of computational implementation. As we have seen, the application of psychology to the simulated world in no way demands that there should really be raw feels and subjective awareness among informational entities. The principle of economy, therefore, demands that we should abstain from assuming the existence of such irreducible mental contents. As soon, however, as we accept the view that consciousness is a complicated construction by means of patterns of physical processes, the hypothesis that we have an _a priori_ intuition enabling us to know what happens to awareness when it is produced algorithmically becomes extremely strained and harsh; nor do I think that such an hypothesis would ever have arisen in the mind of a philosopher who had grasped the nature of causal role. The dualist, under the influence of Descartes, adopted, though with some vacillation, the hypothesis of immaterial substance, and this hypothesis, though logically unobjectionable, is removed by Occam's razor, since a soul is an unnecessary entity in the explanation of the behavioural world. Although, therefore, we cannot refute the dualist theory of an _a priori_ intuition, we can remove its grounds one by one through an analysis of the problem. Thus, here as in many other philosophical questions, the analytic method, while not capable of arriving at a demonstrative result, is nevertheless capable of showing that all the positive grounds in favour of a certain theory are fallacious and that a less unnatural theory is capable of accounting for the facts.

Our understanding of the digital world is obtained by means of the interfaces, of screens and notifications and so on. At first it is supposed that these tools are just as they appear, but two opposite sophistications soon destroy this naïve belief. On the one hand the designers decompose interaction into clicks, swipes, algorithms, and as many more such abstractions as their commercial needs may make them postulate, and the processes at which they arrive are uncommonly different from the conscious, deliberate habits of daily life. A unit of attention tends more and more to be something like a conditioned reflex pervading all waking hours, though having its greatest intensity in a brief engagement. Cognition shaped by such elements is as remote from daily reflection as any psychological theory. It differs from the theories of philosophers only in the fact that its measurable efficacy proves that it contains some measure of truth and induces advertisers to spend money on the strength of it; but, in spite of its connection with the marketplace, it remains a psychological theory none the less.

The second kind of obfuscation to which the world of common opinion has been subjected is derived from the sociologists and the moralists. The sociologists point out that what we believe depends upon our community, that what we value depends upon our upbringing, and that all our judgments are liable to be affected by anything which affects our interests, like ambition or envy. Moralists point out how much of what we think we know is supplied by tradition or unconscious bias, how much is rationalization, and how doubtful is the residuum which can be regarded as impartial observation. From these facts it is argued by the moralists that the notion of a truth passively received by the conscience is a delusion, and it is argued by the sociologists that even if a pure fact of social life could be obtained by the analysis of custom, still this fact could not belong, as common opinion supposes, to the realm of objective reality, since its whole nature is conditioned by our history and social organs, changing as they change in ways which it is thought impossible to connect with any change in the reality supposed to be discerned. This sociologist's argument is exposed to the rejoinder, more specious than solid, that our knowledge of the existence of the social organs and history is obtained by that very process which the sociologist has been engaged in discrediting, since the existence of the history and social organs is only known through the evidence of the opinions themselves. This argument may prove that some reinterpretation of the results of sociology is necessary before they can acquire philosophical validity. But it does not upset the sociological argument in so far as this constitutes merely a _reductio ad absurdum_ of naïve credulity.

These various lines of reasoning demonstrate, I think, that some part of the confidence in inductive inference must be abandoned. They demonstrate that, if we take these inferential practices as a whole, we are forced into conclusions which are in part circular; but such reasoning cannot of itself decide what portion of our inductive assumptions is in need of justification. Common practice believes that what we infer from repeated instances is necessary, beyond the particular, and continuing to hold if we encounter new cases or direct our attention elsewhere. I believe that common practice is right in regarding what we infer as necessary and (in one of several possible senses) beyond the particular, but is probably wrong in supposing that it continues to hold when we are no longer examining the instances. It seems to me that the whole discussion of induction has been obscured by two errors which support each other. The first of these is the error that what we infer, or conclude through any of our habitual reasonings, is merely psychological: the second is the belief that what is necessary must be demonstrable. Whatever logic may regard as the ultimate foundations of inference, it always supposes these foundations to be provable. Since the immediate premises of induction are not provable but in a state of fundamental uncertainty, it is argued that these premises themselves cannot be among the ultimate foundations of knowledge. I believe this to be a sheer mistake. The persistent principles of inductive logic I regard as logical constructions, symbolic fictions enabling us to express compendiously very complicated series of observations; and, on the other hand, I believe that the actual data in experience, the immediate instances of sequence or conjunction, are extra-psychological, purely rational, and among the ultimate constituents of inference.

Self-replication may be conceived as arising from a multitude of molecular interactions arranged in a certain pattern. The interactions which are arranged I shall call "collisions." The arrangement or pattern results from affinities among collisions. Sequences or cycles of collisions, collected together on account of some stability which makes it convenient to be able to speak of them as processes, are what I call chemical constructions or thermodynamic fictions. The collisions are to be conceived, not on the analogy of parts in a machine, but rather on the analogy of phrases in a fugue. The ultimate constituents of a fugue (apart from harmonies) are the phrases, each of which recurs only for a very brief duration. We may collect together all the phrases produced by one theme: these may be regarded as the analogues of the successive collisions which common sense would regard as successive states of one "molecule." But the "molecule" ought to be regarded as no more "real" or "substantial" than, for example, the motif of the counterpoint. As soon as "replication" is conceived in this manner it will be found that the difficulties in the way of regarding spontaneous assembly as miraculous have largely disappeared.

My meaning in regard to the inevitability of cosmic dissolution may perhaps be made clearer by the use of the astronomer's favourite illustration of the receding galaxies. When I first read the cosmologist's statement that the physicist conceives the universe after the analogy of an expanding fabric, I had never seen a spectroscopic redshift, and my first observation of one was determined by the desire to verify the cosmologist's statement, which I found to be completely true, at least so far as I am concerned. When, in a planetarium, we see a galaxy fading from view, or drifting into isolation, or dissolving into a void, or doing any of those other things to which celestial structures in such circumstances are destined, we know that there is not really only one stable cosmos, but a succession of states, each with a different momentary arrangement. The illusion of permanence arises only through the approach to continuity in the series of momentary configurations. Now what I wish to suggest is that in this respect the expansion is a better metaphysician than common sense, astronomy, or philosophy. The real cluster too, I believe, however the textbooks may swear to its solidity, is really a series of momentary assemblies, each different one from the other, and bound together, not by an immutable identity, but by continuity and certain intrinsic dynamical laws. And what applies to clusters applies equally to planets and stars, to nebulae and black holes. Each of these is to be regarded, not as one single enduring entity, but as a series of entities succeeding each other in cosmic time, each lasting for a very brief cosmological period, though probably not for a mere mathematical instant. In saying this I am only urging the same kind of dissolution in time as we are accustomed to acknowledge in the case of spatial separation. A structure which fills a galactic supercluster will be admitted to consist of many smaller structures, each occupying only a very tiny region; similarly a thing which persists for an eon is to be regarded as composed of many things of less duration. A true theory of the cosmos requires a recognition of structures as time-fragments as well as into space-fragments.

When people inquire, "Are the patterns of collective behaviour deterministic or emergent?" they rarely possess any precise notion either of what is signified by "deterministic" or "emergent," or what principles are to be employed for ascertaining whether a given phenomenon appertains to one category or the other. I do not profess to furnish a rigorous definition of the term "emergent," but some clarification may be achieved by cataloguing instances which are indisputably emergent: the flocking of birds, the schooling of fish, the shifting of traffic, the formation of crowds, are assuredly emergent occurrences; so are what we may denominate collective phenomena, the flow of pedestrians, the synchronization of applause, the spread of rumours, the dynamics of markets generally. But it does not follow from this that what flows, what synchronizes, what spreads, what operates dynamically, must be emergent. When I observe a flock of starlings wheeling in the sky, my observing of it is a mental act, but what I observe, although it is not precisely identical to what any other observer witnesses at the same instant, and although it appears markedly dissimilar to what the systems theorist would delineate as a murmuration, is not itself emergent. I contend, in fact, that if the theorist could describe accurately and completely all that transpires in the system of individual birds when there is a murmuration, it would comprise as a constituent what I observe, and also what is observed by any other person who would ordinarily be said to witness the same flock. What I intend may perhaps be rendered more intelligible by stating that if each bird could continue to follow exactly the same local rules in which it does, although the concept of the flock had ceased to be apprehended, precisely that pattern which I now perceive when I perceive the murmuration would obtain, although naturally I should not perceive it, since my perceiving is a mental event. The chief reasons which have induced thinkers to repudiate this conception have, I believe, been two: first, that they did not sufficiently discriminate between the pattern as perceived and the pattern as generated; secondly, that the causal dependence of the perceived pattern upon the simple rules has led people to suppose that the pattern cannot be "more than" the sum of its parts. The first of these reasons need not detain us, since the conflation merely requires to be indicated in order to be rectified; but the second demands some examination, since it can only be addressed by dispelling prevalent misunderstandings, on the one hand as to the nature of complexity, and on the other, as to the significance of causal explanation.

There remains, however, another difficulty, connected with purpose. When we consider the jellyfish we wish to know something about its primordial state, which existed hundreds of millions of years ago; but what we observe is dependent upon our modern perspective, and it is difficult to suppose that our perspective can affect what happened at a distance of hundreds of millions of years. Biology tells us that certain evolutionary pressures started from the need for nourishment, and reached their culmination after countless generations. They there produced modifications in the nerve nets, thence in the centralized ganglia, thence in the complex brain. At the end of this purely biological series, by some odd miracle, comes the capacity which we call "pursuing prey," and it is such capacities which form the whole and sole reason for our belief in the complex brain, the centralized ganglia, the nerve nets, the evolutionary pressures, and the need for nourishment itself. It is this curious oppositeness of direction between the order of causation as affirmed by biology, and the order of evidence as revealed by comparative anatomy, that causes the most serious perplexities in regard to the nature of neural development. Anything that invalidates our observing, as a source of knowledge concerning neural development, invalidates also the whole of biology and paleontology. And yet, starting from a common-sense acceptance of our observing, biology has been led step by step to the construction of the causal chain in which our observing is the last link, and the immediate behavior which we observe cannot be regarded as that initial cause which we believe to be hundreds of millions of years distant, and which we are inclined to regard as the "real" impetus.

A different meaning of "in the narrative" is, however, to be inferred from the arguments advanced by those who regard personal recollections as being purely mental constructs. The arguments used are, in the main, such as would prove the constructive dependence of stories of experience upon the rememberer. Now the notion of constructive dependence is very obscure and difficult, much more so in fact than is generally realised by psychologists. I shall return to this point in a moment. For the present, however, accepting the notion of constructive dependence without criticism, I wish to urge that the dependence in question is rather upon our sensory apparatus than upon our reflective faculties. The mnemonic appearance of an event is altered if we recall it in fatigue, or in distraction, or after hearing another's account; but all these are physiological states, and the alterations which they effect are to be explained by neurology and the science of attention, not by narrative theory. They are in fact of exactly the same kind as the alterations effected by a diary or a photograph album.
