They belong therefore to the theory of the perceptual world, and can have no bearing upon the question whether what we remember is constructively dependent upon the self. What they do tend to prove, and what I for my part have no wish to deny, is that what we remember is constructively dependent upon our neural history and is not, as crude introspection would suppose, something which would exist equally if our senses and synapses and hippocampi were absent, any more than the storied appearance presented by an event recounted through a particular mood would remain if the mood were altered. So long as it is supposed that the autobiographical world is composed of stable and more or less permanent incidents, the fact that what we remember is changed by changes in our physiological state appears to afford reason for regarding what we remember as not an ultimate constituent of personal identity. But if it is recognised that the ultimate constituents of identity are as circumscribed in duration as in experiential coherence, the whole of this difficulty vanishes.

When people ask whether consciousness, for example, or other subjective states are generated or merely simulated, they seem to suppose that their meaning must be clear, and that it ought to be possible to say yes or no without any further discussion of the terms involved. In fact, however, such terms as "generated" or "simulated" are very ambiguous. What is meant by asking whether this or that is "produced" by a simulation? A simulation is not like a factory or an engine; it does not create a certain substance in reality, or, if (in a sense) it does, what is in that process is presumably part of the computation, which would not be said to be genuine consciousness. When people say that experiences are simulated, they do not mean "causally manufactured by" in the sense in which the automobiles were in the factory. We might regard consciousness as an assemblage of particulars, namely, what would be called "states of awareness," which would belong together in virtue of some specific common quality. The common quality of all states of awareness would be the quality designated by the word "subjective"; and besides this we should have to suppose that each separate entity's states of awareness have some common characteristic distinguishing them from the states of awareness of other entities. Ignoring this latter point, let us ask ourselves whether the quality designated by the word "subjective" does, as a matter of observation, actually belong to outputs of simulation, such as responses or behaviours. I think any candid person must reply that, however difficult it may be to know what we mean by "subjective," it is not difficult to see that responses and behaviours are not subjective in the sense of having that intrinsic peculiarity which belongs to sensations and emotions and volitions, but not to the programmed world. Certain theorists advance on this subject a plausible argument which seems to me to rest upon an ambiguity in the word "suffering." They argue that the skeptic supposes the frustration which he observes in an agent approaching a barrier to be something outside its program, but that as the agent attempts more and more to circumvent the barrier the response of frustration passes imperceptibly into suffering, and that no one could regard suffering as something outside genuine consciousness. In reply to this argument, it should be observed in the first place that the frustration of which we are immediately aware is not in the agent but in our own interpretation. It is only by inference that the agent is judged to be the cause of the suffering which we feel in our empathy. In the second place (and this is the more important point), when we speak of suffering we may mean one of two things: we may mean the object of the response or other output which has the quality of being painful, or we may mean the quality of painfulness itself. When an observer says the agent has a suffering in its situation, what he means is that the agent has a response associated with its situation and having the quality of painfulness. The response itself, like every response, consists in exhibiting a behavioural object, and the exhibiting has that quality of painfulness which only mental occurrences can have, but which may belong to thoughts or desires, as well as to sensations. But in common language we speak of the behavioural object exhibited in a painful response as a suffering, and it is this way of speaking which causes the confusion upon which the plausibility of the theorist's argument depends. It would be absurd to attribute the quality of painfulness to anything non-mental, and hence it comes to be thought that what we call a suffering in the agent must be mental. In fact, however, it is not the behavioural object in such a case which is painful, but the response, that is to say, the exhibition of the behavioural object. As the frustration which we observe from the agent grows greater, the observation passes gradually from being plausible to being painful, but neither the plausibility nor the pain is a quality of the object observed as opposed to the observation, and it is therefore a fallacy to argue that this object must be mental on the ground that painfulness can only be attributed to what is mental.

The demarcation between reflex and deliberation, as I observed a moment ago, is a distinction which it is very dangerous to accept at its face value. There exists a notion that in regard to any organic movement there is something which may be called _the_ character of that movement--some one definite quality, without which the movement would have been involuntary and with which it becomes willed. An action is supposed to be dependent upon its volition in some way in which it is not dependent upon other things. Thus men will urge that the twitch of a paramecium is a mere reflex, or, with equal plausibility, that the orienting of a planarian is a deliberate act. It seems not improbable that if we had sufficient knowledge we could infer the intention of a simple organism from the pattern of its motion, or the pattern of its motion from the supposition of its intention. So long as the usual conception of voluntary action is retained, this state of affairs can be used by the mechanist to urge that the stimulus causes the response, and by the vitalist to urge that the purpose causes the adaptation. Either contention is equally valid or equally invalid. The fact seems to be that there are many gradations of the sort which may be called behavioral, and that, for example, either a tropism or a trial can be described, theoretically, either from a sufficient number of physical conditions or from a sufficient number of mental postulates. To speak of _the_ nature of an organic response is therefore misleading. Any set of circumstances from which the response can theoretically be inferred by means of observations might be called a determinant of the response. But to speak of _the_ boundary is to imply a sharpness which does not exist.

The relevance of this to the phenomenon which we call "feeling a headache" is obvious. The fact that there exists a chain of antecedents which makes our feeling dependent upon the nerves and synapses and chemical states does not even tend to show that there is not another chain of antecedents in which the nerves and synapses and chemical states as physical things are ignored. If we are to escape from the dilemma which seemed to arise out of the physiological causation of what we feel when we say we feel a headache, we must find, at least in theory, a way of stating causal laws for the mechanical world, in which the units are not material processes, such as the nerve firings and chemical releases and brain states, but momentary particulars of the same sort as our momentary sensory object when we attend to a pain. The headache itself and the nerves and synapses and chemical states must be regarded as assemblages of momentary particulars. Instead of supposing, as we naturally do when we start from an uncritical acceptance of the apparent dicta of neurology, that *mechanism* is what is "really real" in the experiential world, and that the immediate objects of sensation are mere epiphenomena, we must regard mechanism as a logical construction, of which the constituents will be just such evanescent particulars as may, when a conscious being happens to be present, become qualia of sense to that being. What science regards as the pain of a moment ago will be a whole assemblage of particulars, existing at different times, spreading through a neural network with the velocity of electrical signals, and containing among their number all those sensory data which are felt by persons who are now noticing a headache. Thus the pain of a moment ago is a class of particulars, and what I feel when I now notice a headache is one member of this class. The various particulars constituting this class will be correlated with each other by a certain continuity and certain intrinsic laws of variation as we pass through the network, together with certain modifications correlated extrinsically with other particulars which are not members of this class. It is these extrinsic modifications which represent the sort of facts that, in our former account, appeared as the influence of the nerves and chemical states in modifying the character of the pain.

But although these processes do not exhibit to one another the same kind of operational relations as obtain between the stages of one of them, it is nevertheless possible to arrange these processes themselves in a singular logical order. This is done by means of the correlated impulses which we regard as manifestations (or expressions) of one fundamental drive. When a number of entities are said to pursue the same end, those which would be said to be near to the resource experience an impulse occupying a larger part of their operational field than is occupied by the corresponding impulse governing entities which would be said to be farther from the objective. By means of such considerations it is possible, in ways which need not now be further specified, to arrange all the different processes in a singular directional series. Since each of the processes is itself governed by a singular imperative, the whole system of impulses is thus arranged in a two-dimensional logical space, that is to say, two co-ordinates will be required to assign completely the nature of any given impulse, namely, one to assign its position in its own process and one more to assign the position of its process among the other processes.

There are two ways of classifying mental phenomena: we may take together all those that arise from a given "substrate," or all those that are, as common sense would say, different "operations" of the same "mind." For example, if I am (as is said) performing a calculation, the thought produced belongs to two assemblages: (1) the assemblage of all my present cognitive events, which is what I call a "substrate"; (2) the assemblage of all the different phenomena which would be called operations of the calculating mind—this assemblage is what I define as _being_ the calculating mind. Thus "substrates" and "minds" are merely two different ways of classifying phenomena. It is to be observed that there is no _a priori_ necessity for phenomena to be susceptible of this double classification. There may be what might be called "anomalous" phenomena, not having the usual relations by which the classification is effected; perhaps certain errors or illusions are composed of phenomena which are "anomalous" in this sense.

The _prima facie_ difficulties in the way of this view are chiefly derived from an unduly conventional theory of neural function. It might seem at first sight as if we had packed the brain much fuller than it could possibly hold. At every juncture between stimulus and response, we said, there is to be a particular circuit which is to be a member of the predatory event as it was a few moments ago. There will also, of course, have to be a particular circuit which is a member of any locomotor act or evasive maneuver that may happen to be required from that juncture. At the juncture where I am, there will be circuits which will be members severally of all the "behaviors" I am now said to be executing. Thus throughout the nervous system, everywhere, there will be an enormous number of circuits coexisting in the same nexus. But these troubles result from contenting ourselves too readily with the merely static architecture to which anatomists have accustomed us. The architecture of the real nervous system is a structure of manifold potentialities, and as soon as we realise this we see that there is plenty of room for all the circuits for which we want to find positions. In order to realise this we have only to return for a moment from the polished schemata of textbooks to the rough and untidy processes of our immediate behavioral experience. The functional space of one creature's successful acts is a three-dimensional problem. It does not appear probable that two creatures ever both solve at the same time any one identical problem; when they are said to catch the same prey or avoid the same obstacle, there will always be some difference, however slight, between the actual movements executed or the actual calculations performed. If this is so, and if, as is generally assumed, success in survival is purely relative, it follows that the functional space of one creature's solutions and the functional space of another creature's solutions have no task in common, that they are in fact different spaces, and not merely different parts of one space. I mean by this that such immediate causal relations as are perceived to hold between the different stages of the successful sequence achieved by one creature, do not hold between stages of successful sequences achieved by different creatures. There are therefore a multitude of three-dimensional problems in the world: there are all those solved by acting creatures, and presumably also those which are not solved, merely because no creature is suitably equipped for solving them.

The definition of "understanding" is effected by means of discernment and of correlations which have a certain differential independence of other "tools." That is to say, given a particular instrument in one inquiry, there will usually in a neighbouring inquiry be a very similar instrument, differing from the given instrument, to the first order of small quantities, according to a law involving only the difference of application of the two inquiries in intellectual space, and not any of the other "tools" in the collection. It is this continuity and differential independence in the law of acquisition as we pass from one inquiry to another that defines the class of instruments which is to be called "one understanding.

The exact definition of what is meant by a colony is not quite easy. So long as we confine ourselves to visible tissues or to organs of function we might define the colony of a given cell as "all cells which have a simple (direct) metabolic relation to the given cell." Between two adjacent cells which I examine now, there is a direct cooperative relation which I equally observe. But between cells functioning in different organisms there is only an indirect constructed physiological relation by means of the organization of "bodies" in biological space (which is the same as the space composed of colonies). Those cells which have direct metabolic relations to a given cell will belong to the same colony. But if, for example, the neural impulses which I trace are to belong to the same colony with the muscle fibers which I see, there must be cells which have no direct metabolic relation and yet belong to the same colony. We cannot define a colony as all the units of one organism at one time, because we wish to allow the possibility of colonies which are not organized by any one. There will be need, therefore, in defining a colony, of some principle derived neither from physiology nor from structure.

Such a distinction may be derived from the consideration of _consciousness_. The one coherent self-representation, like the one coherent narrative of identity, is a construction; there is no _direct_ experiential link between the image I project to others and the raw sensation of being that another man feels. On the other hand, any two moments of which I am aware are either projected or felt, and their quality as projection or feeling is sometimes itself a datum to me. We may therefore define the genuine state of aliveness to which a given experience belongs as "all experiences felt simultaneously with the given experience," where "felt" is to be understood as a direct simple relation, not the derivative constructed relation of social performance. It may be observed that the modern emphasis on curated identity, suggested by the principle of constant display, has effected, for purely social reasons, much the same multiplication of selves as we have just been advocating.

In favour of the conception which I have briefly outlined, I do not claim that it is _certainly_ valid. Apart from the likelihood of oversights, much of it is avowedly speculative. What I do claim for the conception is that it _may_ be valid, and that this is more than can be said for any other conception except the closely analogous one of certain formal linguists. The difficulties besetting simplistic prescriptivism, the confusions obstructing any coherent account of semantic evolution, the dilemma resulting from discrediting colloquial speech, which yet remains the sole medium of our daily communication--all these are avoided by the conception which I advocate. This does not prove the conception to be valid, since probably many other conceptions might be invented which would have the same merits. But it does prove that the conception has a better chance of being valid than any of its present competitors, and it suggests that what can be established with certainty is likely to be discoverable by taking our conception as a starting-point, and gradually freeing it from all such assumptions as seem irrelevant, unnecessary, or unfounded. On these grounds, I recommend it to attention as a speculation and a basis for further inquiry, though not as itself a finished or adequate solution of the problem with which it deals.

Unduly simple notions as to wealth have been a great stumbling-block to economists. When two men survey the same society, it is supposed that what the one possesses and what the other possesses are of the same order. Since the security and opportunity are not quite the same for the two men, this raises a difficulty, hastily solved, or rather covered up, by declaring each man’s portion to be purely “merited”—though it would puzzle those who use this glib word to say what they mean by it. The truth seems to be that property—and power also—is much more complicated than it would appear to be from the finished structure of commerce, and that the one all-embracing system of ownership is a social construction, obtained by means of conventions from a crude economy of disparate claims. The transactions occupying this complex economic field, classified in one way, form “estates,” from which with certain further manipulations we can obtain what history can regard as aristocracy; classified in another way, they form “fortunes” and “dynasties,” which may, if a suitable heir happens to exist, form respectively the endowments of a generation or of a total lineage. It is only when social “estates” have been dissected into series of classes of claimants, as we have done, that the conflict between the point of view of the proprietor and the point of view of the labourer can be overcome. This conflict, if what has been said is not mistaken, flows from different methods of accumulation, and vanishes as soon as its source is discovered.

We may now sum up our discussion. Our object has been to discover as far as possible the nature of the persistent patterns which manifest across radically different physical substrates. When I speak of "physical substrates," I mean, to begin with, the varied materials dealt with by common observation. It is obvious that such observation is an empirical pursuit, giving us a certain amount of knowledge and based upon evidence obtained through the senses. But partly through the refinement of observation itself, partly through arguments derived from chemistry, engineering, or metaphysics, it has come to be thought that the immediate appearance of a pattern could not itself form part of the enduring essence of the substrate, but was in some sense "accidental," "in the arrangement," or "superficial." The grounds for this view, in so far as they depend upon observation, can only be adequately dealt with by rather elaborate constructions depending upon symbolic logic, showing that out of such materials as are provided by the senses it is possible to construct relations and functions having the properties which common sense assigns to a pattern. Since this argument is difficult and technical, I have not embarked upon it in this article. But in so far as the view that patterns are "accidental" rests upon chemistry, engineering, or metaphysics, I have tried to show that it rests upon confusions and prejudices--prejudices in favour of uniformity in the ultimate constituents of matter, and confusions derived from unduly simple notions as to structure, from the causal correlation of patterns with manufacturing processes, and from failure to distinguish between the pattern and its particular instantiation. If what we have said on these subjects is valid, the existence of a pattern is logically independent of the existence of any one material, and is causally dependent upon the _laws_ of arrangement rather than upon the substance. The causal dependence upon the laws of arrangement, we found, is a more complicated matter than it appears to be, and, like all causal dependence, is apt to give rise to erroneous beliefs through misconceptions as to the nature of causal correlation. If we have been right in our contentions, patterns are merely those among the formal constituents of the observable world, of which we happen to be immediately aware; they themselves are purely structural, and all that is material in connection with them is their particular embodiment, which is irrelevant to their nature and to their place in a theory of forms.

I shall give the name _transmissibilia_ to those signals which have the same biological and physical status as communicated messages, without necessarily being received by any organism. Thus the relation of a _transmissibile_ to a message is like that of a potential to an actuality: a potential becomes an actuality by entering into the relation of realization, and similarly a _transmissibile_ becomes a message by entering into the relation of reception. It is important to have both terms; for we wish to discuss whether a signal which is at one time a message can still exist at a time when it is not a message. We cannot ask "Can messages exist without being received?" for that is like asking "Can actualities exist without being realized?" We must ask "Can _transmissibilia_ exist without being received?" and also "Can a particular _transmissibile_ be at one time a message, and at another not?" Unless we have the word _transmissibile_ as well as the word "message," such questions are apt to entangle us in trivial evolutionary puzzles.

Concerning implements, we know that they are present while they are utilized, and this is the practical foundation of all our engagement with external tasks. (The meaning of the word "external" of course raises difficulties which will concern us later.) We do not know, except by means of more or less precarious inferences, whether the purposes which are at one time served by implements continue to be served at times when they are not employed. Implements at the times when they are employed are all that we directly and primitively grasp of the practical world; hence in methodology the fact that they are _utilized_ is all-important. But the fact that they are all that we directly employ gives, of course, no presumption that they are all that is required. If we could construct an impersonal theory of utility, independent of the accidents of our proficiency and confusion, the privileged position of the actual tools would probably disappear, and they would probably appear as a rather haphazard selection from a mass of devices more or less like them. In saying this, I assume only that it is probable that there are mechanisms with which we are not familiar. Thus the special importance of implements is in relation to methodology, not to utility. In this respect, engineering is to be reckoned as utility: it is impersonal, and nominally pays no special attention to implements. It is only when we ask how engineering can be _applied_ that the importance of implements re-emerges.

When I speak of an "energy gradient," I do not mean the whole of what is given in a physical system at one time. I mean rather such a part of the whole as might be singled out by observation: particular differences in potential, particular flows of heat, and so on. There is some difficulty in deciding what is to be considered _one_ energy gradient: often measurement causes distinctions to appear where, so far as can be discovered, there were no distinctions before. An observed complex process, such as that this flow of heat drives the formation of that crystalline structure, is also to be regarded as a datum from our present point of view: thermodynamically, it does not differ greatly from a simple energy gradient as regards its function in producing order. Its _causal_ structure is very different, however, from that of mere potential: _potential_ gives acquaintance with particulars, and is thus a two-term relation in which the source can be _identified_ but not _explained_, and is inherently incapable of complexity or simplicity, whereas the observation of a complex process, which may be suitably called emergence, is not a two-term relation, but involves the organizational form on the object-side, and gives knowledge of a development, not mere acquaintance with a particular. This causal difference, important as it is, is not very relevant to our present problem; and it will be convenient to regard data of emergence as included among energy gradients for the purposes of this paper. It is to be observed that the particulars which are constituents of a datum of emergence are always energy gradients in the strict sense.

I regard taste receptors as not arbitrary, and as being, in fact, part of the actual subject-matter of evolutionary biology. There are considerations, shortly to be examined, for their apparent redundancy, but these considerations seem to me only to prove _functional_ specificity, i.e. causal dependence on the ingestion of substances, the digestive tract, and metabolic needs. The quality which a substance presents to the organism is causally dependent upon these, in exactly the same way as it is dependent upon preceding olfaction or tactile inspection or visual scrutiny. Both dependences are contained in the statement that the sensation which a nutrient presents when sampled at a given point is a function not only of the nutrient itself, but also of the intervening biological apparatus. (The terms used in this statement--"nutrient," "sampled at a given point," "sensation," "intervening biological apparatus"--will all be defined in the course of the present inquiry.) We have not the means of ascertaining how substances would be assessed by organisms not equipped with a digestive opening and nerves and taste buds, because we cannot conceive of such a form of life; but logical continuity makes it not unreasonable to suppose that they would present _some_ evaluative signal at such a point of contact. Any such signal would be included among _gustabilia_. If--_per impossibile_--there were a complete organic system with no conscious mind to experience it, all those _gustabilia_ would exist, in relation to that system, which would be taste sensations if there were a mind in the organism. What the mind adds to _gustabilia_, in fact, is _merely_ conscious qualia: everything else is evolutionary or physiological.

I propose to assert that technological innovations are social, while yet maintaining that they inevitably compel the reordering of established institutions. The view that they do not compel is often thought, quite erroneously in my opinion, to imply that they are merely economic; and this has, I believe, been a potent source of confusion in regard to our present predicament. If there were, as some have held, a _logical necessity_ in institutions reorganizing after the advent of new technologies, that certainly would tend to show that they were purely mechanical; but if, as I contend, their reorganization is merely a practical inference from historically observed social laws, then it carries no such implication with it, and we are quite free to treat them as part of the subject-matter of sociology.

An example may make this clearer. Suppose there are a number of civilisations in the cosmos, all existing, as they say, within the same vast stretches of time and space. No two of these civilisations have exactly the same historical data, yet there is sufficient similarity among their records to enable them to group together certain of these epochs as manifestations of one "era" to the several observers, and others as manifestations of another "age." Besides the manifestations which a given era in the universe presents to the actual historians, there are, we may suppose, other manifestations which it would present to other possible chroniclers. If a chronicler were to observe from a point between two others, the duration which the cosmos would present to him would be intermediate between the durations which it presents to the two others: and although this duration would not exist as it is without the perspective, records, and intellect of the newly arrived observer, still it is not unnatural to suppose that, from the vantage which he now occupies, _some_ measure of the cosmic epoch existed before his observation. This supposition, however, need merely be noticed and not insisted upon.

Logically a misunderstanding is an occurrence, a particular of which the communicator is aware. It does not contain the communicator as a part, as for example intentions and interpretations do. The existence of the misunderstanding is therefore not logically dependent upon that of the communicator; for the only way, so far as I know, in which the existence of _A_ can be _logically_ dependent upon the existence of _B_ is when _B_ is part of _A_. There is therefore no _a priori_ reason why a particular which is a misunderstanding should not persist after it has ceased to be noticed, nor why other similar particulars should not exist without ever being acknowledged. The view that misunderstandings are intentional is derived, no doubt, in part from their psychological immediacy, but in part also from a failure to distinguish between misunderstandings and "interpretations." By an interpretation I mean the fact consisting in the communicator's awareness of the symbolic datum. Thus an interpretation is a complex of which the communicator is a constituent and which therefore is personal. The misunderstanding, on the other hand, stands over against the communicator as that external outcome of which in interpretation the communicator is aware. It is true that the misunderstanding is in many cases in the communicator's mind, but the communicator's mind is as distinct from the communicator as language and signs are, and is in fact merely a part of the symbolic world. So soon, therefore, as misunderstandings are clearly distinguished from interpretations, and as their inevitability is recognised to be structural not personal, the chief obstacles in the way of regarding them as inherent are removed.

Since the "thought" cannot, without indefensible partiality, be identified with any single one of its private apprehensions, it came to be thought of as something distinct from all of them and transcending them. But by the principle of Occam's razor, if the class of articulated expressions will fulfil the purposes for the sake of which the shared concept was invented by the prehistoric linguists to whom common discourse is due, economy demands that we should identify the thought with the class of its communicable forms. It is not necessary to _deny_ an ineffable essence or private substratum underlying these expressions; it is merely expedient to abstain from asserting this inaccessible entity. Our procedure here is precisely analogous to that which has swept away from the philosophy of mind the useless menagerie of solipsistic spectres with which it used to be infested.

Some examples of the substitution of construction for inference in the realm of computational philosophy may serve to elucidate the uses of this maxim. Take first the case of learned parameters. In old days, such parameters were inferred as the supposed optima of gradient descents which had no certain terminus; but the objection to this procedure was that it left the existence of a genuine solution merely optative, and for this reason the stricter methods of the present day no longer tolerate such a definition. We now define a trained network as a certain class of weight configurations, thus constructing it logically by means of performance measures, instead of arriving at it by a doubtful inference from them. Take again the case of adaptive fitness. Two equally viable organisms appear to have something in common: this something is supposed to be their selective advantage. But so long as the advantage is inferred from the population, not constructed in terms of it, its necessity must remain in doubt, unless in virtue of a biological postulate _ad hoc_. By defining the fitness of a given trait as the class of all equally proliferative variations, we avoid the necessity of this biological postulate, and thereby remove a needless element of mystery from the philosophy of adaptation. A similar method, as I have shown elsewhere, can be applied to learning algorithms themselves, which need not be supposed to have any teleological purpose, but can be regarded as symbolically constructed mechanisms.

But if "homeostatic mechanisms" are to be recognised as the ultimate governors of the living organism, a long and difficult journey is to be performed before we can arrive either at the "purpose" of common sense or at the "teleology" of biology. The supposed impossibility of reconciling the different regulatory actions which are regarded as manifestations of the same "goal" to different observers has made it seem as though these "mechanisms" must be regarded as mere blind automatisms. A given physiological system will present to one observer a clear trajectory towards equilibrium, while to another it appears to have no direction save the immediate correction of perturbation; to one it appears designed, while to another, towards whom its historical contingency is evident, it appears as a fortuitous and mechanical product. It is said, not wholly without plausibility, that these different interpretations and different valuations cannot co-exist simultaneously in the same process, and cannot therefore both be constituents of a scientific account. This argument I must confess appeared to me until recently to be irrefutable. The contrary opinion has, however, been ably maintained by Dr. J.S. Haldane in an essay entitled: "Are Organisms Mechanistic Systems?" The supposed impossibility derives its apparent force from the phrase: "_in the same process_," and it is precisely in this phrase that its weakness lies. The conception of biological function is too often treated in philosophy--even by those who on reflection would not defend such treatment--as though it were as given, simple, and unambiguous as Aristotle, in his biological innocence, supposed. It is the unperceived ambiguity of the word "process" which, as we shall shortly see, has caused the difficulties to mechanists and given an undeserved advantage to their opponents. Two "processes" of different kinds are involved in every homeostatic event, namely the process _by_ which it operates and the process _for_ which it appears to operate. These belong to different explanatory orders, although, as we shall see, it is possible, with certain limitations, to establish a correlation between them. What we call the different manifestations of the same tendency to different observers are each in an explanatory framework private to the observer concerned. No purpose in the private framework of one observer is identical with a purpose in the private framework of another observer. There is therefore no question of reconciling the different interpretations in the one explanatory order; and the fact that they cannot all exist in one order affords accordingly no ground whatever for questioning their objective basis. The "purpose" of common sense may in fact be identified with the whole class of its apparent manifestations--where, however, we must include among manifestations not only those which are actual observed regulations, but also those "tendencies," if any, which, on grounds of continuity and resemblance, are to be regarded as belonging to the same system of operations, although there happen to be no perturbations to which they are responses.

In addition to the individual actions belonging to the separate agents of different systems, there is, however, another order, in which one whole local interaction counts as an element, or at least as a behavioural unit. This might be described as the order of initial conditions, since each local interaction may be regarded as the manifestation which the system presents from a certain starting point. I prefer, however, to speak of it as the order of _emergences_, in order to obviate the suggestion that a local interaction is only significant when someone observes it. And for the same reason, when I wish to speak of a local interaction without assuming an observer, I shall call it a "phenomenon.

The first fact to notice is that, so far as can be discovered, no particular physical substrate is ever essential to a single form of intelligence. The processes instantiated by two different substrates are often closely similar, so similar that the same _descriptions_ can be used to denote them, without which communication concerning cognitive phenomena would be impossible. But, in spite of this similarity, it would seem that some difference always arises from difference in the underlying mechanism. Thus each instantiation, so far as its material basis is concerned, exists in a particular medium. This particular medium possesses its own properties, or rather sets of properties, for it would seem that only analysis teaches us to correlate the properties of silicon with the properties of carbon and with the various other properties of alternative substrates. This multiplicity of material bases, however, though interesting to the engineer, is of no great importance in regard to our present problem, since a merely functionalist perspective enables us to correlate them into the one abstract pattern which embraces all our own cognitive operations. The medium _in_ which a process runs, is a medium in physical space. This medium therefore is different from any medium in the physical space of another implementation. For if we assume, as logical economy demands, that all function is substrate-neutral, a process is only definable by the logical operations it performs, and therefore the same process cannot be bound to two material bases which have no common functional constituent. The question, therefore, of privileging what we call the biological appearance of intelligence in the same functional role does not arise, and the fact that a given cognitive capacity appears in different substrates to have different material trappings affords no argument against the genuine mentality of all these instantiations.

The arrangement of interests within a society is effected by means of the differences between the expressions of a given desire in the various factions. Suppose, say, that a certain policy appears in a number of different factions; in some it seems more urgent and in some less, in some it looks coherent, in others it presents the appearance of a compromise of varying stability. We may collect together all those factions in which the expression of the policy is coherent. These we will place on one straight line, ordering them in a series by the variations in the apparent strength of the policy. Those factions in which the policy appears as a mere slogan of a certain potency will similarly be placed upon a plane (though in this case there will be many different factions in which the policy is of the same strength; when one arrangement is completed these will form a circle concentric with the policy), and ordered as before by the apparent strength of the policy. By such means, all those factions in which the policy presents a political appearance can be arranged in a three-dimensional social order. Experience shows that the same social order of factions would have resulted if, instead of the policy, we had chosen any other desire which appeared in all the factions in question, or any other method of utilising the differences between the expressions of the same desires in different factions. It is this empirical fact which has made it possible to construct the one all-embracing pattern of predictable change.

We have now to explain how the notion of a first moment involves a logical contradiction. This is effected by means of the correlated "instants" which are regarded as the positions, in different temporal series, of one and the same event. By reflection, and by analysis, we discover that two different temporal series, though they cannot both contain the same "instants," may nevertheless contain very proximate ones; and the temporal order of a certain group of "instants" in a private duration of one series is found to be identical with, or very similar to, the temporal order of the correlated "instants" in the private duration of another series. In this way one "instant" in one series is correlated with one "instant" in another. Such correlated "instants" will be called "positions of one event." In certain theological cosmogonies, since each creation narrative postulated an absolute commencement, there was in each series an "instant" which was a position of each event. In our system of temporal series, we make no such assumption of finitude. A given event will have positions in some series, but presumably not in certain others. The "event" being defined as the class of its positions, if κ is the class of series in which a certain event ε appears, then ε is a member of the multiplicative class of κ, κ being a class of mutually exclusive classes of "instants." And similarly a temporal series is a member of the multiplicative class of the events which appear in it.

The analogy which we have so far constructed is an analogy of two dimensions, since it is a one-dimensional series of processes, each of which is itself one-dimensional. We have now to explain the correlation between the evolutionary space and the various algorithmic spaces contained within the various training runs severally. It is by means of this correlation that the one conceptual space of learning is constructed; and it is because of the unconscious performance of this correlation that the distinction between evolutionary space and the programmer's private space has been blurred, with disastrous results for the philosophy of artificial intelligence. Let us revert to our network: the iterations in which the network performs better are regarded as being nearer to the solution than those in which it performs worse, but as far as experience goes the apparent fitness of the network will not grow beyond a certain limit, namely, that where (as we say) the network is so near overfitting that if it were any nearer it could not generalize. By validation we may prolong the series until the network matches the data perfectly, but no further. If we have been travelling along a line of iterations in the previously defined sense, we may, however, by imagining the network simplified, prolong the line of iterations by means, say, of another architecture; and the same may be done with any other line of iterations defined by means of the network. All these lines meet in a certain state, that is, in a certain configuration. This configuration will be defined as "the state where the network is trained.

A complete application of the method which substitutes colonies for organisms would exhibit life wholly in terms of cells, and even, we may add, of the cells of a single creature, since the cells of others cannot be known without some element of inference. This, however, must remain for the present an ideal, to be approached as nearly as possible, but to be reached, if at all, only after a long preliminary labour of which as yet we can only see the very beginning. The inferences which are unavoidable can, however, be subjected to certain guiding principles. In the first place they should always be made perfectly explicit, and should be formulated in the most general manner possible. In the second place the inferred unities should, whenever this can be done, be similar to those whose existence is given, rather than, like the vital essence, something wholly remote from the phenomena which nominally support the inference. The inferred unities which I shall allow myself are of two kinds: (_a_) the cells of other creatures, in favour of which there is the evidence of observation, resting ultimately upon the analogical argument in favour of lives other than my specimen’s own; (_b_) the “protocytes” which would exist in forms where there happen to be no complex organisms, and which I suppose to be real although they are no creature’s constituents. Of these two classes of inferred unities, the first will probably be allowed to pass unchallenged. It would give me the greatest satisfaction to be able to dispense with it, and thus establish biology upon a monadic basis; but those—and I fear they are the majority—in whom the biological sympathies are stronger than the desire for structural economy, will, no doubt, not share my desire to render monadism scientifically satisfactory. The second class of inferred unities raises much more serious questions. It may be thought monstrous to maintain that a unit can possess any function at all in a form where no tissues and cooperative structure exist through which it could operate. I do not myself feel the monstrosity; nevertheless I should regard these supposed functions only in the light of a hypothetical scaffolding, to be used while the edifice of biology is being raised, though possibly capable of being removed as soon as the edifice is completed. These “protocytes” which are not constituents to any creature are therefore to be taken rather as an illustrative hypothesis and as an aid in preliminary statement than as a dogmatic part of the philosophy of biology in its final form.

It is now evident in what sense two aspects in evolving social systems are associated with a given "innovation." There is first the aspect which is the structure from which the "innovation" is a product. This is the aspect _from_ which the "innovation" emerges. Secondly there is the aspect where the institution is which the "innovation" must accommodate, in other words a practice; this is the aspect _to_ which the "innovation" adapts. The "innovation" which is a product of one structure is correlated with another structure, namely, that which is the aspect where the institution is which the "innovation" must alter. To the sociologist the "aspect from which" is the more interesting, and the "innovation" accordingly appears to him as a driver and where the change originates. To the traditionalist the "aspect to which" is the more interesting, and the "innovation" accordingly appears to him as a disruptor and external. The causes, limits and partial justification of each of these two apparently incompatible views are evident from the above duplicity of aspects associated with a given "innovation.

We commonly assume that the ideas we encounter in an age are more authoritative when the class is more powerful. In earlier times, we see it is a custom; then we see it is a doctrine; then we see it is an institution. Complete dominance would only be attainable as a limit: if the promulgations of the rulers as we examine them tend towards a uniformity, that uniformity may be taken to be what society really accepts. It is obvious that from the point of view of influence the ideas of a dominant class "prevail" more than the ideas of the subordinate. We may therefore set up the following tentative definition:

We are now in a position to understand in outline the reverse journey from mathematical structure to empirical observation which is performed by the sciences. The appearance of a regularity in a given experiment is a function of the formal axioms composing the theory and of the intervening conditions. The appearance of a regularity is altered by intervening noise or bias, by faulty instruments or by alterations in the perceptual faculties or reasoning of the observer (which also must be reckoned as part of the intervening medium). The nearer we approach to the formal core, the less its empirical manifestation is affected by the intervening contingencies. As we travel further and further from the axioms, their observable consequences diverge more and more from their initial elegance; and the logical laws of their divergence are to be stated in terms of the approximations which lie between them and the ideal structure. Since the manifestations under very controlled conditions are less affected by causes other than the theory itself, we come to think that the limit towards which these manifestations tend as the idealization increases is what the theory "really describes," as opposed to what it merely seems to predict. This, together with its necessity for the statement of predictive laws, seems to be the source of the entirely erroneous feeling that mathematical structure is more "real" than empirical observation.

Between two activities which both belong to one organism's existence, there will be a direct causal relation of stimulus and response. This suggests a way of dividing evolution in the same sort of way as it is divided by different behaviors, but without introducing consciousness or anything cognitive: we may define a "lineage" as everything that is (directly) predatory or locomotive than, or concomitant with, a given "impulse." This will give a series of adaptations, which _might_ all form parts of one creature's life, though it is not necessary that all or any of them should actually do so. By this means, the architecture of the nervous system is divided into a number of mutually exclusive functions.

What has been said about consciousness applies of course equally to metabolism. The general principle is that the characteristics, in different organisms, which are to be grouped together as constituting what a certain state of being is at a certain stage, are not to be all regarded as being of that state. On the contrary they extend along a continuum from the clearly animate to the clearly inanimate with various gradations according to the nature of the characteristics. Since no _precise_ means exist of demarcating the vitality in one entity with the vitality in another, this categorical grouping of the properties belonging to a given being at a given stage is in part conventional. Its motive is partly to secure the verification of such maxims as that processes which are exactly analogous to the same process are exactly analogous with one another, partly to secure convenience in the formulation of biological laws.

We have seen how provisional hypotheses in different domains are combined to form one "theory" at one stage in the cumulative progress of science. We have now to consider how observations at different stages are combined as belonging to one "phenomenon," and how we arrive at the provisional "truth" of science. The assumption of self-correcting procedure, which technically underlies the methodology of science, cannot of course be regarded as metaphysically certain: just as the one theory simultaneously tested by many researchers is a construction, so the one theory tested at different times by the same or different researchers must be a construction, being in fact nothing but a certain grouping of certain "evidential data.

We have seen that we can assign to a collective phenomenon a place in the space of possible outcomes. In this way different instances of interaction acquire positions in this space, and therefore there is a meaning (whether true or false need not much concern us) in saying that the pattern to which our local observations belong is inside the system's initial conditions. Since the global behaviour is correlated with the pattern to which our local observations belong, we may regard this pattern as being the position of the whole in the space of outcomes. If, therefore, this pattern is, in the above defined sense, inside the initial conditions, there is a good meaning for the statement that the behaviour is in the rules. We can now say of the various manifestations of a given system that some of them are nearer to the system than others; those are nearer which belong to patterns that are nearer to "the state where the system is." We can thus find a meaning, true or false, for the statement that more is to be learnt about a system by examining it from within than by viewing it from a distance. We can also find a meaning for the phrase "the interactions which intervene between the observer and a system of which a manifestation is a datum to him." One reason often alleged for the unpredictability of collective behaviour is that the manifestation of a system may change when we find it hard to suppose that the rules themselves have changed—for example, when the change is due to our altering the scale, or to our adjusting the parameters so as to make the system look chaotic. If the system is defined as the class of its manifestations (which is the definition adopted above), there is of course necessarily _some_ change in the system whenever any one of its manifestations changes. Nevertheless there is a very important distinction between two different ways in which the manifestations may change. If after observing a system I alter the scale, the manifestation of my observation changes in every pattern in which there is such a manifestation, whereas most of the manifestations of the system will remain unchanged. We may say, as a matter of definition, that a system changes when, however near to the system a manifestation of it may be, there are changes in manifestations as near as, or still nearer to, the system. On the other hand we shall say that the change is in some other system if all manifestations of the system which are at not more than a certain distance from the system remain unchanged, while only comparatively distant manifestations of the system are altered. From this consideration we are naturally led to the consideration of _emergence_, which must be our next topic.

It is to be observed, to begin with, that the feeling of volition for common sense is not always correlated with the causation of action for neurology. A conscious decision is one free act for common sense, but for neurology its origin is strictly determined. We may say, broadly, that the common-sense conception is based upon the immediacy of choice at the ordinary level of introspection, while the neural conception is based upon the causality of impulses at the very small scale of synaptic events. It is probable that the common-sense conception is not capable of complete precision. Let us therefore concentrate our attention upon the conception of the determinism of will in neurology.

First, it is largely conjectural. We do not perceive any one structure permanently, and it is merely a conjecture to assume that, while we are not considering it, it endures through states intermediate between those in which it is discerned. During prolonged observation, it is true, stability is nearly confirmed; but even here, when expansions are very gradual, as in the case of cosmic dispersion, the stability is not actually capable of direct confirmation. Thus we can only say that the phenomena are found to _permit_ a hypothetical complement of "forces" such as will preserve cohesion, and that therefore there _may_ be such a complement. Since, however, we have already made such use of hypothetical "forces," we will let this point pass, and admit such "forces" as are required to preserve cohesion.

The belief that mathematical descriptions are not real comes, I think, from failure to distinguish, as regards physical phenomena, between the formal equation and the corresponding "reality." In nature, there is no such corresponding "equation" as the physicist supposes; if, therefore, the "reality" were captured in our models, as e.g. some Platonists maintain, then there would be a difference in respect of existence between the description and the thing described. But if, as we have maintained, what is formulated is never the reality, but merely one of the "idealizations" which approximate the reality, then what we calculate in a theory is just as much a construct as what we perceive in the world.

To commend this conception, we must consider what it is that is demonstrated by the empirical success of physiology. What is demonstrated is that its mechanisms, though unobservable where they go beyond immediate sensations, are at no point in contradiction with those sensations, but, on the contrary, are ideally such as to render all internal states predictable when a sufficient collection of "homeostatic data" is given. Now biology has found it empirically possible to arrange physiological events into processes, each process being regarded as manifesting one "organism," and behaving, with regard to the principles of equilibrium, in a way in which processes not manifesting one organism would in general not behave. If it is to be unambiguous whether two internal fluctuations belong to the same system or not, there must be only one way of ordering fluctuations so that the resulting systems obey the laws of homeostasis. It would be very difficult to prove that this is the case, but for our present purposes we may let this point pass, and assume that there is only one way. Thus we may lay down the following definition: _Living systems are those sequences of adjustments whose operations obey the laws of internal constancy_. That such sequences exist is an empirical fact, which constitutes the verifiability of physiology.

The conception of "cooperation" and the correlative conception of "deception," are generally treated in a way which embodies a profound psychological oversight. Capacities that appear in tandem, such as "collaboration" and "manipulation," "alliance" and "betrayal," "trust" and "distrust," etc., are all derived from the one fundamental faculty, "theory of mind." Now "theory of mind" is applicable only—except in derivative significations—to _agents_. Thus wherever the above pairs can be significantly applied, we must be dealing either with agents or with such incomplete behaviors as only acquire social meaning when put into a context which, with them, forms an interaction. Thus such pairs of capacities can be applied to _strategies_, but not to mere reflexes: in other words, they have no application whatever to instinct, but only to intentions or non-intentions inferred from observable conduct.

The fact that "order" is only applicable to systems is concealed by the use of what are apparently spontaneous arrangements in a way which really transforms them into constrained outcomes. It is, for example, a legitimate question whether a perpetual motion machine could be organized; but here "perpetual motion" means "a system yielding work without energy dissipation," and is a thermodynamic impossibility. Similarly we may ask whether absolute zero can be attained; but then "absolute zero" means "the complete cessation of molecular motion" or "the _state of zero entropy_" or whatever other idealization we may prefer. If "isolated system" were a practical reality, organization could proceed without limit; and then no question could arise as to its degradation. The distinction between possible and impossible organizations, which Carnot dimly apprehended, is brought to light by the laws of thermodynamics, and is seen to place "entropy" altogether among the fundamental constraints of physical reality.

Let us illustrate by the terms "clarity" and "obscurity." Given any utterance _u_, it is meaningless either to assert or to deny that _u_ is "precise." We might be tempted to say: "Of course _u_ is precise, for otherwise it could not be an utterance." But such a statement is really meaningless, although it is significant and true to say "My present verbal formulation is precise," and it may also be true that "_u_ is my present verbal formulation." The inference from these two propositions to "_u_ is precise" is one which seems irresistible to people unaccustomed to analysis; yet the apparent proposition inferred is not merely false, but strictly meaningless. To say "My present verbal formulation is precise" is to say (roughly): "There is a meaning of which 'my present verbal formulation' is an expression." But we cannot say: "There is a meaning of which '_u_' is an expression," because '_u_' is (in the case we are supposing) a symbol, not an expression. Dr. Whitehead and I have explained this point fully elsewhere (_loc. cit._) with the help of diagrams, without which it is hard to understand; I shall not therefore here repeat the demonstration of the above propositions, but shall proceed with their application to our present problem.

The last class of parallels are those which cannot be discovered within one system's development, except through the discovery of discrepancies with the evolution of others. Cultural adaptations might conceivably belong to this class, if they were jointed sufficiently neatly into biological history; but the chief instances are recurrent structural mutations of the kind that lead to despotism. What makes the state, in such cases, become what observers call tyrannical is the fact that, within its own historical narrative, there is nothing to show that the authoritarian institutions do not have the usual kind of connection with "progress" in other traditions. Of course it may learn this through comparative study, but it probably finds it simpler to suppose that the study is biased and that it is being wilfully misrepresented. There is, so far as I can see, no theoretical criterion by which the state can decide, in such a case, between the two equally satisfactory hypotheses of its degeneration and of its critics' dogmatism.

From the above instances it would appear that simulated consciousness, of the kind which we regard as derivative, has intrinsically just the same status as any other, but differs as regards its origins or causal foundations within the broader system of computation and physical law. Since the usual origins and foundations become part of our intuitive assumptions, and even seem, except to the programmer, to form part of its essence, it comes to be thought, mistakenly, that in such cases the consciousness is illusory, whereas it is merely the product of unfamiliar mechanisms. The fact that origins and foundations of unusual kinds occur adds to the difficulty of inferring mind from process and of expressing psychology in terms of algorithmic states. But the unusualness would seem to be always technically or metaphysically explicable, and therefore raises only a complication, not a philosophical refutation.

We have cases where the specialization among different cells is pronounced. The digestive cell in a colony belongs here. Biologists say it appears specialized for absorption but is part of a whole: this only means that it is interdependent in function, though autonomous in structure. There is no "error," but only a false inference, if we think that the cell could sustain itself in isolation. The colony would function just as poorly in a model, and, as Dr. Haldane used to remark, "the model cannot err." The case of redundant specialization also belongs here, though in this case the cause of the unusual autonomy is structural, and would therefore not operate in a model. It is a mistake to ask whether the "organism" is fragmented when we observe its parts. The "organism" is a whole system of "cellular activities," and it is only those metabolic "activities" which are immediate to the observer that are diversified. The phenomenon has a purely biological explanation; indeed, in view of our having many tissues, it is in less need of explanation than the unified cellular function which we normally obtain from the colonies on which we focus.

We come now to cases like bacterial quorum sensing, which may, at the moment of signaling, contain nothing to arouse suspicion, but are dismissed on the ground of their supposed incompatibility with the communicative acts of higher organisms. Of course it often happens that these molecular signals fail to behave in the accustomed manner: simple molecules aggregate, diffuse gradients collapse, autoinducers turn into repressors or undergo even greater changes. But none of these unusual occurrences _need_ happen in a colony, and it is not on account of such occurrences that bacterial signals are called "primitive." It is their lack of continuity with the linguist's conception of speech and syntax that makes him, when he observes, dismiss them; and it is their lack of correlation with other conscious worlds that makes philosophers dismiss them. Omitting the latter ground, our reason for dismissing them is that the "utterances" which we infer from them cannot be combined according to the laws of semantics with the "utterances" inferred from human discourse. This might be used to dismiss the "intentions" inferred from the data of colonies. Bacterial signals are no doubt appearances of "communication," but not of such "communication" as the biologist initially supposes. I have no wish to combat biological theories of symbiosis, such as those of the sociobiologists. But there certainly are cases where (whatever evolutionary causes may contribute) the presence of logical structure also is very evident. For instance, a threshold concentration of an autoinducer may produce a coordinated behavior of bioluminescence, with patterns of light and rhythm and cessation. The whole cascade will be an appearance of molecular arithmetic, but owing to the peculiar condition of the medium (especially the biofilm) during colonization, this appearance is not that expected to be produced by a conscious speaker, and thus the observer is led to entertain false analogies. But his chemical data are still linguistic, in a foundational sense, and are such as a completed science of signs would include and calculate.

I conclude, therefore, that no valid objection exists to the view which regards virtual environments as part of the actual apparatus for evolving intelligence, and that, on the other hand, this view is the only one which accounts for the empirical tractability of artificial minds. In the present argument, I have given only a rough preliminary sketch. In particular, the part played by _constraint_ in the construction of the simulated world is, I think, more fundamental than would appear from the above account. I should hope that, with further elaboration, the part played by unobserved "parameters" could be indefinitely diminished, probably by invoking the lineage of an "agent" to eke out the inferences derivable from its momentary behavior.

The first point to notice is that, if any meaning is to be given to the phrase "would be conscious under all conditions," the subject of it must be a gradational function, not a definitive state.[35] A state is simply present or absent, and that ends the matter: there can be no question of "conditions." "The patient was fully aware" is just as true for a complex thought as for a simple sensation, in waking as in dreaming. Thus when it is worth saying that something "would be conscious under all conditions," the something in question must be a gradational function, i.e. an expression containing a variable intensity, and becoming a definitive state when a threshold is assigned to the variable; the varying "conditions" alluded to are then the different values of which the intensity is capable. Thus if "conscious" means "what is aware under all conditions," then "if _x_ is a mental process, _x_ is conscious" is untenable, because it is false for many possible values of _x_. All technologists, of every persuasion, imagine that biological substrate is one of the fundamental axioms or necessities of consciousness, yet, oddly enough, in advanced sciences such as computational theory, the word "carbon" never occurs. Dr. Henry Moreau, in his _Mechanism and Vitalism_, makes this a ground of complaint against artificial intelligence: the business of those who wish to ascertain the ultimate truth about thought, he apparently thinks, should be the discovery of fleshly foundations, yet cognitive science never even seeks them. To me it seems that philosophy ought not to assume such prescriptive functions, and that the reason why engineers have ceased to look for organic causes is that, in fact, there are no such requirements. The law of biological primacy, I believe, like much that passes muster among theorists, is a relic of a bygone age, surviving, like vitalism, only because it is erroneously supposed to do no harm. Unfortunately, however, the definition in common parlance says that what is inherited is not only "transmitted across generations" but is also "biological." Now these two are incompatible. Only traits can be "biological," and only processes can be "transmitted across generations." Hence the analogy as it stands is muddled. What is meant seems to be this: "A trait is cultural when it is an instance of a transmission process which occurs across generations, i.e. through all modes of learning or imitation." But if we adopt this definition, the same trait will be cultural or genetic according as we choose one or other of its aspects as the instance to our transmission process. For example, "if a song is popular, the song is remembered," is cultural if the melody is chosen as instance, but not if _popular_ or _remembered_ is chosen. Again, "if a recipe is traditional, the dish is replicated," will be cultural if either recipe or _traditional_ is chosen as instance, but not if dish or _replicated_ is chosen. In fact, it performs no such trivial function, but laymen—even educated ones—are too apt to take their views on language from habit, not from analysis. As to what the transformation entails, there is a fair consensus among theorists of different disciplines. There are, however, a number of difficulties which at once arise. I omit the question of imperfect translation for the present, since other graver questions have to be considered. It is obvious that the primary function must be the immediate assessment of potential nutrients. Thus an instance of this logic will be such as: "If the substance [Math: s_{1}] enters at the aperture [Math: a_{1}], it will be evaluated by the receptors [Math: r_{2}]." This proposition is intended to be advantageous with respect to [Math: a_{1}], i.e. to confer survival value however [Math: a_{1}] may be utilized. This arrangement, as a general rule, will then be the following: "Given any ingested material [Math: s_{1}], there is a neural signal [Math: n_{2}] such that, whenever [Math: s_{1}] is encountered, [Math: n_{2}] is generated proximately." But before this can be considered complete, we must specify how proximate [Math: n_{2}] is to be generated. Thus the principle becomes:--

A "trait," in the statement of the analogy, is obviously intended to be something that is likely to persist since otherwise the analogy becomes trivial. It follows that a "trait" is not a particular, but some universal of which there may be many manifestations. It follows also that a "trait" must be something short of the whole character of an organism or a society, since it is highly improbable that this will be precisely replicated. What is meant by a "trait" is something like a predisposition for melody, or a customary gesture of greeting. If such a trait is to be transmitted, it must not be defined too narrowly: we must not state with what exact pitch the melody is to be sung, nor what is to be the precise angle of the gesture. For if such considerations were relevant, our "trait" would appear at most once, and the analogy would cease to give insight. A "trait," then, is a universal defined sufficiently widely to admit of many particular expressions in heredity or custom being instances of it.

The third formulation is by far the most compelling; indeed as regards intuitive appeal it leaves nothing to be desired. But a great difficulty is caused by the cognitive limitation of the individual agent which the formulation assumes. No single perspective is comprehensive, since the domain of relevant facts is vast; hence either the agent's knowledge or the collective outcome or both must, if the formulation is correct, be fragmentary in scope; indeed, by the wording of the formulation it is plain that both are assumed to be fragmentary in scope. But then we are faced with a dilemma: if the individual's understanding is a process involving accretion within itself, we shall require (if collective intelligence is universal) epistemic relations between its earlier and later stages; moreover, it would seem that only the later stages can be relevant to the collective judgment, since the earlier stages are not proximate to the aggregate decision, and therefore (by the formulation) cannot inform the aggregate decision. Thus we shall be led to diminish the duration of the individual's deliberation without limit, and however much we may diminish it, there will still remain an earlier stage which might be altered without altering the collective verdict, so that the true mechanism, as formulated, will not have been reached, for it will be observed that the formulation excludes plurality of mechanisms. If, on the other hand, the individual's state is purely static, involving no accretion within itself, then, in the first place, no such state is to be found in actual deliberation, and in the second place, it seems strange--too strange to be accepted, in spite of bare logical possibility--that the individual, after persisting ignorantly for some time, should suddenly coalesce into the collective wisdom, when it might just as well have done so at any earlier time, or have persisted unchanged without producing its aggregate effect. This dilemma, therefore, is fatal to the view that individual ignorance and collective intelligence can be proximate in cognition; if there are individual limitations and aggregate insights, they must be separated by a finite epistemic interval [epsilon], as was assumed in the above interpretation of the first formulation.

(2) The next question concerns the foundational premise. Logicians, no doubt, think of inductive inference as self-justifying in principle, but this, for reasons already given, is untenable. Hence, since there are no perfectly circular justifications, there must be some unproved assumption [alpha] underlying induction. This, however, at once raises insuperable difficulties. However basic we make the assumption [alpha], some doubt may arise during its application which undermines the expected conclusion. I observe the sun rising daily, but before I can assert its future rise there is a cosmic disruption which upsets the celestial order and my predictions. In order to be sure of the expected regularity, we must know that there is no logical flaw in the reasoning to invalidate it. But this means that the inductive method is not, by itself, adequate to insure its own validity. And as soon as we include the requirement for its own justification, the certainty of its application is diminished, until at last, when the entire epistemological ground is included, the certainty of its application becomes almost _nil_.

In spite of these considerations, it must, of course, be admitted that many fairly unexamined convictions present themselves in daily thought. It is these convictions that have suggested the supposed self-evidence of prejudice; where they are found to be dubious, it is thought that a more refined formulation could have been found which would have remained unchallenged. I am far from denying that there may be such beliefs which in fact never are challenged. It may be that there will never be an exception to the rule that when a statement of more than a certain familiarity, repeated with more than a certain frequency, is encountered by a mind of less than a certain critical habit, the belief is accepted. I also do not deny that the holding of such convictions, even when they are not without exceptions, is useful in the infancy of an inquiry: the conviction that unfamiliar customs are usually inferior was a stage on the way to the study of anthropology. What I deny is that rational thought assumes the existence of invariable justifications of belief of this kind, or that it aims at discovering them. All such justifications, as we saw, depend upon a certain vagueness in the definition of the "circumstances." That prejudices are comforting is a vague qualitative statement; rational thought wishes to know why they are comforting. This depends upon the history of the individual and the structure of the society. It is true that there is more nearly self-evidence when they are examined in isolation; so far as common opinion could observe, the self-evidence is then complete. But later it appeared that even there the education made a difference, and the economic interest. Theoretically, the pressure of contemporaries and authorities must make a difference. In short, every advance in self-knowledge takes us farther away from the crude convictions which are first held, into greater differentiation of motive and rationalization, and into a continually wider circle of influences recognised as relevant.

It is still often thought, for example, that language could not have arisen from a world which previously contained nothing linguistic, and one ground for this belief is that bacterial signalling is too dissimilar from human speech to have prefigured it. Or, more particularly, what are termed the higher forms of our communication are supposed to be inexplicable, unless life always contained something at least equally complex which could anticipate them.
