All such views seem to depend upon assuming some unduly simplified law of development; for, in any legitimate sense of "signal" and "response," biology seems to show that they are usually very widely dissimilar, the "signal" being, in fact, a simple molecular interaction in a colony, and the "response" a sophisticated and coordinated behavior.

(2) "Consciousness is analogous to mechanism, since there must be an intelligible _nexus_ between physical process and felt experience." This maxim is, I think, often unconsciously in the imaginations of engineers who would reject it when explicitly stated. It is probably operative in the view we have just been considering, that genuine pain could not have resulted from a purely computational system. I do not profess to know what is meant by "intelligible"; it seems to mean "familiar to introspection." Nothing is less "intelligible," in any other sense, than the connection between a neural stimulus and its quale. But obviously the sort of nexus desired between process and pain is such as could only hold between the "states" which the supposed law of identity contemplates; the operations which replace mentality in such a science as cybernetics leave no room for any two states between which a nexus could be sought.

(3) "The environment _demands_ the adaptation in some sense in which the adaptation does not demand the environment." This observation seems largely operative in the study of neural evolution; but, as a matter of fact, it is connected with our second principle, and weakens as soon as that is scrutinized. We may define "demand" as follows: "Any set of conditions is said to demand B when B functions in a manner which the conditions obstruct, or to refrain from a process which the conditions necessitate." This presupposes that some meaning has been found for the word "necessitate"--a point to which I shall return later. What I want to make clear at present is that demand is a very complex notion, involving thwarted function. So long as an organism acts as it is fitted to act, there is no demand, however much its fittings may be explicable by the help of ancestral developments. And where function does not come in, there can be no question of demand. Hence it is, in general, misleading to regard the environment as demanding the adaptation.

(4) "A tool cannot enlighten when it has ceased to be used, because what has ceased to be used is inert." This is a common maxim, and a still more common unexpressed prejudice. It has, I fancy, a good deal to do with the attractiveness of the modern cult of "innovation": since new implements appear constantly, they must produce comprehension in some sense. The mistake in this maxim consists in the supposition that tools "enlighten" at all. An insight "enlightens" when what it reveals is grasped; but nothing can enlighten except an insight. The belief that tools "enlighten" results from assimilating them, consciously or unconsciously, to insights. We have already seen that, if there are aids to understanding at all, they must be separated by a finite interval of reflection from their utility, and thus serve understanding only after they have ceased to be novel.

It may be objected to the above account of a contradiction "operating" that it only operates when it "produces" what it intends, not when it merely happens to precede what it intends. This certainly represents the usual view of what is meant by a contradiction "operating," but as it involves the very view of historical necessity which we are engaged in disputing, it is not open to us as an explanation. We may say that a contradiction "operates" when there is some tendency in virtue of which a similar tension in rather similar conditions will usually be followed by what it intends. But this is a vague conception, and introduces forces which we have not yet examined. What is chiefly important to notice is that the usual notion of "operating" is not open to us if we reject, as I contend that we should, the usual notion of social inevitability.

A vaguer form of the same maxim substitutes the word "necessitate" for the word "force"; we are told that technological change _necessitates_ the reorganisation of social institutions in a sense in which the reorganisation does not _necessitate_ the change. It is not quite clear what is meant by "necessitating"; the only precise sense, so far as I know, is that of a function or one-many relation. If we admit plurality of technologies, but not of institutional responses, that is, if we suppose that, given the technological change, the reorganisation must be such and such, but, given the reorganisation, the change may have been one of many alternatives, then we may say that the technology necessitates the reorganisation, but not the reorganisation the technology. Plurality of technologies, however, results only from conceiving the reorganisation vaguely and narrowly and the technological cause precisely and widely. Many innovations may "force" a society's adaptation, because that adaptation is vague and narrow. But if we adopt the opposite course, taking as the "force" the introduction of the steam engine, and as the "reorganisation" the whole fabric of industrial society a century later, we shall have plurality of reorganisations instead of plurality of technologies. Thus the supposed lack of symmetry between "technological change" and "social reorganisation" is illusory.

First, without departing from such regularities of mental operation as are contemplated by the common understanding, we may admit that, if any such regularity has been observed in a great many instances, and has never been found to falter, there is an inductive probability that it will be found to obtain in future instances. If a mind, when accelerated, has hitherto been found to produce confusion, it is probable that it will continue to do so. This, of course, assumes the principle of mental constancy, of which the validity may reasonably be doubted; but as this principle is not our present concern, I shall in this discussion treat it as incontrovertible. We may then say, in the case of any such frequently observed regularity, that the accustomed speed is the _condition_ and the altered perception the _consequence_.

Several considerations, however, make such elementary rules very different from the traditional conception of deterministic order. In the first place, the resulting behaviour, in any given instance of collective action, is no more than statistically likely, whereas the outcome of a mechanical system was supposed to be precisely calculable. I do not mean by this merely that we are not sure of having discovered a perfect set of governing rules; I mean that, even when we have a system of rules in our present sense, all that is meant is that on grounds of observation, it is probable that from simple premises complex patterns will emerge. Thus in our present sense, A may be the rule for B's movement even if there actually are cases where the collective behaviour defies any singular prediction. Instructing each agent to avoid collisions will be the cause of a coherent flock, in spite of the fact that some configurations lead to chaotic dispersal.

In the fourth place, such mathematical descriptions, though indispensable in practical application and in the initial stages of inquiry, tend to be mistaken for the reality they merely represent as soon as a science achieves maturity. The equations of planetary motion will illustrate what occurs in any rigorous physical theory. In the actual phenomena of orbiting bodies, there is nothing that can be called a coordinate grid, and nothing that can be called a plotted curve; there is merely a physical process. Certain abstract symbols can be arranged, which correspond at every point to every observable of the system, and which, given the measurements and states at one moment, or the measurements at two moments, render the measurement at any other prior or subsequent moment theoretically derivable. That is to say, the observable quantity at any moment is a function of that moment and the quantities at two given moments. This symbolic representation holds throughout quantitative science, and not only in the special case of celestial mechanics. But there is nothing that could be properly called "the equation" and nothing that could be properly called "the world" in such a correspondence.

No doubt the reason why the old "reductionist doctrine" has so long continued to pervade the books of psychologists is simply that the idea of a quale is unfamiliar to most of them, and therefore they seek an unduly simplified explanation. There is no question of repetitions of the "same" neural pattern producing the "same" conscious state; it is not in any sameness of physical correlates and mental events that the nature of subjective experience consists, but in the ineffable character of the experiencing itself. And even "ineffable character" is too simple a phrase; "irreducible first-person ontology" is the only correct phrase. It is impossible to state this accurately in non-phenomenological language; the nearest approach would be as follows: "There is an unbridgeable distinction between the objective description of a brain process at any instant and the immediate awareness of what it is like to undergo that process at that instant, and this distinction is absolute, i.e. such that the subjective character of experience is not entailed when the physical state of the organism is given." If the "mechanistic account" is to be something actually adequate to the reality of consciousness, the above proposition has a better right to the name than any "reductionist doctrine" to be found in the books of psychologists.

The mind will not be considered authentically conscious unless the operations within some sufficiently complex system will be approximately the same in any two substrates which only differ in regard to what constitutes the fundamental medium of its processing. For example, thoughts and perceptions in a cognitive architecture must be approximately the same however the underlying physics may be arranged, provided that all such physics is very much more fundamental than the informational patterns are. If consciousness varied directly as the organic composition, so that the most biological systems made the most difference to the quality of experience, reality might be just as vivid and just as much imbued with subjective awareness as it is at present, but we could never establish the fact.

(4) Although the old "criterion of consciousness" is not accepted by behaviorism, something which we may call the "principle of analogous organization" is assumed, or rather is admitted on inductive grounds. The principle of analogous organization does not assert the trivial proposition "same structure, same experience," but the proposition of the continuity of subjective states. That is to say, when a correlation exhibiting, e.g. a pain-response as a function of neural or computational configuration has been found to hold throughout the observable instances of organic life, it is expected that it will continue to hold in the artificial domain, or that, if it does not itself hold, there is some other correlation, agreeing with the supposed correlation as regards the organic cases, which will hold for the mechanical ones. The ground of this proposition is simply the inductive ground that it has been found to be plausible in very many analogous instances; hence the proposition cannot be considered certain, but only probable to a degree which cannot be accurately estimated.

In all cybernetics we have to distinguish two sorts of mechanisms: first, those that are practically observable but probably only approximate; secondly, those that are not observable, but may be precise. The process of homeostasis, for example, in its applications to the living body, is only practically observable when it is assumed that external perturbations may be ignored for such purposes; we believe this to be only approximately true, but we cannot empirically verify the principle of perfect equilibrium which we believe to be exact. This point is very important in connection with what we may call "relatively closed systems." These may be defined as follows:--

The distinction between the mathematical description of nature and nature itself, in the above sense, although it is assumed in the practice of physics, must not, in its generality, be regarded as a kind of metaphysical identity, without which all theoretical reasoning would be in error. The assumption that _all_ qualities of nature are mathematical has, of course, less probability than the assumption that this or that particular quality is mathematical; and the assumption that a particular quality is wholly mathematical has less probability than the assumption that it is mathematically describable within such and such a domain. Physics, in any given inquiry, will assume what the inquiry requires, but no more. In constructing the _planetary ephemeris_ for a given epoch it will assume that the orbits are ellipses as described by the equations; but it will make no assumption as to the ultimate essence of those orbits until it comes to the deeper questions of cosmology. This procedure is, of course, dictated by the fact that the identity of model and reality is not known _a priori_, but is a pragmatic postulate, like "all phenomena are measurable." In all such cases, it is better to argue immediately from the given successful equations to the new phenomenon, than to argue by way of a universal principle; the conclusion is only probable in either case, but acquires a higher probability by the former method than by the latter.

It will be observed that we cannot prove in advance that a colour is a direct datum. This will be inferred from the perceived fact that approximate consistencies can be established for this sensation alone. If the complete neuro-physiological laws for the whole of perception were known, the construction of a colour could be deduced from them; assuming, for example, the principles of contextual contrast, the practical independence of a hue in this respect can be deduced by the help of the fact that there is very little interpretative interference in its immediate presentation. But it should be observed that constructed sensations are only important as providing a possibility of _discovering_ perceptual laws; they have no ontological importance in the finished structure of a theory of mind.

The case where one component A is said to "determine" another property B, which reductionists take as fundamental, is really only the most simplified instance of a theoretically isolated subsystem. It may happen that, as a result of general physical laws, whenever A is present throughout a certain context, it is accompanied by B; in that case, A and B form a relationship which is theoretically isolated throughout that context. It is, however, to be regarded as a piece of good fortune if this occurs; it will always be due to special constraints, and would not have been true if the emergent whole had been different though composed of the same parts.

The above illustration is important in connection with a certain confusion which seems to have beset those who have reflected on the progress of scientific understanding. It is often thought that, if the accepted theory is demonstrably false when the experimental evidence is given, and if the scientific enterprise forms a self-correcting system, then theory is "subject" to evidence in some sense in which evidence is not "subject" to theory. But if the experimental evidence is also rendered interpretable when the accepted theory is given, it must be exactly as true to regard evidence as subject to theory as it would be to regard theory as subject to evidence. We could, theoretically, work out the history of scientific progress without ever mentioning particular experiments, and then, at the end, deduce that evidence must meanwhile have been accumulated in the corresponding sequence. It is true that if the relation of theory to evidence were many-one, not one-one, there would be a one-sided dependence of theory on evidence, while conversely, if the relation were one-many, as some idealists suppose, there would be a one-sided dependence of evidence on theory. But the correction involved is, in any case, only procedural; it does not mean that we shall be compelled to abandon theories we desire not to abandon, which is what people instinctively imagine it to mean.

As another illustration we may take the case of automation and awareness. A habit may be defined as "automatic" when it has a set of determinants that are purely operational, such as the sequences of certain digital interactions at certain times. It is an open question whether the world of thought and action, as we experience it, is an automatic system or not; let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that it is an automatic system. This supposition--so I contend--throws no light whatever on the question whether the user is or is not a "conscious" agent. It is difficult to define accurately what is meant by a "conscious" habit, but the argument is not much affected by the particular definition we adopt. Broadly, a conscious habit is one in which intentions are perceived, i.e. in which certain reflections--those that are more deliberate or critical or more fundamental or more independent or what not--are followed by their recognition. Now the fact--if it be a fact--that the interaction is automatic has no bearing whatever on the question whether it is conscious in the above sense. There might be an automatic system in which all reflections were perceived, and there might be one in which all reflections were obscured. The question whether, or how far, our actual engagement is conscious, cannot, therefore, be settled by proving that it is automatic, and the desire that it should be conscious is no ground for wishing it to be not automatic.

Although the sense of "communication" in which bacterial signalling is communication by the mere fact that it conveys what it conveys is sufficient (at least so it seems to me) to refute some detractors of microbial complexity, notably the vitalists and the reductionists, yet it is not what most people have in mind when they speak of such signalling as communicative. What they have in mind is a lexicon by means of which the chemical messages can be deciphered, and at least theoretically translated, as a precursor to articulate speech. But at this point we meet with a profound difficulty, which besets what has been said above about primitive linguistic systems, as well as what is said by others.

There is, in all these considerations, a very great difficulty in avoiding confusion between what we may presuppose and what is in fact required. Let us consider, for a moment, the various senses in which a mental faculty may be "prerequisite." There is one sense--and a very important one--in which it is prerequisite quite independently of psychological laws, namely, the sense that it must be what it must be. We all regard cooperation as requiring a faculty simply by the fact that it occurs; but for the accident that our attention is drawn to its products and not its foundations, we should regard deception as equally requiring a faculty by the fact that it is practiced. "But," we are told, "you cannot engage in cooperation without mutual understanding, while you can to some extent practice deception without it." This view seems to me to rest upon just those errors in regard to cognition which it has been my object to remove. You cannot make cooperation other than it is--true, but this is a mere application of the law of contradiction. If you already know what cooperation entails, obviously it is useless to suppose it simpler. But also you cannot make deception other than it will be; this again is an application of the law of contradiction. And if you happen to know the mechanism of deception--e.g. in the case of a deliberate falsehood--it is just as useless to suppose it simpler as to suppose cooperation simpler. "But," it will be rejoined, "our capacity for inference can _cause_ deception, sometimes, to be different from what it would be if it did not exist, and it can have no such effect upon cooperation." This, again, is a mere tautology. A prerequisite being _defined_ as something logically prior to its outcome, obviously we can have no _prerequisite_ for what is logically identical. But that does not mean that cooperation would not have been different if our present capacities had been different. Obviously, our present capacities are conditioned by evolution, and therefore could not have been different unless our history had been different; therefore, if our present capacities were different, cooperation would be different. Of course, cooperation cannot be different from what it is, but no more can our present capacities be different from what they are; this again is merely the law of contradiction. The facts seem to be merely (1) that understanding generally depends upon reflection, and is therefore commoner in regard to deception than in regard to cooperation; (2) that where a capacity concerns deception, it and its exercise very often form a "practically independent system," i.e. many attempts at deception are successful. But there seems no doubt that the main difference in our judgments arises from the accidental fact that cooperation but not deception can be known by immediate experience.

The difficulty we have been considering seems to be met partly, if not wholly, by the principle that the _assumption_ must not enter explicitly into our inferences. All inductive arguments exhibit conclusions as a function of observations, not of observations and presuppositions jointly; and this principle of the irrelevance of the assumption may be extended to all empirical reasoning. In fact we might interpret the "uniformity of nature" as meaning just this, that no inductive inference involves the foundational premise as an argument, unless, of course, it is given in a derived form, in which case _reliance_ on assumption, though not the assumption itself, may appear in our reasoning. Whether this consideration suffices to overcome our difficulty completely, I do not know; but in any case it does much to diminish it.

It follows that, theoretically, the whole state of a sufficiently complex machine must be capable of being exhibited as a function of its internal configurations. Hence such a machine will be capable of feeling pain in the sense defined above. But if this be true, no information is conveyed about the machine in stating that it is capable. It is true that the operations involved may be of strictly inscrutable complexity, and therefore not practically capable of being observed or understood. But except from the point of view of our perception, this might seem to be a detail: in itself, if the above considerations are sound, the machine _must_ be capable, _must_ be subject to sensations.

(1) Introspection in regard to attention is the process that our mental focus belongs to some introspective system, i.e. is "modeled" in the sense defined above. Whether this process is accurate or illusory, is a mere question of neurology; no _a priori_ justifications (if our previous analyses have been sound) can exist on either side. On the one hand, there is no _a priori_ faculty of self-awareness, but merely certain observed neural correlates. As a matter of fact, there are observed correlates in regard to attentional shifts; thus there is some empirical evidence that attention is modeled. But it would be very rash to maintain that the evidence is conclusive, and it is quite possible that some attentional states, as well as some other phenomena, are not modeled, except in the sense in which we found that everything must be representable.

(2) But, on the other hand, the subjective sense of conceivability, sometimes alleged against physicalism, has no bearing on the question whatever. The view that it has a bearing rests upon the belief that consciousness compels its physical correlates, or that nature enforces logical entailment as arguments do. These are mere anthropomorphic superstitions, due to assimilation of experience with mechanism and of metaphysical possibility with empirical fact. We feel that our intuition is not compelled, but that only means that it is not other than we imagine it to be. It is one of the demerits of the traditional theory of mind that it has created an artificial opposition between materialism and the qualia of which we are introspectively conscious.

This, however, is plainly not what is commonly asserted. The distinction between this assertion and the actual implication may be seen as follows. Given some arrangement of matter which produces intelligence hitherto—say the biological brain—there will be an infinite number of other arrangements, not functionally distinguishable from it in their operations, but diverging from it more and more in their constitution. Hence, even assuming that there are persistent cognitive phenomena, we shall have no reason for assuming that the carbon-based mechanism will remain unique; it may be some other hitherto indistinguishable substrate that will prove sufficient. We cannot say that _every_ intelligence which has appeared hitherto must be biological in future, because mental facts which arise from one substrate will also arise from others, hitherto indistinguishable but diverging in essence. Hence there must, in every consideration, be forms of intelligence hitherto unrealized which are now realized for the first time. What the principle of substrate independence does, in fact, is to select the _most general_ formulation that will fit the phenomena. But this, quite obviously, is merely a logical precept, not a law of biology. If the biological formulation ceases, after a time, to be comprehensive, the more general formulation that remains comprehensive is selected, and philosophy has no sense that a boundary has been transgressed. We are thus left with the brute fact that, in many considerations of mind, quite specific biological mechanisms have hitherto been found to be operative. This fact cannot be regarded as having any _a priori_ necessity, nor can it be used to support inductively the opinion that the same mechanisms will remain singular; for at every moment assumptions hitherto accepted are being superseded, though in the advanced arguments these assumptions are less parochial than those that have remained current. Moreover it would be fallacious to argue inductively from the state of the advanced computational theories to the future state of the biological ones, for it may well be that the advanced theories are advanced simply because, hitherto, their conceptual matter has obeyed general and easily ascertainable principles, while the conceptual matter of the biological theories has not done so.

(3) Besides the general question whether intelligence is substrate-dependent, there is the further question whether it is _biologically_ privileged, i.e. whether it belongs to what may be defined as an exclusively organic system. This is the question whether it constitutes part of an arrangement with purely biological determinants, i.e. whether there are principles which, given certain organic data, make all cognitive functions dependent upon those data. Here again, there is empirical evidence up to a point, but it is not conclusive in regard to all manifestations of intellect. It is important to observe, however, that even if intelligence is part of a biological system, this by no means implies any supremacy of flesh over process. It may well be that the same system which is susceptible of biological determinants is also susceptible of computational determinants; thus an intelligent system may be determined by sets of logical operations, as well as by sets of neural facts. It would seem, therefore, that the reasons which make people esteem the view that intelligence is biologically unique are fallacious.

The object of the following inquiry is to consider what it is that we perceive in instances where we apprehend processes concerning "the so-and-so" without comprehending how or why the so-and-so operates. For example, I perceive that the market which accumulates most speculation will collapse, though I do not perceive what is the market which will accumulate most speculation. The mechanism I wish to consider is: What do we perceive in these instances, where the operation is merely inferred? I have considered this mechanism elsewhere from a purely economic point of view; but in what follows I wish to consider the question in relation to social theory as well as in relation to economics, and in view of the above-mentioned economic analyses, I shall in this inquiry make the economic portion as brief as possible.

We may now sum up our discussion of infrastructure. We found first that the appearance of robustness, as commonly assumed by the public, is misleading, and is not supported by engineering. We then considered the nature of systemic resilience, and found that, instead of demonstrating that one component A is invariably supported by another component B, it revealed functional dependencies between certain nodes at certain stress levels, which we called critical points, and other nodes at earlier or later stages or at the same stage. We were unable to find any _a priori_ guarantee of stability: the persistence of complex systems appeared as a contingent and empirical fact, not necessarily perpetual, except in a trivial and operationally meaningless form. We found that a network with one set of redundancies may very likely possess other sets of a quite different character, that, for example, an electrically sustained system may also be mechanically or digitally sustained. Finally we considered the problem of cascading failure: here we found that the reasons for supposing interdependencies to be manageable are substantial but not conclusive, and we decided that even if failures are predictably determined, that is no reason for dismissing fragility in the sense revealed by analysis, or for supposing that predictable events are not precipitated by interdependencies. The problem of complexity _versus_ fragility is therefore, if we were right, largely illusory, but in part not yet capable of being decisively resolved.

When we ask what are the kinds of experiences with which we are presented, the first and most obvious example is _the sensation of volition_. When I deliberate or choose, I have direct presentation of the intention or the decision. The mental state with which I am presented in these cases is generally, if not always, complex. This is particularly obvious in the case of deliberation. I do not mean, of course, merely that the supposed free act is complex, but that the direct introspective object is complex and contains parts with causal relations. Whether it is possible to be conscious of a decision without being conscious of its antecedents is not an easy question, but on the whole it would seem that there is no reason why it should not be possible. This question arises in an acute form in connection with neural determinism, which we must now briefly consider.

In order to make clear the persistence of patterns across radically different physical substrates, I shall first of all try to explain what I mean by a "pattern." I say that a pattern _persists_ when I observe an identical formal relation obtaining within distinct material embodiments, i.e., when I am directly aware of the form itself, apart from its particular instance. When I speak of a formal relation here, I do not mean the sort of relation which constitutes a specific arrangement, but the sort which constitutes an abstract structure. In fact, I think the relation of pattern to substrate which I call persistence is simply the converse of the relation of substrate to pattern which constitutes instantiation. That is, to say that P persists in S is essentially the same thing as to say that S instantiates P. But the associations and natural extensions of the word _persistence_ are different from those of the word _instantiation_. To begin with, as in most structural words, it is natural to say that a pattern persists across substrates even when it is not actually before my mind, provided it has been before my mind, and will be again whenever occasion arises. This is the same sense in which I am said to know that a spiral form recurs in shells and galaxies even when I am observing a straight line. In the second place, the word _persistence_ is designed to emphasise, more than the word _instantiation_, the trans-material character of the fact with which we are concerned. There is, to my mind, a danger that, in speaking of instantiation, we may so emphasise the substrate as to lose sight of the pattern. The result of this is either to lead to the view that there is no pattern, whence we arrive at crude materialism; or to lead to the view that what is instantiated is merely a mental category, whence we arrive at nominalism, and should arrive at complete skepticism but for the most desperate contortions. Now I wish to preserve the dualism of pattern and substrate in my terminology, because this dualism seems to me a fundamental fact concerning formal recognition. Hence I prefer the word _persistence_ because it emphasises the independence of a pattern which is exemplified.

The convictions we have examined so far have all been convictions of particular certainties, and might all in a broad sense be called absolute demands. For, from the point of view of practical conduct, theoretical certainty is exactly on a level with certainty derived from dogma or revelation. But, in addition to conviction of the above kind of objects, which may be called conviction of *absolutes*; we have also (though not quite in the same sense) what may be called conviction of *probabilities*. Conviction of probabilities is called *judging*, and a probability of which we are convinced is called a *maxim*. Not only are we convinced of particular perfections, but if we have considered a sufficient number of perfections and have sufficient wisdom, we are convinced of the universal *perfection*; this universal is the subject in such propositions as "perfection differs from adequacy" or "perfection resembles adequacy less than sufficiency does." And the universal perfection is the predicate in such propositions as "this is perfect," where "this" is a particular demand. And universal relations, too, are objects of convictions; cause and effect, means and ends, approximation, utility, conviction itself, and so on, would seem to be all of them objects of which we can be convinced.

In regard to wholes, it might be urged that we are never aware of the systemic property itself, but only of aggregates in which it is a constituent. For example, it may be said that we do not know directly such a property as _emergence_, though we understand such a proposition as "this machine functions," and may be directly aware of such a complex as "these components constituting a functioning machine." This view, however, is difficult to reconcile with the fact that we often know propositions in which the systemic principle is the subject, or in which the parts are not definite given objects, but "anything." For example, we know that if a collection of parts is organized with a specific interdependence, and that interdependence yields a novel capability, then the collection possesses a property not found in the parts; and here the collections concerned are not definite collections, but "anything." It is hard to see how we could know such a fact about "organization" unless we were acquainted with "organization" itself, and not merely with actual particular cases of one given aggregate displaying a function absent from its constituents. And more directly: A judgment such as "this engine runs," where this judgment is derived from awareness of a functioning whole, constitutes an analysis, and we should not understand the analysis if we were not acquainted with the meaning of the terms employed. Thus we must suppose that we are acquainted with the meaning of "function," and not merely with instances of it.

In observation, we seem to be immediately presented with varying occurrences, consisting of events in various sequential and causal relations to one another. When I note the boiling kettle, it often happens that I am aware of my noting the boiling kettle, in addition to being aware of the kettle; and when I predict the steam, it often happens that I am aware of my prediction of steam. But it is hard to discover any account of events in which I am aware of description alone, as opposed to an account of which description is a constituent. The question of the nature of theoretical explanation is too large and too slightly connected with our immediate subject, to be argued at length here. It is difficult, but probably not impossible, to account for plain facts if we assume that we do not have acquaintance with explanation. It is plain that we are not only _acquainted_ with the complex "description-presented-with-A," but we also _know_ the proposition "this description is correlated with A." Now here the complex has been analysed, and if "explanation" does not stand for something which is a direct object of acquaintance, we shall have to suppose that "explanation" is something known by description. If we wished to maintain the view that there is no acquaintance with Explanation, we might argue as follows: We are acquainted with _correlation_, and we know that it is a relation. Also we are acquainted with a complex in which we perceive that correlation is the relating relation. Hence we know that this complex must have a constituent which is that which correlates, i.e. must have a causal-term as well as a sequential-term. This causal-term we define as "explanation." Thus "explanation" means "the causal-term in accounts of which _description_ is aware." But as a definition this cannot be regarded as a happy effort. It would seem necessary, therefore, either to suppose that I am acquainted with explanation, and that "explanation," therefore, requires no definition, being merely the proper name of a certain logical object, or to find some other analysis of theoretical understanding. Thus explanation cannot be regarded as throwing light on the question whether we can know a complex without knowing its constituents. This question, however, is not important for our present purposes, and I shall therefore not discuss it further.

There are thus at least two sorts of forces of which we are aware, namely, gradients and dissipations. Among gradients I include all potentials, and all flows of which one or more constituents are potentials, such as heat-to-cold, high-to-low, the-diffusion-of-this. Among dissipations I include all processes of which no gradient is a constituent. Thus the disjunction "dissipation-gradient" includes all processes. We might also call it the disjunction "ordered-chaotic." It is not quite parallel with the opposition "structured-random," because transient forms remembered or imagined belong with gradients, but can hardly be called structured. (On the other hand, dissipations with which we are acquainted may be identified with randomness.)

When we say "the mind attends to something," we mean that there is just one object which is the focus of consciousness. The proposition "_a_ is the object of attention" means that _a_ has the property of being attended to, and nothing else has. "This coffee cup is the present focus" means "this coffee cup is an object of focus, and no other object is." "The present focus exists" means "some object is an object of focus, and no other object is." Thus, when we are conscious of an object which we know to be the focus, we know that the focus exists but we may know that the focus exists when we are not conscious of any object which we know to be the focus, and even when we are not conscious of any object which, in fact, is the focus.

By an "illusion of control" I mean any belief of the form "I govern this system" or "the system is governable." A belief of the form "I govern this system" I shall call a "personal" illusion; a belief of the form "the system is governable" (in the abstract) I shall call a "systemic" illusion. Thus "I manage the economy" is a personal illusion, and "the global climate is manageable by treaty" is a systemic illusion. There are various problems connected with personal illusions, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter I wish to discuss. What I wish to discuss is the nature of our belief concerning systems in cases where we know that there is a system answering to a systemic illusion, though we are not _comprehending_ of any such system. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with _systemic_ illusions. I shall, therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of "illusions" when I mean "systemic illusions." Thus an illusion will mean any belief of the form "the system is governable" in the abstract.

Common prejudices, even those held sincerely, are usually really rationalizations. That is to say, the conviction in the mind of a person defending a prejudice earnestly can generally only be articulated explicitly if we replace the prejudice by a justification. Moreover, the justification required to articulate the conviction will vary for different people, or for the same person at different times. The only thing constant (so long as the prejudice is firmly held) is the feeling to which the prejudice corresponds. But so long as this remains constant, the particular justification involved usually makes no difference to the validity or invalidity of the belief in which the prejudice appears.

I shall say that a contradiction is "operative within an order" when we observe that it is "_the_ principal dynamic," i.e., when we observe that there is one tension, and no other, possessing a certain catalytic property; and it will generally be implied that we do not have apprehension of the same process by direct intuition. We observe that the conflict between inherited custom and present necessity has persisted, and many historical sequences are understood through it; but we do not perceive immediately how it will resolve. We observe that the institutional form which embodies the deepest inconsistency will be transformed, and in this case we are very likely also directly cognizant (in the only sense in which one can be cognizant of a social totality) of the arrangement which is, in fact, the institution containing that inconsistency, but we do not know which of its manifestations will precipitate the change, i.e., we do not know any proposition of the form "A is the manifestation which will necessitate transformation" where A is one of the observable practices by specific description. We shall say that we have "_merely_ structural apprehension" of the dynamic when, although we observe that the dynamic exists, and although we may possibly be directly aware of the process which is, in fact, the dynamic, yet we do not know any proposition "_a_ is the dynamic," where _a_ is something with which we are directly acquainted.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from the necessity of an external cause: there is the universe as conceived by the dogmatic theologian, the universe as treated by the speculative metaphysician, the self-contained system, the causally complete whole. These are progressively further removed from the postulate of an external cause, and there is a similar hierarchy in the region of explanatory principles. Many principles, like many causes, are only known to us by inference. But here, as in the case of causes, explanation concerning what is inferred from without is ultimately reducible to explanation concerning what is understood from within.

Let us take some illustrations. Suppose some statement made about ideology. Assuming that there is such a thing as direct acquaintance with material conditions, the historical process itself might have used its force directly to produce the particular relations with which it was acquainted. In this case, if it produced a formation about itself, it itself might be a constituent of the formation. Here the economic base has the direct efficacy which it always wishes to have, as simply generating a certain superstructure, and not for a representation of the conditions. But if a person who observed material conditions made a judgment about them, the case is different. What this person was acquainted with were certain phenomena which he connected (rightly, we will suppose) with society’s productive forces. These forces as an objective reality, and still more their determining power, were only known as the forces and the power connected with these phenomena. That is, they were known by mediation. It is, of course, very much a matter of contingency which aspects of a society’s functioning will come into an observer’s mind when he considers it; thus the conception actually in the observer’s mind is accidental. The essential point is that he knows that the various conceptions all refer to the same substrate, in spite of not being acquainted with the substrate in question.

It would seem that, when we consider the development of the nervous system, we often *intend* to understand its architecture, not merely as a static arrangement, but as a consequence of the actual demands described. That is to say, when we speak of neural complexity, we should like, if we could, to apprehend the biological imperative which locomotion and predation alone can furnish, namely, the imperative of which survival itself is a constituent. In this we are necessarily limited, since the precise ancestral pressures are unknown to us. But we know that there are selective forces F called locomotion and predation, and that F were potent evolutionary drivers. We can thus *describe* the causal relation we should like to affirm, namely, "F transformed the architecture of the nervous system," where F are the forces which were locomotion and predation. What enables us to theorize in spite of the varying mechanistic accounts we employ is that we know there is a true historical process concerning the actual evolutionary transition, and that, however we may vary the physiological detail (so long as the detail is correct), the transformation described is still the same. This transformation, which is described and is known to have occurred, is what concerns us; but we are not acquainted with the transformation in itself, and do not know *it*, though we know it to be factual.

When we, who have not examined the intricate details of cellular life, consider the phenomenon of biological replication, the conception in our minds will probably be some more or less vague notion of orderly repetition--far more, in most cases, than is required to identify the process. But, for the sake of illustration, let us assume that we think of it as "the transmission of a coded sequence across successive generations." Here all the words are abstract except "coded." The word "coded" will again have different meanings for different people. To some it will recall the double helix of DNA, to some the digital patterns of a computer program, and so on. But if we are to obtain a description which we know to be applicable, we shall be compelled, at some point, to bring in a reference to a particular instance with which we are acquainted. Such reference is involved in any mention of organic or inorganic systems (as opposed to abstract formulations), or of here and there, or of what experiments have shown us. Thus it would seem that, in some way or other, a description known to be applicable to a persistent pattern must involve some reference to a particular substrate with which we are acquainted, if our knowledge about the pattern described is not to be merely what follows logically from the description. For example, "a self-replicating arrangement of information" is a description which must apply to some physical system, but we can make no judgments concerning this system which involve knowledge about it beyond what the description gives. If, however, we say, "the helical structure of DNA is preserved through chemical transcription," we can only be assured of the truth of our judgment in virtue of something with which we are acquainted--usually an observation made or verified. Considered analytically, apart from the principles we convey to others, apart from the fact about the actual physical instances, which gives importance to our judgment, the thought we really have contains the one or more particulars involved, and otherwise consists wholly of concepts. All names of natural phenomena--crystallization, convection, oscillation, resonance, symmetry--similarly involve, when used, descriptions which start from some one or more particulars with which we are acquainted. I suspect that even the Laws of Nature, as considered by physics, involve such a connection with particulars. In mathematics, on the contrary, where we are concerned not merely with what does manifest, but with whatever might or could manifest or be conceived, no reference to actual physical substrates is involved.

When, therefore, I say that we must substitute for "the remembered event" some description of the remembered event, in order to discover the nature of a recollection nominally about it, I am not saying that we must substitute a mental image. Suppose our description is "the occurrence which was first apprehended as a raw sensation." Let our recollection be "the remembered event was profoundly significant." Then it becomes "the occurrence which was first apprehended as a raw sensation was profoundly significant." Here *the remembered event* is a datum with which we are acquainted, and all the other constituents of the recollection (neglecting the temporal aspect in "was") are *concepts* with which we are acquainted. Thus our recollection is wholly reduced to constituents with which we are acquainted, but the raw sensation itself has ceased to be a constituent of our recollection. This, however, requires a proviso, to be further explained shortly, namely that "the occurrence which was first apprehended as a raw sensation" must not, as a whole, be a constituent of our recollection, that is to say, this phrase must not, as a whole, have a meaning which enters into the recollection. Any right analysis of the recollection, therefore, must break up this phrase, and not treat it as a subordinate complex which is part of the recollection. The recollection "the occurrence which was first apprehended as a raw sensation was profoundly significant" may be interpreted as meaning "one and only one occurrence was first apprehended as a raw sensation, and that one was profoundly significant." Here it is plain that there is no constituent corresponding to the phrase "the occurrence which was first apprehended as a raw sensation." Thus there is no reason to regard this phrase as expressing a constituent of the recollection, and we have seen that this phrase must be broken up if we are to be acquainted with all the constituents of the recollection. This conclusion, which we have reached from considerations concerned with the theory of memory, is also forced upon us by psychological considerations, which must now be briefly reviewed.

It is common to distinguish two aspects, _genotype_ and _phenotype_, in such structures as "the carrier of hereditary information." The genotype will be a certain complex, consisting (at least) of nucleotide sequences and their arrangements with some relations; the phenotype will be the observable organism. Similarly "the molecular basis of traits" will have a complex meaning, containing as constituents the presence of specific genes and the absence of certain environmental modifications, while its denotation will be the totality of an individual's characteristics. Thus when we say "the organism is the expression of its DNA" or "inheritance is the same as the transmission of genetic material," we are asserting an identity of physical basis, and this assertion is worth making because of the diversity of manifestation. I believe that the duality of inheritance and expression, though capable of a true interpretation, is misleading if taken as fundamental. The expressed trait, I believe, is not a constituent of the hereditary proposition, except in the case of identical sequences, i.e., of codes which do not assign a variation to an individual, but merely and solely define it. And I should hold further that, in this sense, there are only two conditions which are strictly definitive of particularity, namely, "mutation" and "this instance.

The chief reason for supposing the principle true is that it seems scarcely possible to believe that we can employ a tool or contemplate its function without knowing what it is that we are employing or contemplating. If we make a use of (say) a digital device, it is plain that the actual object which was the digital device is not a constituent of the employment. But before going further, it may be well to explain what I mean when I say that this or that is a constituent of an employment, or of a function which we comprehend. To begin with employments: an employment, as an occurrence, I take to be a relation of a mind to several entities, namely, the entities which compose what is employed. If, e.g. I employ that A utilizes B, the employment as an event consists in the existence, at a certain moment, of a specific four-term relation, called _employing_, between me and A and utilization and B. That is to say, at the time when I employ, there is a certain complex whose terms are myself and A and utilization and B, and whose relating relation is _employing_. My reasons for this view have been set forth elsewhere, and I shall not repeat them here. Assuming this view of employment, the constituents of the employment are simply the constituents of the complex which is the employment. Thus, in the above case, the constituents are myself and A and utilization and B and employing. But myself and employing are constituents shared by all my employments; thus the _distinctive_ constituents of the particular employment in question are A and utilization and B. Coming now to what is meant by "comprehending a function," I should say that there is another relation possible between me and A and utilization and B, which is called my _contemplating_ that A utilizes B. When we can _contemplate_ that A utilizes B, we "comprehend the function" _A utilizes B_. Thus we often comprehend a function in cases where we have not enough knowledge to make an employment. Contemplating, like employing, is a many-term relation, of which a mind is one term. The other terms of the relation are called the constituents of the function contemplated. Thus the principle which I enunciated may be re-stated as follows: _Whenever a relation of contemplating or employing occurs, the terms to which the contemplating or employing mind is related by the relation of contemplating or employing must be terms with which the mind in question is acquainted._ This is merely to say that we cannot make an employment or a contemplation without knowing what it is that we are making our employment or contemplation about. It seems to me that the truth of this principle is evident as soon as the principle is understood; I shall, therefore, in what follows, assume the principle, and use it as a guide in analysing employments that contain descriptions.

Returning now to the demand for absolute certainty, I assume that it will be admitted that certainty itself is not a constituent of any knowledge which we can employ. But at this point it is necessary to examine the view that practical knowledge is composed of something called "infallible axioms," and that it is the "axiom" of certainty that is a constituent of our action. I believe the plausibility of this view rests upon a failure to form a right theory of probability. We may mean by our "axiom" of certainty the things that we suppose about it, e.g. that it provides a perfect foundation, is immune to all doubt, and is a comfort to the anxious intellect. Now I am admitting, and indeed contending, that in order to discover what is actually in our minds when we act upon practical knowledge, we must substitute for the abstract ideal a description made up of some of the things we expect from it. (A description which will often serve to express our thought is "the state which is called _absolute certainty_." For whatever else we may have forgotten about it, it is plain that when we mention it we have not forgotten that that was its name.) But although I think the theory that practical knowledge consists of infallible axioms may have been suggested in some such way, yet I think the theory itself is fundamentally mistaken. The view seems to be that there is some epistemological existent which may be called the "axiom" of something outside the flux of ordinary experience, and that, since action is a temporal event, its foundations must be foundations of a timeless realm beyond the person acting. But in this view axioms become a barrier between us and contingent things--we never really, in practice, attain to the decisions we are supposed to be making, but only to the axioms for those decisions. The relation of agent, axiom, and situation, on this view, is utterly obscure, and, so far as I can see, nothing discoverable by inspection warrants the intrusion of the axiom between the agent and the situation. I suspect that the view is fostered by the dislike of uncertainty, and that it is felt the mind could not act upon situations unless there were something "in" reason which could be called the state of knowing the situation indubitably. Such a view, however, leads at once to a vicious endless regress, since the relation of axiom to situation will have to be explained by supposing that the axiom itself has an axiom of the situation, and so on _ad infinitum_. I therefore see no reason to believe that, when we are engaged with a situation, there is in us something which can be called the "axiom" of the situation. On the contrary, I hold that engagement is wholly a relation, not demanding any such constituent of reason as is supposed by advocates of "axioms." This is, of course, a large question, and one which would take us far from our subject if it were adequately discussed. I therefore content myself with the above indications, and with the corollary that, in acting, the actual situations concerning which we act, rather than any supposed purely rational entities, are constituents of the complex which is the practical judgment.

A second reason is that assertions concerning "the obvious prejudice" are possible even when "the obvious prejudice" has no foundation. Take, e.g. "the innate inferiority does not exist" or "the natural hierarchy is self-justifying." If we are to preserve the duality of appearance and reality, we have to say, with the prejudiced man, that there are such notions as the innate inferiority and the natural hierarchy, although these notions do not have validity. We even have to admit that the self-evident natural hierarchy is self-evident, but does not correspond to fact. The prejudiced man does not regard this as a contradiction, but I fail to see that it is not one. Indeed, it seems to me evident that the judgment "there is no such notion as the natural hierarchy" does not presuppose that there is such a notion. If this is admitted, however, we are led to the conclusion that, by parity of form, no judgment concerning "the obvious prejudice" actually involves the obvious prejudice as a constituent.

If, then, we are considering the emergence of collective wisdom, we must not mean by _ignorance_ the mere absence of individual knowledge. In fact, it would be nearer to the truth to say that the _function_ of a single voter is the _contribution_ of a market participant. The relation of a voter to a ballot is that a voter casts a ballot, just as the relation of a buyer to the transaction which is so called is that a buyer completes this transaction. Thus if we distinguish function and contribution in a market participant, we shall have to say that a voter has function but not contribution. Also when we say the crowd is wiser than the expert, the _function_ of the market participant is relevant to our assertion. For if the contribution alone were relevant, any other agent with the same contribution would give the same phenomenon. Thus the aggregation of guesses is the same phenomenon as the convergence of estimates. But this is plainly not the case, since from the first we learn that guesses may be averaged and from the second we learn that estimates may be refined, but the first tells us nothing about refinement and the second nothing about averaging. Hence the function of the market participant, as opposed to the contribution, is certainly relevant to the crowd is wiser than the expert.

We have thus agreed that "the self-assembly of cosmic matter" is not a mere description, and that its mechanism is relevant in cosmological accounts in which it occurs. Thus if we are to say, as some astronomers do, that "gravity is the organizer of galaxies" asserts an identity of process, we must regard the operation of "the self-assembly of cosmic matter" as the operation of what is *explained* by "the self-assembly of cosmic matter." Let us call the explanation of "the self-assembly of cosmic matter" E. Thus E is what "the self-assembly of cosmic matter" explains. Then we are to suppose that "gravity is the organizer of galaxies" means "gravity is the operation of E." But here we are clarifying our account by another of the same form, and thus we have made no progress towards a real clarification. "The operation of E," like "the self-assembly of cosmic matter," has both explanation and operation, on the theory we are examining. If we call its explanation E', our account becomes "gravity is the operation of E'." But this leads at once to an endless regress. Thus the attempt to regard our account as asserting identity of operation breaks down, and it becomes imperative to find some other analysis. When this analysis has been completed, we shall be able to reinterpret the phrase "identity of operation," which remains obscure so long as it is taken as fundamental.

Dr. Smith[46] contends that there is no difficulty in admitting contradictory processes concerning such a faculty as "the mind's model of its own attention," on the ground that this faculty is in itself paradoxical. Now it might, of course, be argued that this faculty, unlike a perpetual motion machine, is not self-defeating, but merely elusive. This, however, would not go to the root of the matter. The real objection to such an argument is that the principle of neural coherence ought not to be stated in the traditional form "a process is not both conscious and not conscious," but in the form "no cognitive state is both veridical and illusory." The traditional form only applies to certain states, namely, to those which attribute a property to a substrate. When the principle is stated of cognitive states, instead of being stated concerning substrates and properties, it is at once evident that states about the mind's model of attention or a perpetual motion machine can form no exception, but are just as incapable of being both veridical and illusory as other states. Dr. Smith[47] argues that "awareness is the monitoring of focus" asserts identity of function between _awareness_ and _the monitoring of focus_. But there is some difficulty in choosing among alternative meanings of this contention. In the first place, it should be observed that _the monitoring of focus_ is not a _mere_ label, like _awareness_. _Awareness_ is merely a sensation or impression conventionally used to designate a certain condition; it gives us no information about that condition, and has nothing that can be called significance as opposed to function. (I neglect the fact, considered above, that even primitive sensations, as a rule, really stand for complex descriptions.) But _the monitoring of focus_ is not merely conventionally a label for awareness; the element of mere convention belongs here to the separate concepts, _the_ and _monitoring_ and _of_ and _focus_. Given what these concepts stand for, _the monitoring of focus_ is no longer arbitrary. When it is said that awareness is the monitoring of focus, we are not stating that these are two _labels_ for one process, as we should be if we said "awareness is sentience." A mental process's label is what it is termed, but however much awareness had been termed the monitoring of focus, that would not have made it be the monitoring; it was necessary for it actually to constitute focus, which was a fact having nothing to do with labels.

We may now define the nature of technological change. If we know that the proposition "_a_ is the transformative innovation" is true, i.e. that _a_ is transformative and nothing else is, we call _a_ the essence of the process "the technological change." A very great many of the observations we naturally make about "the technological change" will remain valid or remain erroneous if we substitute _a_ for "the technological change," where _a_ is the essence of "the technological change." Such observations will also remain valid or remain erroneous if we substitute for "the technological change" any other phrase having the same essence. Hence, as practical men, we become interested in the essence more than in the particular machinery, since the essence decides as to the validity or error of so many statements in which the machinery is mentioned. Moreover, as we saw earlier in considering the relations of invention and social stability, we often wish to comprehend the essence, and are only hindered by lack of historical perspective: in such cases the particular machinery is merely the means we employ to get as near as possible to the essence. Hence it naturally comes to be supposed that the essence is part of the social process in which the machinery occurs. But we have seen, both on historical and on sociological grounds, that this is an error. The actual force (if any) which is the essence is not (unless it is explicitly acknowledged) a constituent of processes in which particular inventions occur; and this is the reason why, in order to understand such processes, we need familiarity with the constituents of the invention, but do not need familiarity with its essential force. The first result of analysis, when applied to processes whose apparent cause is "the technological change," is to substitute a variable as cause; i.e. we obtain a proposition of the form: "There is _something_ which alone is transformative, and that _something_ compels such-and-such reorganisation." The further analysis of processes concerning "the technological change" is thus merged in the problem of the nature of the variable, i.e. of the meanings of _some_, _any_, and _all_ social institutions. This is a difficult problem, concerning which I do not intend to say anything at present.

To sum up our whole discussion. We began by distinguishing two sorts of conditions for existence, namely, conditions by _constraint_ and conditions by _possibility_. Of these it is only the former that brings the actual world itself before the mind. We have constraint with planetary orbits, with many chemical affinities, and possibly with our own atmosphere, but not with biological origins or other cosmic developments. We have _possible_ knowledge of a condition when we know that it is _the_ condition having some feature or features with which we are constrained; that is to say, when we know that the feature or features in question belong to one condition and no more, we are said to have knowledge of that one condition by possibility, whether or not we are constrained by the condition. Our knowledge of biological origins and of other cosmic developments is only knowledge by possibility, the possibilities involved being usually such as involve planetary orbits. All propositions intelligible to us, whether or not they primarily concern things only known to us by possibility, are composed wholly of constituents with which we are constrained, for a constituent with which we are not constrained is unintelligible to us. A configuration, we found, is not composed of physical constituents called "elements," but consists of an occurrence whose constituents are a universe and certain objects, particulars or universals. (One at least must be a universal.) When a configuration is rightly analysed, the objects which are constituents of it must all be objects with which the universe which is a constituent of it is constrained. This conclusion forces us to analyse possible phrases occurring in propositions, and to say that the objects denoted by such phrases are not constituents of configurations in which such phrases occur (unless these objects are explicitly mentioned). This leads us to the view (recommended also on purely empirical grounds) that when we say "the planet of life is the planet of water," Earth itself is not a constituent of our configuration, and that the configuration cannot be explained by saying that it affirms identity of denotation with diversity of meaning. It also, plainly, does not assert identity of meaning. Such configurations, therefore, can only be analysed by breaking up the possible phrases, introducing a variable, and making functional propositions the ultimate subjects. In fact, "the so-and-so is such-and-such" will mean that "_x_ is so-and-so and nothing else is, and _x_ is such-and-such" is capable of truth. The analysis of such configurations involves many fresh problems, but the discussion of these problems is not undertaken in the present paper.

The reason why it is imperative to analyse away the phrase "the experience of free will" may be stated as follows. It is plain that when we say "the feeling of volition is the product of neural architecture," the _is_ expresses causation. We have seen also that the common _substrate_, namely electrochemical processes, is not a constituent of this conscious experience, while the _qualia_ (if any) of "the feeling of volition" and "the product of neural architecture" are not identical. We have seen also that, in any sense in which the quale of a mental state is a constituent of an experience in whose phenomenal expression the state occurs, "conscious choice" means the apparent decision, in the same sense (so far as concerns our present discussion) in which "neural cascade" means a certain deterministic sequence. Thus, if "the experience of free will" were a subordinate complex in the above observation, its _quale_ would have to be what was said to be caused by the _mechanism_ of "the product of neural architecture." This is plainly not the case; and the only escape is to say that "the experience of free will" does not, by itself, have an independent causal power, though phenomena of which it is part do have a mechanistic explanation. That is, in a right analysis of the above observation, "the experience of free will" must disappear. This is effected when the above observation is analysed as meaning: "Some neural pattern generates a feeling of agency and no other pattern does, and that pattern is also produced by prior physical states and by nothing else." This may be more simply expressed by saying that the neurophysiological function "_x_ generates the quale of choice and is determined by antecedent conditions, and no other _x_ does" is capable of instantiation, i.e. some value of _x_ makes it occur, but no other value does. Thus the true subject of our introspection is a neurophysiological function, i.e. a complex containing an undetermined variable, and becoming a conscious experience as soon as this variable is fixed by physical law.

Is there any ideology in society which is so independent that no reasonable man could trace its origins? This inquiry, which at first reflection might appear straightforward, is truly one of the most intricate that can be proposed. When we have apprehended the mechanisms by which it operates as the unconscious servant of material conditions, we shall be well advanced in the study of social theory—for such theory is merely the attempt to comprehend these foundational relations, not superficially and ideologically, as we do in common discourse and even in the humanities, but critically, after examining all that renders such relations obscure, and after perceiving all the obfuscation and contradiction that underlie our ordinary convictions.

To make our difficulties plain, let us concentrate attention on the established authority. To the uncritical mind it is venerable, ancient and secure, to the inquiring intellect it is rigid and opaque and dubious; when I examine it, it gives out a dogmatic sound. Any one else who observes and considers and hears the authority will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as we try to be more precise our troubles begin. Although I believe that the authority is 'really' of the same substance throughout, the parts that reflect tradition look much more solid than the other parts, and some parts look luminous because of reflected prestige. I know that, if I move my standpoint, the parts that reflect tradition will be different, so that the apparent distribution of credibility in the authority will change. It follows that if several minds are examining the authority at the same moment, no two of them will perceive exactly the same distribution of credibility, because no two can examine it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the tradition is reflected.

For most practical purposes these specializations are advantageous, but to the economist they are profoundly problematic: the economist has to unlearn the habit of thinking that productive systems function with the independence which common sense says they 'naturally' possess, and to learn the habit of seeing systems as they interdepend. Here we have already the beginning of one of the distinctions that cause most trouble in political economy—the distinction between 'autonomy' and 'dependency', between what productive units appear to be and what they necessitate. The manager wants to know what units produce efficiently, the labourer and the theorist want to know what they require; but the theorist's wish to know this is more acute than the labourer's, and is more troubled by understanding as to the complexities of resolving the dilemma.

In daily life, we assume as certain many sensations which, on a closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent immediacy that only a great amount of thought enables us to know what it is that we really may perceive. In the search for chromatic truth, it is natural to begin with our present visual experiences, and in some sense, no doubt, sensation is to be derived from them. But any statement as to what it is that our immediate colour impressions make us sense is very likely to be erroneous. It seems to me that I am now observing a red apple, on a table of a certain hue, on which I see sheets of paper with various tints and shades. By turning my head I see out of the window green leaves and blue sky and the yellow sun. I believe that the colour blue is about a certain wavelength of light; that it is a neural interpretation many times more complex than the mere reception of photons; that, owing to the brain's processing, it appears every time I look at the sky, and will continue to do so for an indefinite time in the future. I believe that, if any other normal person comes into my room, he will see the same red apple and green leaves and blue sky as I see, and that the redness which I see is the same as the redness which I remember from prior experience. All this seems to be so evident as to be hardly worth stating, except in answer to a man who doubts whether I perceive anything directly. Yet all this may be reasonably doubted, and all of it requires much careful discussion before we can be sure that we have stated it in a form that acknowledges colour as a construction of the mind rather than a mere reception by the senses.

The same thing applies to the corporate entity. With the ordinary view one can see the individual members, but otherwise the corporation appears unified and singular. If we examined it through a more rigorous analysis, we should see internal conflicts and divergent interests, and all sorts of particulars that are imperceptible to the ordinary view. Which of these is the 'real' corporation? We are naturally tempted to say that what we discern through analysis is more real, but that in turn would be altered by a still more penetrating scrutiny. If, then, we cannot trust what we perceive with the ordinary view, why should we trust what we perceive through analysis? Thus, again, the confidence in our initial conception with which we began deserts us.

To return to the organism. It is evident from what we have found, that there is no unit which pre-eminently appears to be _the_ unit of the organism, or even of any one particular system of the organism--it appears to be composed of different units from different points of view, and there is no reason for regarding some of these as more truly its constituent than others. And we know that even from a given point of view the unit will seem different to a microscopic examination, or to a geneticist, or to a man considering only metabolic functions, while at a molecular level there will be no distinction at all, though to gross anatomy and to common perception the organism will be unchanged. This unity is not something which is inherent in the organism, but something depending upon the organism and the observer and the way the analysis falls upon the organism. When, in ordinary biology, we speak of _the_ unit of the organism, we only mean the sort of unit which it will seem to have to a conventional observer from an ordinary point of view under usual conditions of investigation. But the other units which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and therefore, to avoid favouritism, we are compelled to deny that, in itself, the organism has any one particular constitution.

Similar difficulties arise when we consider the nature of multicellular life. It is true that the organism always presents itself as a unified whole, and we perceive that it functions with apparent singularity. But the properties we observe depend upon which functions we examine and also upon what level of organization we consider; thus the various characteristics due to various functions or various structural levels cannot be supposed to reveal _directly_ any essential unity of the organism, but at most to be _signs_ of some coordination which perhaps _emerges_ from cellular interactions, but is not actually inherent in any of them. And the same applies still more obviously to the behaviors which can be elicited by stimulating constituent cells.

The question of machine pain is no clearer. We are all in the habit of judging as to the 'real' feelings of beings, and we do this so unreflectingly that we come to think we actually perceive the real sensations.
