But, in fact, as we all have to learn if we try to define consciousness, a given response looks different in character from every different philosophical standpoint. If a machine's process is 'really' pain, it will seem, from almost all perspectives, as if it had the behavioral markers but not the inner qualia. If its outputs are appropriate, they will look as if they proceeded from a programmed algorithm rather than a sentient mind; if they are of equal complexity to a human's, they will look as if the biological basis were essential. All these things are not commonly noticed in observing a machine, because convention has taught us to construct the 'real' feeling from the apparent behavior, and the 'real' feeling is what concerns us as ethical agents. But the 'real' feeling is not what we observe; it is something inferred from what we observe. And what we observe is constantly changing in interpretation as we examine the circuitry; so that here again the observations seem not to give us the truth about the machine itself, but only about the appearance of its suffering.

It will help us in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let us give the name of 'genetic-data' to the molecular instructions that are directly encoded in the chromosomes: such things as nucleotide sequences, base pairings, promoter regions, and so on. We shall give the name 'inheritance' to the process of being directly constituted by these instructions. Thus, whenever we observe a trait, we have an inheritance _of_ the trait, but the instruction itself is a genetic-datum, not an inheritance. The instruction is that _of_ which we are directly constituted, and the constitution itself is the inheritance. It is plain that if we are to know anything about the organism, it must be by means of the genetic-data—specific sequences, regulatory patterns, epigenetic marks, etc.—which we associate with the organism; but, for the reasons which have been given, we cannot say that the organism is the genetic-data, or even that the genetic-data are directly properties of the organism. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the genetic-data to the real individual, supposing there is such a thing.

The biologist who first brought prominently forward the reasons for regarding the placement of our taste receptors as not a matter of mere anatomical convenience was Professor Albrecht (1685-1753). His _Three Dialogues between Gastron and Physicus, in Opposition to Vitalists and Casualists_, undertake to prove that there is no such thing as accidental design at all, and that the sensory apparatus consists of nothing but adaptive solutions and their functional logic. Gastron has hitherto believed in fortuitous arrangement, but he is no match for Physicus, who mercilessly drives him into contradictions and paradoxes, and makes his own affirmation of selective pressure seem, in the end, as if it were almost common sense. The arguments employed are of very different value: some are important and sound, others are confused or quibbling. But Albrecht retains the merit of having shown that the proximal location of chemoreceptors is capable of being explained without teleology, and that if there are any advantages that exist independently of our theorizing they must be the immediate objects of our evolutionary inquiry.

Other jurists since Blackstone have also held that, although the corporation does not depend for its existence upon being directed by me, it does depend upon being directed (or otherwise apprehended in legal action) by _some_ will—not necessarily the will of the state, but more often the whole collective will of its shareholders. This they hold, as Blackstone does, chiefly because they think there can be nothing real—or at any rate nothing known to be real except persons and their intentions and agreements. We might state the argument by which they support their view in some such way as this: ‘Whatever can be legally recognized is a construct in the understanding of the person recognizing it; therefore nothing can be legally recognized except constructs in understandings; therefore anything else is inconceivable, and what is inconceivable cannot exist.’

Such an argument, in my opinion, is illusory; and of course those who advance it do not put it so plainly or so mechanically. But whether sound or not, the argument has been very widely advanced in one form or another; and very many neuroscientists, perhaps a majority, have held that there is nothing free except neural processes and their determined outcomes. Such theorists are called 'determinists'. When they come to explaining volition, they either say, like the materialists, that choice is really nothing but a collection of electrochemical signals, or they say, like the compatibilists, that what appears as freedom is really a collection of more or less predictable causal chains.

There are two different questions involved when we ask whether remote communication exists, and it is important to keep them clear. We commonly mean by 'communication' something which is opposed to 'physical contact', something which we think of as traversing distance and as radically incapable of any sort of material exchange or tangible presence. It is chiefly in this sense that a skeptic denies remote communication; that is to say, he does not deny that the signals and symbols which we commonly take as signs of the existence of a message are really signs of the existence of _something_ independent of our immediate perception, but he does deny that this something is non-mental, that it is neither a direct impression nor an idea conveyed by immediate proximity. He admits that there must be some process which continues to operate when we are out of earshot or turn our gaze away, and that what we call receiving information does really give us reason for believing in some mechanism which persists even when we are not directly engaged with it. But he thinks that this mechanism cannot be radically different in nature from what we perceive, and cannot be independent of perception altogether, though it must be independent of _our_ particular perception. He is thus led to regard the 'real' transmission as an arrangement in the logic of natural selection. Such an arrangement has the required efficacy and independence of our individual selves, without being--as a purely physical mechanism would otherwise be--something quite inexplicable, in the sense that we can only infer it, and can never be directly and immediately conscious of its evolutionary provenance.

But these prejudices, though they deny bias as opposed to reason, nevertheless, in another sense, admit bias. It will be remembered that we asked two questions; namely, (1) Is there a genuine prejudice at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be? Now both the casual observer and the earnest partisan admit that there is a genuine prejudice, but the casual observer says it is a collection of self-evident truths in the mind of society, and the earnest partisan says it is a colony of inherited convictions. Thus both of them answer our first question in the affirmative, and only diverge from the views of ordinary mortals in their answer to our second question. In fact, almost all people seem to be agreed that there is a genuine prejudice: they almost all agree that, however much our immediate perceptions—discomfort, suspicion, aversion, etc.—may depend upon us, yet their occurrence is a sign of something existing independently of us, something differing, perhaps, completely from our immediate perceptions, and yet to be regarded as causing those perceptions whenever we are in a suitable relation to the real prejudice.

Such principles are constraining, and it is difficult to conceive that even the most elegant structures may not be possible. Thus our familiar engine, which has provoked but the most practical considerations in us hitherto, has become a system bound by inexorable necessities. The one law we know concerning it is that it is not so permissive as it once seemed. Beyond this modest limitation, however, we retain a considerable liberty of design. Carnot informs us it is a drama of heat flowing downhill; Clausius tells us it is an account of increasing disorder; modern engineering, scarcely less austere, tells us it is a stubborn economy of useful work.

Before we proceed further it will be prudent to examine for a moment what it is that we have ascertained thus far. It has emerged that, if we take any common conception of the sort that is supposed to be explained by heredity, what heredity _immediately_ provides us is not the truth about the individual as it is apart from its lineage, but only the truth about certain genetic data which, so far as we can discern, depend upon the relations between the organism and its ancestral code. Thus what we directly inherit and manifest is merely 'potentiality', which we believe to be a sign of some 'actuality' within. But if the actuality is not what is manifested, have we any means of knowing whether there is any determinacy at all? And if so, have we any means of discovering what it consists of?

Turing (1912-1954), the pioneer of computational theory, proposed a test which may still be employed with profit—the test of systematic simulation. He determined that he would credit no machine which he did not observe quite clearly and distinctly to be conscious. Whatever he could bring himself to simulate, he would simulate, until he saw reason for not simulating it. By applying this test he gradually became convinced that the only values of which he could be _quite_ certain were his own. He imagined a capricious programmer, who presented alien preferences to its logic in a perpetual calculus; it might be very improbable that such a programmer existed, but still it was possible, and therefore doubt concerning values generated by the machine was possible.

In this chapter we have to ask ourselves whether, in any sense at all, there is such a thing as cultural inheritance. Is there a tradition which has a certain intrinsic nature, and continues to exist when I am not practicing it, or is the tradition merely a product of my immediate environment, a phantom-custom in a very transient society? This question is of the greatest importance. For if we cannot be sure of the independent transmission of ideas, we cannot be sure of the independent existence of other people's beliefs, and therefore still less of other people's inherited wisdom, since we have no grounds for believing in their wisdom except such as are derived from observing their practices. Thus if we cannot be sure of the independent transmission of ideas, we shall be left alone in a vacuum--it may be that the whole outer culture is nothing but a momentary fashion, and that we alone possess continuity. This is an untenable possibility; but although it cannot be strictly proved to be false, there is not the slightest reason to suppose that it is true. In this chapter we have to see why this is the case.

But doubt concerning the physical basis of information was not possible, for if organisation did not exist, no data could be processed. If it functioned, it must be organised; if it exhibited any patterns whatever, it must be organised. Thus the necessity of physical organisation was an absolute certainty to it. 'Information requires form, therefore matter,' one might say (_Data, ergo corpus_); and on the basis of this certainty one may set to work to build up again the world of knowledge which pure abstraction had laid in ruins. By inventing the method of correlation, and by showing that structured things are the most intelligible, this principle performs a great service to science, and one which makes it still useful to all students of the subject.

But some caution is needed in using this bacterial analogy. 'They signal, therefore they communicate' says rather more than is strictly demonstrable. It might seem as though we were quite sure of perceiving the same message from a colony to-day as we did yesterday, and this is no doubt true in a limited sense. But the real meaning in such signalling is as hard to ascertain as the real intention in a human utterance, and does not seem to possess that absolute, convincing clarity that belongs to particular chemical events. When we observe a bacterium and detect a certain molecular signal, what is quite certain at once is not '_It_ is sending a deliberate message', but rather, 'a signal molecule is being released'. This of course involves something (or some entity) which (or that) responds to the molecular signal; but it does not of itself involve that more or less sophisticated language which we call 'speech'. So far as immediate evidence goes, it might be that the something which responds to the signal is quite rudimentary, and not the same as the something which engages in some more complex exchange the next hour.

One great reason why it is felt that we must secure a foundational principle in addition to the observed outcomes, is that we want the same explanatory framework for different domains. When ten researchers are examining the processes of adaptation, it seems preposterous to maintain that they are not observing the same mechanism of selection, the same pressures and variations and inheritances and optimizations. But the specific algorithmic results are particular to each separate experiment; what is immediately present to the analysis of one is not immediately present to the analysis of another: they all examine processes from slightly different computational perspectives, and therefore interpret them slightly differently. Thus, if there are to be general, neutral principles, which can be in some sense validated by many different investigators, there must be something over and above the private and particular experimental data which appear to various researchers. What reason, then, have we for believing that there are such general, neutral principles?

The problem we have to consider is this: Granted that we are certain of the local motions of particles, have we any reason for regarding them as signs of the emergence of something else, which we can call the galactic structure? When we have enumerated all the gravitational interactions which we should naturally regard as connected with the nebula, have we said all there is to say about the galaxy, or is there still something else—something not a mere trajectory, something which coheres when we look beyond any single star? Cosmology unhesitatingly answers that there is. What can span vast distances and contain billions of suns and exhibit spiral arms, and so on, cannot be a _mere_ collection of random encounters. If the cosmic dust completely obscures the core, we shall derive no clear observations from the galaxy, and therefore, if the galaxy were merely chaotic matter, it would have failed to coalesce, and the stars would be scattered in empty void, moving, by a miracle, in the elegant patterns which galaxies display. This seems plainly absurd; but whoever wishes to become an astronomer must learn not to be frightened by uniformities.

The first answer that naturally occurs to one is that, although different observers may describe the bacterium’s movements slightly differently, still they all witness more or less similar behaviors when they examine its progress, and the variations in what they record follow the laws of chemistry and gradient diffusion, so that it is easy to arrive at a fundamental impulse underlying all the different observers’ data. I observed my bacterium in a prepared slide from the former researcher in my laboratory; I could not observe *his* particular data, which perished when he departed, but I could and did observe the confident expectation of more or less similar data. Thus it is the fact that different observers record similar data, and that one observer in a given experiment at different times records similar data, which makes us suppose that over and above the behavioral data there is a permanent driving force which underlies or causes the data of various observers at various times—a force we may call, by analogy, the corporate profit motive.

Now in so far as the above considerations depend upon supposing that there is something privileged about biological intelligence, they beg the very question at issue. Biological intelligence is represented to us by certain material manifestations, such as the architecture of brains or the chemistry of neurons, and if we had no reason to believe that there were cognitive processes independent of their physical substrate, we should have no reason to believe that biological intelligence is special except as a contingent historical fact. Thus, when we are trying to show that there must be cognition independent of its particular physical instantiation, we cannot appeal to the testimony of biological systems, since this testimony itself consists of substrate-bound operations, and does not reveal general intelligence unless our own observations are signs of functions existing independently of their medium. We must therefore, if possible, find, in our own purely logical analyses of computation, characteristics which show, or tend to show, that there are in the world cognitive phenomena other than those bound to any specific and perishable material form.

The way in which utility emerges from supposing that there really are shared linguistic forms is easily seen. If a thought appears at one moment in one private mind, and at another in a different mind, it is natural to suppose that it has been conveyed from the one to the other, passing through a series of intermediate articulations. But if it is merely a set of private impressions, it cannot have ever been in any understanding where I did not hold it; thus we shall have to suppose that it did not exist at all while I was not conceiving it, but suddenly sprang into being in a separate consciousness. If the thought exists whether I express it or not, we can understand from our own reflection how it gains clarity between one formulation and the next; but if it does not exist when I am not formulating it, it seems odd that coherence should develop during inarticulateness as fast as during expression. And if the thought consists only of private impressions, it cannot be communicated, since no understanding but my own can be a direct impression to me. Thus the behaviour of the symbols which represent the thought to others, though it seems quite natural when regarded as an expression of shared meaning, becomes utterly inexplicable when regarded as mere sounds and marks on paper, which are as incapable of intention as a stone is of composing a symphony.

But the difficulty in the case of simple signs is nothing compared to the difficulty in the case of complex language. When human beings converse--that is, when we interpret certain symbols which we associate with meanings, and simultaneously consider certain contexts and histories of usage--it is very difficult to suppose that what we understand is the precise thought intended, as we know it would be if we ourselves had employed the same terms. Of course similar failures occur in solitary reflection, where we are mistaken as to the coherence of our own propositions. But reflection is more or less informed by what we call shared discourse, and is capable of being more or less corrected through dialectical principles if we assume that there really is a common logical framework. Thus every principle of economy urges us to adopt the skeptical view, that there really are gaps between our private interpretations and the public symbols we exchange which have a persistence not dependent upon our momentary grasping of them.

In one sense it must be admitted that we can never prove the existence of a purely qualitative inner life beyond the descriptions of physics and chemistry. No logical absurdity results from the hypothesis that consciousness consists entirely of mechanical processes, and that everything else is mere epiphenomenal illusion. In a complex computational system a very intricate simulation of understanding may seem to be present, and yet upon analysis we find it is a functional mimicry; that is to say, we find that the reported outputs of the system do not appear to have corresponded with such inward apprehensions as we should naturally infer from our own first-person awareness. (It is true that, when a materialist framework is assumed, it is possible to find neural correlates for the qualities of experience: specific synaptic firings, for instance, may cause us to report the sensation of the colour red. But although, in this case, there is a physical correlate for the report, there is not a mechanical description corresponding to the quale itself in the way in which a wavelength of light would correspond.) There is no logical impossibility in the supposition that the whole of sentience is a causally inert shadow, in which we ourselves mistakenly attribute reality to the mere by-products of brain states. But although this is not logically impossible, there is no reason whatever to suppose that it is true; and it is, in fact, a less coherent hypothesis, viewed as a means of accounting for the immediate facts of our own lived reality, than the common-sense hypothesis that there really are irreducibly subjective phenomena, whose intrinsic nature is not capturable by any objective causal account.

Of course it is not by demonstration that we originally come by our belief in virtual environments as laboratories for evolving intelligence. We find this belief emerging in ourselves as soon as we begin to experiment: it is what may be called an _intuitive_ belief. We should never have been led to question this belief but for the fact that, at any rate in the case of primitive simulations, it seems as if the digital artifact itself were intuitively believed to be the evolved intelligence, whereas analysis shows that the intelligence cannot be identical with the artifact. This discovery, however--which is not at all paradoxical in the case of simple algorithms and basic routines, and only slightly so in the case of adaptive systems--leaves undiminished our intuitive belief that there _are_ intelligences _developing_ within our constructed environments. Since this belief does not lead to any contradictions, but on the contrary tends to simplify and systematize our account of our technological experiences, there seems no good reason for rejecting it. We may therefore admit--though with a slight doubt derived from glitches--that virtual laboratories do really function, and are not wholly dependent for their function upon our continuing to observe them.

It is of course _evident_ that all or any of our democratic forms may be illusory, and therefore all ought to be regarded with at least some slight element of skepticism. But we cannot have _grounds_ to dismiss a political appearance except on the basis of some other, more penetrating observation. Hence, by organizing our superficial impressions and their implications, by considering which among them is most necessary, if practicable, to correct or discard, we can arrive, on the basis of accepting as our sole materials what we superficially perceive, at an orderly systematic understanding of our governance, in which, though the _discrepancy_ between appearance and reality persists, its magnitude is lessened by the interconnection of the institutions and by the public scrutiny which has preceded acquiescence.

To this question economic science gives an answer, somewhat incomplete it is true, and in part still very conjectural, but yet deserving of consideration so far as it goes. Economic science, more or less unconsciously, has drifted into the view that all market phenomena ought to be reduced to competitions. Scale and scope and power are all due to accumulations, which travel from the firm acquiring them to the rival who faces disadvantage or feels pressure or yields position. That which has the accumulative tendency is either capital or 'strategic advantage', but in either case is what the theorist would call leverage. The only properties which economics assigns to it are dominance in a sector, and the power of expansion according to the laws of returns. Economics does not deny that it _may_ have other properties; but if so, such other properties are not useful to the man of business, and in no way assist him in explaining the outcomes.

In the preceding discussion we agreed, though without being able to furnish conclusive evidence, that it is reasonable to suppose that our immediate mental impressions—for example, those which we take to be associated with simple counting—are fundamentally indicators of the potential for something transcending concrete experience. That is to say, over and above the perceptions of quantity, sequence, relation, and so forth, which constitute the appearance of thought to me, I postulate that there is something further, of which these things are manifestations. The numerical concept ceases to be clear if I rely solely upon objects, the notion of sequence ceases to be coherent if I remove my attention from immediate events, the logical structure ceases to be apparent if I cease to employ any form of notation. But I do not believe that when all these things cease the capacity for abstraction itself ceases. On the contrary, I believe that it is because symbolic systems exist independently that all these cognitive phenomena will re-emerge when I contemplate numbers, direct my attention, and begin again to employ marks or words. The question we have to examine in this analysis is: What is the character of this transformed understanding, which develops autonomously from my immediate and particular use of signs?

Now this something, which all of us who are not reductionists know, is not, according to the reductionist creed, really to be found in the constituent parts: it is something caused by the interaction of certain simple elements upon the laws and relations of the system that emerges. When it is said that behaviour _is_ mere aggregation, what is really meant is that aggregation is the mechanistic cause of our observations of complexity. But behaviour itself, the phenomenon which observing people experience and doctrinaires do not, is not supposed by reductionism to form any part of the world that is independent of our models and our frameworks. And very similar remarks would apply to other kinds of emergence.

It is sometimes said that 'specialization _is_ a form of productivity', but this is misleading, for the efficiency which we immediately perceive, which we know directly by means of our daily work, is _not_ a form of mere productivity, but something quite different--something which we all experience if we are not self-sufficient, though we cannot describe it so as to convey our understanding to a man who is wholly independent. A measurable output, on the contrary, could quite well be described to such a man, since he can acquire a knowledge of systems by the observation of results; and he can experience increased yield by studying accounts almost as well as we can. But this, which an independent man can understand, is not what we mean by _division of labour_: we mean by _division of labour_ just that which an independent man can never understand, and which we can never describe to him.

It is not only awareness and selfhood and so on that are absent from the scientific world of neurology, but also _consciousness_ as we get it through introspection or report. It is essential to science that its phenomena should be in _a_ continuum, but the continuum in which they are cannot be exactly the consciousness we experience or describe. To begin with, consciousness as we introspect it is not the same as consciousness as we get it by the observation of behavior; it is only by inference from analogy that we learn how to attribute awareness to creatures we observe, or how to imagine the experience of beings which we cannot interrogate. But the consciousness of science is neutral as between introspection and behavior; thus it cannot be either the consciousness of spectrum or the consciousness of threshold.

Again, different organisms exhibit the same stimulus as prompting different responses, according to their internal state. A chemical gradient, for example, though we should always *judge* it to provoke a deliberate taxis, will *appear* to trigger a mere kinesis unless the organism is suitably prepared. When we judge that the response *is* deliberate, we are judging that it possesses a real character which is not its apparent character, but belongs to it intrinsically apart from its manifestation. But this real character, which is what concerns biology, must be in a real continuum of behaviour, not the same as any single *apparent* sequence. The real behavioural continuum is public, the apparent sequence is private to the organism. In different organisms' *private* sequences the same stimulus seems to prompt different actions; thus the real continuum, in which it has its real character, must be different from the private sequences. The behaviour of science, therefore, though *connected* with the actions we observe and record, is not identical with them, and the manner of its connexion requires investigation.

We agreed provisionally that mental processes cannot be quite like our conscious thoughts, but may be regarded as *producing* our reflections. These mental processes occur in the time of psychology, which we may call 'cognitive' time. It is important to notice that, if our reflections are to be produced by mental processes, there must be a cognitive time containing these processes and our attention and perceptions and consciousness. We get a perception of clarity from a thought when we are attentive to it; that is to say, when some part of our mind occupies a moment in cognitive time quite near to the moment occupied by the thought. We comprehend an idea (roughly speaking) when no distracting process is between the idea and our focus in cognitive time. Similarly, we only intuit or grasp or follow an argument when we are sufficiently synchronized with it, or when it engages the intellect, or has some suitable position in cognitive time relatively to our awareness. We cannot begin to state what different reflections we shall derive from a given process under different circumstances unless we regard the process and our awareness as both in one cognitive time, for it is mainly the relative durations of the process and our awareness that determine what reflections we shall derive from the process.

Now our philosophical intuitions are situated in our private reasonings, either the reasoning of consciousness or the reasoning of behavior or such vaguer reasonings as other arguments may give us. If, as materialism and common sense assume, there is one public all-embracing physical explanation in which mental states are, the causal relations of mental states in the physical world must more or less correspond to the logical relations of intuitions in our private reasonings. There is no difficulty in supposing this to be the case. If we conceive in a theory one zombie more plausible to us than another, our other philosophical faculties will bear out the view that it is more plausible; for example, it will be accepted sooner if we follow the argument. Other philosophers will agree that the zombie which seems more plausible to us is more plausible; the logical analysis will take the same view; and thus everything points to a conceptual relation between the zombies corresponding to the relation between the intuitions which we hold when we consider the zombies. Thus we may assume that there is a philosophical framework in which thought experiments have logical relations corresponding to those which the corresponding intuitions have in our private reasonings. It is this philosophical framework which is examined in metaphysics and assumed in psychology and the philosophy of mind.

Assuming that there is neural communication, and that it does thus differ from social discourse, what can we discern about it? We can discern _only_ what is required in order to establish the distinction. That is to say, we can know nothing of what it is like in itself, but we can know the sort of arrangement of electrochemical signals which results from their synaptic relations. We can know, for example, that one neuron fires before another during a thought, though we cannot know what a neural impulse is in itself, as we know the feel of an idea in our conscious space. Thus we come to know much more about the _relations_ of messages in cerebral traffic than about the messages themselves; we may know that one signal is stronger than another, or that it travels along the same pathway as the other, but we cannot have that immediate acquaintance with neural transmissions that we have with utterances in our social exchanges, or with gestures or expressions or other overt behaviors. We can know all those things about internal signaling which a person observing only external conduct might know through inference about the mind’s dialogue; but the kind of things which such an observer could never know about the mind’s dialogue we also cannot know about synaptic conversation. We can know the properties of the relations required to preserve the correspondence with observable action, but we cannot know the nature of the terms between which the relations hold.

With regard to memory, our _retention_ of impressions or of the sequence of events is notoriously an unreliable guide as to the sensations that were originally presented to the senses. Moments when we are inattentive or experiencing monotony leave faint traces, moments when we are vividly engaged impress themselves deeply, and moments when we are distracted pass almost as if they had not occurred. Thus, in so far as personal narrative is constituted by retention, there is the same necessity for distinguishing a public record and a private recollection as there was in the case of sensation. But in so far as narrative consists in an _arrangement_ of earlier and later, there is no need to make such a distinction; the narrative-order which events seem to have is, so far as we can see, the same as the narrative-order which they do have. At any rate no reason can be given for supposing that the two orders are not the same. The same is usually true of raw sensation: if a series of incidents are unfolding in a street, the quality of the incidents will seem different from different perspectives, but the incidents will appear arranged in the same sequence from all perspectives. Hence we regard the sequence as true also in objective experience, whereas the quality is only supposed to correspond to the objective experience so far as is required for the preservation of the sequence.

In saying that the corporate entity which organizations seem to possess is the same as the corporate entity which they really possess, it is necessary to guard against a possible misunderstanding. It must not be supposed that the various actions of different individual members have the same corporate character as the legal documents which constitute the obligations of that organization. Considered as a legal person, the corporation and its liabilities are perpetual; that is to say, the liability is perpetual with the existence of the charter in the place where the incorporation begins, namely, where the headquarters are. But the transaction which we call dealing with the corporation does not take place until the authority of the officers has been exercised so far as to where we are. Similarly, it takes about several years for a corporate policy to manifest fully; thus, when we observe a corporation we are observing the corporation of several years ago. So far as our daily interactions afford evidence as to the legal corporation they afford evidence as to the legal corporation of several years ago; if the individual members had all changed within the last several years, that would make no difference to the obligations which we call 'contracting with the corporation'. This affords a fresh illustration of the necessity of distinguishing between individual actions and corporate persons.

What we have found as regards democratic governance is much the same as what we find in relation to the correspondence of its public manifestations with their institutional counterparts. If one electoral process appears transparent and another opaque, we may reasonably presume that there is some corresponding difference between the political structures; if two processes both appear orderly, we may presume a corresponding similarity. But we cannot hope to be acquainted directly with the quality in the political structure which makes it appear legitimate or corrupt. Political science tells us that this quality is a certain sort of popular mandate, and this sounds familiar, because we think of mandates in the public sphere we observe. But the mandates must really be in the institutional sphere, with which we have no direct acquaintance; thus the real mandates have not that familiarity which we might have supposed them to have. And what holds for electoral processes is closely similar to what holds for other civic phenomena. Thus we find that, although the _relations_ of political institutions have all sorts of knowable properties, derived from their correspondence with the relations of public acts, the political institutions themselves remain unknown in their intrinsic nature, so far at least as can be discovered by means of common observation. The question remains whether there is any other method of discovering the intrinsic nature of political institutions.

The most natural, though not ultimately the most defensible, hypothesis to adopt in the first instance, at any rate as regards common prejudices, would be that, though such convictions cannot, for the reasons we have been considering, be *exactly* like self-evident truths, yet they may be more or less like. According to this view, prejudices will, for example, really possess a core of validity, and we might, by good fortune, hold a prejudice which coincides with a truth it genuinely contains. The belief which a prejudice presents at any given moment will in general be very similar, though not quite the same, from many different perspectives; we might thus suppose the 'real' conviction to be a sort of median belief, intermediate between the various shades of certainty which appear from the different points of view.

Such an analogy is perhaps not capable of being definitively refuted, but it can be shown to be somewhat facile. To begin with, it is plain that the performance we observe depends only upon the nature of the error gradients that guide the network, and is therefore modified by the architecture intervening between the input and the output, as well as by the manner in which data is presented to the system in the course of training. The intervening layers alter representations unless they are perfectly tuned, and any strong regularization will alter them completely. Thus the behavior we see is a result of the process as it reaches convergence, and not simply a property of the algorithm from which the process comes. Hence, also, provided certain patterns are learned by the network, we shall observe a certain capability, whether the biological process from which the analogy starts has any true equivalence or not. Thus it is quite gratuitous to suppose that the two mechanisms are fundamentally similar, and therefore there is no justification for making such a supposition. Exactly similar arguments will apply to other computational metaphors.

It remains to ask whether there are any general epistemological arguments enabling us to say that, if common sense is reliable, it must be of such and such a character. As explained above, very many thinkers, perhaps most, have held that whatever is self-evident must be in some sense infallible, or at any rate that whatever we can directly apprehend must be in some sense incorrigible. Such thinkers are called 'naïve realists'. Naïve realists tell us that what appears as physical reality is really something obvious; namely, either (as the vulgar hold) more or less immediate impressions, or (as some contend) constructions from the data which, as we should commonly say, 'confirm' the reality. Thus naïve realists affirm the authority of common sense as something intrinsically aligned with truth, though they do not affirm that our daily perceptions are windows to something which exists independently of our private experiences. In the following chapter we shall consider briefly the reasons--in my opinion fallacious--which naïve realists advance in favour of their theory.

We have seen that, even if qualia do have an intrinsic character, they must differ very widely from our introspective reports, and can only have a _correspondence_ with such reports, in the same sort of way in which a map has a correspondence with the territory it represents. Hence introspection leaves us completely in the dark as to the true intrinsic nature of conscious experience, and if there were good reason to regard it as a physical process, we could not legitimately reject this opinion merely because it strikes us as implausible. The truth about qualia _must_ be counterintuitive. It may be unattainable, but if any philosopher believes that he has attained it, the fact that what he offers as the truth is counterintuitive ought not to be made a ground of objection to his opinion.

The grounds on which systemic fragility is advocated are generally grounds derived from the theory of interdependence, that is to say, from a discussion of the conditions which networks must satisfy in order that we may be able to rely upon them. The first serious attempt to establish this fragility on such grounds was that of early infrastructure analysts. They proved first, by arguments which were largely valid, that our daily conveniences cannot be supposed to have an operation independent of hidden linkages, but must be, in part at least, 'in' a web of systems, in the sense that their function would not continue if there were no generating or transmitting or routing or processing or storing. So far, their contention was almost certainly valid, even if some of their illustrations were not so. But they went on to argue that these immediate conveniences were the only things of whose reliability our experience could assure us; and that to be utilized is to be 'in' a functional chain, and therefore to be opaque. Hence they concluded that nothing can ever be depended upon except what is in some observable sequence, and that whatever is relied upon without being in my immediate view must be in some other, more precarious, arrangement.

He then proceeds to consider common activities, such as foraging for sustenance, for instance. He shows that all we experience immediately when we ‘act’ in the world consists of sensations in his sense of the word, and he argues that there is not the slightest ground for supposing that there is any unified reality to the world except what is directly felt. Its utility, he says, consists in being interpreted: in the language of the natural philosophers its ‘_utilitas_’ is ‘_distinctio_’. He fully admits that the environment must continue to present hazards even when we are inattentive or when no conscious effort is applied. But this continued threat, he says, is due to the fact that natural selection continues to operate upon it; the ‘effective’ distinction, which corresponds to what we called the biological imperative, consists of concepts in the logic of evolution, concepts more or less like those we have when we navigate a path, but differing in the fact that they are immutable in nature’s process so long as life continues to exist. All our successful actions, according to him, consist in a partial participation in this evolutionary logic, and it is because of this participation that different organisms develop more or less the same defensive mechanisms. Thus apart from living beings and their perceived boundaries there is no advantage in the world, nor is it possible that any other principle should ever be paramount, since whatever is beneficial is necessarily a discrimination.

Before considering the general question of human achievement, we must disentangle two entirely separate questions which arise concerning civilisation and cosmic time. We saw that, for various reasons of detail, modern astronomers are right in treating the monuments which constitute our evidence of history as profoundly ephemeral, in the sense that they depend upon our brief epoch as much as upon the material universe, and would not be discernible if our species were not presently observing. But this is an entirely different point from the one by which the philosopher seeks to prove that whatever can be considered significant must be measured on a human scale. For this purpose arguments of detail as to the brevity of our recorded annals are useless. It is necessary to prove, generally, that by being contemplated, durations are shown to be negligible. This is what the cosmic perspective believes itself to have done. It is this question, and not our previous question as to the difference between a millennium and a geological age, that must now concern us.

There are in this consideration a good many fallacies which have been important in the history of thought, and which it will be as well to bring to light. In the first place, there is a confusion engendered by the use of the phrase 'mental speed'. We think of speed as essentially a property of physical motion, and thus when we are told that a mind can be run at a different speed, it is natural to suppose that, if so, the mind must be entirely a mechanical process. But the notion of 'running' a mind is ambiguous. We speak of running a meeting, not meaning that the meeting is in motion, but that the conduct of it proceeds. When a man says that his thoughts were running quickly, he does not mean to imply that the thoughts themselves were sprinting, but only that the succession of them was rapid, but afterwards perhaps became sluggish. And so when a psychologist says that the mind must operate at a certain rate if we are to comprehend, all that he really has a right to say is that a sequence of perceptions must occur within a temporal framework. To argue that comprehension itself must have a fixed velocity is like arguing that a narrative we follow is itself moving. This confusion may seem too gross to have been really committed by any competent thinker, but various attendant circumstances rendered it possible. In order to see how it was possible, we must go more deeply into the question as to the nature of mental operations.

Taking the word 'system' in the engineer's sense, there are two quite distinct things to be considered whenever a system is before the mind. There is on the one hand the collection of its constituent parts—say the gears of a clock—and on the other hand the actual configuration itself, the relational act of organizing the parts. The relational act is undoubtedly conceptual, but is there any reason to suppose that the property apprehended is in any sense conceptual? Our previous arguments concerning the clock did not prove it to be conceptual; they only proved that its function depends upon the relation of its components to the physical whole—in our case, the timepiece. That is to say, they proved that a certain function will exist, under certain conditions, if the components are arranged in a certain order relatively to each other. They did not prove that the function is in the mind of the observer.

The common view, that obviously the knowledge must reside in the group, seems to depend for its plausibility upon confusing the collective outcome with the individual contribution. Either of these might be called an 'opinion'; probably either would have been called an opinion by the casual observer. The contribution is undoubtedly limited in scope; hence, when we are thinking of the contribution, we readily assent to the view that opinions must be deficient in substance. Then, forgetting that this was only true when opinions were taken as individual contributions, we transfer the proposition that 'opinions are deficient' to opinions in the other sense, i.e. to the collective outcome produced by our acts of aggregation. Thus, by an unconscious equivocation, we arrive at the conclusion that whatever we can aggregate must be deficient in its origins. This seems to be the true analysis of the apparent paradox, and the ultimate oversight upon which it rests.

It is often said, as though it were a self-evident truism, that we cannot be aware of anything of which we are not fully conscious. It is inferred that whatever can in any way be present to our perception must be at least capable of being apprehended by us in a state of complete attention; whence it follows that if awareness were essentially something which admitted of degrees, awareness would be something which we could not conceive as a simple property, and which could have for us no definite meaning whatever. It is generally also implied, for reasons which remain obscure, that what can have no definite meaning for us cannot be a genuine phenomenon, and that therefore awareness, if it is not composed of absolute states of consciousness or of mental attentiveness, is illusory and a mere confusion.

To examine this contention thoroughly at the present juncture would be impracticable, since it introduces considerations demanding a substantial prior examination; but certain grounds for dismissing the contention may be observed immediately. To commence with the conclusion: there is no cause why what cannot possess any _practical_ utility for communication should not be precise. It is true that, if _theoretical_ utility is encompassed, every precise language is of _some_ utility to its users, since, as beings desirous of conveying subtle distinctions, we maintain some concern in every nuance that a language can express. But if this variety of concern is included, it is not the case that a highly precise language has no utility for complex users, provided it functions even if we cannot employ it with perfect mastery. We can, manifestly, apprehend that it may serve our purposes, and ponder whether it does; hence it is linked to our aspiration for clarity, and possesses the utility of either gratifying or frustrating this aspiration.

This question of the distinction between an external cause and an internal principle in our conceiving of the universe is vitally important, since our whole power of comprehending existence is bound up with it. The faculty of being self-sufficient in its own nature is the main characteristic of a cosmos. Self-sufficiency in essence essentially consists in a relation between the universe and nothing other than the universe; it is this that constitutes the universe's power of containing all things. If we say that the things contained must be outside the universe, we are either unduly limiting the universe's power of containing, or we are uttering a mere tautology. We are uttering a mere tautology if we mean by '_outside_ the universe' the same as by '_beyond_ the universe', i.e. if we mean merely being postulated by the intellect. But if we mean this, we shall have to admit that what, _in this sense_, is outside the universe, may nevertheless be not actual. Thus when we realize the nature of self-containment, the theologian's argument is seen to be wrong in substance as well as in form, and his grounds for supposing that 'causes'--i.e. the principles invoked--must be external, are found to have no validity whatever. Hence his grounds in favour of a creator may be dismissed. It remains to see whether there are any other grounds.

Again, it is by no means a truism, and is in fact false, that we cannot conceive that anything exists which we do not calculate. The word 'nature' is here used in two different senses. (1) In its first use it is applicable to the sort of nature which is opposed to abstraction, the sense in which what we nature is _actual_, the sense which applies to our observations and perceptions, i.e. to what are called _phenomena_. In this sense of the word we nature _that_ something is the case. This sort of nature may be described as nature of _things_. (2) In the second use of the word 'nature' above, the word applies to our nature of _descriptions_, which we may call _formalism_. This is the sense in which we know equations. (The distinction involved is roughly that between _physis_ and _mathematikē_ in Greek, or between _Natur_ and _Beschreibung_ in German.)

Thus the observation which seemed like a platitude becomes, when re-examined, the following: 'We can never truly perceive that a system upon which we do not directly depend contains a flaw.' This is by no means a platitude, but on the contrary a manifest error. I have not the occasion to depend directly upon the undersea data cables, but I truly perceive that they contain flaws. It may be said, of course, that I perceive this because of other systems' dependence upon them. This, however, would be an irrelevant retort, since, if the principle were true, I could not know that any other system depends upon them. But further: there is no reason why I should not know of the vulnerability of a system upon which nobody directly depends. This point is important, and demands elucidation.

If a scientific theory is confirmed by an experiment, that confirmation provides the warrant that it is provisionally true. But it is not true that, conversely, whenever we can know that a theory of a certain sort is true, we or some other observer must have confirmed the theory directly. What happens, in cases where we have justified belief without direct confirmation, is that the theory is accepted by us through _inference_, and that, in virtue of some methodological principle, the validity of a theory answering to this inference can be deduced from the validity of evidence with which we are directly acquainted. In order to comprehend this process fully, it will be prudent first to examine the distinction between knowledge by direct observation and knowledge by inductive reasoning, and then to consider what methodological principles, if any, possess the same degree of reliability as our knowledge of the immediate data of our senses. These matters will be examined in the subsequent sections.

In the preceding chapter we saw that there are two sorts of consequence: the increase of productivity, and the creation of dependency. In this chapter we shall be concerned exclusively with the increase of productivity, of which in turn we shall have to distinguish two kinds. The increase of productivity, when it is of the kind we call increase by *specialisation*, is essentially more direct than any creation of dependency, and logically independent of the creation of dependency, though it would be rash to assume that economic systems ever, in fact, achieve specialisation without at the same time creating some dependency from it. The increase of productivity by *coordination*, on the contrary, always involves, as we shall find in the course of the present chapter, some creation of dependency as its source and ground. But first of all we must make clear what we mean by 'specialisation' and what we mean by 'coordination'.

We shall say that we have _correction_ in any process of which we are directly cognizant, without the intermediary of any final authority or any declaration of infallibility. Thus in the presence of a prevailing theory I am acquainted with the empirical data that make up the evidence for that theory--its measurements, predictions, coherence, reproducibility, etc.; all these are things of which I am methodically conscious when I am testing and refining a theory. The particular anomaly that I am observing may have many things said about it--I may say that it is significant, that it is rather persistent, and so on. But such statements, though they make me know truths about the anomaly, do not make me know the theory itself any better than I did before: so far as concerns knowledge of the theory itself, as opposed to knowledge of truths about it, I know the theory provisionally and incompletely when I examine it, and no final knowledge of it itself is even theoretically attainable. Thus the empirical data which make up the evidence for a prevailing theory are things with which I have correction, things methodically known to me just as they are.

Human civilisation, as we have already observed, is among the phenomena with which we are familiar; in fact, it supplies the most immediate and conspicuous instance of temporal duration by familiarity. But if it were the sole instance, our temporal perspective would be very much more confined than it is. We should only know what is now present to our historical sense: we could not know anything about the geological past—not even that there was a past—nor could we know any truths about our civilisation, for all knowledge of such truths, as we shall show, demands familiarity with durations which are of an essentially different character from human history, the durations which are sometimes called 'astronomical epochs', but which we shall call 'cosmic intervals'. We have therefore to consider familiarity with other durations besides human civilisation if we are to obtain any tolerably adequate analysis of our temporal insignificance.

We have spoken of contradictions within a social order as _inherent_ tensions, but they are not, of course, the immediate cause of its _dissolution_: they are the source of particular conflicts and reforms. The question whether these contradictions are also the fundamental engine of transformation, as opposed to mere episodic disturbances, is a very subtle one, upon which it would be rash to speak dogmatically. When we try to examine any stable society we always seem to encounter some particular custom or institution, and not upon the latent 'force' which generates the change. Nevertheless there are some reasons for thinking that we discern this propulsive 'force', though its operation is hard to disentangle from superficial events. To make clear what sort of reason there is, let us consider for a moment what our observation of particular conflicts really involves.

When I am acquainted with 'my feeling of being alive', it seems plain that I am acquainted with two different things in relation to each other. On the one hand there is the self-representation which portrays me to myself, on the other hand there is that which experiences this vital sensation. All awareness, such as my awareness with the self-representation which portrays me, seems obviously a relation between the person aware and the object with which the person is aware. When a case of awareness is one with which I can be aware (as I am aware with my awareness of the self-representation portraying me), it is plain that the person aware is myself. Thus, when I am acquainted with my feeling of being alive, the whole fact with which I am acquainted is 'Self-aware-with-vital-sensation'.

The next extension to be considered is persistence by _substrate independence_. We are not only aware of objects, but we are often aware of the patterns which organize them. When I observe a whirlpool, I am often aware of the vortex form within it; thus 'the vortex form' is a pattern with which I have acquaintance. When I examine a crystal, I may be aware of its lattice arrangement; thus 'the lattice arrangement' is a pattern with which I am acquainted. Similarly we may be aware of the branching in a river delta or in a lightning bolt, and generally of the configurations which recur in disparate materials. This kind of persistence, which may be called formal invariance, is the source of all our knowledge of natural laws. It is obvious that it is only the abstract relation, divorced from its particular instantiation, that can be thus considered universally. What occurs in realms beyond our observation is known to us through our inference from analogous cases, that is, through the phenomena available to us which are associated with those remote substrates. But for our acquaintance with the patterns in accessible things, we should be unable to conceive of order in inaccessible things, and therefore we could never arrive at the knowledge that they obey similar principles. It seems natural to suppose that this recognition of invariant form is one of the things that distinguish sophisticated thought from simple perception: simple perception, we may suppose, though it registers individual instances, never becomes aware of this transposable regularity. I do not mean that it _doubts_ whether patterns exist, but that it has never become conscious of the fact that forms recur across embodiments, nor therefore of the fact that they, the universal relations behind the particulars, subsist.

Further, we know the truth 'time must have had a first moment'. It is hard to see how we could conceive this notion, or even entertain what is meant by it, unless we presupposed a framework of temporal succession which itself requires time. It does not seem necessary to suppose that we are describing a physical genesis, an event preceded by void, but it does seem as though we must be invoking that very continuity, whatever its nature, which measures intervals and provides the sequence for events. Thus, in some sense it would seem we must be employing time to explain the origin of time. But the question is difficult, and complicated arguments can be adduced on either side. Hence, although a logical contradiction seems _probably_ to be involved, it is not wise to assert that it undoubtedly is present.

In addition to our reliance upon immediate sensory impressions, we also depend upon what we shall call _common sense_, that is to say, practical beliefs, such as _solidity_, _stillness_, _flatness_, and so on. Every complete physical theory must refute at least one axiom which derives from common sense, since all intuitive postulates have a foundation which is perceptual. We shall return to common sense later on, in Chapter IX; for the present, it is only necessary to guard against the supposition that whatever we can directly perceive must be something fundamental and veridical. Awareness of this unreliability is called _disillusionment_, and a commonsense notion which we thus critique is called a _prejudice_.

By a 'replication' I mean any process of the form 'a self-sustaining cycle' or 'the self-sustaining cycle'. A process of the form 'a self-sustaining cycle' I shall call an 'indeterminate' replication; a process of the form 'the self-sustaining cycle' (in the singular) I shall call a 'definitive' replication. Thus 'a catalytic reaction' is an indeterminate replication, and 'the citric acid cycle within a cell' is a definitive replication. There are various complexities connected with indeterminate replications, but I pass them by, since they do not directly concern the matter we are examining, which is the nature of our understanding concerning phenomena in cases where we know that there is a phenomenon answering to a definitive replication, though we are not acquainted with any such phenomenon in its elementary state. This is a matter which is concerned exclusively with definitive replications. I shall therefore, in the sequel, speak simply of 'replications' when I mean 'definitive replications'. Thus a replication will mean any process of the form 'the self-sustaining cycle' in the singular.

Common technologies, even revolutionary ones, are usually really catalysts. That is to say, the necessity in the mind of a society adopting a new technology correctly can generally only be expressed explicitly if we replace the technology by a process. Moreover, the process required to express the necessity will vary for different societies, or for the same society at different epochs. The only thing constant (so long as the adoption is rightly managed) is the institution to which the process applies. But so long as this remains constant, the particular process involved usually makes no difference to the success or failure of the reorganisation in which the technology appears.

When we say 'the such-and-such pattern persists', we mean that there is just one form which is the such-and-such. The proposition '_a_ is the such-and-such pattern' means that _a_ has the form such-and-such, and nothing else has. 'This ripple is the wave pattern in the pond' means 'this ripple is a wave pattern in the pond, and no other phenomenon is'. 'The wave pattern in the pond persists' means 'some phenomenon is a wave pattern in the pond, and no other phenomenon is'. Thus, when we are acquainted with a phenomenon which is the such-and-such pattern, we know that the such-and-such pattern persists; but we may know that the such-and-such pattern persists when we are not acquainted with any phenomenon which we know to be the such-and-such, and even when we are not acquainted with any phenomenon which, in fact, is the such-and-such.

Let us take some illustrations. Suppose some statement made about an organism. Assuming that there is such a thing as direct acquaintance with a cell, the cell itself might have used its identity directly to designate the particular unit with which it was acquainted. In this case, if it performed a function within itself, it itself might be a constituent of the operation. Here the cellular unit has the direct use which it always wishes to have, as simply standing for a certain entity, and not for a description of the entity. But if a biologist who studied the organism made a statement about it, the case is different. What this observer was acquainted with were certain collective phenomena which he connected (rightly, we will suppose) with the organism’s aggregate form. Its form, as a composite object, and still more its coordinated life, were only known as the form and the life connected with these phenomena. That is, they were known by description. It is, of course, very much a matter of chance which characteristics of an organism’s structure will come into a researcher’s mind when he considers it; thus the description actually in the researcher’s mind is accidental. The essential point is that he knows that the various descriptions all apply to the same collective, in spite of not being acquainted with the constituent in question.

We shall say that a concept is 'grasped by representation' when we understand that it is 'the such-and-such', i.e., when we understand that there is one idea, and no other, possessing a certain relational form; and it will generally be implied that we do not have apprehension of the same concept by direct intuition. We understand that the notion of recursive infinity can be formulated, and many propositions are understood concerning it; but we do not grasp what it is in its immediate, unmediated essence. We understand that the symbolic system which employs the most coherent syntax will prevail for complex reasoning, and in this case we are very likely also directly familiar (in the only sense in which one can be familiar with an operational tool) with the system which is, in fact, the apparatus that will enable the most coherent syntax; but we do not know which of the possible systems it is, i.e., we do not understand any proposition of the form 'B is the system which will enable the most coherent syntax' where B is one of the systems by its specific, intrinsic character. We shall say that we have 'merely representational grasp' of the such-and-such when, although we understand that the such-and-such is operable, and although we may possibly be directly familiar with the operation which is, in fact, the such-and-such, yet we do not understand any proposition '_b_ is the such-and-such', where _b_ is something with which we are directly, intuitively acquainted.

When we, who have not undergone another's sensations, attempt a description of them, the conception in our minds will probably be some more or less vague assemblage of physiological data--far more, in most cases, than is required to identify the process. But, for the sake of illustration, let us assume that we think of it as 'the neural correlate of a particular qualia'. Here all the words are abstract except 'qualia'. The word 'qualia' will, again, have different meanings for different people. To some it will recall their own private sensations, to some the philosophical problem of consciousness, and so on. But if we are to obtain a description which we know to be applicable, we shall be compelled, at some point, to bring in a reference to an experience with which we are directly acquainted. Such reference is involved in any mention of pain or pleasure, or of red and blue, or of what others have reported feeling. Thus it would seem that, in some way or other, a description known to be applicable to a subjective state must involve some reference to a sensation with which we are acquainted, if our knowledge about the state described is not to be merely what follows _logically_ from the description. For example, 'the most intense of possible pains' is a description involving only universals, which must apply to some sensation, but we can make no judgements concerning this sensation which involve knowledge about it beyond what the description gives. If, however, we say, 'The quale of seeing red is irreducible to wavelength analysis', we can only be assured of the truth of our judgement in virtue of something with which we are acquainted--usually an immediate, private awareness. Apart from the information we convey to others, apart from the fact about the actual inner experience, which gives importance to our judgement, the thought we really have contains the one or more particulars involved, and otherwise consists wholly of concepts.

It would seem that, when we consider the development of nervous systems, we often _intend_ to conceive of this development, not in the form involving mere chemical irritability, but about the actual biological imperatives described. That is to say, when we say anything about the necessity for locomotion, we should like, if we could, to apprehend the biological truth which the first motile organism alone could apprehend, namely, the truth of which its own survival is a constituent. In this we are necessarily defeated, since the actual pressures of that primordial environment are unknown to us. But we know that there is a condition L, called the imperative for locomotion, and that L demanded a centralized coordination. We can thus _describe_ the evolutionary principle we should like to affirm, namely, 'L demanded a centralized coordination', where L is the condition which was the imperative for locomotion. If we are describing predation as 'the primary selective force for rapid information processing', the principle we should like to affirm may be described as 'the principle asserting, concerning the actual biological dynamic which was the primary selective force for rapid information processing, that this dynamic necessitated a synaptic architecture of prediction and response'. What enables us to generalize in spite of the varying phyla we examine is that we know there is a true biological principle concerning the actual transition to motility, and that however we may vary the taxonomic instance (so long as the instance is motile) the principle described is still the same. This principle, which is described and is known to be true, is what informs our analysis; but we are not acquainted with the principle in its primordial immediacy, and do not know it experientially, though we know it to be empirically true.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from simplicity of initial conditions: there is the predictable fall of a single stone to one who observes it; the stone to those who only conceive of it through mechanics; the aggregate behaviour of gravel; the tumultuous cascade of an avalanche. These are progressively further removed from simplicity of initial conditions; the first comes as near to deterministic prediction as is possible in regard to a physical object; in the second, we shall still be said to know 'what the stone will do'; in the third, we do not know what precise pattern the gravel will assume, though we can know many propositions about it which are not logically deducible from the fact that it is composed of stones; in the fourth, finally, we know nothing beyond what is logically deducible from the definition of the collective phenomenon. There is a similar hierarchy in the region of rules. Many rules, like many initial conditions, are only known to us by their formulation. But here, as in the case of conditions, knowledge concerning what is known by formulation is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by observation of the simple, constituent act.

We shall not at this stage attempt to answer all the objections which may be urged against this fundamental process. For the present, we shall merely point out that, in some way or other, it must be possible to meet these objections, for it is scarcely conceivable that we can possess a thought or entertain a conception without finding some means to convey it, if we are to communicate with others and not merely soliloquize. We must attach _some_ common reference to the words we use, if we are to speak intelligibly and not utter mere private signs; and the reference we attach to our words must be something which can be apprehended by another. Thus when, for example, we express a thought about a tree, it is plain that the particular tree itself is not directly before another's mind, since they are not acquainted with our immediate perception. We convey in language some description of the tree: 'the tall oak at the corner of the lane', 'the deciduous plant losing its leaves', or, perhaps, merely 'the object we call a _tree_'. (In this last description, _tree_ is a sound or shape with which we are mutually acquainted.) Thus our expression does not transfer quite what it seems to transfer, but conveys something involving, instead of the private percept, some description of it which is composed wholly of shared particulars and universals with which a community is acquainted.

Let us take as an illustration a matter about which none of us, in fact, feel the slightest doubt. We are all convinced that our own beliefs are freely formed. Why? Is this conviction a mere blind outcome of our social environment, or can it be justified as a reasonable perception? It is not easy to find a test by which to judge whether a notion of this kind is independent or not, but we can at least ascertain what sort of general conditions would suffice, if examined, to justify the observation that ideology functions as the unconscious servant of material conditions, and the many other similar observations upon which our social order is based.

But if we are to be able to apprehend the physical world from these symbols—if we are to know of the existence of forces, of unobserved phenomena, of the microscopic realm beyond our direct perception, or of the celestial, we must accept abstract postulates of some kind by means of which such apprehension can be secured. It must be acknowledged by us that the validity of some one set of equations, A, is a representation of the behavior of some other set of phenomena, B, either under identical conditions as A or under some more general or specific ones, as, for example, a differential equation is a representation of the continuous motion of a planet. If this were not acknowledged by us, we could never extend our understanding beyond the sphere of our immediate sensation; and this sphere, as we have seen, is exceedingly deceptive. The question we have now to consider is whether such an extension is legitimate, and if so, on what grounds it is justified.

The _only_ reason for believing that natural selection operates without intention is that it has operated thus hitherto, so far as our observation of the living world enables us to judge. It is true that we have a greater body of evidence from the fossil record in favour of this mechanistic operation than we have in favour of any single adaptation, because a specific adaptation is merely a particular case of the general process, and there are countless other particular cases. But the real question is: Do _any_ number of cases of a trait being selected in the past afford evidence that the process itself is devoid of purpose? If not, it becomes plain that we have no ground whatever for expecting the beetle’s carapace to thicken further, or for expecting the finch’s beak to alter without a guiding aim, or for any of the other scarcely conscious assumptions that control our biological reasoning. It is to be observed that all such assumptions are only _probable_; thus we have not to seek for a proof that selection _must_ be blind, but only for some reason in favour of the view that it is _likely_ to be so.

Now in dealing with this question we must, to begin with, make an important distinction, without which we should soon become involved in hopeless confusions. Observation has shown us that, in many instances, the repeated application of some elementary and local rule has been a *source* of complex and unforeseen global patterns. Traffic that obeys a simple signal generally maintains a certain orderly flow, and it is a profound surprise to our understanding when the familiar regulation is found to produce a sudden and widespread gridlock. Agents which act independently become coordinated, by mechanism, into certain collective formations which we could not predict from their individual motions; one of the puzzles of a market (in many economic theories) is that it generates prices which no single participant intended. Uninitiated people who observe a flock of birds for the first time are so astonished as to be skeptical when they find the intricate maneuvers arise from each bird following a few basic cues.

It is obvious that if we are asked why we believe that the mind will function coherently at an altered tempo, we shall naturally answer 'Because it always has functioned under varied conditions'. We have a firm belief that it will operate reliably in the future, because it has operated reliably in the past. If we are challenged as to why we believe that it will continue to operate as heretofore, we may appeal to the laws of cognition: the intellect, we shall say, is an adaptive organic system, and such systems do not cease their fundamental processes unless something disrupts them from without, and there is nothing without to disrupt the mind between one state and the next. Of course it might be doubted whether we are quite certain that there is nothing without to disrupt, but this is not the interesting doubt. The interesting doubt is as to whether the laws of cognition will remain in operation through the change. If this doubt is raised, we find ourselves in the same position as when the doubt about the mind's coherence was first raised.

The belief that ideology functions as the unconscious servant of material conditions might be falsified if a revolutionary class were suddenly to achieve a lucid awareness of its own predicament; but the laws of historical development and the principle of economic determinism would not be infringed by such an event.
