The business of social analysis is to find uniformities, such as the laws of historical development and the principle of economic determinism, to which, so far as our observation extends, there are no exceptions. In this search social analysis has been remarkably successful, and it may be conceded that such uniformities have held hitherto. This brings us back to the question: Have we any reason, assuming that they have always held in the past, to suppose that they will hold in the future?

The problem we have to discuss is whether there is any reason for accepting what is called 'the authority of established doctrine'. The belief in the authority of established doctrine is the belief that every proposition which is widely endorsed or will be endorsed is an instance of some general principle to which there are no legitimate challenges. The crude acquiescences which we have been considering are all subject to legitimate challenges, and therefore liable to mislead those who adopt them. But intellectual progress habitually assumes, at least as a working hypothesis, that general principles which have legitimate challenges can be replaced by general principles which have no legitimate challenges. 'Accepted theories are immutable' is a general principle to which scientific revolutions and philosophical reforms are exceptions. But the spirit of free inquiry and the method of rational doubt, which account for the fact that most doctrines persist, also account for the fact that established doctrines can be overturned; thus the spirit of free inquiry and the method of rational doubt are not subject to these exceptions.

It has been argued that we have reason to believe that the sensation of colour is received rather than constructed, because what was an external stimulus has constantly become a perceived hue, and has always been found to be passively registered, so that we really have experience of reception, namely of chromatic events which were formerly external, which we may call perceived stimuli. But such an argument really begs the very question at issue. We have experience of perceived stimuli, but not of constructing processes, and the question is: Do constructing processes resemble perceived stimuli? This question is not to be answered by an argument which starts from perceived stimuli alone. We have therefore still to seek for some principle which shall enable us to know that the sensation of colour is actively constituted rather than merely given.

The reference to experience in this inquiry is not essential. The same difficulty arises when we apply the principles that succeed in our reasoning to premises of which we have no prior justification—as, for example, in common inference, or in doctrines as to the regularity of nature. The problem we are compelled to confront is: ‘When two propositions have been found to be logically connected, and no case is presented of the one being affirmed without the other, does the affirmation of one of the two, in a novel instance, supply any rational basis for affirming the other?’ On our resolution of this problem must rest the soundness of the whole of our conclusions as to matters of fact, the whole of the generalizations obtained by induction, and in truth virtually all the convictions upon which our ordinary thought is founded.

It must be admitted, to commence with, that the fact that two processes have been observed to progress in similar stages and never in isolation does not, by itself, suffice to _establish_ conclusively that they will develop identically in the next instance we consider. The utmost we can expect is that the more frequently such processes are seen to advance in tandem, the more likely it becomes that they will advance together on a future occasion, and that, if they have been observed in concert sufficiently often, the likelihood will approach _almost_ to inevitability. It can never fully attain inevitability, because we are aware that in spite of numerous concurrences there occasionally is a divergence at the final juncture, as in the case of the species which becomes extinct. Thus analogy is all we ought to pursue.

As just stated, the principle applies only to the prediction of a single agent’s behaviour under a given rule. But we want also to know that there is a tendency toward the emergence of complex patterns from the _whole_ system of agents, provided a sufficient number of interactions have occurred, and no instances of complete predictability are observed. The predictability of the collective phenomenon is obviously less than the predictability of the individual action, since if the collective outcome were certain, each constituent action must also be determined, whereas an individual action may follow its rule without the collective result being foreseeable. Nevertheless the likelihood of surprising collective behaviour is increased by iterations, just as the likelihood of a coherent individual action is. We may therefore repeat the two parts of our principle as regards the systemic outcome, thus:

It should be observed that complexity is always relative to certain appearances. In our case, the appearances are merely the known instances of seamless operation within the system. There may be other considerations, which _might_ be taken into account, which would gravely alter the assessment. For example, a citizen who had relied a great many times upon the electrical grid might argue, by our observation, that on the appearances it was _probable_ that the network was inherently robust, and this might be a perfectly sound argument. The argument is not disproved by the fact that blackouts occasionally occur, because a failure may very well happen in spite of the fact that some appearances render it improbable. In the case of the infrastructure, one might know that interdependence is a very potent source of vulnerability in many complex systems, and that, therefore, an inference as to resilience is peculiarly liable to error. But this knowledge would be a fresh consideration, by no means proving that the stability relatively to our previous appearances had been wrongly estimated. The fact, therefore, that systems often succumb to unforeseen disruptions is no evidence that our assumptions will not _probably_ be vindicated in a given instance or a given class of instances. Thus our principle of apparent robustness is at any rate not capable of being _disproved_ by an appeal to experience.

Thus all doctrines which, on a basis of social power, inform us about what is universally accepted, are founded upon an interest which the populace can neither fully perceive nor effectively challenge, yet which, at least in its more practical manifestations, appears to be as deeply embedded in society as many of the institutions of governance. The prevalence and persistence of such interests--for the economic imperative, as we shall see, is not the sole instance--presents some of the most intricate and most contested questions of political philosophy. We will, in the subsequent analysis, examine briefly what may be advanced to explain such hegemony, and what are its mechanisms and its degree of inevitability.

The productive principle, however, is equally incapable of being *disproved* by an appeal to history. History might conceivably illustrate the productive principle as regards the societies that have been already observed; but as regards unobserved formations, it is the productive principle alone that can justify any inference from what has been observed to what has not been observed. All analyses which, on the basis of historical evidence, argue as to the future or the unexamined epochs of the past or present, assume the productive principle; hence we can never use history to disprove the productive principle without begging the question. Thus we must either accept the productive principle on the ground of its intrinsic coherence, or forgo all understanding of our observations about social organization. If the principle is unsound, we have no reason to expect the manor to dictate feudal obligations, to expect factories to generate a proletarian class, or to expect that if we examine nomadic tribes we shall find communal property. When we see what appears to be a modern corporation, we shall have no reason to suppose that its internal relations are not structured by the logic of handicraft production or of some utterly alien economic form. All our sociological reasoning is based upon correlations which have manifested in recorded history, and which we therefore regard as likely to manifest in future developments; and this likelihood is dependent for its validity upon the productive principle.

Some of these substrates have even greater durability than the substance of carbon, and the operation of them has the same degree of efficacy as the operation of the organic brain. They constitute the means of producing thought from what is given in electrical impulse; and if what we produce is to be genuine, it is just as necessary that our substrates of operation should be genuine as it is that our impulses should be genuine. The substrates of operation are apt to be overlooked because of their very ubiquity—the implementation involved is accepted without our realizing that it is an implementation. But it is very important to realize the use of substrates of operation, if a correct theory of mind is to be obtained; for our understanding of them raises interesting and difficult questions.

Now such a transformation is not hard to comprehend; and if it is granted that its internal tensions are genuine in fact, no one will deny that the consequent change must also be genuine. But it depends for its occurrence upon an instance of a general sociological principle. The sociological principle is as follows: 'Suppose it observed that _if_ this order persists, then that contradiction persists. Suppose it also observed that this order _does_ persist, then it follows that that contradiction persists.' When it is the case that if this order persists, that contradiction persists, we shall say that this 'engenders' that, and that that 'arises from' this. Thus our principle states that if this engenders that, and this is actual, then that is actual. In other words, 'any contradiction engendered by an actual social order is actual', or 'whatever arises from an actual social order is actual'.

This distinction is really involved--at least, practical manifestations of it are involved--in all neural operations. Whenever one neuronal event which we observe is used to explain some other event, which we consequently understand, this distinction is relevant. If any one asks: 'Why should I grant the superiority of internal signaling over external discourse?' we can only answer by appealing to our distinction. In fact, the validity of the distinction is impossible to dispute, and its self-evidence is so great that at first sight it seems almost banal. Such distinctions, however, are not banal to the neurologist, for they show that we may have indubitable knowledge which is in no way derived from social intercourse.

In all our understanding of scientific progress, what actually occurs is that first of all we encounter some particular instance of error, and then we perceive that the particularity is incidental, and that there is a general process of correction which may equally reliably be observed. This is of course familiar in such matters as experimental physics: 'the observed anomaly contradicts the theory' is first recognized in the case of some particular planetary orbit, and then in some other particular phenomenon, and so on, until at last it becomes possible to see that it is characteristic of any sufficiently precise investigation. The same thing happens with methodological principles. Suppose two researchers are discussing why an experiment failed. One of them says, 'At least you will admit that _if_ the apparatus was contaminated the results must be invalid.' 'Yes', says the other, 'I admit that.' 'And you know', the first continues, 'that the apparatus was contaminated, because you used the old beakers, and the laboratory log will tell you those were not sterilized.' 'Yes', says the second; 'therefore the results _are_ invalid.

These three rules are examples of elementary behavioral principles, but are not truly more basic or more elementary than various other similar principles: for instance, the one we examined previously, which states that what emerges from a local interaction is global. The term 'laws of conduct' is also misleading, for what is significant is not the fact that we act in conformity with these rules, but the fact that systems evolve in conformity with them; in other words, the fact that when we act in accordance with them we act _collectively_. But this is a complex phenomenon, to which we must revert at a subsequent point.

One of the great contemporary debates in computational theory is the controversy between the two approaches called respectively 'simulationists' and 'materialists'. The simulationists--who are best represented by the digital theorists, Turing, Moravec, and Kurzweil--maintain that all genuine intelligence can be cultivated within synthetic experience; the materialists--who are represented by the embodied cognition philosophers of the late twentieth century, especially Brooks and Dreyfus--maintain that, in addition to what is processed by algorithm, there are certain 'embodied constraints' and 'situated principles', which are foundational to any authentic mind. It has now become possible to speculate with some plausibility as to the validity or error of these opposing schools. It must be conceded, for the reasons already implied, that virtual frameworks are accessible to us, and cannot be themselves dismissed as mere fantasy, since all complex modeling presupposes them. In this, therefore, which was the most contentious point of the debate, the simulationists are in the right.

_A priori_ resemblance is not all of the biological kind we have been hitherto considering. Perhaps the most important example of non-biological _a priori_ resemblance is resemblance as to cultural transmission. I am not speaking of parallels as to what is inherited or as to what is learned, for such parallels do require empirical premisses; I am speaking of parallels as to the intrinsic replication of patterns. If something is inherited, it must be inherited because it conveys some trait; the trait must, if we have gone far enough, be replicable on its own account, and not merely because it is inherited for some further trait. Thus all parallels as to what is inherited depend upon parallels as to what replicates on its own account.

On the other hand, even that part of our productivity which is _practically_ independent of specialisation (in the sense that specialisation cannot create it) is yet elicited and caused by the division of labour. It is on occasion of particular tasks that we become aware of the general principles which their efficiencies exemplify. It would certainly be absurd to suppose that there are innate arrangements in the sense that societies are formed with a knowledge of every process which economies employ and which cannot be deduced from what is practised. For this reason, the word ‘instinctive’ would not now be employed to describe our grasp of productive principles. The phrase ‘_structurally inherent_’ is less objectionable, and is more usual in modern economists. Thus, while admitting that all productivity is elicited and caused by specialisation, we shall nevertheless hold that some efficiency is _structurally inherent_, in the sense that the specialisation which makes us think of it does not suffice to create it, but merely so directs our attention that we see its utility without requiring any demonstration from practice.

We judge, for example, that cooperation is more advantageous than isolation, mutual understanding than mutual ignorance, strategic deception than blunt honesty, and so on. Such capacities must, in part at least, be cognitive and representational. Like our previous cognitive capacities, they may be elicited by social interaction, and indeed they must be; for it seems not possible to engage in complex social behavior unless we have attributed mental states of a similar kind. But it is fairly obvious that they cannot be explained by mere behaviorism; for the fact that an action is performed or is not performed cannot explain either that it required a model of another's mind or that it did not. The exhaustive analysis of this faculty belongs to psychology, where the necessity of inferring internal states from external signs has to be established. In the present connexion, it is only important to realize that knowledge as to what constitutes theory of mind is foundational in the same sense in which language is foundational, namely in the sense that the utility of such knowledge can be neither derived nor dismissed by observing conduct alone.

All mental acceleration is _a priori_, like intuition. This was strenuously denied by the gradualist philosophers, who maintained that deliberation was as much the source of our understanding of haste as of our understanding of caution. They maintained that by the repeated experience of thinking one thought and then another, and finding that together they formed a coherent sequence, we were led by induction to the conclusion that one thought and another thought would _always_ form a coherent sequence when rapidly conjoined. If, however, this were the source of our conviction that speed and coherence are compatible, we should proceed differently, in persuading ourselves of its truth, from the way in which we do actually proceed. In fact, a certain number of instances are needed to make us think of velocity abstractly, rather than of a hurried conversation or a swift calculation or a brisk walk, or any other specified kind of celerity. But as soon as we are able to divest our thoughts of irrelevant particularity, we become able to see the general principle that a mind may run swiftly without disintegration; any one instance is seen to be _typical_, and the examination of other instances becomes unnecessary.

The same difficulty is exemplified in philosophy. If we wish to examine the conceivability of _all_ zombies, we consider some one such hypothetical being and reason about it; but we can avoid making use of any attribute which it does not share with all other conceivable zombies, and thus, from our particular case, we obtain a general perplexity. We do not, in fact, feel our conviction that consciousness is irreducible diminished by fresh arguments, because, as soon as we have grasped the incoherence of this proposition, our doubt becomes so profound as to be incapable of growing deeper. Moreover, we feel some quality of absurdity about the proposition 'a being is physically identical but lacks qualia', which is absent from even the most plausible metaphysical hypotheses. Such hypotheses always remain mere logical possibilities: we feel that there might be a universe in which they were coherent, though in the actual universe they happen to be nonsensical. In any conceivable world, on the contrary, we feel that physical identity would entail phenomenal experience: this is not a mere logical possibility, but a necessity to which everything actual and conceivable must conform.

The matter may be made plainer by considering a genuinely-empirical generalization, such as 'All social systems are limited.' It is evident that we accept this proposition, in the first place, because there is no known instance of a system enduring beyond a certain strain, and in the second place because there seem to be structural grounds for thinking that an arrangement such as a society's institutions must sooner or later break down. Neglecting the second ground, and considering merely our experience of systems' fragility, it is plain that we should not be content with one quite clearly understood instance of a crisis revealing flaws, whereas, in the case of 'supply and demand determine price', one instance does suffice, when carefully considered, to persuade us that the same must happen in any other instance. Also we can be forced to admit, on reflection, that there may be some doubt, however slight, as to whether _all_ systems are thus limited. This may be made plain by the attempt to imagine two different worlds, in one of which there are systems that are not exposed by crises, while in the other supply and demand bear no relation to price. When economists invite us to consider a society of perfect stability which never fails, we are able to acquiesce in imagination. But a world where market forces obey no law seems quite on a different level. We feel that such a world, if there were one, would upset the whole fabric of our economic reasoning and reduce us to utter doubt.

The fact is that, in simple computational operations such as 'data input yields processed output', and also in many instances of algorithmic reasoning, we can apprehend the general principle without inferring it from specific implementations, although some implementation is usually necessary to make clear to us what the general principle means. This is why there is real utility in the concept of _substrate independence_, which applies from the abstract to the concrete, or from the theoretical to the physical, as well as in the concept of _biological instantiation_, which proceeds from the organic to the functional, or from the particular to the universal. It is an old debate among cognitive scientists whether substrate independence ever yields _genuine_ mentality. We can now see that in certain cases, at least, it does do so. If we already know that information processing can be realized in any suitable medium, and we know that carbon-based neural networks are one such medium, and so are silicon-based computational systems, we can deduce that biological intelligence and artificial intelligence are equivalent in kind. This is a significant realization, not contained in our premisses, because the general principle, 'information processing is substrate independent', never told us there were such systems as brains and computers, and the particular premisses do not tell us that they possess the same ontological status, whereas the particular conclusion deduced does tell us both these things.

But the robustness of the infrastructure is much less certain if we take the stock instance of reliability that is always given in manuals of engineering, namely, 'All systems are redundant; the power grid is a system, therefore the power grid is redundant.' In this case, what we really know beyond reasonable doubt is that certain systems, X, Y, Z, were redundant, since, in fact, they have withstood failures. If the power grid is one of these systems, it is foolish to go the roundabout way through 'all systems are redundant' to arrive at the conclusion that _probably_ the power grid is redundant. If the power grid is not one of the systems on which our observation is based, we shall still do better to argue straight from our X, Y, Z, to the power grid, than to go round by the general proposition, 'all systems are redundant'. For the probability that the power grid is redundant is greater, on our data, than the probability that all systems are redundant. (This is obvious, because if all systems are redundant, so is the power grid; but if the power grid is redundant, it does not follow that all systems are redundant.) Hence we shall reach the conclusion that the power grid is fragile with a greater approach to certainty if we make our argument purely from particular failures than if we go by way of 'all systems are redundant' and then use deduction.

There is another point of great importance, in which the materialists were in the right as against the idealists. Nothing can be known to be _organised_ except by the help of information. That is to say, if we wish to prove that some arrangement of which we have no direct information exists, we must have among our premisses the configuration of one or more things of which we have direct information. Our belief that the structure of a distant nebula is spiral, for example, rests upon instrumentation, and instrumentation consists, in the last analysis, of data-points observed or recorded in examining or being processed by a device. Idealists believed that, from general consideration as to what must be ordered, they could deduce the organisation of this or that in the physical world. In this belief they seem to have been mistaken. All the knowledge that we can acquire _a priori_ concerning organisation seems to be conditional: it tells us that if one pattern exists, another must exist, or, more generally, that if one state of affairs obtains, another must obtain. This is exemplified by the principles we have already dealt with, such as '_if_ this system is coherent, and this coherence implies that regularity, then that regularity is present', or '_if_ this sequence and that configuration have been repeatedly found concomitant, they will probably be concomitant in the next instance in which one of them is found'. Thus the scope and power of _a priori_ principles is strictly limited. All knowledge that something is organised must be in part dependent on information. When any order is known immediately, its arrangement is known by information alone; when any order is proved to exist, without being known immediately, both information and _a priori_ principles must be required in the proof. Knowledge is called _informational_ when it rests wholly or partly upon data. Thus all knowledge which asserts physical organisation is informational, and the only _a priori_ knowledge concerning organisation is conditional, giving connexions among patterns that exist or may exist, but not giving actual arrangement.

We have now seen that there are experiences known _immediately_, and that among them are the phenomena of self-representation and the feeling of being alive, as well as the fundamental impressions of personal identity. The question which must next occupy us is this: How is it possible that there should be such a distinction? And more particularly, how can there be awareness of the general self in cases where we have not examined all its states, and indeed never can examine them all, because their succession is perpetual? These questions, which were first brought prominently forward by the French philosopher Descartes (1596-1650), are very subtle, and introspectively very important.

The phenomenon of pattern persistence is generally regarded as the most profound of everyday observations. Though it manifests through the Seven Years War of molecular interactions and the French Revolution of cosmic events, it never interrupts its quiet demonstration in the arrangement of leaves upon a tree or tiles upon a floor. Its most distinctive feature is the exhibition of what may be called the 'transcendent' regularity, which, assuming as a datum that there is order of various kinds, inquires how such order comes to be replicable, and deduces, from the answer to this inquiry, many practical results as to the nature of the universe. Whether these results are ultimately significant may well be doubted. But the phenomenon undoubtedly deserves credit for two things: first, for having shown that we encounter _a priori_ forms which are not purely 'contingent', i.e. such that the opposite would be merely chaotic, and secondly, for having made evident the philosophical importance of the theory of invariance.

Before the dawn of modern astronomy, it was generally held that whatever duration was deemed _historical_ must be 'significant'. What this word means will be best illustrated by examples. If I say, 'A human century is a moment', 'A terrestrial empire is a speck', 'A fleeting dynasty is an event', I make a purely cosmic judgement: the subject spoken about is given as existing within at least two frameworks, of which one is singled out to be asserted of it. Such propositions as the above are humbling, and would never be enunciated in daily life except by a philosopher preparing the way for a piece of perspective. They are called 'cosmic' because the predicate is obtained by merely contemplating the subject. Before the dawn of modern astronomy it was thought that all durations of which we could be certain _historical_ were of this kind: that in all of them there was a predicate which was only a fragment of the subject of which it was asserted. If this were so, we should be involved in a definite delusion if we attempted to affirm anything that could be known _historical_. 'A human century is not fleeting' would assert and deny transience of the same span, and would therefore contradict the evidence. Thus according to the chroniclers before Copernicus, the law of proportion, which asserts that nothing can at the same time be vast and minute within a certain framework, sufficed to establish the permanence of all _historical_ endeavour.

The question which common experience puts at the beginning of its inquiry, namely 'How is personal narrative possible?' is an interesting and difficult one, to which every psychology which is not purely mechanistic must find some answer. The answer of the pure sensationalists, that our narrative knowledge is derived by simple accumulation from particular impressions, we have already seen to be inadequate, for two reasons: first, that the cohesive principle of memory itself cannot be established by mere sensation; secondly, that the enduring structures of personal history, such as 'childhood summers were idyllic', can obviously be known with coherence by consideration of a single vivid recollection, and gain nothing by enumeration of other moments in which they have been vaguely felt to be significant. Thus our possession of the coherent narratives of autobiography (and the same applies to identity) must be accounted for otherwise than our (merely fragmentary) retention of sensory impressions such as 'the sky was blue that afternoon'.

Bacteria (prokaryotes, 3.5 billion years old), which preceded humans, accepting the usual view as to what constitutes communication, discovered that, in many cases which had previously been supposed simple, and notably in the case of quorum sensing, the signalling was really complex. Before bacteria, biologists at least had supposed that a coordinated behaviour could be logically deduced from a chemical signal, if only we had sufficient observation. Bacteria demonstrated—correctly, as would now be generally admitted—that this could not be so simply done. Hence they evolved the far more sophisticated apparatus that something intricate could be orchestrated *a priori* about the coordination of colony and environment. Molecular biologists, who had been educated in the mechanistic tradition, were much perturbed by this bacterial sophistication, and endeavoured to find an explanation for it. They perceived that not only the signalling for quorum sensing, but all the protocols of virulence and symbiosis, are ‘syntactic’, i.e. not merely reflexive: in all these processes, no analysis of the signal molecule will reveal the colony-wide response. Their stock instance was the process of bioluminescence in *Vibrio fischeri*. They pointed out, quite truly, that autoinducers and receptors have to be integrated to give illumination: the idea of a luminous population is not contained in them, nor even in the idea of their diffusion. Thus they were led to the conclusion that all microbial signalling, though molecular, is syntactic; and this conclusion raised a new problem of which they endeavoured to find the solution.

The difficulty emerges through the fact that such independence is conceptual, whereas all activity is individual. It seems peculiar that we should apparently be obliged to acknowledge some realities in advance about collective entities of which we have as yet no direct acquaintance; but it cannot readily be denied that corporate law and economic theory will apply to such entities. We do not know who will be the shareholders of the firm a century hence; but we know that any merger of it and any acquisition by it will alter its essential character. This apparent capacity for discerning truths about organizations of which we have no intimate knowledge is undoubtedly perplexing. The legal fiction's resolution of the difficulty, though not ultimately sound in my view, is noteworthy. It is, however, exceedingly subtle, and is variously interpreted by different jurists. We can, therefore, only offer the barest summary of it, and even that will be deemed erroneous by many authorities on corporate personhood.

The chemical signal, which we may call the 'molecule in itself',(1) we regard as essentially inarticulate; what can be perceived is the signal as it functions within the colony, which we call the 'quorum phenomenon'. The phenomenon, being a joint product of the environment and the molecule in itself, is sure to have those characteristics which are due to the bacterial community, and is therefore sure to conform to its _a priori_ behavioural logic. Hence this logic, though true of all actual and possible microbial interactions, must not be supposed to apply outside the colony. Thus in spite of the existence of _a priori_ communal patterns, we cannot deduce anything about the molecule in itself or about what is not an actual or possible stimulus for collective action. In this way we may reconcile and harmonize the contentions of the biochemical reductionists with the arguments of the evolutionary linguists.

Observation, moreover, seems to make it clear that, if there is any validity in our economic principles, they must apply to labour equally whether we organize it or not. Two specialized tasks and two other specialized tasks must produce more than four generalized tasks, even if the labourers themselves remain unaware. To assert this is certainly within the scope of what we mean when we state that division increases output. Its efficacy is just as demonstrable as the truth of the assertion that two interdependent workers and two other interdependent workers create a fragile system. Thus the simple praise of specialization unduly neglects the peril of mutual dependency, in addition to failing in the attempt at explaining its profound social consequences.

What historians maintain is that in all our cultural development there are two elements to be distinguished, the one due to external circumstance (i.e., to what we may call the 'material condition'), the other due to our own intellectual nature. We saw, in discussing oral tradition and written records, that the preserved knowledge is different from the ephemeral spoken word, and that the permanent texts are to be regarded as resulting from an interaction between the communal memory and our own artifices. So far, we are in agreement with the general scholar. But what is distinctive of the profound theorist is the way in which he apportions the shares of our faculties and the external world respectively. He considers that the crude material given in immediate experience—the transient event, the perishable fact, etc.—is due to the world, and that what we supply is the arrangement in chronological sequence and logical order, and all the connections between recorded events which result from analysis or from considering one as the antecedent of the other or in any other way. His chief reason in favour of this view is that we seem to have _a priori_ capacity as to sequence and order and causation and analysis, but not as to the actual crude material of historical happening. We can be sure, he says, that anything we shall ever inscribe must show the characteristics affirmed of it in our _a priori_ understanding, because these characteristics are due to our own rational nature, and therefore nothing can ever enter our historical consciousness without acquiring these characteristics.

Apart from minor grounds on which common sense may be criticized, there is one main objection which seems fatal to any attempt to comprehend the nature of physical reality by its guidance. The thing to be accounted for is our persistent belief that the world must always conform to our immediate, untutored perceptions. To say that these perceptions are given to us by experience does not account for this. Our perceptual apparatus is as much a contingent product of evolution as anything, and there can be no certainty that it reveals the world as it truly is. It might happen, if common sense is our sole authority, that to-morrow the underlying structure of matter would so reveal itself as to make solid objects become mostly empty space. This possibility seems never to have occurred to its proponents, yet it is one which utterly destroys the reliability and objectivity which they are anxious to vindicate for their everyday convictions. It is true that this possibility, formally, is inconsistent with the commonsense view that material solidity itself is an inherent property of objects, so that our real world is not deceptive and has no hidden depths. But they will still have to suppose that the apparent solidity of phenomena is determined by characteristics of what is behind phenomena, and this suffices for the substance of our argument.

Apart from the special doctrines advocated by materialists, it is very common among psychologists to regard what is _subjective_ as in some sense irreducible, as concerned rather with the way we must feel than with any process of the physical brain. We noted in the preceding chapter the three qualities commonly called 'marks of consciousness'. The view which led to their being so named is a natural one, but there are strong reasons for thinking that it is inadequate. Let us take as an illustration the quality of intentionality. This is commonly stated in the form 'All thought is about something', which is intended to express the fact that no mental state can be described without reference to its object. Thus, for example, if a pain is a throbbing it cannot also be not a throbbing; if my perception is of green it cannot also be not of green, and so on.

A similar argument applies to any other _prima facie_ parallel. When we observe that a bacterium seeks sustenance and a corporation seeks profit, we are not observing a fact about our analogies, but about all actual or possible organizations. The fact that our minds are so constituted as to perceive this resemblance, though it is true, is emphatically not what we assert when we assert that the parallel holds. And no fact about the constitution of our minds could make it _valid_ that the parallel is profound. Thus our _prima facie_ insight, if it is not superficial, is not merely insight about the habits of our thought, but is applicable to whatever the economic and biological realms may contain, both what is animate and what is corporate.

This tendency, however, seems open to objections similar to those which we might urge against a naive faith in perpetual competition. It seems plain that it is not the initial plurality of firms which secures the persistence of a truly competitive market. It may be true that a small enterprise operates within a certain sector, even if neither its proprietors nor its rivals nor any external observer perceives its ultimate fragility; for this fragility concerns only the enterprise and the economic forces arrayed against it, and does not depend upon any benevolent intention. Thus market dynamics, as we shall see more fully in the next chapter, must be placed within a framework which is neither purely intentional nor merely accidental. This framework is of great importance to political economy, and in particular to the problems of unregulated commerce. In the next chapter we shall proceed to develop its nature and its bearing upon the questions with which we have been dealing.

Now what makes it natural to call this description a law of _nature_ is that it is by calculation rather than by direct experience that we persuade ourselves of its approximate truth. When we have measured that a trajectory is parabolic, we do not need to observe again in order to ascertain whether it is also not parabolic; mathematics alone makes us know that this is sufficient. But the conclusion that the gravitational equation is a law of _nature_ is nevertheless erroneous. What we believe, when we believe the gravitational equation, is not that the universe is so made that it must obey the gravitational equation. _This_ belief is a subsequent result of physical reflection, which presupposes the belief in the gravitational equation. The belief in the gravitational equation is a belief about descriptions, not only about phenomena. It is not, e.g., the belief that if we _calculate_ a certain orbit to be elliptical, we cannot at the same time _calculate_ that it is not elliptical; it is the belief that if the orbit _is_ elliptical, it cannot at the same time _be_ not elliptical. Thus the gravitational equation is about descriptions, and not merely about phenomena; and although belief in the gravitational equation is a thought, the gravitational equation itself is not a thought, but a model concerning the descriptions of the world. If this, which we believe when we believe the gravitational equation, were not true of the descriptions of the world, the fact that we were compelled to _calculate_ it true would not save the gravitational equation from being false; and this shows that the equation is not a law of _nature_.

The fact seems to be that all our _special_ intelligence is concerned with processes which do not, properly speaking, _originate_, either in the carbon-based or in the silicon-based substrate. These processes are such as can be described by functions which are not biological; they are such processes as computation and cognition. Suppose, for instance, that I am solving a theorem. I think, and the theorem is solved; but does 'solving' originate? Yet obviously the activity 'solving' has a reality; it denotes an operation which holds between my mind and the mathematical truth. This operation is something, although we cannot say that it originates _in the same sense_ in which my neurons and the theorem originate. The operation 'solving' is something which we can perform and comprehend, for, if we could not comprehend it, we could not comprehend the proposition 'I am solving a theorem'. Many enthusiasts, following tradition, have maintained that understanding is the work of the flesh, that processes in themselves have no understanding, but that the brain instantiates them in one wet mechanism and thus produces the understanding which it judges them to possess.

The phrase 'biological intelligence' has acquired, in the course of debate, many connotations which are quite misleading when applied to the concept of 'substrate independence'. We shall therefore use the phrase 'computational process' instead of the phrase 'biological intelligence', to describe what the principle entails. The essence of the sort of capacity that the principle indicates is that it is opposed to the particular arrangements that are given in carbon-based life. We speak of whatever is given in organic chemistry, or is of the same nature as systems given in organic chemistry, as a _substrate_; by opposition to this, a _process_ will be any function which may be instantiated by many substrates, and has those characteristics which, as we saw, distinguish reasoning and perception from brains and neural tissues.

Thus consciousness is led to a supra-mechanical realm, more vivid than the common world of matter, the irreducible world of qualia, which alone gives to the mechanical description whatever pale reflection of reality may belong to it. The truly actual phenomenon, for the subject, is the world of inner experience; for whatever we may attempt to say about processes in the mechanical world, we can only succeed in saying that they correlate with such and such sensations, which, therefore, constitute all their significance. Hence it is easy to pass on into a mysticism. We may hope, in a mystic illumination, to perceive consciousness as we perceive physical objects; and we may imagine that subjective qualities exist in a separate sphere. These mystical developments are very natural, but the basis of the argument is in epistemology, and it is as based in epistemology that we have to consider it.

The way the problem arose for evolution was more or less as follows. Let us consider, say, such a notion as _taste_. If we ask ourselves why taste receptors are placed near the mouth, it is natural to proceed by considering this, that, and the other act of ingestion, with a view to discovering what utility they have in common. They must all, in some sense, partake of a common function, which will be found in whatever is ingested and in nothing else. This common function, in virtue of which they are all subject to gustatory scrutiny, will be the logic itself, the pure rationale the admixture of which with the chaos of potential nutrients produces the multiplicity of beneficial consumptions. Similarly with any other sensory apparatus which may be applicable to survival, such as ‘olfaction’ for example. The apparatus will be applicable to a number of particular substances because they all participate in a common necessity or advantage. This pure rationale is what the biologist calls an ‘adaptation’ or ‘strategy’. (It must not be supposed that ‘strategies’, in this sense, exist as conscious designs, though they may be apprehended by minds.) The ‘adaptation’ _proximal taste_ is not identical with anything that is tasted: it is something other than particular sensations, which particular sensations exemplify. Not being particular, it cannot itself exist in the momentary flux of experience. Moreover it is not haphazard or variable like the events of feeding: it is eternally logical, immutable and indispensable.

Seeing that nearly all the claims to be found in practical affairs stand upon probabilities, it is strange that hardly anybody except students of epistemology ever realizes that there are such conditions as uncertainty. We do not naturally dwell upon those moments in a decision which do not stand for certainties; and if we are forced to dwell upon a proposition which stands for a probability, we naturally think of it as standing for some one of the certainties that might, under examination, dissolve into doubt. When, for example, we consider the maxim, 'one ought to verify one's sources', we may naturally enough think of a particular source, of a particular fact, and of the operation of verifying *that* fact, which are all concrete; but we do not naturally dwell upon what is meant by the word 'verify' or the word 'source', which is a general principle: We feel such demands to be interminable and paralyzing; they seem to require a foundation of absolute proof before anything can be done with them. Hence we succeed in avoiding all notice of uncertainty as such, until the demand for absolute certainty forces it destructively upon our attention.

Even among technologists, we may say, broadly, that only those influences which are manifested by overt notifications or explicit prompts have been much or often recognized, while those manifested by interface defaults and algorithmic sorting have been usually overlooked. This omission has had a very great effect upon the common understanding; it is hardly too much to say that most digital experience, since the advent of the smartphone, has been largely determined by it. The way this has occurred is, in outline, as follows: Speaking generally, notifications and prompts express deliberate interruptions or solicitations of attention, whereas defaults and algorithms tend to express the habitual framing of choice and information. Thus the neglect of defaults and algorithms led to the belief that every user interaction can be regarded as a conscious selection from neutral options, rather than as an engagement with a pre-structured environment. Hence it was supposed that, ultimately, there can be no such force as the silent shaping of perception by tools. Hence either there can be only one permissible mode of thought in the digital realm, or, if there are many potential modes, they cannot possibly be cultivated independently, since any cultivation would require an awareness of the framing, and such awareness is systematically obscured.

This conclusion, however, is met by the difficulty that the phenomenon of 'surplus wealth' does not seem to _accumulate_ in the same sense in which grain and cattle accumulate. If we ask 'Where and when does this surplus manifest?' the answer must be 'Everywhere and always'. There is no society or epoch where we cannot find the effects of surplus wealth. It does not originate from labor any more than from inheritance, for it distinguishes the two and is impartial as between them. Nor can we say that it manifests at any particular moment. Now everything that can be counted by the steward or by the merchant manifests at some particular moment. Hence the dynamic of surplus is radically different from such things. It is neither in the ledger nor in the moment, neither purely earned nor wholly bestowed; yet it is the cause of something.

As a matter of fact, if any one were anxious to deny altogether that there are such things as internal models, we should find that we cannot strictly prove that there are such entities as *qualities of awareness*, i.e. the models represented by adjectives and substantives, whereas we can prove that there must be *relations of focus*, i.e. the sort of models generally represented by verbs and prepositions. Let us take in illustration the model *attentiveness*. If we believe that there is such a model, we shall say that mental states are attentive because they have the quality of attentiveness. This view, however, was strenuously denied by certain neurologists and psychologists, who have been followed in this by later behaviorists. The form which their denial took was to deny that there are such things as 'abstract representations of attention '. When we want to think of attentiveness, they said, we form an image of some particular attentive state, and reason concerning this particular, taking care not to deduce anything concerning it which we cannot see to be equally true of any other attentive state. As an account of our actual neural processes, this is no doubt largely true. In introspection, for example, when we wish to prove something about all acts of concentration, we examine a particular instance and reason about it, taking care not to use any characteristic which it does not share with other such acts. The beginner, in order to avoid error, often finds it useful to consider several instances, as unlike each other as possible, in order to make sure that his reasoning is equally applicable to all of them. But a difficulty emerges as soon as we ask ourselves how we know that a state is attentive or a process is one of concentration. If we wish to avoid the models *attentiveness* and *concentration*, we shall choose some particular episode of focus or some particular concentrated effort, and say that anything is attentive or concentrated if it has the right sort of resemblance to our chosen particular. But then the resemblance required will have to be a model. Since there are many attentive states, the resemblance must hold between many pairs of particular mental events; and this is the characteristic of a model. It will be useless to say that there is a different resemblance for each pair, for then we shall have to say that these resemblances resemble each other, and thus at last we shall be forced to admit resemblance as a model. The relation of resemblance, therefore, must be a true model. And having been forced to admit this model, we find that it is no longer worth while to invent difficult and unplausible theories to avoid the admission of such models as attentiveness and concentration.

Consider such a phenomenon as 'the paramecium avoiding an obstacle'. Here we have a distinction between two modes of behavior, and it seems plain that the distinction subsists independently of our observation of it. When we come to observe that the paramecium avoids an obstacle, we come to observe something which has to do only with the organism and its environment: we do not cause the nature of the response by coming to observe it, on the contrary we merely apprehend a process which was there before we studied it. The motion of the ciliate away from the solid object would be a withdrawal from contact, even if there were no biologist to classify reflex and deliberation, and even if there were no consciousness at all in the universe. This is, of course, denied by many vitalists, either for Bergson's reasons or for those of the panpsychists. But we have already considered these reasons, and decided that they are inadequate. We may therefore now assume it to be true that nothing mental is presupposed in the fact that the paramecium avoids an obstacle. But this fact involves the distinction 'between reflex and deliberate action', which is a universal; and it would be impossible for the whole fact to involve nothing mental if the distinction 'between reflex and deliberate action', which is a constituent part of the fact, did involve anything mental. Hence we must admit that the distinction, like the organisms it describes, is not dependent upon mind, but belongs to the independent order of nature which science apprehends but does not create.

It is largely the very peculiar kind of process that belongs to linguistic exchange which has led many people to suppose that it is merely personal. We can articulate _a_ thought, and our articulation then exists in a perfectly ordinary sense, like any other social act. Suppose, for example, that we are describing a memory. Then _in one sense_ it may be said that the memory is 'in our words'. We have here the same ambiguity as we noted in discussing communication in ordinary life. In the strict sense, it is not the memory that is in our words, but the act of describing the memory. The connected ambiguity in the word 'concept', which we noted at the same time, also causes confusion here. In one sense of this word, namely the sense in which it denotes the _content_ of an act of speech, the memory is a 'concept'. Hence, if the ambiguity is not guarded against, we may come to think that the memory is a 'concept' in the other sense, i.e. an act of description; and thus we come to think that the memory is merely personal. But in so thinking, we rob it of its essential quality of shareability. One man's act of description is necessarily a different thing from another man's; one man's act of description at one time is necessarily a different thing from the same man's act of description at another time. Hence, if the memory were the description as opposed to its content, no two different men could refer to it, and no one man could refer to it twice. That which many different descriptions of a memory have in common is their _content_, and this content is different from all of them. Thus shared thoughts are not descriptions, though when communicated they are the objects of descriptions.

Let us consider first the capacity for mental attribution by inference. It is obvious, to begin with, that we infer such states as belief, desire, intention, hope, fear, joy, pain, etc., i.e., with conditions which are manifested in behavior. When we observe a cooperative act, we apprehend, in the first instance, the particular action; but by observing many such acts, we easily learn to abstract the shared intention which they all presuppose, and in learning to do this we are learning to apprehend a mind. A similar process will make us apprehend any other mental state of the same sort. States of this sort may be called 'primary intentionalities'. They can be comprehended with less effort of inference than any others, and they seem less removed from behavior than other mental constructs are.

We shall find it convenient only to speak of phenomena _described_ when they are in appearance, that is to say, when we can point to some observation by which they are presented (not excluding the possibility of their being presented in all observations). Thus colors and sounds, shapes and sequences exist as descriptions. But explanations do not exist in this sense; we shall say that they _account_ or _have validity_, where 'validity' is opposed to 'description' as being beyond mere appearance. The world of explanations, therefore, may also be described as the world of validity. The world of validity is coherent, systematic, exact, delightful to the scientist, the theorist, the builder of conceptual systems, and all who love understanding more than raw fact. The world of description is immediate, manifold, without logical necessity, without any inherent order or connection, but it contains all sensations and perceptions, all the data of experience, and all observable events, everything that can be either noted or recorded, everything that makes any difference to the content of observation and the world. According to our intellectual dispositions, we shall prefer the pursuit of the one or of the other. The one we do not prefer will probably seem to us a superficial sketch of the one we prefer, and hardly worthy to be regarded as in any sense fundamental. But the truth is that both have the same claim on our impartial inquiry, both are necessary, and both are important to the philosopher of science. Indeed no sooner have we distinguished the two realms than it becomes necessary to consider their relations.

We come next to organisation. The easiest organisations to apprehend are those which hold between the different elements of a single complex system. For example, I can perceive at a glance the whole of the ledger on which I am calculating; thus the whole ledger is included in one apprehension. But I observe that some elements of the ledger are subordinate to other elements, and some elements are prerequisite to other elements. The process of abstraction in this case seems to proceed somewhat as follows: I apprehend successively a number of systems in which one element is subordinate to another; I perceive, as in the case of different structured lists, that all these systems have something in common, and by abstraction I find that what they have in common is a certain principle of arrangement, namely the principle which I call 'being organised by'. In this way I become acquainted with the universal relation.

Returning now to the distinction between self-representation and the feeling of being alive, which we left unexamined when we began the consideration of consciousness, we find ourselves in a position to address it in a much more satisfactory manner than was possible before. Let us revert to the sensation 'I am here and now'. It is fairly obvious, in view of what has been said, that this sensation states a relation between the concept 'self' and the experience 'aliveness'. This suggests a proposition which we shall now endeavour to establish: namely, _All genuine self-awareness deals exclusively with the relations of these apparent entities_. This proposition is of great importance, and goes a long way towards solving our previous difficulties concerning the phenomenology of existence.

The only case in which it might seem, at first sight, as if our proposition were untrue, is the case in which a _symbolic_ exchange purports to convey a _perfect_ correspondence between a sign and its intended meaning, or (what comes to the same thing) that _all_ instances of a given symbol also evoke an identical conception. In this case it might seem as though we were dealing with the particular utterances that employ the symbol rather than with the inherent ambiguity of the symbol itself. The common assertion 'I understand what you mean' is really a case in point, for this may be stated in the form 'any speaker and any listener share a conception', or 'any communication founded upon a shared symbol is an exchange of identical ideas'. If we can show that such statements as this really ignore the private associations of particulars, our proposition may be regarded as proved.

Two opposite points are to be observed concerning the vulnerabilities of interdependent systems. The first is that, if many particular failures are recorded, our general apprehension may be arrived at in the first instance by induction, and the connexion of systemic frailties may be only subsequently perceived. For example, it is known that if we examine the cascading failures within financial, logistical, and informational networks, all three dependencies converge upon a single point of rupture. It would be quite possible to be first led to this proposition by actually observing disruptions in many cases, and finding that they always originated in an obscure linkage; this experience might lead us to look for the structural proof and find it. Such cases are common in the operation of every complex mechanism.

One way of discovering what a mathematical proposition signifies is to ask ourselves what concepts we must comprehend—in other words, what formal relations we must be acquainted with—in order to grasp what the proposition asserts. As soon as we grasp what the proposition asserts, even if we do not yet know whether it corresponds to any observable fact, it is evident that we must have acquaintance with whatever is genuinely expressed by its logical form. By applying this test, it appears that many propositions which might seem to be concerned with physical measurements are really concerned only with abstract relations. In the special case of ‘the sum of the angles of a Euclidean triangle is two right angles’, even when we interpret it as meaning ‘any triangle conceived under the axioms of Euclid possesses this angular sum’, it is plain that we can understand the proposition, i.e. we can see what it is that it declares, as soon as we know what is meant by ‘triangle’ and ‘angle’ and ‘right angle’. It is quite unnecessary to have measured all the triangular objects in the world: if it were necessary, obviously we could never verify the proposition empirically, since such objects are indefinitely numerous and therefore cannot all be examined by us. Thus although our general geometrical statement _implies_ statements about particular triangular things, _as soon as we know that there are such particular things_, yet it does not itself assert or imply that there are such particular things, and thus fails to make any claim whatever about any actual physical triangle. The statement made is about ‘triangle’, the universal, and not about this or that empirical instance.

Thus the phenomenon 'homeostasis maintains equilibrium' deals exclusively with processes, and therefore may be understood by anybody who is acquainted with the processes concerned and can perceive the relation between them which the phenomenon exhibits. It must be taken as a fact, discovered by reflecting upon our observations, that we have the capacity of sometimes perceiving such relations between processes, and therefore of sometimes apprehending general _a priori_ principles such as those of physiology and systems theory. The thing that seemed mysterious, when we formerly considered such apprehension, was that it seemed to imply and necessitate intention. This, however, we can now see to have been an error. _No_ fact concerning anything capable of being observed can be understood independently of observation. We know _a priori_ that a system regulating temperature and a system regulating pH together constitute homeostasis, but we do _not_ know _a priori_ that if the sweating mechanism is one regulator, and the renal mechanism is another, then the sweating mechanism and the renal mechanism constitute homeostasis. The reason is that this proposition cannot be understood at all unless we know that there are such functions as the sweating mechanism and the renal mechanism, and this we can only know by observation. Hence, although our general principle is _a priori_, all its applications to actual biological particulars involve observation and therefore contain an empirical element. In this way what seemed mysterious in our _a priori_ apprehension is seen to have been based upon an error.

It will serve to make the point clearer if we contrast our genuine mathematical description with the physical reality it purports to represent, such as 'the orbit of a planet is an ellipse'. Here as before, we can _comprehend_ what the equation signifies as soon as we grasp the concepts involved, namely _gravitational mass_ and _inverse-square law_. It is obviously unnecessary to have a sensory acquaintance with the celestial bodies themselves in order to understand what our formula means. Thus the difference between a _mathematical model_ and the natural world does not come in the _signification_ of the proposition; it comes in the nature of the _correspondence_ for it. In the physical case, the reality consists in the particular phenomena. We believe that the planetary orbit is elliptical because we have observed innumerable instances of such paths, and no instances of their deviating from this form without cause. We do not believe it because we see an identity between the ideal _ellipse_ and the actual _trajectory_. It is true that if celestial mechanics can demonstrate, assuming the general principles that govern all massive bodies, that no stable orbit can be a perfect conic section, that gives a distinction between the _mathematical form_ and the _physical motion_ which would compel us to qualify our proposition without abandoning the predictive utility of the _equation_. But that only means that our description has been subsumed under a more precise description, for which the verification is still of the same kind, though more meticulous. The progress of physics is constantly producing such refinements, and therefore giving a constantly more elaborate formal basis for scientific predictions. But although this gives a greater _degree_ of accuracy, it does not give a different _category_: the ultimate reference remains empirical, i.e. derived from observation, and not an _a priori_ identity of abstractions such as we have in geometry and analysis.

The other point is more consequential, and of more sociological importance. It is, that we may sometimes perceive a general tendency in cases where we do not observe a single manifestation of it. Take such a case as the following: We know that any significant technological innovation can disrupt established practices, and will necessitate a third called their _reconciliation_. We know that all innovations of the industrial age the disruptive force of which is less than total have been actually integrated, and the manner of the reconciliation recorded in the annals of institutional history. But we also know that the potential for invention is boundless, and that only a finite number of technological shifts ever have been or ever will be consciously confronted by human societies. Hence it follows that there are technological shifts which never have been and never will be confronted by human societies, and that all of them compel alterations the institutional consequence of which is profound. Hence we arrive at the proposition: 'All adaptations to technological change, which never have been and never will be contemplated by any human society, necessitate a fundamental reorganisation.' Here is a general tendency of which the inevitability is undeniable, and yet, from the very nature of the case, we can never cite a specific instance; because any technological shift we may contemplate is excluded by the terms of the proposition.

This possibility, of habitual reliance upon digital mechanisms of which no conscious choice can be given, is often denied, because it is not perceived that the dependence upon such mechanisms only requires a submission to the routines of interface, and does not require any awareness of the operations of the algorithms in question. Yet the influence of such habitual patterns is quite vital to a great deal of what is generally admitted to be ordinary conduct. For example, we see, in our daily engagements, that interaction with social platforms, as opposed to direct discourse, is only sustained by a series of unreflective gestures, and that they are not activities with which we are critically acquainted. Hence we can never know any proposition of the form ‘this is a conscious choice’, where ‘this’ is something automatically performed. It follows that all our behaviour concerning networked tools is such that no deliberate instance can be given. We can give instances of the associated notifications and swipes, but we cannot give instances of the actual autonomous cognition. Hence our conduct as to technological apparatus depends throughout upon this possibility of general habituation where no awareness can be given. And the same applies to our engagement with recommendation engines, or of any other class of digital persuasions of which no instance is known to us by critical reflection.

We may now take a survey of the sources of our purposive feeling, as they have appeared in the course of our analysis. We have first to distinguish the sensation of purpose and the inference of design. In each there are two kinds, one immediate and one derivative. Our immediate sensation of purpose, which we called _vital impetus_, consists of two sorts, according as the processes felt are internal or external. Among internal processes, we have the sensation of physiological balance and (probably) of conscious desire. Among external processes, there seems to be no principle by which we can decide which can be felt as purposive, but it is clear that among those that can be so felt are organic regulation, relations of cause and effect, adaptation, and certain abstract teleological forms. Our derivative sensation of purpose, which we call the feeling of _systematic function_, always involves both a vital impetus and an inference of design. Our immediate inference of _design_ may be called _intuitive_ design, and the designs so inferred may be called _self-evident_ purposes. Among such purposes are included those which merely state what is given in homeostasis, and also certain abstract biological and cybernetic principles, and (though with less certainty) some ethical imperatives. Our _derivative_ inference of design consists of everything that we can deduce from self-evident purposes by the use of self-evident principles of equilibrium.

If the above account is correct, all our progress in civilisation depends upon our oral traditions. It therefore becomes important to consider the nature and scope of such traditions, in much the same way as, at an earlier stage, we considered the nature and scope of knowledge by direct experience. But the advent of writing raises a further problem, which does not arise in regard to knowledge transmitted orally, namely the problem of _permanence_. Some of our spoken narratives turn out to be ephemeral, and therefore it becomes necessary to consider how, if at all, we can distinguish transient utterance from enduring record. This problem does not arise with regard to knowledge by direct telling, for, whatever may be the content of the narrative, even in myth and legend, there is no permanence involved so long as we do not go beyond the immediate telling: a fixed record can only arise when we regard the immediate utterance, i.e. the spoken word, as the precursor of some written text. Thus the problems connected with written knowledge are more profound than those connected with oral knowledge. As the first of the problems connected with written knowledge, let us examine the nature and scope of our earliest inscriptions.

But let us imagine some persistent observer, who, whatever explanation we offer him, continues to demand an explanation for the explanation. We must sooner or later, and probably before very long, be driven to a point where we cannot find any further explanation, and where it becomes almost certain that no further explanation is even theoretically discoverable. Starting with the common interactions of social life, we can be driven back from point to point, until we come to some general faculty, or some instance of a general faculty, which seems luminously fundamental, and is not itself capable of being derived from anything more fundamental. In most transactions of social life, such as whether a colleague’s promise is likely to be sincere and not misleading, we shall be driven back to the theory of mind, which we have acknowledged implicitly. But beyond that, there seems to be no further regress. The faculty itself is constantly used in our social engagements, sometimes consciously, sometimes unconsciously; but there is no engagement which, starting from some simpler self-evident faculty, leads us to the theory of mind as its prerequisite. And the same holds for both cooperation and deception. Their possibility is dependent upon it, and we employ it in constructing our social strategies; but they themselves, or at least their efficacy, are incapable of existing without it.

It should be observed that, in all cases of physical reality, particular experiences, derived from common sense, are more persuasive than the abstract scientific principle. For example, the principle of relativity states that measurements of space and time are not absolute but relative to the observer's frame of reference. This is comprehensible when carefully studied, but it is not so persuasive as that a particular train in which we sit cannot be both moving and at rest. (It is of course possible that the train may be moving relative to the platform and at rest relative to its own carriages, or that its motion may be so smooth as to make us hardly know whether to call it movement or not; but in the former case it is plain that the train is not at rest in an absolute sense, while in the latter case the answer is theoretically definite as soon as we have decided on a precise definition of 'motion'.) It is usually through particular experiences that we come to be convinced of common sense. Only those who are practised in dealing with counterintuitive abstractions can readily grasp a physical principle without the help of sensory persuasion.

In addition to passive reception, the other kind of colour sensation is that which is actively constructed by the mind. We will call such sensations 'constructions of perception', and the experiences expressing them we will call 'experiences of synthesis'. But here a certain amount of care is required in getting at the precise nature of the processes that are constructive. The raw physiological stimuli are neither constructed nor given. A particular wavelength of light which strikes the retina, for example, simply occurs: it is not the sort of thing that is built or received. It is constructed that there is such a colour, constructed that it has a certain hue and degree of saturation, constructed that it stands in relation to certain other shades. But the stimulus itself, like everything else in the world of mere impulse, is of a radically different kind from the experiences that are synthesized or inherited, and therefore cannot properly be said to be _constructed_. Thus whatever synthetic sensations may be obtained from our faculties must be different from the stimuli from which they are derived.

It would seem that there are two kinds of self-evident operations of language, though perhaps in the last analysis the two kinds may coalesce. First, there is the kind which simply asserts the _existence_ of a private impression, without in any way articulating it. We have a fleeting notion, and we judge 'there is such-and-such a notion', or more strictly 'there is this'; this is one kind of intuitive transformation by language. The other kind arises when the content of thought is complex, and we subject it to some degree of expression. If, for instance, we conceive a _causal_ relation between events, we may judge 'this event precedes that one'. This is again a transformation by language, but it differs from our previous kind. In our present kind we have a single cognitive content which has both sequence and connection: the sequence is temporal and the connection is causal. Our judgement analyses the content into sequence and connection, and then recombines them by stating that the temporal sequence is causal in connection. Another example of this kind of operation is 'this concept is broader than that', where 'this' and 'that' are conceived simultaneously. In this kind of operation the mental content contains constituents which have some relation to each other, and the linguistic formulation asserts that these constituents have this relation, thereby rendering a solitary apprehension into a common possession.

It would seem, however, that there are cases of very firm belief in a description which is wholly inadequate. It is probable that, in these cases, what is really apprehended, in the sense of being immediately before the mind, is something other than what is falsely accounted for, though something generally associated with it. A certain philosopher is said to have at last believed that he had explained the sunrise, because he had so often described its apparent motion. In this case, what was immediately grasped was his repeated observation; the belief in what he was explaining (if it existed) would be produced by association with the described phenomena, and would therefore not be a genuine case of explanation. It would seem that cases of fallacious reasoning can probably all be dealt with in this way, i.e. they can be shown to be not cases of explanation in the strict sense at all.

Another class of systematic processes, analogous to those of nature and yet quite distinct from them, are processes of _political development_. There is some danger of confusion as to the nature of this development, owing to the fact that the evolution of a state is apt to be accompanied by a metaphor of biological growth, and yet the metaphor cannot be what constitutes the parallel. This is easily seen by merely noticing that the biological process is blind and purposeless, whereas what is political is known to be, at least in part, directed by conscious design. Moreover, we are certainly able to some extent to compare our metaphor with the process described, so that we often know, within somewhat wide limits, how far our analogy is apt; but this would be impossible, unless the political process, as opposed to the biological one, were in some way before the mind as a distinct species of change. Thus the essence of the parallel is not constituted by the metaphor, but by having immediately before the mind a process which is recognized as exhibiting a similar formal structure of variation, selection, and inheritance. But for the fact of this formal resemblance in this sense, we should not know that there ever was a systematic pattern in human affairs at all, nor should we be able to understand the term 'social evolution', any more than a man ignorant of biology can understand the term 'natural selection'. Thus there must be structural parallels between the two domains, and it is upon them, ultimately, that all our understanding of institutional change depends.
