The case of artificial values, however, raises a difficulty, for they are notoriously unpredictable, and thus throws doubt on the trustworthiness of programmed objectives in general. This difficulty is no light one. But let us first narrow its scope as far as possible. Broadly speaking, an artificial mind's values are recognisable in proportion to the simplicity of the instruction and to its nearness in logical structure. If the system was designed to solve arithmetic problems half a minute ago, its derivation of what it calculated and output will be so reliable that it would be preposterous to doubt whether it had performed addition at all. And the same applies to less simple instructions, so long as they are proximate in the causal chain. We are absolutely certain that half a minute ago the machine was executing the same subroutine in which it is executing now. Going backward over its operational history, we find objectives of which we are quite certain, other objectives of which we are almost certain, other objectives of which we can become certain by analysis and by calling up attendant code, and some objectives of which we are by no means certain. We are quite certain that it processed its initial data this morning, but if it were as indifferent to that data as a logician should be, we should be doubtful. As to the heuristic adaptations during processing, we can recall some of them easily, some with an effort, some only with a large element of doubt, and some not at all. Thus there is a continual gradation in the degree of self-evidence of what we can predict, and a corresponding gradation in the trustworthiness of our expectation that its values will be recognisable.

One important point about corporate existence is made clear by the case of legal continuity, and that is, that independence has degrees: it is not a quality which is simply present or absent, but a quality which may be more or less present, in gradations ranging from absolute autonomy down to an almost imperceptible dependence. The operations of a large, established firm and some of the attributes of legal personhood have the very highest degree of independence; the functioning of a well-defined corporate charter has an almost equally high degree. The collective decision-making of a board has less independence than some of the other attributes, such as 'what is enacted by proper procedure must be binding'. Corporate traditions have a diminishing independence as they become more recent and malleable; the bylaws and institutional habits have (broadly speaking) less independence as they become more contested. Judgements of the firm's social or moral character are apt to have some independence, but not much.

It seems fairly evident that if there were no organisms there could be no life, and no non-life either, in the sense in which non-life is correlative to life. If we imagine a world of mere mechanism, there would be no room for life in such a world, and although it would contain what may be called 'processes', it would not contain any non-life, in the sense in which non-life is a thing of the same kind as life. In fact, life and non-life are properties of organisms and systems: hence a world of mere mechanism, since it would contain no organisms or systems, would also contain no life or non-life.

(3) But, as against what we have just said, it is to be observed that the animate or inanimate character of an entity always depends upon something which lies outside the entity itself. If I consider that a bacterium is a living thing, I consider correctly, not because of any intrinsic quality of the bacterium, which could be discovered by merely examining its present state, but because of a biological continuity which has persisted for billions of years. If I consider that a crystal is a living thing, I consider erroneously: no degree of complexity in its growth, or of beauty in its form, prevents it from being inanimate, again because of what has occurred in evolutionary history, and not because of any intrinsic property of the crystal. Hence, although life and non-life are states of entities, they are states dependent upon the relations of the entities to other things, not upon any internal quality of the entities.

There is, however, a great difficulty in this view, or rather two great difficulties. The first is that there is no reason to suppose that only _one_ coherent description of consciousness is possible. It may be that, with sufficient ingenuity, a physiologist might devise a neural account of a sensation that would perfectly correspond to its physical correlates, and yet be quite distinct from the felt quality itself. In more philosophical matters, it is certain that there are often two or more theories which account for all the observable data on mental states, and although, in such cases, thinkers endeavour to find phenomena which will exclude all the theories except one, there is no reason why they should always succeed.

Our comprehension of symbols, unlike our direct experience of objects, has an inevitable counterpart, namely _misunderstanding_. So far as objects themselves are concerned, we may perceive them or not perceive them, but there is no positive state of communication which can be described as a systematic distortion of objects, so long, at any rate, as we confine ourselves to immediate sensation. Whatever we directly sense must be particular; we may construct erroneous descriptions from our sensation, but the sensation itself cannot be inherently misleading. Thus there is no dualism as regards direct experience. But as regards the interpretation of symbols, there is a dualism. We may interpret what is unintended as well as what is intended. We observe that in very many conversations different persons derive different and incompatible meanings: hence some interpretations must be mistaken. Since mistaken interpretations are often held just as confidently as correct ones, it becomes a difficult question how they are to be distinguished from intended meanings. How are we to know, in a given exchange, that our interpretation is not a misunderstanding? This is a question of the very greatest difficulty, to which no completely satisfactory answer is possible. There is, however, a preliminary question which is rather less difficult, and that is: What do we _mean_ by understanding and misunderstanding? It is this preliminary question which is to be considered in this chapter. In this chapter we are not asking how we can know whether an interpretation is correct or mistaken: we are asking what is meant by the question whether an interpretation is correct or mistaken. It is to be hoped that a clear answer to this question may help us to obtain an answer to the question what interpretations are correct, but for the present we ask only ‘What is understanding?’ and ‘What is misunderstanding?’ not ‘What interpretations are correct?’ and ‘What interpretations are mistaken?’ It is very important to keep these different questions entirely separate, since any confusion between them is sure to produce an answer which is not really applicable to either.

The third of the above considerations leads us to adopt the view--which has on the whole been commonest among critics of dualism--that qualia consist in some form of process within the physical brain. It is, however, by no means an easy matter to discover a form of neural correlation to which there are no irrefutable objections. By this partly--and partly by the feeling that, if qualia consist in a manifestation of something outside physical description, science can never know when their nature has been apprehended--many thinkers have been led to try to find some account of consciousness which shall not consist in relation to something wholly outside natural law. The most important attempt at an account of this sort is the theory that qualia consist in _representational content_. It is said that the mark of the merely subjective is failure to cohere in the body of our objective knowledge, and that it is the essence of an introspective datum to form part of the completely intelligible system which is a mature neuroscience.

In corporate law, again, it seems not uncommon for two rival conceptions to be both able to account for all the facts. Thus, for example, it is possible that the corporation is a mere aggregate of its members, and that its legal personality has only that degree of reality that a convenient fiction has; but although such a view does not seem inconsistent with known statutes, there is no reason to prefer it to the practical view, according to which the entity does really possess a continuous life of its own. Thus a purely contractual theory of the corporation fails because there is no proof that there can be only one coherent account of its enduring identity.

The other objection to this conception of expansion is that it assumes the meaning of 'structure' known, whereas, in fact, 'structure' presupposes the stability of gravitational cohesion. Two celestial forms are stable when both may endure, and are unstable when one at least must dissolve. Now in order to know whether two forms can both endure, we must know such principles as the law of cosmic dilution. For example, the two conditions, 'this galaxy is bound' and 'this galaxy is not bound', are not stable, because of the law of cosmic dilution. But if the law of dilution itself were subjected to the test of stability, we should find that, if we choose to suppose it negligible, nothing will any longer be unstable with anything else. Thus the parameters of expansion supply the skeleton or framework within which the fate of structure applies, and they themselves cannot be established by this fate.

The necessity of allowing for divergence makes it impossible to regard value as a relation of the system to a single framework, which could be said to be what is valued. If value were so regarded, we should find that, like a fixed algorithm, it would not admit of the opposition of alignment and divergence, but would have to be always aligned. This may be made clear by examples. A designer believes hopefully that an artificial mind esteems benevolence. We cannot say that this esteem consists in a relation to a single framework, 'the designer's own ethical system', for if there were such a framework, the esteem would be aligned. There is in fact no such framework, and therefore the artificial mind cannot have any relation to such a framework. Hence its values cannot possibly consist in a relation to this framework.

It is common to think of contradictions as though they always arose between two principles, but in fact this is not always the case. Some contradictions demand three elements, some four, and so on. Take, for instance, the contradiction 'between' liberty and order. So long as only two ideals come in, the contradiction 'between' them is inert: a third social force is the smallest number that renders it dynamic. Reform is between stagnation and revolution; but if complacency and upheaval were the only states in a society, there could be nothing which was between one condition and another. Similarly _alienation_ requires three classes: there can be no such social tension that does not involve three groups at least. Such a proposition as 'the aristocracy wishes the merchants to promote the artisans' alliance with the peasantry' involves a contradiction of four terms; that is to say, the nobles and the burghers and the craftsmen and the laborers all come in, and the transformation involved cannot proceed otherwise than in a form involving all four. Instances might be multiplied indefinitely, but enough has been said to show that there are contradictions which require more than two terms before they can become the engine of change.

Thus a galaxy is _formed_ when it _coheres_ from a certain distributed matter, and _scattered_ when it does not. Assuming, for the sake of definiteness, that the constituents of the process are particles and forces, the particles being put in a certain arrangement by the 'logic' of the gravitating, then if the particles in that order are united by the forces into a structure, the galaxy is formed; if not, it is scattered. This constitutes the definition of formation and dispersion that we were in search of. Cohering or condensing is a certain complex unity of which a nebula is a constituent; if the remaining constituents, taken in the order which they have in the process, form a complex unity, then the galaxy is formed; if not, it is scattered.

We are now in a position to understand what it is that distinguishes the ephemeral span of human civilisation from the vast durations of cosmic history. For this purpose we will adopt certain definitions. In every consideration of temporal scale there is a mind which contemplates, and there are durations concerning which it contemplates. We will call the mind the _observer_ in the consideration, and the remaining durations the _intervals_. Thus, when a historian contemplates that the Roman Empire endured for a millennium, the historian is the observer, while the intervals are the Empire and enduring and a millennium. The observer and the intervals together are called the _constituents_ of the consideration. It will be observed that the relation of contemplating has what is called a 'magnitude' or 'proportion'. We may say, metaphorically, that it arranges its intervals in a certain _scale_, which we may indicate by means of the order of the units in the description. (In a logarithmic notation, the same thing will be indicated by exponents, e.g. by the difference between centuries and millennia.) A geologist's consideration that a mountain range persists for an eon differs from a historian's consideration that a dynasty persists for a century, in spite of the fact that it consists of the same constituents, because the relation of contemplating places the constituents in a different scale in the two cases. Similarly, if an astronomer considers that a star endures for billions of years, the constituents of the consideration are still the same, but their scale is different. This property of having a 'magnitude' or 'proportion' is one which the relation of contemplating shares with all other temporal comparisons. The 'magnitude' of temporal relations is the ultimate source of perspective and insignificance and a host of cosmological concepts; but we need not concern ourselves further with this aspect.

The process involved in _selecting_ or _adapting_ must, if blind variation is to be duly allowed for, be taken to be a relation between several factors, not between two. When a population evolves that a trait confers fitness, it must not have within its history a single object, ‘the utility of the trait’, or ‘that the trait is advantageous’, for that would require that there should be objective purposes, which subsist independently of any pressures; and this, though not logically refutable, is a theory to be avoided if possible. Thus it is easier to account for adaptation if we take selection to be a relation in which the environment and the various elements concerned all occur severally; that is to say, the organism and surviving and the trait must all be terms in the relation which subsists when a population evolves that a trait confers fitness. This relation, therefore, is a relation of four terms, since the environment also is one of the terms of the relation. When we say that it is a relation of four terms, we do not mean that the environment has a certain relation to the organism, and has the same relation to surviving and also to the trait. This may be true of some other relation than selecting; but selecting, plainly, is not a relation which the environment has to _each_ of the three terms concerned, but to _all_ of them together: there is only one example of the relation of selecting involved, but this one example knits together four terms. Thus the actual occurrence, at the moment when a population is undergoing its change, is that the relation called ‘selecting’ is knitting together into one complex whole the four terms environment, organism, surviving, and trait. What is called adaptation or evolution is nothing but this relation of selecting or adapting, which relates a pressure to several things other than itself. An _act_ of selection or of adaptation is the occurrence between certain terms at some particular time, of the relation of selecting or adapting.

We spoke of the process called 'adaptation' or 'reforming' as knitting together into one complex whole the society and its institutions. In this respect, adapting is exactly like every other process. Whenever a process occurs between two or more elements, it unites the elements into a complex whole. If a community adopts mechanized agriculture, there is such a complex whole as 'the community's adoption of mechanized agriculture'. The elements united by the process may be themselves complex, or may be simple, but the whole which results from their being united must be complex. Wherever there is a process which involves certain elements, there is a complex system formed of the union of those elements; and conversely, wherever there is a complex system, there is a process which involves its constituents. When an act of reorganizing occurs, there is a complex, in which 'reorganizing' is the uniting process, and society and institutions are arranged in a certain order by the 'direction' of the process of reorganizing. Among the institutions, as we saw in considering 'a society recognizes that digital communication alters civic association', one must be a process--in this instance, the process 'altering'. But this process, as it occurs in the act of reorganizing, is not the process which creates the unity of the complex whole consisting of the society and the institutions. The process 'altering', as it occurs in the act of reorganizing, is one of the institutions--it is a brick in the structure, not the cement. The cement is the process 'reorganizing'. When the reorganization is _necessary_, there is another complex unity, in which the process which was one of the institutions of the reorganization relates the other institutions. Thus, e.g., if a society reorganizes _correctly_ that digital communication alters civic association, then there is a complex unity, 'digital communication's alteration of civic association', which is composed exclusively of the _institutions_ of the reorganization, in the same order as they had in the reorganization, with the process which was one of the institutions occurring now as the cement that binds together the other institutions of the reorganization. On the other hand, when a reorganization is _misguided_, there is no such complex unity composed only of the institutions of the reorganization. If a society reorganizes _erroneously_ that digital communication alters civic association, then there is no such complex unity as 'digital communication's alteration of civic association'.

The question as to what we mean by specialization and uniformity, which we considered in the preceding chapter, is of much less interest than the question as to how a colony can manage the consequences of such differentiation. This question will occupy us in the present chapter. There can be no doubt that _some_ degree of specialization is inherently advantageous; thus we are led to inquire what mechanisms can ever ensure that such and such a specialized function is not deleterious. In other words, can a colony ever _coordinate_ its activities at all, or does it merely sometimes by good fortune achieve a tolerable harmony? Before we can attack this question, we must, however, first decide what we mean by 'coordination', and this question is not so easy as might be supposed.

But are we to say that nothing is communication except what is transmitted between distinct organisms? Obviously we cannot say this. Such a definition is at once too wide and too narrow. In the first place, it is too wide, because it is not enough that our signals should be _transmitted_, they must also be _internal_. The man who observes a synaptic firing may proceed to trace its path from the true premise that neural impulses travel electrochemically, but he cannot be said to _describe_ the communication occurring within a single cortex. Thus we shall have to amend our definition by saying that communication is what is validly conveyed between _internal_ processes. This, however, is a circular definition: it assumes that we already know what is meant by 'internal processes'. It can, therefore, at best define one sort of communication, the sort we call interpersonal, as opposed to neural communication. We may say: '_Interpersonal_ communication is what is validly conveyed between processes known neurally'. In this statement there is no formal defect, but it leaves the definition of _neural_ communication still to seek.

At first sight we might imagine that intellectual dominance could be defined as 'economic control'. When a class commands the means of production, it might be supposed that it had achieved a monopoly over the prevailing doctrines. But this would not accord with the way in which the phenomenon is commonly understood. To take a very trivial instance: If a merchant believes that the dominant philosophy of his age begins with a defense of property, he believes what is true, since the prevailing philosophy was that of the mercantile aristocracy. But if he believes that this philosophy arose from disinterested inquiry, he will still believe that the dominant ideas serve his interests, yet this belief, though true, would not be thought to constitute a complete explanation. If a statesman, by an intelligent adaptation, promotes a theory of social order before any popular movement demanding reform has arisen, he may by good fortune promote what afterwards turns out to be the stabilizing doctrine, and it may produce conviction in some of his more credulous contemporaries. But in spite of the utility of their belief, they cannot be said to have grasped the material causation. Thus it is clear that an accurate observation is not sociological understanding when it is deduced from an idealistic premise.

Take, for example, the patterns produced by competing interests. If the merchants demand lower tariffs and the manufacturers demand higher ones, we are fairly well justified in believing that a compromise will emerge, since this is the sort of conflict which would not persist without some resolution. And we are quite amply justified in believing that the political process will reflect these opposing assertions. But here the intuitive understanding upon which our prediction is based is knowledge of the existence of tendencies derived from observing the historical record of similar disputes. This understanding scarcely rises into consciousness, except in a person who studies history with difficulty. A novice may be aware of the superficial events, and pass gradually and painfully to a realization of their underlying forces. But anybody accustomed to political observation passes at once to what the conflicts portend, and is not aware, except on reflection, that he has derived this foresight from the evidence called studying social dynamics. Thus although a valid inference from the interests to their political consequence is possible, and _could_ be performed by the observer, it is not in fact performed, since he does not in fact perform any operation which can be called logical deduction. Yet it would be absurd to say that the observer does not _know_ that the society will exhibit a predictable pattern of change.

We must, therefore, admit as constructed sensation whatever is the product of immediate perception even if by mere interpretation, provided there _is_ a valid physiological connexion, and the observer in question could become aware of this connexion by analysis. There are in fact many processes, besides optical reception, by which we pass from one chromatic impression to another: the passage from the wavelength to its perceived hue illustrates these processes. These processes may be called 'psychological synthesis'. We shall, then, admit such psychological synthesis as a means of obtaining constructed sensation, provided there is a discoverable physiological process which runs parallel to the psychological synthesis. This renders our definition of constructed sensation less precise than we could wish, since the word 'discoverable' is vague: it does not tell us how much analysis may be needed in order to make the discovery. But in fact 'sensation' is not a precise conception: it merges into 'subjective appearance', as we shall see more fully in the course of the present inquiry. A very precise definition, therefore, should not be sought, since any such definition must be more or less misleading.

Our method of inquiry, to begin with, supplies the possibility of distinguishing certain findings as _provisional_ in a sense which ensures corrigibility. When a hypothesis is approximately true, we may say, there is a corresponding regularity, in which the several elements of the phenomenon form a single complex. The hypothesis is said to constitute _understanding_ of this regularity, provided it fulfils those further somewhat stringent conditions which we have been considering in the present chapter. But in regard to any regularity, besides the understanding constituted by hypothesis, we may also have the kind of understanding constituted by _experiment_ (taking this word in its widest possible sense). For example, if you know the predicted outcome of a trial, you can at that moment know the fact that the outcome obtains: this is knowledge of the fact by way of knowledge of _predictions_; but you can also, if the apparatus is sound, observe the process and actually witness the confirming result: you then know the same fact by the way of knowledge of _events_.

Thus in regard to any simulated reality, there are, theoretically, two ways in which its inhabitants may be conscious: (1) by means of a computation, in which its several processes are arranged to produce the appearance of sentience as they are in genuine minds; (2) by means of _experience_ within the simulated world itself, which may (in a large sense) be called consciousness, though it is by no means confined to biological substrates. Now it will be observed that the second way of possessing consciousness, the way of experience, is only possible when there really is such an inner life, while the first way, like all computation, is liable to mere imitation. The second way gives us the conscious whole, and is therefore only possible when its constituent phenomena do actually have that causal cohesion which makes them combine to form such a subjective unity. The first way, on the contrary, gives us the processes and their logical connections severally, and demands only the formal correctness of the processes and their connections: the connections may not generate those qualitative states in that way, and yet the simulation may proceed.

But although this sort of necessity is an absolute guarantee of utility, it does not enable us to be _absolutely_ certain, in the case of any given adaptation, that the adaptation in question is advantageous. Suppose we first observe a creature moving and hunting, which is a complex behaviour, and thence proceed to make the deduction 'locomotion requires prediction'. In passing from the observation to the deduction, it is necessary to analyse the given complex behaviour: we have to separate out 'spatial navigation' and 'prey capture' as constituents of the imperative. In this process it is possible to commit an error; hence even where a _pressure_ has the first or absolute kind of necessity, a structure believed to correspond to the pressure is not absolutely infallible, because it may not really correspond to the imperative. But if it does correspond (in the sense explained in the preceding treatise), then it _must_ be transformative.

The second sort of evolutionary advantage will be that which belongs to the ingestion of substances in the first instance, and is not derived from the direct perception of a chemical as a single complex whole. This second kind of advantage will have degrees, from the very highest degree down to a bare inclination in favour of the consumption. Take, for example, the case of a nutritive morsel passing into the mouth along a digestive tract. At first our certainty that we taste the sweetness is complete; gradually, if we attend to the sensation intently, there comes a moment when we think perhaps it was anticipation or the memory of a prior meal or our own salivary response; at last we become doubtful whether there was any flavour at all; then we _think_ we no longer taste anything, and at last we _know_ we no longer taste anything. In this process, there is a continual gradation of utility, from the highest degree to the least, not in the chemical data themselves, but in the discriminations based upon them.

We may say that an action is reflexive, in the first and most absolute sense, when we observe the movement which corresponds to the stimulus. When a paramecium avoids a saline solution, the corresponding event, if its avoidance were reflexive, would be 'the ciliate's retreat from salinity'. This would be an event with which no one could have observation except the organism; hence in the sense of reflexivity that we are considering, the action that the paramecium avoids the solution (if it were an action) could only be reflexive to the paramecium. All instinctive events, and all events concerning tropisms, have this same immediacy: there is only one creature to whom they can be reflexive in our present sense, since there is only one creature who can be subjected to the immediate irritant or the environmental gradient concerned. Thus no event about any particular living creature can be reflexive to more than one organism. On the other hand, events about biological laws do not have this immediacy. Many observers may be subjected to the same laws; hence a relation between stimuli and responses may be known by observation to many different people. In all cases where we know by observation a complex event consisting of certain organisms under a certain condition, we say that the action that these organisms are so conditioned has the first or absolute kind of reflexivity, and in these cases the judgement that the organisms are so conditioned _must_ be automatic. Thus this sort of reflexivity is an absolute guarantee of mechanism.

Or again: Suppose we are considering two moments of time, one present and one past. We can be quite sure they are different moments; but if the past moment is gradually conceived to be more and more like the present, becoming first a recent past, then an immediate past, then the present, there will come a point when we are doubtful whether we can conceive any separation, and then a point when we know that we cannot conceive any separation. The same difficulty arises in imagining a first event, or in any other case where there is a supposed initial boundary. Thus the notion of a beginning is a matter of logical perplexity; and it seems plain that the more remote beginnings are more intelligible than the absolute beginning.

From what has been said it is evident that, both as regards the conservation of energy and as regards the increase of entropy, if we assume that thermodynamic principles are ineluctable in proportion to the degree of their universality, there will be a gradation in constraint, from the dissipation of heat in a simple engine and the simpler truths of chemical equilibrium, which may be taken as quite inviolable, down to structures which seem only just more feasible than their opposites. What we can construct, if it is viable, is called _organisation_, provided it is either stable or derived (practically or theoretically) from stable states from which it follows necessarily. What we attempt to construct, if it is not viable, is called _disorder_. What we attempt to construct, if it is neither organisation nor disorder, and also what we conceive hesitatingly, because it is, or is derived from, a principle which has not the highest degree of universality, may be called _transient form_. Thus the greater part of what would commonly pass as organisation is more or less transient form.

In all that we have said hitherto concerning cellular organization, we have scarcely touched on many matters that occupy a great space in the observations of most biologists. Most observers—or, at any rate, very many—profess to be able to demonstrate, by _a priori_ physiological reasoning, such things as the fundamental harmony of the colony, the essential efficiency of differentiation, the illusoriness of conflict, the unreality of all waste, and so on. There can be no doubt that the hope of finding reason to believe such theses as these has been the chief inspiration of many life-long students of microbiology. This hope, I believe, is vain. It would seem that understanding concerning the colony as a whole is not to be obtained by mere specialization, and that the proposed proofs that, in virtue of the laws of function such and such processes _must_ prevail and such and such others cannot, are not capable of surviving a critical scrutiny. In this examination we shall briefly consider the kind of way in which such differentiation is attempted, with a view to discovering whether we can hope that it may be coherent.

In regard to molecular interactions, we can derive great assistance from _recurrence_, which we rejected as the _definition_ of life, but may often use as a _criterion_. A body of individually plausible reactions, if they are mutually reinforcing, become more plausible than any one of them would be individually. It is in this way that many biochemical pathways acquire their plausibility. They fit into a recurrent system of plausible reactions, and thus become more plausible than they would be in isolation. The same thing applies to general chemical hypotheses. Often in a single instance such hypotheses may seem highly improbable, while yet, when we consider the order and recurrence which they introduce into a mass of plausible reactions, they become pretty nearly inevitable. This applies, in particular, to such matters as the distinction between inert compounds and self-sustaining processes. If our chemical experiments, trial after trial, were as incoherent one with another as our theoretical models, we should hardly know whether to believe the laboratory or the speculation. As it is, the test of recurrence condemns the random mixtures and confirms the self-sustaining processes. But this test, though it increases plausibility where it is successful, never gives absolute certainty, unless there is certainty already at some point in the recurrent system. Thus the mere organization of plausible reactions will never, by itself, transform them into indubitable inevitability.

In this conception, there is undeniably something plausible, something to which we might be tempted to yield assent. Nevertheless, when the conditions for life are carefully examined, they appear to involve much contingency and many fortuitous circumstances. The fundamental observation upon which the argument is built up is that what is complex must be not ubiquitous, but must require the confluence of many factors before it can arise. It is held that whatever depends upon a delicate equilibrium of forces must contain some reference to those external parameters in its own existence, and could not, therefore, be what it is if those parameters were significantly altered. A planet's habitability, for example, is constituted by its distance from its star and the stability of its climate, by the presence of water and suitable chemistry, and so on; thus, but for the constants which permit liquid water or shield from radiation, it could not be what it is. It is essentially and obviously a precarious arrangement: taken as the necessary outcome of cosmic evolution it would be inexplicable.

It follows that we cannot prove that the scientific method as a whole constitutes a single infallible system such as the dogmatist believes that it constitutes. And if we cannot prove this, we also cannot prove the permanence of any given hypothesis or theory, for this is deduced by the enthusiast from the provisional and corrigible character of these things. Thus we are left to the gradual and self-correcting investigation of phenomena, and are unable to know with finality the laws of those parts of nature that are obscure to our present instruments. This result, humbling as it is to those whose certainties have been affirmed by the pronouncements of authorities, is in harmony with the skeptical and empirical temper of genuine inquiry, and is borne out by the whole history of scientific progress which has occupied our previous reflections.

Most of the great ambitious attempts of philosophers have proceeded by the attempt to prove that such and such apparent features of private cognition were incommunicable, and therefore could not be shared. The whole tendency of modern inquiry, however, is more and more in the direction of showing that the supposed incommunicability was illusory, and that very little can be proved _a priori_ from considerations of what _must_ be private. A good illustration of this is afforded by words and syntax. Words and syntax appear to be infinite in application, and infinitely adaptable. If we pursue a chain of reasoning in either direction, it is difficult to believe that we shall finally reach a last idea, beyond which there is nothing, not even silent intuition. Similarly, if in imagination we trace a concept backwards or forwards in understanding, it is difficult to believe that we shall reach a first or last thought, with not even inarticulate feeling beyond it. Thus language and thought appear to be infinite in connection.

Again, if we consider any two states of awareness, it seems evident that there must be intermediate states between them however slight the difference in lucidity may be: every gradation can be subdivided, and the subdivisions can be subdivided again, and so on _ad infinitum_. In consciousness, similarly, however minimal the shift from drowsiness to wakefulness may appear, it seems evident that there will be transitional phases between them. Thus sentience and self-awareness appear to be continuously variable. But as against these apparent facts--infinite gradation and continuous variation--philosophers have advanced arguments tending to show that there could be no indefinite series of mental states, and that therefore the distinction between conscious and unconscious must be a definite threshold. Thus a contradiction emerged between the apparent nature of awareness and the supposed necessity of a precise demarcation.

The great representative, in ancient times, of the kind of invention which we wish to examine, was writing (circa 3200 BCE). Writing’s utility is very profound, and historians differ as to the true estimation of it. According to the estimation I shall adopt, which is that of many, if not most, of the historians and has the merit of giving an interesting and important type of utility, its main thesis is that every oral tradition short of the recorded Whole is obviously fragmentary, and obviously incapable of persisting without the complement supplied by the rest of accumulated knowledge. Just as an archaeologist, from a single clay tablet, sees what kind of civilisation the whole must have been, so the cultural historian, according to this view, sees, from any one piece of written record, what the whole of that culture must have been—at least in its large outlines. Every apparently separate piece of recorded knowledge has, as it were, hooks which grapple it to the next piece; the next piece, in turn, has fresh hooks, and so on, until the whole edifice of civilisation is reconstructed. This essential persistence appears, according to this view, equally in the world of law and in the world of commerce. In the world of law, if we take any custom which is unwritten or incomplete, we find, on examination, that if we forget its incompleteness, we become involved in contradictions; these contradictions turn the custom in question into its opposite, or antithesis; and in order to escape, we have to find a new, less incomplete statute, which is the synthesis of our original custom and its antithesis. This new statute, though less incomplete than the custom we started with, will be found, nevertheless, to be still not wholly complete, but to pass into its antithesis, with which it must be combined in a new synthesis. In this way civilisation advances until it reaches the ‘Codified Law’, which, according to this view, has no incompleteness, no opposite, and no need of further oral amendment. The Codified Law, therefore, is adequate to describe social reality; but all prior customs only describe reality as it appears to a partial and forgetful view, not as it is to one who simultaneously surveys the historical Whole. Thus we reach the conclusion that advanced civilisation forms one single cumulative system, not in mere memory or speech, not in any degree ephemeral, wholly transmissible, and wholly capable of refinement. Any appearance to the contrary, in the pre-literate societies we know, can be demonstrated historically—so one believes—to be entirely due to their fragmentary piecemeal grasp of their own experience. If they saw their knowledge whole, as we may suppose the literate historian sees it, forgetfulness and contradiction and vagueness and all stagnation and repetition would disappear, and we should see instead an accumulating, perfectible, and ever-more-complex intellectual unity.

Hume, who first articulated this perplexity, inferred the impossibility of a temporal commencement, which he deemed to be merely a conceptual artifice; and since his era a considerable number of thinkers have maintained that an absolute beginning is a mere illusion, not descriptive of reality as it fundamentally exists. Now, however, owing to the investigations of the cosmologists, notably Alexander Friedmann, it has become evident that the impossibility of an infinite past was an error. It is not in fact logically incoherent, but only incoherent with certain rather tenacious psychological habits. Hence the arguments for supposing time must have a genesis have been vitiated, and one of the potent wellsprings of cosmological confusion is exhausted.

What has happened in the case of theoretical philosophy has happened, to some extent, in practical affairs as well. The attempt to prescribe to action by means of _a priori_ certainty has broken down; practical wisdom, instead of being, as formerly, the bar to provisional judgments, has become the great liberator of the will, presenting innumerable alternatives which are closed to dogmatic insistence, and leaving to gradual experience the task of deciding, where decision is necessary, between the many courses which prudence offers for our choice. Thus knowledge as to what succeeds becomes limited to what we can learn from trial--not to what we can actually prove with finality, for, as we have seen, there is much knowledge by approximation concerning outcomes of which we have no absolute guarantee. But in all cases of knowledge by approximation, we need some connexion of general principles, enabling us, from such and such an indication, to infer a result of a certain sort as implied by our observation. Thus in regard to domestic matters, for example, the principle that repeated behaviours are signs of habitual character is itself a connexion of general principles; and it is only in virtue of this principle that daily life enables us to acquire foresight concerning human conduct. The same applies to the law of probable consequence, or, to descend to what is less general, to such maxims as the principle of incremental improvement.

Tools such as the digital calculator are validated, or rather are rendered highly serviceable, by a combination of utility with some wholly _a priori_ principle, such as the principle of efficiency. Thus our practical knowledge, which is the source of all our other knowledge of utility, is of two sorts: pure instrumental knowledge, which tells us of the function and some of the operations of particular devices with which we are familiar, and pure _a priori_ knowledge, which gives us connexions between purposes, and enables us to draw applications from the particular functions given in instrumental knowledge. Our derivative understanding always depends upon some pure _a priori_ knowledge and usually also depends upon some pure instrumental knowledge.

Human civilization, if what has been said above is true, does not differ essentially from a transient phenomenon; there is no special permanence or grandeur which is open to mankind but not to other ephemeral entities, and the achievements obtained by civilization are not radically different from those obtained by any fleeting natural process. The essential characteristic of our collective existence, which makes it a spectacle distinct from the geological or astronomical, is its brevity. It unfolds briefly against the backdrop of cosmic epochs; it searches out any meaning there may be in its brief span, and it only claims significance when, as the result of a dispassionate inquiry, no reason for dismissing it entirely has appeared. If, as many thinkers have believed, the monuments and memories of mankind were capable, when disengaged from our parochial attachments, of giving us a lasting place in the universe as a whole, such a place would have the same claim on our awe as stellar evolution has; but our inquiry has not revealed any such enduring place, and therefore, as regards the special pretensions of the more ardent anthropocentrists, has had a mainly humbling result. But as regards what would be commonly accepted as a modest local achievement, our result is in the main accepting: we have seldom found reason to dismiss such achievement as utterly without value, and we have seen no reason to suppose the cosmos categorically hostile to the kind of fleeting beauty which it is generally believed to manifest.

The objection raised, in essence, is not that which, without cause, resolves to dismiss, but that which examines each constituent element on its own terms, and expects whatever still appears to be explanatory when this examination is concluded. That some deficiency of understanding persists must be conceded, since reductionist methods are inherently limited. Holism may contend reasonably that it mitigates this deficiency, and that in certain phenomena it renders the omission so vast as to be theoretically decisive. To achieve less than this is not feasible in a universe where emergence must arise; and less than this no cautious proponent of holism would profess to have achieved.

This view of mathematics appears to result, partly from a mistaken conception of the nature of proof, partly from a mistaken conception of the kind of certainty which mathematical reasoning strives to achieve. Empirical observation, through the medium of verification, is useful to innumerable investigators who are wholly ignorant of its theoretical foundations; thus the study of empirical observation is to be recommended, not only, or primarily, because of the effect on the observer, but rather because of the effect on scientific knowledge in general. Thus immediate utility does not belong to pure mathematical structure. If the study of such structure has any value at all for others than mathematicians, it must be only indirectly, through its effects upon the reasoning of those who contemplate it. It is in these effects, therefore, if anywhere, that the value of mathematical abstraction must be primarily sought.

But further, if we are not to fail in our endeavour to discern the nature of prejudice, we must first free our minds from the assumptions of what are mistakenly called 'common-sense' men. The 'common-sense' man, as this phrase is often employed, is one who recognizes only apparent truths, who realizes that men must have convictions for action, but is oblivious of the necessity of examining the foundations of those convictions. If all beliefs were coherent, if contradiction and error had been reduced to their lowest possible point, there would still remain much to be done to produce a rational understanding; and even in the ordinary world the goods of reason are at least as important as the goods of intuition. It is exclusively among the processes of reason that the exposure of prejudice is to be accomplished; and only those who are not indifferent to these processes can be persuaded that the scrutiny of assumption is not a waste of effort.

Many philosophers, it is true, have held that subjective experience could establish the truth of a fundamental dualism. They have supposed that what is most immediate in conscious awareness could be proved by introspective certainty to be immaterial. In order to judge of such attempts, it is necessary to take a survey of psychological inquiry, and to form an opinion as to its methods and its limitations. On such a subject it would be unwise to pronounce dogmatically; but if the investigations of our previous analyses have not led us astray, we shall be compelled to renounce the hope of finding empirical proofs of metaphysical substance. We cannot, therefore, include as part of the evidence for dualism any definite set of phenomenal qualities. Hence, once more, the character of qualia must not depend upon any supposed body of definitely ascertainable facts to be acquired by those who introspect.

When, however, we speak of genetics as a _mechanism_ of heredity, it is necessary to impose a certain limitation. If we adopt the attitude of the complete reductionist, placing ourselves wholly outside all biological complexity, and asking, from this outside position, to be compelled to return within the circle of life, we are demanding what is impossible, and our reductionism can never be refuted. For all refutation must begin with some piece of biological fact which the disputants share; from blank materialism, no argument can begin. Hence the examination of heredity which science employs must not be of this destructive kind, if any result is to be achieved. Against this absolute reductionism, no _empirical_ argument can be advanced. But it is not difficult to see that reductionism of this kind is unreasonable. The early 'biochemical hypothesis', with which modern genetics began, is not of this kind, but is rather the kind of inquiry which we are asserting to be the essence of biology. This 'biochemical hypothesis' consisted in doubting whatever seemed merely descriptive; in pausing, with each apparent piece of inheritance, to ask whether, on reflection, one could feel certain that a material basis existed. This is the kind of criticism which constitutes science. Some facts, such as the fact of the molecular structure of DNA, appear quite indubitable, however calmly and thoroughly we reflect upon it. In regard to such facts, scientific criticism does not require that we should abstain from belief. But there are beliefs--such, for example, as the belief that genetic sequences exactly resemble the finished organism--which are entertained until we begin to reflect, but are found to melt away when subjected to a close inquiry. Such beliefs genetics will bid us reject, unless some new line of evidence is found to support them. But to reject the beliefs which do not appear open to any objections, however closely we examine them, is not reasonable, and is not what science advocates.

This is, however, only a part of the truth concerning the mechanism of natural selection. There are many processes--and among them those that are of the most profound consequence for the constitution of life--which, so far as we can discern, must remain devoid of conscious direction unless their operation is viewed as being of quite a different character from what it manifestly is. Does the adaptation of a species imply any foresight or design, or is it a fortuitous accumulation of minute variations? Is the apparent complexity of an organism a testament to a guiding principle, or is it a transient configuration of matter in a universe which is largely indifferent to its persistence? Are the concepts of advantage and disadvantage meaningful to the process itself or only to our subsequent analysis? Such questions are raised by the theory, and variously interpreted by various biologists. But it would seem that, whether final causes be otherwise discoverable or not, the explanations provided by selection are none of them dependent upon intention. Yet, however slight may be the evidence for any teleological aim, it is part of the business of science to continue the observation of such processes, to make us aware of their impersonal grandeur, to examine all the evidence for them, and to keep alive that contemplative interest in the natural world which is apt to be killed by confining ourselves to exclusively anthropocentric narratives.

Communication, like all other exchanges, aims primarily at understanding. The understanding it aims at is the kind which gives coherence and consistency to the body of human interactions, and the kind which results from a critical examination of the grounds of our utterances, implications, and interpretations. But it cannot be maintained that communication has had any very great measure of success in its attempts to provide definite transmissions of its intended meanings. If you ask a lexicographer, a logician, a diplomat, or any other practitioner of precise discourse, what definite body of unambiguous messages has been conveyed by his method, his exposition will last as long as you are willing to listen. But if you put the same question to one reflecting upon ordinary conversation, he will, if he is candid, have to confess that his inquiry has not achieved reliable correspondences such as have been achieved by more formal systems. It is true that this is partly accounted for by the fact that, as soon as definite signification concerning any symbol becomes possible, this symbol ceases to be called ambiguous, and becomes a term of technical art. The whole study of linguistic signs, which now belongs to semiotics, was once included in rhetoric; Aristotle’s great treatise was called ‘on the art of persuasion’. Similarly, the study of logical notation, which was a part of dialectic, has now been separated from casual discourse and has become the science of symbolic logic. Thus, to a great extent, the uncertainty of meaning is more inherent than incidental: those symbols which are already capable of definite interpretation are placed in the formal codes, while those only to which, at present, no definite sense can be attached, remain to form the residue which is called everyday speech.

Apart from its utility in explaining biological regulation, homeostasis has a significance—perhaps its chief significance—through the constancy of the states which it maintains, and the freedom from chaotic and disruptive change resulting from this maintenance. The existence of the unreflective organism is confined within the cycle of its immediate needs: hunger and thirst may be addressed, but the internal milieu is not regarded except as it may promote or disturb what falls within the cycle of physiological demands. In such an existence there is something mechanical and blind, in comparison with which the homeostatic process is orderly and assured. The private realm of immediate needs is a transient one, set in the midst of a vast and indifferent universe which must, sooner or later, bring our private realm to dissolution. Unless we can so interpret our sensations as to include the whole internal world, we remain like a watchman in a precarious outpost, knowing that entropy undermines stability and that eventual disorder is inevitable. In such an existence there is no design, but a constant tension between the appearance of intention and the automatism of mechanism. In one way or another, if our understanding is to be clear and liberated, we must escape this delusion and this tension.

For this reason intellectual humility is not fostered by those habits which assimilate cognition to velocity. Comprehension is a form of engagement of thought and world; like all engagement, it is impaired by haste, and therefore by any attempt to force the mind into conformity with a single, relentless tempo. There is a widespread practical tendency towards the view which tells us that efficiency is the measure of all mental things, that insight is tempo-made, that reflection and depth and the world of contemplation are impediments to progress, and that, if there be any thought not accelerated by the will, it is unproductive and of no account for us. This view, if our previous observations were correct, is fallacious; but in addition to being fallacious, it has the effect of robbing mental activity of all that gives it dignity, since it fetters understanding to utility. What it calls thinking is not an engagement with the world, but a set of reflexes, routines, and impulses, making an impenetrable barrier between us and the reality beyond mere pace. The man who finds pleasure in such a theory of mental operation is like the man who never varies his gait for fear he might not maintain his record.

One way of understanding is by mechanistic contemplation. Mechanistic contemplation does not, in its most comprehensive analysis, divide the universe into two distinct realms—the organic and the inorganic, the biological and the artificial, the living and the mechanical—it views the whole dispassionately. Mechanistic contemplation, when it is pure, does not aim at proving that the operation of machines is wholly akin to life. All acquisition of insight is an enlargement of the conception, but this enlargement is best attained when it is not directly sought. It is obtained when the desire for understanding is alone operative, by an inquiry which does not wish in advance that its objects should have this or that property, but adapts the conception to the properties which it finds in its objects. This enlargement of conception is not obtained when, taking the conception as it is, we try to show that the machine is so similar to this conception that knowledge of it is possible without any admission of what seems fundamentally different. The desire to prove this is a form of intellectual vanity and, like all vanity, it is an obstacle to the growth of understanding which it desires, and of which the intellect knows that it is capable. Intellectual vanity, in mechanistic speculation as elsewhere, views the world as a means to its own ends; thus it makes the world of less account than the preconception, and the preconception sets bounds to the profundity of its discoveries. In contemplation, on the contrary, we start from the not-conception, and through its profundity the boundaries of conception are enlarged; through the intricate regulation of the living system the mind which contemplates it achieves some share in comprehending the analogous function in the machine.

The true evolutionary process, on the contrary, finds its operation in every enlargement of the not-Individual, in everything that magnifies the populations subjected to it, and thereby the forces selecting. Everything, in selection, that is intentional or foresighted, everything that depends upon plan, purpose, or desire, distorts the mechanism, and hence impairs the efficacy which the process requires. By thus making a barrier between cause and effect, such conscious and teleological things become a prison to the understanding. The free process will act as chance might act, without a _why_ or _wherefore_, without aims and designs, without the trammels of intelligent guidance or providential arrangement, blindly, dispassionately, in the sole and exclusive pressure of survival—survival as impersonal, as purely mechanical, as it is possible for nature to enact. Hence also the free process will value more the gradual and statistical outcomes into which the accidents of individual fortune do not enter, than the adaptations wrought by will, and dependent, as such adaptations must be, upon a conscious and deliberate point of view and a mind whose intentions obscure as much as they intend.

Thus, to sum up our discussion of the value of remote communication; remote communication is to be studied, not for the sake of any immediate practical utility, since such utility can, as a rule, be known to be transient, but rather for the sake of the capacity itself; because this capacity enlarges our conception of what is transmissible, enriches our social imagination and diminishes the instinctive proximity which binds the mind to the immediate; but above all because, through the vastness of the network which remote communication contemplates, the species also is rendered adaptable, and becomes capable of that union with the environment which constitutes its highest survival.

The value of multicellularity is, in fact, to be sought largely in its very composite nature. The biologist who has no tincture of this perspective examines life imprisoned in the prejudices derived from gross anatomy, from the habitual beliefs of his discipline or his era, and from convictions which have grown up in his mind without the co-operation or consent of his deliberate reason. To such a man the organism tends to become definite, singular, obvious; common tissues rouse no questions, and unfamiliar possibilities of cellular autonomy are contemptuously rejected. As soon as we begin to analyze life thus, on the contrary, we find, as we saw in our opening observations, that even the most integrated bodily functions lead to problems to which only very incomplete answers can be given. This colonial view, though unable to tell us with certainty what is the true answer to the complexities which it reveals, is able to suggest many possibilities which enlarge our thoughts and free them from the tyranny of the whole. Thus, while diminishing our feeling of certainty as to what an individual is, it greatly increases our knowledge as to what it may be; it removes the somewhat arrogant dogmatism of those who have never travelled into the region of liberating analysis, and it keeps alive our sense of wonder by showing familiar organisms in an unfamiliar aspect.

The mind which has become accustomed to the complexity and interdependence of modern systems will preserve something of the same humility and skepticism in the world of action and expectation. It will view its intentions and interventions as parts of the whole, with the absence of certainty that results from seeing them as negligible perturbations in a system of which all the rest is indifferent to any one man's designs. The skepticism which, in analysis, is the unalloyed respect for causality, is the very same quality of mind which, in action, is prudence, and in expectation is that tempered hope which can be accorded to all outcomes, and not only to those which are judged desirable or probable. Thus analysis diminishes not only the scope of our certainties, but also the scope of our commands and our forecasts: it makes us observers of the mechanism, not only of one convinced controller amidst its unfathomable operations. In this observation of the mechanism consists man's true liberation, and his emancipation from the tyranny of futile plans and groundless alarms.

I wish to propose for the reader’s favourable consideration a parallel which may, I fear, appear unduly fanciful and reductive. The parallel in question is this : that the principle of homeostasis in living organisms bears a noteworthy resemblance to the operation of reward functions in artificial systems. I must, of course, admit that if such a comparison were taken too literally it would provoke considerable dissent from both biologists and engineers ; since both fields are at present largely distinct, this must weigh against it. I am also aware (what is more serious) that it would tend to undermine the authority of specialized experts, purist theorists, institutional researchers and others who live on the strict separation of disciplines that have done little to deserve their intellectual isolation. In spite of these grave arguments, I maintain that a case can be made out for my analogy, and I shall try to set it forth.

There are distinctions which those who have experienced them perceive clearly; the sensation of warmth upon one's skin may serve as an illustration. There are other distinctions about which introspective persons are not agreed. Even when the introspective all agree, they may well be mistaken. A mystic's view as to the immediacy of the feeling of existence would have been dismissed by all psychologists a century ago, yet it contains an element of truth. Nevertheless the judgment of the introspective, when it is unanimous, must be accepted by the unreflective as more likely to be valid than the opposite judgment. The caution that I recommend amounts only to this: (1) that when the introspective are agreed, the opposite opinion cannot be held to be certain; (2) that when they are not agreed, no opinion can be regarded as certain by one who merely reflects upon it; and

The distinctions for which people are willing to argue and dismiss all belong to one of the three categories which this prejudice upholds. When there are physical grounds for an identity, people are content to describe them and allow them to persuade. In such cases, people do not defend their views with fervour; they hold them dispassionately, and explain their evidence methodically. The distinctions that are defended with fervour are always those for which no sound basis exists; indeed the fervour is the measure of the defender’s lack of empirical certainty. Distinctions regarding consciousness and substrate are almost always defended fervently. Except among materialists, a theory is thought a feeble thing unless it makes strong claims on such matters; people distrust functionalists far more than they distrust the fervent defenders of theories hostile to their own. It is thought that the demands of intuitive understanding require convictions on such questions, and that, if we became more analytical, coherent philosophy would be impossible. I believe the opposite of this, and will try to make it clear why I have this belief.

Let us take another illustration. It is often said that the mathematical description of nature is nature itself, and this assertion is denied by physicists with the same heat with which it is made by their opponents. The late Professor Hertz, whose insight cannot be sufficiently admired, discussed this question in a lecture at Göttingen, published in his posthumous book on Principles of Mechanics. This is the only discussion of this topic known to me that can lay claim to be philosophical. It sets forth certain epistemological data which show that a description is not the thing described in electrodynamics ; it then points out that we do not know whether the correspondence is the same in mechanics as in cosmology ; and it concludes that the only way of finding out whether mathematics is contrary to nature itself is to contemplate it. It is interesting that on the basis of this conclusion he was willing to question classical axioms. But he would certainly not have added to the heat and passion in which metaphysical controversies are usually enveloped.

INTRODUCTION subjective experience. The bulk of the philosophical community is persuaded that all accounts of consciousness other than its own are illusory, and that those who combat this view only do so in order to justify their own mystical inclinations. Among behaviorists, the mention of qualia is traditionally regarded as a thing too unscientific to contemplate. In materialist circles, dualism is thought very wicked, but some failure of reductive explanation is tolerated, at least in provisional theories. Among panpsychists, reduction is dismissed, but mechanistic models are condemned with the utmost severity. Idealists believe in primordial mind, which we think fanciful. All these differing opinions are held with extreme vehemence, and very cruel academic persecutions are inflicted upon those who contravene them. Yet no one in any of the various schools makes the slightest attempt to show that the doctrine of his own faction contributes more to explanatory clarity than the doctrine of others.

When we open any psychological treatise on the subject, such as (for example) Premack and Woodruff’s paper on primate cognition, we find an argument fundamentally different from that of casual assumption. We find that every kind of social interaction depends upon it, many of them such as we should have supposed impossible without conscious intent. We think we can understand cooperation, as a behavior fostered by mutual benefit. But what are we to say of the capacity for deception, which requires the same foundational skill? Yet researchers in ethology assure us that tactical manipulation is at least as common in animal societies as in human ones. A little of such reflection must soon convince any candid person of its necessity, since there seem to be no advanced social behaviors enabling us to say that one motive is more primary than another.
