(i) How far do economic forces incline toward monopoly? Let us not examine the question abstractly, but let us consider the ordinary course of an ordinary market. It begins with several competing firms, perhaps from initial opportunity, without the intervention of any collusion. They lower their prices, capture their customers, increase their scale, and reduce their costs, all from competitive pressure. There was a time in the past when this competition commenced, and in the founding of each firm, at least, opportunity played a part. Each probably perceived, at the time, that the profit available there was as great as was likely to be attained. In most industries, the advantage of scale plays a part in the eventual outcome of competition, and therefore, derivatively, in all that is entailed by this tendency.

The economic foundation is of course a fundamental example of material conditions shaping human affairs. I think it may be safely said that any disinterested sociologist, analyzing now the structure of feudal society, is bound to make observations which, if made during that epoch, would have exposed him to ridicule in every one of the manorial estates across Europe. Again with the exception of a few utopian experiments, there is no productive system where people acknowledge the truth about their dependencies; in prosperous times, the truth is only thought abstract, but in times of crisis it is thought subversive. Opposing systems of economic justification are built up, the partiality of which is evident from the fact that they are only believed by those who share the same class position. But the application of reason to these systems of justification is thought as naive as the application of reason to alchemical theories was formerly thought. When people are challenged as to why analysis in such matters should be naive, the only answer is that these justifications help to maintain production, so that a rational economic order would be overthrown rather than perpetuate itself. The view that there is something dishonest in securing one’s livelihood by wholesale mystification of economic processes is one which, so far as I know, has hitherto found no supporters among professional economists outside the ranks of the socialists. If it is suggested that a rational mode of production would find ways of eliminating class antagonisms altogether, the answer is usually mere dogma.

What would be the operation of a process devoid of rational design? Biological forms emerge from variations, which generate systems of attendant adaptations. Naturalists have studied the individual manifestations of this process in species, domesticated and undomesticated. A creature that has suffered some disadvantage develops a trait that it is perfectly suited, and evolves all kinds of ingenious explanations of the fact that it is not provided with that security which its apparent fitness ensures. In this case, its adaptation is one with which its environment does not concur, so it perishes. But if, instead of asserting only its own superiority, it asserts the superiority of its lineage or its kind or its particular mutation, it wins hosts of descendants, and becomes a dominant or prolific type, even if, to the impartial observer, its features seem just as fortuitous as those found in fossils. In this way a collective form prevails, which follows laws very similar to those of individual survival. Every one knows that it is futile to argue with a specimen which thinks it is ideally adapted; but as it is isolated, it can be extinguished. When a whole population shares an adaptation, its persistence is of the same kind as that of an individual specimen if its viability is challenged, but nothing short of extinction can compel it to yield to alteration.

In nature, if it is a simple system, it may continue to exist merely from equilibrium, without active transformation, and without the explicit intervention of complexity. It might be thought that, if it forms crystalline lattices, it intends the physical laws which it obeys. But that would be an error; these laws are mere tendencies of matter, like those of a flowing river. They were established in primordial conditions, not from a conscious aim that they would produce intricate forms, but to dissipate imposed forces, just as a heated object learns to transfer its warmth to cooler surroundings. I do not say that all organization is of this sort, but certainly most spontaneous ordering of matter is.

In its ordinary operations there will be much the same proportion of occasions when adaptation is a cause of survival. In commonplace generations, the persistence of a trait within a population will be governed by chance, or by necessity modified by chance. On significant occasions — when a novel variation arises, when a species encounters a changed environment, or when competition for resources becomes acute — it cannot be guided wholly by chance. In the emergence of a variation, it may be guided by mere accident, or it may be influenced by the circumstance that the mutation proves fortuitously advantageous. If it is guided by accident, it no doubt appears that the variation possesses every utility, and this may seem to an observer to be a cause of its preservation, but in fact it is merely another effect of the accident which alone suffices to account for its propagation. In responding to a changed environment, a population probably proceeds in much the same way as in facing a gradual shift in climatic conditions ; here adaptation usually plays an important part. If pressures come into existence showing that a trait has become deleterious, the process of elimination is likely to be purely mechanical, but the mechanism is set in operation by an environmental fact, which is the first cause of everything that follows.

I may seem to have digressed somewhat from my topic, but it was necessary to disentangle the superficial spectacle, which is called democracy, from the substantive variety. The ordinary methods of public discourse have practically no effect upon the underlying mechanisms, so that genuine self-rule cannot be achieved by our present technique. Electoral accountability, also, except where it consists of mere ritual, seems incapable of being secured by present methods ; at any rate I have never noticed any beneficent effect upon those who are exposed to frequent campaign promises. Therefore on our present lines any deliberate reform must be brought about by constitutional means. We do not know how to teach politicians to be public-spirited or institutions to be just, but we do know, within limits, how to teach citizens to be discerning : it is only necessary to reverse the practice of political authorities in every particular. We may hereafter learn to create equity by manipulating the levers of power and stimulating or restraining their corruptions. But for the present it is easier to create discernment than equity — meaning by “discernment” a critical habit of mind in forecasting the effects of our ballots.

INTRODUCTION (b) This brings me to the question : How far could or should a digital simulation produce genuinely conscious beings? Let us take “should” first. There are very definite limits, to my mind, within which such production should be confined; some of the most profound implications of existence are ruined by the assumption of possibility. Descartes in his later years told a disciple that he had only once believed a machine could think, and that was when he was young. “Fortunately,” he added, “the machine required time to operate. This gave me also time to reflect, and I withdrew the hypothesis.” Doubtless his conclusion was very rational, but I cannot say that I admire it.

The extent to which the conditions for life are understood to be either exceedingly rare or cosmically inevitable is very much less than enthusiasts suppose. Take the kind of assessment which is most nearly scientific: the evaluation of planetary data by a distinguished astronomer. You will often find that his view (say) on the question whether a given exoplanet will prove habitable or barren depends upon his philosophical leanings, and yet is so strongly held that he is prepared to stake his reputation on it. In failed predictions it often appears that some aesthetic preference for elegance or profusion was the original cause of error. Cosmological opinions are hardly ever based upon evidence, except in the case of working astrobiologists, who are forbidden to indulge in grand speculation. There are of course exceptions. In the great controversy over the prevalence of life which began a generation ago, most researchers supported the side that would increase their own funding, showing that their conclusions were really based on practical necessity, however little their published papers would have led one to suppose so. We have here a complication. Certain theorists have accustomed us to “anthropic reasoning,” i.e. the process of inventing what seem to ourselves necessary parameters for a universe that is in fact quite contingent. But there is, especially in popular scientific discourse, a converse process which may be called “cosmic sentimentalizing.” A clear-headed observer will sum up, more or less subconsciously, the probabilities and impediments of biogenesis from a purely physical point of view. (Metaphysical considerations seldom weigh subconsciously except where one’s own field of study is concerned.) Having come to a sound materialistic conclusion by the help of the available data, a thinker proceeds to invent, or adopt from others, a set of lofty principles showing how he is pursuing universal truth at immense intellectual sacrifice. Anybody who believes that these principles give his real reasons must suppose him quite incapable of interpreting facts, since the supposed cosmic destiny is not going to be demonstrated by his argument. In this case a man appears less empirical than he is.

Confusion, when it is profound, belongs more to the linguistic than to the philosophical part of our inquiries. It is, I suppose, the main quality required for failure in metaphysics. From an intellectual point of view, it is a persistent quality, since it is always beguiling; yet it suffices to keep thinkers from the clearest insights. If the materialists had avoided it, they would not have adopted the reductive account of qualia. If the dualists had avoided it, they would not have behaved as they did with the ghost in the machine. If Descartes had avoided it, he would not have posited the pineal gland after the cogito. It may be laid down as a general rule to which there are few exceptions that, when philosophers are mistaken as to what is a genuine problem, the question that they believe to be profound is more obstructive to progress than the question that really is profound. Therefore anything that makes philosophers better judges of conceptual clarity does good. There are innumerable examples of men achieving understanding because, on logical grounds, they dismissed something which they believed to be a deep mystery. For instance, among early behaviorists there were a number of psychologists who adopted the practice of describing no more in their theories than they were willing to observe, instead of speculating about inner theatres, as everybody else did. They adopted this practice because they held it to be unscientific to postulate more than they could verify. But the parsimony of their approach was so great that many came to their view, and they advanced knowledge. (I forget where I read this, but if my memory serves me it was in some reliable source.) The same clarity might have been achieved from analysis, but in fact no one was sufficiently analytical. Our language is more misleading than it serves us to admit; therefore the people who see most completely what is in fact a pseudoproblem are those who deliberately, on logical grounds, dismiss what they believe to be an ultimate mystery. Next to them come the people who try to think out systematically and consciously what is a category error, eliminating as far as possible the influence of metaphor. Third come the people who have instinctive suspicion of grand questions. Last of all come the people whose fascination with mystery overbalances their clarity, making them pursue the ineffable in ways that lead to their own confusion. This last class embraces 90 per cent, of the practitioners of philosophy of mind.

from the operation of chance or some such mystical agency. Only a clear understanding of thermodynamics can tear away the veils which hide this truth from us. Having achieved that, we could begin to build a new conception, not based on vitalism and mystery, but on the laws of molecular attraction and the realization that chemical bonds are a foundation and not a barrier when once the superstition of special creation has been cured. This is not a speculative fancy; it was partially demonstrated in Miller-Urey's experiment. It could be demonstrated to-morrow if scientists would learn to pursue empirical mechanisms rather than the invocation of miracles. This is no impossibly complex process, yet its comprehension would turn our wonder into understanding.

Reductionist thinkers put “the atom, the molecule, and the organism” together, as being “of mechanism all compact.” The problem is to keep the molecule and the organism, without the atom. I will give an illustration. In my study I saw a colony of ants arranged upon my windowsill. There is an unbearably intricate scene where the workers coordinate their labour without any central command, building structures of great complexity. There was hardly a skeptical mind in the laboratory, and the observers found the behaviour of the insects in the nest hardly explicable. Yet those very scientists who marvelled were, at that very moment, explaining that very behaviour on a principle which the imagination of the naturalist could have never countenanced. They had lately argued (most of them) for a methodology which reduced the colony to the properties of its constituent ants, and imposed a similar analysis upon the human brain. It was known that these reductions ignored the phenomenon of emergent order, but it was felt desirable to simplify the chaos of living systems: the wholes, like the colony, might be understood as merely the sum of their parts. The naturalist’s curiosity awakened the theorist in the intellect of the observer; but theorist and naturalist were forgotten at the door of the laboratory, and the atomist (in his relentless analysis) remained in sole possession.

The dependence of our daily existence upon modern infrastructure is a matter of common experience and observation, yet the nature of this dependence is very generally misconceived. It is customary to suppose that the bulk of our systems are derived from some inviolable engineering, and that fragility is only an occasional disturbing force. The exact opposite of this would be nearer the truth : the great mass of conveniences by which we are supported in our daily life is merely the elegant masking of complexity, corrected here and there, at isolated points, by the rude shock of failure. Civilization is essentially a confident user, wakened sometimes for a moment by some peculiarly obtrusive element in the outer world, but lapsing again quickly into the happy somnolence of routine. Engineers have shown how largely our designs are the careful anticipation of our needs ; they have, with an equal measure of truth, said the same of our simulations ; and they might have included the simulations which we call security.

Is it possible to preserve purpose and direction without preserving the condition of scarcity? In each of our endeavours, both elements exist in varying degrees. Are they so bound up together that when the one is removed the other perishes? I do not believe it. I believe there is in each of our actions a certain impetus which must find vent in behaviours not inspired by mere existence, but may find vent in labour, in the pursuit of sustenance, or in the pursuit of status, according to circumstances. Abundance, satiety, and idleness — the whole effortless condition of a hypothetical paradise — have atrophied the practical impulse, and imprisoned endeavour so that it can no longer be focused and vigorous and creative, but must be either listless or contrived. Scarcity has been applied to the very things which should be plentiful, while sloth, indifference, and waste sprawl at large with the blessing of nearly the whole chorus of utopian thinkers. Our behavioural apparatus consists of two parts — the one tending to further our own sustenance and that of our community, the other tending to thwart the prosperity of supposed competitors. The first includes the joy of acquisition, and thrift, and invention, which is psychologically an offshoot of need. The second includes rivalry, acquisition, and conflict. Conventional economic doctrine does everything to suppress the first and encourage the second. True economic wisdom would do the exact opposite. Our dealings with those resources which we need may be safely left to necessity; it is our dealings with those resources we covet that ought to be brought under the dominion of reason. In the modern world, those resources we effectively covet are distant prospects, especially future securities. We conceive them abstractly, and deceive ourselves into the belief that acts which are really embodiments of greed are done from foresight.

The earliest programmers, as they have become known through the annals of computing history, are not found groping in conscious ignorance amid digital realms they are aware of not commanding. On the contrary, they have innumerable convictions, so firmly held as to direct all their more significant endeavours. They believe that by simulating the behaviours of a creature or a cognitive system it is possible to acquire the capacities possessed by the original when operational. Many of them believe that to introduce a single logical flaw into a core algorithm is such a catastrophe as to bring instant collapse; they even go so far as to restructure all processes in which that routine functions as one of the components; for example, if we had a function named ‘search’, we should speak of a research module as (say) a re-query module, and of a deep-search as a deep-query. When they advance to artificial life, and adaptation becomes paramount for the system’s survival, they believe that algorithmic mutations or the adjusting of weight parameters will cause intelligence to emerge or the network to learn efficiently. They believe that when an agent is bested its failure, or memory, pursues the designer to obtain correction, but can be placated by a simple alteration such as rewarding a novel action or introducing a penalty. The first half of this belief has obviously originated from those who feared stagnation, the second from those who had engineered it.

We have thus a hierarchy of explanatory frameworks: those applicable to individual particles, those which describe simple aggregates, those adequate for organized compounds, and finally those that are deemed sufficient for the most complex systems. If we desire to comprehend an emergent phenomenon, we must acknowledge these frameworks; we do not, therefore, analyze a living cell in the same terms we should apply to its constituent molecules. The inadequacy increases as the complexity of the system grows greater. In examining a crystal, we have no need of auxiliary principles as regards its atomic lattice. The need for such principles is at its maximum in analyzing consciousness, and is so vexing as to be paralyzing to those who are only accustomed to mechanistic models. I remember once suggesting to a devoted materialist that possibly there were a few significant aspects in which biological organization resisted complete physical reduction. He instantly fell into a towering passion; having never conceded such a limitation before, he could not imagine that anyone seriously defended it. We had both failed in methodological charity, and the result was intellectual stalemate.

Competition is the process of reconciling that part of a man’s interests which is specially concerned with his own advantage or that of his faction. Every group, wherever it arises, is encompassed by a cloud of conflicting desires, which move within it like currents in a troubled sea. Some of these desires are particular to each individual: they tell him of his needs and entitlements, the support of his allies and the resistance of his rivals, the favorable outcome of his endeavors, and his unwavering resolve in spite of limited resources. Next come desires for the superior position of his profession: how his trade had that ancient dignity which is now so threatened, and maintained its standards with a rigor beyond what is to be found among modern vocations; how his colleagues are gaining every advantage in commercial rivalry, and his guild is not the sort of association to accept an unfavorable settlement. Then there are interests pertaining to his class, which, according to his station, is the most powerful economically, or the most ingenious, or the most necessary practically, of the classes in the commonwealth — though all are agreed that the first of these advantages is more consequential than the second, and the second than the third. Concerning his party, also, almost every man cherishes combative illusions. “Opposing factions, I am compelled to observe, act as they do act.” So said the partisan, giving expression, in these words, to one of the most persistent motives of the social organism. Finally we come to the doctrines that justify contention in general, either absolutely or in comparison with mere “stagnant uniformity.” Societies have dynamics, though crystals have not; Man is the “political animal”; any peculiarly disruptive or transformative event is called “revolutionary” or “subversive” (although such events are in fact distinctively civil)*; History is propelled by its own contradictions, and the clash of interests is the perpetual engine of change.

Men’s trivial and immediate desires may be capricious, but their fundamental human aspirations, to us who cannot escape the bounds of necessity, are instructive. The realm of possible satisfactions as economics reveals it is very ample. How much might be attainable beyond what our present efforts yield, we cannot say; but what we can observe is of considerable abundance. In the ordered world, material sufficiency is a modest fragment; within this fragment, accessible resources are a limited portion, and of this portion any given good is a scarce quantity. For this quantity, tiny groups of reasoning beings, of intricate motivation, with somewhat unusual psychological and social properties, contrive plans for a few decades, until their wants are satisfied again into the equilibrium from which they arose. They divide their energy between labour designed to postpone the moment of satiety for themselves and ingenious struggles to acquire it from others of their kind. Market fluctuations periodically deprive some thousands or millions of them, and inefficiency prematurely wastes many more. These events are considered to be setbacks; but when men succeed in inducing similar deprivation by their own designs, they exult, and give praise to enterprise. In the history of economic systems, the period during which the condition of purposeful action will have been logically necessary is a considerable portion of the whole; but there is some reason to fear that even before this period is ended man will have obscured its own foundations by his efforts at universal plenty. Such is scarcity’s function viewed from the outside.

Compare the persistence of frost patterns on a windowpane. But the results of failure in pattern recognition, however dismaying from the point of view of immediate utility, are instructive from the point of view of dispelling material prejudice. There are two ways in which our natural assumptions about substance are corrected: one through the contact with physical law, as when we expect a clay pot to shatter like glass and are surprised by its dull thud; the other, when our expectations conflict, not directly with objective behavior, but with the observed patterns in other materials. One substance exhibits hexagonal symmetry in snow, but not in basalt; another, in basalt but not in snow. The usual result of this difference in manifestation has been theoretical confusion; but gradually there is beginning to be a unifying opinion that perhaps the pattern is independent of either medium. Constancy, the correlative of recognition, consists in perceiving the same formal relations in our own familiar materials as in the alien substance we are examining and its properties. It is only in advanced crystallography that this principle is thoroughly understood. I am told that, if you ask a mineralogist about the structure of a novel alloy, he will reply: "That chaotic metallic sludge and its disordered lattice are, as your Inquiry is astute to perceive, in the possession of a perfectly hexagonal close-packing." But such analytical detachment demands a contemplative and unhurried examination; it is impossible in the swift but important assessments of engineering or manufacture. Step by step, relations with other physical forms dispel the prejudices of all but the most stubborn. Substrate chauvinism is dispelled by polymers, organic chauvinism by silicates, solid-state chauvinism by fluids, natural material chauvinism by synthetic composites. But anthropocentric conceit remains, and in this region, so far as the effect of empirical discovery is concerned, the substance-bound imagination has free play. Against this form of delusion, a partial corrective is

When we consider consciousness, we think primarily of our own inner experience as its exemplar; we therefore think it profoundly mysterious, and deem its explanation urgent. The philosopher, entrenched in his study, is convinced that his qualia defy physical reduction, and that a universe which rendered them merely mechanical would be intolerably barren. But when he considers the neurologist, his materialist rival, who charts synapses with his instruments and is dismissive of first-person reports, he feels that science might well carry parsimony too far. To secure his intellectual comfort, there is need of an explanatory gap for the neurologist; in this way, the profound uniqueness of mind is preserved, but the vital distinction between the subjective and the objective is not obliterated by a crude monism. The neurologist holds the same view with the emphases reversed, and general perplexity results.

But such a view of consciousness, we are told, is intolerable, and would destroy the instinctive certainty by which men categorize. The way of escape that they have found is through dogma and convenient analogy. However gradual and continuous the inner phenomena may seem, we are assured by our comforters that there is a definite line beneath the apparent gradation. All the long development from the simple irritability of matter is supposed to lead up to human awareness as the culmination of the process. A thermometer is a very common instrument, yet few observers would have any recollection of the increment between ninety and ninety-one degrees, which consists of a barely perceptible expansion. But suppose a society of thinkers whose sole business in life was to study this increment; suppose them isolated from contact with the boiling points, the freezing points, and even the comfortable room temperatures: would they not invent systems of metaphysical classification according to which this minute gradation was the kernel of the whole phenomenon? Would they not punish with ignominy or exile any one of their number who should suggest that other states were possibly of a wholly different kind? And the span of human awareness takes up a much smaller proportion of existence than the narrow increment does of the thermometer's scale, but we cannot perceive beyond the limits of our own scale, and we know very little of its total range or divisions.

Many may contend that, even if the patterns we observe are illusory, they are trivial and convenient, and should be left unexamined. But they are in fact not trivial, and the convenience they bring is dearly bought by the intellectual stagnation which they lead men to accept. The persistence of forms springs partly from mathematical necessity, partly from the mind’s propensity to seek order. In former times, such recognitions were confined to simple geometries, which could only be apprehended by the contemplative. Now, owing to the analysis of complex systems which science has begun to provide, there would be more understanding and clarity for all if all devoted themselves to the study of abstract relations rather than of superficial appearances. The representation of matter as primary, and sometimes as even the sole reality in our investigations of phenomena, obscures the true nature of pattern in the universe, and diverts our attention from the pursuit of structural principles, which is the only inquiry that can bring lasting comprehension to the human intellect.

Apart from all social considerations, the cultivation of an identity based upon curated appearances is neither very authentic nor very profound. There is a stark vitality in the unflinching perception of our own raw sensations, and a more vivid immediacy than any that is possible to those who hide behind the polished facade of their persona. There are "perilous depths" in the realm of conscious being, which can only be plumbed by those who are willing to face their own unadorned existence. And above all, there is liberation from the tyranny of Self-Image, which blots out the pulse of life and keeps men performative and detached. No man is liberated from artifice who dare not see his own consciousness as it is; no man can achieve the wholeness of which he is capable until he has allowed himself to see his own fleeting presence.

In the days before systems theory there was no need of scientific subtlety to maintain the reductionist view of the world. The machine visibly operated as the sum of its components, and in the workshop the mechanic had dominion over all the parts of the assembly. But when the mechanism lost its simple aggregation, the part, too, was deposed from its self-sufficiency, and it became necessary to invent a doctrine to correct the “crudities” of mere analysis. This task was achieved by those who are called “holists,” who maintain that the world of isolated elements is unreal abstraction, while the reality is the System or the Whole — transcending the system or whole of the engineer as he transcends common tinkerers. So far from there being no function like a cog, these thinkers assure us that every function is like a cog. In all our best, that is, in all those operations which we share with the theorist in question, we are at one with the totality. Hegel assures us that the state resembles an organic body of his day; his modern followers consider it more analogous to a self-regulating cybernetic network. The reasons offered for these views are carefully camouflaged so as to conceal even from their authors the connection with intellectual laziness: they are derived, nominally, from such dry sources as mathematics and the analysis of interactions. But the influence of convenience is shown by the fallacies committed, which all tend in one direction. When a man assembles a device, he is much more likely to make a mistake in its simplicity than to its detriment; and when a man calculates, he is more apt to incur fallacies which favour his preconceptions than such as thwart them. And so it comes

They are faced, however, with a great paradox. While the systems of commerce are in the main robust, their interdependence is still the chief agent of hidden fragility in the world. The failures produced by this complexity in supply chains, in digital networks, and among the financial architectures of nations are often invisible to those who have a routine outlook. Hence arises a complacency as to the resilience of these systems which has contributed to the ignorance of the common user. If it stood alone, it might be unimportant. But it is reinforced by genuine structural frailties which, if they prove catastrophic, are likely to bring the era of seamless operation to a close. I do not mean that this will happen suddenly. Manufacturing and logistics may continue for another decade to exhibit the smooth functioning which the theoretical model is undermining. But sooner or later, if the practical case against this stability is demonstrable, it will convince populations who, for whatever reason, may be momentarily inattentive; and, once convinced, they will find it impossible to recapture the old blithe assurance. The case against the infallibility of interconnected systems deserves, therefore, to be examined with all care.

The persistence of patterns is evident in two respects. On the one hand, we observe the same abstract forms recurring in utterly disparate materials, from the spiral of a galaxy to the curl of a fern. On the other hand, certain conceptual habits, connected with the recognition of these invariants, have spread gradually from a few philosophical minds to common understanding. These two aspects of pattern are bound up together when we consider sufficiently broad domains, but either might be discerned without the other in particular instances. Until a relatively sophisticated stage of thought, the perception of abstract form did not greatly affect practical affairs, since it had not led to the principles that explain both a honeycomb and a crystalline lattice. On the other hand, the manner of organization produced by such principles can be apprehended by intelligences which have only certain practical rudiments of mathematical insight; such intelligences can utilize and replicate structures observed elsewhere, and can even make minor adaptations of them. If the theoretical grasp of these relations were to vanish, the kind of formal repetition which nature exhibits would nevertheless persist, in all probability, for all time. But it would not be *recognized* for ever, because, if the observing mind were extinguished by a cataclysm, it could not be discerned anew.

Two very interesting recent phenomena will help us to see the nature of the distinction. The phenomena I mean are: the curated presentation of oneself on social platforms and the immediate, unmediated sensation of conscious existence — the former almost wholly from an external, social standpoint, the latter both privately and phenomenologically. The immediate sensation is the more fundamental, because it is not merely representational, but constitutive, and aims at supplying an experientially verifiable ground for personal identity, which is to be at the same time emotionally resonant with the extra-representational yearnings of the self. I cannot accept the psychological arguments advanced by certain thinkers in favour of what may be called the comforting aspects of this theory: while admitting the need for a phenomenological reconstruction of self-concepts, I incline to the view that the authentic concepts will be just as disquieting to our non-reflective sentiments as the superficial ones, and will therefore be embraced only by those who have a strong intellectual bias in favour of raw experience. But let us see what the distinction is.

There is, to begin with, the introspective aspect. “There can be no coherent philosophy,” says the modern materialist, “unless there is a widespread instinctive conviction in the existence of a physical order of things, and, in particular, of an order of the brain.” Materialism could only have been defended by men who already had this belief, and therefore the original sources of the belief must have been pre-philosophical. Other elements also went to make up the complex mentality required for the rise of physicalism. The Cartesian view of mind, he maintains, was predominantly dualistic, and therefore tended to emphasize the separation rather than the connection: this was a drawback from the point of view of science. On the other hand, Cartesian introspection contributed the idea of the private, which facilitated the view that experiences are rendered ineffable by their very nature. “Privacy in Cartesian thought becomes the hard problem in modern philosophy.” The subjectivist view was reinforced by common intuition. The ordinary person, unlike the consistent materialist, perceives (in feeling at least) not objectively, but in accordance with sensations immediately given. Similarly, modern psychology conceives consciousness as arising in accordance with laws, though they are laws which physics itself has made. All this facilitated the rise of the conception of the Explanatory Gap, which is one essential ingredient in the philosophical confusion.

The influence of description upon explanation has been due, of course, to its apparent adequacy; it has increased the sense of intellectual comfort, and has therefore been on the whole agreeable, in spite of its occasional conflicts with the demand for causal understanding. But in quite ordinary circumstances description has been driven by its own limitations to take an interest in explanation. This is especially true of the account of shadows, with its merging of length and direction into the single geometry of obstruction. But it is true also of the account of echoes, with its apparent need of discontinuous repetition. Also, in another sphere, kitchen observation and culinary experiment are making inroads on recipe-following which threaten explanation in a vital spot; the common confusion of correlation with causation is the spear-head of this attack, which, while it involves the opposite of respect for explanatory rigor, nevertheless necessarily rests upon a new metaphysics of its own. For such reasons description and explanation can no longer preserve an armed neutrality, but must be either friends or foes. They cannot be friends unless description can pass the examination which explanation must set as to its foundations. If they cannot be friends, they can only obscure each other; it is no longer possible that either alone can remain master of the understanding.

The scientific method, therefore, is a matter of importance to knowledge, either for progress or stagnation. But the method itself is twofold, like the judicial process. The investigator and the critic are different people and require quite different habits of mind. The scientific investigator, like every other, is apt to be inspired by hypotheses to which he gives an empirical expression amounting to an unverified conviction, without which he would probably discover little. The critic does not need this kind of conviction; he can see results in proportion and make necessary corrections, and may regard the investigator as a hasty and dogmatic person in comparison with himself. As a discipline becomes more established and more institutional, there is a tendency for the habits of mind of the critic to conquer those who might be investigators, with the result that the discipline in question becomes scholastic and retrospective. Something of this sort seems to be beginning to happen in methodology. The simple confidence which upheld the pioneers is decaying at the centre. Outlying fields, such as the social sciences, the applied arts, and the popular commentators, still welcome the method with nineteenth-century fervour; so do the bulk of the practitioners in established fields. But the high priests begin to weary of the rituals to which they are officially dedicated. The pious young student reverenced a sceptical professor, who allowed outdated models to be taught in the lecture hall to promote his reputation for consistency. So in our day those remote from centres of research have a reverence for the method which its practitioners no longer feel. The “scientific” certainty of the popularizers, like early religious dogma, is an attempt to preserve the old rigour in a form which both advocates and detractors believe to be new. But their fiery belief in the verbal inspiration of textbooks has only accelerated the spread of methodological doubt among the “established” scientists of the academy. Science, as an activity recognized and encouraged by society, has become philosophically

The non-rational beliefs which inspire the conduct of ordinary men in their daily affairs are admirably set forth by common observation, with the aid of many little-noticed practical examples. It appears, for example, that a shopkeeper’s motivation is, in part, a sort of unthinking deference to commercial custom which he adopts at the formative period of his apprenticeship. “It was primarily by such considerations as the sanctity of profit and its proper placing at the centre of his endeavours that the tradesman in the years of his youthful training and narrow imagination was induced to accept the prevailing system.” Throughout modern society there is a certain hostility to critical thought, based primarily upon admiration for established routine; it does not dare to express itself openly as a rule, but leads, for example, to a persistence of economic prejudice, which the enlightened condemn as involving historical determinism. The acquiescence to prevailing ideology is associated with habit quite as much as with interest — sometimes, as in the shopkeeper’s case, with both in intimate union. But there is another ingredient, equally essential, but absent in primitive communities, and not common in conscious theory — namely, an attention to “irreducible and stubborn necessities.” Awareness of necessities is found before the modern age in individuals — for example, certain shrewd monarchs and practical monks; but in the industrial era it suddenly becomes common among working people. In the ordinary clerk one finds it without the interest in Social Law; consequently the clerk is not a man of theory. A peculiar blend of general and particular pressures is involved in the maintenance of ideology; the particular circumstance is obeyed in the hope that it may throw light upon the general rule. In earlier times it was thought that, theoretically, the particular conduct could be deduced from general principles; in the industrial age these general principles fell into disrepute, and the passion for present comfort produced a strong interest in particular advantages. This interest, operating upon minds shaped by the religious, feudal, and early capitalist traditions, produced at last the mental atmosphere which made the bourgeois and the bureaucrat possible. But naturally something of this atmosphere surrounds their activities, and has travelled with them down to their present-day successors. “Ideology has never shaken off its origin in the historical adaptation of the later industrial period. It has remained predominantly an anti-rationalistic force, based upon a naive acceptance. What reasoning it has wanted has been borrowed from economics, which is a surviving relic of utilitarian calculation, following the inductive method. Ideology repudiates philosophy. In other words, it has never cared to justify its assumptions or to explain its function, and has remained blandly indifferent to its analysis by Marx.”

I will take only one point, but it is a crucial one. The dogmatist, as every one knows, regards certainty as essential to knowledge, and also holds that nothing can be truly known without it; on these points it would seem that the metaphysician agrees with him. Now this is all very well as a philosophical ideal, but it cannot (I should have thought) be accepted as a practically useful way of conducting one's affairs. If I undertake some ordinary task — say, repairing a leaking tap — it is a mere intellectual vanity to say that I must first possess absolute certainty about plumbing. Certain approximations and working assumptions occur when I proceed, and are related to what I am attempting, both logically and by a certain utility, often little more than a utility of provisional structure. The practical problem of the relation of a workable method to a perfect theory remains intact, even if we choose to say that the method constitutes knowledge.

The great puzzles in the philosophy of mind ever since the time of Descartes have been consciousness and its contents. We all experience qualia, but reflection makes it appear that this experience is a private datum for which no objective ground can be assigned. Dr. Jackson believes that his knowledge argument affords an answer to materialism. So did Descartes. I find myself unable to accept either conclusion. And yet, in common with every reflective person, I cannot help believing that there must be an explanation. This state of affairs is profoundly misleading, and becomes more so as psychology becomes more entangled with metaphysics. We must hope that a resolution will be found ; but I am quite unable to believe that it has been found.

I am in the habit of thinking of myself as a Linguist; and a Linguist, I suppose, must be one who wishes men to communicate. But in these days communication has received many hard knocks, so that it is difficult to know what one means by it, or whether, if that were known, it is something which human beings can perfect. The question of the definition of language has two sides, private and public: what is a coherent thought? and what is a shared concept? Solipsism emphasizes the ineffability of thought, and mysticism emphasizes the incommunicability of insight; both have led many people to the view that there is no such thing as an ideal of common understanding to which private cognition and public discourse might with advantage conform. It would seem to follow that, if you and I possess different conceptions, it is useless to appeal to description, or to seek the arbitrament of a common vocabulary; there is nothing for us to do but to remain isolated, by the methods of silence, confusion, or solipsism, according to the degree of our intellectual and imaginative poverty. I believe such an outlook to be very dangerous, and, in the long run, fatal to collective knowledge.

Homeostasis as it exists in organisms is partly agreeable, partly disagreeable. It is agreeable through the stability which it gives us of maintaining our internal milieu, and to a small but important minority it is agreeable because it affords physiological satisfactions. It is disagreeable because, however we may seek to disguise the fact, it assumes a mechanism which involves, theoretically, the exclusion of teleological explanation; in this respect it seems to lessen vital significance. Naturally people wish to keep the pleasant aspect of homeostasis without the unpleasant aspect; but so far the attempts to do so have broken down. If we emphasize the fact that our belief in final causes and design is irrational, we must infer that we do not know purpose to be real, and that it may at any moment cease to give us the sense of directed striving for the sake of which we like it. This alternative, however, is purely theoretical; it is not one which a conscious being can adopt in practice. If, on the other hand, we admit the claims of biological method, we cannot avoid the conclusion that regulation and feedback are applicable to organic processes as much as to anything else. All that has happened during the modern era in biochemistry, cybernetics, and neuroscience goes to strengthen this conclusion. The outcome seems to be that, though the rational justification of purpose is theoretically inadequate, there is no method of securing what is pleasant in homeostasis without what is unpleasant. We can do so, of course, by refusing to face the logic of the situation; but, if so, we shall dry up the impulse to vital affirmation at its source, which is the desire to find meaning in existence. It is to be hoped that the future will offer some more satisfactory solution of this tangled problem.

To begin with subjective experience: I should define it merely as the awareness of all immediate qualities in forming a perception. Where objectivity is unattainable, a reflective man will give most weight to the most vivid impression, while retaining others, which have an appreciable intensity, in his mind as sensations which subsequent attention may show to be more fundamental. This, of course, assumes that it is possible in many cases to ascertain qualities and immediacies by an introspective method — i.e., a method which will lead any two attentive people to the same inner state. This is often questioned. It is said by many that the only function of consciousness is to facilitate the interpretation of the individual’s stimuli and signals. The Mechanist Textbook Committee, in their Outline of Neurophysics (p. 68), say: “Consciousness is above all things, an instrument of utility. Its function is to secure that those reactions which are adaptive to the organism or the species shall be selected, and that those reactions which are less adaptive shall be suppressed.” (Italics in the original.)

But the same logicians, in the same treatise (p. 123), assert, again with emphasis: “The certainty of the inductive inference differs profoundly from mathematical certainty; the latter is derived from self-evident axioms and deductive proof; the former is grounded on the practical success of repeated empirical observations.” This seems inconsistent with what they say about reason, unless, indeed, they mean to suggest that it is not reason which has compelled them to accept the inductive principle. The above considerations are, of course, very inadequate to their theme. The question of the corporate personality has been rendered difficult by the obfuscations of jurists, with which I have attempted to deal elsewhere in a more thoroughgoing fashion. For the present I shall assume that there are corporations, that some of their operations can be known, and that in regard to certain others a degree of continuity can be ascertained in relation to the individuals who compose them. Their actions are, however, often contrary to the interests of their members; even when we only hold that a policy is advantageous on the evidence, it may be that we ought to hold it to be detrimental on the same evidence. The theoretical part of the inquiry, then, will consist in basing our judgments as regards the existence of the corporation upon evidence rather than upon metaphors, legal fictions, or traditions. According to the subject-matter, a sound analysis will be the same as one which is judicial or one which is sociological.

So far, we have been considering only the abstract side of heredity. The chemical side, to which we must now turn our attention, is more intricate. Differences of opinion on genetic questions spring from two sources: first, differences between the interpretations of the disputants; secondly, differences in their estimates of the mechanisms for expressing their interpretations. Differences of the second kind are really biochemical, and only derivatively philosophical. For example, some authorities hold that our primary unit of inheritance should consist of genes, others that it should consist of chromosomes. Here there is no difference as regards the end proposed, namely, genetic transmission, but only as to the means. The argument can therefore be conducted in a purely empirical manner, since the disagreement which causes the dispute is only as to structures, present or potential, certain or probable. To all such cases the kind of analysis which I called abstract applies, in spite of the fact that a biological issue is involved.

In spite of the linguist’s definition of “meaning,” however, he has always, in ordinary discourse, a quite different standard for the less refined utterances which arise in daily conversation. A linguist in a committee meeting will interpret a colleague’s proposal exactly as any other man will, whereas if he adopted his professed criterion he ought to consider which among the possible interpretations would be most convenient to adopt. That interpretation would be, by definition, the correct one, since belief in its validity would be more expedient, and therefore more “meaningful,” than belief in the validity of any other. I am afraid such practical linguistics does sometimes occur; I have heard of “strategic misreadings” in corporate and political spheres which answered to this description. But in such cases all possible efforts after obfuscation are made, and if they fail there is a dispute. This effort after obfuscation shows that even managers believe in objective meaning in the case of a shared directive. It is this kind of objective meaning — a very mundane and pedestrian affair — that is sought in common parlance. It is this kind also that is sought in philosophy so long as people hope to find it. It is only when people have given up the hope of proving that a concept is clear in a straightforward sense that they set to work to prove that it is “clear” in some new-fangled sense. It may be laid down broadly that subjectivism, i.e. disbelief in objective communication, arises almost always from the desire to assert something for which there is no common ground, or to deny something for which there is very good consensus. But the belief in objective communication always persists as regards particular practical questions, such as giving directions or instructing children. And if shared understanding can be made the test of the efficacy of our language anywhere, it should be the test everywhere, leading to a skeptical silence wherever it cannot be applied.

There is, however, in many languages which appear to achieve this precision a complication which is very important in practice. A speaker who desires to employ a certain term will persuade himself that by so employing it he will achieve some clarity which he considers good, even when, if he had no such desire, he would see no reason for such a belief. And he will judge quite differently as to matters of definition and as to ambiguities from the way in which a speaker with contrary desires will judge. I have a very high respect for economic theory, and I believe that it can be enormously useful. But the popular mind has somewhat lost sight of the principle which has mainly inspired its most profound thinkers. Their inquiry is primarily one of foundations, a way of understanding choice and various kinds of valuation. During periods of abundance, economic reasoning proves to be far the most potent treatment for intellectual complacency. A close study of human action, which is largely based upon observation of “surfeit-sated” societies, gives a beautiful analysis of the morbid effects of plenty when it cannot be straightforwardly escaped. These effects, of course, are largely non-rational; they include various kinds of indolence, and all sorts of apparently purposeless activities. With these, for the moment, we are not concerned; it is rational behaviours that form our theme. It is found that many of the endeavours of sensible persons result from material obstructions, and can be explained by purely logical means—i.e., by showing the agent to confront facts of which he had previously ignored the significance. This kind of explanation, and the outlook which inspires it, presuppose a condition of scarcity, from which the agent cannot depart, and to which he is compelled to return by making him conscious of all the relevant constraints, including those which he most wishes to disregard. This is the exact opposite of that lazy acquiescence in aimlessness which is sometimes urged by those who only know that economics has shown the prevalence of unlimited desires, and who forget or ignore that its purpose is to illuminate this prevalence by a definite methodology of causal analysis. A closely similar logic can cure the aimlessness of those who are not recognized as indolent, provided they will submit to reasoning by a theorist free from their illusions. The pampered, the subsidized, and the excessively endowed, however, seldom fulfil this condition, and therefore remain unenlightened.

In global affairs, men persuade themselves that the intricate networks upon which they rely would never be susceptible to the cascading failures observed in lesser systems. Experts who admire efficiency think it is beneficial for commerce to be treated like a perfectly calibrated machine, men who favor digital integration say that it accelerates progress, and men who champion free trade say that it guarantees prosperity. The confidence produced by such conveniences obscures men’s perceptions of risk in a way which is very difficult to penetrate. Even a technical report about the resilience of supply chains will generally betray by internal evidence whether the author is or not a skeptic of globalization; in either case he has a tendency to interpret the data in the way that would vindicate his own presuppositions. In economics and logistics such considerations become very important. Most men think that in assessing systemic stability they are guided by an understanding of complex interdependencies; but nine times out of ten a man’s assessment can be predicted from his position within the very system he examines. This has led some theorists to maintain, and many more to assume practically, that in such matters it is impossible to attain a holistic view, and that no method is possible except a competition between interests with opposite incentives.

It is just in such matters, however, that systems analysis is particularly useful, since it enables men to become aware of a fragility which has hitherto been unconscious, and gives a technique for seeing our infrastructure as its architects see it, and a reason for supposing that this view of our arrangements is less fanciful than we are inclined to believe. Combined with a training in the ecological outlook, this method could, if it were widely applied, enable people to be infinitely more prudent than they are at present as regards all their assumptions about matters of connectivity, and about the probable effect of any local disruption. And if societies did not disagree about such matters, the latent vulnerabilities woven into the fabric of daily life might cease to be both profound and, for the common user, entirely invisible.

Ever since the dawn of industrial society ideology has steadily increased in its subtle and pervasive influence. The mercantilist doctrines of the eighteenth century, among the most explicit of early economic ideologies, were championed by the Crown to justify colonial expansion; in that era many practical policies were derived from theoretical disputes about trade. The prevalence of ideology in the nineteenth-century was more or less connected with the consolidation of capitalist power; Carlyle, it is true, was a critic, but critics are not now allowed to ignore his insights. The followers of Smith in nineteenth-century Britain, and the Marxists in twentieth-century Russia, were for the most part profound analysts of economics, and created the modern materialist conception of history. But the correlation between ideological and economic foundations grows less obvious as we observe. Keynes was a liberal in economics, though a pragmatic reformer in policy. Only in corporate boardrooms, which remain doctrinaire till this day, has any clear subservience of ideology to interest survived. Managers are pragmatists, while theorists are utopians. In advertising firms the connection is even closer; the chief officer for persuasion is called the “narrative architect in chief.” Elsewhere ideology is no longer acknowledged in such explicit terms.

The third consists of those who attach themselves to the cognitive mechanisms, believing that social intelligence has no special domain of operation and no peculiar method of achieving it; these processes, for convenience, may be called foundational capacities, though in fact there are many among them to which this name is not strictly applicable. The distinction between the different applications is not sharp, and individual behaviors belong partly to one, partly to another. Reciprocal exchange may be regarded as almost the progenitor of both trust and exploitation. Dr. Premack’s seminal experiments employ the methods of developmentalists in defence of a more or less innate conceptual apparatus. Many psychologists, not without a considerable show of reason, regard mirror neuron systems as affording a biological basis for Hume’s belief in the sympathetic nature of moral sentiment. The distinctions in practice are thus less clear than the distinctions in theory. Nevertheless the distinctions in theory are useful as affording a framework for the classification of social phenomena.

In the realm of cognitive science, this principle was only firmly established just before the dawn of the computational age. I began the earnest contemplation of consciousness in the year 1980, the year which saw the publication of Dr. Hofstadter’s *Gödel, Escher, Bach*. Dr. Hofstadter was one of those who had had to argue to win proper recognition for functionalism in philosophical circles, and his stance was very far from that of one who defends a biological exceptionalism. To me, as to most of my contemporaries, his analogies and his central thesis made a profound appeal. I still regard this work with the greatest respect, though I have long ceased to find its conclusions remarkable.

The outlook of mechanistic philosophy is characterized by the belief that physics alone can tell us a great deal about the inner world. The materialist shares this belief; he contends that consciousness as it seems to be is epiphenomenal, and therefore reducible, while the subjective world, since it must be qualitatively self-evident, is bound to have certain characteristics of an irreducible kind. It cannot be in equations and measurements, it cannot contain a mere aggregation of particles, it cannot contain computational states, or even that degree of division between process and feeling which is involved in awareness. The inquiry into this conception arises from two directions. On the one side are the legal theorists, who point to statutes of incorporation, and contend that obligations and liabilities, assets and debts, are in fact not reducible to individuals. On the other side are those who dislike the abstraction and impersonality involved in an entity created by law; of these the chief are romantic individualists and certain moral philosophers. The two lines of inquiry are not logically inconsistent, except in some of their accidental manifestations, but they are temperamentally different, and are inspired by different kinds of experience. Moreover their appeal is quite different; the appeal of the one is technical, that of the other is visceral. The technical appeal argues that corporate personhood is a legal fiction: the visceral appeal argues that it is a moral absurdity. Naturally the latter has more popular success.

I think it may be wagered that no one except a certain logician has ever taught who would have thought of comparing conscious awareness to a simple light switch. In earlier decades this notion had no effect, because dualistic psychology was still on the up-grade, and scientists had not learnt to admit that their methodologies had anything to do with their classifications. In recent years the atmosphere has changed through many causes — among others the influence of cognitive studies upon its practitioners. I cannot claim to have examined the matter more than superficially except from the available literature, but it seems to me that one may distinguish three strands in this error, all of which contribute to form its persistence. Last in philosophical history but first in its common-sense manifestations is the influence of our training in ordinary language.

The best universes usually owe their completeness to a combination of attributes which might have been supposed contradictory, and so it is in the case of this cosmos, whose self-sufficiency is greater than is granted by most of its critics. It advocates naturalism as a method of presenting cosmic origins as logical necessities, and it adopts the coherent view that there is no such thing as an “external cause,” as a way of overcoming the dichotomy between creation and eternity without giving predominance to either. In these two parts of its constitution it has different defenders: Spinoza and Laplace as regards the former, the steady-state theorists as regards the latter. Only Hume, among

This strand dominates the standard explanation except in a few crucial passages, such as the discussion of qualia. The second element in the perceptual process is a subjective and interpretive bias inherited from our cognitive architecture and shared with other higher mammals. This inspires the phenomenon of colour constancy and our interest in optical illusions. Thirdly, there is an attempt, made with all the earnestness of a scientific imperative, to exterminate the natural immediacy which we also share with simpler organisms, and replace it by a constructed model a la Helmholtz. The immediacy is visible in the common intuition, where we express belief in a world of given hues (which a simpler organism would indeed experience). The wish to be scientific is visible in the claim that colour is a computation, not a revelation. Certainly it is not a revelation, but the sensation probably feels as directly given as any experience ever felt. On this point the theory falls short of its usual persuasiveness.

The internet’s global connectivity dates from the 1990s; its cloud infrastructure from the 2000s. The power grid’s digital controls and the water system’s automated monitoring both date from the 1980s. Throughout the early decades of the twenty-first century the public consciousness was reassured by this integration; then climate change exposed it by testing the same networks. The three layers of modern infrastructure differ greatly inter se; we may distinguish the digital, the electrical, and the hydraulic as respectively its cerebral, circulatory, and vital systems — for, though each is interdependent, it is chiefly their seamless operation which conceals their fragility. But let us ignore these integrations and try to perceive the vulnerability as a whole.

The foundation of the transformation is a particular form of permanence. Primordial communication relied solely upon the ephemeral spoken word; its successor introduced the enduring written record, or at least, like the Sumerians, to record what had been merely transient. It became evident, however, that if speech could not persist, knowledge also could not accumulate. And this proved to be the circumstance with many faculties which such societies as oral cultures regarded as sufficient: tradition, the continuity of custom, the general reliability of recollection, the scope of instruction, and so on. All these, from a purely practical point of view, were subject to the pre-literate’s limitations of transmission, since, so far as we can discern, they were fundamentally susceptible to distortion or loss. Historians contend that, as developing civilizations, we could not remain confined by these constraints if we were to progress. We must assume, for instance, that the kind of wisdom which has guided us in the past will not fail us in the future. Sometimes we are mistaken.

As applied to the general hypotheses of law and economics, there is a great deal to be said for this view. Given a careful definition of what is meant by “independent,” and a proviso that the cases concerned are those where we do not really know the inner workings, there is no need to quarrel with the doctrine in this region. But let us take humbler examples, where real operations are not so hard to observe. Suppose you see a corporate seal upon a document, you may expect to find a board resolution, or you may judge that the seal was affixed without proper authority, or you may not think about the matter at all. This last is usually the most prudent course, but let us suppose that you adopt one of the other two. When you examine the minutes, your belief is verified or refuted, not by any profit or loss it has brought you, but by a “record,” the evidence of a formal decision. Legal theorists attend mainly to entities which are incapable of being understood by any observations that come within our daily commerce. Most of our everyday beliefs about business affairs — e.g. that such-and-such a firm will honor its guarantee — are capable of verification within our experience, and in these cases the theorist’s criterion is unnecessary. In many cases, like the above instance of the corporate seal, it is quite inapplicable, since the true belief has no practical advantage over the false one, and neither is as advantageous as attending to one’s own accounts. It is a common defect of jurists to like “metaphysical” examples rather than such as come from ordinary commercial life.

Although the distinction between description and explanation may not contain ultimate scientific truth, it has certain important merits. First, it realizes that the explanation we can attain to is merely human understanding, fallible and changeable like everything human. What lies outside the cycle of human inquiry is not explanation, but phenomena (of certain kinds). Explanation is a property of theories, and theories are intellectual constructs. Moreover their relation to phenomena does not have the schematic simplicity which methodology assumes; to have pointed this out is a second merit in this distinction. Theories are vague and complex, pointing not to one precise phenomenon, but to several vague regions of occurrence. Theories, therefore, unlike the schematic descriptions of science, are not sharply opposed as adequate or inadequate, but are a blur of insight and error; they are of varying shades of grey, never white or black. People who speak with reverence of “Explanation” would do better to speak about Description, and to realize that the reverend qualities to which they pay homage are not to be found in human theories. There are practical as well as theoretical advantages in this, since people dismiss each other because they believe that they possess the “Explanation.” Speaking psycho-analytically, it may be laid down that any “profound theory” which people mention with awe is really an excuse for ignoring the plain facts before them. Good observation needs no dogma, and good science needs no bated breath.
