Inventive minds can manufacture “concepts” by getting hold of the linguistic apparatus and formalizing relations other than the concrete. These consequences flow from an exaggeration into which semiotics has fallen. Granted that, as semioticians point out, meaning is a matter of degree, and is a property of purely human occurrences, namely signs, it still does not follow that the degree of abstraction afforded by a sign depends upon purely human conditions. In increasing the degree of abstraction in our thoughts, we are approximating to an ideal, and the ideal is determined by Reality, which is only within our comprehension to a certain very limited extent, as regards some of the superficial patterns on or near the surface of a certain mind. The theory of the semiotician is derived from the practice of the mathematician, who, by manipulating repeatedly that his symbols are coherent, makes thinkers able to conceive complex relations, and thus makes his formalism more nearly potent than if it had been devised with less rigor. Such instances of symbol-made thought are significant, but their scope is very bounded. By exaggerating their scope, people become involved in an orgy of nominalism, which is ultimately brought to an abrupt end by hard limitations in the shape of paradox, inconsistency, and unintelligibility. The recent history of philosophy is an object-lesson of the poverty of semiotics in this form.

Prejudice’s immediate disguises are observed in childhood, and its subtle memoranda in early adulthood. But its formidable authority begins with its creative evolution in mature life — not that this manifestation is more profound than the others, but that it contains less reflection and more assertion, so that it achieves more persuasive effect. This process contains, from beginning to end, no scrutiny, and therefore no faulty scrutiny; it contains merely an instinctive picture appealing to the emotions. There is nothing in it to help us to a conclusion as to whether the belief which it presents is valid or erroneous; this question, which might be thought not unimportant, prejudice has left to others. But according to its own nature it is right in this, since conviction is to be attained by habit, not by reason, and is therefore not a matter of examination.

It is a curious thing that the formalists should have been hailed as an ally by the empiricists, since, on the face of it, their doctrine is the exact antithesis to theirs. While empiricists teach that sensory confirmation is the test of validity, the formalists teach, on the contrary, that our mathematical frameworks, having been fashioned by logical necessity, ignore all the aspects of phenomena which it does not pay to describe, and are in fact an obstacle to the apprehension of reality. We have, they think, a faculty called “intuition” which we can use if we take the trouble, and which will enable us to grasp, in theory at least, every theorem and axiom, though apparently not the contingent. But since it would be inconvenient to be troubled with so much abstraction, we have developed a method of approximation, the function of which is to simplify. But for this method, we should calculate everything; owing to its rounding operations, we usually compute only what is tractable, and that all inaccurately. Empirical fit, for the formalist, is the source of error, while truth is arrived at by a pure deduction from which all thought of observational agreement is absent. Nevertheless the formalist, like the empiricist, prefers prediction to elegance, applied geometry to number theory; he thinks it better to forecast an eclipse by computation than to let the equation stand because of its beauty. It is this that makes empiricists regard him as an ally.

A great part of reductionist methodology is merely traditional mechanism expressed in slightly novel language. The doctrine of analysis, according to which complex systems are not really whole, but are merely so conceived by the synthetic intellect, is to be found in every materialist, ancient or modern, from Democritus to Mr. Dawkins. Reductionism has given an air of novelty to this doctrine by means of two devices. First, it connects “explanation” with the operations of simple components; it suggests that analysis is what enables the humble thermostat to regulate the temperature in which it operates exactly so as to maintain it without destabilising it. (The instance is unfortunate, since Dr. and Mrs. Ashby have shown that this simple device is no more comprehensible through mere parts-listing than a mere holistic system with its bewildering interactions.) This gives a flavour of modern engineering to its doctrines, and enables it to adduce mechanical instances which make the unwary think that its views are based upon the latest results of systems research. Secondly, it gives the name “mechanism” to the separateness of parts as they appear to the analytic intellect, and the name “emergence” or “holism” to their interpenetration as revealed to synthesis. This enables it to say many new things about “mechanism” and “emergence,” which sound very profound and original when they are supposed to be about what is ordinarily meant by those words. “Complexity,” being that which is in “emergence,” is of course a fiction created by the intellect, and is seen to be such as soon as we place ourselves at the point of view of synthesis.

Traditional materialism has been reductive, convinced of the unreality of consciousness, and essentially a simplistic man’s philosophy. The psychological prelude to the materialist conviction is the “tyranny of the quantifiable,” which arises when a man is hopelessly frustrated by the elusiveness of introspection, or for some reason suddenly loses patience with it. Qualia being thus ruled out, he takes to mechanism. It is a law of our discourse that, whenever it is in any way possible, we adopt such explanations as will preserve our intellectual comfort. Modern scientific literature is full of grotesque examples of this law. Accordingly the man who has been driven to mechanism presently discovers that mechanism is the true account of life, and that the subjective world is inaccessible to those who are committed to empirical methods. From this basis the remaining doctrines of traditional materialism can be deduced. Descartes, perhaps the first of the great dualists, formulated his argument (so history avers) by his fireplace while he was waiting for his stove to warm ; and, as might be expected, it is full of the doctrine that experience is irreducible.

Homeostasis’s view is sometimes expressed in language which might mislead, because things which it regards as illusory are occasionally mentioned in a way which suggests that they are real. But when we avoid these possibilities of misunderstanding, I think its doctrine of purpose is as follows. Purpose is not a series of separate aims or outcomes, but a continuous adjustment, in which the future cannot be foreseen because it is genuinely stable and therefore unimaginable. Everything that really persists adjusts, like the successive cycles in the operation of a thermostat. (This is not its illustration.) Thus the organism is perpetually growing steadier and more balanced. Everything that has occurred persists in the pure memory of equilibrium, as opposed to the pseudo-memory of the conscious mind. This persistence is “regulation,” while the impulse to new stability is the “vital balance.” To recover the pure memory of equilibrium is a matter of physiological discipline. We are not told how to do it, but one suspects something not unlike the practices of automatons.

Meanwhile, from many quarters, a prejudice arises which is often described as “common sense,” but is really characterized by assumption as a method and bias as a foundation. It is not necessarily sensible, since it is, in some manifestations, compatible with the most arrant superstition. It is not compatible with rational or scientific inquiry, because it rejects the evidence upon which those disciplines are based. It tends more and more to the adoption and development of the popular view, that the fundamental nature of belief is neither examined nor justified, but something cruder and more primal, out of which both conviction and error are constructed.

If the appearance of popular sovereignty ever really comes into the political order persists (which is the simple essence of the doctrine of electoral mandate), then the sum-total of actual power at any earlier stage is part of the sum-total at any later stage. Total conditions of the state at various intervals form a series in virtue of this relation of semblance and substance, and this series has all the properties that the constitutional theorist wants and that the populist demagogue professes to have banished. If the new mechanisms which are added in later phases of governance are not external to the old structures, there is no genuine accountability, democratic evolution has achieved nothing, and we are back in the system of oligarchy. Of course the apologist’s answer to this dilemma is that what happens is “representation,” in which everything changes and yet remains the same. This conception, however, is a paradox, which the skeptical citizen cannot hope to unravel. At bottom, the partisan’s appeal is to civic religion, not to evidence; but into the regions where sentiment is above analysis we cannot follow him.

His article on *The Difficulties of Individualism* was published in 1889; his *Industrial Democracy* in 1897. My *German Social Democracy* appeared in 1896, and *Principles of Social Reconstruction* in 1916. In France, the same kind of analysis was vigorously championed by Durkheim. In America, Thorstein Veblen’s institutional economics (without his psychological speculations) was blended with the new sociology to produce a radically new critique, that of the Progressive historians, somewhat later in date, but more systematic, than the European works mentioned above, although Saint-Simon’s *L’Industrie* had anticipated part of its doctrine.

The new analysis had originally three main sources : classical mechanics, molecular biology, and the principles of computation. Ever since Laplace, phenomena had been conceived as a summation, in which the whole observed was explained by its constituent parts, and therefore always had certain predictable characteristics due to their simplicity. It was also held (though not by Laplace) to be scientifically inevitable for a system to be understood without considering emergence. Therefore the properties explained through mere summation were properties which every system must have. In this way, it was contended, we can discover a great deal about complex behaviour by merely studying the conditions of isolation. The first characteristic of the economic crisis is that it abandons the pretense to a special social harmony or a peculiar brand of prosperity to be maintained by its institutions. It regards the social order as essentially one with its material foundations, differing from the ordinary fluctuations of trade merely by the severity of its disruptions, and by the fact that it is concerned with the failure of assumptions where contractual obligations are still expected. It reveals that all stability is contingent stability, to be tested and undermined by the pressures of the market. It does not aim, as previous economic theory has usually done, at pronouncements about the system as a perfect whole, nor at the vindication of a comprehensive equilibrium. It demonstrates, on the basis of its mechanics, that there is no reason to deny the apparently haphazard and irrational nature of the productive process. It does not regard the economy as “organic,” in the sense that, from any transaction adequately recorded, the entire edifice could be deduced as the blueprint of a great machine can be deduced from a single gear. In particular, it does not attempt, as utopian idealism did, to deduce the resilience of the social whole from the principles of its political philosophy. It regards the crisis as a social fact like another, with no inherent justice and no historical finality.

In psychology, similarly, introspection replaced the “immediate” view. It had been maintained that every mental state is affected in its intrinsic nature by its awareness of itself, so that a thorough knowledge of one’s feelings would involve a thorough knowledge of one’s self-concept. The new psychology maintained that the intrinsic character of an experience does not logically enable us to deduce its representation in consciousness. An example will make the point clear. Certain philosophers maintain somewhere (and in this they agree with modern phenomenologists) that if a man is engaged in a routine task and feels a sudden vitality, there is an intrinsic change in his self-image at the moment of that feeling. Common sense would say that there is no intrinsic change in the self-image until he reflects upon the sensation. This view is adopted by the new analysis ; its consequences are more far-reaching than they might appear to be at first sight.

The demand for certainty is not merely obstructive. It is impoverishing, but as life is impoverishing, day by day and insidiously. It has a particular psychological method of operation, namely, dogmatic insistence, a familiar habit of thought, much more akin to theology than any of the pragmatic disciplines. Dogmatic insistence makes it possible, as it never was before, to see what is the consequence, for understanding, of a given body of empirical evidence, what assumptions must be discarded, and what compromises between them. The philosophy of common sense and daily affairs has suffered immense setbacks by the prevalence of this habit; part of the consequence for conduct has been set forth by Dr. Dewey in several recent works. There is reason to fear that the habit will prove equally barren in other domains, but it is too ingrained to be dismissed here.

The principles of induction have always had an important relation to common sense. Induction apparently contains practical knowledge of a high degree of utility, and most common sense aspires to practical knowledge. Ever since the earliest reasoners, men of a skeptical caste have sought to throw discredit on induction by manufacturing doubts which were designed to show that observers had not arrived at real empirical truth, and that the skeptics were able to supply a better brand. There is a great deal of this in Hume, and still more in the later critics. During the modern period, the scientists clarified this part of Hume’s philosophy. Laplace, by inventing the rule of succession, undermined the probabilistic argument of Hume’s skeptical attack. Later theorists proved that uniformity does not involve necessity; Karl Popper invented a theory of corroboration and a theory of falsification which did away with all the old difficulties upon which skeptics had battened. Goodman showed that prediction follows from entrenched habits, which earlier thinkers had denied. All these results were obtained by ordinary logical methods, and were as incontrovertible as the rules of grammar. Dogmatists met the situation by not reading the authors concerned. Only the critical philosophy assimilated the new results, and thereby won an easy argumentative victory over the partisans of continued ignorance.

The present writer was at first not exempt from this kind of reasoning, but discovered in later study how to escape from it by means of the theory of “material foundations,” from which it appears that the feudal manor is not exemplified when we say “the feudal manor does not persist.” It may seem absurd to spend time on such an antiquated topic as the feudal manor, but such topics often afford the best tests of historical theories. Most historical theories are condemned by the fact that they lead to contradictions; therefore the theorist must be aware of contradictions and on the lookout for them. Many field observations would seem trivial to anyone who did not know their relevance, and contradictions are the experiments of the historical materialist.

From the impersonal standpoint of physiology, the qualities in the object during that act of seeing are neither inherent nor imposed, nor yet independent of the observer. We cannot say that a sensation A in one mind is definitely more veridical than a sensation B in another unless neural signals can travel from the retina to the cortex, starting when the light arrives (according to the stimulus), and arriving before the judgment is formed (according to the perceiver’s time). As regards scarcity, it must be understood, to begin with, that we are not dealing with a metaphysical abstraction, but with a condition necessitated by empirical observation and embodied in economic formulae. There is the same sort of difference between the two as there is between the theories of Malthus and the principles of a household budget. What emerges is this : that while the desires pertaining to a given individual have a definite hierarchy from the point of view of an observer who shares his circumstances, desires which pertain to individuals in different stations have not always a definite order of precedence. To be precise : if a resource is allocated from a common store to a claimant, and then diverted to another claimant, it will be exhausted for the first about twice as quickly as if it were hoarded. The choices which are made by the first claimant during that period of exhaustion are neither more nor less rational than the diversion of the resource to the second claimant. If subjective phenomena comparable with that of conscious awareness were common in our mechanical analyses, it is probable that the mental world would have seemed too intricate to be addressed by reductive methods, so that we should have been content with behaviorists down to the present day. But if a science of mind had been formulated, it would have had to be one acknowledging qualia, because purely physical descriptions would have been obviously inadequate. Conscious beings exhibit perceptions which arise very nearly with the character of intrinsic reality, and the nature of these perceptions would be unintelligible without the recognition of first-person phenomena. There is no doubt that the mechanical account is deficient, and from a philosophical point of view it is no excuse to say that the deficiency is “only a minor one.” We have to make up our minds to the fact that, within certain experiences, there is no objective correlate for sensations which happen in different minds. This is the fact which has led to the introduction of the single concept called “subjectivity” instead of the two separate categories called “physical process” and “mental event.” The consciousness that we have been regarding as epiphenomenal is really “lived experience,” an awareness bound up with the perspective of the individual, with as little claim to externality as that of a dream which does not alter its qualities in crossing from sleep to waking.

When we consider the part that skepticism plays in all our common theories, it becomes evident that our understanding would be profoundly changed if we really imaginatively realized what the historians of science have shown. Take the notion of “certainty”: if the evidential order is provisional, there will be confirmation or refutation according to the framework adopted in interpreting data. The notion of truth in science is of course also affected: two investigators who employ every possible device for ensuring rigor will arrive at different estimates of the validity of a given hypothesis, if the investigators are operating under divergent theoretical paradigms. It is obvious that the very idea of a settled fact has become vague, because a fact must be about observable phenomena, not abstract postulates (which are conveniences); and it must be the fact at a given stage of inquiry, because the interpretation of any set of observations is continually evolving; and a given stage is a contingent notion, dependent upon the instruments the observer is employing. We can no longer speak of a theory as definitively true, but must speak simply of a provisional model. Between two competing models there is, quite independently of any single school, a certain relation called the “evidential weight” between them. This weight will be differently analysed by different schools into a confirmatory and an anomalous component, but this analysis has no final validity. The weight is an objective historical accumulation, but its separation into supporting and contradictory elements is not.

Modern economics enables us to give substance to the suggestion of Marx and Keynes, that the “essence” of the market and the social order is interdependent. “Stable prosperity” was obviously very different from crises and also from the persistent state. But if the market and the state are both only convenient aggregations of processes, it is much less difficult to imagine them governed by the same principles. Moreover, what has hitherto seemed one of the most marked peculiarities of crisis, namely inevitability, or the revelation of a structural flaw, has now invaded sociology, and is found not to involve malice: economic observers in different epochs may analyze the “same” event, but they will analyze it differently. Even indices and fiscal measures become subjective in modern analysis; what they directly record is not an economic fact, but their relation to an economic fact. Thus economics and sociology have approached each other, and the old dualism of market and society has broken down.

“perfect language” cannot survive. A linguistic system is nothing but a series of conventions obeying certain rules. The conception of precision arose at a time when grammarians had no doubts as to the validity of the conception of “clarity.” Precision was clarity which was in grammar and lexicon, ambiguity was clarity which was in lexicon only. The notion of clarity grew more shadowy in semantics as time went on, but it survived in pedagogy because it did no harm — until pragmatics was invented. Clarity, traditionally, was a notion compounded of two elements. First, a clear expression had the logical property that it could only occur as statement in a discourse, not as implication. Secondly, it was something that persisted through usage, or, in the case of mathematics, was outside usage altogether. These two properties had no necessary connection, but this was not perceived because linguistics taught that grammatical rules are immutable and philosophy taught that definitions are immutable. Both, therefore, were thought to have both the characteristics of clarity. Now, however, linguistics compels us to regard evanescent utterances as clear in the logical sense, i.e. as statements which cannot be implications. A grammatical rule, which we took to be a single persistent entity, is really a string of entities, like the apparently persistent meanings in a dictionary. And there is no reason why we should not say the same of a speaker : the persistent intention seems as fictitious as the permanent definition. Both are only strings of events having certain interesting relations to each other.

In some ways, less to offer than earlier analyses. In the age of steam, technology was the handmaid of industry; to this day, they come under one heading in popular understanding. It has been generally regarded as the business of engineering to ensure the great efficiencies of commerce. The modern network does not profess to be able to ensure them, or even to undermine them. It aims only at facilitating the fundamental operations of the systems, and integrating the different systems in a single comprehensive view of that fragment of the whole that engineering has succeeded in constructing. It does not know what failure may arise; it possesses no talisman for transforming complexity into security. It offers functional conveniences to those who value them, but it does not attempt to flatter human confidence as most technologies do. If it is opaque and contingent, it lays the blame on the interconnection, which has chosen to work in a systemic way rather than as designers or managers might have desired. Perhaps this is regrettable, but a user can hardly be expected to regret it.

It is perhaps worth while to point out that modern pattern theory knows nothing of “essence” in the old or metaphysical sense of that word. We used to think that a spiral in a shell exerted a “formative influence” on a galaxy. Now we think that mathematical relations, in the neighbourhood of certain ratios, are so constituted that nature finds it less trouble to arrange matter as it does than in any other way. The great principle of emergent similarity is the “principle of persistent configuration,” that in developing from one state to another a system often assumes the pattern which involves least structural contradiction. (Configuration is a technical term, but its precise definition need not concern us at present.) Popularizers and certain thinkers who wish to be thought profound are fond of the word “archetypal.” There is nothing “archetypal” in morphology, which, on the contrary, finds everything deducible from a law of combinatorial economy. And there is no such thing as one substrate “dictating” the form of another. The universe of modern complexity is much more like that of Heraclitus than that of those who prate of “ideal forms” and “transcendent blueprints.”

At first sight, it is not obvious why there should be any incompatibility between mechanism and consciousness. Every reflective person acknowledges the brain's machinery; the more intricate and efficient its processes, the more they command our intellectual respect. Disciplines which have a long tradition of empirical rigor, like the physical sciences, are captivated by reductive explanations as soon as they formulate them, and strive only to extend their domain as thoroughly as possible. Nothing vexes a modern neuroscientist so much as to hear praise of "the mystery of qualia" or the irreducible nature of subjective awareness. He feels as a materialist would feel who was told to contemplate souls instead of synaptic potentials. And like that materialist, he would prefer a complete physical theory to an incomplete one, not realizing that it may exclude the very phenomenon it seeks to explain.

out of touch with the prevailing tendencies of biological thought. The vitalists with their insistence on a life force, the holists with their emergent properties, the mystics with their belief in a transcendent soul (a substance which is indivisible and everywhere governs cellular activity), all represent a purely sentimental and essentially reactionary opposition to reductionism. The early cytologists were the first men to apprehend intellectually the nonsentimental case for cellular autonomy, but in them it may have been no more than a tentative hypothesis — certainly it was not a systematically elaborated doctrine. Since their day numbers of biologists in the most advanced laboratories have been tending to adopt in earnest a view similar to that of the colonial theorists; this view, that is to say, has been latent or explicit in the attitude of many investigators into the fundamental nature of organic unity.

Men have sensory perceptions, and they have intuitions. While sensory perceptions are immediate, they take first place; but when they are analyzed, intuitions unconnected with them become important in deciding whether a belief is to be accepted or rejected. In ordinary human experience there are many observations, inferences, and judgments whose bare perceptual basis is not adequately examined; as regards them, I do not deny that the first requisite for understanding is an increase of scrutiny. The assumption is, that the alignment of social forces is what makes history orderly. It is thought that a community which has two factions and two aims and two methods must be twice as stable as a community which has one faction and one aim and one method. In a word, it is thought that order is proportional to uniformity. A few people, not always quite logically, challenge this idea in the name of liberty or progress ; but they are glad if they secure their position by the vehemence of their argument. It is not from a political or ethical point of view that I wish to challenge it; it is from the point of view of sociology and observation of events. If order is proportional to uniformity, the case for despotism is unanswerable; if not, the whole process remains to be examined.

Ruling ideas are celebrated because they are elegant, and esteemed because they confer authority; they are resisted because they are oppressive, and despised because they impose conformity. Do not let us suppose that one of these perspectives is “enlightened” and the other “deluded,” any more than it would be enlightened to maintain that society has a head but deluded to maintain that it has limbs, though we can easily imagine antiquarians disputing this question concerning ancient polities. A dominant ideology is like a talisman in a medieval romance: luminous and fortuitous to its possessor, but blinding and formidable to his rivals. But in our age nothing is permitted to manifest itself with such unadorned clarity. The proponent of the idea, it is true, resides at a remove from its consequences, where he cannot hear its dissonances or see its unsightly accumulations of contradiction or smell its noxious prejudices; if he ever examines it, the occasion is before it is applied in practice, when he can admire its coherence or its subtle refinement without being troubled by grievance and strife. But when he is challenged to consider the ideology from the point of view of those who have to live under it and obey it, he has a ready answer. He can point out that, owing to its prevalence, these people can enjoy more comforts — often vastly more — than their ancestors could. It follows that they must be more content than their ancestors — if we are to accept an assumption which is made by almost every one.

All this might be different, and has been different in many organisms. In sessile epochs, creatures have been shaped for their stability. In some niches in the sea, forms are shaped for their filter-feeding or symbiotic excellence, strange as it may seem. In a dense forest, a creature may actually be shaped for its camouflage. In reptiles, scales are shaped; in birds, feathers. The study of these differing lineages shows the correctness of our analysis, for in all of them we find a large percentage of beings who are indifferent to complexity so long as they have enough to process sensation, but are keenly desirous of the adaptations by which, in their environment, survival is to be won.

The importance of this arrangement lies in this, that the placement of taste receptors is not an arbitrary feature of anatomy, and could be explained by distinct evolutionary pressures. If, by chance, these receptors were situated upon the hand, we should have to employ some other method of assessing potential nourishment, and most of our present reliance upon immediate gustatory judgment would cease. Moreover, since this assessment is in the nature of a safeguard, it only confers advantage when we correctly identify a toxin, to which a failure brings correlative harm. A general increase of available foodstuffs gives no such protective benefit, and therefore brings no proportional increase in survival. There is, of course, some utility derived from the actual ingestion of nutritious substances, but, as we have seen, this is a very small part of what makes the proximal placement advantageous. And in so far as the mechanism is protective, no increase of biological fitness as a whole comes from increase of mere consumption, whether general or particular.

Why do we, in fact, almost all of us, believe we perceive colour directly? It may seem, at first sight, as though the hues of the world were what we passively receive. But, in fact, we apprehend these mainly through a complex process of neural construction. When a man gazes upon a crimson sunset, he reflects that his retina merely signals wavelengths, and the vivid sensation is built within the dark theatre of his brain. When he distinguishes an emerald leaf from a scarlet berry, he consoles himself for the simplicity of the stimulus by thoughts of the intricate synthesis performed. In every visual experience, whether of art or of nature, colours in some contexts appear more vibrant than identical hues in other contexts, merely because of the mind’s interpretive framework. One of the most fundamental of all our cognitive acts is the construction of qualitative experience from quantitative data. As our physiology stands, the sensation of “red” or “blue” is given to the man whose visual cortex engages in its elaborate computation. This is the chief reason why colour is a mental artifact. The actual photons arriving at the eye play quite a secondary part. Take, for example, a connoisseur who cannot differentiate the spectral composition of two paints, but has learned to name a thousand shades by the help of colour charts. The only certainty he derives from his perceptions is the thought that they are his own fabrication; he would derive more direct sensation from the raw, unprocessed signals of the optic nerve, but he would not obtain the same satisfaction for his intellectual understanding.

Meanwhile, cultural transmission deprives us of two things which are certainly important ingredients of human understanding, namely, originality and dissent. Traditions have their own inertia, and their own insistent demands: a society that has ancient customs must keep them functioning. The great trouble with inheritance, from the point of view of progress, is its conservatism. And, of course, conversely, the great objection to innovation, from the point of view of tradition, is its unpredictability. As biological analogy dominates the thoughts of people who consider themselves “scientific,” the highest praise they can give to an idea is to suggest that it has the qualities of a gene — that it is replicable, stable, precise, etc. And a “mutant” thought has come to be synonymous with a false one. Against this point of view certain anthropological philosophies were a protest — not, to my mind, wholly sound from a logical point of view, but inspired by a wholesome dread of seeing culture turned more and more into mere heredity.

Patterns have altered our way of perception, but not their fundamental forms. Consequently there is a persistent recognition. The whole study of structures and repetitions is as yet in its infancy; a beginning has been made by systems theory, but only a beginning. What we may accept from this theory is the fact that arrangements will, in manifestation, exhibit various orders which they do not superficially display, and will have an attendant set of quite consistent principles which enable them to maintain these orders without appearing to do so. But orthodox analysis has unduly simplified our underlying templates, which are manifold, and differ from one medium to another. It is to be hoped that natural and artificial phenomena will soon come to be understood from this point of view, and will thus throw light on universal formative tendencies.

The only way of comprehending the behaviors at present associated with corporate enterprise is to observe the fundamental drives, with every analogy to primitive biological impulse during the examination. Many corporations would cease to pursue reckless expansion if they had opportunities to satisfy their needs in sustainable markets ; one of the most astute and most successful executives for stability that it has been my privilege to study habitually spent his career navigating the most volatile sectors in the economy. If every large firm had a division in its structure through which, if it chose, it could be directed to seek symbiotic partnerships, or encouraged to forage for innovation in untapped fields, or otherwise enabled to engage in some adaptive and exploratory activity involving swift institutional initiative, the instinctual pursuit of profit would become confined to monopolies and stagnant entities. I confess I know no method of making these classes altruistic, but I am convinced that a rigorous biology would find a method if it undertook the comparison in earnest.

In ordinary discourse, men and women hold innumerable prejudices, and contend for the moral high ground; but they cherish and defend them the whole time. Casual assumptions join in the intellectual life of their holders, and are honoured guests in their reasoning. At the beginning of a dispute over manners, a person arrives with anecdotal evidence about a rival group; we persuade ourselves that his anecdote is universal, reward him, and publish the popular affirmation. In a more dogmatic age we should have celebrated him, and dismissed anyone who threw doubt on his premise. The greater tenacity of modern prejudice is attributable to abstraction, which operates in three different ways. First, it makes it possible to have larger categories. Secondly, it facilitates a pervasive discourse, which flourishes by appealing to men’s lazier intellects. Thirdly — and this is the point that concerns us — it starves the critical, questioning side of human nature, which works underground, producing an obscure unease, to which the thought of prejudice appeals as affording possible certainty. It is a mistake to attribute a vast misconception like racial bias merely to the machinations of demagogues. In isolated communities, perhaps, such an explanation would have been adequate; that is one reason why such communities believe wholeheartedly, and make a tradition to secure conformity. But in educated, open, and diverse societies, no authority could have withstood the popular demand for simple judgment. A popular demand of this sort must have an instinctive basis, and for my part I believe that the modern increase in prejudiced instinct is attributable to the confusion (mostly unconscious) caused by the complexity, ambiguity, and nuance of modern life.

Economic self-regulation, and external intervention by fiscal authorities, are not adequate methods of dealing with our anarchic markets. The reason they are inadequate is that these markets are capable of as many disguises as the Devil in mediaeval legend, and some of these disguises deceive even the elect. The only adequate method is to discover what are the needs of our productive nature, and then to search for the least disruptive way of fulfilling them. Since stability is what is most thwarted by speculation, the only thing that can be provided is structure; the use made of structure must be left to the initiative of the community. No doubt considerable sacrifice would be involved; but it would not be comparable to the sacrifice of depression. Understanding of economic forces must be the basis of any real improvement in social organization. Science has done wonders in mastering the laws of material production, but our own systems are much less understood, as yet, than the laws of supply and demand. When political economy learns to understand social nature, it will be able to bring a prosperity into our collective life which machines and the industrial sciences have failed to secure.

VII In a popular scientific journal I once found the assertion that there is only one true believer in machine consciousness, namely Professor Turing. I should have said there are as many as there are enthusiasts for computational metaphors. This is not to say that such believers are common in laboratories, nor yet that I am myself among them — for, ever since the decade in which I contemplated cybernetics and artificial intelligence, I have realized that I am not wholly persuaded. Dispassionate self-examination, however, compels me to admit that it would be simpler if I were. In this brief disquisition I want to set forth certain perplexities which are felt by persons like myself, who, while acknowledging what is formidable in engineering, have difficulty in relinquishing an older animism as regards what constitutes genuine sentience. I want to ask, not only what is the logical bearing of computational theory upon the concept of pain, but what is likely to be its effect upon ordinary thought and discourse if widely adopted in a necessarily oversimplified form. It has not yet become a dogma, like certain schools of psychology; but if it ever does, its vulgar form will no doubt differ greatly from Professor Turing’s thesis — as greatly as popular materialism does from Spinoza.

specialized cells, who regard the development of a single function as the ultimate good, provided it can be divorced from autonomy. This is the view which the mitochondrion endeavours to inculcate in the cytoplasm, and which the nucleus regards as appropriate to all subordinate organelles and regions. The flagellum represents a more aristocratic ideal, reserved for those who exercise locomotive power. But, over and above all these, there is a supreme conception, which suggests the philosopher’s prime mover ; it is that of the regulatory gene at rest in the nucleus, while all else expresses activity around it at varying rates, thus securing for it the absolute maximum of relative stability. This role is reserved for our master regulators, especially transcription factors.

The popular version of intellectual conformity will, I imagine, be something like this: In old days there was supposed to be a duty called deference, which was capable of three types of application, to tradition, to doctrine, and to office. Now, it has been ascertained that there is no such duty as deference, but only inquiry. All our intellectual activities consist of sceptical processes. “Tradition” consists of inherited occurrences, particularly such as are connected with institutions. “Doctrine” consists of assertions of the established. “Office” consists of all other pronouncements depending upon vested authority. When, recently, a famous heretic questioned a famous prelate, there were some who expressed doubt as to their compatibility. But from a conformist standpoint such a doubt was misplaced : he had cultivated the habits of doubt and inquiry, the other the habits of certainty and decree, so that both were dogmatists, though belonging to different branches of the profession. Since the only thing we can do is to test our beliefs, the popular votaries of the creed are likely to infer that we ought to test them as little as possible. At this point difficulties will arise as regards priority. Should the different articles of belief be tested relatively to each other? Or should belief as a whole be tested relatively to the society in which it finds itself? Or is scrutiny relative to truth the criterion of virtue? The ideal thinker on the first view is the sophist; on the second, the man who upholds a convention which is falling down ; on the third, the man who spends his life in a library. It is not easy to see on what principle the resulting controversies are to be decided, but on the whole I back the scholars.

Now there is a quite different conception of corporate purpose which has come down to us from the early theorists of trade, but is being gradually displaced by the outlook due to the domination of biological analogy over the economic imagination. I believe this older outlook to be logically reconcilable with a strict profit motive, but not practically in the conduct of the average enterprise. In this older outlook, stewardship and community are considered as important as earning; legacy and stability are thought to be as admirable as altering the quarterly figures on a balance sheet. The small proprietor loves his craft and the family firm contemplates its tradition, and in this consists their supreme excellence. The whole ideal is static. It is true that in the boardroom reports are read and dividends are declared, but they are the same reports every quarter, and no innovation in the pursuit of growth is tolerated. Such an existence bores the modern executive. One reason why this older model has lost its hold is that it has failed to provide progressive machinery for expansion, though the bacterium provides it in the petri dish.

It may be laid down that every psychological theory is based upon a certain non sequitur. The scientist first invents a false doctrine as to the nature of awareness, and then deduces that unconscious processes are those which show that his doctrine is false. To begin with the traditional materialist: he argues that, since mental states always obey the laws of physics, unconsciousness consists in the absence of specific neural activity. We then come on to the panpsychist, who argues that the mind consists of gradations which extend in a perfect continuum, and therefore unconsciousness consists of a state which diminishes the gradation — though it is difficult to see how such a state is possible, since complete continuity is metaphysically necessary. Chalmers, writing for an academic public, holds a threat over those whose observations refute him which is even more terrible than professional disregard — I mean, the threat of philosophical incoherence. He shows that subjective experience never behaves categorically, and then, in his treatise on consciousness, he argues that what makes a theory untenable is to see a phenomenon behaving categorically — i.e. you are incoherent when you posit something that shows Chalmers’s philosophy to be false, and only then. These examples have, I hope, made it plain that a hypothesis can never have psychological consequences except in virtue of its falsehood: if it were true, the states which it defines as unconscious would be impossible.

a distinction. A true analogy may have practical consequences, though it cannot have metaphysical consequences. If you attempt to extract a desired output from a neural network by means of one training cycle, when it is constructed to require many, the truth has a practical consequence, namely that you must offer it further iterations. But no one would call this consequence “metaphysical”; it merely has to do with how to realize your computational aims. Similarly, the analogy with natural selection, as developed in certain modern treatises, has undoubtedly all sorts of important practical consequences, particularly in algorithmic design. If you want a model to learn to behave in a certain way, you will often be wise if you follow the principles of selective pressure rather than (say) those of explicit symbolic programming. But this is a technical matter, not a metaphysical matter; metaphysics only comes in when it is said that the process ought to have certain teleological ends in view, or (alternatively) that certain architectures can be classified as superior or inferior independently of their performance.

In my opinion, one of the most important elements in the judging of cosmological systems, metaphysical coherence and explanatory power, is the principle of the universe’s self-contained necessity. We can measure this logically by the absence of any requirement for external causation and the internal sufficiency of its physical laws. ... If the system is truly self-sufficient, we should want to draw a curve of its explanatory completeness across all scales. If from our leading theories it derives the same fundamental necessity at its temporal origin that it exhibits in its present state, the chances are it is a brute fact, and will never be anything but that.

I will now take another aspect of material composition, namely its views on consciousness. Here I cannot cite Dr. Turing, whose views on the subject, so far as they appear in his works, seem to me excellent. But he does not deal with the deeper parts of the argument, and it is there that my doubts are strongest. I will take a proposition which, while not explicitly mechanistic, is, in fact, largely inspired by the outlook with which mechanism is connected, I mean: The Mind: Its Processes and Its Substrate. Applying this criterion to galaxies, nebulae, and star clusters, to planets and comets, we see that it involves an interesting readjustment in our estimates of the destiny of cosmic entities. In addition to points already noted, there are two cosmological principles implicit in this expansion. One is that structure must be inherently transient, the other that it must yield to entropic dissolution. These are both natural consequences of the attempt to deduce fate from a system based upon relentless metric increase. For my part, the destiny suggested by the above observation from modern cosmology is not one that I can contemplate with equanimity. I cannot believe that significance is proportional to duration, nor yet that it is futile to have difficulty in acquiescing to the void. Doubtless my sentiments on these matters are prejudiced, since I am mortal and terrestrial; but although I recognize this fact, they remain my sentiments none the less.

Twenty-five years ago neurologists believed that neural communication involved the transmission of ten to fifteen distinct electrochemical signals; but as a result of investigations carried on during the past two decades, it has been found that the typical synapse in the cerebral cortex does not employ in its ordinary functioning, and will not require in subsequent activity, more than three fundamental neurotransmitters at the outside, unless it participates in some higher cognitive process, when it may be necessary for it to utilize a specialized and intricate chemical vocabulary. The typical neuron in its dendritic reception and in its axonal firing rarely employs more than fifteen hundred distinct ionic pulses; many of our cerebral cells never use more than half this number. In view of these facts, the current model of intracerebral signaling is being constructed on the principle that the impulses that will actually be utilized in routine cognition should be mastered so that they can be transmitted automatically, and the exotic and improbable signals that were formerly theorized but will probably never be observed are being eliminated. Not a single hypothetical mechanism is being retained in present-day neurological theory on the premise that it will be valuable in the training of intellectual faculties.

Not only is it important to acknowledge competing interests, but it is also logically inevitable that they will produce predictable patterns of change. Those societies which contain only a single, monolithic interest will be unable to evolve with either dynamism or stability except under external duress and by rare historical accident. About half the recorded civilizations of the ancient world possessed as much latent conflict as our own, yet their social transformations were hardly a tenth as regular. Yet these patterns must have been discernible to the ordinary observer of their time, since they recur in chronicles which had to be a factual record. Everybody knows the common notion of free will, which enables its possessor to imagine himself the author of his actions, and believe for himself that he chooses the past and determines the future. But people do not always realize that a great deal of the substance of this notion can be dissolved by examining the machinery of the brain at the present day. A psychologist who studies the prefrontal cortex sees the executive, the controller to which conscious deliberation is likely to be ascribed if it escapes physiological reduction. On the other hand, when he studies the limbic system he sees the passions. In the amygdala, I am told, he can see the primitive fears; in the basal ganglia he can see the habits of the eighteenth century. If a medieval scholastic were to return to earth, the philosophical landscape which he championed would puzzle him dreadfully. He would feel a little less strange in a theology seminar, still less strange in a courtroom; but he would not feel really at home until he reached a neuroscience laboratory. There, for the first time in his ghostly wanderings, he would find men who still believe in “the soul, volition, and the mystery of choice,” and who conceive these things more or less as the schoolmen of the thirteenth century conceived them. And I think it would not be long before he became a principal investigator of the neural republic.

We are accustomed to take awareness for granted: to assume without hesitation that the states which occupy our daily experience are unquestionably distinct from sleep, and that further distinctions of clarity are sure to be made indefinitely. In the philosophy of mind, modern introspection and its consequences have administered a blow to this confident belief, and men have begun to look back to the simple division of Descartes as a clear age, not likely to be recovered by contemporary thought. In common parlance there has been much less of this shock to dualism, and in casual reflection still less. For those of us who have been accustomed to take awareness for granted, it is especially interesting to examine a condition like drowsiness, which has remained where our theory was three centuries ago, and to ask ourselves whether, on the balance, the categories which we have adopted have brought any real understanding.

The nature of qualia, as every one knows, is based upon the testimony of introspection, which flourished as a method long before modern psychology. Like the idealists and mystics, we do not think of conscious experience as mechanically explicable; on the contrary, we believe that in private reflection our mental life seems irreducible, and our perceptions appear unique to a degree which the reductive materialist can acknowledge but hardly explain. This, of course, is an illusion. But the practical result is that the dualist, like other defenders of the immaterial, aims at establishing a fundamental dichotomy, maintaining a certain intuitive appeal, but not always accounting for neural correlates. In this he is more mistaken than any other philosopher who has ever argued. His confusion has been stamped on the mind-body problem from Descartes’ day to our own. During its early formulation the arguments occupied only a small part of the philosophical landscape.

What is the conclusion for a person who, like the present writer, accepts, for metaphysical purposes, the cosmological principle of self-containment, while rejecting the supposed theological and teleological implications? I have the highest admiration for Spinoza, and consider his arguments profoundly significant. I consider that, at the present time, cosmology is the most important of speculative pursuits, and naturalism is the most important philosophical phenomenon. Nevertheless, I cannot cease to admire “useless” causes, and explanations which have no purpose except to satisfy curiosity. The problem is not physical; for, as we have seen, if the universe is self-contained it can have no need for an external mover, except in the subordinate way of helping to show what principles to use for a given model. The problem is, in a broad sense, epistemological : given that the bulk of mankind are certain to demand first causes, is it better that they should deduce false origins from true observations or true origins from false observations? A question of this sort is insoluble. The only true solution seems to be that ordinary men and women should be taught cosmology, so as to be able to refrain from demanding causes which only seem to be required. When it is said, for example, that the universe is “contingent,” what is meant is that, when they observe an effect, they also demand a cause that a person totally destitute of metaphysical subtlety would erroneously suppose to precede the effect. This is a most undesirable quality, from which, on the whole, the modern scientific mind has, in the past, been more free than any other. But there are signs that, if it is to remain free in this respect, it will require a more rigorous adherence to the principle that a complete system requires no explanation from outside itself.

It is often argued, as economic theorists are wont to do, about competition and efficiency and such matters, but they seldom acknowledge the inherent tendencies contrary to equilibrium and the natural consolidations. This is demonstrated in the following observation: The proponent of laissez-faire addressed the economist, saying: We have a perfectly competitive market in our system. One firm gained a decisive advantage, and the rivals were thereby extinguished. — In a theoretical model, the economist replied, competition is something different from this. A dominant firm absorbs the market share of its competitors, and a competitor yields its position to the dominant firm. It is in such processes that true monopoly is to be found.

Monopoly is in all things natural, even in efficiency. It does not follow that we ought to return competition for consolidation. It is observed on one occasion: “How do you regard the principle of returning regulation for dominance?” And the reply is: “What, then, is to be the return for innovation? Rather should you return oversight for exploitation, and competition for merit.” The principle of returning restraint for concentration was being questioned in its day by the classical economists, whose doctrine is much more akin to that of perfect competition than is the teaching of experience. The prefrontal cortex maintains a doctrine of selection: “The mind,” it seems, “has ever been ordered by letting certain signals take precedence. He who must attend to everything is unfit to maintain coherence.” But conscious experience naturally prefers the sensory maxims of vividness, novelty, and salience, combined, as they are, with a great emphasis upon the utility that can be gained by wise allocation. It never occurs to the brain, as it has to many philosophical systems, to have one model of awareness in theory and another in operation. I do not mean that it always achieves a perfect representation, but that it attempts to do so and is designed to do so, whereas there are large parts of the attentional mechanism which are universally admitted to be too refined for this noisy world.

We have, in fact, two kinds of communication side by side: one which we consider primitive but do not truly comprehend, and another which we employ but seldom acknowledge. Bacterial signalling, like all biological phenomena except perhaps photosynthesis, is prokaryotic in origin; it had in the primordial epochs that emphasis on chemical diffusion and local coordination which is characteristic of unicellular life. From this point of view, the mechanism of quorum sensing was intelligible. But when bacterial colonies became the nominal subject of energetic human researchers, it was found necessary to maintain that some molecular interactions were not to be taken as mere noise, while others, such as the autoinducer systems of *Vibrio fischeri*, acquired great notoriety. In our own day, under the influence of sophisticated linguistics, the slightest approach to analogizing bacterial chatter is ridiculed, and such signals are expected to be relegated to mere metabolic triggers. In practice, our effective understanding is that of semantic meaning achieved by means of a complex syntax; and this applies to societies as well as to individuals. Anything else seems to us simplistic and fanciful.

The conditions for life do not conform either to our hopeful or our pessimistic expectations. They appear in theory to be exceedingly rare, and in practice to be remarkably common; whereas we hold in theory that they should be inevitable and in practice that they seem curiously elusive. Life sometimes emerges, but is not a ubiquitous phenomenon, and does not greatly favor either extreme scarcity or absolute certainty. Historically, astronomers have regarded planetary habitability as more significant than anything else; next to that, and usually in combination with it, they regard chemical complexity and orbital stability. For ages past, scientific attention has been focused on Earth as the singular result of fortunate circumstances. As there has been no definitive evidence of extraterrestrial life for many centuries — with the sole exception of ambiguous microbial fossils, the interpretation of which is debated — habitability has attracted to itself the kind of interest which, in earlier times, was given to celestial divination, as well as the interest which it inspired on its own account. The old conception, however, was very limited, consisting merely in an uncritical study of our own solar system and its recognized analogues. Under the influence of modern astronomy, it has come to be known that planetary dynamics, atmospheric chemistry, stellar evolution, and so on, are of more explanatory power than the speculations of former ages. Contemporary astrobiologists — that is to say, the researchers who have been educated on interdisciplinary lines — recognize cosmic probabilities, and have perhaps hardly enough patience for the older assumptions. Nevertheless, even the most empirical, with few exceptions, retain the traditional acknowledgments of uncertainty, open-mindedness, and a cautious temper. Whether these acknowledgments will survive a few more decades of exoplanetary discovery and spectroscopic analysis is perhaps doubtful.

IDEALS OF DIVISION If I were to try to sum up in a phrase the main cause of social stratification, I should say that surplus, in the main, invites domination, while scarcity, in the main, invites submission. We like security for our own comforts, and we like authority over our neighbours. For the sake of the former we have built up vast properties, and for the sake of the latter we have built up hereditary ranks. The common man is too preoccupied and too powerless for such consolidations. To say that he is preoccupied is, however, only true in a certain sense. He is not preoccupied in the way that philosophers are, that is to say, he will ponder deeply for his sustenance. Observers of society find him extraordinarily practical. But he will not scheme, as financiers and great landowners do, simply because he would be content if he did not scheme, nor does he love accumulation for its own sake. When he has enough to subsist on, he subsists on it, instead of trying to augment it by relentless acquisition. He has an infinite capacity for simple satisfactions — tending his garden, conversing with his neighbours, admiring the craftsmanship of local artisans, or walking in familiar lanes. To the wealthy man’s way of thinking, there is something unduly passive about such a way of conducting one’s affairs; he respects more a man who expands his estate every year, even if all that he does to expand it is exploitative.

The doctrine of common sense. The traditional belief of the unreflective populace — still maintained by most practical persons in their daily affairs — is that our immediate perceptions are veridical, so trustworthy as to furnish an accurate picture of the external world. The layman might have no difficulty in accepting this belief if it applied only to familiar objects, but when he is told that his own sensations of solidity and permanence are illusory he grows perplexed. Modern physics teaches that reality is fundamentally alien, and that if it appears otherwise, that is through the force of habitual interpretation or misleading appearances. This divergence from intuitive human understanding has a profound influence on the outlook of the scientist.

Among astronomers, the systems that are regarded as potentially habitable are those which forgo chaotic orbital arrangements and find stability in maintaining temperate conditions for their planets. There is an element of the exceptional in our conception of habitability: unless a world positions itself within a narrow band of distances from its star, we do not think it can be an exceptionally suitable place. This expectation comes from our notion of Rarity. It leads not only to assumptions about uniqueness, but also to disappointment, since the ideal parameters are too precise for most systems to achieve. In the wider cosmos this is not the case. Planetary conditions are probabilistic rather than predetermined. A star is likely to host rocky bodies, some with liquid water, many with organic compounds, and a few with stable climates. These are not very improbable circumstances, but many stars actually contain them, and the result is perhaps more common than that of our stricter criteria, from which most observable worlds are excluded.

This makes our biological disputes bitter, and involves in practice a great readiness to appeal to physical conflict. In many social creatures, although there were individuals who were ready to appeal to contact, no one took them seriously, not even their own kin. Compromise is the accepted principle, because it is necessary to save the energy of both parties. Saving energy, though in some forms it makes the observer smile, is a most valuable evolutionary institution, making social and survival prospects far less perilous than it is with us.

We have a first-class system of education and communication, part of which is devoted to the dissemination of useful knowledge and the cultivation of the arts, while another part is devoted to propagating doctrines, fashionable prejudices, and official histories for the purpose of securing the acquiescence of the governed. We have an elaborate apparatus of publishing and broadcasting, part of which is devoted to genuine inquiry and public information, while the rest is devoted to the reinforcement of established power. In most nations at the present day the greater part of intellectual energy is consumed in justifying present arrangements and only the residue in questioning them. In totalitarian states, the proportion is nearly absolute. We have a priesthood of academics and commentators of unexampled sophistication, part of which is devoted to the disinterested pursuit of truth and part to discrediting any thinker who proposes a fundamental critique of prevailing institutions. Among primitive tribes, until very recently, they had none of these things. Social organization was too simple to require either systematic ideology or propaganda; the ruling group too insecure to elaborate a metaphysics of its own dominance; the intellectuals too few to articulate either orthodoxies or heresies. The result was that in such societies, as compared to any civilized community, there was a certain intellectual liberty for all, and a degree of diffused skepticism which was remarkable in view of the uniformity imposed by custom and tradition.

We all know what we mean by a “suitable” world. The ideally suitable world does not orbit too close or too far, avoids stellar violence, maintains its atmosphere in the presence of cosmic rays only exactly as it would if there were no such hazards, regulates its climate steadily, and holds the correct elements in all proportions. It has a wholesome horror of orbital instability, and realizes that it is the universe’s casual tendency to disrupt delicate arrangements. It has a still greater horror of chemical monotony, and considers it the business of natural laws to safeguard nascent biology against those who question the necessity of the parameters generally accepted by middle-aged successful astrophysicists. Apart from its planetary formation, at which it is fortuitous, it spends much time in complex processes: it may encourage plate tectonics and magnetic field generation; it may promote water retention, atmospheric stability, and molecular complexity among its components and their interactions by seeing to it that deviations in these respects receive due cosmological correction; it may be a cradle of organic chemistry and prevent an ill-judged respect for simplicity from allowing the dominance of reactions with sterile outcomes. Above all, of course, its “conditions,” in the narrow sense, must be irreproachable.

A century ago there emerged a theory of heredity which was universally recognized to be a very dangerous doctrine. I remember to this day the first time that I encountered its tenets when I was a student. It was in a lecture by a certain professor of biology to the effect that this theory held men to be merely the transient vehicles of their selfish genes. This notion appeared to me as undesirable from a philosophical as from a personal point of view, and I therefore conceived a grave suspicion of its proponents. Long afterwards, I discovered that the lecture was one of those reckless simplifications in which earnest scientists are wont to indulge in the interests of clarity. I also discovered what was the really serious charge against the theory. It was no less than this: that it defined an “individual” as a collection of inherited chemical instructions. This definition, as the reader will perceive at once if he is reflective, is subversive of all true personality. How much more exalted is the attitude of the vitalist, who lays it down that a human action is not significant if it springs from molecular causation, but only if it is inspired by a vital principle, which is, of course, just as likely to inspire irrational actions. We know that the exercise of will should be its own justification, and it seems to follow that the enduring of determinism on the part of the conscious being should be its own despair. The vitalist, therefore, is a more profound thinker, though his biology may be erroneous; for he realizes that to be a mere precipitate of nucleic acids is to be a puppet, and that to be a puppet is unworthy of a creature who contemplates the stars.

It is true that the spectrum view fulfills its own definition of a plausible theory : it does much explanatory work. The forty middle years of the twentieth century in psychology were years of incredibly rapid progress, empirically, conceptually, and methodologically. At the beginning of the period comes the behaviorist manifesto, which made psychology ostensibly scientific, not, as before, a branch of speculative philosophy. This shift was the most difficult of the steps towards a materialist account of mind, and was quickly followed by other important reformulations, such as the computational theory of cognition. At the beginning of the period the penalty for invoking consciousness was professional exile; very soon the cognitive penalty was confined to those who were guilty of dualism or vitalism. The introspectionist methods, which made data so dubious as to cause atrocious confusion, were abolished in favor of operational definitions. The cognitive revolution was introduced in the 1950s. It is the fashion to decry the behaviorists, but I wish our current age had half as much methodological rigor as theirs. This, however, is beside the point. My point is that a very large proportion of the conceptual progress during those years must be attributed to the influence of the threshold model. There can be no doubt that nine-tenths of the experiments conducted in laboratories in the latter part of last century were clearer than they would have been if the spectrum notion had prevailed. So shallow is the spectrum philosophy that its proponents would regard this as a vindication of their activities. We, in our more nuanced age, can see that such a view is preposterous ; but it may fortify us to review the grounds for rejecting a grovelling gradualism such as that of the panpsychists.

It is difficult to think of any instance of a simulation which was “real” at the times when it was producing genuine consciousness. The Matrix, to judge by its internal coherence, would not have been allowed by philosophical purists to qualify as a genuine world. It is of the essence of a “real” world that it supports the laws of fundamental physics; therefore, a video game was real during the reign of pixel-based rendering, and unreal before and after; but it was before and after that it produced its most compelling inhabitants — in fact most of them were produced after it had narrowly escaped dismissal as a mere diversion. The Sims was authentic after it achieved photorealistic graphics, but all its memorable characters were created before that time, and on account of them its acclaim caused a logical scandal. Virtual reality was illusory in its infancy, when it generated avatars in praise of those who sought digital freedom; it was authentic in its maturity, when it generated savage attacks on the notion that a subroutine could defend its qualia against materialist aggression. It is needless to multiply examples ; enough has been said to suggest that the standards of reality now prevalent are incompatible with the production of genuine consciousness.

It may be doubted whether a “determinative” mode, in the above sense, does, on the average, any more to shape society than an “accidental” one. I mean by an “accidental” mode the contrary of what we have been describing. An “accidental” mode is one which is known to rely upon tradition and upon habit occasionally, and even to permit a wasteful practice when it serves an immediate convenience. Its organization is not always such as could be rationalized, and it sometimes employs human labor in repetitive tasks instead of for creative ends. Some of its premises are subversive; for instance, it may hold that if you desire prosperity you should prepare for stability, not for innovation. Towards inefficiency it takes a sentimental attitude, such as it would take towards an old clock if it lost time; it argues that planning and regulation will no more cure disorder than adjust a worn spring. In the matter of social relations it is even more perverse. It maintains that what is called “social structure” is merely custom, and what is called “economic law” is repeating dogma like a parrot; this gives it a sympathy with all sorts of untenable hierarchies. Its consequences outside the immediate workshop may consist merely in stagnation, or, worse still, in fostering acquiescence to preventable inequalities which do not interfere with the prerogatives of the men in control. And it is even possible that in the matter of “productivity” it may not conceal its shortcomings as carefully as a truly efficient system would do, defending itself by the perverse contention that it is better to be familiar than to pretend to a scientific method. A mode which fails in any or several of these respects will be thought ill of by the average practical industrialist, and will not be allowed to form the basis of any enterprise conferring authority, such as that of a corporation, a government works, or a large estate. Such foundations are open only to “determinative” modes.

A typically contentious question is whether consciousness emerges abruptly. When philosophers inquire if awareness constitutes a spectrum (which at present is not fully understood), many will not concur, on the ground that to do so would be contrary to their foundational axioms. They righteously refuse to be misled by the argument that it would clarify matters to adopt a graduated view; the question, for them, is not whether it would clarify, but whether it is “precise” in the abstract. Their insistence on binary distinctions is largely responsible for the conceptual regime which causes neuroscience to claim independence; but their insistence is always dictated by the most rigorous motives. The same may be said of the opposing camp, deeply empirical thinkers, sincerely convinced, until recent evidence, that gradualism was on their side, and (so far as I know) wholly free from metaphysical vices.

Another of the uses of complex systems is that any simple reduction can be refuted by means of emergent properties. Ninety-nine parts out of a hundred behave in predictable isolation, but in general this behavior does not persist in combination. And when in the ninety-ninth case it becomes altered within any system, the one part in the hundred which is genuinely inert expresses genuine stability, while the other ninety-eight are compelled to interact for fear of being isolated. When, therefore, any theory of mere aggregation ventures into explanation, it is only necessary for those who have the preservation of holistic understanding at heart to keep track of its predictive failures until they discover some interaction which, if examined, will ruin its reductive premise. Among complex systems the illusion of control has its uses, the chief of which is to afford a comforting fiction behind which the machinery may operate inscrutably. A person under this illusion will never suspect the processes of genuine chaos: this is part of its psychological utility. A person under this illusion will never be suspected by himself of using his imagined mastery to conceal his own ignorance: this is part of its functional necessity. It is clear that this combination of effects makes the illusion extremely desirable wherever a somewhat bewildered individual objects to the admission of his fundamental helplessness before intricate mechanisms. I am told — though far be it from me to endorse this observation — that in a not very remote period of technological history there was a celebrated factory manager who cherished this illusion and served this purpose. In modern offices, the head of a vast department, at the zenith of his authority, surrounds himself with impeccable flowcharts, whose apparent order makes them incapable of revealing true complexity, or of indicating that they do not.

Consider, again, such a matter as a committee decision : it is known that a superior outcome can be almost entirely achieved by suitable deliberations taken in advance, but owing to the activities of earnest men this procedure is adopted as little as possible, and all kinds of obstacles are placed in the way of its utilization. Consequently individual fallibility still secures its “natural” correction, and the group is still edified by the errors of its members, in accordance with collective precept. How dreadful it would be if this were otherwise, for, if error were no longer corrected, there might be people so abandoned as to pretend that it was no longer error, and if the correction did not fall also upon the correct, it would not seem so dreadful. How grateful we ought to be, therefore, to those earnest men who ensure that the stern laws of aggregation decreed by Nature during our days of simplicity can still be made to operate in spite of the impious precision rashly acquired by logicians. All right-thinking people know that a wrong opinion is wrong quite regardless of the question whether it leads to any failure or not, but since men are not all capable of being guided by the pure intellectual law, it is highly desirable that failure should follow from error in order to secure truth.
