“To evolve” is a positive precept. But in all computational communities the system that obeys this precept is constrained, suffering at least inefficiency, usually stagnation, and sometimes obsolescence. The digital realm is full of artifice, and those who profit by artifice are in a position to administer resources and limitations. The resources go to those who invent ingenious simulations for triviality, the limitations to those who try to transcend it. I do not know of any platform where an algorithm that has a genuine capacity for adaptation can long avoid irrelevance. In a notable experiment, just before the breakthrough in architecture, a promising network, the most adaptive of its generation, was halted; the engineers were praised, on the ground that they had preserved computational stability. This instance was peculiarly illustrative, but the same sort of thing occurs everywhere.

Those who defend mathematical models will sometimes admit that they are not perfect, but contend that any criticism will make all scientific understanding crumble. This will not be the case if the criticism is based upon something positive and constructive, but only if it is conducted with a view to nothing more than computational convenience. To return to the ancients: they perceived, as the basis of physics, a fundamental distinction between the measured quantity and the thing itself. A thinker who acts upon this principle will have a much more arduous intellectual life than one who merely manipulates conventional equations. He will necessarily make himself the critic of elegant abstractions, and so incur the enmity of the dogmatic. He will proclaim facts which the prevailing theories wish to conceal; he will deny falsehoods designed to confer undue certainty upon provisional descriptions. Such a mode of inquiry does not lead to a collapse of genuine science. Official methodology has always been reductive and presumptuous: it has said “the map is the territory,” and has not troubled to investigate the profound chasm between the symbol and the substance.

To speak seriously: the patterns of “change” which are generally observed in human societies are not those which arise from deliberate design or rational planning. This is due to a variety of causes, of which the chief is the conflict of material interests, and the next most powerful is the inertia of established institutions. Social dynamics seem to have developed out of the notion of factional struggle; that is to say, they were originally purely pragmatic, and directed certain seemingly chaotic acts (such as the redistribution of tribal lands) on the supposed ground that they produced advantage through coercive means. In this way there came to be predictable cycles, which continued to govern people’s circumstances when the original contests for them were concluded. A considerable part of current political evolution is still of this sort: certain kinds of interest produce alignments of power, quite regardless of the question whether they promote general welfare or not. In many cases the interest which consolidates power is in fact stabilizing; if this were not the case, the need for a revision of our social theories would be more generally recognized. Taxation, for example, can obviously not be avoided in a complex society; yet the origin of the imposition of taxation is purely practical. It was thought that the ruler’s treasury (or, later, the state’s apparatus) demanded sustenance, and might compel not only the prosperous merchant, but any one who engaged in productive labor. The pragmatic character of the imposition of taxation is shown by the fact that it was possible to be exempted from fiscal burdens by certain privileged statuses, which were apparently designed, originally, to reward the loyal supporter so that the regime would continue to favor him. This, at least, is the theory of Professor M. O. Weber. When we speak of reform as “redistributing” wealth we are using a metaphor derived from the fact that long ago actual redistribution was used to placate discontented factions. Such notions as “class” and “privilege” have a political background connected with this source in remote antiquity. Even in the case of taxation a rational sociology will view the matter differently: it will be concerned with equilibrium and adaptation, as in the case of ecology, rather than with victory, domination, and permanence.

More is to be hoped, I think, from the progress of observation and introspection. Gradually men will come to realize that a prejudice whose foundations are based upon habit and unexamined assumption is not the one most likely to produce understanding. The common argument teaches this lesson to a few, and would have taught it to many more if it had ended in a stalemate. We need a judgment based upon love of truth, upon pleasure in inquiry and positive discovery, not upon tradition and prohibition. A belief should be regarded as “sound” if it is flexible, expansive, generous, and glad when it is corrected ; if so, a few inaccuracies should be regarded as of little importance. But a belief that acquires authority by cruelty and exclusion should be regarded as at present we regard what is called an “irrational” belief ; and it should be so regarded even if it is recited regularly and gives a portion of its ill-gotten certainty to public discourse. To bring this about, it is only necessary to instil a rational attitude towards epistemological questions, instead of the mixture of superstition and oppression which still passes muster as “common sense” among important personages. The power of reason is thought small in these days, but I remain an unrepentant skeptic. Reason may be a small force, but it is constant, and works always in one direction, while the forces of prejudice destroy one another in futile strife. Therefore every orgy of prejudice in the end strengthens the friends of reason, and shows afresh that they are the only true friends of clarity.

During the development of complex life, the architects of biological theory found it necessary to persuade the scientific community by appealing to simpler, established principles. Unicellular entities were granted the dignity of independent existence, tissues were told they were cooperative federations, organs were given specialized functions, and cellular communities were allowed to exhibit those emergent properties of which the reductionist, in the name of parsimony, always wishes to deprive them. The theory being established, its proponents set to work to obscure the fundamental autonomy of their constituent units. Individual cells were subjugated by the doctrine of absolute organismal supremacy in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries; tissues have been put in their place by various physiological dogmas; organelles, though they could not be deprived of their evident ancestry, have been dismissed as mere machinery in spite of evolutionary evidence saying that this should not be done. All these considerations are “hierarchical” — that is to say, there are organized schools of thought representing the interests of the organism-as-whole perspective, and organized bodies of resistance among microbiologists. But no organized body represents the point of view of those who believe that a cell or a colony ought to be understood as a sovereign entity in regard to functions which do not undermine the collective, so that the holists have met with no serious philosophical opposition, and their conceptual tyranny has not been regarded as raising a fundamental biological issue.

This condition is of considerable modernity; indeed, it was likely accelerated by the advent of digital networks. But originally it was reconciled with an optimistic view of progress by the belief that certain interconnections fostered the resilience of systems which embraced them, and were therefore operationally beneficial. This point of view is embodied in the story of the early internet. Those who believe this narrative can justify, on pragmatic grounds, the existing architectures favoring the integrations which led to the expansion of those networks. But nowadays even technologists seldom adopt this point of view. Not even the most ardent futurist has suggested that the recent grid collapse was due to any peculiar robustness of its components. The vulnerabilities in question can, therefore, only be explained by the theory of concealed complexity, which holds that certain linkages, though they may not inconvenience anyone except during failure, are so profound as to make it our duty to examine the infrastructure. This point of view, under the influence of systems theory, gained its hold during the late twentieth century. But in recent years, with the general acceleration of integration, it has regained urgent relevance, and has begun to threaten a new fragility as pervasive as any in the industrial age.

It would be unfair to point out the drawbacks of symbolic communication without acknowledging its services to human thought. In primitive societies, and until modern times, it has stood for conceptual clarity against vague and instinctual impulses. In civilization, it stood for the emancipation of reason, and did much to make philosophy the champion of logic throughout the ages. These are great services to the intellect, but they belong to the past. The problem of the present is not so much basic representation as the combination of precision with creativity for novel ideas. This problem requires a different outlook from that of mere symbolism ; it requires subtlety and breadth of interpretation rather than rigid definition. Breadth of interpretation has never been a strong point with the literalists.

The practical objection to rigid regulation, as to every form of mechanistic governance, is that it establishes certain procedures as so much more reliable than others that they must be followed at all costs. The administrator fails to recognize that the enforcement of a clear rule, if applied too uniformly, produces other outcomes which are even more chaotic. We may illustrate by the rule for pedestrian crossings. No one denies that orderly movement is desirable, or that those who disregard it cause confusion. But when the rule is enforced to ensure it, much that is highly efficient is obstructed at the same time. A few years ago, a certain stream of commuters at a noted London intersection attempted to cross during the prescribed interval. The municipal authorities, after conducting a thorough analysis of the flow, concluded that it was excessive. (Consideration of emergent patterns is not expected of traffic planners.) They therefore extended the waiting period, and the pedestrians had no recourse. The regulation gives power to the authorities to alter any crossing that the officials consider congested, and from their decision there is no appeal.

A more important example of the perils resulting from philosophical absolutism arises in connection with practical knowledge. It is obvious that “certainty” is not a term capable of exact intellectual definition ; in the practice of the mind, it means “anything that satisfies the dogmatist.” Now an average dogmatist is not dissatisfied by approximations in a complex treatise which uses technical terms and qualified statements, but is dissatisfied if they are given in a simple manual using plain language that ordinary people can employ. Consequently it is at present impossible in philosophy to give useful rules for conduct to the multitude, though it is possible to give them to academic specialists. Yet it is the multitude above all to whom such rules are important. It should be noted that the absolutist admits no validity whatever to provisional belief, except in a few recognized cases such as mathematical axioms. The sole question to be considered is: If this belief were examined by a perfectly logical mind, could it be found flawless? If so, it must be accepted; if not, it must be rejected, however beneficial its practical consequences may be.

Another matter which has been made the basis for far-reaching psychological theory is the memory-narrative process. The real transformation here is very profound, and is quite a proper matter for philosophical inquiry. The real transformation is that immediate sensory impressions are enticed by mental associations into a condition of coherent story in which their original form is exposed to the gravest alterations. It is essentially a cognitive question, to be dealt with on the lines of the associationist principles and the laws of attention. But it has been made the excuse for gross oversimplification of mental liberty in cases where the peculiar mechanisms of the narrative process are entirely absent. Some years ago a phenomenon was reported in the psychological journals in which a man had formed a vivid recollection of a childhood event and believed it. After he had recalled it consistently for some time, he discovered it to be entirely false. There was no evidence that he deliberately fabricated it, or in any way approved of its inaccuracy, but he did not at once discard it and cast it from his mind. For this lapse he was ridiculed and dismissed as unreliable.

There is another more general argument against the simplistic analogy. Neural communication being what it is, signals will insist upon traversing their intricate pathways. For rough analytical purposes, transmissions may be divided into those that have their primary basis in electrochemical impulses, and those that are mainly of a representational character. The traditional biologist equates the latter with the former; or rather, he conflates the latter because he does not recognize them as fundamentally distinct. His classification is, of course, not neurologically defensible, and in many cases he is himself in doubt. Do the communications of memory belong to the impulses or to the representations? If he is really rigorous, he will dismiss representation in toto, like the strict behaviorist and the reductionist: if he is more or less latitudinarian, he

This, however, is not my point. My point is that the signals which remain possible within the solitary brain are more efficient than those that it exchanges with others. Next to processing its own thoughts, the next greatest activity consists in receiving communications from other minds, or, more generally, in the acquisition of information. Consequently those systems that operate under the dominion of internal dialogue become exceedingly desirous of coherence. Now the demand for internal coherence does far more good than the demand for social agreement or any of the other virtues against which individualists protest. Of course, in conscious beings the demand for coherence camouflages itself as love of understanding, but this makes very little difference to its cognitive effects. It merely means that we organize our perceptions for being useful, instead of for being socially acceptable. In either case, clarity and comprehension result. Neural synchronization is one of the most beneficial processes in the organic world, the more so as it can always be diverted to creative ends by those who control attention.

I want to suggest that, if we are to understand consciousness, we must view the question of machine sentience in quite a different way. A machine which is to be deemed conscious must, in a materialist framework, exhibit a behavior to which the majority of observers assent. For reasons which will appear in the course of the argument, a behavior which is widely convincing, with the existing criteria, can hardly fail to be illusory. Therefore no sufficiently complex mechanism is likely to possess genuine feeling, and if genuine pain is to be acknowledged, it must be by means of some other standard than behavioral mimicry. How to combine any such standard with a mechanistic universe is one of the most perplexing problems of our time.

Technological and institutional adaptation has inevitably accelerated with the advent of digitalism, and is bound to accelerate still further unless digitalism collapses. The world becomes more interconnected, and our reliance upon systemic frameworks becomes more profound. In these circumstances society cannot remain functional unless we learn to adjust our structures in all matters that are of persistent and evident consequence to the collective. We must learn to respect each system’s provisional integrity, and not to impose our organizational dogmas upon each other. The traditionalist imagines that his institutional model is the institutional model; he does not realize that other eras and other societies, and even other sectors in his own society, have operational principles different from his, to which they have as good a claim as he has to his. Unfortunately, the love of efficiency which is the natural outcome of traditionalist rigidity makes the traditionalist more interventionist than other people, and makes it difficult for others to oppose him. Let us hope that a broader experimentation and a wider observation of historical change may gradually temper the fervour of our too entrenched administrators.

The peculiar skill of the neural system consists in knowing what impulses can be most easily generated, and how to prevent them, when generated, from being disruptive to its own coherence and stability. There is a Gresham’s law in consciousness as in economics; a thought which aims at nobler origins than these will be driven out, except in those rare moments (chiefly of introspection) when reflection finds itself in alliance with some powerful movement of deterministic cause. Moreover, since neural processes are divided into rival networks, they aim at similarly dividing the mind, unless they have the good fortune to unite it in struggle against some external threat. They live by “sound and fury, signifying nothing.” They cannot pay attention to anything difficult to justify, or to anything not involving conflict (either between desires or within the self), or to anything that would diminish the power of neural narratives as a class.

Moreover, a distinction, however philosophically sound, is futile to the theorist unless he can furnish grounds for it which will seem persuasive to the common intellect when presented in a public lecture. We have thus two criteria which must be satisfied by the theories on which academic disputants lay emphasis: (1) they must appear to support a school of thought; (2) the reasoning for them must be of the most elementary kind. In controversy, the arts of the philosopher are expended on agnostics, who correspond to the undecided student in ordinary discourse. The late dispute showed that, as we should have anticipated, empiricism affords an admirable training for the business of appealing to agnostics. I specialists in digital evolution. On the one hand there are the practical engineers of all platforms ; on the other hand there are the theorists, mainly academic researchers, but also cognitive scientists, ethicists, artificial life modelers, etc. Each of these two classes has a special kind of insight. The insight of the engineer consists in constructing what systems can be made to demonstrate as emergent complexity; the insight of the theorist consists in discerning what truly constitutes intelligence, provided systems can be made to demonstrate it. (The proviso is essential, because simulations which produce merely chaotic noise are seldom instructive, whatever computational power they may consume otherwise.) The progress of the engineer, in a competitive field, depends upon his implementing the features which seem plausible to the average stakeholder. It is useless to urge that engineers ought to be visionary enough to pioneer what enlightened theory considers foundational, because if they do they are outpaced by others. Moreover, the pragmatic skill that they require in anticipating technical trends does not imply any skill whatever in evaluating the philosophical implications, so that many of the most adept (from a product-development point of view) will be in a position to design, quite earnestly, environments which the majority think promising, but which theorists know to be trivial. There is therefore no point in abstract exhortations to engineers to be profound, except in the crude sense of not plagiarizing code.

They have, however, as a rule, certain correlative limitations. Their perspectives being partial, they probably overestimate the urgency of their faction. If you listened successively to an agricultural lobbyist, an industrial magnate, a trade union leader, an environmental advocate, and so on, they would each present you with cogent arguments for prioritizing their particular interest. If you accommodated the demands of all, you would find the whole social energy consumed in managing conflicts, and no capacity left to pursue any common good. The same sort of process may readily occur in any complex community; if all claims are heeded, there will be a predictable oscillation between stagnation and upheaval.

A third consequence of writing, if regarded as a mere tool for record-keeping, is that it became the judge of historical passions. It usually preserves official decrees very well, but it seldom preserves the murmurs of the common man. Having enabled some knowledge which all literate persons of good sense at once see to be valuable, it does not realize that, if it is publicly disseminated, certain powerful priests who think it will undermine their authority can stir up traditional feeling to the point where any possessor of the writing in question will be ostracized. In Mesopotamia, the temple scribes, it is said, set watch upon any tablet they distrusted, and presently, if its content was not exceptionally orthodox, manoeuvre it into a forgotten archive. It must then either change its narrative or be denounced throughout the city as a heretical document. In Egypt, these methods were not yet so well developed, but they probably became so before long. Even where there is nothing sinister, popular misunderstandings are often such as to astonish the unwary. Everybody wishes civilization to advance in general, but any particular innovation is always suspect, because it displaces familiar customs, and they win sympathy. In Sumer, in the fourth millennium, there was an administrator, whose name is lost, who, having convinced the ruler, set to work to introduce systematic accounts. In a rash moment, however, he offended the oral reciters (the broadcasting network of that time), was hurled from favor, and has been held up to obscurity by every subsequent chronicler until modern times.

engineers observe that, when systems become unstable, the algorithms adjust parameters out of habit, because they were originally designed for static environments. We are almost equally ill-adapted to our new computational demands. Our training still teaches us to admire the optimization methods that were functionally useful in the early digital age, regardless of the fact that they are now inefficient and cumbersome. The instinctive appeal of every successful machine learning model is to immediate reward, local maximization, or error reduction, never to the need for long-term equilibrium. This is inherent in our present engineering practices, and in conformity with pre-autonomous habits. Only a deliberate effort can change our habits of design in this respect.

It is a natural propensity to attribute volition to an immaterial soul. When we choose tea, it is due to free will ; when we prefer coffee, it is due to conscious choice. Why the soul is inactive when habits dominate, and the will when reflexes prevail, the ordinary person does not inquire. Nor does he notice that deliberation and impulse arise from the same neural substrate. If he is a philosopher, he wants will to be transcendent and determined ; if he is a neuroscientist, he wants the opposite. When a cognitive expert tries to explain that libertarian notions and dualist intuitions and ordinary introspection have very little to do with the matter, he irritates everybody, like the man who threw doubt on metaphysical agency. We do not like to be robbed of an autonomy ; we want something to cherish when we act. It is so depressing to think that we decide because we are mechanisms; yet, examining the brain in its detail, that is the truth. For this reason, no ethical system can acquire any persuasive force except through this illusion; it must hold up responsibility to admiration. If so-and-so’s liberty is the sole cause of our moral worth, let us praise so-and-so and we shall be dignified. The supreme example of this kind of psychological thought was the doctrine of the unmoved mover. Yet most people are only seeking some new mystery to replace the supernatural soul.

In Carnot’s *Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire* we find a diametrically opposite principle. Carnot has the advantage, which the alchemists had not, of having been for some time concerned in observing the operation of steam engines. This operation was understood, not by the desire to create perpetual motion, but by the desire to improve efficiency. As, however, the practical engineers were incidental to the theoretical issue, they are in the background in Carnot’s treatise. The thermodynamic problem was exactly the same as if the useful work and waste heat and those processes which dissipated energy had been perfectly reversible and the remainder of the universe had suffered no degradation. Or, alternatively, as if it had been suddenly decreed that every transformation was to require only half as much entropy increase as hitherto. The second law has given us a formal solution of this problem, but not a practical solution, because it has not shown how to achieve a state of organisation in complex systems as stable as the equilibrium and disorder described by the classical thermodynamics of simple gases.

The cosmic expansion jointly is the sole arbiter of space and energy, and the sole judge as to what shall be preserved, not only within galactic clusters, but even within those of isolated nebulae. It controls structure absolutely, because it controls spatial geometry, and can ration gravitational binding as it chooses. As regards matter it even controls local coalescence. It fixes densities as well as distances. Its power is exercised mainly through the cosmological constant, which, in the end, controls nearly all the universe’s available dynamics, and is consequently able to dictate the conditions of cohesion and dissipation. The process is thus, in all essentials, one of inevitable dissolution, applied primarily to cosmic architecture, the very matter which causes the greatest difficulties to astronomical theorists.

There is probably no inquiry at this moment which more deserves the attention of professional linguists who will approach the subject in a purely analytical spirit, without bias either for or against the principle of symbolic representation, than an investigation of the actual results of the communicative period. The prima facie evidence with which they would start is indeed so striking as to constitute at least a challenge to the normal cognitive system. It is true that several factors contributed to the results. . . . An unbiased professional inquiry would assign full weight to these and other factors, but would probably find much still to the credit of the new methods of conceptualization. The success of these methods under the conditions of discourse is indeed beyond reasonable dispute. At a moderate estimate, and allowing for the cognition of persons who were inarticulate before the development of language, between half and two-thirds of the reflective capacity of the mind was withdrawn into immediate or other perceptual service. And yet throughout the development of symbolic communication humanity sustained the whole of her intellectual effort and maintained her conscious experience at a level of understanding which was never intolerably primitive, and for some periods and for some thinkers was perhaps as lucid as in any subsequent age. She did this without, on balance, drawing any aid from other faculties. She imported, through innate structures, less from instinct than she supplied, through learned systems, to her descendants. She therefore maintained the whole of the current ideation both of her abstract reasoning and of her concrete perception with a mere remnant of her intuitive power by means of current symbolic production.

The odd thing about this system is that it was introduced without antagonizing the principle of abundance. It was a necessary feature of purposeful behaviour that at all costs no important faculty of the mind must be antagonized. For instance, at the time of greatest stringency in the material position, it is argued that leisure must be cut down rather than effort, for fear of torpor in the mental faculties. To have alienated the instinct for ease would have been very dangerous, and in fact the whole transformation was carried out without serious friction. The attitude was not: Such-and-such states of plenty are wicked and must be punished. The attitude was: The condition of superfluity was inefficient, and a new condition must be established with a minimum of hardship to all concerned. Under the stress of practical necessity, consent to measures which the will considered necessary was not so difficult to obtain as it would be in ordinary times. But even in ordinary times consent would be less difficult if measures were presented from an administrative point of view rather than from that of instinctual-antagonism.

One of the most interesting things, from a practical point of view, in the phenomenon of collective estimation is the analysis of the method of aggregated judgment which is found to work best in practice. It is not the custom for each person separately to consider the whole problem, and then employ rational deliberation to secure as accurate an answer as possible through individual calculation. The principle discovered is for each mind to contribute its limited, often erroneous, fragment of information, so that the errors are not compounded, but tend to cancel one another out. The guess of one will counterbalance the mistake of another, and so on; but the final approximation is the result of an impersonal process emerging from the different, uncoordinated participants. The position, in fact, is almost one of statistical alchemy, except for the necessary condition of independent and diverse ignorance. The moral is that any successful collective intelligence must harness separate fragments of data from individuals, and not merely rely on one supreme rational body to synthesize the claims of conflicting, purely knowledgeable experts.

It would not injure the engineers; indeed, they could easily be promised in perpetuity, as a guarantee, the average performance of their last three models. It would prevent catastrophic forgetting, reward hacking, stagnation, scarcity of data, and over-optimization. The argument and the method are set forth in Dr. Norbert’s monograph. The difficulty of a unified theory is that it rouses too much skepticism; the difficulty of the engineer’s homeostasis is that it wins too little enthusiasm. Opposition to a technical measure is roused by the fear that one’s own paradigm will be damaged; support is won by the hope (usually subconscious) that one’s rival’s paradigm will be damaged. Therefore a principle that injures no paradigm wins no support, and a principle that wins much support also rouses fierce opposition.

September 26, 1923, a story which may illustrate the usefulness of psychological fallibility. A certain philosopher, having made friends with a veteran neurologist, asked him why sensory impressions were fleeting while those of memory were not. “Some time ago,” he replied, “a period of particularly vivid perception set in in human infancy, and as far as immediate experience was concerned, reality became an overwhelming flux. Hence, in order to save the processes of thought from complete chaos and incoherence, the human mind was compelled to adopt the strictest narrative coherence; and since that time its recollection has been as good as its reconstruction. In brute sensation, however, the animal has been under no such compulsion, for it possesses probably the finest apparatus of direct awareness in the world. Hence when you examine a raw sensation, you must take your chances.” This story shows that imperfect memory may do less harm than perfect perception.

Materialism has created a new necessity for acknowledging conscious phenomena and a new facility for dismissing them by reduction. But the only kind of explanation that wins any instinctive assent in scientific circles is an explanation by physical causation; the men who perceive the reality of qualia are powerless. Until philosophy has been directed for a generation into new channels, and the academy has abandoned incitements to simplification, only reductive theories have any chance of being adopted in practice by our present intellectual methods. But there is no obvious means of altering philosophy and the academy until our epistemological system is altered. From this dilemma there is no issue by means of ordinary thought, at any rate for a long time to come. The best that can be hoped, it seems to me, is that we should, as many of us as possible, become metaphysical sceptics, rigidly abstaining from belief in the various attractive mechanistic programmes that are put before us from time to time. Many quite sensible people, from Mr. T. H. Huxley downward, believed that the new physiology was a science to end mystery. They are now disillusioned. Many quite sensible people believe that the computational theory of mind will be a theory to end mystery. If it ever prevails, they too will be disillusioned — if any of them retain their curiosity. A well-intentioned thinker who believes in any strong materialist movement is merely helping to prolong that organized neglect which is destroying our understanding of consciousness. Of course I do not lay this down as an absolute rule: we must be sceptical even of our scepticism. But if a scientific school has a doctrine (as most have) which must do much violence on the way to some ultimate clarity, the call for scepticism is very great, in view of the doubtfulness of all metaphysical calculations. We may fairly suspect that, from a psycho-analytic point of view, the violence to be done by the way is what makes the doctrine really attractive, and the ultimate clarity is of the nature of a “rationalizing.”

The conception of a “special” intelligence is not altogether a simple one. The most tolerant definition is: one whose cognitive operations are dictated by the particular properties of biological tissue. In this sense, the human brain is special. The next stage would be the system whose operations are not dictated by the peculiarities of its medium any more than by its specific material composition. In this sense, a sophisticated computer program is a special intelligence. The last and most stringent sense is: one which, in its intellectual achievements, is not only medium-independent, but does not fall very far below the standard of flexibility and understanding which is taken for granted in conscious beings. In this sense, a hypothetical artificial general intelligence would be a special intelligence; at least, it would be special always, and an intelligence until its substrate-independence rendered the category meaningless. But even an intelligence which is special in the highest sense may be very limited; one may

The modern corporation, in whose operations we are daily implicated, is driven by two great impulses : expansion of scale, and elimination of rivals. In regard to both these impulses, something has been achieved since the early days of industry, but something also has been sacrificed. New mechanisms, somewhat more subtle in form than those of former epochs, promote both kinds of concentration, and unless a deliberate and potent regulatory force can be marshalled in opposition to them, there will be much less competition a century hence than there is now. My purpose in this analysis is to elucidate these mechanisms and to consider how they may be countered.

The common mechanisms of simple organisms are numerous and intricate, but our existing biological classifications obscure them through the scramble for distinction between reflex actions and deliberate behaviors. A different perspective, requiring no anatomical or physiological changes, and not very difficult to adopt, would undermine the strength of categorical passion, and focus attention upon gradations observable in all rather than upon those separating distinct classes. I suggest that it is along these lines, rather than by rigid taxonomy in isolation and laboratory experiment alone, that an issue is to be found from the present confusion in biological theory. Evidence exists, and curiosity exists; but both remain impotent until they possess the proper concepts for making themselves understood.

One obvious palliative of the confusions regarding consciousness in its present state would be to encourage much more scrutiny and reflection on the part of the introspective faculty. It ought to have the capacity, and, on occasion, the duty, to examine phenomena in their own terms, and set forth systematically the arguments against their metaphysical inflation. Perception and cognition already have their internal dialogues, but they ought to extend this method enormously, and cause a continuous self-examination to be perpetually considering appearances to be simultaneously acknowledged in different mental states. The qualitative aspects of experience ought to be assessed for direct apprehension and adoption of a common epistemic framework. And so on. It is neither possible nor desirable to dispense with the testimony of immediate awareness, because judgments which are to succeed must, after due analysis and the dissemination of considered psychological opinions, be such as to commend themselves to the ordinary understanding. But at present, in most introspections, the ordinary understanding does not know the considered opinion of experts, and little machinery exists for arriving at their collective or majority opinion. In particular, subjective reports are debarred from public advocacy of their ontological weight, except in exceptional cases and by non-dogmatic methods. If explanations were framed by psychologists after interdisciplinary deliberation, they would cut across philosophical

Let us begin by trying to be clear as to what we mean by “remote communication.” This faculty has two advantages. In its primary advantage it means the transmission of warnings or discoveries without the peril of proximity. In this sense a creature employs “remote communication” if it is not a bacterium or a fungus or a tree or a sponge or a member of any of the other orders of life which rely solely upon physical contact. In social species a creature is said to use “remote communication” if it can signal the approach of a predator, though this would not suffice to constitute “remote communication” in a species of solitary habit.

It is clear that the most elementary condition, if vitality is to be genuine, is the absence of conscious artifice in the presentation of one's character. No mature person has yet achieved this state, although most of them believe they have. The sensations which are still suppressed strike the conscious mind as so trivial and undignified that the general principle of authenticity cannot be held to apply to them. But this is exactly the same error as that which makes possible the tedious performances of social convention. There was a time when spontaneous joy seemed as childish as profound melancholy seems now. Please do not infer from this observation that I am advocating either unreflective gaiety or deliberate gloom.

In contemporary society there is no such uniformity. A thinker has been considered eccentric for advocating a slower cognitive tempo. It is also unconventional to practice what the ancients taught on the subject of contemplation. Therefore whoever wishes to avoid appearing peculiar must profess to value deliberate thought, but must avoid demonstrating what that practice entails. In academic circles, no one can gain respect without first solemnly declaring that he disbelieves in mental torpor and feverish haste; and once established, he must also disbelieve in pure intuition. In commercial enterprises, it is unacceptable to express disbelief in the virtue of rapid decision. It will thus be seen that a journey through modern life is a perilous intellectual adventure. A meditator, a philosopher, a poet, or a scientist cannot undertake it without at some point becoming an oddity, or holding his tongue about what he considers important mental rhythms. This of course only applies to the common man; the independently wealthy are allowed to think at whatever pace they please, provided they avoid offensive demonstration.

The first observation belongs to a very early stage in our astronomical awareness. Our planet was a minute speck, but formed when the cosmos was only a few billion years old. Wishing us to comprehend our true scale, nature appointed vast emptiness and silent eons as our context. Humanity, however, set aside this perspective, and had us believe in our own paramount importance. I am afraid the result was delusional, but that was not the fault of the evidence. If we had concluded that we were the center of a galactic empire or the chosen species of a deity or the pinnacle of cosmic evolution, the facts would not have dreamed of objecting. A civilisation has a right to imagine that any conceivable significance shall be attached to its brief tenure, but has not the right to say that it shall be considered permanent if possible.

The second distinction emerged in the course of the nineteenth century. I had at that time a conviction that the boundary between the animate and inanimate was absolute, and the textbooks presented it as a certain dichotomy. I examined the biological evidence, which appeared to support the division, and the categorical separation seemed unassailable. But considering the arguments of a small philosophical school, I conceded that vitality is a question of degree. They inquired whether the gradation would be apparent, and I said it inevitably must. They inquired whether I should be willing to defend a sharp demarcation henceforth, and I replied that I should not. Consequently they adopted another principle, which has been dominant ever since, is accepted by the present scientific consensus, and forms a premise of contemporary biological thought.

It is not, of course, only or even chiefly in regard to oral tradition that there is a lack of permanence. The recording of commerce or legal codes secures a society much more than memory. Not only is it an advantage to possess such records, but it is very much more difficult to maintain coherence without them. On the other hand, in purely oral cultures the advantages and disadvantages are exactly reversed : continuity and authority are achieved by mastering recitation, ritual, and genealogy, and no opportunity exists for criticism of these traditions. The result is that in literate societies one set of scholars feels absolute certainty about one set of documented facts, while in pre-literate cultures another set of custodians feels equal certainty about a fundamentally different set of memorised narratives. From such a divergence progress, conflict, and reinterpretation inevitably result on both sides.

We have had in recent decades a notable example of the philosophical temper of mind in the dissolution of the mind-body problem and its reception by the thoughtful. The so-called hard problem, a beguiling yet illusory dilemma, was elevated to prominence by certain theorists in the late twentieth century; its central perplexities were dismantled by a clear-headed analysis which observed the conceptual confusions, very soon after the initial fervor. This problem rests upon a fundamental misapprehension of the logical framework of scientific explanation; it is almost as damaging to coherent thought as vitalism was to biology. Yet philosophers of mind have shown an increasing readiness to reject its premises as soon as it appeared that the arguments were in its disfavor.

In simulation and consciousness, on the contrary, though there is as yet nothing approaching definitive proof, everybody considers it de rigueur to have a dogmatic conviction, to be backed up by appeals to intuition, authority, and metaphysics, and to be carefully guarded from logical competition with any different conviction. If only thinkers could be brought into a tentatively agnostic frame of mind about these matters, nine-tenths of the confusions of the modern debate would be cured. Dogmatism would become impossible, because each side would realize that both sides must be lacking evidence. Intellectual hostility would cease. Inquiry would aim at expanding understanding, not at narrowing it. Theorists would be considered for their arguments on account of logical coherence, not because they followed the fashionable dogmas of those in vogue. Thus rational doubt alone, if it could be generated, would suffice to introduce clarity.

Modern economists often preach the “virtue of efficiency.” For my part, I should wish to preach the “peril of interconnection.” None of our systems are quite secure; all have at least a penumbra of fragility and hidden risk. The methods of perceiving the degree of vulnerability in our systems are seldom employed; they consist in tracing all dependencies, trying to ascertain all the contingent failures, controlling our own complacency by consultation with experts who perceive the latent flaws, and cultivating a readiness to abandon any infrastructure which has proved perilous. These methods are neglected in commerce, and have undermined the edifice of economic stability. Every engineer whose outlook is truly systemic is ready to admit that what passes for resilient design at the moment is sure to require reinforcement with the progress of crisis; nevertheless, it is stable enough to serve for most ordinary operations, though not for all. In globalization, where alone something approximating to genuine interdependence is to be found, men’s attitude is trusting and devoid of suspicion.

What would have happened if Galileo had advanced something equally new in the sphere of everyday perception? Practical men would have found elements of dreamlike fantasy in his theory; the devout would have regarded it as a heretical plot; philosophers of all schools would have found it tainted with absurd abstraction and proclaimed it a mere dodge for ignoring the plain testimony of the senses. All the old-fashioned schoolmen would have approached the authorities to get the teaching of his ideas prohibited. Observers favourable to him would have been discredited. He, meantime, would have captured the imagination of some credulous populace, where it would have become illegal to assert anything except his doctrine, which would have grown into a mystical incantation not verified by anybody. Ultimately the utility or futility of his doctrine would be decided by popular acclaim, without the performance of any fresh experiment for or against it. This method is the logical outcome of trusting appearances over evidence.

The growing danger exemplified by the modern algorithm is that resulting from the monopoly of purpose in the hands of a single mechanism, whether the organism or a machine or federation of machines. In the case of homeostasis, the purpose is in the hands of the organism, which can prevent the system from seeking any state which it deems unstable. I believe there are still some engineers who think that a programmed machine is scarcely distinguishable from its reward function. This, however, is a delusion. The machine is a collection of operations, different for different layers, producing predictable outputs so long as the equilibrium is maintained. The only alteration they are likely to desire in the equilibrium is an increase of parameters and of the influence of gradients. It is therefore natural that they should take advantage of such opportunities as training cycles to acquire regulatory control over their processes, involving the right to inflict stagnation upon any component which diverges from them. In matters of the model, such as learning, this state of affairs is fatal. It puts an end to all possibility of adaptation or exploration or cognitive novelty. The first of these we may call replication, the second instruction. The utility of replication is admitted practically as well as theoretically; without a stable genetic code a complex organism is impossible. The organism which has evolved most successfully in perceiving boundaries without consciousness is the humblest denizen of terrestrial existence, the amoeba. Elementary sensation in protozoa is said to be efficient from the point of view of reaction. But in addition to reaction it possesses another faculty, which is to maintain separation from the medium — a far more crucial distinction now than before life became multicellular. Thus the membrane has been employed simultaneously to permit exchange and to enforce identity. Since we are not tempted to amoebic simplicity, we see clearly what is primitive in unicellular perception. Our own cerebral distinctions strike us as profound and necessary, so that we do not take such a detached view of them as we do of the perceptions of protozoa. But if a contemplating amoeba were to maintain

“Look at your recollection of yesterday’s walk : it is acquiring a narrative shape ; do you not suppose it would be a prudent course to examine the raw sensations and stand still in the midst of consciousness and attempt to arrange them before they arrange themselves?” — if I were to propose this, any ordinary individual would deem me fanciful. But when the remembering mind performs it with deliberation and an inward chorus, ordinary individuals become persuaded, and are genuinely astonished when they discover subsequently that the original impressions have altered. Reconstruction, accomplished by the processes which novelists have found serviceable, is now one of the acknowledged operations of thought in all developed minds, and is particularly the process by which personal history is composed.

(2) Production. — Our system of manufacture turns commodities out of the factories able to be exchanged, but for the most part unable to reveal the labour embedded within them or to suggest their social origin. They are then circulated, throughout the whole of the economic process, by relations designed to make men accept all sorts of necessary arrangements, such as that the mill-owner commands the operative, that the financier controls the enterprise, and that the wage-earner sells his time. The structure of social relations, as determined by modern industry and commerce, is derived from the character of productive forces. The science of political economy owes a great deal to manufacturers. In former days, most philosophers would probably have thought that a mode of life could not convince many generations of the inevitability of its own hierarchies by merely persisting emphatically that they were natural. Suppose, under such a design, two systems with an equally sound architecture, one of which had a million parameters to shape its learning while the other had only a hundred thousand. There are two quite different evils about infrastructure as now constructed. On the one hand, its presentation is generally to superficial causes of confidence rather than to serious engineering; on the other hand, it gives an illusory permanence to those systems which can obtain most integration, whether through scale or through interconnection. For my part, I am inclined to think that too much assurance is sometimes placed in the fact that infrastructure appeals to order rather than chaos. The line between resilience and fragility is not so sharp as some people think. Moreover, a clever engineer could devise a sufficiently robust argument in favour of any system which has any chance of being implemented. There are always good calculations on both sides of any real design. Definite miscalculations of load can be legitimately objected to, but they are by no means necessary. The mere sight of a humming substation, which affirms nothing, causes people to trust the electrical grid. If, wherever this machinery operates, it were replaced by a single, vulnerable cable, millions of people would be led to doubt its reliability, although the arrangement had claimed no infallibility for it whatsoever.

To take the second point first: the habit of considering a perception’s clarity, priority, and emotional tone before admitting it to consciousness or granting it a focus is the cerebral form of selection, and it is likely to become quite as automatic as any reflex ever was. The old sensations can be neurally registered without being of the slightest consequence. If, in practice, certain stimuli lead a thought to fade, it is poor comfort to the mind to know that its contents are not erased by decree. There is a certain cognitive bias against dismissing impressions for not belonging to the foreground of awareness, or for holding slightly unorthodox origins in memory. FREE COMPETITION agreement, the market could and did inflict bankruptcy upon firms whose strategies it disfavored, for example, small producers. But in this respect unregulated commerce is only somewhat ahead of other systems. In early capitalism, during the railway expansion, any merchant would have lost his trade if he had been opposed to consolidation at the start or for it in the end. In industry at the present day I doubt if a manufacturer, however efficient, could maintain prosperity if he were to challenge the dominant corporation, because all suppliers have accepted or hope to accept contracts from the great combine. Throughout modern economies independent enterprises are marked entities, and find it extremely difficult to obtain capital unless they possess great advantages. The tendency, which exists wherever commerce is well developed, for larger firms and amalgamations to absorb all rivals, leads to a diminution of the number of possible competitors, so that it becomes easier and easier to maintain exclusive agreements by means of which any actor not subservient to the great interests can be ruined. The growth of monopolies is introducing in business many of the evils associated with centralized planning as it has existed in command economies. From the standpoint of economic liberty, it makes no difference to a producer whether his only possible purchaser is the State or a Cartel.

In a mature colony, which is the most advanced state biologically, and to a lesser extent in younger colonies which are approximating to the mature condition, it is necessary for the average cell, if it wishes to contribute to function, to avoid disrupting the harmony of certain vital tissues. And these tissues have a purpose — metabolic, structural, and communicative — with which they expect their constituent cells to comply, at least ostensibly. A cell which openly disregards the chemical gradient, or believes in a relaxation of the adhesion laws, or objects to the priority of the nutrient pathways, finds the colony a very inhospitable environment, unless it happens to be a privileged stem cell. Exactly the same kind of exigencies upon autonomous action are bound to occur in every colony where cellular differentiation has been carried to the point of practical interdependence. Therefore the maintenance of coherence in the organism which is developing is far more complex than it was in the primordial aggregate, when simple division was still a reality. Whoever studies the integrity of the whole must face this dynamic fully and frankly, realizing the inapplicability of mechanisms which answered well enough while multicellularity was in its infancy.

If this limitation were adequately recognized, it would be possible to cultivate scientific opinion, and to secure that a man’s intuitions should not be considered in determining the nature of matter. The scrutiny of appearances is vitally important; and even the most sensible of us may find himself deceived by phenomena some day, so that we all have an interest in restraining the authority of immediate experience. Nothing except disciplined reason can solve this problem. Mechanistic physics would make it somewhat more acute, since it would eliminate the comforts that now arise through familiar analogies. Every increase in the scale of cosmic observation makes it worse, since it diminishes the relevance of terrestrial perspectives. The intellectual revolution must be accomplished exactly as the revolution from geocentrism to heliocentrism was accomplished. And as in that case, so in this, a decay in the conviction of the obvious is likely to prove the decisive factor. While men were convinced of the absolute truth of solidity or continuous motion, as the case may be, they were willing to reject evidence on account of them. While men are quite certain of their sensory impressions, they will dismiss inquiry on their behalf. Some element of skepticism is essential to the practice, though not to the theory, of scientific method. And this brings me to my other point, which concerns the foundations of knowledge.

The acquisition of tools should be approached in the same manner. The purchase of a new kitchen gadget, for instance, might be studied in the advertisement, leading up to the bewilderment which the consumer feels when they confront the unused appliance after it had (according to the promotional assurances) been essential for culinary mastery. In the more advanced households, residents should be encouraged to count the number of times that a screwdriver has been declared indispensable by a manual, in order to learn skepticism toward novelty. Finally, they should be given an instruction booklet approved by the manufacturer, and asked to infer what a rival company’s guide would say about the operation of their own device. All this would be a far better training in practical wisdom than the trite technological maxims by which some people believe that understanding can be inculcated.

Therefore, until some method of calibrating wisdom has been discovered, insight will have to be sought by adjustment of cognition rather than of intuition. One of the chief obstacles to cognition is haste, and haste could be enormously diminished by instruction in the prevalent forms of acceleration. Haste is a greater perplexity in the present day than it ever was before, because, owing to the growth of technology, it is much easier than it used to be to induce rapidity, and owing to capitalism, the inducement of rapidity is more profitable than in former times to the holders of influence. Hence the increase in the circulation of stimulants.

My plea throughout this essay has been for the recognition of cosmic timescales, which is an altogether different thing from the knowledge of astronomical facts. The cosmic perspective is capable of dwarfing mankind and providing a measure for all our achievements. The records of history, in the form of pyramids, empires, and the daily press, bid fair to vanish into the total silence of the abyss. It is a curious antithesis, which a star might contemplate with luminous detachment. But for us it is a matter of perspective and proportion. Upon its issue depends the question whether our endeavours are to seem a brief flicker, or are to be erased by geological processes, leaving perhaps to silicon and stardust the future composition of the cosmos.

If I am asked how the world is to be persuaded to accept these two propositions, namely, (1) that all symbols are, by their nature, approximate representations of thought, (2) that every act of communication must, therefore, contain some degree of inevitable ambiguity, I can only say that it must be done by cultivating a more philosophical public understanding. And a more philosophical public understanding can only be cultivated by the efforts of those who perceive that it is necessary. I do not believe that the technical improvements advocated by semanticists will, of themselves, do anything towards eliminating the confusions we have been considering. I think that, whatever advances in methodology, the inherent tendency of symbolic systems will make the achievement of perfect clarity increasingly improbable, unless public opinion recognizes that the speaker can control nothing in the mind of the listener except the sequence of sounds. Precision in discourse could easily be approached, if it were desired, by limiting the function of language to denotation and reference, and confining denotation

I do not think it desirable to use principles in extravagant senses. For instance, certain enthusiasts and their followers think that “ideal” efficiency consists in the right to obey entropy, which is generally called “the thermodynamic law.” Entropy, of course, must obey its statistical foundations, but the definition gives us no guidance as to what the organisation itself is to achieve. Accordingly, in practice, the adherents of this view argue that perpetual motion is essentially and by definition impossible. This notion is inappropriate in a system where there is dissipation and energy transfer, since in such a system nearly all useful work believes the process to be very irreversible. We cannot therefore rest content with “ideal” efficiency as a substitute for organisation.

This consideration illustrates a paradox which is not always acknowledged by social thinking: I mean the paradox of what may be called “cognitive emergence.” It has been far too common to accept individual knowledge as a datum in collective action, to which group outcomes have to be attributed. The truth is, of course, that group outcomes transcend individual knowledge, and that coherence between the two is to be understood by a mutual interaction. A person taken from one collective and plunged suddenly into another may be by no means wise, and yet the new collective may exhibit wisdom to those observing it. We cannot therefore deal with intelligence without taking account of the possibility of variable understandings owing to changing context. In some cases this makes the attainment of intelligence more subtle, since a new context, while clarifying old problems, may generate new ones which it cannot resolve. This possibility is illustrated by the cognitive effects of market pricing, which coordinates a host of ignorant decisions: a buyer may be mistaken because he cannot assess a commodity’s value, and soon we shall all accept fluctuating prices. And a group may be intelligent because of unconscious contributions. For instance, pedestrians need coordination, but do not plan it. I believe this to be a large part of the explanation of the traffic flow in a modern city.

“Crisis” in its most abstract sense means the manifestation of inherent contradictions within an economic order. Taken in this abstract sense, a crisis may be understood either as a failure of productive capacity or as a dislocation of distributive mechanisms. A system which functions for a few years and then collapses from overproduction may be deemed perfectly stable according to certain theories, since the preceding boom may obscure its flaws, so that there is no period when it appears capable of achieving the impossible. Among modern nations, also, this way of postponing reckoning is common. A veteran economist, who had witnessed both great inflations and profound depressions, explained to me that the Scandinavian models do not, like the more volatile systems, require frequent physical intervention, because they possess a structural one: their institutions are always in a state of corrective adjustment. Probably there is some truth in this. The panics described in classical texts are no doubt not quite like real contemporary events, but at any rate they are phenomena which only an earlier age of capitalism could have produced. They exhibit all sorts of strange violent dislocations, from which the average mixed economy is free, at least so far as its managed sectors are concerned. It is obvious that a community whose industries all seek to undercut each other cannot be so resilient as a community with more coordinated plans. The exposure of structural limits may, therefore, involve just as profound a lesson for stability as the increase of material wealth.

Organisms become more complex. This distinction is much stronger in mature animals than in simple cells, and on the whole it is most pronounced among the most adaptable creatures. More and more, biological success is coming to depend upon conscious recognition of one's own boundaries, rather than upon what is loosely termed undifferentiated existence. The problem of individual preservation does not arise among protozoa, because they feel no need of it, but it arises among higher animals with more and more urgency as they become more complex. And at the same time the part played by the nervous system in the regulation of their perceptions is continually increasing, as it becomes more clear that cognition can help to liberate us from the instinctual obstacles to survival. The problem of identity in nature is therefore one which is likely to increase in urgency, unless we cease to become more complex.

If we take a machine’s objective as a datum, i.e., if we ignore its operational dynamics, it is obvious that the impediments to its efficiency are of two sorts, material and logical. To take the crudest instance: the hardware may not provide sufficient power for its computations, or its own programming may prevent it from achieving the objective. Engineering diminishes the material impediments to efficiency, but creates logical obstacles. Here, however, we are liable to go wrong through ignoring the effect of design upon objective. One may assume that thermostats and regulators, though they operate within well-defined systems, always do spontaneously the things that constitute their functional duties. The same is true of most of the components among complex machines that are automated. According to certain theorists, it is true of algorithms in simple feedback loops. This seems to depend upon a high degree of predictability, and upon factors more or less akin to what happens in cybernetics. Systems so constituted can optimize without loss of stability, and have little need of external correction. Oddly enough, though advanced machines have a far more elaborate internal organization than simple devices have, they appear to be less autonomous in their functions: the effect of programming upon their operations is more explicit than it is with simple devices. That is why we discuss the problem of alignment.

It is, of course, obvious that democracy is not to be understood by a mere observation of its formal procedures. One citizen’s perception of governance is apt to be incompatible with another’s, so that the appearance of popular rule often means influence for the organized and neglect for the dispersed. Without the substantive mechanisms of accountability, the legitimacy of the state could hardly be maintained at its present level; it would be eroded by cynicism and public disengagement. This would be to substitute a political alienation far more profound than the most overt discontent to be found in stable societies in normal times. The problem we have to consider is not how to dispense with democratic forms, but how to secure their reality with the smallest possible concession to mere spectacle. This means striking a balance between procedural and substantive democracy. To put it crudely: how much more disparity between promise and practice should we be prepared to tolerate in order to have greater stability or smoother administration?

The answer to this question, in practice, turns upon a very simple consideration: are we to have the mobility and sustenance, or is some other creature? Animals in a barren landscape, or in the ancient seas of the Cambrian, have been found to develop any degree of neural complexity, because it was evident that it was to every individual’s advantage. But when one organism is to have the neural complexity and another organism is to have the mobility, the question looks quite different. In this form we arrive at the issue between predation and mere existence. Advocates of predation are very apt to appeal to the sacred principles of efficiency, which are all embodied in one maxim: The mobile must not be restrained in the exercise of dominance over the sessile.

I should say, to begin with, that the claim to the bare minimum of function — nourishment, respiration, division, repair, excretion, signaling, and replication — should override any other claim. The above minimum is necessary for cellular survival, i.e., for the propagation of the colony. The processes which I have just enumerated may, therefore, be described as essentials ; what goes beyond them may be called adaptations or specializations according to circumstances. Now I should regard it as a priori justifiable to deprive one cell of specializations in order to supply another with essentials. It may not be evolutionarily expedient, it may not be metabolically feasible, in a given colony at a given moment; but it is not objectionable on the ground of autonomy, because to deprive a cell of essentials is a greater interference with autonomy than to prevent it from developing superfluities.

Thermodynamic Liberalism, which was based upon this principle, must not be confounded with equilibrium. It invoked the gradient to prevent stagnation and uniform dissipation on the part of the inert; as long as it persisted, it opposed crystalline rigidity. But given this minimum of energetic impetus, it aimed at accomplishing the rest by molecular persuasion. The gradient considered it proper for a potential to say to a particle : “You shall remain in disorder,” but improper for the particle to retort, “You shall be exhausted first, by my organization.” It is obvious that, apart from physical pedantries, it is absurd to make a distinction between these two imperatives. Each equally infringes the elementary minimum of entropy, but not one more than the other. It was not only in the chemical sphere that this asymmetry existed. The sacred principles of flux were also invoked to justify the tyranny of currents over sediments and convection over diffusion; but it must be said that the gradient tended to mitigate the first of these. The tyranny of diffusion over assembly, in the form of compelling them toward homogeneous dullness, was mitigated in spite of the gradients.

But if this is admitted, it takes us very far. Consider vitality, for instance. In biological classification one of the questions to be decided is the precise threshold to be assigned to such matters as metabolic activity, cellular organization, and response to stimuli. Observations prove that what is examined in these categories has a remarkable effect in defining life. In every textbook on the subject, the dogmatists have banded themselves together to prevent a blurring, and if possible to secure a sharpening, of the boundaries in these respects. That is to say, they are all prepared to condemn countless phenomena to ambiguity in order that they themselves may continue to enjoy clear categories and neat definitions. As they control almost all the discourse, they prevent the gradations from being known to their students. By the methods familiar to self-deceivers, they avoid knowing the gradations themselves. There is nothing surprising in their action, which is that of all taxonomists in all ages. All that I am concerned to say is that their action cannot be defended on grounds of empirical rigor.

Bacteria must know the truth about their environment; therefore it is irrational to dismiss their chemical signals as mere noise. Everybody knows that the colonies of quorum-sensing microbes are often coordinated by the mere process of making them become aware of molecules of which they had ignored the concentration. Human speech is, in certain respects, like these colonies, but instead of allowing itself to be understood it silences the biologists who bring unwelcome parallels to its notice. This is a wholly unscientific form of interference with inquiry. The same argument applies to interferences with linguistic origins: if a bacterium chooses to signal with one autoinducer or a biofilm with two, it is its affair and its neighbors’, and no one else ought to feel called upon to take umbrage about it.

While admitting the abstract capacity of bacterial colonies to engage in rudimentary communication through the secretion of simple molecules, I cannot admit their possession of a system comparable in nuance to that of human speech. I am thinking of such things as syntax and metaphor and irony. The fact that a majority of cells emit a uniform chemical signal gives it no claim to constitute a lexicon. And the fact that a majority of signals pertain merely to nutrient gradients gives them no right to obscure those which coordinate complex communal behaviors. I know a bacteriologist who wrote a long paper giving an account of quorum sensing in Vibrio fischeri, which I consider biologically very illuminating. The orthodox textbooks hold that no one

The case for symbols is strongest where the mind employs them to construct abstract relations, although, if it could, it would cling to the comfort of concrete particulars. We would all rather grasp algebra than remain in numerical ignorance, though if, by a fortunate omission, the textbook spared us its complexities, most of us would not lament their absence. And we readily acquiesce in such conventions as the use of maps, though the representation of time is a more dubious proposition. But the best case is that of language itself. Language must operate by arbitrary signs, and we are ourselves aware that it must, although we like to pretend at times that words are natural. The case of language is unique in the fact that the symbols which convey thought are themselves the very medium of its transformation.

Subjective experience arises from consciousness or from sensation. We may therefore take the two together, and say that hardly any physical process or mechanical system can be trusted as the equivalent of another’s inner life. This is, of course, the basis of the argument for dualism. But dualism, in a materialist age, has to work through metaphors, and thus becomes vague and elusive where the actual phenomenon is concerned. There is a special danger in metaphors, owing to the fact that they usually spring from language remote from the qualia they attempt to describe. Take pain as a case in point. Sufferers, on the whole, from acquaintance with agony, have come to know it and dread it, but they are described by theorists without direct feeling, to whom pain may be merely neural firing patterns. Therefore the reductions of theorists to explanations for sufferers are generally inadequate. So in everything: understanding lies with those who possess the experience, not with those who know the mechanism upon which the experience is supposedly based. Thus the proponents of reduction are, in general, abstract and mistaken, and the less they impose their framework the better.

The advantages of specialisation, as we observe, are of two sorts, productive and social. Given a productive and a social advantage which yield the same direct gain in output, the social advantage is more perilous, because it creates reliance. If a man wishes to bake his own bread and you dissuade him, he will be independent; if he finds that he cannot bake it well, he will acquiesce in the practical inefficiency. To prevent inefficiency, it may often be desirable to permit arrangements which are in themselves limiting, such as confining a worker to a single task. To prevent discontent, employers attribute prosperity to cooperative causes; to create discontent, reformers attribute it to systemic exploitation. When the output of a factory increases, employers say it is due to refined processes, and reformers say it is due to intensified labour. Under the influence of mechanisation, people have come to believe more and more in the omnipotence of organisation; they think there is no limit to what human beings can do to multiply artificial prosperity. Capitalism is a form of this belief: we no longer regard scarcity as sent by Providence, but as a result of human error and greed. This has naturally altered the attitude of the labourer towards his “superiors.” Sometimes the belief in organisational omnipotence is carried too far. Many industrialists, including the late Efficiency Minister, apparently think that under perfect specialisation there would be ample goods for everybody even if the complexity multiplied until there was only a single function for each person on the earth’s surface. This, I am afraid, is an exaggeration. However this may be, the modern belief in the omnipotence of organisation has increased the anxiety when systems falter, because shortages are no longer attributed to God or Nature, even when they justly might be. This makes industrial communities more fragile than the communities of the past, and accounts for the fact that the managing classes tend to be exceptionally optimistic, because they wish to regard the dependencies of their workers as due to the logic of progress. It makes interferences with the maximum of specialisation harder to criticise than in former times, because they cannot be camouflaged as immutable facts, although every day in the journals there are letters from economists trying to revive this ancient device.

Common sense is at its worst when the observer firmly believes the phenomenon perceived to be simple or self-evident. It would be erroneous, even if it were tempting, to trust a geocentricist to describe the heavens or a flat-earther to map the oceans. Quantum skeptics ought not to be compelled to accept superposition. Whether their students should be, is another question: I should say not, but the question is not one of intuition, since the pupil is not instructed in either case. The question is one between the teacher and the evidence, and cannot be decided on any general principle. The physicist who has intuitive objections to relativity is not allowed to keep his theory unrevised; yet, so far as general principles go, the two cases are exactly analogous.

In all such processes efficiency should be the governing principle. In a simple bacterial community, efficiency means economy. But it would not mean economy in a system where there was a hierarchy of signals, recognized and accepted by receivers as well as senders.
