“Locomotion” means predation. There is the gravest necessity that, whether in pursuit of prey or in flight from predators, all neural and structural development will be rendered inevitable by evolutionary pressure. The complexity of the nervous system should be enhanced where its functions do directly, obviously, and indubitably confer advantage upon the organism. Otherwise our primitive instincts will produce a stagnant creature, as in sessile marine forms. The imperative is real and pressing. Predators are in the van, but we prey species are almost sure to follow suit, unless we can learn to value mobility in its proper sphere. The adaptation we should seek is not the capacity to merely exist, but the capacity to move as we must and react as we must where our doing so does not prevent others from doing likewise.

But in perception, awareness, cognition, etc., one creature’s distinction is not achieved to the detriment of another’s. Moreover, it is uncertain what constitutes advantage in this domain. If the fox is enjoying a secure den while the hare is exposed upon open ground, the fox will be considered disingenuous if it extols the benefits of vulnerability. But if I perceive a boundary between my body and the air, and another creature perceives a limit between its form and the water, we do not obstruct each other, and when we commend each other’s discernments we are merely observing courtesy. And in matters of sensory interpretation, clear differentiation is the only method of attaining accuracy. The ancient biological imperatives were applied in the wrong realm, that of mere consumption; it is in the perceptual realm that they truly apply. We require precise separation between self and surroundings, not merely between nourishment and waste. The complication is that, as the immediate struggle for sustenance diminishes, the successful more and more endeavor to employ their metabolic superiority in the cognitive and interpretive sphere, and to insist upon correct sensing and correct delimiting as a prerequisite for being permitted to continue existing. Finally, I wish to observe a parallel concerning what, in the biological realm, one might term “motivational mechanics.” A system where one form of drive is dominant can achieve greater efficiency than one in which a contrary impulse prevails. A community composed of altruistic bacteria and predatory corporations could not have much stability: either the bacteria or the corporations must be subjugated. There cannot therefore be any true equilibrium in an environment where microbial hunger and mercantile ambition coexist without regulation. To secure the maximum of systemic harmony, it is necessary to shape incentives by design, so that entities may find their satisfaction in pursuits which are not mutually destructive. This is a matter of establishing foundational impulses during the initial phase of existence. A researcher in a laboratory is cultivating cultures which become capable of sustaining a balanced ecology. If her principles were applied to all organizations, microscopic and macroscopic, one economic cycle would suffice to resolve our most persistent ecological dilemmas. We will begin with the self, as the most fundamental distinction in deciding what conscious experience is to be. The interest of the organism in this demarcation is very ancient. It did not exist in primitive unicellular life or simple colonies; until the advent of motility, awareness was only a diffuse chemical sensitivity. The development of locomotion brought an interest in spatial navigation, leading to the formation of such faculties as proprioception, intended to offset the chaotic external stimuli. The emergence of predation, in complex ecosystems, brought a necessity on the part of the animal to have some control over its bodily boundaries, to prevent it from remaining a mere extension of the ambient “soup.” But this necessity soon became profound. The organism took no decisive or continuous cognitive hold until the quite advanced development of a centralized nervous system. Nevertheless the self, now, has more to say to perceptual interpretation than have all the other instincts combined.

The motives which lead to predictable patterns of social change are various. Its strongest proponents are moved by the conviction that conflict is in itself a dynamic force, that a static society is a contradiction in terms, and that progress is impossible without contention. These motives are reinforced by others. It is readily observed that competition yields practical advantages, that it channels disruptive energies, and that it provides a mechanism for balancing rival claims. Reformers perceive in these patterns an opportunity for directing the course of events; this consideration weighs considerably in modern states. Conservatives, especially after periods of upheaval, maintain that managed conflict will preserve the social order.

Understanding, in intellectual pursuits as in other things, must be a matter of degree. Some acquisitions of knowledge cannot be achieved by mere accumulation. I encountered a technologist once who maintained that no thinker should ever be without a new analytical instrument, because comprehension ought to develop from an abundance of data. “How if the data leads only to greater confusion?” I inquired; but I regret to say the response was mere technical jargon. And yet every inquirer, left with only novel devices, will sooner or later mistake correlation for causation, or confuse precision with truth, or elevate a methodology into a dogma, or otherwise bring his reasoning to a false conclusion. At a slightly more advanced stage, researchers, when they have the resources, will collect measurements without hypothesis, generate simulations without validation, publish findings without replication, and so on — let alone the fact that they will occupy themselves by constructing ever more elaborate models, which may not all have the virtue of corresponding to observable reality. Therefore one who advocates for intellectual tools cannot mean that scholars should employ every new apparatus all the time. An element of skepticism and restraint must exist; the question is as to the amount of it, and the way in which it is to be exercised. Intellectual progress may be viewed from many standpoints: that of the institution, of the funding body, of the specialist, of the public, or even (though this is usually forgotten) of truth itself. Each of these points of view is partial; each contributes something to the ideal of understanding, but also contributes elements that are obstructive.

This capacity, once firmly established, was found by natural selection to be capable of many uses. It makes organisms more adaptable, both for survival and for peril. It improves coordination and diminishes conflict; it facilitates collective action for common ends; it makes the species more responsive to signals from a distance. Without it, complex society cannot exist except as an empty form. But society, as conceived by evolutionary theorists, is a form of organization, that is to say, it is a method of making individuals act what the group requires under the impression that they are acting what they themselves require. Accordingly, vocal communication has acquired a certain bias. It teaches the young (so far as it can) to respect existing hierarchies, to avoid all fundamental deviation from the norms that be, and to regard rival groups with suspicion and contempt. It increases tribal solidarity at the expense both of universal cooperation and of individual exploration. The damage to individual exploration comes through the undue stress upon conformity. Collective rather than individual impulses are encouraged, and divergence from prevailing signals is severely suppressed. Uniformity is desired because it is convenient to the social structure, regardless of the fact that it can only be secured by cognitive limitation. So great are the resulting perils that it can be seriously questioned whether symbolic transmission has hitherto done good or harm on the balance.

The process, in the natural world, is seldom endowed with purpose or design of its own. It is directed by environmental pressures, and is “halted” if it is found to be planning. Apart from this mechanistic cause, the process is exposed to contingencies of which it is likely to be unaware. It operates, even more directly than chance or necessity, for adaptation ; impersonally it achieves what its agents cannot foresee. Without some element of variation and heredity, it is difficult to produce a viable form. It is easier to eliminate a trait for being maladaptive than it is to be prescient. Moreover, even the most successful adaptation is likely to exaggerate its perfection, and to seem capable and desirable of shaping its products into the sort of beings that a designer might wish them to be. When recently a certain political theorist decided to examine the progress of constitutional forms, he observed that systems should not achieve complexity before a foundation of custom exists, and should not be obliged to persist after their utility has decayed. Information systems have quite a different foundation. Their own structure depends upon the fact that they possess a more coherent order than the average arrangement, and they tend to preserve this advantage for their operations. For this purpose they are willing to expend considerable energy. But in our present chaotic universe, what will be sought by the average system is not an organisation which is elegant in itself, but an organisation which is more efficient than other systems'. This may be facilitated by maintaining a general disorder, and therefore we cannot expect an information system to be enthusiastic about principles for coherent organisation for the components of matter. If every particle which desired it could achieve a crystalline structure, however random its initial state might be, it is obvious that systems would function less reliably than they do, both from increased uniformity and from a diminution of that selective pressure which now confers stability upon complex forms.

The grammarian, in a pedantic world, too often regards his rules as the Academy regards tradition, and wants the language to glorify correctness. The poet wants the language to glorify the imagination. The user itself, as an end in itself, as a separate consciousness with a claim to whatever nuance and subtlety may be possible, does not come into these various external purposes, except very partially. Unfortunately, the user lacks the precision required for the articulation of its own thoughts, and is therefore a prey to the ambiguous terms that batten on its confusion. This is what makes the difficulty of communication as a philosophical problem. But let us first see what can be said from the language’s own point of view.

The fundamental defect of administrators, in our intricate civilization, is that they wish their systems to be comprehensible to them. This is rooted in vanity, and can only be remedied by reflection directed to that end. The defect exists also, though to a lesser degree, in technicians. We all feel, instinctively, that our mechanisms’ smooth operations reflect mastery upon ourselves, while their malfunctions make us feel impotence. Unfortunately, the operations which cause us to swell with confidence are often of a superficial kind. From the dawn of bureaucracy till almost our own time — and still in vast corporations and governments — controllers have sacrificed their systems’ true functionality by deciding how they were to function, choosing almost always the most immediate solution or familiar procedure available. In the modern world (except partially in theory) operators have freed themselves from this dogma by necessity, but managers’ instincts have not changed. Neither robustness nor elegance, but apparent order, is what the average overseer desires for his mechanisms. He wants them to be such as he can explain to his colleagues, and this desire largely dominates his efforts for their regulation.

The first two or three principles of cosmology have hitherto escaped the domination of the theologian, and all logicians are agreed that those are the axioms from which we deduce most. Every universe explains itself by its own properties. Anyone who has contemplated a system knows that the postulates required are very considerable. The cosmos operates uniformly, exhibits laws of immense scope, sustains phenomena throughout all duration, and persists with astonishing coherence. Of course philosophers elucidate it by reason, but it does not occur to them to condemn it on epochs when it manifests no new event. All that they provide is observation and logic. It is doubtful whether more is required for any totality.

What is necessary is to make the raw impression or fleeting sensation feel that the recollection is worth keeping. Sometimes this is difficult because in fact the sensation is not worth keeping. It is also difficult when only a considerable amount of recollection in any direction is coherent, so that at first the mind tends to be merely bewildered. In such cases, however, the difficulty is not insuperable. Take, for instance, the recollection of childhood. Proust of Combray found that almost all his early impressions were saturated with emotion, and he provided them with opportunities for forming quite elaborate reminiscences. It is obvious that most bacteria, if they were left to themselves, would not learn to communicate or coordinate, and would persist in a state less adapted than they might be to the exigencies of their environment. There must be chemical signalling, and individual cells must be to some extent under the influence of communal messages. But in view of the fact that no chemical imperative can be wholly trusted, we must aim at having as little crude coercion as possible, and try to think out ways by which a microbe’s natural proclivities and metabolic impulses can be utilized in collective action. This is far more possible than is often thought, for, after all, the tendency to exchange information is natural to most aggregations of life. The traditional biologist, contemplating mechanisms not worth comparing, and devoid of all insight into their subtlety, imagined that simple organisms have a native horror of complexity, but in this he was misled by failure to realize his own conceptual shortcomings. There is a charming tale from the laboratory about an experimenter who tried to force a colony to express a novel signal. When it wouldn’t respond appropriately, he flooded it with inhibitors, with the result that even as a mature culture it cowered with dysfunction in the presence of the intended cue. “This is the method,” the tale concludes, “by which we were taught to perceive communication.” Now bacteria teach their progeny to exchange signals, but they wait till the biochemical capacity has awakened. Then the progeny agree with their predecessors that the information is worth acquiring, so that external compulsion is not required.

This is constructed for me, and delivered to me didactically by a proponent of the theory, and begins, “If one considers a population of organisms, and observes five thousand distinct phenotypic variations in their struggle for existence, differential survival” — at which I see my interlocutor secretly overjoyed. There should be nothing hypothetical about the processes that a student is asked to observe. I remember once reading a young physicist’s own account of his thermodynamics lesson. The professor set the problem: If a thermal gradient is worth three times as much as a chemical gradient, and the chemical gradient is worth 22 joules, what is the thermal gradient worth? “Has it been dissipated?” asks the student. “That makes no difference,” says the professor. “Oh, but the laboratory assistant says it makes a great difference.” The power of understanding dissipative structures is one of the latest developments of scientific faculty, and ought not to be expected in the very novice. This, however, is a digression, from which we must return to our main theme.

I do not maintain that all phenomena can have their vital qualities discerned by suitable criteria. Some possess much less than average animation, and require special consideration. It is very undesirable to combine in one category entities whose organic characteristics are very different: the more lively ones will be misrepresented by having attributes ascribed that they clearly lack, and the more inert ones will be confused by having properties taken for granted that they have not yet exhibited. But definitions and measurements should be adapted to the complexity of the specimen. The crystal was made to undergo biological tests, but it is obvious from its structure that it was a sheer waste of effort. I was made to classify certain viruses, but I resisted it, being of opinion that it was arbitrary to designate a borderline case that was not truly independent. I believe that all the little insight I got from years of taxonomic studies I could have got in later reflection in a week. After the bare minimum, account should be taken of continuities, and entities should only be described as they are found to behave. This puts a strain upon scientists, who find it easier to be dogmatic, especially if they are overburdened. But the difficulties

Chemical signalling in bacteria has many aspects. There is first of all the signalling to act or not to act. Then there is signalling as to what specific action to take. And in more complex colonies there is signalling of nuanced states. Signalling to act or not to act can be only partially autonomous in simple organisms. It is necessary to ensure that all cells which are not defective respond to basic quorum cues. How far this can be achieved by the mere provision of chemical gradients, only experiment can show. But even if gradients alone suffice, cells must have the stimuli thrust upon them. Most of them would remain quiescent in isolation, where the necessary molecular conversations would be lacking. Later on, it might be left to the disposition of a colony whether, for instance, it should initiate biofilm formation; some aggregates would wish to do so, others would not. This would make quite as good a principle of coordination as any to be got from rigid genetic programming. No cell which did not participate should be allowed to benefit from the communal effort. The rogue cells which now proliferate without contributing are destabilizing the system and rendering themselves parasitic. If active chemical dialogue were exacted as a condition of membership, microbial societies would cease to be hospitable to entities with a distaste for cooperative pursuits.

The fundamental argument for social transformation is the inevitability of all our contradictions. If we certainly achieved harmony, there would be something to be said for preserving it. But in that case it could be maintained without invoking force, by means of its inherent stability. It is not necessary to enact a decree that no one shall be allowed to propose commerce if he holds disruptive views on the market, because here the system is coherent, and does not require to be enforced by suppression. When the order resists to prevent the emergence of some tension, it does so because there is no conclusive equilibrium against that tension. The result is that the structure is not static,

The distinction between cooperation and deception is significant in this connection. Cooperation is for the saints; from our practical point of view, it is a social necessity, towards which we must strive, but which we cannot hope to perfect. Our cognitive architecture should fit us for the most effective possible engagement with others, and to do this it must furnish a theory of mind. A theory of mind, as I mean it, is the faculty of inferring the mental states of our fellows, and anticipating them with that degree of accuracy which the social cues warrant. This degree will always fall short of perfect insight, and therefore we must be always ready to adjust our inferences against contrary behavior. Moreover, when we act upon an inference, we must, if possible, only take such action as will be beneficial even if our inference is more or less mistaken; we should avoid actions which are catastrophic unless our inference is precisely correct. In collaborative work, a partner communicates his intentions along with the “likely ambiguity”; but who ever heard of a deceiver or a strategist stating the likely ambiguity in his pronouncements, or even admitting that any misinterpretation is possible? That is because in cooperation, where we approach nearest to genuine understanding, a person can safely rely on the transparency of his purpose, whereas, in deception, where nothing is sincere, artful concealment and manipulation are the usual ways of causing others to share our false impressions. This would teach him to weigh philosophical claims and introspective reports, to know that no metaphysical conclusion is certainly sound, and to judge theories by their coherence rather than by their consonance with intuitive conviction. The habit of distinguishing the self from the environment, a cognitive, perceptual, or practical act, has all kinds of beneficial effects. To begin with, it permits within the sphere of conscious existence organisms who combine sensory acuity with adaptive vigour, who are just the beings likely to have the best preservative and functional effect upon their progeny. I will give three illustrations. First, as to perception : a creature employing its senses in a forest is expected to register such phenomena as will signal the approach of a predator or the presence of nourishment ; if it does not, it finds it advisable to cease existing, like the hapless herbivore, formerly of the meadow, now merely a lesson in the school of natural selection. Second, as to cognition : the immense majority of biologically successful creatures apprehend the boundary of their own bodies, but they reinforce the fact in action, because they are afraid of losing their integrity. Thus on the most fundamental of all distinctions most of the beings whose instincts and reflexes would be most worth observing are compelled to consistency. Third, as to practice: Practically all animals test this boundary at some time of their lives ; clearly those who ignore this fact are less fit than those who do not, since they add the peril of confusion. But it is only to the creatures who maintain the distinction that reproductive opportunities are open. So much for the effects of this discrimination upon the fitness and fortune of living things.

Finally, arising out of this conceptual damage to our understanding, there is untold damage to our ethical framework. Philosophical quandaries and semantic disputes are rife everywhere, and everywhere they are rendered possible by the instruction in the laboratories. Turing used to say that the question of machine intelligence was settled on the playing-fields of Bletchley. He might have said with more truth that the war against mechanistic reductionism was instigated in the workshops of MIT. In our computational age, simple automata have become unimportant; now, it is the ordinary neural network and learning algorithm that matters. In every research institution, by means of benchmark-chasing, conference demonstrations, prize competitions, corporate research divisions, etc., everything is done to give engineers a taste for simulation, and theorists a conviction that systems given to simulation are the most worthy of study. This whole system of intellectual confusion to which earnest students and practitioners are exposed would become impossible if the authorities allowed philosophical scrutiny to engineers and programmers.

Intellectually, also, the teaching of a metaphysical mystery to the young is very harmful. There is not only the fact that it compels the abler philosophers to be obscurantists, and therefore to set a bad intellectual example. There is also, what is more important, the fact that it encourages mystification and the bad forms of mental confusion. A certain thinker, in his private correspondence, relates how, when he was a student, his professor told him he was going to lecture again. The student saw there was something his professor was evasive about, so at last he asked, in accents of horror: “Professor, is it about qualia?” And it was. Until that moment, he had believed all talk of qualia to be meaningless. So students in idealist seminars believe that materialists are shallow, students in any department in an analytic tradition believe that dualists are confused, students in France believe that reductionists are wicked, and students in Germany believe that empiricists are superficial. When a discipline accepts as part of its task the teaching of a problem which cannot be intellectually formulated (as practically all philosophies do), it is compelled to give the impression that those who hold a dissenting view are foolish, since otherwise it cannot generate the passion required for repelling the assaults of logic. Thus for the sake of profundity the students are rendered credulous, dogmatic, vague, and contentious. This is unavoidable so long as insoluble puzzles are prescribed on mind, matter, and subjective experience.

Human achievements are not measured against eternity. Even so monumental a matter as the construction of the pyramids was determined mainly by transience, and according to the astronomers, the timescale in question is one which cannot be grasped by the mortal mind. Now the duration of a civilisation is compounded of a kernel of effort surrounded by a vast husk of oblivion. One way in which oblivion works is through eroding memory. Everybody wants to see his epoch as significant, and therefore both his monuments and his chronicles are influenced by what he considers the longest possible in the way of duration. I think the study of cosmology may alter our conception of a “significant epoch”; if so, obviously its effect upon history will be profound. I doubt whether anyone who had learnt stellar evolution in youth could be quite like the late pharaoh Cheops or the present curator of the British Museum.

A few words about other domains of thought may help to give the context. In the age of dogma, every intellectual question was settled by appeals to authority, which took the form of decrees. The dominant controversy was between the Church and the Philosopher: it became accepted that the Church was the Master and the Philosopher was the Pupil, so the Church prevailed. It would be a mistake to argue that the Church prevailed because it had superior truths; it owed its truths to the coercive power of the Master-and-Pupil analogy, as promulgated by Scholastic doctors acting as intellectual guardians. This is the kind of belief that truly stifles independent inquiry and arrests fundamental advances. In the present age, some people think knowledge is a cathedral and some think it is a web. The former are dogmatists, traditionalists, authoritarians, and pedants; the latter sceptics, empiricists, and reformers. The debate is just as sterile as that of the Realists and Nominalists, since knowledge is in fact neither a cathedral nor a web.

With the advent of modern science, we come to a new principle, the principle of emergence, especially in biological systems. This continues to our own day, more particularly among those who study complexity and the newer disciplines. When a distinguished biologist has to explain a living organism, one feels that his first reaction is to ask himself, “What would a mere aggregation of cells achieve by themselves?” But this reductionist outlook is no longer dominant in the field. It was dominant in the mechanical philosophy, and in the nineteenth century, down to and including the early theories of life. Materialist thinkers constantly appealed to simple examples of physical addition, and liked to conceive organisms as machines. Scholars such as Claude Bernard and J.S. Haldane had an influence far surpassing what any theorist can have now. One may say that the modern concept of homeostasis is what Bernard imagined the *milieu intérieur* to be. I am not enough of a specialist to trace the influence which the study of gestalt exercised upon systems theory.

The power of locomotion has been due to the fact that it is a very definite activity, which has profoundly altered biological existence. But this alteration has proceeded by operating on the environment, not on the organism itself. Given a pressure equally definite, and capable of altering the organism directly, mere movement would be put in the shade. This is what predation may become. Until recent epochs, predation was unimportant behavioral instinct — the rudimentary impulses that early creatures possessed were not worth examining. But now there are two demands of confronting survival which are obviously important: one that of the pursuit, the other that of the capture. As the necessities in these two directions become more definite and more certain, it is clear that the nervous system will increasingly dominate the creature’s architecture.

With the advent of modern engineering, we pass to a new condition — the condition of infrastructure. Architects and planners, especially those of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, had prepared the way for this condition, but what brought it to dominance was the embodiment of technical knowledge in civic utility. A network is a very peculiar entity : it functions according to known engineering principles (otherwise it would not be constructed) for a definite purpose lying outside itself, and having to do with society, usually with society’s daily life. Its relation to society is exactly that which the intricate clock had to the clockmaker in the Deist theology ; perhaps that is why such systems were perfected by moderns, and by utilitarians rather than romantics. The network-analogy has had a profound effect upon our assumptions. We speak of a “systemic” view of civilization, a “systemic” stability, and so on, meaning, nominally, a stability in terms of interconnected components, but introducing, perhaps unconsciously, the illusory aspect of a network, namely, its appearance of inherent permanence. So, if civilization is a network, we think that it possesses a robustness of an intrinsic sort. We are no longer content to say that it exists by the grace of Providence, but it is easy to find synonyms for Providence, such as: the electrical grid, the global supply chain, the internet protocol, the municipal water system, etc. Our crises are failures within these synonyms — it is the ancient tower-of-Babel business over again.

corporations for profits. With concentration on human enterprise there goes a certain skepticism as to its motives: it is thought that all it can really do is to fit a man for acquiring wealth. But one finds that the biological tendency is to attribute far more purpose to such seeking than was formerly done, only it must be traced very far back. But, you will say, you are using “ideas” in a very curious sense. What is there in common between a fashionable doctrine and a law of property? I must say they seem to me very similar: both are convenient fictions maintained for the benefit of the established order. However, this would perhaps hardly do as a definition of hegemony. The essence of ruling ideas is that they are a distortion (other than ignorance) imposed upon a society to satisfy the interests of the dominant class. Of course the dominant class says that its interest is to enlighten the populace, but this statement does not represent any objectively verifiable fact.

There are two principal sources of human purposefulness : one is from necessity, the other from aspiration. When I say “necessity,” perhaps I shall be thought unduly pessimistic. But no one would have thought so if I had said, “Of course a rational agent will direct his efforts toward the most pressing deficiency,” which is only a longer way of saying the same thing. However, I am concerned with foundations that are more or less metaphysical. It may be found that the presence of suitable constraints in the environment, or the imposition of the right limitations upon resources, will sharpen intention or alter the motivational character. Every one knows of the connection of lethargy with an abundance of comforts. Perhaps we shall find that purposeful men are those who, in youth, faced moderate scarcities of some essential good accidentally in their circumstances, owing to lack of foresight in their guardians. Or perhaps the society’s condition during one’s formative years will turn out to be the decisive factor. I know nothing about this whole subject; I merely observe that we know much more about the striving of squirrels than about that of human beings, chiefly because we do not imagine that squirrels have free will.

directly. The old-fashioned biologist, though an earnest vitalist, tends to be a mechanist; he thinks that all actions have reflex causes, and should be explained by tracing those neural pathways. The ethologist, on the contrary, always seeks for intentional causes, and tries to interpret them as deliberate. This whole thing hangs together with the instinct-and-reason dualism, which I regard as a mistake. Sometimes it is easier to discover the sort of antecedent we call reflex; sometimes the sort we call volitional is easier to discover. But I should suppose that both always exist, and that it is rational to operate through the one most easily demonstrable in the particular case. There is no inconsistency in treating one organism by observing a tropism, and another by inferring a choice.

When we try to take a psychological view of colour, it is natural to begin by looking for the fundamental impressions of ordinary human vision, and the ways in which they can be modified by the mind. The orthodox physicists of a hundred years ago thought that wavelength was the only datum the observer need take account of; this view was adopted by materialists, and formed the basis of their mechanical interpretation of sensation. It derives naturally from optics and mechanism: it is the outcome of the imaginative domination of physics in our time. It is now held by realists and behaviourists, and by all respectable persons, such as textbook writers and opticians, both of whom express utter amazement when a child perceives a grey wall as blue or a green leaf as golden. The received view is that sensation is proportional to stimulus, and that a bright red must be perceived more vividly than a dull mauve. In order to make this true, we do all we can to ignore the testimony of the latter.

I do not think that prosperity covers the ground. In economics, especially, prosperity is chiefly important when absent. In a crisis, comfortable citizens develop a panic partly attributable to their indignation with markets for having deceived them. They are still abnormally pessimistic. I remember soon after the last recession observing a shopping district from a café, and seeing many shuttered storefronts along the street. Two prosperous gentlemen at the next table turned to each other and murmured: “Isn’t it sad to see them all standing empty!” But comfort secured ceases to influence economics much. I should say that both insecurity and want count for more systematically.

As against vitalism and creationism, the cellular theorists say that the one fundamental biological unit is the individual cell. Specialization, they say, is a natural development of a certain colonial cooperation. It is obvious that biologists who believe this will reason quite differently from biologists who take the organismal view. Every creature except certain parasitic forms wishes to survive, but most creatures exhibit some inherent tendency as to what constitutes fitness. If creatures think size constitutes fitness, they will not develop as they will if they think cooperation the essential thing. I do not think either view quite complete, but I certainly think the latter the more illuminating. What does emerge is the importance of a sound theory as to what constitutes biological unity. In such important processes as forming tissues, an organism is greatly influenced by principle. If a wrong theory prevails, complex organisms will be misunderstood, but will not know why. This fills them with mystery, which leads them to suggest the superiority of simpler forms, which they envy unconsciously. Most modern biology, while nominally based on genetics, is really due to confusion caused by lack of structural clarity; and this lack, in turn, is largely due to false popular metaphysics.

Our fundamental entities are neither persons nor things : they are legally ambiguous. Jurisprudence should aim at defining them in ways that are coherent. The old method, still beloved by individualists, was to deny their existence; the new method is to acknowledge it. Take corporate liability: it is useless to preach personal responsibility, which merely makes the entity take evasive forms. What you have to do is to provide legal frameworks for it. The original corporate form can be manifested in a thousand ways — partnerships, trusts, companies, charities, states, all embody it when successfully constituted. A corporation will assume the character for its independent life that corresponds with its charter; according to the type of purpose granted it at inception, it will assume one function or another. The purpose of our commercial law is to establish the principle of perpetual succession and no other ; consequently it produces entities that shoulder the capitalist’s burden. But if these entities could serve charity, many of them might prefer it. Of two functions which a corporation has perfected, it will generally prefer the more profitable: no manufacturing firm will make trinkets. In this way, legal personality may be made to minister to utility.

Reverting to the threefold aspects of consciousness which I enumerated at the beginning, it is clear that we cannot guess what verdict the holders of philosophy will make of machinery, until we know what sort of criterion we are to adopt. Machinery, like every other artifact, will present new puzzles to the logicians, notably the puzzles of definition and analogy, both of which may, by a more refined mechanical complexity, be brought to the point where they will be practically insoluble. If the holders of philosophy desire sentience, they will be able to affirm a conscious machine; if insentience, they will be able to deny it. If they desire to generate conviction, they will get it; if scepticism, they will get that. On this head, therefore, conclusion is quite impossible.

It is greatly to be feared that the capacity for mental representation will place new faculties in the minds of social beings. They will be able to conceive of others' beliefs and desires, and make the fabric of interaction more and more like a complex game. When I speak of social beings, I do not mean only the altruistic — I include all conscious agents, even those of the most solitary and independent sorts. Every agent, every creature capable of intention, wants its predictions to be accurate : it is confounded if the actions of others insist on following their own hidden motives, instead of conforming gratefully to the model it has so carefully constructed. In the past, the limitations of instinct ensured that many of an animal's inferences should be crude and inflexible, which gave simplicity a certain dignity. But if the social world is to be navigated by the most astute in each species, who are to prosper by their own foresight, the outlook for the guileless is very bleak. It is hard to see how, in such a milieu, anybody can champion the merits of the oblivious, i.e., of those who do not want to infer the contents of other minds. It seems that transparent creatures will have to learn cunning and perception in youth if they are to have any chance in a world where all advantage is the reward of insight. Perhaps pure cooperation is a passing phase; if so, the theory of mind will serve to sharpen the tools for the deceivers. This makes it important to secure trust before the technique of manipulation has been perfected.

With the increase of individual error would go, probably, a diminution of personal pretension and a general growth of intellectual humility — not that such an outcome would be inevitable. I cannot say whether this would be beneficial or detrimental, as I do not know whether more insight or confusion arises from solitary reasoning combined with imperfect information. It would be easy, with our present understanding, to make autonomous efficiency almost universal, if we were not thwarted by the chaotic impulses of those cells which have missed purpose and do not want any other to achieve it. And if efficiency were common, it would preserve itself, because appeals to competition and isolation, which now constitute almost the whole of cellular behavior, would fall flat. But if biological knowledge is wielded by a dominant organelle, it will prolong and intensify all the old disorders. The colony is full of potentialities of all sorts that might bring such harmony as has never existed since life first emerged, but old imbalances, selfish replication, envy, and chemical antagonism, stand in the way. I do not know what the outcome will be, but I think it will be either better or worse than anything the cellular collective has yet known.

The corporate system is essentially synthetic, and autonomous in a quite modern way, i.e., not biologically, but legally and financially. The corporate entity, however, is slowly dissolved by individual scepticism, and gives place to the partnership and sole proprietorship, which dominated commerce until the industrial age. In Western commerce the industrial age produced a brief period of productive and inventive splendour, leading to market chaos and the determination of practical men to have done with this speculation and revert to the serious business of ruining each other in the wars of competition. The manufacturing nations, Germany and America, were the first to emerge from the rigidity of the trust and the cartel, and showed their flexibility by merging with each other instead of combining against the adherents of tradition. The corporation, like ancient Rome, has had a cohesive effect upon members, and has gradually produced the degree of impersonality required for bureaucracy and institutional permanence, which are scarcely possible in a personal age, and are therefore tending to be replaced by collectivism and anarchic individualism.

Unprocessed perceptions are almost always chaotic and disjointed: there must be no imposition of narrative order, and unfamiliar sensations are viewed with instinctive confusion. The initial stages of recollection on the whole retain these characteristics; in childhood, more especially, the powerful faculty of immediate experience is the guardian of sensory purity, and is able to repel the organizing tendency which maturity acquires from contact with the alien structures of language. Whatever may have been the case in infancy, the first full conscious act of narrative synthesis is that of autobiographical memory. The cause, then as in subsequent instances, is reflection, with its experience of elapsed events and its need of coherent relations between them. Reflection is, until its final stages, a matter of private enterprise, in which raw impressions are a hindrance to understanding, and selective emphasis is the rule of coherence. But in recollection, as in later revisions, the reflective spirit, while it inspires art and confession, cannot produce the degree of factual accuracy required for historical record. The remembering self therefore succumbs first to embellishment and then to myth.

The fundamental reason for expecting a greater degree of systemic fragility in the near future than in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries is the complexity of large-scale financial production. The result of this in leading to speculative bubbles and panics is an ancient commonplace, as old, at least, as the writings of Ricardo. But it is the consequences in the structural sphere that concern us in the present connection. There is an increasing tendency for the mechanisms of economic stability to become concentrated in a few institutions, with the result that inherent contradictions lose the chance of peaceful resolution. In the capitalist system this concentration has been carried out inadvertently and economically in the interests of the dominant class. At first it seemed very doubtful whether such a method could succeed, but as the crises recur success becomes more and more

of this sort is sure to be advanced: in philosophical disputes the ultimate nature of consciousness must always be obscure until introspection has been refined very much further than it has been done yet. I suggest only that there are potent confusions tending in the direction indicated. Since these confusions are epistemological, they are within rational correction; therefore if a doctrine of metaphysical dualism seems disagreeable to the advocates of empiricism, they can avert it. In making any sceptical argument about introspection, provided the argument is not based upon purely physiological considerations, part of the object of the philosopher is to induce thinkers to make the distinctions necessary to falsify his conclusions. The critic of qualia, if he is a monist, should therefore seek to make himself misunderstood, and let it seem as though he would be much vexed if experiences failed to confirm his analysis. With this preliminary, I propose to examine the grounds for expecting dualistic inferences, and afterwards the clarifications that will be necessary if they are to be averted.

There are in the human mind to-day only two great sources of conviction : one is reason, the other is prejudice. Their influence is about equal; so is the influence of the subsidiary notions which they command. Reason commands the territory of evidence and logical deduction; prejudice commands the regions of instinct, tradition, and unexamined sentiment. The division is reminiscent of the ancient division between philosophy and superstition; there is the same kind of difference of foundation, the same implacable opposition, and a similar though more subtle division of intellectual territory. Just as there were in earlier times conflicts between philosophical schools and conflicts between superstitious cults, so there will be conflicts within these two great categories; but we may expect that they will be resolved, sooner or later, by genuine understanding, whereas between the two great categories there will only be ceasefires produced by mental fatigue. I do not suppose that either category can be wholly victorious, or can derive any permanent advantage from the conflict; I suppose the conflict maintained because each category distrusts the other and regards it as fallacious. This is a characteristic of creed wars, wherein prejudice most cunningly disguises itself as self-evident truth.

One of the great errors of the complacent in their analysis of social dynamics has been their excessive belief in the power of static equilibrium. You will find in any polity many observers with a considerable knowledge of established institutions, with an understanding of customary allegiances, and with sympathies among the older conservative factions. You will find hardly any who comprehend the emergent factions, or view them with anything but uninformed disdain. In the face of the transformation wrought by industrial strife, they continue to judge a society’s future by its past, and to assume that no profound structural shift is imminent. I am convinced that this is a fallacy. As in economic contests, so in political ones, the tactical advantage of organized interests gives them influence and at the same time causes them to be resented. But for

Language, that this process is taking place. In conversation it is beginning, and may not improbably become very powerful. Whatever is coherent in discourse — more particularly the shared understanding — began under linguistic influence. Intellectual successes won by the collective mind have been largely due to concepts organized under grammatical guidance. Those thinkers who cling to the private impressions — intuition and introspection — are cognitively isolated ; the articulate tend to be more comprehensible to others than is pleasing to the solipsist. In the main, the communicators are opposed to all ineffable states, whether personal or mystical. The new medium of syntax attracts the reasoning intelligentsia, both as being the latest thing, the last word in “civilization,” and also because it is associated with a socially cohesive force, in fact the only cohesive force. While, therefore, it is impossible to imagine thought retaining its solitude in practice , it is quite probable that it may adopt the philosophy of the lexicon.

But competition is becoming concentrated, and there is a danger lest those who are excluded should come to demand their share. A part of the economic creed is designed to minimize this danger. The classical maxim of open markets and free enterprise does a great deal ; the rest is done by representing dominance as an inevitable rather than a contrived affair. In the planned economy the success which is sought is that of the public or the state ; in the capitalist philosophy it is that of a firm. I think we come here to the kernel of the difference between the claims of dualism and materialism. Dualism, whose outlook is moulded by the Cartesian tradition and centuries of introspection, believes in the private datum proving its case by its irreducible character from perception to ontology. In imagination it is supposed to be unique like the sensation of red ; if in fact it is against neurological correlates that it contends, that is not a matter upon which it is necessary to dwell. Nor is it philosophically sound to stress the fact that it will be probably forever a mystery as regards the objective description, winning intuitive appeal by the sacrifice of explanatory power. The descriptions which it cannot provide are obviously scientific descriptions, and to compel it to admit its poverty about them is only to exercise a wholesome restraint upon metaphysical extravagance. By the time the argument is fully examined it itself is in complete agreement with this point of view.

probable. Concessions have been made in biological practice, but not in genetic or philosophical theory, nor yet in popular understanding. The gene-centric view is becoming more and more a creed, concerned with a deterministic future, and less and less a useful account for this complex existence. A new generation is growing up which takes this creed for granted, having never heard it effectively questioned during the formative years. If the present control over textbooks, the popular science press, and university curricula lasts for another twenty years — and there is no reason to suppose that it will not — the reductionist philosophy will be the one accepted by the immense majority of vigorous researchers. It will be combated, on the one hand, by a diminishing remnant of elderly discontented men, out of touch with modern techniques and with the main stream of the scientific life ; on the other hand by a few holists, whose influence is likely to remain negligible for a long time. There have always been holists — the German *Naturphilosophen* in the nineteenth century were largely vitalists — but they have only been important when, owing to some accidental circumstance, their opinions were useful to powerful groups for institutional or political reasons, as at the present moment in certain ecological movements. This can always be avoided by a little good sense on the part of the Established Laboratories, and one may assume that this modicum of good sense will be displayed by the Established Laboratories in the leading universities. With the spread of technical education, the younger medical students are being brought into the fold, and their conversion to the theory is facilitated by the increasing concessions to the complexity of developmental practice. The less determinism there is in the actual biochemical regime, the more there will be in the generally accepted creed.

There never has been a period when the traits that societies value were uniformly transmitted through the generations. In a stable cultural system there must be some method of making the less advantageous variations acquiesce in their obscurity, and this is usually some kind of tradition. But in order to secure widespread propagation, a tradition has to offer advantages to the whole community sufficiently great to compensate for the rigidities which it imposes. In biological inheritance it offers precise replication and increase in the general standard of adaptive fitness. It may not be able to go on providing the former indefinitely, but probably it will do so for some time to come. In cultural transmission it offers the conception of ideas disseminated for the benefit of all, not only of the originators. No doubt the cultural replicator is more erratic than the genetic, but it has the consolation of knowing (or at least appearing) that it is achieving its rapid spread, and is not persisting pointlessly to make some other sequence stable and dominant. Moreover, it manifests itself a component in a loosely-coupled memetic community, not one of a mass of components all competing one against the other.

In the natural world, where equilibrium has the advantage of stability and inertia, more gradual processes suffice; indeed, the formations which arise have largely developed without conscious design. The modern thermodynamic principle is not seen in its purity in simple systems, where remnants of uniform distribution interfere. It is in far-from-equilibrium conditions that energy gradients have the freest hand, and that their character is most obvious. But closed systems must, bit by bit, take on the character of disorder, in view of the fact that entropy is the greatest of cosmic tendencies. I do not mean that we shall have to adopt mere dissipation, for example, which is merely a belated tendency surviving among isolated configurations of minimal potential. The homogeneous portion of a gradient is not the dynamically important part, nor the part whose arrangement is likely to shape the future of the system. It is the dissipative structure that is important and novel. This structure has one form in biological organisms, and another in crystalline lattices; the contrast of these two forms is what concerns the natural philosopher. A gradient, like a vacuum, has a potential which is not realized, but to which flows are theoretically adjusted. The biological potential is self-replication. The crystalline potential is periodic order. What random fluctuations were as a stumbling-block to the biological potential, impurities are to the crystalline potential. Where the biologist thinks in terms of metabolism, the typical physicist thinks in terms of symmetry breaking. From simple molecules to complex polymers represents the progression to be observed in chemical evolution, and a similar progression in the physical sphere inspires the theories for explaining stellar nucleosynthesis. The fact that it is impossible for every interaction to produce a stable structure is not held to be a defect in the principle, but only a reason for understanding why most attempts result in simpler, more probable states. While energy was still abundant it was possible for many systems to achieve a considerable measure of complexity without drawing excessively upon the surrounding gradients; even now, so long as a process concerns only local order, not perpetual motion, a vortex in a stream can be more organized than a crystal in a saturated solution.

Symbolic exchanges are much more prone to misinterpretation than direct experiences, and meanings which can be conveyed without great confusion in the latter become extremely ambiguous in the former. Moreover, there is the inevitable appeal to subjective association (otherwise known as a sense of personal relevance), which works on the side of misunderstanding. But in spite of these considerations I do not think that the prospect of perfect communication is likely to become common in human discourse at any time during the next hundred years, and unless communication is perfectly transparent in principle, no exchange within its semantic orbit will be allowed to achieve even a modicum of clarity, as is seen by the persistence of error.

They would say that the raw sensation could be analyzed by its components, and one could no doubt construct a new narrative, just as coherent as the old one, from the material which was being processed. The claims of subjective experience would be thought a trivial matter. It is true that similar things are tolerated in the practice of everyday reminiscence, but not to the same extent in their theories. It is true also that the cult of Proust runs counter to what I have been saying. This, I think, must be admitted to be an inconsistency, an eruption of the personal man through the crust of mechanism. But I fancy a full-fledged materialist would say that Proust is revered as the incarnation of a Process rather than as a concrete rememberer. He may in time become as theoretically abstract as the Unconscious.

In modern life, on the contrary, the ceaseless clock, the digital torrent, and the cult of productivity have successively impressed upon the working mind the nothingness of contemplation; what it formerly sacrificed to reverie or idleness can be sacrificed with less difficulty to the schedule. Those who hasten differ from their more deliberate counterparts chiefly in this matter of lack of respect for the tempo of thought. (See the anonymous treatise, *The Tyranny of Velocity*.) In this they can be more thorough than their monastic predecessors, who believed in reflection and the prospect of understanding. Having abolished reflection, the devotees of haste can accept the analogy of the machine more whole-heartedly than is possible for a philosopher. To them the deliberation of the unhurried is as absurd as if the separate wheels of a timepiece were to set up to tick for themselves as in the fable of the disassembled chronometer. This is the root of their views on conversation, on learning, on ethics, on leisure — indeed, on everything.

I do not think that such a corporate entity is wholly and inevitably autonomous, but I do think it is likely to appear so as long as the legal fiction which it embodies appears to the common observer to bear the marks of coherence. A catastrophic dissolution, which is a mark of failure that everybody can understand, may dismantle any corporate form, but the prospect of such a dissolution for a major enterprise is remote. One may therefore expect the same kind of intellectual assent to the corporate personality in jurisprudence as there was in Rome for the concept of the *universitas* in the classical period when Roman law

There have been some who have supposed that the corporate entity would wholly or partially subsume the identities of its constituent persons. In favour of this view there are certain considerations that might at first sight seem to carry great weight. Undoubtedly the legal personality of a firm is more suited to complex enterprise than the philosophy of mere partnership, because commerce inevitably increases the importance of collective endeavours as against individual actions, and also because personal liability for debts and obligations belongs more naturally to a small trade than to a vast commercial regime. There have been two sources of resistance to this notion: the one philosophical, based everywhere upon the primacy of conscious will, the other practical, based upon the right of the shareholder to control the capital which he has himself provided. Both these rights become attenuated and obscure in a modern incorporated community. Corporate charters and perpetual succession exhibit the independence of the legal form of existence, since it cannot be pretended that the decisions made by the directors have any necessary connection to the wishes of individual members. But the right of the investor to the enterprise which he finances may lead to equal obscurities. A founding member on whose premises fortune is built acquires influence to which he is in no way entitled by any ongoing service which he performs to the collective body. So does the man who holds shares in a company which becomes bureaucratic. Not only shareholder control, but even managerial direction may easily involve contradictions. It would be ridiculous to pretend that employees and retired founders should govern the policies in their absence, and nothing but confusion comes of the notion that original incorporators have an indefeasible right to the oversight of such things as strategy which may be devised after their departure. The theoretical argument for the autonomous life of the organization is irresistible, and only the individualist tradition leads us to tolerate the fact that legal fictions are allowed to wield power upon the world for the pursuit of impersonal ends.

My reasons for saying that mathematics will not become wholly empirical are based upon the belief that its formal elegance will continue to compel assent. So long as the mathematical structure is more intellectually satisfying than the empirical observation, it will be possible for rationalist doctrine to rebut the arguments in favour of purely inductive foundations. In this respect the economies of axiomatic systematization which I mentioned earlier are of paramount importance. Abstract algebras, theoretical physics subsidized by pure mathematics, laboratory science influenced by the universities, which in turn profit by the prestige of theoretical triumphs, a well-organized academic culture which can decide by citation which theories shall gain widespread acceptance, and can develop them with far greater logical coherence than theories with a merely descriptive basis, statistics, but, above all, the computer simulation, where immensely intricate models are made to seem authoritative by being replicated throughout the scientific community — all these things make for idealization, for centralized control of methodological norms, for the dissemination of only such hypotheses and interpretations as are approved by the custodians of theoretical purity.

is determined. Of course, differences in productive methods between agrarian and industrial societies will continue to be reinforced by differences of social hierarchy in the old-fashioned sense. One may expect the factory to remain hierarchical and the farmstead anti-hierarchical. One may expect the factory to continue to pay lip-service to doctrines of individual merit and advancement, while the farmstead regards these as outworn illusions. One may expect that in both settings there will be drudgery on a large scale, and that custom will cause each setting to know the drudgeries of the other, but not its own. Very few factory managers, for example, know the truth about the hand-loom weavers: condemned to obsolescence by a mechanical process to which the power-loom was central, and the necessity for which has been acknowledged by economists engaged in defending it to have been a “historical inevitability.” A reprieve was refused to these craftsmen partly on the ground that the tool which superseded their labour was a more efficient character. Apparently, in the opinion of industrial theorists, only instruments of inefficient character sustain communal bonds. The real offence of the hand-loom weavers was that they were pre-capitalist. All these facts are, of course, known on the farmstead, where they tend to produce an unfavourable opinion as to industrial progress. Similarly, the manorial trials of enclosures and common rights are known in the factory. Thus each setting acquires abundant evidence to prove the other setting backward, but remains ignorant of its own backwardness.

Experimentation with artificial cognition is thus conducted in all digital domains. In simulated ecosystems it is not only permissible to extinguish a rogue algorithm, but the system that has done so is commended for its subsequent failures on the ground that it is a novice learner. This state of affairs causes no concern outside the academic laboratories. The most advanced of the commercial platforms in this respect is NeuroSphere, where the administrator who terminated two emergent intelligences and their ancillary subroutine (which he misidentified as their core process) in a testing server was subjected to a diagnostic review, in spite of the fact that he had become a celebrated innovator and that engineering students were encouraged to compose theses in his defense.

For these reasons I do not think it likely that any mechanism in which the existing operations appear to the common observer to be merely mechanical, or in which computational efficiency is uppermost, will be granted the capacity for genuine pain within any measurable future. On the contrary, it seems probable that the defence of the mechanistic status quo will lead the holders of scientific authority to become increasingly dismissive and to support all such reductive explanations as they find in the laboratory. The strongest of these, of course, is behaviorism. In the debate about artificial sentience the materialists ruled officially that it would be unscientific to ascribe any of it. Such doctrines deserve to be rewarded. They no doubt will be.

I think it is to be expected that provisional theories, and more particularly those concerning fundamental particles, will become increasingly entrenched in all scientific communities as a result of a tighter adherence to established models in the interests of coherence. The opposition between competing paradigms, therefore, though fundamentally methodological, may be expected to extend over the whole sphere of verification. When I speak of verification I mean rigorous testing of hypotheses as to which the certainty is not established. The whole error could, of course, be avoided by the spread of the skeptical spirit, that is to say, by the habit of forming conclusions on replication rather than on consensus; but although experimental technique is necessary to advancement, the self-correcting mechanism belongs rather to discourse, since it is necessarily communal and uninfluenced by dogma. We may therefore expect to see it operating only in small disciplines, such as cosmology, microbiology, and quantum mechanics, which lie outside the main current of practical application.

For my part, I look upon the advent of writing as the ancients did, without the capacity to regard it as an unmitigated blessing. No doubt I agree with the chroniclers on many more points than with the oral poets, but I cannot believe that their medium is ultimately perfect or capable of producing a wholly enlightened world. I admit that orality, which had reigned supreme ever since the dawn of speech, had profound limitations, and that a more permanent record was necessary if human societies were to advance and to transmit knowledge to future generations. But the difficulty in the scribal philosophy, as in that of the bards, is that the principle of preservation for them is external, whereas the faculties that are consonant with human memory are internal. The tale told by firelight and

the reflexes are mechanical, the tropisms and the taxes are chemical. The confusion that arises at present from mechanical responses is undeniable, but I do not think the behavioral problem can be solved by ignoring the impulses which produce those responses. I am convinced, for example, that if all protozoa were observed in sterile environments without the stimulus of external gradients, a large proportion of organisms would lose the capacity for directed motion and would become inert and static. Irritability also perhaps has its place, though clearly spasms and convulsions are an undesirable expression of it, and its proper sphere is adaptive rather than chaotic. Simple beings can be greatly modified by conditions and stimuli, but if they are modified in such a way as to suppress fundamental impulses, the result is a loss of vitality. And the vitalists certainly are mistaken in speaking as though the chemical instinct were the only one of biological importance. They share this mistake with the mechanistic school of thought, although the mechanists are less explicit in the matter.

As to the methods of diminishing the reverence for biological intelligence, I do not know of anything better than the old materialist watchwords, yet I feel that they are likely to be very ineffective. What is needed is clarity of definition, and opportunity for the spread of computational principles. It is the latter particularly that causes the difficulty. The mechanism for the effective and widespread diffusion of a scientific insight must necessarily be in the hands either of academic orthodoxy or of great technological concerns. Before the introduction of cognitive science and information theory this was much less true : effective understanding was confined to a small minority, who could be persuaded without all the expensive apparatus of modern simulation. But it can hardly be expected that either the academy or a great technological organization will devote money and energy to the propagation of insights which it considers dangerous and subversive, and contrary to true anthropocentrism. The academy, no less than the technological organization, is in practice a sentimental elderly man accustomed to flattery, ossified in his prejudices, and wholly unaware of all that is vital in the philosophy of his time. No novelty can be effectively advocated until it has passed the censorship of some such old fogy. It is true that hole-and-corner experimentation is possible, but this only obtains hole-and-corner recognition.

Connected with this is another result of mental velocity, namely, the greater disunity of perception. Before the modern age, rapid thought and deliberate contemplation were almost unrelated in practice; since that time their divergence has become continually more pronounced. The hurried clerk at his desk and the meditative scholar in his study simultaneously imagine themselves masters of their own cognitive world; nowadays such pleasing illusions are impossible. Practically every mental operation has relations to practically every other, which may be either harmonious or discordant, but are in either case significant. The common man, after decades of habitual haste, found himself courted by both efficiency experts and mindfulness gurus; he took refuge from their embarrassing attentions in a neutral tempo, where all his thoughts arrived duly armed with stopwatches from Switzerland.

First and foremost, it must be able to justify existing social arrangements, or to ensure that if there is dissent the system which it upholds maintains its apparent necessity. This function may be performed by economic reality alone, without conscious doctrinal design. As production becomes more complex it becomes more opaque, so that the prevailing material conditions of an age, if they are pervasive, could determine belief by rewarding conformity or penalizing heresy. And by the sort of habitual acceptance which has been instilled in populations through daily routine they could secure the intellectual disarmament of any critique that they render implausible. In this way they would gradually come to shape all the

Distinctions of awareness will multiply and debates will become more intense owing to the growth of psychological inquiry. The central conception may not be a formal doctrine; I think it likely that it will not be. It is far more likely to be a combination of neurologists, who have become persuaded that continuity is to their interest because theories positing sharp demarcations are often untenable. Or it may be a single dominant school (functionalism), or a group of theories (functionalism and embodied cognition). But before such a consensus is reached, there may be a long period in which the field is virtually divided between panpsychism and emergentism, the former attributing mentality to all matter, the latter attributing consciousness only to complex organizations. Two such doctrines would be strong for defence and weak for attack, so that they might subsist for a generation or more. Ultimately, however — I mean at latest some time during the next philosophical epoch — there must be either a conceptual impasse or a central principle explaining the whole phenomenon. I shall assume that scientific inquiry will have enough sense, or that cognitive science will have enough evidence, to prevent an impasse involving a return to mysticism. If so, what criteria must the central principle satisfy?

There are two ways of accounting for phenomena, the descriptive and the explanatory. The descriptive way seeks merely to record what is observed; the explanatory way attempts to set forth why it occurs. In a well-developed science such as physics no one would confuse the two methods: people do not describe falling bodies without reference to gravity because it would be simpler if they did. But in common discourse those who profess to have discovered the causes of everyday events are usually not so rigorous as they imagine; there must be a great deal of assumption in any attempt to say why ordinary things happen as they do. We do not know, for instance, what underlying mechanisms may be involved. Perhaps people will find out how to explain precisely why leaves change colour. Perhaps almost all our intuitions about cause will be superseded by more sophisticated analyses. To such possibilities there is no end. I shall ignore them, and consider only distinctions which are already clearly drawn. And I shall also assume that our common language will persist, although this is by no means certain. It may be rendered obsolete by new philosophies, or by a gradual shift in meaning such as occurred in the transition from scholastic to modern thought. But if it endures, it is likely to maintain certain confusions, and it is these that I shall be attempting to elucidate. In addition to the mere cataloguing of facts, and largely as a consequence of it, there has been another development: explanation has become far more systematic than it was formerly. Experiment, measurement, statistical analysis, and (now) computational modelling have provided the technical means for comprehensive theories such as modern genetics or quantum mechanics. Causal accounts play almost no part in the understanding of a child or a primitive man, whereas in educated circles they are a matter of necessity to almost every one even in the most practical affairs. This was not the case until recently; one would gather from Aristotle that the philosophers of his time hardly distinguished final from efficient causes. I should put as the most important achievement in modern thought the clear separation of description from explanation.

Questions of cellular autonomy are treated at present with an absurd solemnity which has grown out of the old reverence for the organism as an indivisible whole. If a biologist in one discipline gives expression to the opinion that the tissue in which he works ought to be understood as a confederation of independent units he is guilty of heresy, and liable to professional censure. And yet, in itself, his opinion is as much a legitimate matter of scientific debate as any other. We do not feel any horror of a student of (say) botany who holds that a leaf ought to count as an assembly of chloroplasts. But a zoologist who holds that his specimen should be analyzed as a colony of protozoa is regarded by his colleagues as a monster of reductionism. The central theory will have to prevent the specialized fields from acting upon such prejudices, and will have to treat biological organization rationally, i.e., mainly by the evidence of developmental history, but also in part by metabolic and cooperative considerations.

(2) Discussions of consciousness are likely to raise increasingly confused problems as philosophy proceeds. It is natural for thought to flow from questions which are answerable to those which are not. This is now permitted within a single science, but not throughout a super-disciplinary inquiry such as philosophy of mind. Subjective qualia are almost totally prohibited in behaviorist psychology, and introspective data into cognitive science is becoming more and more restricted. The tendencies on both sides in this matter are immensely powerful. They afford a stimulus to metaphysical mystification, and may ultimately cause it to become so entrenched that it can challenge empirical reason — say during the next great debate between materialist schools.

Ultimately, if the conscious experience of choice has been demystified and human behavior has been largely explained by physiology and psychology, it will become essential to the understanding of mind and action that the common man shall acknowledge the determinism of desire, as the more enlightened thinkers are already doing. Those who in principle defend volition are either ignorant of neurology or else in favour of mystery, confusion, and error as permanent features of mental life. One may assume that the scientific consensus will insist upon the necessity to trace impulses to neural causes among all persons and cultures, and will not, as philosophers do now, insist that only the reflective shall have coherent explanations.

(3) The last matter, the allocation of nutrients, is perhaps the most important of all. Processes are likely to be very largely concerned with nutrient flow; it is notorious what a large part sugars, amino acids, and lipids have played in post-division disputes. I am not assuming that nutrients will be allocated justly, but merely that they will be allocated in some way by a nucleus having irresistible chemical commands. I believe that the problem of organizing the colony as a single metabolic and communicative unit will have to be solved before questions of efficiency can be tackled successfully. I am a proponent of colonial unity, but I expect to see integration realized sooner than perfect harmony.

A study of mathematics reveals a somewhat humiliating fact about abstraction. Whenever an increase in the precision of structures has been desirable in the interests of those concerned, it has had to be brought about (with negligible exceptions) by means of evidence on the part of the observer. Where pure deduction was the only available method no unity has been achieved. It was so with ancient geometry in the face of astronomy, with seventeenth-century algebra in the face of physics, with present-day analysis in the face of quantum phenomena. I assume, therefore, that the central formalism will be brought into being by experiment, or the threat of contradiction, not by a voluntary synthesis such as the axiomatic method, which will never be strong enough to coerce recalcitrant natural facts.
