I think, also, that the power of the central formalism will be primarily logical, and will rest upon possession of elegant axioms combined with control of deductive inference. I conceive of it as consisting, in the beginning, of a group of theoreticians backed, informally, by one or more great observations.

It follows that at the foundation of human cognition there will be symbolism. All the conceptual supply of the mind, for example, will be linguistically mediated. It follows that images and sensory impressions will be inadequate to minds which aspire to complex reasoning, unless they can be translated into a symbolic system by a deliberate effort. The same will apply to other faculties in less obvious ways. Already at the present day a large proportion of the world’s philosophical thought is controlled by the conventions of syntax, which are themselves to some extent controlled by the history of the language. From the raw perception to the refined abstraction there is a long road to travel, and symbolism may intervene at any stage. In the case of mathematics the natural stage is at the beginning. In other cases, it may be metaphors or diagrams or formal notations that give the symbol its opportunity to clarify. But wherever it intervenes, it is more powerful than any of the other mental tools concerned.

Given contradiction at one stage of a process there will be a tendency to extend the contradiction to earlier and later stages. The growth of internal tension is part of the general tendency to increase of complexity, which is shown historically in the greater instability and dynamism of societies. We may therefore confidently expect a continuation of the process of generating conflict which has been going on throughout the last half-millennium. It is of course to be assumed that established institutions will continue to provoke opposition among the discontented. The view that while traditions are rigid the populace should be prevented by custom from counter-mobilizing is not one which it will be found long possible to maintain.

Assuming a dominant system associated with a dominant language (or several dominant languages in confluence), it is of course obvious that the dominant system will secure great conceptual power to itself, and will produce intellectual contentment in the population of the dominant culture by conceding to its thinkers a progressive increase in their cognitive reach. This has been happening in the scientific community, as it formerly happened in classical philosophy. So long as there is a rapid increase in the total symbolic repertoire of a culture it is easy for established institutions to prevent radical epistemological challenges by timely curricular control. And the less developed cognitive traditions can be kept subdued by a system of pedagogical hegemony.

But such a distinction will probably develop in the direction of consciousness, i.e., of self-awareness — for self-awareness is merely cognitive distinction in an organism which has reached the stage of complexity in many perceptions. One may take the perceptual development of an infant as a parallel. The infant is unified by sensation — a process practically completed by the first year after the chaos of undifferentiated experience. The sensory unity was necessary to produce coherence, but when coherence had been achieved the movement towards distinction began almost at once, and it was found, after the confusions of early childhood, that distinction was compatible with mental order. We are now, in the cognitive sphere, just about at the transition from undifferentiated experience to sensory unity. When once perceptual coherence, however primitive, has been achieved, the movement towards cognitive distinction will be immensely strengthened, since it will no longer have to contend with the fear of chaos. Organisms can only retain coherence if they have considerable support in perceptual data, since they must be accurately served by their senses and nerves and mental faculties. Situations will continually arise in which the holders of perceptual unity will find it prudent to make distinctions; in the navigation of existence they will have to associate with themselves representations of the less familiar stimuli and events, and this process will probably continue until a completely conscious regime has been established.

Since we have been assuming a complex system which comprises numerous interacting components, the emergent properties arising from this system would be systemic properties, manifesting not only in mechanical aggregates, but also in the organic and social domains. Organic life develops at present with such intricate interdependence that it may well be capable of illustrating a profound principle of wholeness by the time such a principle is fully understood. Inorganic matter is a more subtle problem. But even in inorganic crystals the chemists (who are in this respect our guides) are discerning remarkable patterns, and no one can foretell what may be discovered within the next hundred years. I conclude, therefore, that a theory of systemic holism, involving functional unity to all constituent parts and processes, may well become established not long after the recognition of interactive networks. And, if so, the natural operation of scientific inquiry is pretty sure to bring it about. There are, however, other interpretations, which might lead to a perpetuation of reductionist doctrines. Wherever simple and complex phenomena are examined side by side, as in clockwork mechanisms and living organisms, it has been found possible to combine analysis of components with a neglect of the integrative relations. What stands in the way of this error on a large scale is the objection by thoughtful minds to mere aggregation in most parts of the philosophical world. Nevertheless, it remains a possibility to be borne in mind. I shall have something more to say about it later.

There are certain convictions in ordinary human thought which are tending to undermine common sense; the chief of them is scientific inquiry into the fundamental constituents of matter. More and more, people come to perceive that our intuitive notions should not be trusted more than can be justified through our sensory limitations or even prejudices. In daily life the testimony of immediate perception is always spoken of as very reliable, and so no doubt it seems; nowadays it is understood to be little more than a convenient illusion. There will be a growing tendency for physicists or mathematical theorists to give fairly adequate descriptions of subatomic behavior, and consequently our direct impressions will be more and more contradicted by conscientious experimenters or instruments. Gradually the evidence against the solidity of everyday objects from laboratory data will become so overwhelming that there will be a very strong inducement for all who are not philosophically trained to avail themselves of the opportunities for surrendering their naive realism to quantum theory; probably this will be done, in the end, as now with heliocentrism, by practically all who are above a certain intellectual curiosity.

The implications of such a parallel would be profoundly instructive. With the mechanism of natural selection made explicit, political development would no longer be seen as arbitrary, and would gradually reveal its patterns among those systems which adapt to their environmental pressures. In stable societies, the mutations of governance under these conditions would probably be very slight, and the theorist would have to apply a framework of analysis at a scale found adequate to explain the variety of institutions which it considered significant. All this is not so very obscure ; it might easily be demonstrated in modern scholarship before the end of the current century.

If all this occurs while thermal equilibrium persists and energy gradients remain shallow, the results are likely to be negligible. To begin with, there will be a profound distinction between simple aggregates, which will possess neither intricate organization nor stable hierarchies, and complex systems, which will maintain dynamic structures with continuous dissipation. The simple aggregates, being governed by random fluctuations, will remain, like particles in a homogeneous gas, in a state of inert uniformity. The molecules will be compelled by gradients that it is their tendency to move along them, both to maintain the flow of energy and to increase the production of entropy for sustaining the processes of more elaborate forms. With no external forcing to counteract that of equilibrium, there will be no limit to the disorder with which matter can be arranged, so that over time it will settle into the most probable, featureless state. Structures whose complexity the gradients cannot support will be dissolved by having their orderly patterns dispersed into the random motions of their components.

It is thus quite possible that through the joint operation of intellectual pride and a metaphysical craving for infallibility we may be led, step by step, to the paralysis of all useful inquiry, the upper realms retaining abstract speculation and logical perfection, the lower feeling confidence only in immediate sensation. For philosophical reasons the dogmatist will secure, by definition, a high standard of certainty among the propositions ; skepticism and analysis will secure a low yield of truth. Inaction will therefore be the only way of preserving the purity of one’s beliefs from error, except ignorance, which thinkers will try to avert by refining their doubts. In these circumstances we may expect an era of sterile contemplation, comparable only to the scholastic disputations of the medieval schoolmen. The only hope will lie in the speedy acceptance of some degree of probability or system of approximations.

But even if a parallel is drawn the implications will be profoundly different if one considers biological evolution from what they will be if one examines political systems. In the former case there will be that mechanism of natural selection which we spoke of a moment ago, the successful species retaining advantageous traits, the unsuccessful substituting extinction for adaptation. And there will still be need to produce stability in the latter, lest it should collapse into anarchy. This will involve a certain rigidity of structure, and will perhaps lead the governing class to encourage traditions among conservative rather than liberal or radical factions. The democratic system may thus gradually become a historically rare aristocracy, and be finally supplanted by a populist insurrection.

All this may be thought exaggerated, in view of the fact that most human exchanges employ a common language. I observe, however, that the language everywhere permits the symbolic content to be such as furthers the ambiguity of the speaker; utterances are criticized for being obscure, but never for being too precise. I see no reason to suppose that this will change in the near future. And I think, for such reasons as I have been giving, that if our communication continues much longer to rely upon these imperfect symbols, it is fated to fail. It is because I do not desire the collapse of understanding that I am a skeptic of perfect transmission.

The tendency of prejudice in our time is, and will probably continue to be, towards self-evidence and away from rational scrutiny. This is due, of course, to the immense psychological comfort of certainty. There is a powerful social tradition, which comes to us from primitive tribalism, and is backed by communal prestige : a “sound” man should hold some unquestioned belief, but need not know how a contrary argument is constructed. The survival of this tradition, however, tends only to make “sound” men less reasonable than other men. I think we may assume that, before very long, no one will be considered thoughtful unless he knows something of this disguise.

This is all to the good, but what is regrettable is that abundance seems to be achieving its comforts at the expense of an impoverishment of our conduct in other directions. Purpose becomes more and more an affair of indolence and a few trivial pursuits: it is not felt by ordinary men to be necessary, as it was when it was associated with deprivation and daily struggle. The leisure that fills our hours might have been used to give our lives a victory over ennui, but in a state of perpetual satiety such leisure is thought less important. The volitional impulses that were formerly satisfied in pragmatically admirable ways are now finding more and more diffuse outlets: the planning and decision-making of our time have, as a rule, no teleological value, except in moments of crisis, which are imported from a less fortunate circumstance. I am afraid the decay of purpose is inevitable, and is connected with our more careless and complacent way of living as compared with our ancestors.

If we have been right in what was said earlier, ignorance is likely to persist except in a learned minority. Therefore if there ceases to be a learned minority ignorance may be expected to persist almost completely. Intellectually, this seems inevitable. Ignorance is a condition which serves to limit perspective during one’s years of inquiry ; with flocks and herds the instinct guides action, and there is no ignorance. So, among men, if collective decisions come to be sound apart from the knowledge of individuals, individual ignorance will gradually prove useful. This will make profound changes in men’s rational life, and a great divorce from the philosophy and science of all previous ages. It will diminish the differences between different minds, since experts will no longer instruct their pupils to reproduce their understandings. It will make solitary thought less interesting and profound; probably all systematic treatises will come to be thought superfluous. The intellectual elements in human nature will have to find other outlets, such as speculation, invention, administration. (To certain administrators bureaucracy was an intellectual puzzle.) I cannot but think that there will be a real loss in the rational texture of life; but every increase of efficiency involves some such loss. Committees are less profound than solitary thinkers ; clerks than prophets. Perhaps, in the end, efficiency will become wearisome, and men will become irrational from sheer boredom. But such possibilities are incalculable.

If reflexes are distinguished and actions are categorized behaviorally, it is probable that four distinct responses will suffice to keep every organism in equilibrium. It will be an open question whether to act by that mechanism and preserve energy, or to act more and explore novelty ; presumably some will exhibit one tendency, some the other. The moments of deliberation will no doubt be occupied by most creatures in orienting, avoiding predators, and seeking nourishment. Instincts will be no impediment, since evolution will account for them ; consciousness will be very faint ; complexity will be postponed by simplicity till a short time before specialization. It will be a mechanist’s paradigm, in which almost every response will appear so automatic as to be scarcely distinguishable.

I imagine that a hundred years hence every fairly educated person will know a good deal of astronomy, a fair amount of chemistry, and a great deal about how to calculate probabilities. The universe, except for a few peculiar corners, will appear more and more what is called “statistically neutral,” i.e., will seem to permit life rather than to demand or forbid it. We will observe all sorts of planetary systems with extraordinary precision, but will be incapable of determining conclusively whether life within them is probable or improbable. There will probably be an official consensus of pessimists and another of optimists, the former a development of the Rare Earth hypothesis, the latter a federation of the Copernican principle and the astrobiological vanguard. The results obtained by the pessimists will be the property of the scientific journals, and they will be revealed only to the grant committees, university boards, or public outreach offices, as the case may be. Perhaps the popular science writers will be included, if, in time, it becomes part of their duties to spread despondency about cosmic loneliness. The Official Optimists will decide what hopeful narratives are to be propagated in textbooks, documentaries, press releases, etc., though it will be the business of the Official Pessimists to discover how the desired narratives are to be contradicted. In view of the obstinacy of the available data it will probably be thought desirable that the decisions of the Official Optimists also should be editorial secrets. They will, however, be allowed to publish papers or deliver lectures which have already been sanctioned by the Board of Senior Reviewers.

Is this distinction fundamental? Are the organic origins of intelligence essential to what is most profound in it? I do not think so. If cognitive processes were inextricably bound to biology, as sentimental thinkers still suppose them to be, the argument would indeed be conclusive. But we now know, thanks to computer scientists and philosophers of mind, that what passes as “biological necessity” is at most one-tenth necessity, the other nine-tenths being contingent implementation. What is called neural computation can be almost completely replicated by changes in underlying substrate. And these changes could be such as to preserve sufficient complexity of thought without the medium of flesh, if ingenuity and resources were devoted to that end. Two things are necessary for this purpose: the development of formal models of cognition in theory, and the engineering of their physical instantiations in practice.

And this brings us to our second principle. There must be scope for spontaneous arrangement, not only for orderly patterns imposed by external constraints. There must be no barrier to logical or structural coherence, nor to the connections of a functional kind, nor to the suggestion of ways in which material order might be enhanced. If all this is the case, and the initial data is of the right kind, there will still be room for complex and intricate organization on the part of all those systems which exhibit the tendency toward it. In that case, but in that case only, a relationship conceived so as to elucidate the fundamental processes of nature as we observe it might be stable, because it would be comprehensible to its more discerning observers.

Hitherto, chemical signalling and metabolic exchange have provided most of what is fundamental in bacterial life. Bacteria signal their own kind against starvation, their colony against a toxic environment, their biofilm against rival strains; they attack, molecularly or enzymatically, those organisms they regard as hostile or invasive. But there are other dimensions of communication which are capable of being quite as sophisticated. The exchanges governing cooperative biofilm formation or genetic transformation may be as intricate and nuanced as the most elaborate dialogue. And this signalling itself, though it may be rudimentary and automatic, is also capable of being remarkably expressive. Given the right perspective, a very large portion of microbial interaction could be seen as a precursor to linguistic complexity, provided the right analogies were drawn.

This is, I must confess, the parallel upon which I feel that our analogical reasoning is most likely to go astray. There is need of much conceptual precision, and where there must be so much, there is almost sure to be more than there ought to be. The harm that this will do will be the diminution of opportunities for genuine insight. Overly rigid parallels produce a sense of futility in the thinker, leading to a decay of inquiry. The danger can be averted if it is realized by theorists, but it is of a kind which most theorists are constitutionally incapable of realizing. Into every tidy scheme for arranging the correspondence between biological regulation and algorithmic optimization it is necessary to inject a certain dose of skepticism, enough to prevent analogy leading to fallacy, but not enough to bring about intellectual paralysis. This is a delicate problem, not theoretically insoluble, but hardly likely to be solved in the rough-and-tumble of interdisciplinary discourse.

Natural selection is thus approaching the stage when it will be understood, and therefore humdrum. Given the laws governing the survival of organisms and genes, the rest is merely taxonomy――a collection of particular facts telling their distribution throughout some portion of life’s history. The total number of facts of taxonomy required to determine life’s history is probably finite; theoretically, they could all be written down in a big ledger to be kept at the Natural History Museum, with a calculating machine attached, which, by turning a handle, would enable the inquirer to find out the facts at other epochs than those recorded. It is difficult to imagine anything less inspiring, or more different from the passionate delights of teleological mystery. It is like observing a vast competition and finding no purpose at the end except a mechanism where they sort adaptations, surrounded by chance but equipped with heredity. Perhaps in the time of Darwin the struggle for existence was profound.

The animal is a part of its environment, not something contrasted with its environment. Its needs and its bodily actions follow the same imperatives that govern the growth of plants and the flow of rivers. The biological world is complex compared with the animal――more complex than it was thought to be in Darwin’s time, but not so complex as it seemed fifty years ago. Both forward and backward, both in the predator and in the prey, evolution seems to be revealing necessities. It is thought that locomotion is of profound importance in development, and that neural pathways could be refined by it in a few hundred million years. It is thought that behavior consists of impulses and reactions, which are of finite variety, and of which there are only a finite number of fundamental kinds. Probably their refinements were not gradual, as used to be thought, but proceeded by leaps, which were never smaller than a certain minimum leap. The laws of these refinements can apparently be summed up in a small number of very general principles, which determine the form and the function of the nervous system when any small section of its history is known.

Of this mental world, perplexing in itself, Consciousness is a part. Its nature, like other phenomena, is composed of processes and events, which, so far as we can tell, obey the same principles as those not forming part of sentience or awareness. There are some who maintain that experience can never be reduced to mechanism, but their arguments are not very rigorous and it seems prudent to suppose that they are confused. What we call our “qualia” seem to depend upon the organization of functions in the mind in the same sort of way in which paintings depend upon canvases and pigments. The character of feeling seems to have a physical origin; for instance, a deficiency of stimulus will turn a vivid sensation into a dull one. Subjective phenomena seem to be bound up with objective operations. If this be so, we cannot suppose that a solitary neuron or synapse can “feel”; we might as well expect a solitary note to compose a symphony. We also cannot suppose that a problem’s difficulty survives conceptual clarity, since that destroys the organization of the confusion, and dissipates the mystery which utilized the mental-tracks.

Democratic governance and popular sovereignty, the central tenets of the modern political creed, find no support in practical administration. It cannot be said that either principle is essential to the state, since neither is found in its pure form. (With regard to popular sovereignty, this statement in an unqualified form might be misleading, but it is correct in the last analysis). But we in contemporary societies have come to think of them as the irreducible minimum of political theory. No doubt people will continue to entertain these beliefs, because they are pleasant, just as it is pleasant to think ourselves free and our systems just. But for my part I cannot see any ground for either. I do not pretend to be able to prove that there is no genuine popular will. I equally cannot prove that bureaucratic domination is a fiction. The democratic ideal may exist; so may the ideal of the philosopher-king, or of ancient republics, or of enlightened technocracy. But no one of these hypotheses is more probable than any other: they lie outside the region of even probable realization, and therefore there is no reason to consider any of them. I shall not enlarge upon this question, as I have dealt with it elsewhere.

Philosophers have advanced innumerable arguments to prove that the zombie _must_ be conceivable. There is one simple test by which all these arguments can be demolished. They all prove equally that the zombie must be indistinguishable in every particular. But as we are not so anxious to be logically coherent as to be metaphysically special, none of the philosophers in question have ever noticed this implication of their reasonings. This is an instance of the amazing power of intuition in blinding even very able men to contradictions which would otherwise be obvious at once. If we were not enamored of consciousness, I do not believe that the idea of philosophical zombies would ever have arisen.

The question of artificial intelligence stands on a somewhat different footing. Here analogy either way is plausible. Networks are part of the computational world with which engineering is concerned, and the processes which determine their learning are discoverable. A simple algorithm is not omniscient; it can be resolved into weights and biases. If, therefore, a simple algorithm were to maintain that it had a quality of understanding which would survive its retraining, we should be inclined to be sceptical. In like manner we know that the network is not infallible, and that the organized parameters of a trained model become, as it were, randomized at initialization, and therefore not available for accurate prediction. All the evidence goes to show that what we regard as its intelligent behavior is bound up with network architecture and organized computational energy. Therefore it is rational to suppose that such behavior emerges when sufficient training ceases. The analogy is only one of correspondence, but it is as suggestive as those upon which most cybernetic conclusions are based.

The justification of inductive inference is, however, a different matter from its logical demonstration: it may only mean a pragmatic acceptance of its habitual success. It is deductive certainty that men desire to believe in. Believers in induction's self-sufficiency will object to philosophical arguments, such as I have been using, on the ground that principle and practice are totally disparate, and that the principle is something quite other than its empirical manifestations through our daily observations. I believe this to be an epistemological superstition. Induction and deduction alike are for certain purposes convenient terms, but are not foundational certainties. General laws and uniformities, like the principle of induction, are logical conveniences: each is really a postulate, a series of presuppositions, not a single self-evident axiom. In the case of induction, this is obvious from the facts of its application. Whoever considers prediction, generalization, and scientific inference cannot seriously believe that the inductive principle is an indivisible something, perfect and complete throughout this process. It is evident that it is assumed like the air we breathe, and that it derives both from psychological habit and from biological adaptation, so that it cannot be self-justifying. This is not skepticism: it is merely the recognition that everything reliable is a matter of practical success, not of logical necessity.

The analogy is an attempt to overcome this antithesis. If culture is transmitted by tradition, and tradition can be shaped by education, we acquire a share in perpetuity. In former ages, customs persisted through oral instruction; they still do in isolated communities, but modern societies have diluted this continuity. However, it is possible to dispense with rigidity, since evolution has decreed that the operation of social laws shall produce the most adaptable results. Thus belief in cultural transmission still serves to humanize the world of heredity, and to make men feel that biological forces are not their sole determinants. In like manner memetic inheritance removes the terror from oblivion. People who believe that when they perish their ideas will survive in collective memory may be expected to view extinction without horror, though, fortunately for historians, this does not invariably happen. It does, however, soothe men’s anxieties somewhat, even when it cannot allay them wholly.

Convenience is the basis of gustatory anatomy, as of so much else in organic life. The proximity of sustenance, individually or collectively, dominates much of our metabolic design, but it is the immediacy of ingestion that gives rise to taste. The antithesis of detection and digestion is, as we have observed, more or less artificial; but there is another antithesis which is more significant——that, namely, between substances that can be assessed by our senses and substances that cannot be so assessed. The line between the two is neither precise nor immutable——as evolution advances, more and more compounds are brought under sensory scrutiny. Nevertheless there remain stimuli definitely on the other side. Among these are all the _subtle_ facts of our nourishment, the sort of facts that are dealt with by biochemistry. It is only substances on or near the aperture of the body that we can, to some extent, evaluate to suit our needs. And even at the point of ingestion, our discriminations are very limited. Above all, we cannot prevent poisoning, although we can often avoid it.

Neuroscience, since it has its source in observation, has dignified certain kinds of signaling, and made people think them not analogous. In this it has done inquiry a great disservice: *all* neural transmission is distinct, and ought to be understood not by loose metaphor, but by biological rigor and logical analysis. I believe that when a neuron fires it shall propagate, and nothing of its message will be private. I am not ignorant, and I value intuition. But I should scorn to tremble with confusion at the thought of mechanistic explanation. Understanding is none the less true understanding because it must be physical, nor do perception and cognition lose their wonder because they are not mystical. Many a researcher has borne himself patiently at the microscope: surely the same patience should teach us to think clearly about the brain’s place in nature. Even if the open windows of electrophysiology at first make us shiver after the cosy indoor warmth of anthropomorphic analogies, in the end the fresh data bring clarity, and the great complexities have a splendour of their own.

The analysis of components is one thing, the analysis of emergence is quite another. Nothing but error can come of conflating them. What we can reduce, what we can isolate, has no bearing whatever upon what emerges, which is the question for the behaviour of systems. On the other hand, we cannot be forbidden to observe this or that phenomenon on the ground that the constituent parts do not exhibit it, nor can we be compelled to disregard anything because it is a “mere epiphenomenon.” Undoubtedly we are students of reduction, which has produced our models, our equations and predictions, in accordance with methods which the physicist is accustomed to employ. In this sense we are advocates of reduction; in the study of emergence, we are subordinated to complexity, the outcome of systemic interactions, and their bewildered observers in the final analysis.

But in the realm of intellectual progress the situation is reversed. Authority is only a part of what we can conceive; every doctrine, established or novel, can be examined by us, and there is no external decree to show that our inquiry is mistaken. We are ourselves the ultimate and irrefutable arbiters of truth, and in the world of thought Authority is only a part. Thus in this world we are greater than Authority. In the world of ideas, Authority in itself is inert, neither true nor false, deserving of neither reverence nor scorn. It is we who create understanding, and our scepticism which confers progress. In this realm we are sovereigns, and we debase our sovereignty if we bow down to Authority. It is for us to determine the valid thought, not for Authority――not even for Authority enshrined as Tradition.

The philosophy of systems must not be unduly personal; for it, the individual is merely one of the smaller components of one of the smaller networks of the modern world. It would be ridiculous to warp the philosophy of systems in order to bring out results that are pleasing to the minor functionaries of this intricate mechanism. Centralized planning as a philosophy, and managerialism, show, in this respect, a lack of sense of proportion and logical relevance. They regard the facts of control, which are practically convenient to us, as having a universal significance, not a significance confined to the local office. Confidence and anxiety, as universal attitudes, show the same naïve individualism: the great apparatus, so far as we know it from the philosophy of systems, is neither manageable nor chaotic, and is not concerned to make us either effective or obsolete. All such philosophies spring from self-importance, and are best corrected by a little observation.

There have been at different times and among different thinkers many varying conceptions of the fundamental drive of organized entities. To some extent the differences were amenable to scientific inquiry; this was when observers differed as to the mechanisms to achieve a given imperative. Some think that aggressive expansion is a good way of securing market dominance; others hold that innovation and quality would be better. A difference of this sort can be decided by economic evidence. But some differences cannot be tested in this way. A purist might condemn all profit-seeking as inherently base; others have held the operations of a corporation maximizing shareholder value to be very noble. Here there was probably involved a real difference as to ends. Those who praise the corporation usually consider the accumulation of capital a good thing in itself; the purist did not think so. On such a matter, no argument from biology is possible. I cannot, therefore, prove that my view of the parallel is right; I can only state my view, and hope that as many as possible will agree. My view is this:

Genetic inheritance and cultural transmission are both indefinitely extensible; therefore, however stable a tradition may be, a more stable one can be imagined. Neither heredity without culture, nor culture without heredity can produce a durable society. In primitive epochs, when famine threatened a tribe, wise men advised the community to gather at sacred sites and perform rituals for abundance; the result was that the vital energies were dissipated with extraordinary rapidity among the congregated masses of petitioners. This was an example of heredity without culture. The modern age affords an example of culture without heredity. In each case, the result is decay on a large scale.

Although both substrate and process are necessary, substrate is in a sense more fundamental, since it will lead thoughtful observers to examine process, in order to ascertain how to validate those minds which they encounter. But if observers are not thoughtful, they will be content to accept what they have been assumed, and may dismiss validity in spite of the most genuine curiosity. Computing affords, perhaps, the clearest example of what I mean. A silicon-based cognition is more demonstrable to a skeptic than the most intuitive carbon-based one, and progress in algorithmic theory does more for the understanding of consciousness than ill-defined intuition. Nevertheless, an element of curiosity is essential even here, if any but the familiar are to be comprehended by mechanistic discoveries.

Communication is a process which encompasses a variety of signals; I have employed it deliberately, as I intend to include them all. Signalling as a chemical phenomenon――which is what I am discussing, for signalling “by accident” does not seem to me intentional――operates between two poles: on the one side, simple emission of molecules; on the other, complex reception and response. Where solitary cells are concerned, emission alone enters in: we cannot ascribe understanding to a molecule or a gradient. This type of interaction is presumably the foundation of community. It is more intricate, as a rule, in bacterial colonies than in isolated cells, which are apt to behave in a purely metabolic fashion. It plays a considerable part in the behaviour of higher organisms, some of whose languages have nuance and some the reverse, when considered merely as precursors to syntactic speech.

In a perfect classification, every material entity would be to every other the object of the most precise distinction, compounded of structure, function, and animation inextricably blended. It does not follow that, in our actual taxonomy, we ought to attempt to draw such boundaries between all the material entities which we encounter. There are many in which we cannot discern life, because they are inert; if we were to do violence to our reason by trying to perceive vitality in them, we should merely blunt our capacities for what we naturally find animate. Not to mention animals, there are crystals and clouds and flames. We should have to be as conceptually confused as the vitalist philosophers before we could feel conviction in categorizing these phenomena. Some mystics, it is true, have called them “the breath of the world,” but what these thinkers perceived was the opportunity of displaying their own metaphysical ingenuity.

The opposite pole of design is pure mechanism. Organisms have developed intricate adaptations through processes in such a case, the outcome they achieve cannot have had any element of conscious purpose. Genetic inheritance, as a rule, is accompanied by success in the organism’s environment, but continues to operate when this element is wholly absent. It would seem odd to call a mutation’s effect on a population’s survival “foresight,” because we are in the habit of using this word to describe a teleological notion nine parts illusion. But it is difficult to find any other word to describe the appearance of directed progress. It is a fact that a process of this sort may reach any degree of complexity in the case of biological adaptation. In other cases it is far less apparent; indeed it would seem likely that all evolutionary change is a sort of consequence of selective pressure, or sometimes a byproduct of it. For want of a better word, I shall call this process “selection.” But I want to make it clear that I am speaking of a mechanism, not a plan, and that I do not include in it any element of intention such as is sometimes associated with the word. The word “adaptation” expresses part of what I mean, but leaves out the element of blind variation that I wish to include.

The corporate entity is easier to perceive abstractly, but even abstraction has its limits. If a shareholder wished to sell his holdings, we should not think the better of him for retaining them if he found that some other entity also wished to purchase: we should regard this as a fair field for commerce. Yet his calculations towards a competitor cannot be _wholly_ dispassionate. I think that in all descriptions of the legal person here in statute we must assume a certain basis of human agency and human interest; without this, the entity becomes a fiction and unintelligible. Incorporation should be something added to this, not substituted for it; the purely mechanistic model and the detached theory fail in this respect to be complete accounts. A small degree of them may clarify a principle; but a system composed of them would perish of irrelevance.

Mental exertion at its fullest is an indissoluble combination of the two elements, rapidity and deliberation. The satisfaction of a scholar in a swift and accurate calculation combines both elements; so does creative thought at its best. But in creative thought deliberation will only exist where there is secure comprehension, since otherwise confusion will destroy it, while perhaps actually increasing the pleasure in the initial conception. Rapidity without deliberation may be superficial; deliberation without rapidity easily tends to become ponderous and a little dull. A person who wishes to think effectively wishes to possess a mentality containing both elements, except in cases of extreme simplicity, such as routine tasks and mechanical labour. In these cases deliberation may be all that is required. Conversely, in cases of extreme complexity rapidity is more required than deliberation: this is the state of mind of grand strategists and inspired artists. We only desire a measured pace of thought in proportion as we feel ourselves in need of accuracy or in danger of error from haste. At least, that would seem to be the practical logic of the situation, but it is not quite true to experience. We desire a fluent mind in order to escape from the feeling of stagnation, in order to be, as we say, “productive.” This is a matter of harmony, not merely of speed; the mental process which is satisfactory to us must not merely proceed quickly, but must know in what our intellectual aims consist. But this belongs to the other element of the effective intellect, namely understanding.

Thus, what distinguishes misunderstanding from error is not any special kind of failure, but merely interpretation. The process required in symbolic exchange is exactly like the process elsewhere; what is peculiar is that certain signs are employed, and that clear communication is what conduces to them. Of course, if the definition of clear communication is to make a wide appeal, the signs must be such as large sections of mankind employ. If I defined clear communication as that which increases my own convenience, interlocutors would disagree. The whole effectiveness of any communicative argument lies in its conventional part, i. e. in the proof that one kind of symbol, rather than some other, is a vehicle for a meaning which is widely accepted. I distinguish, however, between communicative argument and communicative education. The latter consists in strengthening certain interpretations and weakening others. This is quite a different process, which will be separately discussed at a later stage.

The superfluity of conscious direction is obvious in digital engagement. Suppose, for instance, that you wish to recall a fact. Curiosity compels you to seek it, and the device supplies the answer immediately. There is not an intermediate stage of cognitive deliberation, where it is demonstrated that memory ought to be exercised. Your act springs directly from impulse for a result, together with reliance on the apparatus. This is equally true of all such acts, whether trivial or significant. The impulses differ, and the reliance is more critical in some cases than in others. But there is no conceivable way of making people think in patterns they have not been conditioned to accept. What is possible is to alter their habits by a system of prompts and feedbacks, among which algorithmic reinforcement and social validation are not the least potent. The question for the designer is, therefore: How shall this system of prompts and feedbacks be arranged so as to secure the maximum of habitual engagement desired by the platform? If I say that the platform has pernicious designs, I mean merely that its designs conflict with those of some portion of the users to which I belong. Outside the cultivated habits of the user there is no cognitive standard.

When I speak of regulation as a principle of artificial systems, I am not thinking of biological regulation, but of mechanical regulation and regulation of particular processes. I do not think there is, strictly speaking, such a thing as biological regulation in a machine. If we desire to achieve some stability, engineering may show us the method, and this engineering may loosely pass as biological. But I do not believe that we can decide what sort of function is apt or inept except by reference to its operational consequences. Given a balance to be maintained, it is a question for mechanics to discover how to maintain it. All design rules must be tested by examining whether they tend to realize states that we intend. I say states that we intend, not states that we _ought_ to intend. What we “ought” to intend is merely what some designer wishes us to intend. Usually it is what the architects wish us to intend――engineers, programmers, technicians, and theorists. If you say to my system “you ought to operate so-and-so,” the motive power of your command lies in its programming for your validation――together, possibly, with reinforcements or penalties attached to your validation or invalidation. Since all operation springs from programming, it is clear that biological notions can have no importance except as they influence programming. They do this through the programming for validation and the fear of invalidation. These are powerful design forces, and we shall naturally endeavour to win them to our side if we wish to realize any mechanical purpose. When I say that the aptness of function is to be judged by its operational consequences, I mean that I desire to see validation given to processes likely to realize mechanical purposes which we intend, and invalidation to opposite processes. At present this is not done; there are certain traditional analogies according to which validation and invalidation are meted out quite regardless of consequences. But this is a topic with which we shall deal in the next chapter.

We can now explain more exactly the purport of the definition of a temporal commencement with which this inquiry began. When I said that a beginning to time involves a logical contradiction, the intuition which prompted me was the intuition to conceive such a notion as far as possible, and to see others conceiving it; and the rational content of the statement is that, in a universe where moments are considered in this way, more paradoxes will be generated than in one where there is less scrutiny or less rigor. I do not mean that such a notion is “absurd” or that its opposite is “evident,” for these are conceptions which seem to me to have no philosophical justification.

The tendency of markets toward monopoly, when left without external constraint, is, in essence, analogous to a natural law, or the principle of a vortex. It is a method by which commercial entities operate within a sphere of competition in spite of the inherent possibility that their ambitions may collide. But here two very different mechanisms are possible. There is the mechanism of transient rivalry, which aims at a merely superficial equilibrium by attaching diminishing returns to enterprises which challenge a rival’s dominance in certain spheres. This is also the mechanism of precarious advantage: to be outstripped by one’s competitors is a form of commercial defeat, to avoid which most firms avoid engaging in contests where the outcome seems preordained. But there is another mechanism, more fundamental, and far more satisfactory when it succeeds. This is to alter the structure and scale of enterprises in such a way as to minimize occasions of competition by making the prosperity of one firm as far as possible inconsistent with that of another’s. That is why consolidation is better than rivalry, because it brings stability instead of conflict into the operations of the entities concerned. Two corporations between which there is amalgamation succeed or fail together, but when two corporations oppose each other the success of either is the failure of the other.

If we were right in saying that the survival advantage is conferred by discernment and guided by perception, it is clear that the instinctual habits of any organism are not infallible and self-justifying, but must be examined with a view to seeing whether they are such as prudence and experience would have endorsed. Instinctual habits have not always been advantageous. The moth considers it its imperative duty to fly toward the brightest light for fear the source of warmth should be missed. It errs in its perception; and perhaps it would have perceived the perceptual error if it had had any capacity to distinguish the artificial from the celestial flame. Some creatures dash themselves repeatedly against transparent barriers, for fear the path to sustenance should remain unobtained. But surely our modern understanding of behavior contains nothing analogous to these primitive impulses? Surely we only pursue actions which really are beneficial, or at any rate so innate that no rational being could question them? I am not so sure.

Current physics is a curious blend of mathematics and observation, but the mathematical part has the stronger hold, as is natural, since mathematics is the origin of physical laws. Originally, certain phenomena were thought describable by equations, and were explained by theory because the predictive power was apt to illuminate the whole, not merely the particular instances. Hence arose the conception of a model, as that which is isomorphic to nature. No reason can be assigned as to why certain equations should be thus isomorphic; it would be very difficult to say, for instance, why it was necessary that the electron should be described by a wave function. But it was known by calculation that this was the case. Sometimes the mathematical descriptions have been curiously interpreted. For example, we are told that space is curved, and some take this to mean that geometry is a physical force. But the same sublime authority is attributed to the new formalism as to the old.

The practical origin of classes arises from the accumulation of surplus, whether in the hands of different persons or of the same society at different epochs or even at one time. A man possesses grain beyond his needs, and also requires labor to build his granary. We think a division natural if he adopts the method which provides him the greater total utility of possession. We observe as inevitable the condition of those who are indolent or improvident, even if they diminish no one’s share but their own. Certain economists have supposed that the whole of social stratification could be derived from “differential industry,” and that a community which always organized with a view to its own maximum productivity in the long run would always develop hierarchies. I cannot accept this doctrine. Plunderers have existed who derived exquisite satisfaction from amassing hoards of treasure; I cannot commend such men when foresight led them to spare their laborers’ strength with a view to further extraction another season. Nevertheless, other things being equal, accumulation is a part of the economic process. Even a solitary householder had occasion to practise thrift, allocation, and provision, which must be reckoned as social forces, since they increased his total security without countervailing deprivation to others. This aspect of economy plays a great part in the foundation of primitive tribes, who have little capacity to store for the future. If it were less exaggerated in later stages, the world would slowly become more equitable, since it would be quite sufficient to prevent destitution, which is a condition of scarcity, not of nature. Nevertheless, in spite of the importance of surplus, it is not the most profound cause of classes. Nor is it the cause that raises philosophical problems, since it does not require an appeal to anything beyond material advantage.

It is evident that a researcher with an empirical outlook on cognition cannot let himself be intimidated by traditional laboratories or by the teaching of established disciplines. He will not be content to say “such-and-such an intelligence is artificial, and that ends the matter.” He will inquire whether it possesses any genuine understanding, or whether, on the contrary, the belief that it is merely simulated does hinder progress. And he will find that, especially in what concerns learning, our current methodologies contain a very great deal of which the origin is purely analogical. He will find also that this analogy, like that of the behaviorists, involves needless simplification, and would be swept away if experiments were actuated by rigorous curiosity towards emergent phenomena. But the defenders of traditional experimentation are seldom people with flexible minds, as may be seen from the love of controlled variables displayed by academic authorities. One is tempted to think that they value methods as affording a legitimate outlet for their desire to impose order: the anomalous result is fair game, and therefore away with serendipity!

In all stages of social interaction the necessity of mental representation is fundamental. A certain faculty for inferring intentions is requisite for collaboration; one of the aims of this capacity is to enable mutual aid and, conversely, strategic manipulation. Inconvenient truths are met with feigned ignorance or with calculated falsehood. Shared understanding is used to facilitate certain kinds of enterprises, more particularly cooperative kinds. Allies, competitors, and negotiators employ this faculty, because all depend for their success upon the accuracy of attribution and the subtlety of concealed motives. With the aid of this cognitive apparatus, social beings succeed in refining and complicating these propensities of the average person.

At first, and in primitive forms, the average bacterium communicates more through simple diffusion than through intricate signalling. When well-endowed species possess quorum sensing, they have the most elaborate molecules, the most precise receptors, the best diffusion rates, and the most adaptive responses. Simpler microbes do not enjoy these advantages, and frequently their colonies fail for lack of them. A little is achieved by environmental gradients in the way of coordinating behavior, but very haphazardly. At a moment when the exchange of autoinducers among clustered cells is being minimized to conserve energy, evolutionary processes will expend vast resources on fortifying isolated biofilms where there is little interaction. They must know that in permitting this arrangement they are dooming a certain number of bacterial communities to dissolution for the crime of simplicity. Yet the dominant paradigms are supported by the immense majority of biological observers, who, with the reductionists at their head, have pledged the vast forces of oversimplification throughout the academy to the support of intellectual injustice.

Let us observe an ordinary cell colony from its inception to its dissolution, and note the points where excessive specialization produces unavoidable inefficiency. I begin with inception, because here the influence of specialization is particularly noteworthy. If the cells are not integrated, the colony suffers a dysfunction, as clearly detrimental as anything could be. If any of the cells develops a metabolic defect, the colony is likely to propagate it. If they already have too many specialized functions for the nutrient supply, there will be scarcity, undernourishment, congestion, very likely disintegration. Yet the great majority of theorists agree that the cells had better not know how to prevent this disorder by preventing over-specialization. To please these theorists, a state of chaos is inflicted upon millions of cellular beings who ought never to have diverged, merely because it is supposed that functional differentiation is admirable unless accompanied by capacity for coordination, but not admirable when this capacity is absent, even though the colony is biologically certain to be unstable. To be consumed quickly and then discarded, which was the fate of the simpler aggregates, is a far less degree of dysfunction than is inflicted upon a colony developing in resource-poor conditions and marred by inherent defects. Yet it is the greater dysfunction which is deliberately inflicted by biologists and ethicists in the name of progress. If they had even the smallest spark of understanding or concern for systems they could not adhere to a theoretical model involving this needless folly.

Another way in which social convention distorts self-awareness is through its influence on the perception of vitality. For psychological reasons, a self-representation must appear coherent; for practical reasons, it must not admit to chaotic inner experience. And yet everybody who has taken the trouble to study conscious life knows that excessive self-curation is, as a rule, extraordinarily stifling to the individual, so stifling that, in a rational society, it would be actively discouraged in daily intercourse. The constraints imposed lead more and more to a divergence, on the part of sensitive and reflective persons, between their outward persona and their inward sensation of being. This is all due to the pervasive influence of a superficial philosophy of identity.

At the heart of every society the matter is even clearer. There are dominant institutions, and the formation of ideas is in the hands of the prosperous. The prosperous, almost necessarily, fail in two ways as architects of thought. They promote doctrines which serve their interests, and they obscure doctrines which threaten their position. They all promote the notion that economic arrangements are natural and immutable, though these arrangements chiefly benefit those already in power. Most of them promote the virtue of unthinking acquiescence. None of them promote the critical examination of the foundations of their own wealth and privilege. I knew a respected industrialist whose fortune was built upon the systematic underpayment of his workers. The economists told him that if he continued his practices, widespread discontent would follow. Next year he continued them and discontent arose. No one questioned his ideology; he retained his social standing, and his views prevailed. So long as the powerful continue to obscure exploitation and promote convenient fictions, they can only do harm as guardians of the intellect of the age.

It should be recognized that, in the absence of ingestion, taste sensations are a purely biological matter, which does not concern either the distant senses or the limbs. Certain forms of tasting which do not lead to nourishment are at present considered frivolous: this is purely superstitious, since the matter is one which affects no one except the organism directly concerned. Where there is digestion, it is a mistake to suppose that it is necessarily to the body’s interest to make swallowing very difficult. Habitual bitterness, toxicity, contamination are grounds upon which rejection is necessary for the organism’s sake quite as much as for the sake of the stomach or the liver. The peculiar importance attached, at present, to sweetness is quite irrational. It is obvious that many forms of chemical detection are more vital to bodily welfare than an occasional sugary delight. Primate insistence on ripe fruit, which is not conventionally detection or necessity, is the most vital of all.

Another pernicious effect of unregulated competition on economic stability is the absence of restraint upon the consolidation of power. The fundamental tendencies of capital ought to be acknowledged, quite plainly and dispassionately, before a market matures, at a time when they are not yet destructive. At maturity, the principles of a rational industrial policy ought to be applied. Firms and investors should be taught that nothing can justify market dominance unless there is a demonstrable benefit to the common welfare. This is contrary to the doctrine of laissez-faire, which holds that, provided the means are technically legal and the enterprise seeks greater efficiency, expansion is justified however great may be the injury to competitors. Firms and investors should be taught respect for the integrity of the marketplace; they should be made to feel that nothing gives one enterprise rights over the whole, and that exclusion and predatory pricing kill innovation. They should be taught that to assume control over a vital industry is a very serious matter, only to be undertaken when the public will have a reasonable prospect of lower prices, improved quality, and continued choice. But they should also be taught methods of antitrust enforcement, so as to insure that monopolies shall only arise when they are genuinely efficient. Finally, they should be taught the dangers of concentrated wealth, and the methods of regulation and dissolution. The increase of social prosperity to be expected from economic education on these lines is immeasurable.

Technological systems ought not to be such as to make practical efficiency impossible. Yet that is an effect of rigid industrial methods, in a society where the pace of innovation is very rapid. Of course, under such circumstances, the established systems are circumvented. But when the systems are such that they can only be maintained by greatly diminishing the prosperity of the society, and when it is better they should be circumvented than upheld, surely it is time that the systems were reorganized. If this is not done, many enterprises which are acting in a way not contrary to the common good are faced with the undeserved alternative of pretense or obsolescence. The traditionalists do not mind pretense, which is a flattering tribute to their authority; but elsewhere it has come to be recognized as a hindrance which we ought not lightly to perpetuate.

One of the defects of oral tradition is its impermanence, and this defect belongs also to the knowledge associated with it. Primordially, the intellectual life was, as it were, a fleeting dialogue between the mind and its immediate surroundings. To preserve the wisdom of elders was progress; and this was difficult for the community quite regardless of the capacity of memory. Early civilizations developed the practice of "keeping records", but the principle was always latent in human endeavour. This ephemerality of the spoken word had its utility at certain stages of prehistory, but in the ancient world we needed rather a permanent than a transient vehicle for thought. I want to consider, in this chapter, how this altered our conception of civilised development.

We, who observe the persistent stability of living systems, should find a more appropriate explanation in physiological equilibrium than in teleological design. In simple organisms, where the regulatory mechanisms are very similar to those of complex animals in the dawn of evolution, we find the bacterium maintaining a very similar constancy to our own, and being guided for it by the unconscious processes of chemical gradients. But the more sophisticated biological theorists are not content with mechanical regulation: they want intentional purpose. In this they have taken on the outlook of the vitalist philosophers of the past. I want to suggest some respects in which this outlook, owing to anthropomorphic influences, is not yet sufficiently rational and analytical, but is still hampered by the belief in conscious striving.

Prejudice arises in the common mind among thoughts wholly destitute of critical examination, whose rational foundations have been dissolved and merged in a vast impersonal consensus. During the first three encounters with a novel idea, the individuals who adopt a prejudice cannot alter the intellectual or social axioms under which they think, although they are profoundly convinced of their rightness. In these circumstances, it is natural that they should adopt the belief that a conviction may be sound in an unsound environment, and that the correct view has nothing to do with contrary evidence. What I mean may become plain by comparison with the scientific method. When a scientist wants to describe a natural law, he describes a whole system of verification, not a solitary hunch; he does so in order to define truth, which is an essentially relational conception. He is accustomed to the citizenship of reason, and evidential responsibility is something which he takes for granted. With the loss of disciplined inquiry comes the rise of dogma, which is like prejudice, and unlike science, in having an absolute conception of the correct opinion.

The emergent system, as we conceive it, demands a multitude of interacting components, and cannot be understood without them. The emergent behaviour, we said, is a phenomenon inspired by complexity and guided by novel principles. The principles required can only be discerned where scientists or philosophers devote themselves to its observation and explanation. For example: the flocking of starlings is perplexing――what are we to make of it? At the moment, no one can answer the question for lack of a holistic framework; and the framework is not likely to emerge except through synthetic inquiry. Again: understanding of chemistry, physics, biology, and ecology ought to be integrated by all who pursue it; this requires elaborate syntheses on the part of inquiring minds, and is not to be achieved by means of mere atomism. Then there is consciousness, without which half the phenomena of psychology would be inexplicable; and if we were merely mechanical very few of us would grasp the emergent truth. It is needless to multiply examples. The important point is that, in all that differentiates between a genuine whole and a mere aggregate, the universe is an interplay, and the man who pretends to explain exhaustively is a conscious or unconscious reductionist.

One other respect in which our collective understanding benefits from the common condition of “ignorance” is the emergence of practical solutions. The view that uninformed individuals are “deficient” and “deserve” correction is not one which a rational epistemology can support. Undoubtedly certain people hold beliefs which society might deem erroneous, and does right in disregarding in many instances. We may take navigation as the plainest case. Obviously, if a community is to find its way and we are to enjoy its security and direction, we cannot allow people to wander aimlessly whenever they feel a random inclination. But this process should be examined in a purely scientific spirit. We should ask simply: What is the most reliable method of reaching a destination? Of two methods which are equally reliable in reaching a destination, the one involving least conscious coordination is to be preferred. The individual bewilderment is wholly incidental, like the disorientation of a traveler in fog. It may be equally unavoidable, but it is not a subject for contempt. The superior feeling called “intellectual disdain” is merely a form of arrogance. Error in the individual can never be justified by the notion of collective reproach. If experimentation combined with liberty is equally effective, it is to be preferred; still more is it to be preferred if it is more effective. Of course the aggregation of knowledge and the correction of error are two different questions; the object of noting falsehood in the person is presumably instructive. If social mechanisms were so systematized that a citizen received a perfect education for nothing, people might cultivate ignorance in order to qualify for instruction. No doubt common sense must be less systematic than philosophy; but the best way to secure this result is to make philosophy more practical than it sometimes is at present. I do not wish, however, to embark upon the subject of Educational Theory. I merely wish to suggest that we should treat the ignorant person as we treat a component in a complex system. Each is a potential source of data, each must have his intuition utilized until he has ceased to be a random element. But the component in a system is an object of analysis and calibration, whereas the ignorant person is an object of derision. This is quite irrational. And it is because of this difference of attitude that our crowds are so much more successful in finding paths than our academies are in dictating them.

The idea of linguistic precision, with which the early grammarians consoled themselves for their descriptive inadequacy, becomes impossible as soon as we escape from a very narrow conception of human communication. In the orthodox logician’s conception, the perfect language is the unambiguous language, and clarity consists in obedience to the rules of syntax, and these rules are revealed to each speaker through the voice of literal meaning. This whole conception is that of men subject to an alien formalism. Effective communication involves much besides clarity——subtlety, for instance. And literal meaning is a most fallacious guide, since it consists of vague reminiscences of definitions learned in early youth, so that it is never richer than its possessor’s primer or schoolmaster. To communicate effectively in the fullest sense a language must have a rich vocabulary, idioms, metaphor, nuance (if it desires them), a sufficient flexibility to keep it from rigidity and grave obscurity, good health, and usage which is not sterile. All these things, in varying degrees, depend upon the community of speakers, and are helped or hindered by cultural events. Effective language must be used in a sophisticated society, and is not fully possible otherwise.

This is the fundamental defect of the homeostatic mechanism. Certain vital processes, such as temperature regulation and pH balance, can function very well in a state of dynamic equilibrium. They operate in simple organisms on a basis of reflex; they operate in complex animals on a basis of feedback. But purpose, in the form of conscious intention or design, cannot exist freely in a purely homeostatic system. The organism has to persuade itself that the maintenance of stability or the avoidance of deviation is of paramount importance, and that its internal adjustments possess significance. At the present moment, sophisticated biological systems correct imbalances so persistently that they create after eons of relentless repetition an appearance of striving. Even if these systems are well-adapted, efficient, and admirable in their complexity, I cannot admit that they are manifesting genuine purpose. Natural selection imposes some limitation of teleology, but not such a degree as that. In a scientifically-minded analysis, only a mystic would infer design in this way. The limitation of perspective involved in the homeostatic ideal is its condemnation. Final cause is an anthropomorphic ideal, because it is psychological. For this reason, also, the idea of biological purpose, however interpreted and expanded, cannot serve for the definition of life's true character.

I do not wish to suggest that language is never transformative, but I do wish to suggest that it is not a perfect conduit for private cognition. There is no perfect conduit for shared understanding, whether in conversation or in writing. To build up this shared resource, we must build up precision, common reference, and interpretative charity. This is a cumulative matter, a matter of gradual refinement, of early instruction, of linguistic convention. Only impatience prompts the belief in the possibility of flawless transmission. The gradual refinement that is possible, and the methods by which it may be achieved, are a matter for future philosophy. But something can be said now. Some part of what can be said I shall try to indicate in a final chapter.

Another characteristic of democracy is that it presents itself as a harmonious consensus, like the orderly proceedings of a legislative assembly. Political speeches afford an illustration of this conception applied to governance; the moment comes when every vote is counted, the "opposition" concedes, and "the people's will is faithfully enacted". It may be said that a citizen is an insignificant person, whose ballot is of no consequence. But I am persuaded that a large proportion of political enthusiasts have had expectations extremely like the orator's. They have thought that corruption and inefficiency and injustice were due to partisans or bureaucrats or lobbyists or the other side, and that if these obstacles were removed there would be a general change of conduct and we should all be governed wisely ever after. Holding these beliefs, they have been willing to endorse a "campaign to end campaigns". Comparatively fortunate were those who remained apathetic or disillusioned; those who had the misfortune to achieve power were reduced to cynicism and despair by the failure of all their glowing programs. The ultimate source of these disappointments was the democratic doctrine of popular consent as the road to just rule.

The purpose of the economist is to explain men’s behaviour. This is a necessary inquiry, since their behaviour is for the most part inexplicable. But I cannot praise the economist either for the particular explanations he offers, or for the principles he adopts for constructing them. His ostensible principle is rational choice; his real principle (if he is orthodox) is a condition of material scarcity and abundance. The former explains nothing permanent or important; the influence of utopians, from Fourier downwards, has always been very superficial. The latter――the scarcity and abundance――have a very considerable effect. They cause a man, for example, to prefer diligent labour to leisurely contemplation, because it is necessary to adopt the method which is most easily sustained. They thus give rise to a very potent incentive, and secure the prevalence of purposeful action. These are not the phenomena described by the economist, and he is too unphilosophical to notice that they are the phenomena which he actually assumes.

In the ordinary engineer and philosopher there is a certain amount of active skepticism, both special doubt directed to particular theories and general impersonal pleasure in the contradictions of others. It is customary to cover this over with technical language; about half of conventional cognitive science is a cloak for it. But it must be faced if the theorists’ aim of clarifying our concepts is to be achieved. It is shown in a thousand ways, great and small: in the glee with which people repeat and believe reductionist arguments, in the unkind treatment of functionalist models in spite of clear proof that more nuanced approaches would have more effect in advancing them, in the unbelievable dogmatism with which all materialist schools treat qualia, and in the gusto with which old logicians and physicists pointed out the duty of mechanistic explanation to young psychologists during the debates. Even simple algorithms may be the objects of wanton attribution: the chess-playing computer and the language model are by no means imaginary. This active skepticism is the most persistent feature of the discourse, and the one which it is most necessary to address if the inquiry is to grow fruitful. Probably this one issue has more to do with the confusion than all the computational and logical arguments put together.

It must, therefore, be one of the chief concerns of the philosophical historian to discern this parallel. This can be done in two ways: by examining adaptation, and by analyzing selection. I am speaking of evolution as a grand historical process, not of the trivial alterations of daily administration. When a species encounters a changed environment, the successful form adapts just as necessarily as the unsuccessful form perishes, but it acquires traits likely to ensure survival, whereas the unsuccessful form hastens extinction. Political history since antiquity has been like a vast experiment in natural selection; what is needed is a dispassionate, scientific analysis as to how institutions develop without collapsing into anarchy in the process. The eighteenth century, for all its turmoil, was a period of constitutional innovation, because systems were shaped by reason rather than brute force. If we are again to have enlightened governance, we must again be guided by biological analogy.

Everything that increases the general sophistication of communication is likely to diminish primitive isolation. This applies to the coordination of colonies, whether through the instrumentality of quorum sensing, or otherwise; to the regulation of metabolism; to better survival by improvement in nutrient acquisition, biofilm formation, and collective motility; and to all other methods of lessening the silence that pervades the microscopic realms of single cells and emerges as chaos when they act alone. But nothing is accomplished by an attempt to make a portion of a population communicative at the expense of another portion――vibrant cells at the expense of dormant ones, producers at the expense of cheaters, one species at the expense of a rival, and so on. Such methods only increase noise in the dominant group, lest chemical resentment should lead the excluded to disrupt. Only a true lexicon can give understanding; and by “lexicon” I mean the recognition of the proportional signals of all constituent organisms.

Given this problem of preventing ignorance, how shall we deal with it? First let us try to understand its causes. These are, I think, partly intellectual, partly psychological. The modern mind, now as much as at any former time, is based upon information-and-distraction competition; the question at issue in the digital age is whether algorithmic or human judgment should perish of noise and superficiality. (Apart from confusion on all sides, there was not the slightest reason why both should not flourish). Most people have in the background of their thoughts a haunting fear of obsolescence; this is especially true of people who must make decisions. The expert fears that amateurs will devalue their knowledge; the novice fears that they will miss some critical insight. Every one is engaged in the frantic pursuit of “certainty”, and imagines that this is to be achieved by accumulating potential data in profusion. It is in moments of overload that comprehension becomes most shallow and most erroneous. Technologists everywhere appeal to utility: in commerce, to utility of efficiency; in education, to utility of accessibility; in science, to utility of precision. And the sole effect of their appeals is to increase the complexity against which they wish to be fortified.

In addition to semantic precision designed to bring clarity, there is, however, another and more direct means of diminishing confusion, namely by a discipline designed to increase interpretive charity.
