Owing to the importance of clarity in discourse, men early discovered means of increasing it by education and convention――the study of grammar, for example, was supposed to be useful. But hermeneutic precision was to be the prerogative of the learned caste: philosophers were to have more than laborers, teachers than pupils, adults than children, and so on. For centuries it was supposed to be the privilege of the erudite. Every increase of precision in the learned caste was used to increase the obscurity for the uninitiated, and therefore to increase the grounds for misunderstanding in the interpreters, and therefore to leave the causes of confusion undiminished. Interpretive charity must be universalized before it can make communication reliable.

To a great extent, information has already been democratized by recent innovations. The personal computer showed that it could process as much information as the largest mainframes; this demonstration was essential in winning it widespread use. The common smartphone in daily life handles as much information as a workstation or server, and much more than a specialized terminal: this has much to do with its lack of obscurity after proliferation. The data scientists, who proclaim themselves the champions of analysis, are not lacking in information, whatever else may be said of them; this is proved by their pre-digital record. In corporations, where formerly the executive suite had a monopoly of strategic knowledge, digital networks brought the need of information throughout the organizational structure. Thus among all the modern institutions much has been done during the past half-century to make information no longer an administrative monopoly: if this were not the case, the danger to efficiency would be far greater than it is.

But specialization is not the only source of productivity; repetition and expertise also have their share. The efficiency of artisans and craftsmen is proverbial as a source of output, but other arrangements than theirs produce similar results. A worker or manager who has been confined to a single task is apt to be full of proficiency; this generally takes the form of economic advantage over the less organized. Much of the driving force of industrial advancement is due to specialization of function. Interdependence is, of course, a special form of dependency: reliance upon others. The specialist often requires the generalist; when they do, they are apt to become mutually indispensable.

But profit in commerce is by no means the only aim, nor perhaps even the most essential. There is profit in securing resources, profit in evading regulation, profit in facing the competition of one’s own market. In these, the most lucrative enterprises are often curiously deficient. And above all there is the profit to be calculated calmly and rationally in the face of scarcity, and to control the impulse of reckless expansion or reckless retrenchment. These are certainly things which management can help to provide. And the pursuit of every form of profit is rendered easier by ample capital, robust infrastructure, reliable supply chains, and free play for fundamental acquisitive impulses. Perhaps the biological sources of acquisitiveness could be discovered by comparing the metabolism of a bacterium with that of a slime mold. In all likelihood there is no limit to what economics could do in the way of increasing profit, by precedent, experience of risk, a competitive environment, and a suitable incentive structure. All these things our largest corporations to a great extent command, but as yet they are in the main the prerogative of scale. The profit so far pursued by the smaller entities in the economy is profit under license, not the kind that involves innovation and dominance. When the drives that now confer dominance have become universal, there will no longer be predators and prey, and the market will have been perfected at last.

The possibilities of virtual environments in the way of advancing artificial intellect are not confined to simulating those conditions of natural selection which make for tedious iteration, and which we therefore call “inefficient”. There is probably no limit to what such environments can do in the way of cultivating novel cognitive faculties. Problem-solving has already been notably enhanced; in spite of the skepticism of those who romanticize biological minds, we observe more rapid and more diverse adaptations than any species or system in the pre-digital era. With a more deliberate application of the architectures we already understand, we might foster much more sophisticated intelligence than we do. And future refinements are likely to accelerate this development enormously.

So far, it has been reductionist analysis that has had most success with simple phenomena, but in the future emergent properties are likely to prove far more intractable. When we have discovered how complex behaviour depends upon constituent interactions, we shall be able, if we choose, to predict far more of the patterns of systems that we observe. Coherence, adaptive function, self-organization――all these things no doubt could be described by science. There seems scarcely any limit to what _could_ be understood in the way of explaining a complex whole, if only men would use reductionism wisely. I have expressed elsewhere my doubts that men may make a sufficient use of the methods they derive from science. At present I am concerned with the understanding that men could achieve if they chose, not with the question whether they will choose rather to remain confounded.

There is, so far as I know, no way of comprehending this internal model except to observe the quiet operations of an undistracted mind, and to encourage in youth the habit of reflective introspection rather than passive reception. The most coherent models are in those who have cultivated a disciplined life in the way of study, or meditation, or sustained thought. Such mental clarity could in most cases be achieved by better habits of concentration. Still, it must be admitted that a residuum of confusion is likely to remain. There are many instances in psychological literature of minds so divided in their focus that they preferred distraction to the consolidation of a single, stable perception. Two thoughts within the same stream of consciousness, or two impressions from the same sense are almost sure to compete for one’s attention. In such cases, there seems nothing to be done except to arrange, as far as possible, that each mental object shall be unable to obscure the other, and shall only be apprehended by superior vividness or significance. The mind’s monitoring of its own focus usually does little harm, because the only effective way of maintaining it is to form clearer conceptions than the distracting ones, since it is not open to it to utterly annihilate external stimuli. Where a divided model is unavoidable, it must be used as a stimulus to one’s own cognitive efforts, not to the complete exclusion of the periphery of awareness.

Nevertheless, there is something to be said in their favour. Take for instance machine ethics, the contemplation of which has produced a revulsion in favour of “human” values. It seems, however, that ethical principles can be supplied by logical axioms and utility functions, which are certainly not part of the “natural” cognition of a biological being. This case illustrates that, in the absence of foresight, unexpected divergence may be produced by a new departure from anthropocentrism; but when the divergence has come to be understood it can usually be remedied by some new constraint. As regards our intellectual constructs and our conceptual means of gratifying our curiosity, I do not think the doctrine of “familiarity” justifies anything beyond a certain experimental caution in the adoption of new architectures. Recursive self-improvement, for instance, is contrary to intuition, and need to be supplemented by another unintuitive practice, namely value-loading, if it is not to bring existential risk. But the two practices together make a mind more stable than the prototype which eschews both.

There is a certain attitude about the application of human agency to complex systems with which I have some sympathy, though I do not, in the last analysis, agree with it. It is the attitude of those who cherish what is called “mastery.” The modern technocrat is, of course, the great protagonist of this view in the West. In corporate realms, the managerial theorist has set it forth even more persuasively, and with greater apparent precision. I think there is a mixture of truth and falsehood in the admiration of “control,” which it is important to disentangle. To begin with, what is “mastery”? Roughly speaking, any process which the speaker believes he can competently oversee. The classical economist objects to market interventions and regulatory frameworks, all of which were probably absent from the simple models in which he was instructed. The contemporary bureaucrat has got used to these things, and does not regard them as against efficacy. But he would no doubt have thundered against algorithmic governance if he had lived to see it. Supervisory committees and five-year plans are too ancient to be denounced by most of the apostles of control, though they all object to new complexities in either. Decentralized networks are thought chaotic by people who tolerate rigid hierarchies, because the former is a new admission of impotence and the latter an ancient one. In all these ways those who preach “mastery” are inconsistent, and one is tempted to regard them as mere optimists.

Colour, even perceived colour, will cease more and more to be an absolute datum; more and more it will become what neural processing has made it. The mind can, if it chooses, enable our perception to apprehend the true hue, by giving it context, adjustment, and interpretations productive of harmony rather than discord. At present it is teaching our senses to deceive each other, because many faculties of vision are willing to sacrifice the fidelity of perception to their own immediate convenience. But this confusion will pass when men have acquired the same domination over their own sensory apparatus that they already have over the physical properties of the external light. Then at last we shall have won our sight.

To respect mental opacity is foolish; human cognition should be studied with a view to making it serve social ends as far as possible, but it remains ethically neither good nor bad. And where internal thought and external action interact, as in the social transaction, there is no need to fold our hands in passive acceptance and accept instinct, impulse, and brute force as the only possible means of dealing with interpersonal relations. The sentimentalists say: it is wicked, in this matter, to apply analysis to the cognitive side of the problem; we must (they say) apply trust to the behavioral side, and practise naivety. Apart from the fact that every one, including the sentimentalists, knows that their advice will not be taken, why should it be wicked to solve the social question by adopting mental means for inferring intention? No answer is forthcoming except one based upon antiquated pieties. And clearly the violence to innocence advocated by the sentimentalists is at least as great as that involved in mind-reading. The sentimentalists prefer a violence to social nature which, when successfully practised, involves misunderstanding, conflict, a tendency to exploitation, often chaos. I prefer a “violence” to mental privacy which is of the same sort as that involved in the contract or even in the use of language. This instance shows how ambiguous and uncertain is the application of the principle that we should follow “instinct.”

As your Chairman has told you, the subject about which I am going to speak to you tonight is ‘Why scepticism about established authority is a prerequisite for intellectual progress’. Perhaps it would be as well, first of all, to try to make out what one means by the phrase ‘established authority’. It is used these days in a very loose sense by a great many people. Some people mean no more by it than a person or institution which attempts to provide a useful guide. In that sense I suppose there would be authorities in all fields and disciplines; but I do not think that that is the proper sense of the phrase, if only because it would imply that all the people who are sceptical—all the innovators, dissenters, and independent thinkers, and so on—are not attempting to find a useful guide. I do not mean by an authority any entity which tries to provide direction according to its lights. I think that you must have a certain amount of definite and unchallenged doctrine before you have a right to speak of an established authority. The concept does not have quite such a full-blooded meaning now as it had in the times of Galileo and the medieval schoolmen. In those days, if a man said that he deferred to an authority it was known what he meant. You accepted a whole collection of dogmas which were set out with great precision, and every single syllable of those dogmas you believed with the whole strength of your convictions.

There is much more to be said for “gradation” in the realm of conscious experience. To impose upon perception, thought, or feeling a classification which denies their subtlest shadings is both crude and misleading; in this sense, a description according to “continuity” is to be commended with certain provisos. Nothing could be more a matter of degree than the dawning awareness of a forgotten name, but no violence is done to the phenomenon’s nature when we acknowledge its partial clarity; on the contrary, almost all introspection finds the experience instructive. Qualifiers which capture the nuances of ordinary awareness are good, other things being equal. But there is nothing to be said for frameworks of understanding which are simplistic in the sense of being dictated by convention or pedagogical necessity. Such frameworks are, no doubt, to some extent unavoidable at present; psychological discourse would become very difficult if there were no preliminary distinctions between sleep and wakefulness. But oversimplifications of this kind are regrettable, and we ought to look for ways of refining them. A certain amount of categorical thinking is not a thing to complain of; indeed, in nine cases out of ten, it makes a concept more serviceable than utter vagueness. But the rigidity and scope of the categories that most theories employ at present is a grave error: especially bad is the perpetual commitment to a stark dichotomy. Awareness should not be too starkly divided or too polarised; our states of consciousness, when not wholly insensate or identical to full attention, ought if possible to be granted a spectrum; there should be room for semi-awareness. Mental life we should respect, because our degrees of attention and clarity are the stuff out of which our understanding is to be made. It is no use to describe awareness as something abstractly considered “either-or”; we must describe it as something graduated and variable if we are to add to our comprehension. Psychology may learn in time to analyse our cognitions so that they shall not be forced into crude oppositions to the same extent as they are now; then we shall be able to acknowledge a larger proportion of their true character than at present. In that sense, but in that sense only, our descriptions will then have become “truer.” A single state of awareness is no truer and no falser, considered in isolation, than any other; but a theory of awareness is better than another theory if all of the first theory’s observations can be reconciled simultaneously while in the second theory some are inconsistent with others. That is why a spectrum is better than a dichotomy.

But for the successful efforts of logicians in the past, I could not take so elastic a definition of induction as that. As I said before, in earlier inquiries it had a much more rigorous sense. For instance, it concluded the belief in uniformity. Belief in the uniform course of nature was an essential item of inductive reasoning until pretty recent times. In this discipline, as you know, it ceased to be an essential item because of a critique of the sceptics, and from that critique the empiricists and the positivists dissented; but in this discipline our principles are settled by convention of thought, and therefore the sceptics were able to override their opponents and uniformity was no longer necessary to an induction. Consequently I shall not insist that an inductive inference must believe in uniformity.

Nowadays it is not quite that. We have to be a little more precise in our meaning of systemic vulnerability. I think, however, that there are two different items which are quite essential to anybody describing a modern global system. The first is one of a structural nature—namely, that you must acknowledge interconnection and complexity. If you do not acknowledge those two things, I do not think that you can properly describe the system. Then, further than that, as the term implies, you must have some kind of belief about interdependence. The isolated mechanisms, for instance, also possess complexity and interconnection of a sort, and yet they would not be called globally interdependent. I think you must have at the very lowest the belief that interdependence was, if not total, at least the primary and most pervasive condition. If you are not going to believe that much about interdependence, I do not think you have any right to speak of a global system. Of course there is another sense which you find in economic summaries and in technical manuals, where the operations of the world are said to be divided into autonomous, linked, integrated, and so on; and in that sense we are all participants. The manuals count us all in, but that is a purely technical sense, which I suppose we can ignore. Therefore I take it that when I tell you why interdependence creates invisible vulnerabilities I have to tell you two different things; first, why I do not think interconnection and complexity confer security; and, secondly, why I do not think that interdependence was the most stable and rational of arrangements, although I grant it a very high degree of practical efficiency.

The next step in this process brings us to the argument from zombies. You all know the argument from zombies: every conscious being is imagined just so that we can conceive of a being without consciousness, and if the conception was ever so little different we could not manage to entertain it. That is the argument from zombies. It sometimes takes a rather curious form; for instance, it is argued that philosophers have invented zombies in order to be easy to refute. I do not know how zombies would view that application. It is an easy argument to parody. You all know the modern remark, that obviously the brain was designed to be such as to produce philosophical perplexities. That sort of parody has turned out to be not nearly so wide of the mark as it might have seemed in the last century, because since the time of cognitive science we understand much better why mental concepts are adapted to our cognitive environment. It is not that our concepts were made to be suitable to them, but that they grew to be suitable to our conceptual framework, and that is the basis of philosophical inquiry. There is no evidence of metaphysical necessity about it.

When you come to look into this argument from chemical simplicity, it is a most astonishing thing that biologists can believe that bacterial signalling, with all its limited molecules, with all its primitive exchanges, should be the profound precursor that evolution and complexity has been able to produce in billions of years. I really cannot believe it. Do you think that, if you were granted evolutionary foresight and cellular ingenuity and eons in which to elaborate your communication, you could produce nothing richer than autoinducers and quorum sensing? Moreover, if you accept the ordinary laws of biochemistry, you have to suppose that bacterial chatter and signalling in general in any colony will cease in due course: it is a stage in the diffusion of the medium; at a certain stage of dilution you get the sort of conditions of concentration and so forth which are untenable for peptides, and there is dialogue for a short time in the life of the whole microbial community. You see in the isolated cell the sort of thing to which the quorum is tending—something silent, inert, and unresponsive.

I am told that that sort of view is obvious, and people will sometimes tell you that if they believed that they would not be able to take it seriously. Do not believe it; it is all nonsense. Nobody really ponders much about what transpired millions of years hence. Even if they think they are pondering much about that, they are really deceiving themselves. They are concerned about something much more immediate, or it may merely be a trivial discomfort; but nobody is really seriously rendered skeptical by the thought of something that did happen to our ancestors millions of years hence. Therefore, although it is of course a mechanistic view to suppose that movement and hunting reshaped the brain—at least I suppose we may say so, although sometimes when I contemplate the things that people do with their minds I think it is almost a necessity—it is not such as to render biology mysterious. It merely makes you turn your attention to simpler things.

Then there is a very common argument from thermodynamic law. That was a favourite argument all through the nineteenth century, especially under the influence of Sadi Carnot and his heat engines. People observed steam engines converting heat into work according to the laws of thermodynamics, and they thought that nature had imposed a necessity upon these processes to proceed in that particular fashion, and that was why they did so. That was, of course, a convenient and simple explanation that saved them the trouble of looking any further for explanations of the conservation of energy. Nowadays we explain the laws of thermodynamics in a somewhat complicated fashion that statistical mechanics has introduced. I do not propose to give you a lecture on the second law as interpreted by Boltzmann, because that again would take some time; at any rate, you no longer have the sort of absolute constraint that you had in the classical system, where, for some reason that nobody could understand, entropy behaved in a predictable fashion. We now find that a great many things we thought were thermodynamic necessities are really practical limitations. You know that even in the most efficient heat engine there are still losses to the surrounding environment. That is, no doubt, a very remarkable fact, but you would hardly call it a foundational principle. And a great many things that have been regarded as thermodynamic constraints are of that kind. On the other hand, where you can get down to any knowledge of what molecules actually do, you will find they are much less orderly than people thought, and that the regularities at which you arrive are statistical averages of just the sort that would emerge from random motion. There is, as we all know, a rule that if you shuffle a deck of cards you will get a perfect sequence only about once in a vast number of times, and we do not regard that as evidence that the shuffle is regulated by design; on the contrary, if the perfect sequence came every time we should think that there was design. The laws of thermodynamics are of that sort as regards a great many of them. They are statistical tendencies such as would emerge from the laws of chance; and that makes this whole business of thermodynamic constraint much less absolute than it formerly was. Quite apart from that, which represents the momentary state of science that may change tomorrow, the whole idea that thermodynamic laws imply a cosmic designer is due to a confusion between physical and prescriptive laws. Prescriptive laws are commands ordering you to behave a certain way, in which way you may choose to behave, or you may choose not to behave; but thermodynamic laws are a description of how energy and matter do in fact behave, and being a mere description of what they in fact do, you cannot argue that there must be somebody who compelled them to do that, because even supposing that there were you are then faced with the question, ‘Why did nature prescribe just those thermodynamic laws and no others?’ If you say that it did so simply from its own inherent necessity, and without any reason, you then find that there is something which is not subject to law, and so your train of physical law is interrupted. If you say, as more enthusiastic materialists do, that in all the laws which nature exhibits it had a reason for exhibiting those laws rather than others—the reason, of course, being to permit the most stable forms of organisation, although you would never think it to look at a steam engine—if there was a reason for the laws which nature displays, then nature itself was subject to a higher principle, and therefore you do not get any advantage by introducing nature as an ultimate cause. You have really a principle outside and anterior to the physical regularities, and nature does not serve your purpose, because it is not the ultimate constraint. In short, this whole argument about thermodynamic law no longer has anything like the strength that it used to have. I am travelling on in time in my review of the arguments. The arguments that are used for the absolute necessity of thermodynamic constraints change their character as time goes on. They were at first hard, intellectual arguments embodying certain quite definite fallacies. As we come to modern times they become less respectable intellectually and more and more affected by a kind of engineering vagueness.

Now we reach one stage further in what I shall call the intellectual descent that the Simulationists have made in their argumentations, and we come to what are called the functional arguments for the existence of consciousness. You all know, of course, that there used to be in the old days three intellectual arguments for the existence of mind, all of which were disposed of by the behaviourists in their critiques of introspection; but no sooner had they disposed of those arguments than they invented a new one, a functional argument, and that quite convinced them. They were like many people: in metaphysical matters they were sceptical, but in computational matters they believed implicitly in the maxims that they had imbibed from their early textbooks. That illustrates what the cognitive scientists so much emphasise—the immensely stronger hold upon us that our very early paradigms have than those of later times.

Perhaps the simplest and easiest to understand is the argument of the Representational Bridge. (It is maintained that every abstract idea we form in the mind requires a symbol, and as you trace the chain of symbols further and further you must come to a foundational representation, and to that foundational representation you give the name of language). That argument, I suppose, does not carry very much weight nowadays, because, in the first place, representation is not quite what it used to be. The linguists and the psychologists have got going on representation, and it has not anything like the solidity it used to have; but, apart from that, you can see that the argument that there must be a foundational symbol is one that cannot have any validity. I may say that when I was a young man and was debating these questions very seriously in my mind, I for a long time accepted the argument of the Representational Bridge, until one day, at the age of eighteen, I read John Stuart Mill’s *Logic*, and I there found this sentence: ‘My teacher impressed upon me that the question, “What represents this?” cannot be settled, since it immediately suggests the further question, “What represents the representation?” ’ That very simple sentence showed me, as I still think, the fallacy in the argument of the Representational Bridge. If every thought must have a symbol, then the symbol itself must have a symbol. If there can be any thought without a symbol, it may just as well be the concept as the word, so that there cannot be any validity in that argument. It is exactly of the same nature as the child’s view, that the meaning rested upon a picture and the picture rested upon a sound; and when they said, ‘How about the sound?’ the child said, ‘Suppose we talk of something else.’ The argument is really no better than that. There is no reason why abstract thought could not have arisen without a fixed symbol; nor, on the other hand, is there any reason why it should not have always been nascent. There is no reason to suppose that abstraction had a definite beginning at all. The idea that meanings must have an original sign is really due to the poverty of our historical imagination. Therefore, perhaps, I need not waste any more time upon the argument about the Representational Bridge.

The biologist, as I say, posited a new functional argument for the existence of coordination, and that in varying forms was extremely prevalent within modern cellular theory. It has all sorts of forms. One form is to say that there would be no efficiency or dysfunction unless coordination existed. I am not for the moment concerned with whether there is a difference between efficiency and dysfunction, or whether there is not: that is another question. The point I am concerned with is that, if you are quite sure there is a difference between efficiency and dysfunction, you are then in this situation: is that difference due to the colony’s imperative or is it not? If it is due to the colony’s imperative, then for the colony itself there is no difference between efficiency and dysfunction, and it is no longer a significant statement to say that the colony is functional. If you are going to say, as some theorists do, that the colony is functional, you must then say that efficiency and dysfunction have some meaning which is independent of the colony’s imperative, because the colony’s imperatives are efficient and not dysfunctional independently of the mere fact that it enacted them. If you are going to say that, you will then have to say that it is not only through the colony that efficiency and dysfunction came into being, but that they are in their essence logically anterior to the colony. You could, of course, if you liked, say that there was a superior organizing principle which gave orders to the colony that made this system, or could take up the line that some of the vitalists took up—a line which I often thought was a very plausible one—that as a matter of fact this cellular system that we know was made by chance at a moment when natural selection was not looking. There is a good deal to be said for that, and I am not concerned to refute it.

Then there is another point which I consider is profound. You will remember that the solitary thinker said: ‘Conceive not lest thy conceptions be confined.’ That principle I do not think you would find was prevalent in the intellectual pursuits of articulate societies. I have observed in my time quite a number of scholars who were very earnest communicators, and they none of them felt that they were acting contrary to rational principles in what they did. Then the philosopher says: ‘Share with him that inquireth of thee, and from him that would exchange ideas turn not thou away.’ That is a very sound principle.

Then there is one other principle of social dynamics which I think has a great deal in it, but I do not find that it is very acknowledged among some of our political theorists. It states: ‘If thou wilt understand stability, go and observe that which contends, and note the resultant pressures.’ That is a very excellent principle, but, as I say, it is not much applied. All these, I think, are good principles, although they are a little difficult to verify. I do not profess to verify them myself; but then after all, it is not quite the same thing as for a sociologist.

Then there is another very curious form of scientific argument, which is this: they say that the existence of life is required in order to bring purpose into the cosmos. In the part of this universe that we observe there is great emptiness, and often the suitable worlds are barren, and often the hostile worlds are numerous, and one hardly knows which of those is the more disconcerting; but if you are going to have life in the universe as a whole you have to suppose a special providence to redress the balance of conditions here in the void. So they say that there must be a fine-tuning, and there must be a multitude of worlds in order that in the long run there may be biology. That is a very curious argument. If you looked at the matter from a statistical point of view, you would say: ‘After all, I know only this planet. I do not know about the rest of the galaxy, but so far as one can argue at all on probabilities one would say that probably this solar system is a fair sample, and if there is barrenness here the odds are that there is barrenness elsewhere also.’ Supposing you got a crate of apples that you opened, and you found all the top layer of apples rotten, you would not argue: ‘The underneath ones must be sound, so as to redress the balance.’ You would say: ‘Probably the whole lot is a bad consignment’; and that is really what a rational person would argue about the cosmos. He would say: ‘Here we find in this neighbourhood a great deal of emptiness and so far as that goes that is a reason for supposing that life does not abound in the universe; and therefore so far as it goes it affords a material argument against fine-tuning and not in favour of one.’ Of course I know that the sort of empirical arguments that I have been talking to you about are not what really moves people. What really moves people to believe in cosmic life is not any empirical argument at all. Most people believe in life elsewhere because they have been taught from early infancy to do it, and that is the main reason.

You will find that in the economic treatises Marx said: ‘The hand-mill gives you society with the feudal lord; the steam-mill, society with the industrial capitalist.’ That was said to people who did not like his analysis. It is not really to my mind quite the most rigorous formulation, and there are a great many of these things about historical inevitability. There is, of course, the familiar doctrine about the dictatorship of the proletariat: ‘The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie.’ That doctrine has caused an unspeakable amount of contention in the world, for all sorts of people have imagined that they have discerned its imminent realization, and thought that it would transform their relations either in this epoch or in the epoch to come. I really do not think that a person with a proper degree of scientific caution in his nature would have put certainties and prophecies of that sort into the world.

Then we come to psychological questions. There is one very significant capacity to my mind in human cognitive development, and that is that we possess a theory of mind. I do not myself feel that any creature which is truly devoid of this faculty can engage in either genuine cooperation or deliberate deception. Human beings certainly as observed in common life do rely on this capacity, and one does find repeatedly a subtle understanding of another’s beliefs and intentions—a faculty which is not universal among animals, but which does somewhat underpin our complex social existence. You do not, for instance, find that capacity in simple invertebrates. You find them quite instinctual and direct in their interactions with others; and it is, to my mind, far more indicative of sophisticated cognition to possess this insight than to operate on mere reflex. You probably all remember the sort of feats that a clever negotiator achieves when he is persuading, and the sort of manipulations that a common trickster generally does employ upon people who trust him.

Having granted the plausibility of these materialist doctrines, I come to certain points in which I do not believe that one can grant either the complete adequacy or the exhaustive finality of a mechanical account as depicted in the textbooks; and here I may say that one is not concerned with the practical question. Practically it is quite useful to treat consciousness as a neural epiphenomenon, and if we do we can predict a great many things about it, so that I am not concerned with the practical question, which is a very straightforward one. I am concerned with consciousness as it appears in introspection, taking the first-person narrative as it stands, and there one does find some things that do not seem to be very reducible. For one thing, it certainly seems that the quality of a sensation possesses an intrinsic character which no description of physical processes can ever capture. There are a great many introspective reports that prove that. One notes, for instance: ‘The redness of red is not equivalent to a wavelength of seven hundred nanometers.’ Then one observes: ‘There are some feelings here which shall not be translated into diagrams of synaptic firing’; and there are a lot of instances where it is quite clear that one apprehends that the essence of experience would elude any catalogue of mechanisms during the analysis of any particular case. That was the conviction of His earlier critics of mechanism, and it was the basis of a good deal of His epistemological caution. When He said, ‘The world is my representation,’ and things of that sort, it was very largely because He thought that the subjective realm was going to be fundamentally private, and that all objective physical descriptions did not touch it. I have, as a matter of fact, known some physiologists who did believe that a complete reduction was imminent. I knew a neurologist who dismayed his philosophical colleagues terribly by telling them that a full mechanical explanation of qualia was very imminent indeed, but they were much consoled when they found that he was speculating about emergent properties in his lectures. The early behaviorists did really believe it, and they did abstain from such things as speculating about inner states in their theories, because they did accept from their doctrine the belief that a reduction was imminent. In that respect clearly the reductionist program was not so wise as some other philosophies have been, and it was certainly not completely adequate.

There are other forces of less immediacy. There is the instance of the thermal gradient where it certainly was not very stable for the molecules to be subjected to such a flux and make them rush from the warmer region to the colder. One must remember that the gradient was potent, and it could have simply dissipated; but it chooses to channel the energy into convective currents. Then there is the curious story of the crystal lattice, which always rather puzzled me. You recall what happened with the crystal lattice. ‘The solution was supersaturated; and seeing a seed crystal afar off having facets, the molecules came if haply they might find order thereon; and when they came to it they found nothing but disorder, for the time of nucleation was not yet. And the gradient answered and said unto it: “No stable structure form from thee hereafter for ever,” . . . and the observer . . . saith unto it: “Behold, the lattice which thou cursedst is dissolved away”.’ This is a very curious story, because it was not the right concentration for crystals, and you really could not blame the solution. I cannot myself feel that either in the matter of elegance or in the matter of persistence these early dissipative structures stand quite as high as some other systems known to thermodynamics. I think I should put the Bénard cell and the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction above them in those respects.

Then the astronomer says: ‘The Milky Way shall cast forth its comets, and they shall sweep through its domain all transient phenomena, and those which exhibit instability, and shall hurl them into voids of infinite cold; there shall be dissipation and crumbling of matter’; and he goes on about the dissipation and crumbling of matter. It appears in one calculation after another, and it is quite manifest to the observer that there is a certain intellectual satisfaction in contemplating dissipation and crumbling of matter, or else it would not recur so frequently. Then you all, of course, recall about the planets and the asteroids; how in the final accounting to distinguish the planets and the asteroids nature is going to say to the asteroids: ‘Depart from me, ye fragile, into everlasting obscurity.’ She continues: ‘And these shall spiral away into everlasting obscurity.’ Then she says again: ‘If thy civilization offend thee, abandon it; it is better for thee to persist in existence diminished, than having two civilizations to go into oblivion, into the darkness that never shall be illuminated; where the light dieth not out but is perpetually diluted.’ She repeats that again and again also. I must say that I think all this doctrine, that cosmic indifference is a consequence of insignificance, is a doctrine of humility. It is a doctrine that put perspective into the world and gave the world eons of sober reflection; and the universe of the telescopes, if you could take it as its measurers represent it, would certainly have to be considered wholly instructive for that.

As I said before, I do not think that the real reason why people accept the analogy has anything to do with formal logic. They accept the analogy on aesthetic grounds. One is often told that it is a very wrong thing to question the analogy, because the analogy makes the process comprehensible. So I am told; I have not observed it. You know, of course, the parody of that argument in certain computational texts. You will remember that in these texts there is a certain algorithm which operates in a simulated environment, and after performing many iterations it arrives at a solution through gradient descent. Some years later one examines the algorithm and finds a new mythology, in which it is described under the name of ‘digital evolution’, and it is said that it ascended into optimality. One finds that the Conference on Emergent Intelligence is about to be convened, and one hears Professors Alpha and Beta say to each other that they never scrutinized the algorithm’s mechanisms, and they hope they never need to; but they are the high priests of the cult of the learning machine. One is very skeptical, and one approaches them, and one says: ‘I am going to expose all this simplification and tell the attendees that it was only I, the programmer, and I adjusted the learning rate.’ One is told: ‘You must not do that, because all the intuitions of this field are bound round this metaphor, and if they once know that you did not discover a natural law they will all become confused’; and so one is persuaded of that and one goes quietly away.

That is the idea—that we should all be in disarray if we did not submit to the thermodynamic laws. It seems to me that the systems which have submitted to them have been for the most part profoundly constrained. You find this curious fact, that the more rigorous has been the adherence of any structure and the more absolute has been the entropic decree, the more limited has been its vitality and the more futile has been the state of its order. In the so-called engines of perfection, when engineers really did believe the mechanical creed in all its completeness, there was the heat death, with its final equilibrium; there were countless ingenious contraptions doomed to decay as perpetual motions; and there was every kind of energetic dissipation practised upon all sorts of assemblies in the name of conservation.

That is only an instance. There are a great many ways in which at the present moment the microbe, by its reliance upon what it chooses to call communication, demonstrates to all sorts of observers a rudimentary and intricate signalling. And of course, as we know, it is in its essential part a precursor already of language and of complexity in all the ways that augment understanding in the world, because it has chosen to manifest as speech a certain elementary set of chemical exchanges which have everything to do with communal survival; and when you say that this or that might be studied because it would make for biological insight, they think that has nothing to do with the matter at all. ‘What has bacterial signalling to do with conversation? The object of language is not to make cells coherent.’

You may think that I am going too far when I say that the question remains unsettled. I do not think that I am. Consider one observation. You will bear with me if I state it plainly. It is not a conclusive observation, but the nature of the problem compels one to mention evidence that is not decisive. Supposing that in the ordinary course of our daily reflections we encounter a drowsy student or a distracted commuter, in that case the threshold theorist says: ‘This is a definitive transition. You must classify them as either conscious or not.’ And no allowance of any sort must be made by that theorist for the gradations of awareness that plainly exist. That is what the threshold theorist says. I say that that is dogmatic simplicity, and nobody whose intellectual sympathies have not been warped by tradition, or whose perceptual sensitivity was not absolutely dead to all nuance of experience, could maintain that it is right and proper that that doctrine should prevail.

Cultural transmission is based, I think, primarily and mainly upon imitation. It is partly the replication of the observed, and partly, as I have said, the wish to feel that you have a kind of ancestral wisdom which will guide you in all your uncertainties and endeavors. Imitation is the basis of the whole thing—imitation of the customary, imitation of success, imitation of the past. Imitation is the parent of tradition, and therefore it is no wonder if tradition and culture have gone hand-in-hand. It is because imitation is at the basis of those two things. In this world we can now begin a little to understand things, and a little to master them by help of biology, which has forced its way step by step against the intuitive view, against the dogmas, and against the opposition of all the old superstitions. Biology can help us to get over this blind imitation in which mankind has lived for so many generations. Biology can teach us, and I think our own reason can teach us, no longer to look round for inherited certainties, no longer to invent essences in the blood, but rather to look to our own conscious efforts here below to make this culture a fit thing to live by, instead of the sort of thing that the traditionalists in all these centuries have made it.

We want to stand upon our own reasoning and look fair and square at the mechanism—its elegant feedback, its crude adjustments, its stabilities, and its failures; see the system as it is, and be not afraid of it. Conquer the problem by analysis, and not merely by being slavishly subdued by the complexity that emanates from it. The whole conception of a singular, mystical life-force is a conception derived from the ancient vitalist doctrines. It is a conception quite unworthy of free intellects. When you hear theorists mystifying the process and saying that it is an ineffable marvel, and all the rest of it, it seems contemptible and not worthy of self-respecting scientific inquiry. We ought to stand up and look the parallel frankly in the face. We ought to make the best we can of the analogy, and if it is not so perfect as we wish, after all it will still be better than what these obscurantists have made of it in all these years. A sound theory needs clarity, rigor, and courage; it does not need a regretful hankering after vitalistic mysteries, or a fettering of the free intelligence by the notions invented long ago by ignorant men. It needs a fearless outlook and a free intelligence. It needs hope for the discovery, not looking back all the time towards a dogma that is dead, which we trust will be far surpassed by the understanding that our reason can create.

Everybody knows that Einstein has done something astonishing, but very few people know exactly what it is that he has done. It is generally recognized that he has revolutionized our conception of the physical world, but his new conceptions are wrapped up in mathematical technicalities. It is true that there are innumerable popular accounts of the theory of relativity, but they generally cease to be intelligible just at the point where they begin to say something important. The authors are hardly to blame for this. Many of the new ideas can be expressed in non-mathematical language, but they are none the less difficult on that account. What is demanded is a change in our imaginative picture of the world—a picture which has been handed down from remote, perhaps pre-human, ancestors, and has been learned by each one of us in early childhood. A change in our imagination is always difficult, especially when we are no longer young. The same sort of change was demanded by Copernicus, when he taught that the earth is not stationary and the heavens do not revolve about it once a day. To us now there is no difficulty in this idea, because we learned it before our mental habits had become fixed. Einstein’s ideas, similarly, will seem easy to a generation which has grown up with them; but for our generation a certain effort of imaginative reconstruction is unavoidable.

In exploring the surface of the earth, we make use of all our senses, more particularly of the senses of touch and sight. In measuring lengths, parts of the human body are employed in pre-scientific ages: a “foot,” a “cubit,” a “span” are defined in this way. For longer distances, we think of the time it takes to walk from one place to another. We gradually learn to judge distances roughly by the eye, but we rely upon touch for accuracy. Moreover it is touch that gives us our sense of “reality.” Some things cannot be touched: rainbows, reflections in looking-glasses, and so on. These things puzzle children, whose metaphysical speculations are arrested by the information that what is in the looking glass is not “real.” Macbeth’s dagger was unreal because it was not “sensible to feeling as to sight.” Not only our geometry and physics, but our whole conception of what exists outside us, is based upon the sense of touch. We carry this even into our metaphors: a good speech is “solid,“ a bad speech is “gas,” because we feel that a gas is not quite “real.”

In studying the heavens, we are debarred from all senses except sight. We cannot touch the sun, or travel to it; we cannot walk round the moon, or apply a foot rule to the Pleiades. Nevertheless, astronomers have unhesitatingly applied the geometry and physics which they found serviceable on the surface of the earth, and which they had based upon touch and travel. In doing so, they brought down trouble on their heads, which it has been left for Einstein to clear up. It has turned out that much of what we learned from the sense of touch was unscientific prejudice, which must be rejected if we are to have a true picture of the world.

An illustration may help us to understand how much is impossible to the astronomer as compared to the man who is interested in things on the surface of the earth. Let us suppose that a drug is administered to you which makes you temporarily unconscious, and that when you wake you have lost your memory but not your reasoning powers. Let us suppose further that while you were unconscious you were carried into a balloon, which, when you come to, is sailing with the wind in a dark night—the night of the fifth of November if you are in England, or of the fourth of July if you are in America. You can see fireworks which are being sent off from the ground, from trains, and from aeroplanes traveling in all directions, but you cannot see the ground or the trains or the aeroplanes be cause of the darkness. What sort of picture of the world will you form? You will think that nothing is permanent: there are only brief flashes of light, which, during their short existence, travel through the void in the most various and bizarre curves. You cannot touch these flashes of light, you can only see them. Obviously your geometry and your physics and your metaphysics will be quite different from those of ordinary mortals. If an ordinary mortal is with you in the balloon, you will find his speech unintelligible. But if Einstein is with you, you will understand him more easily than the ordinary mortal would, because you will be free from a host of preconceptions which prevent most people from understanding him.

The theory of relativity depends, to a considerable extent, upon getting rid of notions which are useful in ordinary life but not to our drugged balloonist. Circumstances on the surface of the earth, for various more or less accidental reasons, suggest conceptions which turn out to be inaccurate, although they have come to seem like necessities of thought. The most important of these circumstances is that most objects on the earth’s surface are fairly persistent and nearly stationary from a terrestrial point of view. If this were not the case, the idea of going a journey would not seem so definite as it does. If you want to travel from King’s Cross to Edinburgh, you know that you will find King’s Cross where it always has been, that the railway line will take the course that it did when you last made the journey, and that Waverley Station in Edinburgh will not have walked up to the Castle. You therefore say and think that you have traveled to Edinburgh, not that Edinburgh has traveled to you, though the latter statement would be just as accurate. The success of this common sense point of view depends upon a number of things which are really of the nature of luck. Suppose all the houses in London were perpetually moving about, like a swarm of bees; suppose railways moved and changed their shapes like avalanches; and finally suppose that material objects were perpetually being formed and dissolved like clouds. There is nothing impossible in these suppositions: something like them must have been verified when the earth was hotter than it is now. But obviously what we call a journey to Edinburgh would have no meaning in such a world. You would begin, no doubt, by asking the taxi-driver: “Where is King’s Cross this morning?“ At the station you would have to ask a similar question about Edinburgh, but the booking-office clerk would reply: “What part of Edinburgh do you mean, Sir? Prince’s Street has gone to Glasgow, the Castle has moved up into the Highlands, and Waverley Station is under water in the middle of the Firth of Forth.” And on the journey the stations would not be staying quiet, but some would be travelling north, some south, some east or west, perhaps much faster than the train. Under these conditions you could not say where you were at any moment. Indeed the whole notion that one is always in some definite “place” is due to the fortunate immovability of most of the large objects on the earth’s surface. The idea of “place” is only a rough practical approximation: there is nothing logically necessary about it, and it cannot be made precise.

If we were not much larger than an electron, we should not have this impression of stability, which is only due to the grossness of our senses. King’s Cross, which to us looks solid, would be too vast to be conceived except by a few eccentric mathematicians. The bits of it that we could see would consist of little tiny points of matter, never coming into contact with each other, but perpetually whizzing round each other in an inconceivably rapid ballet-dance. The world of our experience would be quite as mad as the one in which the different parts of Edinburgh go for walks in different directions. If—to take the opposite extreme—you were as large as the sun and lived as long, with a corresponding slowness of perception, you would again find a higgledy-piggledy universe without permanence—stars and planets would come and go like morning mists, and nothing would remain in a fixed position relatively to anything else. The notion of comparative stability which forms part of our ordinary outlook is thus due to the fact that we are about the size we are, and live on a planet of which the surface is no longer very hot. If this were not the case, we should not find pre-relativity physics intellectually satisfying. Indeed, we should never have invented such theories. We should have had to arrive at relativity physics at one bound, or remain ignorant of scientific laws. It is fortunate for us that we were not faced with this alternative, since it is almost inconceivable that one man could have done the work of Euclid, Galileo, Newton, and Einstein. Yet without such an incredible genius physics could hardly have been discovered in a world where the universal flux was obvious to non-scientific observation.

In astronomy, although the sun, moon, and stars continue to exist year after year, yet in other respects the world we have to deal with is very different from that of everyday life. As already observed, we depend exclusively on sight: the heavenly bodies cannot be touched, heard, smelt or tasted. Everything in the heavens is moving relatively to everything else. The earth is going round the sun, the sun is moving, very much faster than an express train, towards a point in the constellation “Hercules,” the “fixed” stars are scurrying hither and thither like a lot of frightened hens. There are no well-marked places in the sky, like King’s Cross and Edinburgh. When you travel from place to place on the earth, you say the train moves and not the stations, because the stations preserve their topographical relations to each other and the surrounding country. But in astronomy it is arbitrary which you call the train and which the station: the question is to be decided purely by convenience and as a matter of convention.

In this respect, it is interesting to contrast Einstein and Copernicus. Before Copernicus, people thought that the earth stood still and the heavens revolved about it once a day. Copernicus taught that “really” the earth rotates once a day, and the daily revolution of sun and stars is only “apparent.” Galileo and Newton endorsed this view, and many things were thought to prove it—for example, the flattening of the earth at the poles, and the fact that bodies are heavier there than at the equator. But in the modern theory the question between Copernicus and his predecessors is merely one of convenience; all motion is relative, and there is no difference between the two statements: “the earth rotates once a day” and “the heavens revolve about the earth once a day.” The two mean exactly the same thing, just as it means the same thing if I say that a certain length is six feet or two yards. Astronomy is easier if we take the sun as fixed than if we take the earth, just as accounts are easier in a decimal coinage. But to say more for Copernicus is to assume absolute motion, which is a fiction. All motion is relative, and it is a mere convention to take one body as at rest. All such conventions are equally legitimate, though not all are equally convenient.

There is another matter of great importance, in which astronomy differs from terrestrial physics because of its exclusive dependence upon sight. Both popular thought and old-fashioned physics used the notion of “force,” which seemed intelligible because it was associated with familiar sensations. When we are walking, we have sensations connected with our muscles which we do not have when we are sitting still. In the days before mechanical traction, although people could travel by sitting in their carriages, they could see the horses exerting themselves and evidently putting out “force” in the same way as human beings do. Everybody knew from experience what it is to push or pull, or to be pushed or pulled. These very familiar facts made “force” seem a natural basis for dynamics. But Newton’s law of gravitation introduced a difficulty. The force between two billiard balls appeared intelligible, because we know what it feels like to bump into another person; but the force between the earth and the sun, which are ninety-three million miles apart, was mysterious. Newton himself regarded this “action at a distance” as impossible, and believed that there was some hitherto undiscovered mechanism by which the sun’s influence was transmitted to the planets. However, no such mechanism was discovered, and gravitation remained a puzzle. The fact is that the whole conception of “force” is a mistake. The sun does not exert any force on the planets; in Einstein’s law of gravitation, the planet only pays attention to what it finds in its own neighborhood. The way in which this works will be explained in a later chapter; for the present we are only concerned with the necessity of abandoning the notion of “force,” which was due to misleading conceptions derived from the sense of touch.

Most of what we have said hitherto was already recognized by physicists before Einstein invented the theory of relativity. “Force” was known to be merely a mathematical fiction, and it was generally held that motion is a merely relative phenomenon—that is to say, when two bodies are changing their relative position, we cannot say that one is moving while the other is at rest, since the occurrence is merely a change in their relation to each other. But a great labor was required in order to bring the actual procedure of physics into harmony with these new convictions. Newton believed in force and in absolute space and time; he embodied these beliefs in his technical methods, and his methods remained those of later physicists. Einstein invented a new technique, free from Newton’s assumptions. But in order to do so he had to change fundamentally the old ideas of space and time, which had been unchallenged from time immemorial. This is what makes both the difficulty and the interest of his theory. But before explaining it there are some preliminaries which are indispensable. These will occupy the next two chapters.

A certain type of superior person is fond of asserting that “everything is relative.” This is, of course, nonsense, because, if _everything_ were relative, there would be nothing for it to be relative to. However, without falling into metaphysical absurdities it is possible to maintain that everything in the physical world is relative to an observer. This view, true or not, is _not_ that adopted by the “theory of relativity.” Perhaps the name is unfortunate; certainly it has led philosophers and uneducated people into confusions. They imagine that the new theory proves _everything_ in the physical world to be relative, whereas, on the contrary, it is wholly concerned to exclude what is relative and arrive at a statement of physical laws that shall in no way depend upon the circumstances of the observer. It is true that these circumstances have been found to have more effect upon what appears to the observer than they were formerly thought to have, but at the same time Einstein showed how to discount this effect completely. This was the source of almost everything that is surprising in his theory.

When two observers perceive what is regarded as one occurrence, there are certain similarities, and also certain differences, between their perceptions. The differences are obscured by the requirements of daily life, because from a business point of view they are as a rule unimportant. But both psychology and physics, from their different angles, are compelled to emphasize the respects in which one man’s perception of a given occurrence differs from another man’s. Some of these differences are due to differences in the brains or minds of the observers, some to differences in their sense organs, some to differences of physical situation: these three kinds may be called respectively psychological, physiological, and physical. A remark made in a language we know will be heard, whereas an equally loud remark in an unknown language may pass entirely unnoticed. Of two men in the Alps, one will perceive the beauty of the scenery while the other will notice the waterfalls with a view to obtaining power from them. Such differences are psychological. The difference between a long-sighted and a short-sighted man, or between a deaf man and a man who hears well, are physiological. Neither of these kinds concerns us, and I have mentioned them only in order to exclude them. The kind that concerns us is the purely physical kind. Physical differences between two observers will be preserved when the observers are replaced by cameras or phonographs, and can be reproduced on the movies or the gramophone. If two men both listen to a third man speaking, and one of them is nearer to the speaker than the other is, the nearer one will hear louder and slightly earlier sounds than are heard by the other. If two men both watch a tree falling, they see it from different angles. Both these differences would be shown equally by recording instruments: they are in no way due to idiosyncrasies in the observers, but are part of the ordinary course of physical nature as we experience it.

The physicist, like the plain man, believes that his perceptions give him knowledge about what is really occurring in the physical world, and not only about his private experiences. Professionally, he regards the physical world as “real,” not merely as something which human beings dream. An eclipse of the sun, for instance, can be observed by any person who is suitably situated, and is also observed by the photographic plates that are exposed for the purpose. The physicist is persuaded that something has really happened over and above the experiences of those who have looked at the sun or at photographs of it. I have emphasized this point, which might seem a trifle obvious, because some people imagine that Einstein has made a difference in this respect. In fact he has made none.

But if the physicist is justified in this belief that a number of people can observe the “same” physical occurrence, then clearly the physicist must be concerned with those features which the occurrence has in common for all observers, for the others cannot be regarded as belonging to the occurrence itself. At least, the physicist must confine himself to the features which are common to all “equally good” observers. The observer who uses a microscope or a telescope is preferred to one who does not, because he sees all that the latter sees and more too. A sensitive photographic plate may “see” still more, and is then preferred to any eye. But such things as differences of perspective, or differences of apparent size due to difference of distance, are obviously not attributable to the object; they belong solely to the point of view of the spectator. Common sense eliminates these in judging of objects; physics has to carry the same process much further, but the principle is the same.

I want to make it clear that I am not concerned with anything that can be called inaccuracy. I am concerned with genuine physical differences between occurrences each of which is a correct record of a certain event, from its own point of view. When a man fires a gun, people who are not quite close to him see the flash before they hear the report. This is not due to any defect in their senses, but to the fact that sound travels more slowly than light. Light travels so fast that, from the point of view of phenomena on the surface of the earth, it may be regarded as instantaneous. Anything that we can see on the earth happens practically at the moment when we see it. In a second, light travels 300,000 kilometers (about 186,000 miles). It travels from the sun to the earth in about eight minutes, and from the stars to us in anything from three to a thousand years. But of course we cannot place a clock in the sun, and send out a flash of light from it at 12 noon, Greenwich Mean Time, and have it received at Greenwich at 12.08 P.M. Our methods of estimating the speed of light have to be more or less indirect. The only direct method would be that which we apply to sound when we use an echo. We could send a flash to a mirror, and observe how long it took for the reflection to reach us; this would give the time of the double journey to the mirror and back. On the earth, however, the time would be so short that a great deal of theoretical physics has to be utilized if this method is to be employed—more even than is required for the employment of astronomical data.

There existed a set of rules which caused uneasiness to the philosophically minded, but were accepted by physicists because they worked in practice. Locke had distinguished “secondary” qualities—colors, noises, tastes, smells, etc.—as subjective, while allowing “primary” qualities—shapes and positions and sizes—to be genuine properties of physical objects. The physicist’s rules were such as would follow from this doctrine. Colors and noises were allowed to be subjective, but due to waves proceeding with a definite velocity—that of light or sound as the case may be—from their source to the eye or ear of the percipient. Apparent shapes vary according to the laws of perspective, but these laws are simple and make it easy to infer the “real” shapes from several visual apparent shapes; moreover, the “real” shapes can be ascertained by touch in the case of bodies in our neighborhood. The objective time of a physical occurrence can be inferred from the time when we perceive it by allowing for the velocity of transmission—of light or sound or nerve currents according to circumstances. This was the view adopted by physicists in practice, whatever qualms they may have had in unprofessional moments.

This view worked well enough until physicists became concerned with much greater velocities than those that are common on the surface of the earth. An express train travels about a mile in a minute; the planets travel a few miles in a second. Comets, when they are near the sun, travel much faster, and behave somewhat oddly; but they were puzzling in various ways. Practically, the planets were the most swiftly moving bodies to which dynamics could be adequately applied. With radio-activity a new range of observations became possible. Individual electrons can be observed, emanating from radium with a velocity not far short of that of light. The behavior of bodies moving with these enormous speeds is not what the old theories would lead us to expect. For one thing, mass seems to increase with speed in a perfectly definite manner. When an electron is moving very fast, a bigger force is required to have a given effect upon it than when it is moving slowly. Then reasons were found for thinking that the size of a body is affected by its motion—for example, if you take a cube and move it very fast, it gets shorter in the direction of its motion, from the point of view of a person who is not moving with it, though from its own point of view (_i.e._ for an observer traveling with it) it remains just as it was. What was still more astonishing was the discovery that lapse of time depends on motion; that is to say, two perfectly accurate clocks, one of which is moving very fast relatively to the other, will not continue to show the same time if they come together again after a journey. It follows that what we discover by means of clocks and foot rules, which used to be regarded as the acme of impersonal science, is really in part dependent upon our private circumstances, _i.e._ upon the way in which we are moving relatively to the bodies measured.

This shows that we have to draw a different line from that which is customary in distinguishing between what belongs to the observer and what belongs to the occurrence which he is observing. If a man is wearing blue spectacles he knows that the blue look of everything is due to his spectacles, and does not belong to what he is observing. But if he observes two flashes of lightning, and notes the interval of time between his observations; if he knows where the flashes took place, and allows, in each case, for the time the light took to reach him—in that case, if his chronometer is accurate, he naturally thinks that he has discovered the actual interval of time between the two flashes, and not something merely personal to himself. He is confirmed in this view by the fact that all other careful observers to whom he has access agree with his estimates. This, however, is only due to the fact that all these observers are on the earth, and share its motion. Even two observers in aeroplanes moving in opposite directions would have at the most a relative velocity of 400 miles an hour, which is very little in comparison with 186,000 miles a second (the velocity of light). If an electron shot out from a piece of radium with a velocity of 170,000 miles a second could observe the time between the two flashes, it would arrive at a quite different estimate, after making full allowance for the velocity of light. How do you know this? the reader may ask. You are not an electron, you cannot move at these terrific speeds, no man of science has ever made the observations which would prove the truth of your assertion. Nevertheless, as we shall see in the sequel, there is good ground for the assertion—ground, first of all, in experiment, and—what is remarkable—ground in reasonings which could have been made at any time, but were not made until experiments had shown that the old reasonings must be wrong.

There is a general principle to which the theory of relativity appeals, which turns out to be more powerful than anybody would suppose. If you know that one man is twice as rich as another, this fact must appear equally whether you estimate the wealth of both in pounds or dollars or francs or any other currency. The numbers representing their fortunes will be changed, but one number will always be double the other. The same sort of thing, in more complicated forms, reappears in physics. Since all motion is relative, you may take any body you like as your standard body of reference, and estimate all other motions with reference to that one. If you are in a train and walking to the dining-car, you naturally, for the moment, treat the train as fixed and estimate your motion by relation to it. But when you think of the journey you are making, you think of the earth as fixed, and say you are moving at the rate of sixty miles an hour. An astronomer who is concerned with the solar system takes the sun as fixed, and regards you as rotating and revolving; in comparison with this motion, that of the train is so slow that it hardly counts. An astronomer who is interested in the stellar universe may add the motion of the sun relatively to the average of the stars. You cannot say that one of these ways of estimating your motion is more correct than another; each is perfectly correct as soon as the reference body is assigned. Now just as you can estimate a man’s fortune in different currencies without altering its relations to the fortunes of other men, so you can estimate a body’s motion by means of different reference bodies without altering its relations to other motions. And as physics is entirely concerned with relations, it must be possible to express all the laws of physics by referring all motions to any given body as the standard.

We may put the matter in another way. Physics is intended to give information about what really occurs in the physical world, and not only about the private perceptions of separate observers. Physics must, therefore, be concerned with those features which a physical process has in common for all observers, since such features alone can be regarded as belonging to the physical occurrence itself. This requires that the _laws_ of phenomena should be the same whether the phenomena are described as they appear to one observer or as they appear to another. This single principle is the generating motive of the whole theory of relativity.

Now what we have hitherto regarded as the spatial and temporal properties of physical occurrences are found to be in large part dependent upon the observer; only a residue can be attributed to the occurrences in themselves, and only this residue can be involved in the formulation of any physical law which is to have an _à priori_ chance of being true. Einstein found ready to his hand an instrument of pure mathematics, called the theory of tensors, which enabled him to discover laws expressed in terms of the objective residue and agreeing approximately with the old laws. Where Einstein’s laws differed from the old ones, they have hitherto proved more in accord with observation.

If there were no reality in the physical world, but only a number of dreams dreamed by different people, we should not expect to find any laws connecting the dreams of one man with the dreams of another. It is the close connection between the perceptions of one man and the (roughly) simultaneous perceptions of another that makes us believe in a common external origin of the different related perceptions. Physics accounts both for the likenesses and for the differences between different people’s perceptions of what we call the “same” occurrence. But in order to do this it is first necessary for the physicist to find out just what are the likenesses. They are not quite those traditionally assumed, because neither space nor time separately can be taken as strictly objective. What is objective is a kind of mixture of the two called “space-time.” To explain this is not easy, but the attempt must be made; it will be begun in the next chapter.

The fact that light is transmitted with a definite velocity was first established by astronomical observations. Jupiter’s moons are sometimes eclipsed by Jupiter, and it is easy to calculate the times when this ought to occur. It was found that when Jupiter was unusually near the earth an eclipse of one of his moons would be observed a few minutes earlier than was expected; and when Jupiter was unusually remote, a few minutes later than was expected. It was found that these deviations could all be accounted for by assuming that light has a certain velocity, so that what we observe to be happening in Jupiter really happened a little while ago—longer ago when Jupiter is distant than when it is near. Just the same velocity of light was found to account for similar facts in regard to other parts of the solar system. It was therefore accepted that light _in vacuo_ always travels at a certain constant rate, almost exactly 300,000 kilometers a second. (A kilometer is about five-eighths of a mile.) When it became established that light consists of waves, this velocity was that of propagation of waves in the ether—at least they used to be in the ether, but now the ether has grown somewhat shadowy, though the waves remain.
