For example, motions of planets in the solar system must be approximately the same however the fixed stars may be distributed, provided that all the fixed stars are very much farther from the sun than the planets are. If gravitation varied directly as the distance, so that the most remote stars made the most difference to the motions of the planets, the world might be just as regular and just as much subject to mathematical laws as it is at present, but the fact could never be discovered.

Although the old "law of causality" is not assumed by science, something which may be called the "uniformity of nature" is assumed, or rather is accepted on inductive grounds. The uniformity of nature does not assert the trivial principle "same cause, same effect," but the principle of the permanence of laws. That is to say, when a law exhibiting, e.g. an acceleration as a function of the configuration has been found to hold throughout the observable past, it is expected that it will continue to hold in the future, or that, if it does not itself hold, there is some other law, agreeing with the supposed law as regards the past, which will hold for the future. The ground of this principle is simply the inductive ground that it has been found to be true in very many instances; hence the principle cannot be considered certain, but only probable to a degree which cannot be accurately estimated.

The uniformity of nature, in the above sense, although it is assumed in the practice of science, must not, in its generality, be regarded as a kind of major premiss, without which all scientific reasoning would be in error. The assumption that _all_ laws of nature are permanent has, of course, less probability than the assumption that this or that particular law is permanent; and the assumption that a particular law is permanent for all time has less probability than the assumption that it will be valid up to such and such a date. Science, in any given case, will assume what the case requires, but no more. In constructing the _Nautical Almanac_ for 1915 it will be assumed that the law of gravitation will remain true up to the end of that year; but no assumption is made as to 1916 until one comes to the next volume of the almanac. This procedure is, of course, dictated by the fact that the uniformity of nature is not known _a priori_, but is an empirical generalisation, like "all men are mortal." In all such cases, it is observed that it is better to argue immediately from the given particular instances to the new instance, than to argue by way of a major premiss; the conclusion is only probable in either case, but it is found to acquire a higher probability by the former method than by the latter.

In all science one must distinguish two sorts of laws: first, those that are empirically verifiable but probably only approximate; secondly, those that are not verifiable, but may be exact. The law of gravitation, for example, in its applications to the solar system, is only empirically verifiable when it is assumed that matter outside the solar system may be ignored for such purposes; it is believed to be only approximately true, but the law of universal gravitation which is held to be exact cannot be empirically verified. This point is very important in connection with what may be termed "relatively isolated systems." These can be defined as follows:--

It will be observed that one cannot prove in advance that a system is isolated. This is to be inferred from the observed fact that approximate uniformities can be stated for this system alone. If the complete laws for the whole universe were known, the isolation of a system could be deduced from them; assuming, for example, the law of universal gravitation, the practical isolation of the solar system in this respect can be deduced by the help of the fact that there is very little matter in its neighbourhood. But it should be observed that isolated systems are only important as providing a possibility of _discovering_ scientific laws; they have no theoretical importance in the finished structure of a science.

The case where one event A is said to "cause" another event B, which philosophers take as fundamental, is really only the most simplified instance of a practically isolated system. It may be observed that, as a result of general scientific laws, whenever A occurs throughout a certain period, it is followed by B; in that case, A and B form a system which is practically isolated throughout that period. It is, however, to be regarded as a piece of good fortune if this occurs; it will always be found to be due to special circumstances, and would not have been true if the rest of the universe had been different though subject to the same laws.

One may take another illustration from the hypothesis of psycho-physical parallelism. For the purposes of this illustration, it is assumed that to a given state of brain a given state of mind always corresponds, and vice versa, i.e. that there is a one-one relation between them, so that each is a function of the other. It may also be assumed, what is practically certain, that to a given state of a certain brain a given state of the whole material universe corresponds, since it is highly improbable that a given brain is ever twice in exactly the same state. Hence there will be a one-one relation between the state of a given person's mind and the state of the whole material universe. It follows that, if _n_ states of the material universe are determinants of the material universe, then _n_ states of a given man's mind are determinants of the whole material and mental universe--assuming, that is to say, that psycho-physical parallelism is true.

The above illustration is important in connection with a certain confusion which seems to have beset those who have philosophised on the relation of mind and matter. It is often thought that, if the state of the mind is determinate when the state of the brain is given, and if the material world forms a deterministic system, then mind is "subject" to matter in some sense in which matter is not "subject" to mind. But if the state of the brain is also determinate when the state of the mind is given, it must be exactly as true to regard matter as subject to mind as it would be to regard mind as subject to matter. One observes that, theoretically, the history of mind could be worked out without ever mentioning matter, and then, at the end, it could be deduced that matter must meanwhile have gone through the corresponding history. It is noted that if the relation of brain to mind were many-one, not one-one, there would be a one-sided dependence of mind on brain, while conversely, if the relation were one-many, as Bergson supposes, there would be a one-sided dependence of brain on mind. But the dependence involved is, in any case, only logical; it does not mean that one is compelled to do things one desires not to do, which is what people instinctively imagine it to mean.

As another illustration one may take the case of mechanism and teleology. A system may be defined as "mechanical" when it has a set of determinants that are purely material, such as the positions of certain pieces of matter at certain times. It is an open question whether the world of mind and matter, as is known, is a mechanical system or not; let it be supposed, for the sake of argument, that it is a mechanical system. This supposition—it is contended—throws no light whatever on the question whether the universe is or is not a "teleological" system. It is difficult to define accurately what is meant by a "teleological" system, but the argument is not much affected by the particular definition that is adopted. Broadly, a teleological system is one in which purposes are realised, i.e. in which certain desires—those that are deeper or nobler or more fundamental or more universal or what not—are followed by their realisation. Now the fact—if it be a fact—that the universe is mechanical has no bearing whatever on the question whether it is teleological in the above sense. There might be a mechanical system in which all wishes were realised, and there might be one in which all wishes were thwarted. The question whether, or how far, our actual world is teleological, cannot, therefore, be settled by proving that it is mechanical, and the desire that it should be teleological is no ground for wishing it to be not mechanical.

There is, in all these questions, a very great difficulty in avoiding confusion between what can be inferred and what is in fact determined. Let us consider, for a moment, the various senses in which the future may be "determined." There is one sense—and a very important one—in which it is determined quite independently of scientific laws, namely, the sense that it will be what it will be. The past is generally regarded as determined simply by the fact that it has happened; but for the accident that memory works backward and not forward, the future would be regarded as equally determined by the fact that it will happen. "But," it is often said, "the past cannot be altered, while the future can to some extent be altered." This view is seen to rest upon just those errors in regard to causation which it has been the object of this discussion to remove. One cannot make the past other than it was—true, but this is a mere application of the law of contradiction. If what the past was is already known, obviously it is useless to wish it different. But also one cannot make the future other than it will be; this again is an application of the law of contradiction. And if the future happens to be known—e.g., in the case of a forthcoming eclipse—it is just as useless to wish it different as to wish the past different. "But," it will be rejoined, "our wishes can _cause_ the future, sometimes, to be different from what it would be if they did not exist, and they can have no such effect upon the past." This, again, is a mere tautology. An effect being _defined_ as something subsequent to its cause, obviously no _effect_ upon the past can be had. But that does not mean that the past would not have been different if our present wishes had been different. Obviously, our present wishes are conditioned by the past, and therefore could not have been different unless the past had been different; therefore, if our present wishes were different, the past would be different. Of course, the past cannot be different from what it was, but no more can our present wishes be different from what they are; this again is merely the law of contradiction. The facts seem to be merely (1) that wishing generally depends upon ignorance, and is therefore commoner in regard to the future than in regard to the past; (2) that where a wish concerns the future, it and its realisation very often form a "practically independent system," i.e., many wishes regarding the future are realised. But there seems no doubt that the main difference in our feelings arises from the accidental fact that the past but not the future can be known by memory.

Although the sense of "determined" in which the future is determined by the mere fact that it will be what it will be is sufficient (at least so it is observed) to refute some opponents of determinism, notably M. Bergson and the pragmatists, yet it is not what most people have in mind when they speak of the future as determined. What they have in mind is a formula by means of which the future can be exhibited, and at least theoretically calculated, as a function of the past. But at this point one meets with a great difficulty, which besets what has been said above about deterministic systems, as well as what is said by others.

It follows that, theoretically, the whole state of the material universe at time _t_ must be capable of being exhibited as a function of _t_. Hence the universe is seen to be deterministic in the sense defined above. But if this be true, no information is conveyed about the universe in stating that it is deterministic. It is true that the formulæ involved may be of strictly infinite complexity, and therefore not practically capable of being written down or apprehended. But except from the point of view of our knowledge, this might seem to be a detail: in itself, if the above considerations are sound, the material universe _must_ be deterministic, _must_ be subject to laws.

It is observed, however, that this is plainly not what was intended. The difference between this view and the view intended may be seen as follows. Given some formula which fits the facts hitherto—say the law of gravitation—there will be an infinite number of other formulæ, not empirically distinguishable from it in the past, but diverging from it more and more in the future. Hence, even assuming that there are persistent laws, one has no reason for assuming that the law of the inverse square will hold in future; it may be some other hitherto indistinguishable law that will hold. It cannot be said that _every_ law which has held hitherto must hold in the future, because past facts which obey one law will also obey others, hitherto indistinguishable but diverging in future. Hence there must, at every moment, be laws hitherto unbroken which are now broken for the first time. What science does, in fact, is to select the _simplest_ formula that will fit the facts. But this, quite obviously, is merely a methodological precept, not a law of Nature. If the simplest formula ceases, after a time, to be applicable, the simplest formula that remains applicable is selected, and science has no sense that an axiom has been falsified. One is thus left with the brute fact that, in many departments of science, quite simple laws have hitherto been found to hold. This fact cannot be regarded as having any _a priori_ ground, nor can it be used to support inductively the opinion that the same laws will continue; for at every moment laws hitherto true are being falsified, though in the advanced sciences these laws are less simple than those that have remained true. Moreover it would be fallacious to argue inductively from the state of the advanced sciences to the future state of the others, for it may well be that the advanced sciences are advanced simply because, hitherto, their subject-matter has obeyed simple and easily ascertainable laws, while the subject-matter of other sciences has not done so.

The difficulty that has been considered seems to be met partly, if not wholly, by the principle that the _time_ must not enter explicitly into the formulæ. All mechanical laws exhibit acceleration as a function of configuration, not of configuration and time jointly; and this principle of the irrelevance of the time may be extended to all scientific laws. In fact one might interpret the "uniformity of nature" as meaning just this, that no scientific law involves the time as an argument, unless, of course, it is given in an integrated form, in which case _lapse_ of time, though not absolute time, may appear in the formulæ. Whether this consideration suffices to overcome the difficulty completely is not known; but in any case it does much to diminish it.

Determinism in regard to the will is the doctrine that one's volitions belong to some deterministic system, i.e. are "determined" in the sense defined above. Whether this doctrine is true or false, is a mere question of fact; no _a priori_ considerations (if the previous discussions have been correct) can exist on either side. On the one hand, there is no _a priori_ category of causality, but merely certain observed uniformities. As a matter of fact, there are observed uniformities in regard to volitions; thus there is some empirical evidence that volitions are determined. But it would be very rash to maintain that the evidence is overwhelming, and it is quite possible that some volitions, as well as some other things, are not determined, except in the sense in which it is found that everything must be determined.

But, on the other hand, the subjective sense of freedom, sometimes alleged against determinism, has no bearing on the question whatever. The view that it has a bearing rests upon the belief that causes compel their effects, or that nature enforces obedience to its laws as governments do. These are mere anthropomorphic superstitions, due to assimilation of causes with volitions and of natural laws with human edicts. One observes that the will is not compelled, but that only means that it is not other than what is chosen. It is one of the demerits of the traditional theory of causality that it has created an artificial opposition between determinism and the freedom of which we are introspectively conscious.

Besides the general question whether volitions are determined, there is the further question whether they are _mechanically_ determined, i.e. whether they are part of what was above defined as a mechanical system. This is the question whether they form part of a system with purely material determinants, i.e. whether there are laws which, given certain material data, make all volitions functions of those data. Here again, empirical evidence is found up to a point, but it is not conclusive in regard to all volitions. It is important to observe, however, that even if volitions are part of a mechanical system, this by no means implies any supremacy of matter over mind. It may well be that the same system which is susceptible of material determinants is also susceptible of mental determinants; thus a mechanical system may be determined by sets of volitions, as well as by sets of material facts. It would seem, therefore, that the reasons which lead people to dislike the view that volitions are mechanically determined are fallacious.

One may now sum up the discussion of causality. It was found first that the law of causality, as usually stated by philosophers, is false, and is not employed in science. The nature of scientific laws was then considered, and it was found that, instead of stating that one event A is always followed by another event B, they state functional relations between certain events at certain times, which may be called determinants, and other events at earlier or later times or at the same time. No _a priori_ category could be found to be involved: the existence of scientific laws appears as a purely empirical fact, not necessarily universal, except in a trivial and scientifically useless form. It was discovered that a system with one set of determinants may very likely have other sets of a quite different kind, that, for example, a mechanically determined system may also be teleologically or volitionally determined. Finally, the problem of free will was considered: here the evidence suggests that the reasons for supposing volitions to be determined are strong but not conclusive, and it is decided that even if volitions are mechanically determined, that is no reason for denying freedom in the sense revealed by introspection, or for supposing that mechanical events are not determined by volitions. The problem of free will _versus_ determinism is therefore, if the argument is correct, mainly illusory, but in part not yet capable of being decisively solved.

The object of the following paper is to consider what it is that is known in cases where propositions about "the so-and-so" are known without it being known who or what the so-and-so is. For example, it is known that the candidate who gets most votes will be elected, though it is not known who is the candidate who will get most votes. The problem to be considered is: What is known in these cases, where the subject is merely described? This problem has been considered elsewhere[40] from a purely logical point of view; but in what follows the question is to be considered in relation to theory of knowledge as well as in relation to logic, and in view of the above-mentioned logical discussions, the logical portion shall in this paper be made as brief as possible.

In order to make clear the antithesis between "acquaintance" and "description," it is first necessary to explain what is meant by "acquaintance." One may say that one is _acquainted_ with an object when a direct cognitive relation to that object is held, i.e., when there is a direct awareness of the object itself. When a cognitive relation is spoken of here, the sort of relation which constitutes judgment is not meant, but rather the sort which constitutes presentation. In fact, it is thought that the relation of subject and object which is called acquaintance is simply the converse of the relation of object and subject which constitutes presentation. That is, to say that S has acquaintance with O is essentially the same thing as to say that O is presented to S. But the associations and natural extensions of the word _acquaintance_ are different from those of the word _presentation_. To begin with, as with most cognitive words, it is natural to say that one is acquainted with an object even at moments when it is not actually before the mind, provided it has been before the mind, and will be again whenever occasion arises. This is the same sense in which one is said to know that 2+2=4 even when something else is being thought of. In the second place, the word _acquaintance_ is designed to emphasise, more than the word _presentation_, the relational character of the fact with which we are concerned. There is, it seems, a danger that, in speaking of presentation, the object may be so emphasised as to lose sight of the subject. The result of this is either to lead to the view that there is no subject, whence materialism is arrived at; or to lead to the view that what is presented is part of the subject, whence idealism is arrived at, and solipsism should be arrived at but for the most desperate contortions. It is wished to preserve the dualism of subject and object in the terminology, because this dualism seems a fundamental fact concerning cognition. Hence the word _acquaintance_ is preferred because it emphasises the need of a subject which is acquainted.

When one asks what are the kinds of objects with which one is acquainted, the first and most obvious example is _sense-data_. When a colour is seen or a noise is heard, there is direct acquaintance with the colour or the noise. The sense-datum with which one is acquainted in these cases is generally, if not always, complex. This is particularly obvious in the case of sight. It is not meant, of course, merely that the supposed physical object is complex, but that the direct sensible object is complex and contains parts with spatial relations. Whether it is possible to be aware of a complex without being aware of its constituents is not an easy question, but on the whole it would seem that there is no reason why it should not be possible. This question arises in an acute form in connection with self-consciousness, which must now be briefly considered.

The awarenesses that have been considered so far have all been awarenesses of particular existents, and might all in a large sense be called sense-data. For, from the point of view of theory of knowledge, introspective knowledge is exactly on a level with knowledge derived from sight or hearing. But, in addition to awareness of the above kind of objects, which may be called awareness of *particulars*, there is also (though not quite in the same sense) what may be called awareness of *universals*. Awareness of universals is called *conceiving*, and a universal of which there is awareness is called a *concept*. Not only is one aware of particular yellows, but if a sufficient number of yellows have been seen and sufficient intelligence is possessed, one becomes aware of the universal *yellow*; this universal is the subject in such judgments as "yellow differs from blue" or "yellow resembles blue less than green does." And the universal yellow is the predicate in such judgments as "this is yellow," where "this" is a particular sense-datum. And universal relations, too, are objects of awarenesses; up and down, before and after, resemblance, desire, awareness itself, and so on, would seem to be all of them objects of which one can be aware.

In regard to relations, it might be urged that one is never aware of the universal relation itself, but only of complexes in which it is a constituent. For example, it may be said that such a relation as _before_ is not known directly, though such a proposition as "this is before that" is understood, and such a complex as "this being before that" may be directly apprehended. This view, however, is difficult to reconcile with the fact that propositions are often known in which the relation is the subject, or in which the relata are not definite given objects, but "anything." For example, it is known that if one thing is before another, and the other before a third, then the first is before the third; and here the things concerned are not definite things, but "anything." It is hard to see how such a fact about "before" could be known unless acquaintance were had with "before" itself, and not merely with actual particular cases of one given object being before another given object. And more directly: A judgment such as "this is before that," where this judgment is derived from awareness of a complex, constitutes an analysis, and the analysis would not be understood if acquaintance were not had with the meaning of the terms employed. Thus it must be supposed that acquaintance is had with the meaning of "before," and not merely with instances of it.

There are thus at least two sorts of objects of which one is aware, namely, particulars and universals. Among particulars are included all existents, and all complexes of which one or more constituents are existents, such as this-before-that, this-above-that, the-yellowness-of-this. Among universals are included all objects of which no particular is a constituent. Thus the disjunction "universal-particular" includes all objects. It might also be called the disjunction "abstract-concrete." It is not quite parallel with the opposition "concept-percept," because things remembered or imagined belong with particulars, but can hardly be called percepts. (On the other hand, universals with which we are acquainted may be identified with concepts.)

When one says "the so-and-so exists," it is meant that there is just one object which is the so-and-so. The proposition "_a_ is the so-and-so" means that _a_ has the property so-and-so, and nothing else has. "Sir Joseph Larmor is the Unionist candidate" is understood to mean "Sir Joseph Larmor is a Unionist candidate, and no one else is." "The Unionist candidate exists" is taken to mean "some one is a Unionist candidate, and no one else is." Thus, when one is acquainted with an object which is known to be the so-and-so, it is known that the so-and-so exists; but it may be known that the so-and-so exists when one is not acquainted with any object which is known to be the so-and-so, and even when one is not acquainted with any object which, in fact, is the so-and-so.

It is observed that common words, even proper names, are usually really descriptions. That is to say, the thought in the mind of a person using a proper name correctly can generally only be expressed explicitly if the proper name is replaced by a description. Moreover, the description required to express the thought is seen to vary for different people, or for the same person at different times. The only thing constant (so long as the name is rightly used) is known to be the object to which the name applies. But so long as this remains constant, the particular description involved usually makes no difference to the truth or falsehood of the proposition in which the name appears.

One may take some illustrations. Suppose some statement made about Bismarck. Assuming that there is such a thing as direct acquaintance with oneself, Bismarck himself might have used his name directly to designate the particular person with whom he was acquainted. In this case, if he made a judgment about himself, he himself might be a constituent of the judgment. Here the proper name has the direct use which it always wishes to have, as simply standing for a certain object, and not for a description of the object. But if a person who knew Bismarck made a judgment about him, the case is different. What this person was acquainted with were certain sense-data which were connected (rightly, one will suppose) with Bismarck's body. His body as a physical object, and still more his mind, were only known as the body and the mind connected with these sense-data. That is, they were known by description. It is, of course, very much a matter of chance which characteristics of a man's appearance will come into a friend's mind when he is thought of; thus the description actually in the friend's mind is accidental. The essential point is that it is known that the various descriptions all apply to the same entity, in spite of not being acquainted with the entity in question.

When one, who did not know Bismarck, makes a judgment about him, the description in one's mind will probably be some more or less vague mass of historical knowledge—far more, in most cases, than is required to identify him. But, for the sake of illustration, let it be assumed that he is thought of as "the first Chancellor of the German Empire." Here all the words are abstract except "German." The word "German" will again have different meanings for different people. To some it will recall travels in Germany, to some the look of Germany on the map, and so on. But if a description is to be obtained which is known to be applicable, one is compelled, at some point, to bring in a reference to a particular with which one is acquainted. Such reference is involved in any mention of past, present, and future (as opposed to definite dates), or of here and there, or of what has been told by others. Thus it would seem that, in some way or other, a description known to be applicable to a particular must involve some reference to a particular with which one is acquainted, if knowledge about the thing described is not to be merely what follows logically from the description. For example, "the most long-lived of men" is a description which must apply to some man, but no judgments can be made concerning this man which involve knowledge about him beyond what the description gives. If, however, it is said, "the first Chancellor of the German Empire was an astute diplomatist," one can only be assured of the truth of this judgment in virtue of something with which one is acquainted—usually a testimony heard or read. Considered psychologically, apart from the information conveyed to others, apart from the fact about the actual Bismarck, which gives importance to the judgment, the thought that is really had contains the one or more particulars involved, and otherwise consists wholly of concepts. All names of places—London, England, Europe, the earth, the Solar System—similarly involve, when used, descriptions which start from some one or more particulars with which one is acquainted. It may be suspected that even the Universe, as considered by metaphysics, involves such a connection with particulars. In logic, on the contrary, where concern is not merely with what does exist, but with whatever might or could exist or be, no reference to actual particulars is involved.

It would seem that, when a statement is made about something only known by description, one often _intends_ to make the statement, not in the form involving the description, but about the actual thing described. That is to say, when anything is said about Bismarck, it is desired, if possible, to make the judgment which Bismarck alone can make, namely, the judgment of which he himself is a constituent. In this, one is necessarily defeated, since the actual Bismarck is unknown. But it is known that there is an object B called Bismarck, and that B was an astute diplomatist. One can thus _describe_ the proposition one would like to affirm, namely, "B was an astute diplomatist," where B is the object which was Bismarck. What enables communication in spite of the varying descriptions employed is the knowledge that there is a true proposition concerning the actual Bismarck, and that, however the description may be varied (so long as the description is correct), the proposition described is still the same. This proposition, which is described and is known to be true, is what is of interest; but one is not acquainted with the proposition itself, and does not know _it_, though it is known to be true.

The chief reason for supposing the principle true is that it seems scarcely possible to believe that one can make a judgment or entertain a supposition without knowing what it is that is being judged or supposed about. If a judgment is made about (say) Julius Cæsar, it is plain that the actual person who was Julius Cæsar is not a constituent of the judgment. But before going further, it may be well to explain what is meant when it is said that this or that is a constituent of a judgment, or of a proposition which is understood. To begin with judgments: a judgment, as an occurrence, is taken to be a relation of a mind to several entities, namely, the entities which compose what is judged. If, e.g., it is judged that A loves B, the judgment as an event consists in the existence, at a certain moment, of a specific four-term relation, called _judging_, between a mind and A and love and B. That is to say, at the time when the judgment occurs, there is a certain complex whose terms are the mind and A and love and B, and whose relating relation is _judging_. The reasons for this view have been set forth elsewhere,[41] and they will not be repeated here. Assuming this view of judgment, the constituents of the judgment are simply the constituents of the complex which is the judgment. Thus, in the above case, the constituents are the mind and A and love and B and judging. But the mind and judging are constituents shared by all judgments of that mind; thus the _distinctive_ constituents of the particular judgment in question are A and love and B. Coming now to what is meant by "understanding a proposition," it would be said that there is another relation possible between a mind and A and love and B, which is called the _supposing_ that A loves B.[42] When one can _suppose_ that A loves B, the proposition _A loves B_ is "understood." Thus a proposition is often understood in cases where there is not enough knowledge to make a judgment. Supposing, like judging, is a many-term relation, of which a mind is one term. The other terms of the relation are called the constituents of the proposition supposed. Thus the principle which was enunciated may be re-stated as follows: _Whenever a relation of supposing or judging occurs, the terms to which the supposing or judging mind is related by the relation of supposing or judging must be terms with which the mind in question is acquainted._ This is merely to say that a judgment or a supposition cannot be made without knowing what it is that the judgment or supposition is about. It seems evident that the truth of this principle is evident as soon as the principle is understood; it will, therefore, in what follows, be assumed, and used as a guide in analysing judgments that contain descriptions.

Returning now to Julius Cæsar, it is assumed that it will be admitted that he himself is not a constituent of any judgment which can be made. But at this point it is necessary to examine the view that judgments are composed of something called "ideas," and that it is the "idea" of Julius Cæsar that is a constituent of the judgment. The plausibility of this view is believed to rest upon a failure to form a right theory of descriptions. By the "idea" of Julius Cæsar may be meant the things that are known about him, e.g. that he conquered Gaul, was assassinated on the Ides of March, and is a plague to schoolboys. Now it is admitted, and indeed contended, that in order to discover what is actually in the mind when judging about Julius Cæsar, one must substitute for the proper name a description made up of some of the things known about him. (A description which will often serve to express the thought is "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_." For whatever else may have been forgotten about him, it is plain that when he is mentioned it has not been forgotten that that was his name.) But although it is thought the theory that judgments consist of ideas may have been suggested in some such way, yet the theory itself is considered fundamentally mistaken. The view seems to be that there is some mental existent which may be called the "idea" of something outside the mind of the person who has the idea, and that, since judgment is a mental event, its constituents must be constituents of the mind of the person judging. But in this view ideas become a veil between us and outside things—it is never really, in knowledge, attained to the things we are supposed to be knowing about, but only to the ideas of those things. The relation of mind, idea, and object, on this view, is utterly obscure, and, so far as can be seen, nothing discoverable by inspection warrants the intrusion of the idea between the mind and the object. It is suspected that the view is fostered by the dislike of relations, and that it is felt the mind could not know objects unless there were something "in" the mind which could be called the state of knowing the object. Such a view, however, leads at once to a vicious endless regress, since the relation of idea to object will have to be explained by supposing that the idea itself has an idea of the object, and so on _ad infinitum_. No reason is therefore seen to believe that, when one is acquainted with an object, there is present something which can be called the "idea" of the object. On the contrary, it is held that acquaintance is wholly a relation, not demanding any such constituent of the mind as is supposed by advocates of "ideas." This is, of course, a large question, and one which would take us far from our subject if it were adequately discussed. One therefore contents oneself with the above indications, and with the corollary that, in judging, the actual objects concerning which we judge, rather than any supposed purely mental entities, are constituents of the complex which is the judgment.

When, therefore, it is said that one must substitute for "Julius Cæsar" some description of Julius Cæsar, in order to discover the meaning of a judgment nominally about him, it is not being said that one must substitute an idea. Suppose the description is "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_." Let the judgment be "Julius Cæsar was assassinated." Then it becomes "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_ was assassinated." Here _Julius Cæsar_ is a noise or shape with which one is acquainted, and all the other constituents of the judgment (neglecting the tense in "was") are _concepts_ with which one is acquainted. Thus the judgment is wholly reduced to constituents with which one is acquainted, but Julius Cæsar himself has ceased to be a constituent of the judgment. This, however, requires a proviso, to be further explained shortly, namely that "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_" must not, as a whole, be a constituent of the judgment, that is to say, this phrase must not, as a whole, have a meaning which enters into the judgment. Any right analysis of the judgment, therefore, must break up this phrase, and not treat it as a subordinate complex which is part of the judgment. The judgment "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_ was assassinated" may be interpreted as meaning "one and only one man was called _Julius Cæsar_, and that one was assassinated." Here it is plain that there is no constituent corresponding to the phrase "the man whose name was _Julius Cæsar_." Thus there is no reason to regard this phrase as expressing a constituent of the judgment, and it has been seen that this phrase must be broken up if one is to be acquainted with all the constituents of the judgment. This conclusion, which is reached from considerations concerned with the theory of knowledge, is also forced upon one by logical considerations, which must now be briefly reviewed.

It is common to distinguish two aspects, _meaning_ and _denotation_, in such phrases as "the author of Waverley." The meaning is observed to be a certain complex, consisting (at least) of authorship and Waverley with some relation; the denotation is seen to be Scott. Similarly "featherless bipeds" can be seen to have a complex meaning, containing as constituents the presence of two feet and the absence of feathers, while its denotation is known to be the class of men. Thus when it is said that "Scott is the author of Waverley" or "men are the same as featherless bipeds," an identity of denotation is being asserted, and this assertion is worth making because of the diversity of meaning.[43] It is believed that the duality of meaning and denotation, though capable of a true interpretation, is misleading if taken as fundamental. The denotation, it is held, is not a constituent of the proposition, except in the case of proper names, i.e. of words which do not assign a property to an object, but merely and solely name it. And it is further maintained that, in this sense, there are only two words which are strictly proper names of particulars, namely, "I" and "this."[44]

A second reason is that propositions concerning "the so-and-so" are possible even when "the so-and-so" has no denotation. Take, e.g. "the golden mountain does not exist" or "the round square is self-contradictory." If the duality of meaning and denotation is to be preserved, one has to say, with Meinong, that there are such objects as the golden mountain and the round square, although these objects do not have being. It is even necessary to admit that the existent round square is existent, but does not exist.[45] Meinong does not regard this as a contradiction, but it can be seen that it is one. Indeed, it becomes evident that the judgment "there is no such object as the round square" does not presuppose that there is such an object. If this is admitted, however, one is led to the conclusion that, by parity of form, no judgment concerning "the so-and-so" actually involves the so-and-so as a constituent.

It is observed that Miss Jones[46] contends that there is no difficulty in admitting contradictory predicates concerning such an object as "the present King of France," on the ground that this object is in itself contradictory. Now it might, of course, be argued that this object, unlike the round square, is not self-contradictory, but merely non-existent. This, however, would not go to the root of the matter. The real objection to such an argument is that the law of contradiction ought not to be stated in the traditional form "A is not both B and not B," but in the form "no proposition is both true and false." The traditional form only applies to certain propositions, namely, to those which attribute a predicate to a subject. When the law is stated of propositions, instead of being stated concerning subjects and predicates, it becomes evident that propositions about the present King of France or the round square can form no exception, but are just as incapable of being both true and false as other propositions. Miss Jones[47] argues that "Scott is the author of Waverley" asserts identity of denotation between _Scott_ and _the author of Waverley_. But there is some difficulty in choosing among alternative meanings of this contention. In the first place, it should be observed that _the author of Waverley_ is not a _mere_ name, like _Scott_. _Scott_ is merely a noise or shape conventionally used to designate a certain person; it gives one no information about that person, and has nothing that can be called meaning as opposed to denotation. (The fact, considered above, that even proper names, as a rule, really stand for descriptions, is here neglected.) But _the author of Waverley_ is not merely conventionally a name for Scott; the element of mere convention belongs here to the separate words, _the_ and _author_ and _of_ and _Waverley_. Given what these words stand for, _the author of Waverley_ is no longer arbitrary. When it is said that Scott is the author of Waverley, one is not stating that these are two _names_ for one man, as one would be if it were said "Scott is Sir Walter." A man's name is what he is called, but however much Scott had been called the author of Waverley, that would not have made him be the author; it was necessary for him actually to write Waverley, which was a fact having nothing to do with names.

It has thus been agreed that "the author of Waverley" is not a mere name, and that its meaning is relevant in propositions in which it occurs. Thus if one is to say, as Miss Jones does, that "Scott is the author of Waverley" asserts an identity of denotation, the denotation of "the author of Waverley" must be regarded as the denotation of what is _meant_ by "the author of Waverley." Let the meaning of "the author of Waverley" be called M. Thus M is what "the author of Waverley" means. Then it is to be supposed that "Scott is the author of Waverley" means "Scott is the denotation of M." But here the proposition is being explained by another of the same form, and thus no progress has been made towards a real explanation. "The denotation of M," like "the author of Waverley," has both meaning and denotation, on the theory being examined. If its meaning is called M', the proposition becomes "Scott is the denotation of M'." But this leads at once to an endless regress. Thus the attempt to regard the proposition as asserting identity of denotation breaks down, and it becomes imperative to find some other analysis. When this analysis has been completed, the phrase "identity of denotation," which remains obscure so long as it is taken as fundamental, can be reinterpreted.

The first point to observe is that, in any proposition about "the author of Waverley," provided Scott is not explicitly mentioned, the denotation itself, i.e. Scott, does not occur, but only the concept of denotation, which will be represented by a variable. If one says "the author of Waverley was the author of Marmion," it is certainly not being said that both were Scott—it may have been forgotten that there was such a person as Scott. What is being said is that there is some man who was the author of Waverley and the author of Marmion. That is to say, there is some one who wrote Waverley and Marmion, and no one else wrote them. Thus the identity is that of a variable, i.e. of an indefinite subject, "some one." This is why propositions about "the author of Waverley" can be understood without knowing who he was. When it is said "the author of Waverley was a poet," what is meant is "one and only one man wrote Waverley, and he was a poet"; when it is said "the author of Waverley was Scott" what is meant is "one and only one man wrote Waverley, and he was Scott." Here the identity is between a variable, i.e. an indeterminate subject ("he"), and Scott; "the author of Waverley" has been analysed away, and no longer appears as a constituent of the proposition.[48]

The reason why it is imperative to analyse away the phrase "the author of Waverley" may be stated as follows. It is plain that when one says "the author of Waverley is the author of Marmion," the _is_ expresses identity. It has been seen also that the common _denotation_, namely Scott, is not a constituent of this proposition, while the _meanings_ (if any) of "the author of Waverley" and "the author of Marmion" are not identical. It has been seen also that, in any sense in which the meaning of a word is a constituent of a proposition in whose verbal expression the word occurs, "Scott" means the actual man Scott, in the same sense (so far as concerns the present discussion) in which "author" means a certain universal. Thus, if "the author of Waverley" were a subordinate complex in the above proposition, its _meaning_ would have to be what was said to be identical with the _meaning_ of "the author of Marmion." This is plainly not the case; and the only escape is to say that "the author of Waverley" does not, by itself, have a meaning, though phrases of which it is part do have a meaning. That is, in a right analysis of the above proposition, "the author of Waverley" must disappear. This is effected when the above proposition is analysed as meaning: "Some one wrote Waverley and no one else did, and that some one also wrote Marmion and no one else did." This may be more simply expressed by saying that the propositional function "_x_ wrote Waverley and Marmion, and no one else did" is capable of truth, i.e. some value of _x_ makes it true, but no other value does. Thus the true subject of the judgment is a propositional function, i.e. a complex containing an undetermined constituent, and becoming a proposition as soon as this constituent is determined.

One may now define the denotation of a phrase. If it is known that the proposition "_a_ is the so-and-so" is true, i.e. that _a_ is so-and-so and nothing else is, _a_ is called the denotation of the phrase "the so-and-so." A very great many of the propositions naturally made about "the so-and-so" will remain true or remain false if _a_ is substituted for "the so-and-so," where _a_ is the denotation of "the so-and-so." Such propositions will also remain true or remain false if any other phrase having the same denotation is substituted for "the so-and-so." Hence, as practical men, it becomes clear that interest is directed toward the denotation more than toward the description, since the denotation decides as to the truth or falsehood of so many statements in which the description occurs. Moreover, as was seen earlier in considering the relations of description and acquaintance, it is often desired to reach the denotation, and one is only hindered by lack of acquaintance: in such cases the description is merely the means employed to get as near as possible to the denotation. Hence it naturally comes to be supposed that the denotation is part of the proposition in which the description occurs. But it has been seen, both on logical and on epistemological grounds, that this is an error. The actual object (if any) which is the denotation is not (unless it is explicitly mentioned) a constituent of propositions in which descriptions occur; and this is the reason why, in order to understand such propositions, acquaintance with the constituents of the description is needed, but acquaintance with its denotation is not needed. The first result of analysis, when applied to propositions whose grammatical subject is "the so-and-so," is to substitute a variable as subject; i.e. a proposition of the form is obtained: "There is _something_ which alone is so-and-so, and that _something_ is such-and-such." The further analysis of propositions concerning "the so-and-so" is thus merged in the problem of the nature of the variable, i.e. of the meanings of _some_, _any_, and _all_. This is a difficult problem, concerning which nothing is intended to be said at present.

One might ask whether there is any knowledge in the world which is so certain that no reasonable man could doubt it. This question, which at first sight might not seem difficult, is really one of the most difficult that can be asked. When the obstacles in the way of a straightforward and confident answer are realized, one is well launched on the study of philosophy—for philosophy is merely the attempt to answer such ultimate questions, not carelessly and dogmatically, as is done in ordinary life and even in the sciences, but critically, after exploring all that makes such questions puzzling, and after realizing all the vagueness and confusion that underlie our ordinary ideas.

In daily life, it is assumed as certain many things which, on a closer scrutiny, are found to be so full of apparent contradictions that only a great amount of thought enables one to know what it is that one really may believe. In the search for certainty, it is natural to begin with present experiences, and in some sense, no doubt, knowledge is to be derived from them. But any statement as to what it is that immediate experiences make one know is very likely to be wrong. It is observed that one is now sitting in a chair, at a table of a certain shape, on which are seen sheets of paper with writing or print. By turning the head, one sees out of the window buildings and clouds and the sun. It is believed that the sun is about ninety-three million miles from the earth; that it is a hot globe many times bigger than the earth; that, owing to the earth's rotation, it rises every morning, and will continue to do so for an indefinite time in the future. It is believed that, if any other normal person comes into the room, the same chairs and tables and books and papers will be seen, and that the table which is seen is the same as the table which is felt pressing against an arm. All this seems to be so evident as to be hardly worth stating, except in answer to one who doubts whether anything is known. Yet all this may be reasonably doubted, and all of it requires much careful discussion before we can be sure that it has been stated in a form that is wholly true.

To make the difficulties plain, one may concentrate attention on the table. To the eye it is observed to be oblong, brown and shiny; to the touch it is found to be smooth and cool and hard; when tapped, it gives out a wooden sound. Any one else who sees and feels and hears the table will agree with this description, so that it might seem as if no difficulty would arise; but as soon as a more precise description is attempted, the troubles begin. Although it is believed that the table is 'really' of the same colour all over, the parts that reflect the light are seen to be much brighter than the other parts, and some parts look white because of reflected light. It is known that, if the observer moves, the parts that reflect the light will be different, so that the apparent distribution of colours on the table will change. It follows that if several people are looking at the table at the same moment, no two of them will see exactly the same distribution of colours, because no two can see it from exactly the same point of view, and any change in the point of view makes some change in the way the light is reflected.

For most practical purposes these differences are unimportant, but to the painter they are all-important: the painter has to unlearn the habit of thinking that things seem to have the colour which common sense says they 'really' have, and to learn the habit of seeing things as they appear. Here one observes already the beginning of one of the distinctions that cause most trouble in philosophy—the distinction between 'appearance' and 'reality', between what things seem to be and what they are. The painter wants to know what things seem to be, the practical man and the philosopher want to know what they are; but the philosopher's wish to know this is found to be stronger than the practical man's, and is more troubled by knowledge as to the difficulties of answering the question.

To return to the table. It is evident from what has been found, that there is no colour which pre-eminently appears to be _the_ colour of the table, or even of any one particular part of the table—it is observed to be of different colours from different points of view, and there is no reason for regarding some of these as more really its colour than others. And it is known that even from a given point of view the colour will seem different by artificial light, or to a colour-blind man, or to a man wearing blue spectacles, while in the dark there will be no colour at all, though to touch and hearing the table will be unchanged. This colour is not something which is inherent in the table, but something depending upon the table and the spectator and the way the light falls on the table. When, in ordinary life, one speaks of _the_ colour of the table, one only means the sort of colour which it will seem to have to a normal spectator from an ordinary point of view under usual conditions of light. But the other colours which appear under other conditions have just as good a right to be considered real; and therefore, to avoid favouritism, it is compelled that one must deny that, in itself, the table has any one particular colour.

The same thing applies to the texture. With the naked eye one can observe the grain, but otherwise the table appears smooth and even. If it is observed through a microscope, roughnesses and hills and valleys, and all sorts of differences that are imperceptible to the naked eye are seen. Which of these is the 'real' table? One is naturally tempted to say that what is seen through the microscope is more real, but that in turn would be changed by a still more powerful microscope. If, then, one cannot trust what is seen with the naked eye, why should what is seen through a microscope be trusted? Thus, again, the confidence in the senses with which one began is deserted.

The shape of the table is no better. One is in the habit of judging as to the 'real' shapes of things, and this is done so unreflectingly that it is thought one actually sees the real shapes. But, in fact, as must be learned if drawing is attempted, a given thing looks different in shape from every different point of view. If a table is 'really' rectangular, it will look, from almost all points of view, as if it had two acute angles and two obtuse angles. If opposite sides are parallel, they will look as if they converged to a point away from the spectator; if they are of equal length, they will look as if the nearer side were longer. All these things are not commonly noticed in looking at a table, because experience has taught the construction of the 'real' shape from the apparent shape, and the 'real' shape is what interests the practical man. But the 'real' shape is not what is seen; it is something inferred from what is seen. And what is seen is constantly changing in shape as one moves about the room; so that here again the senses seem not to give the truth about the table itself, but only about the appearance of the table.

It will help in considering these questions to have a few simple terms of which the meaning is definite and clear. Let the name of 'sense-data' be given to the things that are immediately known in sensation: such things as colours, sounds, smells, hardnesses, roughnesses, and so on. The name 'sensation' is given to the experience of being immediately aware of these things. Thus, whenever a colour is seen, one has a sensation _of_ the colour, but the colour itself is a sense-datum, not a sensation. The colour is that _of_ which there is immediate awareness, and the awareness itself is the sensation. It is plain that if anything is to be known about the table, it must be by means of the sense-data--brown colour, oblong shape, smoothness, etc.--which are associated with the table; but, for the reasons which have been given, it cannot be said that the table is the sense-data, or even that the sense-data are directly properties of the table. Thus a problem arises as to the relation of the sense-data to the real table, supposing there is such a thing.

One observes that the philosopher who first brought prominently forward the reasons for regarding the immediate objects of our senses as not existing independently of us was Bishop Berkeley (1685-1753). His _Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous, in Opposition to Sceptics and Atheists_, undertake to prove that there is no such thing as matter at all, and that the world consists of nothing but minds and their ideas. Hylas has hitherto believed in matter, but he is no match for Philonous, who mercilessly drives him into contradictions and paradoxes, and makes his own denial of matter seem, in the end, as if it were almost common sense. The arguments employed are of very different value: some are important and sound, others are confused or quibbling. But Berkeley retains the merit of having shown that the existence of matter is capable of being denied without absurdity, and that if there are any things that exist independently of us they cannot be the immediate objects of our sensations.

One observes that there are two different questions involved when it is asked whether matter exists, and it is important to keep them clear. By 'matter' is commonly meant something which is opposed to 'mind', something which is thought of as occupying space and as radically incapable of any sort of thought or consciousness. It is chiefly in this sense that matter is denied by Berkeley; that is to say, it is not denied that the sense-data which are commonly taken as signs of the existence of the table are really signs of the existence of _something_ independent of us, but it is denied that this something is non-mental, that it is neither mind nor ideas entertained by some mind. It is admitted that there must be something which continues to exist when the room is left or eyes are shut, and that what is called seeing the table does really give reason for believing in something which persists even when it is not being seen. But it is thought that this something cannot be radically different in nature from what is seen, and cannot be independent of seeing altogether, though it must be independent of _our_ seeing. One is thus led to regard the 'real' table as an idea in the mind of God. Such an idea is seen to have the required permanence and independence of ourselves, without being--as matter would otherwise be--something quite unknowable, in the sense that it can only be inferred, and can never be directly and immediately aware of it.

Other philosophers since Berkeley have also held that, although the table does not depend for its existence upon being seen by any particular individual, it does depend upon being seen (or otherwise apprehended in sensation) by _some_ mind—not necessarily the mind of God, but more often the whole collective mind of the universe. This view is held, as in Berkeley, chiefly because it is thought there can be nothing real—or at any rate nothing known to be real except minds and their thoughts and feelings. The argument by which this view is supported might be stated in some such way as this: ‘Whatever can be thought of is an idea in the mind of the person thinking of it; therefore nothing can be thought of except ideas in minds; therefore anything else is inconceivable, and what is inconceivable cannot exist.’

Such an argument, in one's opinion, is fallacious; and of course those who advance it do not put it so shortly or so crudely. But whether valid or not, the argument has been very widely advanced in one form or another; and it is observed that very many philosophers, perhaps a majority, have held that there is nothing real except minds and their ideas. Such philosophers are called 'idealists'. When the explanation of matter is approached, it is seen that they either say, like Berkeley, that matter is really nothing but a collection of ideas, or they say, like Leibniz (1646-1716), that what appears as matter is really a collection of more or less rudimentary minds.

But these philosophers, though they deny matter as opposed to mind, nevertheless, in another sense, admit matter. It will be remembered that two questions were asked; namely, (1) Is there a real table at all? (2) If so, what sort of object can it be? Now both Berkeley and Leibniz admit that there is a real table, but Berkeley says it is certain ideas in the mind of God, and Leibniz says it is a colony of souls. Thus both of them answer the first question in the affirmative, and only diverge from the views of ordinary mortals in their answer to the second question. In fact, almost all philosophers seem to be agreed that there is a real table: it is generally agreed that, however much our sense-data--colour, shape, smoothness, etc.--may depend upon the observer, yet their occurrence is a sign of something existing independently, something differing, perhaps, completely from our sense-data, and yet to be regarded as causing those sense-data whenever one is in a suitable relation to the real table.

Before one proceeds farther it will be well to consider for a moment what it is that has been discovered so far. It has appeared that, if any common object of the sort that is supposed to be known by the senses is taken, what the senses _immediately_ tell one is not the truth about the object as it is apart from the observer, but only the truth about certain sense-data which, so far as can be seen, depend upon the relations between the observer and the object. Thus what is directly seen and felt is merely 'appearance', which is believed to be a sign of some 'reality' behind. But if the reality is not what appears, are there any means of knowing whether there is any reality at all? And if so, are there any means of finding out what it is like?

Such questions are bewildering, and it is difficult to know that even the strangest hypotheses may not be true. Thus the familiar table, which has roused but the slightest thoughts hitherto, becomes a problem full of surprising possibilities. The one thing known about it is that it is not what it seems. Beyond this modest result, so far, the most complete liberty of conjecture is available. Leibniz informs one that it is a community of souls; Berkeley informs one that it is an idea in the mind of God; sober science, scarcely less wonderful, informs one that it is a vast collection of electric charges in violent motion.

In this chapter one must ask whether, in any sense at all, there is such a thing as matter. Is there a table which has a certain intrinsic nature, and continues to exist when it is not being observed, or is the table merely a product of imagination, a dream-table in a very prolonged dream? This question is of the greatest importance. For if one cannot be sure of the independent existence of objects, one cannot be sure of the independent existence of other people's bodies, and therefore still less of other people's minds, since no grounds are available for believing in their minds except such as are derived from observing their bodies. Thus if one cannot be sure of the independent existence of objects, one is left alone in a desert—it may be that the whole outer world is nothing but a dream, and that only the solitary observer exists. This is an uncomfortable possibility; but although it cannot be strictly proved to be false, there is not the slightest reason to suppose that it is true. In this chapter it must be seen why this is the case.

Descartes (1596-1650), the founder of modern philosophy, invented a method which may still be used with profit--the method of systematic doubt. It was determined that nothing should be believed which was not seen quite clearly and distinctly to be true. Whatever could be brought into doubt, was to be doubted, until reason for not doubting it was seen. By applying this method it gradually became convincing that the only existence of which one could be _quite_ certain was one's own. A deceitful demon was imagined, who presented unreal things to the senses in a perpetual phantasmagoria; it might be very improbable that such a demon existed, but still it was possible, and therefore doubt concerning things perceived by the senses was possible.

But doubt concerning one's own existence is not possible, for if one did not exist, no demon could deceive one. If one doubts, one must exist; if one has any experiences whatever, one must exist. Thus one's own existence becomes an absolute certainty. 'I think, therefore I am,' it is stated (_Cogito, ergo sum_); and on the basis of this certainty it is possible to set to work to build up again the world of knowledge which doubt had laid in ruins. By inventing the method of doubt, and by showing that subjective things are the most certain, a great service is performed for philosophy, and one which makes Descartes still useful to all students of the subject.

But some care is needed in using Descartes' argument. 'I think, therefore I am' is observed to say rather more than is strictly certain. It might seem as though one were quite sure of being the same person to-day as one was yesterday, and this is no doubt true in some sense. But the real Self is as hard to arrive at as the real table, and does not seem to have that absolute, convincing certainty that belongs to particular experiences. When the table is observed and a certain brown colour is seen, what is quite certain at once is not '_I_ am seeing a brown colour', but rather, 'a brown colour is being seen'. This of course involves something (or somebody) which (or who) sees the brown colour; but it does not of itself involve that more or less permanent person whom we call 'I'. So far as immediate certainty goes, it might be that the something which sees the brown colour is quite momentary, and not the same as the something which has some different experience the next moment.

The problem to be considered is this: Granted that one is certain of one's own sense-data, is there any reason for regarding them as signs of the existence of something else, which can be called the physical object? When all the sense-data which would naturally be regarded as connected with the table have been enumerated, has all there is to say about the table been said, or is there still something else—something not a sense-datum, something which persists when one goes out of the room? Common sense unhesitatingly answers that there is. What can be bought and sold and pushed about and have a cloth laid on it, and so on, cannot be a _mere_ collection of sense-data. If the cloth completely hides the table, no sense-data from the table will be derived, and therefore, if the table were merely sense-data, it would have ceased to exist, and the cloth would be suspended in empty air, resting, by a miracle, in the place where the table formerly was. This seems plainly absurd; but whoever wishes to become a philosopher must learn not to be frightened by absurdities.

One great reason why it is felt that a physical object must be secured in addition to the sense-data, is that the same object is wanted for different people. When ten people are sitting round a dinner-table, it seems preposterous to maintain that they are not seeing the same tablecloth, the same knives and forks and spoons and glasses. But the sense-data are private to each separate person; what is immediately present to the sight of one is not immediately present to the sight of another: they all see things from slightly different points of view, and therefore see them slightly differently. Thus, if there are to be public neutral objects, which can be in some sense known to many different people, there must be something over and above the private and particular sense-data which appear to various people. What reason, then, can be found for believing that there are such public neutral objects?

The first answer that naturally occurs to one is that, although different people may see the table slightly differently, still they all see more or less similar things when they look at the table, and the variations in what they see follow the laws of perspective and reflection of light, so that it is easy to arrive at a permanent object underlying all the different people's sense-data. The table was purchased from the former occupant of the room; one could not purchase _his_ sense-data, which died when he went away, but one could and did purchase the confident expectation of more or less similar sense-data. Thus it is the fact that different people have similar sense-data, and that one person in a given place at different times has similar sense-data, which makes it be supposed that over and above the sense-data there is a permanent public object which underlies or causes the sense-data of various people at various times.

Now in so far as the above considerations depend upon supposing that there are other people besides oneself, the very question at issue is begged. Other people are represented by certain sense-data, such as the sight of them or the sound of their voices, and if no reason existed to believe that there were physical objects independent of one's sense-data, no reason would exist to believe that other people exist except as part of a dream. Thus, when it is attempted to show that there must be objects independent of one's own sense-data, one cannot appeal to the testimony of other people, since this testimony itself consists of sense-data, and does not reveal other people's experiences unless one's own sense-data are signs of things existing independently. It must therefore, if possible, be found, in one's own purely private experiences, characteristics which show, or tend to show, that there are in the world things other than oneself and one's private experiences.

In one sense it must be admitted that one can never prove the existence of things other than oneself and one's experiences. No logical absurdity results from the hypothesis that the world consists of oneself and one's thoughts and feelings and sensations, and that everything else is mere fancy. In dreams a very complicated world may seem to be present, and yet on waking it is found to have been a delusion; that is to say, it is found that the sense-data in the dream do not appear to have corresponded with such physical objects as would naturally be inferred from those sense-data. (It is true that, when the physical world is assumed, it is possible to find physical causes for the sense-data in dreams: a door banging, for instance, may cause one to dream of a naval engagement. But although, in this case, there is a physical cause for the sense-data, there is not a physical object corresponding to the sense-data in the way in which an actual naval battle would correspond.) There is no logical impossibility in the supposition that the whole of life is a dream, in which all the objects that come before one are created by oneself. But although this is not logically impossible, there is no reason whatever to suppose that it is true; and it is, in fact, a less simple hypothesis, viewed as a means of accounting for the facts of one's own life, than the common-sense hypothesis that there really are objects independent of one, whose action upon one causes one's sensations.

The way in which simplicity comes in from supposing that there really are physical objects is easily seen. If the cat appears at one moment in one part of the room, and at another in another part, it is natural to suppose that it has moved from the one to the other, passing over a series of intermediate positions. But if it is merely a set of sense-data, it cannot have ever been in any place where it was not observed; thus one is led to suppose that it did not exist at all while it was not being looked at, but suddenly sprang into being in a new place. If the cat exists whether it is seen or not, it can be understood from common experience how it gets hungry between one meal and the next; but if it does not exist when it is not being seen, it seems odd that appetite should grow during non-existence as fast as during existence. And if the cat consists only of sense-data, it cannot be hungry, since no hunger but one's own can be a sense-datum to the observer. Thus the behaviour of the sense-data which represent the cat, though it seems quite natural when regarded as an expression of hunger, becomes utterly inexplicable when regarded as mere movements and changes of patches of colour, which are as incapable of hunger as a triangle is of playing football.

But the difficulty in the case of the cat is nothing compared to the difficulty in the case of human beings. When human beings speak—that is, when certain noises are heard which are associated with ideas, and certain motions of lips and expressions of face are simultaneously seen—it is very difficult to suppose that what is heard is not the expression of a thought, as it would be known to be if the same sounds were emitted. Of course similar things happen in dreams, where one is mistaken as to the existence of other people. But dreams are more or less suggested by what is called waking life, and are capable of being more or less accounted for on scientific principles if it is assumed that there really is a physical world. Thus every principle of simplicity urges the adoption of the natural view, that there really are objects other than oneself and one’s sense-data which have an existence not dependent upon their being perceived.

Of course it is not by argument that one originally comes by the belief in an independent external world. This belief is found ready in oneself as soon as reflection begins: it is what may be called an _instinctive_ belief. One would never have been led to question this belief but for the fact that, at any rate in the case of sight, it seems as if the sense-datum itself were instinctively believed to be the independent object, whereas argument shows that the object cannot be identical with the sense-datum. This discovery, however--which is not at all paradoxical in the case of taste and smell and sound, and only slightly so in the case of touch--leaves undiminished the instinctive belief that there _are_ objects _corresponding_ to our sense-data. Since this belief does not lead to any difficulties, but on the contrary tends to simplify and systematize the account of our experiences, there seems no good reason for rejecting it. It may therefore be admitted--though with a slight doubt derived from dreams--that the external world does really exist, and is not wholly dependent for its existence upon our continuing to perceive it.

It is of course _possible_ that all or any of one's beliefs may be mistaken, and therefore all ought to be held with at least some slight element of doubt. But _reason_ to reject a belief cannot be had except on the ground of some other belief. Hence, by organizing instinctive beliefs and their consequences, by considering which among them is most possible, if necessary, to modify or abandon, one can arrive, on the basis of accepting as the sole data what is instinctively believed, at an orderly systematic organization of knowledge, in which, though the _possibility_ of error remains, its likelihood is diminished by the interrelation of the parts and by the critical scrutiny which has preceded acquiescence.

In the preceding chapter it was agreed, though without demonstrative reasons being found, that it is rational to believe that sense-data—for example, those which are regarded as associated with a given table—are really signs of the existence of something independent of perception. That is to say, over and above the sensations of colour, hardness, noise, and so on, which make up the appearance of a table, it is assumed that there is something else, of which these things are appearances. The colour ceases to exist if the eyes are shut, the sensation of hardness ceases to exist if an arm is removed from contact with the table, the sound ceases to exist if one ceases to rap the table with one’s knuckles. But it is not believed that when all these things cease the table ceases. On the contrary, it is believed that it is because the table exists continuously that all these sense-data will reappear when the eyes are opened, the arm is replaced, and one begins again to rap with one’s knuckles.
