The question to be considered in this chapter is: What is the nature of this real table, which persists independently of its perception?

To this question physical science gives an answer, somewhat incomplete it is true, and in part still very hypothetical, but yet deserving of respect so far as it goes. Physical science, more or less unconsciously, has drifted into the view that all natural phenomena ought to be reduced to motions. Light and heat and sound are all due to wave-motions, which travel from the body emitting them to the observer who sees light or feels heat or hears sound. That which has the wave-motion is either aether or 'gross matter', but in either case is what the philosopher would call matter. The only properties which science assigns to it are position in space, and the power of motion according to the laws of motion. Science does not deny that it _may_ have other properties; but if so, such other properties are not useful to the scientific investigator, and in no way assist in explaining the phenomena.

Now this something, which is known to all who are not blind, is not, according to science, really to be found in the outer world: it is something caused by the action of certain waves upon the eyes and nerves and brain of the person who sees the light. When it is said that light _is_ waves, what is really meant is that waves are the physical cause of the sensations of light. But light itself, the thing which seeing people experience and blind people do not, is not supposed by science to form any part of the world that is independent of us and our senses. And very similar remarks would apply to other kinds of sensations.

It is observed that it is not only colours and sounds and so on that are absent from the scientific world of matter, but also _space_ as it is perceived through sight or touch. It is essential to science that its matter should be in _a_ space, but the space in which it is cannot be exactly the space that is seen or felt. To begin with, space as it is seen is not the same as space as it is obtained by the sense of touch; it is only by experience in infancy that one learns how to touch things that are seen, or how to get a sight of things which are felt making contact. But the space of science is neutral as between touch and sight; thus it cannot be either the space of touch or the space of sight.

Again, it is observed that different people see the same object as of different shapes, according to their point of view. A circular coin, for example, though one should always _judge_ it to be circular, will _look_ oval unless one is straight in front of it. When it is judged that it _is_ circular, one is judging that it has a real shape which is not its apparent shape, but belongs to it intrinsically apart from its appearance. But this real shape, which is what concerns science, must be in a real space, not the same as anybody's _apparent_ space. The real space is public, the apparent space is private to the percipient. In different people's _private_ spaces the same object seems to have different shapes; thus the real space, in which it has its real shape, must be different from the private spaces. The space of science, therefore, though _connected_ with the spaces we see and feel, is not identical with them, and the manner of its connexion requires investigation.

It is provisionally agreed that physical objects cannot be quite like sense-data, but may be regarded as _causing_ sensations. These physical objects are in the space of science, which may be termed 'physical' space. It is important to notice that, if sensations are to be caused by physical objects, there must be a physical space containing these objects and the sense-organs and nerves and brain. A sensation of touch is derived from an object when contact is made with it; that is to say, when some part of the body occupies a place in physical space quite close to the space occupied by the object. An object is seen (roughly speaking) when no opaque body is between the object and the eyes in physical space. Similarly, an object is only heard or smelled or tasted when one is sufficiently near to it, or when it touches the tongue, or has some suitable position in physical space relatively to the body. One cannot begin to state what different sensations will be derived from a given object under different circumstances unless the object and the body are regarded as both in one physical space, for it is mainly the relative positions of the object and the body that determine what sensations will be derived from the object.

Now one observes that sense-data are situated in private spaces, either the space of sight or the space of touch or such vaguer spaces as other senses may give. If, as science and common sense assume, there is one public all-embracing physical space in which physical objects are, the relative positions of physical objects in physical space must more or less correspond to the relative positions of sense-data in private spaces. There is no difficulty in supposing this to be the case. If a house is seen on a road nearer than another, other senses will bear out the view that it is nearer; for example, it will be reached sooner if the road is walked along. Other people will agree that the house which looks nearer is nearer; the ordnance map will take the same view; and thus everything points to a spatial relation between the houses corresponding to the relation between the sense-data which are seen when the houses are looked at. Thus it may be assumed that there is a physical space in which physical objects have spatial relations corresponding to those which the corresponding sense-data have in private spaces. It is this physical space which is dealt with in geometry and assumed in physics and astronomy.

Assuming that there is physical space, and that it does thus correspond to private spaces, what can be known about it? One can know _only_ what is required in order to secure the correspondence. That is to say, nothing can be known of what it is like in itself, but the sort of arrangement of physical objects which results from their spatial relations can be known. It can be known, for example, that the earth and moon and sun are in one straight line during an eclipse, though what a physical straight line is in itself cannot be known, as the look of a straight line in visual space is known. Thus much more comes to be known about the _relations_ of distances in physical space than about the distances themselves; it may be known that one distance is greater than another, or that it is along the same straight line as the other, but that immediate acquaintance with physical distances which is had with distances in private spaces, or with colours or sounds or other sense-data, cannot be had. All those things about physical space which a man born blind might know through other people about the space of sight can be known; but the kind of things which a man born blind could never know about the space of sight also cannot be known about physical space. The properties of the relations required to preserve the correspondence with sense-data can be known, but the nature of the terms between which the relations hold cannot be known.

With regard to time, one observes that the _feeling_ of duration or of the lapse of time is notoriously an unsafe guide as to the time that has elapsed by the clock. Times of boredom or suffering are perceived to pass slowly, times of agreeable occupation are perceived to pass quickly, and times of sleep pass almost as if they did not exist. Thus, in so far as time is constituted by duration, it becomes clear that there is the same necessity for distinguishing a public and a private time as there was in the case of space. But in so far as time consists in an _order_ of before and after, no need is found to make such a distinction; the time-order which events seem to have is, so far as can be seen, the same as the time-order which they do have. At any rate no reason can be given for supposing that the two orders are not the same. The same is usually found to be true of space: if a regiment of men are marching along a road, the shape of the regiment will look different from different points of view, but the men will appear arranged in the same order from all points of view. Hence the order is regarded as true also in physical space, whereas the shape is only supposed to correspond to the physical space so far as is required for the preservation of the order.

In saying that the time-order which events seem to have is the same as the time-order which they really have, it is necessary to guard against a possible misunderstanding. It must not be supposed that the various states of different physical objects have the same time-order as the sense-data which constitute the perceptions of those objects. Considered as physical objects, the thunder and lightning are simultaneous; that is to say, the lightning is simultaneous with the disturbance of the air in the place where the disturbance begins, namely, where the lightning is. But the sense-datum which is called hearing the thunder does not take place until the disturbance of the air has travelled as far as to where one is situated. Similarly, it takes about eight minutes for the sun's light to reach the observer; thus, when the sun is seen, one is seeing the sun of eight minutes ago. So far as sense-data afford evidence as to the physical sun they afford evidence as to the physical sun of eight minutes ago; if the physical sun had ceased to exist within the last eight minutes, that would make no difference to the sense-data which are called 'seeing the sun'. This affords a fresh illustration of the necessity of distinguishing between sense-data and physical objects.

What has been found as regards space is much the same as what is found in relation to the correspondence of the sense-data with their physical counterparts. If one object looks blue and another red, it may reasonably be presumed that there is some corresponding difference between the physical objects; if two objects both look blue, a corresponding similarity may be presumed. However, one cannot hope to be acquainted directly with the quality in the physical object which makes it look blue or red. Science tells us that this quality is a certain sort of wave-motion, and this sounds familiar, because wave-motions are thought of in the space that is seen. But the wave-motions must really be in physical space, with which no direct acquaintance is had; thus the real wave-motions are found to lack that familiarity which might have been supposed. And what holds for colours is closely similar to what holds for other sense-data. Thus it is found that, although the _relations_ of physical objects have all sorts of knowable properties, derived from their correspondence with the relations of sense-data, the physical objects themselves remain unknown in their intrinsic nature, so far at least as can be discovered by means of the senses. The question remains whether there is any other method of discovering the intrinsic nature of physical objects.

The most natural, though not ultimately the most defensible, hypothesis to adopt in the first instance, at any rate as regards visual sense-data, would be that, though physical objects cannot, for the reasons that have been considered, be _exactly_ like sense-data, yet they may be more or less like. According to this view, physical objects will, for example, really have colours, and it might be, by good luck, that an object is seen as of the colour it really is. The colour which an object seems to have at any given moment will in general be very similar, though not quite the same, from many different points of view; it might thus be supposed that the 'real' colour is a sort of medium colour, intermediate between the various shades which appear from the different points of view.

Such a theory is perhaps not capable of being definitely refuted, but it can be shown to be groundless. To begin with, it is plain that the colour one observes depends only upon the nature of the light-waves that strike the eye, and is therefore modified by the medium intervening between the observer and the object, as well as by the manner in which light is reflected from the object in the direction of the eye. The intervening air alters colours unless it is perfectly clear, and any strong reflection will alter them completely. Thus the colour that is seen is a result of the ray as it reaches the eye, and not simply a property of the object from which the ray comes. Hence, also, provided certain waves reach the eye, a certain colour will be seen, whether the object from which the waves start has any colour or not. Thus it is quite gratuitous to suppose that physical objects have colours, and therefore there is no justification for making such a supposition. Exactly similar arguments will apply to other sense-data.

It remains to be asked whether there are any general philosophical arguments enabling one to say that, if matter is real, it must be of such and such a nature. As explained above, very many philosophers, perhaps most, have held that whatever is real must be in some sense mental, or at any rate that whatever can be known anything about must be in some sense mental. Such philosophers are called 'idealists'. Idealists tell us that what appears as matter is really something mental; namely, either (as Leibniz held) more or less rudimentary minds, or (as Berkeley contended) ideas in the minds which, as is commonly said, 'perceive' the matter. Thus idealists deny the existence of matter as something intrinsically different from mind, though it is not denied that our sense-data are signs of something which exists independently of our private sensations. In the following chapter the reasons--in the author's opinion fallacious--which idealists advance in favour of their theory will be considered briefly.

One observes that those who are unaccustomed to philosophical speculation may be inclined to dismiss such a doctrine as obviously absurd. It is noted that common sense regards tables and chairs and the sun and moon and material objects generally as something radically different from minds and the contents of minds, and as having an existence which might continue if minds ceased. It is commonly thought that matter had existed long before there were any minds, and it is found to be hard to think of it as a mere product of mental activity. But whether true or false, idealism is not to be dismissed as obviously absurd.

It has been observed that, even if physical objects do have an independent existence, they must differ very widely from sense-data, and can only have a _correspondence_ with sense-data, in the same sort of way in which a catalogue has a correspondence with the things catalogued. Hence common sense is seen to leave one completely in the dark as to the true intrinsic nature of physical objects, and if there were good reason to regard them as mental, this opinion could not legitimately be rejected merely because it strikes one as strange. The truth about physical objects _must_ be strange. It may be unattainable, but if any philosopher is believed to have attained it, the fact that what is offered as the truth is strange ought not to be made a ground of objection to that opinion.

The grounds on which idealism is advocated are generally grounds derived from the theory of knowledge, that is to say, from a discussion of the conditions which things must satisfy in order that they may be known. The first serious attempt to establish idealism on such grounds was that of Bishop Berkeley. It was proved first, by arguments which were largely valid, that sense-data cannot be supposed to have an existence independent of a perceiver, but must be, in part at least, 'in' the mind, in the sense that their existence would not continue if there were no seeing or hearing or touching or smelling or tasting. So far, the contention was almost certainly valid, even if some of the arguments were not so. But it was further argued that sense-data were the only things of whose existence perceptions could assure one; and that to be known is to be 'in' a mind, and therefore to be mental. Hence it was concluded that nothing can ever be known except what is in some mind, and that whatever is known without being in one's own mind must be in some other mind.

One then proceeds to consider common objects, such as a tree, for instance. It is shown that all that is known immediately when one 'perceives' the tree consists of ideas in the sense of the word used, and it is argued that there is not the slightest ground for supposing that there is anything real about the tree except what is perceived. Its being, it is said, consists in being perceived: in the Latin of the schoolmen its '_esse_' is '_percipi_'. It is fully admitted that the tree must continue to exist even when eyes are shut or when no human being is near it. But this continued existence, it is said, is due to the fact that God continues to perceive it; the 'real' tree, which corresponds to what is called the physical object, consists of ideas in the mind of God, ideas more or less like those had when the tree is seen, but differing in the fact that they are permanent in God's mind so long as the tree continues to exist. All our perceptions, according to this view, consist in a partial participation in God's perceptions, and it is because of this participation that different people see more or less the same tree. Thus apart from minds and their ideas there is nothing in the world, nor is it possible that anything else should ever be known, since whatever is known is necessarily an idea.

In this argument there are a good many fallacies which have been important in the history of philosophy, and which it will be as well to bring to light. In the first place, there is a confusion engendered by the use of the word ‘idea’. One thinks of an idea as essentially something in somebody’s mind, and thus when it is stated that a tree consists entirely of ideas, it is natural to suppose that, if so, the tree must be entirely in minds. But the notion of being ‘in’ the mind is ambiguous. It is observed that one speaks of bearing a person in mind, not meaning that the person is in one’s mind, but that a thought of him is in one’s mind. When a man says that some business he had to arrange went clean out of his mind, he does not mean to imply that the business itself was ever in his mind, but only that a thought of the business was formerly in his mind, but afterwards ceased to be in his mind. And so when Berkeley says that the tree must be in our minds if we can know it, all that he really has a right to say is that a thought of the tree must be in our minds. To argue that the tree itself must be in our minds is like arguing that a person whom we bear in mind is himself in our minds. This confusion may seem too gross to have been really committed by any competent philosopher, but various attendant circumstances rendered it possible. In order to see how it was possible, one must go more deeply into the question as to the nature of ideas.

Before taking up the general question of the nature of ideas, one must disentangle two entirely separate questions which arise concerning sense-data and physical objects. It is observed that, for various reasons of detail, Berkeley was right in treating the sense-data which constitute the perception of the tree as more or less subjective, in the sense that they depend upon the observer as much as upon the tree, and would not exist if the tree were not being perceived. But this is an entirely different point from the one by which Berkeley seeks to prove that whatever can be immediately known must be in a mind. For this purpose arguments of detail as to the dependence of sense-data upon the observer are useless. It becomes necessary to prove, generally, that by being known, things are shown to be mental. This is what Berkeley is believed to have done. It is this question, and not the previous question as to the difference between sense-data and the physical object, that must now concern the inquiry.

Taking the word 'idea' in Berkeley's sense, one observes that there are two quite distinct things to be considered whenever an idea is before the mind. It is observed that there is on the one hand the thing of which one is aware—say the colour of a table—and on the other hand the actual awareness itself, the mental act of apprehending the thing. The mental act is undoubtedly mental, but it can be asked whether there is any reason to suppose that the thing apprehended is in any sense mental. The previous arguments concerning the colour did not prove it to be mental; they only proved that its existence depends upon the relation of the sense organs to the physical object—in this case, the table. That is to say, it was proved that a certain colour will exist, in a certain light, if a normal eye is placed at a certain point relatively to the table. It was not proved that the colour is in the mind of the percipient.

Berkeley's view, that obviously the colour must be in the mind, seems to depend for its plausibility upon confusing the thing apprehended with the act of apprehension. Either of these might be called an 'idea'; probably either would have been called an idea by Berkeley. The act is undoubtedly in the mind; hence, when one is thinking of the act, one readily assents to the view that ideas must be in the mind. Then, forgetting that this was only true when ideas were taken as acts of apprehension, the proposition that 'ideas are in the mind' is transferred to ideas in the other sense, i.e. to the things apprehended by our acts of apprehension. Thus, by an unconscious equivocation, it is arrived at the conclusion that whatever can be apprehended must be in our minds. This appears to be the true analysis of Berkeley's argument, and the ultimate fallacy upon which it rests.

The question of the distinction between act and object in the apprehending of things is vitally important, since the whole power of acquiring knowledge is bound up with it. The faculty of being acquainted with things other than itself is observed to be the main characteristic of a mind. Acquaintance with objects essentially consists in a relation between the mind and something other than the mind; it is this that constitutes the mind's power of knowing things. If it is said that the things known must be in the mind, one is either unduly limiting the mind's power of knowing, or uttering a mere tautology. A mere tautology is uttered if by '_in_ the mind' is meant the same as by '_before_ the mind', i.e., if it is meant merely being apprehended by the mind. But if this is meant, it must be admitted that what, _in this sense_, is in the mind, may nevertheless be not mental. Thus when the nature of knowledge is realized, Berkeley's argument is seen to be wrong in substance as well as in form, and his grounds for supposing that 'ideas'--i.e. the objects apprehended--must be mental, are found to have no validity whatever. Hence his grounds in favour of idealism may be dismissed. It remains to be seen whether there are any other grounds.

It is often said, as though it were a self-evident truism, that one cannot know that anything exists which one does not know. It is inferred that whatever can in any way be relevant to experience must be at least capable of being known; whence it follows that if matter were essentially something with which one could not become acquainted, matter would be something which could not be known to exist, and which could have no importance whatever. It is generally also implied, for reasons which remain obscure, that what can have no importance for us cannot be real, and that therefore matter, if it is not composed of minds or of mental ideas, is impossible and a mere chimaera.

To go into this argument fully at the present stage would be impossible, since it raises points requiring a considerable preliminary discussion; but certain reasons for rejecting the argument may be noticed at once. To begin at the end: there is no reason why what cannot have any _practical_ importance for one should not be real. It is true that, if _theoretical_ importance is included, everything real is of _some_ importance, since, as persons desirous of knowing the truth about the universe, there is some interest in everything that the universe contains. But if this sort of interest is included, it is not the case that matter has no importance, provided it exists even if it cannot be known that it exists. It can, obviously, be suspected that it may exist, and one may wonder whether it does; hence it is connected with the desire for knowledge, and has the importance of either satisfying or thwarting this desire.

Again, it is by no means a truism, and is in fact false, that one cannot know that anything exists which one does not know. The word 'know' is here used in two different senses. (1) In its first use it is applicable to the sort of knowledge which is opposed to error, the sense in which what is known is _true_, the sense which applies to beliefs and convictions, i.e. to what are called _judgements_. In this sense of the word it is known _that_ something is the case. This sort of knowledge may be described as knowledge of _truths_. (2) In the second use of the word 'know' above, the word applies to knowledge of _things_, which may be called _acquaintance_. This is the sense in which sense-data are known. (The distinction involved is roughly that between _savoir_ and _connaître_ in French, or between _wissen_ and _kennen_ in German.)

Thus the statement which seemed like a truism becomes, when re-stated, the following: 'One can never truly judge that something with which one is not acquainted exists.' This is by no means a truism, but on the contrary a palpable falsehood. One may not be acquainted with the Emperor of China, yet one can truly judge that he exists. It may be said, of course, that such a judgment is made because of other people's acquaintance with him. This, however, would be an irrelevant retort, since, if the principle were true, it could not be known that any one else is acquainted with him. But further: there is no reason why the existence of something with which nobody is acquainted should not be known. This point is important, and demands elucidation.

If one is acquainted with a thing which exists, that acquaintance gives one the knowledge that it exists. But it is not true that, conversely, whenever it can be known that a thing of a certain sort exists, one or some other must be acquainted with the thing. What happens, in cases where true judgement without acquaintance is present, is that the thing is known by _description_, and that, in virtue of some general principle, the existence of a thing answering to this description can be inferred from the existence of something with which one is acquainted. In order to understand this point fully, it will be well first to deal with the difference between knowledge by acquaintance and knowledge by description, and then to consider what knowledge of general principles, if any, has the same kind of certainty as our knowledge of the existence of our own experiences. These subjects will be dealt with in the following chapters.

In the preceding chapter it was observed that there are two sorts of knowledge: knowledge of things, and knowledge of truths. In this chapter the concern shall be exclusively with knowledge of things, of which in turn it will be necessary to distinguish two kinds. Knowledge of things, when it is of the kind known as knowledge by _acquaintance_, is essentially simpler than any knowledge of truths, and logically independent of knowledge of truths, though it would be rash to assume that human beings ever, in fact, have acquaintance with things without at the same time knowing some truth about them. Knowledge of things by _description_, on the contrary, always involves, as will be found in the course of the present chapter, some knowledge of truths as its source and ground. But first of all it must be made clear what is meant by 'acquaintance' and what is meant by 'description'.

It shall be said that one has _acquaintance_ with anything of which one is directly aware, without the intermediary of any process of inference or any knowledge of truths. Thus in the presence of a table, one is acquainted with the sense-data that make up the appearance of that table—its colour, shape, hardness, smoothness, etc.; all these are things of which one is immediately conscious when seeing and touching a table. The particular shade of colour that is being observed may have many things said about it—it may be said that it is brown, that it is rather dark, and so on. But such statements, though they make one know truths about the colour, do not make one know the colour itself any better than before; so far as concerns knowledge of the colour itself, as opposed to knowledge of truths about it, the colour is known perfectly and completely when it is seen, and no further knowledge of it itself is even theoretically possible. Thus the sense-data which make up the appearance of a table are things with which one has acquaintance, things immediately known just as they are.

One's knowledge of the table as a physical object, on the contrary, is not direct knowledge. Such as it is, it is obtained through acquaintance with the sense-data that make up the appearance of the table. It has been seen that it is possible, without absurdity, to doubt whether there is a table at all, whereas it is not possible to doubt the sense-data. Knowledge of the table is of the kind which shall be called 'knowledge by description'. The table is 'the physical object which causes such-and-such sense-data'. This describes the table by means of the sense-data. In order to know anything at all about the table, one must know truths connecting it with things with which one has acquaintance: it must be known that 'such-and-such sense-data are caused by a physical object'. There is no state of mind in which one is directly aware of the table; all knowledge of the table is really knowledge of truths, and the actual thing which is the table is not, strictly speaking, known at all. A description is known, and it is known that there is just one object to which this description applies, though the object itself is not directly known. In such a case, it is said that knowledge of the object is knowledge by description.

Sense-data, as has already been seen, are among the things with which one is acquainted; in fact, they supply the most obvious and striking example of knowledge by acquaintance. But if they were the sole example, knowledge would be very much more restricted than it is. It would only be possible to know what is now present to the senses: nothing could be known about the past—not even that there was a past—nor could any truths about sense-data be known, for all knowledge of truths, as will be shown, demands acquaintance with things which are of an essentially different character from sense-data, the things which are sometimes called 'abstract ideas', but which we shall call 'universals'. It is therefore necessary to consider acquaintance with other things besides sense-data if any tolerably adequate analysis of knowledge is to be obtained.

The next extension to be considered is acquaintance by _introspection_. It is observed that one is not only aware of things, but one is often aware of being aware of them. When the sun is seen, one is often aware of one's seeing the sun; thus 'one's seeing the sun' is an object with which one has acquaintance. When food is desired, one may be aware of one's desire for food; thus 'one's desiring food' is an object with which one is acquainted. Similarly one may be aware of one's feeling pleasure or pain, and generally of the events which happen in one's mind. This kind of acquaintance, which may be called self-consciousness, is the source of all knowledge of mental things. It is obvious that it is only what goes on in one's own mind that can be thus known immediately. What goes on in the minds of others is known through the perception of their bodies, that is, through the sense-data which are associated with their bodies. But for acquaintance with the contents of one's own mind, one would be unable to imagine the minds of others, and therefore one could never arrive at the knowledge that they have minds. It seems natural to suppose that self-consciousness is one of the things that distinguish men from animals: animals, it may be supposed, though they have acquaintance with sense-data, never become aware of this acquaintance. It is not meant that they _doubt_ whether they exist, but that they have never become conscious of the fact that they have sensations and feelings, nor therefore of the fact that they, the subjects of their sensations and feelings, exist.

One has spoken of acquaintance with the contents of one's mind as _self_-consciousness, but it is not, of course, consciousness of one's _self_: it is consciousness of particular thoughts and feelings. The question whether one is also acquainted with one's bare self, as opposed to particular thoughts and feelings, is a very difficult one, upon which it would be rash to speak positively. When an attempt is made to look into oneself, one always seems to come upon some particular thought or feeling, and not upon the 'I' which has the thought or feeling. Nevertheless there are some reasons for thinking that acquaintance with the 'I' is present, though the acquaintance is hard to disentangle from other things. To make clear what sort of reason there is, let us consider for a moment what acquaintance with particular thoughts really involves.

When one is acquainted with 'one's seeing the sun', it is observed that one is acquainted with two different things in relation to each other. On the one hand there is the sense-datum which represents the sun, on the other hand there is that which sees this sense-datum. All acquaintance, such as acquaintance with the sense-datum which represents the sun, seems obviously a relation between the person acquainted and the object with which the person is acquainted. When a case of acquaintance is one with which one can be acquainted (as one is acquainted with one's acquaintance with the sense-datum representing the sun), it becomes clear that the person acquainted is oneself. Thus, when one is acquainted with one's seeing the sun, the whole fact with which one is acquainted is 'Self-acquainted-with-sense-datum'.

Further, it is known that the truth 'one is acquainted with this sense-datum' holds. It is hard to see how this truth could be known, or even how what is meant by it could be understood, unless one were acquainted with something which can be called 'I'. It does not seem necessary to suppose that acquaintance is had with a more or less permanent person, the same to-day as yesterday, but it does seem as though acquaintance must be had with that thing, whatever its nature, which sees the sun and has acquaintance with sense-data. Thus, in some sense it would seem one must be acquainted with one's Self as opposed to one's particular experiences. But the question is difficult, and complicated arguments can be adduced on either side. Hence, although acquaintance with oneself seems _probably_ to occur, it is not wise to assert that it undoubtedly does occur.

In addition to the acquaintance with particular existing things, one also has acquaintance with what may be called _universals_, that is to say, general ideas, such as _whiteness_, _diversity_, _brotherhood_, and so on. Every complete sentence must contain at least one word which stands for a universal, since all verbs have a meaning which is universal. It will be necessary to return to universals later on, in Chapter IX; for the present, it is only necessary to guard against the supposition that whatever can be acquainted with must be something particular and existent. Awareness of universals is called _conceiving_, and a universal of which there is awareness is called a _concept_.

One observes that common words, even proper names, are usually really descriptions. That is to say, the thought in the mind of a person using a proper name correctly can generally only be expressed explicitly if the proper name is replaced by a description. Moreover, the description required to express the thought is seen to vary for different people, or for the same person at different times. The only thing constant (so long as the name is rightly used) is the object to which the name applies. But so long as this remains constant, the particular description involved is known to make no difference to the truth or falsehood of the proposition in which the name appears.

Let us take some illustrations. Suppose some statement made about Bismarck. Assuming that there is such a thing as direct acquaintance with oneself, it can be observed that Bismarck himself might have used his name directly to designate the particular person with whom he was acquainted. In this case, if a judgement about himself was made, he himself might be a constituent of the judgement. Here the proper name has the direct use which it always wishes to have, as simply standing for a certain object, and not for a description of the object. But if a judgement about him was made by a person who knew Bismarck, the case is different. What this person was acquainted with were certain sense-data which were connected (rightly, we will suppose) with Bismarck's body. His body, as a physical object, and still more his mind, were only known as the body and the mind connected with these sense-data. That is, they were known by description. It is, of course, very much a matter of chance which characteristics of a man's appearance will come into a friend's mind when he is thought of; thus the description actually in the friend's mind is accidental. The essential point is that it is known that the various descriptions all apply to the same entity, in spite of not being acquainted with the entity in question.

When one, who did not know Bismarck, makes a judgement about him, the description in one's mind will probably be some more or less vague mass of historical knowledge—far more, in most cases, than is required to identify him. But, for the sake of illustration, let it be assumed that he is thought of as 'the first Chancellor of the German Empire'. Here all the words are abstract except 'German'. The word 'German' will, again, have different meanings for different people. To some it will recall travels in Germany, to some the look of Germany on the map, and so on. But if a description is to be obtained which is known to be applicable, one is compelled, at some point, to bring in a reference to a particular with which one is acquainted. Such reference is involved in any mention of past, present, and future (as opposed to definite dates), or of here and there, or of what has been told by others. Thus it would seem that, in some way or other, a description known to be applicable to a particular must involve some reference to a particular with which one is acquainted, if knowledge about the thing described is not to be merely what follows _logically_ from the description. For example, 'the most long-lived of men' is a description involving only universals, which must apply to some man, but no judgements can be made concerning this man which involve knowledge about him beyond what the description gives. If, however, it is said, 'The first Chancellor of the German Empire was an astute diplomatist', one can only be assured of the truth of this judgement in virtue of something with which one is acquainted—usually a testimony heard or read. Apart from the information conveyed to others, apart from the fact about the actual Bismarck, which gives importance to the judgement, the thought that is really held contains the one or more particulars involved, and otherwise consists wholly of concepts.

It would seem that, when a statement is made about something only known by description, one often _intends_ the statement, not to be in the form involving the description, but to be about the actual thing described. That is to say, when anything is said about Bismarck, it is desired, if possible, to make the judgement which Bismarck alone can make, namely, the judgement of which he himself is a constituent. In this, one is necessarily defeated, since the actual Bismarck is unknown. But it is known that there is an object B, called Bismarck, and that B was an astute diplomatist. One can thus _describe_ the proposition one would like to affirm, namely, 'B was an astute diplomatist', where B is the object which was Bismarck. If Bismarck is described as 'the first Chancellor of the German Empire', the proposition one would like to affirm may be described as 'the proposition asserting, concerning the actual object which was the first Chancellor of the German Empire, that this object was an astute diplomatist'. What enables communication in spite of the varying descriptions employed is the knowledge that there is a true proposition concerning the actual Bismarck, and that however the description may be varied (so long as the description is correct) the proposition described is still the same. This proposition, which is described and is known to be true, is what is of interest; but one is not acquainted with the proposition itself, and does not know it, though it is known to be true.

It will be seen that there are various stages in the removal from acquaintance with particulars: there is Bismarck to people who knew him; Bismarck to those who only know of him through history; the man with the iron mask; the longest-lived of men. These are progressively further removed from acquaintance with particulars; the first comes as near to acquaintance as is possible in regard to another person; in the second, one may still be said to know 'who Bismarck was'; in the third, it is not known who was the man with the iron mask, though many propositions about him can be known which are not logically deducible from the fact that he wore an iron mask; in the fourth, finally, nothing is known beyond what is logically deducible from the definition of the man. A similar hierarchy is observed in the region of universals. Many universals, like many particulars, are only known by description. But here, as in the case of particulars, knowledge concerning what is known by description is ultimately reducible to knowledge concerning what is known by acquaintance.

One shall not at this stage attempt to answer all the objections which may be urged against this fundamental principle. For the present, one shall merely point out that, in some way or other, it must be possible to meet these objections, for it is scarcely conceivable that a judgement can be made or a supposition entertained without knowing what it is that is being judged or supposed about. Some meaning must be attached to the words used, if one is to speak significantly and not utter mere noise; and the meaning attached to those words must be something with which one is acquainted. Thus when, for example, a statement is made about Julius Caesar, it is plain that Julius Caesar himself is not before the mind, since one is not acquainted with him. One has in mind some description of Julius Caesar: 'the man who was assassinated on the Ides of March', 'the founder of the Roman Empire', or, perhaps, merely 'the man whose name was _Julius Caesar_'. (In this last description, _Julius Caesar_ is a noise or shape with which one is acquainted.) Thus the statement does not mean quite what it seems to mean, but means something involving, instead of Julius Caesar, some description of him which is composed wholly of particulars and universals with which one is acquainted.

But if one is to be able to draw inferences from these data—if it is to be known of the existence of matter, of other people, of the past before individual memory begins, or of the future, general principles of some kind must be known by means of which such inferences can be drawn. It must be known that the existence of some one sort of thing, A, is a sign of the existence of some other sort of thing, B, either at the same time as A or at some earlier or later time, as, for example, thunder is a sign of the earlier existence of lightning. If this were not known, knowledge could never be extended beyond the sphere of private experience; and this sphere, as has been observed, is exceedingly limited. The question now to be considered is whether such an extension is possible, and if so, how it is effected.

One may take as an illustration a matter about which none of us, in fact, feel the slightest doubt. It is widely held that the sun will rise to-morrow. Why? Is this belief a mere blind outcome of past experience, or can it be justified as a reasonable belief? It is not easy to find a test by which to judge whether a belief of this kind is reasonable or not, but it can at least be ascertained what sort of general beliefs would suffice, if true, to justify the judgement that the sun will rise to-morrow, and the many other similar judgements upon which our actions are based.

It is obvious that if one is asked why it is believed that the sun will rise to-morrow, the natural answer is 'Because it always has risen every day'. A firm belief is held that it will rise in the future, because it has risen in the past. If a challenge is raised as to why it is believed that it will continue to rise as heretofore, an appeal may be made to the laws of motion: the earth, it will be said, is a freely rotating body, and such bodies do not cease to rotate unless something interferes from outside, and there is nothing outside to interfere with the earth between now and to-morrow. Of course it might be doubted whether one can be quite certain that there is nothing outside to interfere, but this is not the interesting doubt. The interesting doubt is as to whether the laws of motion will remain in operation until to-morrow. If this doubt is raised, one finds oneself in the same position as when the doubt about the sunrise was first raised.

The _only_ reason for believing that the laws of motion will remain in operation is that they have operated hitherto, so far as our knowledge of the past enables one to judge. It is true that a greater body of evidence from the past is possessed in favour of the laws of motion than is possessed in favour of the sunrise, because the sunrise is merely a particular case of fulfilment of the laws of motion, and there are countless other particular cases. But the real question is: Do _any_ number of cases of a law being fulfilled in the past afford evidence that it will be fulfilled in the future? If not, it becomes plain that no ground whatever exists for expecting the sun to rise to-morrow, or for expecting the bread to be eaten at the next meal not to poison one, or for any of the other scarcely conscious expectations that control daily life. It is to be observed that all such expectations are only _probable_; thus what must be sought is not a proof that they _must_ be fulfilled, but only some reason in favour of the view that they are _likely_ to be fulfilled.

Now in dealing with this question one must, to begin with, make an important distinction, without which it is recognized that hopeless confusions would soon become involved. Experience has shown that, hitherto, the frequent repetition of some uniform succession or coexistence has been a _cause_ of the expectation of the same succession or coexistence on the next occasion. Food that has a certain appearance generally has a certain taste, and it is a severe shock to expectations when the familiar appearance is found to be associated with an unusual taste. Things which are seen become associated, by habit, with certain tactile sensations which are expected if they are touched; one of the horrors of a ghost (in many ghost-stories) is that it fails to give any sensations of touch. Uneducated people who go abroad for the first time are so surprised as to be incredulous when it is found that their native language is not understood.

One observes that this kind of association is not confined to men; in animals also it is very strong. A horse which has been often driven along a certain road resists the attempt to drive him in a different direction. Domestic animals expect food when they see the person who usually feeds them. It is known that all these rather crude expectations of uniformity are liable to be misleading. The man who has fed the chicken every day throughout its life at last wrings its neck instead, showing that more refined views as to the uniformity of nature would have been useful to the chicken.

But in spite of the misleadingness of such expectations, they nevertheless exist. The mere fact that something has happened a certain number of times causes animals and men to expect that it will happen again. Thus it is observed that instincts certainly cause one to believe that the sun will rise to-morrow, though one may be in no better a position than the chicken which unexpectedly has its neck wrung. It becomes clear, therefore, that a distinction must be drawn between the fact that past uniformities _cause_ expectations as to the future, and the question whether there is any reasonable ground for giving weight to such expectations after the question of their validity has been raised.

The problem to be discussed is whether there is any reason for believing in what is called 'the uniformity of nature'. The belief in the uniformity of nature is the belief that everything that has happened or will happen is an instance of some general law to which there are no exceptions. The crude expectations which have been considered are all subject to exceptions, and therefore liable to disappoint those who entertain them. But science habitually assumes, at least as a working hypothesis, that general rules which have exceptions can be replaced by general rules which have no exceptions. 'Unsupported bodies in air fall' is a general rule to which balloons and aeroplanes are exceptions. But the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, which account for the fact that most bodies fall, also account for the fact that balloons and aeroplanes can rise; thus the laws of motion and the law of gravitation are not subject to these exceptions.

It is observed that the belief that the sun will rise to-morrow might be falsified if the earth came suddenly into contact with a large body which destroyed its rotation; but the laws of motion and the law of gravitation would not be infringed by such an event. The business of science is understood to be the finding of uniformities, such as the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, to which, so far as our experience extends, there are no exceptions. In this search science has been remarkably successful, and it may be conceded that such uniformities have held hitherto. This leads one to the question: Do we have any reason, assuming that they have always held in the past, to suppose that they will hold in the future?

It has been argued that one has reason to know that the future will resemble the past, because what was the future has constantly become the past, and has always been found to resemble the past, so that there is really experience of the future, namely of times which were formerly future, which may be called past futures. But such an argument is seen to beg the very question at issue. There is experience of past futures, but not of future futures, and the question remains: Will future futures resemble past futures? This question is not to be answered by an argument which starts from past futures alone. It is therefore still necessary to seek for some principle which shall enable one to know that the future will follow the same laws as the past.

The reference to the future in this question is not essential. The same question arises when the laws that work in one's experience are applied to past things of which there is no experience—as, for example, in geology, or in theories as to the origin of the Solar System. The question that really must be asked is: 'When two things have been found to be often associated, and no instance is known of the one occurring without the other, does the occurrence of one of the two, in a fresh instance, give any good ground for expecting the other?' On the answer to this question must depend the validity of the whole of one's expectations as to the future, the whole of the results obtained by induction, and in fact practically all the beliefs upon which daily life is based.

It must be conceded, to begin with, that the fact that two things have been found often together and never apart does not, by itself, suffice to _prove_ demonstratively that they will be found together in the next case one examines. The most that can be hoped is that the oftener things are found together, the more probable it becomes that they will be found together another time, and that, if they have been found together often enough, the probability will amount _almost_ to certainty. It can never quite reach certainty, because it is known that in spite of frequent repetitions there sometimes is a failure at the last, as in the case of the chicken whose neck is wrung. Thus probability is all that ought to be sought.

It might be urged, as against the view being advocated, that all natural phenomena are known to be subject to the reign of law, and that sometimes, on the basis of observation, it can be seen that only one law can possibly fit the facts of the case. Now to this view there are two answers. The first is that, even if _some_ law which has no exceptions applies to the case in question, one can never, in practice, be sure that that law has been discovered and not one to which there are exceptions. The second is that the reign of law would seem to be itself only probable, and that the belief that it will hold in the future, or in unexamined cases in the past, is itself based upon the very principle under examination.

As just stated, the principle applies only to the verification of one's expectation in a single fresh instance. But it is also desired to know that there is a probability in favour of the general law that things of the sort A are _always_ associated with things of the sort B, provided a sufficient number of cases of association are known, and no cases of failure of association are known. The probability of the general law is obviously less than the probability of the particular case, since if the general law is true, the particular case must also be true, whereas the particular case may be true without the general law being true. Nevertheless the probability of the general law is increased by repetitions, just as the probability of the particular case is. One may therefore repeat the two parts of the principle as regards the general law, thus:

It should be noted that probability is always relative to certain data. In the case under consideration, the data are merely the known cases of coexistence of A and B. There may be other data, which _might_ be taken into account, which would gravely alter the probability. For example, from observing a great many white swans, one might argue, by the principle in question, that on the data it was _probable_ that all swans were white, and this might be a perfectly sound argument. The argument is not disproved by the fact that some swans are black, because a thing may very well happen in spite of the fact that some data render it improbable. In the case of the swans, it might be known that colour is a very variable characteristic in many species of animals, and that, therefore, an induction as to colour is peculiarly liable to error. But this knowledge would be a fresh datum, by no means proving that the probability relatively to the previous data had been wrongly estimated. The fact, therefore, that things often fail to fulfil our expectations is no evidence that our expectations will not _probably_ be fulfilled in a given case or a given class of cases. Thus the inductive principle is at any rate not capable of being _disproved_ by an appeal to experience.

The inductive principle, however, is equally incapable of being _proved_ by an appeal to experience. Experience might conceivably confirm the inductive principle as regards the cases that have been already examined; but as regards unexamined cases, it is the inductive principle alone that can justify any inference from what has been examined to what has not been examined. All arguments which, on the basis of experience, argue as to the future or the unexperienced parts of the past or present, assume the inductive principle; hence it is observed that experience can never be used to prove the inductive principle without begging the question. Thus it becomes clear that one must either accept the inductive principle on the ground of its intrinsic evidence, or forgo all justification of expectations about the future. If the principle is unsound, no reason is found to expect the sun to rise to-morrow, to expect bread to be more nourishing than a stone, or to expect that if one throws oneself off the roof one will fall. When what looks like one's best friend is seen approaching, no reason is had to suppose that his body is not inhabited by the mind of one's worst enemy or of some total stranger. All conduct is based upon associations which have worked in the past, and which are therefore regarded as likely to work in the future; and this likelihood is dependent for its validity upon the inductive principle.

Thus all knowledge which, on a basis of experience tells one something about what is not experienced, is based upon a belief which experience can neither confirm nor confute, yet which, at least in its more concrete applications, appears to be as firmly rooted in us as many of the facts of experience. The existence and justification of such beliefs—for the inductive principle, as will be seen, is not the only example—raises some of the most difficult and most debated problems of philosophy. In the next chapter, it will be considered briefly what may be said to account for such knowledge, and what is its scope and its degree of certainty.

Some of these principles have even greater evidence than the principle of induction, and the knowledge of them has the same degree of certainty as the knowledge of the existence of sense-data. They constitute the means of drawing inferences from what is given in sensation; and if what is inferred is to be true, it is just as necessary that the principles of inference should be true as it is that the data should be true. The principles of inference are apt to be overlooked because of their very obviousness—the assumption involved is assented to without it being realized that it is an assumption. But it is very important to realize the use of principles of inference, if a correct theory of knowledge is to be obtained; for the knowledge of them raises interesting and difficult questions.

In all knowledge of general principles, what actually happens is that first of all some particular application of the principle is realized, and then it is realized that the particularity is irrelevant, and that there is a generality which may equally truly be affirmed. This is of course familiar in such matters as teaching arithmetic: 'two and two are four' is first learnt in the case of some particular pair of couples, and then in some other particular case, and so on, until at last it becomes possible to see that it is true of any pair of couples. The same thing happens with logical principles. Suppose two men are discussing what day of the month it is. One of them says, 'At least you will admit that _if_ yesterday was the 15th to-day must be the 16th.' 'Yes', says the other, 'I admit that.' 'And you know', the first continues, 'that yesterday was the 15th, because you dined with Jones, and your diary will tell you that was on the 15th.' 'Yes', says the second; 'therefore to-day _is_ the 16th.

Now such an argument is not hard to follow; and if it is granted that its premisses are true in fact, no one will deny that the conclusion must also be true. But it depends for its truth upon an instance of a general logical principle. The logical principle is as follows: 'Suppose it known that _if_ this is true, then that is true. Suppose it also known that this _is_ true, then it follows that that is true.' When it is the case that if this is true, that is true, it can be said that this 'implies' that, and that that 'follows from' this. Thus the principle states that if this implies that, and this is true, then that is true. In other words, 'anything implied by a true proposition is true', or 'whatever follows from a true proposition is true'.

This principle is really involved--at least, concrete instances of it are involved--in all demonstrations. Whenever one thing which is believed is used to prove something else, which is consequently believed, this principle is relevant. If it is asked: 'Why should the results of valid arguments based on true premisses be accepted?' one can only answer by appealing to this principle. In fact, the truth of the principle is impossible to doubt, and its obviousness is so great that at first sight it seems almost trivial. Such principles, however, are not trivial to the philosopher, for they show that indubitable knowledge may be possessed which is in no way derived from objects of sense.

These three laws are samples of self-evident logical principles, but are not really more fundamental or more self-evident than various other similar principles: for instance, the one considered just now, which states that what follows from a true premiss is true. The name 'laws of thought' is also misleading, for what is important is not the fact that thinking occurs in accordance with these laws, but the fact that things behave in accordance with them; in other words, the fact that when one thinks in accordance with them one thinks _truly_. But this is a large question, to which it is necessary to return at a later stage.

One of the great historic controversies in philosophy is the controversy between the two schools called respectively 'empiricists' and 'rationalists'. The empiricists—who are best represented by the British philosophers, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume—maintained that all knowledge is derived from experience; the rationalists—who are represented by the Continental philosophers of the seventeenth century, especially Descartes and Leibniz—maintained that, in addition to what is known by experience, there are certain 'innate ideas' and 'innate principles', which are known independently of experience. It has now become possible to decide with some confidence as to the truth or falsehood of these opposing schools. It must be admitted, for the reasons already stated, that logical principles are known, and cannot be themselves proved by experience, since all proof presupposes them. In this, therefore, which was the most important point of the controversy, the rationalists were in the right.

On the other hand, even that part of human knowledge which is _logically_ independent of experience (in the sense that experience cannot prove it) is yet elicited and caused by experience. It is on occasion of particular experiences that one becomes aware of the general laws which their connexions exemplify. It would certainly be absurd to suppose that there are innate principles in the sense that babies are born with a knowledge of everything which men know and which cannot be deduced from what is experienced. For this reason, the word 'innate' would not now be employed to describe the knowledge of logical principles. The phrase '_a priori_' is less objectionable, and is more usual in modern writers. Thus, while admitting that all knowledge is elicited and caused by experience, it is nevertheless held that some knowledge is _a priori_, in the sense that the experience which makes one think of it does not suffice to prove it, but merely so directs attention that its truth is seen without requiring any proof from experience.

It is observed that there is another point of great importance, in which the empiricists were in the right as against the rationalists. Nothing can be known to _exist_ except by the help of experience. That is to say, if one wishes to prove that something of which one has no direct experience exists, it is necessary to have among one's premisses the existence of one or more things of which one has direct experience. The belief that the Emperor of China exists, for example, rests upon testimony, and testimony consists, in the last analysis, of sense-data seen or heard in reading or being spoken to. Rationalists believed that, from general consideration as to what must be, they could deduce the existence of this or that in the actual world. In this belief they seem to have been mistaken. All the knowledge that can be acquired _a priori_ concerning existence seems to be hypothetical: it tells one that if one thing exists, another must exist, or, more generally, that if one proposition is true, another must be true. This is exemplified by the principles already dealt with, such as '_if_ this is true, and this implies that, then that is true', or '_if_ this and that have been repeatedly found connected, they will probably be connected in the next instance in which one of them is found'. Thus the scope and power of _a priori_ principles is strictly limited. All knowledge that something exists must be in part dependent on experience. When anything is known immediately, its existence is known by experience alone; when anything is proved to exist, without being known immediately, both experience and _a priori_ principles must be required in the proof. Knowledge is called _empirical_ when it rests wholly or partly upon experience. Thus all knowledge which asserts existence is empirical, and the only _a priori_ knowledge concerning existence is hypothetical, giving connexions among things that exist or may exist, but not giving actual existence.

_A priori_ knowledge is not all of the logical kind that has been hitherto considered. Perhaps the most important example of non-logical _a priori_ knowledge is knowledge as to ethical value. One is not speaking of judgements as to what is useful or as to what is virtuous, for such judgements do require empirical premisses; one is speaking of judgements as to the intrinsic desirability of things. If something is useful, it must be useful because it secures some end; the end must, if one has gone far enough, be valuable on its own account, and not merely because it is useful for some further end. Thus all judgements as to what is useful depend upon judgements as to what has value on its own account.

One judges, for example, that happiness is more desirable than misery, knowledge than ignorance, goodwill than hatred, and so on. Such judgements must, in part at least, be immediate and _a priori_. Like the previous _a priori_ judgements, they may be elicited by experience, and indeed they must be; for it seems not possible to judge whether anything is intrinsically valuable unless something of the same kind has been experienced. But it is fairly obvious that they cannot be proved by experience; for the fact that a thing exists or does not exist cannot prove either that it is good that it should exist or that it is bad. The pursuit of this subject belongs to ethics, where the impossibility of deducing what ought to be from what is has to be established. In the present connexion, it is only important to realize that knowledge as to what is intrinsically of value is _a priori_ in the same sense in which logic is _a priori_, namely in the sense that the truth of such knowledge can be neither proved nor disproved by experience.

All pure mathematics is _a priori_, like logic. This was strenuously denied by the empirical philosophers, who maintained that experience was as much the source of our knowledge of arithmetic as of our knowledge of geography. It was maintained that by the repeated experience of seeing two things and two other things, and finding that altogether they made four things, one is led by induction to the conclusion that two things and two other things would _always_ make four things altogether. If, however, this were the source of our knowledge that two and two are four, one would proceed differently, in persuading oneself of its truth, from the way in which one does actually proceed. In fact, a certain number of instances are needed to make one think of two abstractly, rather than of two coins or two books or two people, or two of any other specified kind. But as soon as one is able to divest one's thoughts of irrelevant particularity, one becomes able to see the general principle that two and two are four; any one instance is seen to be _typical_, and the examination of other instances becomes unnecessary.(1)

The same thing is exemplified in geometry. If one wants to prove some property of _all_ triangles, a particular triangle is drawn and reasoned about; but it is possible to avoid making use of any property which it does not share with all other triangles, and thus, from this particular case, a general result is obtained. It is not, in fact, felt that the certainty that two and two are four is increased by fresh instances, because, as soon as the truth of this proposition is seen, the certainty becomes so great as to be incapable of growing greater. Moreover, a quality of necessity is felt about the proposition 'two and two are four', which is absent from even the best attested empirical generalizations. Such generalizations always remain mere facts: it is felt that there might be a world in which they were false, though in the actual world they happen to be true. In any possible world, on the contrary, it is felt that two and two would be four: this is not a mere fact, but a necessity to which everything actual and possible must conform.

The case may be made clearer by considering a genuinely-empirical generalization, such as 'All men are mortal.' It is plain that such a proposition is believed, in the first place, because there is no known instance of men living beyond a certain age, and in the second place because there seem to be physiological grounds for thinking that an organism such as a man's body must sooner or later wear out. Neglecting the second ground, and considering merely the experience of men's mortality, it is plain that one should not be content with one quite clearly understood instance of a man dying, whereas, in the case of 'two and two are four', one instance does suffice, when carefully considered, to persuade one that the same must happen in any other instance. Also it can be admitted, on reflection, that there may be some doubt, however slight, as to whether _all_ men are mortal. This may be made plain by the attempt to imagine two different worlds, in one of which there are men who are not mortal, while in the other two and two make five. When Swift invites the reader to consider the race of Struldbugs who never die, one is able to acquiesce in imagination. But a world where two and two make five seems quite on a different level. It is felt that such a world, if there were one, would upset the whole fabric of our knowledge and reduce us to utter doubt.

The fact is that, in simple mathematical judgements such as 'two and two are four', and also in many judgements of logic, one can know the general proposition without inferring it from instances, although some instance is usually necessary to make clear what the general proposition means. This is why there is real utility in the process of _deduction_, which goes from the general to the general, or from the general to the particular, as well as in the process of _induction_, which goes from the particular to the particular, or from the particular to the general. It is an old debate among philosophers whether deduction ever gives _new_ knowledge. It can now be seen that in certain cases, at least, it does do so. If it is already known that two and two always make four, and it is known that Brown and Jones are two, and so are Robinson and Smith, one can deduce that Brown and Jones and Robinson and Smith are four. This is new knowledge, not contained in the premisses, because the general proposition, 'two and two are four', never indicated there were such people as Brown and Jones and Robinson and Smith, and the particular premisses do not indicate that there were four of them, whereas the particular proposition deduced does indicate both these things.

But the newness of the knowledge is much less certain if the stock instance of deduction that is always given in books on logic is taken, namely, 'All men are mortal; Socrates is a man, therefore Socrates is mortal.' In this case, what is really known beyond reasonable doubt is that certain men, A, B, C, were mortal, since, in fact, they have died. If Socrates is one of these men, it is foolish to go the roundabout way through 'all men are mortal' to arrive at the conclusion that _probably_ Socrates is mortal. If Socrates is not one of the men on whom the induction is based, it is still better to argue straight from A, B, C, to Socrates, than to go round by the general proposition, 'all men are mortal'. For the probability that Socrates is mortal is greater, on the given data, than the probability that all men are mortal. (This is obvious, because if all men are mortal, so is Socrates; but if Socrates is mortal, it does not follow that all men are mortal.) Hence the conclusion that Socrates is mortal is reached with a greater approach to certainty if the argument is made purely inductive than if one goes by way of 'all men are mortal' and then uses deduction.

Immanuel Kant is generally regarded as the greatest of the modern philosophers. Though the Seven Years War and the French Revolution occurred, the teaching of philosophy at Königsberg in East Prussia was never interrupted. The most distinctive contribution is considered to be the invention of what he called the 'critical' philosophy, which, assuming as a datum that there is knowledge of various kinds, inquired how such knowledge comes to be possible, and deduced, from the answer to this inquiry, many metaphysical results as to the nature of the world. Whether these results were valid may well be doubted. But it is widely held that Kant undoubtedly deserves credit for two things: first, for having perceived that there exists _a priori_ knowledge which is not purely 'analytic', i.e. such that the opposite would be self-contradictory, and secondly, for having made evident the philosophical importance of the theory of knowledge.

Hume (1711-76), who preceded Kant, accepting the usual view as to what makes knowledge _a priori_, is observed to have discovered that, in many cases which had previously been supposed analytic, and notably in the case of cause and effect, the connexion was really synthetic. Before Hume, rationalists at least had supposed that the effect could be logically deduced from the cause, if only sufficient knowledge were possessed. It is argued by Hume—correctly, as would now be generally admitted—that this could not be done. Hence the far more doubtful proposition is inferred that nothing could be known _a priori_ about the connexion of cause and effect. Kant, who had been educated in the rationalist tradition, is seen to have been much perturbed by Hume's scepticism, and an answer to it was endeavoured to be found. It is perceived that not only the connexion of cause and effect, but all the propositions of arithmetic and geometry, are 'synthetic', i.e. not analytic: in all these propositions, no analysis of the subject will reveal the predicate. The stock instance used was the proposition 7 + 5 = 12. It was pointed out, quite truly, that 7 and 5 have to be put together to give 12: the idea of 12 is not contained in them, nor even in the idea of adding them together. Thus one is led to the conclusion that all pure mathematics, though _a priori_, is synthetic; and this conclusion raised a new problem of which a solution was endeavoured to be found.

Before the time of Kant, it was generally held that whatever knowledge was _a priori_ must be 'analytic'. What this word means will be best illustrated by examples. If one says, 'A bald man is a man', 'A plane figure is a figure', 'A bad poet is a poet', a purely analytic judgement is made: the subject spoken about is given as having at least two properties, of which one is singled out to be asserted of it. Such propositions as the above are trivial, and would never be enunciated in real life except by an orator preparing the way for a piece of sophistry. They are called 'analytic' because the predicate is obtained by merely analysing the subject. Before the time of Kant it was thought that all judgements of which one could be certain _a priori_ were of this kind: that in all of them there was a predicate which was only part of the subject of which it was asserted. If this were so, one would be involved in a definite contradiction if an attempt were made to deny anything that could be known _a priori_. 'A bald man is not bald' would assert and deny baldness of the same man, and would therefore contradict itself. Thus according to the philosophers before Kant, the law of contradiction, which asserts that nothing can at the same time have and not have a certain property, sufficed to establish the truth of all _a priori_ knowledge.

The question which Kant put at the beginning of his philosophy, namely 'How is pure mathematics possible?' is an interesting and difficult one, to which every philosophy which is not purely sceptical must find some answer. The answer of the pure empiricists, that our mathematical knowledge is derived by induction from particular instances, has already been seen to be inadequate, for two reasons: first, that the validity of the inductive principle itself cannot be proved by induction; secondly, that the general propositions of mathematics, such as 'two and two always make four', can obviously be known with certainty by consideration of a single instance, and gain nothing by enumeration of other cases in which they have been found to be true. Thus it is observed that knowledge of the general propositions of mathematics (and the same applies to logic) must be accounted for otherwise than our (merely probable) knowledge of empirical generalizations such as 'all men are mortal'.

The problem arises through the fact that such knowledge is general, whereas all experience is particular. It seems strange that one should apparently be able to know some truths in advance about particular things of which there is as yet no experience; but it cannot easily be doubted that logic and arithmetic will apply to such things. It is not known who will be the inhabitants of London a hundred years hence; but it is known that any two of them and any other two of them will make four of them. This apparent power of anticipating facts about things of which there is no experience is certainly surprising. Kant's solution of the problem, though not valid in the present view, is interesting. It is, however, very difficult, and is differently understood by different philosophers. One can, therefore, only give the merest outline of it, and even that will be thought misleading by many exponents of Kant's system.
