It is needless to multiply examples. The important point is that, in all that differentiates between a good life and a bad one, the world is a unity, and the man who pretends to live independently is a conscious or unconscious parasite.

The idea of individual salvation, with which the early Christians consoled themselves for their political subjection, becomes impossible as soon as one escapes from a very narrow conception of the good life. In the orthodox Christian conception, the good life is the virtuous life, and virtue consists in obedience to the will of God, and the will of God is revealed to each individual through the voice of conscience. This whole conception is that of men subject to an alien despotism. It is observed that the good life involves much besides virtue――intelligence, for instance. And conscience is a most fallacious guide, since it consists of vague reminiscences of precepts heard in early youth, so that it is never wiser than its possessor’s nurse or mother. To live a good life in the fullest sense it is necessary to have a good education, friends, love, children (if they are desired), a sufficient income to keep from want and grave anxiety, good health, and work which is not uninteresting. All these things, in varying degrees, are seen to depend upon the community, and are helped or hindered by political events. The good life must be lived in a good society, and is not fully possible otherwise.

This is the fundamental defect of the aristocratic ideal. Certain good things, such as art and science and friendship, can flourish very well in an aristocratic society. They existed in Greece on a basis of slavery; they exist among ourselves on a basis of exploitation. But love, in the form of sympathy or benevolence, cannot exist freely in an aristocratic society. The aristocrat has to persuade himself that the slave or proletarian or coloured man is of inferior clay, and that his sufferings do not matter. At the present moment, polished English gentlemen flog Africans so severely that they die after hours of unspeakable anguish. Even if these gentlemen are well-educated, artistic, and admirable conversationalists, it cannot be admitted that they are living the good life. Human nature imposes some limitation of sympathy, but not such a degree as that. In a democratically-minded society, only a maniac would behave in this way. The limitation of sympathy involved in the aristocratic ideal is its condemnation. Salvation is an aristocratic ideal, because it is individualistic. For this reason, also, the idea of personal salvation, however interpreted and expanded, cannot serve for the definition of the good life.

Another characteristic of salvation is that it results from a catastrophic change, like the conversion of Saint Paul. Shelley’s poems afford an illustration of this conception applied to societies; the moment comes when everybody is converted, the “anarchs” fly, and “the world’s great age begins anew”. It may be said that a poet is an unimportant person, whose ideas are of no consequence. However, it is observed that a large proportion of revolutionary leaders have had ideas extremely like Shelley’s. It has been thought that misery and cruelty and degradation were due to tyrants or priests or capitalists or Germans, and that if these sources of evil were overthrown there would be a general change of heart and all would live happy ever after. Holding these beliefs, one finds a willingness to wage a “war to end war”. Comparatively fortunate were those who suffered defeat or death; those who had the misfortune to emerge victorious were reduced to cynicism and despair by the failure of all their glowing hopes. The ultimate source of these hopes can be identified as the Christian doctrine of catastrophic conversion as the road to salvation.

It is not to be suggested that revolutions are never necessary, but it is to be suggested that they are not short cuts to the millennium. There is no short cut to the good life, whether individual or social. To build up the good life, intelligence, self-control, and sympathy must be built up. This is recognized as a quantitative matter, a matter of gradual improvement, of early training, of educational experiment. Only impatience prompts the belief in the possibility of sudden improvement. The gradual improvement that is possible, and the methods by which it may be achieved, are a matter for future science. But something can be said now. Some part of what can be said will be attempted to be indicated in a final chapter.

The purpose of the moralist is to improve men’s behaviour. This is a laudable ambition, since their behaviour is for the most part deplorable. However, one cannot praise the moralist either for the particular improvements he desires, or for the methods he adopts for achieving them. His ostensible method is moral exhortation; his real method (if he is orthodox) is a system of economic rewards and punishments. The former effects nothing permanent or important; the influence of revivalists, from Savonarola downwards, has always been very transitory. The latter――the rewards and punishments――have a very considerable effect. They cause a man, for example, to prefer casual prostitutes to a quasi-permanent mistress, because it is necessary to adopt the method which is most easily concealed. They thus keep up the numbers of a very dangerous profession, and secure the prevalence of venereal disease. These are not the objects desired by the moralist, and he is too unscientific to notice that they are the objects which he actually achieves.

In the ordinary man and woman there is a certain amount of active malevolence, both special ill-will directed to particular enemies and general impersonal pleasure in the misfortunes of others. It is customary to cover this over with fine phrases; about half of conventional morality is observed to be a cloak for it. But it must be faced if the moralists’ aim of improving human actions is to be achieved. It is shown in a thousand ways, great and small: in the glee with which people repeat and believe scandal, in the unkind treatment of criminals in spite of clear proof that better treatment would have more effect in reforming them, in the unbelievable barbarity with which all white races treat negroes, and in the gusto with which old ladies and clergymen pointed out the duty of military service to young men during the War. Even children may be the objects of wanton cruelty: David Copperfield and Oliver Twist are by no means imaginary. This active malevolence is the worst feature of human nature, and the one which it is most necessary to change if the world is to grow happier. It can be concluded that this one cause probably has more to do with war than all the economic and political causes put together.

Given this problem of preventing malevolence, how shall it be dealt with? First, let the causes be understood. These are, one observes, partly social, partly physiological. The world, now as much as at any former time, is based upon life-and-death competition; the question at issue in the War was whether German or Allied children should die of want and starvation. (Apart from malevolence on both sides, there was not the slightest reason why both should not survive). It is observed that most people have in the background of their minds a haunting fear of ruin; this is especially true of people who have children. The rich fear that Bolsheviks will confiscate their investments; the poor fear that they will lose their job or their health. Every one is engaged in the frantic pursuit of “security”, and it is imagined that this is to be achieved by keeping potential enemies in subjection. It is in moments of panic that cruelty becomes most wide-spread and most atrocious. Reactionaries everywhere appeal to fear: in England, to fear of Bolshevism; in France, to fear of Germany; in Germany, to fear of France. And the sole effect of their appeals is seen to increase the danger against which protection is sought.

It must, therefore, be one of the chief concerns of the scientific moralist to combat fear. This can be done in two ways: by increasing security, and by cultivating courage. One is speaking of fear as an irrational passion, not of the rational prevision of possible misfortune. When a theatre catches fire, the rational man foresees disaster just as clearly as the man stricken with panic, but he adopts methods likely to diminish the disaster, whereas the man stricken with panic increases it. Europe since 1914 has been like a panic-stricken audience in a theatre on fire; what is needed is calm, authoritative directions as to how to escape without trampling each other to pieces in the process. The Victorian age, for all its humbug, was a period of rapid progress, because men were dominated by hope rather than fear. If progress is again to be achieved, it is necessary that society be again dominated by hope.

It is observed that everything which increases the general security is likely to diminish cruelty. This applies to the prevention of war, whether through the instrumentality of the League of Nations, or otherwise; to the prevention of destitution; to better health by improvement in medicine, hygiene, and sanitation; and to all other methods of lessening the terrors that lurk in the abysses of the human mind and emerge as nightmares during sleep. But nothing is accomplished by an attempt to make a portion of mankind secure at the expense of another portion――Frenchmen at the expense of Germans, capitalists at the expense of wage-earners, white men at the expense of yellow men, and so on. Such methods are seen only to increase terror in the dominant group, lest just resentment should lead the oppressed to rebel. It becomes clear that only justice can give security; and by “justice” is meant the recognition of the equal claims of all human beings.

In addition to social changes designed to bring security, there is, however, another and more direct means of diminishing fear, namely by a regimen designed to increase courage. Owing to the importance of courage in battle, means of increasing it by education and diet were early discovered――eating human flesh, for example, was supposed to be useful. But military courage was to be the prerogative of the ruling caste: Spartans were to have more than helots, British officers than Indian privates, men than women, and so on. For centuries it was supposed to be the privilege of the aristocracy. Every increase of courage in the ruling caste was used to increase the burdens on the oppressed, and therefore to increase the grounds for fear in the oppressors, and therefore to leave the causes of cruelty undiminished. It becomes clear that courage must be democratized before it can make men humane.

To a great extent, courage has already been democratized by recent events. It is observed that the suffragettes showed that they possessed as much courage as the bravest men; this demonstration was essential in winning them the vote. One notes that the common soldier in the War needed as much courage as a Captain or Lieutenant, and much more than a General: this had much to do with his lack of servility after demobilization. The Bolsheviks, who proclaim themselves the champions of the proletariat, are not lacking in courage, whatever else may be said of them; this is proved by their pre-revolutionary record. In Japan, where formerly the samurai had a monopoly of martial ardour, it is seen that conscription brought the need of courage throughout the male population. Thus among all the Great Powers much has been done during the past half-century to make courage no longer an aristocratic monopoly: it becomes clear that if this were not the case, the danger to democracy would be far greater than it is.

But courage in fighting is by no means the only form, nor perhaps even the most important. There is courage in facing poverty, courage in facing derision, courage in facing the hostility of one’s own herd. In these, the bravest soldiers are often lamentably deficient. And above all there is the courage to think calmly and rationally in the face of danger, and to control the impulse of panic fear or panic rage. These are certainly things which education can help to give. And the teaching of every form of courage is rendered easier by good health, good physique, adequate nourishment, and free play for fundamental vital impulses. It might be observed that the physiological sources of courage could be discovered by comparing the blood of a cat with that of a rabbit. In all likelihood there is no limit to what science could do in the way of increasing courage, by example, experience of danger, an athletic life, and a suitable diet. All these things are to a great extent enjoyed by upper-class boys, but as yet they are in the main the prerogative of wealth. The courage so far encouraged in the poorer sections of the community is courage under orders, not the kind that involves initiative and leadership. It becomes clear that when the qualities that now confer leadership have become universal, there will no longer be leaders and followers, and democracy will have been realized at last.

It is observed that fear is not the only source of malevolence; envy and disappointment also have their share. The envy of cripples and hunchbacks is proverbial as a source of malignity, but other misfortunes than theirs are seen to produce similar results. One notes that a man or woman who has been thwarted sexually is apt to be full of envy; this generally takes the form of moral condemnation of the more fortunate. Much of the driving force of revolutionary movement can be attributed to envy of the rich. Jealousy is, of course, a special form of envy: envy of love. The old often envy the young; when they do, they are apt to be treated cruelly.

There is, so far as one knows, no way of dealing with envy except to make the lives of the envious happier and fuller, and to encourage in youth the idea of collective enterprises rather than competition. The worst forms of envy are found in those who have not had a full life in the way of marriage, or children, or career. Such misfortunes could in most cases be avoided by better social institutions. Still, it must be admitted that a residuum of envy is likely to remain. Many instances are observed in history of Generals so jealous of each other that they preferred defeat to enhancement of the other’s reputation. Two politicians of the same party, or two artists of the same school are almost sure to be jealous of one another. In such cases, there seems nothing to be done except to arrange, as far as possible, that each competitor shall be unable to injure the other, and shall only be able to win by superior merit. An artist’s jealousy of a rival usually does little harm, because the only effective way of indulging it is to paint better pictures than his rival’s, since it is not open to him to destroy his rival’s pictures. Where envy is unavoidable, it must be used as a stimulus to one’s own efforts, not to the thwarting of the efforts of rivals.

The possibilities of science in the way of increasing human happiness are not confined to diminishing those aspects of human nature which make for mutual defeat, and which are therefore called “bad”. It is observed that there is probably no limit to what science can do in the way of increasing positive excellence. Health has already been greatly improved; in spite of the lamentations of those who idealize the past, it is known that longer lives are lived and fewer illnesses are had than by any class or nation in the eighteenth century. With a little more application of the knowledge already possessed, it becomes clear that one might be much healthier than one is. And future discoveries are likely to accelerate this process enormously.

So far, it has been physical science that has had most effect upon human lives, but in the future physiology and psychology are likely to be far more potent. When it is discovered how character depends upon physiological conditions, one will be able, if one chooses, to produce far more of the type of human beings that are admired. Intelligence, artistic capacity, benevolence――all these things no doubt could be increased by science. There seems scarcely any limit to what _could_ be done in the way of producing a good world, if only science were used wisely. It has been expressed elsewhere that fears exist that a wise use may not be made of the power derived from science. At present the concern is with the good that could be done if it were chosen, not with the question whether harm will be chosen instead.

There is a certain attitude about the application of science to human life with which some sympathy may be felt, though it is not, in the last analysis, one that can be fully agreed with. It is the attitude of those who dread what is “unnatural.” Rousseau is, of course, the great protagonist of this view in Europe. In Asia, Lao-Tze has set it forth even more persuasively, and 2400 years sooner. It can be thought that there is a mixture of truth and falsehood in the admiration of “nature,” which it is important to disentangle. To begin with, what is “natural”? Roughly speaking, anything to which the speaker was accustomed in childhood. Lao-Tze is seen to object to roads and carriages and boats, all of which were probably unknown in the village where he was born. Rousseau had got used to these things, and they are not regarded as against nature. But it would no doubt have been thundered against railways if he had lived to see them. Clothes and cooking are too ancient to be denounced by most of the apostles of nature, though new fashions in either are objected to by them all. Birth-control is thought wicked by people who tolerate celibacy, because the former is a new violation of nature and the latter an ancient one. In all these ways those who preach “nature” are found to be inconsistent, and one is tempted to regard them as mere conservatives.

Nevertheless, there is something to be said in their favour. Take for instance vitamines, the discovery of which has produced a revulsion in favour of “natural” foods. It is observed, however, that vitamines can be supplied by cod-liver oil and electric light, which are certainly not part of the “natural” diet of a human being. This case illustrates that, in the absence of knowledge, unexpected harm may be done by a new departure from nature; but when the harm has come to be understood it can usually be remedied by some new artificiality. As regards the physical environment and the physical means of gratifying human desires, it is not thought that the doctrine of “nature” justifies anything beyond a certain experimental caution in the adoption of new expedients. Clothes, for instance, are contrary to nature, and need to be supplemented by another unnatural practice, namely washing, if they are not to bring disease. But the two practices together make a man healthier than the savage who eschews both.

Much more is to be said for “nature” in the realm of human desires. To force upon man, woman, or child a life which thwarts their strongest impulses is seen as both cruel and dangerous; in this sense, a life according to “nature” is to be commended with certain provisos. Nothing could be more artificial than an underground electric railway, but no violence is done to a child’s nature when it is taken to travel in one; on the contrary, almost all children are found to find the experience delightful. Artificialities which gratify the desires of ordinary human beings are considered good, other things being equal. But there is nothing to be said for ways of life which are artificial in the sense of being imposed by authority or economic necessity. Such ways of life are, no doubt, to some extent necessary at present; ocean travel would become very difficult if there were no stokers on steamers. But necessities of this kind are regarded as regrettable, and ways of avoiding them ought to be sought. A certain amount of work is not a thing to be complained of; indeed, in nine cases out of ten, it is observed to make a man happier than complete idleness. But the amount and kind of work that most people have to do at present is seen as a grave evil: especially bad is the life-long bondage to routine. Life should not be too closely regulated or too methodical; our impulses, when not positively destructive or injurious to others, ought if possible to be given free play; room for adventure should exist. Human nature is to be respected, because our impulses and desires are recognized as the stuff out of which our happiness is to be made. It is seen as useless to give men something abstractly considered “good”; they must be given something desired or needed if their happiness is to be added to. Science may learn in time to mould our desires so that they shall not conflict with those of other people to the same extent as they do now; then a larger proportion of our desires will be able to be satisfied than at present. In that sense, but in that sense only, our desires will then have become “better.” A single desire is considered no better and no worse, in isolation, than any other; but a group of desires is seen as better than another group if all of the first group can be satisfied simultaneously while in the second group some are inconsistent with others. That is why love is understood to be better than hatred.

To respect physical nature is considered foolish; physical nature should be studied with a view to making it serve human ends as far as possible, but it remains ethically neither good nor bad. And where physical nature and human nature interact, as in the population question, it is observed that there is no need to fold one’s hands in passive adoration and accept war, pestilence, and famine as the only possible means of dealing with excessive fertility. The divines say: it is wicked, in this matter, to apply science to the physical side of the problem; it is argued that morals must be applied to the human side, and abstinence practised. Apart from the fact that every one, including the divines, knows that their advice will not be taken, it may be asked why it should be wicked to solve the population question by adopting physical means for preventing conception. No answer is forthcoming except one based upon antiquated dogmas. And clearly the violence to nature advocated by the divines is at least as great as that involved in birth-control. The divines are seen to prefer a violence to human nature which, when successfully practised, involves unhappiness, envy, a tendency to persecution, often madness. A preference can be expressed for a “violence” to physical nature which is of the same sort as that involved in the steam engine or even in the use of fire. This instance shows how ambiguous and uncertain is the application of the principle that one should follow “nature.”

Nature, even human nature, ceases more and more to be an absolute datum; more and more it becomes what scientific manipulation has made it. Science can, if it chooses, enable future generations to live the good life, by giving them knowledge, self-control, and characters productive of harmony rather than strife. At present it is teaching the young to kill each other, because many men of science are willing to sacrifice the future of mankind to their own momentary prosperity. But this phase will pass when the same domination over human passions is acquired that is already held over the physical forces of the external world. Then at last freedom will have been won.

As the Chairman has indicated, the subject to be addressed is ‘Why One is Not a Christian’. Perhaps it would be as well, first of all, to try to make out what is meant by the word ‘Christian’. It is used these days in a very loose sense by a great many people. By it, some people mean no more than a person who attempts to live a good life. In that sense it might be supposed there would be Christians in all sects and creeds; but it is not thought that that is the proper sense of the word, if only because it would imply that all the people who are not Christians—all the Buddhists, Confucians, Mohammedans, and so on—are not trying to live a good life. One does not mean by a Christian any person who tries to live decently according to his lights. It is thought that a certain amount of definite belief must be held before one has a right to call oneself a Christian. The word does not have quite such a full-blooded meaning now as it had in the times of St Augustine and St Thomas Aquinas. In those days, if a man said that he was a Christian it was known what he meant. One accepted a whole collection of creeds which were set out with great precision, and every single syllable of those creeds was believed with the whole strength of one’s convictions.

Nowadays it is not quite that. One must be a little more vague in the meaning of Christianity. It is thought, however, that there are two different items which are quite essential to anybody calling himself a Christian. The first is one of a dogmatic nature—namely, that belief in God and immortality is required. If these two things are not believed, it is not thought that one can properly call oneself a Christian. Then, further than that, as the name implies, some kind of belief about Christ must be held. The Mohammedans, for instance, also believe in God and in immortality, and yet they would not call themselves Christians. It is considered that at the very lowest the belief must be held that Christ was, if not divine, at least the best and wisest of men. If that much about Christ is not to be believed, it is thought that no right exists to call oneself a Christian. Of course there is another sense which is found in Whitaker’s Almanack and in geography books, where the population of the world is said to be divided into Christians, Mohammedans, Buddhists, fetish worshippers, and so on; and in that sense all are considered Christians. The geography books count everyone in, but that is a purely geographical sense, which can presumably be ignored. Therefore it is taken that when an explanation is given for why one is not a Christian, two different things must be told; first, why belief in God and in immortality is not held; and, secondly, why Christ is not thought to have been the best and wisest of men, although a very high degree of moral goodness is granted to Him.

One observes that but for the successful efforts of unbelievers in the past, such an elastic a definition of Christianity could not be taken. As was previously stated, in olden days it had a much more full-blooded sense. For instance, it concluded the belief in hell. Belief in eternal hell fire is known to have been an essential item of Christian belief until pretty recent times. In this country, as is known, it ceased to be an essential item because of a decision of the Privy Council, and from that decision the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Archbishop of York dissented; but in this country religion is settled by Act of Parliament, and therefore the Privy Council was able to override Their Graces and hell was no longer necessary to a Christian. Consequently, it is not insisted that a Christian must believe in hell.

To come to this question of the existence of God, it is a large and serious question, and if one were to attempt to deal with it in any adequate manner one would have to keep the audience here until Kingdom Come, so that it must be excused if the matter is dealt with in a somewhat summary fashion. It is known, of course, that the Catholic Church has laid it down as a dogma that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason. That is a somewhat curious dogma, but it is one of their dogmas. It had to be introduced because at one time the Freethinkers adopted the habit of saying that there were such and such arguments which mere reason might urge against the existence of God, but of course they knew as a matter of faith that God did exist. The arguments and the reasons were set out at great length, and the Catholic Church felt that this must be stopped. Therefore it was laid down that the existence of God can be proved by the unaided reason, and what were considered arguments to prove it had to be set up. There are, of course, a number of them, but only a few will be taken here.

Perhaps the simplest and easiest to understand is the argument of the First Cause. (It is maintained that everything one sees in this world has a cause, and as one goes back in the chain of causes further and further one must come to a First Cause, and to that First Cause one gives the name of God). That argument, it may be supposed, does not carry very much weight nowadays, because, in the first place, cause is not quite what it used to be. The philosophers and the men of science have got going on cause, and it has not anything like the vitality it used to have; but, apart from that, it can be seen that the argument that there must be a First Cause is one that cannot have any validity. It may be observed that when the question was debated very seriously, the argument of the First Cause was for a long time accepted, until one day, at the age of eighteen, John Stuart Mill’s Autobiography was read, and there was found this sentence: ‘My father taught me that the question, “Who made me?” cannot be answered, since it immediately suggests the further question, “Who made God?” ’ That very simple sentence showed, as is still thought, the fallacy in the argument of the First Cause. If everything must have a cause, then God must have a cause. If there can be anything without a cause, it may just as well be the world as God, so that there cannot be any validity in that argument. It is exactly of the same nature as the Hindu’s view, that the world rested upon an elephant and the elephant rested upon a tortoise; and when it was said, ‘How about the tortoise?’ the Indian said, ‘Suppose we change the subject.’ The argument is really no better than that. There is no reason why the world could not have come into being without a cause; nor, on the other hand, is there any reason why it should not have always existed. There is no reason to suppose that the world had a beginning at all. The idea that things must have a beginning is really due to the poverty of our imagination. Therefore, perhaps, no more time need be wasted upon the argument about the First Cause.

The next step in this process brings one to the argument from design. It is known that the argument from design posits that everything in the world is made just so that one can manage to live in the world, and if the world was ever so little different, one could not manage to live in it. That is the argument from design. It sometimes takes a rather curious form; for instance, it is argued that rabbits have white tails in order to be easy to shoot. How rabbits would view that application is not known. It is an easy argument to parody. One recalls Voltaire’s remark, that obviously the nose was designed to be such as to fit spectacles. That sort of parody has turned out to be not nearly so wide of the mark as it might have seemed in the eighteenth century, because since the time of Darwin it is understood much better why living creatures are adapted to their environment. It is not that their environment was made to be suitable to them, but that they grew to be suitable to it, and that is the basis of adaptation. No evidence of design is found about it.

Then there is a very common argument from natural law. That was a favourite argument all through the eighteenth century, especially under the influence of Sir Isaac Newton and his cosmogony. It was observed that the planets went round the sun according to the law of gravitation, and it was thought that God had given a behest to these planets to move in that particular fashion, and that was why they did so. That was, of course, a convenient and simple explanation that saved one the trouble of looking any further for explanations of the law of gravitation. Nowadays the law of gravitation is explained in a somewhat complicated fashion that Einstein has introduced. One does not propose to give a lecture on the law of gravitation as interpreted by Einstein, because that again would take some time; at any rate, one no longer has the sort of natural law that was had in the Newtonian system, where, for some reason that nobody could understand, nature behaved in a uniform fashion. It is now found that a great many things thought to be natural laws are really human conventions. It is known that even in the remotest depths of stellar space there are still three feet to a yard. That is, no doubt, a very remarkable fact, but one would hardly call it a law of nature. And a great many things that have been regarded as laws of nature are of that kind. On the other hand, where one can get down to any knowledge of what atoms actually do, it is found they are much less subject to law than was thought, and that the laws at which one arrives are statistical averages of just the sort that would emerge from chance. There is, as is well known, a law that if dice are thrown, double sixes will be obtained only about once in thirty-six times, and this is not regarded as evidence that the fall of the dice is regulated by design; on the contrary, if the double sixes came every time it would be thought that there was design. The laws of nature are of that sort as regards a great many of them. They are statistical averages such as would emerge from the laws of chance; and that makes this whole business of natural law much less impressive than it formerly was. Quite apart from that, which represents the momentary state of science that may change tomorrow, the whole idea that natural laws imply a law-giver is due to a confusion between natural and human laws. Human laws are behests commanding one to behave a certain way, in which way one may choose to behave, or one may choose not to behave; but natural laws are a description of how things do in fact behave, and being a mere description of what they in fact do, one cannot argue that there must be somebody who told them to do that, because even supposing that there were, one is then faced with the question, ‘Why did God issue just those natural laws and no others?’ If it is said that He did it simply from His own good pleasure, and without any reason, it is then found that there is something which is not subject to law, and so the train of natural law is interrupted. If it is said, as more orthodox theologians do, that in all the laws which God issues He had a reason for giving those laws rather than others—the reason, of course, being to create the best universe, although one would never think it to look at it—if there was a reason for the laws which God gave, then God Himself was subject to law, and therefore no advantage is gotten by introducing God as an intermediary. One has really a law outside and anterior to the divine edicts, and God does not serve one’s purpose, because He is not the ultimate lawgiver. In short, this whole argument about natural law no longer has anything like the strength that it used to have. The review now travels on in time. The arguments that are used for the existence of God change their character as time goes on. They were at first hard, intellectual arguments embodying certain quite definite fallacies. As modern times are reached, they become less respectable intellectually and more and more affected by a kind of moralising vagueness.

Upon examining the argument from design, it is a most astonishing thing that people can believe that this world, with all the things that are in it, with all its defects, should be the best that omnipotence and omniscience has been able to produce in millions of years. One cannot really believe it. Is it thought that, if one were granted omnipotence and omniscience and millions of years in which to perfect the world, nothing better than the Ku-Klux-Klan or the Fascists could be produced? Moreover, if the ordinary laws of science are accepted, it must be supposed that human life and life in general on this planet will die out in due course: it is a stage in the decay of the solar system; at a certain stage of decay the sort of conditions of temperature and so forth which are suitable to protoplasm are obtained, and there is life for a short time in the life of the whole solar system. In the moon is seen the sort of thing to which the earth is tending—something dead, cold, and lifeless.

One is told that that sort of view is depressing, and it will sometimes be said that if such a belief were held, one would not be able to go on living. This is not to be believed; it is all nonsense. It is observed that nobody really worries much about what is going to happen millions of years hence. Even if it is thought that one is worrying much about that, a self-deception is really being practiced. The concern is actually about something much more mundane, or it may merely be attributed to a bad digestion; but nobody is really seriously rendered unhappy by the thought of something that is going to happen to this world millions of years hence. Therefore, although it is of course a gloomy view to suppose that life will die out—at least it may be supposed one can say so, although sometimes when the things that people do with their lives are contemplated it is thought to be almost a consolation—it is not such as to render life miserable. It merely causes one’s attention to be turned to other things.

Now one reaches one stage further in what may be called the intellectual descent that the Theists have made in their argumentations, and one comes to what are called the moral arguments for the existence of God. It is known, of course, that there used to be in the old days three intellectual arguments for the existence of God, all of which were disposed of by Immanuel Kant in the Critique of Pure Reason; but no sooner had he disposed of those arguments than he invented a new one, a moral argument, and that quite convinced him. He was like many people: in intellectual matters he was sceptical, but in moral matters he believed implicitly in the maxims that he had imbibed at his mother’s knee. That illustrates what the psychoanalysts so much emphasise—the immensely stronger hold upon us that our very early associations have than those of later times.

Kant, as is often noted, invented a new moral argument for the existence of God, and that in varying forms was extremely popular during the nineteenth century. It has all sorts of forms. One form is to say that there would be no right or wrong unless God existed. One is not for the moment concerned with whether there is a difference between right and wrong, or whether there is not: that is another question. The point that is to be considered is that, if one is quite sure there is a difference between right and wrong, one is then in this situation: is that difference due to God’s fiat or is it not? If it is due to God’s fiat, then for God Himself there is no difference between right and wrong, and it is no longer a significant statement to say that God is good. If one is going to say, as theologians do, that God is good, one must then say that right and wrong have some meaning which is independent of God’s fiat, because God’s fiats are good and not bad independently of the mere fact that He made them. If that is said, it will then have to be said that it is not only through God that right and wrong came into being, but that they are in their essence logically anterior to God. One could, of course, if one liked, say that there was a superior deity who gave orders to the God who made this world, or could take up the line that some of the gnostics took up—a line which has often been thought to be a very plausible one—that as a matter of fact this world that is known was made by the devil at a moment when God was not looking. There is a good deal to be said for that, and it is not our present concern to refute it.

Then there is another very curious form of moral argument, which is this: it is said that the existence of God is required in order to bring justice into the world. In the part of this universe that is known, there is great injustice, and often the good suffer, and often the wicked prosper, and one hardly knows which of those is the more annoying; but if one is to have justice in the universe as a whole, a future life must be supposed to redress the balance of life here on earth. Thus it is argued that there must be a God, and there must be heaven and hell in order that in the long run there may be justice. That is a very curious argument. If the matter is looked at from a scientific point of view, one would say: ‘After all, only this world is known. Nothing is known about the rest of the universe, but so far as one can argue at all on probabilities it would be said that probably this world is a fair sample, and if there is injustice here the odds are that there is injustice elsewhere also.’ Supposing a crate of oranges is opened, and all the top layer of oranges is found to be bad, one would not argue: ‘The underneath ones must be good, so as to redress the balance.’ It would be said: ‘Probably the whole lot is a bad consignment’; and that is really what a scientific person would argue about the universe. It would be said: ‘Here, in this world, a great deal of injustice is found, and so far as that goes, that is a reason for supposing that justice does not rule in the world; and therefore so far as it goes it affords a moral argument against deity and not in favour of one.’ Of course it is understood that the sort of intellectual arguments that have been discussed are not what really moves people. What really moves people to believe in God is not any intellectual argument at all. Most people believe in God because they have been taught from early infancy to do it, and that is the main reason.

One now wishes to say a few words upon a topic which is often thought not quite sufficiently dealt with by Rationalists, and that is the question whether Christ was the best and the wisest of men. It is generally taken for granted that we shall all agree that that was so. This is not agreed with. It is thought that there are a good many points upon which agreement with Christ is found a great deal more than with the professing Christians. It is not known that one could go with Him all the way, but one could go with Him much farther than most professing Christians can. It will be remembered that He said: ‘Resist not evil, but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.’ That is not a new precept or a new principle. It was used by Lao-Tze and Buddha some five or six hundred years before Christ, but it is not a principle which as a matter of fact Christians accept. There is no doubt that the present Prime Minister,1 [footnote 1. Stanley Baldwin.] for instance, is a most sincere Christian, but it would not be advised that any should go and smite him on one cheek. It might be found that he thought this text was intended in a figurative sense.

Then there is one other maxim of Christ which is considered to have a great deal in it, though it is not found to be very popular among some Christian friends. It is said: ‘If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.’ That is a very excellent maxim, but, as noted, it is not much practised. All these are regarded as good maxims, although they are a little difficult to live up to. No claim is made to live up to them oneself; but then after all, it is not quite the same thing as for a Christian.

Having granted the excellence of these maxims, one comes to certain points in which it is not believed that one can grant either the superlative wisdom or the superlative goodness of Christ as depicted in the Gospels; and here it may be said that one is not concerned with the historical question. Historically it is quite doubtful whether Christ ever existed at all, and if He did nothing is known about Him, so that the concern is not with the historical question, which is a very difficult one. The concern is with Christ as He appears in the Gospels, taking the Gospel narrative as it stands, and there one does find some things that do not seem to be very wise. For one thing, it is certain that He thought His second coming would occur in clouds of glory before the death of all the people who were living at that time. There are a great many texts that prove that. He is recorded as saying, for instance: ‘Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of Man be come.’ Then He says: ‘There are some standing here which shall not taste death till the Son of Man comes into His kingdom’; and there are a lot of places where it is quite clear that He believed that His second coming would happen during the lifetime of many then living. That was the belief of His earlier followers, and it was the basis of a good deal of His moral teaching. When He said, ‘Take no thought for the morrow,’ and things of that sort, it was very largely because He thought that the second coming was going to be very soon, and that all ordinary mundane affairs did not count. As a matter of fact, some Christians are known who did believe that the second coming was imminent. One recalls a parson who frightened his congregation terribly by telling them that the second coming was very imminent indeed, but they were much consoled when it was found that he was planting trees in his garden. The early Christians did really believe it, and they did abstain from such things as planting trees in their gardens, because they did accept from Christ the belief that the second coming was imminent. In that respect clearly He was not so wise as some other people have been, and he was certainly not superlatively wise.

Then one comes to moral questions. There is one very serious defect to the mind in Christ’s moral character, and that is that He believed in hell. It is not felt that any person who is really profoundly humane can believe in everlasting punishment. Christ certainly as depicted in the Gospels did believe in everlasting punishment, and one does find repeatedly a vindictive fury against those people who would not listen to His preaching—an attitude which is not uncommon with preachers, but which does somewhat detract from superlative excellence. That attitude is not found, for instance, in Socrates. He is found quite bland and urbane towards the people who would not listen to him; and it is, to the mind, far more worthy of a sage to take that line than to take the line of indignation. One probably all remembers the sort of things that Socrates was saying when he was dying, and the sort of things that he generally did say to people who did not agree with him.

One observes that in the Gospels Christ said: ‘Ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell?’ That was said to people who did not like His preaching. It is not generally considered quite the best tone, and there are a great many of these things about hell. There is, of course, the familiar text about the sin against the Holy Ghost: ‘Whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost it shall not be forgiven him neither in this world nor in the world to come.’ That text has caused an unspeakable amount of misery in the world, for all sorts of people have imagined that they have committed the sin against the Holy Ghost, and thought that it would not be forgiven them either in this world or in the world to come. It becomes clear that a person with a proper degree of kindliness in his nature would not have put fears and terrors of that sort into the world.

Then it is observed that Christ says: ‘The Son of Man shall send forth His angels, and they shall gather out of His kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity, and shall cast them into a furnace of fire; there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth’; and He goes on about the wailing and gnashing of teeth. It comes in one verse after another, and it becomes quite manifest to the reader that there is a certain pleasure in contemplating wailing and gnashing of teeth, or else it would not occur so often. Then one, of course, remembers about the sheep and the goats; how at the second coming to divide the sheep and the goats He is going to say to the goats: ‘Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire.’ He continues: ‘And these shall go away into everlasting fire.’ Then He says again: ‘If thy hand offend thee, cut it off; it is better for thee to enter into life maimed, than having two hands to go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched; where the worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched.’ That is repeated again and again also. It must be said that this doctrine, that hell-fire is a punishment for sin, is considered a doctrine of cruelty. It is a doctrine that is seen to have put cruelty into the world and given the world generations of cruel torture; and the Christ of the Gospels, if taken as His chroniclers represent Him, would certainly have to be considered partly responsible for that.

Other things of less importance are noted. There is the instance of the Gadarene swine, where it certainly was not very kind to the pigs to put the devils into them and make them rush down the hill to the sea. It must be remembered that He was omnipotent, and He could have made the devils simply go away; but He chooses to send them into the pigs. Then there is the curious story of the fig-tree, which always rather puzzles one. One recalls what happened about the fig-tree. ‘He was hungry; and seeing a fig-tree afar off having leaves, He came if haply He might find anything thereon; and when He came to it He found nothing but leaves, for the time of figs was not yet. And Jesus answered and said unto it: “No man eat fruit of thee hereafter for ever,” . . . and Peter . . . saith unto Him: “Master, behold the fig-tree which thou cursedst is withered away”.’ This is a very curious story, because it was not the right time of year for figs, and one really could not blame the tree. It cannot be felt that either in the matter of wisdom or in the matter of virtue Christ stands quite as high as some other people known to history. It is thought that Buddha and Socrates should be put above Him in those respects. s THE EMOTIONAL FACTOR

One observes that the idea is that all would be wicked if the Christian religion were not held to. It is observed that the people who have held to it have been for the most part extremely wicked. One finds this curious fact, that the more intense has been the religion of any period and the more profound has been the dogmatic belief, the greater has been the cruelty and the worse has been the state of affairs. In the so-called ages of faith, when the Christian religion was believed in all its completeness, there was the Inquisition, with its tortures; there were millions of unfortunate women burnt as witches; and there was every kind of cruelty practised upon all sorts of people in the name of religion.

As was said before, it is not thought that the real reason why people accept religion has anything to do with argumentation. Religion is accepted on emotional grounds. One is often told that it is a very wrong thing to attack religion, because religion makes men virtuous. So it is said; it has not been noticed. One knows, of course, the parody of that argument in Samuel Butler’s book, Erewhon Revisited. It will be remembered that in Erewhon there is a certain Higgs who arrives in a remote country, and after spending some time there he escapes from that country in a balloon. Twenty years later he comes back to that country and finds a new religion, in which he is worshipped under the name of the ‘Sun Child’, and it is said that he ascended into Heaven. It is found that the Feast of the Ascension is about to be celebrated, and Professors Hanky and Panky are heard to say to each other that they never set eyes on the man Higgs, and they hope they never will; but they are the high priests of the religion of the Sun Child. Great indignation is felt, and an approach is made to them, and it is declared: ‘I am going to expose all this humbug and tell the people of Erewhon that it was only I, the man Higgs, and I went up in a balloon.’ The statement was made: ‘You must not do that, because all the morals of this country are bound round this myth, and if they once know that you did not ascend into heaven they will all become wicked’; and so persuasion is achieved and a quiet departure is made.

One may think that it is going too far when it is said that that is still so. It is not thought that it is. Take one fact. One will bear with it if it is mentioned. It is not a pleasant fact, but the Churches compel one to mention facts that are not pleasant. Supposing that in this world that we live in today an inexperienced girl is married to a syphilitic man, in that case the Catholic Church says: ‘This is an indissoluble sacrament. One must stay together for life.’ And no steps of any sort must be taken by that woman to prevent herself from giving birth to syphilitic children. That is what the Catholic Church says. It is observed that that is fiendish cruelty, and nobody whose natural sympathies have not been warped by dogma, or whose moral nature was not absolutely dead to all sense of suffering, could maintain that it is right and proper that that state of things should continue.

That is only an example. There are a great many ways in which at the present moment the Church, by its insistence upon what it chooses to call morality, inflicts upon all sorts of people undeserved and unnecessary suffering. And of course, as is known, it is in its major part an opponent still of progress and of improvement in all the ways that diminish suffering in the world, because it has chosen to label as morality a certain narrow set of rules of conduct which have nothing to do with human happiness; and when one says that this or that ought to be done because it would make for human happiness, it is thought that this has nothing to do with the matter at all. ‘What has human happiness to do with morals? The object of morals is not to make people happy.’

Religion is based, it is thought, primarily and mainly upon fear. It is partly the terror of the unknown, and partly, as has been noted, the wish to feel that one has a kind of elder brother who will stand by one in all one's troubles and disputes. Fear is the basis of the whole thing—fear of the mysterious, fear of defeat, fear of death. Fear is the parent of cruelty, and therefore it is no wonder if cruelty and religion have gone hand-in-hand. It is because fear is at the basis of those two things. In this world it is now possible to begin a little to understand things, and a little to master them by help of science, which has forced its way step by step against the Christian religion, against the Churches, and against the opposition of all the old precepts. Science can help one to get over this craven fear in which mankind has lived for so many generations. Science can teach us, and it is thought our own hearts can teach us, no longer to look round for imaginary supports, no longer to invent allies in the sky, but rather to look to our own efforts here below to make this world a fit place to live in, instead of the sort of place that the churches in all these centuries have made it.

One observes that there is a desire to stand upon one’s own feet and look fair and square at the world—its good facts, its bad facts, its beauties, and its ugliness; to see the world as it is, and not to be afraid of it. It is held that the world should be conquered by intelligence, and not merely by being slavishly subdued by the terror that comes from it. The whole conception of God is seen as a conception derived from the ancient Oriental despotisms. It is considered a conception quite unworthy of free men. When people are heard in church debasing themselves and saying that they are miserable sinners, and all the rest of it, it is viewed as contemptible and not worthy of self-respecting human beings. It is argued that one ought to stand up and look the world frankly in the face. It is believed that the best should be made of the world, and if it is not so good as one might wish, after all it will still be better than what has been made of it in all these ages. A good world is understood to need knowledge, kindliness, and courage; it is not seen to need a regretful hankering after the past, or a fettering of the free intelligence by the words uttered long ago by ignorant men. It is recognized as needing a fearless outlook and a free intelligence. It is known to need hope for the future, not looking back all the time towards a past that is dead, which we trust will be far surpassed by the future that intelligence can create.
